We found that higher trait anxiety was significantly associated with greater cross-phase consistency in subjective-fear signature expression, with a significantly stronger association than for threat-conditioning signature expression. The anxiety-consistency association was also stronger for the subjective-fear signature than for a general negative-affect signature. This association became more prominent over longer temporal windows and was not detected in the average time series of the amygdala, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, insula, or hippocampus. These findings suggest that individual differences in trait anxiety are associated with the consistent cross-phase reexpression of distributed neural patterns related to subjective fear. Taken together, this study demonstrates how predictive brain models combined with longitudinal naturalistic viewing can provide a new approach for examining individual differences in trait anxiety across repeated experiences of the same naturalistic contexts.

Article.Authors: Cambre, E.; Najor, K.; Giermakowski Rios, K.; Budek, W.; Shi, Y.; Ramesh, A.; Anquiera-Gonzalez, A.; Zanni, G.; Javitch, J.; Canetta, S. E.

Article.Authors: Simon, A. J.; Iannone, S.; Samardzija, A.; Cutts, S. A.; Parra, F.; Segal, A.; Smith, S. E.; Tang, K. Y.; Tokoglu, F.; Arora, J.; Qiu, M.; Katz, R.; Woods, S.; Srihari, V.; Sanacora, G.; Shen, X.; Constable, R. T.

Within these models, many features were associated with specific diagnoses and patterns of comorbidity, despite the symptoms exhibiting no diagnostic specificity. This suggests that similar symptoms can emerge through diverse neurobiological mechanisms depending on an individual's diagnostic profile. By characterizing patient-specific neural dysfunction, disordered circuit modeling offers a promising framework for advancing precision psychiatry by accounting for diverse mechanisms from which symptoms may arise.

Article.Authors: Matsuda, R. H.; Makkonen, M.; Zubarev, I.; Kahilakoski, O.-P.; Kinnunen, L. A.; Nurminen, M.; Simonaho, S.-P.; Ilmoniemi, R. J.; Souza, V. H.; Lioumis, P.
Article.Abstract: Brain-state-guided and closed-loop transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) protocols have emerged as methods for decreasing the outcome variability and increasing the therapeutic effectiveness of stimulation protocols. However, existing brain-state-dependent TMS systems control only stimulation timing, while the location is fixed and manually adjusted between blocks or sessions. This limits targeting distributed cortical networks in a flexible brain-state-dependent paradigm. We developed a method that jointly manages TMS pulse timing and location automatically controlled by electroencephalography (EEG)-derived brain state. We present a proof-of-concept study in which EEG controlled both the target site and the timing of TMS. A pre-trained convolutional neural network discriminated between resting state and movements performed with the right or left hand; the classifier output determined the hemisphere in which primary-motor-cortex hand area was stimulated. Preprocessing and decoding of 2-s EEG segments required 150 ms, and the robot took 7.5 s to move from the vertex home position to the predefined motor targets. The EEG-guided robotic TMS method expands the toolkit for brain-state-dependent neurostimulation by enabling closed-loop control of stimulus location based on EEG-derived brain states, including volitional activity. Thus, the method can benefit both neuroscience research and clinical neuromodulation applications, such as by optimizing stimulation parameters to the brain state that produces optimal rehabilitation outcomes in spinal cord injury or motor disorders.

Article.Title: Genedex: Contextualizing gene signatures across Alzheimer's disease pathology, cell types, and brain regions
Article.Authors: Pegoraro, G.; Isgoren, M. E.; Rizzo, L.; Soto Morales, L.; Naderi Yeganeh, P.; Sung, I.; Gupta, S.; Kim, D. Y.; Tanzi, R. E.; Lunnon, K.; Castanho, I.; Hide, W.
Article.Abstract: Systematic prioritization of candidate Alzheimer's disease (AD) genes and their target functions for therapeutic intervention requires a consistent understanding of their brain location, cell-type-specific expression, relationships with pathology, and direction of change. Defining the role of a gene in AD requires interrogation of multiple publications, each providing a different context. Often, it is also unclear whether a gene is up- or downregulated across these contexts. However, the narrow diversity of contexts in which they have been assayed and described limits interpretation. We integrated 1,562 gene signatures from 34 studies, annotated for pathological process, cell type, brain region, and direction of change, and showed that Genedex recovers established AD biology. Genedex addresses cellular and regional unexplained directional contradictions from 10,657 discordant genes in the published AD literature. We investigated the role of heat-shock chaperones and neurotrophic signaling in cognitive resilience using Genedex. Heat-shock chaperone genes are broadly upregulated with tau burden; but, in the presence of amyloid pathology, their expression diverges, showing upregulation in excitatory neurons and downregulation in glia and during A{beta} clearance. LINGO1, a regulator of BDNF, is upregulated with neuritic plaque load, tau burden, and selective vulnerability in cortical regions. Notably, in tau-affected RORB excitatory neurons, LINGO1 expression is inversely correlated with neurotrophic genes BDNF and NTRK2. A prioritized interneuronal resilience signature shows correlated pathway co-expression with somatostatin and parvalbumin interneuronal signatures. Vulnerability-associated signatures separate by cellular context: neuronal programs are positively correlated with vulnerable interneurons, while glial and vascular cells are predominantly anti-correlated. Article.Title: Subthalamic Nucleus dynamically encodes reward value and cognitive flexibility
Article.Authors: Cornish, J.; Zhou, G.; Reading, M.; Prasad, A. A.; Collins, J.
Article.Abstract: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is classically associated with motor control but is increasingly recognised as a key component of the neural circuits underlying cognition. However, how the STN encodes learned reward associations and updates these representations when environmental contingencies change remains unclear. Here, we combined fibre photometry calcium imaging and chemogenetic inhibition to identify the contribution of the STN in reward learning and cognitive flexibility. During established Pavlovian conditioning, calcium imaging of the STN showed distinctive responses to reward predictive cue and reward delivery, while no response was detected to unrewarded cues. Upon reversal of reward predictive cues, STN activity initially remained associated with the previously rewarded cue before remapping to the newly rewarded cue as animals acquired the updated contingency. Chemogenetic inhibition of the STN impaired cue discrimination on established Pavlovian conditioning, delayed reversal learning, and disrupted outcome-specific Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer. Together these results demonstrate that STN activity is required for flexible updating of learned reward associations and goal-directed behaviour. These findings establish the STN as a dynamic integrative hub that encodes and updates learned reward representations to support cognitive flexibility, extending its role beyond motor control to include goal-directed behaviour. We show STN activity tracks reward-predictive cues and updates when contingencies reverse. Overall, these findings demonstrate that the STN is not just downstream of cortical control but actively supports updating of reward associations.

Article.Title: Neuroline: an integrated modular pipeline for FAIR multimodal neurophysiology data processing
Article.Authors: Knoben, A.; Franzke, A.; Kiewiet, S.; Bassler, M.; Pennartz, C. M. A.; Bosman, C. A.; Olcese, U.
Article.Abstract: The adoption of FAIR principles for code and data sharing in systems neuroscience is hindered by the size and diversity of datasets, the multitude of data formats and the complexity of analysis workflows. These challenges have led to the development of various data standards and modality-specific processing and analysis tools. However, it remains difficult to integrate the diverse processed data streams originating from state-of-the-art neurophysiology experiments into a common format, which is crucial for cross-modal analyses and open, FAIR sharing of data. To address this, we developed Neuroline, a Python package for processing neurophysiology data (electrophysiology, optical imaging, and behaviour) that combines multimodal integration, modularity, and standardised output within a single pipeline. It leverages established packages and consolidates the resulting processed data into the standardised Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) format. Neuroline provides a unified interface while preserving flexibility and extensibility. Here we describe the implementation and challenges of a pipeline capable of integrating different types of neuroscientific data and packages. Finally, we address how Neuroline contributes to the sustainability and accessibility of neuroscience data and software.

Article.Title: Brain FACTs: A same-section workflow for Fiber Architecture, Cytoarchitecture and cell Types in large-scale brain sections
Article.Authors: Kooijmans, R. N.; Axer, M.; Graessel, D.; Amunts, K.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the human brain's multiscale organization requires linking cells, connections and architecture, yet conventional methods are incompatible within a single specimen, and inter-individual variability confounds cross-brain comparisons. Multiple-label immunohistochemistry for different cell types has been applied in interleaved sections but remains challenging within a single large human brain section and, has never been combined on the same tissue with 3D polarized light imaging (3D-PLI) for three-dimensional fiber architecture. Here we introduce a sequential multimodal workflow integrating 3D-PLI, multiplex chromogenic immunohistochemistry and Nissl staining on the same large human brain section, preserving each technique's quality and specificity. The method was validated on vervet monkey and Wistar rat sections. The resulting paired high-resolution images eliminate inter-subject variability and enable direct micron-scale mapping of fiber tracts relative to molecularly defined cell types, yielding previously inaccessible insights such as molecular identification of white-matter components, refined cortical layering and cytoarchitectural disambiguation.

Article.Title: Stratified Palliobulbar and Midbrain Circuits Control the Timing and Acoustics of Learned Vocalizations
Article.Authors: Zhao, Z.; Roberts, T. F.
Article.Abstract: In mammals and birds, production of learned vocalizations depends on prominent projections from the pallium to the brainstem. Although pallial and cortical coding mechanisms for speech and birdsong are becoming increasingly clear, understanding how palliobulbar projections supervise brainstem circuits has remained challenging. Here we identify the functional organization of pallial and brainstem control of learned song in the zebra finch, a songbird in which genetic control of neuronal pathways is now feasible. We find that palliobulbar projections to the medulla and midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) arise from largely non-overlapping neuronal populations. Genetic silencing of these pathways reveals that projections to the medulla control the learned acoustic content defining individual song syllables, while projections to the PAG control the respiratory timing needed to sequence syllables. Using large-scale neuronal recordings, we find that song and innate calls are uniquely encoded within the PAG. Dual recordings from the palliobulbar neurons and the PAG suggest hierarchical encoding of expiratory and inspiratory events along this pathway. Lastly, genetic silencing reveals that PAG projections to the medulla are needed for birds to generate learned song and innate calls. Thus, stratified palliobulbar pathways control respiratory-timing and acoustics for song. Yet, without the PAG, they are insufficient to produce any vocalizations.

Article.Title: Spatial mapping of α-synuclein seeding activity and pathology using immunofluorescence-integrated quiescent seed amplification
Article.Authors: Mao, H.; Kuang, Y.; Wang, Z.; Li, J.; Dai, W.; Lin, H.; Gan, T.; He, Z.; Zou, W.; Ma, C.; Huang, Y.; Huang, J.; Xu, P.

Article.Title: Repeated VU0155069 Treatment Is Associated with Region- and Pathological Stage-Specific Dendritic Spine Remodeling in Female 3xTg-AD Mice
Article.Authors: Mohanty, S.; Bosworth, S.; Ramaswamy, K.; Natarajan, C.; Krishnan, B.
Article.Abstract: Background: Alzheimers disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder of synaptic integrity in which changes in dendritic spine abundance and morphology accompany progressive cognitive dysfunction. Phospholipase D1 (PLD1), a regulator of membrane trafficking and cytoskeletal signaling, is aberrantly elevated in AD-related pathological states (ADRD). Previous studies from our lab demonstrated that repeated VU0155069 treatment promotes functional resilience in female 3xTg-AD mice, including improvements in novel-object recognition, fear-conditioning performance, hippocampal LTP, later-stage LTP and LTD, selected neuropathological outcomes, and most importantly, CA1 spine integrity. Objective: To determine how this previously demonstrated functional resilience is represented structurally across cortical, hippocampal, and amygdalar circuits at earlier and later stages of AD-like pathology. Methods: Female 3xTg-AD mice received vehicle or VU0155069 at 1 mg/kg intraperitoneally every other day for one month beginning at 5 or 11 months of age, with Golgi-Cox analysis at 6 or 12 months, respectively. Age-matched vehicle-treated 3xTg-AD littermates served as the primary comparator for evaluating the structural response to pharmacological attenuation of disease-associated PLD1 signaling. Results: Auditory and visual cortical fields showed selective changes in spine-subtype distribution and morphometry. Hippocampal cornu ammonis (CA)2, CA3, and dentate gyrus (DG) exhibited distinct patterns involving spine abundance, density, and geometry, whereas the central, lateral, and basolateral amygdalar nuclei showed nucleus- and stage-dependent remodeling. Across the multiregional dataset, recurring responses comprised spine-subtype redistribution, changes in spine abundance, and morphometric remodeling rather than uniform structural rescue. Conclusions: VU0155069 engages circuit- and pathological stage-specific forms of dendritic spine remodeling across distributed recognition- and associative-memory networks.

Article.Title: Proteomic analysis in Alzheimer's disease with psychosis reveals a shared AD proteomic landscape and a separate molecular signature of postsynaptic density disruption
Article.Authors: Ku, T. S.-H.; Mullet, S. J.; Sui, Z.; Zeng, L.; Ding, Y.; Yocum, A. K.; MacDonald, M. L.; Gelhaus, S. L.; Kofler, J. K.; Sweet, R. A.
Article.Abstract: Background and Hypothesis: Alzheimer's disease with psychosis (AD+P) is a subgroup of AD patients with more rapid cognitive deterioration. While our previous study showed that AD+P is associated with loss of prefrontal cortex postsynaptic density (PSD) proteins, identifying proteins in the broader cellular environment that influence PSD loss addresses a critical knowledge gap about synaptic dysfunction mechanisms in early disease stages. Study Results: AD+P showed the most pronounced alterations relative to controls (178 proteins with q<0.05), although alterations in AD-P and AD+P relative to controls were highly similar (R2=0.965, p<0.001). Weighted-gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA) identified four modules significantly associated with disease status comparing AD subjects to controls, but none differed significantly between AD+P and AD-P. We identified 15 proteins significantly correlated with PSD yield across all samples, including ENPP6, linked to AD+P by GWAS. Additionally, PSD yield-associated proteins showed minimal overlap with altered AD proteins (1 of 137). Proteins negatively correlated with PSD yield were enriched for presynaptic endocytosis, whereas the one WGCNA module significantly correlated with PSD yield was enriched for inflammatory terms. Conclusions: Our findings suggest a model in which AD+P arises from the combination of quantitative alterations within a shared AD proteome profile and a superimposed set of protein alterations correlated with PSD yield that confer distinct mechanisms of synaptic vulnerability and psychosis risk.

Article.Title: One placement, many fields: robust voxel-wise mapping with multichannel TMS
Article.Authors: Numssen, O.; Qiu, R.; Souza, V.; Laine, M.; Matsuda, R. H.; Buchberger, L.; Martin, C. W.; Weise, K.; Knoesche, T. R.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the human brain at the individual level is central to understanding its function and a prerequisite for personalized therapy. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can map structure-function relationships at high resolution by regressing trial-wise variation in the TMS-induced electric field (E-field) against a response such as motor evoked potentials (MEPs). This requires distinct E-fields across pulses at different cortical locations, which single-coil TMS (sTMS) achieves by physically repositioning the coil (typically supported by neuronavigation software such as InVesalius Navigator; Souza et al., 2018)--increasingly reliant on robotic guidance and capped by the coil geometry. Multichannel TMS (mTMS) instead steers the E-field electronically via independent currents in several coils, opening a design space of high variability without physical repositioning. We adapt determinant-based sequence optimization from discrete sTMS coil-placement sets to the continuous mTMS current space (D-optimal design), identifying pulse sequences whose induced cortical E-fields are as mutually dissimilar as biophysical constraints allow. We benchmarked optimized mTMS sequences against random baselines and optimized sTMS placements in virtual motor mapping across multiple head models, assessing three mTMS array geometries (5-channel planar, 6- and 12-channel spherical), two figure-of-eight sTMS coils, and varying pulse counts, response noise, and cortical depth. D-optimal mTMS currents substantially outperformed random currents and optimized sTMS at matched pulse counts. The gain was modest without noise but increased significantly with it: at the highest noise level, optimized sTMS failed to converge after 100 pulses (~20-22 mm error), whereas all mTMS arrays reached median errors at or below 6 mm. mTMS also recovered deep targets better than sTMS (up to 35 mm skin-cortex distance, versus 25 mm) and performed uniformly across the region of interest. A coil-space scheme based only on the magnetic vector potential, precomputable once per array without per-subject MRI, captured most of the benefit, matching subject-specific optimization at 100 pulses. mTMS thus makes voxel-wise mapping robust throughout a region of interest without coil repositioning.

Article.Title: Older Adults Show Preserved Neural Signatures of Audiovisual Integration but Altered Links to Speech Comprehension
Article.Authors: Reynolds, C.; Jensen, O.; Segaert, K.; Park, H.
Article.Abstract: Older adults often experience difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments despite relatively preserved hearing. Auditory and visual tagging responses were modulated by task relevance similarly across age groups, indicating largely preserved modality-specific sensory processing in older adults. Intermodulation responses, reflecting nonlinear interactions between auditory and visual speech signals, also remained sensitive to task relevance and did not differ in their condition-dependent modulation between age groups. Greater Task-Relevant versus Task-Irrelevant differences in intermodulation coherence were also associated with greater comprehension benefits in younger adults; no significant association was found in older adults, and this relationship differed significantly between age groups. These findings suggest that the absence of a comprehension benefit in older adults is linked to a change in the relationship between audiovisual intermodulation and behaviour, despite largely preserved task-sensitive brain responses.

Article.Title: Intrinsic Goals for Autonomous Agents: Hierarchical Exploration Captures Future Volitional Action in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Kutscher, D.; Keller, R.; Pei, F.; Kirsch, A.; Nayebi, A.
Article.Abstract: Animals have a remarkable ability to act autonomously---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. To understand how biological autonomy may emerge from optimizing intrinsic goals, we use recent whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (\textit{Drosophila melanogaster}) that identify neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than $10$ seconds in advance. Combined with a neuromechanical digital twin of \textit{Drosophila}, these recordings allow us to test whether intrinsically motivated artificial agents with realistic embodiments quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. We implement a hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agent whose policy operates over a discrete library of motor primitives---fixed low-level controllers that actuate joint dynamics---closely matching ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents with no external reward using $20$ intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. We evaluate frozen policies in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled after the fruit-fly experiment, allowing us to compare spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decode future turn direction from both kinematics and neural activations on the same timescales observed in flies. We find that DIAYN---a hierarchical competency algorithm that learns a discrete set of policies maximizing behavioral entropy and the separability of their induced sensory observations---achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance with the fruit fly. Surprisingly, DIAYN's learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this behavioral diversity optimizes a concrete computational goal of maximizing state-space coverage at the \emph{population} level. Furthermore, DIAYN agents' latent activity closely captures the specific sum-difference rule in interhemispheric encoding of future kinematics in biological flies. Together, these results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.

Article.Authors: Chupina, I.; Roos, N. M.; Sierpowska, J.; Oostenveld, R.; Tuladhar, A. M.; Westner, B. U.; Piai, V.

Article.Authors: Flook, E. A.; Shafiei, G.; Cieslak, M.; Horien, C.; Luo, A. C.; Meisler, S. L.; Salo, T.; Sydnor, V. J.; Tong, T. T.; Barch, D. M.; Goldsmith, J.; Gur, R. E.; Somerville, L. H.; Uddin, L. Q.; Alexander-Bloch, A.; Shinohara, R. T.; Satterthwaite, T. D.

Article.Title: Loss of PEA-15 Alters ERK/MAPK Signaling and Circadian Function in the Suprachiasmatic Nucleus
Article.Authors: Wheaton, K.; Halloy, N.; Formanowicz, M.; Ramos, J. W.; Hoyt, K. R.; Obrietan, K.
Article.Abstract: Circadian rhythms are a fundamental biological process that coordinates physiological functions, behavior, and metabolism with an approximately 24-hour periodicity. At the center of the mammalian circadian timing system is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, which generates robust, clock-gated neuronal output that establishes the temporal organization of cellular and physiological processes throughout the body. Our previous work demonstrated that the scaffold protein PEA-15 (phosphoprotein enriched in astrocytes 15) is highly expressed in the SCN and dynamically interacts with ERK, a key effector kinase of the MAPK pathway, to regulate its subcellular localization. Thus, loss of PEA-15 alters multiple properties of the SCN clock, including its intrinsic period and its responsiveness to photic input, with effects that depend on the direction of phase resetting. Collectively, these findings identify PEA-15 as an important regulator of SCN circadian function and implicate ERK/MAPK signaling as one mechanism through which PEA-15 modulates clock timing and photic entrainment.

Article.Title: Predictable Timing Enhances the Use of Predictable Content
Article.Authors: Magnusson, O.; Hobbelen, H.; Berkhof, W.; Sack, A. T.; Leunissen, I.; ten Oever, S.
Article.Abstract: As events unfold, they carry structure in both their timing and content, with these dimensions often interrelated. Most research has treated these dimensions separately, although processing them jointly may provide important computational benefits. It is an open question whether the brain processes a sequence's timing and predictable content structure independently, or integrates these two sources of information to guide prediction. We hypothesised that predictable timing would allow listeners to better exploit structure in the content, with this effect increasing as content structure becomes stronger. To test this, we presented tone sequences with pitch trajectories following a 1/f^{beta} structure, where {beta} determines how strongly the content of each tone persists, while independently varying the temporal periodicity of the sequence. Performance was quantified using response errors relative to outcome predictions of a Gaussian Process Regression model and a model-free measure of how strongly preceding tones influenced responses. Response error decreased and reliance on preceding tones increased with higher {beta} and periodic timing. Moreover, the influence of preceding tones showed an interaction between timing and content, such that the effect of periodicity grew with increasing {beta}. The response error showed no such interaction, although the effect of periodic timing was reliable only for the most structured sequences. Our findings suggest an interdependency between content and timing, where predictable timing helps listeners make greater use of predictable content.

Article.Title: Memory erasure by dopamine-gated retrospective learning
Article.Authors: Jeong, H.; Zsembik, L.; Farouq, F.; DiSanto, J. A.; Jin, C.; Chakraborty, R.; Belur, N.; Zhou, M.; Sanders, A. D.; Wang, S. X.; Srinivasan, A.; Cox, S. M. L.; Garr, E.; Brooke, S.; Janak, P. H.; Leyton, M.; Chen, R.; Namboodiri, V. M. K.

Yet once a cue-outcome association is learned, repeated cue exposure without outcome suppresses conditioned behavior without erasing the underlying memory. This allows rapid behavioral recovery when outcomes are reintroduced. Here, we confirm this limitation for standard prospective extinction protocols that present cues without the associated outcome, but show that true memory erasure is achieved by inverting the paradigm: presenting outcomes without associated cues, i.e., retrospective extinction. We demonstrate that orbitofrontal cortex activity at outcome is necessary for the rapid behavioral recovery following prospective extinction, and that mesolimbic dopamine activity at outcome is necessary for retrospective extinction. Article.Authors: Nakamura, T.; Okubo, L.; Miyoshi, K.; Murakami, I.
Article.Abstract: What we see at one location depends on what surrounds it. Such contextual effects are thought to arise from neural signals that travel across the retinotopic representations. Because these signals need more time to travel longer distances, a more distant surround should influence perception most strongly when presented earlier, compensating for its delay. We tested this prediction in human observers using a visual illusion in which a central target appears tilted away from the orientation of its surround (tilt illusion). Measuring the temporal window of this illusion using psychophysical reverse correlation revealed the opposite: the most effective surround occurred progressively later as distance increased. Computational modelling demonstrated that this reversal is explained if the visual system sends out a query that recruits contextual information on demand. Article.Authors: Parameshwarappa, V.; Rastoldo, G.; Franceschini, E.; Macherey, O.; Norena, A.

Article.Title: Linking cross-species hemodynamics with neuronal activity in prefrontal cortex during abstract sequence viewing
Article.Authors: Conen, K. E.; Stewart, B.; Rivera Nunez, M. V.; Hyde, H.; Yusif Rodriguez, N.; Ahuja, A.; Basu, D.; McKim, T.; Desrochers, T. M.

However, neuronal activity does not directly mirror hemodynamic responses, and abstract sequence responses are found both near and far from fMRI peaks. In contrast, distinct dynamics of spiking activity are selectively present near fMRI peaks, suggesting that temporal coordination across neurons may influence hemodynamic activity in prefrontal cortex. Together, these experiments establish a link between human brain activity, macaque fMRI, and single neuron responses, providing a window into the neural processes that mediate abstract sequence detection.

Article.Title: Habitual sleep duration is associated with the cortical organisation of brain network controllability

Article.Title: Familiarity synchronizes brain rhythms during natural viewing
Article.Authors: Noad, K. N.; Kaiser, D.
Article.Abstract: Our perception of the world is shaped not only by sensory information, but also by prior experience. Across participants, all brain rhythms showed reliable intersubject synchrony and related to activity across large-scale brain networks. Familiarity selectively enhanced intersubject synchronisation in beta and gamma rhythms, with these effects reflected in visual and default mode brain regions. Moreover, beta and gamma band activity were modulated by similar aspects of the movie, suggesting coordinated familiarity-related processing. These findings show that familiarity selectively shapes rhythmic neural dynamics across the cortex, providing a mechanism through which prior experience alters the coordination of neural representations during naturalistic perception.

Article.Authors: Kwon, J.-S.; Wang, L.; Ganti, N. R.; Li, J.; Xia, S.; Al-Dalahmah, O.; Yoo, A. S.

HD-LINC knockdown cleared neuritic LD accumulation, restored soma-enriched LD distribution, and reduced lipid peroxidation. Finally, we developed antisense oligonucleotides that effectively reduced HD-LINC and reversed HD-LINC-associated phenotypes, nominating HD-LINC lowering as a potential therapeutic strategy in HD. These results identify HD-LINC as a human-specific regulator of neuronal LD spatial organization, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal degeneration in HD. Article.Title: Neuroscience in Conversation: Tracking Scientific Change Through an Open Seminar Archive
Article.Authors: Bellin, I.; Tulner, L. K.; Beyh, A.; Wearn, A.; Forkel, S. J.
Article.Abstract: Scientific talks capture how researchers frame questions, debate ideas, and communicate emerging methods, providing a complementary record of scientific change to the published literature. We investigated whether an open neuroscience seminar archive could reveal shifting scientific attention and contain predictive information about subsequent discourse. We analysed 470 English-language transcripts from the Clinical Neuroanatomy Seminars YouTube channel, spanning 2010-2026 and approximately 2.6 million words, using longitudinal vocabulary analysis, unsupervised topic clustering, conceptual comparisons, and rolling temporal forecasting. The archive captured sustained discussion of language, white matter anatomy, connectivity, clinical neuroscience, and neurobiological mechanisms, alongside changes in their relative prominence. Network-related terminology became more prominent than localisation-related terminology, references to individual variability and computational approaches increased, and open science practices became more visible in scientific discussion. Beyond retrospective description, a regression model predicted keyword frequencies one and two years ahead with approximately 12% and 17% lower mean absolute error, respectively, than a persistence baseline. This modest gain is better explained by smoothing of year-to-year fluctuations than by genuine prediction: terms showing the strongest recent growth tended to fall back rather than continue rising. These findings suggest that spoken scientific discourse shows clear longitudinal change but offers limited evidence of information about subsequent shifts in attention. Interpretation remains grounded in the archive curated scope and changing content composition. By making nearly two decades of freely accessible neuroimaging education amenable to systematic analysis, this study connects open educational practice with the study of science itself. Open seminar archives can serve as reusable research resources, preserving the conversations through which scientific communities develop and revise their ideas.

Article.Title: Early life adversity enhances prosocial helping towards a cagemate and reshapes brain-wide neural activity and network organization
Article.Authors: Breton, J. M.; Lynch, A.; Chiang, J.; Wijethunga, S.; Abdallah, I.; Hickman-Maynard, J.; Poon, Z.; Ben-Ami Bartal, I.; Brenhouse, H.

Network analyses further revealed altered functional connectivity in ELA-reared animals, with heightened connectivity in stress-related regions such as the lateral habenula. Together, these findings demonstrate that ELA impacts prosocial helping behavior and is associated with widespread changes in neural activity and network organization. This work provides insight into how early adversity shapes social motivation and the neural systems supporting prosocial behaviors.

Article.Authors: Dimou, M.; Beumer, S.; Pigorini, A.; Mikulan, E.; Calcagno, A.; Spinelli, L.; Momjian, S.; Seeck, M.; Vulliemoz, S.; Roehri, N.

These findings indicate that ESI only partially captures spontaneous intracranial dynamics and define spatial and temporal constraints for interpreting EEG-based source reconstructions.

BH4 promotes recovery of OL maturation programs, including restoration of translation-related networks and OLIG1 nuclear localization, providing mechanistic insight into BH4-supported white matter maturation under chronic hypoxic conditions.

Article.Authors: Pando-Naude, V.; Kuang, V. H.; Christensen, K. L.; Stupacher, J.; Vuust, P.; Keller, P. E.

These findings suggest that sensorimotor synchronization deficits in PD reflect reduced use of recent timing errors to guide upcoming movements and less precise internal timekeeping. Article.Authors: Jung, J.; Gim, J.-A.; Lambon Ralph, M.
Article.Abstract: A fundamental challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the molecular and neurochemical architecture of the human cortex gives rise to sophisticated higher cognitive functions. ATL GABA+ and Glx concentrations were positively associated with semantic memory performance, and GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor-subunit expression showed selective relationships with semantic memory accuracy. Crucially, mediation analyses revealed that GABA+ mediated associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and semantic performance, whereas Glx mediated both glutamatergic and widespread GABAergic receptor associations. Together, these findings reveal a coupled molecular-neurochemical architecture of the human ATL, linking neurotransmitter receptor organisation to regional neurochemical state and individual differences in semantic memory. Article.Title: Heterogeneous plasticity rules generate diverse structures in recurrent networks
Article.Authors: Cusseddu, C.; Festa, D.; Miehl, C.; Gjorgjieva, J.
Article.Abstract: How do local changes at individual synapses give rise to structured recurrent connectivity? Experiments have revealed diverse forms of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) across the brain, making it difficult to predict which circuit structures different rules will generate. We developed an analytical framework mapping excitatory Hebbian, anti-Hebbian, and symmetric STDP rules to directed three-neuron motifs. Individual homogeneous rules generate restricted subsets of motifs, and no single rule produces all motifs. Combining different rules generates motifs inaccessible to individual rules and yields the full motif repertoire, and these predictions generalize to larger recurrent networks. The mapping is nevertheless highly non-unique, with distinct rules and parameters producing similar motif distributions, including distributions compatible with experimental connectivity. Thus, circuit structure constrains candidate plasticity rules but does not uniquely identify them. Finally, networks with similar motif distributions can nonetheless differ in their firing rates and pairwise correlations, suggesting that activity may provide an additional constraint on candidate plasticity rules.

Article.Title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
Article.Authors: Delaney, C.; Herrejon, I.; Magalhaes, T. N. C.; Jackson, T. B.; Hicks, T. H.; Bernard, J. A.
Article.Abstract: The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been relatively understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson's Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network, which has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. In a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86 we looked at network connectivity in cognitive and motor sub-circuits. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI). This data was analyzed using the CONN toolbox with an ROI-ROI approach targeting the CB-BG circuit. We replicated the previously mapped cognitive subcircuit and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adult hood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity as it relates to performance on the Stroop task showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. We also explored sex differences and found higher functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. Together, we have replicated motor and cognitive CB-BG subcircuits and further demonstrated that this network has altered connectivity associated with age, sex, progesterone, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential new step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson's Disease.

Article.Title: Ms4a4a loss preferentially remodels microglia with limited, compartment-specific effects across central and peripheral immune compartments in 5xFAD mice
Article.Authors: Danhash, E.; Verbeck, A.; Iyer, A.; Karch, C. M.
Article.Abstract: Background: Genome-wide association studies have identified the MS4A locus as a major modifier of Alzheimers disease (AD) risk and resilience. MS4A4A is enriched in microglia, and we previously demonstrated that loss of Ms4a4a reduces amyloid plaque pathology and attenuates amyloid-associated tau spreading. However, MS4A4A is also expressed in peripheral myeloid populations, raising the possibility that its effects extend beyond brain-resident microglia. Here, we sought to define how constitutive Ms4a4a loss alters immune populations across central nervous system (CNS), CNS-border, and peripheral compartments in the context of amyloid pathology. Methods: We performed multicompartment immune profiling by flow cytometry in 5xFAD Ms4a4a wild-type and 5xFAD Ms4a4a-deficient mice. Myeloid and lymphoid populations were characterized in the brain, dural meninges, skull bone marrow, tibial bone marrow, and spleen. Results: Ms4a4a loss produced its strongest immune effects in brain microglia. 5xFAD Ms4a4a-deficient mice exhibited increased microglial abundance, increased frequency and expression of CD86, increased MHC class II expression intensity, and enrichment of CXCR4-high microglia, whereas P2RY12 and TREM2 were unchanged. Brain macrophages showed increased MHC class II expression, whereas conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) in the brain showed reduced MHC class II expression, with limited changes in other infiltrating immune populations. Immune composition in the dura and skull bone marrow was largely preserved, although MHC class II expression was increased in skull bone marrow cDCs. Peripheral immune composition in tibial bone marrow and spleen was similarly preserved, with selective increases in M2-like macrophages in tibial bone marrow and splenic CD8 T-cell frequency. Conclusions: These findings identify microglia as the immune population most strongly remodeled by Ms4a4a loss in the setting of amyloid pathology. Constitutive Ms4a4a deficiency does not produce broad systemic immune remodeling but instead preferentially alters microglial state, accompanied by more limited, cell type- and tissue-specific effects across other central and peripheral immune compartments. These findings establish MS4A4A as a context-dependent regulator of immune responses to AD pathology with particularly prominent effects on microglia.

Article.Title: Very Early Cortical Auditory Responses to Speech in Humans
Article.Authors: Lerud, K. D.; Fisher, C. D.; Commuri, V.; Anderson, S.; Simon, J. Z.
Article.Abstract: A foundational measure of the auditory system's ability to process sound correctly is the auditory brainstem response (ABR) and middle latency response (MLR) complex, but their dependence on stimulus complexity and behavioral relevance is poorly understood. Here we recorded noninvasive, simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) in adults listening to both naturalistic speech and clicks, and computed the resulting temporal response functions (TRFs). The TRF's ABR-MLR complex for speech listening contains a very early cortical peak (11 ms latency), which has not been well-characterized, and is absent for click stimuli. Other significant differences in latency and source between the speech and click MLR complexes point to further differences in their auditory processing, in thalamus and cortex. In contrast, the speech and click TRF's ABR complex both share a similar, prominent wave V response. In summation, the use of naturalistic speech reveals how early auditory responses reflect its ethological relevance.

Article.Title: Information coding strategies in biological reservoir computing for multiclass time-series classification
Article.Authors: Nishi, Y.; Yamamoto, H.; Katori, Y.; Sato, S.
Article.Abstract: Physical reservoir computing (RC) using biological neural networks (BNNs) offers a framework for probing how high-dimensional dynamics arising from multicellular systems support complex information processing in the brain. However, how electrical inputs and extracellular readouts should be designed to suit different task demands remains unclear. Here, using primary rat cortical neurons cultured on a high-density microelectrode array, we investigated how input encoding and spike detection methods influence neural representations and the resulting RC performance in BNNs. Comparison of pulse amplitude modulation and latency coding revealed that the latter exhibited superior performance in demanding multiclass conditions, including a 10% improvement in a 10-class spoken digit classification task. Spike sorting further improved classification performance by enhancing class separability, while largely preserving the low-dimensional structure of population activity. These findings highlight the importance of designing information coding strategies according to task difficulty.

Article.Title: Focal neuronal loss and cell replacement in a connectome model of fly steering
Article.Authors: Habib, P.; Petr, M.; Rust, R.
Article.Abstract: Focal neuronal loss after stroke, traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury can disrupt circuits and result in persistent motor deficits. Which cells and connections must be restored to recover a specific behavior is difficult to establish experimentally. Here we use a connectome-constrained spiking model of the fruit-fly nervous system and decode motor-neuron output to simulate visually guided steering. After loss of 4,000 neurons, path straightness ranged from 0.04 to 0.95 depending on lesion location. At a fixed sensorimotor site, a 2,000-neuron lesion reduced simulated displacement to 6.5% of intact. Across 100 stochastic simulation realizations of the connectome, replacing 100 cells with their original connections increased displacement to 62.5% of intact when motor-control pathways were prioritized, compared with 10.1% after random selection of 100 cells and 48.5% after random selection of 1,000 cells. When connections were instead inferred from cell type, the same 100 intended replacements reached 60.0% of intact with matched identities and 6.7% with non-target identities, indicating that cell identity and type-dependent integration are required for recovery. Our model generates testable predictions for genetic ablation experiments in fruit flies and identifies candidate cellular and circuit requirements for motor repair that can inform cell replacement therapies and future models of mammalian locomotion.

Article.Title: Appellian Neural Networks
Article.Authors: Bahdasariants, S.; Parola, L.; Kacker, K.; Feldman, A. K.; Zdobinski, Z.; Kang, I.; Weber, D. J.
Article.Abstract: The movement of articulated bodies, whether biological or robotic, involves two interrelated computational challenges. Inverse dynamics determines the forces or torques required to achieve a specified movement, while forward dynamics computes the resulting accelerations from given forces or torques. Although both computations are governed by the same equations of motion, they are typically implemented as separate inverse and forward mappings in both model-based and data-driven approaches. This division can obscure the underlying structure common to both problems. Here, we introduce the Appellian Neural Network (ANNet), a physics-informed neural network that unifies both computations through a shared learned representation by modeling a single scalar quantity from classical mechanics, specifically Appell's acceleration energy. Inverse dynamics is obtained by differentiating the learned energy function with respect to acceleration to recover joint torques. Forward dynamics is computed without retraining by embedding the same learned energy landscape into an optimization objective, where the unregularized minimum satisfies the Gibbs-Appell equation. The resulting accelerations are then integrated forward in time. ANNet is evaluated using a double pendulum paradigm. For trajectories not encountered during training, both inverse and forward simulations demonstrate accuracy and real-time capability. Both computations propagate input noise similarly to their analytical counterparts, and adaptation of the inverse dynamics to a modified pendulum generalizes to forward simulation without additional forward-specific training. These results establish a first-principles approach for employing a single learned representation to support both inverse and forward dynamic computations.

Article.Title: A canonical input to the head direction compass carries predominantly eye movement signals
Article.Authors: Stott, J. J.; Chang, H. H. V.; Bao, C.; Zhang, K.; Cullen, K. E.; van der Meer, M. A.
Article.Abstract: The mammalian head direction (HD) system is thought to update its internal compass using angular head velocity (AHV) signals relayed from the brainstem. We tested this canonical interpretation by recording from the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi (NPH), a proposed AHV relay known to be important for accurate HD tracking, while simultaneously measuring eye and head movements in mice. Neurons classified as AHV-tuned instead predominantly encoded eye movements: most showed saccade-related bursts or pauses, and apparent AHV tuning was largely explained by eye rather than head motion. Optotagging showed that even NPH neurons projecting directly to the HD circuit predominantly encoded eye movements. Empirically constrained population models reconstructed eye position and gaze direction, but head-direction readouts failed when eye and head motion were dissociated. These findings overturn the canonical view of NPH as a dedicated AHV relay, revealing eye movements as a major, previously unmeasured component of the signals entering the mammalian HD circuit and thereby changing the computational problem that the HD system must solve to maintain a stable representation of heading.

Article.Title: Lower Levels of Task-Induced Hippocampal Activation Predict Better Performance on a Separate Verbal Memory Evaluation
Article.Authors: Sisk, C. A.; McDermott, K. B.; Elison, J. T.; Swanson, M. R.; Wig, G. S.; Gilmore, A. W.; Nelson, S. M.
Article.Abstract: Inter-individual differences in learning-related activation in the hippocampus and its subregions predict specific differences in memory abilities. The complexity of these relationships creates a setting that is ripe for theoretically informative investigation, but that can also yield reports of spurious relationships that do not reflect underlying neurobiological associations. Across-study replication is therefore a critical step toward understanding how individual differences in hippocampal activity drive individual differences in memory ability. In the domain of verbal memory, Wig et al. (2008) identified a negative relationship between task-induced activation in right posterior HPC (pHPC) and out-of-scanner verbal memory test performance. Replicating this result in an independent sample of 86 participants, we identified the same negative correlation between pHPC activation during an in-scanner Lithuanian-English paired associate learning task and out-of-scanner California Verbal Learning Test (CVLT-II) performance. In a follow-up exploratory voxel-wise association analysis, we observed the same negative correlation between CVLT-II performance and task-induced activity across three regions of the medial temporal lobe: the left perirhinal/entorhinal cortex, right parahippocampal gyrus, and left posterior hippocampus. This replication and accompanying extension represent a critical step toward understanding how pHPC supports verbal memory by answering basic questions concerning the reliability and selectivity of this previously identified relationship.

Article.Title: High-content imaging of live microglia-containing Alzheimer's disease brain organoids
Article.Authors: Quang, D.; Summers, R.; Dooling, B. R.; Esquer, H.; Zhou, Q.; LaBarbera, D. V.; Vergara, M. N.; Chial, H. J.; Potter, H.; Johnson, N. R.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common progressive neurodegenerative disease for which there is currently no safe and effective treatment. AD is characterized by the pathological aggregation of amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) in the brain resulting in neuronal dysfunction/death and cognitive decline. Modeling these processes in vitro remains challenging due to the lack of an immune-competent 3D in vitro human model of AD amenable to high-throughput analyses. Conventional cerebral organoids (COs) lack microglia and are optically dense which precludes real-time longitudinal analyses. Here, we employ the fluorescent amyloid probe PyrPeg to selectively monitor A{beta} aggregation, and calcein AM and propidium iodide to assess cellular viability within microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We identify age-dependent DS-AD-associated phenotypes within T21 MCOs including A{beta} neuropathology, neurodegeneration, and glial cell dysregulation. Our platform supports real-time, multiplexed tracking of disease progression and provides a scalable platform for longitudinal analyses studying disease mechanisms and targeted approaches to treatment.

Article.Title: Scalp EEG detects motor sequence replay signatures during wakeful rest
Article.Authors: Dash, D.; Sugata, H.
Article.Abstract: Brief wakeful rest may support motor-memory processing through replay of recently practiced neural sequences, but human motor replay has been demonstrated mainly with invasive recordings or magnetoencephalography. Here we tested whether ordered motor-sequence replay can be detected from scalp EEG across wakeful rest during motor skill learning. During rest, participants received no cue, regular or accelerated auditory targeted-memory reactivation (TMR), or randomized tones. Neural states re-emerged in the practiced sequence order, revealing forward replay across conditions. Accelerated TMR enhanced total learning; within this condition, stronger forward replay showed the clearest exploratory relationship with micro-offline gains, while forward and reverse replay also covaried with gains across the cohort. The apparent replay timescale shifted systematically with decoder temporal resolution, showing that measured timing reflects both neural dynamics and the observation model. These findings support scalp EEG as a scalable approach for studying ordered motor-sequence reactivation during wakeful rest.

Article.Title: Auditory tracking magnitude, temporal alignment, and anatomical distribution during wakefulness and propofol-based anesthesia in human sEEG
Article.Authors: Zhu, H.; Yao, C.; Han, Z.; Zhou, W.; Wang, Y.; Li, S.; Wong, P. C. M.; Tian, X.; Teng, X.
Article.Abstract: General anesthesia attenuates auditory responses, but response magnitude alone does not describe how residual activity aligns with sound over time or varies across the brain. We jointly characterized these aspects of auditory tracking using stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG) in 13 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy during wakefulness and clinically defined unresponsiveness under propofol-based anesthesia. The same rhythmic humming sequences were presented at approximately 1.61 Hz in both sessions. During anesthesia, stimulus-rate power showed widespread reductions and phase alignment with the stimulus rhythm was less consistent, although responses remained detectable at some recording channels. During wakefulness, response strength decreased with cortical surface distance from posteromedial Heschl's gyrus; this distance-response relationship was weaker during anesthesia. In a contrastive learning analysis (CEBRA), low-dimensional embeddings derived from anesthesia recordings yielded lower acoustic-envelope decoding accuracy on held-out data and lower consistency across model fits. Together, these findings characterize how attenuated auditory tracking is expressed jointly in response magnitude, temporal alignment, and anatomical distribution.

Article.Title: Brain Age Gap Associations with Externalising Behaviours in Youth: A Longitudinal Investigation in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Cohort
Article.Authors: Asikin, A.; Visontay, R.; Devine, E. K.; Squeglia, L. M.; Byrne, H.; Mewton, L.
Article.Abstract: Background. Early adolescence is a period of heightened risk for the emergence of externalising psychopathology, making it an important window for identifying neurodevelopmental risk markers. Differences between predicted brain age and chronological age - termed the brain age gap - reflect variation from age-typical patterns of brain structure. While brain age gap has been closely linked with internalising behaviours in adolescence, less is known about its relationship with externalising symptoms. This study examined whether brain age gap in late childhood/early adolescence (9-11 years) is associated with current externalising symptoms and whether it predicts externalising trajectories over seven-year follow-up. Methods. Participants were 10,516 adolescents (aged 9-11 at baseline; up to 18 years at follow-up) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study who met inclusion/exclusion criteria. Brain age gap for each participant was derived from an external validated prediction model (Drobinin et al., 2022) applied to baseline measurements of cortical volume, area, and subcortical volume. Linear mixed-effects models were used to test cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline brain age gap and externalising symptoms, as assessed using the Child Behaviour Checklist. Primary models were adjusted for age, sex, pubertal status, and prior to inclusion of sociodemographic covariates (ethnoracial identity and caregiver highest education). Results. A higher/more positive brain age gap was associated with greater externalising symptoms at baseline (B[SE]=0.067[0.033], p=.042), but this association was removed following sociodemographic adjustment (B[SE]=0.056[0.033], p=.088). Longitudinally, a significant brain age gap x age interaction was identified that remained evident after sociodemographic adjustment, with this relationship weakening across adolescence (B[SE]=-0.007[0.003], p=.033). Conclusions. These findings suggest that a more positive brain age gap, indicating more mature-appearing brain structure for age, in late childhood/early adolescence may be associated with externalising psychopathology, but this relationship is likely to be age- and context-dependent rather than a stable marker of persistent behavioural risk.

Article.Title: Scalable hardware and software for high-density, multi-regional electrophysiology in non-human primates
Article.Authors: Dubey, A.; Xu, Q.; Khazali, M. F.; Choi, J.; Wingel, K.; Haggerty, J.; Stefanowicz, J.; Pesaran, B.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how distributed neural circuits generate complex behaviors requires long-duration recordings from populations of individual neurons across multiple brain regions. High-density Neuropixels probes have revolutionized rodent systems neuroscience. Extending these capabilities to non-human primates (NHPs) for chronic, multi-regional recordings requires compact, implantable microdrive hardware and reliable automated spike-sorting software. NHPs provide access to complex and flexible behaviors that are difficult to study in other model systems. Extending the Neuropixels revolution to NHPs therefore depends on integrating hardware and software for long-duration, multi-regional recordings. Here, we present a scalable hardware-software platform co-designed for high-density neural data acquisition and reliable single-unit identification in NHPs. The Multi-regional Implantable NeuroDrive (MIND) is a lightweight, implantable microdrive that provides stable recordings from multiple independently positioned Neuropixels probes and is designed to support chronic, ambulatory, head-free recordings. We paired MIND with UnitAssay, an automated post-sorting curation framework that identifies and curates characteristic spike-sorting errors with minimal computational cost. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide an integrated platform for implanted, multi-regional recordings in NHPs performing complex and naturalistic behaviors. We tested MIND and UnitAssay across parietal, prefrontal, and motor cortices in rhesus macaques performing reaching and eye-movement tasks. MIND enabled stable multi-probe recordings across cortical regions and durations. UnitAssay enabled automated curation of large-scale spike-sorting output and improved reliable single-unit identification relative to Kilosort 4 labels and standard SpikeInterface quality control. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide a scalable solution for high-density, multi-regional, long-duration electrophysiology in NHPs.

Article.Title: Enhancing working memories using repetitive TMS
Article.Authors: Pagnotta, M. F.; D'Esposito, M.
Article.Abstract: Working memory, the ability to retain and manipulate information no longer present in the environment, is fundamental for goal-directed behavior (Baddeley, 2012; Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; D'Esposito, 2007; D'Esposito & Postle, 2015). Alpha oscillations (~8-12 Hz) have two apparently contradictory roles in working memory. Alpha activity gates irrelevant information through inhibition, a role causally supported by rhythmic transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of parietal cortex at alpha frequency when a retrospective cue renders a memory item irrelevant (Bonnefond & Jensen, 2012; Riddle et al., 2020). Yet alpha activity also tracks the content of memory and binds the features of memorized objects during maintenance (Foster et al., 2016; Pagnotta et al., 2026). Whether alpha oscillations causally support the fidelity of memory representations during maintenance is untested. Here, 24 participants received short trains of repetitive TMS (rTMS) at theta (6 Hz) or alpha frequency (10 Hz), or in an arrhythmic control pattern, during the second half of the delay of a color working memory task, over the left posterior inferior frontal sulcus or the left intraparietal sulcus. A mixture model separated memory precision from swap errors and guesses. Alpha stimulation of the intraparietal sulcus specifically increased memory precision, whereas rhythmic stimulation of either site reduced response error, guesses and swaps irrespective of frequency. These results provide causal evidence that alpha oscillations support the fidelity of working memory representations during maintenance, and show that rhythmic stimulation at the appropriate frequency, site and time can enhance human working memory.

Article.Title: Manifolds for the neural representation of 3D spatial experience
Article.Authors: Doudlah, R.; Xiao, M.; Postlewaite, S.; Kim, B.; Cowan, N.; Rosenberg, A.
Article.Abstract: The precision with which animals navigate and interact with objects depends in part on how their brains represent position and orientation in three dimensions. A central challenge is to explain within a common framework how neural systems ranging from insects to primates represent three-dimensional (3D) pose. Here we develop a framework based on the hypothesis that neural representations of pose lie on manifolds derived from the Special Euclidean Group, SE(3), which describes the full space of rigid-body positions and orientations in three dimensions. The framework shows how movement constraints, object geometry, and visual features jointly determine the topology of the resulting pose manifold, yielding a taxonomy that guides experimental tests. We apply the framework to derive low-dimensional manifolds for neural representations of 3D object orientation in macaque parietal cortex and head direction in the limbic systems of fruit bats, mice, and monkeys. This analysis also guides the construction of neuronal tuning functions that respect the topology determined by experimental conditions. Together, these results provide a common approach for linking the geometry of 3D pose to neural coding across species and brain systems.

Article.Title: Dissociable episodic memory performance and subjective experience across the aphantasia imagery spectrum
Article.Authors: Duckett, W.; Simons, J.
Article.Abstract: Mental imagery is often assumed to support episodic memory, yet whether this relationship depends on conscious access to imagery, and how reduced imagery differs from total aphantasia, remains unclear. The present study compared objective episodic memory performance, subjective trial-by-trial vividness, confidence, and response times in people reporting normal imagery, reduced imagery, or total aphantasia, across younger and older age groups. Participants completed an incidental-encoding episodic memory task requiring identification of visual or spatial changes in targets within scenes, alongside trial-by-trial vividness and confidence ratings. Across the full imagery spectrum, trial-level fluctuations in vividness were related to memory performance, whereas trait-level and averaged vividness measures were not. Moreover, reduced imagery and total aphantasia showed dissociable patterns of episodic memory performance and subjective experience. In the reduced-imagery group, vividness was a stronger predictor of accuracy and response times, vividness judgements were slower, and confidence was lower, suggesting greater metacognitive uncertainty when imagery is weak and inconsistent. Controls outperformed reduced and aphantasic groups on visual but not spatial changes, and both groups responded more slowly than controls; confidence did not differ between control and aphantasic groups. Age-related memory decline was observed in the control and reduced groups but not in the aphantasic group. Exit questionnaire data highlighted limited awareness of aphantasia among typical imagers and a persistent belief among aphantasic participants that their memory was inferior. Together, these findings show that reduced imagery should be distinguished from total aphantasia rather than treating both as a single population, and that trial-level fluctuations in vividness reveal relationships with episodic memory that trait-level and averaged measures do not capture.

Article.Title: Daylight exposure improves sleep and subsequent sleepiness
Article.Authors: Yang, M.; van Bergeyk, T.; Hut, R. A.; Lok, R.
Article.Abstract: Study Objectives: The causal effects of daylight exposure on sleep remain poorly understood, particularly under real-world conditions. This study aimed to address this gap by examining the effects of an afternoon daylight intervention on subsequent sleep. Methods: Ten healthy participants (4 males; 19 to 28 years) completed two randomized 3-h afternoon outdoor walks under high-intensity light (HIL; clear goggles) or attenuated light (AL; neutral-density-filtered goggles; ~10 photopic lux) conditions. Light exposure was centered around the estimated crossover between the phase-advancing and phase-delaying portions of the light phase-response curve, individually determined from baseline dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). Subsequent nocturnal sleep was assessed using at-home polysomnography (PSG), and subjective sleepiness and sleep quality were assessed using the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale and Groningen Sleep Quality Scale, respectively. Differences between conditions and across time were examined using linear mixed-effects models. Results: There were no significant differences between conditions in DLMO timing or the phase angle between DLMO and sleep onset, indicating that the light manipulation did not produce a detectable shift in circadian phase. Sleep duration and self-reported sleep quality were also unchanged. However, nighttime delta power accumulated more rapidly following HIL exposure, accompanied by greater NREM sleep and reduced wakefulness after sleep onset (all p < 0.01). Participants were also significantly less sleepy upon awakening following HIL compared with AL exposure (p < 0.05). Conclusions: High-intensity natural daylight exposure may promote greater sleep intensity and reduce sleepiness upon awakening. These findings highlight a potential role for daytime light exposure in modulating subsequent sleep physiology and next-morning sleepiness, independent of changes in circadian phase.

Article.Title: A vagal-to-sympathetic reflex controls lung vascular leak
Article.Authors: Robinson, E.; Ibanez, E. M.; Santibanez Ocampo, B.; Li, J.; Ballal, N.; Miller, J. M.; Shivdikar, K.; Umans, B. D.; Prescott, S. L.
Article.Abstract: Dynamic regulation of the vascular barrier is required for an effective inflammatory response, allowing delivery of plasma proteins and immune cells to sites of insult. Although normally protective, sustained leak becomes costly in organs like the lung, where swelling stiffens tissue and impairs breathing, yet many upstream regulators remain unidentified. Using a chemogenetic screen of vagal afferent subtypes, we identify a neural reflex that drives lung vascular leak. The reflex originates in an orphan population of neurons expressing Cysltr2 that innervates alveolar capillary beds and senses both mechanical and inflammatory stimuli, fitting classic definitions of pulmonary 'J' receptors, an afferent subtype described anatomically since the 1950s whose function has remained speculative. Activating CYSLTR2 neurons increases lung vascular leak within minutes and causes perivascular edema and respiratory dysfunction, whereas silencing them during inhaled allergen challenge reduces leak and improves lung mechanics. Rather than acting locally through antidromic peptide release, this reflex engages brainstem relays and sympathetic efferents to broadcast its effects throughout lung vasculature. Vagal control of the vascular barrier thus forms an axis of organ defense that can go awry in disease, revealing new ways to regulate organ fluid balance upstream of the endothelium

Article.Title: Lateral-eyed tree shrews combine panoramic vision with an expanded oculomotor repertoire
Article.Authors: Pal, R.; Kempkes, E.; Aeleti, R.; Tubbs, E.; Biswas, A.; Sedigh-Sarvestani, M.
Article.Abstract: Mammals differ in how they redirect gaze. Primates shift and hold gaze with rapid, precise eye movements that can be decoupled from the head. In lateral-eyed mammals studied to date, gaze is organized around the head: saccades are coupled to head rotation in freely moving animals and typically accompanied by attempted head movements even under head fixation. These observations suggest a trade-off: animals that keep a panoramic field give up the precise, eye-driven control of gaze typical of frontal-eyed animals. But because lateral eyes and head-centered gaze co-occur in every lateral-eyed species studied, it is unknown whether one follows from the other. Here we test this in the tree shrew, an arboreal mammal with laterally placed eyes. Using real-time eye tracking in head-fixed animals, we find that tree shrews saccade frequently under head fixation and that most saccades occur without detectable attempted head movement. Tree shrews make visually evoked saccades, along both the horizontal and vertical axes of the visual field, toward targets. They can also fixate on visual targets. Using widefield calcium imaging, we show that visual cortex over-represents the central visual field. Lastly, we show that extraocular muscles contain morphologically elaborate palisade endings, specialized nerve endings that are a constant feature of frontal-eyed species. Lateral eyes therefore do not preclude eye-driven gaze control. The two are separable dimensions of visual system design, a combination that may suit animals whose locomotion routinely points the head away from where they need to look.

Article.Title: Natural scene segmentation dynamics reveal iterative Bayesian inference
Article.Authors: Biswas, T. K.; Vacher, J.; Molholm, S.; Mamassian, P.; Coen-Cagli, R.
Article.Abstract: The visual system operates by segmenting visual inputs into distinct perceptual objects. Segmentation is dynamic, as revealed by the tempo of perceptual choices and neural activity in the visual cortex. Dynamics for natural stimuli however, are poorly understood because natural scene segmentation is ambiguous and subjective. We measured subjective human segmentation maps for natural images using an innovative paradigm, and uncovered richer spatiotemporal dynamics than predicted by current theories of segmentation. To explain these dynamics, we introduced Iterative Bayesian Inference algorithms for segmentation that iteratively integrate visual inputs with the prior expectation for local smoothness. When visual inputs were consistent with such a spatial prior, iterative inference was faster. Such a predicted relationship between spatial prior and inferential dynamics was evident in our data and correctly reflected each individual participant's spatial biases. We conclude that iterative Bayesian inference sets the tempo for a fundamental function of natural vision.

Article.Title: The remarkable complexity of the brain microbiome in health and disease
Article.Authors: Hu, Z.; McKenzie, C.-A.; Smith, C.; Haas, J. G.; Lathe, R.
Article.Abstract: Microbes in human brain and their potential contribution to neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) have long been debated. We recently developed a new method (the electronic tree of life, eToL) based on small subunit ribosomal RNA (rRNA) probes, further confirmed by large subunit rRNA analysis, to comprehensively address the spectrum of microorganisms in control and AD brain. We report a remarkable diversity of brain microbes in control brain. The most abundant are fungi, bacteria, and chloroplastida, and we report detailed identification of representative microbial species. The pattern is substantially conserved across different bilateran species from Drosophila to human. In terms of diversity, the human brain microbiome appears to be a subset (~20%) of the gut microbiome. Adenovirus type C was the major virus found in human brain; other viruses were not well represented. However, the spectrum of brain microbes differed between individuals as well as between brain regions examined from single individuals (amygdala, cingulate cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus); of these four regions, the highest microbial burden was in cingulate cortex. There was evidence of spreading of pathogens between brain regions in single individuals. Some microbes are over-represented in AD brain according to two measures: (i) absolute number of microbes normalized to endogenous human transcripts, and (ii) the number of brain specimens showing overabundance versus control. Species over-represented in AD brain according to both measures notably include bacteria (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus/Bacillus, Sphingomonas/Ralstonia) and fungi (Acrocalymma/Altenaria/Aureobasidium of the Aspergillus group; Komagataella of the Candida group, Cortinarius of the Schizophyllum group, and Tausonia of the Cryptococcus group), that are all related to known human pathogens. In addition, an uncharacterized chloroplastida (algae-related) species was more abundant in AD brain samples. Although these findings point to diverse microbial species, indicative of multiple causation, similar absolute levels of bacteria and fungi in AD brain samples could suggest synergy between pathogens. However, it is important to stress that not all AD samples were positive for these microbes, but this could be because the affected brain region(s) was not examined. These findings support the contention that infection, perhaps associated with declining immunity with age, may contribute to AD development.

Article.Title: Chronic In Vivo Imaging of a Focal Cortical Dysplasia Mouse Model Reveals Progressive Neuronal Loss with No Senolytic or Antiseizure Efficacy Following Dasatinib-Quercetin Treatment
Article.Authors: Olson, C. V.; Shariati, N.; Prochazkova, N.; Cizek, K.; Rehorova, M.; Populova, J.; Rozlivkova, J. T.; Wang, S.; Ricketts, B.; Kucerova, B.; Kudlacek, J.; Straka, B.; Jiruska, P.; Novak, O.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) type II is a common cause of pediatric drug-resistant epilepsy with no disease-modifying treatment. It arises from somatic mutations in the mTOR pathway that produce a mosaic population of mTOR-hyperactive dysmorphic neurons (DNs) with a senescence phenotype. A recent report showed that oral dasatinib-quercetin (DQ), both putative senolytics, selectively eliminates these neurons and abolishes seizures in an Mtorp.S2215F model. However, this has not been tested in a second FCD model and neuron loss was shown only by cross-sectional histology. Methods: Using chronic cranial windows and longitudinal in vivo two-photon imaging, we tracked genetically labeled neurons over eight weeks. In a mosaic MTORp.L2427P FCD model on a C57BL/6J background, we combined imaging with continuous video-EEG, immunohistochemistry (IHC), and LC-MS/MS pharmacokinetics in 47 mice. Seizure and pharmacokinetic sampling were extended to a smaller Swiss/CD1 cohort, the strain used previously. Results: Imaging revealed progressive loss of mTORmut (16.7%) and non-mTORmut (13.1%) neurons, with minimal loss in unmatched non-FCD controls. In IHC, lesions contained Beta-galactosidase-positive (B-Gal+) cells, but oral DQ showed no evidence of eliminating DNs or reducing seizure frequency, duration, or burden; seizures also persisted in CD1 mice. B-Gal+ cells tended to be less dense after DQ, but not significantly after correction. These data are more consistent with a senomorphic than a senolytic effect. Brain dasatinib (median 8.5 nM) exceeded its Src/ABL IC50, whereas quercetin (median 12 nM) was nearly two orders of magnitude below its BCL-XL affinity. Significance: Longitudinal tracking of single neurons shows progressive loss of labeled neurons in an FCD model, whereas the reported senolytic and antiseizure effects of DQ were not reproduced. DQ should not be assumed to act as a senolytic across FCD models, strains, or MTOR variants. Dependence on strain, mutation, or brain exposure bears on clinical translation.
