Article.Title: Glutamatergic and Redox Abnormalities in Major Depressive Disorder: Links to Childhood Maltreatment and Perceived Stress
Article.Authors: Syed, S.; Dan, R.; Hutson, L. M.; Brown, A. R.; Wang, C.; Stein, A.; Chen, X.; Du, F.; Pizzagalli, D. A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Childhood sexual abuse (CSA) increases the risk for major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain poorly understood. We examined (1) associations of medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) glutamatergic metabolites and redox balance with childhood maltreatment and MDD; and (2) whether these neurochemical measures predicted future perceived stress. Methods: Using proton and phosphorus 4T magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we quantified glutamate, glutamine, their sum (Glx), and the NAD/NADH ratio within the same mPFC voxel in 71 women across four groups: healthy controls (HC; n=27), current MDD without CSA (n=14), current MDD with CSA (n=14), and remitted MDD with CSA (n=16). Results: Glutamate and Glx levels were lower in both CSA-exposed groups (n=30) compared with HC (n=27), whereas women with MDD without CSA did not differ significantly from HC. Among CSA-exposed women, greater maltreatment severity was associated with lower glutamine, and greater maltreatment multiplicity with lower glutamate and Glx, specifically in women with current MDD. The association between depressive symptom severity and glutamine differed by CSA history. A significant interaction between baseline NAD/NADH ratio and clinical group predicted perceived stress at 6-month follow-up, adjusting for baseline perceived stress. Specifically, lower baseline NAD/NADH ratio predicted greater subsequent perceived stress in MDD without CSA, but not in the other clinical groups. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that mPFC glutamatergic metabolites and redox balance show distinct patterns of association with CSA history, depression status, and subsequent perceived stress, highlighting neurochemical heterogeneity in MDD and molecular markers of risk.

Article.Title: Measuring conscious tactile perception without report: pupil, blink, and microsaccade signatures of a tactile no-report paradigm
Article.Authors: Sharma, A. A.; Senjalia, R.; Woodworth, A.; Jin, D.; Aerts, S.; Cormier, D.; Khalaf, A.; Blumenfeld, H.
Article.Abstract: Conscious perception is often inferred from behavioral reports, which conflate awareness-related neural signals with the motor and decision processes required to respond. No-report paradigms address this by using spontaneous physiological signals, such as eye movements, to infer perception. Although our group developed a no-report visual paradigm, we had not applied this approach to touch. We developed a no-report tactile paradigm using the Galileo stimulation system to deliver pneumatic air puffs to non-thumb fingers on both hands while tracking eye movements. Participants reported sensations from the Report hand while receiving threshold-level puffs on both hands; eye metrics were used to infer perception in the No-Report hand. Perceived threshold-level stimuli elicited greater pupil dilation and more post-stimulus blinking than identical unperceived stimuli, with effects lasting 1 - 2 seconds. Microsaccade rate decreased after stimulus onset, but this suppression did not reach statistical significance. A stacked support vector machine trained on the Report eye-tracking measures was applied to classify No-Report trials and successfully separated [Predicted] Perceived from [Predicted] Not Perceived trials (AUC = .92; cross-validated accuracy = 72%; sensitivity = 90% at 80% specificity; label-permutation p < .001). These findings show that eye tracking can detect conscious tactile perception without overt responses and offer a noninvasive, scalable approach for studying tactile perception in patients with self-reported disabilities, including comatose or intubated patients.

Article.Title: Theta-Phase Targeted Encoding Gates Memory Sensitivity
Article.Authors: Raissle, A.; van de Ven, V.; Leunissen, I.; Fang, Z.; Valente, G.; Naseri, P.; Ten Oever, S.
Article.Abstract: Theta phase has been proposed to play an important role in memory. It may gate encoding and retrieval, such that certain phases are more favorable for memory processing than others, or become part of the memory representation, such that reinstating the encoding phase benefits retrieval. To test and distinguish these competing accounts, we used a closed-loop EEG system, allowing us to control the phase at which items were presented at encoding and retrieval. In an associative memory task, visual targets were presented at predefined phases of the ongoing mid-frontal theta rhythm, thereby pairing individual memory items with specific encoding phases. During retrieval, targets appeared either at the same phase as during encoding or at an alternative phase. We show that theta phase during encoding predicted subsequent memory sensitivity, while finding no evidence that retrieval phase nor the match between encoding and retrieval phases influenced performance. Therefore, our findings are consistent with a gating account, in which the rhythmic state at the moment of encoding influences the efficacy of memory formation.

Article.Title: Cortical organoid diffusion MRI reveals protocol-associated spatial reproducibility and increasing apparent diffusivity with diffusion time
Article.Authors: le Boeuf Flo, A.; Taskin, E.; Lavielle, O.; Grigoriou, A.; Pierzchala, K.; Le, T. P.; Jelescu, I.; Krsnik, Z.; Ribierre, T.; Thiran, J.-P.; Rafael Patino, J.; Canales Rodriguez, E. J.; Fischi Gomez, E.
Article.Abstract: Early human cortical development involves rapid cytoarchitectural changes that are difficult to study non-invasively. Diffusion MRI can probe developing microstructure and membrane water exchange, but model assumptions are difficult to validate in human tissue. Cortical organoids provide a tractable platform for relating diffusion measurements to tissue architecture. We scanned six fixed cortical organoids at 9.4 T, three grown under directed and three under undirected differentiation protocols, at three diffusion times and b-values up to 7000 s/mm2 Center-to-periphery profiles of diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI) metrics were reproducible across directed organoids but more variable across undirected organoids, consistent with nuclear staining. Unexpectedly, DKI-derived apparent mean diffusivity (MD) increased with diffusion time in more than 80% of tissue voxels in both batches, opposite to previous organoid measurements. Across 12,348 analytically simulated two-compartment substrates and Monte Carlo diffusion simulations in sphere packings, this trend emerged in permeable substrates with a marked contrast between extracellular and apparent intracellular diffusivities. Detailed Monte Carlo trajectory analysis of a representative substrate showed that fitted MD increased despite decreases in displacement-derived and second-cumulant diffusivities, revealing an exchange-sensitive finite-b effect involving higher-order signal contributions. These findings support using cortical organoids to probe early microstructure, test diffusion models, and investigate potential emerging diffusion biomarkers.

Article.Title: Pregnancy History and Loss of Normal PSEN2 Function Impact Female Late-Life Cognitive Processing, Inhibitory Signaling, and Gliosis
Article.Authors: Fang, J. I.; Lehmann, L.; Prater, K. E.; Barker-Haliski, M.
Article.Abstract: Background. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is well-documented to be more progressive in affected females. It is thus critical to define how female-specific life experiences interact with AD-related risk factors to impact disease trajectory and functional burden. For example, pregnancy exerts dramatic influences on the maternal immune system, behavior, and neuroplasticity, specifically in hippocampal and limbic structures. The long-term clinical impacts from pregnancy history (parity) on late-life AD outcomes are, however, conflicting. Thus, we investigated the late-life functional impacts of parity on rodent cognitive function, inhibitory neuron density, and glial biology with loss of normal function of the AD-related risk factor, presenilin 2 (PSEN2). Methods. Female PSEN2 knockout (KO) and wild-type (WT) mice with (multiparous) and without (nulliparous) pregnancy history were challenged at 10-15 months-old in the T-maze (TM) and Open Field Test (OFT), followed by immunofluorescence for neuronal signaling and gliosis markers. Results. Neither parity history nor PSEN2 deficiency impacted hippocampally-mediated spatial working memory of aged female mice in the TM. However, both PSEN2 KO and multiparous mice exhibited decreased OFT locomotor behavior. Multiparous mice also showed reduced OFT center zone exploration (p=0.0045) suggesting a more anxious phenotype. Parity history generally increased inhibitory marker expression in dorsal hippocampus (p=0.017), prefrontal cortex (p=0.021), and amygdala (p=0.035). Parity generally blunted oligodendrocyte marker expression in CA1 (p<0.05), while boosting astrocyte and microglia marker expression in CA3 of dorsal hippocampus. Conclusion. This work suggests that although parity history and PSEN2 deficiency exert individual differing age-related effects on cognition and neurobiology, they do not act synergistically.

Article.Title: EEG decodability of facial expressions and their stereoscopic depth cues in immersive virtual reality
Article.Authors: Klotzsche, F.; Nasim, A.; Hofmann, S. M.; Villringer, A.; Nikulin, V.; Sommer, W.; Gaebler, M.
Article.Abstract: Face perception typically occurs in three-dimensional space, where stereoscopic depth cues enrich the perception of facial features. Yet, most neurophysiological research on face processing relies on two-dimensional displays, potentially overlooking the role of stereoscopic depth information. Here, we combine immersive virtual reality (VR), electroencephalography (EEG), and eye tracking to examine the neural representation of faces under controlled manipulations of stereoscopic depth. Thirty-four participants viewed computer-generated faces with neutral, happy, angry, and surprised expressions in frontal view under monoscopic and stereoscopic viewing conditions. Using time-resolved multivariate decoding, we show that EEG signals in immersive VR conditions can reliably differentiate facial expressions. Stereoscopic depth cues elicited a distinct and decodable neural signature, confirming the sensitivity of our approach to depth-related processing. Yet, expression decoding remained robust across depth conditions, indicating that under controlled frontal viewing, the neural representation of behaviorally distinguishable facial expressions is invariant to binocular depth cues. Eye tracking showed that expression-related gaze patterns contained comparable information but did not account for neural representations, while depth information was absent in gaze patterns--consistent with dissociable representational processes. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of EEG-based neural decoding in fully immersive VR as a tool for investigating face perception in naturalistic settings and provide new evidence for the stability of expression representations across depth variations in three-dimensional viewing conditions.

Article.Title: Neural mechanisms for resilient sensory computation under metabolic stress
Article.Authors: Castedo, S. H.; Padamsey, Z.; Rochefort, N. L.; Monasson, R.
Article.Abstract: Food-restricted mice can solve visual discrimination tasks despite reduced synaptic currents and increased noise resulting from cellular changes in the primary visual cortex. Combining neural recordings and modeling, we study the population structure of the noise and show it is mainly concentrated along task-irrelevant directions in high-dimensional population activity, hence preserving coding on the low-dimensional stimulus manifold. In addition, we predict that food restriction shortens decision times, conserving energy but limiting the evidence accumulation needed for fine discrimination.

Article.Title: In vivo imaging of autophagy dynamics in the intact mammalian brain using a fluorescence lifetime-based sensor
Article.Authors: Maman, M.; Ando, K.; Fisher, N.; Thomas, C.; Levy, Y.; Bond, G.; Kagan, T.; Malchenko, N.; Desbois, M.; Ben Zaken, S.; Orovan, S.; Uzan, G.; Eid, S.; Naftachi, G.; Sarji, S.; Lapidot, M.; Rapaport, R.; Break, E. Article.Abstract: Autophagy regulates neuronal development, plasticity, and metabolism, yet our ability to monitor its spatial and temporal organization within intact mammalian neural circuits remains limited. We developed an imaging approach combining a pH-sensitive fluorescence lifetime readout with independent morphological labeling to quantify autophagic vesicle state, abundance, and trafficking in vivo. Following pharmacological, genetic, and ultrastructural validations, we resolved compartment-specific autophagy levels across somata, dendrites, and axons of layer 2/3 cortical excitatory neurons in the intact mouse brain. We uncovered distinct patterns of dendritic autophagy in vivo, revealing faster autophagic vesicle trafficking in distal than proximal dendrites, that were preferentially sensitive to sensory experience. Using a newly generated transgenic mouse line, we found distinct cell-type-specific basal autophagy in excitatory neurons, interneurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. These findings reveal the spatial, cell-type-specific, and activity-dependent organization of autophagy in the brain and establish a framework for investigating its regulation during development, plasticity, and disease.

Article.Title: Interactions of Sleep and Repetitive Behavior in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Autism, and Intellectual Disability
Article.Authors: Niedernhuber, M.; Michelini, G.; Malanchini, M.; Ali, A.; Noreika, V.
Article.Abstract: Objective: Sleep problems and restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) feature in neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disabilities (ID). It is unclear whether their interaction differs between conditions, and whether symptom dimensions might capture differences better than diagnostic categories. Method: In a preregistered cross-sectional analysis of the Healthy Brain Network community sample enriched for neurodevelopmental conditions (n = 2,394, 5-21 years), linear regression modeled parent-reported sleep disturbance and RRBs by diagnostic category and symptom dimensions (autistic traits, ADHD traits, IQ). Results: All symptom dimensions predicted sleep disturbance (p < .001), whereas only ADHD consistently predicted greater sleep disturbance (d = .35, 95% CI [.24, .47]) among diagnostic categories relative to typical development. All diagnostic categories and symptom dimensions were associated with RRB severity. Sleep disturbance and RRBs were associated in the entire sample (beta = .30, p < .001). Sleep disturbance predicted RRBs at all levels of autistic and ADHD traits, but most strongly with high autistic and low ADHD traits (beta = .16) and least strongly when both were high (beta = .13). Dimensional measures explained more variance than diagnoses for sleep disturbance (R square = .14 vs .03) and RRBs (R square = .38 vs .21), and provided better model fits in all comparisons. Conclusion: Autistic and ADHD traits shaped the relationship between sleep disturbance and RRBs, whereas diagnoses did not. Neurodevelopmental symptom assessments might be more informative than diagnoses to manage sleep and RRBs, though the cross-sectional design and parent report limit inference.

Article.Title: Comparative Proteomics Reveals Cell-Type-Specific Heterogeneity of Human Neural Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles
Article.Authors: Chen, X.; Lo, C. H.; Zeng, J.
Article.Abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly explored as biomarkers and as drug delivery vehicles for the brain, yet how EV cargo differs among neural cell types at baseline remains poorly defined. This gap limits both the interpretation of disease-associated EV changes and the rational choice of EV source for therapeutic use. Here, we compared EVs from human neuronal-like SH-SY5Y cells (N-EV), astrocytes (AS-EV), and HMC3 microglia (MG-EV) side by side using tandem mass tag (TMT)-based quantitative proteomics, with all samples analyzed in a single multiplexed batch. EV identity was supported by TEM, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and canonical MISEV2023 markers. Size, zeta potential, and protein content per vesicle were comparable across EV types, whereas N-EV showed the highest particle concentration and protein yield. Enrichment analyses and consensus clustering showed cargo consistent with parental-cell functions: neuronal connectivity and structural remodeling in N-EV, extracellular support and cellular interaction in AS-EV, and immune surveillance in MG-EV. Cross-comparison also revealed patterns beyond these canonical roles, including complement-associated cargo shared by N-EV and MG-EV and a Glial-EV signature of chromatin-associated and epigenetic regulatory proteins shared by AS-EV and MG-EV. We further defined cell-type-specific signature proteins; interaction networks of the larger sets were consistent with the enrichment results. Overall, these data provide a baseline comparative reference of EV proteomes from human neural cell models for interpreting disease-associated alterations, selecting EV sources for therapeutic use, and generating hypotheses on selective cargo sorting.

Article.Title: Dynamic brain states during encoding and their post-encoding reinstatement predict episodic memory in children
Article.Authors: Zeng, Y.; Chakravartti, S. P.; Ryali, S.; Li, L.; Qin, S.; Menon, V.
Article.Abstract: Episodic memory, the ability to rapidly learn and explicitly remember past events and experiences, plays a critical role in children's academic learning and knowledge acquisition. The formation of lasting memories relies on the brain's ability to dynamically organize its activity. How these neural configurations unfold moment-by-moment across encoding and offline phases remains poorly understood. To probe these dynamics, we applied a novel Bayesian Switching Dynamic Systems approach, a hidden Markov model with automatic state detection, to fMRI data from children performing scene encoding followed by an offline post-encoding rest. We identified four distinct brain states during encoding with unique activation modes between visual, medial temporal lobe, and frontoparietal and default mode network nodes. An 'active-encoding' state with integrated visual-hippocampal and frontoparietal activity dominated encoding and predicted individual memory performance, while an inactive state negatively predicted performance. State transition dynamics revealed that flexible shifts into the active-encoding state enhanced memory formation, whereas transitions toward inactive states impaired it, demonstrating that memory success depends on dynamic neural flexibility. Critically, encoding states spontaneously reemerged during post-encoding rest. A 'default-mode' state characterized by enhanced default mode network activity showed sustained maintenance during rest and robustly predicted memory outcomes, an effect specific to post-encoding, not pre-encoding rest. These findings establish that episodic memory emerges from coordinated brain state sequences bridging online encoding with offline consolidation, providing a computational framework for how moment-to-moment neural dynamics support memory formation in children.

Article.Title: Evolutionary tuning of complexin-synaptotagmin fusion clamp governs regulated neurotransmitter release
Article.Authors: Wang, Y.; Bose, D.; Griffith, D.; Dittman, J. S.; Krishnakumar, S. S.
Article.Abstract: Synaptic vesicles must be held in a fusion-ready but restrained state until calcium influx triggers release. Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) and Complexin (CPX) both contribute to this fusion clamp, yet removing either protein produces opposite effects in different species. Whether this reflects genuine divergence in their molecular roles, or species-specific tuning of a conserved mechanism, has remained unresolved. Here we address this by comparing mammalian and C. elegans orthologs in a reconstituted single-vesicle assay that isolates clamping from upstream docking and priming. We find that clamping in both species requires the combined action of CPX and Syt1, with neither sufficient on its own. CPX clamps only with its cognate SNARE complex, a specificity conferred entirely by its accessory helix. The Syt1 orthologs differ markedly in intrinsic clamping strength, which maps to C2B mediated higher-order oligomerization and sets the functional dependence on CPX in each system. These results support a dual-regulator model of exocytosis in which Syt1 and CPX act sequentially and cooperatively through discrete molecular states to control vesicle clamping and calcium-triggered release. This framework reconciles long-standing functional discrepancies across species and reveals how evolutionary divergence modulates conserved mechanisms governing synaptic fidelity.

Article.Title: Rapid switching of in-phase and anti-phase interhemispheric rhythms within a single theta cycle: a mechanistic explanation
Article.Authors: Kailasa, S.; Jedrasiak-Cape, I.; Booth, V.; Avitabile, D.; Ahmed, O. J.
Article.Abstract: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) supports memory consolidation and spatial navigation. In vivo recordings of local field potential (LFP) from RSG reveal coexisting gamma (30-80 Hz) and spline (100-160 Hz) oscillations, coupled to distinct phases of the background theta ([~]8 Hz) rhythm. Remarkably, bilateral recordings reveal that gamma and splines exhibit divergent interhemispheric phase relationships: gamma is in-phase across hemispheres, while splines are anti-phase. Here, using numerical bifurcation analysis of next-generation neural mass models, we show that RSG oscillations within a single hemisphere can be understood as alternation of PING (pyramidal-interneuron gamma) and ING (interneuron gamma) mechanisms in an excitatory-inhibitory network. Theta-frequency external drive to the inhibitory population switches the network between these two rhythms. Next, we build canonical interhemispheric circuits, composed of two such excitatory-inhibitory modules, delay-coupled across hemispheres. These circuits switch between in-phase gamma and anti-phase splines within a single theta cycle, reproducing the cross-spectral statistics of experimental RSG recordings. Finally, we present analytical results for threshold-linear neural mass models, showing cross-hemispheric phase patterning is governed by the ratio of cross-hemispheric delay to local inhibitory delay; we obtain explicit ranges of this ratio for which RSG-like patterning could be expected. Our work establishes that the unique oscillatory profile of RSG can be explained parsimoniously by minimal interhemispheric circuit configurations and provides a framework for experimental interrogation of interhemispheric rhythms.

Article.Title: Asymmetric Adaptation of Catch-up Saccades with Artificial Central Scotomas
Article.Authors: Dore, S.; Black, J.; Blohm, G.; Khan, A. Z.
Article.Abstract: In fully-sighted individuals, pursuit and saccadic eye movements work together to foveate moving targets; pursuit attempts to match target velocity, while catch-up saccades re-align the fovea to the target if it deviates during pursuit. Although saccade-pursuit interactions are well understood in healthy individuals, much less is known about how these mechanisms adapt in the presence of central vision loss. Here, we simulated central vision loss in healthy young adults to examine plasticity in saccade-pursuit mechanisms and investigated whether and how catch-up saccades adapted over five days of visual tracking. Twenty-five fully sighted participants performed a task in which they pursued a moving target that stepped position randomly (designed to elicit catch-up saccades) while viewing with a gaze-contingent central scotoma. The scotoma was shaped like a bitten cookie to encourage use of a specific preferred retinal locus (PRL) corresponding to the peripheral location with the highest acuity. By the end of the five days of repetition, most participants showed catch-up saccade endpoints shifted towards the PRL rather than the fovea. On average, endpoints shifted 0.5 deg towards the PRL between days 1 and 5 (range=0.3-1.5 deg), with significant shifts in 13 of the 25 participants. Adaptation was asymmetric; shifts were largest when the target moved in the direction opposite the scotoma bite and smallest when it moved towards it. In summary, we observed adaptation of saccade-pursuit interactive mechanisms through the re-referencing of catch-up saccades from the fovea to PRL. These results provide a promising avenue for rehabilitation in central vision loss aimed at improving eye movements and encouraging PRL use. Ultimately, such an approach may enhance residual visual function and quality of life.

Article.Title: Coherence from Context - Two-Point Neuron Models for Contextual Integration in Visual Information Processing
Article.Authors: Schmid, D.; Neumann, H.
Article.Abstract: The integration of contextual information is crucial for coherent perception and cognition. The morphology and conductance properties of cortical pyramidal cells suggest that they operate as ''two-point neurons'' (TPNs), asymmetrically combining driving sensory input at basal dendrites with modulating context at apical compartments. We present a mechanistic rate-based TPN model of layer V pyramidal cell populations and their local PV, SOM, and VIP interneuron circuits. The model rests on asymmetric feedforward-feedback integration and pooled inhibition to implement local competition and global cooperation supporting the selective amplification of coherent signals. Fitted to multi-compartment pyramidal cell simulations, it reproduces their basal-apical input-output map and, unlike static transfer functions, shows how apical amplification unfolds over time under interneuron control. Asymmetric apical-basal coincidence integrates context during processing and tags TPNs for reward-driven learning with a local four-factor rule. A pool of TPNs thereby learns to use flanker context to decide ambiguous orientations. Context-driven VIP cells gate apical integration and learning through dis-inhibition. We connect TPN populations with joint spatial and feature selectivity into networks. Contextual signals from lateral recurrence and top-down feedback yield coherence formation and evidence propagation. This propagation disambiguates visual motion and requires apical-basal coupling. For larger-scale simulations, we show how established simpler models follow from reducing the TPN's complexity while retaining its core principles. Overall, context in the TPN amplifies sensory evidence but cannot create it without feedforward input. Finally, we discuss when dynamics and interneurons matter, the model's testable predictions for VIP silencing, and implications for artificial neural networks.

Article.Title: Neural mechanisms by which spaced learning promotes understanding
Article.Authors: Liang, Y.; He, Y.; Cheng, Z.; Li, Y.; Liu, L.; Wu, Y.; Sun, Y.; Ren, F.; Shuai, M.; Luo, W.; Yang, X.; Zhang, L.
Article.Abstract: Human learning must build understanding that can be reconstructed and extended, especially as artificial intelligence advances. Spacing improves retention, with neural mechanisms studied for memory; a few studies show benefits for understanding, yet none has examined its neural basis. Here, learners inferred unfamiliar word meanings from familiar component words, reconstructing an intrinsic explanatory relation. Schedules were equated at a criterion-verified immediate endpoint before delayed EEG retrieval. Spaced learners revised written explanations more often, in smaller steps converging on shared formulations, and later reported greater explanatory retrieval fluency than massed learners. Spacing showed greater differentiation from once-learning than massing over right frontocentral and temporal sensors (520-740 ms); a right-temporal subset was indirectly associated with the fluency advantage. A visual word-recognition model matched early-stage activity only under once-learning and massing, but word identity under all schedules. Earlier encoding-stage similarity and retrieval-stage differentiation may be successive windows on the reorganisation making understanding reconstructable.

Article.Title: Mental replay rescales the subjective duration of past events via alpha and theta oscillations
Article.Authors: Yue, W. W. Y.; Mu, Z.; Yao, Z.; Chen, D.; Zhang, Y.; Liu, J.; Hu, X.
Article.Abstract: Human memory recall is flexible in time, allowing past events to be mentally replayed at variable speeds. However, it remains unclear whether temporally rescaled replay distorts the perceived duration of remembered events, and whether such distortion is tied to changes in the retrieved content. Here we instructed participants to mentally replay previously encoded naturalistic videos at compressed, expanded, or self-paced (free) speeds while recording scalp electroencephalography (EEG). Replaying an event at an expanded pace lengthened participants' subsequent judgments of its original duration relative to free and compressed replay, and the longer an event had been replayed, the longer it was judged to have lasted. Crucially, recalled memory content was unaffected, with gist accuracy and recalled detail comparable across speed conditions. During replay, alpha and theta power were reduced under compression, and both interacted with the speed instruction in predicting reported duration. Specifically, alpha power exhibited a stronger positive relationship with duration judgments under compressed replay than under free or expanded replay. Conversely, the relationship between theta power and reported duration was significantly more positive under expanded replay than under free or compressed replay. Neural pattern similarity between instructed and later spontaneous replay varied with replay speed, yet this reinstatement neither predicted reported duration nor mediated the oscillatory effects. These findings suggest that remembered duration is not read out from the amount of content retrieved but reconstructed at retrieval through oscillatory dynamics, decoupling the subjective scaling of time from the content of memory.

Article.Title: Representational geometry of punishment learning across basolateral amygdala neurons
Article.Authors: Jean-Richard-dit-Bressel, P.; Huang, N.; Choi, L.; Millan, Z.; Occelli Hanbury-Brow, C.; Killcross, S.; McNally, G. P.
Article.Abstract: Punishment learning allows animals to suppress actions that cause harm while maintaining actions that earn reward. Although the basolateral amygdala is necessary for punishment learning, how its population activity changes across learning, and how this activity reflects an action's consequences, remain unknown. We used longitudinal calcium imaging to track 1,147 basolateral amygdala neurons in male mice across instrumental training, punishment, choice test, and punishment extinction. Punishment learning transformed basolateral amygdala neuron activity associated with the punished action. This activity diverged from that associated with the unpunished action and became aligned with activity evoked by the punisher itself. This alignment was action and contingency specific. It preserved the direction of individual neurons' responses to the punisher: neurons activated by the punisher become more activated by the punished action alone, whereas neurons inhibited by the punisher become more inhibited by the punished action alone. We then asked whether reward and punishment were encoded separately or on a common value dimension across basolateral amygdala neurons. Punishment added a strong shock component to action-related activity without reducing its reward component, while reward and shock themselves occupied largely orthogonal population directions. Thus, during punishment learning, basolateral amygdala population activity can encode opposing consequences of the same action instead of simply changing what that action is worth.

Article.Title: Bridging Sensory Extraction and Decision Dynamics: Face Pareidolia Emergent from Bottom-Up and Top-Down Interactions
Article.Authors: Karimi-Rouzbahani, H.; Mattingley, J. B.
Article.Abstract: Face pareidolia-the illusory perception of faces in everyday objects-provides a unique window into how the human brain resolves visual ambiguity. Whether pareidolia arises from bottom-up sensory processing or top-down, expectation-driven feedback, is currently debated. Here we recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while participants viewed rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) streams of images, each of which was an object-to-face morph generated along a 21-image continuum via text-to-image diffusion models. Time-resolved representational similarity analyses revealed a clear spatiotemporal dissociation, in which early occipitotemporal areas tracked physical feature changes linearly, while later frontocentral channels collapsed this structural gradient into a sharp, sigmoidal profile reflecting discrete categorical decisions (face-like versus object-like). To characterise information transmission between these regions, we implemented a novel transformation-based representational connectivity analysis. These analyses uncovered an initial feedforward flow of information that transferred and transformed posterior linear traces into anterior sigmoidal representations. Crucially, partitioning the image continuum revealed that unambiguous stimuli (faces or objects) were predominantly resolved via feedforward information flow, whereas ambiguous pareidolic images recruited prolonged top-down feedback. Furthermore, perceptual decision sensitivity was biased by animacy priors and directly predicted individual behavioural reaction times during the task. Together, the findings help reconcile prior debate by establishing that face pareidolia is neither a feedforward process nor an isolated top-down projection, but an active, multi-stage recurrent process driven by feedforward feature extraction and top-down categorical resolution.

Article.Title: Brain and kidney Extracellular Vesicle Morphology and Complementary Brain proteomics after Inflammatory Challenge
Article.Authors: Brown, K.; Wang, Y.; Shan, Z.; Bi, L.
Article.Abstract: Shape, size variation, and protein composition describe different properties of tissue extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations. We compared brain and kidney EV shape and size using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We also assessed repeated protein detection and reanalyzed a deposited brain proteomics cohort, with attribution to its original source. The study used intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and an intravenous miRNA-associated EV formulation. Each group contained three biological samples, as labelled in the source data. Source morphometry summaries included 385 brain and 101 kidney profiles. Kidney circularity was 0.9225, 0.8977, and 0.9288 in the control, LPS, and treatment groups, respectively. The corresponding values for diameter quartile dispersion, a measure of size variation, were 0.2603, 0.5334, and 0.6018. Thus, near-control outline shape coexisted with persistent size variation. None of the six primary morphology tests remained significant after Holm correction. Independent recalculation confirmed 1,527 eligible rat protein accessions across individual searches. The complete quantitative matrix contained 953 features. The main peptide filter combined unique and razor peptides. A stricter analysis retained 916 features. PTGFRN and LAMB2 remained the only significant treatment-versus-LPS findings. In the main analysis, PTGFRN increased 14.71-fold (q = 0.0365), and LAMB2 increased 6.23-fold (q = 0.00585). Their LPS levels were already close to control values. Exploratory normalization used the geometric mean of four measured EV-associated markers. The resulting treatment-versus-LPS increases were 16.43-fold and 6.96-fold, respectively. These ratios support selective changes in relative protein representation within the recovered mixture. They do not establish protein copies per EV. Analysis of the full protein profile and calibration of the complete selection process did not support an overall return to control. This study compares morphology and composition as separate outcomes. It identifies membrane and matrix associations as priorities for validation. Original TEM measurements were unavailable, sample matching remained unresolved, and kidney proteomics were absent. These limitations prevent causal conclusions and individual-sample comparisons between morphology and protein composition.

Article.Title: Behavioral Markers of Essential Tremor Correlate with Distributed Alteration of Brain Functional Connectivity
Article.Authors: Blondiaux Pirson, F.; Kim, C.; Colmant, L.; Lebrun, L.; Jankovski, A.; Gaëtan, D.; Dricot, L.; Bernard, H.; Crevecoeur, F.
Article.Abstract: Essential Tremor (ET) is a common motor disorder characterized by involuntary oscillations of the upper limbs during voluntary movement. Although increasing evidence implicates dysfunction of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway, ET remains a diagnosis of exclusion, as no definitive biological marker currently exists. To better characterize ET, we recently hypothesized that impaired compensation of sensorimotor delays within the long-latency feedback pathways may generate the tremor-like oscillations observed in ET. This theory suggests that the mean spectral amplitude (MSA), derived from limb kinematics, may serve as a potential marker of ET. Here we investigated the relationship between MSA, standard clinical assessment (Fahn Tolosa Marin Tremor Rating Scale; FTM-TRS), and brain connectivity derived from resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). Using seed-based analyses, we replicated previous findings of reduced functional connectivity between the dentate nucleus and components of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway in ET patients compared with neurologically intact (NI) age-matched participants. Graph-theoretical analyses of whole-brain functional networks revealed distributed alterations in network topology across motor-related cortical and subcortical regions. Several graph metrics correlated with FTM-TRS scores and/or MSA, particularly within motor-related cortical and subcortical circuits, including the thalamus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum in ET. These findings indicate that ET is characterized by distributed alterations in functional brain networks beyond reduced connectivity of dentate nucleus and highlights MSA as a candidate quantitative marker linking altered brain connectivity to sensorimotor delay-driven tremor oscillations.

Article.Title: TMEM106B C-Terminal fragment aggregation exacerbates α-synuclein and TDP-43 proteinopathy phenotypes.
Article.Authors: Riordan, R.; Saxton, A.; Han, M.; Parrot, K.; Kraemer, B.
Article.Abstract: Genetic variation in the human gene encoding the lysosomal transmembrane protein 106B (TMEM106B) drives risk of neurodegenerative dementia. A C-terminal fragment of TMEM106B (TMEM CT) accumulates in lesions across neurodegenerative disease, potentially contributing to neurotoxicity and hampering efficacy of therapeutic interventions. Previously, we developed the first transgenic organism model of TMEM CT neuronal aggregation in Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans). We demonstrated that TMEM CT neuronal aggregation drives severe neuronal dysfunction and neuronal loss. To investigate the potential synergistic interaction of TMEM CT aggregation with other types of aggregated neurotoxic proteinopathies occurring in dementia, we assessed neuronal degeneration and pathogenic protein accumulation in bigenic C. elegans expressing TMEM CT and other key proteinopathies of neurodegeneration including a-synuclein, tau, and TAR DNA binding protein 43 (TDP-43). Our results showed strong neurotoxic synergy of TMEM106B with TDP-43 or -synuclein. However, we detected only mild synergy between TMEM106B and tau. This work provides evidence in support of TMEM CT aggregation as a significant participant in the neurodegenerative process attributed to other toxic protein aggregates. The work also highlights the importance of considering secondary proteinopathy contributions including TMEM CT aggregation when developing interventions against primary TDP-43 or -synuclein proteinopathies.

Article.Title: Concussive Injury in Human Forebrain Organoids Alters Neurogenesis and Neuroimmune Signaling
Article.Authors: Jaberi, R.; Okoro, P. D.; Taitano-Johnson, C.; Contreras, E. M.; Chidambaram, R.; Babakhanins, P. O.; Noshadi, I.; zur Nieden, N. I.; Santhakumar, V.
Article.Abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of long-term neurological disability, yet the mechanisms underlying human-specific injury responses remain poorly understood. Rodent models of TBI have yielded significant insights into mechanisms and pathophysiology of TBI but may not capture human-specific developmental and molecular responses. Here, we establish a human forebrain organoid (hFBO) injury paradigm to examine developmental stage and region-specific responses to concussive injury. Dorsal and ventral hFBOs, enriched in glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, respectively, showed progressive physiological maturation with rudimentary firing characteristics at 80 days in vitro (DIV) and spontaneous synaptic activity by 150 DIV. Injury to dorsal and ventral hFBOs at 25 DIV, when neural progenitors dominate, caused cell death that scaled with severity and increased expression of neural proliferation markers and TLR4/NF-{kappa}B associated neuroimmune signaling. Injury to physiologically mature organoids at 150 DIV produced severity-dependent acute intracellular calcium dysregulation. Together, these findings establish a human organoid-based platform that captures developmental stage-dependent neurogenic, molecular, and cellular dysfunction in responses to concussive injury.

Article.Title: Defining cell type-specific diurnal gene expression in the mouse retina
Article.Authors: Marlin, M. N.; Meng, G.; Alqahtani, S.; Kerstein, P. C.; Weake, V. M.
Article.Abstract: The mammalian retina exhibits daily oscillations in gene expression that contribute to retinal physiology and visual function. However, the extent to which these temporal patterns differ among retinal cell types remains incompletely understood. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing in the mouse retina over the day and night, identifying rhythmic genes in the six major retinal cell types. Distinct diurnal gene expression patterns across photoreceptors, interneurons, retinal ganglion cells, and Muller glia correspond to their diverse functions across the light cycle. Even core circadian clock genes exhibited differences in paralog expression and rhythmicity across the retina. In contrast, dopamine signaling via the DRD4 receptor is highly rhythmic across most retinal cell types, suggesting dopamine signaling may be a key rhythmicity cue in the retina under diurnal conditions. This dataset highlights the complexity of daily transcriptional regulation in the retina and provides a resource to explore cell-type-specific diurnal rhythms.

Article.Title: Alterations in phototransduction timing, dark adaptation and GNAT1 trafficking in GNAT1-edited Xenopus laevis.
Article.Authors: Skitsko, D.; Tam, B. M.; Chiu, C. N.; Burns, P.; Moritz, O. L.
Article.Abstract: GNAT1 (also called -transducin) is the -subunit of a heterotrimeric G-protein present in rod photoreceptors that plays a critical role in phototransduction. Photoactivated rhodopsin binds GNAT1, which stimulates phosphodiesterase to hydrolyze cGMP, closing ion channels and hyperpolarizing the rod cell. To examine the effects of GNAT1 ablation on light-induced autophagy and light-exacerbated retinal degeneration, we previously generated genetically chimeric, GNAT1-edited Xenopus laevis using CRISPR technology. Here, we interbred these F0 animals to produce F1 animals with defined genotypes, including full knockouts, and characterized the F1 generation by Western blot, histology, and electroretinography (ERG). In X. laevis tadpoles with nonsense mutations in all four GNAT1 alleles, the GNAT1 protein was absent, and the scotopic ERG was absent, indicating full knockout. In animals with reduced GNAT1 expression, we observed increased A- and B-wave implicit times. Greater GNAT1 protein reduction was associated with greater ERG delay, demonstrating a role for GNAT1 in the timing of phototransduction. We also identified two unexpected phenotypes linked to distinct gene edits. The Q184L-GNAT1.L mutation conferred an ERG phenotype similar to that of a full knockout, but with minimal reduction in GNAT1 protein levels, consistent with loss of function. This mutation is also present in the human population. A three-base-pair deletion (T183,Q184[->]K183) in GNAT1.S caused dominantly inherited diminished ERG response and defective dark adaptation, and was associated with photoreceptor structural abnormalities and GNAT1 accumulation at the connecting cilium, consistent with a dominant-negative effect on GNAT1 trafficking.

Article.Title: The Parkinson's disease-associated A53E mutation decreases alpha-synuclein aggregation and phosphorylation in vivo
Article.Authors: Irving, W. L.; Meredith-Andrews, S.; Nguyen, K. T.; Schainker, K. L.; Brockway, N. L.; Unni, V. K.; Weissman, T. A.
Article.Abstract: Abnormal -synuclein aggregation is the defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD) and related synucleinopathies. Rare disease-causing alpha-synuclein mutations either accelerate or slow fibrillization in vitro, however their effects in vivo are less well understood. Interestingly, the A53E mutation slows fibrillization in vitro but causes a more virulent form of PD. We use an in vivo model to examine the aggregation dynamics of disease-causing A53E and E46K alpha-synuclein mutations. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching within presynaptic terminals shows that A53E-alpha-synuclein is significantly more mobile than E46K- or wild-type (WT)-alpha-synuclein. Longitudinal analysis in vivo reveals that E46K- and WT-alpha-synuclein become progressively less mobile over days, while A53E maintains high mobility, suggesting delayed progression toward aggregated states. We also find that A53E-alpha-synuclein lacks detectable disease-relevant phosphorylation at serine-129, unlike E46K-and WT-alpha-synuclein. To mechanistically test whether this unique lack of phosphorylation drives its high mobility, we genetically modified A53E-alpha-synuclein to mimic S129 phosphorylation, and show that this manipulation indeed decreases its mobility, directly implicating the phosphorylation status of this residue in mobility.

Article.Title: Odor representations are structured by heterogeneous tuning and concentration-dependence of functionally distinct olfactory sensory neuron subpopulations.
Article.Authors: Castro, J.; Burton, S. D.; Hallkaj, J.; Wachowiak, M.
Article.Abstract: Olfactory stimuli (odorants) are represented by combinatorial patterns of olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) activation that are translated into spatially-organized glomerular maps at their input to the CNS. How glomerular maps relate to odorant features - including chemical structure and concentration - remains a key question in understanding the neural mechanisms of odor coding. Here, we compared glomerular response maps for the same 59 odorants across three concentration regimes, using GCaMP6 imaging from OSN axon terminals in the olfactory bulb (OB) of the anesthetized mouse. At the lowest regime, in which concentrations were chosen to distinguish the most sensitive glomeruli for each odorant, glomeruli were exceptionally narrowly tuned and responses across glomeruli were extremely sparse. We then compared responses at two higher-concentration regimes, 'low' and 'high', differing by 25-fold from each other and 2 - 5 log units higher than the 'most-sensitive' regime. Increasing concentration broadened tuning of OSN inputs; this broadening was heterogeneous across chemical space and was well-described by classifying glomeruli into several subpopulations with distinct consensus tuning profiles. Each subpopulation was selectively tuned to one or a few odorant chemical classes and spatially clustered in a manner consistent with the projection patterns of receptor-defined OSN classes. Glomerular subpopulations retained distinct tuning and spatial localization even at the highest concentrations. OSN subpopulations thus sample chemical space nonuniformly across a large concentration range. These results suggest a lower-dimensional structure in the representation of odorant information that largely reflects OSN subpopulations which, in turn, map to olfactory receptor subfamilies. This organization may enable distinct odor coding strategies for different OSN classes and for parts of chemical feature space with distinct ethological relevance.

Article.Title: Direct cortical feedforward and feedback pathways differentially shape visual responses and selectively engage looped circuits
Article.Authors: Vasile, F.; Oude Lohuis, M.; Mazo, C.; Shah, D. P.; Mastrogiuseppe, F.; Machens, C.; Petreanu, L.
Article.Abstract: Nearly every computational account of hierarchical cortex rests on assumptions about the influence of direct cortico-cortical inputs and which neurons they act upon. Yet, disentangling their direct functional contributions from indirect, multisynaptic influences remains difficult. We examined how feedforward (FF) and feedback (FB) pathways between mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and posteromedial cortex (PM) modulate visual responses, combining retrograde labelling, multi-area two-photon imaging and optogenetic perturbations. High or low activity in either pathway was associated with both excitation and inhibition of neurons in the targeted areas. FF activity was associated with stronger additive changes, while FB activity was related to stronger multiplicative modulations and improvements in visual decoding. Optogenetic manipulations causally confirmed these asymmetries. Both pathways preferentially modulated reciprocating "looped" neurons, with FF exciting them and FB either exciting or inhibiting them. These findings demonstrate that feedforward and feedback pathways serve distinct functional roles within recurrent cortical loops.

Article.Title: The human circular Tau 12->7 RNA is translated in mouse neurons and promotes tau aggregation
Article.Authors: Bagheri, N.; Cai, W.; El-Amouri, S.; Dobler, M.; Cochran, C. J.; Turner, A. K.; Lahiri, A.; Fister, S.; Rodgers, D. W.; Wen, Y.; Nelson, P. T.; Stamm, S.

Despite using a ubiquitously active promoter, circTau 12->7 protein and a control circEGFP protein were only observed in mouse neurons, indicating neuron-specific translation of these circular RNAs. Article.Title: Movement refinement and cholinergic regulation of outcome-dependent updating during skilled reaching.
Article.Authors: Yeh, N.-H.; Prokop, L.; Marshall, J. J.; Contractor, A.
Article.Abstract: Motor skill learning transforms initially variable actions into precise and reproducible movements, yet conventional measures of task success can obscure the distinct processes through which this refinement occurs. We combined detailed outcome scoring and kinematic analysis of single-pellet reaching in mice to resolve how individual components of the action change with practice. Decomposing reaching into successive stages revealed improvements in targeting and retrieval, while grasp success after pellet contact did not change detectably. Paw trajectories became more consistent across both successful and unsuccessful reaches, whereas changes in the mean speed profile were detected in successful reaches. To examine how striatal cholinergic signaling contributes to movement refinement and the influence of recent outcomes on subsequent actions, we monitored acetylcholine (ACh) in vivo and inhibited cholinergic interneurons (CINs) during training. ACh was elevated before reach onset and declined during execution across all reach outcomes, with no detectable change between early and late training. CIN inhibition had little effect on movement refinement across days, but altered how recent outcomes influenced the next reach, most clearly following attempts in which the pellet was grasped and then lost. These findings distinguish refinement of the practiced movement from outcome-dependent adjustments to its execution. Together, they raise the possibility that the pre-reach ACh elevation plays a role in enabling the evaluation of recent outcomes to update the execution of the next reach.

Article.Title: Projection Neurons from Infralimbic (IL) to the Basolateral Amygdala (BLA) are Critical for the Expression of Social Familiarity induced Anxiolysis (SoFiA) in rats
Article.Authors: Majumdar, S.; Burke, A. R.; Dustrude, E. T.; Lungwitz, E. A.; Andrews, K. D.; Dietrich, A. D.; Truitt, W. A.
Article.Abstract: Mental health is crucially linked to social behavior. Healthy social behavior involves learning to adapt emotional responses to social cues, for example learning to suppress anxiety through social familiarity, or social familiarity-induced anxiolysis (SoFiA). SoFiA is well documented and forms the basis for interpersonal therapy, however, the neural mechanisms of SoFiA are unclear. SoFiA is modeled in rats by employing the social interaction habituation (SI-hab) protocol. Using SI-hab protocol, it has been determined that SoFiA represents social safety learning, which requires both anxiogenic stimulus and social familiarity during training sessions (5-6 daily SI sessions), and SoFiA expression is dependent on infralimbic subdivision (IL) of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the basolateral amygdala (BLA). Here we investigated the role of IL in SoFiA acquisition and expression, using chemogenetics to inhibit IL neurons. Male Wistar rats received bilateral viral injections targeting the IL or BLA and left undisturbed for 5-7 weeks to allow for viral expression. We chemogenetically inhibited via low doses of ip. clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) either the IL, the BLA, or the projections neurons from the IL to the BLA during expression of SoFiA in rats. We found that projection neurons from IL to the BLA are critical for the recovery SI behavior from the attenuation caused by the bright light (expression of SoFiA). Furthermore, CNO inhibited IL neurons with projections to the BLA and there were no off target effects of CNO on the behavioral measures. Article.Authors: Gandelman, M.; Figueroa, K. P.; Classen, A.; Scoles, D. R.; Pulst, S. M.
Article.Abstract: Background and Objectives: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 4 (SCA4) is caused by a GGC-repeat expansion in ZFHX3 encoding an expanded polyglycine tract causing p62- and ubiquitin-positive neuronal intranuclear inclusions (NIIs). In multiple polyglycine diseases NIIs sequester tRNA-splicing ligase complex (tRNA-LC) proteins, causing downstream functional defects linked to neurodegeneration. We assessed the localization of tRNA-LC proteins in SCA4 pontine neurons. Methods: Postmortem brain tissue from a genetically confirmed SCA4 patient was examined across multiple regions using immunofluorescence confocal microscopy for p62, ubiquitin and tRNA-LC proteins FAM98B, RTRAF, and RTCB. Results: In pontine neurons, FAM98B, RTRAF, and RTCB were incorporated into NII, accumulating in a distinct outer layer respective to a ubiquitin inner layer. This redistribution was accompanied by depletion of all three proteins from the soluble nucleoplasm. Discussion: Our findings link SCA4 to a tRNA-LC dysfunction phenotype shared by multiple GGC-repeat disorders, further supporting a unified pathological mechanism in polyglycine diseases.

Article.Title: Coordinated orienting behavior emerges following unilateral optogenetic activation of Superior Colliculus GABAergic neurons
Article.Authors: Suyama, H.; Lupashina, T.; Hamon, M.; Sibille, J.; Teh, K. L.; Liebert, K.; Larkum, M. E.; Sachdev, R.; Kremkow, J.
Article.Abstract: Orienting coordinates movements of the eyes, whiskers, nose, and other effectors, but how the superior colliculus (SC) recruits these components over time remains unclear. Recordings from the SC contralateral to the stimulated hemisphere revealed heterogeneous neuronal responses comprising short-latency excitation and delayed excitation or inhibition. Short-latency excitation was similar on trials with and without evoked movements, whereas delayed excitation was greater on trials that evoked eye or nose movements. Neurons modulated during spontaneous nose movements showed corresponding optogenetically evoked responses, linking stimulation-induced activity to endogenous movement-related activity. Thus, activation of SC GABAergic neurons initiates evolving population activity that recruits a coordinated sequence of orienting movements.

Article.Title: Imbalance between RNA-binding proteins and the WAVE regulatory complex underlies the toxic gain-of-function effects of the CYFIP2 Arg87Cys variant in neurodevelopmental disorders
Article.Authors: Kim, U. S.; Jun, Y.; Kim, H.; Yang, Y.; Kang, M.; Ma, R.; Kang, H. R.; Ju, S.; Jeong, H.; Kim, S. Y.; Kim, Y.; Oh, J. Y.; Kim, E.; Kim, K.; Kang, H.; Kim, J. Y.; Han, K.
Article.Abstract: Pathogenic variants in cytoplasmic FMR1-interacting protein 2 (CYFIP2) cause neurodevelopmental disorders, with hotspot substitutions at arginine 87 (Arg87) associated with particularly severe symptoms. Quantitative proteomic analysis of the CA1 region uncovered an imbalance between CYFIP2-associated protein networks, characterized by increased RBPs and reduced WRC components. Moreover, the cell adhesion molecule Eph receptor A3 was reduced, possibly as a result of RBP dysregulation. Article.Title: Impact of heat and sex on embryonic brain growth in dragons with temperature induced sex-reversal (Pogona vitticeps, Lacertilia: Agamidae)
Article.Authors: Hoops, D.; Ceddia, A.; Peters, R.; Whiteley, S. L.; Collin, S. P.; Crowe-Riddell, J.
Article.Abstract: Climate warming can influence sex determination and embryonic growth in oviparous reptiles that rely on external temperatures during development. Although incubation temperature significantly influenced growth rate and body size during development, overall brain size was not significantly different across temperature treatments. Our results indicate that the effects of genotypic sex on brain development are more important than thermal influences, and thus the brain may be somewhat buffered to the effects of warm incubation temperatures in this arid-adapted dragon.

Article.Title: Blue light compromises cellular fate of intrinsically photosensitive M&uumlller glial cells in the developing chicken retina.
Article.Authors: Marchese, N. A.; Rios, M. N.; Yaneff, A.; Davio, C.; Guido, M. E.
Article.Abstract: M&uumlller glial cells (MCs), the predominant glial population in the retina, interface with all neuronal types to form the structural and functional core of the tissue. Beyond their established homeostatic roles, MCs have emerged as promising endogenous neural stem cells with remarkable regenerative potential. Our recent work identified MCs as novel photosensitive elements of the vertebrate inner retina that express non-visual opsins and respond to brief light stimuli. Direct photic responses manifest as a sustained increase in intracellular calcium levels driven by a G protein-mediated signaling cascade that primarily recruits calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, highlighting MC photoreception and its roles in retinal physiology. In the present work, we characterize expanded light-directed responses in primary chicken MC cultures, identifying a blue light (BL)-triggered signaling cascade. BL stimulation induces a peak in cAMP levels at 10 min, followed by CREB activation (p-CREB) within 30 min, a temporal profile consistent with observations in ex vivo retinal explants. BL exposure (1 h) at the onset of each cell cycle dampens proliferative capacity and migration while lengthening the cell cycle in both primary chicken MCs and an immortalized human MC cell line compared to dark controls. Furthermore, over time (24, 48, and 72 h), BL exposure reduces the proportion of pluripotent cells (Sox2 positive cells), concomitant with an increase in neuronal progenitors (Tbr2) and no change in glial markers (GS, RGR, GFAP). Finally, mature neuronal markers (TUJ-1 and Brn3) increase in MC cultures 120 h post-BL stimulation. Overall, this work broadens our understanding of BL-triggered signaling cascades in MCs and uncovers photoreception as a potential mechanism driving cell fate in the developing retina.

Article.Title: Spatially resolved single-cell atlas reveals cortical glial reactivity associated with regions of neuronal growth programs in both hemispheres after stroke
Article.Authors: Kenwood, M.; Betz, D.; Guttierez-Kuri, E.; Derebery, B.; Rhoton, P.; Palavicinni, J. P.; Ramirez, D. M. O.; Goldberg, M. P.
Article.Abstract: Post-stroke recovery relies on structural remodeling of neuronal circuits in both the spared ipsilesional and contralesional cortices. Together, these findings identify spatially organized neuronal growth and glial activation states in both hemispheres after stroke and nominate regions for investigating spatial relationships between complex cell types and functional recovery.

Article.Abstract: Milk-derived extracellular vesicles (MEV) represent a naturally derived, potentially scalable platform for immunomodulation, yet their effects on central nervous system (CNS) glial inflammation at defined particle-to-cell ratios remain insufficiently characterized. At 7 months postpartum, both PROKs were elevated in the cortex, and these increases were prevented by PC1. Article.Authors: Damiani, F.; Di Antonio, G.; Epifanio, J.; Vinci, G. V.; Galluzzi, A.; Mattia, M.
Article.Abstract: The hierarchical organization of the brain underlies its ability to process information across multiple time scales and support flexible behavior through context-dependent computation. Compared to models with heterogeneous time constants, our approach achieves comparable performance with more parsimonious synaptic modifications, while preserving scale-invariant dynamics.

Article.Title: Quantitative spatial connectomics of liver reveals a partially exposed sympathetic network that integrates multiple cell types across the portal tract
Article.Authors: Noon, L. A.; Casal, G.; Soriano-Navarro, M.; Cattin, A.-L.; Camacho, R.; Acosta Umanzor, C.; Rojo Sanz, C.; Leal Tassias, A.; Fernandez-Rodriguez, J.; Verboven, E.; Gomez Sanchez, J. A.; Darsinou, M.; Power, A.; Riccio, A.; Andersson, E. R.; Burden, J. J.; Lloyd, A. C.
Article.Abstract: Peripheral tissues are innervated by sparse axonal networks that regulate homeostasis, regeneration and disease, yet their three-dimensional architecture and cellular targets remain largely unknown. Here, we present an EM workflow for quantitative 3D spatial connectomics to define these networks. We identify the mouse liver connectome as a meshwork, rather than a tree-like structure, of mainly sympathetic axons, in which partial Schwann cell coverage is associated with exposed varicosities along the length of individual axons with large regions of the network devoid of glial coverage. Axon tracing identified axonal terminals throughout the network, but the vast majority of cellular contacts involved exposed 'en passant' varicosities. While both terminals and varicosities innervated the vasculature, most synaptic-like contacts involved hepatocytes, fibroblasts, macrophages, and the stem-cell niche, with all individual axons contacting different cell types along their length, highlighting the network nature of liver innervation, the potential for co-ordinating tissue function and demonstrating the power of this approach for decoding connectivity in peripheral tissues.

Article.Title: Estrogen remodels large-scale cortical dynamics to promote behavioral persistence
Article.Authors: Asokan, M. M.; Le, A.; Tsin, D.; Sirrs, L.; Cramer, M.; Oline, S. N.; Rogers, F. D.; Falkner, A. L.
Article.Abstract: Sex-steroid hormones remodel the brain on slow timescales of hours to days to coordinate adaptive behaviors with changing bodily physiology. Yet how this slow remodeling reorganizes and constrains neural computations that govern behavior on a moment-to-moment timescale remains poorly understood, particularly in cortical regions that support flexible social decision-making. Here we combined longitudinal high-density neural recordings, quantitative behavioral phenotyping and estrogen-receptor manipulation in female mice across low and high estrogen states. Tracking behavior and neural dynamics using this dense sampling approach revealed that high estrogen increased signatures of behavioral and neural persistence. High estrogen reversibly increased male-directed social preference and behavioral persistence, effects that were abolished by estrogen receptor alpha knockdown in the medial prefrontal cortex. In the mPFC high estrogen produced more persistent neural states that were more closely aligned with ongoing behavior, increased state discriminability, and compressed within-state dimensionality. At the single-neuron level, estrogen increased tuning selectivity, lengthened intrinsic timescales, and stabilized social representations across days, even within the same neurons tracked longitudinally. High estrogen also strengthened recurrent connectivity during the resting state, exhibiting preferential connectivity between similarly tuned ensembles. Finally, incorporating these connectivity changes into a mean-field dynamical-systems model was sufficient to reproduce increased behavioral and neural-state persistence. Together, these findings show that estrogen oscillates cortical computations across multi-day timescales, flipping the prefrontal cortex from flexible to persistent regimes that play a role in sustaining potentially costly social behaviors.

Article.Title: Single-AAV Delivery of the SpCas9 Nickase Improves CAG/CTG Repeat contraction in a mouse model of Huntington's disease
Article.Authors: Murillo, A.; Aston, A. N.; Lelos, M.; Dion, V.
Article.Abstract: The best studied Cas9 enzyme, from Streptococcus pyogenes, is thought to be too large to be efficiently packaged into a single adeno-associated virus (AAV) together with a single-guide (sg) RNA cassette, requiring a dual-vector system. Here we have circumvented this limitation and packaged the full CRISPR system into a single AAV by using a single promoter driving the expression of both the Cas9 enzyme and a sgRNA. We compared the ability of the dual and single vector systems to induce contraction of CAG/CTG repeats in the striatum of a Huntington's disease model. We show that the all-in-one system led to larger contractions of the CAG/CTG repeats. This approach provides a more efficient and less costly approach for in vivo gene editing and improves the translational potential of AAV-mediated delivery of Cas9.

Article.Title: The role of deficient action knowledge in unawareness (anosognosia) of tool-action errors after left-hemisphere stroke
Article.Authors: Thibault, S.; Williamson, R.; Wong, A. L.; Buxbaum, L. J.
Article.Abstract: Many individuals with limb apraxia after left-hemisphere stroke exhibit a lack of awareness of their tool-related action errors, i.e., unawareness of apraxia (UA; also called anosognosia of apraxia). Little is known about the prevalence of UA, the relationship between UA and apraxia severity, or its underlying mechanisms. Here, we assessed both the causes and consequences of UA. Based on a mechanistic model, we hypothesized that UA may arise because of deficits in representations signaling how tool-related movements should look and feel - a component of action knowledge - and that degradation of this knowledge impedes the detection of mismatches between planned and actual tool-related actions. We further predicted that a consequence of UA is a reduction in error-correction attempts. Fifty-six individuals with chronic LCVA gestured to show how to use tools. Immediately after the gesture production task, participants were asked if they made any errors. All participants also completed an action knowledge task to measure the integrity of tool-related movement goals. Individuals were denoted as exhibiting UA if they performed below a normative cutoff for apraxia yet reported making no errors. Our sample included 21 individuals with apraxia; of these, nearly half (48%) exhibited UA. These two groups made a comparable number of gesture errors and were of equivalent stroke severity, yet individuals with UA had significantly more impaired action knowledge. Additionally, individuals with UA were less likely to attempt to correct their errors compared to individuals who were aware of their apraxia. These data are consistent with the hypothesis that action knowledge (how tool actions look and feel) serves a key role in error detection and awareness of apraxia and may contribute to the difficulties with everyday tasks experienced by many people with apraxia.

Article.Title: Hill-Based Reformulation of the Hodgkin-Huxley Model for Mapping Gating Changes to Neuronal Excitability
Article.Authors: Saab, B.; Fahs, J.; Daou, A.
Article.Abstract: Conductance-based models link ion-channel gating to neuronal excitability, but mutation reports often provide steady-state voltage shifts without sufficient kinetic measurements to specify a unique model. We introduce a Hill-based reformulation of selected Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) gating relationships and evaluate its usefulness under this low-information constraint. The hybrid formulation retains canonical HH-like spike waveforms and frequency-current behavior after a modest remapping of applied current, while providing an explicit mapping from reported activation descriptors to model parameters under specified assumptions. An A863P kinetic-sensitivity analysis shows how steady-state constraints and kinetic assumptions jointly shape excitability predictions in both classical HH and Hill-based implementations. The Hill formulation makes this mapping reproducible through explicit parameter relations, whereas refitting classical HH rates requires additional fitting choices; both approaches still require kinetic assumptions. Retrospective benchmarks using the Nav1.7 mutations A863P, F1449V, and A1632G show that the Hill-based model captures the qualitative increase in excitability but overestimates the magnitude of threshold reduction. Classical HH comparisons for A863P demonstrate that similar qualitative predictions can also be obtained under specified kinetic assumptions. These findings support the Hill formulation as a reproducible framework for mapping reported gating changes onto HH-like excitability, without establishing superior quantitative prediction of mutation effects. Quantitative transfer to mutation-specific neuronal behavior requires additional kinetic and cellular constraints.

Article.Title: Neural and Gait Adaptations to Dual-Task Demands in Children and Young Adults: A Mobile Brain-Body Imaging (MoBI) Study.
Article.Authors: Nicklas, P. R.; Freedman, E.; Foxe, J. J.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive-motor interactions describe the complex interplay underlying how the brain manages concurrent demands on motor and cognitive processing. Yet, how cognitive-motor interactions present across childhood and young adulthood remains understudied, particularly through multi-modal methods which include neurophysiology. We investigated development of cognitive-motor interactions using a dual-task study design including simultaneous motor (walking) and cognitive (visual Go-NoGo) tasks. Using mobile brain-body imaging, (MoBI), we recorded simultaneous EEG, gait kinematics, and task performance. 61 neurotypical 8-to-30-year-olds completed the Go-NoGo while seated or walking on a treadmill. With increased age, participants became faster and more accurate on the task, walking became less variable, and N200 and P300 ERP amplitudes increased. Two distinct effects of cognitive-motor interactions emerged with age. An N200 amplitude attenuation when walking became exaggerated with age, suggesting older participants engaged greater neurophysiological flexibility to support their improved task performances, whereas children performed less well and may not have needed to recruit the same adaptive neural mechanisms. Additionally, an attenuation of stride variability during dual-task walking lessened with age, demonstrating robust motor development under dual-task conditions. These findings demonstrate a distinct pattern of changes to cognitive-motor interactions through development. Future research can examine how this pattern varies in different developmental conditions.

Article.Title: A hypothalamic circuit links hunger to mesolimbic dopamine to drive feeding
Article.Authors: Bacharach, S. Z.; Zappetti, K. A.; Coutinho, L. O.; Bacherer, A.; Wahba, J. I.; Schneps, H. M.; Liu, Z.-W.; Dietrich, M. O.; Alhadeff, A. L.
Article.Abstract: Hunger enhances the motivational value of food, but the neural circuits linking homeostatic hunger neurons to dopamine systems remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a hypothalamic-midbrain neural circuit through which AgRP neurons engage the mesolimbic dopamine system. We demonstrate that AgRP neuron activity is both necessary and sufficient for the potentiated dopamine response to food by hunger, and that they achieve this by reducing inhibitory drive onto midbrain dopamine neurons. Importantly, this AgRP neuron-evoked dopamine signaling is required for subsequent food intake. Mechanistically, we find that AgRP neuron projections to NPY-sensitive paraventricular hypothalamic neurons selectively amplify food-evoked dopamine release to promote feeding behavior. These findings reveal a circuit mechanism through which hunger recruits dopamine signaling to transform physiological need into motivated feeding behavior.

Article.Title: ResXR: infrastructure for quality-controlled, reproducible studies of human behavior in Extended Reality
Article.Authors: Bergstein, Y.; Barel, N.; Shai Basson, G.; Bromberg, O.; Schonberg, T.
Article.Abstract: Extended Reality (XR) combines experimental control and ecological validity, yet behavioral XR research lacks shared infrastructure: building immersive experiments demands specialized engineering, and custom tools yield data in custom formats that other laboratories cannot readily reanalyze. We present ResXR (Research with XR), an open-source toolkit providing a path from immersive experiment to standardized dataset and quality report, running on standalone Meta Quest headsets. A Unity template records head, hand, eye, and face tracking with per-sample software development kit (SDK) timestamps and status flags; an independent Python pipeline checks data quality, can mask flagged intervals, and exports raw and derivative datasets in Motion-BIDS, the motion extension of the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS), with self-contained quality reports. Three ready-to-run paradigms, covering discrete choice, spatial navigation, and free visual exploration, let researchers collect and process data without programming. ResXR grounds its default schema and the signals its quality checks read in stress tests rather than in vendor documentation: when we induced tracking failures on Meta Quest Pro headsets, several status flags kept marking the data as valid. With its code, stress-test protocols and example datasets openly available, ResXR provides a transparent, community-extensible foundation for reproducible XR experimentation.

Article.Title: Multimodal Connectome Markers of Disruptive Behavior Problems in Youth: Distinct Patterns of Concurrent Severity and Prospective Symptom Change
Article.Authors: Christofilea, E.; Mai, K.; Liang, Q.; Rodriguez, R. X.; Lloyd, C.; Zhao, Y.; Scheinost, D.; Sukhodolsky, D. G.; Ibrahim, K.
Article.Abstract: Disruptive behaviors problems, such as irritability/anger and maladaptive aggression, are associated with altered connectivity across networks supporting emotion regulation. However, multimodal connectome markers of concurrent severity and prospective symptom change, including sex-specific patterns, remain unclear. Using a large, sex-balanced sample from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, we applied multimodal connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) to test whether resting-state functional (n = 7,556; 49.3% female) and structural (N = 8,978; 48.4%) connectivity predicted baseline disruptive behavior severity (at ages 9-10) and 2-year symptom change (from ages 9-10 to 11-12). Models were adjusted for covariates, permutation-tested, and FDR corrected. Secondary analyses tested sex-stratified models separately in males and females. In models emerging as significant, follow-up analyses tested for distinct vs shared predictive edges. Functional and structural connectomes predicted baseline severity ({rho} = 0.087 and {rho} = 0.071, respectively). Functional connectivity also predicted prospective symptom change ({rho} = 0.038), whereas prospective structural prediction was predominately with negative edges ({rho} = 0.026). Functional connectivity models were significant in both sexes, while prospective structural connectivity models were significant in males, but not females. Frontoparietal, medial frontal, sensorimotor, salience, cerebellar, and visual networks contributed across models. Cross-sectional models showed a more distributed pattern while prospective models showed a more focal pattern. These findings identify complementary, largely distinct functional and structural connectome patterns associated with current disruptive behavior risk and subsequent symptom change, supporting the importance of developmental timing, sex, and imaging modality in developing brain-based biomarkers of disruptive behavior risk in youth.
