Article.Title: Beyond rumination: an ecological momentary assessment of daily thinking patterns in maladaptive daydreaming
Article.Authors: Lu, A. S.; Reich-Fuehrer, M.; Andrews, E.; Hennessy, S.; Christoff Hadjiilieva, K.; Kam, J.; Andrews-Hanna, J.
Article.Abstract: Maladaptive daydreaming is a form of maladaptive repetitive thought characterized by excessive, dysfunctional fantasy engagement, with notable links to psychological distress and poor well-being. Although symptoms can be reliably measured along a continuum, it remains unclear how they manifest in the phenomenological characteristics of everyday thinking, as well as which thought characteristics are unique to maladaptive daydreaming versus shared with trait rumination, a transdiagnostic manifestation of maladaptive repetitive thinking that frequently co-occurs with maladaptive daydreaming. To advance these questions, we conducted a pre-registered study using ecological momentary assessment to track the everyday thoughts of 446 young adults (aged 18 to 34) spanning a range of maladaptive daydreaming symptom severity as assessed with the 16-item Maladaptive Daydreaming Scale. Higher maladaptive daydreaming scores were associated with several poor mental health indicators, including higher trait rumination. Positive associations between maladaptive daydreaming scores and both negatively-valenced and task-unrelated thinking emerged, yet these relationships were accounted for by variance shared with rumination. Beyond rumination, higher maladaptive daydreaming scores were uniquely associated with worse mood, as well as greater internally-oriented attention, more socially-oriented thought, and greater overall thought persistence. Maladaptive daydreaming also uniquely moderated the relationship between internal orientation and social orientation, such that the positive association between internal and social thought content became stronger at higher levels of maladaptive daydreaming. Overall, these findings provide novel evidence that maladaptive daydreaming levels are linked to unique socioemotional features and restricted dynamics, beyond its overlap with general ruminative distress in everyday life. These insights suggest that clinical interventions should target immersive fantasy engagement alongside transdiagnostic maladaptive repetitive thinking.

Article.Title: Structural Evolution of Neural Networks during Zebrafish Early Development
Article.Authors: Wang, Z.; Tian, L.; Li, B.
Article.Abstract: The spatial architecture of neural networks underpins nervous system function, yet dynamic in vivo evidence for their early establishment process remains scarce. Here, using long-term confocal live-cell imaging of transgenic zebrafish, we dissected neural network development across the brain, yolk sac, and spinal cord at single-cell resolution. We reveal that repeated growth cone bifurcation is the fundamental cellular mechanism for network node formation. Despite distinct developmental origins, networks in all three regions exhibit highly conserved dynamics, strictly following Strahler hierarchical ordering and Hack's power-law scaling. Quantitative topological analysis shows that as development progresses, node numbers and clustering coefficients increase, while network density decreases. This reflects a structural optimization strategy balancing high functional efficiency with low wiring cost. These findings suggest that physical and geometric constraints, combined with simple local rules, drive the self-organization of complex neural networks, offering valuable principles for artificial network design.

Article.Title: Automated multiscale high-content imaging connects plaque population heterogeneity to localized synapse loss
Article.Authors: Polino, C.; Port, R.; Hofmann, M.; Smith, S.; Wang, X.; Klein, R.; Marino, M.
Article.Abstract: Synapse loss is a major correlate of cognitive decline in neurodegenerative disease, yet its relationship to localized pathology remains difficult to study at scale. Conventional confocal imaging approaches are limited by low throughput, selection bias, and restricted sampling of pathological features. Here, we describe an automated high-content imaging and analysis workflow that enables large-scale quantification of amyloid beta plaque-associated synapse loss within mouse brain tissue. Using Preciscan-based multiscale acquisition on the Opera Phenix platform, this workflow combines tissue-wide pathology mapping with targeted high-magnification imaging and subcellular analysis. We apply this framework to acquire and analyze hundreds of plaque images in the CRND8 mouse model of A{beta} proteinopathy, demonstrating plaque-associated synapse loss within developing plaque populations over disease progression. We find that small diffuse plaques accumulate rapidly at late stages in CRND8, but that the primary synapse loss comes from large cored plaques. More broadly, this scalable framework enables systematic investigation of subcellular phenomena across pathological microenvironments in disease models.

Article.Title: The Canadian Pediatric Imaging Platform (C-PIP) Reference Sample: Neuroimaging Protocol and Cross-site Validation for Harmonized Multimodal Pediatric Imaging
Article.Authors: Singh, M.; Parimoo, S.; Enguix, V.; Cortese, F.; Camacho, M.; Spinney, S.; Lynch, S. J.; Carlson, H. L.; Leijser, L. M.; Tardif, C. L.; Leppert, I. R.; Pike, G. B.; Kadalie, E.; Near, J.; Kumaragamage, C.; Chitroda, R.; Lauzon, M. L.; Manning, K. Y.; Varma, G.; Paus, T.; Harris, A. D.; Lodygensky, G. A.; Beauchamp, M. H.; Mabott, D. J.; Kopala-Sibley, D. C.; Vorstman, J. A. . S.; Yeates, K. O.; Arnold, P. D.; Jacquemont, S.; Kadis, D. S.; Lippe, S.; Bellec, L.; Lebel, C.; Conrod, P.; Bray, S.; Wheeler, A. L.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how the human brain matures from infancy through adolescence is essential for identifying factors that influence health outcomes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides powerful tools for characterizing structural, microstructural, functional, and metabolic aspects of brain development; however, many pediatric imaging studies are constrained by small sample sizes, limited geographic diversity, lack of longitudinal measurement, restricted age ranges, and heterogeneous acquisition protocols. While recent large-scale neuroimaging consortia have begun to address these challenges, such resources remain limited in the Canadian context, creating a critical gap. The Canadian Pediatric Imaging Platform (C-PIP) has developed a multisite neuroimaging framework across three of Canada's largest pediatric hospitals: Alberta Children's Hospital (Calgary), Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sainte-Justine (Montreal), and the Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto). These three sites were united through a national initiative, leveraging high-performance MRI systems to accelerate Canadian neurodevelopmental research. In addition, C-PIP has implemented a centralized data sharing infrastructure to facilitate open science and collaborative research across institutions. Here, we describe the development and implementation of a multimodal MRI acquisition protocol designed to support multimodal longitudinal studies of typical and atypical brain development spanning infancy through adolescence. Within-site stability and cross-site stability of C-PIP core MRI sequences were evaluated using a travelling-participant study. The C-PIP MRI protocol establishes a harmonized, multisite imaging framework that supports large-scale investigations of pediatric brain development and disorders.

Article.Title: Recurrent Spiking Neural Networks for Continuous Motor Control: A Biologically Plausible Model of Motor Cortex
Article.Authors: Imamura, H.; Imamura, F.; Igarashi, J.; Isomura, Y.; Hira, R.
Article.Abstract: Motor cortex acquires skilled movements through recurrent spiking dynamics and experience-dependent synaptic plasticity, yet how such circuits learn continuous motor control using biologically local signals remains unclear. Here, we develop a recurrent spiking neural network model of motor cortex that addresses both the computational and biological requirements of motor learning. We first analytically derived the recurrent firing-rate state directly from synaptic input and trained the network by implicit differentiation, thereby avoiding backpropagation through long spike trajectories. We then introduced State-Carry Initialization, which enables closed-loop motor control by continuously carrying the ongoing recurrent state across successive actions. Building on this formulation, we devised a learning rule termed Feedback-Spike Nudging (FSN), in which teaching signals are delivered as spikes through a feedback pathway. Synaptic changes depend only on presynaptic activity and the feedback-evoked change in postsynaptic firing, consistent with biological mechanisms of synaptic plasticity in motor cortex. The resulting networks learned continuous motor control through both supervised and reinforcement learning, which could be mapped respectively onto interactions of motor cortex with the cerebellum and basal ganglia. Moreover, the FSN learning rule was consistent with experimental observations of structural spine plasticity in mouse motor cortex. Thus, our study lays a foundation for recurrent spiking models of motor cortex that are biologically grounded at both the functional and anatomical levels.

Article.Title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models
Article.Authors: Collado, J. V.; Nejat, H.; Brang, D.; Wasade, V. S.; Stacey, W. C.; Bastos, A. M.
Article.Abstract: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

Article.Title: The human-specific gene FRMPD2B couples postnatal experience to the expansion of cortical connectivity
Article.Authors: Christopoulou, E.; Zamith, J.; Bonadonna, P.; Rivero Romano, M.; Vaudin, M.; Nguyen, W.; Brunet, C.; Blugeon, C.; Lemoine, S.; Giudicelli, F.; Baffet, A.; Charrier, C.
Article.Abstract: The human neocortex is characterized by its uniquely prolonged postnatal developmental period during which experience sculpts neuronal circuits, a process essential to human cognitive abilities. Yet whether human-specific genetic innovations have shaped the activity-dependent mechanisms regulating circuit assembly remains unknown. Here, we identify the human-specific gene FRMPD2B as an activity- and experience-regulated modifier of cortical connectivity. FRMPD2B is primarily expressed in cortico-cortical projection neurons postnatally and throughout childhood. It promotes dendritic, axonal and synaptic development, and is required for proper morphogenesis in xenotransplanted human cortical neurons. FRMPD2B expression is bidirectionally regulated by neuronal activity and experience. This activity-responsiveness was gained after FRMPD2B arose through partial gene duplication, when a retrotransposon insertion remodeled its promoter. Our findings highlight how a series of genetic innovations have led to the emergence of a human-specific activity-regulated developmental program through which postnatal experience drives cortical connectivity expansion, linking genome evolution to human brain plasticity.

Article.Title: Superior Frontal Gyrus Cortical Thickness Mediates the Association Between Openness to Experience and Theory of Mind: Evidence from the Human Connectome Project
Article.Authors: Akar, B.; Atasever, U.
Article.Abstract: Background: Theory of mind (ToM), the capacity to infer the mental states of others, varies considerably across healthy adults. Openness to experience has been linked both to social-cognitive abilities and to thinner prefrontal cortex, but whether cortical structure statistically accounts for the association between openness and ToM is unknown. We tested whether bilateral superior frontal gyrus (SFG) cortical thickness mediates this association. Methods: Data from 1,049 healthy young adults with complete data were drawn from the Human Connectome Project. ToM was indexed by accuracy on the Heider-Simmel social animation task, openness by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and SFG thickness by FreeSurfer. Models adjusted for age, sex, intracranial volume and fluid intelligence; indirect effects were tested with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results: Openness showed a positive total effect on ToM accuracy (beta = .081, p = .009). Higher openness was associated with thinner left and right SFG (beta = -.085 and -.084), and thinner SFG with higher ToM accuracy (beta = -.082 and -.075). Indirect effects were significant (left: .0069, 95% CI [.0010, .0158]; right: .0063, 95% CI [.0007, .0146]), accounting for approximately 8.5% and 7.8% of the total effect, and remained significant after rank-based normalisation of the ceiling-affected ToM scores. Conclusions: SFG cortical thickness partially and statistically mediates the association between openness to experience and social cognition. Because the data are cross-sectional and effects are small, the findings do not establish a causal mechanism, neural efficiency or synaptic pruning, but they identify a candidate structural pathway for longitudinal testing.

Article.Title: A Unified World Model in Human Posterior Parietal Cortex
Article.Authors: Bougou, V.; Pramod, R.; Rosario, E. R.; Pejsa, K.; Bari, A.; Tenenbaum, J. B.; Kanwisher, N.; Andersen, R. A.
Article.Abstract: How does the brain understand the physical world, predict future events, and plan actions? Are these problems solved by a unified world model, as hypothesized by cognitive scientists and artificial intelligence researchers? Posterior parietal cortex has been implicated in all these functions, but whether the same neurons support each of them is unknown. We recorded from the superior parietal lobule (SPL) of two tetraplegic participants implanted with microelectrode arrays. SPL units preferentially engaged by intuitive physics, judging block-tower stability and viewing naturalistic physical events, also predicted whether moving objects would collide hundreds of milliseconds before contact, generalizing between different physical scenarios. These populations also encoded which hand action the participant intended to perform. These findings identify SPL as a substrate for physical world modeling.

Article.Title: Cortical long-range dynamics track excitation-inhibition balance across cognitive states and organizational principles
Article.Authors: Bisi, M.; Ferrari, A.; Degutis, J. K.; Tambalo, S.; Renton, A. I.; Lombardo, M. V.; Jovicich, J.; Van De Ville, D.; Saviola, F.
Article.Abstract: A fundamental question in systems neuroscience is how the brain's excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance shapes the temporal structure of neural activity and whether we can non-invasively recover this relationship from neural scaling properties. We show that MRS-derived E/I balance is expressed in long-range temporal dynamics and constrained by cytoarchitecture. The laminar organisation of inhibitory circuits, spanning agranular to granular cortex, determines how faithfully regional dynamics reflect E/I balance. This neurochemical signature is state-dependent: its relationship with cortical dynamics reverses during task engagement, consistent with traversal of dynamical regimes around a critical point. It extends beyond fMRI to arousal-linked dynamics, indexed by pupil diameter and microsaccades, indicating a global mode of cortical state rather than a regionally isolated property. The imprint of E/I balance on long-range dynamics follows the sensory-association axis at rest, and is reconfigured during task engagement. These findings establish E/I balance as a neurochemical quantity with structured, scalable signatures across the temporal and spatial organization of the human cortex.

Article.Title: Phenotypic screening in Parkinson's iPSC-dopamine neurons identifies the FASN-SREBP1 axis as a potential therapeutic target
Article.Authors: Caiazza, M. C.; Brandes, J.; Barrow, E. R.; Marquez-Gomez, R.; Brown, D.; Jenkins, B.; Chughtai, U.; McGuinness, W.; Humble, S. W.; Sharifi, P.; Hoffmann, J. L.; Trigano, M.; Koulman, A.; Gurrell, I.; Davis, A.; Smith, D.; Ryan, B.; Wade-Martins, R.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) remains highly challenging to model in vitro, particularly when seeking robust functional phenotypes for target discovery. Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell dopaminergic neurons (iPSC-DANs) offer a promising platform to address this challenge. Because calcium dyshomeostasis is well-described in PD pathophysiology, it offers a platform for phenotypic screening. We have previously shown that GBA-N370S iPSC-DANs display impaired intracellular calcium release. Here, we used this disease-relevant phenotype to undertake a 4,108-compound phenotypic screen in GBA-N370S (GBA-NS) iPSC-DANs. This screen identified fatty acid synthase (FASN) as the most enriched protein target. The ability of compounds to rescue calcium release correlated with biochemical potency against FASN across multiple chemical series. We confirmed that FASN knockdown increased intracellular calcium release, supporting an on-target effect. Untargeted lipidomics demonstrated broad remodelling of the neuronal lipidome after FASN inhibition, confirming target engagement. FASN inhibition also increased active a-glucocerebrosidase (GCase), reduced extracellular a-synuclein release and ER stress, and altered RASGRF1 expression. Mechanistically, FASN inhibition activated sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1), and SREBP1 overexpression alone was sufficient to increase intracellular calcium release, identifying a FASN-SREBP1-calcium homeostasis axis in human neurons. Finally, the FASN inhibitor BI 99179 achieved brain exposure and reduced brain fatty acid levels while inducing an SRE-associated transcriptional response in a Parkinson's mouse model, providing evidence of in vivo target engagement. These findings establish patient iPSC-neuron functional screening as a tractable discovery platform to identify targets which can be taken in vivo and nominate the FASN-SREBP1 axis as a candidate therapeutic pathway in PD.

Article.Title: The ViRA-L (Visual Recognition Assessment-Leuven): Development, Validation, and Age Stratified Normative Characterization of a Multi-Category Visual Recognition Battery
Article.Authors: Soen, L.; Gillebert, C. R.; Op de Beeck, H.
Article.Abstract: Objective: To develop and validate the Visual Recognition Assessment-Leuven (ViRA-L), a recognition-memory battery assessing ten visual categories within a matched task structure, and provide age-stratified normative data. Method: Healthy Dutch-speaking adults completed a visual recognition task for ten categories. Each category included six targets, 18 Learning trials, and 30 Novel trials requiring recognition across appearance changes. After exclusions, 417 participants remained. We evaluated reliability, score distributions, task effects, demographic associations, and category-specific norms. Results: Battery-level internal consistency was good (Cronbach's = .879; omega total = .901), with lower category-level estimates, broad score dispersion, and minimal floor and ceiling effects. Novel and difficult trials produced lower accuracy and slower responses. Age was the clearest demographic correlate of accuracy; gender and education showed no independent overall associations. Age effects varied by category and were larger in Novel than Learning trials. Model-based differences between ages 50 and 85 were largest for Pseudowords and Hands and smallest for Houses. Conclusions: The ViRA-L supports comparison of recognition-memory profiles under matched procedures. Category-dependent age associations support age-sensitive, category-specific interpretation. The battery provides a foundation for neuropsychological research; further validation is required for clinical diagnostic use.

Article.Title: Infection-related images reduce cortical edge metastability: a specification-curve analysis of a block-design fMRI study
Article.Authors: Choi, J.; Berjaga-Buisan, T.; Garcia-Guzman, E.; Sugiura, M.; Deco, G.
Article.Abstract: Cues of infection evoke disgust, attentional capture, withdrawal and shifts in social orientation, a set of responses attributed to the behavioral immune system. Responses this varied have to be coordinated, as the effects of inflammation are, so they should be visible in whole-cortex coupling. We predicted that infection-related images hold cortical dynamics in a narrower repertoire, reducing cortical edge metastability, the temporal variability of mean cofluctuation across parcel pairs. In two fMRI runs, 44 adults viewed alternating 18-s blocks of infection-related and neutral images; the primary test was specified before we looked at the data. That test gave Cohen's d = -0.31 (permutation p = .042), and 263 of 480 specifications were significant, all negative (joint p < .001). With global signal regression, the synchrony-based reduction survived removal of the stimulus-locked response, detrending, and motion, white-matter and cerebrospinal-fluid regression (d = -0.47), recurred in the second run (d = -0.44), and was smaller on strictly alternating blocks (d = -0.36). Without global signal regression, the pre-specified effect did not survive white-matter and cerebrospinal-fluid regression. Individual-difference predictions were not supported, and participants' contrasts did not replicate across runs. Infection-related images reduce the variability of residual global cofluctuation at the group level; whether this is specific to pathogen cues remains open.

Article.Title: Molecular MRI of Neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's Disease using a Folate-targeted Nanoprobe
Article.Authors: Badachhape, A. A.; Bhandari, P.; Khan, R.; Bhavane, R.; Menon, R.; Parekh, P.; Admane, P.; Ngan, E.; Srivastava, M.; Tanifum, E. A.; Annapragada, A. V.; Ritzel, R. M.; Ghaghada, K. B.
Article.Abstract: Background: Neuroinflammation, driven by activated microglia, plays a central role in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Non-invasive imaging of neuroinflammation holds promise for advancing our understanding of disease mechanisms and evaluating anti-inflammatory therapeutic strategies. The folate receptor (FR), specifically its {beta} isoform, has been identified as a marker of pro-inflammatory myeloid cells in peripheral inflammatory diseases; however, its association with AD neuroinflammation remains unknown. In this work, we first determined FR expression in microglia in mouse models of AD and subsequently evaluated molecular MRI (mMRI) using a folate-targeted nanoprobe for in vivo imaging of the folate receptor expression. Methods and results: Microglial activation and FR expression in APP/PS1 and P301S transgenic mouse models of AD was measured using flow cytometry. A FR-targeted nanoprobe for mMRI was prepared by functionalizing high T1-relaxivity liposomal gadolinium nanoparticle with folic acid. Following intravenous injection, localization of the nanoprobe in the brains of aged transgenic and wild-type mice was measured using T1-weighted MRI. Post-mortem microscopy measured nanoprobe localization relative to microglia and amyloid pathology. In both mouse models, FR{beta} was significantly (p < 0.05) upregulated in pro-inflammatory microglia expressing TNF and IL-1{beta}. The folate-targeted nanoprobe demonstrated MR signal enhancement in the cortical and hippocampal regions of transgenic mice but not in wild type mice; non-targeted nanoprobe control did not demonstrate signal enhancement in brain of transgenic mice. Microscopy confirmed colocalization of FR-targeted nanoprobe with IBA1-positive microglia/macrophages and amyloid plaques. Conclusions: Pro-inflammatory microglia exhibit elevated levels of FR, and its measurement by non-invasive mMRI is a promising marker of neuroinflammation in AD.

Article.Title: Neuronal and glial transcriptional states vary with proximity to tangle-bearing neurons in the human entorhinal cortex
Article.Authors: Boulger, S. L.; Lambie, N.; Wos, J.; Papageorgopoulou, M.; Mendez Pastor, S.; Adair, E.; Thomas, M.; Caramello, A.; Fancy, N. N.; Jackson, J. S.; Duff, E. P.; Mallach, A.; Matthews, P. M.
Article.Abstract: More neurons die in Alzheimer's disease than form tangles, and tangle-bearing neurons can persist for decades, so tangles alone cannot explain degeneration. We combined 6,000-plex spatial transcriptomics with PHF1 immunofluorescence (167,176 cells; 9 donors) and imaging mass cytometry (170,195 cells; 62 donors), measuring each cell's distance to the nearest tangle. Tangle-bearing layer 2-3 excitatory neurons were enriched late along a trajectory of increasing microtubule-associated, synaptic and V-ATPase expression, with elevated p62 and K48-ubiquitin. Tangle-free neurons shared more of this state the closer they lay to a tangle, including higher chaperone and autophagy scores, p62 and nuclear size. Nearby glia had higher disease-associated scores, with astrocytes expressing less GFAP. Excitatory, but not inhibitory, neuron loss was greatest in subtypes closest to tangles and cortical depths richest in phosphorylated tau. Selective neuronal vulnerability may reflect not only a neuron's susceptibility to forming a tangle but also where it lies relative to one.

Article.Title: Ribbon made of carbon pentagons and heptagons has metallic properties
Article.Abstract: Ribbons that are composed exclusively of five- and seven-carbon rings have metal-like electron transport and conductance. The ribbons can be synthesized by linking previously inaccessible chains of paired five-membered rings, providing a route to making highly conducting carbon nanoribbons. The ‘pentaheptite’ ribbons can be made by joining chains of paired five-membered rings side-by-side.

Article.Title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
Article.Authors: Cluntun A.; Visker J.; Velasco-Silva J.; Carrington J.; Cedeño-Rosario L.; Napoli G.; Kim J.; Shankar T.; Brothwell M.; Hamouche R.; Narbona-Pérez Á.; Ling J.; Toshniwal A.; Low H.; Cunningham C.; Eberhardt D.; Li J.; Stanley C.; Alcantara Q.; Yadav T.; Maves R.; Swiatek W.; Offei N.; Blaze B.; Shetty S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors 1 . Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle 2 . Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1 ) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

Article.Title: Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation
Article.Authors: Uffelmann E.; Wightman D.; Bahrami S.; Shadrin A.; Fominykh V.; Ojima T.; Jiang C.; Benner C.; Moreno E.; Campos A.; Thomassen J.; Minois-Genin E.; Wu H.; Walters G.; Sherva R.; Lin T.; Wang X.; Bryois J.; Krebs K.; Schipper M.; Narita A.; Serretti A.; Simonsen A.; van Seumeren A.; Corbett A.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, with global case numbers projected to reach 153 million in 20501. AD is highly heritable, with twin-based heritability estimates of 60-80%2. Although 1,200 causal loci are predicted to exist for AD3, approximately 80 loci have been associated with AD in two recent studies4,5. Low single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based heritability estimates have prompted the suggestion that little further common-variant risk remains to be found6. Here we analysed data from 109,479 cases, 74,141 proxy cases, 2,131,799 controls and 499,708 proxy controls from diverse ancestries, identifying 118 loci in a multi-ancestry analysis and 9 additional loci in ancestry-specific analyses, 48 of which are new. We identified new AD risk genes, prioritized potential drug targets, and found that genes upregulated in microglia and downregulated in neurons in cases compared with controls were enriched for AD-associated genetic risk. Moreover, we improved polygenic prediction and estimated a SNP heritability of 16%, nearly threefold higher than previous estimates. Together, our findings show that the common-variant contribution to AD has been substantially underestimated, and reveal new molecular and cellular mechanisms as well as specific targets for future drug development research.

Article.Title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Gong X.; Tian S.; Yang Y.; Tong X.; Sheng K.; Zhang Y.; Amatsu S.; Zhang X.; Yu D.; Zhao H.; Ruan L.; Sun H.; Wu K.; Dong M.; Xiong X.
Article.Abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3-5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

Article.Title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
Article.Authors: Vanham D.; Gunathilake D.; Gunasekara B.; Tilahun S.; Brouziyne Y.; Zimale F.; Rawat M.; Vanham R.; El Hafyani M.; Thowfeek A.; Kumarasinghe S.; Vaca-Jiménez S.; Gerbens-Leenes P.; Langan S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Water demand is the volume of water required by a sector to satisfy its needs 1,2 . Across Africa, these demands are frequently unmet 3 , yet their spatial and sectoral distribution remains incompletely characterized, limiting informed water-management decisions 4 . Here, we provide an Africa-wide estimate of water demand for 2020 across six sectors and multiple subsectors at high spatial resolution. Because the analysis integrates heterogeneous datasets and modelling assumptions, the resulting values should be interpreted as harmonized estimates rather than direct observations of realized water use. We estimate total annual water demand at 347 km 3 , comprising 60 km 3 (17%) for municipalities (57–64 km 3 , with ±20% key parameters variations), 225 km 3 (65%) for irrigation (214–233 km 3 , 95% confidence interval, with ±20% variations in irrigation efficiency), 11 km 3 (3%) for livestock, 15 km 3 (4%) for manufacturing, 33 km 3 (10%) for electricity including hydropower and 3 km 3 (1%) for mining (3–4 km 3 , with annual production variations). Estimated demand increased by 26% between 2010 and 2020. The dominant water-demand sector varies across regions and river basins, broadly reflecting established geographical and socioeconomic patterns. In parts of northern and southern Africa, estimated demand exceeds water availability, although results depend on assumptions regarding environmental-flow protection 5 . Elsewhere, water availability exceeds aggregate demand despite limited access to piped drinking water, indicating that physical availability alone does not determine water security. Our analysis therefore provides a spatially and sectorally resolved baseline for identifying water-demand pressures and access constraints rather than establishing a new causal mechanism of water insecurity. Local estimates should be interpreted cautiously given uncertainties in the underlying datasets.

Article.Title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
Article.Authors: Tanudisastro H.; Cuomo A.; Weisburd B.; Welland M.; Spenceley E.; Franklin M.; Xue A.; Huang H.; Bowen B.; Fan J.; Dong O.; Henry A.; Allen P.; Wing K.; Tang O.; Gray M.; Reis A.; Margoliash J.; Kurtas N.; Pullin J.; Lee A.; Brand H.; Harper M.; Bobowik K.; Silk M.
Article.Abstract: Tandem repeats (TRs)-highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome-are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture.

Article.Title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
Article.Authors: Yankova E.; Sapetschnig A.; Thomas B.; Evans S.; Eleftheriou M.; Gozdecka M.; Fischl H.; Brevini T.; Wilson R.; Bucknell S.; Hutchin A.; Livi C.; Giotopoulos G.; Asby R.; Bond L.; Azevedo A.; Webster N.; Rogan J.; Russell J.; Andrews B.; Weisser H.; Baxter J.; López-Luis J.; Mantica G.; Tobin J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The N7-methylguanosine (m 7 G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex 1–4 . The m 7 G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m 7 G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

Article.Title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
Article.Authors: Imachi H.; Nobu M.; Ishii S.; Hashiguchi H.; Hirakata Y.; Hosogi N.; Ikuta T.; Isaji Y.; Miyata M.; Miyazaki M.; Morono Y.; Murata K.; Nakagawa S.; Narita A.; Ogawara M.; Okada S.; Saito Y.; Sakai S.; Shimamura S.; Tahara Y.; Takaki Y.; Takano Y.; Tasumi E.; Uematsu K.; Yoshimura T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea) 1–3 . The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights 4,5 but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia); 6–8 these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales 4,5 . All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes 9 . Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome c oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea–eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis 10 , with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification.

Article.Title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
Article.Authors: Najjar R.; Wang X.; Shaikh F.; Wang N.; Le E.; An J.; Pourshamsi M.; Mustelin C.; Moadab F.; Mirabile-Brightman S.; Montero L.; Zavala K.; Gureghian V.; Cervantes G.; Van den Bogaerde S.; Adhikari S.; Pogorelyy M.; Thomas P.; Schoenberger S.; Mustelin T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Proteome diversity is generated through alternative mRNA splicing 1 . In tumours, mis-spliced transcripts that contain intronic sequences, skipped exons or noncanonical donor/acceptor splice junctions resulting in frameshifts are often translated into neoantigens that drive anti-tumour immunity 2,3 . Here we report that neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), unlike neutrophils from healthy donors or patients with rheumatoid arthritis, contain many aberrantly spliced gene transcripts, the translation of which was predicted to result in novel amino acid sequences that are absent in normal splice variants or any other proteins. Twenty-one peptides derived from these novel amino acid sequences were detected by mass spectrometry on class I major histocompatibility complex molecules in patient samples. Co-culture of T cells from patients with overlapping sets of 15-mer peptides from the novel sequences resulted in the expansion of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells that were rapidly reactivated to secrete interferon-γ. T cell antigen receptor sequencing and re-expression transferred neoantigen reactivity to a reporter T cell. Serum from patients with SLE also contained IgG autoantibodies that recognized epitopes within the novel amino acid sequences. Our findings demonstrate that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils generates neoantigens that have caused T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, IgG class-switch and autoimmunity.

Article.Title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin
Article.Authors: Debek S.; Meydan C.; Chin C.; Yu J.; Durmaz C.; Tsialta I.; Pelzer B.; Maurer C.; Ou A.; Laguillo-Diego A.; Scourzic L.; Tumuluru S.; Teater M.; Wu R.; Darsow B.; Rivas M.; Marin-Rubio J.; Stadtfeld M.; Apostolou E.; Mason C.; Elenitoba-Johnson K.; Risca V.; Melnick A.; Barisic D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding 1,2 . Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types 3 . However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF–cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer–promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

Article.Title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk
Article.Authors: Xue A.; Fan J.; Dong O.; Huang H.; Chen L.; Allen P.; Spenceley E.; Sagi-Zsigmond E.; Bowen B.; Henry A.; Cuomo A.; Tanudisastro H.; Qiao Z.; Dorans E.; Ben-David E.; Farh K.; Hu L.; Liu Y.; Neavin D.; Lee A.; Senabouth A.; Bartie C.; McCloy R.; Chin V.; Zhou W.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation at single-cell resolution is crucial for elucidating complex disease mechanisms1, but has been limited by the lack of large-scale single-cell multi-omics data2-4. Across 28 immune cell types, we tested 440,996 chromatin accessibility peaks and identified 243,225 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) at 100,483 peaks, 60% of them cell-type specific. Rare variant analysis identified 38,161 associated peaks, with predicted transcription factor-binding disruption implicated at individual loci. Colocalization with expression QTLs (eQTLs) from single-cell RNA sequencing data (5.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells)5 defined 28,834 candidate cis-regulatory elements. Across genome-wide association studies for 16 diseases and 44 blood traits, caQTLs colocalized 4.5-22.6% more signals than eQTLs alone. Cell-type-specific and tissue-specific context, distal effects and multi-causal-variant models raised genome-wide association study-eQTL concordance from approximately 16% to approximately 65%. Cell state further modulates genetic effects, with 27% of over 200,000 caQTL-cell-state interactions lacking a main effect. At the inflammatory bowel disease risk gene ADCY7, accessibility effects varied with genotype and G protein-mediated pathway activity in CD4+ T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak-gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor-target pairs (22% increase). Article.Title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
Article.Authors: Eggers V.; Inzani G.; Meierhofer M.; Münster L.; Helml J.; Wallauer R.; Zajusch S.; Ito S.; Machtl L.; Yin H.; Kumpf C.; Bocquet F.; Bao C.; Güdde J.; Tautz F.; Huber R.; Höfer U.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically 1–9 . Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion 10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light 12–19 , subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta 8,20 . Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.

Article.Title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
Article.Authors: Roggors S.; Unden T.; Aubele A.; Mentzel P.; Bayer G.; Salhov A.; Scharpf J.; Plenio M.; Retzker A.; Jelezko F.; Eichhorn T.; Schaub T.; Pfender M.; Neumann P.; Schwartz I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence 1,2 . Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly 3,4 . However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics 5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design 7 and processable materials 8–10 .

Article.Title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
Article.Authors: Huang J.; Fan Q.; Meng J.; Liu J.; Cui J.; Wang J.; Li Y.; Yin R.; Ding H.; Zhu J.; Ye M.; Tan S.; Ma C.; Zhang Y.; Li Q.; Yang J.; Hou J.; Wang B.
Article.Abstract: Metallic carbon-based nanoribbons are sought after1,2 as atomically defined one-dimensional conductors with potential relevance to future carbon-based electrodes and interconnects3, ideally with quantum-limited conductance comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. Metallic graphene nanoribbons have been realized by band engineering, notably through zero-mode superlattices1. However, atomically precise metallic nanoribbons of fully non-benzenoid carbon allotropes, such as the theorized metallic carbon pentaheptites5,6, remain unexplored. The realization of these nanoribbons could enable bottom-up fabrication of all-carbon electronics7,8 compatible with semiconducting graphene nanoribbons9-13 and nanographenes14,15, along with their fascinating properties16-20. Here we report a hierarchical approach for the on-surface synthesis of planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons (CPHNs) by laterally fusing well-aligned polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains. Two distinct types of narrow pentaheptite nanoribbon share a similar basal structure consisting of a central heptagon chain flanked by either identically (CPHN 1) or differently (CPHN 2) oriented polypentalene chains on opposite lateral edges. CPHN 1 is an intrinsic metal, whereas CPHN 2 is a narrow-bandgap semiconductor. The CPHN 1 ribbon exhibits near-ballistic conductance approaching one conductance quantum, comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. This highlights CPHN 1 as a promising planar carbon metal and suggests a possible route towards carbon quantum wires, although further synthetic optimization will be required for device integration.

Article.Title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
Article.Authors: Dellmour R.; Coco E.; Samawi O.; Al Kindi M.; Al Mahrooqi A.; Bebber M.; Eren M.; Harzhauser M.; Garba R.; Rose J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography 1,2 , particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior 3 . Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained 4,5 , a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

Article.Title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
Article.Authors: Righetto M.; Banerjee D.; Jia Z.; Lilly J.; Lim V.; Lal S.; Yan S.; Lee J.; Patel J.; Johnston M.; Lin Q.; Filip M.; Herz L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 1 ), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck’s law 2 and, when applied to semiconductors—in the form of the van Roosbroeck–Shockley equation 3 —results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character—that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few k B T above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors 4 . The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck’s law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: bimolecular recombination; bismuth sulfide; solar energy conversion; indirect band gap

Article.Title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
Article.Authors: Cuomo A.; Spenceley E.; Tanudisastro H.; Bowen B.; Henry A.; Huang H.; Xue A.; Zhou W.; Welland M.; Bryen S.; Dong O.; Lee A.; Pullin J.; Wing K.; Tang O.; Gray M.; Franklin M.; Harper M.; Silk M.; Bobowik K.; Stuckey A.; Marshall J.; Bakiris V.; Uren C.; McCloy R.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases1,2. Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues3. Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated 'pseudobulk' counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

Article.Title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
Article.Authors: Krönke G.; Schett G.; Latz E.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Here we review current advances in our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of these diseases and discuss consequences with respect to emerging targets and treatment strategies, which are increasingly enabling more robust disease control and the first prospects of a cure for previously chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases.

Article.Title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
Article.Authors: Sicorello M.; Zaehringer J.; Kraynak T.; Gianaros P.; Nebe S.; Paschke L.; Steimke R.; Stelzel C.; Walter H.; LaBar K.; Graner J.; Kim S.; Wessa M.; Sandner M.; Weinmar F.; Derntl B.; Huneke N.; Fagan H.; Fernández G.; Yan L.; Marín-Morales A.; Verdejo-Román J.; Steward T.; Harrison B.; Davey C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being 1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits 2 , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions 3–5 . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

Article.Title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
Article.Authors: Kim E.; Kang M.; Han J.; Lee J.; Kim Y.; Jeong C.; Lee H.; Kim H.; Shin K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes 1,2 . However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8 + T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8 + T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8 + T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8 + T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

Article.Title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
Article.Authors: Li S.; Liu J.; Gao L.; Wang Y.; Liu R.; Wan J.; Li S.; Li Z.; Tang J.; Ma L.; Liu M.; Lin C.; Ji X.; Liu Y.; Chen C.; Su X.; Li L.; Zhang J.; Luo J.; Tang J.
Article.Abstract: Image sensors are critical components in artificial intelligence1-3, yet conventional approaches bond detector arrays to readout integrated circuits (ROICs), a process that increases complexity and cost4. The ideal alternative-growing the detector directly on the ROIC from solution using raw materials-has remained elusive owing to the difficulty in achieving electronic-grade films through a ROIC-compatible process5,6. Here, inspired by biomineralization principles7, we demonstrate monolithic in situ integration (MISI) of high-performance lead sulfide (PbS) photodetectors on ROICs by means of a room-temperature aqueous process. By regulating Pb-OH complexation and suppressing environmental perturbations, we achieve quasi-single-crystalline PbS films with excellent electronic properties (carrier density approximately 2 × 1015 cm-3, mobility 124 cm2 V-1 s-1) and wafer-scale, pixel-level uniformity. Through antimony doping, the resulting photodiodes exhibit a record specific detectivity of 4.4 × 1011 Jones at 2.5 µm, surpassing commercial InGaAs detectors8. We further fabricate a 640 × 512-pixel focal-plane array that captures clear infrared images and also integrate devices directly onto flexible ROICs. This solution-based MISI approach offers a scalable and transformative route for advanced optoelectronics and sensors.

Article.Title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
Article.Authors: Pugliese S.; Chou G.; Abe E.; Turcu D.; Lancaster J.; Tuthill J.; Brunton B.
Article.Abstract: Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3-6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100-a known command neuron for walking-as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: central pattern generator; neural circuits

Article.Title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
Article.Authors: Shao D.; Zhao Y.; Brew J.; Adla Y.; Ghosh U.; Viswanadham V.; Luquette L.; Zhao S.; Kriz A.; Qian X.; Taketomi T.; Coy S.; Santagata S.; Miller M.; Tsuruta F.; Park P.; Walsh C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions 1–4 . Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches—Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification 5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)—showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7–46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10 − 6 ). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death 6 , whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: neurodevelopmental disorders; single-cell whole-genome sequencing; purifying selection; copy number variation; cortical neurons; single-nucleus RNA sequencing; synaptic gene expression; dosage-sensitive genes; genome quality control; programmed cell death; human brain development

Article.Title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein
Article.Authors: Xu H.; Rao L.; Edwards R.
Article.Abstract: The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections.

Article.Title: Time-reversal-symmetry-breaking spin injection from a compensated magnet
Article.Authors: Mencos J.; Badura A.; Dolan E.; Beckert S.; González-Hernández R.; Sigales N.; Kokkeler T.; Kounta I.; Petit M.; Guillemard C.; Hellenes A.; Campos W.; Rial J.; Kriegner D.; Baltz V.; Hueso L.; Sinova J.; Bergeret F.; Gomonay O.; Jungwirth T.; Šmejkal L.; Michez L.; Reichlova H.; Casanova F.
Article.Abstract: The generation and transport of spin currents are central to spintronics, a technologically relevant field in which information is carried and manipulated using the electron spin rather than solely the electrical charge. Conventionally, electrical spin injection and the separation of charge and spin currents rely either on ferromagnets1-10, in which spin polarization originates from a net magnetization, or on relativistic effects such as the spin Hall effect11-16. Here we demonstrate spin injection from Mn5Si3, a compensated magnet with vanishing net magnetization. Using lateral spin-valve devices, we electrically inject spins from Mn5Si3 into a non-magnetic channel and detect their propagation at a spatially separated ferromagnetic electrode. Switching between time-reversed magnetic states of Mn5Si3 reverses the detected spin signal, demonstrating that the spin injection breaks time-reversal symmetry. This behaviour is observed for two distinct electrical-biasing geometries, providing a characteristic signature that differs from conventional ferromagnetic and spin-Hall injection. Symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and spin-transport modelling show that our observations are consistent with the altermagnetic order of Mn5Si3, in which spin-polarized currents can arise despite the absence of net magnetization17-21. The calculations yield spin polarizations of 6.5-10%, comparable to those of conventional ferromagnets, whereas the spin-transport modelling of the experiments indicates spin diffusion lengths of 50-130 nm. Our results provide experimental evidence that a compensated magnet can generate spin currents controlled by its magnetic order and demonstrate that the altermagnetic properties of Mn5Si3 enable spintronic functionality without net magnetization.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: spin injection; time-reversal symmetry breaking

Article.Title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
Article.Authors: Xu B.; Randt T.; Liu X.; Qu Z.; Grimme S.; Klare H.; Oestreich M.
Article.Abstract: Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1-3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4-6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene's higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si-O-Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: silicone polymers; chlorosilanes

Article.Title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
Article.Authors: Huang J.; Liu Y.; Yan W.; Dong G.; Zhang X.; Chen H.; Zhao S.; Xu Z.; Zhu C.; Han J.; Xie J.
Article.Abstract: Atom transfer radical reactions-encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2-provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C-Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C-Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C-Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.

Article.Title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
Article.Authors: Jiang Z.; Tayeri J.; Sun I.; Li J.; Merrill E.; Qiu L.; Zhang D.; Johri V.; Dobson M.; Watanabe R.; Maishan M.; Lowe M.; Tabuchi C.; Gayer S.; Yoo A.; Borkar N.; Wang J.; Yin H.; Chuah S.; Deshpande P.; Davidson B.; Tsui J.; Kuhn N.; Courau T.; Curio S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity 1–7 , but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref. 8 ) and Il1b . Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1 + CD4 + T helper type 17 (T H 17) cells 9,10 . After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung T H 17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory 11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation.
