Article.Title: ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2
Article.Authors: McGrath L.; Kar G.; Bonanno L.; Guisier F.; Insa A.; Liberman M.; Bylicki O.; Livi L.; Egenod T.; Corre R.; Kim D.; Garcia Campelo M.; Provencio Pulla M.; Shim B.; Metro G.; Bennouna J.; Bielska A.; Yohannes A.; Shaju J.; He Y.; Dowson A.; Grenga I.; Spicer J.; Forde P.; Cascone T.
Article.Abstract: Patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain at high risk of relapse despite perioperative treatment1-3. NeoCOAST-2 (NCT05061550), a phase 2, randomised platform trial, tested novel perioperative treatments in patients with stage IIA-IIIB NSCLC. At primary analysis, combining standard chemotherapy plus durvalumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) with oleclumab (Arm 1, n = 76), monalizumab (Arm 2, n = 72) or datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd; Arm 4, n = 54) resulted in pathological complete response (pCR) rates of 20.3%, 25.7%, and 35.2%, respectively4. Here, we present the first report of prespecified secondary endpoints of event-free survival (EFS) and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) clearance, and exploratory analyses of associations between ctDNA dynamics and clinical outcomes. The 24-month EFS rates were 70.5%, 75.7% and 77.9% in Arms 1, 2 and 4, respectively. Using a tumour-agnostic assay, ctDNA clearance at neoadjuvant Cycle 3 Day 1 was highest in Arm 4 (50.9%, 54.5%, and 72.5% in each arm, respectively). ctDNA clearance correlated with prolonged EFS versus non-clearance (pooled hazard ratio (HR) 0.22; 95% CI = 0.11-0.45, P = 0.0000443). Patients with both ctDNA clearance and pCR had favourable EFS outcomes versus those with neither (EFS HR 0.10, 95% CI = 0.02-0.42, P = 0.002). These findings suggest combined assessment of ctDNA clearance and pCR may improve risk stratification, and that the numerically highest pCR4 and EFS rates with the Dato-DXd combination warrant further evaluation.

Article.Title: Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance
Article.Authors: Singh A.; Martin L.; Sršen M.; Guttesen F.; Hu B.; Ito Y.; Pedersen S.; Kamounah F.; Pauly F.; Pittelkow M.; Lü J.; Hedegård P.; Tal O.
Article.Abstract: For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage's polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4-6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: molecular machines; helicenes; molecular junctions

Article.Abstract: Embedding enzymes that break down ester bonds into compostable polyesters enables rapid and complete biodegradation even in microbe-scarce environments. Polyesters containing ester-bond-breaking enzymes could help to reduce plastic pollution in marine environments.

Article.Title: Cave stalagmites document global patterns in monsoon rainfall over the past 450,000 years
Article.Abstract: A 450,000-year stalagmite record of rainfall in the Amazon Basin , combined with existing Asian records, shows that the global monsoon system has oscillated regularly, strengthening in one hemisphere while weakening in the other. However, during intervals of warmth and warming climate, monsoons in both hemispheres failed for millennia. The South American and Asian monsoons have both weakened during past periods of rapid warming.

Article.Title: The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology
Article.Authors: Xing S.; Wu Z.; Shao Q.; Ge J.; Bennett E.; Rao H.; Lin S.; Zhao Y.; Liu F.; Liu Y.; Zhou K.; Feng X.; Jiangzuo Q.; Fu Q.
Article.Abstract: The taxonomy and phylogeny of late Middle Pleistocene hominins in East Asia remain highly debated1. Xujiayao, a key representative assemblage with many fossils and a clear stratigraphy dating to around 199-138 thousand years ago, has been extensively studied, but its evolutionary position remains uncertain. Here, to clarify this, we analysed Xujiayao material through both palaeoproteomic analysis and morphological comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo. Proteomic analysis of two specimens identified 18 endogenous proteins, and the Denisova-specific COL1A2-996 R>K mutation strongly supported their affiliation with the Denisovan lineage. Extended analysis identifies a set of shared morphological traits between Denisovan fossils (Xujiayao and Harbin) and other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong), indicating that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage. This analysis provides a comprehensive view of Denisovan features, showing both traits reminiscent of Homo erectus (such as a thick cranial vault) and those characteristic of modern humans (for example, a strongly arched temporal squama). They also share features with late Neanderthals, such as the structure of the temporal labyrinth and the presence of a suprainiac fossa. Notably, Denisovans are distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.

Article.Title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes
Article.Authors: Kim K.; Gardner C.; Cullen A.; Stelzer J.; Cho K.; Sharma A.; Nemera M.; Law T.; Naz H.; Zhao G.; Gabel H.; Patti G.; Musiek E.; Ahn T.; Yi J.
Article.Abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.

Article.Title: Functional architecture of the human insula
Article.Authors: Quabs J.; Pantis S.; Chen G.; Huang W.; Ma E.; del Vecchio M.; Lyu D.; Wang C.; Avanzini P.; Buch V.; Ramayya A.; Caspers S.; Vogel H.; Parvizi J.
Article.Abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7-10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal-posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral-posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior-polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

Article.Title: Additive manufacturing of ultralong and architected single crystals
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Cui Y.; Wang J.; Han X.; Ji Z.; Liang Z.; Zhang C.; Marian J.; Li Z.; Lu T.; Xu T.; Zhang J.; Cui W.; Liu W.; Fang D.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Single-crystal materials are indispensable for high-performance applications, yet their deployment remains constrained by conventional manufacturing techniques that depend on strict quasi-steady thermal conditions1. This requirement fundamentally conflicts with the intense cyclic thermal fluctuations inherent to additive manufacturing2, historically preventing the 3D printing of large or architected single crystals. Here we present a free-form additive manufacturing approach that resolves this contradiction by using delicately controlled alternating and pulsed heat inputs to govern and direct single-crystal growth. Using this method, we demonstrate the fabrication of metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V alongside, to our knowledge, the first single-crystal lattice structures containing complex zigzag ligaments, effectively eliminating theoretical size constraints for single-crystal components. The resulting bulk single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V exhibits an order-of-magnitude increase in creep resistance over standard grain-size scaling predictions, driven by the synergistic elimination of grain boundaries and an additive manufacturing-induced hierarchical α/β-architecture that regulates dislocation density, mobility and void evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broad applicability of this technique by printing single crystals of hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys. Our work introduces a large-scale method for single-crystal additive manufacturing, expanding the accessible materials library and enabling high-performance, complex geometries previously unattainable by classical methods.

Article.Title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root
Article.Authors: Oliva M.; Stuart T.; Tang D.; Khan A.; Clement O.; Makosa D.; Poppe D.; Pflueger J.; Jabbari J.; Gigante S.; Dragwidge J.; Petterson M.; Whelan J.; Lewsey M.; Lister R.
Article.Abstract: Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1. Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types.

Article.Title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
Article.Authors: Battini L.; Slough M.; Kaur R.; Guo L.; Florez C.; Serris A.; Meola A.; Lasso G.; Tischler N.; Alvarez R.; Lambe U.; Khera L.; Wang J.; Scott R.; Garrido J.; Barria M.; Josleyn N.; Rey F.; Herbert A.; McLellan J.; Jangra R.; Chandran K.; Guardado-Calvo P.
Article.Abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms-occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus-receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.

Article.Title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation
Article.Authors: Meier R.; Morgand E.; Mezine F.; Mengel M.; Mangiola M.; Mohiuddin M.; Montgomery R.; Loupy A.
Article.Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

Article.Title: Octupole-driven spin torque switching of antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions
Article.Authors: Kang J.; Hamdi M.; Cheung S.; Yuan L.; Elekhtiar M.; Matt E.; Rogers W.; Meo A.; Lim P.; Tey M.; D’Addario A.; Konakanchi S.; Athas J.; Arpaci S.; Devincenti A.; Wan L.; Mehta S.; Zogbi N.; Sangwan V.; Incorvia J.; Fowlie J.; Upadhyaya P.; Carpentieri M.; Dravid V.; Hersam M.
Article.Abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions based on ferromagnets are canonical devices in spintronics, with wide-ranging applications in data storage, computing and sensing. They simultaneously exhibit mechanisms for electrical detection and control of magnetic order through the tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR)1-5 and spin-transfer torque6-9 effects, respectively. It was long assumed that neither of these effects could be sizeable in all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions (AATJs), considering that they have no net magnetization. However, it was recently shown that AATJs based on chiral antiferromagnets do exhibit TMR due to their non-relativistic momentum-dependent spin polarization and cluster magnetic octupole moment, which are manifestations of their spin-split band structure10-13. However, the reciprocal effect, that is, the antiferromagnetic counterpart of spin-transfer torque, has been assumed non-existent due to the total electric current being spin-neutral. Here we report nanoscale AATJs that display this reciprocal effect, which we term octupole-driven spin-transfer torque (OTT). We demonstrate current-induced OTT switching of PtMn3|MgO|PtMn3 AATJs, with a TMR value of 363% at room temperature and switching current densities of the order of 10 MA cm-2. Our theoretical modelling explains the origin of OTT in terms of the imbalance between intra- and inter-sublattice spin currents across the AATJ, and, equivalently, in terms of the non-zero net cluster octupole polarization of each PtMn3 layer. This work establishes a new materials platform for antiferromagnetic spintronics and provides a pathway towards deeply scaled magnetic memory and room-temperature terahertz technologies.

Article.Title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
Article.Authors: Woo J.; Williamson M.; Choi D.; Akdemir E.; Zlatkov T.; Yu K.; Kwon W.; Maleki E.; Ko Y.; Sanchez K.; Maleki H.; Choi J.; Serin-Harmanci A.; Deneen B.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51- astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51- astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.

Article.Title: Amazon carbon emissions driven by human actions amplified by droughts
Article.Authors: Gatti L.; Cunha C.; Blas J.; Denning A.; Reis M.; Marani L.; Arai E.; Messias C.; Conciani D.; Miller J.; Schumacher V.; Naccarato K.; Marengo J.; Alencar A.; Soler L.; Almeida C.; Domingues L.; Correia C.; Neves R.; Nobre C.; Corrêa S.; Campbell E.; Johnson J.; Berry J.; Sanchez A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation 1–5 , rising tree mortality 6–8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest 9–11 . Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions 1–4,11,12 . Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable 1,9,13 . Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts 9,14–17 . Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO 2 measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 , with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 ) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr −1 ) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.

Article.Title: WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry
Article.Authors: Vuillemenot L.; Morales L.; Dragoi C.; Pennycook B.; Harris E.; Lin L.; Weston W.; Brown J.; Graham E.; Moulin L.; Andrew I.; Roumelioti G.; Montoya A.; Game L.; Young G.; Datta K.; Shliaha P.; Novák B.; Yamano H.; Barr A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint 1–3 . Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53- mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in TP53- wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Reduced expression of APC/C CDH1 or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.

Article.Title: Touch-sensing digital pixel fibre enables interactive garment GUI
Article.Authors: Fu H.; Li Z.; Chaturvedi S.; Zhang X.; Li X.; Li Q.; Khudiyev T.
Article.Abstract: Wearable computing promises to transform human interaction with information, yet conventional graphical user interfaces (GUIs) rely on planar, rigid displays incompatible with textiles, which are composed of one-dimensional fibres. Despite recent progress1,2 in flexible and fibre-based displays, bridging this fundamental dimensional mismatch remains challenging because existing approaches do not naturally provide the digitally addressable, high-throughput, information-rich interfaces required for interactive GUIs. Here we present a digital pixel fibre integrating addressable pixels, a common propagation-axis interconnection for scalable in-fibre circuitry and a coaxial sensing layer for fibre-level touch localization. Microelectronic components and a touch-gated resistive path system form a linear circuit that acts as both an interactive display backbone and a computational bus, while peripheral multimodal fibre sensors and actuators enable physiological, inertial, optical, and acoustic input and output. We integrate these fibres into the forearm portion of a garment sleeve to realize a GUI with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30-frame-per-second refresh rate and 8-bit colour depth. It supports dynamic graphics, integrated audio-video playback, wireless data exchange and interactive computing functions, while maintaining the flexibility, washability, breathability and mechanical robustness of everyday textiles. By merging display, sensing and computation within a single fibre, this work establishes a scalable platform for intrinsically interactive textiles, opening pathways toward garments that operate as fully integrated computational systems.

Article.Title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
Article.Authors: Huang Q.; Iida N.; Isobe N.; Kabe T.; Omura T.; Ilangovan M.; Kimura S.; Seok J.; Nomaki H.; Kasuya K.; Iwata T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The accumulation of persistent plastics in the ocean is causing wide-ranging environmental problems 1–3 . Some commercially available compostable plastics 4–7 , developed to address these issues, degrade efficiently under industrial composting conditions; however, their degradation in marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains limited 8–10 . Here we demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate- co -adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate- co -terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m. Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months. Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m. In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation. The mechanical properties of enzyme-embedded polyesters were similar to those of enzyme-free polyesters. Chemical analysis confirmed the formation of low-molecular-mass degradation products and biochemical oxygen demand measurements supported the mineralization of the enzyme-embedded polyesters. The enzyme-embedding strategy enables enhanced marine degradation of compostable polyesters and represents a potential solution to marine plastic pollution.

Article.Authors: Qi L.; Sheng Y.; Zhang W.; Ni Y.; He L.; Li B.; Wang A.; Zhu W.; Bell A.; Liu Z.
Article.Abstract: Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1-5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6-12. Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13. Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14-18. Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation. We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h. The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively. Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation. Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes.

Article.Title: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
Article.Authors: Sergio F.; Natsukawa H.; Tanferna A.; Chicano J.; Carro F.; Soriguer R.; Hiraldo F.; Blas J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Interactions among species are increasingly recognized as key determinants of climate change impacts on ecosystems 1–5 . However, we know little about how climatic perturbations affect interactions among top vertebrate predators. Here we show that, when an emergent disease caused the decline of shared prey (rabbits), after decades of neutral co-existence a mammalian carnivore (lynx) started to prey heavily on a top predatory raptor (kites). These predation bouts occurred exclusively under drought conditions and when lynx found rabbit remains under the raptor nests, consistent with the removal of a potential competitor. Drought-induced lynx predation depressed lifetime reproductive success and triggered territory abandonment and dispersal by the raptor, suggestive of a new arms race among predators. A reduction in raptor abundance was associated with an increase in an insectivorous bird (a small owl), showing that the new interaction had the potential to reach lower trophic levels. These results underline the importance of diet flexibility and mobility as important mediators of resilience to stressors. In the future, synergistic effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors may reshape the interactions and ecological roles of many apex predators, with potential cascading consequences for whole ecosystems. A key to forecasting the future impact of global change may reside in understanding how behavioural flexibility and interacting keystone species respond to interacting shocks.

Article.Title: The anatomy of a personal health agent
Article.Authors: Heydari A.; Gu K.; Srinivas V.; Yu H.; Paruchuri A.; Zhang Z.; Zhang Y.; He Q.; Palangi H.; Hammerquist N.; Metwally A.; Winslow B.; Kim Y.; Ayush K.; Yang Y.; Narayanswamy G.; Xu M.; Garrison J.; Schmidgall S.; Armento Lee A.; Vafeiadou J.; Graef B.; Galatzer-Levy I.; Schenck E.; Barakat A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored 1,2 . Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

Article.Title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis
Article.Authors: Yi Y.; Cao Z.; Wu K.; Ding H.; Fu L.; Gao W.; Li L.; Zhou L.; Zhou Z.; Dai L.; Lu Y.; Cheng L.
Article.Abstract: Anaerobic degradation of complex organic compounds to methane and carbon dioxide is common in the deep subsurface biosphere and has long been considered to require syntrophic cooperation, with methanogens confined to the terminal use of simple C1 and C2 substrates. However, experimental validation in pure culture was lacking. Here we report the isolation of a thermophilic archaeon, Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75, affiliated with Archaeoglobi, from a Chinese petroleum reservoir. Strain AA-75 not only converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, but also uses saturated fatty acids varying from C7:0 to C18:0 and unsaturated fatty acids including C16:1, C18:1 and C18:2 to produce methane. We term the latter lipotrophic methanogenesis, which integrates β-oxidation of fatty acids with the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway and the canonical methyl-tetrahydromethanopterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase complexes, together with an intracellular electron transfer system. A formaldehyde-methanol branch probably functions as an auxiliary route for C1 metabolism during methanogenesis. Methane produced from stearate is moderately 13C-enriched (δ13C-CH4 = -40.0‰ to -36.3‰), distinct from the strong 13C depletion characteristic of canonical methanogenic pathways. These findings demonstrate that methanogens can function as primary degraders of complex organic matter, challenging the classical syntrophic paradigm and calling for refinement of current models of carbon cycling in the deep subsurface biosphere.

Article.Title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
Article.Authors: Willemsen P.; Mason V.; Zelst V.; van Bergeijk V.; Breteler M.; Muller J.; Dermentzoglou D.; Vouziouris A.; van Veelen T.; Dzimballa S.; Wijnberg K.; Hoitink A.; Buring P.; Paul M.; Antonini A.; Bouma T.; Borsje B.
Article.Abstract: Salt marshes protect coastlines by attenuating wind waves with their elevated marsh platform and above-ground vegetation1. A unique experiment was conducted by transferring intact salt marsh to one of the world's largest wave flumes, and subsequently exposing it to increasingly higher waves that reach up to 2 m significant wave height. Our global assessment supports the differentiation between low- and high-energetic conditions resulting from the flume experiment. Our results suggest that the marsh platform remains stable under extreme wave events and that substantial wave attenuation by marsh vegetation is limited to low-energy marsh coasts.

Article.Title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
Article.Authors: Lee H.; Doğan C.; Koyuncu S.; Wehrmann M.; Artan M.; Petrovic D.; Loureiro R.; Sahu A.; Schnubel J.; Grobushkin P.; Prymidis D.; Georgomanolis T.; Sokol A.; Yang M.; Hoppe T.; Frezza C.; Vilchez D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species 1–3 , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans . Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2–BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

Article.Title: GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control
Article.Authors: Yu F.; Jiang L.; Liu H.; Yang S.; Yuan Y.; Jin H.; Liu J.; Liu X.; Dong Y.; Ren D.; Kang J.; Huang Y.; Meng Q.; Bai F.; Li Y.; Li S.; Liu H.; Zhao W.; Xiao J.; Chen Q.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondria are bound by a double membrane and are semiautonomous organelles, rendering them highly vulnerable to global and internal proteostatic stress1. Multiple surveillance mechanisms at proteostatic and inter-organellar levels have evolved to maintain mitochondrial integrity and cellular health2-7. However, the precise mechanisms by which proteostatic damage relays stress signals across organelles and how the quality surveillance machinery coordinates these functions remain unknown. Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network. Quantitative proteomic and correlative light-electron microscopy analysis revealed that SIMPA mediates inter-organellar communication via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes. Mechanistically, GRP75 coordinates SIMPA biogenesis and focally activates endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response pathways via mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes for the targeted clearance of SIMPAs. Functionally, in both cellular and liver disease models, we found that a GRP75-dependent SIMPA signalling cascade attenuates mitochondrial stress and preserves mitochondrial integrity under proteotoxic stress. Overall, we show that SIMPAs, functioning as protein condensates, serve as a central cross-compartment communication hub for mitochondrial quality control, supporting cellular and organismal fitness.

Article.Title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language
Article.Authors: Dai F.; You S.; Zhu Y.; Gao Y.; Fu L.; Zhou X.; Su J.; Wang C.; Fan Y.; Tan Q.; Ma X.; Deng X.; Yu L.; Qian H.; He Y.; Ke Y.; Zhang Z.; Han C.; Chang X.; Zheng L.; Wang S.; Ji Y.; Hao K.; Cao L.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Programming biological function-designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks-is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1-3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein-text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks-a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein-and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.

Article.Title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
Article.Authors: Mishra S.; Payal N/A.; Evans D.; Bortey K.; Bootwala H.; Gonzalez-Gutierrez G.; Vázquez R.; Baker D.; Lewis J.
Article.Abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1-5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6-8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

Article.Title: Cortex-wide imaging in naturally behaving mice with 1-gram wireless mesoscopes
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Li A.; Yuan L.; Wang M.; Zhao W.; Wang Z.; Zang B.; Zhou Y.; Yu T.; Gao L.; Wu Y.; Zhu R.; Tian M.; Li K.; Wu J.; Dai P.; Dai Q.
Article.Abstract: Revealing how distributed cortical circuits coordinate behavior in freely moving animals remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience, constrained by limited fields of view, low throughput, and the tethering required by current miniaturized microscopes1-4. Here, we present Airscope, a wireless mesoscope delivering 4 μm lateral resolution across a 6 mm field of view at 12.5 Hz, weighing 1.0 gram. An aspheric-lens design achieves a 2.84× shorter total track length than previous miniaturized microscopes1,2,5,6 while matching the neuron yield of benchtop one-photon mesoscopes; a tailored wireless link supports cable-free calcium imaging from >8,500 neurons per animal (25‑fold increase). Paired with a zero-shot behavior analyzer, Airscope enables cortical imaging across rich behavioral conditions, including room-scale enriched arenas, swimming assays, and multi-organ implantation, with concurrent recording from multiple animals. Using Airscope, we demonstrate versatile applications of untethered cortical imaging across diverse behavioral paradigms. We identify cortical activity patterns across multiple dorsal regions that correlate with behavioral signatures of social dominance, and show dorsal-cortical population activity prospectively decodes competition outcomes across paired animals. We observe reward-location-associated cortical activity patterns during maze exploration, and characterize Granger-causal influence from spinal cord to cortex during fear conditioning, enabled by simultaneous brain-spinal recordings. By uniting large-scale, cellular-resolution recording with unconstrained behavior, Airscope makes naturalistic, multi-animal cortical recording experimentally practical, and provides a broadly accessible technology for systems neuroscience.

Article.Title: Nearly half of reef-building corals face elevated relative risk of extinction
Article.Authors: Obura D.; Polidoro B.; Cabada-Blanco F.; Linardich C.; Carpenter N.; Gutierrez L.; Kemppinen K.; Pettersson E.; Strongin K.; Aeby G.; Alliji K.; Alvarado J.; Alvarez-Filip L.; Casado de Amezua P.; Banaszak A.; Bayley D.; Bluemel J.; Cortés J.; Couce E.; Cowburn B.; Crabbe M.; Croquer A.; Dellisanti W.; DeVantier L.; Edwards A.
Article.Abstract: Coral reefs are diverse marine ecosystems that provide ecological functions and economic and social benefits across over 100 tropical countries. Warming driven by climate change is a primary threat to coral reefs and is increasing the frequency of global coral bleaching events. Here we reassessed the IUCN Red List status of 892 reef-building coral species, first assessed in 2008 1. Because species-level population trends are unavailable for most reef-building corals, population reductions were inferred using proxies based on global coral cover trends and projected annual severe bleaching under SSP2-4.5, both over three decades, adjusted using trait-based estimates of species vulnerability. Of the 774 species with sufficient data to be assessed, 340 (44%) were classified as threatened under IUCN Red List criteria. Thirty-three species were assessed as Critically Endangered, 251 as Endangered, and 56 as Vulnerable, most due to risk of population reduction associated with projected thermal stress. These findings predate the three hottest years on record and the fourth global coral bleaching event (2023-2025), and the first exceedance for an annual mean of the 1.5oC global warming threshold. The findings reinforce the importance of limiting further warming to maintain coral biodiversity and reef ecosystem function. The Red List assesses the relative extinction risk of species, whereby species are placed in categories of increasing risk by comparing their population size, decline and geographic range against standardised thresholds. The Red List does not predict whether or when a species may go extinct. As the ranges of coral species remain under-surveyed, future assessments would be strengthened by species-level population data and thermal-stress and recovery metrics that better capture range-representative dynamics.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: reef-building corals; extinction risk assessment

Article.Title: Evaluating space-based methane detection through a one-year blind test
Article.Authors: Reuland F.; Adams T.; Sherwin E.; El Abbadi S.; Kort E.; Brandt A.
Article.Abstract: Space-based remote sensing allows detection and monitoring of large, concentrated methane sources worldwide1. However, independent evaluation of instruments and algorithms is limited, and new satellites and artificial intelligence techniques have not been tested under controlled, single-blind conditions2. Here we conduct a year-long, single-blind test involving 746 events: 481 methane releases of 9.5-1,183.7 kg h-1 and 265 blank controls. We released metered methane quantities in Arizona, USA, coinciding with overpasses from 12 government, commercial and non-profit satellites. Fifteen analysis teams from nine countries generated more than 2,250 estimates, making this, to our knowledge, the largest controlled test so far and one of the first evaluations of the instruments EMIT, Tanager-1 (Carbon Mapper) and GHOSt. Performance is heterogeneous: 'built-for-purpose' instruments designed to target methane demonstrate excellent detection performance (92-100% true positive rate, 0-11% false positive rate) and quantification accuracy (slope 0.83-1.00, 44% mean absolute percentage error). Instruments repurposed for methane sensing perform more variably (detection rates 62-88%, 46% mean absolute percentage error); still, many demonstrate significant skill. Broad land scanners detect poorly at tested rates but have consistent global coverage and historical archives, motivating additional work. Artificial intelligence-based methods show promise, but caution is warranted; 79% of false positives emerge from these methods. Ground-measured cloud cover >20% degraded performance across systems, raising concerns for use in some locations. Our findings show that satellite-based measurements can achieve accurate detection and quantification of methane point sources when the source location is approximately known.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: methane detection; satellite remote sensing; blind test
Article.TopicFields: Environmental Science > Global and Planetary Change > Atmospheric and Environmental Gas Dynamics; Chemistry > Spectroscopy > Spectroscopy and Laser Applications; Environmental Science > Ecology > Remote Sensing in Agriculture

Article.Title: Intrinsic physicochemical activity at microplastic–water interfaces
Article.Authors: Qian N.; Zhao R.; Chan K.; Vuong V.; Gao X.; Zhao Z.; LaCour R.; Dai Y.; Stapleton P.; Yan B.; Head-Gordon T.; Min W.
Article.Abstract: Plastics have become an integral part of our modern society, largely because they are generally regarded as chemically inert under normal circumstances. However, plastics fragmented into microplastics (less than 5 mm in size) have recently raised significant public concerns, and have been detected widely across ecosystems and human tissues with increasing environmental and health risks1-5. Here we show that commodity microplastics exhibit intrinsic physicochemical activity in water, manifested by the spontaneous generation of reactive oxygen species that increases with interfacial hydrophobicity and strongly correlates with interfacial electrostatics. Ab initio calculations support these observations and reveal that hydroxide oxidation becomes energetically more favourable at increasingly hydrophobic microplastic-water interfaces through the combined effects of partial solvation and electrostatics. These interfacial properties and the resulting oxidative chemistry have direct implications for biomolecular adsorption, protein aggregation, and even cellular damage. Together, our findings challenge the prevailing paradigm of plastic inertness, identify a possibly overlooked mechanism for the detrimental effects of microplastics on health and the environment, and contribute to a fundamental understanding of the structure-activity relationship of interfacial water, which may inform the design of safer and more sustainable plastic materials.

Article.TopicFields: Environmental Science > Pollution > Microplastics and Plastic Pollution; Environmental Science > Water Science and Technology > Minerals Flotation and Separation Techniques; Chemistry > Physical and Theoretical Chemistry > Electrostatics and Colloid Interactions

Article.Title: Hidden reaction pathways inform additive engineering for perovskite LEDs
Article.Authors: Baek S.; Yang Y.; Wu P.; Yang H.; Ali M.; Kok H.; Luo X.; Shao W.; Choi H.; Kim J.; Guo L.; Huang L.; Rand B.; Dou L.
Article.Abstract: Perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) have emerged as a promising class of solution-processed light-emitting devices, combining high efficiency with facile fabrication1-5. Amino-acid-based molecular additives are widely used to regulate crystallization and suppress defects in perovskite thin films6-8, yet these molecules are chemically reactive in precursor solutions, in which their transformations and products remain poorly understood. Here we resolve and control the hidden solution-phase chemistry of a ubiquitous additive, 5-aminovaleric acid (5AVA), whose solution-phase reactivity has remained unclear6,9-15. We show that 5AVA undergoes competing in situ reactions during precursor preconditioning, yielding two chemically and functionally distinct products: a beneficial organoamidinium zwitterion and a detrimental Lewis-base lactam. By explaining this reaction dichotomy and establishing targeted reaction-pathway control, we selectively use the beneficial species. Direct synthesis and incorporation of the purified zwitterion decouple its intrinsic passivation function from confounding by-products, yielding perovskite films with a near-unity mean peak photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of 97.2% and PeLEDs with a champion external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 37.1%, alongside a mean peak EQE of 32.8%. Finally, we demonstrate that this reaction-pathway control concept can be extended to further additive chemistries and emission colours, highlighting its potential as a chemistry-driven strategy for rational additive design in PeLEDs.

Article.Title: Evidence for multi-Li+ clustering in lithium-ion battery electrolytes
Article.Authors: Stevenson J.; Agarwal G.; Debnath S.; Goldsmith Z.; Mondal M.; Svirinovsky-Arbeli A.; Yeu I.; Metlay A.; Kwon Y.; Bhai L.; Guha R.; Keeler E.; Weber J.; Steingart D.; Marbella L.; Urban A.; Jacobson L.; Halls M.; Friesner R.
Article.Abstract: In lithium-ion batteries, the bulk solvation structure of the electrolyte is a major determinant of the physical and electrochemical properties of the cell, for example, conductivity, viscosity, salt dissociation and subsequent reactivity, the electrochemical stability window (and thus solid electrolyte interphase formation), and the composition of the electrochemical double layer1-3. However, elucidation of this structure at an atomic level of detail has been challenging to accomplish via a purely experimental approach. Here we combine machine-learning-enabled atomistic simulations4-16, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, electrochemical data3,17-20 and quantum-chemical calculations to reveal previously unstudied multi-Li+ complexes without bound anions that are uniquely facile for reduction. This insight explains the success of empirically chosen ethylene-carbonate-containing solvent mixtures and provides a foundation for the rational design of improved electrolytes. Furthermore, our machine-learning force-field-based lithium-ion-battery electrolyte simulations accurately reproduce a wide range of condensed-phase experiments3,21-24, despite being parameterized to only quantum-chemical gas-phase cluster calculations, and hence provide a compelling demonstration that machine-learning force-field-based models developed from first principles can robustly represent a complex chemical system to atomic resolution.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: lithium-ion battery electrolytes; electrolyte conductivity
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advancements in Battery Materials; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advanced Battery Materials and Technologies; Engineering > Automotive Engineering > Advanced Battery Technologies Research

Article.Title: Clasping folds enable superior elastic strength of graphene films
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Liao Y.; Huang J.; Shen C.; Chen L.; Li X.; Ding D.; Zhang M.; Peng L.; Li K.; Li P.; Liu Y.; Xu Z.; Pang K.; Xu Z.; Gao C.
Article.Abstract: Two-dimensional graphene sheets show strong potential for use in fabrication of macroscopic films, as they have exceptional mechanical properties owing to their in-plane strength1-6. Improvements in the stacking order of flat two-dimensional sheets have led to corresponding improvements in the strength and toughness of such films7-11. In addition, modulation of the spatial conformation of individual units has enabled the development of benchmark materials with superior properties12,13; however, this has remained elusive in the case of two-dimensional sheets. Here we report a strategy for preparation of graphene films with a combination of high strength (2.9 GPa), toughness (84.5 MJ m-3) and elastic strain (5%). We attribute these performance gains to a fold-clasping lamellar structure achieved by modular assembly of surface-folded multilayer graphene oxide flakes. We identify a pull-to-push transition of force chain topology and propose a shear-lock stress transfer strategy in the fold-clasping lamellar graphene film that enables advances in mechanical properties. This work demonstrates the modular design of spatial conformation of two-dimensional flakes on a large scale and further improves the performance of macroscopic films for potential applications in lightweight structural components.

Article.Title: Alveolar stem cells go beyond making gas-exchange cells to repair damaged airways
Article.Abstract: Alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells are the stem cells of the lung’s air sacs and are responsible for maintaining alveolar structure and gas exchange. A study that tracked AT2 cells shows that, after injury to the airway, they can also migrate between lung compartments and become bronchiolar cells to help repair damaged airways. Alveolar type 2 cells can migrate from the lung’s air sacs into the airways to repair damage there.

Article.Title: Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K
Article.Authors: Cook D.; Chen X.; O’Leary M.; Rao S.; Wang W.; Belcher C.; Payne M.; Borges P.; Lee T.; Devaraj A.; Asta M.; Lavernia E.; Apelian D.; Minor A.; Liu D.; Kumar P.; Ritchie R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Plastic deformation in body-centred cubic (bcc) metals and alloys is conventionally mediated by screw dislocations. Their temperature-sensitive motion is attributed to a steep rise in strength with decreasing temperature that constricts plastic zones at crack tips, leading to a ductile-to-brittle transition 1 . Here we evaluated the mechanical properties of group IV–V bcc refractory alloys with similar electronic structures at 20 K and found that these materials instead exhibit a plateau in tensile yield strength and fracture toughness as a function of temperature, with no apparent ductile-to-brittle transition. This behaviour arises from the global activation of twinning and an ω-phase transformation, which nucleate dislocations at interfaces before global dislocation motion. The initial mechanism is temperature insensitive and controls yielding, thereby preventing a crack-tip plastic zone from constricting with decreasing temperature.

Article.Title: Parity-dependent coupling of molecular spin chains to a superconductor
Article.Authors: Vaxevani K.; Ortuzar J.; Trivini S.; Monninger G.; Wang D.; Vilas-Varela M.; Gómez-Rodrigo L.; Peña D.; Pascual J.
Article.Abstract: Collective behaviour in quantum materials can produce excitations carrying only a fraction of the quantum numbers of their constituents. A notable case occurs in chains of spin-1 units1, in which a topological gap protects the interior of the chain, whereas spin-1/2 states, half the spin of the units that form it, emerge at the ends2. In short chains, these fractional edge spins couple to each other and their topological protection makes them attractive for hybrid spin-superconductor devices. Whether such fractionalization survives the proximity of a superconducting condensate, however, remains an open question. Here we grow molecular Haldane chains of antiferromagnetically coupled spin-1 triangulene units on a proximitized Au(111)/Nb(110) surface and resolve a parity-dependent coupling of their spin-1/2 edge states to the superconductor by scanning tunnelling spectroscopy. Odd-length chains host Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) bound states inside the superconducting gap, originating from a global S = 1 ground state, whereas even-length chains form an S = 0 ground state decoupled from the superconductor. A two-site model attributes this alternation to the sign and strength of inter-edge interactions, independently confirmed by extra-gap spin excitations in tunnelling spectra. Many-body spin excitations of the S = 1 chain are also detected, decoupled from the superconductor by the much larger Haldane gap. The length-tunable coupling of the edge spins to superconductors opens a route towards molecular spin qubits based on π-conjugated carbon architectures.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: Yu-Shiba-Rusinov bound states; collective spin excitations; triangulene; molecular spin qubits; topological edge states; superconducting proximity effect; antiferromagnetic chains; spin fractionalization; Haldane gap

Article.Title: Interhemispheric monsoon dynamics over the past 450,000 years
Article.Authors: Olson E.; Gillikin D.; Parmenter D.; Burns S.; Verheyden A.; Miyawaki O.; Vuille M.; Piccirillo L.; Castro R.; Yurivilca G.; Edwards R.; Rodbell D.
Article.Abstract: The global monsoon system provides freshwater to much of Earth's biota, including its human population1. The Milankovitch theory predicts changes in Earth's solar insolation over geologic time, and these variations are expected to result in changes to the global monsoon2. Internal climate forcings, such as ice cover and sea surface temperatures, may also affect the system. However, few records of monsoon variability in the Southern Hemisphere over glacial-interglacial cycles exist to test our understanding of the factors that drive variations in the global monsoon. Here we show that monsoons in both the Southern and Northern Hemispheres vary with Milankovitch forcing, and with internal boundary conditions over the past 450,000 years. We present a record of South American Summer Monsoon (SASM) variability, based on speleothem oxygen-isotope data from the Amazon Basin. South American Summer Monsoon variability and that of a major Northern Hemisphere monsoon-that is, the Asian monsoon3,4-have been strikingly out of phase. However, we observe occasional synchronous behaviour in regions impacted by both monsoons. We identify a synchronicity threshold that is exceeded during ten events, including during glacial terminations. Comparison with palaeoclimatic forcing factors during these intervals indicates that greenhouse gas concentrations, cross-equatorial thermal gradients and sea surface temperatures in both the Atlantic and Pacific probably influence these events. This record demonstrates that the global monsoon can reorganize itself, especially during intervals of rapidly changing planetary boundary conditions.

Article.Title: Targeted stimulation of motor cortex ensembles drives learned movements
Article.Authors: Chen Q.; Wu A.; Yu B.; Chae S.; Tan Z.; Ramot A.; Aljadeff J.; Komiyama T.
Article.Abstract: During the execution of learned motor skills, the neural population in layer 2/3 (L2/3) of primary motor cortex (M1) expresses a reproducible spatiotemporal activity pattern1. It is debated whether M1 actively participates in generating this learned pattern and whether this pattern causally drives the learned movement2-5. Here we combined in vivo two-photon calcium imaging and holographic optogenetic stimulation of functionally defined M1 L2/3 ensembles in mice performing a skilled lever-pressing task. Brief synchronous stimulation of about 20 neurons whose activity onset precedes voluntary movement onset induced movements resembling the learned movement, while producing activity patterns in other M1 neurons resembling the learned activity. Moreover, trial-by-trial variability of optogenetically triggered population activity correlated with variability in the induced movements. These variabilities were predicted by the initial state of M1 activity preceding stimulation. In some trials, stimulation induced the learned activity without inducing movements, indicating that the learned activity is not simply a reflection of movements but can arise internally. Stimulation failed to generate movements or learned activity in task-disengaged mice. Stimulation of neurons whose activity followed movement onsets failed to induce the learned movement in task-engaged mice. Together, the learned activity in M1 L2/3 can be generated when M1 is prepared at the optimal initial state and receives precise triggering inputs, supporting the active role of M1 in generating learned activity and learned movements.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: motor learning; motor cortex; neuronal ensembles; brain-computer interface

Article.Title: Divergent genomic evolution in astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas
Article.Authors: Chowdhury T.; Tesileanu C.; Kocakavuk E.; Johnson K.; Lee J.; Erson-Omay Z.; Heo C.; Aldape K.; Amin S.; Anderson K.; Ashley D.; Barthel F.; Barnholtz-Sloan J.; Brat D.; Brodbelt A.; Castro A.; Claus E.; Connelly J.; Costello J.; Datta I.; Elliott C.; Finocchiaro G.; French P.; Gan H.; Garofano L.
Article.Abstract: Astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas are isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas that most commonly arise in adults under the age of 50 and exhibit variable responses to treatment1-3. To understand the genetic drivers of disease progression, here we used whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing to characterize longitudinally collected tumour specimens from 183 patients with IDH-mutant glioma. Samples were collected through the Glioma Longitudinal Analysis (GLASS) Consortium4. Most primary surgery samples were classified as grade 2 on the basis of histology (73% for astrocytomas and 93% for oligodendrogliomas). We validated known genomic markers of tumour progression, including hypermutation and homozygous deletion of CDKN2A or CDKN2B (hereafter, CDKN2A/B)5, and discovered genetic alterations that distinguish between the evolutionary trajectories of astrocytomas and those of oligodendrogliomas. Mutations in phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and NOTCH1 were newly acquired in recurrent oligodendrogliomas, regardless of treatment, and were associated with an increased tumour mutational burden. In recurrent astrocytomas, however, again irrespective of treatment, acquired focal oncogene amplifications and CDKN2A/B homozygous deletions were associated with an increase in chromosomal imbalances, which converged with markers of chromosomal instability such as chromothripsis and whole-genome doubling. In both types of IDH-mutant glioma, we observed a convergence of acquired alterations, genome-wide changes and worse patient outcomes, suggesting that treatment-refractory clones were being selected. Treatment with temozolomide was associated with the mutational signatures SBS11 and SBS119 in both tumour types, whereas the radiotherapy-associated ID8 signature increased in astrocytomas specifically. We show that the genomes of oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas adapt to the selective pressures of tumour progression and treatment in distinct ways, suggesting that oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas differ in their responses to treatment-induced DNA damage.

Article.Title: Modelling mouse embryogenesis from chemically induced totipotent stem cells
Article.Authors: Wu H.; Hu Y.; Yu H.; Huang N.; Shi L.; Gao M.; Du X.; Lu X.; Zhang Y.; Sun X.; Xu X.; Liu Z.; Yuan J.; Zhou W.; Shao Q.; Wang D.; Zhao Y.; Ma T.; Ding S.
Article.Abstract: The ability to faithfully initiate embryogenesis from a single, induced non-germline cell type, akin to the totipotent blastomeres, remains a considerable challenge in developmental and synthetic biology1-14. Here we established conditions that enable the continuous ex utero development of mouse embryo models (EMs), starting solely from the chemically induced totipotent-like stem cells (ciTotiSCs)15 and spanning the pre-implantation morula, blastocysts and post-gastrulation stages with both embryonic and extraembryonic compartments. These ciTotiSCs self-organized into blastocyst-like structures that closely resembled natural blastocysts in both morphology and lineage segregation. The resulting ciTotiSC-derived EMs (ciToti-EMs) successfully progressed through key developmental milestones, including gastrulation, embryonic axis formation, haematopoiesis and early organogenesis, closely resembling embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) natural embryos (NEs). Furthermore, extended culture led to the development of functional cardiac tissues in ciToti-EMs, highly comparable to those of E10.5 NEs. These findings demonstrate an extraordinary ability of a single induced cell type, ciTotiSCs, to autonomously recapitulate the complete spectrum of early mouse embryogenesis. Our ciToti-EM system provides a powerful model for investigating mammalian embryonic development and opens new avenues for creating multicellular organisms from non-germline cells.

Article.Title: Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning
Article.Authors: Guan H.; Mouatadid S.; Orenstein P.; Cohen J.; Dong H.; Ni Z.; Berman J.; Flaspohler G.; Lu A.; Schloer J.; Talib J.; Weyn J.; Mackey L.
Article.Abstract: Decision-makers rely on weather forecasts to plant crops, manage wildfires, allocate water and energy and prepare for weather extremes1-3. Today, such forecasts enjoy unprecedented accuracy as far as 2 weeks thanks to steady advances in physics-based dynamical models and data-driven artificial intelligence models4-10. However, model skill drops precipitously at subseasonal timescales (2-6 weeks ahead) due to compounding errors, systemic model biases and the chaotic nature of the atmosphere11-15. To counter this degradation, we introduce probabilistic bias correction, a machine learning framework that substantially reduces systematic error by learning to correct historical probabilistic forecasts. When applied to the leading dynamical and artificial intelligence models from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), probabilistic bias correction doubles the modest subseasonal skill of the AI Forecasting System16 and improves the skill of the operationally debiased dynamical model17 for 91% of pressure, 92% of temperature and 98% of precipitation targets. We designed probabilistic bias correction for operational deployment, and, in the 2025 real-time forecasting competition of ECMWF18, its global forecasts were the best for all weather variables and lead times, outperforming the dynamical models from six operational forecasting centres, an international dynamical multimodel ensemble, the AI Forecasting System of ECMWF and the forecasting systems of 34 teams worldwide. These probabilistic skill gains translate into more accurate prediction of extreme events and have the potential to improve agricultural planning, energy management and disaster preparedness in vulnerable communities19.

Article.Title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation
Article.Authors: Parada G.; Bretschneider H.; Li J.; Fine J.; Dupas S.; Ellis J.; Braunschweig U.; Bonnal S.; Dalal T.; Engchuan W.; Zarrei M.; Wei W.; Zafar N.; Hemberg M.; Attisano L.; Ellis J.; Irimia M.; Wainberg M.; Trost B.; Scherer S.; Morris Q.; Blencowe B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neuronal microexons are a highly conserved class of alternative splicing events enriched in genes with critical functions in nervous system biology 1,2 . Microexon splicing is often disrupted in the brains of autistic individuals, and mice with microexon deficiencies display autism-like phenotypes 1,3,4 . However, the full landscape of microexons is not known, and the impact of genetic variation on these exons has not been systematically investigated. Here, through extensive transcriptome profiling, we detect hundreds of new microexons, including many with neuronal subtype-specific splicing patterns, and others that activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Using machine learning, we define a sequence code predictive of neuronally spliced microexons and use this to identify critical regulatory elements surrounding the expanded microexon repertoire. This code further reveals genomic variants predicted to alter microexon splicing in individuals affected by autism, with rare variants having the strongest estimated impact. These variants are mostly detected in idiopathic individuals and are associated with autism status. They also converge on synaptic and other autism-linked genes, as well as genes not previously linked to autism. Our results collectively define an expanded repertoire of microexons, delineate their regulatory code, and pinpoint variants predicted to affect their splicing, with implications for the disruption of functions central to neuronal biology and brain disorders.

Article.Title: Wave coarsening drives time crystallization in mechatronic metamaterials
Article.Authors: Veenstra J.; Binysh J.; Seinen V.; Solé Borràs R.; Naber R.; Robledo-Poisson D.; Hunt A.; van Saarloos W.; Souslov A.; Coulais C.
Article.Abstract: When metals are magnetized1, emulsions phase separate2, or galaxies cluster3, domain walls and patterns form and irremediably coarsen over time. This coarsening is universally driven by diffusive relaxation towards equilibrium. Here we discover a vibrational counterpart-wave coarsening-in active elastic media4-13: vibrations emerge and spontaneously grow in wavelength, period and amplitude, before a globally synchronized state called a time crystal14-17 forms. We observe wave coarsening in one- and two-dimensional mechatronic metamaterials and capture its dynamical scaling. We further arrest the process by breaking momentum conservation and reveal a far-from-equilibrium nonlinear analogue to chiral topological edge modes18-24. Our results open new questions about the transient physics of systems with non-potential interactions15,25-28 and suggest an organizing principle for nonlinear waves in acoustics29,30, optomechanics31,32, living matter6,33 and soft robotics9.

Article.Title: Capillary-selective vasodilation through myosin inhibition halts ischaemic cascades
Article.Authors: Pénzes M.; Winternitz M.; Horváth Á.; Mastitskaya S.; Awan U.; Szimler T.; Glaser C.; Kikuti C.; Juillé M.; Heidsieck L.; Rauscher A.; Bálint T.; Nagy D.; Radovits T.; Sayour A.; Gibson C.; Houdusse A.; Gyimesi M.; Málnási-Csizmadia A.
Article.Abstract: In acute myocardial infarction and acute kidney injury, capillary no-reflow denotes that capillary blood flow is still blocked despite successful arterial reperfusion. This is associated with substantially increased mortality and reinfarction risk; nevertheless, no targeted therapy exists so far1,2. Because capillary no-reflow is driven by smooth muscle myosin-mediated hypercontraction of capillary pericytes, we developed R(+)2501, a myosin-specific and capillary-selective vasodilator. In reperfused animal models of acute myocardial infarction and acute kidney injury, direct in vivo imaging showed that R(+)2501 rapidly restored capillary flow, an effect sustained even after rapid drug clearance. Ex vivo experiments confirmed reversal of pericyte constriction directly. Restoration of capillary blood flow, together with clearance of trapped neutrophils, linked resolution of capillary no-reflow to attenuation of an early driver of reperfusion injury. R(+)2501 enhanced capillary perfusion while preserving coronary autoregulation and systemic haemodynamics, and markedly improved survival during acute reperfusion. We further found that acute myocardial infarction induced renal capillary no-reflow, which was reversed by R(+)2501, suggesting that capillary no-reflow contributes to the pathophysiology of cardiorenal syndrome type I. These findings establish pericyte-targeted smooth muscle myosin inhibition as a therapeutic strategy to restore microvascular perfusion and halt the ischaemic cascade across organs, while defining a specific physiological role for capillaries and pericytes in circulatory regulation.

Article.Title: Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat
Article.Authors: Gómez-Banoy N.; Barrero J.; Pinheiro de Carvalho L.; Jiang C.; Lama T.; Karandikar N.; Koenen M.; Lam T.; Plucińska K.; Morozova K.; Chahwan S.; Barraza G.; Agridag Ucpinar B.; Liu J.; Sharma R.; Lafontaine D.; Schöder H.; Cohen P.
Article.Abstract: Adipose tissue has a central role in systemic energy balance and the pathogenesis of obesity and its sequelae1,2. In contrast to white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue (BAT) uses energy to produce heat3. Detectable BAT in humans is associated with decreased prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases4. However, the complete spectrum of health conditions associated with BAT remains unknown, and high-throughput methods to quantify BAT activity in humans are lacking5,6. Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre. Our unbiased analyses revealed that, across all diagnoses, cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases were less prevalent in people with BAT. Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution. People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices. Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence. As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure. Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans.
