Article.Title: Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates
Article.Authors: O’Neill H.; Beeken J.; Bingham H.; Golden Kroner R.; He Y.; Stewart J.; Ali A.; Beltran J.; Bull J.; Canney S.; Dharmaratne N.; Eghenter C.; Fitzsimons J.; Hill S.; Jenkins C.; Julianty C.; Leon Y.; MacKinnon J.; Mallya A.; Marnewick D.; Maurer G.; Milkovic M.; Mohammed A.; Pantaleo Y.; Parsons B.
Article.Abstract: Conservation areas are critical for tackling the global environmental crisis1. These sites are reported as covering 18.5% of the terrestrial realm2 and governments have committed through Global Biodiversity Framework Target 3 to increase this to at least 30% by 2030 (ref. 3). There are concerns that this potential near-doubling of conservation area coverage will negatively affect vulnerable people and over-stretch conservation resources4. However, nationally available datasets indicate that more conservation areas exist than are reflected in global figures5-7. We evaluated progress towards the area component of Target 3 using a globally representative sample across 25 countries and territories that incorporated these national datasets8. Extrapolating from this sample, we show that conservation areas likely already cover 26.81% of the terrestrial realm. We may be much closer to achieving 30% terrestrial coverage than previously thought. However, we also show that the extra land does not substantially address gaps in ecological representativeness, indicating that solely meeting the area component of Target 3 will do little to solve continuing global biodiversity loss. More focus and resources are needed to achieve the other components of the target, using a more strategic and inclusive approach to fill present gaps and produce equitable and effective conservation area networks.

Article.Title: De novo design of cysteine proteases
Article.Authors: Choi H.; Bauer M.; Coventry B.; Venkatesh P.; Chen A.; Kim D.; Bera A.; Kang A.; Nguyen H.; Sadre S.; Decarreau J.; Joyce E.; Shankaran B.; Thompson T.; Greenstein G.; Didi K.; Schaaf L.; Gershon J.; Shida A.; Lee G.; Hilvert D.; Pellock S.; Baker D.
Article.Abstract: Despite advances in de novo enzyme design, success has been largely limited to low-energy-barrier model reactions. Amide bonds such as those linking amino acids along the peptide backbone are stable for hundreds of years in neutral aqueous solution because of the high energy barrier to hydrolysis1. Here we describe the de novo design of enzymes that use an activated cysteine nucleophile to hydrolyse the polypeptide backbone in a sequence-dependent manner, with a success rate of 13/69 = 19% and rate enhancements over the background reaction (kcat/kuncat) of up to 3 × 107. The designed proteases have folds that are very different from proteases in nature (TM score < 0.50), and six crystal structures are very close to the design models (Cα root mean squared deviation of <1.2 Å), highlighting the capacity for generalization and the accuracy of the design methodology. Experimental and computational analyses suggest that the remaining gap in activity to the most active native cysteine proteases arises from imperfections in active-site preorganization and substrate positioning. The designed proteases efficiently cleave their targets in mammalian cells, opening the door to a wide range of synthetic biology applications.

Article.Title: Sexual dimorphism in epidermal stem cell dynamics
Article.Authors: Engelman D.; Hochstetter J.; Bauduin A.; Patil S.; Valenti M.; Song Y.; Lian Q.; Toniolo A.; Ghiasloo M.; Bansaccal N.; Delaunois A.; Liagre M.; De Luca M.; Hoste E.; De Rosa L.; Shwartz Y.; Simons B.; Blanpain C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The epidermis is a stratified epithelium comprising proliferative basal cells and differentiated suprabasal cells that are continuously renewed throughout life. Conflicting theories have been proposed regarding the heterogeneity of the basal cell layer, with some studies proposing that all proliferative cells have self-renewal potential during homeostasis 1–5 . Meanwhile, others posit a model in which stem cell differentiation occurs through an intermediate transit-amplifying-like progenitor state with strictly limited proliferative potential 6–10 . Here, to determine the heterogeneity and pattern of cell fate, we performed intravital time-lapse imaging to track the fate of lineage-labelled cells in the skin interfollicular epidermis. Results from quantitative analyses of clonal dynamics support a two-compartment model of epidermal homeostasis, whereby basal cells are organized in a stem cell–transit-amplifying cell hierarchy. Critical to these conclusions was the discovery of sexual dimorphism in epidermal fate, with female mice showing a highly synchronized pattern of cell division, differentiation and delamination that contributes to accelerated wound healing. Single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptional profiling and clonal analyses of castrated mice revealed that male sex hormones promote stem cell differentiation and delamination. In summary, our study provides insight into the functional identity of the stem cell population and identifies sex-specific differences in the regulation of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cell fate.

Article.Title: Jurassic flightless bird reveals early ecological diversity of avialans
Article.Authors: Xu L.; Wang M.; Lin G.; Dong L.; Deng K.; Xu X.; Du H.; Lin M.; Chen R.; Zhou Z.
Article.Abstract: The origin and early diversification of birds remain highly debated in vertebrate evolution. Although estimates of the evolutionary timescales suggest a Jurassic period radiation1,2, a profound scarcity of fossils from this period has hampered how the distinctive bird bauplan was assembled3-5. Selection for powered flight has been viewed as the primary driver of early avialan skeletal modifications3,6,7, attesting to the independent occurrences of aerodynamic features among paravian lineages8. Here we report on the discovery of a Late Jurassic avialan, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, gen. et sp. nov., from the Zhenghe Fauna of southeastern China9. As one of the earliest diverging avialans, Y. yangyuanensis exhibits a striking mosaic of features, combining a mixture of avialan- and troodontid-like cranial characters, paired with derived postcranial traits and a deinonychosaur-like hyperextensible second pedal digit. Phylogenetically informed analyses show that Y. yangyuanensis possesses markedly short forelimbs-a condition present widely among non-avialan theropods. These findings provide strong evidence for a terrestrial, flightless lifestyle of Y. yangyuanensis. Our study demonstrates that evolution works intensively as exemplified by the occurrence of several, divergent ecological pathways being exploited in the initial diversification of birds.

Article.Title: Computational design of metalloproteases
Article.Authors: Chen A.; Wu K.; Choi H.; Venkatesh P.; Pellock S.; Hanikel N.; shin H.; Evans D.; Didi K.; Schaaf L.; Díaz-Perlas C.; Coventry B.; Kim D.; Woodbury S.; Ji P.; Honda S.; Bera A.; Nguyen H.; Kang A.; Wang Y.; Li X.; Gerben S.; Chang L.; Yan X.; Oller-Salvia B.
Article.Abstract: De novo design of enzymes that cleave amide bonds represents a major challenge1,2. Here we use RFdiffusion methods3,4 to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket. Of 135 designs tested, 36% catalyse cleavage of their cognate peptide substrates at the targeted scissile bond. The best design accelerates peptide-bond hydrolysis by more than 108-fold relative to the uncatalysed reaction; four substitutions increase this acceleration to more than 1010-fold by improving active-site preorganization5. We use this approach to design metalloproteases that selectively cleave the human disease-associated proteins TDP-43, amyloid-β and serum amyloid A, with rate enhancements of up to 109-fold. We further design caged cytokines and receptor antagonists that are selectively activated by the designed proteases, enabling bioorthogonal control of cell state. Thus, de novo design can yield highly active, programmable proteases with applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation.

Article.Title: Rh3+ stabilized in KRh@MFI catalyses regioselective hydroformylation
Article.Authors: Zhao M.; Millán R.; Skorynina A.; Simonelli L.; Haro M.; Calvino J.; Concepción P.; Corma A.
Article.Abstract: Hydroformylation has been a cornerstone of industrial organometallic catalysis, with regioselectivity being a critical aspect in this process1,2. Present industrial systems use homogeneous Rh-based catalysts with expensive and toxic phosphine-containing ligands, underscoring the need to develop alternative heterogeneous catalysts that could compete with the actual homogeneous ones3. In this direction, atomically dispersed Rh catalysts have been proposed as promising candidates for hydroformylation4,5. However, achieving high regioselectivity at high conversion is still a big challenge. Here subnanometre Rh2O3 clusters are confined inside the channels of the MFI zeolite, which under reaction conditions disrupt into isolated Rh3+ and Rh+ species. Density functional theory (DFT) investigations combined with spectroscopic and catalytic studies demonstrate that Rh3+-mediated hydroformylation is energetically plausibly similar to Rh+, with Rh3+ being intrinsically more selective for hydroformylation and less selective for double-bond isomerization than Rh+. In the coexistence of both Rh3+ and Rh+ species, we demonstrate the possibility to selectively inhibit Rh+ sites through the addition of N-containing molecules such as N-methylpyrrolidine (MP) or 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), which preferentially coordinate to Rh+ inside MFI zeolite channel, thereby suppressing its isomerization function while leaving Rh3+ sites catalytically accessible. This strategy results in a notable enhancement of regioselectivity, with a state-of-the-art reported highest linear to branched aldehydes (l/b) ratio of 817 with 96% undecanal selectivity at 99.8% 1-decene conversion, using NMP as additive.

Article.Title: Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
Article.Authors: Canaria D.; Nguyen T.; Huang H.; Xu H.; Yue L.; Fu Y.; Truong H.; Patel K.; Xing W.; Ravichandar J.; Xing C.; Martin A.; Delidakis G.; Wong S.; Pae A.; Yu Y.; Macdonald R.; Huang Z.; Main M.; Rodriguez A.; Lin X.; Mouchess M.; Hung M.; McGlinchey E.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is a central anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses immune responses in myeloid cells but can also activate T cells, limiting its therapeutic use in chronic inflammatory diseases owing to narrow efficacy windows and dose-limiting toxicities 1–5 . Here we show that myeloid and T cells differ in their dependence on JAK-family kinase pairing for IL-10 signalling and function. We took advantage of this differential kinase dependence to engineer a tetravalent nanobody-based myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonist (msIL-10R agonist) that fully recapitulates IL-10’s potent suppression of monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells while avoiding stimulation of T cells. Cryo-electron microscopy structural analysis reveals a distinct receptor cross-linking geometry of the msIL-10R agonist compared with native IL-10 family cytokines. This tetravalent architecture renders signalling strictly TYK2-dependent and highly sensitive to IL-10Rα and IL-10Rβ receptor abundance, thereby conferring selective activity in myeloid cells. This msIL-10R agonist reduces inflammation in humanized mouse models of lipopolysaccharide challenge, delayed-type hypersensitivity and colitis. A humanized version exhibits IgG-like pharmacokinetics, sustained receptor occupancy and durable myeloid suppression up to 30 days without T cell activation or haematological toxicities in non-human primates. These findings establish a geometry-based strategy for achieving cell-type-selective cytokine signalling and identify the msIL-10R agonist as a therapeutic candidate for myeloid-driven inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel diseases.

Article.Title: Elp1 is required for myeloid differentiation and brain repopulation
Article.Authors: Mader M.; Li W.; Scavetti A.; Yoo Y.; Neumayer G.; Han K.; Shibuya Y.; Haney M.; Wyss-Coray T.; George L.; Lefcort F.; Bassik M.; Nakauchi H.; Wilkinson A.; Wernig M.
Article.Abstract: Haematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) transplantation-mediated replacement of microglia-the reconstitution of the central nervous system microglial niche with donor-derived myeloid cells-represents a promising strategy for brain cell therapies1-7. However, the cell-intrinsic molecular regulators of HSPC-derived myeloid lineage commitment in the brain have remained largely uncharacterized. This is partially because the scarcity of primary HSPCs has rendered large-scale genetic interrogation intractable. Here we explored whether ex vivo expansion of primary cultured HSPCs (cHSPCs) enables unbiased genetic interrogation of haematopoietic differentiation. We established that cHSPCs can be genetically manipulated and readily differentiate into myeloid cells and repopulate microglia niches of the brain after transplantation. Moreover, primary neonatal astrocytes contained strong signals to induce myeloid specification of cHSPCs in vitro. To identify genes that regulate glia-induced myeloid differentiation, we successfully screened around 20,000 individual genetic perturbations and characterized genes involved in the regulation of cell signalling, cell cycle, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Among these genes was elongator acetyltransferase complex subunit 1 (Elp1), which suppressed the unfolded protein response during myeloid specification and was essential for the generation but not maintenance of myeloid cells. Our work establishes a platform to investigate the molecular mechanisms of brain myeloid biology.

Article.Title: Early tetrapod neck mobility modelled using an extant analogue
Article.Authors: Korneisel D.; Donatelli C.; Han L.; Stewart T.; Traynor A.; Otoo B.; Martinez M.; Miyashita T.; Standen E.; Maddin H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Tetrapods arose from lobe-finned fishes with a notochord-dominated axial column 1–3 . During this transition, the skull became separated from the shoulder girdle 4–6 , giving rise to a neck region. This head–shoulder separation has generated hypotheses suggesting that neck mobility increased during the origin of tetrapods, facilitating the ecological transition towards more terrestrial habitats 4,5,7–9 . However, incompletely co-ossified vertebral components 10 have posed a challenge to modelling the mobility of these early tetrapod necks. Here we used material tests on the similarly configured axial columns of sturgeon to predict the capacities of the tetrapod neck region for lateral flexion, extension and rotation across the tetrapod stem. Our model indicates that the soft tissue-dominated axial column was surprisingly rigid, despite lacking co-ossified vertebral components. We estimate that most stem tetrapods could move their heads less than 6° laterally and less than 3° dorsally but could not rotate them. Notably, mobility did not shift in conjunction with the head–shoulder separation that occurred between the origin of tristichopterids (represented by Eusthenopteron ) and that of more crownward stem tetrapods. Therefore, mobility in the tetrapod neck did not serve as a functional driver of head–shoulder separation. Instead, forelimb-driven locomotion, implicated in early tetrapods 11–14 , provides a better functional explanation for the head–shoulder separation.

Article.Title: Educational intervention can rewire village social networks
Article.Authors: Papamichalis M.; Forastiere L.; Airoldi E.; Christakis N.
Article.Abstract: Social networks shape behaviour, affect information dissemination and undergird collective action. And they can be exploited in the design of interventions in these domains1-7. Although social networks obey fundamental principles, such as the degree distribution8,9, they can nevertheless evolve as ties form and break. Here, through a randomized controlled trial involving a total of 8,331 people in 110 remote Honduran villages, we evaluate the secondary effects of a 22-month public-health intervention1 on pre-existing social-network structure. We used a design in which a varying fraction of village households received the intervention, and villages in which no one received the intervention were used as the primary reference group. In 'low-dosage' villages (in which 5-30% of households received the intervention), people who received the intervention tended to sever ties with untreated individuals to whom they previously went for health advice. Conversely, in high-dosage villages (50-100%), treated individuals increased their ties. These average changes are explained mainly by tie dynamics; that is, treated-treated pairs persist and form new links, whereas treated-untreated ties dissolve. A mediation analysis indicates that absorption of health information increases the likelihood of tie formation and persistence. The rewiring patterns generally lasted for three years after the intervention ceased. Moreover, although the intervention delivered health information, it reshaped friendship and financial ties, not just health-advice connections. In aggregate, the introduction of a new information regime acted as a kind of social institution, rewiring individuals' connections even though the overall degree distribution of village-wide networks remained relatively stable.

Article.Title: Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs
Article.Authors: Xu L.; Wang X.; Quan X.; Ferguson S.; Liu D.; Chen J.; Wang S.; Liang S.; Huang G.; Huang K.; Liu F.; Pan X.
Article.Abstract: Ionotropic receptors (IRs) are essential for insect olfaction, enabling the detection of carboxylic acids, amines, moisture, and temperature cues that mediate critical behaviors, including mosquito host-seeking 1,2. However, the structural mechanisms underlying ligand specificity and channel activation in these receptors remain unclear. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures and functional validation of the IR8a-IR75k complex from the malaria mosquito Anopheles stephensi, a carboxylic acid detector, captured in four states: the ligand-free full-length closed form (apo state), the ligand induced full-length open state, and the nonanoic acid (NA)- and octanoic acid (OA)-bound extracellular domains. These structures reveal a dynamic ligand-binding pocket in IR75k, in which specificity is determined by alkyl chain length and carboxylate geometry. Ligand binding triggers closure of IR75k's bilobed ligand binding domain (LBD), and this conformational change propagates through conserved mechanical linkers to the transmembrane domain (TMD), functioning as a molecular lever that dilates the pore via outward displacement of transmembrane helices. This gating mechanism was further corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations and electrophysiology. These insights provide an atomic resolution view of IR mediated host detection in mosquitoes and establish a foundation for the rational design of next generation mosquito control strategies targeting host-seeking behavior.

Article.Title: Catalytic transfer of carbon atoms enables spirofusion of C–C σ-bonds
Article.Authors: Fujimoto H.; Mizutani M.; Imachi K.; Nishioka T.; Ikeda R.; Tobisu M.
Article.Abstract: Spirocyclic frameworks, polycyclic structures in which two rings share a single carbon atom, constitute key structural motifs across diverse areas, including optoelectronic and hole-transporting materials1-3, ligand design for coordination complexes4-6, and numerous natural products7. In a spiro skeleton, the two molecular units adopt an orthogonal arrangement, generating a rigid three-dimensional (3D) architecture. Introducing a single carbon atom to join two components to form the spiro centre therefore represents a direct strategy for constructing such frameworks. Previous carbon-atom-transfer approaches have largely relied on π-bond reactivity, whereas controlled insertion of a carbon atom into C-C σ-bonds remains challenging8-11. Here we report a rhodium-catalysed spiro-carbon-atom insertion reaction that converts biphenylene substrates into spirocyclic structures through sequential C-C bond activation. Using N-isocyanoiminophosphorane (PINC)12-14 as an atomic carbon equivalent, the reaction forms four new C-C bonds at a spiro centre. The transformation enables both homo- and cross-spirofusion of biphenylenes and can be extended to reactions combining σ- and π-bond activation. These results establish a catalytic strategy for constructing structurally complex spirocyclic frameworks through C-C σ-bond activation, with a single carbon atom serving as a central linchpin.

Article.Title: Atomic-scale spin sensing of a 2D d-wave altermagnet via helical tunneling
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Yu S.; Cheng X.; Xiao X.; Ma W.; Ma Y.; Quan F.; Song H.; Zhang K.; Zhang Y.; Liu W.; Yadav P.; Sheng H.; Wang A.; Shi X.; Wang Z.; Niu Q.; Gao Y.; Xiang B.; Liu J.; Wang Z.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Altermagnets simultaneously possess momentum-dependent nonrelativistic spin splitting and zero net magnetization (1-6). Their defining crystalline symmetry connects opposite-spin sublattices in real space and imposes alternating spin polarization on the symmetry-related electronic states in momentum space (1-3). Identifying such an order and its associated spin response therefore calls for atomic-scale spin-sensitive measurements in both real and momentum space, an experimental milestone yet to be achieved. Here we show that the helical edge modes of the higher-order topological insulator α-Bi4Br4 can serve as a spin-selective scanning tunnelling microscopy probe of the two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetic order in the surface layer of KV2Se2O. Atomically registered mapping reveals the spatial relationship between the two V sublattices and a density-wave lattice modulation, as well as real-space patterns consistent with the checkerboard antiferromagnetic order. Field-dependent spectroscopy further finds opposite energy shifts of the unidirectional quasiparticle excitations extending along two orthogonal crystal axes and a predominantly out-of-plane magnetic response. In momentum space, spin-sensitive quasiparticle interference imaging reveals a bias-reversing d-wave anisotropy between the symmetry-paired X and Y valleys. These results provide converging evidence for two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetism on the surface of KV2Se2O and demonstrate helical-edge-mode tunnelling as a route for atomic-scale spin sensing in quantum materials.

Article.Title: Selective, Catalytic Oxidation of Polyethylene Surfaces
Article.Authors: Woroch C.; Klivansky L.; McCarthy D.; Miao H.; Fink Z.; Zuo X.; Guthrie C.; Wang C.; Helms B.; Hartwig J.
Article.Abstract: Polyethylene (PE) accounts for more than a quarter of all plastic produced, owing to its exceptional material properties and scalable production.1 However, pristine PE lacks critical properties, such as adhesion, that are needed for many additional commercial applications.2 Selective post-polymerization functionalization of PE can impart properties that are absent in the pristine polymer, but global functionalization in a uniform medium perturbs bulk properties.3-5 Here, we demonstrate catalytic functionalization of solid PE at a solid-liquid interface. The resulting materials possess enhanced surface properties while maintaining bulk properties, such as melting temperature or tensile strength. The method selectively converts methylene units to ketones with just 0.001 mol% iron catalyst below 80 °C with inexpensive oxidants. PE functionalized at the solid-liquid interface adheres to polar surfaces up to 90-fold more strongly than does pristine PE and up to 4-fold more strongly than does PE functionalized in a uniform medium at a comparable level. We demonstrate that the surface ketones can be modified to enhance adhesive strength further and that the augmented surface properties persist for longer than they do after other unselective functionalizations. Thus, selective C-H bond functionalization at the solid-liquid interface produces materials inaccessible by bulk functionalization methods or by traditional surface oxidations.

Article.Title: Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria
Article.Authors: Tang S.; Ramirez J.; He Q.; Rodríguez Mestre M.; Wiegand T.; Zhang D.; Wang M.; Lampe G.; Wang J.; Ma Y.; Jovanovic M.; Pinilla-Redondo R.; Fernández I.; Sternberg S.
Article.Abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) employ diverse and distinctive mechanisms of cDNA synthesis to protect bacteria against viral infection1. However, the functions and mechanisms of many DRTs remain unknown2. Here we identify a new antiviral defense system, DRT10, that associates with a noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to catalyze processive, protein-primed synthesis of tandem-repeat DNA. Reverse transcription is templated by a defined ncRNA region with a characteristic sequence pattern and template boundary elements, both of which are conserved and essential for DNA repeat addition. Cryo-EM reconstructions reveal an unanticipated 2:1 architecture, wherein two RT monomers bind opposite sides of a pseudo-symmetric ncRNA. Biochemical experiments further demonstrate that each RT monomer reverse transcribes the template encoded on its respective side of the ncRNA, but only one generates the long repetitive product, whose template is defined by the distance between two flanking stem-loop anchors. This mode of iterative, boundary-delimited cDNA synthesis exhibits direct parallels to the mechanism of telomeric repeat addition by eukaryotic telomerase, and phylogenetic analyses of RTs across domains of life place telomerase in a monophyletic clade with the DRT family, suggesting a common origin for their DNA polymerization activities. Together with earlier studies of DRT2, DRT3, and DRT93-5, our findings identify a conserved mechanistic logic underlying RNA-templated DNA repeat addition across diverse DRTs, despite vastly different architectural solutions, and expand the repertoire of reverse transcription-based strategies for antiviral immunity in bacteria.

Article.Title: Genome accessibility reveals disease risk that gene expression misses
Article.Abstract: Most disease-associated genetic alterations do not affect the genes themselves, but instead change how strongly they are expressed, often by modifying genome accessibility. The effects of disease-associated genetic variants on gene expression and genome accessibility have been analysed together.

Article.Title: How to control where semiconductor crystals start growing
Article.Abstract: Semiconductor crystals grow from tiny nuclei, but the position of these nuclei is difficult to control precisely and can affect the crystal’s properties. An approach using ‘etching flux’ has now been developed that constrains the position at which a nucleus forms, enabling spatially programmable growth of large single crystals of semiconducting material. Single crystals of a semiconductor can be formed in a spatially programmable way.

Article.Title: Structural basis for regulating lipopolysaccharide transmembrane transport
Article.Authors: Taylor R.; Pahil K.; Caruso A.; Plaman B.; Early S.; Rowe S.; Baidin V.; Wilson A.; Ruiz N.; Walsh R.; Harrison S.; Kahne D.
Article.Abstract: Gram-negative bacteria are surrounded by a multilayered cell envelope with a mostly impermeable outer membrane that provides intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics1-5. The outer membrane is an asymmetrical bilayer with phospholipids in the inner leaflet and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet6,7. An LPS transport (Lpt) machine called LptB2FGCADE moves LPS across a protein bridge from the inner membrane to the outer membrane8,9. LPS biosynthesis is regulated to prevent toxic accumulation of LPS molecules in the inner membrane during growth10-12. Whether LPS transport across the Lpt bridge is also regulated has been unclear. Here we present three structures of the trans-envelope Lpt complex in LPS-free, LPS-bound and ATP-bound states, along with a structure of a partial bridge. These structures, combined with biochemical experiments, show that Lpt bridge assembly triggers movement of the transmembrane helix of LptC (TM-LptC) in an LPS-dependent manner, resulting in increased ATP binding and hydrolysis. We also show that LPS transport in vivo requires bridge formation and movement of the TM-LptC. Our data support a model in which assembled Lpt bridges respond to the presence of LPS in the inner membrane to turn on transport by moving the TM-LptC, thus coordinating LPS transport activity with bridge assembly and the presence of LPS at the inner membrane.

Article.Title: Mechanism of spliceosome termination
Article.Authors: Boreikaite V.; Faraway R.; Vorländer M.; Phillips A.; Opitz L.; Wanke M.; Yakoub G.; Raffl G.; Fin L.; González-Prieto R.; Luijsterburg M.; Ameres S.; Plaschka C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract After excising an intron from pre-mRNA, the spliceosome remains trapped in a non-productive complex bound to the intron 1–5 . Termination of this complex is critical for spliceosome recycling and intron decay 6 , but the mechanism remains unknown. Here we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of human spliceosomes at two sequential stages of termination. First, the RNA helicases DHX15 and Aquarius unwind the RNA active site of the spliceosome, releasing bound components including U2 snRNA and extracting the buried intron–lariat branch point. The branch point is then debranched by the spliceosome-tethered enzyme DBR1, generating the previously unknown debranched intron spliceosome. This state recruits the RNA helicase DHX35 with its co-factors GPATCH1–WDR83, assisted by YJU2B. DHX35 ejects the debranched intron from the U6 snRNA–5′ splice site duplex, driving spliceosome disassembly and intron turnover. In defective spliceosomes stalled on aberrant introns, YJU2B partners with LENG1 to guide DHX35–GPATCH1–WDR83 for termination through spliceosome quality control. Together, we reveal the mechanism of regular spliceosome termination and its parallels with spliceosome quality control, ensuring accurate and efficient pre-mRNA splicing.

Article.Title: Prehistoric global migration of vanishing gut microbes with humans
Article.Authors: Carter M.; Liu Z.; Olm M.; Martin M.; Sprockett D.; Ghadermazi P.; Trumble B.; Kaplan H.; Stieglitz J.; Rodriguez D.; Relman D.; Sonnenburg E.; Gurven M.; Good B.; Sonnenburg J.
Article.Abstract: The gut microbiome is crucial for health and is affected strongly by lifestyle1. Many microorganisms commonly found in non-industrialized populations are disappearing or have become extinct in industrialized populations2-6. Studying which microorganisms have been long-term residents of the human gut and may have co-evolved with humans2,7,8 could provide insights into how microbial biodiversity loss affects human health. However, the genetic complexities of microbial evolution and the plasticity of gut microbiome composition have made it challenging to resolve the evolutionary history of these long-term associations. Here we performed deep metagenomic sequencing of the Tsimane horticulturalists of Bolivia and compared their gut microbiomes with those of the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania3. These two populations, whose ancestors have been separated for tens of thousands of years, share 1,231 microbial species, most of which are rare in or absent from industrialized populations. Population genetic analyses of 636 of the shared species revealed patterns of microbial divergence and gene flow consistent with prehistoric human co-migration, with estimated split times that approximately align with human migration out of Africa and into the Americas. Our findings indicate that a diverse gut microbiome co-migrated with humans worldwide and has persisted over millennia. However, many of these species are now vanishing from industrialized populations and the consequences for human health remain uncertain.

Article.Title: Dynamics of human cardiogenesis and its disruption in trisomy 21
Article.Authors: Cranley J.; Kanemaru K.; Bayraktar S.; Knight-Schrijver V.; Hulbert R.; Lana-Elola E.; Aoidi R.; Pett J.; Wilbrey-Clark A.; Polanski K.; Dabrowska M.; Mulas I.; Johnson H.; Combemorel N.; Yu Y.; Palmer J.; Lee W.; Van Wauwe J.; Ng-Blichfeldt J.; Richardson L.; Semprich C.; Kapuge R.; Perera S.; He X.; Ho S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Developmental dynamics involve the specification of diverse cell types and their spatial organization into multicellular niches 1 . Here we combine single-cell and spatial multiomics to define 21 distinct tissue niches in the developing heart, which we use to develop a context-aware, resolution-agnostic niche classification tool (TissueTypist). Applying high-resolution spatial profiling to the developing sinoatrial node, we resolve three pacemaker cell subtypes arrayed along a linear axis. First trimester subpopulations, such as pacemaker cells in the sinus horn and sinoatrial node head region, display neuroattractant programs and interact with parasympathetic neurons via interactions that include Eph–ephrin and semaphorin–plexin signalling. Temporal trajectories map the maturation of atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes and uncover a lipid–metabolic switch and potential key regulators of cell-type identity. In the ventricle, we identify cellular and transcriptional gradients along both pseudotime and transmural axes, which provide molecular insights into myocardial compaction and maturation. Comparative profiling revealed that hearts with trisomy 21 are depleted in compact cardiomyocytes and exhibit increased apoptosis relative to euploid hearts. This finding was validated in isogenic-matched trisomy 21 and euploid cardiomyocytes derived from induced pluripotent stem cells. These early developmental perturbations may contribute to the increased risk of congenital heart disease associated with Down’s syndrome. In summary, we present a spatially resolved framework of human cardiac development to enable systematic explorations of developmental niches in health and disease.

Article.Title: A split attractor design for rapidly writing a navigational goal
Article.Authors: Lanz A.; Kathman N.; Hao E.; Ermentrout B.; Nagel K.
Article.Abstract: Recurrent attractor networks are widely thought to form the basis of working memory1-3, but how they can be rapidly switched on and off is unclear4-7. Here we investigate stability and switching in a recurrent circuit of the fly navigation centre8. h∆K and PFG neurons are recurrently connected in a ring structure and exhibit shared persistent bump activity that turns on with odour and terminates at the end of a goal-directed run. Using whole-cell recordings, we show that persistence in h∆K depends on recurrence, and that h∆K receives slow recurrent excitation and fast inhibition from its synaptic partners. Computational modelling reveals that these synaptic dynamics yield persistent attractor dynamics over a range of synaptic strengths. Next we examine the mechanisms of rapid switching. We find that whereas both populations show similar activity during runs, they become decoupled during turns and rest. We can reproduce these differential dynamics in our model by using inhibition to dynamically uncouple activity in h∆K from PFG. When h∆K is inhibited, PFG neurons follow their inputs from the compass system; when h∆K is disinhibited, recurrent interactions lock this input into place, forming a heading memory. Consistent with this model, we find that inhibitory inputs onto h∆K increase during turns and are suppressed during odour and goal-directed runs. Our work reveals how disinhibition can serve as a gate to rapidly write an ongoing measurement to a recurrent circuit.

Article.Title: Observation of critical topological phase transition
Article.Authors: Cheng Z.; Zhang X.; Yu X.; Zhou L.; Gong J.; Zhang B.
Article.Abstract: Phase transitions are traditionally understood within two seemingly incompatible theoretical paradigms. Landau-Ginzburg phase transitions1,2 are continuous, occurring at critical points where microscopic details become irrelevant and universal behaviour emerges, driven by gapless fluctuations with scale-invariant correlations3. By contrast, topological phase transitions connect gapped phases characterized by quantized topological invariants4,5 and, in doing so, necessarily pass through gapless phase boundaries where such invariants become ill-defined6-9. Here using an acoustic metamaterial platform, we experimentally demonstrate a unifying scenario-a critical topological phase transition-in which topology becomes well-defined at criticality10-13, overcoming this conventional incompatibility, and reorganizes critical behaviour by driving a phase transition along critical phase boundaries14. This transition gives rise to a topology-enforced multicritical point at an isolated intersection of critical boundaries with distinct topology. Along these boundaries, we observe topological edge states and diagnose criticality by means of logarithmic entanglement-entropy scaling15-17. At the multicritical point, the entanglement entropy shows additive logarithmic scaling given by the sum of contributions from adjacent boundaries, directly evidencing topology-enforced multicriticality. These findings establish a hierarchical organization of phase transitions, in which topology shapes criticality beyond the conventional Landau-Ginzburg paradigm and standard topological phase transitions.

Article.Title: A 7-eV bandgap semiconductor based on silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1−x)2O3
Article.Authors: Steele J.; Bhattacharya D.; Nomoto K.; Pieczulewski N.; Sorensen P.; Ha V.; Pant N.; Shukla I.; Das S.; Kilic U.; Ramesh M.; Giustino F.; Mazumder B.; Senevirathna M.; Williams M.; Schubert M.; Muller D.; Xing H.; Jena D.; Schlom D.
Article.Abstract: In rectifying power electronics, wider-bandgap (Eg) semiconductors allow higher efficiency and power density with the Baliga figure of merit proportional to Eg5.5 (refs. 1,2). Unfortunately, the unique ability of semiconductors to have their conductivities controllably modulated over orders of magnitude by equilibrium doping methods becomes increasingly elusive as the bandgap increases. Increasing demand for wider-bandgap semiconductors has led to many materials previously considered insulators-including GaN, SiC, AlN, Ga2O3 and GeO2-to emerge as useful semiconductors after decreasing defect densities and finding appropriate dopants. Here we report silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1-x)2O3 films with bandgaps exceeding 7.0 eV grown by suboxide molecular-beam epitaxy, surpassing that of cubic boron nitride, the next-widest-bandgap semiconductor known3-5. In the colossal-bandgap regime, >6 eV, our silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1-x)2O3 films have room-temperature conductivities over 100 million times higher than all previous reports6. We fabricate a Schottky diode and a field-effect transistor (the AlphaFET) with colossal-bandgap channels. These α-(AlxGa1-x)2O3 films and devices use sapphire, an abundant, inexpensive substrate with excellent quality that is produced at massive scale, facilitating the development and adoption of colossal-bandgap electronics. Our achievement breaks the trend of increasing synthesis difficulty, cost and small size of ever-wider-bandgap semiconductors, for example, diamond and cubic boron nitride.

Article.Title: Spatially deterministic nucleation of 2D semiconductors by etching flux
Article.Authors: Park J.; Kim J.; Kang S.; Oh J.; Sunwoo Y.; Oh S.; Shin S.; Yang S.; Jo S.; Lee J.; Lee D.; Kim M.; Eom C.; Jeong S.; Lim C.; Moon G.; Kang M.; Kim M.; Kim J.; Yun C.; Noh G.; Park D.; Kim D.; Kwon S.; Hong C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nucleation control is fundamental to semiconductor deposition, governing when, where and how crystalline materials form. Conventional strategies can regulate nucleation density and, through area-selective growth, confine deposition to designated regions 1–13 . However, they generally do not determine where an individual nucleus forms within the growth regions, leaving even single-nucleation events spatially stochastic and limiting deterministic construction of crystalline materials. Here we report etching-flux-mediated single-centred nucleation of two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors to deterministically localize a single nucleation event. The etching flux released from the barrier suppresses nuclei near the pattern boundary, leaving a single surviving nucleus at the pattern centre, and systematic experiments elucidate the mechanism and establish nucleation design rules for zero, single and multiple nucleation regimes. Etching-flux-mediated single-centred nucleation enables single-crystal molybdenum disulfide growth at the 10-μm scale, field-effect mobilities of up to 117 cm 2 V −1 s −1 and large-area uniformity with process compatibility. This in-plane chemical-flux strategy realizes spatially programmed growth, demonstrating nucleation–growth decoupling for line-shaped single crystals, multiple transistors integrated within a large common crystal, and aligned 2D lateral heterostructures for self-aligned contacts. These capabilities open a path towards advanced 2D electronic integration and expand semiconductor deposition from controlling where materials grow to controlling where and how crystals can begin to form.

Article.Title: Human lung organoid modelling of tissue-resident antiviral T cell responses
Article.Authors: Rathkey J.; Choi S.; van Unen V.; Zhang H.; Liu M.; Ding J.; Alwahabi S.; Santos A.; Mallajosyula V.; Chan J.; Mohsin A.; Elsheikh M.; Rustagi A.; Lam B.; Chirieleison S.; Wallen B.; Solis D.; Mah J.; Horn H.; Röltgen K.; Nair R.; Trope W.; Guh-Siesel A.; Lin Z.; Powell H.
Article.Abstract: Tissue-resident immunity constitutes a first line of defence against pathogens and enables rapid innate and adaptive memory responses1-3. However, experimental studies have been hindered by a lack of holistic human in vitro models that enable epithelial infection in the context of tissue-resident immune subsets. In lung, differing notions of transient versus sustained residency of tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM cells) have challenged the extent to which anamnestic recall immunity to respiratory pathogens occurs locally or in concert with secondary lymphoid organs4-6. Here we generated long-term adult human distal lung organoids from intact tissue fragments in 3D air-liquid interface culture, which co-preserved epithelial and stromal components with endogenous lung-resident immune cells (T cells, B cells, natural killer cells and myeloid cells). The organoid T cells expressed residency and memory markers and preserved T cell receptor repertoires of cognate fresh tissue. SARS-CoV-2 infected the organoid lung epithelium, stimulated inflammatory cytokine production and, crucially, induced SARS-CoV-2-specific, tissue-resident T cell responses. Furthermore, boosting T cells within intact organoids with SARS-CoV-2 peptide pools blunted subsequent SARS-CoV-2 infection, consistent with a component of virus-specific protective TRM cell function in the absence of secondary lymphoid tissues. Overall, this immunocompetent lung organoid system demonstrates functional control of viral infection by lung-intrinsic memory T cell responses, provides a rationale for local vaccination strategies and validates a general platform for investigation of human tissue-resident immunity in health and disease.

Article.Title: A chiral superlattice route to spin-split topological antiferromagnetism
Article.Authors: Dinh T.; Liu M.; Qiu J.; Mardanya S.; Sung S.; Le X.; Broyles C.; Zhu C.; Xu Q.; Chen H.; Rehfuss Z.; Liu Y.; Zeng X.; Li H.; Guo P.; Liu J.; Huang T.; Shi J.; Smith M.; Blawat J.; Singleton J.; McDonald R.; Arvizo I.; Cui D.; Zheng S.
Article.Abstract: Chirality has emerged as a new mechanism for inducing spin and Berry-curvature phenomena in quantum materials and molecular chemistry1-7. Collinear antiferromagnets (AFMs) are promising for spintronics and topological magnetism, yet realizing large Berry curvature and spin-split bands remains challenging8,9. Here we report a chiral-superlattice route to spin-split topological phenomena from collinear antiferromagnetism. We study the collinear AFM UOTe, in which we show a spontaneous chiral superlattice arising from frozen chiral phonons at a finite wave vector. Without the superlattice, the pristine collinear AFM in UOTe has neither Berry curvature nor spin-split bands. When electrons move through the chiral superlattice, their orbital Bloch wavefunction and quantum geometry are modulated by the strong chiral superlattice potential, generating large Berry curvature, which we detect by the nonlinear Hall effect. At 150 K, the chiral-superlattice-induced Berry curvature couples to the collinear AFM order, leading to an anomalous Hall angle of about 0.14 abruptly near the Néel temperature TN which is among the largest in bulk magnets. Moreover, our spin Hanle precession measurement shows that the chiral superlattice also generates spin-polarized current from the collinear AFM, a long-standing goal in spintronics. We shed light on the supermodulation formation mechanism based on chemical ion size and physical interlayer-intralayer energy competitions, which we use to propose a design principle to discover similar bond-mismatch superlattices, providing a chiral superlattice pathway through real-space engineering of quantum geometry10,11.

Article.Title: Cryo-EM structure of a methanogen nitrogenase–PII protein supercomplex
Article.Authors: Kashyap R.; Deere T.; Dhamad A.; Chanderban M.; Tokmina-Lukaszewska M.; Bothner B.; Lessner D.; Antony E.
Article.Abstract: Nitrogenases are metalloenzymes that catalyse the reduction of atmospheric dinitrogen to ammonia, sustaining the global nitrogen cycle1,2. Although bacterial nitrogenase has been extensively characterized, the architecture and regulation of archaeal nitrogenases have remained unknown despite longstanding evidence of nitrogen fixation in methanogens. Here we report a cryo-electron microscopy structure of a native nitrogenase-PII protein supercomplex from Methanosarcina acetivorans. The structure reveals an assembly of three NifDK heterotetramers bridged by six NifI1,2 heterotrimeric PII complexes, which sterically block NifH association and lock the enzyme in an inactive state. The PII complexes show asymmetric binding of ADP and 2-oxoglutarate, coupling nitrogenase inhibition directly to cellular energy and nitrogen status. Addition of 2-oxoglutarate and ATP releases the NifI complexes, stimulating a threefold increase in NifDK activity in vitro. This higher-order architecture identifies a regulatory strategy in methanogens in which PII proteins drive nitrogenase oligomerization to control activity. The finding that nitrogenase activity may be modulated through direct assembly into higher-order structures indicates future directions for the exploration of nitrogenase evolution, regulation and biotechnological applications.

Article.Title: A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop
Article.Authors: Toscani De Col L.; Riebner T.; Morawetz I.; Schneider F.; Sempelmann N.; Schlachet-Lépinay J.; Schaden F.; Bartokos M.; Kazakov G.; Beeks K.; Gerstenecker B.; Pimon M.; Lahs S.; Hellerschmied A.; Lercher T.; Denker H.; Premper J.; Niessner A.; Matus M.; Čížek M.; Číp O.; Lal V.; Zitzer G.; Petrov V.; Tiedau J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The laser-accessible nuclear transition in the thorium-229 isotope has been identified as a candidate for realizing an optical nuclear clock 1 that might outperform current optical clocks based on electron-shell transitions in atoms or ions 2 . Improvements to the instability by several orders of magnitude are projected for future devices. Article.Title: Hydrogen bonding in water under extreme confinement
Article.Authors: Xu X.; Kuehne M.; Walker H.; Bao D.; Jin X.; Tu Y.; Ritt C.; Martis J.; Idrobo J.; Pantelides S.; Strano M.; Hachtel J.; Majumdar A.
Article.Abstract: Fluids under extreme confinement or near interfaces exhibit molecular structures and intermolecular bonding distinct from their bulk analogues. Optical vibrational studies have shown that interfacial and confined water can exhibit altered intramolecular O-H stretching frequencies, a sensitive spectral signature of changes in intermolecular hydrogen bonding1-4. Investigating confined water experimentally at the length scale of intermolecular and surface forces has, however, remained a challenge. Here we report direct molecular-level observations of hydrogen bonding in water confined inside individual carbon nanotubes (CNTs), enabled by in situ vibrational electron energy loss spectroscopy (vEELS) with nanoscale resolution. Water in larger CNTs exhibits the bonded O-H vibrations of bulk water, but at smaller diameters, and the frequency blueshifts to near the free O-H stretch found in water vapour and water located near hydrophobic surfaces, indicating a highly dispersed, non-H-bonded environment. Theoretical analysis based on quantum vibrational oscillators links the observed spectral features to local hydrogen-bonding configurations, consistent with the experimental observation. Furthermore, cryogenic experiments provide insights into complex structural phase transitions of confined water. This research reveals the quantum and dynamic nature of hydrogen bonds under confinement and the potential impact of unveiling molecular-level structure and bonding in confined fluids.

Article.Title: Australia’s current wildfire crisis linked to colonial land-use change
Article.Authors: Fletcher M.; Romano A.; O’Shea C.; Maezumi S.; Magee H.; Connor S.; Mullett R.; Menéndez P.; Gadd P.; Mariani M.; Chevalier M.; N/A N/A.; Mullett R.
Article.Abstract: The global wildfire crisis1 is often attributed to climate change, a framing that overlooks crucial historical drivers. Biomes at the forefront of this crisis, such as the temperate eucalypt forests of Australia, have seen alarming increases in large, intense wildfires in recent decades. Yet evidence of how colonial land-use change and the disruption of Indigenous fire use altered vegetation structure and fuel dynamics remains scarce. Here we reconstruct 1,000 years of vegetation and fire change in a temperate eucalypt forest in southeastern Australia. Before the British invasion (from 1788 CE), fire use by the Indigenous Gunaikurnai people maintained stable, open woodlands through frequent, fine-grained, low-temperature cultural burning. Colonial disruption drove cascading changes: increased fire temperature, a fourfold rise in eucalypt cover, a shift from open woodland to forest and increased soil erosion. These transformations preceded anthropogenic warming, indicating that the vulnerability of these forests to wildfire is shaped by colonial land-use legacies. By creating more flammable landscapes, colonial land use amplified the influence of climate change, suggesting a reinforcing feedback (the 'catastrophic wildfire loop') in which high-intensity wildfires raise fuel loads and further increase the likelihood of climate-driven fire. Integrating Indigenous knowledge into fire management is therefore essential to restoring resilience and mitigating future wildfire risk.

Article.Title: Experimental observation of critical topology
Article.Authors: Lin Z.; Wang L.; Kong Z.; Zhou Y.; Lin H.; Yu X.; Zhang S.; Jiang J.
Article.Abstract: Understanding phases of matter and their transitions stands as a central pursuit in physical sciences, representing a continuously evolving frontier that drives fundamental discovery. Conventional phase transitions are marked by continuous order-parameter evolution and universal critical behaviour, whereas topological phase transitions are defined by abrupt changes of quantized topological invariants-two frameworks long viewed as distinct and even incompatible1,2. Recent theories have predicted quantum criticality endowed with nontrivial topology mostly in one-dimensional (1D) systems3-5, pointing to a potential unification of the two patterns. Yet experimental observation of such critical topology, that is, topology at phase boundaries and its extension to higher dimensions, remain outstanding. Here we report experimental evidence indicating that critical gapless topological states can be characterized by the entanglement spectrum (ES) and entanglement wavefunctions in both one and two dimensions, complemented by direct imaging of the topological boundary modes in gapless bulk continuum using engineered phononic crystals. Although implemented in a classical platform, our experimental approach gives results equivalent to those in the quantum limit and is in fact readily extensible to quantum systems. Through entanglement-based analysis, we illustrate that transitions among phase boundaries with distinct critical topology lead to multi-critical points in the phase diagram, evidencing topology-driven multi-criticality and a hierarchical structure of topological phases. Our work demonstrates a fundamental connection between topology and criticality, paving the way for an experimental route towards exploring topological physics at phase transitions.

Article.Title: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes
Article.Authors: Minixhofer B.; Murray T.; Limisiewicz T.; Korhonen A.; Zettlemoyer L.; Smith N.; Ponti E.; Soldaini L.; Hofmann V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have largely been driven by large language models, deep neural networks that operate over discrete units called tokens. To represent text, most large language models use words or word fragments as the tokens, known as subword tokenization 1 . Subword tokenization obscures fine-grained information, which is problematic, especially for scientific data—such as computer code or biological sequences—where meaning depends on the individual characters or bytes 2 . Models that instead operate directly on the byte encoding of text avoid these limitations, but until now they have lagged behind subword-based models in performance. Here we introduce a general method for creating byte-level large language models through byteification that approach the capabilities of subword-based systems. We use a two-stage conversion procedure to retrofit existing subword-based models into byte-level models with minimal extra training. The resulting models outperform earlier byte-level approaches and excel on character-level reasoning tasks, achieving practical inference speeds by efficiently processing byte-level information and adaptability by reusing the existing ecosystem around the source large language model. Our results remove a long-standing performance barrier to end-to-end byte-level language modelling, demonstrating that models operating on raw text encodings can scale competitively while offering advantages in domains requiring fine-grained textual understanding.

Article.Authors: Liu K.; Liu Z.; Meng X.; Tang M.; Di F.; Wang Z.; Li C.; Yang S.; Zhang Y.; Yang X.; Lv Z.; Li X.; Jin H.; Pu W.; Zhao H.; Li F.; Sui P.; Zhou B.
Article.Abstract: The lung consists of two anatomically distinct compartments: the airways and the alveoli. This transdifferentiation process is accompanied by an intermediate stage marked by Cldn4 expression. Functional blockade of either SPP1 or ITGB1 impairs AT2 cell migration, whereas inhibition of Notch signalling prevents their transdifferentiation into club cells. Collectively, our findings reveal a cross-compartmental cellular mechanism for bronchiolar epithelial repair, expanding the current understanding of lung regenerative plasticity and potentially informing therapeutic strategies for airway injury.

Article.Title: 5-oxoETE links redox control of epithelial damage detection and resilience
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Lengyel M.; Hui K.; Ambaw Y.; Gelashvili Z.; Kim L.; Ly R.; Peng S.; Quraishi M.; Walther T.; Farese R.; Niethammer P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Organisms harness oxidative stress to rapidly attract white blood cells to wound sites and to kill pathogens 1–3 . In undamaged tissue, where NADP + is low, DHRS7 quenches unnecessary inflammation. Mechanistically, 5-oxoETE induces the expression of NUDIX hydrolases, which protect the cytoplasmic nucleotide pool from oxidation and prevent apoptosis in zebrafish and human intestinal cells. Thus, our data reveal a conserved mode of redox sensing and signalling—beyond classic thiol oxidation—that leverages NADPH metabolism to orchestrate the antimicrobial and pro-resilience functions of oxidative stress.

In patients, tRNA1Arg(UCU) is downregulated in neuroendocrine prostate cancer and its loss is associated with accelerated metastasis and poor survival. Article.Title: A Jurassic mammaliaform swimmer and transformation of the mammalian pharynx
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Li P.; Neander A.; Zhang H.; Zhou C.; Martin T.; Luo Z.
Article.Abstract: The discovery of a well-preserved mammaliaform fossil from the Middle Jurassic period of China reveals evidence on the evolutionary transformation of the feeding apparatus and the ecological diversity of Mesozoic era mammals. Mammaliaforms are evolutionary predecessors to modern Mammalia1-3, and their morphologies provide primary insights into the evolutionary origin of mammals. The rare preservation of a therian-like pharyngeal vault (throat passage) and hyoid skeletal anatomy (throat bones) in this mammaliaform suggests that critical soft-tissue anatomy for therian-like swallowing, drinking and suckling behaviours had evolved in the common ancestors of Docodonta and Mammalia, long before the rise of modern mammals. This fossil exhibits a wealth of features specialized for swimming, filling in a major gap of anatomical knowledge of pelvis and hindlimb for early mammals. It is characterized by highly distinctive canines and pseudo-carnassial sectorial teeth for a faunivorous diet. We interpret that this mammaliaform was semiaquatic, swimming and foraging in water, with a lifestyle analogous to the extant platypus. This species is the largest of Jurassic mammaliaforms. It expands the body size range of docodontans, and adds to a growing body of evidence that multiple docodontans exploited diverse niches with semiaquatic and other ecomorphotypes. Docodontans are an early example of replicated evolution of the semiaquatic and other ecomorphotypes in the Mesozoic ecosystem dominated by dinosaurs, long before the diversification of extant mammals.

Article.Title: Overcoming key challenges in the evolutionary transition to multicellularity
Article.Authors: Ozan Bozdag G.; Tong K.; Yunker P.; Herron M.; Ratcliff W.
Article.Abstract: Dozens of independent origins of multicellularity have profoundly shaped Earth's evolutionary and ecological history. These transitions have given rise to massive radiations encompassing thousands to millions of species and the evolution of increasingly complex bodies. Multicellular taxa now constitute the majority of Earth's biomass and have fundamentally transformed global ecosystems, underpinning diverse biomes from forests and grasslands to coral reefs. While these macroevolutionary patterns have long been recognized, the microevolutionary processes driving the transition to multicellularity have remained unclear. Questions remain on how solitary cells form cohesive groups, how these groups become evolutionary units capable of adaptation at the multicellular level, and how novel cell types and developmental patterns emerge. Recent discoveries of previously unknown multicellular species and the development of experimental models have provided important insights into these questions. This work reveals that seemingly insurmountable evolutionary hurdles are often readily overcome either through the repurposing of ancestral unicellular traits or through emergent properties of multicellular collectives that arise spontaneously. Here we review key breakthroughs in our understanding of the microevolutionary processes that underpin the evolution of increasingly complex multicellularity, focusing on mechanisms through which single cells can evolve into functionally integrated multicellular organisms.

Article.Authors: Yakushev A.; Khuyagbaatar J.; Düllmann C.; Pershina V.; Schädel M.; Ballof J.; Bartl P.; Block M.; Cantemir R.; Dietzel D.; Giacoppo F.; Hermainski K.; Herzberg R.; John J.; Krier J.; Kurz N.; Löchner S.; Maiti M.; Mošať P.; Raeder S.; Sato T.; Schausten B.; Uusitalo J.; Wieczorek P.

Article.Title: A preinvasive regulatory T cell axis for lung cancer interception
Article.Authors: Gamble S.; Whiteman Z.; Peinador-Marín C.; Lebrusant-Fernandez M.; Shurr A.; Enica A.; Sahwangarrom T.; Ung S.; Rogers A.; Fessas P.; Khaw C.; Kalinke L.; Ahlmann-Eltze C.; Alhendi A.; Otter K.; Hu X.; Thakkar K.; Gration B.; Newsham I.; Uddin I.; Musson E.; Lazarus K.; Przybilla M.; Pennycuick A.; Hall H.

Tracking and targeting preinvasive T cell regulation may inform new approaches to detect and intercept lung cancer development. Here we explore how the T cell network is remodelled during NSCLC development via multi-omic, cross-tissue immune profiling in patients with preinvasive lung lesions surveilled by autofluorescence bronchoscopy and computed tomography (CT) imaging. Effector regulatory CD4 + T cells (eT reg cells) expressing basic leucine zipper ATF-like transcription factor (BATF) accumulated in high-grade premalignant airway lesions and were clonally related to circulating eT reg cells. Circulating eT reg cells were increasingly elevated during preinvasive progression, enabling lung tumorigenesis to be tracked through analysis of peripheral blood. Emergence of this clonally coordinated eT reg cell circuit defined rapid progression in patients with early-stage NSCLC detected during CT screening. In mice, carcinogen-driven lung tumorigenesis triggered an analogous preinvasive eT reg cell axis across the blood, airways and draining lymph nodes (dLNs). This culminated in an expansion of lung BATF + T reg cells and T reg cell-rich peribronchial immature tertiary lymphoid structures (iTLSs). Immune interception via phosphoinositide 3-kinase-δ (PI3Kδ) inhibition abrogated formation of T reg cell-rich iTLSs, reduced circulating and pulmonary T reg cells, increased local conventional type 1 dendritic cells (cDC1s) and reduced lung tumour incidence and size. These data reveal a conserved eT reg cell network that emerges across tissues during early pulmonary tumorigenesis and provide a theranostic framework to track and target preinvasive immune regulation for lung cancer interception.

Article.Title: RNA catalysis emerges from dynamic structural ensembles
Article.Authors: Degenhardt M.; Degenhardt H.; Bhoge B.; Lee Y.; Yu P.; Zhang J.; Deme J.; Stagno J.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The dynamic interplay between RNA structure and its associated Mg 2+ ions is central to RNA function yet remains poorly understood at a near-atomic level 1–4 . Here, using a heterogeneity-focused protocol for cryo-electron microscopy data analysis of conformationally flexible RNA particles, we determined the structures of RNase P RNA ensembles composed of 76 coexisting active and inactive conformers that differ in a transient tertiary interaction that is critical for activity. The binding of the accessory protein does not change the local structure but induces thermodynamic allostery that enhances catalysis by altering the dynamics of the tertiary interaction. Four distinct classes of Mg 2+ ions have critical roles in the structure, dynamics and catalysis of the conformational ensembles. Together, these findings establish a new paradigm in which catalysis is regulated through multimodal communications coupled with the dynamics of RNA–Mg 2+ conformational ensembles, rather than a single static catalytic structure in a single action mode.

Article.Title: In-cell structures visualize human pre-ribosome assembly in the nucleolus
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Hayashi Y.; Fung H.; Cuylen-Haering S.; Mahamid J.; Müller C.
Article.Abstract: In eukaryotes, ribosome biogenesis initiates within the nucleolus, a hallmark multilayered compartment of the nucleus. Structures of pre-ribosomes have been characterized ex situ, but their assembly pathways within human nucleoli have not been described. Here, we used cryogenic correlative light and electron tomography to visualize molecular landscapes within HeLa cell nucleoli and obtained in-cell structural snapshots of both ribosomal subunit precursors, the small subunit processome and the pre-60S. These recapitulate major states resolved previously ex situ and reveal additional critical interaction partners, including the RNA exosome, rixosome, and nuclear export receptor CRM1-RanGTP. We further show how pre-ribosome assembly landscapes are altered upon RNA polymerase I inhibition. Our study combines molecular structures with cellular context to elucidate the spatiotemporal assembly pathway of the human ribosome.

Article.Abstract: A Chern metal is a two-dimensional metallic state of matter carrying chiral edge states. Article.Abstract: Martian meteorites provide a record of the planet’s geological history. Article.Authors: Jost D.; Regmi R.; Lomeli E.; Sahel-Schackis S.; Scheufele M.; Neuhaus M.; Nickel R.; Yakhou F.; Kummer K.; Brookes N.; Shen L.; Dakovski G.; Ghimire N.; Geprägs S.; Kling M.

Article.Authors: Brabant C.; Pollock L.; Geldmann J.; Bendixen M.; Comte L.; Farooq H.; Hébert K.; Lehner B.; Sayer C.; Iversen L.
Article.Abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Article.Authors: Faure Q.; Bounoua D.; Balédent V.; Gukasov A.; Garlea V.; Ribeiro A.; Rau J.; Petit S.; McClarty P.

Article.Title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
Article.Authors: Chandrasekhar S.; McMinimy R.; Manford A.; Wehri E.; Gee C.; Miller C.; Bingol B.; Kuriyan J.; Schaletzky J.; Rapé M.
Article.Abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. Article.Title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm

Article.Title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
Article.Authors: Thorp H.
Article.Abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

Whereas optical BICs have been realized in photonic systems, achieving electronic bound states embedded in a metallic background remains an ongoing challenge. In this study, we used scanning tunneling microscopy to identify two defect-induced electronic states that remain localized within the metallic continuum of Pd 5 AlI 2 , a two-dimensional van der Waals metal. Our calculations suggest that electron-hopping interference on the decorated checkerboard lattice of Pd 5 AlI 2 gives rise to a (quasi) flat band built from spatially localized eigenstates that are orthogonal to the dispersive continuum. Atomic defects within this frustrated lattice shift the associated flat-band localized states into the metallic continuum, forming robust, symmetry-protected BICs.

Article.Title: Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity
Article.Authors: Maity D.; Guha Ray P.; Buchmann P.; Charpin-El Hamri G.; Fussenegger M.
Article.Abstract: Lifestyle-related type 2 diabetes and associated obesity (diabesity) affect >2.5 billion people worldwide and impose nearly $3 trillion in annual health care costs. We developed an implantable, wirelessly powered electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization (ECHO) device containing platinum-decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in graphite felt that enabled selective, electrically tunable oxidation of blood glucose to renally cleared gluconate. In type 2 diabetic mice, wireless, low-power activation (0.75 volts, 10 milliamperes) restored glucose homeostasis within 1 hour, shifted metabolism from glucose to lipid utilization, reduced body weight and triglycerides, and increased circulating free fatty acids and ketone bodies without detectable hypoglycemia or adverse physiological, inflammatory, or behavioral effects during 6 weeks of treatment. Coupling this ECHO device to a commercial continuous glucose monitoring system enabled autonomous, smartphone-controlled, drug-free closed-loop management of experimental diabesity.

Article.Title: BAK and BAX form a multiprotein complex to drive mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Kim H.; Liao G.; Ta N.; Tu H.; Ramani S.; Chen C.; Li Z.; Tanno N.; Hsieh J.; Cheng E.
Article.Abstract: The apoptotic regulators BAX and BAK, once activated, form homo-oligomers to trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), activating the apoptosome and caspases. However, the molecular basis of mtDNA efflux remains unclear. We purified a macromolecular complex comprising BAK, BAX, activator BH3-only molecules, voltage-dependent anion channels 1 and 2 (VDAC1 and VDAC2), and prohibitins that released mtDNA from mitoplasts. BAX-BAK activation resulted in VDAC closure, mitochondrial calcium influx, and mtDNA efflux. Loss of VDAC1, VDAC2, or prohibitins prevented BAX-BAK activation–induced mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death without affecting MOMP or mitochondrial inner membrane herniation. These findings support differential regulation of cytochrome c and mtDNA efflux by distinct BAX-BAK complexes.

Article.Authors: Englander R.; Brugiolo M.; Devoucoux M.; Wu T.; Kostich M.; Leclair N.; Walawalkar I.; Kang H.; Park S.; Marches F.; Peeples M.; Chen P.; Banchereau J.; Yu P.; Salner A.; Banchereau R.; Palucka K.; Anczuków O.

Article.Title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet
Article.Authors: Young N.; Miller G.; Raynolds M.; Bueltmann H.; Lehman S.; Raberg J.; Seward K.; Pendleton S.; Andrews J.; Webber P.; Schaefer J.
Article.Abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The new LIS reached maximum dimensions in ~1960 CE, after which anthropogenic summer warming resulted in a negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.

Article.Title: Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain
Article.Authors: Schmidbauer P.; Nieder A.
Article.Abstract: Perceptual decision-making is well studied in mammals, but its operation in other vertebrates remains unclear. We show that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy. Recordings from the pallial endbrain reveal that direction-selective neurons encode the upcoming choice as early as about 70 milliseconds after stimulus onset and about 170 milliseconds before the response, with ramping activity scaling with sensory evidence and converging at response onset. These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decision-making circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control.

Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Kang Y.; Feng F.; Hu T.; Xu R.; Yu H.; He K.; Yang Z.; Wang Z.; Lau C.; Low Z.; Gu Q.; Liu J.; Wang H.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Nanochannels capable of fast and selective mass transport are central to applications in energy, resources, biomedicine, and the environment. However, extreme nanoscale confinement, often coupled with rigid channel environments, imposes substantial frictional and adhesive barriers, causing sluggish transport and constrained selectivity. Through a combination of experiments and simulations, we demonstrated that such dynamics reshape transport by promoting kinetic energy transfer and enabling more efficient molecular relays, thereby improving separation performance beyond current benchmarks. Article.Abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Article.Title: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting
Article.Authors: He M.; Tsui Y.; Peng R.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Vafek O.; Yazdani A.
Article.Abstract: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Article.Abstract: The power conversion efficiency (PCE) and stability of flexible perovskite solar modules (PSMs) are less than those of their rigid devices because surface hydroxyls desorption on flexible substrates, which disrupts self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anchoring and perovskite crystallization. Article.Abstract: We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Article.Title: Gate-tunable chiral spin mode in WSe <sub>2</sub> /WS <sub>2</sub> moiré superlattices
Article.Authors: Shan Z.; Su W.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Zhu S.; Xu Y.; Tang Y.
Article.Abstract: The interplay between many-body and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) effects can lead to previously unobserved phenomena in solids. Chiral spin modes (CSMs) are collective spin excitations that arise from such interplay and connect states with opposite chirality. Here, we report a gate-tunable CSM that occurs between conduction SOC-split minibands in near-0°-twisted WSe 2 /WS 2 bilayers. This mode manifests as a sharp resonance with giant Raman efficiency in the pseudovector-symmetry channel of the Raman spectra. The spin-flip nature is directly confirmed by the Zeeman effect, and the filling dependence indicates a charge-transfer insulator at unity filling. Article.Title: Empirical constraints on ice cliff calving
Article.Authors: Needell C.; Walker C.; Bassis J.
Article.Abstract: When calving cliffs at the margins of Earth’s ice sheets exceed a critical height, runaway retreat may be initiated in a process called the marine ice cliff instability. However, sufficiently tall ice cliffs have rarely been observed. To address this gap, we measured the characteristics of 15,330 ice cliffs across Earth’s ice sheet margins using laser altimetry. We show that cliff height is highly correlated with mélange thickness, water depth, and crevassing. We found that tall cliffs calve more rapidly than parameterizations assume, but dynamic thinning and retreat into regions with low ice thickness gradients prevent runaway retreat. These observations suggest that model projections may underestimate subannual rates of cliff calving, but that the potential for instability will depend sensitively on additional quantities, not cliff height alone.

Article.Authors: Bezold A.; Köbrich M.; Vollhüter J.; Feng L.; Amon L.; Karpstein N.; Wang Y.; Spiecker E.; Göken M.; Mills M.; Neumeier S.
Article.Abstract: Defects in crystals are usually considered to be consequences of deformation, but they can also be engineered as strengthening features. Article.Authors: Tan D.; Xie G.; Zhang L.; Xu Y.; Liu C.; Yuan H.; Chen Z.; Hu C.; You J.; Liu S.; Lutz E.; Kippenberg T.; Yu D.
Article.Abstract: Generating complex multimode entanglement is a central goal of quantum information science. Article.Abstract: In two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), the local electrostatic field of the chalcogen p -orbitals dictates the crystal field splitting of the transition metal d -orbitals, stabilizing diverse electronic states from semiconducting and semimetallic to exotic topological phases. Article.Title: To reverse nature loss, change what drives it
Article.Authors: Cooper D.; Díaz S.
Article.Abstract: This week, at the 17th Meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), delegates from 195 countries and the European Union are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, for a global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, an international set of goals and targets adopted in 2022 to tackle the biodiversity crisis. The urgent question before them is clear: What must change now to halt and reverse nature’s decline and put it on a path to recovery by 2030? COP-17 comes as international cooperation is under increasing strain. Extreme weather is intensifying, ecosystem deterioration is creating new security risks, and geopolitical tensions are rising. Yet nature’s decline does not pause for geopolitical instability—it deepens it. That makes effective multilateralism, with North and South as equal partners, more important, not less.
