Article.Title: Recent strengthening of eastern Pacific ENSO in the last millennium paleorecord
Article.Authors: Cole J.; Thompson D.; Dyez K.; Tripp C.; Tudhope A.; Lofverstrom M.; Stevenson S.; Okun J.; Lawman A.; Conroy J.; Overpeck J.; Jimenez G.; Edwards R.
Article.Abstract: The Pacific El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) generates climate extremes that endanger ecosystems, infrastructure, and human well-being worldwide. The response of this system to climate warming is poorly constrained, owing to both data scarcity and uncertainties in climate models. The geochemistry of Galápagos coral skeletons across the past millennium reveals a large recent increase in interannual variability of sea surface temperature in the eastern equatorial Pacific compared with that in existing paleorecords that exceeds simulated natural variability. This increase parallels rising global temperature and results from stronger El Niño events. Central Pacific coral data also show increased variability, although less distinctly than in the Galápagos. Article.Title: High-capacity associative memory in a quantum-optical spin glass
Article.Authors: Marsh B.; Schuller D.; Ji Y.; Hunt H.; Ganguli S.; Gopalakrishnan S.; Keeling J.; Lev B.
Article.Abstract: The Hopfield neural network stores memories using all-to-all-coupled spins and recalls those memories through equilibrium dynamics. Storing too many hampers recall because frustration causes an exponential number of spurious patterns to arise as the network becomes a spin glass. Despite this, we show that memory recall can be restored, and even enhanced, under quantum-optical nonequilibrium dynamics that convert spurious patterns into reliable memories. We experimentally observe associative memory with high storage capacity in a driven-dissipative spin glass made of atoms and photons. The capacity surpasses that of the Hopfield model under Hebbian learning by up to sevenfold in a 16-spin network. Atomic motion boosts capacity by dynamically modifying connectivity akin to short-term synaptic plasticity in neural networks, realizing a precursor to learning in a quantum-optical system.

Article.Abstract: Bacterial degradation of marine snow aggregates is a major component of global carbon cycling. These observations revealed systematic correlations between fountaining and summit inflation, enabling unprecedented quantitative forecasts. Article.Authors: Zhou Y.; Ge Y.; Harrison W.; Zhao H.
Article.Abstract: Enzymatic carbon-phosphorus bond formation is extremely rare in nature, limiting biocatalytic access to phosphorus-containing compounds that are widely used in pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Article.Authors: Evered S.; Xu M.; Li S.; Geim A.; Bonilla Ataides J.; Kalinowski M.; Bluvstein D.; Maskara N.; Kokail C.; Greiner M.; Vuletić V.; Lukin M.

Article.Abstract: Vast amounts of new data are fundamentally shaping how people manage their lives and do their work. The volume is overwhelming—Google Dataset Search discovers 2 million new datasets every month—and so are the uses by scientists, governments, and the public. Governments across the world are treating data as a strategic asset. But data alone are not enough. Infrastructure must be developed that can provide signals about which data are “fit for purpose” for the increasingly vast number of potential uses. Informed and appropriate use is, after all, the ultimate objective of making data available for the public good.

Article.Title: A fast radio burst at redshift 2, three billion years after the Big Bang
Article.Authors: Caleb M.; Nanayakkara T.; Stappers B.; Pastor-Marazuela I.; Khrykin I.; Glazebrook K.; Tejos N.; Prochaska J.; Rajwade K.; Mas-Ribas L.; Driessen L.; Fong W.; Gordon A.; Hoffmann J.; James C.; Jankowski F.; Kahinga L.; Kramer M.; Simha S.; Barr E.; Bezuidenhout M.; Deng X.; Lin Z.; Marnoch L.; Martin C.
Article.Abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients from extragalactic sources. Their frequency and polarization properties are affected by plasma and magnetic fields along the line of sight to Earth. We report radio observations of FRB 20240304B and near-infrared follow-up to identify its host galaxy. The host is a low-mass, clumpy, star-forming galaxy at redshift 2.148 ± 0.0013, corresponding to 3 billion years after the Big Bang. This FRB occurred during the peak of cosmic star formation and probes ionized gas over approximately 80% of cosmic history. The highly scattered burst emission implies that there is a population of FRBs that are undetected by current surveys.

Article.Authors: Jauhal A.; Cordazzo-Vargas B.; Sunko D.; Niroula P.; Deng L.; Toe L.; Muhammad A.; Pasha A.; Shafiq Y.; Iqbal N.; Khan W.; Mertens A.; Fehr K.; McDermid J.; Manus M.; Shu C.; Hampel D.; Shahab-Ferdows S.; Beggs M.; Lagerborg K.; Jain M.; Lachat C.; DeBoer M.; Van Eyk J.; Rodriguez N.
Article.Abstract: The mammary gland produces nutrient-rich human milk (HM), yet how mammary functional state shapes HM composition and infant outcomes remains poorly understood. Article.Title: A DNA Typewriter records the cell lineage history of a mouse, from zygote to late organogenesis
Article.Authors: Yu Q.; Kim H.; Seidel S.; Acosta-Clark J.; Martin B.; O’Connor K.; Daza R.; Gasperini M.; Nathans J.; Lam M.; Gamo E.; Vijay Kumar S.; Kuo L.; Lalanne J.; Simeonov K.; Pepper M.; Trapnell C.; Gray J.; Choi J.; Qiu C.; Shendure J.
Article.Abstract: Mammalian biology unfolds over time, within tissues and organs opaque to our eyes and instruments. We applied DNA Typewriter, a sequential molecular recorder, to record the cell lineage of a mouse over nearly two weeks of development. From one embryo, we reconstruct a time-calibrated, parsimony-supported, zygote-rooted phylogeny of 1.28 million transcriptionally profiled cells. A burst of editing unequivocally marks the daughters of the first cleavage, which serve as inline replicates. We quantify clonal dominance arising during gastrulation. Tree siblings share cell type far above chance; heterotypic siblings mark terminal differentiations. Temporal sweeps of clade co-occurrence recover a dated hierarchy of cell-type couplings; imputed labels for internal nodes recapitulate known state paths. A lineage-anchored ontogeny of mammalian development, long out of reach, is coming into view.

Article.Authors: Dailey-Chwalibóg T.; Mertens A.; Fehr K.; Shu C.; Jauhal A.; Manus M.; Deng L.; Toe L.; Muhammed A.; Pasha A.; Shafiq Y.; Iqbal N.; Khan W.; Nisar M.; Baxter J.; Beggs M.; Sundararaman N.; Van Eyk J.; Bode L.; Hubbard A.; Lagerborg K.; Jain M.; Hampel D.; Shahab-Ferdows S.; Allen L.

Article.Title: Interneurons and network activity in the cerebral cortex: a developmental dialogue
Article.Authors: Moissidis M.; Marín O.
Article.Abstract: The mammalian cerebral cortex undergoes profound functional changes during early postnatal development. During this period, neurons generate spontaneous electrical activity long before sensory experience, coordinating into distinct patterns of synchronous activity. Traditionally, neuronal activity has been viewed as instructing interneuron development by modulating transcriptional programmes, morphology and connectivity. However, accumulating evidence in rodents reveals that this relationship is bidirectional: cortical interneurons are not merely passive recipients of activity-dependent signals but also active architects of developing network dynamics. They regulate spontaneous activity transitions from gap-junction-mediated synchronous events to large, synaptically driven bursts, and later to sparse firing characteristic of mature circuits. Critically, different interneuron subtypes mature at distinct timelines and orchestrate transitions in network activity. Activity-dependent mechanisms, in turn, regulate interneuron wiring, programmed cell death, diversification and terminal differentiation. This reciprocal dialogue between interneurons and network activity is essential for establishing functional cortical circuits.

Article.Title: The endocannabinoid system and the ageing brain
Article.Authors: Zimmer A.
Article.Abstract: Ageing is accompanied by a progressive decline in homeostatic resilience that increases vulnerability to chronic disease, disability and cognitive impairment. Although unhealthy brain ageing can often be prevented by managing the underlying risk factors, the molecular, cellular and physiological mechanisms that connect risk factors to late-life brain dysfunction remain incompletely understood. This review examines the role of the endocannabinoid system in brain ageing. The endocannabinoid system is a short-range lipid signalling network that helps to maintain neuronal, glial, metabolic and inflammatory homeostasis. Endocannabinoid signalling follows a dynamic lifespan trajectory, with relatively high activity during early adulthood and functional decline during ageing. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of endocannabinoid system activity impairs several processes linked to hallmarks of brain ageing, including neuroinflammatory control, adult neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, cognitive performance, metabolic regulation and epigenetic stability. Conversely, low-dose Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) treatment can ameliorate several ageing-related brain phenotypes in old animals. However, clinical evidence in older humans remains limited, and the therapeutic potential of cannabinoid-based interventions requires further evaluation.

Article.Title: Sensing the skeleton: sensorineural regulation in bone
Article.Authors: Li Z.; Zhu M.; Thottappillil N.; Ramesh S.; James A.
Article.Abstract: The traditional view of bone tissue as an inert mechanical scaffold has been fundamentally revised over time. Perhaps nowhere is this more clear than in the emerging field of 'skeletal neuroscience', which has revealed the skeleton to be a densely innervated organ that senses and integrates mechanical, immune and metabolic stimuli. Here, we review recent evidence for bidirectional crosstalk between somatosensory neurons and the bone microenvironment, and highlight how techniques such as whole-tissue clearing, genetic tracing and single-cell transcriptomics have mapped osteo-neural interactions with molecular precision. Nerve growth factor (NGF)-TrkA signalling coordinates somatosensory nerve growth and survival during skeletal development and repair, yet the same pathways can drive pathological nerve sprouting, skeletal pain and disease progression in skeletal pathologies ranging from osteoarthritis to heterotopic ossification and bone malignancies. We further discuss neuro-immune-bone interactions, conserved neuroregulatory mechanisms in the skeleton, and emerging neuromodulatory strategies. Finally, we identify topics for future investigation, including the effects of age-related neural decline on the skeleton, sex differences in skeletal innervation and bone pain, and translational gaps between rodent and human biology, that may guide the design of precision medicine interventions.

Article.Title: Spatial single-cell mapping of transcriptional differences across genetic backgrounds in mouse brains
Article.Authors: Hemminger Z.; Tam G.; De Ocampo H.; Wang A.; Underwood T.; Xie F.; Zhao Q.; Song D.; Li J.; Dong H.; Wollman R.
Article.Abstract: Genetic variation can alter organ structure and function. Comparative statistical analysis of organs across genetic backgrounds requires spatial, single-cell, atlas-scale data in replicates. Here we introduce atlas-scale transcriptome localization using aggregate signatures (ATLAS), a scalable tissue mapping method that learns transcriptional signatures from single-cell RNA sequencing data, encodes them in situ with tens of thousands of oligonucleotide probes and decodes them to infer cell types and imputed transcriptomes. We validated ATLAS against direct MERFISH measurements of marker genes and through quantitative comparisons to four other technologies. We profiled 40 million cells across more than 400 coronal sections from central brains of five male and five female C57BL/6J mice and five male BTBR T+tf/J mice, an idiopathic autism model. Our analysis revealed more than 40 significant differences in cell-type distributions and identified 16 regional composition changes across male-female and B6-BTBR comparisons. ATLAS thus enables systematic comparative studies, facilitating organ-level structure-function analysis of disease models.

Article.Title: Enhanced cfDNA methylation profiling by detection and correction of jagged ends
Article.Authors: Wang R.; Hamilton E.; Almanza D.; Bonilla R.; Sugio T.; Hui A.; Tian F.; Phillips N.; Liu C.; Yoo C.; Alig S.; Rossi C.; Juul N.; Chen E.; Liu K.; Shen E.; Shi W.; Olsen M.; Kang X.; Nair V.; Wakelee H.; Shrager J.; Shi S.; Desai T.; Esfahani M.
Article.Abstract: Analysis of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation can enable noninvasive disease detection by leveraging tissue-specific epigenetic differences between malignant and nonmalignant cells. However, such analyses can be confounded by the repair of jagged DNA fragment ends during double-stranded sequencing library preparation, which introduces spurious methylation signals into cfDNA molecules. Here we present JEEPERS, a framework to detect and correct jagged-end-induced methylation errors while preserving duplex integrity and native methylation patterns. We showed high fidelity for measuring tumor burden and demonstrated allele-specific methylation differences at recurrent somatic mutations, revealing a link between adjacent CpG methylation and EGFR/TP53 driver and resistance mutations. We further demonstrated enhanced diagnostic performance across liquid biopsy applications, including tumor-type-specific methylation profiles, hemimethylation profiling, epigenetic-clock-based age estimation and cell type deconvolution. By faithfully correcting end-repair errors, JEEPERS provides a versatile framework for integrating mutations and methylation features in cfDNA at high resolution, enabling more precise molecular profiling and disease monitoring.

Article.Title: Advancing morphological profiling with self-supervised learning through comparative insights into representation learning of cellular perturbations
Article.Authors: Abdelmoula W.; Albuquerque T.; Jaensch S.; Pati P.; Van Dyck M.; Allen S.; Zhang L.; Mansi T.; Liao R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Self-supervised learning (SSL) enables scalable, label-free foundation models (FMs) that learn task-agnostic representations directly from images, bypassing cell segmentation and feature engineering inherent to classical morphological profiling. We present a large-scale evaluation of SSL FMs for image-based phenotypic profiling, covering contrastive (DINO), masked-based generative (MAE, iTPN) and hybrid (DINOv2) learning mechanisms, pretrained on all unannotated chemical perturbations from the Joint Undertaking for Morphological Profiling–Cell Painting (JUMP–CP) dataset (119,876 compounds, ~1.77 million images, 7 laboratories). Here we show that top-performing SSL models outperformed CellProfiler in compound-replicate retrieval on the held-out JUMP–Target2 set (302 annotated compounds, P ≤ 0.001). DINO and DINOv2 generalized across diverse perturbations and cell types, outperforming CellProfiler with 31–37% gains in site-averaged mean average precision for mechanism-of-action retrieval on EU-OPENSCREEN Bioactives (2,464 compounds), and consistently surpassing masked-based models across all benchmarks. This study provides a systematic assessment of SSL approaches for advancing morphological profiling and offers pretrained FMs to accelerate drug discovery.

Article.Title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain
Article.Authors: Santra K.; Barber K.; Logiacco F.; Frechou M.; Bellafard A.; Liou J.; Vaziri A.
Article.Abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca2+) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

Article.Authors: Zhu H.; Zhou Y.; Huang R.; Wang Y.; Hu Y.; Wang L.; Jin J.; Ye Q.; Liu X.; Wang Z.; Xie H.; Li J.; Pang D.; Liu S.
Article.Abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)-an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. By optimizing aptamers targeting the Zα domain of ADAR1 p150 and embedding them in a circular RNA scaffold, MARRS enables near-complete adenosine-to-inosine editing of RNA targets in cultured cells and mouse models, achieving efficiencies up to 100% in vitro and 84% in vivo. MARRS also exhibits remarkable versatility across a range of transcript targets while maintaining high specificity with minimal off-target effects. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform.

Article.Title: Continuous mass photometry by single-molecule trapping
Article.Authors: Loewenthal D.; Asor R.; Thorpe S.; Peters J.; Zouboulis K.; Kaplan M.; Thiele J.; Bardzil J.; Helmi S.; Burnap S.; Tan T.; Struwe W.; Benesch J.; Kukura P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The dynamic choreography of biomolecular interactions underpins the processes of life, but its direct observation remains challenging. Here we introduce continuous mass photometry, enabling hour-long, mass-resolved observation of individual biomolecules tethered to supported lipid bilayers, their complexes and interactions, with up to sub-kilodalton mass precision and millisecond temporal resolution. Our approach represents a quantitative time-resolved single-molecule measurement modality for studying complex biomolecular mechanisms in action.

Article.Title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics
Article.Authors: Martínez-de-Morentin X.; Khan S.; Maillo A.; Lehmann R.; Kiani N.; Lagani V.; Gomez-Cabrero D.; Tegner J.
Article.Abstract: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Benchmarking reveals substantial variation in performance across datasets, technologies and evaluation criteria, highlighting trade-offs among segmentation completeness, transcriptomic fidelity and biological interpretability. Cross-technology analyses further demonstrate that segmentation choice critically shapes downstream analyses, including cell-type specificity, transcript contamination and ligand-receptor inference. Together, our unified Nextflow pipeline provides a scalable foundation for standardized evaluation of segmentation and method selection in spatial transcriptomics.

Article.Title: CauTrigger: deciphering biological system state transitions by hierarchical causal decomposition
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Cai D.; Aihara K.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Biological systems exhibit complex hierarchical regulation, with interactions across multiple layers governing transitions between states. Identifying the causal architecture underlying these state transitions remains challenging because confounding can produce spurious associations in observational data. Here we present CauTrigger, a hierarchical deep latent variable model that integrates do-calculus to identify potential causal triggers and predict perturbation outcomes across multiple regulatory layers. By disentangling causal and spurious latent factors, CauTrigger recursively reconstructs the underlying regulatory hierarchy and enables interpretable reasoning from observational data. Across synthetic and real-world datasets with multilayer regulatory structures, CauTrigger outperforms existing methods in identifying causal triggers and forecasting system-level responses. Applied to single-cell multi-omics and gut microbiome datasets, CauTrigger prioritizes candidate causal triggers and uses in silico perturbations to generate testable hypotheses about biological state transitions and inform potential strategies for state navigation. Together, these results establish CauTrigger as a general-purpose framework for causal discovery in complex biological systems.

Article.Title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics
Article.Authors: Nimo J.; Fritzsche S.; Valdes D.; Trinh M.; Pentimalli T.; Klingeberg M.; Schallenberg S.; Klauschen F.; Herse F.; Florian S.; Rajewsky N.; Coscia F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

Article.Title: Multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM): a reconfigurable platform for high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy
Article.Authors: Chen B.; Millett-Sikking A.; Chang B.; Gałecki S.; Daetwyler S.; Jiou J.; Monistrol J.; Shen Q.; Zhou F.; Lin H.; Jenkins E.; Stein M.; Marlar-Pavey M.; Sturm G.; Li A.; Tang Q.; Feng B.; Diaz U.; Chen Y.; Shalizi A.; Gillich A.; Friedman J.; Tomer R.; Marshall W.; Shahmoradian S.
Article.Abstract: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) enables gentle, rapid and efficient volumetric imaging of biological specimens. Despite its potential, LSFM has fragmented into multiple variants, each narrowly optimized for specific samples or imaging regimes, limiting its broad applicability. Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains diffraction-limited performance across a refractive index range of 1.33 to 1.51. It is compatible with standard sample mounting, current clearing protocols and high-throughput 3D imaging. We leverage miOPM to image diverse biological specimens at multiple spatial scales. By expanding the adaptability and ease of use of LSFM, miOPM is poised to democratize advanced 3D imaging.

Article.Title: Recent developments of fluorescent proteins and biosensors driven by cross-disciplinary insights
Article.Authors: Gest A.; Mehta S.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Since the discovery and application of green fluorescent protein for use as an optical tag, fluorescent proteins (FPs) have changed the way we observe biological signals and processes. FP and fluorescent biosensor design has continued to advance, facilitated by new technologies and developments in chemistry, physics, engineering and screening technologies. We summarize some of the recent developments in FP engineering, focusing on insights that have led to improved photostability or longer wavelengths, among other improvements, highlighting mScarlet as a case study. We also discuss the engineering of new fluorescent biosensors, focusing on the ways in which screening, quantitative imaging, spatial resolution and multiplexing have been improved in recent years. Finally, we conclude with a perspective on what the future holds for the next generation of FPs and biosensors.

Article.Title: LoL-align: sensitive and fast probabilistic protein structure alignment
Article.Authors: Reifenrath L.; van Kempen M.; Kim G.; Kim S.; Radnezhad M.; Gilchrist C.; Mirdita M.; Steinegger M.; Söding J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The ubiquitous availability of protein structures permits replacing sequence alignment with more accurate and sensitive structure alignment algorithms. LoL-align maximizes a local log-odds score for proteins to be homologous, given their intra-protein C α − C α distances. Here we show that LoL-align is markedly more sensitive in detecting remote homologs than TM-align and Dali on single- and multidomain benchmarks and achieves better alignment quality at 5–20 × their speed. LoL-align is fully integrated into Foldseek.

Article.Title: MassNet: billion-scale AI-ready mass spectral corpus empowering scalable deep learning in proteomics
Article.Authors: A J.; Zhang X.; Zhang X.; Wei J.; Zhang T.; Deng Y.; Liu P.; Nie Z.; Yu Y.; Chen Y.; Dong N.; Gao Z.; Sun S.; Guo T.
Article.Abstract: Here we present MassNet, inspired by large-scale data corpora of text and images; MassNet is an artificial intelligence (AI)-ready data corpus for mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics. The corpus contains 1.5 billion tandem MS spectra from high-quality data-dependent acquisition (DDA) MS data across 35 species. Approximately 1.7 million peptide precursors are from human samples. We further present an AI-ready DDA data format called Mass Spectrometry DDA Tensor (MSDT) for compact and standardized storage, curation and reuse of data from multiple sources, which can be optionally converted to a Lightning Memory-Mapped Database for accelerated input/output in deep learning. On the basis of MassNet, we develop XuanjiNovo, a nonautoregressive transformer model that leverages a curriculum learning strategy for de novo peptide sequencing. XuanjiNovo achieves 38.35-143.57% improvement over state-of-the-art methods on human Astral data. MassNet also supports additional downstream tasks, including retention time prediction and PSM rescoring. MassNet represents a foundational MS-based proteomics data resource, marking a critical milestone for AI proteomics research.

Article.Title: Near-infrared photochromic miniprotein enables photoacoustic molecular imaging of acute inflammation and intracellular antigens
Article.Authors: Oliinyk O.; Xu Y.; Luo J.; Tokarchuk K.; Manoilov K.; van de Klashorst J.; Eyring M.; Wang M.; Chen M.; Song P.; Hickey J.; Yao J.; Verkhusha V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Using near-infrared photoswitchable photochromic genetically encoded probes, differential photoacoustic tomography (PAT) enables deep-tissue imaging with high resolution and sensitivity; however, current bacteriophytochrome-based probes are bulky multidomain proteins exceeding 55 kDa, which constrains their use for designing PAT molecular reporters. Here we engineer rsmiRFPnano, a compact cyanobacteriochrome-derived photoswitchable PAT probe. With a molecular weight below 19 kDa, rsmiRFPnano efficiently incorporates biliverdin, exhibits high extinction coefficients in both photochromic states and demonstrates robust performance in live cells. We established rsmiRFPnano-based reporters for NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, which display low basal activity and strong activation-dependent responses. These reporters effectively visualized acute inflammation using noninvasive PAT in vivo, further validated through cellular-level spatial omics mapping. We then created photoswitchable nanobody probes, rsNIR-Fbs, stabilized upon antigen binding and rapidly degraded otherwise, enabling selective photoacoustic immuno-imaging of intracellular antigens in vivo. Together, these results establish rsmiRFPnano as an ultracompact and versatile platform for molecular PAT.

Article.Title: Accurate and well-powered case–control analysis of spatial molecular data
Article.Authors: Reshef Y.; Sood L.; Curtis M.; Rumker L.; Stein D.; Palshikar M.; Nayar S.; Filer A.; Jonsson A.; Korsunsky I.; Raychaudhuri S.
Article.Abstract: As spatial molecular data grow in scope, there is a pressing need to identify disease-associated spatial structures. Current approaches typically make restrictive assumptions such as representing tissue regions by abundances of discrete cell types and samples by abundances of discrete niches; this risks overlooking important signals. Here we introduce variational inference-based microniche analysis (VIMA), a method combining deep learning with principled statistics to discover disease-associated spatial features with greater flexibility and precision. VIMA trains an ensemble of variational autoencoders to summarize the contents of every small tissue patch in a dataset via numeric 'fingerprints'. It uses these to define many data-dependent, overlapping 'microniches' and meta-analyzes them to identify microniches whose abundance correlates significantly with case-control status. We confirm VIMA's calibration, power and spatial accuracy in simulations. We then apply VIMA to spatial datasets spanning three diseases and spatial modalities, recapitulating known biology and identifying new spatial features of disease.

Article.Title: Serotonin signaling enhances phagocytosis by brain macrophages through Htr2b and alleviates brain injury after stroke
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Chen Y.; Cheng Y.; Li R.; Chen W.; Li Y.; Fan Q.; Zhou Y.; Huang T.; Xie W.; Guo Y.; Liesz A.; Wan J.; Ginhoux F.; Li P.
Article.Abstract: Brain myeloid cells, including infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and microglia, play critical roles in ischemic brain injury, clearing debris and shaping neuroinflammation and neurological outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, using single-cell RNA sequencing and fate mapping with an MDM-specific Ms4a3creERT2-Ai14 mouse line, we identified serotonin receptor Htr2b+ MDMs as a crucial cell population involved in resolving neuroinflammation within the ischemic penumbra. Htr2b+ MDMs significantly accumulate in the peri-infarct region and exhibit enhanced phagocytosis and inflammation-resolving gene signatures. Mechanistically, Htr2b activation promotes nuclear translocation of Tfe3, a key lysosomal regulator, enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and supporting phagocytic activity. MDM-specific Htr2b ablation impairs debris clearance, exacerbates neuroinflammation and ischemic injury, whereas pharmacological agonism or Tfe3 activation restores lysosomal biogenesis in brain MDMs and improves post-stroke outcomes. Thus we demonstrate a previously unrecognized Htr2b+ MDM subset that integrates serotonin signaling to license intrinsic phagocytic function, alleviating ischemic brain injury.

Article.Title: Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success
Article.Authors: Xiao J.; Daume J.; Salimpour Y.; Kurilenko N.; Mosher C.; Anderson W.; Valiante T.; Mamelak A.; Rutishauser U.
Article.Abstract: Controlling whether an experience is encoded into long-term memory and thus later remembered is a crucial aspect of memory. Here we examined single-neuron activity in the human brain while participants formed memories for novel visual stimuli and later retrieved them with confidence ratings. Category-selective amygdala neurons exhibited elevated firing during encoding of later remembered items relative to later forgotten items. This effect was predictive of the episodic aspect of the memory, was restricted to the preferred category of each cell, emerged earlier and was stronger in the amygdala compared to the hippocampus, and did not depend on stimulus valence and arousal. Successful memory formation was accompanied by enhanced spike-field coherence between the activity of amygdala category cells and hippocampal field potentials. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-specific recruitment of the amygdala predicts memory formation and suggest category cells in the right amygdala as a target for interventions to treat disorders affecting episodic memory in humans.

Article.Title: Circuit mechanisms for disentangled representations and generalization in the hippocampus
Article.Authors: Tang W.; Chang H.; Liu C.; Perez-Hernandez S.; Zheng W.; Park J.; Karaba L.; Oliva A.; Fernandez-Ruiz A.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how the heterogeneous activity patterns of individual neurons give rise to coherent population dynamics and cognition is a central challenge in neuroscience. In the hippocampus, neurons are tuned to spatial location, yet their activity is also modulated by multiple external and internal variables and appears to drift randomly over time, making it difficult to link hippocampal computations to behavior. By analyzing hippocampal population dynamics in behaving mice, we reveal a structured organization underlying the diversity of single-neuron responses-the hippocampus encodes different aspects of experience as disentangled variables represented in the co-activity dynamics of cell assemblies. The temporal and contextual components of these representations are governed by local inhibitory interactions and input-driven cell-assembly dynamics, respectively. Our findings reveal the circuit basis of disentangled hippocampal representations, offering a unifying geometric principle of population coding that supports flexible memory representations and enables rapid generalization of prior knowledge to new situations.

Article.Authors: Berghoff S.; Spieth L.; Vitale S.; Schlaphoff L.; Zirngibl M.; Junker N.; Dean A.; Liu L.; Damkou A.; Roth S.; Hurler C.; Hosang L.; Perez Anderson K.; Besson-Girard S.; Reich M.; Feiten A.; Huber L.; Müller C.; Kislinger G.; Dinkel L.; Nkeh Y.; Groh J.; Williams A.; Liesz A.; Schifferer M.

Our findings uncover a pro-inflammatory microglial state characterized by lysosomal dysfunction and increased myelin reactivity, highlighting a novel therapeutic target for chronic demyelinating disorders.

Article.Title: Microglial NUS1 deficiency drives dopaminergic neurodegeneration through intercellular iron dysregulation in Parkinson’s disease models
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Hong Y.; Wang X.; Huang X.; Ma Y.; Wang R.; Sun Q.; Sun H.; Hao Z.; Mu C.; Lu X.; Hu L.; Guo J.; Tang B.; Wang G.; Ren H.
Article.Abstract: The selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. NUS1, which encodes neurite outgrowth inhibitor-B receptor (NgBR), was recently identified as a PD risk gene. Here we show that NgBR is highly expressed in microglia, where its deficiency drives progressive PD-like motor deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration via the LCN2-SLC22A17 iron-transport axis in mice. NgBR deficiency in mouse and human microglia triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress and PERK-ATF4-NUPR1 signaling, which preferentially induces LCN2-mediated iron efflux over cytokine release. Subsequently, microglia-derived iron-loaded Holo-LCN2, but not iron-free Apo-LCN2, is internalized by SLC22A17, a receptor highly expressed in dopaminergic neurons, leading to iron overload and ferroptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of LCN2-SLC22A17 axis or ferroptosis alleviated dopaminergic neuron loss and PD-like symptoms caused by microglial NgBR deficiency in vitro and in vivo. Our findings identify disrupted intercellular iron homeostasis as a pathological driver of PD and highlight the LCN2-SLC22A17 axis as a potential therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Identification of candidate markers for the isolation of neuron-specific extracellular vesicles
Article.Authors: Ter-Ovanesyan D.; Whiteman S.; Gilboa T.; Kowal E.; Trieu W.; Iyer S.; Budnik B.; Babila C.; Han C.; Vance D.; Heimberg G.; Burgess M.; Keshishian H.; Carr S.; Regev A.; Church G.; Walt D.

We first selected transmembrane proteins suitable as cell type-specific EV markers based on gene expression and EV proteomic data. We developed a high-purity EV isolation method and cataloged the proteins present on EVs in human cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Using ultrasensitive immunoassays against several predicted neuron-specific proteins, we confirmed one marker, NRXN3, as present on EVs in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Finally, we developed efficient EV immuno-isolation methods and applied them to isolate NRXN3 + EVs. Our work provides a general methodology for the isolation of cell type-specific EVs, advancing the goal of using EVs to study brain diseases.

Article.Title: Sustained antidepressant-like effects of psychedelics through 5-HT2AR–β-arrestin signaling
Article.Authors: He L.; Tang L.; Cao D.; Duan W.; Yu J.; Zhang P.; Li H.; Wang Y.; Meng B.; Wang H.; Zhou Y.; Li W.; Li X.; Liu Z.; Zhang L.; Cheng J.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Psychedelics produce long-lasting antidepressant effects, but their hallucinogenic properties limit clinical use. Using structure-guided design of 5-HT2AR-β-arrestin-biased agonists, we identified β-arrestin signaling as a critical driver of prolonged antidepressant-like effects in mice. Here we show that the slow-dissociation kinetics of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) enable progressive accumulation of 5-HT2AR engagement during repeated low-dose administration, approaching the receptor occupancy achieved by an acute high dose while avoiding its high peak concentration. This kinetic separation sustains β-arrestin signaling while limiting robust Gαq-mediated Ca2+ responses. Consistent with this framework, repeated low-dose LSD and repeated low-dose psilocybin pretreatment followed by a high-dose psychedelic challenge produced sustained antidepressant-like behavioral effects in mice. In parallel, these regimens produced no detectable psychedelic-associated behavioral disruption in mice and cynomolgus macaques. Together, these findings uncover the signaling basis of sustained psychedelic efficacy and provide a rational framework for developing nonhallucinogenic psychedelic therapies for psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Behavioral genomics identifies Creld1 as a cross-modal regulator of somatosensation
Article.Authors: Jiang Y.; Huang W.; Yao H.; Chen Y.; Bi C.; Ye T.; Wang S.; Yin H.; Cui Y.; Xiao B.
Article.Abstract: Somatosensation is mediated by dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, which convert physical and chemical stimuli into electrical signals. However, the full repertoire of molecular components underlying somatosensation remains incompletely identified. Here we developed an efficient postnatal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout platform for interrogating DRG-expressed genes (such as Piezo2, Trpv1 and Scn9a) in mice using AAV9-mediated single-guide RNA delivery. Combining this approach with somatosensory behavioral assays, we performed a targeted screen of 20 genes and identified Creld1 as a cross-model regulator of somatosensation. Either single-guide RNA-mediated postnatal knockout or tamoxifen-induced Cre-mediated deletion of Creld1 in DRG neurons resulted in profound behavioral deficits in touch, temperature, pain and itch, whereas its overexpression enhanced touch and thermal responses. Mechanistically, CRELD1 functions as an auxiliary regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) for controlling DRG neuron excitability. Together, this work establishes a robust postnatal screening platform for behavioral genomics and identifies Creld1 as a master regulator of somatosensory function.

Article.Title: Network geometry shapes the transformation of task representations across the human cortex
Article.Authors: Chakravarthula L.; Ito T.; Tzalavras A.; Cole M.
Article.Abstract: Flexible cognition requires the brain to generalize across tasks while preserving task-specific information. Previous work showed that task representations are compressed in the association cortex and expanded in sensory and motor systems, but the mechanisms underlying these transformations are unclear. Here we test whether the geometry of intrinsic brain connectivity constrains how representations change between cortical regions. We analyzed functional MRI acquired during 16 diverse cognitive tasks together with activity flow modeling, finding that connectivity dimensionality predicts representational changes across the cortex. Low-dimensional connectivity compressed task representations and increased similarities across tasks, whereas high-dimensional connectivity expanded representations and supported conjunctive coding of task features. Activity flow modeling reproduced the observed compression-to-expansion pattern along the sensory-association-motor hierarchy and generated representational geometries that more closely matched targets than sources, consistent with transformation rather than transfer of information. These findings identify network geometry as a systems-level principle that shapes cortical representations and supports flexible cognition.

Article.Title: A corticohypothalamic circuit that mediates maternal awakening to pup cries
Article.Authors: Tang P.; Wu K.; Pan Y.; Yang S.; Cai Z.; Liang Y.; Mai F.; Chen P.; Peng M.; Wang Y.; Chen X.; Song C.; Ji X.; Liang F.
Article.Abstract: Maternal caregiving requires sensory vigilance to ensure offspring survival, particularly during sleep. Infant cries are salient sensory cues that reliably trigger maternal arousal and caregiving responses in both humans and dams, but the underlying neural circuitry remains poorly defined. Here we identify a corticohypothalamic circuit in mice that mediates maternal awakening in response to pup calls. We show that layer 6 (L6) neurons in the temporal association cortex and ectorhinal cortex (TeA/Ect) projecting to the preoptic area (POA) exhibit enhanced responsiveness to pup calls after the transition to motherhood. This enhanced responsiveness is mediated by increased expression of dopamine receptor D1 (Drd1) in TeA/Ect → POA neurons. Additionally, we reveal a pathway from the auditory thalamus to L6 TeA/Ect neurons that transmits pup cues during sleep. Together, these findings identify a dedicated neural circuit that grants infant cries privileged access to arousal systems, likely representing a fundamental adaptation for caregiving across mammals.

Article.Title: SIK3 controls synaptic localization of NMDA receptors by phosphorylating GluN1
Article.Authors: Lu R.; Morishita W.; Han X.; Temkin P.; Malenka R.; Südhof T.
Article.Abstract: Synaptic NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs) are central components of all neural computations. NMDAR levels critically vary between synapses but how the synaptic localization of NMDARs is controlled remains unclear. Here we show that SIK3, a serine-threonine protein kinase, localizes to synapses where it phosphorylates the obligatory NMDAR subunit GluN1 at a single site. This single phosphorylation event controls NMDAR recruitment to synapses. Genetic deletion of SIK3 severely and selectively decreases synaptic GluN1 levels by ~60% without altering AMPA-type glutamate receptor levels or inducing major transcriptional changes. Pharmacological inhibition of SIK3 impairs synaptic NMDAR responses within 45 minutes. Mutating the SIK3-phosphorylation site inhibits GluN1 synaptic recruitment. 'Sleepy', a gain-of-function mutation in SIK3 that increases sleep, selectively enhances synaptic NMDAR levels by increasing GluN1 phosphorylation. Thus, SIK3 phosphorylation of GluN1 provides a key signal for recruiting NMDARs to synapses.

Article.Title: Early lineage divergence segregates sensory and motor-associative identities in the thalamus
Article.Authors: Puche-Aroca L.; Andrés-Bayón B.; Wilson E.; Javed A.; Torregrosa-Mira A.; Rodríguez-Malmierca L.; López-Atalaya J.; López-Bendito G.
Article.Abstract: The thalamus integrates sensory, motor and associative functions through distinct nuclei, yet the developmental principles driving their specification remain unclear. Here we generate a spatiotemporal single-cell multiomic and spatial transcriptomic atlas of the embryonic mouse thalamus, combined with barcoding-based lineage tracing. We identify two major glutamatergic lineages, sensory-related and motor-associative, each governed by different gene regulatory programs and temporal dynamics. These lineages arise from spatially and molecularly distinct progenitor domains, revealing an early segregation of functional identities. Within the sensory lineage, we resolve branching sensory trajectories leading to first-order visual and somatosensory neurons, both emerging from a shared higher-order-like state. Using in silico predictions and in vivo perturbation, we identify Sp9 as a key regulator of visual thalamic fate. Together, our findings define the molecular architecture and developmental trajectories that underpin thalamic modality specification, providing a framework to understand how functional circuits emerge in the mammalian brain.

Article.Title: Dysregulated cholesterol trafficking through ABCA1 drives neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s disease
Article.Authors: Ma F.; Zhao X.; Wang X.; Fang S.; Xu S.; Wang M.; Liu Y.; Wang C.; Wang Q.; Lu M.; Cao L.
Article.Abstract: Although brain cholesterol dysregulation is implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), targeting cholesterol synthesis has shown limited efficacy. Here we identify ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) as a critical regulator of cholesterol homeostasis in PD. We show that ABCA1 expression is elevated in the substantia nigra of postmortem PD brains and in a PD mouse model, with regional analyses revealing preferential alterations in nigral and striatal circuits. Mechanistically, astrocytic ABCA1 drives excessive cholesterol efflux in mice, promoting neuronal cholesterol overload. In neurons, ABCA1 localizes to lysosomes, where it facilitates cholesterol import, leading to cholesterol accumulation, autophagy impairment and α-synuclein pathology. Genetic silencing of Abca1 in either astrocytes or dopaminergic neurons attenuates neurodegeneration and behavioral deficits in vivo. Furthermore, we identify magnesium citrate as an ABCA1 inhibitor and show that it reduces dopaminergic neuronal loss in a PD mouse model. Our findings identify an ABCA1-dependent cholesterol pathway underlying PD pathogenesis and support ABCA1 inhibition as a potential disease-modifying strategy.

Article.Title: An amygdala-mediated simulation-to-decision cascade aligns interbrain dynamics to solve social dilemmas
Article.Authors: Ni J.; Meng F.; Zhang C.; Tan H.; Zeng X.; Yang J.; Li H.; Qi Y.; Yan Y.; Zhang Y.; Zhang K.; Ma Y.
Article.Abstract: Mutual cooperation (MC) requires independent decision-makers to coordinate under uncertainty about each other's intentions. Using simultaneous intracranial electroencephalography from epilepsy-patient dyads playing a real-time iterated prisoner's dilemma, we identified neurocognitive mechanisms that enable interacting brains to align during mutual cooperation. Amygdala interbrain representational alignment (IBRA), similarity in fine-grained neural spectral patterns across partners, emerged selectively during MC and predicted trial-by-trial outcomes. Early θ-suppression-characterized IBRA reflected rapid, history-sensitive alignment, whereas later IBRA, characterized by low-frequency suppression and γ increases, supported coordinated commitment and action. Furthermore, mutual cooperation relied on an amygdala-mediated, simulation-to-decision cascade, operationalized here as a model-based prospective estimate of partner cooperation that guided self-choice. Amygdala low-frequency suppression tracked this prospective estimate of partner cooperation and θ-γ coupling linked this partner estimate to self-decision processes. Conditional cooperators strategically relied on partner tracking, whereas unconditional cooperators leveraged dispositional tolerance of uncertainty to transition into anticipatory neural alignment. These findings reveal the neural interdependency underpinning MC, redefining cooperation not as isolated decision-making but as a dynamic, interbrain, cognitive alignment.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal remodeling in habenula marks the onset of depression-related phenotypes
Article.Authors: Molina P.; Osypenko D.; Garnica J.; Amossé Q.; Bouteldja F.; Camelot L.; Mondoloni S.; Congiu M.; Kathe C.; Mameli M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

Article.Title: An aging-sensitive secreted phospholipase confers neuroprotection and cognitive resilience
Article.Authors: Vicidomini C.; Goode T.; Yu R.; Mehta I.; McAvoy K.; Beveridge C.; Randolph C.; Iyer S.; Victor M.; Leary N.; Evans L.; Steinbaugh M.; Lai Z.; Lyon M.; San Silvestre M.; Tosoni G.; Ayyildiz D.; Ho Sui S.; Yamamoto K.; Murakami M.; Salta E.; Tsai L.; Chopra G.; Sahay A.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive reserve theory posits that compensatory mechanisms during aging stave off cognitive decline and lower risk for Alzheimer's disease. Here, in a screen for hippocampal dentate granule cell (DGC) synapse loss-induced factors in mice, we identified a secreted phospholipase, Pla2g2f, whose expression increases in DGCs during aging and is associated with cognitive resilience in humans. Pla2g2f deletion in DGCs exacerbates aging-associated pathophysiological changes, including synapse loss, inflammatory microglia, reactive astrogliosis, impaired neurogenesis, lipid dysregulation, lipid droplet accumulation and hippocampal-dependent memory loss. Conversely, boosting Pla2g2f in DGCs during aging is sufficient to prevent these pathophysiological alterations in hippocampal-cortical circuits, protect memory and prophylactically modify trajectory of cognitive decline. Mutagenesis of the catalytic site of PLA2G2F prevented lipid droplet mobilization and reduction of reactive gliosis and inflammatory microglia. Neuronal PLA2G2F mediates intercellular signaling to decrease lipid droplet and cholesterol ester load in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia. Our findings implicate PLA2G2F as a compensatory neuroprotective broadcast signal that maintains lipid homeostasis to counteract aging-associated cognitive decline.

Article.Title: Periventricular gradient pathology is linked to ependymal reactivity and cell adhesion disruption in multiple sclerosis
Article.Authors: Groh A.; Afanasiev E.; Thevakumaran R.; Creeggan F.; Callahan-Martin L.; Bigotte M.; Yaqubi M.; Gertsvolf J.; Pei J.; Wu H.; de Vos J.; Aalders M.; Zandee S.; Prat A.; Rudko D.; Stratton J.
Article.Abstract: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-adjacent brain areas are especially vulnerable to diffuse degeneration in multiple sclerosis (MS). Surface-in gradients arising from CSF-borne cytotoxic factors have been proposed to predict disease relapses independent of white matter lesions. Yet, whether such factors disrupt ependymal cells to penetrate the ventricular border in MS remains unknown. Here, using ultra-high-field magnetic resonance imaging-guided histology, electron microscopy and single-nucleus multiomics, we found that ependymal pathology correlates with periventricular gradients and involves an immune-reactive state marked by transporter and junctional protein dysregulation. We further defined the gene regulatory networks underpinning the MS ependymal state and predicted ligands known to be enriched in MS CSF that could drive the emergence of this state. One of the candidates, IFNγ, increased murine ependymal permeability in vivo, indicating that CSF ligands can modulate ependymal function and regional inflammation. These findings identify CSF-driven ependymal dysfunction as a contributor to periventricular pathology in MS.

Article.Title: A half-center oscillator regulates sleep pressure
Article.Authors: Hasenhuetl P.; Sarnataro R.; Vrontou E.; Rorsman H.; Talbot C.; Brain R.; Miesenböck G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Changes in oscillatory neural dynamics reflect—but may not necessarily determine—transitions between sleep stages and variations in sleep pressure. Here we show that sleep-control neurons innervating the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila (dFBNs) produce slow-wave activity (SWA) that is causally linked to sleep. The dFBN ensemble contains bistable cells whose membrane voltages oscillate between hyperpolarized DOWN and depolarized UP states. The oscillations rely on interhemispheric competition of two half-centers connected by inhibitory glutamatergic synapses. dFBN-restricted interference with glutamate release disrupts SWA and baseline as well as rebound sleep, whereas the optogenetic replay of SWA induces sleep. dFBNs generate SWA throughout the sleep–wake cycle (despite mutual antagonism with arousing dopaminergic neurons) and adjust its power to sleep need via sleep history-dependent increases in excitability and homeostatic synaptic depression. The oscillatory format permits a continuous encoding of sleep pressure but requires mechanisms that convert the amplitude-modulated signal into binary sleep–wake states.

Article.Title: 5-HT2A receptors in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediate the neuroplastic but not the hallucinogenic effects of psilocybin
Article.Authors: Baker J.; Kogan E.; Ma S.; Lu J.; Zuo Y.
Article.Abstract: It is unclear how serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2ARs) in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons differentially contribute to psilocybin-induced hallucinations versus neuroplasticity. Here we show that psilocybin promotes synapse formation and maturation while accelerating the elimination of pre-existing synapses. Cell type-specific manipulation further demonstrated that 5-HT2AR signaling in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for psilocybin-induced synaptic remodeling but dispensable for the head-twitch response, a rodent proxy of hallucination.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal AI-based modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain using Seal
Article.Authors: Hao Y.; Park C.; Theesfeld C.; Troyanskaya O.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 regions, 30 cell types and 7 developmental stages. Seal predictions provide mechanistic interpretation by linking variants to transcriptional regulators in a spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole-genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing cell-type-specific and stage-specific effects. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.

Article.Title: Symmetries and continuous attractors in disordered neural circuits
Article.Authors: Clark D.; Abbott L.; Sompolinsky H.
Article.Abstract: A core challenge in neuroscience is reconciling idealized models with experimental data. Classical continuous-attractor models describe neural representations of continuous variables such as head direction. Symmetry in the weights generates a manifold of stable states, with tuning curves identical up to shifts. Rodent head-direction cells, by contrast, are markedly heterogeneous. Such heterogeneity, we show, is nevertheless compatible with these models. Here we build, directly from head-direction cell data, recurrent networks that behave as quasicontinuous attractors. A generative process then reproduces the heterogeneous tuning of these cells while making connectivity and dynamics tractable at large N. Although the weights appear disordered, they carry a circular symmetry whose eigenvalue degeneracies could signify continuous-attractor organization in connectome data. Dynamical mean-field theory recovers the ingredients of classical ring attractors, namely, Mexican hat interactions and a spontaneously broken symmetry producing bump states. Continuous-attractor mechanisms may thus operate in complex mammalian circuits.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: continuous attractors

Article.Title: Investigating molecular and hemodynamic effects of LSD in the human brain
Article.Authors: McCulloch D.; Larsen K.; Johansen A.; Reveles Jensen K.; Nykjær C.; Holze F.; Falck N.; Neufeld V.; Steenstrup E.; Skov-Andersen P.; Spanggård A.; Geisler M.; Randrup P.; Jensen P.; Shalgunov V.; Johansen S.; Nielsen M.; Andersen T.; Stenbæk D.; Svarer C.; Fisher P.; Knudsen G.
Article.Abstract: Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) is a potent psychedelic with increasing therapeutic interest, yet qualification of target engagement using in vivo neuroimaging has not yet been performed. Using simultaneous positron emission tomography-magnetic resonance imaging technology, we describe multiple brain actions of LSD in seven healthy volunteers blinded to LSD dose received. Here we show that LSD occupies 5-HT2AR with a high affinity and increases both global cerebral blood flow (CBF) and internal carotid artery flow. LSD also decreases global connectivity, which was negatively associated with changes in CBF. We observe an anticlockwise hysteresis loop between plasma drug levels and subjective effects, suggesting atypical pharmacodynamic mechanisms. We contrast our CBF and global connectivity findings and their relation in a separate cohort of 25 participants administered psilocybin, highlighting key consistencies and differences. By establishing the dose-occupancy relation of LSD in humans, our findings provide insights for the clinical development of psychedelic compounds and demonstrate unique neurophysiological effects that distinguish LSD from psilocybin.

Article.Title: Genome-wide analysis of common structural variants in Alzheimer’s disease identifies a risk-associated regulatory CCG repeat in FAM193B
Article.Authors: Cao H.; Fu Y.; Zhou X.; Duan Y.; Ip F.; Chen Y.; Hu S.; Liu S.; Kwok T.; Mok K.; Cheung T.; Hardy J.; Fu A.; Ip N.
Article.Abstract: Although Alzheimer's disease (AD) has a polygenic architecture, with numerous associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) identified, the contribution of structural variants (SVs) is unclear. In this study, using long-read (n = 11) and short-read (n = 3,190) sequencing data from the Chinese population, we show that common SVs contribute to AD heritability beyond common SNPs. We identify an expanded CCG repeat in the FAM193B promoter that shows a genome-wide significant association with increased AD risk (odds ratio = 2.20 per 10-repeat increase, P = 5.5 × 10-13). The expanded FAM193B-CCG repeat increases FAM193B expression and mediates the pleiotropic association between brain FAM193B expression and AD risk. Analyses of postmortem human brains and cultured neuronal cells show that elevated neuronal FAM193B expression is associated with DNA damage and cell death-related pathways. These findings establish the common FAM193B-CCG repeat as an AD risk genetic factor and highlight the contribution of common SVs to AD heritability.

Article.Title: Alzheimer’s disease target and drug discovery by leveraging multiomics and electronic health data
Article.Authors: Hou Y.; Li Y.; Zhang P.; Lorincz-Comi N.; Gohel D.; Fan F.; Qiu Y.; Yang J.; Chen X.; Song W.; Yang X.; Tan Z.; Liu Z.; Fang X.; Rivera Paz I.; Martin W.; Feng Y.; Zhou Y.; Xu J.; Dou L.; Border J.; Zhang H.; Mazique J.; Hwang S.; Roman R.
Article.Abstract: Despite prolific genomic data from individuals with Alzheimer's disease (AD), translation into treatments has lagged. Here we applied Mendelian randomization to multiple AD genome-wide association studies and functional multiomics datasets to nominate druggable targets, identifying 19 targets for individuals of European ancestry and 7 for African ancestry. This included epoxide hydrolase 2 (EPHX2), for which we identified a protective missense variant (p.Arg287Gln). Experiments in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons and cerebral organoids from patients with AD validated the protective role of p.Arg287Gln via reduced levels of EPHX2 and phosphorylated tau (pTau-181). Pharmacological inhibition of EPHX2 improved cognitive performance in the 5xFAD mouse model of AD. Finally, by leveraging electronic health data from 111,680 patients with mild cognitive impairment, we identified 12 drugs associated with reduced AD incidence, including trazodone (targeting ADRA1A) and baclofen (targeting GABBR1). Thus, integrating multiomics data, functional validation and electronic health data identifies new approaches for treating AD.

Article.Title: Modality-specific reactive and predictive responses in the human superior colliculus
Article.Authors: Chen D.; Barton-Zuckerman M.; Kross Z.; Kragel P.; Savoca P.; Wald L.; Bianciardi M.; Wager T.; Choi J.; Zhang J.; Quigley K.; Satpute A.; Barrett L.; Theriault-Brown J.
Article.Abstract: Inspired by recent theoretical work emphasizing predictive neural processing, we tested whether a midbrain structure for multimodal sensory integration-the superior colliculus-would show predictive responses to both visual and somatosensory stimulation. A multi-stage experimental design allowed us to test predictive activity in the human superior colliculus while 7-Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) allowed us to map its sensory response across superior colliculus layers (N = 80). As expected from non-human animal work, visual and somatosensory stimulation elicited distinct depth-dependent responses. We also observed a predictive response: these same modality-specific and depth-dependent effects occurred during task periods preceding direct stimulation, when sensorimotor input was identical between visual and somatosensory conditions. Further analyses rule out cross-trial carryover and show corresponding effects in the thalamic sensory nuclei. Here our results confirm that, in humans, the superior colliculus is sensitive to both visual and somatosensory input, and they demonstrate that it carries predictive signals for upcoming sensory events.

Article.Title: Astrocytes regulate axonal mitochondrial transport deficits in C9ORF72 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis motor neurons
Article.Authors: Stavrou M.; Heffernan Á.; Carter R.; Dando O.; Jiwaji Z.; Burr K.; Nanda J.; Villarroel-Campos D.; Masoud Abdelhafid A.; Cholewa-Waclaw J.; Soong D.; Story D.; Schiavo G.; Hardingham G.; Chandran S.; Selvaraj B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Disrupted axonal transport and astrocyte dysfunction are implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here we show these processes are linked—human-induced pluripotent stem-cell-derived astrocytes carrying the C9ORF72 mutation disrupt mitochondrial axonal transport and mitochondrial function in cocultured motor neurons (MNs). Conversely, isogenic gene-corrected astrocytes or boosting astrocytic mitochondrial bioenergetics rescue axonal mitochondrial transport deficits in C9ORF72 MNs. Our results delineate a non-cell-autonomous role for astrocytes in regulating mitochondrial transport along axons in ALS models.

Article.Title: Human claustrum neurons encode uncertainty and prediction errors during aversive learning
Article.Authors: Hu M.; Dalvit R.; Medina-Pizarro M.; Dougherty M.; Zhou Y.; Barreto-Nieves J.; Obaid S.; Afrasiyabi A.; Krishnaswamy S.; Kaye A.; Günel M.; Krystal J.; Sheth K.; Gu X.; Pittenger C.; Wise T.; Damisah E.
Article.Abstract: Flexible behavior depends on continuous updating of internal models, yet the neural circuits coordinating this process remain poorly understood. The claustrum, which is reciprocally connected to nearly the entire neocortex, is uniquely positioned to influence cortical processing. Here we report single-neuron recordings from the human claustrum during aversive learning, with anterior cingulate cortex and amygdala recordings for comparison. Claustrum and anterior cingulate neurons displayed structured, task-related responses. Distinct subpopulations encoded stimulus onset and action-contingent outcomes, with outcome representations diverging between regions. Critically, both regions encoded model-derived latent variables, including uncertainty and prediction error, but with different temporal profiles; only the anterior cingulate carried uncertainty signals during the intertrial period, whereas both regions encoded uncertainty and prediction error during the active-avoidance period. By contrast, the amygdala showed minimal latent-variable modulation. These findings provide evidence that human claustrum neurons track higher-order cognitive variables not directly observable from sensory input and reveal dissociable roles for the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex in tracking latent task states.

Article.Title: Phase separation of SMARCAL1 orchestrates epigenetic reprogramming and methionine metabolism to foster radioresistance and immunosuppression
Article.Authors: Zheng C.; Cui Q.; Li J.; Chen J.; He L.; Zhang X.; Liu Z.; Chen T.; Lyu Y.; Liang C.; Ma S.; Li M.; Shi X.; Jia Y.; Li Z.; Wang X.; Xu W.; Li B.
Article.Abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation has emerged as a key mechanism governing cellular organization and function, but its role in pathological processes and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely elusive. Here we show that SMARCAL1 forms nuclear condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation to enhance histone H4 lactylation and chromatin accessibility. This SMARCAL1‑driven epigenetic reprogramming not only facilitates the recruitment of DNA repair proteins, leading to radiotherapy resistance, but also regulates methionine adenosyltransferase transcription, thereby promoting the methionine cycle and inducing T cell exhaustion and immune therapy tolerance. Intriguingly, SMARCAL1 is identified as a biomarker for predicting therapy response and patient stratification. Importantly, pharmacological disruption of SMARCAL1 condensates by digoxin sensitizes tumours to both radiotherapy and anti-PD1 therapy in multiple models. These findings highlight the crucial role of condensates centred on SMARCAL1-histone H4 in governing DNA repair and immune microenvironment remodelling, as well as propose an innovative strategy to overcome radioimmunoresistance.

Article.Title: Methylated eEF1A selectively decodes mRNA to shape cancer proteomes
Article.Authors: Liu S.; Cruz-Navarrete F.; Hausmann S.; Szkop K.; Ikram S.; Brady R.; Lu X.; Dong R.; Vu J.; Flores N.; Zahn E.; Thompson J.; Garcia B.; Larsson O.; Topisirovic I.; Blanchard S.; Gozani O.; Mazur P.
Article.Abstract: Although mRNA decoding efficiency influences protein synthesis, it remains unknown whether the translation elongation machinery harbours intrinsic mechanisms that selectively modulate codon decoding to shape proteomes. Here we show that METTL13-catalysed dimethylation of the elongation factor eEF1A at lysine 55 (eEF1AK55me2) enhances decoding of select codons, preferentially increasing pro-oncogenic protein synthesis to promote tumorigenesis and targeted therapy resistance. Proteomic profiling and single-molecule imaging reveal that eEF1AK55me2 increases decoding efficiency, particularly for under-represented codons with weak wobble-position base pairing. In cancer cells, METTL13 knockdown reduced translation of oncogenic mRNA enriched in eEF1AK55me2-dependent codons, including KRAS; synonymous recoding with eEF1AK55me2-independent codons reversed this effect. METTL13 loss inhibited the growth of KRASG12C inhibitor (sotorasib)-resistant lung adenocarcinoma syngeneic tumours and patient-derived xenografts. In relapsed autochthonous KRASG12C-driven lung adenocarcinoma, METTL13 ablation mitigated sotorasib resistance and significantly extended survival in vivo. Among patients receiving a KRASG12C inhibitor, inferred METTL13 activity was associated with inferior clinical response. These findings identify an eEF1AK55me2-mediated mRNA decoding mechanism promoting selective oncogenic protein synthesis and suggest METTL13 targeting may counteract KRAS-inhibitor resistance.

Article.Title: Motile vesicles (MoVes) are a cancer cell migration-associated extracellular vesicle population
Article.Authors: Tsering T.; Nadeau A.; Ghasemi M.; Mousovich-Neto F.; Tobias G.; Chen Y.; Kienzle L.; Dickinson K.; Douanne N.; Serganova I.; Zappasodi R.; Matei I.; Lyden D.; Burnier J.
Article.Abstract: Migrating cancer cells release diverse extracellular vesicles (EVs) that carry cargo capable of influencing tumour progression and intercellular communication. However, the mechanisms by which intracellular components are incorporated into EVs remain poorly understood. Here we identify and characterize a previously undescribed population of large EVs (2-5 μm), termed motile vesicles (MoVes), that are generated during active cancer cell migration and associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Comparative analyses across EV populations show that MoVes display distinct ultrastructural features, molecular composition and sedimentation behaviour. Live-cell imaging and scanning electron microscopy reveal that MoVes arise from trailing-edge retraction during mesenchymal migration and are actively shed by cancer cells but rarely by non-transformed cells. MoVes contain genomic DNA spanning the genome of the parent cell, recapitulating its mutational landscape, as well as organelles and proteins associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Moreover, MoVes-associated mitochondrial cargo can enhance oxidative phosphorylation in recipient cells. Together, these findings identify MoVes as a cancer cell migration-associated EV population capable of disseminating genomic DNA and organelles.

Article.Title: Tubulin acetylation regulates nuclear shape fluctuations and DNA repair
Article.Authors: Wallis S.; Tse W.; Donker L.; Baxter A.; Dave N.; Weber A.; Gillespie E.; Chen B.; Burden J.; Friskes A.; Medema R.; Charras G.; Calado D.; Godinho S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Genome stability depends on the accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). While chromatin-based mechanisms have been well studied, emerging evidence reveals that nuclear mechanics actively shape repair outcomes, although the mechanisms remain unclear. Here we identify microtubule acetylation as a regulator of nuclear mechanics that promotes DSB repair via homologous recombination (HR). DNA damage induces progressive tubulin acetylation, leading to displacement of the perinuclear vimentin cage. Loss of the vimentin cage softens the nucleus and renders the nuclear envelope responsive to microtubule forces, which drives transient nuclear shape fluctuations, localized DSB mobility and repair. Inhibiting tubulin acetylation abolishes these fluctuations, restricts DSB mobility and negatively impacts the homology search during HR, leaving non-homologous end joining intact. Consequently, persistent DSBs coalesce and cluster at the nuclear periphery, triggering cell-cycle arrest and senescence and increasing sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents. Removal of the vimentin cage is sufficient to rescue these effects, with restored nuclear fluctuations and repair efficiency. Thus, we propose that nuclear fluctuations act as a mechanical strategy to accelerate error-free repair. These findings reveal how cytoskeletal forces shape nuclear function and establish nuclear fluctuations as a fundamental principle for maintaining genome stability.

Article.Title: A three-dimensional human co-culture system reveals reciprocal embryo–endometrial adaptation at implantation onset
Article.Authors: Bi Y.; Tu Z.; Zhang X.; Hu J.; Chen C.; Xu Y.; Zheng Y.; Song Y.; Chen Y.; Lin T.; Wang H.; Che X.; Li J.; Huang G.; Gao S.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Human embryo implantation begins with dynamic, tightly coordinated interactions between embryonic and endometrial compartments, yet the earliest trophoblast-endometrial interface dynamics remain poorly resolved in vivo. Here, using an endometrial assembloid-based three-dimensional co-culture system with human blastoids and natural blastocysts, we analyse implantation-like progression by time-series single-cell transcriptomics and functional perturbation. Importantly, we identify co-culture-induced trophoblast subsets marked by SDC1+MMP7+ and enriched for transcriptional features associated with extracellular matrix remodelling and cell migration. These subsets are reproducibly detected across independent implantation-like systems, emerge specifically within a decidualized stromal co-culture context, and are further linked to stromal-derived CSF3 signalling by intercellular communication analysis and targeted perturbation. In parallel, the endometrium displays transcriptional changes associated with enhanced decidualization and a glandular hypersecretory transition. Together, our study provides a tractable framework for dissecting reciprocal embryo-endometrial adaptation at the onset of implantation.

Article.Title: Keratin 9 regulates mechanosensitive YAP1 signalling in palmoplantar epidermis
Article.Authors: Steiner S.; Horst E.; Chiu E.; Athaiya M.; Johnson C.; Shen J.; Kerns M.; Kirma J.; McCarthy R.; Shah S.; Sarig O.; Samuelov L.; Sprecher E.; O’Toole E.; Gudjonsson J.; Mehta G.; Iglesias-Bartolome R.; Coulombe P.
Article.Abstract: The palmoplantar epidermis, in adapting to the exceptional mechanical strain it bears during locomotion, is histologically and molecularly distinct from other skin body sites. The mechanisms specifying and maintaining its unique identity remain incompletely defined. Here we identify the type I keratin 9 (KRT9/K9), a protein uniquely expressed in palmoplantar epidermis, as a key modulator of mechanosensitive YAP1 signalling in response to postnatal mechanical compression. K9 loss-of-function variants driving KRT9-pEDD, a palmoplantar epidermal differentiation disorder, result in aberrant YAP1 subcellular partitioning and elevated levels of the stress-induced keratin 16 (KRT16/K16). Krt9 null mice recapitulate these molecular phenotypes as early as postnatal day 3. We further identify dynamic, YAP1-dependent regulation of Krt16/K16, upstream of and necessary for Krt9/K9 expression, during early postnatal development in situ and in response to mechanical compression of keratinocytes ex vivo, highlighting the role of mechanical stress in epidermal specification. Mechanistically, K9 interacts with the YAP1 binding protein 14-3-3σ and sequesters YAP1 in the cytoplasm, inhibiting its transcriptional activity; these functions are disrupted by KRT9-pEDD-causing variants in K9. Finally, we show that genetic or pharmacological inhibition of YAP1 ameliorates palmoplantar keratoderma in Krt9 null mice. These findings reveal a role for mechanical cues in specification and maintenance of palmoplantar skin and suggest new therapeutic interventions for inherited palmoplantar epidermal differentiation disorders.

Article.Title: The rise of reducing reagent-resistant TfR1 dimer marks ferroptosis
Article.Authors: He J.; Kelleher M.; Veeckmans G.; Zhang Y.; Reynolds L.; Tanczos H.; Huang Z.; McLaughlin B.; Martinez Molina M.; Lightburn A.; Zamarro M.; Huang W.; Owusu S.; Walravens M.; Willemart C.; Hassannia B.; Pope L.; Gager C.; Vaughan A.; Wang Z.; Weaver S.; Boggess W.; Lu X.; Papagiannakopoulos T.; Flores-Mireles A.
Article.Abstract: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent type of cell death caused by excessive membrane lipid peroxidation. It remains a challenge to detect ferroptotic cells, especially in in vivo settings, hindering translational studies. Here we discover that a reducing reagent-resistant (3R) dimer of the transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) is a highly specific indicator for lipid peroxidation. The 3R dimer is elevated in cells when ferroptosis is induced, either by pharmacological agents or by genetic perturbations. Furthermore, the 3R dimer can be used to detect disease-associated ferroptosis in tissue and in extracellular vesicles isolated from mouse or patient plasma. Given the near-ubiquitous expression of TfR1, we posit that the 3R dimer may function as a ferroptosis marker with widespread potential utility for basic and translational studies.
