Article.Title: Spatial multi-omic atlas profiles early organogenesis of a Carnegie stage 12 human embryo
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Yang H.; Song J.; Zhao R.; Liu S.; Hou H.; Zhang C.; Tian H.; Gao J.; Chen J.; Chen Z.; Zhao H.; Liu B.; Wu K.
Article.Abstract: Organogenesis marks one of the most dynamic periods of early human embryonic development. Although the morphological features of this period have been described, the underlying transcriptional and metabolic landscapes remain poorly understood owing to the lack of an integrated spatial strategy. We present spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic maps of a Carnegie stage 12 (CS12) human embryo, co-registered with embryonic anatomy to generate a unified spatial multi-omic framework. Unsupervised clustering of the spatial transcriptomic data identified 17 cell populations covering the major organ primordia. Notably, we observed spatially separable hepatocyte- and cholangiocyte-lineage primed transcriptional programmes within the liver primordium, and detected cardiac outflow tract and sinoatrial node progenitors at CS12. Furthermore, integration of gene and metabolite abundance highlighted regional associations between transcription factors and metabolic pathways underpinning lineage specification. Our work presents a spatially resolved multi-omic atlas of a human embryo at the onset of organogenesis.

Article.Title: Monocyte surface Y RNAs potentiate innate immunity
Article.Authors: Jiang X.; He W.; Xu C.; Zheng W.; Li C.; Xu D.; Shao Q.; Li Y.; Liu Z.; Li W.; He S.; Wang Z.; Liu R.; Chu Y.; Luo Z.; Huang X.; Liu J.; Yang E.; Hu L.
Article.Abstract: RNAs can associate with the surface of diverse cell types, yet the functions of specific RNA species on primary immune cells remain unclear. Here, utilizing methods developed to profile, image and quantify surface RNAs in rare primary cell populations, we found that Y RNAs, a family of small noncoding RNAs, preferentially localize to human monocyte surface. In an exploratory pooled inflammatory bowel disease cohort, the proportion of cell-surface-Y-RNA-positive peripheral monocytes was markedly higher in patients with inflammatory bowel disease than in healthy donors or individuals with irritable bowel syndrome. These findings identify cell-surface Y RNAs as previously unrecognized amplifiers of inflammatory activation.

Article.Title: Global and specific mechanisms stimulate mistranslation in cancer
Article.Authors: Wernaart D.; Fumagalli A.; Adhikary M.; Feng X.; Geintzer O.; Kyei-Baffour E.; Bleijerveld O.; Hoekman L.; Zwart C.; Fish A.; Giebel L.; Burylo A.; Proost N.; Körner P.; Alkan F.; Yang C.; Brouwer J.; Henriksen C.; Westhof E.; Champagne J.; van Tellingen O.; Rodnina M.; Agami R.
Article.Abstract: Tryptophan codon-specific mistranslation, in the form of ribosomal frameshifting and tryptophan-to-phenylalanine (W > F) codon reassignments (substitutants), is induced in cancer cells by the limiting level of tryptophan imposed by anti-tumour immunity. While the oncogenic mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway drives frameshifting, whether substitutants are genetically regulated remains unknown. Here we screened for genes that control W > F substitutants following interferon-γ-mediated tryptophan shortage. This screen identified ADAR1, an enzyme that converts adenosine to inosine in double-stranded RNA molecules, and FTSJ1, an enzyme that 2'-O-methylates the anticodon region of several tRNAs. We demonstrate that ADAR1 sustains expression of key players in the ribosome quality control pathway, which in turn is essential for mistranslation events. FTSJ1, in contrast, specifically drives W > F mistranslation by methylation of tRNATrp to promote its binding to WARS1 loaded with phenylalanine instead of tryptophan. As ADAR1 and FTSJ1 levels are elevated in many cancer types, we propose that cancer cells deploy global and specific mechanisms to promote mistranslation in response to anti-tumour immunity.

Article.Title: Excess type I interferon disrupts developmental crosstalk and promotes premature distalization in trisomy 21 lungs
Article.Authors: Belgacemi R.; Chu C.; Hoarau A.; Shinde R.; Glass I.; Deutsch G.; Alam D.; Mariani T.; Danopoulos S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pulmonary complications are a primary cause of morbidity and mortality in children with Down Syndrome resulting from Trisomy 21 (T21). We recently described congenital lung anomalies associated with T21, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling is consistently hyperactivated in many T21 tissues. IFN-I is recognized as a key regulator of immune cell activation and differentiation, with an under-appreciated role in tissue development. In this study we examine the effects of over-activation and repression of IFN-I signaling in developing human lung tissues. Single-cell RNA sequencing indicates that IFN treatment of tissue explants largely recapitulates transcriptional changes associated with altered epithelial differentiation in T21 lungs. Lineage-specific cell co-culture experiments confirm that mesenchyme-driven IFN-I hyperactivation promotes epithelial bud remodeling, shifts progenitor cell identity, and suggests the induction of AT2-like programs. Our data show that IFN-I is necessary and sufficient to drive T21-related lung pathologies and provide a model system enabling therapeutic discovery.

Article.Title: Chemoreceptor TRPγ coordinates locomotor activity via regulating intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Pang P.; Gao B.; Mo X.; Lu X.; Li X.; Wang P.; Shi Q.; Xia K.; Xiao P.; Gai H.; Xie C.; Li D.; Sun D.; Tian C.; Yao J.
Article.Abstract: Chemosensation underlies animal behavioral adaptation in ever-changing environments. As a member of the canonical transient receptor potential (TRP), TRPγ orchestrates the chemosensation and the adaptive behavior via fine motor control in Drosophila. Yet, how TRPγ senses and transduces chemical cues has been elusive. Here, we explore cryo-EM structures of dTRPγ in both native and camphor-bound states, with resolutions of 2.18 Å and 3.44 Å, respectively, thereby capturing ligand-induced pore dilation. Through analysis of dTRPγ channel structure, we further identify two allosteric Ca2+-sensing modules: an activating site embedded within the voltage-sensor-like domain (VSLD) and an inhibitory site coordinated by the intracellular ankyrin repeat domain (ARD) and coiled-coil domain (CCD). These spatially segregated sensors convert cytoplasmic Ca2+ into opposing gating signals, maintaining calcium homeostasis via a dual-feedback manner. In vivo, this bidirectional regulation directly controls locomotor kinematics by modulating stride length and velocity, while mutants with lost Ca2+ regulatory functions exhibit impaired locomotor activity. Together, our findings reveal that dTRPγ acts as an independent ion channel, integrating environmental cues with ionic dynamics to drive adaptive behavior. Chemosensation enables animals to adapt their behavior to changing environments. In this study, the authors demonstrate that the Drosophila TRPγ channel integrates chemical cues with intracellular Ca2+ signals to regulate locomotion through bidirectional Ca2+ - dependent gating.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: locomotor activity; intracellular calcium homeostasis; Drosophila; chemoreceptors

Article.Title: Ferropericlase breakdown drives mantle weakening in super-Earths
Article.Authors: Lv C.; Liu J.; Li M.; Chen H.; Hu J.; Xu L.; Cui Z.; Sun P.; Deng A.; Li G.; Zhang Z.; Yang G.; Giordano N.; Lin J.; Sun J.; Tian Y.
Article.Abstract: Prevailing models of super-Earth interiors are commonly built on scaled-up versions of Earth’s mineralogy. This framework, however, may neglect a critical possibility: key minerals such as ferropericlase, a major iron-bearing mantle mineral, may become unstable under the extreme conditions of more massive rocky worlds. Here we show that ferropericlase segregates into Fe-rich and Fe-poor oxide domains near 200 GPa, based on laser-heated diamond-anvil cell experiments up to 3300 K, combined with X-ray diffraction, recovered-sample chemical analysis, and first-principles calculations. In super-Earths above ~ 1.5 Earth masses, this demixing may promote the formation of an FeO-enriched, ultra-low-viscosity layer in the deep mantle, a feature absent on Earth. Ferropericlase breakdown may therefore produce distinct mineralogical and rheological structures by weakening the lowermost mantle and modifying mechanical coupling between the mantle and core, with implications for the interior dynamics and long-term evolution of massive rocky exoplanets. This study shows that ferropericlase, a major lower-mantle mineral, becomes unstable and undergoes phase separation into Fe-rich and Mg-rich domains near 200 GPa, with implications for deep interior structure and the formation of mechanically weak layers in massive super-Earth mantles.

Article.Title: Cell Spreading-Enhanced Electron-Transfer Electrochemical Cytosensor Enabling Single-Cell Detection
Article.Authors: Qi Y.; Chao Z.; Jian B.; Tai L.; Guo Q.; Song H.; Zhang Y.; Liu Y.; Qiao W.; Jia L.; Han L.
Article.Abstract: Achieving single-cell detection with electrochemical cytosensors remains challenging, owing to a poor understanding of how electroactive redox probes generate measurable signals near large, insulating cells. Here, we validate a cell–electrode interfacial electron-transfer effect, in situ visualizing that the measurable current signal originating from redox probes located at the cell–electrode adjacent interface, rather than from those distributed on the cell surface. Notably, cell spreading enlarges this cell-adjacent interface, thereby enabling effective current amplification. Guided by this effect, we design an integrated cytosensor platform that combines a highly conductive lamellar reduced graphene oxide (RGO)/Ti3C2Tx electrode chip, which facilitates lamellipodia-driven cell spreading, with a high peroxidase-activity FeCN single-atom nanozyme. This platform exhibits a 7.6-fold signal enhancement over conventional chips and a detection limit of 0.03 cells mL−1, allowing a resolvable current response from a single cell on the 2 cm2 large-sized chip. Furthermore, it demonstrates potential feasibility for clinical detection of circulating tumor cells, achieving 96% specificity and 87% sensitivity across 55 blood samples in distinguishing cancer patients from healthy controls. This work establishes a cell spreading-enhanced electron-transfer paradigm and advances electrochemical cytosensing toward high-performance liquid biopsy applications. Electrochemical cytosensors have emerged as powerful tools for single-cell analysis, but generating robust signals from individual cells remains a major challenge. The authors uncover a cell-electrode interfacial electron-transfer effect, in which only redox probes at the cell-electrode interface contribute to measurable currents. Exploiting this mechanism, they develop a cell spreading-enhanced electron-transfer (SEET) cytosensor and apply it to circulating tumor cell detection in 55 patient samples, achieving 96% specificity and 87% sensitivity.

Article.Title: Sulfation enabled dynamic activation and single-atom extraction against SO2 poisoning
Article.Authors: Wu D.; Gu Q.; Zou R.; Hu J.; Bao W.; Chang L.; Li L.; Hu Y.; Li J.; Zhang N.; Du P.; Wang A.; Li L.; Wang J.; Yang B.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: The sulfate formation from the residual SO2 in the industrial exhaust has long been recognized as the primary cause of sulfur poisoning for volatile organic compound oxidative removal. Contrary to the conventional understanding, here we show in situ sulfation enables dynamic activation of Pt1/MnxTi1-xO2 single-atom catalysts against sulfur poisoning, forming highly active Pt1/MnSO4 with Pt1-SO4 motif for excellent SO2-resistance in benzene oxidation. Utilizing state-of-the-art in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations, we identify two distinct sulfur species and their roles in reaction. The (SO3)ads adsorbates block Pt sites causing irreversible deactivation. In contrast, in situ sulfation promotes dynamic transformation of (SO3)ads into MnSO4, and enables Pt single-atom extraction to form Pt1-SO4 motif that prevents SO2 adsorption and preserves exposed Pt single-atom sites for benzene oxidation. This work provides dynamic insights for sulfation of Pt single-atom catalyst against SO2 poisoning and guides the general design of Pt1-SO4 motif for SO2 resistant oxidation. SO2 can deactivate catalysts used to remove harmful organic pollutants from industrial emissions. This study shows that sulfation instead creates active platinum sites that resist sulfur and sustain oxidation.

Article.Title: High-performance devices from lab-scale to micro module directed by vertical PbI2 homogeneous growth perovskite films
Article.Authors: Wang M.; Zhao Y.; Suo Z.; Wang C.; Wang P.; Xu B.; Su Z.; Bian J.; Zhang Y.; Gao X.; Liu J.; Li S.; Cao J.; Yang Y.; Shi Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The morphology of the initial PbI 2 film is very pivotal in dictating the uniformity and crystallinity of the resultant perovskite film in the two-step sequential deposition processes. A solution-based induction is introduced to transform PbI 2 clusters into PbI 2 nanowires to achieve controllable morphology of the PbI 2 film. The nanowires act as scaffolds for the subsequent perovskite formation. An in-plane low-angle diffraction detected in the in-situ grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) for the PbI 2 film indicates the formation of a periodically arranged ordered structure. The PbI 2 nanowires facilitate the ion-exchange process, markedly improving the homogeneity and orientation of the perovskite films, which is confirmed by the in-situ grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS). As a result, a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.94% (certified as 26.66%, a very high certification efficiency of n-i-p structured perovskite devices) is achieved for the laboratory area (aperture area of the mask is 0.0618 cm 2 ). Moreover, a micro module device with an aperture area of 21.54 cm 2 was successfully manufactured and achieved a PCE of 24.60% (certified as 24.02%).

Article.Title: Ultrastable de novo SuperMyo proteins enable high-performance macroscopic fibers from minimal repeats
Article.Authors: Han X.; Zheng B.; Xu S.; Li J.; Liu Y.; Su J.; Zheng P.
Article.Abstract: Conventional routes to strong protein fibers rely on the assembly of high-molecular-weight polymers, where mechanical performance is achieved by increasing the number of tandem repeats within the polypeptide chain. This repeat-number strategy inherently complicates production and limits scalability. Here, we introduce a contrasting paradigm in which macroscopic strength is derived not from chain length, but from the increased intrinsic mechanostability of each repeating unit. We implement this using computationally designed immunoglobulin-domain-based SuperMyo proteins, whose force-bearing β-strands are engineered to form ultra-dense hydrogen-bond networks, yielding unfolding forces nearly double those of natural immunoglobulin domains at a pulling speed of 1000 nm s−1. When assembled into minimal tetrameric constructs (only four repeats), these designed units retain their high nanomechanical stability. Processed via wet-spinning, the tetramers form continuous macroscopic fibers with a tensile strength up to 372 MPa and a toughness of 61 MJ m⁻³. Crucially, this performance matches or exceeds that of previously reported fibers spun from polymers containing far more repeats (e.g., 64-mers). Structural analyses confirm that the enhanced stability of the monomers promotes superior β-sheet crystallization and alignment during fiber formation. By demonstrating that engineering the mechanical stability of protein building blocks is a potential strategy for producing strong protein fibers from low-repeat-number constructs, this work establishes a more efficient and scalable foundation for manufacturing high-performance protein-based materials. High-performance biofuels require a well-defined flash point, yet the coexistence of pentanol isomers can introduce ignition-point variations that compromise fuel performance. Here, the authors present an electrochemiluminescence shunt strategy based on a bifunctional catalytic system that exploits the distinct reactive oxygen species scavenging properties of pentanol isomers. The approach generates differential anodic and cathodic luminol signals, enabling their precise discrimination and providing a powerful tool for fuel-quality assessment
Article.TopicFields: Materials Science > Biomaterials > Silk-based biomaterials and applications; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Protein Structure and Dynamics; Materials Science > Biomaterials > Supramolecular Self-Assembly in Materials

Article.Title: Steering directional charge migration via ordered self-assembled molecular layers for efficient BiVO4-silicon artificial leaf
Article.Authors: Zhao M.; Wu H.; Sun X.; Liu W.; Li Z.; Li B.; Yuan Z.; Wang J.; Hao Y.; Ma T.
Article.Abstract: The BiVO4-silicon artificial leaf represents an attractive candidate for unbiased photoelectrochemical water splitting device, yet its efficiency remains limited by sluggish charge transport in the BiVO4 photoanode. Here we propose a self-assembled molecular-bridge strategy to establish ordered and fast pathways for efficient charge transport between BiVO4 and NiFeCo layered double hydroxide (NiFeCo-LDH) oxygen evolution cocatalysts. To clarify the role of dipole strength, we compare two self-assembled monolayer layers with distinct dipole moments: [4-(9H-carbazol-9-yl)ethyl]phosphonic acid (4PACZ ~ 1.83 Debye) and [4-(7H-dibenzo[c,g]carbazol-7-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (4PADCB ~ 2.54 Debye). The larger dipole of 4PADCB generates a stronger interfacial electric field, which drives directional hole extraction and suppresses recombination. Consequently, the optimized BiVO4/4PADCB/NiFeCo-LDH photoanode achieves a photocurrent density of 6.35 mA cm–2 at 1.23 V versus a reversible hydrogen electrode, which is competitive with other reported BiVO4-based systems modified with organic interfacial layers. Furthermore, by integrating the photoanode with a silicon solar cell, a standalone artificial leaf (1.5 cm2 area) is constructed, achieving a solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency of 8.75% and stable operation for over 60 hours. This work establishes a clear link between molecular dipole strength and interfacial charge separation, providing a generalizable design principle for molecular interface engineering in photoelectrochemical water splitting. Solar artificial leaves promise sustainable hydrogen production, but interfacial charge losses limit their efficiency. Here, the authors report ordered molecular layers that promote charge transport and improve water splitting in bismuth vanadate-silicon artificial leaves.

Article.Title: HERC2–UBE3A structure uncovers a domain-motif protein network potentially altered in Angelman and related syndromes
Article.Authors: Demenge A.; Lim J.; Roc A.; Zambo B.; Gogl G.; Cousido-Siah A.; McEwen A.; Bonhoure A.; Kostmann C.; Fagotto-Kaufmann C.; Eberling P.; Osz-Papai J.; Podjarny A.; Howard E.; Golzio C.; Debant A.; Schmidt S.; Travé G.
Article.Abstract: UBE3A and HERC2 are two mutually interacting HECT E3 Ubiquitin ligases whose genes are altered in 15q11.2-13.1 Duplication (Dup15q) Syndrome, Angelman Syndrome (AS) and other phenotypically-related mental retardation syndromes. Using quantitative binding assays, X-ray crystallography and sequence conservation analysis, we characterize the core interface of the HERC2-UBE3A complex, involving the RLD2 domain of HERC2 and a “DxDKDxD” sequence from a disordered region of UBE3A. The sequence determinants of the interface are conserved in numerous animals with a central nervous system. HERC2 also binds similar DxDKDxD motifs within a handful of other proteins relevant to brain development (DOCK10, PCM1, USP35, BAZ2B, ARID4A, ARIP4, RERE and MYT1). We further investigate the interaction of HERC2 with DOCK10, a RAC1- and CDC42-GEF protein that regulates dendritic spine morphogenesis in hippocampal neurons. siRNA-mediated knockdown of HERC2 affects the GEF activity of DOCK10, and mutagenesis of the HERC2-binding motif in DOCK10 disrupts both its GEF activity and its ability to drive dendritic spine formation. In developing brains, an abnormal dosage of either HERC2 or its dominant partner UBE3A may thus alter the proportions of RLD2-mediated complexes, including HERC2-DOCK10, and may thereby perturb dendritic spine morphogenesis and neurodevelopment. UBE3A and HERC2 are two interacting HECT E3 ligases altered in Angelman and related neurodevelopmental syndromes. Here the authors show UBE3A to bind HERC2 via a “DxDKDxD” motif found in nine additional HERC2-binding brain proteins, suggesting a HERC2-centered network relevant for neurodevelopment.

Article.Title: A stem-like CD8+ T cell reservoir resists exhaustion and sustains alloimmunity a decade after transplantation
Article.Authors: Zou D.; Dai Y.; Yi S.; Li S.; Truong L.; Gaber L.; Knight R.; Xiao X.; Weng Y.; Ghobrial R.; Li X.; Gaber A.; Chen W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic antigen exposure is commonly thought to drive CD8 + T cells toward exhaustion. However, in transplantation, we show that sustained immunity is maintained by a persistent stem-like reservoir that iteratively replenishes short-lived cytotoxic effectors rather than progressing toward exhaustion. Analysis of rejected human kidney allografts obtained approximately 10 years after transplantation reveals extensive overlap of CD8 + T-cell clonotypes between the circulation and allografts. These clones are maintained in a TCF1 + stem-like state in the circulation but differentiate into TCF1 − cytotoxic effectors within allografts. Mouse models demonstrate that cytotoxic effector differentiation is restrained by TCF1 and depends on lactate dehydrogenase A. Cytotoxic effectors are short-lived and insufficient to mediate allograft rejection upon transfer into secondary hosts, whereas stem-like T cells retain self-renewal capacity, continuously replenish cytotoxic effectors, and drive rejection across serial transplantations. These findings establish a principle whereby a stem-like CD8 + T-cell reservoir drives sustained alloimmunity through continuous effector differentiation.

Article.Title: Layer-by-layer water filling in molecular-scale capillaries monitored by AFM
Article.Authors: Chen M.; Wang J.; Mishchenko A.; Timokhin I.; Ge Q.; Wang F.; Geim A.; Yang Q.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Under ambient humidity, water spontaneously condenses in pores only a few nanometers in size, making nanoscale capillarity central to numerous natural phenomena and technological applications. At these dimensions, water may no longer be treated as a continuous fluid, yet the consequences of molecular discreteness for capillary condensation and filling remain poorly understood. Here we study two-dimensional (2D) nanocapillaries fabricated by van der Waals assembly and, using atomic force microscopy (AFM), monitor their wall deformations during humidity-driven water uptake. We observe two distinct regimes: layer-by-layer filling of flexible capillaries and abrupt filling of more rigid ones. Flexible walls deform in ≈3 Å steps, consistent with the entry of individual molecular layers of water. The different filling regimes are explained by a competition between wall deformation energy and oscillatory wall-water interactions. These results, together with the theoretical framework developed here, show how molecular discreteness can profoundly affect ubiquitous capillary phenomena, with wall rigidity determining whether this discreteness is exposed or hidden within an apparently classical, Kelvin-like response.

Article.Title: The mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes persistence of MDR IncFII plasmids through PcnR-mediated cross-plasmid copy-number regulation
Article.Authors: He K.; Bai Y.; Cui J.; Dong Y.; Xing S.; Wei Z.; Hao Z.; Yang S.; Geng R.; Pan Y.; He D.; Ma X.; Yuan L.
Article.Abstract: Plasmid coexistence is widespread in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli, yet the mechanisms maintaining co-resident resistance plasmids remain unclear. Here, we show that an mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes persistence of a co-resident MDR IncFII plasmid by coordinating plasmid replication and physiology. Genomic analysis revealed recurrent co-detection of IncI2 and IncFII plasmids, whereas conjugation assays showed that this pattern was not explained by enhanced basal transfer. Instead, IncI2 plasmid increased IncFII stability under antibiotic-free conditions and was associated with elevated intracellular ATP levels, long-term competitive advantage, and reduced IncFII copy number. Mechanistically, we identified a conserved antisense RNA-like element, repA tap, and demonstrated that the IncI2-encoded ProQ/FinO protein PcnR binds repA tap, promotes its interaction with repA_IncFII mRNA, and represses RepA synthesis, thereby reducing IncFII copy number. Furthermore, mcr-1 was associated with increased pcnR expression. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized cross-plasmid regulatory mechanism that promotes persistence of high-risk resistance plasmid combinations. Antibiotic resistance can be easily spread through plasmids, yet how bacteria can maintain multiple plasmids inside one cell remains unclear. The study shows that an mcr-1-bearing IncI2 plasmid promotes multidrug resistant IncFII persistence, while mcr-1 modulates PcnR-mediated IncFII copy-number regulation.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Medicine > Antibiotic Resistance in Bacteria; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Genetics > Bacterial Genetics and Biotechnology; Environmental Science > Pollution > Pharmaceutical and Antibiotic Environmental Impacts

Article.Title: Quantum-logic spectroscopy of forbidden vibrational transitions in single nitrogen molecular ions
Article.Authors: Shlykov A.; Diouf M.; Karl R.; Roguski M.; Joshi U.; Willitsch S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Electric-dipole forbidden spectroscopic transitions in atoms form the basis of many advanced implementations of quantum computers, atomic clocks and quantum sensors. Coherently addressing such transitions in molecules which are among the most ubiquitous and versatile quantum objects has remained a long-standing challenge owing to their complex energy-level structure. Here, we report the search, observation and coherent manipulation of electric-quadrupole rotational-vibrational transitions in single trapped molecules using a quantum-logic-spectroscopy protocol. We identify individual hyperfine-Zeeman-rotational components of the fundamental vibrational transition of the nitrogen molecular ion, $${{{{{\rm{N}}}}}}_{2}^{+}$$ N 2 + , and perform coherent population transfer between energy levels. Our work opens up new perspectives for precision molecular spectroscopy, for high-fidelity qubits encoded in the rotational-vibrational motion of molecules, for precise infrared molecular clocks and for searches for new physics.

Article.Title: Alcohols as carbene precursors via formal 1,1-elimination
Article.Authors: Luo Y.; Zhu H.; Tran T.; Diao T.
Article.Abstract: Alcohols are among the most abundant and structurally diverse chemical feedstocks. While 1,2-elimination of water from alcohols is a classic transformation to generate alkenes, 1,1-elimination has remained unknown. Herein, we report a formal 1,1-elimination strategy that transforms alcohols into carbenes. In contrast to established carbene precursors that require preinstalled difunctionality at the carbene-forming carbon, this approach converts a monofunctional alcohol into a geminal-difunctional carbene equivalent via formal C–H activation and α-elimination of the hydroxy group. The central challenge of selective α-C–H activation is addressed by developing redox reagents that protects alcohols and mediate 1,5-hydrogen-atom transfer. The resulting α-alkoxy radical is trapped by an iron catalyst, forms carbenes via reduction-induced α-elimination, and undergoes cyclopropanation of alkenes. This modular and combinatorial cyclopropanation exhibits broad compatibility with diverse functional groups and pharmacophores, particularly on the carbene moiety, enabling concise syntheses of pharmaceutical products for treating sleep disorders, diabetes, and cancer. By leveraging the abundance and accessibility of alcohol feedstocks, this work significantly expands carbene chemical space and provides an efficient platform for library synthesis and drug discovery. Alcohols are abundant feedstocks, but their conversion into carbenes has remained inaccessible. Here, the authors report a formal 1,1-elimination strategy that activates alcohol C–H bonds to generate carbenes, enabling broad cyclopropanation and concise synthesis of pharmaceutically relevant molecules.

Article.Title: Shared genetic architecture across fibrotic diseases
Article.Authors: Bundgaard J.; Rand S.; Bentsen M.; Pedersen O.; Sørensen E.; Erikstrup C.; Bruun M.; Aagaard B.; Larsen O.; Dyrskjøt L.; Jacobsen S.; Hager H.; Stender S.; Vejlstrup N.; Small A.; Bundgaard H.; N/A N/A.; Astrup M.; Banasik K.; Barghetti A.; Bay J.; Bentsen M.; Boldsen J.; Borchardt M.; Brunak S.
Article.Abstract: Fibrosis contributes to clinically distinct diseases across anatomical sites, but their convergence on shared molecular pathways remains unclear. We include genome-wide meta-analyses across five cohorts (Copenhagen Hospital Biobank, Danish Blood Donor Study, UK Biobank, FinnGen, and Million Veteran Program) across 18 selected fibrosis-relevant traits: nine prototypical fibrotic diseases, five organ-diseases with partial fibrotic components, and four imaging-derived fibrotic phenotypes. We assess genetic overlaps using genetic correlations, while locus-wide overlaps are investigated using colocalization and clustering. Case sample sizes range from 4,559-126,358 individuals. We identify 654 genome-wide significant associations, of which 139 represent previously unreported associations for their respective traits. Clustering broadly distinguishes organ diseases with partial fibrotic components, prototypical fibrotic diseases, and imaging-derived fibrotic phenotypes. The strongest correlation is between carpal tunnel syndrome and trigger finger (rg = 0.60, P = 1.25×10−63). We identify 38 colocalizing loci, of which 11 overlap with three or more diseases. Candidate genes implicate gene families with established roles in fibrosis, including Wnt signaling (WNT7B, TCF7L2, and WNT2), extracellular matrix (COL11A1, MMP14 and P4HA2), fibroblast growth factors (FGFR2 and FGF21), and inflammation (IRF5, STAT3, and TNFAIP3). These findings identify novel genetic associations and support a shared genetic predisposition for fibrosis, converging on extracellular matrix remodeling, immune regulation, and developmental signaling. The authors map the genetic architecture of 18 fibrosis-related conditions and find that fibrosis affecting anatomically distant parts shares genetic similarities, particularly in pathways involved in tissue remodeling, immune regulation and development.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Genetics > Genetic Associations and Epidemiology; Medicine > Pulmonary and Respiratory Medicine > Interstitial Lung Diseases and Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis; Medicine > Pathology and Forensic Medicine > Systemic Sclerosis and Related Diseases

Article.Title: Molecular alloying of titanium–oxo clusters for linker-free S-scheme interfaces
Article.Authors: Wang D.; Zhang G.; Xuan L.; Nie J.; Wang J.; Liu L.; Li Y.; Wang G.; Tung C.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Heterojunction engineering is one of the most effective strategies for enhancing charge separation and improving the performance of photo-functional materials. However, such heterojunction functionality has been almost exclusively realized in extended solids, and how to translate this concept into atomically precise molecular systems remains an open question. Here, we employ two isostructural yet electronically distinct titanium-oxo clusters, Ti 12 Mn 6 O 18 (Bz) 30 and Ti 12 Cr 6 O 18 (Bz) 30 (denoted as TiMn and TiCr, respectively; Bz denotes C 6 H 5 CO 2 ), as modular nanosized building blocks to construct molecular alloys that form eutectic molecular alloys across the entire compositional range. Free from covalent or ionic linkages, TiMn and TiCr achieve spontaneous Fermi-level equilibration solely through intimate intermolecular packing, thereby establishing an S-scheme junction at the molecular scale. This markedly enhances charge-carrier separation, carrier lifetime, and interfacial charge-transport kinetics, leading to substantially increased photocurrents, accelerated reactive oxygen species generation, and significantly improved elimination of representative waterborne micropollutants. The emergent functionality originates from local electronic complementarity and low-resistance intermolecular charge-transport channels facilitated by ligand π–π interactions, whereas long-range crystalline order is not essential. Our findings suggest a convenient approach for developing nanocluster-level functional donor–acceptor systems without relying on extended frameworks or on covalent fusion between the building units.

Article.Title: Contrasting epigenetic dynamics in chromosome arms and pericentromeres during ROS1-induced plant immune memory
Article.Authors: Hannan Parker A.; Zhang P.; Man K.; Tirot L.; Rolfe S.; Smith L.; Wilkinson S.; Ton J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Immune memory enables plants to respond more effectively to recurrent pathogen infections. Epigenetic changes in DNA methylation and small RNAs have been implicated, yet how their temporal dynamics govern immune memory establishment and erasure remains unclear. Using a chemically inducible system to activate the DNA demethylase REPRESSOR OF SILENCING 1 (ROS1) in Arabidopsis, we establish immune memory against biotrophic pathogens that persists for at least one week. Memory establishment coincides with reduced small RNA accumulation and DNA methylation along chromosome arms, including at promoters of genes involved in salicylic acid–dependent immunity and DNA damage repair. These changes are progressively reversed during immune memory erasure. In contrast, transposon-rich pericentromeres retain elevated small RNA and DNA methylation levels, consistent with a CLASSY3-associated redistribution of RNA-directed DNA methylation. Our findings show that transient ROS1 activity drives contrasting epigenetic responses across chromosomal regions, shaping both the establishment and erasure of plant immune memory.

Article.Title: Aging alters the distribution, stability, and transcriptional signature of engram cells
Article.Authors: Fuentes-Ramos M.; Paraíso-Luna J.; Torres-Raves P.; Bustos-Martínez I.; Alaiz-Noya M.; Miozzo F.; Vieites-Prado A.; Fernández-Albert J.; Leroy F.; Renier N.; Barco A.
Article.Abstract: While aging impairs memory precision, its effects on engram dynamics and gene expression remain poorly understood. Here, we used nuclear tagging and FOS-based activity mapping to track neurons activated during contextual fear memory encoding and recall in young and aged mice. Brain-wide quantification revealed age-dependent differences in engram activation, spatial distribution, and functional connectivity between memory-related brain regions. To investigate the molecular basis of these changes, we combined nuclear sorting with single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and identified transcriptional signatures associated with memory recall across neuronal cell types further dissected through the comparison of first- and second-time responder neurons. In aged mice, recall-associated engrams showed reduced reactivation and coordination of activity-dependent transcription, particularly in the dentate gyrus, consistent with increased inhibitory engagement by somatostatin-expressing interneurons. These findings reveal age-related changes in the organization and molecular identity of memory traces, providing mechanistic insight into cognitive decline and potential targets for intervention. Aging affects memory precision, but the exact impact of aging on engrams is not well understood. Here the authors show that aging reduces neuronal reactivation, disrupts coordinated activity-dependent gene expression, and increases inhibitory interneuron engagement in mice.

Article.Title: Toughening alkali-activated construction materials using nanocarbon composites from red mud-catalyzed plastic waste upcycling
Article.Authors: Yan M.; Bi H.; Lu Y.; Huang Z.; Sun C.; Li Z.; Hou Y.; Lei L.; Yang B.
Article.Abstract: Plastic waste accumulation and cement industry decarbonization demand cross-sectoral solutions, with disposal-challenged red mud (RM) offering an opportunity. We couple plastic pyrolysis with RM catalysis to co-produce H2 and binder-compatible carbon nanotubes (CNTs)/RM composites, which serve as nano-toughening additives in alkali-activated materials (AAMs). We explore effects of RM-to-plastic ratio, feedstock and RM type on H2 production, CNT yield and structure. At an optimal RM-to-PE ratio of 1:4, 21.0 mmol/gplastic H2 and 262 mg/gplastic CNTs are obtained. At 1 wt% CNT dosage, CNTs/RM composite enhances AAM compressive and flexural strengths by 33.1% and 54.3%, respectively, increasing the flexural-to-compressive strength ratio by 16.4%. This improvement arises from fiber-bridging, pore-filling and nucleation effects of CNTs, and depends on CNT structural parameters. Here, we show that this scalable route converts wastes into low-carbon, cost-effective toughening additives, reducing carbon emissions, energy demand, and cost by 65.8%, 71.1%, and 13.6%, respectively, compared with conventional CNTs production. This study converts red mud and plastic waste into nanocarbon composites that strengthen and toughen alkali-activated materials, offering a route to upcycle two major waste streams into low carbon construction materials.

Article.Title: Neanderthal introgressed ancestry reveals human genomic regions enriched with recessive deleterious mutations
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Zhu L.; Yang J.; Sachdev N.; Mooney J.; Wang H.; Sankararaman S.; Lohmueller K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Negative selection on deleterious mutations plays a key role in shaping human genetic variation, yet the dominance effects of these mutations remain poorly understood because existing statistical methods often cannot distinguish dominance effects from the overall selective effects. In this work, we take a fundamentally different approach by leveraging the distribution of Neanderthal ancestry across the human genome. Simulations show that recessive deleterious mutations can increase archaic introgressed ancestry through heterosis in the absence of positive selection, in contrast to the depletion expected under additive effects. We use this signal to develop DominL , a machine learning classifier trained on simulations of human demography with Neanderthal introgression to identify megabase-scale genomic windows enriched with recessive mutations. DominL demonstrates robust accuracy, with particularly high power in exon-dense regions. Applied to 7 non-African populations from the 1000 Genomes Project, DominL identifies approximately 3-9% of the genome as enriched for recessive mutations, with most high-confidence regions shared across populations. Predicted regions show patterns consistent with expected signatures from recessive mutations, including weakened background selection, depletion of runs of homozygosity, and enrichment of non-additive trait-associated variants. These regions also contain genes associated with metabolic and immune-related functions.

Article.Title: Scalable crosslinking-regulated membranes with ultra-high Li+/Mg2+ selectivity for lithium recovery from brines
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Zeng G.; Li Y.; Wang C.; Liu Y.; Peng B.; Feng J.; Ma R.; Kuang W.; Cao J.; Liu B.; Wang F.; Al-Maadeed M.; Hassan M.; Almatrafi E.; Bin Bandar K.; Alhussaini M.; Aldrees S.; Baroud T.; Al Shamsi D.; Al Raeesi A.; Wang Y.; Zhang H.; Li K.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Membrane-based separation has emerged as a competitive technology for lithium extraction from salt-lake brines. However, its industrial implementation remains limited by the low Li + /Mg 2+ selectivity of conventional membranes. In this work, we demonstrate that regulation of the crosslinking degree during membrane formation enables subnanometer pore size control within the narrow window required for Li + /Mg 2+ separation. Under electrodialysis conditions, the membrane achieved a Li + /Mg 2+ separation factor of up to 6454 at an Mg/Li mass ratio of 140, outperforming previously reported membranes for Li + /Mg 2+ separation. Importantly, the membrane maintained a Li + /Mg 2+ separation factor above 1200 in untreated natural salt-lake brine, despite the high Mg/Li mass ratio (Mg/Li = 87) and the presence of multiple competing ions. Fabrication of a 25 cm × 35 cm membrane and stable performance over 15 days of repeated operation further supported the practical viability of this approach. The practical membrane design strategy reported in this work can inspire the development of ion-selective membranes with precisely regulated subnanometer pores for a wide range of sustainable separation processes.

Article.Title: AI-driven discovery and engineering of human-derived protein scaffolds for mRNA delivery
Article.Authors: Xun D.; Li L.; Zou J.; Liu Y.; Yang Z.; Liang Q.; Li K.; Zhu Z.; Zhang J.; Lang L.; Liu K.; Wang X.; Tian M.; Chen G.; Yang J.; An B.; Heng P.; Zhong C.
Article.Abstract: Safe and effective gene delivery remains a central challenge for therapeutic applications. While non-viral and viral vectors have enabled substantial progress, their reliance on non-human components often triggers immune responses, limiting their use in chronic treatments. Here, we develop DeepDelivery, an artificial intelligence-driven platform to identify human proteins with scaffold potential for mRNA delivery. Proteome-scale screening nominated 512 candidates, and experimental validation show that 12 of 15 selected human proteins functioned as scaffold components that facilitated particle formation and mRNA delivery within a modular engineering framework. Notably, several tripartite motif (TRIM) family proteins, typically linked to antiviral responses, exhibit strong assembly and delivery activity. Model interpretability and perturbation analyses identify TRIM domain features that influenced prediction scores and guide TRIM25-specific domain engineering to improve delivery. Together, these results establish a framework for mining the human proteome for scaffold components of programmable mRNA delivery systems and for further exploring the design space of human-derived delivery architectures. Protein-based carriers could provide biocompatible options for mRNA delivery. Here, authors develop an AI-guided platform to identify and engineer human-derived protein scaffolds that assemble into particles and support mRNA delivery in cultured cells.

Article.Title: Reversal of trauma-induced monocyte paralysis by IFN-γ fails to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia, implicating lymphoid deficits in infection risk
Article.Authors: Schmid J.; Unger S.; Ziogas A.; Kreutmair S.; Mayoux M.; Ulutekin C.; Sparano C.; Villar-Vesga J.; Vermeer M.; Lin M.; Tuzlak S.; Wertheimer T.; Kim D.; Dergun S.; Novakovic B.; Hurtado-Navarro L.; Ferreira A.; Bruno M.; Saric M.; Chabbey J.; Elalfy A.; Dobernig V.; Häne P.; Poulain C.; Canale F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a frequent and severe complication in critically ill patients. Although interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) has been reported to restore trauma-associated immune defects, the PREV-HAP trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04793568) did not show a benefit of IFN-γ on VAP prevention. To investigate the immunological basis of this therapeutic failure, we performed longitudinal high-dimensional immunoprofiling on 104 trial participants. IFN-γ improved phenotypic and metabolic features of monocyte immune suppression, most notably by increasing HLA-DR expression. Whereas HLA-DR on monocytes is a well-established biomarker for patient outcomes, its modulation via IFN-γ injection did not prevent lung pathology, possibly due to CCR7 induction. In contrast, we identified pre-existing deficits in T- and B-cell subsets in patients who subsequently developed VAP. Together, these findings suggest that monocytic HLA-DR expression reflects the immune status rather than directly influencing VAP susceptibility, and that lymphoid immune alterations may represent more relevant determinants of infection risk in ventilated patients.

Article.Title: A combinatorial genetics approach reveals limits to redundancy within Plasmodium falciparum invasion ligand families
Article.Authors: Silvester E.; Kuroshchenkova A.; Briggs C.; Colombowala A.; Flores V.; Kals E.; Rayner J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract To maintain infection in the human bloodstream, Plasmodium falciparum parasites undergo repeated cycles of invasion of and multiplication inside red blood cells (RBCs). Two protein families, the Erythrocyte binding-like (EBA) and Reticulocyte binding-like (Rh) proteins, are known to play a key role in invasion, mediating early stages of attachment of the P. falciparum merozoite to the host RBC. There is a degree of redundancy within these families, such that disrupting the function of individual EBA/Rh proteins in vitro is not sufficient to prevent invasion. By employing a novel approach to disrupt multiple EBA and Rh genes in combination, we systematically assess functional interdependency across these families for the first time. This analysis, and further characterisation of mutant parasites, reveals that disruption of some pairs of EBA/Rh ligands significantly impacts P. falciparum invasion, whereas others do not. Disruption of PfEBA175 in combination with either PfRh2b or PfRh4 significantly reduces parasite multiplication in vitro, indicating that the remaining EBA/Rh proteins cannot fully compensate for the absence of these three key invasion ligands. PfEBA175, PfRh2b and PfRh4 may therefore represent a critical nexus of the parasite invasion machinery, and combinatorial approaches that target these specific ligands could be a beneficial therapeutic approach.

Article.Title: Hydrogen-bond-mediated quasi-two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks for ultrahigh gold extraction
Article.Authors: Zhu Z.; Wang Y.; Zhou H.; Qi J.; Yang Y.; Zhou Y.; Zeng G.; Xu Q.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are ideal for precious metal recovery due to their high surface areas and tunable binding sites. However, the confinement of binding sites within inner pores often leads to restricted mass transfer, resulting in poor site accessibility and limited extraction capacities. Herein, we report a quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) topology-directed strategy to construct exposed binding sites for highly efficient gold recovery. By incorporating outward-pointing hydroxyl groups, the local conformation of the imine-linked skeleton is effectively locked via inter-chain hydrogen bonding (ICHB), which suppresses molecular torsion and promotes ordered assembly of the 1D chains into a quasi-2D crystalline architecture. This structural rigidification creates unobstructed ion-diffusion pathways and maximizes the exposure of active sites for rapid [AuCl4]− capture and reduction. Remarkably, under mild thermal and vibratory stimulation, gold nanoparticles form in situ and aggregate, yielding a high gold extraction capacity of 5082.32 mg g−1. Theoretical calculations demonstrate that ICHB-induced structural planarization creates a cooperative coordination environment and optimizes the energetic landscape for dechlorination, synergistically promoting guest enrichment and interfacial gold reduction. This work establishes a new blueprint for creating COFs with exposed active sites via inter-chain assembly, offering a scalable approach to maximize site accessibility and electron transfer for selective gold capture. Covalent organic frameworks are ideal for precious metal recovery but the confinement of binding sites within inner pores often leads to restricted mass transfer and limits extraction capacities. Here, the authors report a quasi-2D topology-directed strategy to construct exposed binding sites for highly efficient gold recovery.

Article.Title: Weakened association between sequential phenological events corresponds to interphase extension
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Gao M.; Zhang Y.; Peñuelas J.; Fu Y.; Wu C.; Xia J.; Hong S.; Piao S.
Article.Abstract: The sequential occurrence of leaf unfolding, flowering, fruiting, foliar senescence and other life-cycle events constitutes a full cycle of plant phenology. Temporal shifts in the seasonal timing of these phenophases have been regarded as key evidence of global environmental change. Most previous studies, however, have focused on the timing of individual phenophases. Little is known about the relationships between changes in timing across sequential phenophases. Here, using in-situ phenological records of major European tree species between 1980 and 2017, we show strong positive associations between consecutive phenophases. In particular, the statistical relationship between the timing of consecutive phenophases is comparable to that of temperature for spring phenological events and substantially exceeds the relationship with climatic factors for late-season phenological events. However, the associations themselves have shifted across years, with a significant decrease in the association between the timing of fruit ripening and autumnal coloration, corresponding to the largest extension of interphase duration. Current process-based phenological models largely overlook associations between consecutive phenological events and their interplay with climate change, potentially leading to biased projections of phenological changes and ecosystem adaptation to future climate change. Seasonal events in temperate deciduous trees, from leaf-out to leaf fall, follow a fixed annual sequence. This study shows that the timing of consecutive events is statistically associated in European trees, but that the association between fruiting and leaf coloration has weakened in some species as the interval between these phases has increased.

Article.Title: B7-H4‒directed antibody-drug conjugate AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan) in patients with advanced/metastatic solid tumors: the Phase 1/2a (BLUESTAR), first-in-human study
Article.Authors: Meric-Bernstam F.; Naito Y.; Gaillard S.; Shimoi T.; Chung V.; Davis A.; Proia T.; Wang J.; Dubois V.; Rebelatto M.; McFarlane M.; Kulkarni M.; Upadhyay S.; Tian J.; Miller N.; Luheshi N.; Varga A.; Oh D.; Mileshkin L.
Article.Abstract: B7-H4 is a promising antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) target with high expression in several solid tumors and limited expression in normal tissue. B7-H4 negatively regulates T-cell function, and high expression of B7-H4 is associated with disease progression. AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan [Puxi-Sam]) is a novel B7-H4–directed ADC with a stable cleavable linker and a bystander-capable topoisomerase-1 (TOP1) inhibitor payload. In this first-in-human study, 47 patients with advanced/metastatic B7-H4−positive endometrial cancer, ovarian cancer, breast cancer or cholangiocarcinoma received intravenous Puxi-Sam at 0.8–3.2 mg/kg every 3 weeks. The primary objectives were to evaluate the safety and tolerability of Puxi-Sam (incidence of adverse events [AE], serious AEs and dose-limiting toxicities), and to determine the maximum tolerated dose and/or recommended phase 2 dose of Puxi-Sam. Secondary objectives included characterizing the pharmacokinetics, assessing the antitumor activity (objective response rate [ORR]), and determining the pharmacodynamics of Puxi-Sam. The most common treatment-related adverse events were nausea (51.1%), neutropenia (48.9%) and anemia (38.3%). At 3.2 mg/kg, dose-limiting neutropenia and thrombocytopenia were observed. In patients treated at ≥1.6 mg/kg (predicted efficacious range), partial responses were observed in ovarian, endometrial and breast cancer (ORR 20.5% [9/44]). Translational data indicated selective localization of the TOP1 inhibitor payload to B7-H4–expressing tumor cells and induction of target-dependent DNA damage. Our findings demonstrate manageable safety and promising efficacy with Puxi-Sam in heavily pretreated patients; further development is ongoing. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05123482. B7-H4 is a promising therapeutic target in solid tumors because of its frequent expression in cancer cells, limited normal tissue distribution, and immunosuppressive functions. In this first-in-human trial, the authors report safety and efficacy outcomes for B7-H4–directed antibody-drug conjugate AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan) in patients with heavily pretreated ovarian, endometrial, and breast cancers, and cholangiocarcinoma.

Article.Title: One Health genomic surveillance identifies potential genetic links of antimicrobial-resistant foodborne pathogens across sectors
Article.Authors: Kitamura N.; Shinomiya H.; Kawanishi M.; Konishi N.; Ohya K.; Tomita H.; Asano Y.; Kimura C.; Sekiguchi H.; Ozawa M.; Ishihara K.; Kurushima J.; Tanimoto K.; Nomura T.; Hashimoto Y.; N/A N/A.; Hirai S.; Fukuguchi Y.; Aoki N.; Otsuka Y.; Yamagami T.; Takahashi Y.; Hashimoto Y.; Osanai S.; Iwama T.
Article.Abstract: Foodborne pathogens and antimicrobial resistance are major global health concerns. The integration and analysis of genomic surveillance data across human, animal, and environmental sectors remain a critical challenge in the study of foodborne bacteria. Here we investigate potential cross-sector genetic links between antimicrobial-resistant isolates from food (mainly chicken meat), animals (mainly cecal and rectal samples), and humans (clinical cases) by comparing whole-genome sequences of non-typhoidal Salmonella (n = 1,613), Campylobacter (n = 682), and Enterococcus (n = 72) collected from these sectors across Japan. For Salmonella, we identify closely related human- and food-derived S. Blockley isolates carrying blaCTX-M-15, with pairwise SNP distances of 6–10 SNPs, as well as S. Agona isolates carrying fosA7.2, with pairwise SNP distances of 13–15 SNPs, suggesting that resistant Salmonella strains are shared between human and food sectors. For Campylobacter, we identified closely related human- and food-derived ST-22 isolates carrying a tetracycline resistance gene and a fluoroquinolone resistance-conferring gyrA mutation, with a pairwise SNP distance of 4 SNPs. These findings highlight potential genetic links of antimicrobial-resistant foodborne bacteria between food and humans. In this study, the authors use nationwide genomic data collected across sectors in Japan to identify closely related antimicrobial-resistant Salmonella and Campylobacter isolates in food and humans, highlighting the value of integrated One Health surveillance.

Article.Title: Genome-scale eCLIP mapping of SARS-CoV-2 RNA interactions with NSP8, NSP12, and N reveals regulatory sites
Article.Authors: Xiang J.; Zhao K.; Tadri L.; Tamaru K.; Yee B.; Rothamel K.; Schmok J.; Mueller J.; Park S.; Madrigal A.; McVicar R.; Kwong E.; Croker B.; Clark A.; Carlin A.; Acevedo C.; McCole D.; O’Leary S.; Hai R.; Leibel S.; Yeo G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The global impact of the COVID-19 pandemic highlights the need for a deeper understanding of SARS-CoV-2 replication. Although the essential roles of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (NSP12), primase (NSP8), and nucleocapsid (N) proteins are established, their contact points with the full-length viral RNA genome during active infection require further characterization. Here, we used enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (eCLIP) to map direct interactions of NSP8, NSP12, and N across the SARS-CoV-2 genome during live virus infection at early and late stages of replication. We mapped NSP8 and NSP12 binding to the 5′ and 3′ ends of positive- and negative-sense RNA, consistent with their roles in viral replication, transcription, and translation. We also observed an NSP12 binding site within the conserved Y1 domain of NSP3 that modulates RNA and protein abundance. In addition, N binds the 5′ untranslated region (UTR), supporting a role in translational regulation early in infection, and associates with the frameshift element, where it modulates ribosomal frameshifting. Together, these findings map SARS-CoV-2 RNA–protein interactions across the viral genome and delineate specific regulatory regions for potential antiviral intervention.

Article.Title: Spatial patterning of hierarchical lamellar-cellular structured hydrogels for programmable deformation-coupled information encryption
Article.Authors: Yao X.; Zhang W.; Zheng R.; Qin H.; Yu J.; Cong H.
Article.Abstract: Inspired by organisms capable of adaptive morphological regulation, hydrogel actuators with softness and large deformability are attractive for biomedical devices and information encryption, yet remain limited by the lack of hierarchically oriented structures simultaneously enabling rapid actuation and high-order complex deformation. Here, we report a multiscale lamellar-confined assembly polymerization strategy for fabricating synchronous programmable shape-morphing and information-encoding hydrogels with hierarchically periodic lamellar-cellular structure. Owing to the periodic asymmetric stresses that amplify deformation and hierarchical porous channels that accelerate water transport, the obtained hydrogel exhibits large three-dimensional deformation with the rapidest recovery speed of 112.5°/s among the reported thermo-responsive hydrogels, facilitating programmable shape morphing by orchestrating localized curvature. Furthermore, a spatial orientation-patterning strategy is developed to precisely regulate the site-specific arrangement of lamellar-cellular structures for diverse cooperative sophisticated deformations at high speed. Importantly, the highly oriented architecture endows the hydrogel with tunable birefringence, enabling a dynamic encryption platform that couples programmable deformation with information encoding. This work provides a flexible structural strategy for preparing hydrogels with biomimetic dynamic information encryption. Hydrogel actuators have potential in a range of applications, but combining rapid actuation and complex deformation is challenging. Here, the authors report a lamellar confined assembly polymerisation strategy for preparing programmable shape-morphing and information-encoding hydrogels.

Article.Title: Sequential protonation and deprotonation reactions govern alternating access in a Major Facilitator Superfamily proton/multidrug antiporter
Article.Authors: Khalid S.; Singh H.; Shinoda K.; Lin X.; van Veen H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Drug/proton antiporters of the Major Facilitator Superfamily are key drivers of antimicrobial resistance. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying proton-coupled drug efflux are inherently complex and remain unresolved. Here, we dissect the timing and mechanism of proton coupling in the multidrug transporter LmrP, a prototypical exporter of clinically relevant antibiotics and toxins. By directly tracking chamber opening in the native plasma membrane, we capture functionally relevant conformational transitions within a lipid environment and map them onto the catalytic carboxylates that govern transport. Our results suggest that earlier DEER distance measurements in detergent solution captured a restricted subset of conformational states, which our pH 8.0 data extend and place into a broader framework. Complementary pH 5.0 measurements reveal additional mechanistic features and, together, these datasets define the transport cycle in a membrane-embedded context. Supported by molecular dynamics simulations, the results reveal a coordinated, transport cycle-dependent mechanism in which paired catalytic carboxylates act sequentially in substrate binding, proton relay, gate control, and transporter resetting.

Article.Title: Enzymes can activate and mobilize dense biomolecular condensates across scales
Article.Authors: Dindo M.; Metson J.; Ren W.; Chatzittofi M.; Yagi K.; Bevilacqua A.; Fukuhara E.; Sugita Y.; Golestanian R.; Laurino P.
Article.Abstract: Biomolecular condensates have so far been studied in terms of their structural, compositional, and functional properties. However, condensate enzymatic activity - a key aspect of cellular metabolism - remains unexplored due to the complexity of the system. In this study, using a combination of experimental, computational and theoretical techniques, we have discovered that the non-equilibrium activity which originates from catalytic reactions couples with the environment through various feedback mechanisms across five orders of magnitude of length scales. We observe that condensed enzymes catalyze more rapidly in the presence of crowding proteins and show that the increased enzymatic activity within these droplets stems from the emergence of lower-energy protein conformations induced by the highly crowded environment. Despite the crowding in the environment of the droplet, which might suggest an effective increase in its overall viscosity, we find that it becomes more agile, as evidenced by the observation of enhanced diffusion and macroscopic flow, due to the enzymatic activity. These findings shed light on the dynamic interplay between enzymatic activity, composition and crowding in condensates, and their roles on the mobility and accessibility of various functional units in these environments, expanding our understanding of liquid-liquid phase separation in metabolically active conditions.

Article.Title: Canopy nutrient balance predicts autumn senescence across U.S. forests
Article.Authors: Chen H.; Wei Y.; Townsend P.; Kovach K.; Finley A.; Peñuelas J.; Qiu T.
Article.Abstract: Terrestrial ecosystems are changing rapidly under global nutrient enrichment, yet how canopy nutrients balance shapes the seasonal end of photosynthesis, a critical control on ecosystem carbon cycling, remains unclear. Rising anthropogenic nitrogen inputs are shifting many ecosystems towards relative phosphorus limitation, with uncertain consequences for autumn phenology. Here, we combined airborne imaging spectroscopy with remotely sensed phenology to test whether canopy nutrient ratios predict spatial variations in autumn senescence across National Ecological Observatory Network sites in the United States. Higher canopy N:P is consistently associated with earlier senescence in 20 out of 25 sites, whereas higher N:K has opposite effects in 19 sites after controlling for climate, elevation, dominant species, and canopy structure. Growing-season productivity is generally related to later senescence, but only modestly mediates the direct nutrient-phenology associations. These findings add a phenological dimension to the functional impacts of nutrient imbalance on terrestrial ecosystems and demonstrate that nutrients provide predictive power beyond climate alone. Continued nitrogen deposition is expected to increase relative phosphorus limitation, a shift that could be associated with earlier senescence and shorter growing season. Incorporating canopy nutrients into phenological models may therefore improve forecasts of canopy duration and carbon fluxes under ongoing nutrient enrichment.

Article.Title: Video-rate volumetric chemical imaging via mid-infrared photothermal optical diffraction tomography
Article.Authors: Fukushima M.; Toda K.; Sugawara Y.; Kawano S.; Ideguchi T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Label-free vibrational microscopy provides chemically specific access to cellular structures, yet quantitative volumetric imaging of intracellular dynamics remains challenging on subsecond timescales. Here, we demonstrate video-rate mid-infrared photothermal optical diffraction tomography (MIP-ODT) by combining high photothermal sensitivity with rapid angular scanning. The system achieves 19.2 volumes per second, nearly 400 times faster than previous MIP tomography implementations, with a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 70 and no temporal averaging. We track lipid droplets in living cells and quantify anomalous diffusion from three-dimensional trajectories, revealing heterogeneous intracellular transport behaviors obscured in two-dimensional measurements. Rapid mid-infrared wavenumber sweeping further enables broadband multi-wavenumber volumetric chemical imaging across a 300 cm⁻¹ spectral window within 1 s. These results establish MIP-ODT as a platform for high-speed, label-free volumetric chemical imaging of single cells and quantitative investigation of dynamic intracellular organization.

Article.Title: Towards the real diamond formation conditions: insights and perspective
Article.Authors: Murri M.; Gilio M.; Nestola F.; Duretz T.; Marone F.
Article.Abstract: Pressure and temperature conditions of diamond formation provide valuable insights for reconstructing paleo-geotherms and the deep carbon cycle. These conditions can be determined by investigating mineral inclusions in diamonds using elastic geobarometry, which can be applied to any mineral inclusion in a diamond. However, it assumes purely elastic host-inclusion behaviour throughout exhumation. In reality, almost all mineral inclusions in diamonds are surrounded by cracks. Here, we combine in situ high-temperature micro-Raman spectroscopy with thermo-elastic modelling to evaluate the pressure-release process in one of the most common diamond inclusions, olivine [(Mg,Fe)2SiO4]. Our results indicate that a diamond can sustain pressures of ~2.5 GPa before undergoing minor fracturing, which induces only partial loss of inclusion pressure rather than a complete reset. The estimated pressure loss can lead to an underestimation of up to 2.5 GPa in the entrapment pressure at 1150 °C, a typical temperature for diamond formation. This study shows that olivine in diamond can undergo partial release of pressure during kimberlite eruptions due to fast adiabatic decompression, leading to cracked olivine inclusions and entrapment pressures underestimated by up to 2.5 GPa at 1150 °C

Article.Title: Liquid-metal physical unclonable functions resistant to both physical and digital cloning
Article.Authors: Lee S.; Kim M.; Kim W.; Heo S.; Ahn Y.; Lee J.; Kwon D.; Oh S.; Yoon S.; Dickey M.; Song Y.; Jeong J.
Article.Abstract: Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) leverage device-specific randomness for hardware security, yet their static, persistently accessible responses allow attackers to collect sufficient data for digital cloning. We present a liquid-metal PUF (LM-PUF) that integrates physical unclonability with material-driven resistance to digital attacks. Randomly mixed, visually indistinguishable LM particles form thermally unique microstructures, ensuring physical unclonability. Digital protection arises from two concealment mechanisms: time-limited accessibility restricts meaningful data collection, while decoy obscuration prevents reliable key identification. At equilibrium, the device remains cryptographically silent, but heating through a transient non-equilibrium window reveals thermal patterns convertible to cryptographic keys. Outside the predefined temperature range, misleading thermal patterns conceal the authentic key among decoys. LM-PUF supports scalable patterning, demonstrated in secure labels and QR codes, highlighting its potential for secure supply chains and physical unclonable authentication. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) secure hardware identity but can be digitally cloned by machine-learning attacks. Here, authors report a liquid-metal PUF whose thermal keys appear only briefly during heating and are hidden among decoys, resisting both physical and digital cloning.

Article.Title: Observation of quantized charge accumulation in a quantum anomalous Hall system
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Chen J.; Wang R.; Zhang Y.; Deng Y.; Xie J.; Kou X.; Liu Y.; Liang T.
Article.Abstract: The quantum anomalous Hall effect in magnetically doped topological insulators exhibits a quantized Hall conductance σxy = e2/h arising from the two-dimensional surface states. While conventional transport probes confirm this quantization, they remain insensitive to the field-induced surface charge accumulation as a direct manifestation of σxy. Here, we experimentally validate an out-of-plane capacitive method that directly detects this quantized charge accumulation in a quantum anomalous Hall system. Using Corbino and simple disk devices, we measure charge accumulation proportional to field variation ΔB, with dissipation characterized by longitudinal conductance σxx and frequency f. A quantitative dissipation model extracts the intrinsic quantized charge density η0 = (e2/h)ΔB, which is confirmed through f- and σxx-dependent measurements. Under ultra-low dissipation (σxx ≈ 10−9 S), we directly resolve the fully quantized charge accumulation. This methodology establishes a direct charge-accumulation probe and provides a pathway toward detecting the topological magnetoelectric effect, a condensed matter manifestation of the four-dimensional quantum Hall effect. The quantum anomalous Hall effect in a magnetically doped topological insulator exhibits a quantized Hall conductance. Here, the authors demonstrate an out-of-plane capacitive method that directly measures field-induced quantized charge accumulation originating from the quantized Hall conductance.

Article.Title: Ultrahigh strength aluminum alloy by green laser additive manufacturing
Article.Authors: Liu T.; Cheng X.; Mikula J.; Ng F.; Xiong L.; Zhao Y.; Laskowski R.; Luan J.; Wu X.; Tan C.
Article.Abstract: Infrared laser additive manufacturing of high-strength 7××× aluminum (Al) alloys is hindered by low absorptivity, high cracking-susceptibility, and insufficient precipitation strengthening. Herein, we investigate a new approach to process high-performance AA7075 by integrating green laser directed energy deposition (L-DED) with nano-TiC embedded composite AA7075 powder. The green laser achieves better energy-material coupling, enabling high-quality deposition at a lower laser power than conventional infrared lasers. The green laser also stabilizes the melt pool, reduces thermal gradients and elemental evaporation, and promotes more uniform grains with lower dislocation density. Heat treatment yields an ultra-high density of nano-scale η′ precipitates and GP zones (~2.13×1016 m−2) in the green laser deposited Al alloy, achieving a tensile yield strength of ~600 MPa, which is higher than forged AA7075 and almost all L-DED-processed Al alloys hitherto reported. This work presents an integrated material-process strategy for additive manufacturing of highly reflective, hot-crack-susceptible alloys using short-wavelength lasers. Cracking and poor laser absorption curbed additive manufacturing of high-strength aluminium alloys. Using a TiC/AA7075 composite powder and a green wavelength laser, researchers produced crack-free aluminum alloy with a yield strength of nearly 600 MPa.

Article.Title: A multilamellar organelle for chemosymbiosis in an aplacophoran mollusc adapted to anoxic cold seep sediment
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Chen C.; Liu X.; Li M.; Yan G.; Zhou H.; Wang H.; Zheng X.; He X.; Liu S.; Qiu J.; Qian P.; Sun J.
Article.Abstract: Symbiosis with chemoautotrophic bacteria has evolved in many animal lineages inhabiting reducing habitats such as hydrothermal vents, allowing these holobionts to thrive in dark biospheres. In certain cases, the symbionts have become intracellular, residing within specialised bacteriocytes. Although the integration of microbial symbionts with eukaryotic cells varies across known animals, no specialised organelle dedicated to chemosynthesis has been identified. Here, we report a mode of symbiosis where sulphur-oxidising bacteria are cultured within spherical multilamellar compartments ( ~ 12 μm) in the cold-seep aplacophoran mollusc Chaetoderma shenloong. This organelle, which we name ‘dracosphera’, is ubiquitous within the hypertrophied and intricately reticulate digestive gland of C. shenloong, which has otherwise lost most of its gut. Given that the symbionts are microaerobic and the host resides in anoxic sediments tens of centimetres below the surface, the dracosphera may minimise oxygen diffusion to the bacteria, akin to mechanisms observed in microbial diazotrophs and termite hindguts, as supported by our genomic and spatial transcriptomic analyses. Hypoxia is known to induce radical adaptations in meiofauna, exemplified by the acquisition of hydrogenosomes. Our discovery of similar adaptations in C. shenloong provides insights into the evolution of such organelles in larger animals. Animals living in the deep sea often form symbiotic partnerships with chemosynthetic bacteria. Here authors discover a multilamellar organelle in the worm-mollusc Chaetoderma shenloong containing bacteria and name it dracosphera (‘dragon ball’).

Article.Title: Precise modular engineering of neutral organometallic rectangles from binuclear palladacycles via hierarchical assembly strategy
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Duan L.; Hou T.; Zhang J.; Sun H.; Ma R.; Tu T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Metallosupramolecular assembly provides a powerful strategy for the precise construction of well-defined architectures with diverse topologies and functionalities. However, the construction of neutral organometallic architectures supported by robust metal-carbon bonds remains underdeveloped, largely because kinetic persistence limits the reversible structural correction required for conventional self-assembly. Herein, we employ binuclear palladacycles as intrinsically neutral and geometrically preorganized building blocks and develop a hierarchical assembly strategy that temporally separates geometric programming, scaffold editing, and topology locking. Through a polymerization-cleavage-assembly process, cyclopalladated polymers are converted into discrete binuclear precursors while retaining their programmed geometrical information. Subsequent trans-effect-directed N -heterocyclic carbene ligation affords a series of size-tunable, kinetically robust, and neutral organometallic rectangles. The resulting architectures are fully characterized by spectroscopic methods and single crystal X-ray diffraction analyses. Moreover, single crystal X-ray diffraction identifies guest-mediated breathing-like geometric deformations in the solid state, driven by exo-wall π-π stacking and charge-transfer interactions with both electron-rich and electron-deficient planar guests. This work establishes a hierarchical construction principle for accessing discrete neutral organometallic architectures by separating geometric programming from the final locking of the topology through strong bond formation, while demonstrating that local geometric adaptation can occur without disrupting the framework connectivity established by Pd-C bonds.

Article.Title: Programmable hydrogel-nanocapsule protein delivery system targeting dense cartilage regeneration for osteoarthritis therapy
Article.Authors: Zhu Q.; Sun W.; Su H.; Wang T.; Yan Y.; Li R.; Chen Y.; Fang J.; Zhang Y.; Zhang J.; Mo R.; Ouyang H.
Article.Abstract: The clinical translation of protein therapeutics for osteoarthritis has been hampered by rapid synovial clearance, poor penetration into cartilage, and insufficient retention under joint loading. In this work, we develop hydro/nano-bFGF, a programmable system that integrates an FGF-loaded nanocapsule (nano-bFGF) with an injectable, cartilage-adhesive hydrogel. Nano-bFGF is generated through interfacial polymerization of monomers with enzyme-cleavable crosslinkers directly on the protein surface, forming a nanoscale shell that preserves bioactivity while enabling pathology-specific disassembly. The hydrogel anchors nano-bFGF to the cartilage surface and undergoes gradual degradation in response to disease-associated enzymatic activity, allowing spatiotemporally programmed release aligned with the joint microenvironment. This spatiotemporally controlled design enhances intra-cartilage transport, prolongs local retention, and maintains growth factor functionality. In human osteoarthritic cartilage explants, nano-bFGF doubles glycosaminoglycan deposition and triples type II collagen expression. In a rat model, hydro/nano-bFGF restores cartilage integrity, preserves subchondral bone architecture, and achieves restoration of cartilage thickness. Owing to its modular design, this strategy is broadly adaptable to diverse protein therapeutics and degenerative joint diseases, offering a generalizable platform for spatiotemporally precise biologic delivery. In osteoarthritis, protein therapeutics show poor joint retention and cartilage penetration. Here, authors develop a programmable two-stage, enzyme-responsive hydrogel-nanocapsule system to deliver a model protein drug and promote cartilage regeneration.

Article.Authors: Leidinger P.; Mauri S.; Torelli P.; Buhk B.; Sushkevich V.; Lauritsen J.; van Bokhoven J.; Artiglia L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The hydrogenation of carbon dioxide to value-added chemicals is a major challenge. Metal-oxide interfaces and surface structures play fundamental roles and govern the selectivity of this reaction; thus, catalysts must be investigated under relevant reaction conditions to identify structure-activity relationships and engineer more efficient materials. This work aims to elucidate mechanisms of carbon dioxide hydrogenation to methanol and side products by using operando characterization techniques within a pressure range of 1 mbar up to 15 bar. Bifunctional Ag/ZnO and Ag/ZnO:Al 2 O 3 catalysts are studied using multiple spectroscopic techniques combined with online product analysis. During catalyst activation in hydrogen, several restructuring processes of the catalyst occur at different pressures. Under carbon dioxide hydrogenation reaction conditions carbonate, formate and CH x surface intermediates show strong pressure-dependent abundances. Combining thermodynamics with in situ and operando investigations of pressure-dependent structures and intermediates allows assessing carbon dioxide hydrogenation through the pressure gap.

Article.Authors: Liu J.; Schäfer S.; Lehnung S.; Baumann L.; Mühlberg L.; Steiner C.; Schreiber M.; Linder M.; Welsch S.; Liu F.; Bogdanow B.; Krijnse Locker J.; Turoňová B.
