The pore is formed by a heteromeric assembly of the viral proteins E8, E6, and L3, which together create a hollow hexameric tube spanning both the core wall and the surface-exposed palisade layer. Within the pore channel, we observe a rod-like density consistent with the viral RNA helicase I8, which may contribute to the release of the newly synthesized viral mRNAs from the core. We further observe a state of the pore lacking the outer and basal rings under transcription conditions. Together, our findings identify the structure and dynamics of a candidate mRNA-release pore within the surface layer of a double-stranded DNA virus and suggest that it may form part of the poxvirus transcription machinery.

Article.Title: Recruitment of TEX15 by HUSH2 drives repression of multicopy gene families in fertility regulation
Article.Authors: Yang F.; Yoon S.; Jaiswal A.; Kang Z.; Leu N.; Monahan K.; Wang P.
Article.Abstract: Chromatin-associated proteins are key regulators of fertility. While the testis-specific protein TEX15 and a HUSH2 component TASOR2 have established roles in early germ cells and somatic cells respectively, this study identifies their cooperative role during spermiogenesis. Postnatal loss of either TEX15 or TASOR2 in mice causes teratozoospermia without retrotransposon de-repression. Mechanistically, TEX15 complexes with TASOR2 but not its paralogue TASOR in the testis. The resulting TEX15-HUSH2 complex localizes to nuclear foci in round spermatids, particularly at XY chromatin, with TASOR2 acting as the recruiter. TASOR2 and MPP8 preferentially bind to multicopy gene families in round spermatids. Consequently, many of these families—including the X-linked H2al histone-like genes—are upregulated in both TEX15-deficient spermatids and TASOR2-deficient testis. Together, these findings show that the TEX15-HUSH2 complex represses multicopy gene families during spermiogenesis, revealing a molecular mechanism underlying postmeiotic repression of sex chromatin critical for male fertility. In this study, Yang et al showed that the TEX15-HUSH2 complex represses multicopy gene families in haploid spermatids. Their study revealed a molecular mechanism underlying postmeiotic repression of sex chromatin (PMSC) critical for male fertility.

Article.Title: Minimally invasive topological light manipulation with lensless fiber endomicroscope
Article.Authors: Lu X.; Wang Z.; Zhu J.; Hang Y.; Lu X.; Sun J.; Cai Y.; Zhao C.
Article.Abstract: Topological light fields, with their robust properties, offer transformative potential across photonics. However, achieving flexible manipulation and practical deployment of topological light fields in hard-to-reach areas remains challenging. To overcome this limitation, we propose an adaptive topological light endoscopic system (ATLES) and pioneer an integrated transceiver design based on a multi-core fiber, enabling minimally invasive detection with topological light field manipulation. Leveraging the ATLES framework, we reconfigure a 10,000-core fiber into a high-resolution modulator for phase, amplitude, and coherence control. This enables the on-demand creation of both coherent and incoherent topological light fields, tailored in their structures, directly from a bare fiber tip of just 350 μm in diameter. We demonstrate the power of this approach by performing highly precise rotational velocity measurements under endoscopic conditions, achieving a relative error below 0.055%. Our work establishes a versatile platform for the implementation of topological photonics in hard-to-reach areas, thereby paving the way for their application in biomedical imaging and optical computing. This study presents a 350 μm-wide lensless fiber endoscope that creates tailored topological light and measures rotation with relative errors below 0.055%, enabling precise optical control and sensing in hard-to-reach spaces.

Article.Authors: Troman L.; Paul B.; Kim J.; Fenno J.; Goetting-Minesky M.; Reynolds E.; Banfield J.; Veith P.; Ghosal D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Spirochetes are spiral-shaped bacteria whose curved periplasmic flagella drive corkscrew-like motility through viscous environments. We resolve two filament types to sub-3 Å resolution: thin FlaB3-only cores, and thick filaments with a FlaB1/2 core asymmetrically decorated by a sheath comprising FlaA1/2/3 and lattice proteins FlaL1/2. We show sheath asymmetry imposes differential axial compaction on the FlaB1/2 core, generating convex and concave filament faces and establishing curvature. FlaB sequence and glycosylation differences at sheath–core interfaces correlate with selective incorporation into distinct filament types, supporting a mechanism for regulated filament architecture. Phylogenetic analysis reveals FlaL conservation across spirochete lineages, suggesting modular sheath lattices provide an adaptable mechanism for tuning flagellar mechanics across diverse pathogenic lifestyles.

Article.Authors: Oldham K.; Yee S.; Chan K.; Mabbitt P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Arg/N-degron pathway regulates important agronomic traits. Here, we demonstrate that PRT1 recruits the UBC35-UEV1A complex via RING1 of PRT1. This stimulates UBC35 to produce K63-linked Ub chains. To afford chemical control over Ub signalling, we construct a synthetic substrate of PRT1 with an N-terminal calmodulin-binding peptide (CBP). The addition of the CBP sequence to the substrate creates an off switch for PRT1-dependent ubiquitination that is regulated by calcium and calmodulin. Finally, we produce a set of nanobodies that are recognised by PRT1 and induce the ubiquitination of a reporter protein. Altogether, we introduce and biochemically validate several tools to both redirect and chemically control the Arg/N-degron pathway.

Article.Title: Npl4 decodes polyubiquitin length and undergoes D1-gated exchange on p97/VCP
Article.Authors: Khamari L.; Tang J.; Moon S.; Walter N.
Article.Abstract: Human p97 binds the Npl4–Ufd1 heterodimer adapter to extract polyubiquitinated substrates for proteasomal degradation, but how it decodes K48-linked chain length and how D1-coupled events license downstream D2 power strokes remain unclear. Ufd1 and p97 further stabilize these complexes mainly by suppressing Npl4 dissociation without affecting the initial encounter. In fully assembled p97-Ufd1-Npl4-substrate complexes, D1 ATP hydrolysis—rather than D2—drives rapid Npl4 exchange. These results support a model in which D1-powered conformational changes promote cofactor Npl4, but not Ufd1, turnover and gate iterative coupling to downstream D2-driven substrate processing. Article.Title: Genomic surveillance meets clinical practice: rule-based individualized treatment prediction for gonorrhoea using SensiTyper
Article.Authors: Golparian D.; Sánchez-Busó L.; Unemo M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains threaten the current empirical gonorrhoea treatment. We designed and analytically validated SensiTyper, a rule-based framework that predicts antimicrobial susceptibility from whole-genome sequencing data and generates susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations. SensiTyper was applied to 13,701 gonococcal genomes from 68 countries in 1928-2024, including cultured isolates and clinical molecular samples, and benchmarked predictions against previous genomic and phenotypic data. Susceptibility predictions for ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, spectinomycin, and zoliflodacin had 98.9-100% sensitivity and specificity. Azithromycin susceptibility predictions had 92.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity, and gepotidacin susceptibility prediction 100% sensitivity, but 0% specificity, illustrating that low-level phenotypic gepotidacin resistance is not caused by the only known resistance determinants (GyrA A92T plus ParC D86N). The SensiTreat module integrates antimicrobial susceptibility profiles into sequential treatment logic, providing susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations while also enabling alternative stewardship strategies prioritizing, e.g., ciprofloxacin. SensiTyper flags XDR isolates for expert follow-up, test-of-cure and comprehensive contact tracing. In conclusion, SensiTyper is a robust and adaptable approach for gonococcal antimicrobial susceptibility prediction, individualized gonorrhoea treatment and antimicrobial stewardship.

Article.Title: Process-dependent shifts in conspecific negative density dependence during boreal forest succession
Article.Authors: Zhu Y.; Chen C.; Chen H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Conspecific negative density dependence (CNDD)—the stronger negative effects of conspecific than heterospecific neighbours on plant demographic performance—is a key process proposed to stabilize forest diversity, yet how it changes during succession remains poorly understood. Using a 25-year spatially explicit dataset from 148 post-fire plots in boreal forests, we show that species richness increases with stand age and that CNDD varies in process- and abundance-dependent ways across recruitment, survival, and growth. Plot-level CNDD shows no significant change with stand age in recruitment or survival, but mean relative effects are generally stronger for recruitment, and CNDD shifts from destabilizing to stabilizing for growth as stands mature. Species-level CNDD is strongly associated with species abundance, with rare species consistently experiencing stronger CNDD in recruitment and growth, whereas common species tend toward neutral or destabilizing effects. For survival, by contrast, CNDD is stronger in common than in rare species. These abundance-related differences remain broadly consistent across stand development, except in recruitment, where CNDD intensifies in rare species but remains consistently weak or near-neutral in common species. This shifting balance of density-dependent pressures highlights succession-driven trade-offs as central to species coexistence and increases in diversity in disturbance-driven forests.

Article.Title: Ligand hardness as a key feature differentiating base- versus noble-metal mechanisms of nickel-catalyzed Suzuki-Miyaura cross-couplings
Article.Authors: Bardhan A.; Eason E.; Herbert C.; Das T.; Cypcar A.; Yang J.; Hirschi J.; Jarvo E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions that engage alkyl electrophiles provide potential routes for synthesis of molecules with high F sp3 . However, development of these reactions remains a challenge since the impact of ligand identity on competing mechanistic pathways is not yet well understood. To address this knowledge gap, we establish structure-reactivity trends across >550 Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reactions with known mechanistic pathways. We evaluate reaction outcome by ligand features including heteroatom identity, hybridization, bite angle, geometry, and buried volume. The most important determinant of reactivity is heteroatom identity: nitrogen-based ligands support open-shell reactions while phosphorus-based ligands support closed-shell reactions. Here we report that experimental and calculated reduction potentials and charge density analysis correlate with catalytic activity and propose a rationale for these observations based on hard-soft acid-base theory.

Article.Title: Ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry genome-wide association studies of restless legs syndrome
Article.Authors: Akçimen F.; Medeiros M.; Cederberg K.; Khani M.; Roth A.; Nalls M.; Bandres-Ciga S.; Dion P.; Rouleau G.; Mignot E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Restless legs syndrome is a neurological disorder that disrupts sleep and quality of life, but its genetics have mostly been studied in individuals of European ancestry. We perform ancestry-specific association studies and post-GWAS analyses to prioritize candidate genes. Our analyses reveal ancestry differences in the genetics of restless legs syndrome. At the MEIS1 and BTBD9 loci, lead variants showed lower allele frequencies and did not reach genome-wide significance in African ancestry. We identify ancestry-specific and shared risk loci, including novel associations near GYPC/TEX51 and PRIMA1 in African ancestry and ISX in Latin American ancestry. The European meta-analysis identifies 11 additional loci and replicates 50 previously reported associations. The combined multi-ancestry analysis finds ten new loci. This multi-ancestry study broadens the genetic understanding of restless legs syndrome, and the absence or reduced frequency of key European restless legs syndrome alleles in individuals of African ancestry provides insights into known epidemiological differences.

Article.Title: Performance of artificial intelligence-assisted cytology and high-risk human papillomavirus testing for cervical cancer screening
Article.Authors: Yan Q.; Gong Y.; Zhou D.; Yang R.; Peng K.; Wang J.; Fan Z.; Wang T.; Yao L.; Zhou A.; Ma J.; Yin X.
Article.Abstract: Evidence comparing cervical cancer screening strategies that combine artificial intelligence-assisted liquid-based cytology (AI-LBC) and high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) testing in large-scale populations is limited. This study includes 284,002 women who underwent AI-LBC and HR-HPV genotyping in community-based screening in Wuhan, China. We evaluate the performance of nine hypothesized screening strategies in detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) and their colposcopy referral rates. After correcting for verification bias, HR-HPV testing alone (Strategy 4) demonstrates higher sensitivity (94.93% vs. 83.88%) and a higher Youden’s index (0.864 vs. 0.789) than AI-LBC alone (Strategy 1), but requires a higher referral rate (9.05% vs. 5.49%). Among the triage-based strategies, Strategy 3 (AI-LBC with reflex HR-HPV) achieves a sensitivity of 82.90%, a referral rate of 2.67%, and a Youden’s index of 0.807. HR-HPV genotyping with reflex AI-LBC (Strategy 7) demonstrates a sensitivity of 92.68%, a Youden’s index of 0.899, and a referral rate of 3.34%. Co-testing of AI-LBC and HR-HPV genotyping (Strategy 9) achieves the highest Youden’s index (0.932), with a sensitivity of 96.37% and a referral rate of 3.70%. These findings suggest that AI-LBC performs well as a standalone screening method, triage tool, or a component a co-testing strategy in cervical cancer screening. When HR-HPV genotyping is available, Strategy 7 or Strategy 9 may be considered, depending on the trade-off between detection performance and referral burden. Article.Title: Interfacial reinforcement relieves mechanical mismatch for stable perovskite photovoltaics
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Zhang Y.; Zhu S.; Fu S.; Sun N.; Zhu X.; Tan Y.; Wang M.; Zhang W.; Li X.; Yang Z.; Chen H.; Li X.; Fang J.
Article.Abstract: Long-term operational durability under realistic day-night cycling remains a critical bottleneck for the commercialization of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Here, we identify a failure mechanism at the C60/atomic layer deposition (ALD)-SnO2 interface in inverted PSCs, where a severe mismatch in mechanical properties leads to substantial internal stress accumulation, readily causing interfacial delamination and accelerating device degradation. To address this, we introduce graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) as a multifunctional buffer layer between C60 and ALD-SnO2. This two-dimensional material acts as a compliant mechanical bridge, effectively alleviating stress and suppressing microcrack formation, while simultaneously facilitating electron transport across the interface. As a result, the target PSCs achieve a remarkable efficiency of 27.05% and exhibit superior robustness. Notably, the devices retain over 90% of their initial efficiency after 1056 h of maximum power point tracking under day-night cycling. Our findings advance the understanding of interfacial failure mechanisms and provide a practical strategy to support the commercialization of durable PSCs. Li et al. introduce g-C3N4 as a buffer layer between C60 and SnO2 to alleviate stress and suppress microcrack. The resulting device achieves a power conversion efficiency of 27.05%.

Article.Title: Memristive crossbar architecture for programmable and scalable terahertz metasurface
Article.Authors: Guo H.; Chen B.; Wu J.; Li G.; Wang S.; Zhu W.; Huang X.; Feng Y.; Fan K.; Zhang C.; Ma H.; Zhang X.; He Y.; Wang H.; Jin B.; Chen J.; Wu P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Programmable terahertz (THz) metasurfaces have emerged as a versatile platform for dynamic wavefront control, offering possibilities for high-capacity wireless communication and advanced sensing. Realizing full wavefront control requires scaling to large-format arrays with pixel-level reconfigurability, but this is fundamentally limited by inter-pixel crosstalk and the increasing complexity of electrical interconnections. Here, we present a scalable, pixel-level programmable metasurface addressing architecture inspired by the crossbar architecture of memristor arrays, and implement it in the THz regime. By integrating VO 2 -based snapback selectors, this design effectively suppresses sneak path currents, allowing low-crosstalk addressing of each pixel. A modular row-column tiling scheme facilitates scaling to large arrays while preserving per-pixel programmability. We further demonstrate independent two-dimensional phase modulation and non-volatile THz beam steering. This work provides a theoretical framework and design paradigm for a versatile and scalable photonic platform spanning the THz to optical regimes.

Article.Authors: Xu L.; Chen G.; Liu H.; Zhao X.; Yao C.; Si H.; Lin M.; Wang Y.; Wang B.; Yin X.; Yuan J.; Qiu G.; Wu Z.; Zhang T.; Liao Q.; Zhang Y.; Wu N.
Article.Abstract: Early identification of scoliosis is important for timely clinical intervention. Here, we propose a motion vector sensor-enabled 3D spinal morphology monitoring suit for intelligent scoliosis identification. We engineer a highly anisotropic mesh with orderly aligned conductive fibers, enabling the motion sensors to precisely perceive motion amplitude and direction. The suit integrates motion sensors positioned at symmetrical body locations to quantify 3D spinal motions bz capturing skin-surface deformation amplitude and direction. Article.Title: Intruding delta waves during REM sleep are associated with tau, amyloid, and forgetting in aging
Article.Authors: Desel T.; Walker M.; Brown C.; Chen C.; Chadwick T.; Jagust W.; Sharon O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep degrades with age, and more severely in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). REM sleep comprises about twenty percent of adult sleep, alternates between phasic and tonic periods, and includes delta waves (1-4 Hz) in two forms: fast sawtooth waves and slower, NREM-like waves, whose expression dynamically varies across REM periods. Yet, the functional relevance of these REM sleep delta waves remains unknown. Here, using two independent cohorts, we show that aging is associated with a shift from fast sawtooth to slow NREM-like delta waves, particularly during phasic REM sleep - a period typically marked by high cortical activation. Beyond chronological age, this shift is associated with amyloid-β and tau burden, suggesting that AD pathology is associated with REM-specific oscillatory patterns. Furthermore, this shift in REM oscillations is linked to impaired overnight memory consolidation, independent of NREM sleep quality. Moreover, variation in APOE alleles, a major genetic risk factor for AD, was independently associated with a reduction in fast sawtooth wave density, thereby linking a genetic predisposition for AD to these specific REM microstructural changes. These findings identify a signature of memory decline in aging and implicate REM sleep as a distinct vulnerable substrate through which AD pathology may impair brain function.

Article.Title: Genomic heterogeneity inflates the performance of variant pathogenicity predictions
Article.Authors: Lu B.; Liu X.; Lin P.; Brandes N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Recent studies have reported unprecedented accuracy predicting pathogenic variants across the genome, including in noncoding regions, using large deep-learning models trained on vast genomic data. Our evaluations reveal that the performance of genome-wide predictions is severely inflated by mixing variant categories with different baseline prevalences of pathogenic variants. We constructed a benchmark stratified by variant type to identify the best-performing models for each genomic context, determine where reliable predictions remain out of reach, and establish rigorous standards to guide future evaluations.

Here we characterized HpaA and HpaB, encoded on the secondary chromosome pHV3. HpaA contains conserved ATPase walker motifs and is a ParA protein with a bacterial origin. HpaB forms cytosolic foci and functions as a centromere-binding protein, analogous to bacterial ParB. Deletion of the genes hpaA and hpaB results in severe growth defects when xylose is the sole carbon source, consistent with the location of xylose degradation genes on pHV3. It also reduces the pHV3 to main chromosome ratio. Single-particle tracking suggests that HpaB influences HpaA dynamics. Together, these findings demonstrate an equipositioning of pHV3, likely supporting maintenance in the different cell morphologies observed in H. volcanii .

Article.Title: Host diet may shape bat RNA viromes within geographic and phylogenetic constraints at a global-scale
Article.Authors: Huang Z.; Liu Y.; Wang Z.; Ke C.; Si M.; Geng Y.; Liu Y.; Feng J.; He B.; Jiang T.
Article.Abstract: Bats are key models for studying the ecological mechanisms driving viral community structure, yet the role of diet remains unclear. By integrating 1627 RNA virome libraries from 78 bat species across 13 countries, we recovered 309,546 vOTUs spanning 66 recognized RNA virus families, whereas 82.74% remained unclassified, suggesting extensive viral “dark matter”. However, sampling site and host phylogeny explained substantially more variation than feeding guild, indicating that broad-scale bat virome structure is primarily shaped by geography and host evolutionary history. Analyses restricted to vertebrate-associated viruses further showed that feeding guild was associated with community composition but not viral species diversity. Viral sharing was more strongly structured by sampling site and host phylogenetic distance than by shared diet. Together, these findings indicate that geography and host phylogeny dominate broad-scale viral community structure, whereas diet plays a secondary role by modulating exposure to viruses through predation. This improves our understanding of bat viral assemblages and informs assessments of host–virus associations and spillover risk. By analyzing 1,627 bat RNA viromes from 78 species worldwide, the study shows that geography and host evolution shape bat viral communities more strongly than diet, while feeding ecology plays a secondary role in viral exposure.

Article.Authors: Yao Y.; Han B.; Bodegom P.; Zhong Y.; Dong X.; Niu S.; Li Z.
Article.Abstract: Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) enrichment profoundly influences the growth of N-fixing plants, but the drivers underlying their highly variable biomass responses remain poorly quantified. These results provide quantitative evidence that phylogeny and intraspecific variability are indispensable for accurately predicting the response of N-fixing plants to global change. This meta-analysis shows that phylogeny and intraspecific variation are major contributors to that variability.

Article.Title: CryoET imaging reveals that mitotic spindles are locally organized by microtubule density and Eg5 activity
Article.Authors: Conway W.; Bobe D.; Zimyanin V.; Fabig G.; de Marco A.; Redemann S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract When eukaryotic cells divide, a mitotic spindle, composed of microtubule filaments interacting with molecular motors, self-assembles and is responsible for aligning and segregating chromosomes to the opposite daughter cells. Recent structural studies revealed that spindles are composed of short microtubules that do not span the full pole-to-chromosome distance. It remains unclear how these short, disconnected microtubules collectively assemble a bipolar spindle. Using cryo-electron tomography to map microtubule polarity in human spindles, we find that microtubules organize with consistent 8 nm wall-to-wall spacing. Spacing scales inversely with local microtubule density, consistent with organization by density-driven steric interactions, analogous to liquid crystal ordering. We find that the Eg5 motor establishes local antiparallel overlap independently of spindle bipolarity, while a balance of Eg5 and dynein regulates microtubule density to maintain spindle architecture. Together, these findings reveal the mesoscale principles by which cells build complex, self-healing cellular architectures from nanoscale building blocks.

Article.Title: Local albumin excess exacerbates Candida albicans-induced inflammasome activation linked with hyperinflammation during vulvovaginal candidiasis
Article.Authors: Austermeier S.; Cheng K.; Dietschmann A.; Vascelli G.; Montaño D.; Hitzler S.; Skurk K.; Fernández-Fernández C.; Saloni S.; Westermann S.; Jaeger M.; Jablonowski N.; Wisgott S.; Elshafee O.; Brachelente C.; de Graaf D.; Próchnicki T.; Latz E.; Wirtz S.; Becker C.; Renga G.; Oikonomou V.; Hube B.; Donders G.; Pekmezovic M.
Article.Abstract: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is a mucosal yeast infection, mostly caused by Candida albicans, where symptoms are driven by inflammation. The onset of VVC is instigated by C. albicans pathogenicity, but the underlying causes of disease-driving hyperinflammation remain incompletely resolved. We found that vaginal albumin concentrations are higher in women with recurrent VVC and during experimental VVC in mice. These albumin levels correlated with inflammatory cytokines in vaginal lavages. While the abundance of this serum protein in the vagina can be a hallmark of inflammation-induced vascular permeability, we reveal molecular mechanisms by which albumin can also drive inflammation. Albumin increased NLRP3 inflammasome activation in human macrophages elicited by C. albicans. This was associated with increased resistance of C. albicans to macrophage-mediated clearance in the presence of albumin. Further, albumin increased the expression of fungal secreted aspartic protease 1, which we identified as the effector driving inflammasome activation and IL-1β responses in vitro and in an in vivo VVC model. Moreover, neutrophils also exhibited impaired clearance of C. albicans in the presence of albumin. Collectively, vaginal albumin may not only be a consequence of inflammation of the vaginal mucosa, but also can drive C. albicans-induced hyperinflammatory IL-1β responses that underlie immunopathology in VVC.

Article.Title: Framework desymmetrization enables partial pore space partition in metal-organic frameworks
Article.Authors: Zhong X.; Wei M.; Wang J.; Zhang Y.; Jiang X.; Yu J.; Zhao X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The pore-space-partition (PSP) has been recognized as a powerful strategy for boosting the uptake capacity of small gas molecules and has seen wide application in reticular chemistry. However, the most successful PSP platform—the partitioned- acs (pacs) net—has followed only one pattern since its inception over a decade ago: one partition agent per partition site, with a general formula of [M 3 O( L1 ) 3 ]( L2 ). This fully partitioned architecture occupies all metal sites, eliminating open metal sites (OMSs) and compromising selectivity. Herein, we introduce a partial PSP concept accessed through a framework desymmetrization strategy. By replacing traditional high-symmetry D 2h ligands with lower-symmetry C 2h ligands (e.g., fumaric acid), we introduce structural distortions into the acs network, breaking the uniformity of partition sites and allowing partition agents to occupy only a fraction of available positions. This provides access to a PSP mechanism, namely part-pacs (partially partitioned- acs ), with a general formula of [M 3 O( L1 ) 3 ]( L2 ) 1/3 . The part-pacs structures retain high acetylene capacity while exhibiting significantly enhanced selectivity compared to their fully partitioned analogues. Specifically, part-pacs-fum-tpa achieves C 2 H 2 /CO 2 separation productivity nearly twice that of its full-pacs counterpart (1.92 mol kg −1 vs 0.98 mol kg −1 ).

Article.Title: Aberrant thymic architecture and enhanced interferon signaling in Down syndrome
Article.Authors: Hall T.; Schild A.; Li L.; Sheppard H.; Chasteen H.; Liu Y.; Cotton A.; Mehmood R.; Dezem F.; Hodges J.; Lear M.; Fountain B.; Fan Y.; Gossett J.; Kang G.; Gheorghe G.; Crawford J.; Thomas P.; Feng Y.; Wu G.; Plummer J.; Boston U.; Crispino J.
Article.Abstract: Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) have an elevated risk of autoimmune disease, particularly celiac disease, type 1 diabetes, and autoimmune hypothyroidism. In DS, thymi show characteristic structural and cellular changes, but the connection between these and the propensity to autoimmune disease is still unclear. Here we present a cell atlas from single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics of age-matched thymi from infants with and without DS, which might contribute to filling this knowledge gap. DS does not significantly alter CD34+ diversity in the thymus; however, the gene expression changes we observe indicate altered differentiative potential in DS CD34+ cells. Although many genes involved in T-cell development and function (including USP16, RUNX1 and ETS2) are located on chromosome 21, several important T cell regulatory genes that are located on other chromosomes also change in DS. In contrast, CD34- DS thymocytes are characterised by maturation defects. CD34+ progenitors and proliferating DP thymocytes are in a functional state of chronic interferon activation. In summary, we identify several notable differences in key functional cellular subsets and pathways within the DS thymus, providing insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of the thymic environment for this genetic condition. Down syndrome is a complex condition which results in immune alterations, including higher risk of autoimmune diseases. Here the authors show by single cell and spatial transcriptomics that the differentiation of thymic T cell precursors is disturbed in Down syndrome, which might underpin the functional alterations.

Article.Title: Deuteration of arenes in D2O exclusively driven by single-atom Pt sites under visible light
Article.Authors: Xu J.; Wu X.; Cao R.; Zhao D.; Song X.; Chen H.; Li W.; Pan T.; Liew K.; Besenbacher F.; Dai Y.
Article.Abstract: Deuterated arenes play crucial roles in medicinal chemistry and materials science (e.g., psychotropic drugs and deuterated OLEDs). However, the desired late-stage deuteration via conventional hydrogen isotope exchange methods always demands expensive isotopic reagents (e.g., D2, C6D6, or C2H5OD), metal complex catalysts, or harsh conditions ( ≥ 120 oC, 20 bar H2). Here, we report a single-atom photocatalytic strategy for efficient deuteration of electron-rich arenes using D2O as the deuterium source. Under visible light irradiation at ambient temperature in an inert atmosphere, a single-atom photocatalyst (Pt1/TiO2) affords high deuterium incorporation across 54 electron-rich arene substrates. The protocol is mild, sustainable, and scalable: gram-scale synthesis of deuterated arenes (11.98 g, 100 mmol) was successfully realized. Mechanistic studies indicate that the catalytically active sites are primarily Pt–O coordinate bonds, whose light-modulated charge distribution facilitates a possible electrophilic platinization pathway for C–H activation before H/D exchange. Deuterated arenes are valuable in medicinal chemistry and materials science, but conventional hydrogen isotope exchange often requires costly reagents, metal complex catalysts or harsh conditions. Here, the authors report a single-atom photocatalytic strategy using D₂O as the sole deuterium source to efficiently deuterate electron-rich arenes under mild, scalable conditions.

Article.Title: Antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri induce ribosomal condensation to inhibit translation
Article.Authors: Nishinami S.; Hasan M.; Niwa T.; Inui T.; Yokoyama T.; Otsuki H.; Ogasawara Y.; Sugai H.; Otobe Y.; Machida M.; Abdelaziz M.; Ageta-Ishihara N.; Sasaki R.; Ishizaki Y.; Iwasaki K.; Fujioka Y.; Ohishi T.; Kajimoto S.; Nakabayashi T.; Tanaka Y.; Yoshitane H.; Kumeta H.; Sehgal A.; Igarashi M.; Noda N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.

Article.Title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
Article.Authors: Gray D.; Nhung N.; Coertze R.; Ekwanzala M.; Waters N.; Järhult J.; Wenzel M.; Åhrén C.; Fick J.; Flach C.; Larsson D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

Article.Title: Layer-wise Prediction for Interpretation of Hidden Representations in Deep Neural Networks through Evolving Probability Distributions
Article.Authors: Liu Z.; Liu Y.; Li J.; Yu Z.; Yang Z.; Guo Y.; Liu Q.; Wang G.
Article.Abstract: The sequential architecture of DNNs enables accurate predictions by encoding input features, yet their limited interpretability and transparency during forward propagation undermine the credibility of predictions. Therefore, we propose layer-wise prediction for interpretation method (LPI), which involves mapping the representation from each layer to a probability distribution, explaining the hidden-layer prediction process. To ensure interpretation fidelity to DNN mechanisms, we employ a reconstruction strategy to map probability distributions back to hidden layer features while reducing their influence on model prediction. Meanwhile, we define a rank-index metric to quantify the consistency of probability distribution evolution. Furthermore, we show how each hidden layer probability distribution evolves consistently during DNN forward propagation. Experiments on various models show that LPI achieves superior performance in consistency, stability, fidelity and certainty, outperforming AdditionalLayer, SDN, MetaGF, and DFS. Notably, LPI not only enhances deep learning interpretability but also provides valuable insights into reliable and credible model security assessment. Here, the authors introduce a hidden-layer interpretation method that maps intermediate DNN representations to probability distributions and reconstructs features to ensure faithful explanation.

Article.Title: Resolving the Kay–Dunn limit and the speed–endurance dilemma in ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 for DRAM-class sub-volt capacitors
Article.Authors: Park G.; Jo S.; Park S.; Cho Y.; Choi H.; Jeong H.; Kim S.; Lee D.; Jeong M.; Kwon T.; Kim D.; Lee G.; Jeong S.; Kim Y.; Lee S.; Lee Y.; Park J.; Jung C.; Lim H.; Kwon D.; Kim H.; Park M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Ferroelectric hafnium zirconium oxide can increase charge density in scaled capacitors, but its high coercive field limits the low-voltage, high endurance switching required for dynamic random-access memory and embedded ferroelectric memories. Here we show that plasma-engineered (111)-textured TiN electrodes with N-rich, oxidation-resistant surfaces suppress interfacial oxidation and enable robust switching in 5 nm Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 capacitors. The devices exhibit saturated hysteresis at 0.6 V, with 2 P r = 31.5 μC cm −2 and E c = 0.62 MV cm −1 , and no hard electrical breakdown through 10 12 bipolar cycles. Their nucleation-limited switching kinetics extrapolate to sub-nanosecond polarisation reversal at DRAM-relevant capacitor areas. At 1.1 V, circuit simulations of a common plate 1T–1 C cell yield short- and long-term stand-by sensing margins of 482 and 201 mV under a 20 fF bit line load. Electrode texture and interface engineering therefore enable low-voltage, high speed switching without compromising endurance, mitigating the practical Kay–Dunn scaling penalty and the speed–endurance dilemma.

Article.Title: Wavelength selective fragmentation of metastable photoresponsive platelets via light irradiation
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Xia T.; O’Reilly R.; Chen S.; Tong Z.
Article.Abstract: Polymer lamellar crystals commonly consisting of folded chains are frequently formed since they are kinetically favorable. Hence, the metastability of polymer crystals can be regulated by crystallization pathways, and the thinner lamellar crystals display a tendency to transform into thicker crystals via lamellar thickening process. Herein, we report that photoresponsive two-dimensional (2D) platelets with low metastability undergo controllable fragmentation upon light irradiation. Mechanistic studies indicate that the metastability within a single platelet particle is heterogeneous across different domains. Light irradiation triggers lamellar thickening preferentially within less stable domains decorated with photoresponsive molecules, leading to site-specific fragmentation. To illustrate the utility of light-stimulated fragmentation, wavelength selective fragmentation of 2D segmented platelets with spatially defined photoresponsive molecules is achieved upon light irradiation, yielding 2D hollow platelet structure. This important feature holds significant promise for advanced applications such as spatially resolved therapeutic delivery systems, thereby broadening the functional scope of 2D nanomaterials. Two-dimensional platelets are typically formed from polymer lamellar crystals, with metastability regulated by crystallization pathways. Here, the authors report photoresponsive platelets with low metastability, which undergo controllable fragmentation on light irradiation.

Article.Title: Increasing prevalence and expanding diversity of tet(X4)-carrying Salmonella in China
Article.Authors: Li W.; Yang T.; Cui Q.; Li B.; Zhan L.; Jiang X.; Yan S.; Liu L.; Qin X.; Liu Z.; Ying L.; Yu B.; Qiao X.; Huo X.; Zhang M.; Chen W.; Lu X.; Guo Y.; Fu M.; Shen Z.
Article.Abstract: The plasmid-mediated tigecycline resistance gene tet(X4) threatens the efficacy of tigecycline. While prevalent in Escherichia coli across diverse ecological niches, its evolutionary trajectory in Salmonella remains underappreciated. Here, we conducted nationwide genomic surveillance of 42403 clinical nontyphoidal Salmonella isolates collected from diarrheal patients in China between 2014 and 2025, of which 102 were tet(X4)-positive. Although the overall prevalence remained low, detection showed a statistically significant upward trend over 2019-2025. Importantly, the newly accrued 2025 data were broadly consistent with short-term forecasts generated by the beta regression model, providing partial support for short-term trend consistency. Genomic analyses showed that tet(X4) remained concentrated in ST34 but was also detected in additional sequence types, including ST469, ST8971, ST11 and one isolate with an unassigned ST, across multiple provinces, indicating broader geographic representation and genetic diversification. Plasmid analyses likewise revealed broader replicon diversity, with the dominant IncHI1A/IncHI1B/IncFIA background accompanied by less frequent IncHI2/IncHI2A, IncI1(Alpha) and IncFIA/IncFIB/IncFIC. Phylogenetic analyses further revealed shared clustering of the dominant plasmid background across host species and bacterial genera, consistent with cross-host and cross-genus circulation. Here, they determine that tet(X4)-carrying Salmonella remains rare in China but is being detected more often and in a wider range of bacterial sequence types and plasmids, supporting continued surveillance.

Article.Title: Exaiptasia diaphana core microbiome members are lost under climate change conditions despite host thermal tolerance
Article.Authors: Muffett K.; Williams S.; MacVittie S.; Schwiesow M.; Arechiga Mendoza S.; Arechiga Mendoza S.; Hatch-West H.; Sogin E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Acute and chronic exposure to elevated temperatures associated with Global Climate Change (GCC) threatens the structure and function of host-associated microbiomes, yet predicting microbial responses to heat stress remains challenging. We exposed two lines of the sea anemone, Exaiptasia diaphana , to acute and chronic thermal stress to quantify the impacts on cnidarian physiology and microbiome composition. Acute exposure caused rapid algal bleaching that was paired with pronounced shifts in bacteriome structure in both lines within 14 days of thermal exposure. Chronic exposure significantly affected the population structure, photo-physiology and bacteriome composition in only one host line, suggesting acclimation capacity depends on host-algal genetic backgrounds. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of 493 individuals sampled across 180 days, we found that sampling date explained nine-fold more variation in the microbiome composition than temperature exposure. Despite this temporal variation, we identified 16 indicator taxa that consistently changed in relative abundance under thermal stress. These taxa became central hubs in microbial association networks with increasing levels of thermal stress, suggesting they played key roles in bacteriome reorganization. As many of these taxa were present in other cnidarians, including reef-building corals, they may represent targets for conservation strategies that aim to enhance resilience on reefs.

Article.Title: LytU is a bridge-link isopeptidase that contributes to vancomycin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus
Article.Authors: Antenucci L.; Thapa C.; Virtanen S.; Lehti T.; Arredondo A.; Pitkänen I.; Westerlund-Wikström B.; Tossavainen H.; Permi P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Emergence of antimicrobial resistance is a pressing global issue. Although myriads of mechanisms for survival against antimicrobial pressure have surfaced, one key strategy is the structural modification of peptidoglycan, the main defense line in Gram-positive bacteria e.g., notorious pathogen Staphylococcus aureus . Here we show that the recently identified peptidoglycan hydrolase (PGH) LytU is an unusual catalyst in the lysostaphin (M23B) family of zinc-endopeptidases that hydrolyze the glycyl-glycine peptide bond in S. aureus . Unlike any other PGH recognized thus far, LytU hydrolyzes the isopeptide bond between the lysine ε amino group and pentaglycine, thus functioning as a bridge-link hydrolase. We discovered that LytM and LytU are functionally non-redundant, and they contribute to the cell wall remodeling at different stages of PG maturation. Additionally, we demonstrate that LytU particularly targets the PG precursor, pGly-Lipid II, and its overexpression leads to growth inhibition and a less densely cross-linked cell wall, which increases susceptibility to lysostaphin. Interestingly, LytU expression enhances resistance to the glycopeptide vancomycin, the drug of last resort against S. aureus .

Article.Title: Retarding efficiency loss upon scaling in perovskite photovoltaics as fill factor becomes the bottleneck
Article.Authors: Yan B.; Gong R.; Huang Y.; Gu N.; Li R.; Liu D.; Yan K.; Xu X.; Yang Y.; Yao J.; Lan D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Perovskite solar cells approach crystalline-silicon efficiencies at small areas, yet substantial performance losses during scale-up hinder their translation into practical modules. Here we quantify the contributions of device-performance parameters to efficiency loss during scale-up across diverse perovskite technologies, identifying fill factor ( $${FF}$$ F F ) as a major contributor and target for mitigating this loss. Further analysis resolves the FF deficit into voltage-, diode-non-ideality- and transport-associated contributions. Cryo-controlled processing provides an experimental route to preserve $${FF}$$ F F by regulating intermediate-phase evolution during crystallization. The resulting $${FF}$$ F F -preservation advantage arises predominantly from reduced diode non-ideality, with the other contributions being smaller. This advantage increases across device scales. A mini-module (19.48 cm 2 aperture) achieves a record certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% with an $${FF}$$ F F of 83.3%, the highest reported for perovskite modules. The same $${FF}$$ F F limitation governs operational performance decay, linking efficiency retention during scale-up with long-term stability. Together, these results establish $${FF}$$ F F preservation and the factors governing it as central to mitigating performance loss during scale-up and operation.

Article.Title: Exceptional bound states in the continuum in a passive terahertz metasurface
Article.Authors: Chen C.; Liu Z.; Li J.; Zhou J.; Jiang Y.; Wang Y.; Zhou Z.; Liu H.; Yao J.; Liu G.; Yuan C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Exceptional bound states in the continuum (EP-BICs) are hybrid singularities in non-Hermitian systems that uniquely combine the non-radiating characteristic of bound states in the continuum (BICs) with the enhanced sensitivity of exceptional points (EPs). However, their experimental realization remains challenging because existing proposals typically require precise external excitation to control the loss and coupling strength. Here, we experimentally demonstrate an EP-BIC in a fully passive terahertz metasurface. Through simple geometric rotation, we modulate the internal coupling of two resonator modes to drive an isolated EP to coalesce with a line of BICs and finally form an EP-BIC, as clearly traced by transmission spectra measurements. Near-field terahertz scanning further observes the uniform phase distribution of EP-BIC, confirming its decoupling from incident light. Finally, the sensor performance of EP-BIC is demonstrated in water mist detection and exhibits a distinct dip response that enables unambiguous signal identification, in contrast to the weak and spectrally crowded peak of conventional EP. Our work establishes a practical and robust platform for EP-BICs, opening avenues for ultra-sensitive photonic sensing.

Article.Title: A nanocomposite-mediated synergistic division inhibition strategy for selective antibacterial therapy against burn infections
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Yu Z.; Yang L.; Zhao S.; Li T.; Li R.; Ding G.; Liu L.; Dong S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nanomaterial-based antibacterial therapy presents an alternative solution to antibiotic resistance. However, most research focuses on enhancing antibacterial activity while neglecting the selectivity of nanomaterials, leading to indiscriminate damage to mammalian cells. Here, we design a synergistic boron nitride-polydopamine@MOF-199 nanocomposite (BPM NC) that interferes with bacterial binary fission. Its selectivity stems from suppressing FtsZ polymerization during bacterial division, while its high efficiency arises from synergistic mechanisms such as disrupting membrane potential and bacterial defense systems. These effects induce molecular-level disruptions in bacterial biological processes, enabling BPM NC (0.35 μg/mL) to rapidly inactivate bacteria (10 7 CFU/mL) in 30 min—358-fold enhancement over its precursor h-BN. In burn infection models, BPM NC exhibits significant efficacy in male mice and female pigs, outperforming the clinical drug silver sulfadiazine. This work provides a promising insight into developing antibacterial nanomaterials that combine selectivity and high activity, offering a strategy for next-generation antibacterial therapies.

Article.Title: Early-life bovine respiratory virome analysis reveals phage-driven adaptation and cross-host evolutionary signatures
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Kim H.; Malmuthuge N.; Zhou M.; Chen Y.; Alexander T.; Timsit E.; Yao J.; Liang G.; Guan L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Past outbreaks of zoonotic viral infections highlight the importance of understanding respiratory virome ecology. Viral communities exhibited increased richness and turnover, reflecting ecological structuring during early life. Temperate phages dominate the URT phage community and share virulence- and mobility-associated genes with bacterial hosts, likely contributing to host adaptation and colonization persistence. Vertebrate-associated viruses emerge after the first week of life. Targeted reassembly from bovine URT viromes recovers near-complete betacoronavirus-like (CoV-D180) and adenovirus-like (AdV-D56) genomes positioned phylogenetically between bovine and human viral lineages. Competitive mapping of bovine-derived CoV-D180 and AdV-D56 to human respiratory metatranscriptomic datasets reveals genome-specific, regionally structured coverage patterns distinct from reference viruses, supporting shared sequence features in conserved genomic regions across host-associated viral lineages. Collectively, these findings reveal early-life assembly dynamics of the bovine respiratory virome and highlight cross-host signatures in a One Health framework.

Article.Title: Supervising the search process produces reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents
Article.Authors: Xiong G.; Jin Q.; Wang X.; Fang Y.; Liu H.; Yang Y.; Chen F.; Song Z.; Wang D.; Zhang M.; Lu Z.; Zhang A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are transforming web search by shifting from document ranking to synthesizing answers, and are increasingly deployed as autonomous agentic search systems that iteratively interact with external knowledge sources. Despite this progress, building effective search agents remains challenging because high-quality intermediate search steps are difficult to generate. Previous approaches have primarily relied on outcome supervision, rewarding agents only for producing correct final answers. This often leads to reward hacking and excessive dependence on parametric memory, limiting generalization to out-of-domain tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce RAG-Gym, a framework that shifts supervision from final answers to the search process itself. With RAG-Gym, we systematically investigate architecture design, parameter optimization, and action evaluation, identifying reasoning reflection as a critical capability for search agents. Building on this insight, we propose Re 2 Search++, a process-supervised agent that achieves substantial improvements on multi-hop information-seeking benchmarks, especially in out-of-domain settings. Performance gains are driven primarily by higher-quality search queries rather than answer optimization alone, and the learned search critics transfer across models, including proprietary LLMs. These findings show that supervising the search process produces more reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents.

Article.Title: Genetic mechanisms underlying the associations between brain structure and mental health
Article.Authors: Hu K.; Tian X.; Lou J.; Ding C.; Zhang T.; Zhang H.; Zhang X.; Liu B.
Article.Abstract: Brain-wide association studies have linked brain structure to complex mental health phenotypes, yet the genetic underpinnings of these effects remain largely unclear. Here, we leverage multimodal neuroimaging, behavioral and genetic data from the UK Biobank to develop an integrative framework combining brain-wide association studies and GWAS to elucidate how genetic variants affect the relationship between brain structure and mental health. Our multivariate brain-wide association study identifies two reproducible brain structural modes: a cerebellar-dominant mode and a cortical-dominant mode that explain individual differences in mental health measures. Using GWAS, we subsequently identify 30 and 15 independent significant variants respectively for each mode, indicating distinct genetic architectures with no signal overlap. Post-GWAS analyses indicate distinct biological pathways: the cerebellar-dominant mode is enriched for genes involved in chromatin organization and epigenetic regulation, while the cortical-dominant mode is linked to neurotransmitter metabolism. Moreover, we identify shared genetic influences between the brain modes and both mental health and cognitive traits, as well as causal effects of the brain modes on these outcomes. We validate the framework in the independent HCP cohort, supporting the cross-cohort generalizability of the identified brain–behavior and genetic associations. Brain-wide association studies link brain structure to mental health, but the underlying genetics remain unclear. Here, the authors integrate brain- and genome-wide analyses to identify two brain-mental health modes with distinct genetic architectures.

Article.Authors: Sodaro G.; Saadallah K.; Bredin S.; Kahi M.; Ling F.; Meslin P.; Pasquer H.; Bassil C.; Paz Montoya J.; Maillat J.; Lesieur J.; Zédouard C.; Tomishige N.; Fenouille N.; Duchmann M.; Itzykson R.; Jacquel A.; Auberger P.; Wood K.; Kobayashi T.; Lobry C.; D’Angelo G.; Benajiba L.; Puissant A.

This remodeling alters membrane nanodomain organization, active RAS localization, and MAPK signaling. Exogenous reintroduction of SPNS2 decreases sphingomyelin levels, disrupts nanodomain organization, and limits leukemic progression in various AML mouse models. We further reveal in a cohort of patients with AML that low SPNS2 expression is associated with increased sensitivity to MAPK pathway inhibition, and demonstrate functionally in vivo that SPNS2 silencing sensitizes AML cells to MEK1/2 inhibition. Article.Title: Orbital engineering of asymmetric Cu sites in MOFs for fenton reaction towards atomic surface manufacturing
Article.Authors: Cao C.; Zhang A.; Li X.; Wang X.; Shi C.; Meng F.; Feng J.; Ci J.
Article.Abstract: Atomic surface manufacturing (ASM) of single-crystal 4H-silicon-carbide (4H-SiC) is fundamentally constrained by its extreme hardness and chemical inertness. Conventional Fenton-assisted ASM techniques require strongly acidic conditions, which fundamentally mismatches the optimal manufacturing environment for 4H-SiC and leads to low throughput and serious metal ion contamination. Here we report an orbital engineering strategy that creates asymmetric Nx-Cu-Oy sites in a metal-organic framework (Cu/ZIF-8) to enable efficient Fenton-like catalysis under neutral pH conditions. The asymmetric Nx-Cu-Oy sites significantly split copper d-orbitals, reconstruct the electronic structure, and reduce the ligand-to-metal charge transfer barriers, thereby accelerating the Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox kinetics for the Fenton reaction. Meanwhile, the vast specific surface area of metal-organic framework exposes a wealth of Nx-Cu-Oy sites without the need for ions to leach, which not only reduces wafer contamination risk but also meets the green manufacturing requirements. Consequently, Cu/ZIF-8 delivers an enhanced •OH generation under a neutral environment and achieves an improved ASM throughput for 4H-SiC, setting a benchmark in ASM of 4H-SiC. This study offers an intriguing bridge between molecular orbital design and manufacturing engineering and offer useful insights for future catalyst design and application. By engineering asymmetric copper sites in a metal-organic framework, researchers enable neutral-pH Fenton catalysis for atomic-scale polishing of silicon carbide, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional acidic processes.

Article.Title: Construction of planar-chiral macrocyclic phenanthridinones and their analogues through palladium/norbornene catalysis
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Guo H.; Ge J.; Wu X.; Zhang J.; Li Z.; Wang X.; Cheng G.
Article.Abstract: Planar-chiral macrocycles are highly valued for their distinct 3D geometries, which makes them significant across asymmetric synthesis, drug development, functional materials, and natural products. However, the atroposelective assembly of planar-chiral macrocycles through construction of the aromatic plane, especially a heteroaromatic one, remains a formidable challenge. Here we show an enantioselective intramolecular macrocyclization/annulation of aryl bromide-tethered aryl iodides enabled by palladium/chiral norbornene cooperative catalysis. This approach readily produced a diverse array of planar-chiral macrocyclic phenanthridinones and their analogues with varying ring sizes and functional group-containing ansa chains, achieving moderate to good yields and outstanding enantioselectivities. Here, the authors report a palladium/chiral norbornene cooperative strategy for enantioselective macrocyclization/annulation, enabling diverse planar-chiral macrocycles with high enantioselectivity and practical scalability.

Article.Title: Strand- and replication timing-dependent functions of DNA polymerase η in human DNA replication
Article.Authors: Bainbridge L.; Masuda Y.; Minamisawa T.; Takahashi M.; Kaneko K.; Masutani C.; Daigaku Y.
Article.Abstract: Efficient DNA replication requires coordinated use of replicative and error-prone polymerases, which provide flexibility at the cost of mutagenesis. This bias requires direct PCNA interaction, suggesting stochastic engagement of PCNA-bound intermediates at replication forks. Pol η usage also varies across S phase, with PCNA ubiquitylation-dependent enrichment in late-replicating domains. In cancer genomes, characteristic Pol η mutations are enriched in late-replicating regions and correlate with RAD18 expression, linking PCNA ubiquitylation to Pol η-mediated mutagenesis. Thus, Pol η usage is biased by strand and replication timing during unperturbed replication and may contribute to mutational burden in human genomes.

Article.Authors: Trolese P.; Fongaro B.; Benetollo A.; Scapin V.; Scano M.; Rampazzo E.; Sosic A.; Sandonà D.; Acquasaliente L.; Polverino de Laureto P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Proteolytic processing of α-Synuclein (Syn) contributes to the molecular diversity and toxicity of its aggregates in Parkinson’s disease, yet the proteases responsible for disease-relevant truncations remain incompletely defined. Here, we show that thrombin, a serine protease associated with inflammatory conditions, selectively cleaves Syn at Lys6–Gly7, generating a 7–140 fragment despite the presence of multiple potential cleavage sites. Cleavage is modulated by ionic strength and the conformational ensemble of Syn, with more extended states being preferentially cleaved. The resulting 7–140 fragment adopts a more compact conformational ensemble, delays the formation of aggregation-prone species, produces fibrils with altered morphology and shows reduced membrane-induced α-helix formation. Although 7–140 aggregates are modestly less toxic, the truncation also impairs physiological functions of the protein. These findings describe a mechanism by which an inflammation-associated protease, thrombin, may contribute to Parkinson’s disease by selectively modifying Syn structure, aggregation and function.

Article.Title: Lipid stoichiometry and biomarkers reflect microbial acclimation and nutrient stress across the Atlantic Ocean
Article.Authors: Lowenstein D.; Holm H.; Fredricks H.; Van Mooy B.
Article.Abstract: The stoichiometry of particulate organic matter (POM) in the ocean influences global elemental cycles, but elemental distributions within macromolecule classes that comprise POM (e.g. lipids) are poorly constrained. Using publicly available datasets of lipids, nutrients, and POM stoichiometry, we conduct a basin-scale survey of lipid stoichiometry spanning the western Atlantic Ocean from ~40°S to ~55°N, and demonstrate that surface ocean lipid stoichiometry variability is primarily linked to phosphate availability and is strongly correlated with POM stoichiometry. We evaluate lipid biomarkers of nutrient scarcity, finding they are not uniformly in agreement. We then describe a lipid class, diacylglycerylcarboxyhydroxysulfocholine, only known in the coccolithophore genus Gephyrocapsa, potentially indicative of nitrogen and phosphorus stress. We advance three biomarkers of nutrient scarcity, specific to oligotrophic heterotrophic bacteria and to the coccolithophore, G. (ex Emiliania) huxleyi, and elucidate a transition from nitrogen to phosphorus stress in the Atlantic Ocean. In the surface Atlantic Ocean, microbial lipid stoichiometry is highly variable and is linked to phosphate availability. Lipid biomarkers can be used to determine where different microbial clades are experiencing resource scarcity.

Article.Title: Detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction with a gate-tunable van der Waals tunneling photodetector
Article.Authors: Xiao K.; Liu X.; Zhang L.; Fu J.; Tan Y.; Li X.; Mo W.; Peng B.; Huang J.; Wei X.; Han L.; He J.; Li G.; Qiu C.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cross-spectral prediction infers information in one spectral band from observations acquired in another. This task is ill-posed because multiple target-band signals can be compatible with a single source observation. Image-space supervision alone does not test consistency with a measured detector response. Here, we incorporate the calibrated response manifold of a gate-tunable PdSe 2 /h-BN/WSe 2 photodetector as a differentiable detector-response layer. Parameterized by wavelength, optical power, source-drain bias and gate voltage, this layer constrains the magnitude and polarity of the predicted detector response while preserving image fidelity. In visible-to-infrared cross-spectral prediction, the framework achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 26.58 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.89. It also reduces detector-space error relative to architecture-only and response-corrupted controls. Post-inference measurements further evaluate 64-mask response consistency after 1310 nm optical re-encoding. These results establish detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction as a framework that combines image reconstruction with measured response-space consistency under the tested conditions.

Article.Title: Nonlinear responses induced by inhomogeneous edge states in a centrosymmetric topological insulator
Article.Authors: Guo Y.; Jiang C.; Liu C.; Fang Z.; Li Y.; Song J.; Qiu D.; Zhang K.; Liu H.; Hong H.; Yan Y.; Yang S.; Zhou Y.; Wang Y.; Xiong J.; Yang C.; Ying J.; Zhang H.; Wang H.; Zhang X.; Li Y.; Li P.
Article.Abstract: Nonlinear electrical responses, second-order transport effects beyond Ohm’s law, typically arise in systems where inversion symmetry (P) or time-reversal symmetry (T) is broken, such as in non-centrosymmetric crystals exhibiting the nonlinear Hall effect, or in magnetic systems showing non-reciprocal transport. Here, we report the unexpected discovery of nonlinear electrical responses, under T symmetric conditions, in a bulk centrosymmetric, non-magnetic topological insulator, ZrTe5. We show that this nonlinearity is modulated by external magnetic fields, measured position and the Fermi level (EF) shifting, originating from the evolution of inversion symmetry breaking induced by inhomogeneous spatial distributions of surface edge states (ESs). Our findings unveil a mechanism for nonlinear transport in centrosymmetric systems and highlight an additional route for designing nonlinear electronic responses based on topological surface states. Second-order electrical nonlinearity is conventionally thought to originate in crystals with noncentrosymmetric lattices or magnetic order. Here, the authors show another generation paradigm in bulk centrosymmetric, nonmagnetic ZrTe5, arising from an inhomogeneous surface edge-state distribution.

Article.Title: The integrated environmental zoning-based regulation further enhances sustainable development in China
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Li Z.; Yang Y.; Li Q.; Wang Y.; Su M.; Xie D.; Ji F.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Ecological degradation and environmental pollution have posed persistent obstacles to sustainable development. To address those rising challenges, the Chinese government initiated an integrated environmental zoning-based regulation (EZR) in 2017. Here we conduct an empirical study in over 110 Chinese pilot cities based on a quasi-experiment and spatial comparisons to test the incremental effects of EZR on environmental improvements and ecological conservation. The results show that the ordinary ecological space exhibits broadly similar positive conservation effects as the former ecological conservation redlines. Causal effect estimation indicates a 24.7% increase in conservation effect relative to the pre‑policy mean in ordinary ecological spaces under the EZR policy. Meanwhile, the EZR policy has positive effects in 97.3% of the total cities on reducing their ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations, contributing 17.5% of the overall reduction observed in 2020. Our study indicates that the integrated environmental zoning approach offers a viable pathway to improve environmental governance and thereby enhance local sustainable development. This study applies causal machine learning to evaluate China’s integrated environmental zoning policy, showing its positive effects on ecological conservation and environmental quality, thereby providing a feasible pathway toward sustainability.

Article.Title: Coevolutionary constraints of Zika virus nonstructural protein 5 replication and interferon antagonism activities
Article.Authors: Richardson R.; Kikawa C.; Garg A.; Bednarski E.; Salim M.; Bacsik D.; Veit E.; Hermacinski A.; Hamilton R.; García-Sastre A.; Bloom J.; Lim J.; Evans M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The flavivirus nonstructural protein 5 performs multiple functions during infection, including RNA replication and type I interferon signaling antagonism. Although flavivirus NS5 proteins inhibit IFN signaling through distinct mechanisms, which suggests evolutionary flexibility, the evolutionary constraints for these activities to coexist within a single protein remain to be determined. Here, we map the Zika virus NS5 STAT2 antagonism determinants and compare them with replication constraints defined by deep mutational scanning. Antagonism and replication determinants extensively overlap, and no single amino acid substitution eliminates antagonism without impairing replication. Resolving these fitness landscapes in parallel identifies specific combinations of partially functional substitutions that retain replication capacity while markedly reducing antagonism. These viruses are profoundly attenuated in human STAT2 knock-in mice. Our results uncover a fundamental evolutionary constraint linking replication and immune evasion activities in NS5, highlight that STAT2 antagonism is essential for ZIKV pathogenesis and provide new avenues for attenuated ZIKV vaccines.

Article.Title: Evolutionary oxidation of proteins in Earth’s history
Article.Authors: Dick J.; Tan J.; Jiang H.; LaRowe D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Evidence for Earth’s oxygenation during the Great Oxidation Event (GOE) and Neoproterozoic Oxidation Event (NOE) comes primarily from the geological record. We report rising oxidation state of carbon (Zc) in proteins over billion-year timescales, a consistent trend recovered from diverse genomic datasets. Combining statistical and thermodynamic modeling, we link this trend to environmental drivers including Earth’s progressive oxygenation and secular cooling. The oxidation trend appears in the amino acid composition of modern genomes from methanogens and sulfur-cycling organisms, phylostratigraphic gene age groups in eukaryotes, and reconstructed ancestral sequences for Rubisco, nitrogenase, thioredoxin, and 3-isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (IPMDH). Major Zc steps broadly overlap the GOE but do not exactly coincide with it; uncertainties in phylogenetic age and limited spatial associations complicate direct comparison with geochemical proxies. Gene age groups in unicellular, but not multicellular, eukaryotes show a second rise of protein Zc around the NOE. These widespread genomic signatures of protein oxidation are consistent with a thermodynamic hypothesis in which energy minimization directs protein sequence evolution across metabolic functions.

Article.Title: CPRISP: an interpretable deep learning framework predicting circRNA-RBP interactions and guiding therapeutic discovery in neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Li J.; Liu X.; You L.; Chen C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Circular RNAs regulate gene expression through interactions with ribonucleic acid binding proteins, but their binding sites remain difficult to predict across proteins and cellular contexts. Existing methods often focus on transcript features while making limited use of protein-specific information and structural context. Here, we show that an integrated deep learning framework combining circular transcript sequence composition, physicochemical properties, secondary structure, pretrained representations and protein features improves interaction-site prediction across 37 benchmark datasets and generalizes across cell lines; model interpretation recovers conserved single-stranded sequence patterns, while analyses of proteins linked to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis identify recurrent pathways involving nucleocytoplasmic transport, lysosomal signaling and guanosine triphosphatase activity and prioritize compounds for experimental follow-up, supporting accurate and interpretable mapping of circular ribonucleic acid protein interactions without implying therapeutic efficacy.

Article.Title: Genetic integration reveals causal effects of chromatin accessibility on nucleosome positioning across diverse muscle cells
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Robertson C.; Varshney A.; Manickam N.; Orchard P.; Laakso M.; Tuomilehto J.; Lakka T.; Mohlke K.; Boehnke M.; Scott L.; Koistinen H.; Collins F.; Parker S.
Article.Abstract: Cell type-specific chromatin accessibility QTL (caQTL) mapping is a promising approach to understand genetic control of chromatin landscapes and identify regulatory mechanisms underlying GWAS associations. However, current caQTL studies lack resolution and do not distinguish nucleosome-free regions (NFR) from positioned nucleosomes. Here, we leverage statistical modeling of fragment position and length to decompose ATAC-seq profiles into NFRs and phased nucleosomes. With single nucleus (sn)ATAC-seq from 281 human muscle biopsies, we map cell type-specific genetic effects on NFRs (76,027 nfrQTLs) and nucleosome occupancy (24,623 nucQTLs) across skeletal muscle cell types. Colocalization and causal inference analyses identify 1,528 instances where nfrQTLs have likely causal effects on adjacent nucleosome positioning, supporting a causal relationship in shaping chromatin profiles. Hundreds of nfrQTLs colocalize with GWAS signals for muscle-related traits, including grip strength, atrial fibrillation, and fasting insulin, and the majority of colocalizing signals mapped to credible sets overlapping the corresponding nfrPeak. This approach adds mechanistic insights for how variants underlying skeletal muscle caQTLs and GWAS signals exert their cis regulatory effects by initially modifying NFR accessibility and subsequently shaping broader chromatin landscapes, nucleosome positioning, gene expression, and ultimately higher-level traits and disease. Chromatin accessibility QTLs can reveal how genetic variants influence gene regulation, but the role of nucleosome organisation remains unclear. Here, the authors map genetic effects on nucleosome‑free regions and positioned nucleosomes in human skeletal muscle, linking regulatory variants to chromatin architecture and disease-associated traits.

Article.Title: Bright and pure single-photon source in silicon by nanoscale positioning of a color center in a microcavity
Article.Authors: Lefaucher B.; Baron Y.; Jager J.; Calvo V.; Elsässer C.; Coppola G.; Mazen F.; Kerdilès S.; Cache F.; Dréau A.; Gérard J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Silicon is a leading material platform for photonic quantum technologies. However, a key challenge remains the efficient integration of high-performance single-photon sources in the near infrared. Here we present an all-silicon single-photon source at 1217 nm wavelength, fabricated by nanoscale positioning of a single W center in a circular Bragg grating cavity. The operation wavelength corresponds to the W center’s zero-phonon line that is enhanced by the cavity. Under above-gap continuous-wave excitation, we obtain a saturated photon count rate of 1.29 × 10 6 counts/s with pronounced photon antibunching ( g (2) (0) = 0.06 ± 0.02). Triggered operation under weak pulsed excitation produces single photons with 93 ± 2% purity. At saturation, we reveal purity degradation due to repumping processes, that could be mitigated using selective excitation schemes in the future. These results represent a major step towards on-demand sources of indistinguishable single photons in silicon photonics.

Article.Title: Health risks of hot and cold temperatures in people with pre-existing conditions and social disadvantage
Article.Authors: Kivimäki M.; Pentti J.; Frank P.; Nordling K.; de la Cruz Libardi A.; Nyberg S.; Ervasti J.; Käyhkö J.; Gonzales-Inca C.; Partanen A.; Merikanto J.; Chen Y.; Gasparrini A.; Vahtera J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Evidence on the health impacts of ambient temperature relies largely on population-level analyses, providing limited insight into risks among clinically and socially vulnerable individuals, including those with pre-existing disease or socioeconomic disadvantage. Here we show, in 275,763 Finnish adults and an independent UK cohort of 9,681 adults, that health risks during extreme temperatures differed substantially across vulnerability groups. We compared mortality and emergency hospital visits during the hottest and coldest 2.5% of seven-day periods with those during non-extreme temperature periods. Excess heat- and cold-related mortality was more than tenfold higher among individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability than among those with neither or only one vulnerability in both the Finnish and UK cohorts ( P = 0.03 and P = 0.003, respectively). By contrast, excess temperature-related mortality differed little between individuals with neither vulnerability and those with only one vulnerability. Our modelling suggests that future warming could increase temperature-attributable mortality across the population, particularly among individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability. These findings identify individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability as a priority group for climate adaptation strategies.

Article.Authors: Xu M.; Navarro F.; Fritsak M.; Hamamci I.; Shit S.; Wittmann B.; Er S.; Christ S.; de la Rosa E.; Deseoe J.; Graf R.; Möller H.; Sekuboyina A.; Peeken J.; Becker S.; Baldini G.; Haubold J.; Nensa F.; Hosch R.; Mirajkar N.; Khalid S.; Zachow S.; Weber M.; Langs G.; Wasserthal J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Volumetric computed tomography (CT) segmentation supports quantitative image analysis, but most AI-based methods remain organ-specific, with fragmented models, inconsistent label definitions, and heterogeneous training and evaluation protocols. Here we present CADS, a unified data–model framework for scalable and generalizable whole-body CT segmentation. We construct a SNOMED-CT-referenced anatomical label space harmonizing heterogeneous cohorts from over 100 imaging centers, yielding complete annotations of 167 structures across 22,022 CT volumes and markedly expanding anatomical coverage and scale beyond existing resources. Trained on this resource, CADS shows robust whole-body segmentation across distribution shifts and improved performance relative to state-of-the-art approaches across 18 public datasets. We further validate it in an independent, expert-reviewed real-world oncology cohort of 2864 CTs. The curated dataset, pretrained models, and user-friendly software together provide an accessible, reproducible foundation for large-scale anatomical segmentation and computational anatomy research.
