Article.Authors: Modrusan P.; Brkic A.; Buttelli A.; Leibundgut M.; Zivkovic I.; Ban N.; Longo L.; Gruic-Sovulj I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are the guardians of translational fidelity. Their complex function is mirrored by an elaborate structure, which includes multiple nested domains. While the evolutionary pressures that promoted the emergence of some domains, such as the editing domain, are clear, the pressures acting on other domains, particularly those at the C-terminus, are not. Here, we combine kinetic analysis, X-ray crystallography, and bioinformatics to unveil the history and evolutionary forces that have shaped isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase (IleRS) domain structure. We find that the traditional classification of IleRSs based on the C-terminal tRNA-recognition domains is incomplete, as it fails to capture features of the synthetic domain. Guided by a crystal structure of the Priestia megaterium IleRS2:tRNA Ile complex, we removed key interactions between IleRS2 and its cognate tRNA and characterised their impact on enzyme activity. We found that D-loop interactions with the IleRS2 C-terminal domains are non-essential in prokaryotes, and their loss can even increase catalytic turnover. Further, we show that the zinc-binding domain of IleRS1 recognises the anticodon less stringently than the canonical C-terminal domain of IleRS2. Our data suggest that C-terminal evolutionary remodelling of IleRSs is an ongoing process with a historical precedent and is consistent with selection for faster aminoacylation rate.

Article.Title: Global rise of a wheat pathogen through two-stage evolutionary emergence coupled with aerial dispersal
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Li Y.; Zhan G.; Zhao J.; Zhang Z.; Liu H.; Basu U.; Kanyuka K.; Davis H.; Qucuo Z.; Tao F.; Gao H.; Li G.; Ma J.; Yao Q.; Jia Q.; Cao S.; Hu Y.; Li Y.; Huang W.; Bai Y.; Tadesse W.; Jonas-Levi A.; Song W.; Huang L.

Our analyses support a two-stage emergence model: P. striiformis sensu stricto originated and diversified in the Himalayan region, subsequently a P. striiformis s. str. lineage jumped to domesticated wheat in the Fertile Crescent, giving rise to epidemic lineage (Pst) and spreading worldwide with wheat cultivation. This host jump triggered demographic expansion and selective sweeps, while GWAS identified region-specific virulence loci shaped by resistant cultivars. Overlay of air trajectory and dispersal simulations identified atmospheric corridors consistent with genomic migration patterns, supporting a historical role for long-distance aerial transport in the pathogen’s global spread. Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici, an obligate fungal pathogen, threatens wheat production worldwide. Using 319 genomes and virulence data from 234 isolates globally, this study constructs its two-stage emergence and global dissemination, supporting a historical role for long-distance aerial transport.

Article.Authors: Yan T.; Hou X.; Watzlawik J.; Dickson D.; Fiesel F.; Springer W.
Article.Abstract: Tau propagation is a key driver of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet selective markers of seeding-competent tau remain elusive. Tau species isolated with pS65-Ub antibodies exhibit seeding activity, whereas removal of pS65-Ub-associated material markedly reduces seeding from AD brain extracts. Together, these findings identify pS65-Ub as a disease-enriched molecular feature of a seed-competent tau population and link cellular stress signaling with pathological tau propagation in AD. Not all selective markers of seeding-competent Tau are known. Here, the authors identify pS65-Ub-associated tau linked to pathological Tau spreading and elevated in Alzheimer’s disease. Removal of pS65-Ub reduces tau seeding activity.

Article.Title: Discrete subdomains establish epigenetic diversity in subtelomeric heterochromatin in fission yeast
Article.Authors: Mazumder A.; Cooper J.; Goksal C.; Brockhausen R.; Schauß J.; Khanduja J.; Joh R.; Amine A.; Groos J.; Kanoh J.; Motamedi M.; Finkelstein I.; Al-Sady B.; Braun S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Subtelomeres are imperfect repeats adjacent to telomeres that are transcriptionally repressed by heterochromatin. Although essential for genome integrity, their repetitive nature has thwarted dissection of local heterochromatin assembly and maintenance mechanisms. By engineering fission yeast strains carrying fluorescent reporters at a single subtelomere, we uncovered distinct subdomains. These subdomains have different silencing requirements: telomere-proximal regions rely on canonical shelterin- or RNAi-dependent nucleation pathways, whereas telomere-distal regions involve nucleosome remodelers, histone chaperones, and boundary-associated factors. Subdomains also exhibit discrete epigenetic states emerging both at homologous loci on different chromosome arms and along the same subtelomeric sequence. We document these epigenetic states using multi-generational live imaging and targeted perturbations. These analyses show that subtelomeric subdomains display position-specific, clonally variable silencing across a spectrum from robust to fragile epigenetic states. Interestingly, structural variants, common in subtelomeric sequences across eukaryotes, dictate local epigenetic stability. These findings reveal that subtelomeres, long recognized for their sequence variability, form a dynamic mosaic of coexisting epigenetic domains. This implies a wide range of gene-repressive regulatory logic at the chromosome ends, from environmental responsiveness to silencing stability.

Article.Title: Asymmetric bloom lengthening drives high-latitude ocean chlorophyll accumulation imbalance
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Chen P.; Jamet C.; Zhang S.; Shi K.; Pan D.
Article.Abstract: Terrestrial ecosystems maintain a stable time-allocation budget between growth and senescence, but whether this applies to the ocean remains unclear. Using fused satellite LiDAR and ocean-color data (2007–2022), we show that marine phenology is variable and asymmetric. In high latitudes ( > 50°N), the bloom growth-to-decline ratio (RGD) is declining by ~5.3% per decade. While the chlorophyll-increase phase has lengthened by 2.3–5.5 days, the post-peak chlorophyll-decline phase has extended disproportionately by 5.7–6.2 days. Environmental sensitivity analyses reveal distinct hemispheric patterns in the statistical associations between phenological variability and multiple co-varying physical and biogeochemical factors, consistent with contrasting nutrient regimes between the Northern and Southern high-latitude oceans. We further show that these shifts are associated with spatially heterogeneous changes in marine chlorophyll accumulation patterns. Our results identify bloom asymmetry as an important dimension of marine phenological change, providing an observational baseline for evaluating future links between chlorophyll phenology, ecosystem timing, and polar biogeochemical processes under climate change. This study shows that unequal changes in bloom duration between hemispheres contribute to contrasting high-latitude ocean chlorophyll trends, linking asymmetric phytoplankton phenology to marine ecosystem changes under climate warming.

Article.Title: In situ reduction-driven formation of sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures
Article.Authors: Huang Y.; Ren Z.; Gao Y.; Li H.; Xiao H.; Liu Q.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures provide a platform for modulating electronic structure and interfacial reactivity through strong atom-level coupling, with potential applications in energy conversion. However, their precise construction remains challenging. Here we show a strategy for constructing sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures through confined spinodal decomposition and ligand-mediated in situ reduction. Oleylamine ligands adsorbed on NiMoO4 sub-nanowires act as mild reductants, selectively reducing Ni2+ to spatially confined metallic Ni domains and forming coherent Ni/NiMoO4 heterointerfaces. Experimental and theoretical analyses suggest that the Ni/NiMoO4 interfaces modify the local electronic structure and facilitate the adsorption and activation of hydrogen evolution intermediates. The resulting catalyst requires an overpotential of 14.4 ± 2.9 mV to reach 10 mA cm−2 in 1 M KOH and delivers 2 A cm−2 at 1.62 V in an anion-exchange membrane electrolyzer at 80 oC, with stable operation over 2200 h at 25 °C. These findings provide insights into the construction and interfacial regulation of sub-nanometer heterostructures through in situ reduction. Sub-nanometer heterostructures offer opportunities to tune interfacial reactivity, but their precise construction remains challenging. Here, the authors report alternating Ni/NiMoO₄ heterostructures that promote hydrogen evolution and sustain durable high-current electrolysis.

Article.Title: A method quantifying soil melanin to understand fungal impacts on soil carbon stability
Article.Authors: Adamczyk S.; Adamczyk B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Fungal necromass, particularly dead microbial cells rich in melanin, is an important contributor to long-term soil carbon stabilization. Progress in understanding the role of soil melanin is limited by the lack of validated analytical methods. DNA-based approaches estimate only the genetic potential for melanin production and therefore provide indirect evidence of melanin occurrence. To directly assess soil melanin, we evaluated spectroscopic and spectrophotometric assays; however, both approaches proved insufficiently specific due to interference from chemically related compounds. Here, we introduce a liquid chromatography method that enables quantification of major fungal melanin types in soils. By enabling direct quantification of fungal melanin in soil, this framework allows longstanding hypotheses regarding melanized fungal necromass and soil carbon stabilization to be tested mechanistically. Here, we show with the proposed method that soil melanin concentrations are strongly correlated with total soil carbon, supporting a central role for fungal melanin in long-term soil carbon stabilization.

Article.Title: A supergene and genomic mosaicism are associated with phenotypic evolution in Galápagos tree finches
Article.Authors: Sebastianelli Arbelaez M.; Enbody E.; Rubin C.; Valle C.; Keller L.; Grant B.; Grant P.; Andersson L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Adaptive radiations provide powerful models to study the origins of phenotypic novelty and species diversity. Darwin’s finches constitute a classic example of adaptive radiation, in which beak morphology is a key trait related to fitness. Here, we focus on Camarhynchus tree finches by analyzing whole genomes in combination with morphological data to revisit long-standing questions regarding their origins raised before genetic evidence became available. Camarhynchus diversified over the last 100,000 years, yielding some striking morphological differences despite shallow genetic divergence. We identify several highly differentiated loci, including G03 , a supergene affecting beak and body size. We reveal a striking example of genomic mosaicism, in which autosomal differentiation between two sympatric species is restricted primarily to a single locus -( G03 )- that approaches fixation, shifting them from one phenotypic optimum to another. Contextualized in a broader phylogenetic framework, we also reveal an unexpected diversity of G03 haplotypes and show that the small and large G03 alleles diverged early in the radiation, suggesting a key genetic innovation enabling ecological expansion among species of Darwin’s finches. Our results further establish Camarhynchus as a model example of speciation with gene flow, underscoring the broader role of hybridization in generating biodiversity.

Article.Title: HCV incidence and prevalence trends among people who use drugs in France 2004 to 2023
Article.Authors: Sabbatini C.; Le Strat Y.; Bonaldi C.; Brouard C.; Audran M.; Saboni L.; Richard J.; David A.; Gaudy-Graffin C.; Chevaliez S.; Barin F.; Stefic K.; Jauffret-Roustide M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains a key public health challenge, particularly among people who use and inject drugs (PWUD, PWID). While direct-acting antivirals (DAA) have revolutionized HCV treatment, meeting the WHO’s 2030 elimination target requires accurate estimation of incidence and prevalence to guide prevention and care. We analyze cross-sectional surveys conducted in France in 2004, 2013, and 2023, recruiting PWUD at harm reduction services and collecting behavioral and biological data. We estimate age-and time-dependent prevalence of HCV antibodies and HCV RNA using multivariate regression models while incidence was estimated from two-state transmission models. The demographic profile of PWUD has aged over time (mean age 35 years in 2004 vs. 44 in 2023) while injection prevalence remained stable (61.7% in 2023). Between 2013 and 2023, HCV burden declined substantially: HCV RNA prevalence fell from 19.4% (95% CI 16.3–23.0) to 9.5% (7.2–12.3) among all PWUD, and from 29.6% to 14.5% among PWID. Incidence among PWID decreased from 6.5 (4.1–8.0) to 2.4 (1.4–4.2) per 100 person-years. These reductions likely reflect the combined impact of DAA scale-up and harm reduction policies, marking substantial progress toward elimination targets. However, ongoing transmission highlights persistent barriers requiring targeted public health actions.

Article.Title: Time-lapse RESOLFT nanoscopy empowered by deep learning
Article.Authors: Minet G.; Ray A.; Pennacchietti F.; Coceano G.; Jug F.; Testa I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

Article.Title: Intensification of near-inertial currents in the Atlantic Ocean over the past two decades
Article.Authors: Zheng Y.; Zhai X.; Stevens D.; Wu W.; Gong W.; Du Y.
Article.Abstract: Near-inertial currents (NICs) play a key role in surface material redistribution and ocean mixing, yet their long-term variability remains poorly known. Using in situ current measurements from surface drifters, we provide observational evidence for a pronounced intensification of surface NICs in the Atlantic Ocean over the past two decades (2003–2022). Basin–mean NIC strength increases at a rate of 3.8 ± 1.7% per decade, with a spatial pattern characterized by strengthening in the South Atlantic and the high-latitude North Atlantic, and weakening in the low-latitude North Atlantic. We further show that these trends in Atlantic NICs are primarily driven by changes in near-inertial wind forcing, particularly those associated with mesoscale weather systems, while variations in mixed-layer depth playing a minor role. This observed intensification of Atlantic NICs may have important implications for ocean transport and mixing, and needs to be properly represented in the current generation of climate models. Ocean drifter observations reveal that Atlantic near-inertial currents intensified by almost 4% per decade during 2003–2022. This intensification is primarily driven by changes in wind forcing associated with mesoscale weather systems.

Article.Title: An automated operon refactoring workflow for heterologous expression of non-ribosomal peptide biosynthetic gene clusters
Article.Authors: Li Z.; Liu L.; Sun X.; Wu H.; Fu S.; Jin J.; Zhang Y.; Zhang X.; Zeng Z.; Tao Z.; Chen N.; Wang X.; Lv J.; Luo P.; Hu D.; Gao H.; Keasling J.; Luo X.
Article.Abstract: Microbial genomes encode numerous biosynthetic gene clusters, yet most remain experimentally uncharacterized, particularly large non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) clusters that resist conventional cloning. Here we show that OSAR (One-Step Assembly and Refactoring)—an automated platform integrating algorithmic primer design with yeast homologous-recombination cloning—directly assembles and refactors NRPS clusters without custom DNA synthesis. Existing approaches for biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) discovery are labor-intensive, depend on de novo DNA synthesis and are difficult to scale. Here we show that an automated platform for one-step assembly and refactoring of BGCs facilitates facile novel product discovery.

Article.Title: ETSAM: effectively segmenting cell membranes in cryo-electron tomograms
Article.Authors: Selvaraj J.; Cheng J.
Article.Abstract: Cryogenic Electron Tomography (cryo-ET) is an emerging experimental technique used to visualize cell structures and macromolecules in their native cellular environment. However, several inherent limitations in cryo-ET, including the very low signal-to-noise ratio, missing wedge artifacts from limited tilt angles, and other noise artifacts, collectively hinder the reliable identification and delineation of these structures. In this study, we present ETSAM, a two-stage Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2)-based fine-tuned AI method that effectively segments cell membranes in tomograms. It is trained on a diverse dataset comprising 83 experimental tomograms from the CryoET Data Portal (CDP) database and 28 simulated tomograms generated using PolNet. On an independent test set of 17 experimental tomograms for which ground-truth annotations are available, ETSAM outperforms other deep learning based methods by robustly identifying cell membranes with high sensitivity while also maintaining better precision. Cell membranes are hard to distinguish in the noisy 3D volumes from cryo-electron tomography. Here, authors adapt a video segmentation foundation model to the task, segmenting membranes across diverse organisms more accurately than existing tools.

Article.Title: Inhomogeneity of negative enthalpy enables excellent mechanical properties in nanosized single crystals of multi-principal element alloys
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Wang Z.; Zhang J.; Xu N.; Duan Z.; Li D.; Wu Z.; Chang X.; Shao R.; Huang T.; Wang X.; Sun Z.; Wang C.; An Z.; Yang C.; Zhang J.; Liao X.; Wang L.; Han X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Many nanosized metals with limited dislocation nucleation and multiplication usually exhibit poor plasticity. Previous studies have demonstrated that multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) can achieve a combination of strength and plasticity. However, whether these mechanical properties extend to their nanosized counterparts and how nanosized MPEAs accommodate plastic deformation remains unknown. Using a homemade in-situ device, we captured the atomic-scale tensile process and measured the stress-strain curve of Fe 48 Mn 32 Co 10 Cr 10 nanosized single crystals (NSCs). We find that NSCs achieve a strength of ~3 GPa and a uniform elongation of ~20%. We show that this combination arises from the inhomogeneous distribution of enthalpy, which produces a broad spectrum of energy barriers for the nucleation of full dislocations, partial dislocations, and nanotwins. Consequently, dislocations and nanotwins are randomly generated throughout MPEA NSCs, effectively suppressing local stress concentration and leading to both high strength and large uniform elongation.

Article.Title: GlycoStamp-seq: Single-cell nascent sialoglycometabolomics captures sialylation dynamics in immune cells of an oxaliplatin-treated bladder cancer mouse model
Article.Authors: Wu X.; Zhao Z.; Ouyang S.; Hao X.; Li J.; Zhu W.; Zhang T.; Lu S.; Dong T.; Jiang N.; Yang X.; Guo H.; Li J.; Tian T.; Yang R.
Article.Abstract: Dynamic remodeling of immune cell-surface glycans reflects cellular state and immune activity. Furthermore, elevated nascent sialoglycan levels mark antigen-reactive CD8⁺ T cells with increased anti-tumor efficacy in vitro and in vivo. GlycoStamp-seq may thus serve as a versatile platform for profiling nascent sialoglycan dynamics in complex tissues, thereby expanding the single-cell multi-omics toolkit and providing insights into sialoglycan dynamics during therapeutic response. Glycosylation is critical for an effective immune response, but immune cell glycan dynamics are not fully understood. Here, the authors present GlycoStamp-seq to track sialoglycan dynamics, and apply GlycoStamp-seq in an oxaliplatin-treated subcutaneous bladder cancer mouse model.

Article.Title: Twisted superconducting quantum diodes for high fidelity anharmonic qubits
Article.Authors: Zhong H.; Kochan D.; Žutić I.; Wu Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In superconducting circuits, bidirectional signal propagation can cause back-reflections and back-action that couple environmental noise back to coherent elements, degrading fidelity. Nonreciprocal superconducting diodes provide an intrinsic route to suppress such back-scattering at the circuit level. However, their diode efficiency and quantum integration remain limited. Here, we realize a quantum diode in twisted NbSe 2 under in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields. A mere 1 ∘ twist yields an efficiency enhancement over pristine devices, reaching 27.6%. Quantum simulations reveal that this intermediate efficiency, well below 100% ideal, is both experimentally practical and optimal for preserving qubit anharmonicity and stabilizing two-level systems. These findings show that maximal rectification is not always beneficial for quantum information, establishing a new principle for designing the fundamental properties of twisted superconductors towards low-power, high-fidelity quantum circuits.

Article.Title: Intrinsically flexible inorganic piezoelectric subnanowire enables wireless wearable bioelectronics for non-invasive multimodal human-machine interfacing
Article.Authors: Xu X.; Wang X.; Cui Y.; Liu Q.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Piezoelectric electronic skin (PE-skin) offers a significant advantage in detecting minute forces, making it highly promising for human-computer interaction in health management and medical rehabilitation. However, PE-skin often faces challenges in real-time, wireless transmission of sensing data, which can compromise both data accuracy and user comfort. Here, we report the synthesis of an inorganic piezoelectric polyoxometalate-based subnanowire, ZnBiPMo12, which possesses intrinsic flexibility and chirality, a piezoelectric coefficient of 24.9 pC/N, and notable ferroelectricity. Leveraging its piezoelectric response, ZnBiPMo12-based PE-skin (1) demonstrates high elasticity and sensitivity to tiny pressures in the range of 0.045-0.319 N. Building on this, a wireless, wearable bioelectronic (WBE) device (1A) is fabricated through multi-level assembly, enabling non-invasive, multimodal monitoring of human physiological signals, including subtle muscle contractions, blinking, breathing, and all-day heart rate. By integrating a machine learning system, a 1-based facial-computer interface (1B) can accurately recognize nine emotional expressions and twelve spoken words. This work not only introduces a typical inorganic piezoelectric material with intrinsic flexibility but also demonstrates scalable manufacturing from subnanomaterials to wireless WBEs, paving the way for non-invasive, multimodal monitoring of human physiological signals and advanced human-computer interaction. Piezoelectric materials enable bioelectronic sensing by converting mechanical stimuli into electrical signals. Xu et al. introduce intrinsically flexible polyoxometalate-based subnanowires and demonstrate their scalable integration into wireless wearable systems for human physiological monitoring.

Article.Authors: Jiao A.; Maghrouni A.; Gutierrez A.; Annett A.; Manokaran C.; Wen T.; Grassl N.; Chan J.; Nguyen S.; Bou-Tayeh B.; Jawhar W.; Le Dily F.; Kleinman C.; Di Croce L.; Jabado N.; Shi Y.

Mechanistically, ASCL1 synergizes with H3K27M to redistribute the chromatin remodeler BRG1 to regulatory elements co-enriched for ASCL1 and SOX motifs, promoting expression of stem and neural progenitor genes at the expense of mesenchymal genes in DMGs. Article.Title: Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda)
Article.Authors: Funston G.; Dudgeon T.; Simon D.; Dufault D.; Boyd C.; Fowler D.; Currie P.; Evans D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The diversification of herbivorous dinosaurs and the rise of angiosperms in the Late Cretaceous are each well established, but the link between them is debated. Broad-scale diversity patterns in the two groups appear not to closely align, and there is no direct evidence of dinosaur adaptation to angiosperm-based diets. Here we describe Infernogallus jamesi gen. et. sp. nov., a diminutive caenagnathid oviraptorosaur, and show that these theropods were specialised herbivores that originated alongside the rise of fleshy angiosperm fruits. The nearly complete, articulated skull of Infernogallus jamesi —the first for the clade—reveals drastic changes to the adductor musculature organisation, unique in non-avian theropods but converged upon by extant frugivorous parrots. These modifications enabled extensive oral processing of soft food using anteroposterior movement of the mandible and occlusion of ridges and grooves on opposed elements. Altogether, this attests to a highly specialised herbivorous diet in caenagnathids, which likely consisted in large part of fleshy angiosperm fruits, which increased in size and diversity in concert with the radiation of oviraptorosaurs. Caenagnathids thus provide one of the strongest candidates for angiosperm-based diet adaptations in dinosaurs, but their role in the Late Cretaceous proliferation of fruit—which shaped early Cenozoic flora—remains unclear.

Article.Title: Large-scale identical-location electron microscopy enables quantifying nanoparticulate electrocatalyst degradation
Article.Authors: Kamšek A.; Ruiz-Zepeda F.; Tabernik D.; Vidergar J.; Logar A.; Kregar A.; Skočaj D.; Dražić G.; Hodnik N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Fuel cells convert chemical energy into electricity, and their performance relies on electrocatalysts whose durability during operation remains poorly understood. Deep mechanistic insight into electrocatalyst stability is essential to design durable, resource-efficient fuel cells. Nanoparticulate electrocatalysts degrade via diverse nanoscale processes, yet particle-to-particle heterogeneity in structure, support interaction, and local microenvironment make true particle-level quantification and understanding impossible with classical approaches. Here we scale up identical-location scanning transmission electron microscopy, which repeatedly images the very same nanoparticles, to track the structural evolution of hundreds of carbon-supported platinum-cobalt nanoparticles, a prototypical oxygen reduction reaction electrocatalyst. We present a three-step image analysis workflow comprising segmentation, tracking, and degradation-event classification with progressive automation, including machine-learning-assisted detection of overlapping particles. By pairing nanoscale resolution and local history with population-level statistics, the pipeline enables unbiased identification and quantification of degradation pathways across statistically meaningful particle sets. We reveal particle size- and shape-dependent effects, showing that smaller and irregular nanoparticles are more prone to detachment, and provide a data-driven framework for probing electrocatalyst degradation at scale.

Article.Title: Quantum-sensing-based super-resolution live cell microenvironment imaging
Article.Authors: Lu Y.; Yang Y.; Xu K.; Mao Z.; Yin L.; Xu Y.; Zhou Z.; Wang X.; Zhang C.; Zhu W.; Feng J.
Article.Abstract: Direct monitoring the multifaceted intracellular microenvironment is fundamental for deciphering localized cellular behavior and function. However, performing nanoscale spatiotemporal sensing of the dynamic physiochemical environment within a live cell has remained challenging, mainly limited by the lack of robust, biocompatible method which satisfies the requirements for spatiotemporal resolution, sensitivity, multi-physical sensing capability and long-term viability. Here we present a super-resolution-based quantum biosensing approach, namely Super-resolution Multi-physical field Imaging with Deconvolution, implemented in our custom-built setup which integrates nitrogen vacancy center-based quantum sensing with structured illumination microscopy. This enables quantitative, super-resolved, and long-term tracking of intracellular physical fields, featuring spatial resolution of 136 nm, temporal resolution of 150 ms, and field of view of 180×180 μm2. We further perform super-resolution multimodal imaging in a live cell, revealing the spatially heterogeneous reactive oxygen species dynamics under external stimulation. Our work enables the dynamic assessment of localized physiochemical dynamics under super-resolution quantum biosensing. This work presents a super-resolution quantum biosensing approach by integrating nitrogen vacancy (NV) center-based quantum nanodiamond sensors with structured illumination microscopy, which achieves super-resolution multi-physical imaging within live cells.

Article.Title: A dual-attribution framework reveals how foreign investment and trade redistribute cobalt availability
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Zhang L.; Jiang S.; Li Y.; Li R.; Mei Z.; Yuan Z.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Global resource allocation is increasingly shaped by foreign direct investment (FDI) and international trade, yet their combined effects on distribution of critical mineral availability across countries remain poorly quantified. Although these mechanisms do not alter the global total amount of cobalt available, they reduce its concentration across countries. Article.Title: PRPF19 drives hepatic stellate cell activation and liver fibrosis via PKM2-mediated glycolytic reprogramming
Article.Authors: Zhang G.; Zi S.; Ye B.; Ma Y.; Chen J.; Zhu J.; Liu T.; Yin J.; Shen X.; Yu X.; Dong L.

Article.Title: Corpus Callosum Dysgenesis is concomitant with reduced metacognitive efficiency and sensitivity across multiple cohorts and modalities
Article.Authors: Barnby J.; Dean R.; Burgess H.; Dayan P.; Richards L.
Article.Abstract: The corpus callosum is the largest commissure in the mammalian brain and has been implicated in supporting cognitive processes required for adapting to complex environments. Metacognition is a key cognitive process that supports these functions; however, it has yet to be tested comprehensively in individuals with Corpus Callosum Dysgenesis. Article.Title: A self-limiting mechanotransduction feedback loop ensures robust organ formation
Article.Authors: Mori Y.; Robin P.; Briggs A.; Levic D.; Wang J.; Jain-Sharma V.; Heikes K.; Bagnat M.; Hannezo E.; Munjal A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Organ morphogenesis uses mechanotransduction feedback loops to convert forces into gene expression changes that regulate cell mechanics. How these loops integrate with developmental programs to ensure robust outcomes remains unclear. Canal development proceeds through bud initiation, extension, and fusion within the otic epithelium. Local swelling of hyaluronan-rich extracellular matrix (ECM) in the bud activates Yap in a spatial pattern. Yap induces its target ccn1l1 , promoting further ECM expansion to sustain bud extension. This feedback loop confers developmental robustness: graded knockdown of ccn1l1 reduces extension rate, yet canal formation persists and fails only with strong disruption. Critically, the loop contains its own termination mechanism. During bud fusion, PKA-CREB signaling, activated by an adhesion GPCR, gpr126, suppresses ccn1l1 , ending the loop. Article.Authors: Pennisi F.; Buzzoni C.; Gervasi F.; Greco M.; Signorelli C.; Russo A.; Renzi C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Individuals with disabilities may experience disparities in cancer diagnosis, but population-based evidence remains limited. A fused data-driven framework further uncovers regime-dependent HONO reduction strategies, prioritizing NOx control in summer and co-reduction of NOx, PM2.5 and direct combustion emissions in winter, to accelerate O3 and PM2.5 joint mitigation. Article.Authors: Chen X.; Liu D.; Zhang X.; Chen X.; Pei F.; Zhang Y.; Yan P.; Ai Y.; Chen G.; Wu Y.; Qiu Z.; Zhu Z.; Yang M.; Li Q.
Article.Abstract: Control of magnetization reversal is crucial for spintronic memory and logic devices. In Type I, reversal initiated in a thicker region propagates rapidly across the step boundary, reducing the coercivity of an adjacent thinner region by up to 59.3%. Article.Authors: He R.; Li Y.; Chen J.; Dinh T.; Stevens C.; Gilchrist A.; Xue Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Multimodal fluorescence and phase imaging provides complementary information about biological samples. Here, we introduce fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography (FDT), which reconstructs the 3D RI of label-free and fluorescence-labeled objects from diffracted fluorescence images acquired in reflection mode under two-photon excitation. FDT uses the transport of intensity equation and a self-supervised neural network based on explicit neural fields. Compared with state-of-the-art implicit neural fields, this approach improves computational speed, reconstruction accuracy, and interpretability. Article.Authors: Montanera K.; Lee A.; Yun W.; Ialongo Del Prete A.; Yeh S.; Jung I.; Rhee H.

Article.Authors: Wang S.; Yang F.; Zhao W.; Lang S.; Chen Z.; Wang Y.; Yang Y.; Zhang X.; Wan D.; Song J.; Liu Y.; Li Y.; Yu Y.; Ju X.; Wu J.; Ni Z.; Lu J.; Liu H.

Article.Abstract: Abstract Urban zones are rapidly expanding worldwide, exposing organisms to complex and multidimensional stressors. Article.Title: Consecutive waves of NODAL inhibition are required for epiblast patterning
Article.Authors: Wang M.; Hou T.; Villagrana J.; Kijima Y.; Dias N.; Altus R.; Brueckner M.; Aktaş T.; Sumigray K.; Kretzmer H.; Smith Z.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The mouse genome encodes two Lefty genes that antagonize NODAL signaling to break symmetry during gastrulation. Despite their central regulatory role, accurately describing and comparing their embryonic function remains unclear. Here, we generated high replicate powered single-cell transcriptional atlases of Lefty1 and Lefty2 mutant embryogenesis to evaluate the effects of perturbed NODAL signaling during gastrulation. We find that both mutants exhibit phenotypes beginning with the earliest primitive streak derivatives, suggesting a sequential shift from anterior Lefty1 to posterior Lefty2-based control that prevents spurious differentiation into extraembryonic and axial mesoendoderm at the cost of embryonic mesoderm and, in the case of Lefty1, rostral forebrain specification. By phasing bulk SMAD2/3 ChIP-seq data into single-cell-resolved descriptions of signal transduction, we identify distinct NODAL-responsive modules that track the context-specific use of this morphogen over gastrulation time. Collectively, our work highlights the potential of single-cell assays to decode how complex differentiation processes resolve morphogen signals in space and time.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: LEFTY2; Lefty1; gastrulation; Nodal signaling; embryonic mesoderm; Smad2/3; morphogen signaling

Article.Title: Pipeline infrastructure for hydrogen transport in the United States
Article.Authors: Singh A.; Zhai H.; Holubnyak E.; Biggs C.
Article.Abstract: Pipeline infrastructure is crucial for regional hydrogen transport. However, existing pipeline models have remarkably underestimated the construction-related material and labor costs compared to U.S. historical data. To cope with this problem and establish sustainable infrastructure, we develop integrated performance, economic and life cycle emissions models to comparatively evaluate dedicated pipelines and repurposed natural gas pipelines for hydrogen transport across the country. We find that the levelized cost of hydrogen transport via dedicated pipelines varies with numerous factors, such as location, capacity, and distance; there are similar variabilities in the cost of hydrogen transport via repurposed natural gas pipelines; and although leveraging existing natural gas pipelines can substantially reduce upfront capital expenditures, it may involve tradeoffs in cost and life cycle emissions. Here, we show that the integrated pipeline models and multi-criteria analysis can better guide engineering design, planning, and investment decisions on building nationwide hydrogen transport networks. This study compares new and repurposed gas pipelines for nationwide hydrogen transport, showing how costs and life-cycle emissions vary across options and highlighting trade-offs for infrastructure planning and investment.

Article.Title: Periodontal pathogen Tannerella forsythia promotes liver fibrosis via ICAM-1⁺ neutrophil–dependent hepatic stellate cell activation
Article.Authors: Tang D.; Wei J.; Liu M.; Cui L.; Chen J.; Li H.; Lin M.; Li X.; Ou Q.; Li Q.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis is a key driver in the development and progression of liver fibrosis. Nevertheless, how specific periodontal pathogens contribute to liver fibrosis remains elusive. Here, we identify Tannerella forsythia as the crucial mediator in the link between periodontitis and liver fibrosis, which can translocate to the gut and aggravate liver fibrosis. Mechanistically, Tannerella forsythia promotes the infiltration of ICAM-1+ neutrophils and inflammatory response in the liver via disrupting intestinal barrier integrity. ICAM-1+ neutrophils secrete TNF-α, which activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway in hepatic stellate cells, triggering collagen deposition and fibrogenesis. Conditional knockout of ICAM-1 in neutrophils or global deletion of TNF-α significantly attenuates inflammatory response and liver fibrosis caused by Tannerella forsythia. Taken together, this study identifies an oral-gut-liver axis driven by Tannerella forsythia and provides a prospective therapeutic target for periodontitis-related liver fibrosis. Peridontitis has been linked in the development and progression of liver fibrosis. Here the authors suggest that Tannerella forsythia is linked to the promotion of liver fibrosis by ICAM-1+ neutrophils activating hepatic stellate cells.

Article.Title: A cross-layer 2D photodetection framework for standardized readout and signal fusion
Article.Authors: Sun X.; Liu X.; Liu J.; Wang Y.; Lu X.; Wang P.; Zhao M.; Xu Y.; Wu H.; Peng D.; Wang L.; Tan C.; Hu G.; Cui H.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Beyond improving device responsivity, a central challenge in photodetectors based on two-dimensional (2D) materials is to resolve the information-interface mismatch and delayed system translation caused by trap-governed persistent photoconductivity (PPC). Here we present a cross-layer engineering route oriented towards practical implementation that integrates defect-mechanism analysis, non-stationary signal definition, dynamic distortion compensation and readout-interface engineering, thereby establishing a conversion pathway from physical response to system output in 2D MoS2, WSe2 and PtSe2 photodetectors. In this context, drift, hysteresis and fatigue accumulation in time-varying photoresponses are no longer treated merely as non-ideal perturbations, but are reformulated as state-dependent information that can be defined, compensated and interfaced. Through interface restructuring and stable readout, nW-level state-dependent photocurrents are systematically mapped onto a mixed-signal readout interface. We further extend this strategy to array-level unified output and multisensor fusion, with its frequency-guided representation evaluated in a machine-vision task. Our results show that the history-dependent nonlinear response governed by PPC is not simply a local device non-ideality, but a state-encoded signal linking defect dynamics, readout pathways and system-level tasks. This work provides an engineering route for translating 2D photodetectors from device-level studies to system-level applications. Persistent photoconductivity usually complicates the readout of 2D photodetectors, limiting the stability and speed of the signal representation and processing. Here, the authors introduce a cross-layer signal engineering approach to analyse and stabilize the dynamic outputs of 2D MoS2, WSe2 and PtSe2 photodetectors, showing its extension to multi-sensor image recognition tasks.

Article.Title: Antisense oligonucleotides targeting transcription termination windows disrupt mRNA 3’ end processing and decrease gene expression
Article.Authors: Winczura K.; Joenson L.; Koller E.; Grzechnik P.; Jan Kiełpiński Ł.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are short, synthetic nucleic acids that bind to complementary RNA sequences and alter gene expression, making them versatile therapeutic agents. Here, we identify transcription termination windows of protein-coding genes as previously unrecognized targets for ASOs. We show that ASOs can act on nascent RNA synthesised downstream of the annotated genes, leading to a pronounced decrease in the corresponding mRNA levels. These downstream-of-gene ASOs (DG-ASOs) induce RNase H1-dependent cleavage, impairing mRNA 3’ end processing, directing the unprocessed mRNAs for exosome-dependent degradation and creating early entry points in the nascent RNA for the XRN2 exonuclease termination factor. Altogether, we show that termination windows are genuine ASO targets which can be exploited to suppress gene expression. Importantly, we also reveal an underappreciated source of off-target effects which may arise from ASOs binding downstream of genes. Our findings indicate the necessity to expand ASO design and off-target assessment guidelines to include termination window sequences, thereby improving therapeutic efficacy and safety.

Article.Title: Non-sewered sanitation systems reshape microplastics into chemically complex and reactive contaminants
Article.Authors: Liu N.; Li Z.; Cheng S.; Zhang P.; He C.; Ye Z.; Ma T.; Wang S.; Liu J.; Campos L.; Guo Z.; Lynch I.
Article.Abstract: Non-sewered sanitation systems (NSSSs) are gaining global attention as decentralized solutions, yet the transformation of microplastics (MPs) within these systems remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate MP characteristics in the influent and effluent of two NSSSs using laser direct infrared spectroscopy, Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS), and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Both systems substantially reduce MP abundance (retention: 53.7–77.1%) but also alter MP characteristics. MPs exhibit fragmentation, reduced particle size, increased morphological irregularity, and surface oxidation, evidenced by decreased spectral matching scores and emerging oxygen-containing functional groups. FT-ICR MS reveals molecular-level oxidation enrichment, and over 260 candidate plastic additives are identified. LC-MS/MS confirms elevated phthalate ester concentrations, including DBP and DEHP. Statistical analyses link MP fragmentation, oxidation, and additive release as coupled processes. These findings suggest that NSSSs reshape MPs into more chemically reactive forms, highlighting the need to evaluate transformation-associated risks beyond retention efficiency. Microplastics are known to be present within non-sewered sanitation systems, but how treatment processes alter their physicochemical properties is not well understood. Here, the authors use a range of techniques to study the fate and transformation of microplastics with treatment.

Article.Title: High-throughput spatial proteomics from cellular to subcellular scales via a hanging droplet workflow
Article.Authors: Chen H.; Guzman U.; Olsen J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples are central for clinical research and spatial proteomics (SP), yet liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) remains challenging due to protein extraction losses, evaporation during decrosslinking, and inefficient sample preparation. Current methods often involve complex protocols or specialized equipment, limiting scalability, throughput, and proteome depth. We present a streamlined micro-FFPE proteomics protocol for laser-capture microdissection (LMD) that enables high-throughput processing in a 96-well format, completing the workflow from tissue lysis to LC-MS-ready tryptic peptides on Evotips in just 2-hours. By integrating whole-slide imaging, LMD, and narrow-window data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (nDIA-MS), our approach optimizes lysis, decrosslinking, and digestion within nano-wells leveraging the hanging droplet concept. This design minimizes surface adsorption, enhances sample processing efficiency, reduces preparation time by ~30% compared with reference methods, and enables parallel handling of up to 192 samples with standard equipment. This enables the quantification of >5,500 protein groups (PGs) from 50,000 µm² regions (~250 cells), with robust performance down to 1000 µm2 (~5 cells) with ~2,500 PGs identified. Application to breast cancer (BC) tissue resolves BC subtypes and microenvironments via biomarkers (TP53, HER2, PR). Even from ~60 µm² regions of single nuclei identify ~1,800 protein groups, enabling microscale spatial proteomics approaching near-organelle resolution.

Article.Title: Precious metal free tunable manganese oxides for sustainable anion exchange membrane fuel cells
Article.Authors: Zhong X.; Ge C.; Zhang S.; Wei H.; Yang M.; Zhang X.; Wang J.; Zhao Y.; Li J.; Xu N.; Sui L.; Koketsu T.; Gao C.; Zhuang L.; Alonso-Vante N.; Zhou J.; Xu J.; Yin W.; Pao C.; Huang W.; Kan W.; Li X.; Hu Z.; Strasser P.; Ma J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Eliminating platinum group metals from cathode catalysts in low-temperature polymer electrolyte fuel cells is highly important for addressing the sustainability challenge fuel cell systems face. Here, we propose modifying the electronic structure of Li-intercalated layered Mn-oxide as a cathode catalyst to overcome the activity/stability tradeoff in anion exchange membrane fuel cells. To achieve this goal, we deploy a precious metal free catalyst design strategy involving atomically dispersed p -block metal Sn doped in Li 2 MnO 3 , in addition to d -block metals, which has been poorly explored in the research thus far. Operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy and rapid freeze-quench 119 Sn Mössbauer methodology are employed to visualize the catalytic dynamics, revealing that part of Mn 4+ ions are converted into Mn 3+ ions, whereas Sn 4+ ions remain unchanged during the oxygen reduction reaction. Under H 2 /O 2 conditions, anion exchange membrane fuel cells employing Li 2 Mn 0.9 Sn 0.1 O 3 cathodes achieve peak power densities above 1.0 W cm -2 geo and 3.96 W mg -1 Pt . This work demonstrates the beneficial modulation of the electronic structure through p -block metal substitution in earth-abundant Mn-enriched oxide materials.

Article.Title: Multi-model collaborative early warning for battery systems with integrated fiber optic sensors
Article.Authors: Zhu J.; Yu C.; Jiang Y.; Schade W.; Angelmahr M.; Wei X.; Dai H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The safety assessment of battery systems is constrained by sparse temperature measurements and monolithic diagnostic frameworks in conventional battery management systems (BMS). To address this, we propose a multi-model collaborative thermal-runaway early-warning framework using distributed temperature sensing. An integrated sensing scheme increases temperature sensing points within the battery pack from 32 to 540 with minimal wiring complexity and is validated in real-world vehicle operation. We establish a functional relationship between temperature Shannon entropy (SE) and average temperature variation to derive a dynamic warning boundary incorporating error tolerance. Integrating this boundary with thresholds for temperature, temperature change rate, and SE change rate enables collaborative early warning. Compared with conventional BMS warning benchmarks, the framework provides maximum warning lead times of 706 s in laboratory modules and 554 s in real-world vehicle operation. These findings demonstrate the potential of distributed sensing and collaborative diagnostics for proactive thermal-runaway risk identification.

Article.Title: Human-specific morphoregulatory signatures in basal radial glia characterise neocortex evolution
Article.Authors: Schütze T.; Kolodziejczyk A.; Ditzer N.; Vangelisti S.; Capra E.; Lee J.; Chiaradia I.; Kufrin V.; Yamada S.; Peters J.; Krause M.; Eugster Oegema C.; Derihaci R.; Birdir C.; Namba T.; Wurm A.; Martin U.; Wimberger P.; Long K.; Lancaster M.; Kalebic N.; Bonev B.; Albert M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract As the seat of our cognition, the human neocortex is an object of immense fascination. Human neocortex expansion during evolution has been attributed to an increase in the proliferative capacity of neural progenitor cells during development, particularly basal radial glia. Despite their evolutionary relevance, the genomic changes driving human basal radial glia biology remain uncharacterised. We use comparative chromatin and transcriptional profiling of neural progenitor cells isolated from gorilla, chimpanzee and human cerebral organoids to identify cis-regulatory elements that have gained activity in humans. Focusing specifically on basal radial glia, we discover that morphoregulatory enhancer activity and gene expression signatures distinguish human basal radial glia from other great apes. Functional analysis of the morphoregulatory genes FAM107A and CNGA3 in human organoids reveals that these genes contribute to the morphological complexity of human basal radial glia. Taken together, our inter-species comparison of basal radial glia suggests that human-specific morphoregulatory signatures characterise neocortex evolution.

Article.Title: De novo design of miniprotein inhibitors of bacterial adhesins
Article.Authors: Chazin-Gray A.; Thompson T.; Lopatto E.; Magala P.; Erickson P.; Hunt A.; Manchenko A.; Aprikian P.; Tchesnokova V.; Basova I.; Sanick D.; Tamadonfar K.; Timm M.; Pinkner J.; Dodson K.; Kang A.; Joyce E.; Bera A.; Schmitz A.; Ellebedy A.; Hvorecny K.; Interlandi G.; Cartwright M.; Vernet A.; Bardales S.
Article.Abstract: The rise of multidrug-resistant bacterial infections necessitates the discovery of novel antimicrobial strategies. Here, we show that protein design provides a generalizable means of generating new antimicrobials by neutralizing the function of bacterial adhesins, which are virulence factors critical in host-pathogen interactions. We de novo designed high-affinity miniprotein binders to FimH and Abp chaperone usher pili adhesins from uropathogenic Escherichia coli and Acinetobacter baumannii, respectively, which are implicated in mediating both uncomplicated and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTI) responsible for significant morbidity worldwide. The designed antagonists have high specificity and stability, disrupt bacterial recognition of host receptors, block biofilm formation, and are effective in treating and preventing murine models of uncomplicated and catheter-associated UTIs in vivo. Here, the authors show that protein design is a generalizable strategy to generate new antimicrobials by neutralizing the function of bacterial adhesins to combat two causative agents of urinary tract infections, E. coli and A. baumannii.

Article.Title: A co-evolved peptide-GPCR system senses host entry to drive fungal infection
Article.Authors: Mendoza-Rojas G.; Nakonz P.; Lu M.; Kühne N.; Postma J.; Shtakser N.; Heinen M.; Patel M.; Arguello-Miranda O.; Heimel K.; Billerbeck S.; Altegoer F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A successful infection requires pathogens to recognize the specific host environment in order to reprogram their physiology accordingly. One major way in which eukaryotic cells sense their surroundings is via G-Protein Coupled Receptors (GPCRs), which share a seven-transmembrane architecture and G-protein-mediated downstream signaling. While mammalian GPCRs are well-characterized and represent important drug targets, their fungal counterparts remain poorly understood. Here we uncover a GPCR-based mechanism that allows the corn pathogen Ustilago maydis to sense whether it has entered plant tissue. During infection, the fungus secretes the protein Pit2, which is cleaved by host apoplastic cysteine proteases, releasing a peptide ligand ‘hidden’ within the protein core. This ligand activates the fungal GPCR Gpe1, thus promoting fungal proliferation after initial host penetration. We elucidate the crystal structure of Pit2 and model the complex formed by Gpe1 and the Pit2-derived peptide. Structure-guided mutational analysis supports that disrupting this interaction reduces fungal virulence. The Gpe1/Pit2 system is conserved in related fungal species, with co-evolutionary signatures apparently preserving receptor-ligand specificity. Furthermore, this system shows mechanistic similarities to mammalian receptors, suggesting an evolutionary link between fungal and mammalian GPCRs.

Article.Title: A cryptic binding pocket regulates the metal-dependent activity of Cas9
Article.Authors: Ahsan M.; Knight A.; Saha A.; Ramos D.; Strohkendl I.; Skeens E.; West M.; Luo J.; Dresser C.; Taylor D.; Lisi G.; Palermo G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cas9 is a metal-dependent nuclease used for genome editing across diverse cells and organisms exhibiting distinct ionic environments, yet how metal ions regulate its catalytic function, and consequently its editing efficiency remains unclear. Here, molecular simulations, Markov state models, and mixed quantum–classical approaches reveal that divalent metals promote activation of the catalytic HNH domain through formation of a divalent metal-binding pocket (DBP) at the HNH–RuvC interface. This cryptic pocket emerges dynamically during HNH activation and is supported by NMR measurements revealing metal-dependent structural perturbations within the HNH–L2 region. Mutations targeting the DBP disrupt HNH activation and impair the coupled catalytic activity of both nucleases, identifying the pocket as a key regulator of Cas9’s metal-dependent activity. Together with quantum–classical simulations revealing distinct catalytic behaviours among divalent metals, these findings uncover an ion-dependent regulatory mechanism in Cas9 with insights for genome editing across diverse biological environments.

Article.Title: Lipid-organized tetramerization of PLPP1 defines the molecular basis of spatial lipid phosphate signaling
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Yuan Q.; Cao Z.; Zhu L.; Xu J.; Guo C.; Wang J.; Xu Y.; Li S.; Li T.; Li Y.; Li Y.; Xu H.; Wu C.
Article.Abstract: Bioactive lipid phosphates, such as lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) and sphingosine-1-phosphate, are potent membrane-embedded signals that regulate fundamental processes in development, immunity, and cancer. The termination of these signals is mediated by phospholipid phosphatases (PLPPs), yet the molecular principles governing their function at the membrane interface have remained poorly understood. Here we report high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structures of human PLPP1 in apo (1.87 Å) and product-bound (2.21 Å) states. The structures reveal a highly ordered, C4-symmetric homotetramer with ordered lipid densities—including densities assigned to phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidic acid, and phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate—at inter-subunit interfaces. Structure-guided mutagenesis shows that residues surrounding these interfacial lipid densities affect enzymatic activity, whereas oligomerization analysis indicates that activity loss does not simply correlate with tetramer disruption. The product-bound structure defines the catalytic pocket and a membrane-facing tunnel that suggests a possible route for LPA access, while electrophysiological recordings detected no PLPP1-associated ion conductance under the conditions tested. Together, these findings provide a structural framework for PLPP1 tetramer assembly, lipid phosphate hydrolysis, and product recognition. Lipid phosphate phosphatases regulate bioactive lipids involved in cell signalling. Here, the authors reveal how human PLPP1 assembles and recognizes lipids, providing a structural framework for its membrane-associated activity.

Article.Title: Spinons, solitons and random-singlet-like behaviours in the spin-chain compound copper benzoate
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Duan G.; Zhao Y.; Xi N.; Pan B.; Xu X.; Wu Z.; Du K.; Li S.; Hu Z.; Shi X.; Bian R.; Wang X.; Li W.; Cui Y.; Zhang L.; Li S.; Yu R.; Yu W.
Article.Abstract: The S = 1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain is a paradigmatic quantum system hosting exotic excitations. Using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) on copper benzoate, we characterise three distinct types of excitations by tuning the magnetic field at ultra-low temperatures. At 0.2 T, a nearly constant spin-lattice relaxation rate (1/T1) and a divergence-like spin-spin relaxation rate (1/T2G) upon cooling provide experimental evidence for spinon excitations. Below 0.4 K, an additional relaxation channel, characterised by 1/T1 ∝ T with spectral weight growing as $$-\ln (T/{T}_{0})$$ and a divergence of the NMR Knight shift (Kn), reveals random-singlet-like behaviours. Above 1 T, a field-induced spin gap Δ ∝ H2/3 signifies the onset of soliton excitations. This work offers NMR identification of spinons, solitons, and the low-energy behaviours of a random-singlet-like state in copper benzoate, and establishes this material as a unique platform for studying the interplay of quantum integrability and disorder. A detailed low-temperature NMR study on copper benzoate reveals spinon excitations, low-temperature random-singlet-like behaviours and field-induced solitons, highlighting the interplay between crystal structure and weak disorder in a spin-chain system.

Article.Title: Topological diversity and scintillating dynamics of dipolar surface twists in a van der Waals magnet
Article.Authors: Lv X.; Qin J.; Hu Y.; Wang Q.; Hao H.; Pei K.; Zhang S.; Fu X.; Cheng H.; Hou Z.; Che R.
Article.Abstract: Realizing diverse configurations and dynamics of skyrmionic solitons offers additional topological and dynamical degrees of freedom for energy-efficient, topology-based spintronic devices. Extending these solitons into three dimensions further amplifies their potential, enabling the selective exploitation of surface- or bulk-topological characteristics, a regime that remains largely unexplored. Here, we report high-density dipolar-interaction-stabilized surface twists atop bulk stripe domains under zero magnetic field, through a systematic investigation of three-dimensional domain architectures in the room-temperature van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2. Unlike conventional skyrmions with integer topological charges, these surface twists carry fractional charges and assemble into diverse composite configurations under field swapping, including aggregates of up to 13 surface twists and ring-like structures. Current-driven experiments uncover two distinct dynamic modes: scintillation, marked by the nucleation, annihilation, and helicity switching of surface twists, and ordered motion of bulk skyrmion strings. These behaviors arise from the interplay between spin-transfer torque and local pinning, establishing surface twists as tunable surface-localized topological states whose dynamics are decoupled from their bulk counterparts, thereby enabling versatile hybrid spintronic functionalities. Authors investigate the field- and current-driven dynamics of three-dimensional magnetic textures in Fe3GaTe2, revealing topological diversity and distinct dynamical behaviors at the surface and in the bulk.

Article.Title: Freezing-induced solid-liquid microphase separation for self-assembly of functional nucleic acid nanoparticles
Article.Authors: Zeng T.; Fang J.; Hao J.; Cao X.; Li S.; Bai S.; Chen J.; Li C.; Yang H.; Lu C.
Article.Abstract: In nature, nuclear DNA complexed with histone form highly condensed chromatin via loop extrusion and microphase separation, yielding physically constrained solid-like structures. Inspired by this natural compaction, here we demonstrate that freezing-induced crystallization pressure and freeze-concentration effects trigger solid-liquid microphase separation for efficient DNA compression. Freezing compress various nucleic acids (single stranded DNA, molecular beacons, siRNA, plasmid DNA) into high-density states that self-assemble into nanoparticles (DNA-NPs, MB-NPs, siBcl-2-NPs, siPLK1-NPs, pEGFP-NPs). Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that ice crystal growth increases solute concentration, enhancing DNA intermolecular interactions to form supramolecular chains. Stress at advancing ice-liquid interfaces further orders and compacts these supramolecular chains into nanoparticles. In breast cancer cells, MB-NPs detect miRNA-21; siBcl-2-NPs downregulate Bcl-2 protein; siPLK1-NPs exhibited antitumor effects; and pEGFP-NPs mediate green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression. This freeze-induced self-assembly strategy replaces chemical synthesis with physical constraints, establishing a versatile platform for facile production of nucleic acid nanoparticles. Efficent delivery of various nucleic acids in vitro and in vivo remains challenging. Here, the authors use freezing-induced condensation and microphase separation to compress nucleic acids into functional nanoparticles, without excipients, validated the bioactivity in vitro and in vivo.

Article.Title: CROSS: A cross-species chromosome substitution platform for dissecting chromosome architecture and activity
Article.Authors: Mao Y.; Yang N.; Zhao Y.; Wang L.; Xu K.; Chen Y.; Ding Y.; Zhong B.; Ma S.; Liu J.; Zhang Y.; Ni Q.; Feng G.; Zhou Q.; Zhou Q.; Li W.
Article.Abstract: The functional integrity of a mammalian chromosome depends on its long-term co-evolution with species-specific nuclear environment. How chromosomes co-adapt with their native environment to define 3D architecture and transcription remains unclear, largely due to a lack of experimental models that dissect this co-evolution. Here, we report cross-species chromosome substitution (CROSS), a method enabling stable, scarless replacement of host chromosomes with divergent orthologs. We integrate microcell-mediated chromosome transfer with CRISPR/Cas9 to import the intact 152-Mb rat X chromosome into male mouse embryonic stem cells, and subsequently replace the mouse X chromosome, maintaining its stability and integrity. Rat-specific LINE1 and RatSatRep2 repeats recruit mouse SETDB1 inefficiently, causing local H3K9me3 loss. This triggers 3D remodeling, characterized by de novo topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries that aberrantly activate adjacent genes, including Rhox5, impairing differentiation. We provide a platform for dissecting sequence and epigenome cooperation in chromosome regulation, and evaluating fidelity of large-scale heterologous DNA. Chromosome function depends on coevolution with nuclear environment, but how is unclear. Here, authors use CROSS to stably and scarlessly replace mouse chrX with rat chrX. Rat repeats poorly recruit SETDB1, causing H3K9me3 loss, new TAD boundaries, that dysregulate genes, impairing differentiation.

Article.Title: FtmOx1-catalyzed diverse C(sp3)-H oxyfunctionalization enables versatile late-stage diversification of phenethylamines and tetrahydroisoquinolines
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Liang H.; Shang A.; Wu C.; Yu J.; Zhang G.; Chen Y.; Wang M.; Tang G.; Sun A.; Zhou S.; Liu H.
Article.Abstract: The enzymatic late-stage functionalization of C(sp3)-H bonds has emerged as a transformative strategy in medicinal chemistry. Verruculogen synthase (FtmOx1) is known to catalyze the endoperoxidation of its native substrate, fumitremorgin B. Here, we demonstrate the catalytic versatility of FtmOx1 by showing its ability to mediate diverse C(sp3)-H transformations on non-native substrates—phenethylamine and tetrahydroisoquinoline derivatives (1) —including β-hydroxylation, β-ketone formation, dealkylation, and α,β-desaturation. A total of 48 structurally diverse substrates prove suitable for this method, substantially expanding the biocatalytic repertoire of FtmOx1. Mechanistic studies, combined with crystallographic and mutagenesis analyses, reveal the distinct molecular basis for this diverse C(sp3)-H oxyfunctionalization compared to native pathway. Notably, the relative flexibility of the phenethyl and benzyl chains of 1, assisted by specific substitutions that allow the two chains to swing, enables high β-selectivity for hydroxylation and prevents secondary oxidation. This C(sp3)-H activation platform efficiently generates structurally diverse oxyfunctionalized derivatives, including 1,2-amino alcohols (2), 1,2-amino ketones (3), and enamines (4), accelerating lead discovery for modulators of the human relaxin family peptide receptor 4 (RXFP4). Collectively, our work establishes FtmOx1 as a powerful biocatalytic tool, expanding the frontiers of C–H functionalization in drug discovery. Enzymatic late-stage functionalization of C(sp3)-H bonds is an important strategy in medicinal chemistry, and verruculogen synthase (FtmOx1) is an enzyme that catalyses endoperoxidation of its native substrate, fumitremorgin B. Here, the authors report the catalytic versatility of FtmOx1 in mediating diverse C(sp3)-H transformations of non-native substrates, including phenethylamines and tetrahydroisoquinolines, through β-hydroxylation, β-ketone formation, dealkylation, and α, β-desaturation.

Article.Title: Genotype-phenotype single-cell transcriptomics for massive parallel assessment of genetic variants
Article.Authors: Vaccaro L.; De Santis R.; Panariello F.; Grimaldi A.; Gandolfo G.; Massa M.; Fusco T.; Salvi M.; Capuana R.; Riccardo S.; Annunziata P.; Colantuono C.; Martone G.; Bamundo M.; Xanthopoulou E.; Schertler L.; Damon C.; Gambardella G.; Arnese R.; Agolini E.; Cesario C.; Abdelrazek I.; AbdelGhany H.; Novelli A.; Salvatori B.
Article.Abstract: Predicting the pathogenic effect of rare genetic variants is significantly hampered by the limited cohort of diagnosed patients and the difficulty in functionally evaluating the effect of existing and novel variants. To address this issue, we leveraged a protein Multiplexed Assay of Variants Effect (MAVE) to functionally assess the effect of ~ 2200 missense variants of the TP63 gene, some of which cause autosomal dominant developmental disorders. The activity of each variant was measured using an optimized fibroblast-to-keratinocyte conversion protocol, and a subset of mutants was validated through multiple orthogonal biochemical and genomics functional assays to assess consistency and robustness. To systematically expand MAVEs beyond predefined assay, we here introduce SCRAMseq (Single Cell RNAseq Associated with MAVEs by sequencing). This generalizable platform leverages full-length scRNAseq for high-throughput, single-cell genotype-to-phenotype mapping. We validate SCRAMseq across different experimental and genetic contexts to demonstrate its reproducibility and accuracy. SCRAMseq provides a robust and versatile workflow poised to accelerate the discovery and dissection of gene variant effects on any potential disease-driving pathway, thereby significantly broadening MAVEs applicability to virtually any possible disease-driving gene. This work introduces SCRAMseq, a generalizable single-cell platform that pairs full-length transcriptomics with genotyping to test the functional effect of thousands of genetic variants simultaneously, bypassing the need for gene-specific functional assays.

Article.Title: APOE2 attenuates APOE4-associated amyloid pathology and related toxicity in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Chen K.; Chen Y.; Ren Y.; Wang Z.; Huang Y.; Pan M.; Li Z.; Casey M.; Qiao W.; Shi J.; Kong D.; Xhafkollari G.; Santhakumar H.; Wetmore A.; Thompson E.; Wang X.; Dickson D.; Holtzman D.; Bu G.; Han X.; Peng J.; Zhao N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The apolipoprotein E ( APOE ) gene is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease (AD), influencing amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregation, clearance, and glial function. While APOE4 promotes Aβ pathology and APOE2 is protective, how these opposing alleles interact in the heterozygous APOE2/4 state remains unknown. Here, using littermate-controlled heterozygous APOE mice ( APOE2/3 , APOE3/4 , and APOE2/4 ) alongside APOE3/3 controls crossed with 5xFAD mice, we show that APOE3/4 mice exhibit increased Aβ deposition, maladaptive microglial activation, and reduced microglial interactions with plaques. These changes were attenuated in APOE2/4 mice, accompanied by a brain proteomic profile more similar to those of APOE3/3 and APOE2/3 mice. Increased myelin basic protein (MBP) abundance was observed in APOE2/3 but not APOE2/4 mice. Plasma lipidomics revealed shared alterations in APOE3/4 and APOE2/4 mice, with distinct signatures in APOE2/3 mice. These findings define allele interaction-dependent effects of APOE on brain and systemic phenotypes and provide a framework for understanding the biological consequences of the APOE2/4 genotype.

Article.Title: Targeting CD28 on T lineage malignancies with chimeric antigen receptor T cells
Article.Authors: Willier S.; Färber J.; Ispyrlidou T.; Wilhelm J.; Mayer E.; Stenger D.; Seiferling J.; Brien A.; Nikolaides S.; Ferrada-Ernst P.; Maile J.; Vick B.; Carr A.; Blaeschke F.; Busch D.; Spieler P.; Nerreter T.; Lotfi R.; Rudelius M.; Kaeuferle T.; Klein C.; Escherich G.; Jeremias I.; Burk U.; Feuchtinger T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Currently, no immunotherapy is approved for T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T‑ALL). High initial response rates to CD7‑directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are limited by profound T cell aplasia and CD7‑negative immune escape, underscoring the need for alternative targets. Here, we show that CD28 is overexpressed on T‑ALL blasts from children and adolescents compared with lymphoid progenitors from healthy donors and is uniformly upregulated in nodal T-follicular helper cell lymphomas (nTFHL-AI, nTFHL-F). Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated CD28 knockout to prevent fratricide, we generate highly functional anti‑CD28 CAR T cells with selective cytotoxicity against CD28⁺ T‑ALL. Anti‑CD28 CAR T cells match anti‑CD7 CAR T cells in vitro and in vivo, but cause markedly less lymphodepletion, largely sparing CD8 T cells and NK cells while preferentially depleting CD4 T cells, particularly TH2 and TH17 subsets. These findings establish CD28 as an actionable target for CAR T cell therapy of T cell malignancies.

Article.Title: Pregnancy establishment in cattle without embryonic interferon tau
Article.Authors: Ali A.; Zakhartchenko V.; Güngör T.; Nüske S.; Stöckl J.; Hecken S.; Hauser A.; Krebs S.; Reese S.; Suchowski M.; Friedl R.; Schwanitz S.; Scholz A.; Blutke A.; Protschka M.; Büttner M.; Fröhlich T.; Reichenbach H.; Wolf E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In ruminants, embryonic interferon tau (IFNT) is widely considered the indispensable signal for maternal recognition of pregnancy, driving endometrial gene expression to prevent luteolysis. However, this canonical paradigm has never been directly tested using genomic loss-of-function models. Here we show that IFNT is completely dispensable for pregnancy recognition, luteal maintenance, and full-term gestation in cattle. Using CRISPR-Cas9, we generate bovine fibroblasts lacking all functional copies of the multigene IFNT locus for somatic cell nuclear transfer. IFNT -null embryos develop into blastocysts in vitro at normal rates and exhibit typical elongation at day 18 post-transfer without inducing endometrial interferon-stimulated genes. Crucially, these IFNT -null conceptuses successfully prevent luteal regression, establish normal placentation, and progress through full-term gestations, culminating in the birth of healthy female calves. These findings provide the first direct genetic evidence that embryonic IFNT is dispensable for pregnancy recognition and establishment in cattle, fundamentally revising the long-standing model of ruminant reproduction and uncovering alternative embryo-maternal signaling mechanisms.

Article.Title: Reward function compression facilitates goal-dependent reinforcement learning
Article.Authors: Molinaro G.; Collins A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Humans can uniquely assign value to novel, abstract outcomes to support reinforcement learning. However, this flexibility is cognitively costly and reduces learning efficiency. We propose that goal-dependent learning initially relies on capacity-limited working memory. With consistent experience, learners create a compressed reward function — a simplified rule — that transfers to long-term memory for automatic evaluation upon receiving feedback. This automaticity frees working memory resources, thereby boosting learning efficiency. Across six experiments, we demonstrate that learning is impaired by the size of the goal space but improves when this space allows for compression. Additionally, faster reward processing correlates with better learning. Although the algorithmic details remain to be established, computational modeling revealed that individual differences in compression efficiency, proxied by reward processing speed, led to higher choice accuracy. Together, our behavioral results and computational models suggest that efficient goal-directed learning relies on compressing complex goals into stable reward functions.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: goal-directed learning; working memory; intrinsic motivation; long-term memory; learning efficiency

Article.Title: Olaparib plus tremelimumab in women with recurrent ovarian cancer and a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation: a phase I/II study
Article.Authors: Adams S.; Gimotty P.; Rutledge T.; O’Malley D.; Ring K.; Wenham R.; Finkelstein K.; Lokich E.; Falcon D.; Yeckes A.; Oyebamiji O.; Brayer K.; Paskus E.; Falk N.; Richards R.; Lee J.; Eberhardt S.; McCance D.; Paliard X.; Boyle S.; Chen R.; Kang H.; Conejo-Garcia J.; Rixe O.; Muller C.
Article.Abstract: Response rates to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in ovarian cancer are low. In preclinical studies, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibition (PARPi) synergized with CTLA4 ICB to achieve long-term survival in Brca1-deficient ovarian cancer models. Here we evaluated the safety and efficacy of combined treatment with the PARPi olaparib and the CTLA4 ICB tremelimumab for recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer in a multi-site single-arm phase I/II study enrolling 50 women with germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations (NCT02571725). In phase I, no new toxicities were identified (n = 3). In the combined phase I and II safety cohort (n = 49), 57% of subjects experienced grade 3 or 4 non-hematologic toxicity, with tremelimumab discontinuation in 34.7%. The primary phase II endpoint, overall response rate was 32.7% (95% CI 19.5-45.8%), and disease control rate was 47.7% (95% CI 33.0-62.5%). Secondary outcomes were progression-free survival (PFS, 3.0 months, 95% CI 2.7-5.9), and overall survival (24.3 months, CI 14.9-30.4). In exploratory post-hoc biomarker analyses, low VSTM5 or IFIT1B expression was associated with treatment benefit and improved PFS (p < 0.001). Although the trial did not meet its prespecified efficacy endpoint, PFS > 12 months in 6 subjects among this heavily pre-treated cohort highlight the need for biomarkers to select regimens for patients with recurrent ovarian cancer. Response rate to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in ovarian cancer remains low and combinatorial strategies are needed. Here the authors report the results of a phase I/II study of the PARP inhibitor olaparib and the anti-CTLA4 antibody tremelimumab in women with recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer and a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation.

Article.Title: Modulate adsorption via Co2+-O-Coδ+ asymmetric pairs toward efficient upcycling of plastic waste to commodity chemicals
Article.Authors: Chang X.; Yu T.; Wang H.; Jiang J.; Yan D.; Chang J.; Jin Y.; Yang Y.; Hou C.
Article.Abstract: The conversion of polyethylene terephthalate waste into valuable bulk chemicals through electrochemical upcycling represents a viable strategy for waste valorization. The direct involvement of hydroxyl species is crucial for C-C bond cleavage during ethylene glycol oxidation in polyethylene terephthalate hydrolysate, thereby enhancing catalytic efficiency. However, excessive or competitive hydroxyl adsorption often suppresses ethylene glycol adsorption and activation, impeding the formation of key intermediates toward formic acid. Here we show a crystal boundary engineering strategy to construct an asymmetric Co2+-O-Coδ+ bridged electrocatalyst within cobalt oxides. This design integrates two catalytic sites: Co2+ sites preferentially facilitate hydroxyl adsorption, while Coδ+ sites exhibit enhanced affinity for ethylene glycol, thereby reducing the energy barrier for formic acid formation. Consequently, the Asy-Co2+-O-Coδ+ exhibits a high Faradaic efficiency of 96.12% and selectivity of 93.75%. It delivers an industrial-level current density of 1000 mA cm−2 under membrane electrode assembly conditions, with competitive stability over multiple polyethylene terephthalate hydrolysate electrolysis cycles. This study provides valuable insights for the design of advanced catalysts in the upcycling of polyethylene terephthalate waste. Electrochemical oxidation of ethylene glycol offers a sustainable route for upcycling polyethylene terephthalate waste. Here, the authors report a grain boundary-engineered asymmetric dual-site catalyst whose synergistic adsorption can be modulated, rendering it promising for plastic waste upcycling.
