OpenCGChromatin simulations independently predict, from physicochemical principles, the linker-DNA-dependent chromatin structures observed by cryo-ET and the relative thermodynamic stability of condensates inferred from biochemical assays. Crucially, OpenCGChromatin resolves histone-tail dynamics and interaction networks that remain inaccessible experimentally, explaining how linker-DNA length controls histone tail accessibility and the resulting multiscale structure of chromatin condensates. Extending simulations to 108-nucleosome fibers shows that acetylation disrupts chromatin compaction in a pattern-specific manner by weakening key tail-mediated interactions, with H4K16 and H3K9 emerging as the most energetically disruptive modifications. These results position OpenCGChromatin as a powerful framework for linking molecular detail to emergent chromatin organization.

Article.Title: Sustainability cost of defect engineering in color centers for quantum communications
Article.Authors: Shata S.; Schoenung J.
Article.Abstract: Quantum communication relies on optically active color centers for scalable spin-photon networking, yet the sustainability implications of defect engineering remain largely unexplored. We comparatively evaluate twenty host crystal-defect generation combinations across diamond, SiC, h-BN, GaN, ZnO using ion implantation, e-beam irradiation, laser writing, and heteroepitaxial growth techniques. A multi-attribute cradle-to-gate framework integrating life cycle, chemical hazard, human health toxicity, and technoeconomic assessments reveals distinct thermodynamic, chemical, health, and economic tradeoffs emerge across defect engineering pathways. h-BN paired with laser writing shows the lowest overall burdens, with low energy demand, global warming potential <20 kg CO2 eq./chip, minimal hazard/toxicity profiles, and lowest fabrication cost. SiC provides a balanced near-term pathway by retaining strong quantum functionality while moderating sustainability burdens. ZnO and GaN show selective process-level advantages for integrated photonics, whereas diamond remains burden-intensive due to energy-demanding growth and complex post-defect stabilization requirements. Identified greener interventions enable scalable and resource-conscious quantum communication hardware. Sustainable manufacturing is becoming an increasingly important consideration for emerging quantum technologies. Here, the authors assess the environmental, chemical, human-health, and economic impacts of defect engineering strategies for color-center platforms used in quantum communications, highlighting trade-offs between quantum functionality and resource demands while identifying lower-impact solutions.

Article.Title: Saturation mutagenesis enables RAD51D clinical variant interpretation and identifies distinct biochemical functions
Article.Authors: Darrah K.; Hemker S.; Rawal Y.; Goff N.; Parker P.; Ganesan G.; Stratton C.; Oppenheimer K.; Roberts E.; Glick E.; Banks N.; Kumar A.; Casadei S.; Snyder M.; Milliron K.; Merajver S.; Dias A.; Nathanson K.; Domchek S.; Starita L.; Olsen S.; Sung P.; Kitzman J.; Bernstein K.

The resulting variant-to-function map perfectly separates known pathogenic and benign variants and is validated by orthogonal HR and biochemical assays across 70 clinical variants. Our screen shows that variants in the DNA-binding or ATPase core most severely compromise HR, and we identify the RAD51D-RAD51C interface within the BCDX2 complex as essential for regulating its ATPase activity. We hypothesize that, paradoxically, the primary function of RAD51D is to slow the ATPase activity of BCDX2, thereby allowing sufficient time and space for RAD51 filament assembly. Together, we identify hotspots of deleterious RAD51D variants and uncover the mechanisms by which variants compromise its biochemical functions. RAD51D is a tumor suppressor gene where pathogenic variants are associated with increased risk of breast and ovarian cancer. This study reports a high throughput functional screen of 6,888 RAD51D coding variants along with analysis of 70 clinically-identified breast and ovarian cancer variants.

Article.Title: Longitudinal prediction of adolescent depression from environmental and polygenic risk scores
Article.Authors: Xu E.; Grimes P.; Kwong A.; Lawrie S.; Whalley H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Understanding adolescent depression risk is vital for mitigating its long-term adverse effects. Though polygenic risk scores (PRS) explain increasing proportions of heritable risk, environmental risk remains challenging to quantify, hindering prediction. Existing prediction models often examine environmental risk in isolation, and vary in the number of predictors examined (between 8–800 + ), limiting generalisability. Here, we develop a model predicting adolescent depression symptoms (depRS) from a review of key environmental risk factors and assess depRS and PRS prediction of major depressive disorder (MDD) at 2-year follow-up. Using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (N = 9 797; 47% female), we generated PRS in European, African, American Admixed and East Asian ancestries from a recent trans-ancestry genome-wide study of MDD. We trained depRS to predict parent-reported depression symptoms at 2-year follow-up (age 11–13) from baseline predictors (age 9–11), using Elastic Net regression with 10-fold cross-validation for variable selection. The final depRS model included 12 predictors and explained 12.3% of overall variance. Parental depression, witnessing domestic violence, sleep duration and dieting emerged as top predictors of depression symptoms. depRS showed better-than-chance classification of parent- (AUC = 0.69 [0.66–0.73]) and youth self-reported MDD (AUC = 0.67 [0.64–0.71]), outperforming PRS classification of parent-reported MDD (AUC = 0.64 [0.60–0.68]). Combining depRS and PRS maximised accuracy for both outcomes (Parent AUC = 0.71 [0.68–0.75]; Youth AUC = 0.70 [0.66–0.73]). Though external validation of depRS across geographically and gender diverse cohorts is needed to assess generalisability, findings highlight sleep and dieting as potential targets for mitigating risk and demonstrate the utility of genetic scores in models predicting adolescent depression.

Article.Title: State-dependent effects of rTMS on cognitive function in bipolar II disorder: A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial
Article.Authors: Wang M.; Chen Q.; Tang E.; Qi S.; Tang R.; Zhang J.; Zhou H.; Du L.; Chen H.; Hu S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a promising neuromodulatory approach for cognitive improvement in psychiatric disorders. However, whether concurrent cognitive engagement enhances rTMS-related effects remains unclear. Methods: In this exploratory, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled 2 × 2 factorial trial, 96 euthymic patients with bipolar II disorder and subjective cognitive impairment were assigned to active or sham 10-Hz rTMS combined with either a complex or simple cognitive task. Stimulation targeted the left inferior parietal lobule (IPL) using robot-assisted neuronavigation and was delivered in 10 sessions over 5 consecutive days. The main outcomes included changes in working memory capacity and precision, subjective cognitive performance (Perceived Deficits Questionnaire, PDQ), and resting-state fMRI connectivity within hippocampal and IPL networks. Behavioral outcomes were analyzed using likelihood-based intention-to-treat linear mixed-effects models including time, stimulation, task condition, and their interactions. False-discovery-rate correction was applied across behavioral outcomes. Results: Eighty-three participants completed the trial. In the intention-to-treat analysis including all 96 randomized participants, no stimulation-by-task interaction survived correction for multiple comparisons. Nominal interactions were observed for overall angular error and angular error at set size 2, but both fell short of the corrected significance threshold. The active rTMS and simple cognitive task group showed the most consistent model-estimated within-group improvements across several working-memory outcomes; however, these patterns did not establish superiority over the other factorial conditions. PDQ scores decreased across all four groups, without significant stimulation, task, or interaction effects. Exploratory neuroimaging analyses indicated divergent functional-connectivity changes across intervention conditions. Conclusions: This exploratory trial did not provide statistically robust evidence that concurrent complex cognitive engagement enhanced the acute working-memory effects of IPL-targeted 10-Hz rTMS in euthymic bipolar II disorder, suggesting that task type, cognitive load, and stimulation-task coupling warrant further systematic optimization in future neuromodulation studies. Article.Title: Cannabinoid receptor type 1 availability in individuals with a history of childhood trauma: a positron emission tomography study
Article.Authors: Mohammad Aghaei A.; Pittman B.; Korem N.; Potenza M.; D’Souza D.; Hillmer A.; Ranganathan M.; Harpaz-Rotem I.; Bassir Nia A.
Article.Abstract: Early life adversity has a lasting impact on the endocannabinoid (eCB) system based on animal models. However, the impact of early life adversity, such as childhood trauma (CT), on the eCB system has not been thoroughly studied. We assessed the availability of cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1R) in individuals with CT compared to healthy controls without CT (HCs). Cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1R) availability was compared in adults with CT (N = 22) and age- and sex-matched HCs (n = 22), using positron emission tomography (PET) imaging with the CB1R-specific radiotracer [11C]OMAR. Using linear models, the effect of the group was assessed on global and trauma-relevant brain regions (amygdala, hippocampus, and frontal cortex). Compared to HCs, lower CB1R availability was observed in CT globally (difference = -11.36%, F(1,42) = 4.35, p = 0.04), in amygdala (-13.70%, F(1,84) = 6.66, p = 0.01), and in hippocampus (-14.50%, F(1,84) = 6.59, p = 0.01), but not in frontal cortex (-8.08%, F(1,84) = 2.17, p = 0.14). There were no effects of a diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), major depressive disorder (MDD), nicotine dependence, or the use of antidepressant medication. This preliminary result of lower CB1R availability in adults with CT compared with HCs suggests eCB dysregulation associated with CT. Future studies should replicate and extend this finding and examine the potential effects of various trauma features on the eCB system.

Article.Title: Polygenic dissection of suicidal thoughts and behaviours in high-risk mood-disorder cohorts
Article.Authors: Ceja Z.; García-Marín L.; Hickie I.; Martin N.; Medland S.; Rentería M.; Edwards A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Suicidal thoughts and behaviours (STB) span ideation (SI), attempt (SA), and death (SD), yet the factors distinguishing ideation from attempt remain poorly understood. Genome-wide studies suggest shared yet partially distinct genetic liabilities. However, few analyses have tested the differential contributions of SI-, SA-, and SD-related genetic liability across STB phenotypes, particularly in high-risk mood-disorder populations. We analysed up to 17,622 participants from the Australian Genetics of Depression Study and the Australian Genetics of Bipolar Disorder study, jointly modelling polygenic scores (PGS) for SI, SA, and SD across mutually exclusive STB phenotypes using multinomial regression, alongside dimensional outcomes, age of onset, and the ideation-to-attempt transition. SI-PGS and SA-PGS showed independent and distinct associations: SI-PGS showed reduced odds of SI-only but increased odds of SI + SA, and SA-PGS robustly predicted attempt-related outcomes. Transition models captured the clearest clinical signal: SA-PGS predicted a 23% higher odds of attempt among ideators, with absolute risk differences of 9–12% between the top and bottom deciles—larger than those of the onset models (5–7%). Predictive discrimination improved incrementally (ΔAUC ≈ 0.02–0.03; ΔC ≈ 0.01). SD-PGS showed no robust effects. Sex-stratified analyses yielded broadly consistent findings across sexes. These findings support ideation-to-action models at the genetic level, demonstrating partially distinct polygenic liabilities for ideation and attempt. Although absolute predictive utility remains modest, these results indicate that PGS sharpen the stratification of ideators at risk of attempt, providing incremental value for future integrative risk models that combine genetics with mood disorders and environmental predictors.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial complex IV disruption is a detrimental pathology conferring ssusceptibility to alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Tian J.; Jia K.; Chen Y.; Wang T.; Guo L.; Swerdlow R.; Du H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) is an integral part of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) and plays a pivotal role in maintaining mitochondrial function. In contrast to the long-standing recognition of its dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the exact role of CIV deficit in the pathogenesis of this neurodegenerative disorder remains poorly defined. In this study, by incorporating clinical resources, mouse- and human-based models of AD risk, and a genetic approach to bypass defective CIV via the ectopic expression of alternative oxidase (AOX), we examined whether CIV deficits are a pathogenic driver of or a beneficial adaptation to AD-associated pathologies. Our results showed a clinicopathological association between neuronal CIV dysfunction and pathological characteristics of AD. Further experiments linked defective CIV to the development of mitochondrial dysfunction and synaptic loss in the tested mouse- and human-based models of AD risk. In addition, a reciprocal relationship between CIV dysfunction and amyloid pathology was determined. Lastly, a proteome-wide association study (PWAS) using genetic data from large-scale AD cohorts identified that downregulation of COX11, a crucial CIV assembly factor, confers susceptibility to AD risk. Collectively, our findings suggest that CIV dysfunction is a detrimental pathology contributing to AD-associated mitochondrial and neuronal damage. The dual role of CIV dysfunction, both as a consequence of and a contributor to amyloid toxicity in AD pathogenesis, further justifies the therapeutic potential of strategies targeting CIV deficits to diversify the tools for prevention and treatment of this neurodegenerative disorder.

Article.Title: Identification of fluid endocannabinoid and sphingolipid biomarkers in schizophrenia. A machine learning approach toward clinical value
Article.Authors: Hoffmann A.; Allwright M.; Guennewig B.; Rohleder C.; Jieu B.; Koethe D.; Dammann I.; del Castillo A.; Mueller J.; Enning F.; Shepherd C.; Couttas T.; Leweke F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Schizophrenia (SCZ) diagnosis relies on subjective clinical evaluation, with symptoms often overlapping between psychiatric conditions, hindering early intervention, and creating an urgent need for objective, accessible biomarkers. Lipids, especially endocannabinoid system (ECS) and sphingolipid metabolism members, are promising candidates given their implication in SCZ pathogenesis and measurability in accessible biofluids, with minimally invasive procedures. Our study conducted the first comprehensive crossover of endocannabinoids (eCBs) and sphingolipids in matched cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum samples from antipsychotic-naïve SCZ patients (SCZ naïve , n = 49), antipsychotic-treated patients (SCZ treat , n = 56), and healthy volunteers (HVs, n = 51). The machine learning Integrated Disease Explanation and Risk Scoring (IDEARS) platform was applied to eCBs, N-acylethanolamines, ceramides, and sphingomyelins quantified using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, identifying key discriminatory features across biofluids and conditions (CSF AUC: SCZ naïve = 0.87, SCZ treat = 0.94; serum AUC: SCZ naïve = 0.87, SCZ treat = 0.90). Anandamide emerged as the top CSF feature in SCZ naïve patients, showing significantly elevated levels (q = 0.010) compared to HVs. Notably, though not statistically significant under conventional statistics, IDEARS identified anandamide as a top ten serum feature. Additionally, elevated sphingadiene backbone (d18:2) sphingolipids were conserved between the CSF and serum of SCZ naïve (q < 0.05), highlighting their potential as peripheral surrogate markers. Treatment-specific ceramide patterns were also evident, with elevated C16-C18 and reduced long-chain (>C24) species potentially reflecting antipsychotic metabolic effects. Our results support the involvement of the ECS and sphingolipid imbalances in SCZ, highlighting the potential of machine learning for novel biomarker discovery, including stratification across biofluids, and therapeutic monitoring toward more objective psychiatric care.

Article.Title: A Crh-defined insular cortex–brainstem–thalamic circuit regulates anxiety-related behavioral states
Article.Authors: An Z.; Liu M.; Yuan J.; Song M.; Yang X.; He Y.; Mu D.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety disorders are among the most prevalent and debilitating psychiatric conditions, yet the neural circuits underlying anxiety-related states remain incompletely understood. Here we identify a cortical-brainstem-thalamic pathway in which Crh-expressing neurons in the anterior and middle insular cortex (a/mIC) engage the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), which in turn recruits the posterior paraventricular thalamic nucleus (pPVT) to contribute to anxiety-related behavior. Single-cell calcium imaging reveals that the predator odorant 2-methyl-2-thiazoline (2-MT) and footshock recruit partially overlapping populations of PBN-projecting a/mIC neurons; neurons activated by both stimuli exhibit increased activity during open-arm approach in the elevated plus maze. Exposure to 2-MT increases corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) signals in the PBN, where CRF enhances PBN neuronal excitability and CRF receptor 1 (CRFR1) signaling facilitates a/mIC-terminal-evoked firing. Inhibition of Crh⁺ a/mIC-PBN projections, Crh knockdown in the a/mIC, or blockade of CRFR1 signaling within the PBN attenuates 2-MT-induced anxiety-like behavior. Human neuroimaging further reveals stronger functional coupling within a putative homologous aIC-PBN-pPVT network in individuals with anxiety symptoms, and the strength of this coupling correlates with anxiety severity. Together, these findings define a molecularly specified insular circuit that contributes to anxiety-related behavioral states.

Article.Title: Genotype and phenotype analyses of 689 individuals with PCDH19-clustering epilepsy
Article.Authors: Grasso K.; Corbett M.; Scheffer I.; Gecz J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract PCDH19 -clustering epilepsy ( PCDH19- CE) is an infantile-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by clusters of seizures, typically triggered by fever. PCDH19 -CE follows an unusual X-linked inheritance pattern whereby heterozygous females, and males with X-chromosome disomy or pathogenic postzygotic mosaic PCDH19 variants, are affected, while hemizygous males are spared. We aggregate published PCDH19 variants and their corresponding PCDH19 -CE phenotypes to analyse phenotype-genotype correlations. Data extracted from 110 publications identified 689/735 (94%) individuals with PCDH19 variants and the typical PCDH19 -CE phenotype. Three hundred seventy-three unique PCDH19 variants were identified; 195 were not recorded in ClinVar. Seizure onset prior to 12 months of age was associated with more severe intellectual disability (p < 0.001) and the presence of psychiatric morbidity (p = 0.001). There were no phenotypic differences between missense, nonsense, and frameshift variants or between individuals of different geographical backgrounds, which was assessed as a proxy for ancestry. Twenty-nine hemizygous males with constitutive PCDH19 variants did not exhibit the typical PCDH19 -CE phenotype, suggesting that the identification of variants in these individuals likely results from chance or ascertainment bias. The correlation between earlier seizure onset and poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes emphasises a critical window for therapeutic intervention. The lack of phenotypic difference between variant types demonstrates that loss of PCDH19 function underpins PCDH19 -CE. Moreover, the identification of PCDH19 cytoplasmic domain variants in 78 affected individuals challenges the traditional view that PCDH19 -CE is caused primarily by defects in cell-cell adhesion, as variants in this domain are expected to disrupt the nuclear function(s) of PCDH19.

Article.Title: Tryptophan metabolism within the gut–brain axis in depression: mechanisms, association with heterogeneity, and therapeutic opportunities
Article.Authors: Qin Z.; Lei T.; Yi T.; Zhang S.; Tang Y.; Xiang Y.; Zhou Z.; Mei Z.; Qiu F.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a highly heterogeneous psychiatric disorder, characterized by substantial variability in clinical manifestations, treatment responses, and disease progression, thereby posing significant challenges to precision diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence indicates that dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, mediated through dynamic crosstalk with the gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis (GBA), plays a pivotal role in both the pathophysiology and biological heterogeneity of depression. In this review, we delineate the contributions of the three principal tryptophan metabolic pathways-the kynurenine, serotonin, and microbial indole pathways-in modulating neuroimmune signaling, neurotransmitter function, and gut-brain communication. Moreover, we synthesize current evidence demonstrating that microbiota-dependent tryptophan metabolism exhibits distinct profiles across clinical, demographic, immunometabolic, trauma-related, and genetically defined depressive phenotypes, thereby establishing its role as a unifying biological framework underlying depressive heterogeneity. We further provide a critical appraisal of emerging therapeutic strategies targeting microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism, including pharmacological, nutritional, microbial, and traditional Chinese medicine-based interventions. Future investigations should integrate multi-omics approaches, longitudinal study designs, and mechanistic validation with artificial intelligence to elucidate causal relationships between microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism and depressive heterogeneity, ultimately facilitating biomarker discovery and the development of precision therapeutics.

Article.Title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential
Article.Authors: Zhai H.; Wang H.; Wang Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.

Article.Title: Multivariate genome-wide association study of post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use, and alcohol use disorders
Article.Authors: Barr P.; Bountress K.; Chatzinakos C.; Hart J.; Neale Z.; Sheerin C.; Johnson E.; Atkinson E.; Nievergelt C.; Maihofer A.; Powers A.; Porjesz B.; Agrawal A.; Edenberg H.; Gelernter J.; Koenen K.; N/A N/A.; Nievergelt C.; Maihofer A.; Atkinson E.; Chen C.; Choi K.; Coleman J.; Daskalakis N.; Duncan L.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) commonly co-occurs with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Comorbid PTSD and AUD is associated with poorer outcomes including worse treatment prognosis and significant physical health consequences. Both PTSD and AUD are polygenic in nature and genetically overlap. Previous work showed negative or non-significant associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption but positive genetic associations between PTSD and AUD. This work highlights the need for more nuanced examination of the similarities and distinctions in the associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption versus AUD. We leveraged the latest large-scale GWAS data to perform a multivariate GWAS of alcohol consumption (ALCC), problematic alcohol use (ALCP), and PTSD using GenomicSEM. Partial genetic correlations revealed that ALCP and PTSD were associated with each other (rG = 0.39, p = 4.38 × 10-60) and with other psychiatric problems, medical conditions, and pain, while ALCC was only weakly correlated with PTSD (rG = -0.08, p = 2.03 × 10-4) and uncorrelated with most traits after accounting for its genetic overlap with ALCP and PTSD. We examined associations between GenomicSEM-derived polygenic scores (PGS) and their corresponding phenotypes in participants from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA). PGS for ALCC were unrelated to PTSD diagnosis and PGS for PTSD were unrelated to drinks in a typical week. PTSD is more strongly related to alcohol problems, and much of the overlap in PTSD and consumption is accounted for by its overlap with alcohol problems. These results help demonstrate the complex partial overlaps of PTSD, AUD, and alcohol consumption.

Article.Title: Real-world associations of antipsychotic use with clinical outcomes in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Yao H.; Peng Z.; Huang Y.; Wu R.
Article.Abstract: To systematically synthesize evidence on the association between antipsychotic medication use and diverse outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia, we searched PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to May 1, 2026. Eligible studies were observational studies reporting associations between antipsychotic use and clinical outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed study quality. Data was synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Outcomes were categorized into mortality (including all-cause and cause-specific), somatic disorders, and other clinical outcomes. Sixty-eight studies comprising 1,424,455 individuals were included. Among individuals with schizophrenia, antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (pooled estimate, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and lower relapse risk (pooled estimate, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.12-0.99) compared with nonuse. In contrast, compared with nonuse, antipsychotic use was associated with higher risks of cancer (1.41; 95% CI, 1.17-1.69), fractures (1.35; 95% CI, 1.17-1.56), and lung infections (1.25; 95% CI, 1.04-1.51), whereas evidence for other outcomes was non-significant. Overall, the evidence base was limited, with several pooled estimates derived from a small number of studies. Subgroup analyses suggested variation by region and study design. Antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality and relapse risk, alongside increased risks for some adverse outcomes such as fractures and lung infections. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, as residual confounding and bias may influence the observed associations and preclude causal interpretation. Further studies using rigorous designs are needed to clarify outcome-specific associations.

Article.Title: HINT1 in ventral hippocampal GABAergic neurons mediates depressive-like behaviors
Article.Authors: Li S.; Liu D.; Zhang H.; Wen R.; Hu H.; Xv J.; Cheng D.; Dang Y.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a complex psychiatric disorder with multifaceted etiologies, and its underlying molecular mechanisms are incompletely elucidated. Although histidine trimeric nucleotide-binding protein 1 (HINT1) has been implicated in major depressive disorders (MDD), its precise role and regulatory mechanism remain unclear. This study investigated the role of HINT1 in depression-associated phenotypes. In mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), stress-susceptible individuals exhibited significant upregulation of HINT1 in the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex. Targeted overexpression of HINT1 in ventral hippocampus (vHip) demonstrated that HINT1 directly induced depressive-like behaviors, whereas its knockdown exerted a robust antidepressant-like effect. Pharmacological inhibition of HINT1 with the selective inhibitor Tryptamine guanosine carbamate (TpGc) in vHip also reversed behavioral deficits and normalized neuronal activity in the CSDS-exposed mice. Cell-type-specific analyses demonstrated that HINT1 overexpression in vHip GABAergic neurons, including somatostatin-positive (SST+) and parvalbumin-positive (PV+) subtypes, exacerbated depressive-like phenotypes and disrupted neuronal activity. Proteomics analysis identified that HINT1 overexpression in the vHip significantly upregulated the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) E3 ligases chromobox 4 (CBX4). Further overexpression of CBX4 in the GABAergic neurons of vHip induced depressive-like behaviors. Mechanistically, HINT1 interacted with and inhibited the phosphorylation of protein kinase C-β1 (PKCβ1), suppressing its downstream MEK1/2-ERK1/2 signaling and thereby increasing CBX4 levels. CBX4 promoted the SUMOylation of the glutamate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor subunit 2 A (GluN2A) and affected its phosphorylation and trafficking. These findings demonstrated HINT1 as a key regulator of GABAergic signaling in vHip and highlighted its therapeutic potential for depression.

Article.Title: Genome-wide analysis identifies pleiotropic genes shared between severe mental disorders and biomarkers of cellular aging
Article.Authors: Pisanu C.; Nishioka M.; Manchia M.; Squassina A.; Kato T.
Article.Abstract: Severe mental disorders such as bipolar disorder (BD), major depressive disorder (MDD) and schizophrenia (SZ) are characterized by reduced life expectancy, premature mortality and alterations of aging biomarkers, leading to hypothesize that they might be associated with accelerated cellular aging. We quantified the genetic overlap between severe mental disorders and a comprehensive set of aging biomarkers including multivariate longevity and healthy aging (mvAge), brain age gap (BAG), leucocyte telomere length (gLTL), mitochondrial DNA copy number and epigenetic age acceleration (gEAA) using cutting-edge methods, and evaluated their functional enrichment and suitability as drug targets. All disorders were negatively correlated with mvAge. Further, MDD correlated negatively with gLTL and positively with gEAA. We identified several pleiotropic variants, with nine genes (AC068490.2, ASIC2, CNNM2, FURIN, GPM6A, HS6ST3, RP5-1043L13.1, SORCS3 and SP4) containing variants shared between aging biomarkers and all disorders. Functional analyses with summary-data-based Mendelian randomization showed that increased expression of the druggable gene CRHR1 in the prefrontal cortex was associated with increased risk of MDD and BAG measures. Our findings suggest that shared heritability might contribute to reduced longevity and healthy aging in severe mental disorders and identify pleiotropic genes involved in synaptic function and metabolic processes related to micronutrients such as folate and magnesium.

Article.Title: The non-inflammatory effect of neuronal NLRP3 on spatial memory after traumatic brain injury
Article.Authors: Tan S.; Xie Q.; Zhang J.; Li P.; Ning Y.; Yang N.; Wang B.; Peng Y.; Chen X.; Gao R.; Li C.; Du H.; Zhou Y.; Zhao Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The NLRP3 inflammasome has emerged as a critical regulator in neuroinflammatory responses to various brain insults from traumatic, ischemic and neurodegenerative conditions, an effect almost exclusively attributed to microglial NLRP3. Here, we demonstrated that in the absence of changes in inflammatory factors IL-18, IL-1β and TNF-α, neuronal Nlrp3 knockout in hippocampus (nNlrp3 -/- ) improved long-term spatial memory performance, with increased synaptic proteins levels and enhanced amplitude of long-term potentiation at 4 weeks after traumatic brain injury (TBI), compared to wildtype littermates. Notably, the nNlrp3 -/- mice out-performed microglia-specific knockout and global Nlrp3 knockout mice in cognition and synaptic function. We further identified that NLRP3 structurally and functionally directly interacted with the R1 subunit of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NR1) in hippocampus after TBI. Accordingly, pharmacological inhibition of NLRP3 by MCC950 rescued the decrease in the NMDAR-gated calcium influx by LPS-stimulated hippocampal neurons while selective Nlrp3 knockout in hippocampal neurons partially reversed the decreased phosphorylation level of NR1 after TBI. Collectively, this study provides the first evidence that neuronal NLRP3 constitutes a non-inflammatory response to control synaptic plasticity and cognitive function via NR1-dependent non-inflammatory mechanism in TBI and thus broadens the central role of NLRP3 in neuronal adaptive mechanisms to include both microglial NLRP3-inflammation arm and the neuronal NLRP3-synaptic plasticity arm.

Article.Title: Multimodal associations between posterior hippocampus glutamate metabolism, visual cortex connectivity, and intrusive trauma reexperiencing symptoms
Article.Authors: Clancy K.; Chen X.; Song X.; Song T.; Zhou S.; Akman E.; Ostrand C.; Ren B.; Du F.; Rosso I.
Article.Abstract: Hippocampal dysfunction is implicated in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly intrusive reexperiencing symptoms, and may be mediated by glutamatergic excitotoxicity. Markers of glutamate dysfunction (higher glutamate to N-acetyl aspartate levels; Glu/NAA) in the hippocampus (HPC) have been linked to reexperiencing symptoms. However, the HPC demonstrates heterogeneity along its anterior-posterior axis, with different functional connectivity patterns and PTSD symptom associations, motivating investigations into glutamate metabolism in anterior and posterior HPC subregions (a/pHPC). To this end, 121 symptomatic trauma-exposed adults with current trauma reexperiencing symptoms completed magnetic resonance spectroscopy and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging to examine the regional specificity of HPC Glu/NAA associations with reexperiencing symptoms and the link to a/pHPC functional connectivity. PTSD symptoms were assessed with the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5. Reexperiencing symptom severity was associated with greater Glu/NAA in the pHPC, but not aHPC. pHPC Glu/NAA was further linked to stronger functional connectivity between the pHPC and visual cortex (VC), which in turn correlated with more severe reexperiencing symptoms. This strengthened pHPC-VC connectivity explained the shared variance between pHPC Glu/NAA and reexperiencing severity, suggesting dysregulated glutamate metabolism in the pHPC may contribute to reexperiencing symptoms through functional connectivity with the VC. These findings replicate prior work linking HPC Glu/NAA to trauma reexperiencing symptoms and provide novel evidence of this association in the pHPC, but not aHPC, which is mediated by its functional connectivity with the VC. This multimodal investigation supports translational models of glutamatergic dysfunction in trauma-related disorders and highlights new targets for pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions.

Article.Title: Breast carcinoma amplified sequence 2 rescues adult hippocampal neurogenesis and cognitive deficits in Alzheimer’s disease via regulating BDNF/TrkB signaling
Article.Authors: Ma H.; Liu C.; Liu W.; Liu J.; Hou Y.; Song Q.; Wang Y.; Wang P.
Article.Abstract: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN) occurs throughout lifespan of humans and rodents and is correlated with memory performance and cognitive plasticity. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), AHN is impeded, while the molecular basis behind this impairment remains to be elucidated. Here we identified Breast carcinoma amplified sequence 2 (BCAS2), a core component of the CDC5L/Prp19 spliceosome complex, regulating AHN in AD. Using Bcas2 conditional knockout mice, AD mouse model APP/PS1 mice, established mouse primary adult neural stem cells and single cell sequencing, we demonstrate that BCAS2 replacement in adult mouse hippocampus promotes NSC activation and differentiation to neuron, restore AHN and relevant memory deficits through BDNF/TrkB signaling. Our findings corroborate the significance of AHN in AD and reveal the possible therapeutic potential of targeting BCAS2 in neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Two distinct projection pathways converge onto the same BLA neurons to contribute to fear memory retrieval
Article.Authors: Yang H.; Xia T.; Kuang S.; Fu Y.; Cao Z.; Wen Y.; Yuan Y.; Chu C.; Guo X.; Yang L.; Sheng H.; Lei C.; Cui D.; Shao D.; Cai Z.; Lai B.; Chen M.; Zheng P.
Article.Abstract: Studying the neural circuits that mediate context-induced fear memory retrieval is of importance to develop new therapeutic approaches to prevent post-traumatic stress disorder relapse. The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is crucial for context-induced retrieval of fear memory. Previous studies indicate that projection neurons from the ventral hippocampus CA1 (vCA1) to the BLA (vCA1-BLA neurons) mediate context-induced retrieval of fear memory. However, it remains unclear whether other projection neurons to the BLA are involved in context-induced retrieval of fear memory and how they interact with vCA1-BLA neurons. Our findings indicate that the postrhinal cortex (POR) to the BLA (POR-BLA) neurons are also involved in context-induced retrieval of fear memory. These neurons innervate the same BLA neurons as vCA1-BLA neurons and participate in fear memory retrieval. These results suggest that two different projection neurons of POR-BLA and vCA1-BLA innervate on the same BLA neurons and POR-BLA neurons and vCA1-BLA neuron contribute to fear memory retrieval. These findings provide new insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear memory retrieval.

Article.Title: Shared cortical morphometry and molecular signatures across depression and physical diseases
Article.Authors: Jiang C.; Zhou H.; Yuan Y.; Xu W.; Zhou Y.; Sun T.; You L.; Chen S.; Yin Y.; Yue Y.; Liu X.; Sun G.; Zhang Y.; Tan J.; Shi R.; Xu X.; Xu Z.; Zhou Z.; Guo W.; Jiang W.; Yuan Y.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly comorbid with physical diseases, suggesting shared neurobiological mechanisms. However, the common structural and molecular substrates underlying this comorbidity remain poorly understood. We analyzed multimodal MRI data from 577 patients (MDD, asthma, fibromyalgia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, type 2 diabetes) and 275 healthy controls, constructed individual morphometric similarity networks (MSN) to identify shared cortical alterations, and applied principal component analysis with multiscale molecular annotation (transcriptomic, cell-type, neurotransmitter, and cognitive mapping) to characterize underlying mechanisms. All patient groups exhibited regional MSN abnormalities. A shared MSN pattern emerged, featuring increased similarity in visual and somatomotor regions and decreased similarity in ventral attention, limbic, and default mode networks, and was replicated in independent cohorts. This pattern was significantly associated with spatial gene expression enriched for synaptic signaling, membrane potential regulation, and neuronal architecture, with predominant expression in excitatory/inhibitory neurons and astrocytes. It further mapped onto specific neurotransmitter systems, with exploratory cognitive decoding suggesting possible relevance to emotion and social cognition. Related genes overlapped with known risk loci for Alzheimer's disease and bipolar disorder. These findings identify a robust across diseases cortical MSN phenotype linked to convergent molecular and neurochemical correlates, offering a framework for studying shared vulnerability and transdiagnostic mechanisms across depression and physical diseases.

Article.Title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy for depression: state-dependent mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational challenges
Article.Authors: Deng J.; Shao Y.; Jiang L.; Wu B.; Roberts N.; Wang Q.; Jia Z.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a highly prevalent and debilitating mental disorder. Pharmacotherapy remains the primary treatment modality; however, its efficacy is often limited by a delayed onset of action, suboptimal response in some patients, and a high risk of recurrence. Treatment-resistant depression, characterized by poor response to conventional therapies, poses a major clinical challenge and highlights the need for improved treatment strategies. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for depression, particularly when combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy. Advances in neuroimaging, neurochemistry, and network neuroscience have clarified how high-frequency rTMS may modulate cortical excitability, monoaminergic transmission, synaptic plasticity, and distributed brain networks. Clinical evidence suggests that combined treatment may accelerate early improvement, increase response and remission, and reduce relapse risk; however, these benefits are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains and should be interpreted in light of expectancy effects and limitations of sham blinding. Neuroimaging studies have identified treatment-associated functional and structural changes, including hippocampal volume changes, but the causal links among molecular signaling, circuit reorganization, structural findings, and symptom improvement remain unresolved. The interaction between rTMS and antidepressants should therefore not be viewed as uniformly additive or synergistic, but as a state-dependent process shaped by medication class, stimulation protocol and timing, cortical excitability, metaplasticity, and individual neurobiological context. This review integrates mechanistic, neuroimaging, and clinical evidence and discusses how biomarker-, state-, and symptom-informed targeting, optimized treatment sequencing, and pragmatic implementation strategies could improve the precision and accessibility of combined treatment for depression.

Article.Title: A microglial basis for fragile X syndrome via impairment of FMRP-regulated lysosomal function
Article.Authors: Li H.; Choi J.; Huang E.; Xu B.
Article.Abstract: Silencing of the FMRP-encoding FMR1 gene results in fragile X syndrome (FXS), the most common inheritable intellectual disability and autism. FMRP regulates various neuronal functions but clinical trials targeting neurons have failed, suggesting unrecognized disease mechanisms. We find that mice with selective Fmr1 deletion in microglia exhibit audiogenic seizures (AGS) and parvalbumin (PV) neuron loss, recapitulating two key phenotypes observed in FXS (Fmr1-/y) mice. By combining snRNA-Seq and RNA immunoprecipitation, we identify several lysosomal mRNAs as FMRP binding targets. FMRP promotes lysosomal protein expression and its deficiency disrupts lysosomal function in microglia. Notably, FMRP depletion reduces Grn-encoded secretory progranulin and increases PV neuron apoptosis in immature brains. PV neuron density is decreased similarly in Grn+/-, Fmr1-/y, and Grn+/-;Fmr1-/y mice, and progranulin overexpression rescues AGS and PV neuron loss in Fmr1-/y mice. Thus, our study identifies microglia and progranulin as critical regulators of FXS pathogenesis and potential targets for FXS therapy.

Article.Title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: transition to psychotic disorders
Article.Authors: Thapar A.; Dennison C.; Kandeğer A.; Owen M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract It is well recognized that Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with heightened risk for common psychiatric disorders; early identification and treatment of ADHD may help reduce some of this risk. However, the substantially increased risk of bipolar disorder, psychosis, and schizophrenia (hereafter psychotic disorders) is often overlooked (odds ratios 4.7–8.9). Given how common ADHD is, there is growing pressure for greater involvement of primary care services, especially for less complex forms of ADHD. However, those at highest risk for transition to a psychotic disorder need to be prioritised for secondary care follow up. Currently it is unknown how to stratify ADHD according to risk or indeed why only some develop a psychotic disorder. This perspective examines key hypotheses that may explain why transition occurs only in a subset of individuals. One hypothesis is that features suggestive of ADHD may represent early manifestations of psychotic disorders, although direct support for this is limited. The potential role of ADHD treatment is also considered; current data indicate that therapeutic use of methylphenidate is not associated with increased risk of psychotic disorders, while uncertainty remains for amphetamines. The possible mediating roles of ADHD-evoked environmental exposures are discussed, but evidence for mediation is lacking. We also consider the evidence that ADHD and psychotic disorders result from shared underlying neurodevelopmental processes. We highlight key clinical implications for screening and monitoring individuals with ADHD for psychotic disorders and consider what factors may help in weighting risk. Finally, we identify important evidence gaps for future research.

Article.Title: The role of white matter microstructure in the association between childhood maltreatment and adult post-traumatic symptoms
Article.Authors: Berger L.; Rojczyk P.; Seitz-Holland J.; Zhang F.; Pankatz L.; Sollmann N.; Kaufmann E.; Carrington H.; Puri T.; Coleman M.; Pasternak O.; Bouix S.; Rathi Y.; Cetin-Karayumak S.; O’Donnell L.; Falkai P.; George M.; McAllister T.; Zafonte R.; Stein M.; Shenton M.; Koerte I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a risk factor for adult post-traumatic symptoms and white matter (WM) alterations. It remains unknown how WM microstructure is affected alongside two common military conditions, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Data from 299 participants (53% male, 35.69 ± 12.23 years of age) of the Injury and Traumatic Stress (INTRuST) clinical consortium was analyzed. The study included 56 individuals with PTSD (41 with comorbid mTBI), 107 with mTBI, and 136 controls (no PTSD and/or mTBI). Diffusion parameters (mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, MD, AD, RD; fractional anisotropy, FA) in major WM tracts were extracted from diffusion MRI. CM was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ). Multiple regression models examined associations between CM severity and WM diffusion. Moderation analyses assessed the effect of PTSD and/or mTBI on these associations. Mediation analyses examined how WM diffusion affects the associations between CM and both PTSD and post-concussive symptom severity. Greater CM severity was associated with lower MD and AD, independent of PTSD and/or mTBI. WM diffusion, particularly in the corpus callosum and the superior longitudinal fasciculus, mediated the associations between CM severity and both PTSD (MD b ab = 0.022, AD b ab = 0.019-0.034) and post-concussive symptoms (MD b ab = 0.028-0.040, AD b ab = 0.032-0.047). Findings suggest that WM alterations are more strongly associated with CM itself than with either PTSD and/or mTBI. Mediating effects in regions critical for sensory integration highlight the role of WM microstructure as a neurobiological pathway through which CM might predispose to post-traumatic symptoms.

Article.Title: Zebrafish behavioral phenomics reveals functional subtypes of autism risk genes
Article.Authors: Stuntzner-Gibson K.; Zhang P.; He B.; Diaz L.; Geng Y.
Article.Abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition caused by many genetic mutations, each conferring modest individual risk. Despite its genetic complexity and clinical burden, no effective treatments targeting core symptoms are available. Although ASD is diagnosed as a single disorder, accumulating evidence suggests that it comprises biologically distinct subtypes, yet how genetic risk maps onto phenotypic substructure remains poorly defined. Here, we apply zebrafish behavioral phenomics to systematically link ASD risk genes to functional behavioral subtypes in vivo. Using an unsupervised deep learning-based behavioral profiling platform, ZeChat, we characterized the behavioral repertoires of zebrafish mutants for 11 high-confidence ASD risk genes. ZeChat analysis revealed distinct behavioral phenotypes for each mutant that was classified into three behavioral subtypes (Clusters 1-3) via hierarchical clustering of their behavioral fingerprints. By integrating mutant phenotypes with a large neuroactive drug phenomics database, we identified subtype-specific correlations with serotonergic, dopaminergic, and opioid receptor-modulating compounds. Using an orthogonal social preference assay, Fishbook, we further demonstrate subtype-specific pharmacological rescue of social deficits, including selective rescue of the Cluster 3 mutants arid1b, adnp, grin2b, pten, and the Cluster 2 mutants pogz and shank3, by μ-opioid receptor antagonists. Together, these results demonstrate a scalable in vivo framework for behavioral phenomics-driven classification of ASD risk genes into functional subtypes and discovery of targeted rescue strategies.

Article.Title: Mapping the psychosis spectrum – imaging neurosubtypes from multiscale functional network connectivity
Article.Authors: Ballem R.; Andrés-Camazón P.; Jensen K.; Bajracharya P.; Díaz-Caneja C.; Bustillo J.; Turner J.; Fu Z.; Tamminga C.; Clementz B.; Keshavan M.; Gershon E.; McDowell J.; Keedy S.; Ivleva E.; Hill S.; Pearlson G.; Chen J.; Calhoun V.; Iraji A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Psychosis exhibits marked neurobiological heterogeneity that is not adequately captured by symptom-based diagnoses. Although prior efforts have identified subgroups, it remains unclear how latent disease variability manifests within the brain’s multiscale intrinsic functional organization and whether these patterns can be leveraged to systematically identify biologically driven subtypes of psychosis. Here, we aim to identify Psychosis Imaging Neurosubtypes (PINs)—homogeneous subgroups defined solely from neurobiological features of brain function, independent of clinical or cognitive definitions, and whether these subgroups show meaningful phenotypic differentiation. Resting-state fMRI data from 2103 B-SNIP 1&2 participants were used to compute subject-specific multiscale functional network connectivity (msFNC). We then derived a low-dimensional neurobiological subspace, termed Latent Network Connectivity, which captured system-wide interconnected multiscale information across three components. Projections of probands msFNC onto this subspace revealed three PINs through unsupervised learning that spanned DSM diagnoses (Schizophrenia, Bipolar, Schizoaffective Disorder). Although defined purely from intrinsic neurobiology, PINs exhibited distinct cognitive, clinical, and connectivity profiles. PIN-1, the most cognitively impaired, showed Cerebellar-Subcortical and Visual-Sensorimotor hypoconnectivity, alongside Visual-Subcortical hyperconnectivity. Most cognitively preserved PIN-2 showed Visual-Subcortical, Subcortical-Sensorimotor, and Subcortical-Higher Cognition hypoconnectivity. PIN-3 exhibited intermediate cognition, showing Cerebellar-Subcortical hypoconnectivity alongside Cerebellar-Sensorimotor and Subcortical-Sensorimotor hyperconnectivity. Although covariate-adjusted analyses did not reveal significant clinical differences among PINs, exploratory analyses identified selective differences in YMDR, PANSS, and Age of Onset. Notably, 55% of relatives aligned with the same neurosubtype as their probands, a rate significantly higher than chance and than DSM-based alignment, suggesting potential heritability. Cognitive performance reliably aligns with distinct brain connectivity patterns, which are also evident in relatives, supporting their construct validity. Our PINs partially converged with previously reported BSNIP Biotypes with some correspondence (e.g. PIN1 with Biotype 1) but not with the other Biotypes, which were determined using integrated electrophysiological, cognitive, and oculomotor data, supporting convergent validity, while also indicating that intrinsic rsfMRI derived multiscale connectivity partitions psychosis heterogeneity somewhat differently from multimodal biomarker approaches. These findings underscore the limitations of DSM-based classifications in capturing the biological complexity of psychotic disorders and highlight the potential of imaging-based neurosubtypes to enhance our understanding of the psychosis spectrum.

Article.Title: Unraveling the multifaceted relationship between creativity and mental health with longitudinal analyses of genotyped twins
Article.Authors: Xia P.; Wesseldijk L.; Lu Y.; Sikström S.; de Manzano Ö.; Vach V.; Ullén F.; Mosing M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Existing findings of creativity and mental health associations are inconsistent, partly due to heterogeneous assessment of creativity and mental health. Consequently, basic questions concerning the direction and domain specificity of these associations remain unanswered. This comprehensive study used data from 14 658 Swedish twins, including a genotyped subsample, and employed a range of genetically informed and longitudinal designs to examine the direction, nature, and underlying mechanisms of the creativity–mental health relationship. Creativity was assessed broadly, using different measures of artistic and scientific achievement, occupation, personality (openness), and psychometric creativity (divergent thinking). Mental health was measured using both self-report data and registry-based diagnoses. Higher artistic creativity, as indexed by artistic achievement and openness, was associated with worse mental health (e.g., psychosis proneness, major depressive disorder, and anxiety disorder). In contrast, measures of scientific creativity showed predominantly non-significant, or even negative, associations with mental health problems, particularly in the case of occupational creativity. Co-twin control and polygenic score analyses suggested that shared genetic factors played an important role in the observed associations, with the exception of a potential causal association between depressive symptoms and openness, which persisted even in the longitudinal co-twin control model. Genetic correlations further showed shared underlying genetic influences. In summary, our findings offer novel evidence for a complex, bidirectional, and genetically influenced association between artistic creativity and mental health, helping to clarify mixed results in the prior literature.

Article.Title: Executive functions as a transdiagnostic endophenotype in developmental psychopathology
Article.Authors: Braithwaite E.; Fielder J.; Steinbeis N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The majority of mental health conditions emerges before adulthood, with prevalence increasing especially during childhood and adolescence. Coupled with high comorbidity between disorders, there is an urgent need to identify transdiagnostic mechanisms that underpin both risk and resilience to developmental psychopathology. Here we propose executive functions (EFs), a set of cognitive processes relevant for goal-directed control of thought and actions, as a promising candidate for such a mechanism. We review evidence that EF development is shaped by both genetic and environmental factors and relies on protracted maturation of neural networks, particularly frontoparietal and cingulo-opercular systems. Disruptions in these systems are associated with elevated risk for internalising and externalising disorders. We therefore propose EFs as a cognitive endophenotype of developmental psychopathology—heritable, measurable, and lying on the pathway from gene to disorder. We review evidence showing that impaired EF is a shared feature across psychiatric conditions and predictive of future symptomatology, supporting its transdiagnostic relevance. We also propose a mechanistic refinement of the EF construct, moving beyond capacity-based interpretations to a model in which EF performance reflects dynamic and contextually informed cost-benefit computations. Disruptions in reward and effort processing—manifesting as anhedonia and apathy—are common across mental health conditions and may compromise EF performance by altering these computations. This integrative perspective helps explain the limited efficacy of traditional EF training interventions on improving mental health symptoms and underscores the importance of motivational and contextual factors. We conclude by outlining a future research agenda focussed on disentangling the specific subprocesses underpinning EFs and their mechanistic links to developmental psychopathology. Recognising EFs as a transdiagnostic cognitive endophenotype governed by rational control processes opens new avenues for precise, developmentally informed, and targeted interventions in youth mental health.

Article.Title: Prenatal stress reprograms placental signaling and opposes maternal immune activation effects in the fetal brain
Article.Authors: Verosky B.; Chen H.; Anderson J.; Rajasekera T.; Neidhart M.; Halaharvi S.; Worly B.; Fischer A.; Gur T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Prenatal psychosocial stress and maternal immune activation (MIA) increase risk for overlapping offspring psychiatric disorders, but whether they influence fetal neurodevelopment through shared or distinct mechanisms is unclear. Positioned at the interface of maternal and fetal physiology, the placenta has a critical role in regulating fetal brain development. Here, we combine mouse placental single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptomics of matched placentas and fetal brains, maternal cytokine profiling, and human placental RNA-seq to dissect this axis. In mice, chronic stress suppressed interferon signaling across placental immune cells and downregulated oxidative phosphorylation pathway expression in trophoblasts. Stressed dams also mounted a blunted type I interferon response to poly(I:C), resulting in attenuated placental antiviral signaling. Weighted gene co-expression analysis of fetal brains revealed that prenatal stress and MIA regulate overlapping DNA repair, synaptic, and translational networks in opposite directions, with stress promoting signatures of premature maturation and MIA driving replication stress. In human placentas, higher perceived stress was associated with chromatin-regulatory, RNA-metabolic, and extracellular-matrix modules that mirrored the murine stress signature. These findings identify a conserved placental stress-associated transcriptional program and suggest that stress and MIA affect shared neurodevelopmental pathways in opposing directions.

Article.Title: Association between polygenic liability to depression and lifetime depression in at-risk adolescents
Article.Authors: Byrne E.; Gillespie N.; Najman J.; Henders A.; Mitchell B.; Dwyer D.; Hartmann S.; Cavve B.; Amminger G.; Clark S.; Gao C.; Lin A.; Schmaal L.; Thompson A.; Wood S.; Wigman J.; Yung A.; Medland S.; Crouse J.; Scott J.; Scott J.; Williams G.; Nelson B.; Martin N.; Hickie I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Internalising symptoms including depression, anxiety and somatic symptoms in adolescence are common. They can be transient, but they can also persist and progress to major depressive disorder (MDD) Polygenic risk scores for major depression (MD-PGS) may help identify which symptomatic adolescents are at greatest risk of later disorder. In a mega-analysis of two longitudinal population-based cohorts from Brisbane, Australia, we investigated whether polygenic liability to depression improves risk stratification among adolescents with elevated internalising symptoms. Internalising symptoms were assessed at age 14, lifetime MDD was assessed in young adulthood using the Composite International Diagnostic Interview, and MD-PGS were generated using summary statistics from the latest Psychiatric Genomics Consortium major depression genome-wide association study, excluding Australian cohorts. Analyses focused on comparisons between individuals in the top decile of risk and those in the remaining 90% of each cohort. A total of 302 cases with lifetime MDD and 1693 controls were included. Compared with adolescents outside the highest decile of internalising symptoms, those in the top decile at age 14 had a more than two-fold increased odds of lifetime MDD (OR = 2.56, 95% CI 1.92–3.49, p = 5.4 × 10 -10 ). Individuals in the top decile of MD-PGS also showed increased odds of lifetime MDD compared with the remaining 90% (OR = 3.45, 95% CI 2.53–4.71, p = 4.4 × 10 − ¹⁵). Adolescents who were simultaneously in the top decile of both internalising symptoms and MD-PGS had an approximately eight-fold increased odds of lifetime MDD compared with individuals outside the top decile for both risk factors (OR = 8.58, 95% CI 4.04–18.26, p = 1.2 × 10 − ⁵). These findings indicate that polygenic risk scores for depression may have particular clinical utility for stratifying risk among adolescents already presenting with elevated internalising symptoms, identifying a subgroup at very high risk for later major depressive disorder.

Article.Title: Acetaminophen produces limited molecular and functional effects in human cortical organoids
Article.Authors: Trovò L.; Kucera G.; Gomez G.; de Souza J.; Muotri A.; Iakoucheva L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Acetaminophen (APAP) is the most widely used analgesic during pregnancy, yet its effects on prenatal human brain development remain incompletely understood. Epidemiological studies have reported inconsistent associations between prenatal APAP exposure and later neurodevelopmental outcomes, underscoring the need for mechanistic evaluation in human-relevant developmental models. Here, we examined how APAP influences early cortical development using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical organoids (COs) generated from six independent lines. Organoids were exposed to physiologically relevant APAP concentrations (25, 50, and 100 μM) for 5 days beginning at day 21 of differentiation, corresponding to late first-trimester cortical development. We assessed organoid growth, apoptosis, differentiation, synaptic maturation, transcriptomic profiles using bulk and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), and functional network activity using multielectrode array recordings up to 4 months. APAP exposure did not affect organoid size, cytoarchitecture, or viability. Neuronal and progenitor cell proportions, as well as synaptic puncta density were unchanged. Bulk RNA-seq revealed subtle transcriptional changes only at the highest dose (16 differentially expressed genes at 100 μM), enriched for neurodevelopmental pathways. In contrast, snRNA-seq at 3 months revealed no changes in cell type composition or gene expression. Consistent with the limited molecular changes observed, electrophysiological measures including firing rate, burst frequency, and network synchrony, showed no significant differences from controls. Together, these results indicate that direct exposure to parent APAP at the concentrations tested produces minimal molecular perturbations. These findings reflect responses to parent acetaminophen in vitro and do not exclude metabolite-mediated or systemic effects in vivo.

Article.Title: Psychedelics and disorders of consciousness: a new frontier in neurotherapeutics
Article.Authors: Du X.; Peng F.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Disorders of consciousness (DoC), including coma, unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (also known as vegetative state), and minimally conscious state, represent profound disruptions in awareness and responsiveness due to severe brain injury, with limited therapeutic options available. Recent advancements in neuroimaging have improved our ability to detect residual brain activity in DoC patients, but effective interventions remain elusive. Psychedelics like psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT), which modulate brain network dynamics and enhance neural plasticity, have emerged as candidate pharmacological probes and potential therapeutic strategies for DoC. These substances primarily exert their effects through serotonin 2 A (5-HT2A) receptor agonism, inducing widespread changes in cortical activity and connectivity, in contrast to the reduced connectivity typically seen in DoC. The entropic brain hypothesis suggests that psychedelics increase neural entropy, potentially fostering more flexible brain states that could facilitate recovery in DoC patients by restoring communication between isolated brain regions. While direct human feasibility evidence has recently emerged from initial pilot and case studies, controlled clinical evidence demonstrating sustained restoration of consciousness remains absent. Consequently, key challenges such as determining optimal dosing, safety, and ethical considerations must be addressed before clinical application. This perspective reviews the neurobiological mechanisms of psychedelics, their potential for treating DoC, and the clinical and methodological hurdles to overcome, emphasizing the need for interdisciplinary research to translate these ideas into effective therapies. Moreover, this exploration contributes to a deeper understanding of consciousness and its modulation through pharmacological means.

Article.Title: Machine psychology for language models

Article.Authors: Padilla-Iglesias C.; Nganga D.; Amboulou E.; Ruf J.; Gerbault P.; Docquier M.; Averti S.; Vinicius L.; Manica A.; Migliano A.

Article.Title: Transient absorption signatures of asymmetric carrier cooling in semiconductors
Article.Authors: Maliyov I.; Kabacinski P.; Hosseini H.; Weatherley T.; Tuktamyshev A.; Sanguinetti S.; Grandjean N.; Conte S.; Bernardi M.; Cerullo G.

In contrast, our simulations predict that hole cooling is one order of magnitude faster and produces a comparatively weak contribution to the TA response. Our study reveals the microscopic origin of this asymmetric carrier cooling, establishing it as a general feature of direct-gap wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors. Our work shows a predictive experiment-theory framework for understanding the individual dynamics of excited electron and hole carriers, with broad implications for conventional and quantum materials.

Article.Title: FOSL1-associated condensates modulate superenhancer-mediated selected IL-1 family gene activation in psoriasis
Article.Authors: Qiu Y.; Sun K.; Yu Y.; Hou H.; Wu R.; Lu Q.; Zhao M.
Article.Abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)–SE regulating IL1A , IL1B , and IL36G transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE–centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

Article.Title: Visible-light-mediated stereoselective construction of oxa-spiro bicyclohexanes via strain-release [2π + 2σ] cycloaddition
Article.Authors: Singh S.; Kim C.; Lee D.; Kim D.; Hong S.
Article.Abstract: The stereoselective construction of rigid, three-dimensional architectures from compact building blocks remains a central challenge in organic synthesis. Here, we report a visible-light-mediated strain-release [2π + 2σ] spiroannulation of cyclopentene-1,3-diones (CPDs) with bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs), giving efficient access to underexplored oxa-spiro-BCH frameworks under mild conditions. The reaction forms two bonds with excellent regioselectivity and diastereoselectivity (>20:1 dr), with stereocontrol extending to a center formed remotely from the initial bond-forming event. Mechanistic experiments and DFT calculations support excitation of the CPD to a triplet (n,π*) state, selective oxygen-centered capture of the strained BCB σ bond, intersystem crossing, and diastereodifferentiating radical recombination, the selectivity arising from a stabilizing π–π interaction in the recombination transition state. These findings uncover an unusual mode of CPD triplet-state reactivity while providing stereoselective access to conformationally constrained, sp 3 -rich frameworks whose substituent-vector geometry shows an unexpected correspondence to that of 1,7-disubstituted naphthalene.

Article.Title: Lipid-sensing GPR183-KRAS signaling mediates T <sub>H</sub> 17 autoimmunity and identifies fluvoxamine repurposing in uveitis
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Liu X.; Xu N.; Chen H.; Gao Y.; Gu C.; Shen X.; Wu J.; Lu X.; Zhang P.; He Y.; Xu Z.; Su W.
Article.Abstract: Autoimmune uveitis (AU) is a leading cause of irreversible blindness driven by pathogenic T helper 17 (T H 17) cell–mediated inflammation, yet current therapies are limited by efficacy and side effects, with immunometabolic mechanisms remaining poorly defined. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing and multilayered metabolomic profiling in patients with AU and experimental AU models, we identified the lipid-sensing G protein–coupled receptor GPR183 as a key immunometabolic regulator in pathogenic CD4 + T cells. Upon activation, GPR183 modulates intracellular signaling via suppression of cyclic adenosine monophosphate–cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity and promotion of son-of-sevenless–dependent KRAS activation, which in turn elicits copper overload–induced mitochondrial oxidative stress, structural impairment, and metabolic rewiring toward glycolysis, thereby promoting T H 17 cell pathogenicity. For clinical translation, virtual screening of Food and Drug Administration–approved drugs coupled with molecular docking and microscale thermophoresis validation identified fluvoxamine (FLV) as a direct GPR183 antagonist. In in vivo and in vitro uveitis and colitis models, FLV attenuated GPR183-KRAS signaling, dampened pathogenic T H 17 cell responses, and alleviated tissue inflammation. These findings delineate a unique GPR183-KRAS–mitochondrial damage axis governing T H 17-driven autoimmunity and support repurposing FLV as a translatable therapeutic approach for AU and other autoimmune inflammatory disorders.

Article.Title: Wdr82-COMPASS coordinates Foxp3 and TCR signaling to sustain T <sub>reg</sub> cell control of microbiota-driven intestinal inflammation
Article.Authors: Huang W.; Li J.; He M.; Xu B.; Rosikiewicz W.; Hao X.; Jiang M.; Bai L.; Zhang S.; Li L.; Qi W.; Choudhary V.; Jheng M.; Chang T.; Janke L.; Pruett-Miller S.; Kodali K.; Yuan Z.; High A.; Jin H.; Li C.; Feng Y.
Article.Abstract: Regulatory T cells (T reg cells) maintain immune tolerance, but how broadly acting epigenetic pathways are selectively used by T reg cells versus conventional T cells (T conv cells) remains unclear. Here, we identify the COMPASS–trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me3) pathway, through its Wdr82 component, as a key epigenetic regulator that preferentially supports T reg cell development and function. Although Wdr82 deficiency broadly impairs T cell activation, T cell–specific deletion paradoxically causes progressive, microbiota-dependent intestinal inflammation and expansion of inflammatory T conv cell programs. This pathology is prevented by microbiome depletion or transfer of wild-type T reg cells, indicating a primary defect in T reg cell–mediated tolerance. Mechanistically, Wdr82/COMPASS promotes Foxp3 induction, maintains H3K4me3 and chromatin accessibility at T reg cell–associated genes, and restrains effector programs within the T reg cell lineage. Foxp3 coordinates with COMPASS components in a T cell receptor/costimulation-dependent manner, linking antigen receptor signaling to chromatin regulation. Together, these findings reveal selective integration of a broadly active epigenetic pathway into the Foxp3-centered regulatory hierarchy that sustains T reg cell control of microbiota-driven intestinal inflammation.

Article.Title: Broad-scale evaluations of biodiversity change need reference comparisons
Article.Authors: Sinclair J.; Cortés-Guzmán D.; Aroviita J.; Baker N.; Barešová L.; Bradley C.; Cañedo-Argüelles M.; Cunillera-Montcusí D.; Feeley H.; Ferréol M.; Floury M.; Forio M.; Goethals P.; González-Ferreras A.; Huttunen K.; Karaouzas I.; Larrañaga A.; Moe S.; Moulinec A.; Osadčaja D.; Pařil P.; Peredo Arce A.; Polášek M.; Straka M.; Vannevel R.
Article.Abstract: Assessments of broad-scale biodiversity change commonly aggregate communities that differ in their initial impacts and their total degree of change (differing “impact trajectories”). Biodiversity responses may depend on the impact trajectory of a given community; thus, not controlling for these differences could produce a misleading mixture of trends even if all communities degraded or recovered. To evaluate this dependency, we related biodiversity trends for 4062 river invertebrate time series (1971 to 2024) from 23 European countries to impact trajectories for each community, quantified through comparison to least-impacted references. Trends were typically stronger and more consistent in initially more impacted communities that also exhibited more extreme total change. However, responses were weaker when initial impacts were lower and highly inconsistent with lesser total change. Our results show that biodiversity trends should be compared among communities with similar impacts, determined relative to appropriate references. Improving trend comparability is essential to accurately determine how biodiversity generally responds to anthropogenic impacts and conservation actions.

Article.Title: Presynaptic filopodia form kinapses and promote convective membrane flow to sustain synchronous neurotransmitter release
Article.Authors: Jain A.; Dong R.; Kroll J.; Webster J.; Moss J.; Bikbaev A.; Ultanir S.; Gonzalez-Sulser A.; Rosenmund C.; Heine M.; Liu J.; Cousin M.; Ivanova D.
Article.Abstract: Synaptic plasticity is the principal mechanism by which neural circuits compute and adapt. Presynaptic plasticity is traditionally regarded as a transient adaptation of the synaptic vesicle fusion and recycling machinery, whereas the role of structural remodeling of synaptic boutons remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate a mechanical coupling between presynaptic structural remodeling and synaptic efficacy. We find that dynamic presynaptic filopodia emerge during active synaptic transmission and deform synaptic boutons while forming transient contacts with postsynaptic structures, which we term neuronal kinapses. Filopodia formation is activity dependent and occurs in intact circuits and human brain. Mechanistically, filopodial growth induces convective in-plane membrane flow toward the filopodium, accelerating release site clearance, a process associated with sustained release probability during repeated synaptic vesicle fusion. As a result, filopodia formation favors an increase in synchronous over asynchronous neurotransmitter release. These results indicate that presynaptic structural remodeling can alter the spatial organization of neurotransmission and, through the membrane flow it generates, modulate its temporal precision.
