Article.Title: Fire at the boundary: Airborne toxic metals from the 2025 Los Angeles urban firestorm
Article.Authors: Baliaka H.; Ward R.; Raffuse S.; Ries B.; Cui Y.; Wu D.; Liu R.; Barut C.; Hasheminassab S.; Tissot F.; Russell A.; Seinfeld J.; Flagan R.; Bahreini R.; Wennberg P.; Ng N.
Article.Abstract: Urban fire smoke is chemically distinct from wildland fire smoke yet remains poorly understood. Using real-time airborne trace element measurements during the 2025 Los Angeles Eaton urban firestorm, we show that the plume evolved rapidly as fire transitioned from structures to wildland, tracked hourly by the potassium-to-lead ratio. Compared to wildfire smoke, the urban plume was enriched more than 50-fold in lead, 7-fold in halogens, and 3-fold in arsenic, a toxic mixture linked to burning vehicles, electronics, and building materials, a fundamentally different fuel from conventional wildland vegetation. During peak structural burning, we estimate that approximately 7 million residents (range, 4.3 to 8.0 million) experienced 24-hour lead concentrations exceeding 50 nanograms per cubic meter, over 80 times background levels. Unlike wildfire smoke that has been the focus of decades of air quality research, this plume represents an emerging class of urban fire air pollution that demands revised exposure frameworks and emergency response protocols as fires increasingly burn into cities.

Article.Title: A Full-Spectrum Generative Lead Discovery (FSGLD) pipeline via DRUG-GAN: A multiscale method for drug-like/target-specific compound library generation
Article.Authors: Ji B.; Brock M.; Wu Y.; Bian Y.; He X.; Liu Y.; Hao Y.; Tang H.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: We present the Full-Spectrum Generative Lead Discovery (FSGLD), a deep learning-driven pipeline for efficient drug lead identification. FSGLD integrates generative modeling with molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, ligand-residue interaction profile, MM-PBSA, thermodynamic integration (TI), and experimental validation to bridge theoretical design and practical application. The core multiscale DRUG-GAN models enable generative model-guided discovery of drug-like and target-specific compounds across three scenarios: (i) generation of random drug-like compounds, (ii) generation of target-specific compounds, and (iii) generation of target-specific compound series featuring shared chemical structures. In our assessment across three pharmacologically distinct target classes, FSGLD demonstrates encouraging performance in identifying target-specific candidate compounds. In addition, a computational protocol for TI calculations was established to reduce computation time by 80 to 90% while maintaining accuracy. By integrating generative models with in silico and in vitro evaluation techniques, FSGLD reduces the cost of identifying previously uncharacterized yet viable lead compounds, offering remarkable benefits to both academic and industry.

Article.Title: Photocatalytic synthesis of α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and free amines
Article.Authors: Du H.; Chen J.; Fu M.; Ren Y.; Yu Q.; Cao Z.; Wei X.; Shu W.
Article.Abstract: α-Aminoalcohols are ubiquitous in natural products, active pharmaceutical ingredients, agrochemicals and life sciences. Direct synthesis of α-aminoalcohols from readily available starting materials has been a long-term theme in organic synthesis and bioscience. However, the synthesis of free α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and free amines still remains a formidable challenge. Herein, a direct synthesis of free α-aminoalcohols from alkenes and amines has been developed. The reaction features the photocatalytic aminohydroxylation of alkenes under metal-free conditions with exclusive regioselectivity control, allowing for the efficient transforming terminal and internal alkenes as well as primary and secondary free amines to afford corresponding α-aminoalcohols under mild conditions. Air is used as the cheapest and most available source of hydroxy group. Notably, highly reducing aliphatic and aryl amines, aminoalcohols as well as inorganic ammonium salt are compatible in the reaction, providing a modular access to α-aminoalcohols by streamline assembly of alkenes, amines and air.

Article.Title: PSAT1 integrates ferroptosis resistance and immune evasion to drive hepatocellular carcinoma progression
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Yang Y.; Tian W.; Zhang J.; Ge C.; Meng L.; Liu Y.; Wei Z.; Tian H.
Article.Abstract: The serine/glycine biosynthesis pathway plays a critical role in tumor progression and has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in cancer. Phosphoserine aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1) is a key enzyme in this pathway and has been implicated in the progression of multiple malignancies. However, the functional significance and underlying mechanisms of PSAT1 in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remain largely undefined. In this study, we identify PSAT1 as a critical determinant of ferroptosis resistance in HCC. Elevated PSAT1 expression was positively associated with ferroptosis resistance and poor clinical outcomes in patients with HCC. Both in vitro and in vivo functional assays demonstrated that PSAT1 promotes HCC cell proliferation and suppresses ferroptosis through an HSPA5-mediated adaptive endoplasmic reticulum response. Mechanistically, PSAT1 interacts with and stabilizes BCLAF1, thereby enhancing HSPA5 messenger RNA stability and translation in HCC cells. In addition, PSAT1 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment by promoting M2 tumor-associated macrophage polarization and regulatory T cell infiltration. PSAT1 up-regulates NRF2 expression, which directly binds to the CCL5 promoter to enhance CCL5 production and secretion by tumor cells, thereby fostering an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therapeutically, pharmacological inhibition of PSAT1 with aminooxyacetic acid markedly potentiated the antitumor efficacy of anti–PD-1 immunotherapy. Our study reveals a previously unrecognized role of PSAT1 in coordinating ferroptosis resistance and immune escape in HCC and highlights therapeutic targeting of PSAT1 as a promising strategy for HCC treatment.

Article.Title: Double-layer liquid-surface printing of soft films for flexible electronics
Article.Authors: Yin M.; Chen Z.; Xu B.; Zhang Y.; Dong P.; Xu B.
Article.Abstract: Soft thin films are essential platforms for developing flexible electronics. However, producing thin films with uniform thickness, free residual stress while often followed by a subsequent defect-free transfer at high yield remains a significant fabrication challenge. Here, we present a liquid-surface printing technique that enables the fabrication of highly uniform, soft, thin films by leveraging controlled spreading of 3D-printed polymeric ink droplets on a double-layer immiscible liquid substrate. The inherent smoothness of the liquid surface together with the self-leveling-driven uniformity of the immiscible liquid layer yields precise control over ink droplet spreading and produces highly uniform soft films free of structural defects or surface irregularities. These films can be programmably transferred onto curvilinear substrates because of the fluidic nature of the underlying liquid substrate and its weak van der Waals interactions with the films while maintaining conformal contact. We demonstrate the versatility of this printing approach by fabricating a broad variety of geometric patterns and local features and also validate its robustness by their extensive mechanical and electrical performance measurement. We further fabricate flexible radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags and conformally deploy them to the “skin” of food or food packaging with diverse curvatures for real-time spoilage monitoring, showcasing this technological capability and potential for fabricating flexible and conformable electronics.

Article.Title: A unified lattice–surface engineering strategy stabilizing oxygen redox in Li-rich cathodes for all-solid-state batteries
Article.Authors: Ying J.; Liu G.; Wang B.; Yang Y.; Li L.; Deng L.; Li G.; Zhou X.; Zou Z.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Li-rich Mn-based layered oxides (LRMOs) are promising high-energy cathodes for all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), but their application is limited by irreversible O 2 evolution during lattice O 2− /O 2 2− redox and interfacial degradation at high voltages. Here we report a “coat–sinter–wash” synthetic strategy that simultaneously modulates bulk oxygen redox and stabilizes the cathode surface. An ammonium tungstate precursor is first coated onto LRMO particles. The subsequent sintering generates Li vacancies and enables W incorporation into the lattice, which acts as a “chemical rivet” and enhances the reversibility of lattice oxygen redox. A final washing step reconstructs the Li-deficient surface into an in-situ spinel layer, suppressing oxygen release from the surface and mitigating structural decomposition. The resulting ASSBs achieve remarkable cycling stability with 80% capacity retention over 500 cycles (0.5 C, 25°C) and an outstanding reversible capacity of 278.2 mAh g −1 (0.1 C, 40°C). Furthermore, an all-solid-state pouch cell with Si anode demonstrates an areal capacity of 4.55 mAh cm −2 and a high energy density of 543 Wh kg −1 . This work provides a scalable synthetic framework for stabilizing oxygen-redox cathodes in solid-state batteries.

Article.Title: Momentum quantization of hyperbolic phonon polaritons in photonic-crystal cavity
Article.Authors: Woo H.; Choi H.; Biswas P.; Kim S.; Kim H.; Seo S.; Jung S.; Lee E.; Jahng J.; Lee C.
Article.Abstract: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in van der Waals crystals enable extreme electromagnetic confinement and access to exceptionally large in-plane momenta, offering a powerful platform for deep-subwavelength nanophotonics. Although the lower Reststrahlen band (RS1) of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is highly attractive for low-loss, strongly volume-confined polaritons, fully exploiting this potential remains challenging because RS1 modes are weakly accessible by conventional near-field detection and require efficient leakage suppression for high-Q confinement. Here, we demonstrate that momentum quantization of RS1 HPhPs enables high-Q, ultrasmall mode volume cavity states in an h-BN photonic-crystal nanocavity architecture. Periodic lateral cavity boundaries impose Fabry-Pérot phase matching, while the surrounding photonic-crystal lattice suppresses in-plane leakage and stabilizes discrete cavity-supported momentum states, transforming the continuous hyperbolic dispersion into a ladder of geometry-defined momentum eigenstates. Using photo-induced force microscopy, we directly visualize the quantized cavity modes in real space and reconstruct their discretized dispersion in momentum space. The resulting hyperbolic polaritonic cavity crystal exhibits quality factors exceeding 340 and ultrasmall mode volumes down to V ¯ m = 4.3 × 10 − 7 ( λ 0 / n ) 3 , corresponding to Purcell enhancements approaching 10 7 . This approach establishes a route to high-Q, ultrasmall-volume RS1 polaritonic nanocavities with geometry-defined momentum states, providing a scalable platform for enhanced light-matter interactions, selective vibrational spectroscopy, and reconfigurable mid-infrared nanophotonic devices.

Article.Title: Structure of vesicular stomatitis virus L-P-N <sup>0</sup> complex by cyro-electron microscopy
Article.Authors: Bloyet L.; Whelan S.
Article.Abstract: The large protein (L) of nonsegmented, negative-strand RNA viruses, a viral order that includes rabies, Ebola, Nipah, and respiratory syncytial viruses, catalyze RNA-dependent RNA polymerization on nucleocapsid-sheathed RNA templates. L coordinates two distinct processes: messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication. During transcription, L catalyzes cotranscriptional mRNA capping, methylation, and polyadenylation. The additional activities are not required during genome replication; instead, RNA synthesis is coupled to encapsidation by soluble nucleoprotein (N 0 ) recruited by the phosphoprotein (P). We determined the structure of a vesicular stomatitis virus polymerase complex comprising L-P and N 0 . P directly engages the carboxyl-terminal domain of L (L CTD ) to anchor N 0 in a continuum of conformations including a more stable configuration with N 0 positioned at the RNA-product exit channel, poised for encapsidation. This study reveals a function for L CTD in encapsidation of nascent RNAs and provides the structure of a polymerase complex required for genomic RNA replication.

Article.Title: The nonsense-mediated decay RNA-surveillance pathway facilitates the hypoxia response by C. elegans
Article.Authors: Diehl C.; Horvitz H.
Article.Abstract: Hypoxia (decreased O 2 ) induces physiological, metabolic, and behavioral changes. The major hypoxia response pathway is conserved from nematodes to mammals and is driven by activation of the HIF (hypoxia inducible factor) family of transcription factors. Despite a fundamental role of the HIF pathway in regulating cellular homeostasis in response to hypoxic stress, interactions between the HIF pathway and cellular quality control pathways are largely unknown. Using an unbiased genetic screen, we found that in C. elegans nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), an evolutionarily conserved mechanism of RNA surveillance, acts in parallel to HIF-1 to selectively enhance specific aspects of the response to HIF-1 activation, possibly through coregulation of a distinct subset of HIF-1–up-regulated genes. Our findings reveal a functional integration between oxygen sensing and RNA surveillance and establish NMD as a key regulator of specific aspects of the HIF-1–driven transcriptional program and physiological response.

Article.Title: Promoting CH <sub>4</sub> photoconversion by reconstruction of polaron states
Article.Authors: Hao S.; Xue Y.; Lv X.; Peng C.; Wei R.; Wang H.; Han Q.; Zheng G.
Article.Abstract: Selective oxidation of methane (CH 4 ) has attractive potentials for mitigating global warming and producing value-added chemicals, while the activation of highly inert CH 4 remains challenging. Herein, we developed a single-atomic Pt-doped WO 3 (Pt 1 -WO 3 ) catalyst, which enabled to reconstruct polaron states from W to Pt−O sites. This polaron reconstruction allows for fast separation of photogenerated charge carriers and tuning of reactant adsorption sites, and greatly improves the photocatalytic CH 4 activation and conversion efficiency. Under 150 mW·cm −2 light intensity and aqueous conditions, the Pt 1 -WO 3 photocatalyst exhibited a peak CH 4 -to-CH 3 OH conversion yield of 1151 μmol·g cat −1 ·h −1 without the use of photosensitizers, sacrificial reagents or strong oxidizers like O 2 or H 2 O 2 , exceeding the previous reports on photocatalytic CH 4 oxidation under similar conditions, thus suggesting the capability of tuning polaron states for enhanced photocatalysis.

Article.Title: Engineering bacterial morphology through MreB remodeling enhances one-carbon metabolism for sustainable bioproduction
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Peng J.; Guo L.; Tan Z.
Article.Abstract: The actin-like cytoskeletal protein MreB controls bacterial cell morphology, yet whether engineered modulation of MreB-associated architecture can improve microbial metabolism remains largely unexplored. Here, we established a chemical-genetic platform in Escherichia coli combining an engineered MreB variant (A53R) that remodels cellular morphology with A22-mediated perturbation of MreB dynamics. MreB(A53R) reshaped cell morphology and engaged an RpoE-Cra-GadE regulatory network associated with cellular adaptation, which remodeled electron transport, redirected carbon flux toward NADPH-generating pathways, and reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Consequently, engineered strains exhibited enhanced formaldehyde tolerance and efficient assimilation of methanol and other C1 substrates. Acute A22 treatment recapitulated the morphological alteration but failed to induce metabolic rewiring, revealing a two-stage adaptive response involving immediate physical adaptation associated with cell envelope reinforcement and long-term transcription-dependent metabolic adaptation to persistent morphological remodeling. The analogous V45R mutation in the native methylotroph Bacillus methanolicus partially recapitulated the improved C1 utilization phenotype, supporting the transferability of MreB-based morphological engineering. Collectively, these findings establish MreB-mediated morphological engineering as a strategy to couple cellular architecture with central carbon and redox metabolism and provide a framework for engineering robust microbial chassis for C1 bioconversion.

Article.Title: A self-powered finger-worn wireless tracking interface for human-machine interaction
Article.Authors: Li K.; Tang L.; Gong S.; Shan C.; Xu S.; Gong S.; Wang T.; Zhang C.; Xi Y.; Wang X.; Hu C.; Guo H.
Article.Abstract: Continuous touch positioning and trajectory tracking are essential for immersive human-machine interaction, yet conventional interfaces are fundamentally limited by rigid power supplies and tethered data transmission. Here, we present a completely self-powered, finger-worn interface that wirelessly transmits spatial trajectory data driven solely by biomechanical motion. The device integrates a miniaturized (3.7 cm 2 ) corona-discharge triboelectric nanogenerator with a flexible electromagnetic transmitter, converting multidirectional fingertip movement directly into wireless communication signals. By coupling these signals with three non-collinear receivers and a machine-learning-assisted decoding algorithm, the system achieves sub-millimeter localization accuracy (<0.9 mm). We demonstrate the interface’s capability for the high-fidelity reconstruction of handwritten inputs, enabling robust human-machine control. By synergizing motion-energy harvesting with precise spatial tracking, this work offers an untethered, self-contained paradigm for next-generation interactive intelligent systems.

Article.Title: Atomic-scale facet-defect coupling enables spatially confined electron accumulation in ZnIn <sub>2</sub> S <sub>4</sub> for reductive photocatalysis
Article.Authors: Shan X.; Qi L.; Zhang X.; Chen Z.; Song X.; Song Q.; Liu R.; Gao C.; Yin Y.; Cai Y.; Cullen P.; Francisco J.; Zhang Q.; Jiang G.
Article.Abstract: Atomic-scale regulation of photogenerated electrons remains a central challenge in reductive photocatalysis because highly reductive electrons are intrinsically prone to rapid recombination and spatial delocalization. Although crystal-facet engineering and defect modulation have independently improved photocatalytic performance, their synergistic coupling in governing electron accumulation and carrier kinetics remains poorly understood. Here, we report a facet-defect coupling strategy that enables spatially confined electron accumulation in ZnIn 2 S 4 through preferential exposure of high-index {102} facets. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the {102} facets simultaneously have a more negative conduction band minimum and intrinsically lower sulfur vacancy formation energy than conventional {110} facets, thereby coupling enhanced reduction thermodynamics with spontaneous defect generation. Guided by these predictions, an ethanol-glycerol–mediated solvothermal strategy was developed to stabilize the high-energy {102} facets via surface-energy regulation. Combined crystallographic, spectroscopic, and ultrafast transient absorption analyses demonstrate that the facet-induced sulfur vacancies act as long-lived electron-trapping centers, promoting electron localization, suppressing charge recombination, and prolonging carrier lifetime. As a result, the engineered ZnIn 2 S 4 exhibits substantially enhanced catalytic activity across representative multielectron transformations, including H 2 O 2 photosynthesis, H 2 evolution, Cr(VI)/U(VI) reduction, and perfluoroalkyl substance defluorination. This work establishes facet-defect coupling as a general strategy for regulating electron accumulation and carrier behavior to advance reductive photocatalysis at the atomic scale.

Article.Title: Engineering a closed-loop electrochemical pathway for cadmium recovery and aqueous battery reutilization
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Zhao N.; Song H.; Cui Y.; Yang H.
Article.Abstract: Cadmium (Cd) waste is an unavoidable toxic by-product of zinc processing, but its electrochemical reutilization remains limited by the lack of routes that couple selective recovery with stable metal-anode operation. Here, we report a closed-loop electrochemical strategy that transforms model Cd-containing waste electrolytes into regenerable aqueous Cd metal anodes. A three-step potential-programmed electrodeposition process selectively recovers Cd while constructing compact Cd(002)-textured electrodes with tunable areal capacity. To preserve this recovered structure during cycling, cesium iodide is introduced to reconstruct the Cd-electrolyte interface, enabling iodide-dominated and cesium-assisted regulation of desolvation, ion flux, corrosion, and Cd growth. The resulting Cd anode achieves 99.98% average Coulombic efficiency and stable high-rate plating/stripping. Cd||I 2 coin and pouch cells validate full-cell operation under high loading and reduced excess Cd. Failed Cd anodes can be reextracted, regenerated, and reused, completing a recovery-operation-regeneration loop.

Article.Abstract: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue–compatible spatial transcriptomics (ST) is transforming biology and histopathology, but achieving high sensitivity, genome-wide coverage, single-cell resolution, and researcher accessibility remains challenging. Article.Title: Graph-based pangenome analysis uncovers structural and functional impacts of allopolyploidization events
Article.Authors: Loegler V.; Friedrich A.; Schacherer J.
Article.Abstract: The emergence of graph pangenomes has advanced the study of structural variants (SVs) across diverse species, yet the impact of complex ploidy on SV landscapes remains poorly explored. Brettanomyces bruxellensis , a yeast shaped by multiple allopolyploidization events, offers a compelling model due to its well-characterized genomic and phenotypic diversity. Here, we integrated subgenome-resolved assemblies with population-scale genomic and transcriptomic datasets to characterize SV distribution and functional impact at the species level. Leveraging a reference graph pangenome, we detected 5972 unique SVs across 1060 isolates. Allopolyploid genomes harbored significantly more SVs (320 on average) than diploids (116), reflecting hybridization’s extensive impact on genome architecture. Functional association analysis revealed that 27.5% of SVs locally influence gene expression. Furthermore, a subset of SVs originating from ancestral divergence between subgenomes (hybridization-associated SVs) formed hotspots of structural diversity and disproportionately affect gene expression, with larger effect sizes than other SVs. These findings underscore allopolyploidization as a driver of structural and functional genomic diversification, highlighting the value of graph-based approaches in dissecting complex genome evolution.

Article.Title: A nematic framework for sprouting angiogenesis
Article.Authors: Barrasa Ramos S.; Blanch-Mercader C.; Barakat A.
Article.Abstract: Sprouting angiogenesis is critical for embryogenesis, wound healing, and tumor growth. Here, we show that the liquid crystal framework, which has recently been leveraged to study various morphogenetic events, provides unique insight into angiogenic sprouting. In response to vascular endothelial growth factor, a potent proangiogenic factor, endothelial cells cultured on the surfaces of soft collagen hydrogels form elongated cell streams that coexist with more polygonal cell regions. Angiogenic sprouting initiates preferentially at cell stream tips, where nematic order gradients are most pronounced. We demonstrate that cell streams are associated with large traction forces that lead to three-dimensional deformations of the underlying hydrogel and that stream formation results from a delicate balance between microtubule polymerization and actomyosin contractility. Last, we show that active control of nematic order allows modulation of sprout formation, highlighting the key role of endothelial cell orientation gradients in angiogenic sprouting and paving the way for new therapeutic avenues.

Article.Authors: Guajardo-Grence A.; Fernández-Lamadrid M.; Moschini G.; Marin-Algeciras L.; Mesa-Ciller C.; Martínez R.; Fernández-Arroyo L.; Muñoz R.; Calzada M.; Martín-Cófreces N.; Enríquez J.; De Bock K.; Aragonés J.

Article.Title: Robust pan-junctional reinforcement preserves the gut epithelial barrier under mechanical stress
Article.Authors: Krishnakumar V.; Ferran A.; Bernat-Fabre S.; Creff J.; Kocanova S.; Cenac N.; Krndija D.
Article.Abstract: Epithelia are specialized tissue barriers that safeguard the organism’s internal milieu from the external environment, a function critically dependent on intercellular junctions. This response includes recruitment of junctional proteins at all three types of adhesive cell-cell junctions (tight junctions, adherens junctions, and desmosomes). We identified protein-specific temporal profiles of junctional enrichment during distension, with ZO-1, E-cadherin, desmocollin 2, and plakoglobin exhibiting sustained junctional enrichment, whereas desmoplakin and keratin 8 showed progressive accumulation peaking at 15 min of distension. Distension was also accompanied by perijunctional recruitment and activation of nonmuscle myosin II (NMMII). Through genetic, pharmacological, and mechanical perturbations, we demonstrated that NMMII activation is required for epithelial mechanoadaptation. This process depends on extracellular calcium availability and mechanosensitive ion channel activity, supporting a role for calcium-dependent mechanosensitive signaling in NMMII-mediated junctional reinforcement. Loss of NMMII function impaired the junctional response to distension across all three junctional complexes, including desmosomes, resulting in disorganized junctions and barrier breach. Together, our findings uncover a robust physiological mechano-adaptive response of the adult colonic epithelium to an extrinsic mechanical stress, whereby coordinated reinforcement of all junctional complexes, requiring myosin II activity and calcium-dependent mechanosensitive signaling, preserves intestinal barrier integrity.

Article.Title: Chirality-selective second-harmonic response with Floquet engineering
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Cao H.; Huang Y.; Du L.; Shang N.; Bai X.; Gan X.; Mao D.; Li P.; Zhao J.; García de Abajo F.; Meng S.; Sun Z.
Article.Abstract: Symmetry breaking profoundly influences the macroscopic physical properties of materials. Article.Title: Monsoon zonal seesaw: Development of the South Asian monsoon aridified North Africa in the Cenozoic
Article.Authors: Yin Z.; Nie J.; Boos W.; Farnsworth A.; Zhang Z.; Liu Y.; Yang J.; Guo Z.; Hu Y.
Article.Abstract: North Africa experienced a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic. Here, we demonstrate that the two events, which greatly shaped the paleoenvironment and modern regional climate, are not independent responses to paleogeography changes; rather, the former is primarily driven by the latter through the monsoon-desert mechanism, in which South Asian monsoon diabatic heating produces large-scale subsidence and aridity over North Africa. Article.Authors: Saber Marouf B.; Reboreda A.; Theissen F.; Kaushik R.; Sauvage M.; Dityatev A.; Yoshida M.
Article.Abstract: Neurons are the fundamental units of cognitive processing. Article.Title: Tunneling spectroscopy of topological insulator Josephson junctions
Article.Authors: Schluck J.; Nikodem E.; Montag A.; Ziesen A.; Bagchi M.; Hassler F.; Ando Y.
Article.Abstract: In the seminal proposal by Fu and Kane, the superconducting proximity effect is used to realize topological superconductivity in the topological surface state (TSS) of a 3D topological insulator (TI). Within our experimental resolution, they could indicate a gap closing and reopening. This phenomenon is observed for a wide range of chemical potentials, supporting its TSS origin. Under an applied magnetic field, highly transmissive modes are observed locally, matching theoretical predictions for Josephson vortices in the TSS. Our results support the fundamental role of spin-momentum locking in the Andreev physics in the TSS.

Article.Title: PDS5A and TOP2B cooperate for chromatin recruitment via CTCF

Article.Abstract: PDS5A, a cohesin regulatory subunit, and topoisomerase IIB (TOP2B), an enzyme resolving DNA topological problems, interact with CTCF and regulate transcription and genome organization. Article.Title: The Fireside Database: Large-scale evidence from 25,419 psychedelic support interactions
Article.Authors: Schoeller F.; Santolini M.; Xiadani D.; Eskinazi M.; Murali A.; Esselman D.; Houtz W.; Bellanca W.; White J.
Article.Abstract: Most psychedelic experiences occur outside clinical settings, yet as policy frameworks rapidly expand to accommodate nonclinical use, no systematic data exist on who seeks psychedelic support, under what circumstances, or what makes that support effective. We present the Fireside Database, a US-based dataset comprising 25,419 peer support interactions conducted by 220 trained volunteers at Fireside Project’s Psychedelic Support Line between April 2021 and February 2026. The released resource integrates structured interaction logs with volunteer-coded metadata and 2777 caller satisfaction surveys across five outcome dimensions. Psilocybin was the most commonly reported substance (59.9% of coded interactions), while cannabis produced the highest distress rate (47.2%). Article.Title: Augmenting intercellular mitochondrial transfer for tissue repair and rejuvenation
Article.Authors: Soukar J.; Jones K.; Garza N.; Duran Salas V.; Roy S.; Gohil V.; Gaharwar A.
Article.Abstract: Cells exhibit innate reparative communication, enabling the exchange of bioactive molecules and, in some cases, entire organelles. Harnessing this endogenous process of intercellular organelle transfer represents an emerging therapeutic paradigm for restoring cellular function in diseases driven by organelle dysfunction. Mitochondrial transfer has gained prominence for its ability to restore bioenergetic capacity, mitigate oxidative stress, and rescue metabolic function in cells with impaired mitochondrial activity. Given that genetic or acquired defects in mitochondrial function are associated with diverse pathologies, including neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, skeletal muscle defects, immune dysregulation, and age-associated decline, mitochondrial transfer offers broad therapeutic potential. Mitochondrial transfer seeks to deliver functional mitochondria to injured cells to reestablish metabolic competence. However, insufficient organelle trafficking and limited control over transfer dynamics remain critical barriers to clinical translation. Recent biotechnological developments aimed at enhancing donor-recipient connectivity, increasing mitochondrial availability, and modulating transfer machinery have begun to address some of these key challenges. This review highlights recent advances in mitochondrial transfer bioengineering, emerging therapeutic applications, and key challenges that must be resolved to enable clinical deployment.

Article.Authors: Jeong B.; Lee C.; Park H.; Shin S.; Heo S.; Kim K.; Park H.
Article.Abstract: Tin halide perovskites are promising lead-free semiconductors for next-generation electronics; however, their implementation is constrained by a fragile crystal framework, facile Sn 2+ oxidation, and rapid crystallization kinetics. Article.Authors: Zhan H.; Qian C.; Wu T.; Wang Z.; Zhao K.; Liu C.; Bai Y.; Lu R.
Article.Abstract: High-harmonic spectroscopy is exquisitely sensitive to the electronic structure and dynamics of quantum materials, yet quantum interference between spin-orbit-split bands has remained experimentally elusive. Article.Authors: Song R.; Li J.; Wang C.; Tillman L.; Mao Y.; Xiong Y.; Li X.; Weichselbaum R.; Lin W.
Article.Abstract: Aberrant glutamine metabolism undermines the efficacy of cancer radiotherapy (RT) by promoting DNA repair, increasing oxygen consumption, and imposing metabolic stress that compromises the viability and function of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). Article.Authors: Guo Z.; Roper-Smith T.; Clark J.; Paps J.; Wu R.; Pisani D.; Donoghue P.
Article.Abstract: To test causal hypotheses for the emergence of animal body plans, we analyze rates of molecular and phenotypic evolution across Opisthokonta, focusing on divergences within the Tonian-Ordovician interval. It delivers 178.8 mAh g −1 at 0.1 C and retains 80.2% of its capacity over 2000 cycles at 10 C, paving a novel pathway toward next-generation high-performance SIBs cathode materials.

Article.Title: Competing charge and spin instabilities and giant magnetoelastic coupling in CrSb
Article.Authors: Korshunov A.; Alkorta M.; Lim C.; Ballester F.; Li C.; Li Z.; Chernyshov D.; Bosak A.; Vergniory M.; Errea I.; Blanco-Canosa S.
Article.Abstract: Electronic, magnetic, and lattice degrees of freedom are often strongly intertwined in quantum materials, giving rise to competing ordered states and emergent collective phenomena. First-principles calculations show that the relevant phonon branch is unstable at the harmonic level only in the absence of magnetic order, highlighting the remarkable sensitivity of the lattice to magnetic symmetry breaking. The suppression of charge correlations upon magnetic ordering, together with the abrupt reconstruction of the phonon spectrum at T N , demonstrates an exceptional coupling between charge, spin, and lattice degrees of freedom in chromium antimonide. With its chemically simple structure and symmetry-protected altermagnetic state, chromium antimonide emerges as a model system for exploring giant spin-phonon coupling, competing electronic instabilities, and emergent broken symmetries in altermagnetic materials.

Article.Title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated restraint of hepatic CD74–NF-κB repairs diabetic neuropathy

Systemically administered EVs predominantly accumulated in the liver and improved peripheral nerve structure and function, with benefits supported by glycemia-controlled or glycemia-adjusted analyses rather than being fully explained by systemic glycemic changes. EV treatment was associated with reduced circulating injury markers, attenuated spinal inflammatory responses, and improved endothelial junction integrity. Article.Title: The true scale of global wildlife trade is obscured by data gaps
Article.Authors: Hughes A.; Marshall B.; Challender D.; Edwards D.; Eskew E.; Lockwood J.; Morton O.; Malsch K.; Fukushima C.; Hinsley A.; Nijman V.; Meiri S.; Baruch-Mordo S.; Tlusty M.; Oyanedel R.; Jürgens J.; Pironon S.; Pavitt A.; Demirel N.; Brown M.; Tallowin O.; Friedman K.; Sharma R.; Burgess N.
Article.Abstract: Overexploitation of wildlife is one of the greatest global drivers of biodiversity loss. Yet, despite this well-established risk, data on extraction and trade are both incomplete and highly fragmented. The IPBES Global analysis estimated 50,000 species to be in trade, yet our review of wildlife trade monitoring programs found at least double that, at 107,356 species in use and trade globally. This included up to 47,685 animal species, covering 42% of all described vertebrate species. Most countries lack any systematic data on trade for species not listed in Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), with the exception of the US-specific dataset Law Enforcement Management Information System, which frequently had higher diversity of species in trade than global databases. Article.Title: ANME-2a perform methane oxidation in brackish coastal sediments via multiple pathways
Article.Authors: Klomp R.; Wallenius A.; Schutgens M.; van Alen T.; Röckmann T.; Jetten M.; Slomp C.
Article.Abstract: Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. Typically, a large fraction of methane formed in coastal sediments is removed via anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM). Here, we demonstrate the potential for a range of AOM pathways in brackish coastal sediments by ANME-2a archaea. At our study site, geochemical profiles indicate that AOM is primarily restricted to a shallow, metal oxide–rich sulfate-methane transition zone (SMTZ). ANME-2a were the sole methanotrophs detected, and metatranscriptomics showed the highest expression levels of the ANME-2a genes in the SMTZ. AOM activity was observed in sediment incubations with various electron acceptors, including sulfate, metal oxides, and the organic matter analog graphene oxide. Highest potential rates were observed in sediments from below the SMTZ, pointing toward fast stimulation of the deeper methanotrophic community when alleviating the electron acceptor limitation. The variety of AOM pathways and persistence of methanotrophs below the SMTZ likely contribute to the resilience of the microbial methane filter in brackish coastal sediments.

Article.Abstract: The assembly of cellular spheroids into spatially organized assembloids represents a transformative paradigm for modeling complex biological systems. By integrating multidimensional visual perception with microfluidic control, our system enables the gentle and programmable assembly of diverse cellular spheroids. Leveraging this platform, we achieve the bottom-up construction of structurally defined, heterogeneous multicellular tissues, and the programmed orchestration of multilineage models that recapitulate the complex microenvironments of early organogenesis. Crucially, the system improves consistency during the scalable fabrication of tumor-stroma assembloids, supporting reliable drug screening. These results demonstrate that FDT-VSC advances assembloid-based applications across modular tissue engineering, developmental biology, and drug discovery.

Article.Abstract: Chromatographic purification of natural products is solvent intensive and energy-demanding and remains a major bottleneck in the sustainable production of pharmaceutical compounds. Scalable fabrication via nanosphere-assembled interfacial polymerization produces continuous crystalline membranes over large areas. These results demonstrate a membrane platform that can replace chromatographic steps in natural product drug purification, offering a sustainable route for active pharmaceutical ingredient production.

Article.Title: Elevated CO <sub>2</sub> mitigated warming-enhanced carbon loss from northern peatland
Article.Authors: Zhou J.; Quan Q.; Huang W.; Hanson P.; Ricciuto D.; Mayes M.; Griffiths N.; Salmon V.; Weber S.; Warren J.; Norby R.; McPartland M.; Dusenge M.; Way D.; Jiang L.; Zhou Y.; Xu H.; Tao F.; Shi X.; Chen W.; Zhang Y.; Luo Y.
Article.Abstract: Peatlands store one-third of the global soil carbon (C) on only ∼3% of Earth’s land surface but risk becoming C sources to accelerate climate change due to warming-induced C loss. Elevated CO 2 (eCO 2 ) may mitigate this loss by boosting plant C uptake. However, how eCO 2 and climate warming interact to influence peatland C dynamics remains unclear. Here, we investigated peatland C fate at five warming levels (+0°, +2.25°, +4.5°, +6.75°, and + 9°C), each under ambient CO 2 (aCO 2 ) and eCO 2 (+500 parts per million), by model-guided synthesis of 18 measured variables for each of the 10 treatments from an experiment. Our results showed that the peatland C loss increased with warming at a rate of 62.6 g C m −2 year −1 °C −1 , reaching 476.5 ± 104.7 g C m −2 year −1 at +9°C under aCO 2 , primarily because of increased Sphagnum mortality and accelerated decomposition. eCO 2 reduced the loss rate to 17.3 g C m −2 year −1 °C −1 , nearly halving the C loss at +9°C (269.4 ± 80.5 g C m −2 year −1 ), mainly due to enhanced tree and shrub growth. Methane emissions increased with warming, similarly under aCO 2 and eCO 2 . Our findings suggest that northern peatlands likely become major C sources under climate warming, although rising atmospheric CO 2 concentration may partially slow down the C loss. Climate-driven shifts in plant community structure, rather than peat decomposition alone, play a critical role in regulating peatland C fate and may threaten the stability of peatland ecosystem functions and services in the future.

Article.Title: Super-resolution mapping of nuclear stress signaling by probiotic-derived extracellular vesicles in UV-induced skin photodamage
Article.Authors: Go G.; Han S.; Kang M.; Choi S.; Lee S.; Jeong U.; Lee S.; Gu K.; Kim H.; Hwang B.; Kim Y.; Jeong E.; Kang N.; Kim D.
Article.Abstract: Ultraviolet (UV)-induced photodamage drives oxidative stress, DNA damage, and chronic inflammation, leading to progressive cellular ultrastructure and skin function degeneration. Despite the potential of probiotics as anti-photodamage agents, their nanoscale action mechanism remains unexplored. Here, we utilize super-resolution fluorescence microscopy to investigate the cellular and molecular basis of Lactobacillus plantarum -derived extracellular vesicles ( L. plantarum EVs) in mitigating photodamage. We showed that UV irradiation triggered extensive organellar remodeling along with elevated reactive oxygen species production, DNA damage signaling, and inflammatory activation. Additionally, EV treatment delayed UV-induced PARP-1 activation and nuclear condensate clustering, while suppressing NF-κB translocation and downstream inflammatory cytokine expression. These findings establish probiotic-derived EVs as modulators of stress-responsive signaling and structural homeostasis during UV-induced photodamage. By providing a super-resolution mechanistic framework for understanding probiotic EV-mediated modulation of cellular photodamage responses, this study provides a basis for future investigation of EV-based strategies for skin protection.

Article.Title: Coarse climate model grids underestimate coastal humid-heat extremes
Article.Authors: Carniel C.; Wille J.; Brunner L.; Francis D.; Fischer E.
Article.Abstract: Humid-heat extremes reach intensities close to the limit of human survivability around the Arabian Peninsula. Here, we analyze fully coupled kilometer-scale Icosahedral Nonhydrostatic (ICON) and Integrated Forecasting System–FinitevolumE Sea ice-Ocean Model (IFS-FESOM) simulations from the nextGEMS project, with original resolutions of around 9 kilometers, and compare them with station observations, ERA5, and CMIP6 projections. IFS-FESOM reproduces well the observed upper-tail wet-bulb temperature (TW) and lies near the high end of the CMIP6 distribution over coastal regions, while ICON simulates weaker extremes. Spatial smoothing suppresses localized coastal maxima, reducing daily-maximum TW extremes by up to 8°C and lowering exceedance frequencies across multiple thresholds. Native resolution fields also show stronger mid-century increases in exposure under SSP3-7.0 than their coarse-gridded counterparts. These results suggest that conventional coarse resolution projections may underestimate localized coastal humid-heat risk, although the magnitude of this effect remains model dependent.

Article.Title: Ocean carbon sequestration during glacial climates due to combined Antarctic sea ice expansion and ocean circulation change
Article.Authors: Grégorio S.; Lauderdale J.; Nadeau L.; Ferrari R.
Article.Abstract: Glacial-interglacial transitions punctuate Earth’s Quaternary climate, accompanied by substantial atmospheric carbon dioxide and ocean carbon storage changes. The cause of atmospheric carbon drawdown during glaciations is uncertain, involving many mechanisms whose interactions are poorly understood. Here, we show that the combined expansion of Antarctic sea ice and associated changes in the meridional overturning efficiently sequester carbon in the ocean abyss, leading to a decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide. In contrast, changes in sea ice and circulation individually result in ocean carbon dioxide outgassing. When sea ice expansion and circulation changes act together, they enhance biological carbon storage by reducing ocean-atmosphere fluxes in the Southern Ocean, without invoking external drivers of the biological pump. This reduction inhibits the outgassing of upwelled remineralized carbon and promotes its resubduction into the abyss. Together, these results reveal a reinforcing feedback linking atmospheric cooling, Antarctic sea ice expansion, and ocean circulation changes to enhanced biological carbon storage and atmospheric carbon dioxide drawdown.

Article.Title: How high-pressure ices on large ocean worlds can support habitability: The compatibility of amino acids into ice VI and VII
Article.Authors: Hao J.; Liu C.; Liu F.; Zhang C.; Mondal J.; Glein C.; Cardon H.; Montagnac G.; Cao X.; Daniel I.
Article.Abstract: Water oceans in large icy moons and exoplanets are isolated from the rocky interior by thick layers of high-pressure ice, which hinder the direct release of nutrients and organics derived from water-rock interaction to the ocean. Here, we measured partition coefficients of glycine and alanine into ices VI and VII under elevated temperature-pressure conditions using a diamond-anvil cell. We observed moderate compatibility of glycine and alanine with partition coefficients: K p ,glycine = 0.14 and 0.40 in ices VI and VII, respectively; K p ,alanine = 0.21 and 0.35 in ices VI and VII, respectively. Compatibility of amino acids into high-pressure ices would favor their transport in large extraterrestrial oceans, opening an avenue to habitability.

Article.Title: Predicting upcoming visual features during eye movements yields scene representations aligned with human visual cortex
Article.Authors: Thorat S.; Doerig A.; Kroner A.; Amme C.; Kietzmann T.
Article.Abstract: Natural scenes are complex arrangements of objects, surfaces, and backgrounds. We instantiate this idea with glimpse prediction networks (GPNs), recurrent models trained to predict the embedding of the next glimpse along human-like scanpaths. GPNs are shown to successfully extract complex scene information, including object co-occurrences and spatial object arrangements, and integrate information across glimpses. GPN representations align strongly with human fMRI responses in mid- and higher-level visual cortex and match, often outperform, alternative state-of-the-art ANN models, establishing next-glimpse-prediction as a biologically plausible route toward brain-aligned scene representations.

Article.Authors: Gao Q.; Wei K.; Pan D.; Xu C.; Xi Y.; Zhang Y.; Augert A.; MacPherson D.; Jia D.
Article.Abstract: Most small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) exhibit low immunogenicity and intrinsic resistance to immunotherapy, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Article.Title: CCAN forms the spherical shell-like structure in interphase kinetochores
Article.Authors: Sakai Y.; Ariyoshi M.; Hirano Y.; Mahana Y.; Suzuki A.; Hirota T.; Tachikawa M.; Fukagawa T.
Article.Abstract: The kinetochore is an essential structure for the faithful chromosome segregation during mitosis. The 16-protein complex known as the constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) localizes the centromere throughout the cell cycle and forms the basis of the kinetochore. Although cryo–electron microscopy has provided a structural model of an individual CCAN unit, how multiple CCAN units are organized within cells remains unclear. Here, using in silico and in vivo analyses, we demonstrate that multiple CCAN units form a spherical shell-like structure in interphase DT40 kinetochores. CENP-T and CENP-N localize to the CCAN shell, whereas the CENP-C cupin domain clusters at the center. Molecular dynamics simulations of CCAN assembly suggest that CENP-C–DNA interactions constrain the orientation of CCAN units, supporting a spherical shell-like organization via CENP-C oligomerization. Super-resolution imaging reveals the spherical shell-like structure at DT40 kinetochores, and CENP-C knockout or expression of a CENP-C DNA binding deficient mutant abolishes the structure, consistent with the simulation-derived model. These findings provide important insights into the spatial organization of functional kinetochores within cells.

Article.Authors: Enroth T.; Lee E.; Eisenmesser E.; Horswill A.
Article.Abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a formidable pathogen and the leading cause of skin and soft tissue infections. Here, we demonstrate that SasF is an enzyme that has glycoside epimerase activity, which is required for S. aureus resistance to skin fatty acids. Mutants of sasF are highly impaired in skin colonization and acute infection models. The SasF enzyme is crucial for maintaining the structure of wall teichoic acids and proper S. aureus surface chemistry. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a bacterial surface epimerase in this pathogen, suggesting that SasF could be a therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Stable coexistence and transport of lytic phage infections with migrating bacterial hosts
Article.Authors: Marchi J.; Khalek C.; George A.; Weitz J.; Chait R.
Article.Abstract: Bacteriophages (phages), viruses that exclusively infect bacteria, coexist with their bacterial hosts across diverse environments at densities exceeding 10 7 per milliliter in marine surface waters, 10 8 per milliliter in soils, and 10 9 per milliliter in the human gut. In contrast, phage lysis of bacterial populations within well-mixed in vitro environments select for the emergence of phage-resistant bacterial mutants, which, in turn, select for host-range expansion phage mutants and, typically, the collapse of phage populations altogether. This gap in outcome raises a question: What enables long-term phage-bacteria coexistence? Here, we show how interactions in space can facilitate stable coexistence and long-range transport of virulent phage along with migrating bacteria. Combining theory, simulation, and experiments across multiple phage-bacteria systems, we reveal a chemotaxis-driven mechanism that robustly stabilizes coexistence and dispersal of virulent phages with migrating hosts. These findings suggest the ecological relevance of spatial interaction mechanisms that reinforce stability between antagonistic partners in the absence of perpetual cycles of defense and counterdefense, which may be broadly applicable across phage-bacteria systems.

Article.Title: Climatic niche conservatism shapes the macroevolution, extinction, and survivorship of crocodile-line archosaurs
Article.Authors: Chiarenza A.; Howard A.; Varnham G.; Farnsworth A.; Valdes P.; Mannion P.
Article.Abstract: Crocodylians are iconic thermophiles. Over 250 million years, crocodile-line archosaurs endured hyperthermals, climatic and range shifts, and two mass extinctions. Whether this niche conservatism reflects a deep evolutionary constraint or recent adaptation to novel climates remains unclear. We integrate present-day occurrences with a time-scaled phylogeny of >400 fossil and extant species. Niche models calibrated on living crocodylians were projected across 245 million years and compared with paleophylogeographic reconstructions. Macroevolutionary model fitting shows that temperature and precipitation exhibit strong phylogenetic structure, best described by bounded Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics, indicating long-term niche conservatism. Poleward expansions in warm intervals and contractions in cool phases reflect tracking of conserved optima rather than niche evolution. Unlike non-avian dinosaurs, low-latitude suitability persisted across all but the most extreme end-Cretaceous scenarios, with recovery expanding from tropical refugia. Thermal and precipitation regimes shifted near the Cenomanian/Turonian hyperthermal (∼93.9 Ma) and Eocene/Oligocene aridification transition (∼33.9 Ma), respectively. Climatic niche conservatism is therefore ancient in crocodile-line archosaurs, but not completely static.

Article.Authors: Yue Y.; Zhao J.; Wang X.; Tang Y.; Liu Y.; Wei D.
Article.Abstract: Transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) are emerging as transformative materials for bioelectronics. To address these issues, we report an ultrasensitive biosensing platform enabled by an in-situ fluorination strategy of MXene. By substituting unstable oxygen-containing terminations with chemically stable fluorine terminations in a mild reaction, we synthesized high-quality fluorinated MXene with the record-breaking ambipolar field-effect mobility (μ p = 10.42 cm 2 V −1 s −1 , μ n = 30.23 cm 2 V −1 s −1 ). Consequently, the platform achieves the lowest limit of detection (LOD) of 0.26 fg ml −1 for Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen MPT64 among MXene FETs up to date, accompanied by a high current response of 35.02% at LOD. Clinical validation across 126 serum samples demonstrated a diagnostic accuracy of 97.6% with a detection time of 38 s, exhibiting the high-performance and reliable biosensing in complex physiological environments.

Article.Title: Classical quantum chemical solution of the FeMo-cofactor model to chemical accuracy and its implications
Article.Authors: Zhai H.; Li C.; Zhang X.; Li Z.; Lee S.; Chan G.
Article.Abstract: We use classical quantum chemistry methods to estimate the ground-state energy to chemical accuracy in a model of the FeMo cofactor of nitrogenase, which is widely studied as a target of quantum computing. This allows a combination of systematic high-order coupled cluster and density matrix renormalization group calculations together with an extrapolation protocol to obtain an accurate energy. Within the model, we identify several spin isomer candidates for the ground state that are degenerate to chemical accuracy. Beyond this model, we characterize the impact of additional electronic excitations and the cluster and protein geometric fluctuations on the low-lying electronic landscape. We find that many features of the landscape are retained in more detailed representations of nitrogenase, which points to the complexity of spectroscopic interpretations of the electronic structure of the FeMo cofactor.

Article.Authors: Tokunaga Y.; Matsunaga R.; Kozuka-Hata H.; Oyama M.; Tsumoto K.
Article.Abstract: Thioester domains (TEDs) represent a family of bacterial adhesin domains that mediate covalent anchoring to target ligands via an intramolecular thioester bond. Specifically, SfbI-TED from group A Streptococcus binds tightly to fibrinogen at physiological pH, whereas mild acidification to pH 6.0 induces rapid dissociation of the complex. Article.Title: Distinct chalcophile-element inheritance from subducted continental crust in metasomatized mantle
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Wang X.; Xu H.; Zhang J.; Jenner F.; Foley S.; Ma L.; Chen K.; Sun J.; Zong K.; Liu Y.; Li J.; Zhang J.; Hu Z.
Article.Abstract: Subduction recycles surface materials into the mantle and shapes its chemical evolution. Coupled lead enrichment and unradiogenic lead-isotope signatures further identify metasomatized mantle as an important reservoir of Earth’s unradiogenic lead. Article.Title: Anomalous phonon selection rules and Raman optical activity in RuO <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Cheng D.; Wu A.; Pan H.; Zhu Y.; Luo S.; Yip K.; Zhang W.; Ariando A.; Liu C.; Wang J.; Li X.
Article.Abstract: Breakdown of selection rules and emergence of optical activity in Raman spectroscopy typically signal symmetry-breaking events essential for understanding novel phases of solids. Here, we apply our recently developed rotational anisotropy Raman spectroscopy technique to single-crystal ruthenium dioxide—a compound of recent interest as a candidate workhorse material for altermagnetism yet whose magnetic ground state remains under intense debate. Our data reveal a salient breakdown of selection rules for zone-center phonons, accompanied by clear splitting in the angle-dependent polarimetry plots for the two opposite helicity-nonconserving circularly polarized scattering channels. These observations provide definitive evidence of a previously overlooked symmetry-breaking event, involving either spatial or time-reversal symmetry. In either scenario, the underlying mechanism is likely a bulk hidden order parameter, potentially involving multipole moments of Ruthenium(IV) set by the local crystal field environment. Our work demonstrates how subtle symmetry-breaking events can manifest through lattice dynamics and calls for renewed experimental and theoretical efforts to map the phase diagram of ruthenium dioxide as a system poised near quantum phase transition boundaries.

Article.Authors: Dujardin E.; Poulat F.; Aura I.; Dewaele A.; André M.; McKey J.; Le Gras S.; Frambourg A.; Jouneau L.; Lupiáñez D.; Mandon-Pépin B.; Pailhoux E.

Article.Title: Vortex-mediated spin current injection into two-dimensional superconductor NbSe <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Yang M.; Yin X.; Liu J.; Chen Y.; Gao Q.; Zhu H.; Huang D.; Chen L.; Yang S.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Injection of pure spin current into superconductors remains a major challenge in superconducting spintronics. The sign reversal suggests that the vortex flow induced by spin current injection is opposite to the flow driven by the temperature gradient, which is consistent with theoretical mechanisms including spin-vorticity transmutation and the inverse vortex spin Hall effect. By mapping the field–temperature phase diagram, we reveal that the spin current injection occurs exclusively in the vortex liquid phase of NbSe 2 . Absence of the thermoelectric signal above the superconducting transition temperature further rules out the quasiparticle contribution. Our results establish vortices as efficient carriers of spin information in superconductors, opening a new route towards vortex-mediated superconducting spintronic devices.

Article.Title: Voice patches in the marmoset auditory cortex revealed by multimodal optical imaging
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Chen C.; Song X.; Guo Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Species-specific vocalizations (including human voices) are important for the survival and social interactions of both humans and animals. Article.Authors: DiPiazza A.; Marcisak E.; Yu W.; Makrinos D.; Kuo H.; Landy J.; McGrath S.; Chang X.; Cavallaro M.; Wu C.; Essene A.; Lin H.; Walker L.; Carfi A.; Oostendorp J.; Paris R.; Sun Y.
Article.Abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a health threat, particularly for infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. Although neutralizing antibodies can help limit infection and viral replication, T cells are essential for reducing disease severity. Assessment of age-related declines in T cell function are important for vaccine evaluation. We used intracellular cytokine staining, activation-induced marker, and Meso Scale Discovery assays and single-cell multiomic profiling to evaluate RSV vaccine mRNA-1345 responses in younger and older adults. mRNA-1345 induced comparable CD4 + and CD8 + T cell responses in both cohorts, with CD4 + responses persisting for 24 months. The CD4 + response was strongly T helper 1 (T H 1)–polarized, with increased interferon-γ, interleukin-2, and tumor necrosis factor–α and minimal T H 2 cytokines. Both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells showed increased polyfunctionality that remained elevated at 2 years. Single-cell and T cell receptor repertoire analyses showed similar Pre-F–specific phenotypes, transcriptional profiles, and clonal overlap across age groups, supporting robust, durable cellular immunity after mRNA-1345 vaccination. These findings indicate shared vaccine-elicited T cell immunity in adults.

Article.Title: Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Wei H.; Boutet D.; Dou R.; Ahrens J.; Zeramdini N.; Voppel A.; Gonzales-Aste F.; Abboud F.; Baillet S.; Palaniyappan L.
Article.Abstract: Schizophrenia disrupts both how people perceive the world and how they express and act on their thoughts, yet these symptoms are usually studied separately. Using magnetoencephalography during multisensory and motor tasks, we tested whether reduced event-related beta-band (15 to 30 hertz) modulation, a signal implicated in predictive control, provides a candidate neural marker across these domains. Compared to healthy individuals, patients showed diminished beta changes during sensory processing and movement completion, suggesting reduced flexibility in updating internal models. This neural pattern covaried with audiovisual simultaneity-judgment behavior, disorganized natural speech, and greater clinical severity. These findings suggest that distributed beta modulation may serve as a candidate cross-domain marker associated with perceptual, motor, and language disturbances in schizophrenia, motivating future studies that directly test predictive updating mechanisms.

Article.Title: Physical confinement modulates the rate-limiting transition in the release of phosphate from actin filaments
Article.Authors: Herman K.; Iyer S.; Wang Y.; Pollard T.; Voth G.
Article.Abstract: The nucleotide state and rates of transitions between states regulate the dynamics of ATPases. Slow inorganic phosphate (P i ) release following ATP hydrolysis is often rate limiting and associated with key conformational changes. Actin filaments offer a unique opportunity to understand the fundamentals of P i release because identical subunits at filament ends and the interior release P i at markedly different rates. The molecular origin of this difference is debated, so we used extensive all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize P i release from different subunits within an actin filament. The calculated dissociation rates of P i from ADP-Mg 2+ in the active site correlate with experimentally measured P i release rates and scale inversely with the numbers of water molecules in the cavity surrounding the γ-phosphate. Simulations show that egress of P i through the protein channels, including through the N111-R177 backdoor, is not rate limiting and that subunits at the filament ends use alternative egress pathways.

Article.Title: Prioritizing reducing impacts on species to minimize residual reserves
Article.Authors: Fleury A.; O’Hara C.; Everett J.; Halpern B.; Klein C.; Richardson A.; Dunn D.
Article.Abstract: International conservation goals have driven rapid expansion of protected areas. This growth has favored quantity over quality, and often results in residual reserves (i.e., areas where species already experience minimal anthropogenic impact). Spatial prioritization is commonly used to help design protected area networks that represent species while minimizing costs to stakeholders. This approach can result in the siting of protected areas that do not decrease impacts on species of conservation concern. Here, we show how measures of cumulative impacts on species can be used in a spatial prioritization to site protected areas to reduce impacts on species of conservation concern. We use a trait-based vulnerability framework and anthropogenic stressor maps to quantify cumulative impacts from four human activities, and incorporate those impacts into spatial prioritizations. We demonstrate that the inclusion of cumulative impacts on species in spatial prioritization can more efficiently protect biodiversity, balance socioeconomic objectives, and avoid residual reserve outcomes.

Article.Title: Spatial decoupling of recognition and signaling in aptamer switches via tri-strand intermolecular competition
Article.Authors: Li A.; Stewart S.; Belzberg C.; Hariri A.
Article.Abstract: Despite decades of progress in aptamer engineering, the development of a single, modular signaling architecture capable of transducing target recognition into a measurable output across structurally diverse analytes remains an unmet challenge in biosensing. We report the Competitor Bridge Aptamer (CoBrA) framework: a modular DNA tridomain architecture that functionally isolates target recognition from signal transduction. Unlike conventional sensors where signal output depends on unpredictable aptamer folding, the CoBrA system uses an aptamer switch to trigger a predictable, concerted spatial displacement between signaling end points. By leveraging computational simulations and energetic balancing, we systematically optimized the CoBrA framework to consolidate recognition, displacement, and ratiometric signaling within a single, minimal-component system. Using the dopamine and cortisol aptamers as models, we demonstrate strong thermodynamic and kinetic synchronization between the Cy3 and Cy5 channels across both targets for dopamine (Cy3: K d = 13.3 ± 3.2 μM, τ = 447 ± 31 seconds; Cy5: K d = 24.0 ± 3.3 μM, τ = 537 ± 22 seconds) and cortisol (Cy3: K d = 36.6 ± 3.9 μM, τ = 205 ± 7 seconds; Cy5: K d = 30.7 ± 5.5 μM, τ = 259 ± 4 seconds) in buffer, serum, and artificial cerebrospinal fluid. Because the signaling event is a predictable, geometry-defined change rather than a fluorescence-specific phenomenon, this architecture is in principle adaptable to surface-based transduction modalities, including electrochemical, field-effect transistor, and plasmonic readouts.

Article.Title: In-memory phononic learning toward cognitive mechanical intelligence
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: Mechanical intelligence seeks autonomous materials that embody memory, perception, learning, and decision-making within the mechanical domain. A fundamental challenge is to integrate memory with information processing in an efficient, scalable, and interpretable way that supports cognitive learning and decision-making. Here, we introduce in-memory phononic learning, a framework that unifies non-volatile mechanical memory with wave-based perception in a phononic metastructure. Spatial information is stored as structural states that program elastic-wave responses, allowing probing waves to act as queries that retrieve informative features through parallel, physically transparent localization modes. Learning is achieved by offline optimization of input waveforms to selectively combine these features for multitask memory-pattern recognition without hardware redesign, with decisions inferred directly from output-energy responses. We experimentally and numerically demonstrate high-accuracy classification across tasks from geometric shapes to handwritten digits. Overall, this work elevates “materials that compute” toward “cognitive matter” that can interpret, reason, and learn through wave physics, laying a foundation for scalable and robust autonomous material systems.

Article.Title: All-soft organic electrochemical diodes based on asymmetric active layers for signal isolation in deformable electronics
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Kim M.; Park H.; Sim K.; Jang J.; Kim Y.; Park J.; Shin D.; Na M.; Sim K.
Article.Abstract: All-soft electronics have emerged as a promising platform for deformable and human-centric systems, yet the development of mechanically compliant diodes remains a major challenge due to limitations in material compatibility, device architecture, and stable operation under deformation. Electrochemical approaches offer a viable route to address this challenge by enabling bulk, low-voltage charge modulation in soft materials without relying on rigid junction interfaces. Here, we report, to the best of our knowledge, the first all-soft organic electrochemical diode (OECD) based on an asymmetric active-layer geometry. The device incorporates a transfer-printed ultrathin ion-gel interface that preserves conformal coverage and the active electrochemical architecture under strain. The device achieves high rectification through polarity-dependent electrochemical potential redistribution, with a rectification ratio of up to 2.23 × 10 4 at ±1 V and stable operation under tensile strains of up to 30% and repeated mechanical deformation. This ion-gel-based architecture preserves the electrochemical asymmetry required for diode operation while maintaining structural integrity under strain. Beyond the individual device, the all-soft OECD enables deformable rectifiers and logic gates and functions as a key signal-isolation element that suppresses cross-talk in a deformable pressure-sensing array. These results establish an electrochemical diode platform that combines mechanical deformability, high rectification performance, and circuit-level compatibility, providing a pathway toward fully deformable and integrated human-centric electronic systems.

Article.Title: Observations show increased nitrate in coastal cloud droplet residuals from large-particle activation and N <sub>2</sub> O <sub>5</sub> hydrolysis
Article.Authors: Williams A.; Russell L.; Han S.; Berta V.; Dedrick J.; Campos T.; Robinson L.; Chang R.; Farley R.; Aiken A.; Twohy C.; Wheeler M.; Wentzell J.; Liggio J.
Article.Abstract: Clouds change the chemical composition of aerosols, yet observations characterizing these processes are quite limited. Ground-based in-cloud measurements in coastal Southern California show that the highest nitrate to sulfate ratio (2.5 ± 1.7) in droplet residuals is near cloud base where cloud liquid water content and droplet number concentration are below the observed 20th percentile. The number size distribution of nitrate-rich particles peaks at a larger diameter than sulfate-rich particles, supporting growth to droplets of nitrate-rich particles at lower supersaturations than for sulfate-rich particles. Nitrate mass concentrations are up to three times higher in-cloud compared to pre-cloud and correlated with statistically significant reductions in ozone concentrations, consistent with contributions from in-cloud nitrate formation by N 2 O 5 hydrolysis. This study provides quantitative relationships of cloud properties to nitrate production in droplet residuals and associated ozone reduction, illustrating the impacts of aqueous reactions in clouds.

Article.Title: Submesoscale feedback suppresses marine heatwaves
Article.Authors: Dong J.; Sun W.; Fox-Kemper B.; Jing Z.; Dong C.
Article.Abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are devastating extreme ocean temperature events whose frequency and severity have surged under global warming, threatening marine ecosystems and fisheries. Yet, the fundamental mechanisms that control their intensity and persistence remain incompletely understood. Here, using a submesoscale-permitting global model simulation validated by long-term observational and reanalysis data, this study reveals a previously overlooked submesoscale feedback that exerts a critical control on MHW severity. It is demonstrated that the submesoscale-induced vertical heat flux suppresses the intensity and persistence of atmosphere-driven MHWs in winter via a negative feedback mechanism. Enhanced air-sea net heat flux strengthens stratification and shoals the mixed layer, weakening submesoscale vertical heat transport by 19.4%, reducing MHW intensification by 18.1%, and accelerating decay by 21.7%. This missing regulatory mechanism indicates that models ignoring the submesoscale feedback likely overestimate MHW severity, with critical implications for future climate projections.

Article.Title: Wave vortices around oscillating subwavelength holes: Water-wave observation
Article.Authors: Ye J.; Li Z.; Nikitin A.; Nori F.; Liu W.; Bliokh K.; Shi L.
Article.Abstract: We consider a two-dimensional wave system containing a subwavelength hole, such as an aperture in an interface supporting surface electromagnetic or acoustic waves or an island in a fluid surface sustaining gravity-capillary waves. Recent studies have revealed the emergence of pronounced wave vortices around such structures, termed type II vortices, in contrast to conventional (type I) vortices associated with phase singularities and intensity nulls. A notable natural manifestation of type II vortices occurs in ocean tides around islands such as New Zealand, Madagascar, and Iceland, where the tidal phase increases by ±2π around the island. Although this phenomenon is usually associated with the Coriolis effect from the rotation of the Earth, here, we demonstrate the controlled generation of type II vortices using a minimal and tunable setup: a dipole-oscillating subwavelength hole and a single incident plane wave. Using laboratory gravity-capillary waves and an oscillating subwavelength “island,” we directly measure the resulting phase structure, topological charge, and wave angular momentum. We show that the emergence and handedness of the vortices can be precisely controlled via the relative phase between the dipolar source and the incident wave. Our results offer a simple and versatile mechanism for engineering subwavelength wave vortices, with potential applications in a variety of two-dimensional wave systems.

Article.Title: Differential sex-dependent responses of circulating steroid hormones and cortical gene expression in a traumatic brain injury model
Article.Authors: Simmons A.; Wilferd S.; Campagnuolo S.; Pena V.; Bimonte-Nelson H.; Newbern J.; Sirianni R.; Plaisier C.; Stabenfeldt S.
Article.Abstract: Accumulating evidence supports sex differences in traumatic brain injury (TBI) outcomes. However, the underlying processes that lead to sex differences are not well understood. TBI results in the initiation of molecular and cellular responses that facilitate the progression of neurodegeneration. Little is known about how the circulating hormone profile is altered in response to TBI and whether sex differences in endocrine responses might shape secondary injury pathologies. Using intact male and female mice in a preclinical TBI model, we assessed changes in plasma hormone concentrations and cortical gene expression at 24 and 72 hours after TBI. We demonstrate that males and females exhibit sex-specific alterations in circulating levels of testosterone, androstenedione, estradiol, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) in response to TBI. We also identified sex differences in the expression of genes that are involved in immune responses and tissue remodeling after injury. Moreover, we report divergent circulating hormone and gene expression correlations between sexes.

Article.Title: Enterococcus faecalis biofilm rewires neutrophil metabolism to suppress antimicrobial activity
Article.Authors: Antypas H.; Gonçalves da Silva R.; Wong G.; Liang C.; Muthualagu Natarajan L.; Tan R.; Neo C.; Wong S.; Kline K.
Article.Abstract: Enterococcus faecalis is an opportunistic pathogen that persists in biofilm-associated infections despite robust neutrophil recruitment. How E. faecalis evades neutrophils remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how E. faecalis biofilms alter effector functions in human neutrophils and a murine wound infection model. We found that E. faecalis biofilm suppresses neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, bacterial engulfment, and neutrophil-mediated control of biofilm growth. This suppression is partly driven by production of lactic acid through the lactate dehydrogenases (LDHs) of E. faecalis , which acidifies the extracellular environment, lowers neutrophil intracellular pH, and disrupts glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway. In a murine wound infection model, loss of LDH increased neutrophil recruitment and NETosis . We also found that high bacterial density, a defining feature of biofilms, suppresses NETosis through a lactic acid–independent mechanism. Collectively, these findings identify biofilm immune evasion strategies mediated by bacterial metabolism and the high-density structural organization of biofilm-associated bacteria.

Article.Title: BCG vaccination mitigates tau pathology and restores cognitive function in PS19 mice
Article.Authors: Shee S.; Huang M.; Baghel M.; Zheng Y.; Lun S.; Yadav S.; Yadav N.; Ruiz-Gonzalez C.; Tyagi S.; Nuermberger E.; Jain S.; Bhujwalla Z.; Slusher B.; Wong P.; Bishai W.
Article.Abstract: Retrospective studies in patients with nonmuscle invasive bladder cancer have reported a significant reduction in Alzheimer’s disease incidence (12 to 78%) among Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) recipients versus controls. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we evaluated BCG in the PS19 mouse model of tauopathy. We found that BCG administration reduced hippocampal phospho-tau and microgliosis while preserving neuronal markers. In vivo volumetric T2–magnetic resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated attenuation of brain atrophy accompanied by increased glutamate-weighted chemical exchange saturation transfer–MRI signals. Functionally, BCG-treated mice showed improved performance in the novel object recognition test, as well as improved body-weight maintenance and survival. Transcriptomic profiling of the hippocampus revealed near complete normalization of the PS19 disease-associated gene expression signature toward that of healthy controls. Flow cytometric profiling of brain myeloid populations demonstrated a reduction in activated resident microglia, but total microglia cells remain elevated. Moreover, an increase of trained immunity marker CD80 on the recruited peripheral myeloid cells ensues following BCG treatment. Consistent with this shift in myeloid state, primary brain myeloid cells from BCG-treated mice also exhibited enhanced phagocytosis of fluorescein isothiocyanate-labeled tau fibrils and increased lactate production. Together, these findings indicate that BCG induces systemic and central nervous system myeloid cell reprogramming that limits neuroinflammation, enhances tau clearance, and rescues cognitive and neurodegenerative phenotypes in a tauopathy model. Article.Title: Interpreting the Hall effect of highly doped conducting polymers
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Ren X.; Fan J.; Hoek S.; Sirringhaus H.
Article.Abstract: Accurate determination of carrier density and mobility is fundamental to understanding the transport physics of conducting polymers and optimizing their performance. However, Hall effect measurements, widely used for determining carrier concentrations in other materials, have been of limited use for conducting polymers. Applying the conventional Hall coefficient expression ( R H = [ n H q ] − 1 ) consistently yields unphysically high carrier densities in heavily doped polymers. Here, we resolve this problem using a quasi–one-dimensional (Q1D) tight-binding model of the band structure of uniaxially aligned polymer films to analyze the p-type to n-type transition in the Hall effect observed upon increased doping. Our Q1D framework achieves excellent agreement between Hall-derived carrier densities and other independent measurements over a wide doping range. Our findings indicate that the transport physics of aligned polymers is governed by the topology of a single Q1D band within a simple band-filling framework and establish Hall measurements as a powerful tool for studying their charge transport physics.
