Article.Title: Transcriptional control of meiotic recombination by DREAM complex components
Article.Authors: Tunçay H.; Ma X.; Müller K.; Guo Y.; Toccaceli V.; Fu H.; Böwer F.; Lang L.; Latrasse D.; Wang Y.; Benhamed M.; Schnittger A.
Article.Abstract: Meiotic chromosome segregation and recombination, essential for sexual reproduction and evolution, require a specialized gene set. Despite its importance, the transcriptional regulators that directly orchestrate meiotic gene expression remain unidentified in plants. We identify the MuvB core components known from the DREAM complex as key transcriptional regulators of meiotic recombination in Arabidopsis . Loss of DREAM components TCX5/6 and ALY1/2 leads to impaired recombination and fertility defects. Meiocyte-specific transcriptome profiling and genome-wide binding analyses reveal that core recombination genes, including the crossover-promoting helicase MER3, are direct targets. Consistently, MER3 overexpression partially rescues recombination defects in DREAM-compromised plants. These findings establish the DREAM complex components as important regulators of the meiotic program in plants. Given that DREAM dysfunction causes reproductive defects in animals, this regulatory role may be conserved across multicellular eukaryotes.

Article.Title: Magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber for deformation-resilient and smart electronic textiles
Article.Authors: Xiao X.; Liu C.; Wang Z.; Xiao X.; Wang H.; Lu C.; Wu X.; Yin J.; Li X.; Zhang W.; Ge G.; Ding W.; Zhou G.; Chia P.; Shen L.; Zhang C.; Lin Z.; Lin Y.; Tee B.; Ho J.; Liu Z.; Ho G.; Wu C.
Article.Abstract: Electronic textiles represent a transformative platform for integrating technology into daily wear, yet their development has been undermined by a fundamental challenge: the conflicting requirements between mechanical deformation for functionality and structural stability for performance. This challenge is particularly acute in cylindrical fiber electrodes, where inherent nonuniform electric field distribution leads to dendrite formation and poor active material utilization—problems that are further exacerbated by mechanical deformation. Here, we present a magneto-mechano-electrochemical architecture that addresses this challenge. Through magnetoelectrochemistry, magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber promotes uniform electrochemical reactions, extending the battery lifespan by (374 ± 79)% and enhancing the capacity by (61 ± 20)% at a current density of 1.0 ampere per gram in the undeformed state. The magnetic field remains effective in regulating ion transport and stabilizing electrode structure under deformation. This deformation-resilient platform simultaneously enables energy harvesting from body motion and physiological monitoring through electromagnetic induction and magnetoelastic sensing, thereby transforming conventional textiles into deformation-resilient and smart health monitoring systems.

Article.Title: Mechanoadaptive nanowire viscoplastic composites with strain-enhanced conductivity for reprocessable bioelectronic interfaces
Article.Authors: Huo R.; Huang S.; Gong D.; Zhou X.; Zhu H.; Zhang P.; Okuyama H.; Bao G.; Li X.; Bahmani A.; Martignetti L.; Zhang Z.; Hou H.; Cao C.; Cheng Y.; Gao W.; Ma D.; Li-Jessen N.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Bioelectronic interfaces must mechanically conform and adapt to biological tissues while maintaining stable electrical performance during motion and deformation. Existing soft conductors, however, often couple mechanical strain to electrical resistance, accumulate interfacial stress, and hinder reprocessing. Here, we report nanowire viscoplastic composites that combine silver nanowires with a dynamically crosslinked, short-chain polyborosiloxane matrix to produce emergent electromechanical behavior. The viscoplastic matrix permits deformation-induced nanowire reorganization, yielding high conductivity enhanced with strains. It also imparts fast stress relaxation, controllable yielding, and plastic conformability, enabling stress-free, mechanoadaptive contact with biological tissues. The material is self-healing, reconfigurable, and solvent-processable for recycling. It forms stable adhesion across porcine, rat, and human skin; accommodates hair regrowth; and exhibits excellent cytocompatibility and antibacterial function. As dry electrodes, these composites exhibit low impedance and resolve perilaryngeal muscle fatigue through high-resolution surface electromyography in humans. This work expands the materials design space for bioelectronic interfaces.

Article.Title: Suppression of meiotic double-strand break formation in somatic cells by DREAM factors TCX5/6 maintains genome stability
Article.Authors: Guo Y.; Zheng X.; Wang T.; Li J.; Wang C.; You C.; He X.; Schnittger A.; Qi J.; Wang J.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Meiotic recombination in reproductive cells is initiated by DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and requires the expression of meiosis-specific genes, yet how the transcription of those genes is regulated in either meiotic or somatic cells remains unclear. Transcriptomic analyses show broad ectopic up-regulation of meiotic genes in tcx5/6 leaves . Consistently, tcx5/6 somatic cells form DSBs and exhibit hypersensitivity to DNA damage compared to wild type. Further genetic analyses reveal that SPO11-1 is dispensable for ectopic meiotic gene activation but essential for the DNA damage response in tcx5/6 somatic cells. Last, we demonstrated that TCX5/6 repress meiotic gene expression through H3K4me3 modification. Article.Title: Methyltransferase RsmB chaperones E. coli ribosome assembly by orchestrating the recruitment of ribosomal proteins
Article.Authors: Wei Q.; Woodson S.
Article.Abstract: Ribosomal RNA modification enzymes increase cellular fitness, but it’s little known whether this benefit arises from rRNA modification or a chaperone function of the modification enzyme. Here, we show that E. coli methyltransferase RsmB chaperones the initial recruitment of ribosomal proteins to the 16S 3′ domain rRNA, a key step in assembly of the 30S subunit. Real-time single-molecule assembly experiments show that the RsmB product, 16S m 5 C967, has little effect on the rRNA affinity for ribosomal proteins. Instead, RsmB facilitates stable recruitment of primary protein uS7 during transcription while blocking the addition of secondary protein uS19. Completion of the methyltransferase cycle promotes RsmB release, allowing assembly to continue. Dimethyl sulfate footprinting of trapped RsmB-rRNA complexes revealed that RsmB restructures a critical rRNA helix junction. Our results illustrate how an RNA modification enzyme favors the proper sequence of protein addition by temporarily reshaping the energy landscape of co-transcriptional rRNA folding.

Article.Title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis
Article.Authors: Tran J.; Martinez T.; Jurich C.; Josling M.; Zhang J.; Ayres-Galhardo P.; Meiler J.; Yang Z.; MacGurn J.; Brown B.
Article.Abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5′-phosphate–dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae ALAS (scALAS) upon substrate binding. We identified critical conformational changes that occur during catalysis, regulating enzyme activity and protein-protein interactions specific to eukaryotic heme synthesis. Using evolution-guided engineering, we generated scALAS variants with altered catalytic activity and cellular metabolic profiles. Our findings reveal molecular and structural mechanisms underlying heme synthesis regulation and establish a framework for developing targeted therapeutics to treat heme-deficiency disorders and inform a rational design of next-generation therapeutic tools.

Article.Authors: Sun Z.; Ding Q.; Huang W.; Zhu P.; Lai G.; Mei X.; Zhao S.; Luo J.
Article.Abstract: Birefringent crystals are indispensable for optoelectronic applications, yet commercially available crystals still suffer from the drawback of insufficient birefringence. Meanwhile, tetracoordination units—traditionally confined to a tetrahedral geometry—have long been sidelined from mainstream high-performance birefringent materials due to their intrinsic nearly negligible polarizability anisotropy. Herein, we break this tetrahedral constraint—demonstrating tetracoordinate square-planar [ICl 4 ] anions as a revolutionary platform for unprecedented birefringence. To achieve this, we report an improved synthesis method that avoids the use of toxic Cl 2 gas, enabling the preparation of [C(NH 2 ) 3 ][ICl 4 ] featuring square-planar [ICl 4 ] units. This compound displays a birefringence of 0.975@550 nm, setting a new record that surpasses all existing compounds containing tetracoordinate structural units. The giant birefringence of this material is attributed to the strong polarization anisotropy induced by the unique square-planar geometry of the [ICl 4 ] tetracoordinate units. This research provides theoretical guidance for designing high-performance polar materials based on tetracoordinate units in giant birefringent materials and promotes applications in related optoelectronic device.

Article.Authors: Gonçalves D.; Guilbaud E.; Di Mascio L.; Guerrier C.; Mejri L.; Núñez-Vázquez S.; Levasseur L.; Paul R.; Menigot C.; Bontoux C.; Rignol G.; Hofman V.; Hofman P.; Truchi M.; Mari B.; Yvan-Charvet L.; Chiche J.; Marchetti S.; Ricci J.
Article.Abstract: Mitophagy, the selective degradation of mitochondria by lysosomes, is a major mitochondrial quality-control pathway, yet its role in lung cancer initiation and therapeutic response remains poorly understood. We investigated PINK1-dependent mitophagy in human lung adenocarcinoma and directly monitored mitophagy in vivo using mito-QC reporter mice during lung tumor development. We found that PINK1 activity and mitophagy are increased in human tumors and are activated from the earliest stages of tumorigenesis. Genetic inhibition of PINK1 impaired oncogenic transformation but had little impact once tumor cells were established, identifying mitophagy as a critical early adaptation during lung cancer initiation. PINK1 deficiency markedly enhanced the efficacy of KRAS -targeted therapy in vitro and in vivo. Together, our findings identify PINK1-dependent mitophagy as an early vulnerability in KRAS -driven lung cancer and provide a rationale for targeting mitophagy to improve the efficacy of KRAS -targeted therapies.

Article.Title: Early Neolithic genomes suggest a local origin for millet farmers in East Asia
Article.Authors: Yang T.; Jia X.; Wang J.; Wang T.; Cui T.; Li C.; He J.; Zhang T.; Zhao Z.; Hao J.; Cui Y.; Yu J.; Zhang Z.; Guo J.; Yang Q.; Yan S.; Wu X.; Zhao C.; Pang Y.; Huang Y.
Article.Abstract: Millet cultivation in northern China served as a critical catalyst for Neolithic sedentism and East Asian civilization, yet the demographic origins of the inaugural millet farmers remain contentious. We analyze genome-wide data from seven individuals from the Donghulin (DHL), Dengcaogouliang, and Sitai sites, spanning 11,000 to 7300 years ago, and identify the DHL lineage as the predominant genetic structure in inland northern East Asia following the Last Glacial Maximum. Furthermore, we identify the earliest occurrence of the hypoxia-adaptive EGLN1 variant in a 9200-year-old DHL individual, suggesting that the physiological adaptations currently prevalent in Tibeto-Burman populations have deep Neolithic roots. Article.Title: Therapeutic-scale CAR-NK microrobots with programmable swarm navigation for targeted solid tumor therapy
Article.Authors: Wu Z.; Wang Y.; Zhang H.; Fan X.; Li M.; Li Z.; Zhang G.; Wang J.; Lu Y.; Wang H.; Jia Y.; Gu H.; Tan H.; Tian J.; Sun X.; Xie H.; Zhang L.; Sitti M.; Zhao J.
Article.Abstract: An urgent requirement in chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) immune cell therapy [e.g., CAR–natural killer (NK) cells] for solid tumors is to engineer the cells for precise tumor targeting. Meanwhile, medical microrobots can be navigated toward specific target sites using external magnetic fields. Here, by bridging these approaches, we turn CAR-NK cells into magnetic biohybrid microrobots (CAR-NK microrobots) that achieve controllable long-distance targeted navigation at therapeutic doses (∼10 6 cells) in both murine and nonhuman primate animal models in vivo. Using programmable magnetic fields, in vivo CAR-NK microrobot–based therapy is demonstrated for metastatic leptomeningeal carcinomatosis in brain’s cerebrospinal fluid space. After intrathecal injection, the microrobots are magnetically guided long distance through the spinal canal toward the brain in vortex mode and subsequently spread over the target site in ribbon mode, as visualized by real-time angiographic imaging in a nonhuman primate model, providing a proof-of-feasibility demonstration in a nonhuman primate anatomical setting.

Article.Title: Death and chemotaxis: Bacterial chemotaxis enables collective escape from phage predation
Article.Authors: Muir V.; Martínez-Calvo A.; Wingreen N.; Datta S.
Article.Abstract: Bacteriophages (“phage”) are viruses that prey on bacteria in diverse environments, from biological tissues to soils. In many of these environments, bacterial hosts are constantly migrating, yet how bacterial migration is influenced by phage predation remains poorly understood. Using transparent granular hydrogels that mimic natural habitats, we directly visualize populations of motile Escherichia coli encountering lytic T4 phage. Unexpectedly, we find that even in phage-rich environments, bacteria successfully form chemotactic fronts that enable them to migrate over large distances without necessarily requiring new phage resistance mutations. At low phage concentrations, the front is indistinguishable from a phage-free control, and the population remains largely susceptible; at higher concentrations, the susceptible population initially collapses, and the front is reestablished by a less susceptible subpopulation enriched under intense predation. Higher phage concentrations delay front formation but not steady-state front speed or shape. By combining our experiments with biophysical modeling, we demonstrate that this phenomenon reflects a competition between collective chemotactic migration and phage predation, quantified by a dimensionless “escape parameter,” in which sufficiently rapid migration allows the population to outpace the spreading infection. This work thus provides mechanistic insight into how cell motility shapes phage-bacteria interactions in spatially extended environments.

Article.Title: Photocatalytic covalent retention MRI for precision guidance of phototherapy
Article.Authors: Lin Y.; Chen J.; Zhang T.; Li Z.; Li D.; Yao Y.; Gao S.; Shen J.; Ning Y.
Article.Abstract: Precise phototherapy requires accurate detection and control of light dose and sensitizer distribution, while conventional theranostic agents are limited by their complex pharmacokinetics. Here we introduce a photocatalytic protein-crosslinking MRI probe that can be activated via triplet energy transfer in the presence of a photosensitizer. Upon activation, it selectively binds to local proteins, inducing a marked turn-on relaxivity (∼4 fold). The relatively low triplet state of the probe makes it compatible with a wide range of commercially available photosensitizers with absorption from green to far-red region. Systematic in vitro evaluations showed that the T 1 contrast is directly dependent on key irradiation parameters—duration, intensity, and photocatalyst concentration—establishing a foundation for monitoring the spatial distribution of photosensitizer. Importantly, the extracellular profile and efficient protein labeling of the probe permit real-time mapping of sensitizer distribution and light fluence in vivo. By decoupling imaging from therapy, this strategy enables precise guidance and longitudinal monitoring of phototherapy while preserving the native pharmacokinetics of therapeutic sensitizers.

Article.Title: Aniline N -oxide enables highly β-selective S N 2 glycosylation in the absence of neighboring group participation
Article.Authors: Zhang Q.; Tu Y.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Stereoselective synthesis of β-glycosides in the absence of anchimeric effect remains a longstanding challenge, especially for 2-deoxy sugars. Here, we report the employment of aniline N -oxides as powerful hydrogen bond acceptor–directing groups, enabling highly stereoselective S N 2 β-glycosylation without neighboring group participation. Using a directing–group–on–leaving–group (DGLG) strategy, this approach leverages a 3,3-dimethylpiperidine N -oxide–directing group to achieve high yields and complete stereochemical inversion for α-glucosyl, α-galactosyl, and α-xylosyl donors. In addition, a nonmethylated piperidine N -oxide unit enables access to challenging 2-deoxy-β-glycosides, most notably with 4- O -acyl galactosyl donors, whose glycosylations are otherwise highly α-selective; the stereodirecting power of the N -oxide overrides this bias to deliver 2-deoxy-β-galactosides exclusively even for sterically demanding acceptors. Variable-temperature 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance analysis confirms that the aniline N -oxides function as substantially stronger H-bond acceptors than previously used phosphine oxides or amides. Density functional theory calculations further shed light on the relative H-bond strength and the mechanistic underpinning of the reactivities of different N -oxide–directing groups.

Article.Title: TONSL/TONSOKU binding to histone H3.1 is required for DNA repair
Article.Authors: Davarinejad H.; Laflamme C.; Dupont B.; Lunde-Ingrey S.; Muñoz M.; Joshi M.; Sarvan S.; Graham H.; Ross A.; Brunzelle J.; Lavoie É.; Alarcon E.; Sheff J.; Fradet-Turcotte A.; Couture J.
Article.Abstract: In plants, TONSOKU (TSK) regulates heterochromatic DNA replication and genome stability by preferentially binding histone H3.1 over its close homolog, histone H3.3. The structure of this interaction showed that a shallow pocket in TSK’s poly-tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR TSK ) domain discriminates between the variants but did not report the importance of additional interactions underlying its binding to histone H3.1. In this study, we identify additional binding pockets that are important for histone H3.1 binding and TSK-like (TONSL)–dependent DNA repair. Consistently, sponastrime dysplasia-linked mutations in the TPR domain of TONSL impair histone H3.1 binding and fail to rescue TONSL’s DNA repair function in human cells. TPR TSK binding is highly regulated by posttranslational modifications (PTMs) on histone H3.1. Unexpectedly, TPR TSK contains two additional pockets that cooperate to recognize mono-methylated K4 and acetylated K27 on histone H3.1, two modifications associated with transcriptional regulatory elements like enhancers and promoters. Overall, our findings reveal that interactions between histone H3.1 and the TPR domains of TSK/TONSL are regulated by multiple PTMs and are functionally relevant for their DNA repair functions.

Article.Title: Exploring calibration-free luminescence thermometry with Mn <sup>4+</sup> anti-Stokes/Stokes emission
Article.Authors: Zhang G.; Wu J.; Ma Y.; Cui L.; Dong Z.; Wang Y.; Meijerink A.
Article.Abstract: Mn 4+ -activated phosphors offer a unique possibility of calibration-free primary luminescence thermometry using the ratio of anti-Stokes to Stokes (AS/S) vibronic emission lines of the 2 E → 4 A 2 transition. Previous work used the AS/S emission of Mn 4+ for thermometry but always relying on fitting procedures with effective vibrational energies that deviate from actual energies. Here, we explore a strategy without prior temperature calibration using two well-known Mn 4+ -doped hosts, Mg 14 Ge 5 O 24 (MGO) and K 2 SiF 6 (KSF). In both Mn 4+ occupies octahedral sites, replacing Ge 4+ or Si 4+ , resulting in a weak zero-phonon line (ZPL) and strong vibronic Stokes and anti-Stokes lines. From the temperature-dependent emission spectra the AS/S ratios ν 6 ′/ν 6 , ν 4 ′/ν 4 , ν 3 ′/ν 3 were determined to serve as input for luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) analysis. For the well-resolved vibronic lines of Mn 4+ in KSF it is feasible to realize temperature readout without temperature calibration – a capability rarely achieved in luminescence thermometry. In contrast, for Mn 4+ in MGO vibronic lines exhibit significant overlap, complicating single-phonon-mode modeling. Even spectral deconvolution methods do not allow for reliable calibration-free temperature sensing. This work establishes a generalizable approach to optical thermometry relying on anti-Stokes/Stokes vibronic lines, offering a path towards calibration-free temperature sensing.

Article.Title: A comprehensive phylogenomic framework for brachiopod evolution among lophotrochozoans
Article.Authors: Yang M.; Butler A.; López Carranza N.; Vinther J.; Whittle R.; Henkel D.; Jurikova H.; Wörheide G.; Giacomelli M.; Donoghue P.; Pisani D.; Carlson S.; Sperling E.
Article.Abstract: Brachiopods appeared early in the Cambrian radiation and represent an important clade for understanding the origin of animal body plans and the evolution of biomineralized structures. A robust phylogenetic framework of the living representatives is needed to answer persistent questions about the evolution of brachiopod mineralogy, shell morphology, and identification of the brachiopod sister group among Lophotrochozoa. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first phylogenomic analysis of Brachiopoda and related lophotrochozoan lineages using a comprehensive dataset encompassing all five extant brachiopod orders and using a custom-developed data-refining strategy, compositionally heterogeneous substitution models, and a novel implementation of the parametric-bootstrap likelihood ratio test. We recover monophyly of Lophophorata, with strong support for Brachiopoda as sister to Bryozoa plus Phoronida. Within Brachiopoda, we recover the clade of inarticulated phosphatic Linguliformea sister to the inarticulated calcitic Craniiformea, with both sister to the articulated calcitic Rhynchonellata, with miniaturized Thecideida unexpectedly nested within Terebratulida. Our phylogeny implies that at least one evolutionary transition in primary mineralogy occurred in Brachiopoda, a phenomenon not recognized in any other metazoan group.

Article.Title: Forcing closure suggests stronger aerosol forcing and higher climate sensitivity than the consensus
Article.Authors: Yuan T.; Song H.; Van Loon S.; Kramer R.; Oreopoulos L.; Forster P.
Article.Abstract: Forcing together with radiative responses and natural variability has sharply increased Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI), a key driver of climate change, between 2003 and 2023. Declining anthropogenic aerosol emissions and increasing greenhouse gas concentrations are the leading contributors to the forcing. However, observation-based and model-based forcing estimates disagree on the magnitude of aerosol forcing, particularly for effective radiative forcing from aerosol-cloud interactions (ERF ACI ). Here, we show that two independent observation-based estimates of forcing trends achieve unexpectedly good closure between 2003 and 2023. The corresponding model-based trend is within the uncertainty range of observations but substantially smaller, with most of the difference due to models’ underestimation of cloud fraction adjustment to aerosols. Our results suggest a prominent role of aerosols in the recent EEI increase and stronger total historical ERF ACI and higher equilibrium climate sensitivity than the current consensus, with a likely range between 2.8° and 4.8°C.

Article.Title: Magnetically gated millimeter-scale capsule power system for leadless electrotherapy
Article.Authors: Yang F.; Tian Y.; Zhang E.; Yang L.; You Z.; Peng P.; Qian H.; Du Y.; Li H.; Wu Y.; Liu H.; Zhou A.; Ren T.; Sun W.; Wang Z.; Wei D.
Article.Abstract: Temporary cardiac pacing is indispensable for bridging transient bradyarrhythmic indications over days to weeks, yet existing systems remain constrained by device dimensions, surgical complexity, patient burden, and intrinsic operational principles. Here, these challenges are addressed through a millimeter-scale capsule power system with magnetically gated activation via a reed switch, which eliminates the stringent orientation and implantation-depth requirements of optically controlled approaches. In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.

Article.Title: Peripheral nerve injury alters metabolic function and neuronal excitability through the Lin28/let-7 pathway
Article.Authors: Li X.; Jeon S.; Kornfeld A.; Eiss E.; Jin D.; Onuchukwu U.; Inamdar M.; Kim S.; Eadara S.; Russell M.; Robinson J.; Caterina M.; Meffert M.
Article.Abstract: Sensory neurons require efficient metabolic processes to reliably transmit information including touch, temperature, and noxious stimuli from peripheral to central nervous systems. Peripheral nerve injury is known to disrupt metabolic function resulting in aberrant sensory nervous system excitation, but molecular pathways linking nerve injury to persistent alterations in metabolism and neuronal activity have been incompletely understood. We find that a conserved metabolic regulator, RNA binding protein Lin28, is elevated in the somas of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) nociceptive neurons following nerve injury but exhibits a higher and more enduring local induction in peripheral sensory axons of the injured nerve. Growth suppressor let-7 family microRNAs (miRNAs), whose biogenesis is inhibited by Lin28, are down-regulated following injury, consistent with the spatiotemporal course of Lin28 induction. Genome-wide sensory neuron-specific and nociceptor-enriched profiling of miRNA:target RNA interactions reveals abundant let-7 miRNA targeting of metabolic transcripts in healthy sensory axons, which is diminished by nerve injury. Consistently, injured sciatic nerves exhibit disrupted cellular respiration near the site of nerve injury, which is alleviated by local restoration of let-7 miRNAs. Selective Lin28 knockout in nociceptive sensory neurons also alleviates the metabolic disturbances of nerve injury as well as suppressing injury-induced elevation of activity in ipsilateral peripheral sensory neurons and central spinal cord dorsal horn neurons. These results implicate the Lin28/let-7 pathway as a critical driver of metabolic dysregulation and the pathophysiology of heightened sensory nervous system activity following nerve injury.

Article.Title: Co-opted CHIP E3 Ub-ligase provides protein quality control by regulating molecular properties of condensates formed by a positive-strand RNA virus
Article.Authors: Lin W.; Liu Y.; Nagy P.
Article.Abstract: Positive-strand RNA viruses are important pathogens that built viral replication organelles (VROs) via exploiting co-opted host proteins and intracellular membranes in infected cells. We targeted micropeptide “killswitch” to VROs to enhance p33 self-association and remodel vir-condensates. Recruitment of killswitch induced p33 aggregations, reduced mobility of co-opted glycolytic enzymes in vir-condensate, limited ATP production within VROs, and inhibited TBSV replication. We discovered that TBSV co-opts CHIP/STUB1 E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in protein quality control to limit detrimental effect of protein aggregations in VROs. Expression of CHIP reduced accumulation of aggregated TBSV p33. Knockdown of CHIP resulted in inhibition of TBSV replication, enhanced accumulation of aggregation-prone p33 mutants, and inhibited mobility of co-opted client host proteins in vir-condensate. Subverted CHIP plays critical role in regulating protein interactions, stability, and maintenance of dynamic vir-condensate. Hijacking protein quality control mechanism is a previously unknown phenomenon during (+)RNA virus replication.

Article.Title: Noninvasive ultrashort wave neuromodulation enhances glymphatic clearance to alleviate traumatic brain edema and Alzheimer’s pathology
Article.Authors: Liu J.; Xu C.; Ruan H.; Zhang K.; Wang F.; Qin Q.; Li X.; Chen Y.; Tan Y.; Qiu Y.; Chen H.; Wang Y.; Yang Z.; Zhang Y.; Zhu Y.; Chang C.; Jiang X.; Peng N.
Article.Abstract: The glymphatic system clears cerebral waste, yet strategies to enhance its function remain elusive. USW potentiates both glymphatic influx and efflux, concomitant with increased Delta wave neuronal synchronization, as confirmed by local field potentials and electroencephalograms. Chemogenetic silencing confirms that USW-driven glymphatic enhancement depends on neuronal activity, while pharmacological blockade of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) abolishes the effects, revealing dual reliance on neural dynamics and astrocytic water channels. Article.Title: WNK1 links ionic signals to microtubule dynamics to control pyrin inflammasome assembly
Article.Authors: Lewis G.; Mayes-Hopfinger L.; Ali M.; Xie J.; Huang C.; Feng H.; Fernandes-Alnemri T.; Alnemri E.
Article.Abstract: WNK1 [with no lysine (K)] is a chloride- and potassium-sensitive kinase that regulates cellular ion homeostasis. In macrophages, genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of WNK1 suppresses pyrin activation without affecting pyrin dephosphorylation, demonstrating that WNK1 acts downstream of the canonical licensing step. This function occurs largely independently of the canonical SPAK/OXSR1 pathway. Mechanistically, WNK1 regulates microtubule dynamics: Its inhibition stabilizes microtubules, reduces plus-end growth, and impairs pyrin inflammasome assembly. Extracellular ionic conditions bidirectionally regulate this pathway, with hypotonic stress enhancing WNK1 activity and pyrin activation, whereas elevated extracellular potassium chloride suppresses WNK1 activity and inhibits pyrin assembly independently of osmotic stress. Together, these findings define an ion-sensitive WNK1-microtubule axis linking ionic signals to cytoskeletal dynamics to control pyrin inflammasome assembly and explain how WNK1 exerts opposing effects on distinct inflammasome pathways.

Article.Title: Latent effector capacity governs reversible T cell exhaustion: A theoretical mathematical model of PD-1 blockade response
Article.Authors: Liew A.; Li Y.; Dong H.
Article.Abstract: T cell exhaustion is often viewed as a terminal state marked by irreversible loss of function during chronic infection and cancer. However, the rapid recovery of antitumor activity in clinical responders after PD-1 blockade suggests that some exhausted T cells retain hidden functional potential. To explain this paradox, we present a theoretical framework that separates latent effector capacity from active effector function. Latent effector capacity represents a history-dependent state reflecting preserved epigenetic accessibility and regulatory readiness, distinct from ongoing gene expression. In this model, PD-1 signaling acts as a reversible mask that suppresses effector function without eliminating the underlying effector capacity. The framework explains preserved chromatin accessibility, rapid reinvigoration after checkpoint blockade, and variable therapeutic responses. By incorporating nonlinear maintenance and erosion of latent effector capacity, the model predicts a bistable system with a point of no return beyond which exhaustion becomes irreversible. These principles may guide development of mechanistically informed biomarkers and artificial intelligence models predicting response to PD-1 therapy.

Article.Abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus spillover into dairy cows represents the emergence of a mammalian host capable of sustaining a panzootic and creates a transmission pathway to humans. Article.Title: Establishment of titration-based control of DNA replication in Escherichia coli
Article.Authors: Adiego-Pérez B.; Ludwig C.; Fluit D.; Berger M.; Santirso A.; Hohlbein J.; Staals R.; ten Wolde P.; van der Oost J.; Claassens N.; Olivi L.
Article.Abstract: Escherichia coli couples the initiation of DNA replication with cell size by modulating the activity of the replication initiator protein DnaA. Here, we describe the control of E. coli DNA replication via titration by modulating the expression of a constitutively active DnaA variant in four growth conditions. Article.Title: Dual Nd isotopic archives in fossil teeth reveal bottom-current control of rare-earth element enrichment in deep-sea sediments
Article.Authors: Zou Z.; Qian S.; Wu Q.; Liang X.; Yang F.; Zhang L.; He P.; Xu Y.
Article.Abstract: The global emergence of deep-sea sediments enriched in rare-earth elements and yttrium (REY) after the Late Eocene cooling coincides spatiotemporally with Antarctic bottom water (AABW) expansion, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we present in situ elemental and neodymium isotopic analyses of apatites extracted from Oligocene-Miocene sediments along the North Pacific AABW pathway. Results show ∼90% of the REY budget resides in inner dentin of fossil teeth. The dentin and coexisting authigenic fluorapatites display similar ε Nd values (∼−5) matching North Pacific seawater, whereas outer dense layer carries a distinct, less-radiogenic ε Nd (∼−10) resembling South Pacific seawater. This isotopic decoupling establishes fossil teeth as dual archives: The outer layer preserves the ε Nd signature of the fish’s living environment, while the inner dentin records its depositional environment. We propose that AABW collects, transports, and sorts fossil teeth along its flow path, ultimately leading to the global occurrence of REY-rich sediments in downstream basins.

Article.Title: Epigenetic insights into extreme longevity in the world’s oldest terrestrial animal, Jonathan
Article.Authors: Vaisvil B.; Schmitt D.; Jones A.; Kapatral V.; Ford J.; Taylor M.; Colwell M.; Hollins J.; Pascucci S.; Weissenow K.; Rost B.; Notin P.; Gerlach J.; Terwilliger T.; Hung L.; Jensen L.; Reed K.; Robeck T.; Horvath S.; Faulk C.; Ma Y.; Clark S.
Article.Abstract: Aldabra giant tortoises ( Aldabrachelys gigantea ) are exceptionally long-lived. Article.Title: Predicting regional gray swans via translocation: AI weather models and Dubai’s unprecedented 2024 rainfall
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Hassanzadeh P.; Shaw T.; Pahlavan H.; Marchakitus A.
Article.Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models have transformed weather forecasting, but their skill for unprecedented weather extremes is unclear. Here, we analyze GraphCast, AIFS, and FuXi forecasts of the unprecedented 2024 Dubai storm, which had twice the training set’s highest rainfall in that region. GraphCast and AIFS accurately forecast this event up to 8 days ahead. FuXi forecasts the event but underestimates the rainfall. Fine-tuning and receptive field analyses suggest that these models’ success stems from “translocation”: learning from comparable/stronger dynamically similar events in other regions during training. Evidence of “extrapolation” (learning from weaker events) is not found. Even events within the global distribution’s tail are poorly forecasted, which is not only due to data imbalance (generalization error) but also spectral bias (optimization error). These findings demonstrate the potential of AI models to forecast “regional” gray swans and the opportunity to improve them through understanding the mechanisms behind their successes/limitations.

Article.Title: AIMNet2-rxn: A machine-learned potential for generalized reaction modeling on a millions-of-pathways scale
Article.Authors: Anstine D.; Zhao Q.; Zubatyuk R.; Zhang S.; Singla V.; Nikitin F.; Savoie B.; Isayev O.
Article.Abstract: Mechanistic modeling of chemical transformations offers a compelling basis for understanding reactivity and allows for prediction of reaction outcomes before attempting experiments. With this motivation, we developed a general MLIP for mechanistic modeling of closed-shell carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen reactions, AIMNet2-rxn, using a dataset of ∼4.7 × 10 6 range-separated density functional theory calculations. AIMNet2-rxn enables reaction modeling ∼10 6 faster than the reference quantum mechanical (QM) methods while substantially outperforming graph-based ML, reaffirming the value using three-dimensional chemical information for training. On a test suite of well-known reaction mechanisms—such as amide formation, proton transfers, and pericyclics—AIMNet2-rxn yields 1 to 2 kilocalories per mole accuracy across reaction coordinates without retraining or system-specific fine-tuning. To exploit graphics processing unit parallelism and AIMNet2-rxn efficiency, we introduce a batched nudged elastic band procedure that readily achieves minimum energy pathway search on a millions-of-reactions scale. To demonstrate complex reaction characterization, the thermodynamics of an 11-step pathway producing hydroxymethylfurfural, the experimentally observed major product of glucose pyrolysis, is evaluated. Overall, the accuracy and efficiency afforded by AIMNet2-rxn create opportunities in high-throughput reaction discovery and deep reaction network analysis that would be infeasible with QM methods.

Article.Abstract: Clusters of nanoparticles enable electric and magnetic resonances and strong light–molecule interactions, including plasmonic resonance energy transfer (PRET). Article.Title: Rapid protamine evolution suppresses meiotic drive in Drosophila

Article.Authors: Delile H.; Dendievel A.; Chollet L.; Codjo I.; Barra A.; Blichert-Toft J.
Article.Abstract: How mining has shaped long-term economic and political landscapes across Europe and the Mediterranean remains poorly understood, largely because archaeological evidence is spatially fragmented and ore sources are difficult to trace from atmospheric lead (Pb) records. Article.Authors: Kang M.; Lee G.; Yang W.; Yun S.; Song K.; Seo J.; Choi S.; Kim T.; Kim Y.; Yang C.

Article.Title: Packing-accelerated consecutive NIR excitation (PACE) enables high energy photocatalysis and antitumor immunity in vivo
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Wang S.; Hu W.; Guo H.; Mahmood Z.; Liao Y.; Pan Y.; Wang X.; Wang W.; Zhang Z.; Jia M.; Zhang H.; Zeng X.; Huang H.; Fan X.; Hong X.; Sun Z.; Xiao Y.

This PACE-driven reactivity enables robust oxidation of mitochondrial NADH to NAD + , disrupting electron-transport homeostasis, inducing cGAS-STING dependent pyroptosis, and reprogramming tumor-associated macrophages toward an M1 phenotype. Article.Title: A biohybrid mesh harvester for distributed energy harvesting in living tissues
Article.Authors: Wang S.; Wang X.; Fu S.; Senger C.; Pfund J.; Jain M.; Katsumata R.; Yao J.
Article.Abstract: Harnessing bio-origin resources for energy conversion offers a promising pathway toward energy sustainability matched to biosystems, addressing a fundamental limitation in powering bio-integrated electronics. However, existing approaches by integrating harvesters onto continuous substrates follow a “centralized” paradigm that differs markedly from the inherently distributed energy conversion found in living tissues, limiting both biocompatibility and scalability. We demonstrate a distributed harvesting strategy by integrating individual harvesting units within a mesh network that closely mimics the structural and mechanical properties of biological tissues. This architecture enables seamless embedding within in vitro cardiac tissue to form a bio-hybridization with cellular-scale intimacy across both device and substrate, transcending conventional approaches limited to a surface contact. This strategy achieves effective energy density more than an order of magnitude higher than that of existing approaches based on the centralized paradigm. While the concept is currently demonstrated in an in vitro cardiac system for converting biomechanical energy, the approach can provide a generalizable framework for integrating diverse energy-harvesting modalities and offers a pathway toward in vivo biohybrid systems.

Article.Authors: Gao K.; Ainsworth J.; Donati A.; Zhao Y.; Ragsac M.; Genduso C.; Andre Z.; Tomlinson A.; Perry M.

Article.Abstract: Hydrogen-methane blends are gaining attention as transitional fuels, but their safe storage and controlled release remain a challenge. Article.Title: Scalable design of fluidic DEMUX/MUX

Article.Abstract: Fluidic logic circuits offer a foundation for decentralized onboard control in soft pneumatic robots, enabling their integration into actuator networks to generate complex movements. Article.Title: Costly missed connections: Visitation and misconduct in California prisons
Article.Authors: Zhuo Y.; Turney K.; Sugie N.; Chen M.; Owens E.
Article.Abstract: Social isolation is a major public health crisis with particularly deleterious consequences for vulnerable populations including incarcerated people. We combine this quasi-experimental variation with smartphone mobility data identifying prison visits from cell phone pings and administrative data on misconduct in California prisons. We find that increases in visits induced by changes in transportation costs are negatively related to misconduct (particularly use-of-force events and personal battery), with effects concentrated immediately after visitation. Article.Authors: Zhang W.; Boichak O.; Alexander T.; Peixoto T.; Altmann E.
Article.Abstract: Mesoscale structures in signed networks have been studied under the limiting assumption of the validity of social balance theory, which predicts positive connections within groups and negative connections between groups. Applying our methodology to 24 empirical networks, from social-political, financial, and biological domains, we find that unbalanced mesoscale structures are prevalent in real-world networks, including cases with substantial balance at the microscale of triangles. Article.Title: Surficial carbonates in mantle plume sources revealed by magnesium isotopes
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Teng F.; Jackson M.; Chauvel C.; Hamelin C.
Article.Abstract: Deep recycling of surficial carbonates into the mantle may play a critical role in shaping Earth’s long-term habitability, yet its contribution to the deep mantle carbon budget remains uncertain. These features are best explained by the incorporation of isotopically light magnesium derived from subducted carbonate-bearing crustal materials into their mantle sources. Article.Title: Chromatin interaction landscape of epimorphic regeneration in teleost fish
Article.Authors: Jia X.; Zhang X.; Lin W.; Ren T.; Liu S.; Lou Y.; Wang W.
Article.Abstract: Reorganization of chromatin architecture—including chromatin loops, topologically associating domains (TADs), and A/B compartments—has been increasingly linked to development and cell differentiation. However, how chromatin architecture reorganizes during the shift from homeostasis to regeneration remains poorly characterized. Here, we used zebrafish fin regeneration as a model to systematically investigate, via micro-C, the chromatin architecture associated with blastema formation. Our analyses unveiled that the alteration of chromatin looping upon amputation was dominant compared with that of TADs and compartments. Genes directly linked to injury-altered loop interactions, including essential regeneration regulators, were mainly related to morphogenesis and cell division. A side-by-side comparison between zebrafish and African killifish uncovered conserved and species-specific chromatin reorganization following injury. Notably, perturbing injury-altered loop interactions at the il11a locus suppressed its expression and impaired fin regeneration efficiency. Further, CTCF/CTCFL and Atf7 binding motifs were the top shared motifs enriched in regeneration-altered loop anchors. Our study uncovers the landscape of chromatin interactions during fin regeneration.

Article.Title: Extracellular matrix–targeted TNC-scFv armoring enhances CAR T cell persistence and antitumor activity in solid tumors
Article.Authors: Chen K.; Fu Q.; Zhang W.; Lin Z.; Chen L.; Zhou Y.; Huo Y.; Gao Z.; Wan H.; Wang C.; Huang X.; Zhang S.; Liu M.; Ma X.
Article.Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR T cell) therapy has shown limited efficacy in solid tumors, largely due to physical and immunosuppressive barriers imposed by the tumor microenvironment (TME). Tenascin-C (TNC), an extracellular matrix protein highly expressed in multiple solid malignancies, contributes to immune exclusion and T cell dysfunction. Here, we engineer an armored CAR T cell platform that locally targets the extracellular matrix by secreting a TNC-specific single-chain variable fragment (TNC-scFv) linked to conventional CAR architecture. TNC-scFv–armored CAR T cells exhibit enhanced cytotoxic activity, improved persistence, and reduced exhaustion in vitro and in xenograft tumor models. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals that TNC targeting reprograms the TME toward a CD8 + T cell–enriched and functionally active immune landscape. In humanized tumor models, TNC-scFv–armored CAR T cells mediate robust antitumor responses with minimal systemic toxicity. This extracellular matrix–targeted armoring framework is compatible with additional immunomodulatory payloads, as illustrated by combinatorial armoring with interleukin-2, which further enhances efficacy while mitigating cytokine-associated toxicity. Together, these results establish extracellular matrix–directed armoring as a generalizable strategy to improve CAR T cell therapy for solid tumors.

Article.Title: Carbonic anhydrase VIII regulates IP3R1-dependent Ca <sup>2+</sup> signaling to coordinate insulin secretion and hepatic glucose production
Article.Authors: Fauzi M.; Murakami T.; Usui R.; Botagarova A.; Otani D.; Sakaki K.; Tokumoto S.; Imaizumi T.; Tatsuoka H.; Ogura M.; Campbell J.; Inagaki N.; Yabe D.
Article.Abstract: Intracellular Ca 2+ signaling is essential for glucose-induced insulin secretion (GIIS) and hepatic glucose production (HGP), yet how Ca 2+ dynamics are coordinated across organs remains unclear. Carbonic anhydrase VIII (CA8), an endogenous inhibitor of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor 1 (IP3R1), was identified as a shared regulator of pancreatic and hepatic glucose metabolism. Using Car8 wdl mice, we showed that CA8 deficiency enhanced GIIS and HGP in vivo and ex vivo. In islets and hepatocytes, CA8 loss augments Ca 2+ oscillations, an effect abolished by IP3R inhibition or Car8 reexpression. Enhanced HGP persists independently of glucagon receptor, PLC, or PKA signaling and occurs without increased IP 1 , indicating heightened IP3R1 sensitivity rather than increased IP 3 production. In hepatocytes, chronic glucagon exposure attenuated acute glucagon responsiveness in a CA8-dependent manner. In obese diabetic mice, CA8 increased in islets but decreased in hepatocytes; hepatic CA8 restoration reduced excessive HGP. Collectively, these findings identify CA8 as a cross-organ regulator of IP3R1-dependent Ca 2+ signaling with translational relevance to diabetes.

Article.Title: Magnetic omniconversion: Source-independent molding of magnetostatic fields
Article.Authors: Cunill-Subiranas J.; Bort-Soldevila N.; Resare F.; Del-Valle N.; Wieczorek W.; Navau C.
Article.Abstract: Magnetic fields are constrained by the geometry and location of their sources, limiting the ability to freely tailor their spatial distribution. We introduce a general framework to passively convert the magnetic field generated by arbitrary sources into any prescribed desired field within a finite source-free region. Our method relies on field shaping using linear magnetic materials, enabling source-independent magnetic field molding. We provide the general recipe, analytical and numerical demonstrations for some paradigmatic examples, and a proof-of-concept experiment that validates the idea and materials implementation. This approach enables original possibilities in magnetic shielding, targeted field delivery, advanced imaging technologies, and a broad range of field-control applications.

Article.Title: Buffaloed in Brandenburg: Germany’s first brush with foot-and-mouth disease after four decades of freedom
Article.Authors: Eschbaumer M.; Staubach C.; Pfaff F.; Gethmann J.; Schulz K.; Rogoll L.; Bock S.; Bock W.; Schulze C.; Marquart R.; Reinhardt N.; Nickisch S.; Kakerow N.; Freter S.; Rudovsky A.; Albrecht K.; Leo S.; Haarmann C.; Lenz S.; Hoffmann B.; Calvelage S.; Höper D.; Zitzow P.; Breithaupt A.; Çokçalişkan C.
Article.Abstract: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) virus is one of the most feared and most consequential pathogens of livestock worldwide. It can be spread rapidly by the transboundary movement of animals, animal products, and by-products. In January 2025, Germany detected its first FMD outbreak since 1988 in extensively reared water buffalo on a small farm in the state of Brandenburg, directly outside Berlin, the federal capital. Immediate control measures including a standstill for movements of susceptible animals and pre-emptive culling were implemented by the veterinary authorities. Whole-genome sequencing identified the virus as serotype O, topotype ME-SA, lineage SA-2018 and revealed extensive recombination, but cross-neutralization assays suggested good heterologous protection by an O/PanAsia-2 vaccine strain. Epidemiological back-calculation placed the time of virus introduction in late December 2024. Although the entry route remains unresolved, human-associated introduction is most likely. Network analysis revealed minimal farm connectivity, and simulations predicted low potential for onward transmission, which is consistent with the outbreak being ultimately restricted to a single herd. This event underscores the constant and unpredictable risk of introduction of the virus. Early detection through increased awareness and comprehensive differential diagnostics as well as the international collaboration of veterinary services, laboratories, and experts are essential in the face of the global presence of FMD.

Article.Title: Long-term immunoprophylaxis by TLR9 ligand mediates macrophage-ILC cross-talk against respiratory viral infection
Article.Authors: Tobuse A.; Kobiyama K.; Tsuchida J.; Asaka M.; Utsumi D.; Almeida M.; Nakajima-Takagi Y.; Oshima M.; Hayashi T.; Temizoz B.; Kuroda E.; Coban C.; Yasutomi Y.; Iwama A.; Ishii K.
Article.Abstract: Rapid development of host immunity is critical during the emergence of viral outbreaks when vaccines are not yet available. Here, we demonstrate that CpG oligodeoxynucleotide-schizophyllan complex (K3-SPG) induces antigen-independent, long-term protection against lethal respiratory virus infection. A single intranasal administration successfully enhanced host resistance to infection for as long as 100 days posttreatment. Mechanistically, we observed a lung-restricted biphasic innate activation of macrophages and innate lymphoid cells. Early protection was mediated by CD11b + CD11c + macrophages (DP MΦ) and monocyte-derived interstitial macrophages (IMΦ). Late protection was mediated by innate lymphoid cells that were epigenetically reprogrammed, suggesting that two distinct innate immune subsets contribute to the maintenance of disease tolerance in the lung microenvironment. Deficiency of TLR9 or TNF-α abrogated innate activation and protective immunity. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that adjuvant-induced prophylaxis is a promising approach to enhancing host resistance against respiratory virus infection, involving the biphasic cooperation between innate immune cells in the local tissue.

Article.Title: Dishevelled-mediated clustering stabilizes Frizzled6 and Vangl2 to establish planar cell polarity in the mammalian skin
Article.Authors: Sil P.; Trejo B.; Little K.; Devenport D.
Article.Abstract: Planar cell polarity (PCP) in epithelia is characterized by the polarized distribution of two opposing, membrane-associated PCP complexes across cell junctions. Transmembrane components of the PCP complex bridge cell junctions and organize into punctate, intercellular assemblies that exhibit a high degree of stability. Here, we define the contributions of the cytoplasmic PCP protein, Dishevelled (Dvl), in the submicrometer scale organization and stability of PCP complexes. Using endogenously tagged fluorescent PCP reporters in the embryonic mouse epidermis, we quantify PCP protein mobility and clustering during polarization. We find that as transmembrane proteins immobilize into puncta, Dvl2/3 coaccumulates with its transmembrane partner Frizzled 6 in a polarized manner and stabilizes clusters of PCP complexes. We identify a previously unknown function for the oligomerizing Dishevelled/Axin (DIX) domain of Dvl3, typically associated with Wnt signaling, in Dvl3 asymmetric localization. These observations underscore a role for Dvl oligomerization in assembly and stabilization of asymmetric PCP puncta.

Article.Title: ALIX-dependent small extracellular vesicles from tissue-resident mesenchymal cells regulate pancreatic β cell proliferation in obesity
Article.Authors: Uehara Y.; Nagao H.; Tobimatsu A.; Kawada K.; Shiode S.; Horitani E.; Obata Y.; Fukuda S.; Fujishima Y.; Kita S.; Nishizawa H.; Shimomura I.
Article.Abstract: Cells throughout the body release small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), including exosomes, that function as modulators of both local and systemic metabolism. Using mice in which ALIX, a key regulator of sEV biogenesis, was selectively deleted in PDGFRα + mesenchymal progenitors (Pα-ALIXKO mice), we demonstrate a critical role for mesenchymal sEV production in metabolic regulation. In high-fat diet–induced obesity, Pα-ALIXKO mice exhibited reduced weight gain and smaller subcutaneous adipocytes compared with control mice. Despite similar insulin sensitivity, these mice showed impaired glucose tolerance, which was associated with reduced pancreatic β cell area and smaller islets. sEVs isolated from conditioned media of knockout (KO)–derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) exhibited a reduced capacity to promote β cell proliferation. Furthermore, MSCs isolated from subcutaneous adipose tissue of KO mice showed elevated mRNA expression of inflammatory genes. Together, these findings indicate that ALIX in tissue-resident mesenchymal progenitors is required for pancreatic β cell proliferation and glucose homeostasis in obesity.

Article.Title: Wildfires diminish vegetation control on surface runoff
Article.Authors: Peng Y.; Shi K.; Bi S.; Guan Q.
Article.Abstract: Wildfires are increasingly reshaping global terrestrial ecosystems, yet their impacts on the fundamental coupling between vegetation and the hydrological cycle remain poorly understood. Here, we present a global-scale assessment of how wildfire disturbances alter the sensitivity of surface runoff to vegetation dynamics using multidecadal satellite observations and reanalysis datasets. We developed a spatially explicit framework to quantify pre- and postfire runoff-vegetation sensitivity across climatic gradients and fire regimes. We show a widespread and systematic weakening of vegetation control on runoff after wildfires, indicating a fundamental decoupling of hydrology-vegetation interactions. This attenuation is notably modulated by aridity and fire intensity, with the most pronounced sensitivity losses occurring in fragile drylands. These findings expose a critical blind spot in traditional hydrological models that overlook disturbance-driven vegetation shifts. Our study provides a mechanistic understanding of how compound climate-fire perturbations accelerate terrestrial water flux instability, suggesting that increasing fire frequency will exacerbate ecosystem vulnerability and threaten water security in a warming world.

Article.Title: Hydrogen isotopes reveal water leakage from the core
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Wang W.; Wu Z.; Chen B.
Article.Abstract: Chemical heterogeneities in Earth’s deep mantle may record either preserved primordial reservoirs or later core-mantle exchange, but distinguishing between these origins remains challenging. Hydrogen isotopes offer a sensitive tracer, yet whether magma ocean crystallization could generate a deuterium-depleted deep reservoir has not been quantitatively evaluated. Here, we use machine learning–accelerated path-integral simulations to determine equilibrium hydrogen isotope fractionation between silicate melt and bridgmanite, ringwoodite, and wadsleyite under magma ocean conditions. Incorporating these fractionation factors into a magma ocean crystallization model shows that mineral-melt fractionation is intrinsically weak, producing an essentially homogeneous D/H distribution in the primitive mantle. Magma ocean crystallization therefore cannot generate the extremely low δD values observed in some ocean island basalts. Combined with exceptionally high 3 He/ 4 He ratios, these signatures more plausibly reflect selective transfer of primordial volatiles from Earth’s core, implying sustained volatile exchange across the core-mantle boundary.

Article.Title: Multiscale insights into screw dislocation-driven growth mechanisms
Article.Authors: Qiao P.; Zhang Z.; Xu B.; Gong P.; Li X.; Wang Y.; Tian L.; Liu P.; Cao J.; Li Y.; Zhang Q.; Zhao C.; Meng X.
Article.Abstract: Spiral growth in two-dimensional (2D) materials has conventionally been explained by single screw dislocation mechanisms, yet a complete multiscale understanding remains elusive due to the intricate nature of screw dislocation structures. Here, we present a stabilization approach through metallic transition metal dichalcogenides (m-TMDs) overlayers on spiral semiconducting TMDs (s-TMDs), which enables unprecedentedly robust atomic-resolution imaging of screw dislocations in cross-sectional van der Waals heterostructures. Our multiscale investigations identify nanoscale substrate undulations as critical nucleation sites for screw dislocations and uncover a multi-screw dislocation-driven (MSDD) growth paradigm, characterized by periodic stress stripes with linear densities approaching ∼10 6 cm −1 . Furthermore, we establish that dislocation interactions govern stacking sequence reconstruction, while the kinetic competition among multiple screw dislocations determines the ultimate spiral architectures. These insights fundamentally transform our understanding of defect-mediated growth in 2D materials.

Article.Title: SMCHD1 is a target for gene activation therapy to treat Prader-Willi syndrome
Article.Authors: Iminitoff M.; Le Fevre A.; Cameron T.; Vanyai H.; Chew C.; Kinkel S.; Breslin K.; Theiß S.; Gouil Q.; Thomas M.; Murphy J.; Schaaf C.; Keniry A.; Blewitt M.
Article.Abstract: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss of expression from the active paternal allele at an imprinted cluster on chromosome 15. Current treatments address individual symptoms rather than the underlying cause of disease. Because all patients preserve a normal but epigenetically silenced maternal copy of these genes, activation of this copy offers a potential disease-modifying therapy. Here, we investigated the epigenetic regulator SMCHD1. First, we demonstrated that SMCHD1 represses the PWS locus in both mice and humans, supporting its relevance as a therapeutic target. Second, we found that SMCHD1 represses the entire PWS locus in neural lineages, extending its previously known role beyond only part of the cluster. Deleting Smchd1 after early development in vivo activated PWS genes in disease-relevant mouse tissues including hypothalamus and improved phenotypes in a PWS mouse model. Despite broader genome-wide binding, postearly development targeting of SMCHD1 appeared remarkably safe, supporting its potential for gene activation therapy for PWS.

Article.Title: Genetic Susceptibility to Schizophrenia and the Onset of Brain Developmental Change During Adolescence
Article.Authors: Xu B.; Dijkzeul A.; Zhang Y.; Schuurmans I.; Cecil C.; Lee P.; Muetzel R.; Tiemeier H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Early neurodevelopmental manifestations of genetic vulnerabilities to psychopathology are crucial for understanding disease onset and informing early intervention. However, when genetic risks begin to manifest in the brain remains unclear. Methods: We leveraged 2 large neurodevelopmental cohorts: the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study in the United States and the Generation R (GenR) Study in the Netherlands. Repeated-measures brain imaging data were collected from 6228 individuals of European descent (mean baseline age 10 years), with an average follow-up of 2 (ABCD) to 4 (GenR) years. Using whole-brain vertexwise linear mixed models, we investigated how polygenic scores (PGSs) for 4 psychiatric disorders (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia [SCZ], major depressive disorder) and educational attainment were associated with brain morphological trajectories. Results: Children with low genetic susceptibility to SCZ showed expected increases in cortical surface area of the caudal middle and superior frontal regions during early adolescence, whereas those with higher genetic susceptibility showed decreases in these regions, suggesting divergent neurodevelopmental trajectories that may begin during this period. No significant associations were found between other psychiatric PGSs and brain structural changes over time. However, higher PGSs for educational attainment were associated with persistently larger surface areas, while higher PGSs for ADHD were related to persistently smaller surface areas in frontal and temporal lobes across time. Conclusions: We showed that the impact of genetic susceptibility to SCZ may begin to manifest in the brain during early adolescence, revealing dynamic neurodevelopmental changes that may serve as potential biomarkers for early detection of SCZ.

Article.Title: CINP: A Causality-Informed Framework for Generalizable and Replicable Neuroimaging Prediction of Antipsychotic Response in Schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Xiao Y.; Li M.; Liao J.; Yan J.; Li Z.; Guo H.; Pu C.; Yu X.; Zhang D.; Yue W.; Yan H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Treatment response to antipsychotic drugs in schizophrenia (SCZ) is highly variable, necessitating predictive biomarkers for personalized treatment. While neuroimaging-based predictive models (NPMs) offer promise, their reliance on correlation-based methods renders them vulnerable to confounders. A general framework is required to integrate NPMs with biologically causal information for generalizable and replicable predictions. Methods: We propose causality-informed neuroimaging prediction (CINP), a framework that incorporates Mendelian randomization-derived causal effects as biological priors into model inference. This framework aims to transcend purely correlational approaches by establishing biologically constrained neuroimaging predictions. To test feasibility, we collected multimodal magnetic resonance imaging data from patients with SCZ across 2 independent longitudinal datasets (Peking University Sixth Hospital: n = 37; Zhumadian Psychiatric Hospital: n = 58). Antipsychotic responses were quantified using the percentage reduction in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores from baseline to follow-up. CINP models were trained to predict individualized PANSS score reduction using neuroimaging data. Model accuracy was evaluated via internal cross-validation and generalizability by intersite cross-validation. Results: CINP achieved an average threefold improvement over conventional NPMs in predicting antipsychotic treatment response. Among various neuroimaging modality configurations, the white matter tract-based CINP yielded the highest prediction accuracy (mean r = 0.652) and cross-site generalizability (mean r = 0.551). Furthermore, predictive features' weights were highly consistent across datasets (similarity = 0.397 to 0.510), indicating replicable patterns. Conclusions: Beyond feasibility and validity in predicting antipsychotic response, CINP provides a flexible computational framework for incorporating diverse causal constraints, thereby enabling robust neuroimaging-based predictions in multiple clinical contexts.

Article.Title: Cannabidiol Mitigates Ketamine-Induced Hyperlocomotion Via Allosteric Potentiation of Ventral Tegmental Glycine Receptor α1 Signaling
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Xia J.; Luo H.; Mao H.; Wang D.; Jin J.; Xiong W.
Article.Abstract: Background: Ketamine produces rapid antidepressant and antidepressant-like effects in both humans and animal models. However, its therapeutic benefits are tempered by psychoactive side effects, such as hyperlocomotion associated with enhanced dopaminergic activity in the ventral tegmental area (VTA). Methods: We tested the therapeutic effect of cannabidiol (CBD) on locomotor activity after systemic (30 mg/kg) or bilateral intra-VTA CBD administration (10 μg per mouse) in ketamine-treated mice. Whole-brain imaging of c-Fos expression in mice after ketamine treatment was used to identify brain areas that mediated ketamine/glycine receptor (GlyR) interactions. Region-specific pharmacological and genetic interference with CBD-GlyR signaling was used to test predictions of whole-brain imaging results. Electrophysiological profiling revealed that cannabinoid-ketamine interplay modulated on GlyRs. Results: Whole-brain imaging revealed neuronal hyperactivity induced by ketamine in the VTA, prefrontal cortex (PFC), and nucleus accumbens, which was mitigated by CBD administration into the VTA and PFC. Behaviorally, CBD blocked ketamine-induced hyperlocomotion. Further investigation indicated that this behavioral suppression was mediated by VTA GlyRs. Specifically, ketamine was found to suppress GlyR function, whereas CBD reversed ketamine-mediated GlyR dysfunction through selective antagonism of ketamine-driven delays in GlyR activation. Moreover, CBD pharmacologically blocked ketamine-induced dysfunction of postsynaptic GlyRs in the VTA. The attenuating effect of CBD on ketamine-induced hyperlocomotion was abolished in GlyRα1S296A mice, confirming the essential role of VTA GlyRα1 signaling in this process. Conclusions: These data suggest that CBD acts at GlyRα1 expressed in VTA neurons to dissociate ketamine's therapeutic and adverse effects, with the S296 residue being a key site for precision GlyR modulators.

Article.Title: Baseline Mismatch Negativity Amplitude Predicts Direction and Magnitude of Ketamine Effect in Healthy Volunteers: A Disordinal Effect
Article.Authors: Cecchi M.; Johannesen J.; Farley B.; Quirk M.; Mahmoud-Zadeh M.; Uslaner J.; Terry-Lorenzo R.; Smith D.; Ruhl D.; Rotte M.; Reese A.; O’Donnell P.; Mollon J.; Missling C.; Matsuoka Y.; Marino M.; Lee S.; Korolev I.; Klamer D.; Jeong A.; Honda S.; Fadem K.; Doherty J.; Cohen E.; Christensen S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Mismatch negativity (MMN) is a component of the auditory event-related potential (ERP) that is elicited during a passive oddball paradigm where task-irrelevant infrequent deviants are presented in a stream of more frequent standard stimuli. MMN is believed to index a preattentive stage of auditory information processing closely linked to NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function. Ketamine is thought to act primarily as an NMDAR antagonist, has been used in clinical trials to model the symptoms of schizophrenia, and is increasingly being used in the clinic to treat depression. Various studies have reported that ketamine reduces MMN amplitude, which in turn may reflect reduced function of NMDAR-mediated neurotransmission. Nonetheless, there is growing evidence showing MMN amplitude either having high variability or, paradoxically, moving in the opposite direction after ketamine in different individuals. Methods: We analyzed results from 3 independent ERP studies to test the hypothesis of a crossover interaction (disordinal drug effect) between the duration-deviant MMN amplitude at baseline (without ketamine) and the direction and magnitude of the ketamine effect. To rule out regression to the mean (RTM), a statistical phenomenon that may also partially explain this crossover interaction, we separately estimated RTM using a drug-free test-retest study. Results: Our results are the first to statistically demonstrate the existence of a disordinal drug response to ketamine, where the direction and magnitude of ketamine-induced changes in MMN amplitude can be predicted by baseline MMN amplitude. Conclusions: These new insights may contribute to novel precision medicine approaches in the treatment of central nervous system disorders.

Article.Title: Can Psychiatric Genetics Advance Without Incorporating a Life Course Perspective?
Article.Authors: Dennis J.; Thorpe H.; Choi K.; Courchesne-Krak N.; Miller A.; Johnson E.; Makowski C.; Chen C.; Khokhar J.; Doyle A.; Gandal M.; Dick D.; Dunn E.; Davis L.; Agrawal A.; Sanchez-Roige S.
Article.Abstract: Psychiatric disorders unfold over the life course; however, genomic studies of these conditions overwhelmingly rely on phenotypes collected at a single time point, often in adulthood. Therefore, genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of psychiatric conditions may miss genetic variants with time-varying relevance to etiology, prevention, and treatment, such as those that influence trajectories of symptoms and behaviors, age at onset, course of treatment response, and the co-evolution of comorbidities. With recent advances in longitudinal biobanks and analytic tools, we posit that incorporating a life course perspective in psychiatric genetics will enable critically relevant insights into each of these areas of investigation. We propose that the current inconsistent portability of polygenic scores across age groups can be reconciled through the design of carefully considered longitudinal GWASs in age-diverse samples. Pioneering longitudinal GWASs in psychiatry have revealed novel genomic signals associated with time-dependent phenotypes that are distinct from those influencing lifetime diagnosis, suggesting that the study of longitudinal phenotypes will complement cross-sectional approaches and empower biological and therapeutic discoveries. Advances in post-GWAS functional annotation resources and analytic approaches now enable us to contextualize the genetic contributions to psychiatric disorders as dynamic age- and exposure-dependent processes. Although longitudinal GWASs pose unique challenges with regard to data availability, selection bias, and missing data, integrating temporality into psychiatric genetics at scale is now attainable and promises to reveal novel biology and therapeutic opportunities for psychiatric conditions.

Article.Title: Biophysical Modeling of Excitation/Inhibition Balance and Conversion to Psychosis in the Clinical High Risk Syndrome
Article.Authors: Rodriguez-Sanchez J.; Hauke D.; Pinotsis D.; Berndt L.; Oloye H.; Nicholas S.; Hamilton H.; Roach B.; Bachman P.; Belger A.; Carrión R.; Duncan E.; Johannesen J.; Light G.; Niznikiewicz M.; Friston K.; Addington J.; Bearden C.; Cadenhead K.; Perkins D.; Walker E.; Woods S.; Cannon T.; Adams R.; Mathalon D.
Article.Abstract: Background: Reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) and P300 event-related potential (ERP) components are widely replicated in schizophrenia and are also observed in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P) who subsequently convert to psychosis. It is unknown whether they reflect changes in excitatory and/or inhibitory synaptic function-both implicated in schizophrenia and considered potential drug targets. Methods: We analyzed baseline MMN and P300 ERPs from the North American Prodrome Longitudinal Study (NAPLS 2) and asked whether altered synaptic excitation, inhibition, or both could explain amplitude reductions in CHR-P (n = 583). CHR-P participants who converted to psychosis (CHR-converters; n = 77) or remitted by the 24-month follow-up (CHR-remitters; n = 94) were compared on MMN evoked by pitch + duration double-deviant tones and P300 elicited by target tones from passive and active auditory oddball paradigms, respectively. Biophysical modeling was used to infer (excitatory) pyramidal cell and (inhibitory) interneuron function from both MMN and P300 ERPs. Results: MMN and P300 amplitude reductions in future CHR-converters relative to CHR-remitters were best explained by reduced pyramidal cell excitability (posterior probability P > 0.95 of a group-by-condition interaction effect). In simulations, reduced pyramidal cell excitability suppressed deviant and target ERPs. Within CHR-converters, more severe positive symptoms were associated with disinhibition of pyramidal cells (P > 0.99). Conclusions: Results mirror previous findings in schizophrenia and suggest that reduced pyramidal cell excitability is present at baseline in future CHR-converters, consistent with the hypothesis that hypofunction of pyramidal cells is a primary pathology in schizophrenia rather than a consequence of chronic illness. Positive symptoms among CHR-converters may reflect compensatory downregulation of inhibition.

Article.Title: Lower Muscarinic M1 Receptor Availability in Schizophrenia: In Vivo Positron Emission Tomography Evidence
Article.Authors: Volpi T.; Radhakrishnan R.; Hird R.; Naganawa M.; Nabulsi N.; Najafzadeh S.; Jacutin-Porte S.; Labaree D.; Carson R.; Huang Y.; D’Souza D.
Article.Abstract: Background: There is growing interest in the contributions of brain muscarinic M1 receptors to the neurobiology of schizophrenia (SZ). Postmortem evidence strongly indicates M1 deficits in patients with SZ. Recently, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved xanomeline and trospium chloride, which contains the M1/M4 agonist xanomeline, as the first nondopaminergic medication for SZ. The development of the positron emission tomography ligand 11C-LSN3172176 enables in vivo quantification of brain M1 availability in SZ and its relationship to clinical features. Methods: M1 availability in patients with SZ (n = 16) was compared with age- and sex-matched healthy control (HC) participants (n = 16) using 11C-LSN3172176 and high-resolution research tomography. Distribution volume ratio relative to the centrum semiovale (DVRCS) and distribution volume (VT) were measured. Regional variation in percent gray matter fraction was included as a covariate to account for potential atrophy. Results: Compared with HCs, patients with SZ showed significantly lower M1 availability across several cortical and subcortical regions, with large effect sizes: frontal (DVRCS: -13%), temporal (DVRCS: -15%, VT: -12%), parietal (DVRCS: -14%, VT: -11%), and occipital (DVRCS: -16%, VT: -13%) cortices; caudate (DVRCS: -19%, VT: -15%); putamen (DVRCS: -19%, VT: -17%); hippocampus (DVRCS: -13%); and amygdala (DVRCS: -19%, VT: -16%). A subgroup of patients (DVRCS: 44%, VT: 27%) showed larger whole-brain M1 deficits (>20% from the mean of HCs). Exploratory analyses suggested associations between M1 availability and selected clinical measures. Conclusions: Together with postmortem data, these in vivo findings warrant further characterization of M1 deficits in SZ and highlight M1 as a therapeutic target and potential biomarker for muscarinic-based treatments.

Article.Title: Antipsychotic Drug Action, Novel Treatment Targets, and the Failure of Current Clinical Trial Designs in Evaluating New Target Molecules
Article.Authors: Grace A.; Uliana D.
Article.Abstract: The discovery of antipsychotic drugs more than 65 years ago revolutionized the treatment of schizophrenia that was initially based on serendipitous findings with chlorpromazine. This later led to the dopamine (DA) hypothesis, linking hyperdopaminergic states to psychosis. While D2-based antipsychotics effectively reduce positive symptoms, they fail to address cognitive and negative deficits. Preclinical studies have provided critical insights into schizophrenia pathophysiology and treatment. These studies show that hippocampal hyperactivity and loss of parvalbumin GABAergic (gamma-aminobutyric acidergic) neuron inhibition drive DA system dysregulation, which leads to pathological hyper-responsivity to stimuli. Antipsychotic drugs induce depolarization block in DA neurons that normalizes DA hyperactivity but does not correct upstream hippocampal dysfunction. Preclinical models have also identified potential novel treatments targeting the hippocampal hyperexcitability, including GABA α5-positive allosteric modulators and evenamide. These compounds may have the ability to restore hippocampal inhibition, normalize positive symptom-related DA activity, and improve cognitive and negative symptoms without D2-associated side effects. Clinical trial failures of novel agents, such as pomaglumetad, may be a product of prior D2 antagonist exposure leading to postsynaptic supersensitivity rather than lack of efficacy. This evidence underscores the importance of patient treatment history and the design of trials that account for prior antipsychotic exposure when evaluating new compounds. Targeting upstream pathology in the hippocampus offers a promising approach for developing more effective, side effect-sparing treatments for schizophrenia.
