Article.Title: Compulsive Coping Behavior, Developed Predominantly by Sign-Trackers, Is Exacerbated by Chronic Atomoxetine
Article.Authors: Chernoff C.; Belin-Rauscent A.; Puaud M.; Torrisi S.; Fouyssac M.; Németh B.; Yu C.; Higuera-Matas A.; Jones S.; Belin D.
Article.Abstract: Background: Loss of control over coping strategies can result in the development of impulsive/compulsive spectrum disorders (ICSDs) such as obsessive-compulsive disorder or trichotillomania. Rats, like humans, show individual differences in their tendency to engage in and maintain control over coping behaviors. While most rats exposed to a schedule-induced polydipsia (SIP) procedure develop controlled, moderate, polydipsic coping, some vulnerable individuals engage in excessive, compulsive drinking, or hyperdipsia. The development of hyperdipsia depends in part on noradrenergic mechanisms, as it is prevented by the noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor atomoxetine (ATX) in highly impulsive vulnerable rats. However, whether noradrenergic mechanisms also underlie the expression of well-established hyperdipsia and whether other traits, such as the ICSD-relevant sign-tracking, confer vulnerability to its development are unknown. Methods: In 2 longitudinal studies with male Sprague Dawley rats, we investigated whether well-established hyperdipsia was influenced by ATX and whether its development was predicted by sign-tracking. Results: Sign-tracking was associated with faster acquisition of SIP and the development of high or compulsive levels of SIP. Chronic ATX both exacerbated hyperdipsia and increased the messenger RNA levels of the markers of cellular activity and plasticity cFos and Zif268 across the dorsal striatum as revealed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction assays. ATX also altered the transcriptomic landscape of the nucleus accumbens shell and the pattern of cFos and Zif268 expression in the amygdalo-striatal system. Conclusions: These results provide new insight into the biobehavioral basis of compulsive behaviors, revealing differential noradrenergic control of the development and expression of compulsive coping, with the latter involving recruitment of distinct striatal processes.

Article.Title: Neural Signatures of Bipolar Disorder and Psychotropic Medication Effects: A Multimodal Positron Emission Tomography–Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study
Article.Authors: Asch R.; Fan S.; Cool R.; Boster S.; DellaGioia N.; Naganawa M.; Nabulsi N.; Lacadie C.; Pietrzak R.; Esterlis I.
Article.Abstract: Background: Synaptic loss and altered network function in frontolimbic brain regions have been implicated in the neurobiology of bipolar disorder (BD), but in vivo evidence remains limited. Synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), a biomarker of synaptic density, can be quantified using [11C]UCB-J positron emission tomography (PET). Methods: Nineteen individuals with BD, including BDI (n = 13) and BDII (n = 6), and healthy control (HC) participants (n = 26) completed SV2A PET imaging in parallel with structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging to assess frontolimbic synaptic density, gray matter volume (GMV), and intrinsic connectivity, respectively. Results: Individuals with BD showed lower frontolimbic SV2A density, which exploratory analyses revealed to be seemingly driven by individuals taking psychotropic medications (BD-med). Conversely, group differences in GMV were observed only when accounting for medication status, with higher GMV in BD-med individuals relative to unmedicated individuals with BD (BD-none). Connectivity was higher in the BD group overall, but lower in the BD-med group relative to the BD-none group. SV2A and GMV were positively correlated in HC participants. However, this relationship was absent in individuals with BD, with lower SV2A/GMV ratios being associated with greater impulsivity in BD. Conclusions: These findings provide the first in vivo evidence of synaptic deficits in BD and offer preliminary evidence suggesting that psychotropic medications may differentially influence brain structure and function. These results underscore the importance of accounting for medication effects when interpreting neuroimaging findings in BD and the need to disentangle illness-related changes from medication effects on brain and behavior in BD.

Article.Title: Domain-Specific Efficacy of Accelerated Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in Neuropsychiatric Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Green J.; Dwivedi S.; Chou Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Accelerated repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (arTMS) (≥2 sessions/day) delivers high neuromodulatory doses over compressed timelines. It is increasingly used to target circuit-level dysfunction and treat diverse psychiatric conditions. However, its domain-specific efficacy and dose-dependent neuroplastic mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Methods: We conducted a preregistered systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD42024536096) of randomized controlled trials comparing arTMS with sham stimulation. Searches of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library (through July 23, 2024) identified 44 trials (N = 1671; 46.3% female) across 20 symptom domains. Standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) quantified treatment effects. Meta-regressions examined the moderating effects of stimulation parameters and participant demographics. Results: Compared with sham, arTMS yielded moderate antidepressant effects (g = 0.61; 95% CI, 0.38 to 0.85) and significant improvements in anxiety (g = 0.43; 95% CI, 0.05 to 0.81), obsessive-compulsive symptoms (g = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.88), working memory (g = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.79), and declarative memory (g = 0.30; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.58). Session frequency, intersession interval, cumulative pulse dose, age, and sex significantly moderated outcomes in specific domains, implicating dose- and sex-linked plasticity mechanisms. Risk of bias was predominantly low. Adverse events were mild and transient. Conclusions: arTMS yields rapid, domain-specific, transdiagnostic benefits with a favorable safety profile. Moderator analyses support a mechanistic model wherein stimulation-induced plasticity interacts with individual neurobiology to shape clinical response. These findings highlight arTMS as a scalable, circuit-targeted intervention and provide quantitative parameters to guide precision-medicine trials.

Article.Title: Isolating the Genetic Component of Mania in Bipolar Disorder
Article.Authors: Merola G.; Zvrskovec J.; Wang R.; Li Y.; Castellini G.; Ricca V.; Coleman J.; Vassos E.; Breen G.
Article.Abstract: Background: Bipolar disorder typically features episodes of mania and depression, frequently accompanied by psychosis. While progress has been made in understanding the genetics of depression and psychosis, mania remains underexplored, limiting opportunities for targeted interventions and a fuller understanding of bipolar disorder's heterogeneity. Methods: We used genomic structural equation modeling to subtract the genetic effects of major depressive disorder (MDD) from bipolar disorder, allowing us to isolate a genetic component specific to mania. This approach used genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from large-scale studies of European ancestry, including 576,327 effective samples for MDD and 27,196 cases with 43,792 controls for bipolar disorder. Results: The structural equation model revealed significant loadings for "mania" (0.90, p < .001) and "depression" (0.43, p < .001) factors, with mania and MDD explaining 81.5% and 18.5% of the variance in bipolar disorder, respectively. Seventy-one independent significant single nucleotide polymorphisms associated with mania were identified, spread in 37 genomic loci. Mania exhibited distinct genetic correlations compared with bipolar disorder, including significantly different correlations with psychiatric phenotypes, tiredness (rg = -0.13 vs. -0.17), subjective well-being (rg = 0.08 vs. -0.13), and educational attainment (rg = 0.26 vs. 0.14). Pathway analysis highlighted a significant enrichment in the voltage-gated calcium channel activity pathway. Conclusions: These findings enhance understanding of bipolar disorder's genetic architecture, offering a more bipolar disorder-specific GWAS. Identifying mania-specific loci may inform earlier diagnosis, personalized treatment approaches, and the development of targeted therapies.

Article.Title: The Link Between Weight Gain and Hippocampal Atrophy in Bipolar Disorder: A Longitudinal Investigation in 934 Participants
Article.Authors: Fraiha-Pegado J.; McWhinney S.; Alda M.; Alexander N.; Anmella G.; Abé C.; Altegoer L.; Benedetti F.; Berk M.; Bøen E.; Bond D.; Boye B.; Bravi B.; Cannon D.; Corkum E.; Corley E.; Dietze L.; Dannlowski U.; Elvsåshagen T.; Fuentes-Claramonte P.; Fullerton J.; Goldstein B.; Goltermann J.; Grotegerd D.; Hahn T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Obesity, which is common in bipolar disorder (BD), is associated with smaller hippocampal volumes. We do not know the role of weight/weight gain in relation to longitudinal hippocampal changes among individuals with BD. Methods: In collaboration with the ENIGMA (Enhancing Neuro Imaging Genetics through Meta Analysis)-BD Working Group, we obtained T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and clinical data from 233 participants with BD and 701 healthy control participants (HCs) scanned twice, 2.84 ± 1.63 years apart on average. We estimated subcortical volumes using FreeSurfer longitudinal image processing stream and used linear mixed models to assess the bidirectional relationship between baseline body mass index (BMI) or BMI change and hippocampal volume or volume change. While the hippocampus was our a priori region of interest, we repeated these analyses in other subcortical regions. Results: Baseline BMI predicted future hippocampal atrophy, but baseline brain structure did not predict future weight changes. BMI increased significantly over time (F1,1085 = 15.98, p < .001). Individuals with lower baseline BMI experienced greater weight gain (F1,922 = 105.12, p < .001). Greater weight gain was associated with greater hippocampal atrophy over time (F1,899 = 16.33, p = .001), more so in participants with BD than HCs (F1,898 = 6.91, p = .009). Consequently, lower baseline BMI predicted greater future hippocampal volume loss (F1,904 = 14.77, p < .001). These associations were not observed in other subcortical regions. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that weight gain is a modifiable risk factor for hippocampal atrophy, especially in individuals with lower BMI and those with BD. Prevention of weight gain in general, but especially in people with BD, could provide neuroprotective benefits.

Article.Title: A Population-Based Family Clustering Study of Body Dysmorphic Disorder
Article.Authors: Pol-Fuster J.; Fernández de la Cruz L.; Rautio D.; Crowley J.; Halvorsen M.; Du Rietz E.; Chang Z.; Larsson H.; Phillips K.; Rück C.; Lichtenstein P.; Kuja-Halkola R.; Mataix-Cols D.
Article.Abstract: Background: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a debilitating and understudied psychiatric condition of largely unknown etiology. Emerging evidence suggests that BDD may be a familial and heritable disorder, but family studies of diagnosed individuals and their biological relatives are yet to be conducted. Methods: We identified 4,857,049 individuals born in Sweden between 1960 and 2008 with information on both biological parents who were living in Sweden in 1997. From this cohort, we identified clusters of full siblings, half siblings, and cousins and compared the risk of BDD among those with a relative diagnosed with BDD and those without. Previously validated ICD-10 diagnoses of BDD were identified through the Swedish National Patient Register. To estimate hazard ratios (HRs), we fitted a series of Cox regression models with time-varying exposures and attained age as the underlying time scale. Individuals were considered unexposed before their relative's BDD diagnosis and exposed thereafter. Results: Relatives of individuals with BDD had a higher risk of BDD compared with relatives of individuals without BDD, with the highest risk observed in full siblings (HR, 16.2; 95% CI, 9.2-28.7), followed by half-siblings (HR, 7.8; 95% CI, 2.5-23.9) and cousins (HR, 2.8; 95% CI, 1.3-6.2), showing a gradient by degree of genetic relatedness. Conclusions: Our findings indicate that BDD is a familial disorder and suggest an important role for genetic factors.

Article.Title: Methylome-Wide Association Study of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
Article.Authors: Höffler K.; Stavrum A.; Halvorsen M.; Eide T.; Hagen K.; Høberg A.; Bäckman J.; Chen L.; Crowley J.; de Schipper E.; Pascal D.; Haavik J.; Hagen K.; Halvorsen M.; Hansen B.; Höffler K.; Johansson F.; Karlsson E.; Kvale G.; Lichtenstein P.; Lindblad-Toh K.; Mattheisen M.; Mataix-Cols D.; Rück C.; Eide T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a debilitating psychiatric condition influenced by both genetic and environmental risk factors. Epigenetic modifications, such as DNA methylation, may offer insights into biologically meaningful differences associated with the disorder. Methods: We conducted the largest methylome-wide association study of OCD to date, analyzing saliva DNA samples from 414 adults with OCD (297 female, 117 male) and 384 adult control participants (275 female, 109 male) using the Illumina EPICv2 array. Differentially methylated positions (DMPs) and differentially methylated regions (DMRs) were identified, with additional analyses including sex-stratified comparisons, methylation quantitative trait loci (mQTL) mapping, and assessments of differences in cell type composition. Results: We identified 35 DMPs and 17 DMRs associated with OCD, mapping to genes involved in neurotransmission, neurodevelopment, synaptic function, and gene regulation. Sex-stratified analyses revealed additional sex-specific methylation signals, highlighting biological differences between males and females. Most associated loci were influenced by genetic variation (mQTLs). Differences in estimated cell composition and the identification of immune-related genes suggest a potential role for immune system processes. Correlation analyses between brain and saliva methylation indicated that several findings may reflect brain-relevant biology. Conclusions: Our findings emphasize the importance of integrating epigenetic, genetic, and sex-specific data to advance our understanding of OCD. DNA methylation may ultimately contribute to progress toward clinically relevant precision medicine approaches.

Article.Title: Facilitating Thought Progression: A Neurocognitive Framework Linking Thought Dynamics and Mood Disorders
Article.Authors: Bar M.; Baror S.
Article.Abstract: Mood and thought are tightly coupled, but the mechanisms that link them are not understood. This link is particularly important when considering mood disorders such as depression. We propose the facilitating thought progression (FTP) framework, which characterizes depression as a disorder of thought dynamics, encompassing both the temporal evolution and semantic expanse of mental activity. Five parameters jointly determine the fluency of thought progression: breadth, speed, flexibility, novelty, and scope. Diminished progression, reflected by repetitive, slow, and narrowed thinking, is associated with excessive inhibition, reduced plasticity, blunted reward signaling, and overly deep attractor dynamics. Conversely, interventions that enhance associative expansion, cognitive flexibility, and exploratory behavior restore adaptive brain dynamics. FTP reframes depression as a disorder of cognitive flow rather than content and provides a mechanistic, testable model for translational research.

Article.Title: Structural Brain Network Alterations in Relation to Treatment and Illness Severity in Bipolar Disorder
Article.Authors: Nabulsi L.; Kang M.; Jahanshad N.; McPhilemy G.; Martyn F.; Haarman B.; McDonald C.; Hallahan B.; O’Donoghue S.; Stein D.; Howells F.; Scheffler F.; Temmingh H.; Glahn D.; Rodrigue A.; Pomarol-Clotet E.; Vieta E.; Radua J.; Salvador R.; Karuk A.; Canales-Rodríguez E.; Houenou J.; Favre P.; Polosan M.; Pouchon A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Large-scale T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have established gray matter abnormalities in bipolar disorder (BD), with our group contributing to consensus findings. However, structural connectivity, particularly within emotion- and reward-related circuits, remains poorly understood. Diffusion-weighted MRI (dMRI) enables investigation of white matter pathways, but prior work is constrained by small samples, methodological heterogeneity, and unclear medication effects. We conducted the largest dMRI network analysis in BD, relating symptom burden and polypharmacy to tractography-derived connectivity and graph-theoretical metrics. Methods: Cross-sectional structural and diffusion MRI scans from 450 individuals with BD (mean ± SD = 35.7 ± 12.6 years) and 509 control participants (33.3 ± 12.6 years), ages 18 to 65 years, were analyzed across 16 ENIGMA (Enhancing Neuro Imaging Genetics through Meta Analysis) BD sites. Standardized segmentation/parcellation and constrained spherical deconvolution tractography generated individual structural connectivity matrices. Graph-theoretical metrics of global and subnetwork organization were related to symptom severity and medications. Results: BD showed widespread network alterations (lower density and efficiency, longer path length, and higher betweenness centrality), altered microstructural organization in a limbic-basal ganglia circuit, and abnormal streamline counts in a default mode/salience/frontolimbic-basal ganglia network. Longer illness duration, later onset, and psychosis history were associated with greater abnormalities in network architecture, whereas more manic episodes were associated with greater frontolimbic connectivity. Antidepressant (particularly selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor), anticonvulsant, and antipsychotic use related to poorer global and frontolimbic connectivity; no clear lithium effects emerged. Conclusions: As the largest structural connectivity study in BD, we revealed widespread disruption in reward and emotion-regulation networks influenced by illness severity and medication use. Results show that multisite harmonization is feasible and highlight ENIGMA-BD as a scalable framework for identifying reproducible neurobiological markers.

Article.Title: Dysfunctional Brain Circuits Overlap in Lesional and Idiopathic Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
Article.Authors: Cotovio G.; Descalço N.; Caballero-Insaurriaga J.; Martins D.; Faro Viana F.; Fonseca C.; Ramos J.; Santos B.; Maia A.; Oliveira J.; Loução N.; Barbour T.; Siddiqi S.; Fox M.; Barahona-Corrêa J.; Oliveira-Maia A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) may develop following brain lesions, but lesion distribution and connectivity patterns are unknown. Methods: Cases of OCD associated with focal brain lesions were identified using a systematic literature search and compared with control lesions (n = 608). Connectivity with each lesion location was computed using normative functional connectivity (n = 1000), and a network specific to OCD lesions was identified. The relevance of this network for primary OCD was explored. Results: Among 129 cases of lesion-associated OCD, 40 had clearly defined locations. OCD-associated lesions intersected the orbitofrontal cortex and right temporal pole more than control lesions and were associated with connectivity to a distinct brain network. This network overlapped with abnormal functional brain imaging and with effective brain stimulation targets in primary OCD. Conclusions: Lesion locations associated with OCD map to a common brain network that aligns with brain imaging abnormalities and brain stimulation outcomes in patients with primary OCD.

Article.Title: Executive Function and Self-Injurious Thoughts and Behaviors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Cheek S.; Walsh R.; Barnes S.; Hall T.; Sheehan A.; Carosa C.; Lindley A.; Velotta S.; Liu R.
Article.Abstract: Background: Although executive functioning (EF) deficits have been implicated in self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITBs), the strength of their associations remain unclear. Few mechanisms reliably differentiating between suicidal thoughts and suicide attempts have been identified. The degree to which EF deficits may differentiate suicidal thoughts from behavior is undetermined. Methods: PubMed and PsycInfo were searched from inception through June 4, 2025. Two reviewers independently identified studies on core EFs (inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory) and their subcomponents in relation to SITBs. Associations between each core EF and their composite parts in relation to suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and nonsuicidal self-injury were extracted. Hedges' g was derived from random-effects meta-analyses. Results: A total of 127 studies were included. Deficits in inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory were associated with suicidal ideation (gs = |0.15|-|0.23|) and suicide attempts (gs = |0.21|-|0.28|). Medium pooled effects were observed for cognitive flexibility (g = 0.52, 95% CI [0.10 to 0.93]) and working memory (g = -0.69, 95% CI [-1.00 to -0.38]) in relation to nonsuicidal self-injury. Sensitivity analyses suggested that task switching and response inhibition were specifically related to suicidal ideation, whereas working memory and attentional control were specific to suicide attempts. Conclusions: While other neurocognitive functions have also been associated with SITBs, EF deficits may be particularly promising candidate mechanisms. Future longitudinal work will be important for establishing prognostic value to inform selection of brain regions to target with neuromodulation treatment paradigms.

Article.Title: Kappa Opioid Receptor Availability in Borderline Personality Disorder: An In Vivo Investigation With [11C]EKAP Positron Emission Tomography Imaging
Article.Authors: Weiss E.; Bartlett E.; Naganawa M.; Asch R.; Hart-Derrick V.; Miller R.; Freeman D.; Duraney E.; Nabulsi N.; Radhakrishnan R.; Matuskey D.; Huang Y.; Enferadi M.; Zhang H.; Davis M.
Article.Abstract: Background: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a chronic mental health condition associated with marked elevations in disability. Limited pharmacological treatment options are currently available, and kappa opioid receptors (KORs) have been identified as a promising treatment target. However, the KOR system has not yet been directly examined in BPD. In this study, we examined KORs in individuals with BPD and investigated links between KORs and BPD's clinical features. Methods: Twenty individuals with BPD and 20 demographically matched healthy control (HC) volunteer participants were scanned with [11C]EKAP positron emission tomography (PET) and completed self-report and interview measures. KOR availability (volume of distribution [VT]) was measured in brain regions of interest (ROIs) relevant to the pathophysiology of BPD. Results: No differences in age or sex were observed between HC participants (mean [SD] age = 32.94 [8.45], 60% female) and individuals with BPD (mean [SD] age = 33.30 [9.34], 60% female). In individuals with BPD, KOR VT was significantly lower in the amygdala (mean difference [meandiff] = -8.04, 95% CI [11.40 to -4.69]), anterior cingulate (meandiff = -2.95, 95% CI [-5.22 to -0.68]); hippocampus (meandiff = -2.12, 95% CI [-3.37 to -0.88]), insula (meandiff = -3.58, 95% CI [-5.71 to -1.46]), and frontal ROIs (meandiff = -1.83; 95% CI [-3.28 to -0.38]). VT correlated negatively with specific clinical features including impulsivity (r28 = -0.45 p = .013, 95% CI [-0.72 to -0.11]) and depressive symptoms (r28 = -0.43, p = .021, 95% CI [-0.70 to -0.07]) but not with trauma symptoms. Conclusions: The findings demonstrate differences in KOR availability in BPD and relationships between KOR availability and clinically relevant features. Results highlight the relevance of KOR in BPD pathophysiology and further implicate the opioid system as a promising target for treatment development in BPD.

Article.Title: E3 ubiquitin ligases: a vital component of proteostasis impaired in hereditary neuropathies
Article.Authors: Gonebale M.; Cutrupi A.; Kennerson M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Protein homeostasis is essential for the maintenance of peripheral axons and depends on co-ordinated protein synthesis, folding, ubiquitination and directing protein fate across multiple protein quality-control pathways. E3 ubiquitin ligases are central to this network by conferring substrate specificity and enabling precise spatiotemporal regulation of protein homeostasis. Increasing genetic and functional evidence implicates the disruption of E3 ligase function in inherited peripheral neuropathies, providing a mechanistic link between impaired proteostasis and progressive axonal degeneration. Here, we examine inherited peripheral neuropathies associated with dysfunction of Tripartite Motif-Containing Protein 2 (TRIM2), Leucine Rich Repeat and Sterile Alpha Motif Containing 1 (LRSAM1), Ubiquitin Protein Ligase E3C (UBE3C) and the Cullin-Ring 3 (CUL3) substrate adapter, Gigaxonin (GAN). Although these proteins differ in structure, substrates and disease mechanisms, their dysfunction converges on disruption of proteasomal degradation, autophagy and cytoskeletal homeostasis. By integrating these genetically distinct neuropathies within a common mechanistic framework, we propose this positions E3 ubiquitin ligases as selective regulators of multiple protein quality-control pathways and highlights the specific vulnerability of long peripheral axons to the disruption of ubiquitin-mediated proteostasis.

Article.Title: Peripheral sensory neurons clock genes are a molecular driver of pain rhythmicity
Article.Authors: Wei L.; Wu Y.; Zirpel F.; Flower G.; Vierbergen J.; Wieser V.; Batchelor V.; Zarebska J.; Steponenaite A.; Tanday N.; Brown L.; Pokhilko A.; Li X.; Peirson S.; Vincent T.; Lall G.; Zameel Cader M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain intensity fluctuates across the day in patients, yet the cellular clock mechanisms that generate pain rhythmicity and their therapeutic potential remain poorly defined. Prior studies have established circadian variation in nociception and a requirement for intact clock function, but it has remained unclear the neurophysiological mechanisms which translate clock state into time-of-day changes in pain. The goal of this study was to define the clock component(s) and effector pathway(s) that drive pain rhythmicity and to test whether this axis can be exploited for analgesia. We combined behavioural analyses under circadian conditions with genetic dissection of clock components in sensory neurons, electrophysiological interrogation of nociceptor excitability, and pharmacological modulation of the clock machinery. To establish translational relevance, we used human iPSC-derived nociceptors, including a human pain disease model, to test whether the same clock–excitability coupling operates in human cells. We show that nociceptive behaviours exhibit robust circadian rhythmicity and that this rhythmicity depends on the molecular clock within peripheral sensory neurons. Loss of cryptochromes CRY1/CRY2 disrupts time-of-day differences in nociceptor excitability, identifying cryptochromes as essential clock effectors in the pain pathway. Mechanistically, cryptochrome state controls voltage-gated sodium channel function, providing a direct link from clock machinery to nociceptor responsiveness. Pharmacological stabilisation of cryptochromes using a small-molecule modulator suppresses sodium currents and reduces nociceptive responses across distinct pain paradigms, and this effect is abrogated when cryptochrome function is absent. In synchronised human iPSC-derived nociceptors, we observe concordant clock-state-dependent changes in excitability, and cryptochrome stabilisation reduces hyperexcitability. These findings identify a peripheral sensory neuron clock mechanism that drives pain rhythmicity through cryptochrome-dependent control of sodium channel function and highlight cryptochrome stabilisation as a non-opioid therapeutic strategy for pain disorders with diurnal symptom variation.

Article.Title: Alzheimer’s pathology mediates arteriolosclerosis and cerebral amyloid angiopathy associations with cognition
Article.Authors: Hayes C.; Dharmapuri A.; Agwu C.; Ramirez V.; Newman J.; Chambers M.; Odden M.; Younes K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Vascular and neurodegenerative pathologies frequently co-occur in aging brains, yet the mechanisms linking vascular neuropathologies to cognitive impairment remain incompletely understood. We examined whether Alzheimer’s disease neuropathologic change (ADNC) and Lewy body disease (LBD) mediate or modify associations between vascular neuropathologies and domain-specific cognitive performance. The analytic sample included 1,269 decedents (mean age at death, 84.3 ± 9.1 years; 43.3% female; 94.7% White). At the last evaluation prior to death, 22.5% were cognitively normal, 2.4% were impaired but not mild cognitive impairment (MCI), 14.9% had MCI, and 60.2% had dementia. Vascular neuropathologies included arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis of the circle of Willis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), gross infarcts/lacunes, and microinfarcts. Multivariable linear regression models evaluated associations with harmonized memory, executive function, and language z-scores adjusting for age at death, sex, education, and apolipoprotein E ε4 status. Effect modification by ADNC and LBD was tested. Mediation models estimated indirect and direct effects of vascular neuropathologies on cognition through ADNC or LBD using 5,000 bootstrap samples. Greater arteriolosclerosis severity was associated with worse memory (β=−0.16, 95% CI −0.23 to −0.09), executive function (β=−0.18, 95% CI −0.24 to −0.11), and language (β=−0.18, 95% CI −0.24 to −0.12; all p<0.001). CAA was strongly associated with poorer cognition across domains, including memory (β=−0.26, 95% CI −0.33 to −0.19; p<0.001). Atherosclerosis and infarcts showed more limited associations, while microinfarcts were not significantly associated with cognition. Mediation analyses indicated that ADNC statistically accounted for approximately 13–29% of the associations between arteriolosclerosis and cognition across domains and 64–91% of the associations between CAA and cognition. Direct effects of arteriolosclerosis remained significant, whereas CAA effects were largely explained by ADNC. Effect modification by ADNC and LBD was limited, although LBD attenuated associations of arteriolosclerosis and CAA with executive function. Mediation through LBD was not observed. This novel evidence shows that vascular neuropathologies influence cognition through defined pathways with statistically significant patterns of associations. In this autopsy-confirmed cohort, vascular neuropathologies showed different patterns of association with domain-specific cognitive performance and ADNC. A larger proportion of the association involving CAA was statistically accounted for by ADNC, whereas direct associations remained more apparent for arteriolosclerosis. This study clarifies how vascular and neurodegenerative processes interact to shape cognitive impact and inform mechanistic preventions.

Article.Title: The amygdaloid complex: from morphology to neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Rodrigo H.; Rábano A.; Vyas S.; Herrero M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The amygdaloid complex is one of the most structurally and functionally heterogeneous regions of the mammalian brain, acting as an integrative node between sensory, mnemonic and visceral systems. It comprises a set of subnuclei whose cytoarchitectural differentiation, neurochemical profiles and anatomical boundaries have been debated since the earliest descriptions. This heterogeneity is established during ontogenetic development, assembling progenitors from pallial and subpallial domains, and preoptic and hypothalamic territories, resulting in a highly connected network. Maturation is not complete at birth, the amygdala changes through childhood and adolescence, leaving a protracted window of environmental sensitivity. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have added a molecular layer to this framework, resolving populations that no single marker separates, and set explicit limits on the resolution at which rodent-derived subdivisions can be transferred to the human amygdala. Together these levels of description provide a structural framework for understanding its functions, which include emotional regulation and conditioned fear, social and sexual behaviours, decision-making, reward and punishment processing, empathy and memory modulation. Cross-species comparison reveals further variation, particularly the expansion of the basolateral complex in primates and the redistribution of neurons towards the lateral nucleus in humans. In summary, the amygdala acts as a densely connected hub with a broad role not only in physiological and psychological health but also in disease states; indeed, the amygdala is affected early in several neurodegenerative disorders, and in some (notably limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy and argyrophilic grain disease) it is among the first regions in which pathology is detected.

Article.Title: Cerebellar subregions support social cognition in early behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Chatzidimitriou E.; Yang W.; Leng F.; Syed F.; McEachen B.; Ivry R.; Rosen H.; Seeley W.; Gorno-Tempini M.; Kramer J.; Miller B.; Rankin K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Social cognitive deficits manifest early in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), compromising individuals’ ability to interpret social cues, empathize, and maintain interpersonal relationships. Current neurobiological models emphasize cortical network disruption, particularly within the salience, semantic appraisal, and default mode networks, as primary contributors to social dysfunction. However, despite the increasingly recognized role of the cerebellum in higher-order cognitive and socioemotional processes, its contributions to social deficits remains underexplored in bvFTD. Here, we investigated the unique and network-level influences of cerebellar subregions on social cognition across experimental and real-world assessments in early-stage bvFTD. A total of 107 individuals with bvFTD and 100 healthy controls were evaluated across three social domains: theory of mind (ToM) (The Awareness of Social Inference Test-Social Inference-Enriched, TASIT-SIE; Cognitive Emotional Perspective Taking Test), emotion reading (Dynamic Affect Recognition Test; TASIT-Emotion Evaluation Test; Comprehensive Affect Testing System), and real-life empathy (Revised Self-Monitoring Scale; Interpersonal Reactivity Index). Using a functional cerebellar parcellation, we extracted volumes of posterior cerebellar subregions implicated in social-linguistic and multiple-demand networks from participants’ structural MRIs. To address the high collinearity between cerebellar and cortical atrophy patterns, we applied sequential regression, partial least squares correlation, and dominance analysis to characterize brain-behavior relationships. Additionally, supplementary structural equation modelling (SEM) examined whether the associations between cerebellar integrity and social cognition was mediated by executive functioning. Our results showed that cerebellar subregional integrity contributed to social cognitive deficits in individuals with early-stage bvFTD. Cerebellar subregions, particularly right Crus I and II, showed the strongest and most selective contribution to high-level inferential Theory of Mind performance. Tasks involving dynamic emotion stimuli exhibited a more distributed pattern of cerebello-cerebral involvement. By contrast, questionnaire-based measures of real-world social functioning were less prominently represented in the latent covariance structure. SEM further showed that cerebellar integrity remained directly associated with social cognition after accounting for executive functioning, whereas the indirect association through executive functioning was not significant. These findings highlight the task-dependent nature of cerebellar involvement in social cognition, and demonstrate that time-limited experimental tasks, particularly those involving inferential reasoning about beliefs and affect, are likely to be especially valuable in detecting subtle cerebello-cerebral network dysfunction that questionnaire-based measures may overlook. Our results extend cortex-centric models of social dysfunction in bvFTD by demonstrating that cerebellar subregions contribute to distributed cerebello-cerebral systems associated with social cognitive performance. These findings provide a foundation for future longitudinal and mechanistic studies of cerebello-cerebral dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.

Article.Title: Altered medial prefrontal-striatal connectivity and plasticity in humanized CBLN2 mice
Article.Authors: S Narasimhan K.; Chettiar P.; Sabnis S.; Kola P.; Thakur S.; Shelkar G.; Asati D.; Gawande D.; Jadhav S.; Dravid S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deciphering processes that are responsible for differences in brain development and architecture among species may provide clues to the species-specific program and may facilitate a mechanistic understanding of vulnerability to neuropsychiatric disorders. It has recently been shown that the promoter of the CBLN2 gene, which codes for a synaptogenic factor, cerebellin 2 (Cbln2), has a repressor element in mice but not in humans. A humanized mouse lacking this repressor (hCbln2) reproduces higher spine density in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) neurons and higher corticothalamic connectivity observed in humans. Cbln2 is part of a trans-synaptic complex that includes glutamate delta-1 receptor (GluD1) and neurexins (Nrxn) (GluD1-Cbln2-Nrxn). Interestingly, we have previously reported a contrasting striatal patch-matrix expression pattern of GluD1 in mouse versus monkey, suggesting a potential role of the GluD1-Cbln complex in species differences. In this study, we examined the synaptic organization and function in the cortex and dorsal striatum of hCbln2 mice. Consistent with previous reports, hCbln2 mice exhibited increased vGluT1 expression in the mPFC, indicating enhanced intracortical connectivity. Electrophysiological recordings further revealed an increased mEPSC frequency along with a reduced mIPSC frequency in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, suggesting an increase in excitatory/inhibitory balance. These changes were accompanied by enhanced mTOR signalling and autophagic deficits in the mPFC. Contrasting synaptic changes were observed in the striatum with an increase in vGluT2 and a reduction in vGluT1, together with a decrease in GluD1-Cbln1 and an increase in hevin. Importantly, corticostriatal dysfunction characterized by a reduction in cortical contribution to mEPSCs and impaired DHPG-induced synaptic depression was observed in the hCbln2 medium spiny neurons. Further, hCbln2 mice displayed increased repetitive behaviour together with social and affective-like deficits, consistent with autism-relevant phenotypes. Collectively, these findings identify humanized Cbln2 regulation as a driver of divergent cortical and striatal synaptic remodelling, disrupted corticostriatal synaptic function, and behavioural abnormalities relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: The TBK1-OTUB2-IRF3 signalling complex promotes neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Wang D.; Chen J.; Lu Y.; Deng D.; Xu B.; Xu Y.; Jin K.; Xu J.; Liu B.; Ruan J.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway-mediated chronic inflammation drives neurodegeneration in natural aging and various neurodegenerative diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here, we identify Otubain-2 (OTUB2) as a pivotal regulator that orchestrates the STING signalosome to amplify inflammatory responses. The function of OTUB2 in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration was investigated through genetic deletion and pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 in hTARDBP transgenic mice​, adeno-associated virus-mediated TDP43 overexpression mice, and aged mice. Biochemical assays were performed to dissect underlying molecular mechanisms. OTUB2 inhibited K63 ubiquitination of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), thereby suppressing TBK1 kinase activity and promoting cell death mediated by hyperactivated receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1). Additionally, OTUB2 functioned as a scaffold facilitating assembly of the TBK1-interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) signalling complex, a prerequisite for IRF3 phosphorylation, and enhanced IRF3 dimerization by reducing its K11 ubiquitination. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 significantly ameliorated neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in both ALS and aged mouse models. This study establishes OTUB2 as a critical regulator of cGAS-STING signalling and a potential therapeutic target for neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Short-term outcomes, longer-term disability and relapse risk in LGI1-antibody encephalitis
Article.Authors: Ramanathan S.; Soltys J.; Michael S.; Mackrill S.; Cleaver J.; Williams R.; Makuch M.; Waters P.; Ansizka Y.; Dinoto A.; Farazdaghi M.; Trewin B.; Rudnik J.; Demakakos P.; Yates S.; Thouin A.; Dilwali S.; Son H.; Dale R.; Jacob A.; Lutterotti A.; Easton A.; Handel A.; Geschwind M.; Gelfand J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated-1 antibody encephalitis (LGI1-Ab-E) is a common and immunotherapy-responsive form of encephalitis. However, it is not known which immunotherapy regimens improve short-term outcomes, longer-term disability and relapse risk. Further, it is not known if the widely-utilised modified Rankin Scale (mRS) accurately captures quality of life (QoL) in LGI1-Ab-E, complicating disability measurements and interpretation of immunotherapy responses. A multicentre, international, real-world comparative analysis of patients with LGI1-Ab-E. Retrospective data from patient records evaluated short-term seizure and cognitive outcomes, 1-6 year disability, and future relapse risk associations, by integrating demographics, clinical features investigations and exposures to immunotherapies and antiseizure medications (ASMs). Patient- and neurologist-rated QoL assessments were used to establish an evidence-based mRS threshold for defining clinically significant disability. Cox proportional hazard models, Anderson-Gill, and generalised linear mixed-effects models were employed. 181 patients were included, with median age at onset 63 years (range 23 - 92); 122/181 (67%) were male. Short-term outcomes, evaluated at both five and ten weeks post-treatment initiation, identified exposure to immunotherapies associated with seizure resolution (OR = 13.97, 95%CI = 6.10-32.01; p < 0.0001 and OR = 8.53, 95%CI = 4.14-17.55; p < 0.0001, respectively), notably with corticosteroids, plasma exchange and rituximab, but not ASMs, intravenous immunoglobulins or steroid sparing agents. Conversely, seizure recurrence was observed after discontinuation of oral prednisolone, but not other immunotherapies or ASMs (OR = 39.53, 95%CI = 12.70-122.20, p < 0.0001). To evaluate longer-term disability, first, mRS scores were calibrated using QoL assessments: this identified a significant increase in patient-rated disability at mRS score of 2. Hence, using mRS 0-1 as a favourable outcome, we identified worse mRS at nadir associated with greater one-year disability (OR = 2.56, 95%CI = 1.56–4.20, p = 0.0003), and each month of delayed immunotherapy associated with a 16% increased risk of disability (HR = 1.16, 95%CI = 1.06-1.35, p = 0.004). Additionally, absence of immunotherapy associated both with greater one-year disability (OR = 5.67; 95% CI 1.19-26.54, p = 0.03) and a relapsing course (OR = 7.64, 95%CI = 2.51-21.77, p = 0.0002). Both a relapsing course, observed in 38% of patients, and the number of relapses associated with step-wise worsening of disability and QoL-outcomes. Rituximab exposure was the only identified clinical factor associated with reduced future relapse risk, by 93% (HR = 0.07, 95%CI = 0.01-0.48, p = 0.002). Persistent serum LGI1-IgMs, but not LGI1-IgGs, at one-year, associated with future relapses (HR = 11.69, 95%CI = 1.58-145.80, p = 0.02). Distinctive clinical factors and select immunotherapies, particularly intravenous methylprednisolone and plasma exchange, but not ASMs, associated with favourable short-term outcomes, patient-centric longer-term disability and relapses in LGI1-Ab-E. Our findings provide evidence-based disability thresholds, highlight novel prognostic biomarkers, and pragmatically guide LGI1-Ab-E care, pending randomized clinical trials.

Article.Title: TREM2: friend or foe in glioma?
Article.Authors: Peshoff M.; Hambardzumyan D.; Wu L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a neuroimmune signaling hub involved in key cellular processes including microglial phagocytosis, chemotaxis, and inflammation. Dysregulation of TREM2 has been implicated in a variety of diseases, most notably in the innate immune response to neurodegenerative disorders and cancer. The TREM2 pathway plays a significant role in governing microglia phenotypic transitions in Alzheimer’s disease, as well as in regulating tumor-associated macrophages’ ability to modulate cytotoxic activity. However, TREM2’s role can be dependent on experimental parameters and disease contexts. Due to its intricate involvement in related disorders and the myeloid-dominated microenvironment in brain tumors, TREM2 has emerged as a vital player to better understand neuroimmune contributions to central nervous system malignancies. This review critically evaluates TREM2’s controversial function in gliomas, analyzes experimental and biological variables that may underlie divergent findings, and outlines important considerations for future investigations.

Article.Title: KCNH1 variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit prominent gain of function
Article.Authors: Thompson C.; Simmons C.; He I.; Jairam N.; Desai R.; Cha E.; Hong A.; DeKeyser J.; Laux L.; Jinnette M.; Vanoye C.; George A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pathogenic variants in KCNH1, encoding the human ether-á-go-go voltage-gated potassium channel (EAG1, KV10.1), are associated with the neurodevelopmental disorders Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS), Zimmermann-Laband syndrome (ZLS), epileptic encephalopathy, and other undefined neurodevelopmental disorders. Investigating the functional consequences of KCNH1 variants can provide information about molecular and cellular pathophysiological mechanisms and help guide therapeutic directions. In this study, we determined the functional properties of 26 disease-associated KCNH1 variants including three recurrent and six that were previously unpublished. Findings were compared to the wildtype (WT) channel along with six rare population variants. Our approach used automated patch clamp recording of heterologously expressed KCNH1 variants in both the homozygous state (variant alone) and the clinically-relevant heterozygous state (variant co-expressed with WT channels). We also examined the impact of alternative splice isoforms on functional consequences of specific variants. We demonstrated that the majority of disease-associated KCNH1 variants exhibit features consistent with gain-of-function including hyperpolarized voltage-dependence of activation, accelerated activation kinetics, or both that promote hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential. By contrast, one unique variant discovered previously in an autism cohort had a depolarized voltage-dependence of activation and was associated with a depolarized resting potential in cells. Pharmacological testing of KCNH1 variants demonstrated differences in potency for channel block by imipramine and an investigational non-selective potassium channel blocker (LY97241) for specific variants. Collectively, our findings support gain-of-function as the most common, albeit not exclusive, molecular mechanism underlying KCNH1-related disorders and suggest opportunities for potential therapeutic drug repurposing strategies for these conditions.

Article.Title: Global best practice recommendations for genetic counselling and testing in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Article.Authors: Salmon K.; de Majo M.; Basak N.; Crook A.; Cummings C.; Dratch L.; França M.; Heckmann J.; Higgins P.; Knight D.; Koo A.; Nalini A.; Rouleau G.; Shahrizaila N.; Sokhi D.; Son B.; Thomas P.; Trefiak P.; Van Damme P.; N/A N/A.; Ahmad-Annuar A.; Binet M.; Cochrane T.; Dave K.; Easton A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with substantial clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Advances in ALS genomics, emerging gene-targeted therapies, and genotype-specific clinical trials have increased the importance of genetic counselling and testing for individuals with ALS and their families. However, access to these services remains highly variable globally due to disparities in healthcare infrastructure, laboratory capacity, specialist availability, and funding. Existing guidance has largely been developed in high-resource settings and may not be feasible or equitable worldwide. The International Alliance of ALS/MND Associations convened an international, multidisciplinary Genetics Task Force to develop expert consensus recommendations for genetic counselling, genetic testing, and laboratory practice in ALS across diverse geographic and resource settings. Recommendations were developed through a structured, iterative consensus process incorporating clinical expertise, lived experience perspectives, published evidence, and global representation. Final recommendations were reviewed and approved through anonymous voting at an in-person consensus meeting. The resulting recommendations establish both minimum and aspirational best practices, emphasizing equitable access, informed decision-making, culturally responsive counselling, tiered genetic testing approaches, and context-appropriate laboratory standards. These globally informed recommendations provide a pragmatic framework to support clinicians, laboratories, policymakers, and advocacy organizations in improving access to high-quality ALS genetics services worldwide.

Article.Title: Do psychiatrists have a spider-sense? Clinical impressions as violations of interpersonal Bayesian expectation
Article.Authors: Amad A.; D’Hondt F.; Gauld C.; Bertoux M.; Daoudi M.; Fovet T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Psychiatric diagnosis depends on the clinician’s ability to infer mental states from complex and dynamically evolving interpersonal signals. During the psychiatric interview, clinicians do not only collect explicit symptoms; they continuously sample a rich array of non-verbal and paralinguistic cues including gaze, prosody, affective reciprocity, and interactional timing. These signals are central to psychiatric assessment, yet their contribution to diagnostic reasoning remains poorly formalized. In this Review, we propose a computational account of clinical impressions in psychiatry. We integrate evidence from phenomenological psychopathology, social cognition, and computational neuroscience. We argue that such impressions may arise when the clinician’s generative model of social interaction is persistently disconfirmed by subtle deviations in interpersonal behaviour, generating high-level social prediction errors experienced as a sense of incongruity or failed attunement. We formalize this process as VIBE: Violation of Interpersonal Bayesian Expectation. VIBE denotes a pre-reflective epistemic signal generated when observed interpersonal cues deviate from the clinician’s expected model of social reciprocity. It is not a diagnostic criterion but orients hypothesis generation by drawing attention to disturbances in interpersonal predictability. We hypothesize that VIBE may constitute a transdiagnostic mechanism: different disorders, from schizophrenia to autism spectrum disorder and mood disorders, may disrupt distinct dimensions of interpersonal prediction. The Praecox Feeling, first described by Rümke in 1942, can be read as the earliest clinical formalization of this process and as its schizophrenia-spectrum instance, in which the profile of interpersonal violations is consistent enough to be clinically recognizable. This framework recasts the diagnostic impression as an embodied inferential process rather than an opaque subjective faculty. Teaching clinicians to articulate, examine, and recalibrate these impressions could strengthen diagnostic reasoning, reduce bias, and improve therapeutic attunement. VIBE provides a bridge between phenomenological psychopathology and computational neuroscience, and offers a tractable, empirically testable model for studying the neurocomputational basis of psychiatric clinical judgement.

Article.Title: Clinically unresponsive patients with acute brain injury activate a brain-computer interface
Article.Authors: Shen Q.; Eliseyev A.; Kansara V.; Neves Briard J.; Song Y.; Carmona J.; Gonzales I.; Velazquez A.; Klein A.; Agarwal S.; Park S.; Ghoshal S.; Roh D.; Connolly E.; Claassen J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Brain activation to verbal commands can be detected by EEG in clinically unresponsive patients. These patients with cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) are unable to communicate with the environment despite preserved consciousness. Advanced brain-computer interfaces (BCI) are promising to support motor function in patients with motor neuron disease or spinal cord injury. Our primary objective was to determine if clinically unresponsive patients can control a self-paced, one-way BCI early after acute brain injury. Secondarily, we assessed the association of BCI control with short- and long-term outcomes. We conducted a prospective single-centre cohort study in 41 clinically unresponsive, critically ill and acutely brain injured patients, as well as in a convenience sample of 8 healthy volunteers and 22 conscious critically ill patients. The self-paced BCI analysed EEG in real time and modulated frequency and pitch of a tone that patients controlled by attempting a motor task: patients were provided with instructions ‘to make the beep sound faster, keep opening and closing your right hand’ alternating with ‘to make the beep sound slower, stop opening and closing your right hand’. CMD was detected by applying machine learning to EEG recorded while patients listened to motor commands. Clinical outcomes were recovery of consciousness by hospital discharge, assessed with the Coma Recovery Scale–Revised, and recovery of functional independence at 12 months, defined as a Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended score of 4 or higher (denoting the ability to function independently for 8 h or more). Additionally, we invited conscious patients as well as family members of conscious and clinically unresponsive patients to complete a survey on perceived utility and challenges associated with the BCI. In this study, 13 clinically unresponsive patients (32%) achieved BCI control and 8 of 41 (20%) were CMD-positive. All healthy volunteers and nine conscious patients (41%) were able to control the BCI. Median signal delay for BCI control was 49.8 [interquartile range (IQR) 39.9–75.6] seconds for clinically unresponsive patients, 17.1 (IQR 7.8–19.9) for conscious patients and 15.5 (IQR 12.9–21.2) for healthy volunteers. In the group of 41 clinically unresponsive patients, 4 of 13 patients with (31%) and 1 of 28 without BCI control (4%) recovered clinical consciousness at hospital discharge [odds ratio (OR) 21.2; 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.3–930.7]. At 12 months, 6 of 13 patients with (46%) and 2 of 28 without BCI control (7%) recovered functional independence (OR 9.9; 95% CI 1.8–81.6). None of the patients that were unable to control the BCI and were CMD-negative recovered. Patients with BCI control had shorter times to recovery of functional independence by 12 months than those who did not (hazards ratio 6.0; 95% CI 1.2–30.6). All respondents of the BCI survey (n = 37) expressed strong support for the potential future use of BCI devices. These results suggest that BCI control is a strong predictor of outcomes following acute brain injury and provide initial evidence that a bedside, EEG-based BCI system might permit bidirectional communication in critically ill unresponsive patients.

Article.Title: TMEM106B risk converges on C-terminal fragment homeostasis: genetics, mechanisms and therapy
Article.Authors: Lastra Osua M.; Perneel J.; Vicente C.; Rademakers R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract TMEM106B is a genetic modifier influencing susceptibility to multiple neurodegenerative disorders, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP), Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, as well as contributing to healthy brain aging and neuronal reserve. The gene harbours single nucleotide polymorphisms and structural variants that define risk and protective haplotypes, and despite extensive efforts to identify the functional variant within these haplotypes, consensus remains elusive. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of TMEM106B genetics from human cohorts and mechanistic studies, highlighting how variants may influence its regulatory network and protein levels, with an emphasis on its aggregation-prone C-terminal domain. We further integrate evidence on the roles of TMEM106B within the endo-lysosomal system and beyond, including insights into protein structure, posttranslational modifications, interactors, proteolytic processing, and fibril formation. These findings are contextualized using data from mouse and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, highlighting current gaps in the available models and the advances required to study its functions and cleavage. Finally, we explore therapeutic strategies targeting TMEM106B, focusing on modulation of expression, specific functional pathways, and fibril formation.

Article.Title: Progenitor transcriptional alterations link fetal and adult pathology in Huntington’s disease
Article.Authors: Battistella M.; Damaggio G.; Conforti P.; Scolz A.; Maestri S.; Bocchi V.; Iafolla D.; Galimberti M.; Morrocchi M.; Cordiglieri C.; Vezzoli E.; Lodato S.; Ranzani V.; Viale S.; Thompson L.; Vogt T.; Felsenfeld D.; Chen J.; Besusso D.; Cattaneo E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Huntington’s disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Although the mutant huntingtin protein is expressed from conception, clinical symptoms typically emerge in mid-adulthood. Imaging and molecular studies have raised the possibility that HD may involve neurodevelopmental abnormalities, but direct evidence at the single-cell level in the human fetal brain has been lacking. Here we investigated whether early, cell type–specific transcriptional vulnerabilities arise during neurodevelopment, persist into adult pathology, and might be rescued. To address this, we performed single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the lateral ganglionic eminence (LGE) and cortex from a rare, anatomically intact human HD fetal brain, alongside matched controls. These data were complemented by an allelic series of HD mouse embryos and cross-compared with already published human post-mortem brains and brain organoid models’ datasets. Neural progenitors displayed the highest number of differentially expressed genes in the human fetal brain, and were also impacted in the HD mouse model, where additional cell types displayed transcriptional alterations. Notably, human HD progenitor transcriptional signatures were moderately enriched in the developing mouse LGE. These progenitors exhibited increased expression of synaptic pathways coupled with reduced expression of cell maintenance genes. Cross-comparison with publicly available post-mortem HD datasets revealed that components of this transcriptional signature persist into adulthood. Furthermore, cellular interactions were found to mitigate these alterations, highlighting a potentially rescuable fetal-to-adult transcriptional signature with important implications for HD pathogenesis and therapeutic strategies. Together, these findings reinforce the view of HD as a disorder with developmental origins, in which early transcriptional changes may shape neuronal function while increasing susceptibility to later neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Serum β-synuclein predicts dementia conversion and mortality beyond amyloid-β and phospho-tau
Article.Authors: Oberstein T.; Schwarz J.; Rudtke L.; Jablonowski J.; Marterstock D.; Schmidt M.; Doerfler A.; Kiesel J.; Klement N.; Schulz P.; Lewczuk P.; Maler J.; Kornhuber J.; Oeckl P.; Otto M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Synaptic dysfunction is among the earliest pathological events in Alzheimer's disease and among the strongest neuropathological correlates of cognitive impairment, yet blood-based synaptic biomarkers are lacking. Whether serum β-synuclein provides prognostic information independent of established amyloid-β (A; CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio) and tau (T1; CSF pTau181) biomarkers has not been determined. We studied 259 non-demented individuals with subjective or mild cognitive impairment from a single-centre memory clinic, classified by CSF biomarkers using externally validated cut-offs into A−T1− controls (n = 97), A−T1+ PASSED (‘pTau and Aβ surge with subtle deterioration’, n = 65), and A + T1+ Alzheimer's disease (n = 97), with parallel analyses using Aβ40-normalised pTau181. Endpoints comprised dementia conversion (n = 185, median follow-up 4.1 years), all-cause mortality (n = 258, median 7.0 years), longitudinal MMSE trajectories (n = 185), and regional brain volumes (n = 137). Independence from CSF biomarkers was quantified through systematic effect attenuation analysis. Serum β-synuclein was selectively elevated in the Alzheimer's disease group (Cohen's d = 0.69 vs controls, P < 0.001) but not in PASSED individuals (P = 0.40), and was more strongly associated with CSF pTau181 (r = 0.36) than with the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio (r = −0.20) across the cohort. Each standard deviation increase was associated with higher risk of dementia conversion (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.40; 95% CI: 1.11, 1.77; P = 0.005), faster cognitive decline (−0.11 SD/year, 95% CI: −0.18, −0.04, P = 0.002, corresponding to −0.20 MMSE points/year), and higher mortality (HR = 1.33; 95% CI: 1.07, 1.65; P = 0.010). For dementia conversion and mortality, adjustment for continuous CSF pTau181 and Aβ42/Aβ40 produced minimal attenuation (≤13%). Both associations were preserved under Aβ40-normalised T1 staging but not against continuous pTau181 normalised to CSF Aβ40. For cognitive decline, β-synuclein's effect remained significant after Aβ42/Aβ40 adjustment (25% attenuation; P = 0.007) but was substantially attenuated by pTau181 (58.5%; P = 0.186). Serum β-synuclein was associated with lower bilateral temporal lobe volume—the only lobar regions to survive hierarchical testing—with sub-regional involvement spanning the hippocampi, entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus, and explained 5.0–8.9% of unique variance beyond CSF biomarkers. Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) showed a strong association with β-synuclein, estimated in the PASSED subgroup (β=0.34 per SD, P < 0.001). Serum β-synuclein provided prognostic information largely independent of CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 across all endpoints and of pTau181 for survival outcomes, while sharing substantial prognostic variance with pTau181 for cognitive trajectory, supporting its candidacy as a blood-based synaptic complement to core Alzheimer's disease biomarkers.

Article.Title: Prematurity insults remodel cerebellar development and behaviour
Article.Authors: Sanidas G.; Simonti G.; Ghaemmaghami J.; Woyshner K.; Vidva R.; Bittel D.; Wolff N.; Triantafyllou M.; Polyviou A.; Byrd C.; Lowe C.; Salisbury H.; Goldstein E.; Sathyanesan A.; Koutroulis I.; Stein-O'Brien G.; Sidiropoulos D.; Gallo V.; Kratimenos P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Preterm survivors often develop motor and socio-cognitive impairments that implicate altered cerebellar development, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. A key challenge is that prematurity involves overlapping perinatal insults that converge on the developing brain, making their individual effects difficult to disentangle. Here, we model two major prematurity-associated insults, maternal immune activation (MIA) and neonatal hypoxia (Hx), in mice. By controlling timing and sequence, we define how these insults shape cerebellar assembly during rapid maturation. Comparative analysis with human tissue confirmed that these insults recapitulate key features of the human preterm cerebellum, establishing the translational validity of this model for dissecting insult-specific outcomes. Behavioral and kinematic profiling revealed divergent motor and social phenotypes, which we traced to insult-specific cerebellar remodelling. Hypoxia compromised both granule cell maturation in the internal granule layer and the principal excitatory afferents to Purkinje cells, a circuit state that manifested as impaired motor execution and stereotyped, sensory-disengaged social investigation. Maternal immune activation, by contrast, expanded the granule cell progenitor layer and reduced Purkinje cell dendritic complexity, a phenotype that preserved social preference but reorganized the kinematic structure of social investigation. When hypoxia followed maternal immune activation, it acted on this primed substrate to produce a distinct state in which the features established by prior inflammation were compounded by granule cell proliferative arrest, progressive mitochondrial dysfunction, and aberrant, hyper-interactive social investigation. Together, these findings reframe prematurity-associated insults as cerebellar reprogramming events shaped by both the identity and sequence of insults, linking distinct mechanistic substrates to divergent neurodevelopmental outcomes.

Article.Title: Neuronavigated dual-target transcranial magnetic stimulation for schizophrenia negative symptoms
Article.Authors: Wei Y.; Wang J.; Tang X.; Qian Z.; Xu L.; Cui H.; Song Y.; Zhu H.; Ju M.; Long B.; Zhai W.; Zeng L.; Jiao X.; Lan X.; Wei X.; Tang Y.; Wang J.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Negative symptoms in schizophrenia severely impair function and quality of life, yet respond poorly to current therapies. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial aimed to investigate the efficacy of neuronavigated dual-target repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) and cerebellum for improving negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04853485). Participants with first-episode schizophrenia or clinical high-risk for psychosis were enrolled from Shanghai Mental Health Center and Suzhou Guangji Hospital. Participants were randomly assigned to either a real or sham group under MRI-guided neuronavigation, targeting rDLPFC with 1Hz at 100% motor threshold(MT), cerebellar with intermittent theta burst stimulation(iTBS) at 120% MT for 20 consecutive days. Clinical assessments were conducted at baseline(T0), 10-session(T1), 20-session(T2) and one month after the intervention(T3). Cognition and MRI were evaluated at T0 and T2. The primary outcome was change of negative subscale score of the Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale(PANSS), while secondary outcomes included alterations in other PANSS subscale scores and fronto-cerebellar circuit functional connectivity. In total, 75 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (36 active, 39 sham). The pre-specified primary linear mixed-effects analysis revealed a non-significant group-by-time interaction for PANSS negative subscale scores (F(3,174.6)=1.45, p=0.230). At the 4-week endpoint (T2), the nominal unadjusted between-group p-value was 0.049; after Sidak correction for multiple comparisons, the adjusted mean difference was −2.48 points (95% CI −4.99 to 0.03, adjusted p=0.150, Cohen’s d=−0.51). Descriptive uncorrected t-tests indicated greater negative-symptom reductions in the active group at T1 and T2, and the 4-week negative-symptom response rate (≥50% reduction) was higher under real rTMS (χ2=9.5, p=0.002). A significant group-by-time interaction was observed for PANSS positive subscale scores (F(3,172.0)=3.26, p=0.023). Both groups exhibited substantial within-group symptom improvement. Resting-state fMRI demonstrated group-by-time interactions within cerebello-temporal, parahippocampal, caudate, and parietal networks (FWE-corrected p<0.05), and negative-symptom change correlated with cerebello-caudate connectivity (r=0.33, p=0.026). These findings suggest neuronavigated dual-target rTMS over rDLPFC and cerebellum may be associated with numerical improvements in negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis.

Article.Title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood
Article.Authors: Dutta S.; Atashgaran A.; Sahoo A.; Chatzimichail S.; Kapanidis A.; Tofaris G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Parkinson’s disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34–45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

Article.Title: Biallelic variants in PIKFYVE cause a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with endolysosomal dysfunction
Article.Authors: Averdunk L.; Groß M.; Hamacher A.; Donkervoort S.; Herebian D.; Mohammad S.; Knaus A.; Seibt A.; Schaper J.; Sticht H.; Bryen S.; Bergmann A.; Langener M.; De Simone L.; Markshausen A.; Lenk G.; Ghosh S.; Sandaradura S.; Guthoff T.; Leventer R.; Orbach R.; Rius R.; Morton N.; Gilmour K.; Mayatepek E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The PIKfyve-FIG4-VAC14 lipid kinase complex generates phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2. Pathogenic variants in VAC14 and FIG4 cause neurodevelopmental disorders and PIKFYVE has been linked to autosomal dominant fleck corneal dystrophy. We searched for the underlyging, genetic cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder in five affected individuals from three families using exome- or genome sequencing. Cranial MRI images and clinical phenotypes were analyzed. Size, number and acidity of cellular vacuoles were investigated in patient-derived fibroblasts from family 1 using LysoSensor acidophilic probes. Levels of PI(3,5)P2 were quantified in patient-derived fibroblasts from family 1 using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae were injected with wildtype-mRNA or mutant mRNA harboring the PIKFYVE missense variant identified in family 3. Pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae were treated with metformin, bafilomycin A1, or rapamycin. We identified biallelic PIKFYVE variants in five affected individuals with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, brain hyperintensities of inferior olives, thalami, long tracts, and optic nerves. Clinically, they presented with intellectual disability, spasticity, muscular weakness, and nystagmus. Additional features included feeding difficulties, auditory dysfunction, insulin resistance, microcephaly, peripheral neuropathy, and mild creatine kinase elevations. We detected four distinct PIKFYVE variants: three loss-of-function variants (family 1 & 2), and one p.Arg1156Pro missense variant (family 3). The pathogenicity of the p.Arg1156Pro variant was confirmed by phenotypic rescue of pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae injected with wildtype-mRNA but not with p.Arg1156Pro mRNA. Consistent with the role of PIKfyve in maintaining endolysosomal homeostasis, patient-derived fibroblasts of family 1 accumulated enlarged, hyperacidic vacuoles and showed a reduced PI(3,5)P2 production upon hyperosmotic stimulation. Exposing pikfyve-mutant zebrafisch larvae to the mTORC1 inhibitor and TRPML1 activator rapamycin attenuated cellular vacuolization, highlighting potential therapeutic approaches. Our findings establish PIKFYVE deficiency as a novel cause of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy and endolysosomal dysfunction.

Article.Title: Target engagement and efficacy in disease-modifying trials of synuclein-related disorders
Article.Authors: Artusi C.; Gallo S.; Galli S.; Rinaldi D.; Tinazzi M.; Rascol O.; Espay A.; Fabbri M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Disease-modifying trials in Parkinson’s disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to demonstrate target engagement, de-risk subsequent phases of drug development and provide mechanistic evidence of biological activity. Whether biomarker modulation predicts clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant review of phase II and III disease-modifying trials (2020-2025) that included at least one biomarker intended to assess target engagement. Twenty-six trials met inclusion criteria (PD=19, MSA=4, DLB=3; n=2,195 participants). Target engagement was reported in 14 of 19 PD trials (12 phase II/2 phase III), 1 of 4 MSA trials, and 2 of 3 DLB trials (all phase II). Concordance between target engagement and clinical improvement was uncommon, as only 8/26 studies (7 phase II/1 phase III) demonstrated both target engagement and statistically significant clinical benefit, and just two of these (both phase II, one in PD and one in MSA) were rigorously controlled with low or moderate risk of bias. Nine trials showed target engagement without clinical benefit, whereas two reported clinical improvement without measurable target engagement. Baseline biomarker-guided patient selection was uncommon and rarely aligned with the compound’s mechanism of action. Patient-reported outcomes were widely used but rarely improved. Across recent disease-modifying trials in PD, DLB, and MSA, target engagement was frequently demonstrated, yet clinical benefit rarely followed. These findings question the predictive value of currently used target-engagement biomarkers and highlight the need to biologically align trial populations with the mechanisms targeted by experimental molecular interventions.
