Article.Title: Dynamics of TFIIH and Spt4/5 during the transition from transcription initiation to elongation
Article.Authors: Portman J.; Torrens K.; Giordano G.; Jeon J.; Chung J.; Friedman L.; Gelles J.; Buratowski S.
Article.Abstract: The transition of RNA polymerase II from initiation to elongation requires the timely exchange of many factors. Some initiation factors and elongation factors contact the same RNA polymerase II surfaces in an apparently mutually exclusive manner. For example, space occupied by the initiation factor TFIIH and elongation factor Spt4/5 (also known as DSIF) are predicted to overlap. To determine whether Spt4/5 actively displaces TFIIH, or binds only after TFIIH dissociates, labeled yeast nuclear extracts were combined with single-molecule fluorescence microscopy to observe their dynamics in real time. TFIIH categorically dissociates before Spt4/5 arrives, with a clear interval in between when neither factor is present. Therefore, Spt4/5 binding is not required to dissociate TFIIH from RNA polymerase II.

Article.Title: TEDEdb: A multicohort analysis and resource for transposable element differential expression in cancer
Article.Authors: Calendo G.; Chaunzwa M.; Dehzangi I.; Madzo J.; Issa J.
Article.Abstract: The human genome consists of nearly 50% repetitive DNA, referred to for decades as “junk DNA.” These repetitive sequences, usually under the strict control of epigenetic silencing, can become aberrantly expressed in cancer. Some of these expressed sequences, e.g., transposable elements (TEs), can induce innate immune responses when derepressed following treatment with epigenetic therapies. As a result, epigenetic therapy has been suggested to augment cancer therapies. TEs are traditionally ignored in most RNA-seq studies and their expression is often excluded from publicly available data sources. Thus, the vast amount of publicly available RNA-seq data is an untapped resource for exploring the role of TE expression in cancer and cancer treatment. Here, we present a uniform reanalysis of over 7,000 RNA-seq samples, encompassing more than 2,000 differential expression experiments across 220 cancer cell lines and 700 drug treatments. We observed that TE expression is more prone to batch effects than gene expression alone, necessitating the use of meta-analysis techniques to probe the dataset for global trends. We confirm that DNMTi and HDACis are powerful inducers of TE expression. We also show that nonepigenetic compounds such as cyclin-dependent kinase and topoisomerase inhibitors can also induce robust up-regulation of TE-derived repetitive DNA elements and confirm that this induction is consistent with transcriptional signatures of viral mimicry response. We made all data available through a publicly available database called the Transposable Element Differential Expression Database, or TEDEdb, and created an interactive web application for its exploration located at https://dataexplorer.coriell.org/TEDEdb/

Article.Title: Scaling laws link conserved gene-abundance distributions to adaptive expression in diatom communities worldwide
Article.Authors: Pigani E.; Simoens K.; Bernardi D.; Campese L.; Iudicone D.; Azaele S.; Suweis S.
Article.Abstract: Marine microbes sustain Earth’s major biogeochemical cycles, yet how they maintain stable ecosystem functions across diverse environments remains unclear. We analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data from diatom communities sampled during the Tara Oceans global expedition. While gene abundance distributions remain statistically similar across sample, gene expression varies systematically across geographical locations, a global pattern we show reflects predictable scaling laws. Global distributions, scaling relationships, and variability among sampling stations are captured by a stochastic model linking gene abundance dynamics to gene expression. While colder waters are associated with higher transcriptional activity and warmer regions show more selective gene usage, we find that transcript abundance increases nonlinearly with transcript richness. This general scaling is captured by our model and suggests that diatom communities balance high expression of core genes with specific functional diversity. These scaling relationships hold consistently across ocean basins, with temperature, used as an effective large-scale environmental descriptor whose signature cannot be fully disentangled from spatial structure, sufficing to predict transcriptional patterns from genetic composition. Our findings reveal how the stability of gene-abundance structure in diatom ecosystems coexists with transcriptional variability, enabling flexible functional responses.

Article.Title: Dlx1&2 directly promote expression of Cxcl14 to control synapse development and interneuron survival
Article.Authors: Guo T.; Lindtner S.; Hu J.; Darbandi S.; Wang Y.; Pai E.; Ypsilanti A.; van Velthoven C.; Nord A.; Rubenstein J.
Article.Abstract: Dlx genes have fundamental roles in the generation, differentiation, and functions of virtually all forebrain GABAergic neurons. Here we used scRNA-Seq to identify genes that are dysregulated in Dlx1/2 conditional mutants in mouse immature CGE- and MGE-derived cortical and olfactory bulb GABAergic interneurons. Dlx1/2 -regulated genes included Cxcl14 and Nr2f2 that are important for cortical interneuron (CIN) survival. We also identified DLX2-bound putative regulatory elements (pREs) of these Dlx -regulated genes. Within the Dlx -expressing lineage, some DLX-bound pREs were specific to CINs, others appeared to be constitutively bound; the latter class having activity in mature CINs. One such pRE and its associated gene, Cxcl14 , is strongly activated by Dlx1/2 and is essential for synaptogenesis onto CINs.

Article.Title: Cooperative nature of residue interactions in biomolecular condensates
Article.Authors: Chen L.; Wu X.; Hu G.; Zeng X.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Cooperativity of residue interactions is prevalent in proteins and plays an essential role in protein folding. However, whether cooperativity exists in intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and their assembled biomolecular condensates remains elusive. Here, we reveal the presence of residue interaction cooperativity in various IDP condensates using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. In all these condensates, cooperative residue interactions manifest as packing between finite residue motifs (3 to 5 residues) with lifetimes three orders of magnitude longer than residue contacts. Notably, these higher-order interactions (HOIs) exhibit a significant nonadditive free energy, which originates from a local low-dielectric environment. The underlying sequence patterns like “Y-X-Q”, “D-X-R”, and “S-Y-X” are identified. Furthermore, HOIs dominate the cohesive energy of IDPs and condensates can be treated as HOI-crosslinked networks. This model can successfully reproduce experimental results of condensate physical properties, including saturation concentration, viscoelasticity, and interfacial tension.

Article.Title: Orexin and pupillary modulation for hunger control
Article.Authors: Kosar S.; Bracey E.; Grujic N.; Du Y.; Peleg-Raibstein D.; Burdakov D.
Article.Abstract: Fasting-based interventions improve metabolic health and are also explored as adjuncts in other clinical settings, but hunger remains a barrier to adherence. Fasting activates AgRP/NPY neurons (ANs), a hunger-promoting population whose inhibition reduces eating in hungry animals. Here we identify hypocretin/orexin neurons (HONs), classically associated with arousal, as rapid suppressors of AN activity. HON ablation increased AN population activity, whereas HON optostimulation rapidly suppressed it. Combined recordings of AN activity and pupil size—a direct arousal metric not previously linked to AN dynamics—revealed that HONs contributed to pupil dilation-associated AN suppression. In fasted mice, sensory stimulation rapidly recruited this pupil-HON pathway, and suppressed AN activity and eating. These findings reveal an arousal–hunger pathway through which self-initiated pupil dilations, or dilations driven by salient environmental events, interrupt fasting-induced hunger signals. They also suggest a framework for noninvasive, sensory-, and pupillometry-guided approaches to hunger control during fasting.

Article.Title: The lncRNA-encoded micropeptide ANCHOR promotes lateral root growth and drought tolerance in rice
Article.Authors: He R.; Jiang J.; Yuan C.; Cao X.; Peng K.; Zhang N.; Luo L.; Fang C.; Zhang Z.; Niu X.; Li W.; Mo W.; Liao Y.; Liu Q.; Zhang Y.; Lian J.; Cheng Y.; Chen Y.
Article.Abstract: Lateral roots (LRs) are important components of plant root systems, determining the robustness of root system architecture and influencing water uptake efficiency. Enhancing the phenotypic plasticity of LRs is key to improving crop production under fluctuating environmental conditions. In this study, we identified ANCHOR, a micropeptide encoded by a long noncoding RNA that is predominantly expressed in LR primordia and plumules. Overexpression of ANCHOR resulted in significantly longer and wider LRs, thereby altering root system architecture and enhancing drought tolerance; knockouts of ANCHOR produced the opposite phenotypes. Mechanistically, ANCHOR localized to plastids and directly interacted with the lysine biosynthetic enzyme LL-diaminopimelate aminotransferase 1 (LL-DAPAT). Our results indicate that ANCHOR functions as a “molecular glue” that enhances DAPAT dimerization. Through its influence on lysine metabolism, ANCHOR raises the levels of the auxin biosynthetic precursor tryptophan, thereby affecting auxin homeostasis. These findings show that lncRNA-derived micropeptides, like their precursor RNAs, can function as fine-tuning regulators. This function of micropeptides, together with their small molecular size, may make them suitable for application as bioeffectors to stimulate root growth and improve plant tolerance to abiotic stress without side effects for plants.

Article.Title: piRNA loss unleashes episodic transposition bursts
Article.Authors: Chen P.; Xu P.; Waseem H.; McCormick J.; Pan K.; Aravin A.; Clark A.; Feschotte C.
Article.Abstract: In Metazoa, transposon expression is suppressed by the piRNA pathway, and disruption of this pathway leads to rampant transposon expression. However, it remains unclear whether increased transposon expression results in actual transposition, and if so, which and how frequently transposons mobilize upon piRNA loss. Here, we developed a framework to track transposon copy accumulation across generations on a single set of nonrecombining haploid genome in the Drosophila male germline, with or without the piRNA biogenesis factor HP1D/Rhino. Single-fly Nanopore DNA sequencing revealed that multiple transposon families mobilized after 10 to 45 generations of piRNA loss. Among them, the most prolific across all replicates was copia , producing dozens of new insertions that were distributed across chromosome arms. With genomic DNA collected at every generation, we validated and dated each copia insertion, revealing episodic bursts of transposition that deviated strongly from a Poisson process. Using phylogenetic analysis, we further showed that multiple copia loci—both autonomous and nonautonomous copies—can mobilize. Interestingly, two additional transposon families, mdg3 and invader3 , also mobilized episodically, but with distinct timing and magnitude, highlighting the stochastic nature of transposition bursts. Because we did not observe a single transposition event for these elements in controls, our results provide direct evidence that the piRNA pathway tightly suppresses germline transposition. More importantly, our findings argue that disruption of the piRNA pathway does not simply elevate transposition rates, but it instead unleashes punctuated and stochastic bursts of transposon movement that may radically reshape the timing and magnitude of mutational input during evolution.

Article.Title: Quantifying ancient architecture: Stone-level machine learning reveals architectural variation and settlement growth at Shivta
Article.Authors: Uziel E.; Avni G.; Feinman G.; Bar-Oz G.; Jaffe Y.
Article.Abstract: Built environments provide durable evidence for how ancient settlements were organized, expanded, and transformed over time. Yet quantitative approaches to documenting architectural variability are generally labor-intensive, limited to individual structures, or dependent on aggregate volumetric estimates. We present a scalable, machine-learning-based framework that shifts the unit of analysis to the individual building stone and combines two complementary datasets: low-altitude drone imagery of surface remains and close-range photographs of standing walls. Applied to the Late Antique settlement of Shivta in the Negev Desert, the method automatically digitized approximately 235,000 surface stones and 12,000 stones in 604 walls, quantifying stone size, shape regularity, and masonry arrangement across walls, households, insulae, and the settlement as a whole. Higher masonry scores cluster around churches and parts of the settlement boundary, while the spatial distribution of masonry variation reveals a previously unidentified earlier boundary and provides evidence for outward expansion from a southern core. Combined with architectural sequencing, these patterns indicate the use of larger and more regularly shaped stones during Shivta’s principal phase of growth. The framework combines analytical flexibility with demonstrated robustness, supporting broader application across diverse stone-built archaeological contexts while complementing architectural energetics and enabling settlement-wide and cross-site comparisons of construction practices and settlement change.

Article.Title: Profile of Barbara Sherwood Lollar
Article.Authors: Davis T.
Article.Abstract: In a laboratory nearly 2.4 kilometers under the Canadian Shield, geochemist Barbara Sherwood Lollar has tracked the sustained release of enough hydrogen gas from Earth’s crust to produce 4.7 million kilowatt-hours of energy per year. Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2022, Sherwood Lollar revisited the Kidd Creek Mine in Ontario, Canada where, in 2013, her explorations found that waters flowing from deep fractures were 1.6 billion years old. Reported in her Inaugural Article, the findings, aided by studies of noble gases in the samples, pushed the age of Earth’s oldest waters back by hundreds of millions of years.

Article.Title: Septin binding restricts Shigella growth and triggers intracellular tolerance
Article.Authors: Özbaykal Güler G.; Zhang C.; Brokatzky D.; Das R.; Wheeler R.; Boneca I.; Cortes T.; Manley S.; Mostowy S.
Article.Abstract: Pathogen survival relies on their ability to adapt to changing environments, yet how intracellular bacteria tolerate cell-autonomous immunity remains unclear. Septins assemble into cage-like structures around cytoplasmic Shigella targeted by autophagy, but their antibacterial activity was unknown. Using advanced microscopy and cell-free reconstitution, we show that septins polymerize into circumferentially oriented filaments that inhibit bacterial growth. RNA-sequencing reveals that septin binding to Shigella upregulates type III secretion system (T3SS) effectors and triggers a stress response. Underlying this, septin-bound Shigella possess hyperpolarized membranes, but without lethally damaged cell envelope. We show that exposure to septin binding enhances the impact of the cell envelope-targeting antibiotic polymyxin B. During infection, T3SS effector OspC1 prevents septin recruitment, while stress-response regulator cspC protects against septin-mediated changes to membrane potential. Hence, septin binding is intrinsically antibacterial and is sensed by Shigella as a danger signal to promote mechanisms of intracellular tolerance.

Article.Title: Intraventricular clindamycin enhances interstitial brain fluid drainage and the blood–brain barrier after a traumatic brain injury
Article.Authors: Ashby L.; Crowe M.; Chakravarty D.; Medam S.; Frampton G.; Das A.; Hormuth D.; Yankeelov T.; Wang V.; Noble-Haeusslein L.; Umlauf B.
Article.Abstract: Despite advances in the acute clinical management of severe traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), treating injury-derived secondary pathogenesis remains challenging. We demonstrate intracerebroventricular (I.C.V.) administration of clindamycin alleviates TBI secondary pathogenesis in both focal and diffuse murine models of brain injury. I.C.V. administration of clindamycin increased the motility of ependymal cilia, which line the ventricles and spinal canal, by 30 to 60%, which correlated with interstitial brain fluid drainage through the cortex (r > 0.9 Pearson, n = 4 compounds tested). I.C.V. clindamycin treatment post-TBI also restored the blood–brain barrier (BBB), decreased lesion size, and lowered serum levels of glial fibrillary acidic protein by 2.8-fold. Consistent with these data, a novel objective recognition test revealed an improvement in recognition memory in brain-injured mice treated with clindamycin. These collective findings reveal a counterintuitive finding that I.C.V. clindamycin enhances drainage of toxins from the brain while simultaneously restoring the BBB, potentially providing a new solution for alleviating secondary pathogenesis in brain-injured patients.

Article.Title: Holocene millennial climate variability influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions
Article.Authors: Zhou P.; Shi Z.; An Z.; Cai W.; Braconnot P.; Zhang Q.
Article.Abstract: A prominent unstable feature, millennial-scale climate oscillation (MCO), punctuated the Holocene. Solar activity and deep ocean variability are generally regarded as the origin of the MCO, yet the dynamics remain debated. Using a Holocene transient simulation with the EC-Earth climate model (8 to 0 ka BP), together with a global compilation of 304 temperature reconstructions, here we identify a robust ~1,350-y oscillatory mode that characterizes Holocene climate variability and is self-sustained and crucially influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions. Within each cycle, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) strengthening evolves with the developing warming and an El Niño-like tropical sea surface temperature (SST) response, accompanied by anticyclonic circulation anomalies over the high-latitude Southern Ocean. Northward cold advection of the associated enhanced westerly winds off the Antarctic coast overcomes the effect of sea ice retreat to promote AABW formation, ocean stratification, and warming. Positive feedbacks including sea ice-albedo, tropical air–sea interaction, and SST-AABW magnify surface warming till AABW reaches its peak. Thereafter, reduced brine rejection from sea-ice retreat weakens AABW, counteracts the warming, and commences a switch to its cooling phase. The dominant periodicity, consistent with that inferred from proxy reconstructions, is confirmed by complementary climate simulations. These results provide an alternative physical mechanism for Holocene millennial-scale climate variability. Under future anthropogenic warming, a positive phase of the oscillation may heighten the positive feedbacks, thereby increasing the risk of rapid climate transformation.

Article.Title: Pancreatic δ cells are resistant to auto- and paracrine inhibition in human type-2 diabetes
Article.Authors: Omar-Hmeadi M.; Matuseviciene L.; Liu L.; Lund P.; Barg S.
Article.Abstract: Somatostatin secretion from pancreatic δ cells inhibits nearby α- and β cells and tunes the body’s glycemic set-point. The role of δ cells in diabetes remains unclear, in part due to the difficulty separating intrinsic regulation from intraislet paracrine effects. Here, we compared the function of isolated δ cells of cadaveric nondiabetic and type-2 diabetic donors by single cell total internal reflection microscopy, electrophysiology, and secretion measurements. Elevated glucose stimulated exocytosis of somatostatin, which was further amplified by glucagon, exendin-4, or forskolin, independent of diabetic status. gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) enhanced exocytosis and electrical activity, while insulin had no detectable effect. Adrenaline and somatostatin strongly inhibited δ cell activity, leading to autocrine feedback inhibition of somatostatin exocytosis. In type-2 diabetes, δ cell inhibition by somatostatin and adrenaline was impaired, together with a marked reduction in somatostatin receptor (SSTR2) surface expression. The data suggest that selective loss of inhibitory control of δ cells may dysregulate intraislet somatostatin signaling in type-2 diabetes.

Article.Title: VAP organizes presynaptic Ca <sup>2+</sup> signaling and synaptic vesicle mobilization through Kv2 membrane contact sites
Article.Authors: Paton C.; Cho I.; Hoppa M.
Article.Abstract: In neurons, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) forms an extensive network that establishes membrane contact sites (MCSs) with various organelles including the plasma membrane (PM). While MCSs are known to regulate lipid exchange and Ca 2+ signaling, their specific roles in synaptic transmission remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the ER-resident proteins VAPA and VAPB are essential for organizing presynaptic Ca 2+ exchange and mobilizing synaptic vesicles. We show that the loss of VAP impairs Ca 2+ loading into both the ER and mitochondria during electrical activity. This regulation occurs primarily through VAP interactions with voltage-gated potassium (Kv2) channels at the PM. Our data suggest that the Kv2–VAP complex organizes presynaptic Ca 2+ signaling outside the active zone. Without this scaffold, vesicle mobilization for exocytosis is strongly impaired and a larger fraction remains trapped in the reserve pool. These findings reveal a role for Kv2–VAP MCSs in coordinating organelle Ca 2+ signaling and the synaptic vesicle cycle.

Article.Title: A voltage-gated porin PPE1 regulates secretion and drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Article.Authors: Yadav M.; C. A. N.; Mandal D.; Shukla J.; Sarkar B.; Kumar Mahtha S.; Chandramouli A.; Prasad A.; Kamat S.; Mohanty D.; Dutta S.; Mahendran K.; Gokhale R.

We identify PPE1 as a voltage-gated outer-membrane porin that mediates the secretion of kupyaphores while also facilitating the uptake of the frontline anti-tubercular drug isoniazid (INH). Genome-wide association analysis of 38,038 clinical isolates links ppe1 mutations with INH resistance, highlighting its clinical relevance. Electron microscopy, molecular modeling, and single-channel electrophysiology reveal that PPE1 assembles into an unusual pentameric α-helical channel, distinct from classical β-barrel bacterial porins. Together, our findings identify PPE1 as a key determinant of mycobacterial membrane permeability that coordinates metallophore secretion and also antibiotic influx. This work uncovers a previously unrecognized mechanism governing Mtb physiology, virulence, and drug susceptibility, providing a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

In a stepwise increase of complexity, we first cocultured patient-derived HNSCC cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and endothelial cells within tailored eECMs, revealing extracellular matrix-dependent differences in transcriptional state, multicellular self-organization, and chemotherapeutic sensitivity. Finally, we incorporated trigeminal innervation through injectable 3D human bioengineered trigeminal ganglia, establishing a chip-based innervation–tumor–vasculature tri-interface. Article.Authors: Nilforoshan H.; Reisler J.; Jahanparast E.; Moor M.; Goodman S.; Wager S.; Leskovec J.
Article.Abstract: COVID-19 has been reported to cause multisystem effects lasting years [Z. Al-Aly, E. Topol, Science 383, 830–832 (2024)]. These findings are primarily based on cohort studies comparing test-positive COVID-19 patients to controls without known COVID-19 infection, tested or untested [M. Cai, Y. Xie, E. J. Topol, Z. Al-Aly, Nat. Med. 30, 1564–1573 (2024)]. However, such comparisons can be biased by the reasons people were tested. Using 14.4 billion insurance claims from 244.7 million US patients, we find that most long-term effects attributed to COVID-19 by unrestricted control designs likely reflect bias due to selective testing of individuals with non-COVID conditions, causing long-term effects of those conditions to be misattributed to COVID-19. We removed this bias by analyzing only tested individuals, comparing test-positive to test-negative patients. Across 614 clinical outcomes followed over 2 y, the test-based design resulted in 83.5% fewer symptoms being attributable to COVID-19 between 30 to 119 d after infection (43 attributable symptoms vs. 262 for the unrestricted control design), a 98.2% reduction at 120 to 359 d (5 vs. 286), and a 100% reduction at 360 to 719 d (0 vs. 369). The unrestricted control design also attributed unrelated outcomes (e.g., firearm injuries) to COVID-19 at a high rate, whereas the testing-based design did not. The test-based control design may modestly underestimate some effects. This study does not indicate that symptoms beyond one year are not genuine but that their attributability to COVID-19 is uncertain.

Article.Title: Neuromodulation-inspired gated associative memory networks: Extended memory retrieval and emergent multistability
Article.Authors: Goto D.; Lopez Rios H.; Scholz M.; Vaikuntanathan S.
Article.Abstract: Classical autoassociative memory models have been central to understanding emergent computations in recurrent neural circuits across diverse biological contexts. However, they typically neglect neuromodulatory agents that are known to strongly shape memory capacity and stability. Here we introduce a minimal, biophysically motivated associative memory network in which neuromodulator-like signals are modeled by a self-adaptive, activity-dependent gating mechanism. Using many-body simulations and dynamical mean-field theory, we show that such gating fundamentally reorganizes the attractor structure: the network bypasses the classical spin-glass transition, maintaining robust, high-overlap retrieval far beyond the standard critical capacity. Mechanistically, when the gates act as fully open or fully closed switches, the gate stabilizes transient “ghost” remnants of stored patterns even far above the Hopfield limit, converting a single memory fixed-point attractor into a cluster of fixed points. The retrieved state is set by the initial overlap rather than quantized to the stored pattern. This graded dependence may be exploited for input-driven computation with persistent activity. These results establish that neuromodulation-like gating alone—without modifying synaptic weights or introducing explicit higher-order couplings—can dramatically expand memory capacity, eliminate catastrophic breakdown, and reshape a discrete attractor landscape into a rich continuum, suggesting a general and biologically accessible route to enhanced computational capabilities in neural circuits and neuromorphic architectures.

Article.Title: Hepatitis C viral variants bear signatures of de novo CD8+ T cell and antibody pressure after spontaneous postpartum viral suppression

Article.Abstract: Progression to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection entails loss of HCV-specific CD4+ T cell help, emergence of viral variants that escape recognition by CD8+ T cells and neutralizing antibodies, and exhaustion of CD8+ T cells targeting remaining intact epitopes. However, in some chronically infected women, a surprising postpartum viral load decline has been linked to resurgent functional HCV-specific CD4+ helper T cells. Plasma from controllers also demonstrated a postpartum increase in neutralization of multiple HCV strains. Together, these findings support the hypothesis that postpartum viral control is mediated by CD8+ T cell and antibody pressure.

Article.Title: Viral metagenomics reveals heterogeneity in mammalian virus hosting, sharing, and spillover
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Qu G.; Huang Z.; Zhang X.; Li H.; Wei X.; Hu L.; Xu S.; Becker D.; Wei F.; Xu Y.
Article.Abstract: Zoonotic viruses originating from mammals pose a persistent threat to global health. While rodents and bats are often considered “special reservoirs,” it is debated if spillover risk is driven by specific taxa or merely reflects mammalian species richness. However, most tests have focused on published host–virus association datasets, which can reflect systematic biases in host and virus sampling effort. To address this limitation, we analyzed a comprehensive repository of 4,685 metagenomic datasets, minimizing bias toward any one viral taxon and spanning 296 species across 14 mammalian orders. We characterized the global mammalian virome and found substantial heterogeneity in the capacity of different mammalian orders to harbor and share human-associated viruses. Counter to conventional wisdom, carnivores exhibited significantly higher propensities to carry human-associated viruses, with bats ranked lower in this metric of zoonotic risk. Network analyses of viral sharing further revealed higher cross-order virus sharing among specific mammalian orders (e.g., carnivores and artiodactyls). Phylogenetic comparative analyses revealed that host life-history traits (e.g., longevity) and anthropogenic factors (e.g., urban land use) were key ecological drivers of both virus richness and transmission centrality. Our study provides a data-driven framework that challenges prevailing narratives of zoonotic risk and offers a refined strategy for prioritizing surveillance and mitigating emerging zoonotic threats.

Article.Title: Encoding metal coordination pathways and nuclearity by molecular knotting
Article.Authors: Chi G.; Li B.; Feng H.; Zhang Z.; Wang H.; Li X.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Precise control over the nuclearity and spatial organization of metal ions is a central objective in coordination chemistry. Knotting imposes severe geometric constraints on frameworks but has rarely been exploited to organize inequivalent metal-binding sites within a single ligand. Direct metalation affords Mn(II) 5 -, Fe(II) 5 -, Co(II) 5 -, and Cd(II) 5 -knots through a dinuclear intermediate and an unusual 2-to-5 metal nuclearity progression, even though these metals do not template knot formation. Crystallization of a Mn(II) 2 -intermediate reveals partial demetalation but retains a Mn(II) center displaying a “3 + 3” coordination mode, whereas all Fe(II) ions in the fully metalated Fe(II) 5 -knot adopt a “3 + 2” binding geometry. Together with computational simulations, these observations support a stepwise metalation mechanism in which the dinuclear “3 + 3” coordination environment evolves into the “3 + 2” motif of the pentanuclear knot. Although the Ni(II) 5 - knot cannot be obtained by direct metalation because of slow incorporation, it forms readily via transmetalation from a Zn(II) 5 -knot. Circular dichroism measurements show that chiral expression is dictated by the overall ligand arrangement rather than the identity of the metal ions. The work demonstrates molecular knotting as a strategy for pathway-controlled multi-metallic assembly.

Article.Title: Mechanically driven grain refinement in Mo by nanoindentation pop-ins: A case of transient instability
Article.Authors: Li F.; Mostafa A.; Kauffmann Y.; Abdolrahim N.; Rabkin E.
Article.Abstract: During load-controlled nanoindentation of pristine metals, the homogeneous dislocation nucleation manifests as a sudden displacement burst, or pop-in, associated with shear stresses approaching the theoretical strength, massive dislocation nucleation, and rapid yet uncontrolled indenter penetration. Using single-crystal Mo with different surface orientations, we demonstrate pop-in-induced nucleation of new, highly misoriented grains at room temperature. This nucleation behavior is attributed to two mechanically driven processes: 1) activation of twinning followed by the evolution of twin boundaries into random high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) and 2) rearrangement of dislocations into HAGBs within regions of high local dislocation density during the abrupt deformation accompanying the pop-in. Displacement-controlled atomistic simulations reproduce both twin- and dislocation-mediated grain nucleation within an individual grain when a preexisting grain boundary blocks dislocation glide. However, in the absence of such a grain boundary, nucleated dislocations glide into the surrounding crystal and fail to form new grains. Continued indentation beyond pop-in mechanically erases newly formed grains, as confirmed in both experiments and simulations, explaining why this phenomenon was not detected in previous studies. Together, the observed nucleation and subsequent erasure of the grains establish the nanoindentation pop-in as a simple, widely accessible platform for qualitatively probing transient microstructural evolution in defect-scarce metals.

Article.Authors: Xu Z.; Tse K.; Liu N.; Olson E.
Article.Abstract: Myoblast fusion is essential for skeletal muscle development and regeneration. Myomaker is a muscle-specific fusogen indispensable for this process. Cryoelectron microscopy analysis has shown that Myomaker dimerization is required for myoblast fusion and muscle formation. Article.Title: Imaging real-space chiral rotation of flat-band states in helical trilayer graphene
Article.Authors: Hao C.; Zhou G.; Zhang M.; Guo Z.; Song Z.; He L.
Article.Abstract: Flat bands have been experimentally realized in a wide variety of graphene-based moiré systems with designed stacking configurations. Spatial mapping of the threefold-anisotropic pattern reveals a chiral rotation that varies as a function of energy. Theoretical simulations based on the Bistritzer–MacDonald model reproduce the distinct orientations of the threefold-anisotropic patterns across different low-energy minibands and reveal a systematic correspondence between the direction of local density-of-states rotation and the structural chirality of helical trilayer graphene. Our results demonstrate that real-space electronic textures—previously overlooked—can partially reveal the intrinsic disparities among different flat bands, highlighting that systematic exploration of flat bands across moiré systems is critical for deciphering the origins of distinct correlated phases.

Article.Title: Protein resource allocation across subcellular compartments revealed by large-scale absolute quantitative proteomics in yeast
Article.Authors: Lu H.; Zhang Z.; He S.; Zhang Y.; Wang Y.; Tao F.; Nielsen J.
Article.Abstract: Subcellular compartmentalization within complex membrane-bound organelles is a hallmark of eukaryal life, enabling metabolic specialization through spatial segregation. Leveraging big data analysis, formula fitting, and machine learning, quantitative correlations among protein abundance, resource allocation, and cellular phenotypes were elucidated at a system level. We found that subcellular resource distribution is highly uneven and covaries with specific growth rate. Specifically, at high specific growth rates, the protein mass fraction (PMF) from certain compartments, (e.g., nucleus) is consistently reduced, coinciding with the increasing protein resource demand from ribosomes. Meanwhile, nutrient limitation may induce resource recycling by upregulating protein resources within specific compartments (e.g., vacuole) to sustain stress adaptation. Importantly, our integrative analysis indicates that PMF from a few subcellular compartments (e.g., nucleus and ribosomes) can accurately predict yeast physiological parameters (e.g., specific growth rate, oxygen uptake rate), and a limited protein set (≥ 23) could be used to capture the variation in resource allocation across seven major subcellular compartments. Furthermore, our comparative analysis between Crabtree-positive and Crabtree-negative species across conditions illustrates that subcellular resource allocation could be shaped by multiple factors and the two species differ markedly in their robustness to environmental perturbations. In summary, the high-quality quantitative proteomic dataset for yeast species offers an unprecedented opportunity for understanding the general principles underlying subcellular resource allocation, laying foundations for precision engineering of cell factories in synthetic biology.

Article.Abstract: The end-Permian mass extinction was the most severe biotic crisis of the Phanerozoic, yet temporal synchrony between marine and terrestrial extinctions remains debated due to correlation uncertainties. Here, we present an integrated magnetostratigraphic, cyclostratigraphic, and carbon-isotope and mercury (Hg) chemostratigraphic record from the fluvial Upper Shihhotse, Sunjiagou, and Liujiagou formations at the Sigou section, North China. We identify 14 magnetozones spanning the late Changhsingian to late Olenekian, constrained by a floating timescale based on gamma-ray cyclostratigraphy and subsequently anchored through magnetostratigraphic correlation. Our chronostratigraphy reveals a Hg peak at 252.4 Ma, aligning with the main eruptive phase of the Siberian Traps Large Igneous Province, while the carbon isotope excursion onset (252.1 Ma) and minimum (252.0 Ma) are synchronous with the Meishan Global Stratotype Section and Point. Furthermore, the Induan–Olenekian boundary is positioned below magnetozone SG4n, constraining the Induan Stage duration to 1.6 to 1.8 My. These findings establish a high-resolution chronostratigraphic framework for the Permian–Triassic boundary in North China, supporting a synchronous extinction zenith across marine and low–middle latitude terrestrial ecosystems, with latitudinal diachroneity relative to high-latitude and tropical landmasses.

Article.Title: Predicting birth weights in West Africa using subseasonal to seasonal climate and socioeconomic variables shows potential for an early warning system
Article.Authors: Shukla S.; Davenport F.
Article.Abstract: Past research has shown a negative impact of climate extremes on child birth weight (BW), which is modulated by household socioeconomic and individual maternal conditions as well as the timing and degree of exposure. This study tests the potential of predicting BW using subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) climate predictors and socioeconomic indicators to support early warning systems for BW. Three sets of predictors were tested: a) a suite of biological and socioeconomic indicators from the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), b) S2S climate predictors, and c) a combination of climate predictors and selected socioeconomic indicators. The most accurate models incorporated the full set of DHS variables [predictors set (a)], with within-country (models trained and tested on the same country) predictive errors ranging from 13.5 to 17% for Burkina Faso and 20 to 25% for Mali. Cross-country (models trained on one country and tested on others) errors varied from 14 to 21% in Burkina Faso to 20 to 26% in Senegal. Models using only climate predictors [predictors set (b)] showed comparable skill to those using the full set of DHS indicators, with a relative error difference of 1 to 5%. The predictive skill was highest for children born with the most in-utero exposure to the lean season (months between planting and harvest). The results of this study have important implications for the prospect of implementing child BW early warning systems in data-sparse regions, based solely on climate predictors or based on selected socioeconomic indicators with climate predictors, to support malnutrition surveillance, to improve antenatal/maternal nutrition, policy formulation, and mitigation decisions.

Article.Title: Humid-heat shifts conceptions and increases pregnancy termination risks in Nigeria
Article.Authors: Brooks N.; Tuholske C.; McMahon K.; Andam K.
Article.Abstract: Climate change is increasing the occurrence of dangerous heat events globally with immediate health consequences, particularly in the Global South. In this paper, we spatially integrate Demographic and Healt 9 h surveys with a high-resolution, blended remotely sensed and station-derived dataset of humid-heat events spanning 1983–2016 to examine the effect of humid-heat exposure on fertility in Nigeria, one of the largest and most climate-vulnerable countries in the world. We use discrete-time models to examine the relationship between humid-heat exposure and conception probability and linear probability models to examine the relationship between humid-heat exposure and pregnancy termination (spontaneous and induced). We find that a 1 ° C increase in the current maximum wet bulb globe temperature decreases conceptions (0.2 conceptions per 1,000 woman-months, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.4), but exposure to hotter temperatures 1 to 2 mo prior increases conception probability. Exposure to hot-humid temperatures during pregnancy increases probability of pregnancy termination (1.73 terminations per 100 pregnancies, 95% CI: 0.7 to 2.7). The net effect is an increase in births, but the timing may be shifted. Subgroup analyses reveal that effects of humid-heat on conception were larger for women residing in rural areas or in northern districts, or who are Muslim or have lower educational attainment, while the association between humid-heat and pregnancy termination was larger for women in southern areas, older women, and Christian women. Differences in how humid-heat affects populations may exacerbate existing inequalities. Overall, our analysis contributes to a better understanding of how humid-heat exposure affects fertility and reproductive health among women in the Global South.

Article.Title: Heterogeneous impacts of temperature extremes on climate attitudes and Green voting
Article.Authors: Bassetto J.; Hoffmann R.; Muttarak R.; Peisker J.; Stanig P.
Article.Abstract: In the past decade, the public in Europe has become more concerned about climate change and expresses stronger proenvironmental policy preferences. Based on data from the European Social Survey (2012–2022, 25 countries), we show that the increased exposure to temperature extremes has contributed to the observed changes in climate change attitudes and electoral support for environmentalist policy platforms. For each additional degree of excess temperature experienced during warm spells measured over the previous 12 mo, we find that the probabilities of being worried about climate change, of feeling responsible for climate change, and of voting for Green parties and Green coalitions increase by 4.0 [CI95: 2.5, 5.5], 2.5 [CI95: 1.1, 3.9], and 2.8 [CI95: 0.9, 3.7] percentage points respectively. We also document significant heterogeneity across individuals, based on gender and education, particularly between highly educated women and low-educated men. While the latter group consistently exhibits the lowest proenvironmental attitudes and voting, it is this group that shows the strongest increases when exposed to temperature extremes, converging toward the levels of their more educated counterparts. Further regional heterogeneity analyses reveal that the effects of warm temperature extremes are smaller in less prosperous or economically disadvantaged regions, as well as in regions with greenhouse gas emission levels above the median. The findings suggest a nuanced interplay between individual factors and contextual influences in shaping climate attitudes of European citizens and their motivations or reservations toward greater climate action.

Article.Title: Decoding climate anomalies—From scientifically sound to societally relevant
Article.Authors: Brown M.; Tarnavsky E.; Enenkel M.
Article.Abstract: As climate impacts worsen, decision-makers, researchers, and public sector institutions increasingly need reliable, relevant, and appropriate information about emerging weather and climate anomalies. However, with the ever-expanding choice of datasets based on ground observations, satellite data, and models, it is critical to not only use the best dataset for a specific decision-making need but to avoid misinforming and even derailing decision-making due to dataset selection. The main objective of this perspective is to illustrate the importance of understanding datasets used to translate climate data into actionable knowledge, supporting the next generation of science- and data-driven climate risk management instruments, projects, and global initiatives. Through the lens of three use cases, we illustrate what data quality means for different applications, the implications of choosing, aggregating, and combining different climate datasets, and the potential consequences of dataset and baseline choice on decision-making. Choosing different datasets often leads to trade-offs that decision-makers need to be aware of, for instance, between the spatial resolution of a dataset and length of the data record. Here, we discuss the implications of selecting the appropriate time step, resolution, and dataset and provide examples of how these choices affect the identification of societally relevant anomalies.

Article.Title: Propagating shocks and transitions across networked food systems: Insights from multiplayer microeconomic modeling
Article.Authors: Zaitchik B.; Siddiqui S.; Simane B.; Zhang Y.; Sankaranarayanan S.; Bakker C.; Witkin S.
Article.Abstract: Accelerating global change is affecting coupled natural ecosystems and human activities in every part of the world. The local and regional expressions of these changes are a product of interacting and networked systems such that a shock, trend or development transition in one region, ecosystem, or sector can propagate impacts to other regions, ecosystems, and sectors. Informed adaptation and development strategies require an understanding of how signals propagate through these coupled systems and regions. Here, we synthesize findings from our work in Ethiopia and Mali, where we developed and applied a modeling system designed to capture cross-sector dynamics of networked food, water, and energy systems at subnational scale. We approach the problem using a multiplayer microeconomic model that accounts for diverse objectives through chains of food production, distribution, and consumption that connect resource regions to market regions. This paper draws lessons from three case studies in Ethiopia and one in Mali that are designed to examine impacts of a subnational climate shock (drought), a centralized national policy decision (export restrictions in response to food shortage), a distributed development strategy (solar-powered groundwater irrigation), and an external intervention (food aid). In each case, we consider how an initial signal propagates through the country via markets, infrastructure, and interactions between economic actors. An understanding of this propagation can inform strategies for food security in a changing climate.

Article.Title: Populations, exposures and outcomes: How social media data is poised to advance climate-demography research
Article.Authors: Mikal J.; Chancellor S.; Grace K.; Rajamani S.
Article.Abstract: As the natural environment continues to change, there is a shared sense among researchers, policymakers, and health practitioners that we need to better understand the impacts of those changes on health and health behaviors for individuals and populations. “Big” social media data, including large datasets from platforms like X (formerly Twitter), Reddit, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube, provide access to previously hard-to-reach populations. These data are posed to revolutionize the data landscape in climate change research; however, there are limitations and ethical concerns with data from these platforms, such as ethical questions, biases, noise, and a distinct underrepresentation of marginalized groups. These issues could hamper the adoption of social media data in research on climate change and health. In this commentary, we propose leveraging and augmenting a “human-in-the-loop” approach that uses humans in data extraction, quality assurances, and model testing to ensure data quality and overcome known limitations of social media data. Using examples from health data, we propose new horizons in climate change health research made possible with qualitative research methods.

Article.Title: Equity dimensions of future vulnerabilities to climate hazards: Long-term spatial population projections for New York City consistent with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
Article.Authors: Balk D.; Tipaldo J.; Jiang L.; Zoraghein H.
Article.Abstract: Projections of future population are important for a myriad of reasons. Large cities, states, and countries routinely produce near- and mid-range population projections. In the context of climate change, the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) framework is used at global and national scales to project long-term population to inform future emissions scenarios and understand future climate-related exposures and impacts. Much less consideration has been given to long-term projections at smaller scales, even though climate impacts are place based and cities now host most of the world’s population. Cities and their metropolitan regions are complex, heterogeneous in terms of population, environmental, and built features. Thus, using global or national-scale approaches overlooks important aspects of urban futures. Cities are diverse, fluid population centers home to migrants, with employment opportunities yet substantial inequality. These quintessential city-centric features are ignored in global/national-scale population projection methods, including long-term ones consistent with the SSPs. Leveraging state-level SSP-based projections, here we extend that approach for New York City, currently home to 8.8 million persons. Combining multistate and multiregional demographic projection and spatial downscaling models, we project county-level population by racial/ethnic groups and age–sex to 2100 and downscale to 100 m. Such projections allow for an equity lens to inform assessments of future vulnerabilities to climate hazards. Four of the five SSPs project that the population of New York City will be smaller and much older at the end of the century, though these futures are dependent on demographic assumptions about fertility and especially migration.

Article.Title: Global high rates of anaerobic methane oxidation at marine cold seeps recorded by isotope bonding in seep carbonates
Article.Authors: Wieman S.; Guo W.
Article.Abstract: Microbial anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM) regulates the flux of methane (CH 4 ) released from anoxic marine sediments into the ocean. However, variations in AOM rates, especially at dynamic environments such as cold seeps, are difficult to constrain, hindering robust projections of marine CH 4 flux in a changing climate. Here, we quantify AOM rates at global marine cold seeps based on isotope bonding in methane-derived authigenic carbonates. We show through model simulations that 13 C- 18 O bond abundance in these carbonates quantitatively records AOM rates at marine cold seeps and validate this proxy using compiled datasets of seep carbonate isotope compositions and independent AOM rate measurements. Accordingly, we estimate a mean AOM rate of 6.3 3.9 10.6 mol·m −2 ·yr −1 and a consumption of 2.1 1.3 3.5 Tg·yr −1 CH 4 at modern global cold seeps, but potentially 1.7 0.9 3.1 times as high an AOM rate and CH 4 sink over the last ~100 kyr. Our results highlight the important role of cold seeps in the global marine CH 4 cycle despite their relatively minuscule footprint.

Article.Title: Solid-state laser refrigeration of nanoscale quantum sensors
Article.Authors: Feng Z.; Pant A.; Felsted R.; Bard A.; Xia X.; Dadras S.; Shayan K.; Luntz-Martin D.; Mannikko D.; Forberger L.; Soldatenko A.; Pavlovetc I.; Stoll S.; Kuno M.; Vamivakas A.; Pauzauskie P.
Article.Abstract: Photothermal heating remains a major challenge during the optical excitation of nanoscale quantum sensors [C. Bradac, S. F. Lim, H. C. Chang, I. Aharonovich, Adv. Opt. Mater. 8 , 2000183 (2020)]. At low laser powers, heating of the sensor leads to the thermal drift of quantum electronic transition energies. At high laser powers, sensors degrade due to thermally induced phase transitions, including melting. Here, we report a general approach for mitigating the photothermal heating of nanoscale quantum sensors through solid-state laser refrigeration of the sensors’ underlying substrate. Experimentally, both nanodiamonds and gold nanocrystals are attached separately to a ceramic laser-cooling substrate through van der Waals interaction. A combination of Debye–Waller factor thermometry and optically detected magnetic resonance spectroscopy of nitrogen vacancy centers is used to demonstrate that solid-state laser refrigeration of the substrate can reduce the temperature of attached nanodiamond payloads by 25 ± 3 K below steady-state operating temperatures. Stokes/anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy is used to demonstrate reduced photothermal heating of plasmonic gold nanocrystals by 8.8 ± 2.7 K during surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy sensing of rhodamine-6G molecules. These results suggest that solid-state laser cooling could open up experimental possibilities for rapid feedback-controlled cooling of a wide range of nanoscale quantum resources.

Article.Title: Spontaneous replication fork collapse regulates telomere length homeostasis in wild-type yeast
Article.Authors: Paschini M.; Gillespie A.; Reyes C.; McCoy C.; Lewis K.; Glustrom L.; Sharpee T.; Wuttke D.; Lundblad V.
Article.Abstract: In most eukaryotes, the enzyme telomerase maintains the termini of linear chromosomes through the addition of repetitive telomeric sequences. It is widely assumed that the primary site of action for telomerase is the single-stranded G-rich overhang at the ends of linear chromosomes. However, increasing evidence indicates that a second telomerase substrate is generated in response to replication stress as the replisome traverses duplex telomeric DNA. We show here that this second substrate, created by spontaneous replication fork collapse in wild-type budding yeast, is elongated by telomerase at a much higher frequency than fully replicated chromosome termini. Furthermore, as much as ~200 nucleotides can be added in a single cell division to newly collapsed forks, indicating that replication fork collapse and the subsequent response by telomerase is a major determinant of telomere length homeostasis. This challenges a long-standing model which posits a length-sensing mechanism that assesses individual telomeres to determine whether yeast chromosome ends are in “telomerase-extendible” versus “telomerase-non-extendible” states. We propose that these two states are instead structurally and temporally distinct substrates for telomerase, generated by two different processes (fork collapse versus completion of DNA replication). We also show that fork collapse at telomeres is kept in check by a telomere-dedicated Cdc13/Stn1/Ten1 complex in collaboration with the canonical RPA complex, indicating that these two complexes stabilize single-stranded DNA exposed at the replication fork. Although failures during DNA replication are often genotoxic events, this represents an opposing example in which fork collapse has been co-opted to promote genome stability.

Article.Title: In vitro binding energies capture Klf4 occupancy across the human genome
Article.Authors: Schwager A.; Neipel J.; Savich Y.; Diehl D.; Jülicher F.; Hyman A.; Grill S.
Article.Abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) regulate gene expression by binding to specific genomic loci determined by DNA sequence. Their sequence specificity is commonly summarized by a consensus binding motif. However, eukaryotic genomes contain billions of low-affinity DNA sequences to which TFs associate with a sequence-dependent binding energy. We currently lack insight into how the genomic sequence defines this spectrum of binding energies and the resulting pattern of TF localization. Here, we set out to obtain a quantitative understanding of sequence-dependent TF binding to both motif and nonmotif sequences. We achieve this by first pursuing accurate measurements of physical binding energies of human TF Krüppel-like factor 4 (Klf4) to a library of short DNA sequences in a fluorescence-anisotropy-based bulk competitive binding assay. Second, we show that the highly nonlinear sequence dependence of Klf4 binding energies can be captured by combining a linear model of binding energies with an Ising model of the coupled recognition of nucleotides by a TF. In this model, nucleotide–TF interfaces collectively switch between two states, weak binding and strong nucleotide-specific binding, and the states of neighboring interfaces are coupled with J ∼ 2 k B T . We find that this statistical mechanics model parameterized by our in vitro measurements captures Klf4 binding patterns on an individual long DNA molecule stretched in the optical tweezer, and is predictive for Klf4 occupancy across the entire human genome without additional fit parameters.

Article.Title: Sources and sinks: Geoclimatic dynamics shaped the assembly of endemic fauna in the world’s Third Pole
Article.Authors: Jiang D.; Li M.; Ren J.; Li R.; Lyu Z.; Klaus S.; Jia R.; Xue T.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: The Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), a biodiversity hotspot shaped by tectonic and climatic forces, has seen significant progress in understanding its floristic origins. However, a comprehensive, multitaxon perspective on how its terrestrial fauna assembled remains lacking. Here we integrate time-calibrated phylogenies of over 20,000 species from five major groups (invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals), to reconstruct the evolutionary history of 527 terrestrial animal species endemic to the QTP. Our finding reveals that the QTP has functioned both as a center of in situ diversification and as a “biogeographic sink” that receives species from surrounding regions, however, with pronounced subregional differentiation: the Hengduan Mountains acted primarily as a diversification source, while the Himalaya and the Plateau Platform acted as sinks, accumulating lineages from adjacent regions. The Eocene–Oligocene climatic transition, rather than late Neogene uplift, initiated sustained faunal diversification and biotic exchange. Across subregions, distinct uplift histories and monsoon regimes drove asynchronous evolutionary trajectories, showing that even geographically adjacent regions can exhibit distinct accumulation patterns of lineages. Notably, integrating our faunal evidence with recent floristic assembly data reveals a consistent “plants first, animals later” pattern across the QTP and its subregions, suggesting that early-arriving plant lineages created ecological niches that facilitated subsequent faunal colonization and diversification. This framework advances our understanding of how mountain biotas assemble over time, with implications extending far beyond the QTP.

Article.Title: Spatial reorganization during post-collapse population growth suggests conspecific attraction in baleen whale nursing grounds
Article.Authors: Grundlehner A.; Andrews-Goff V.; Double M.; Smith J.; Brasier M.; Cresswell K.; Corney S.
Article.Abstract: Habitat use is strongly interlinked with population dynamics and plays an important role in population regulation. Animals frequently modify their habitat use behavior in response to major changes in population density. This is well studied in contexts wherein resources are limiting: for example, when changes in habitat use behavior reduce pressure from resource limitations. Situations wherein resource limitations are relaxed, such as upon recovery from severe declines, remain poorly studied. Here, we study how the spatial distribution of a nearly extirpated animal population changed during population recovery. We study a population of southern right whales ( Eubalaena australis ), a migratory species that was nearly extirpated by whaling. Using large-scale annual aerial survey data (1976–2023), we assess how spatial distribution patterns at nursing grounds changed as annual coastal abundances grew from few individuals to a few hundred. This includes assessment of the species’ characteristic site fidelity at a uniquely large spatiotemporal scale. We observed weaker fidelity to specific sites than generally assumed for Australian southern right whales and found strong indications that conspecific attraction influences the species’ coastal habitat selection. Distribution patterns initially displayed strong dispersal but became increasingly clustered coincident with substantial growth in annual whale abundances. This transition captures a rare example of a population crossing a behavioral threshold, possibly reflecting a switch in behavioral strategy or lack of conspecific cues. Our findings suggest that the behavioral processes governing habitat selection can shift with population density, driving substantial reorganization of populations’ spatial structure during substantial demographic change.

Article.Title: circEPSTI1 regulates miR-942-5p–SERPINE1–AKT1 signaling axis to enhance dengue infection and is suppressed by Tiplaxtinin
Article.Authors: Das N.; Krishnamoorthy P.; Junghare K.; Raj A.; Saha P.; Pal K.; Adhya S.; Garg A.; Khetan D.; Kumar A.; Kumar H.
Article.Abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have recently been identified as crucial regulators of gene expression in various diseases. Their role in dengue remains unexplored. In this study, circEPSTI1 induction was observed in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and plasma of dengue patients. The induction of circEPSTI1 is interferon-dependent and enhances DENV infection by sponging the expression of miR-942-5p. The antiviral role of miR-942-5p is mediated by bidirectional inhibition through targeting conserved genomic sequences of the DENV genome of different subtypes across NS1, NS3, and NS5 and the host AKT1 signaling pathway. RNA-seq analysis of DENV-infected circEPSTI1 knockdown A549 cells identified SERPINE1 and AKT1 signaling pathways to be dysregulated significantly. circEPSTI1 relieves the inhibition of miR-942-5p over DENV genomic RNA and the host SERPINE1 to activate AKT1 signaling. The activation of AKT1 signaling facilitates cell survival and enhances DENV replication. The expression of SERPINE1 and circEPSTI1 was upregulated in Dengue patients, and pharmaceutical inhibition of SERPINE1 through Tiplaxtinin inhibits the DENV replication by reducing the expression of circEPSTI1. Overall, our result demonstrates the therapeutic potential of Tiplaxtinin by targeting the circEPSTI1–miR-942-5p–SERPINE1–AKT1 axis in dengue treatment.

Article.Title: Changes in American adolescents’ outdoor time over two decades
Article.Authors: Jarosz E.; Ulset V.; Skirbekk V.
Article.Abstract: Spending time outdoors provides opportunities for physical activity, exposure to natural light, and social contact. Although young people’s time use has changed substantially in recent decades, little is known about long-term trends in adolescents’ outdoor engagement. This question is especially important because adolescence is a period of major life transitions and the development of lasting behavioral habits. This study examines 20-y trends in time spent outdoors among American adolescents using time-diary data from 14,235 individuals aged 15 to 19 in the 2003–2023 American Time Use Survey, a nationally representative survey of the US population. We describe trends in outdoor exposure and examine associations between outdoor time and leisure behaviors, including computer use for leisure, indoor physical activity, and time spent with friends. We find that outdoor engagement among boys has declined sharply, erasing a long-standing male advantage and causing boys’ participation levels to converge with girls’ at similarly low rates. Greater time spent in computer-based leisure was associated with less outdoor time, particularly among boys, whereas time spent with friends was positively associated with outdoor engagement for both sexes. Indoor physical activity did not change over the observation period and did not offset declines in outdoor time. These findings suggest that broader changes in leisure activities may be reshaping how young people engage with outdoor environments. Further research is needed to better understand the factors underlying these trends and their potential long-term implications.

Article.Title: Human organ trafficking and missing persons in China
Article.Authors: Wang X.
Article.Abstract: The persistent shortage of human organs for transplantation has long been a global challenge. The prospect of substantial profit creates strong incentives for illegal organ trafficking, including murder for organ harvesting, yet empirical evidence remains scarce. This study addresses this gap by exploiting a unique quasi-natural experiment created by China’s organ policy reform. From 1984 to 2014, executed prisoners were the primary source of transplant organs in China. In 2015, the Chinese government abolished the use of organs from executed prisoners, sharply exacerbating the organ shortage. Following this policy change, the number of missing persons rose notably nationwide. Employing difference-in-differences and triple-difference strategies, we show that, compared to cases unrelated to organ trafficking (e.g., voluntary disappearances), the number and incidence of involuntary missing persons plausibly related to organ trafficking increased significantly after 2015. The effects are especially pronounced among individuals with mental illness and in regions with higher transplant demand and greater transplant capacity. Although we do not directly observe organ trafficking, the spatial, temporal, and demographic patterns we document are consistent with the hypothesis that increased organ scarcity intensified incentives for illicit organ procurement. More broadly, the findings suggest that severe organ shortages may generate unintended and highly harmful consequences, even in a low-crime setting such as China. These results underscore the importance of accounting for behavioral responses and illicit-market incentives when designing policies that restrict the supply of scarce, high-value goods such as transplant organs.

Article.Title: The scope and severity of bat fatalities at US wind energy facilities
Article.Authors: Labuzzetta C.; Wiens A.; Udell B.; Bohner T.; Diffendorfer J.; Grajal-Puche A.; Hein C.; Johnsen A.; Lopez A.; Mai T.; Reichert B.; Seymour M.; Thogmartin W.; Frid B.
Article.Abstract: Wind turbines are a major source of bat fatalities in the United States, yet the magnitude and species-specific patterns of these fatalities have remained poorly quantified because monitoring has been site-specific, unstandardized, and not designed for landscape-level synthesis. In the most comprehensive analysis to date, we synthesized 499 postconstruction monitoring reports and developed a multispecies Bayesian hierarchical framework with an adapted N-mixture model to pool information across sites and estimate total fatalities for ten bat species across the conterminous United States from 1981 to 2024. Our analysis predicts approximately 18.7 million bat fatalities over this period, with substantially higher species-specific totals than previously estimated. Our framework provides a landscape-level analysis that can predict fatalities for unmonitored locations and years, identify landscape-level drivers of fatalities, produce a multidecade hindcast of cumulative losses due to wind energy, and map where species-specific risk is highest. Although limitations and uncertainty remain, the magnitude of predicted fatalities may be comparable to total losses from white-nose syndrome, another major threat to North American bat populations. These threats affect largely different species, suggesting their impacts may compound, but updated population-level impact assessments could reveal potential cumulative effects. Our estimates of species-specific covariate relationships with rotor-swept area, ground clearance, land cover, and proximity to rivers, highlight opportunities to help reduce impacts through wind turbine design and siting. This work establishes a generalizable landscape-level framework for evaluating wildlife fatalities at wind energy facilities and highlights how coordinated monitoring, data sharing, and population-level impact assessments could further inform conservation efforts.

Article.Title: A spatially deployable iron redox rheostat tunes root growth under nutritional stress
Article.Authors: Clúa J.; Berbel A.; Urbez C.; Madueño F.; Poirier Y.; Blázquez M.
Article.Abstract: Root growth must continuously adjust to fluctuating nutrient availability, yet the mechanisms that quantitatively integrate environmental signals into developmental responses remain poorly understood. Distinct nutrient stresses, including ammonium toxicity and phosphate deficiency, inhibit primary root growth through iron-dependent processes, suggesting that iron acts as a central regulatory node. Here, we show that plants use an antagonistic module composed of CYBDOM ferrireductases and LPR ferroxidases to regulate apoplastic iron homeostasis and control root growth in a graded manner. Genetic perturbation of this module demonstrates that root growth inhibition scales quantitatively with iron accumulation, supporting a proportional control mechanism rather than a binary response. Loss of CYBDOM function causes excessive iron accumulation, elevated reactive oxygen species, and impaired meristem activity, whereas increased CYBDOM activity buffers iron deposition and confers resistance to stress. Mechanistically, iron-induced oxidative stress promotes HYP1 expression, which in turn limits further iron accumulation. Transcriptomic analyses distinguish ammonium-specific responses from Fe-associated transcriptional changes enriched in redox buffering and cell-wall remodeling. Finally, we show that this regulatory module is redeployed in distinct tissues under phosphate deficiency, indicating that plants reuse a conserved iron-based mechanism to coordinate growth across environmental contexts. Together, our findings establish genetically controlled Fe accumulation as a key determinant of developmental plasticity under nutrient stress.

Article.Title: Anchoring Anatolian tree-rings and Mesopotamian chronology with single-year radiocarbon patterns and ice-core evidence
Article.Authors: Pearson C.; Brehm N.; Wacker L.; Brewer P.; Sigl M.; Kuniholm P.; Nicolussi K.; Salzer M.; Bayliss A.
Article.Abstract: The historical chronology of Mesopotamia offers a key chronological bridge to connect the Near East and eastern Mediterranean during the second millennium BCE. It is unusually rich in written records, including king lists, administrative documents, royal inscriptions, and astronomical observations. The latter offer a number of alternate possible absolute anchor points, resulting in competing high, middle, low, and ultra-low temporal frameworks. Establishing which of these is correct has consequences far beyond Mesopotamia. Tree-ring sequences from preserved timbers at archaeological sites in Anatolia, linked directly to Mesopotamia via the Old Assyrian trade network, could provide the answer. However, attempts have been limited by the lack of calendar secured dendrochronological dating for these timbers. Here we develop transferable methodologies in single-year radiocarbon analysis, utilizing patterns of 14 C preserved in single tree rings from Anatolian timbers to anchor their combined chronology 2072 BCE–744 BCE. This provides a calendrically-secured reference chronology for wood samples from Anatolian sites during this period as well as an annually resolved paleoclimatic record. Tree-ring dates are combined with archaeological and high-resolution ice-core evidence to evaluate the competing chronological frameworks for Mesopotamia between 2000 and 1500 BCE. Remaining dating uncertainties are constrained in strong support of the middle–low chronology.

Article.Title: Position-specific isotope signatures evolve during a reversible reaction
Article.Authors: Rasmussen C.; Hoffman D.
Article.Abstract: Position-specific isotope distributions capture information about reaction dynamics, metabolism, and environmental processes, encoding the formation history of organic molecules. Kinetic and equilibrium isotope effects are fundamental drivers of isotope fractionation, yet how these effects are expressed in position-specific isotope distributions remains poorly constrained. Here, we use glucose mutarotation as a model reaction for tracking the evolution of position-specific isotope ratios in a system in disequilibrium. In aqueous solution, α- and β-glucose interconvert through a low-abundance open-chain intermediate, providing an ideal framework for probing isotope effects within a single molecular pool at natural 13 C abundance. Using NMR spectroscopy, we simultaneously measure glucose anomer populations and position-specific 13 C/ 12 C ratios, enabling direct, time-resolved observations of isotope fractionation at the anomeric (C1) carbon. Starting from α-glucose, initial β-glucose formation generates a large transient isotope disequilibrium driven by unequal forward and reverse kinetic isotope effects, producing a temporary divergence in 13 C abundance of more than 30‰ between anomers. Continued interconversion redistributes the isotopes and yields an equilibrium difference of ~7‰ between α- and β-glucose at the C1 position. Together, these results demonstrate how kinetic and equilibrium isotope effects acting within a reversible reaction can generate substantial, time-dependent intramolecular isotope heterogeneity, with potential implications for how position-specific isotope signatures emerge and propagate through (biogeochemical) reaction networks.

Article.Title: Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders
Article.Authors: Geiger N.; Capelle M.; Rosentreter P.; Herberstein M.; Bahl A.; De Agrò M.; Klein B.; Rößler D.
Article.Abstract: Sleep is a fundamental behavioral state found across the animal kingdom, yet most of what we know about sleep is heavily vertebrate-biased. Studies are scarce or nonexistent in all but a few invertebrate lineages. A recent study of an REM sleep-like behavior in a jumping spider has reported unexpected parallels to sleep expression in vertebrates. So far, experimental evidence that these behavioral indicators truly represent sleep was lacking in spiders. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation into sleep behavior in the spider Portia fimbriata (Salticidae). We demonstrate diurnal activity, a free-running circadian rhythm, robust sleep architecture, regularly occurring REM-like behaviors, elevated arousal thresholds during those REM-like states, as well as rebound effects following sleep disruption. We conclude that the behavior we observe in spiders is behavioral sleep, providing evidence for an REM-like sleep substate in a terrestrial invertebrate. These results contribute to fundamental questions about the evolution and function of sleep across animals.

Article.Title: FMRI-guided focal transcranial magnetic stimulation of anterior cingulate cortex reduces opioid seeking and restores connectivity
Article.Authors: Ma Z.; Duan Y.; Nguyen H.; Lin S.; Haque M.; Wang D.; Hoffman S.; Carney A.; Scott T.; Varlas E.; Stein E.; Xi Z.; Shaham Y.; Lu H.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: Relapse remains a major challenge in opioid addiction treatment. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy for addiction, yet results had been mixed due to empirically selected stimulation targets and limited knowledge of neural circuit engagement. Here, we used a focal rat TMS platform to test whether high-density theta-burst stimulation (hdTBS) of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), a corticostriatal node implicated in opioid relapse by prior causal and longitudinal functional MRI studies, decreases relapse-like oxycodone seeking and associated circuit dysfunction. Male rats self-administered oxycodone intravenously for 14 d and then underwent 13 d of electric barrier-induced abstinence, a procedure that suppresses drug taking while preserving drug availability and drug-associated context. During abstinence, the rats received seven daily sessions of sham stimulation or ACC-targeted hdTBS, with relapse tests and longitudinal functional MRI acquired during early and late abstinence to assess the behavioral and circuit-level effects of stimulation. Sham-treated rats showed a time-dependent increase (incubation) in oxycodone seeking and reduced ACC connectivity with dorsal and ventral striatum. In contrast, ACC-targeted hdTBS prevented incubation of oxycodone seeking and reversed abstinence-associated ACC-striatal connectivity reductions. Stimulation-sensitive functional circuits showed spatial correspondence with tracer-defined ACC projection patterns, suggesting that anatomical connectivity is critical to the circuit-level effects of focal stimulation. These findings support ACC-centered corticostriatal circuits as mechanistically informed targets for neuromodulation in opioid addiction and introduce a preclinical framework for linking stimulation, behavior, and longitudinal circuit remodeling.

Article.Title: Fine and ultrafine Martian dust presents additional risks for future crewed missions to Mars
Article.Authors: VanBommel S.; Knight A.; Harrington A.; Do S.; Herd C.; Liu Y.; Berger J.; Clark B.; Connell S.; Elam W.; Hausrath E.; Hecht M.; Hurowitz J.; Johnson J.; Jones M.; Kenney R.; Martínez G.; Morantz C.; Schmidt M.; Shumway A.; Siljeström S.; Steele A.; Uckert K.; Wade L.; Yingst R.
Article.Abstract: Surface dust poses a fundamental challenge to extraterrestrial human exploration, a reality demonstrated by the operational hazards encountered during Apollo lunar missions. On Mars, this challenge is compounded by regional and global dust cycles that coat sensitive hardware. While previous Mars missions have constrained the bulk geochemistry of coarser particulates (≳3 µm), the properties of the fine (≲2.5 µm) and ultrafine (≲0.1 µm) fractions remain largely uncharacterized. This knowledge gap is critical as these respirable particles, defined by their ability to bypass upper respiratory defenses, possess the mobility to penetrate deep into the alveolar regions of biological systems, presenting a systemic toxicity risk to future crews. Here, we report on direct examination of these fine and ultrafine Martian dust fractions using X-ray fluorescence through the analysis and modeling of data acquired by the Perseverance rover. We observe particulates measuring as small as 100 to 200 nm on spacesuit samples and calibration targets. Compositionally, this dust is a phosphorus-, iron-, and sulfur-enriched mafic silicate accumulating on materials analogous to the planned external layers of potential crew systems. Our results emphasize the importance of a thorough characterization of Martian dust properties in terrestrial laboratories to better prepare future crews and crew support systems destined for the surface of Mars.
