Article.Title: Autonomous disproofs of the Erdős unit distance conjecture with GPT-5.5 Pro
Article.Authors: Huang Y.
Article.Abstract: OpenAI’s disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marks a milestone in AI for mathematical research. However, the result relied on an internal model with undisclosed test-time compute, hindering independent reproduction and analysis by the community. Here we present a simple autonomous agent built on the publicly available GPT-5.5 Pro. The agent uses a problem-agnostic three-stage prompting pipeline: brainstorm, execute, and review. We ran eight independent trials with web search disabled. In each trial, the agent produced a correct or essentially correct disproof of the conjecture. The resulting proofs are diverse and do not merely reproduce earlier AI-generated proofs. Since GPT-5.5 Pro was released nearly a month before OpenAI published its disproof, our evaluation is free from data contamination. The system operates efficiently, using an average of 106.7 k reasoning tokens per trial. We release our code and all outputs, providing a publicly accessible AI agent to resolve this conjecture autonomously.

Article.Title: Resource-driven release from lag phase triggers the world’s fastest and largest coastal plant invasion
Article.Authors: Ge Z.; Richardson D.; Pyšek P.; Cai T.; Chen Y.
Article.Abstract: What determines the duration of invasion lag phases remains one of the major unresolved questions in invasion ecology. Lag phases are often attributed to genetic adaptation, propagule limitation, or demographic stochasticity, yet the mechanisms by which environmental conditions regulate establishment success remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the explosive expansion of Spartina alterniflora along the coast of mainland China, the most rapid plant invasion recorded globally. Combining field experiments, demographic theory, and historical invasion records, we identify resource-regulated Allee effects as a mechanism governing the invasion lag phase. Experimentally, sediment accretion substantially increases clonal propagation and sexual reproduction, weakening demographic constraints associated with establishment and accelerating the transition from sparse founder patches to highly reproductive meadows. A theoretical model reveals that sediment-driven positive feedbacks weaken demographic constraints during establishment and shorten the duration of Allee effects. Historical invasion records spanning both sides of the Pacific Ocean support the predicted negative relationship between sedimentation rate and lag-phase duration. Invasion lag phases can arise solely from interactions between species traits and environmental resource availability. Contrary to the prevailing view that Allee effects are fixed properties of species, our results show that their duration is regulated by environmental resource availability. More broadly, environmental resources can govern ecological transitions by controlling transient dynamics during establishment, providing an explanation for why some introduced populations remain dormant for decades, whereas others rapidly become dominant ecosystem engineers.

Article.Title: Evaluation of possibly fabricated references in 500,000 science, engineering, and computing papers
Article.Authors: Topaz M.; Gupta P.; Zhang Z.; Peltonen L.
Article.Abstract: References to nonexistent studies are well documented in biomedical research, but evidence outside biomedicine is limited. We analyzed a stratified random sample of 500,000 peer-reviewed journal papers in chemistry, physics, materials science, engineering, and computer science published from January 2023 through March 31, 2026, using OpenAlex, a large open index of scholarly works and citations. Our automated pipeline classified 1,135 references across 619 papers as fabricated, with 85.8% precision on masked expert review; fabricated is an operational label for a claimed title that could not be located in any of seven bibliographic and open-web sources. Affected-paper prevalence rose from 1 in 1,600 (6.3 per 10,000) in 2023 to 1 in 435 (23.0 per 10,000) in the first quarter of 2026, and full-period rates differed roughly sixfold across fields, from 25.6 per 10,000 papers in physics to 4.3 in chemistry. Most affected papers contained one or two fabricated references, but the 27 papers containing five or more accounted for more than a third of all fabricated references identified. Applying each field’s rate to the approximately 7 million OpenAlex papers indexed in these fields gives an estimated 8,500 papers carrying at least one fabricated reference. Routine automated reference verification at submission, together with retrospective screening of the published literature, can detect fabricated references before and after they enter the scientific record.

Article.Title: New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming
Article.Authors: Berger T.; Naimi A.; Hardes K.; Sachße C.; Gericke R.; Marner M.; Mühlemeyer F.; Pommerening T.; Reher R.
Article.Abstract: Mumia vera aegyptiaca was a mummy-derived medicinal substance widely used in medieval and early modern medicine, yet its material composition and biological activity remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate Egyptological and pharmaceutical-historical analysis of 41 textual sources with LC–MS/MS-based metabolomics, molecular networking, machine-learning-assisted annotation, and bioactivity testing to investigate ancient Egyptian embalming materials and historical Mumia vera samples. We analyzed 24 objects from university and pharmacy museum collections, including historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. Comparative metabolomics revealed substantial heterogeneity among materials labeled as Mumia vera , but also recurrent molecular signatures consistent with aged conifer resins, including oxidized abietane-type diterpenoids. Several samples contained Aloe -associated metabolites, including aloeresin A/D- and aloin-related compounds. These data reveal Aloe -associated metabolites in ancient Egyptian embalming-related materials and support the presence of Aloe spp.-derived exudates in selected samples. The convergence of molecular and textual evidence further raises the possibility that a previously unresolved Egyptian term from the 2nd millennium BC may refer to Aloe sp. or an Aloe -derived product. Comparative metabolomics also linked an inconspicuous powder sample to a specific mummified head, although their curatorial association had not been securely documented. Finally, a historical Mumia vera aegyptiaca extract modestly protected MDCK cells from influenza virus-induced cytopathic effects, whereas the isolated major compound 7-oxodehydroabietic acid was inactive on its own. Together, these findings show how integrating textual scholarship, pharmaceutical history, and molecular analysis can refine the interpretation of ancient Egyptian embalming practices, museum objects, and historical medicines.

Article.Title: Rembrandt through the eyes of the machine: Toward explainable Human–AI collaboration in painting attribution
Article.Authors: Arias-Rosales A.; Wheelock A.; Moritz J.; LeDuc P.; Cagan J.
Article.Abstract: With questions that persist for centuries, art attribution is a complex detective effort that shapes cultural identity. Our goal is to complement human expertise, providing statistical and visual arguments that shed new light on discussions about great masters like Rembrandt and beyond, with long-term implications for art analysis and human–AI collaboration. We present an AI-driven explainable approach to assist painting attribution with up to 97.9% recall, 95.8% accuracy when highly confident, and methods that identify the most relevant areas. This work supports human–AI collaboration by incorporating expert guidance, expanding the outputs with explainable visualizations, tailoring settings to users’ needs, thorough calibrations to avoid overconfidence, and building a dataset that balances quality with quantity and focuses on comparable artists like a master’s pupils and teachers.

Article.Title: Education reduces dementia incidence and mitigates genetic risk
Article.Authors: Barcellos S.; Carvalho L.; Langa K.; Nimmagadda S.; Turley P.
Article.Abstract: There is little causal evidence on factors that can protect individuals against Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) risk. We study the causal effect of education on ADRD, exploiting a regression discontinuity generated by a compulsory schooling reform. ADRD was ascertained based on medical history, hospital records, and death registries, addressing concerns about selective sample attrition. We find that education reduces incidence of ADRD. Using molecular genetic data, we show that the reform weakened the relationship between genetics and ADRD incidence, implying genetic risk of dementia is not immutable and can be modified by social policy.

Article.Title: Capillary physics links HIV capsid geometry to nuclear pore translocation
Article.Authors: Brown A.; Al-Izzi S.; Parker J.; Hertel S.; Jacques D.; Kusumaatmaja H.; Morris R.
Article.Abstract: The protective capsid encasing the genetic material of HIV can traverse the nuclear pore complex (NPC) intact, despite being far larger than conventional passive cargo. This is attributed to the properties of the capsid surface, which promote partitioning into cohesive assemblies of the disordered proteins that form the NPC’s permeability barrier: phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins (FG-Nups). The implication, at the mesoscale, is that capsid–NPC interactions are characterized by the interfacial physics of wetting and capillarity. To capture this, we develop a minimal theory that reduces to an interplay between capsid geometry, effective cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic contact angles, and a ratio of interfacial tensions. By combining analytical calculations, sharp- and diffuse-interface numerics, we make several predictions: A geometry-dependent trade-off between penetration depth and the wetting transition; asymmetric capillary forces that generate torques and lead to metastable “stalled” states that are tilted; a topological classification of the possible mechanisms underlying the largest energetic barrier; and spontaneous symmetry breaking of displaced FG-Nups. These behaviors connect capsid shape and orientation to the topology and symmetry of FG-Nup displacement, and to the molecular compositions on each side of the pore. They are consistent with published cryoelectron tomography orientations, which provide an initial estimate of the cytoplasmic contact angle. Crucially, our results identify a capillary advantage for the HIV capsid’s characteristic broken-symmetry geometry.

Article.Title: High-resolution measurements of thermal conductivity matrix and search for thermal Hall effect in La <sub>2</sub> CuO <sub>4</sub>
Article.Authors: Hu J.; Xu H.; Gu G.; Li Q.; Ong N.
Article.Abstract: We investigated the longitudinal thermal conductivity κ xx and thermal Hall conductivity κ xy in La 2 CuO 4 at temperatures T between 2 and 20 K in magnetic fields H up to 10 T. Within the temperature and field intervals studied, we do not resolve any thermal Hall signal with a conservative upper bound of | κ xy / T | < 1 × 10 − 4 Wm − 1 K − 2 . The longitudinal thermal conductivity κ xx / T agrees well with previous reports, in both its magnitude and T dependence. Both κ xx and κ xy were measured using the field-swept protocol. To achieve high resolution, we carefully took into account relaxation effects after each step-increase in H . At low T , we find a weak linear decrease in κ xx / T vs. H , as well as weak hystereses near the metamagnetic transitions of the spins.

Article.Title: Local growth laws determine global shape of molluscan shells
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Bhattacharya K.
Article.Abstract: Molluscan shells come in various shapes and sizes. Despite this diversity, each species produces a shell with a characteristic shape that is independent of environmental conditions. We seek to understand this robust complexity. We are guided by two principles in the spirit of D’Arcy Thompson. First, the growth is governed by the repeated and continuous application of a fixed growth law, even as the shell evolves in overall shape, without any complex biological machinery to monitor and control the growth. Second, the growth law depends solely on local geometry at the shell’s growing edge. The first principle naturally leads to the mathematical statement that the shape of the shell is generated by the action of a Lie group on a protoconch. The second naturally leads to a particular representation of the Lie group. We use this representation to show that the shapes of nearly all known molluscan shells can be described by essentially three parameters: a scalar (scaling), a vector (orientation), and a curve (edge of the protoconch). We relate these parameters to the phylogenetic tree. In addition to the morphogenetic insight, our results potentially point to a alternative growth-based approach to engineering complex structures.

Assembly from a single ONT flowcell (~35× coverage) consistently produced an assembly more contiguous than GRCh38.p14, providing a foundation for further optimization and scaling. Assembly quality was assessed by direct chromosome-level alignments to a reference genome, variant calling, and annotation of gene-rich regions at Chr22q11, the extended MHC locus, and at several difficult to assemble regions, including the rRNA gene clusters, the subtelomeric region on Chr4q35, ChrY, and the centromeres. Article.Title: Si-scRNA-seq: Enabling ambient-stable single-cell transcriptomics through spatially confined biosilicification
Article.Authors: Zhou L.; Ruan T.; He Y.; Xie G.; Qi J.; Cao X.; Brinker C.; Liu Y.; Zhu W.
Article.Abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is constrained by rapid RNA degradation during sample storage, necessitating cold-chain logistics. Here we present spatially confined biosilicification (SCB), wherein RNA is encapsulated within a nanoscopic layer of amorphous silicon dioxide, as a highly effective methodology enabling ambient-temperature preservation of single-cell transcriptomes. By judiciously incorporating a silicification inhibitor, SCB achieves spatiotemporal control over both intra- and extracellular silica deposition, preventing excessive crosslinking and cell aggregation while preserving RNA biointegrity and accessibility. scRNA-seq performed with biosilicified cells (Si-scRNA-seq) maintained high transcriptomic fidelity with fresh samples (R 2 = 0.95 after 7 d) extending RNA half-life to 54.8 d at 25 °C, a 685-fold improvement compared to unprotected samples. Furthermore, Si-scRNA-seq confers robust resistance against oxidative and UV degradation. Compatible with mainstream platforms at ~0.1 RMB per sample, Si-scRNA-seq successfully resolves cellular heterogeneity in clinical lung, liver, and ovarian cancer specimens after extended room-temperature storage. Si-scRNA-seq provides a scalable and cold-chain–free solution for single-cell transcriptomics in research and clinical settings.

Article.Title: Deconfined criticality between an antiferromagnetic insulator and a nodal d -wave superconductor: A quantum Monte Carlo study

We access a regime of frustrated magnetic order without a sign problem using a parton representation of the electron in terms of fermionic spinons and bosonic chargons. Both partons move in a background π -flux (so the electron experiences no net flux) and are coupled to a quantum fluctuating SU(2) lattice gauge field. In contrast to earlier studies directly on the electronic degrees of freedom, we find evidence for a second-order deconfined quantum phase transition at which both the Néel and d -wave superconductivity orders vanish continuously. We compute correlators of the spinon-chargon composite with the same quantum numbers as the electron: we find a gapless Dirac dispersion inside the d -wave superconductor, turning into a gapped dispersion in the antiferromagnet.

Article.Title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision
Article.Authors: Jung H.; Jain H.; Han X.; Feilong M.; Han J.; Shokeen D.; Van Uden C.; Hanson I.; Connolly A.; Wager T.; Haxby J.; Nastase S.
Article.Abstract: Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. Article.Title: Integrating ecology with genetics to explain gene reuse during repeated evolution
Article.Authors: Nosil P.; Gompert Z.; Montoya J.; Feder J.; Oakley T.; Peichel C.
Article.Abstract: The role of determinism and chance in the evolutionary history of life is often analyzed through the lens of the repeatability of evolution. Although it is now clear that evolution often repeats itself, we are only beginning to understand why this varies in degree. For example, the probability of gene reuse during repeated bouts of adaptation often declines with time since divergence, but the causes of this pattern remain unclear. Here, we explore two core hypotheses for time-dependent variation in the repeatability of gene reuse during adaptation. Specifically, gene reuse depends on the extent to which lineages have 1) similar genomes such that they have similar genetic architectures, mutations, and mutational effects (i.e., a fairly well-appreciated “shared genetics” hypothesis), and 2) similar ecologies such that they have similar environments and patterns of natural selection (i.e., a mostly unexplored “shared ecology” hypothesis). The latter hypothesis emphasizes ecology’s role in gene reuse and has received little explicit attention. In particular, testing the shared ecology hypothesis requires moving beyond a simple dichotomous characterization of ecology to embracing ecological divergence as a multivariate and continuous phenomenon. Although such tests are only beginning to emerge, they already illustrate how integration of ecological factors can help explain variation in gene reuse. Here, we advocate a framework that integrates the influence of both genetic and ecological factors in the repeatability of evolution and can be applied to a range of organisms to better understand the role of determinism and chance in biological diversification.

Article.Title: Contactless continuous guidance of matter in its main states using curved elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields
Article.Authors: Nikolaev D.; Iablonskyi D.; Martinez-Marchese A.; Sirkka M.; Aldea M.; Okwudire C.; Hæggström E.; Marzo A.; Salmi A.
Article.Abstract: Acoustic manipulation uses sound waves to exert force on matter, enabling contactless movement, trapping, and the structuring of particles in bulk media. It offers a contamination-free approach for handling matter in applications spanning across chemistry, biology, and advanced manufacturing. However, state-of-the-art techniques, including acoustic holograms or phased arrays of transducers (PATs) are limited to transporting individual particles or small clusters one by one, and are not suitable for dispersed matter such as gases or aerosols. Here, we introduce a method for guiding a continuous flow of matter along reconfigurable three-dimensional trajectories using elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields (EBAFs). These fields generate converging radial acoustic forces along a programmable path, forming stable mid-air conduits that continuously transport matter. Compared to existing methods such as near-field acoustic levitation, acoustofluidic separation, particle manipulation with vortex and Airy beams, the proposed method offers enhanced versatility, scalability, and real-time control of transport trajectories in mid-air without requiring physical guiding structures. We developed methods to generate EBAFs with PATs tailored to different particle sizes and material properties, and experimentally demonstrated guidance of solids, liquids, aerosols, and gases along programmable trajectories. This technique enables containerless laboratory operations, precise and contamination-free reagent or energy delivery, and integration into advanced additive manufacturing processes that require controlled distribution of matter in different states to target zones.

Article.Title: Susumu Tonegawa (1939–2026): A molecular biologist who transformed immunology and neuroscience
Article.Authors: Lafaille J.; McHugh T.
Article.Abstract: Susumu Tonegawa transformed two fields of biology. His discovery of the genetic mechanism generating antibody diversity established the foundations of modern immunology and earned him the 1987 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Remarkably, he then began a second scientific career in neuroscience, pioneering genetic approaches to dissect the molecular and circuit mechanisms of learning and memory and, ultimately, the neuronal ensembles that store specific memories. He was also an ambitious institution builder whose leadership shaped neuroscience at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and RIKEN. As former trainees from his immunology and neuroscience labs, we remember a scientist of extraordinary curiosity, intensity, and intellectual courage, who was never afraid to leave familiar territory in pursuit of a fundamental question.

Article.Authors: Sonnett M.; Boersma S.; Ward M.; Van Eyndhoven L.; Centofanti E.; Brambach M.; Zhou C.; Knipe D.; Raj A.; Oyler-Yaniv A.; Oyler-Yaniv J.

Article.Authors: Lin W.; Qian S.; Sun Q.; Zhu L.; Liao W.; Li T.; Li F.; Shi X.; Wang T.; Zhao E.; Zhang H.; Li P.

Their planets now reside at orbital separations smaller than the maximum stellar radii attained during the RGB phase, implying that they should not have survived. Among them, 24 Boo b orbits at only 0.183 au with a 30-d period, making it the closest planet known around a red-clump giant. These findings demonstrate that this paradox is not an isolated anomaly but signals the emergence of a class of evolved planetary systems. Their survival defies current models of stellar–planetary coevolution and points to unexplored physics shaping planetary architectures around post-RGB stars.

Article.Authors: Dong Y.; Cao W.; Kamyshinsky R.; Kampf N.; Zhao P.; Schilt Y.; Raviv U.; Klein J.
Article.Abstract: The search for high-performance lubricants is of broad relevance to biomedical applications, including artificial joints, regenerative scaffolds, and osteoarthritis therapies. Here we introduce glycerosomes—phosphatidylcholine (PC)-based vesicles containing glycerol—as a promising boundary lubricant. Using a surface force balance, we show that glycerosomes achieve a friction coefficient as low as 10 − 5 under a high compression pressure of 15.6 MPa, representing a 20-fold reduction compared to conventional PC liposomes. This level of lubrication surpasses any previously reported boundary lubricant system at such pressures in aqueous media. Mechanistically, glycerosomes exhibit substantially lower adhesion energy than PC liposomes, and theoretical simulations reveal enhanced vesicle stability and flexibility. Our findings establish glycerosomes as a superior hydration lubrication platform, with promising implications for both biomedical implants and industrial applications requiring robust lubricity.

Article.Title: Virus transmission required for maintenance and host adaptation mirrors neurophysiological differences in rabies-derived peptides
Article.Authors: Remal A.; Acheson E.; Leighton P.; Rees E.; Rhodes J.; O’Brien B.; Weltzin M.; Hueffer K.
Article.Abstract: Pathogen adaptations to new hosts are central to the disease ecology of cross-species transmission and host switching of viruses. The rabies virus is a model for adaptations to different hosts as it induces behavioral changes that facilitate transmission, while being maintained in distinct species-specific cycles of infection. Here, we demonstrate that the rabies virus requires distinct transmission dynamics in two hosts with different ecologies to establish maintenance, using agent-based modeling, analyses of virus glycoprotein-mediated manipulation of neuroreceptor function, and phylogenetic analysis. Epidemiological models suggest that rabies virus variants adapted to arctic foxes, which sustain rabies virus at very low host densities, require a higher probability of transmission than viruses adapted to raccoons. Using in vitro electrophysiology, we demonstrate that the rabies glycoprotein-derived peptides from arctic fox rabies variants are more potent antagonists of alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. These findings suggest a possible functional basis for the behavioral modifications that drive enzootic rabies transmission in the context of host ecology. In addition, a large proportion of residues that may drive rabies virus adaptation to raccoons and arctic foxes are found within this neurotoxin-like region. Furthermore, a residue in the neurotoxin-like region of the mature rabies virus glycoprotein (residue 183) has been associated with pathogenicity, host switching, and disease ecology in previous studies. We propose the hypothesis that rabies virus transmission dynamics adapt to the ecology and physiology of novel hosts through the selection of glycoproteins that elicit specific degrees of behavioral modification and transmission probability.

Article.Title: Reduction of aflatoxin contamination in maize kernels mediated by host-induced gene silencing
Article.Authors: Ahmed A.; Cavanaugh K.; Baldrich P.; Stergiopoulos I.; Michelmore R.
Article.Abstract: Aflatoxins produced by some species of Aspergillus pose a significant threat to global food safety, because they contaminate a variety of crops including maize. In this study, we used host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) to reduce aflatoxin accumulation in maize upon infection with Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus . Two RNAi constructs were designed and introduced into maize, one targeting two essential fungal genes involved in ergosterol biosynthesis ( CYP51A and CYP51B ) and the other targeting three aflatoxin biosynthesis genes ( AflC , AflD , and AflR ). The presence of RNAi transgenes was confirmed in 17 and 14 independent lines possessing the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi construct and the AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi construct, respectively. Most transgenic lines had single-locus integrations and one or two copies of the transgene. Transgene expression varied considerably among the lines. Small RNA sequencing confirmed the production of siRNAs from the HIGS trigger sequences. Levels of CYP51A , AflC , AflD, and AflR transcripts in Aspergillus spp. were successfully decreased upon infection of transgenic maize. However, significant reduction in the level of CYP51B transcripts was not achieved and the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi transgene had no discernible effect on fungal growth in infected maize. In contrast, we observed significant reductions in aflatoxin accumulation in four AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi transgenic lines infected with A. flavus and in two transgenic lines infected with A. parasiticus . Notably, one AflC/AflD/AflR transgenic line exhibited minimal aflatoxin contamination upon kernel infection with A. parasiticus . These results demonstrate the potential of HIGS to reduce aflatoxin production in mature corn kernels.

Article.Title: System-level reorganization of gene networks underlies the nurse-to-forager transition in honeybees
Article.Authors: Page R.; Bonabeau E.
Article.Abstract: Division of labor in social insects is enabled by coordinated changes in physiology, neural signaling, and gene regulation, yet it remains unclear to what extent behavioral maturation reflects incremental changes in individual genes and/or a reorganization of transcriptomic regulation at the system level. Here, we analyze the nurse-to-forager transition in worker honeybees ( Apis mellifera ) from a network perspective, treating the transcriptome as a gene–gene correlation system whose global organization reflects collective regulatory states. Using fat body gene expression data across five developmental time points that span an interval of behavioral transition, we construct signed gene–gene correlation networks and quantify their macro- and mesostate properties. We then descend to the level of the gene and construct microstate gene lists of interacting genes. Behavioral maturation of worker honeybees is accompanied by coordinated, nonmonotonic changes in global network structure rather than simple global shifts in interaction strength across the network. Early stages exhibit broadly positive, globally synchronized correlations, whereas later stages show increased modular segregation and the emergence of antagonistic gene–gene relationships. Despite this differentiation, networks remain fully connected with high global efficiency, consistent with a flexible small-world–like organization. Positive correlations primarily support global integration, while negative correlations act as localized, boundary-enforcing constraints. Negative correlations form a structured pattern of antagonism that is sparse and module-specific, occurring primarily between functional gene modules rather than within them. Network layouts and module analyses reveal two polarized, attractor-like regulatory states, a structure recapitulated in a vitellogenin-centered subnetwork and consistent with prior experimental perturbation studies.

Article.Title: Blinks are strategically coupled with head movements in unconstrained natural gaze behavior
Article.Authors: Goettker A.; Hayhoe M.
Article.Abstract: Blinks are a ubiquitous yet largely unnoticed aspect of human vision, despite causing frequent interruptions of visual input that can amount to up to 10% of waking time. By leveraging a large dataset of unconstrained gaze behavior during two natural tasks, we found a behavioral strategy to limit the impact of blinks: blinks were strategically coupled with head movements, which minimizes information loss due to unreliable visual input during head movements. Specifically, blink probability increased with higher head velocities and showed strong temporal modulation relative to head movement onset: Blink probability was reduced before head movement initiation and then peaked during the head movement. The strength of this coupling was tailored to the individual needs of participants, with participants with higher baseline blink rates showing stronger synchronization. This indicates that blinks are a part of an individually coordinated strategy when orchestrating eye and head movements during unconstrained natural behavior.

Article.Title: Linguistic intervention unlocks the economic gains of diversity
Article.Authors: Levine S.; Siegenthaler S.; Wilson B.
Article.Abstract: Gains from trade generate prosperity, yet interpersonal exchange can falter along racial lines. We study incentivized experimental economies where participants must spontaneously initiate and sustain trading relationships with others whose race is visible. When the highest gains from trade require cross-race exchange, diverse economies underperform: welfare and specialization suffer as many retreat to autarky. This underperformance reflects not segregation into racial trading blocs, but a collapse in exchange. Opportunities for contact alone do not close the performance gap, which persists and even widens over time. To understand why, we turn to communication itself. Lower welfare is associated with less communication, fewer expressions of affiliation and achievement, and less explicit signaling of needs, deficits, and surpluses. We call this communicative misalignment: differences in shared-language use that raise search, bargaining, and coordination costs. A brief linguistic intervention equips participants with a communicative toolkit. It increases communication volume and the frequency of motivational and state-signaling language. Crucially, when gains depend on cross-race exchange, the intervention restores specialization and cross-race trade, closing the performance gap. Its effects are minimal when efficient trade need not cross race, indicating specificity rather than generic skill training. Language thus operates bidirectionally, both revealing the state of cooperation and causally shaping it. Although we examine racial boundaries, the mechanism may operate along other fault lines where interactional norms diverge, including hierarchy, geography, or culture. Language, a primary conduit of culture, can impede exchange when misaligned and facilitate it when aligned. This suggests a scalable micro-governance tool for reducing transaction costs.

Article.Title: C1ql2 gates stress vulnerability by regulating microglia-mediated synaptic pruning in the BLA-vHPC circuit

Article.Title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands
Article.Authors: Gacetta E.; Laws M.; Aulet L.; Ozaydin T.; Tsay J.; Zapanta C.; Cantlon J.
Article.Abstract: Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners’ spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

Article.Title: Random, fragile, or correlated: Mechanisms of synteny decay in mammals
Article.Authors: Moffett A.; Di Pierro M.
Article.Abstract: We formalize three models of genome evolution, yielding analytical distributions of synteny block sizes between pairs of genomes. To evaluate each model, we fit theoretical synteny block size distributions to empirical distributions from a comparative analysis of nearly 200 mammalian genomes. Between the random breakage model (RBM), with uniformly distributed breakpoints, the fragile breakage model (FBM) with breakpoint hotspots, and what we term the correlated breakage model (CBM) with pairs of nearby breakpoints, we find that the FBM and CBM are far more consistent with mammalian genome evolution than the RBM. Inferred parameters of each model qualitatively agree with previously calculated rates of mammalian genome evolution. The FBM and CBM perform comparably with each other, suggesting that either model could serve as an improved null model of genome evolution to use in statistical tests for syntenic regions that are unlikely to exist due to random chance.

Article.Title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models
Article.Authors: Cullen M.; Biancaniello C.; Taškova K.; Miletić V.; De Simone A.; Mercadante D.
Article.Abstract: With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from C α -only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to explore phenomena such as secondary structure propensity and nucleation in condensates, conformationally selected binding motifs across disordered ensembles or conformational preferences of sequence-specific short-linear motifs.

In many cases, these hotspots exhibit more than an order of magnitude greater genetic diversity than the rest of the Mtb genome, which is otherwise characterized by remarkably low variation. Mutations within these regions display clustered substitution patterns, excess paralog-matching variants, and distinct mutational spectra consistent with ongoing gene conversion. These GCEs occur predominantly within gene families associated with virulence and host–pathogen interactions, including the PE, PPE, and ESX families. Several of the most pronounced diversity hotspots occur in antigens encoded within PRs. Among these, the vaccine candidate PPE18 harbors mutations in validated epitope sequences and predicted alterations in HLA-II binding. Together, these findings demonstrate that gene conversion actively shapes antigenic and virulence-associated diversity in Mtb .

Article.Title: In-cloud motions shape warm-rain production in marine clouds: Evidence from multiyear observations
Article.Authors: Lamer K.; Kollias P.; Kim J.; Zhu Z.; Yang F.; Battaglia A.; Luke E.
Article.Abstract: Despite years of research, the processes controlling warm-rain formation remain uncertain. Precipitation is observed beneath marine stratocumulus in over 56% of cloudy columns with liquid water path (LWP) <130 g m −2 , rising to more than 84% in columns with LWP beyond 130 g m −2 . This indicates that marine stratocumulus routinely support warm-rain formation and suggests that barriers to precipitation onset in this regime are weaker than commonly assumed. For the same LWP, oceanic cumulus precipitate less frequently than stratocumulus but on average produce two times larger and one to two orders of magnitude fewer precipitation drops. This contrast is consistent with cumulus presenting two times stronger updrafts and lower adiabaticity than stratocumulus, both of which can affect drop growth histories. Whereas the precipitation characteristics of stratocumulus are generally consistent with growth by collision–coalescence during gravitational free fall in low LWP clouds, those of cumulus cannot be explained without invoking additional processes. Together, these findings suggest that warm-precipitation parameterizations should more explicitly account for the influence of small-scale dynamical processes on precipitation growth. The apparent importance of drop growth histories further motivates continued exploration of Lagrangian particle-tracking approaches in both models and observations.

Article.Authors: Sun X.; Wei Z.; Shan M.; Peng S.; Wang Z.; Wu P.; Luo Y.; Shen J.; Huai L.; Miao Y.; Ou Z.; Onbasli M.; Wang Z.; Wu T.; He J.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: A new frontier in condensed matter physics is to stack atomically thin layered materials with different properties and create intriguing phenomena which do not exist in any of the constituent layers. Recently, rare phenomena were indeed observed, including chiral superconductivity, two-component nematic superconductivity, topological surface superconductivity, and enigmatic magnetic memory. However, this flat band only exists on the 1T-TaS 2 terminated surface layer with broken translational symmetry, but not on the 1T-TaS 2 subsurface layers buried in the bulk. These results directly challenge the foundation of the current theoretical paradigm. On the 1T-TaS 2 terminated surface layer, we further revealed a pseudogap and an anomalous doping effect. These phenomena and the dichotomy between surface and bulk layers also shed light on the unusual coexistence of distinct electronic orders in this mysterious heterostructure.

Article.Title: CD28 costimulation is organized by signaling condensates and counteracted by PD-1
Article.Authors: Chen H.; Wu S.; Zhang Y.; Hu W.; Lou C.; Chen W.; Lou J.
Article.Abstract: T cell activation relies on the coordinated integration of T cell receptor (TCR) and cosignaling pathways, yet how these signals are physically organized remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that CD28 co-stimulation is driven by a condensation mechanism in which the CD28 intracellular domain (ICD) forms signaling condensates with the Src-family kinase Lck. Ligand engagement promotes CD28 ICD accessibility and triggers rapid CD28/Lck condensation, enhancing CD28 phosphorylation, cytoskeletal polarization, and cytokine production. The downstream effectors of CD28, including PI3K and GRB2, can also be recruited into the CD28-Lck condensates in our reconstituted system. We further identify PD-1 as a graded regulator of this process: Monophosphorylated PD-1 is recruited into CD28/Lck condensates, whereas diphosphorylated PD-1 competitively binds the CD28 ICD and dissolves these assemblies. CD28 and PD-1 ICDs also undergo condensation directly, revealing a dynamic and compositionally heterogeneous signaling system. Guided by this competitive condensation mechanism, we engineer CD28 ICD mutants that preserve Lck condensation while resisting PD-1-mediated disruption. Incorporation of these condensation-selective mutants into Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) constructs confers resistance to inhibitory signaling and enhances antitumor efficacy in vivo. These findings establish condensation as a central organizing principle of CD28 costimulation and provide a biophysical framework for engineering more resilient therapeutic T cells.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial subpopulations promote cellular responses to changes in metabolic demand and signal transduction
Article.Authors: Fung T.; Tzoc-Pacheco E.; Cui R.; Brown S.; Schwörer S.; Lindsten T.; Thompson C.; Ryu K.
Article.Abstract: When mammalian cells are under increased ATP demand, mitochondria segregate into two distinct subpopulations, one capable of oxidative phosphorylation (oxidative subpopulation) and another specialized in reductive synthesis of metabolic precursors (reductive subpopulation). Here we report that mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) along with protein components of the mitochondrial nucleoid segregate to the oxidative subpopulation in response to increased ATP demand. This suggests that formation of the reductive mitochondrial subpopulation might serve to eliminate alternative uses of mitochondrial NAD(P)H when cells are under bioenergetic or nutrient stress. To examine this further, we studied mitochondria in cells exposed to low levels of glutamine. Mitochondria use glutaminase (GLS1) to maintain net glutamine uptake when cytosolic glutamine decreases, by converting glutamine to glutamate. The resulting glutamate can either be oxidized into α-ketoglutarate to enter the TCA cycle or utilized in the reductive synthesis of proline/ornithine. GLS1 can polymerize into hyperactive filaments in response to elevations in inorganic phosphate as might occur when ATP consumption exceeds production. However, when extracellular glutamine is reduced, GLS1 filaments segregated away from mtDNA, becoming colocalized with pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS) filaments in reductive mitochondria lacking ATP synthase markers. This cosegregation supported the ability of TGF-β signaling to enhance reductive proline/ornithine biosynthesis under low glutamine conditions despite compromising oxidative TCA cycle support from glutamine. The cosegregation of GLS1-P5CS filaments depended on continuing mitochondrial fission/fusion and occurred even in cells lacking mtDNA. Together, these data demonstrate that the reductive mitochondrial subpopulation is functional and under regulation by both metabolic demand and intercellular signal transduction.

Article.Title: Validation of targets linked to weight gain in C57BL/6 mice and translational aspects in humans
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; Rudolf A.; Wang L.; Zhang Z.; Niu C.; Xia F.; Li M.; Wang A.; Mitchell S.; Zhang H.; He Y.; Chen C.; Speakman J.
Article.Abstract: Obesity is linked to complex interactions between an organism’s genetic background and its environment. Mouse models have been invaluable research tools to study obesity, with C57BL/6N being widely studied, given its propensity for weight gain on a high-fat diet (HFD). Despite this, the genetic basis of its susceptibility is poorly understood. In a partner paper we have identified SNP variants in 11 genes causing susceptibility to, or protection against, HFD-induced obesity in male C57BL/6N mice explaining 87% of the individual variation in fat gain. Surprisingly, most of them were maximally expressed outside the brain. In this study, we further validate some of these targets. We demonstrate that tissue-specific inhibition of Nova1 and Mchr1 in muscle, Nr1i3 in liver, and Ahr in lung and liver led to resistance to HFD–induced obesity or glucose intolerance. Further RNAseq analysis revealed that mTOR, Acox1, IL-15, and eIF2a signals are positioned downstream of these genes, potentially mediating their effects on obesity susceptibility. Importantly, variants in eight of the genes identified here have been previously implicated in human obesity, suggesting that a deeper understanding of the genetic/environment interactions of model systems can inform this complex human disease. Our work confirms that body fat regulation is likely more complex than current models which focus on the brain–adipose axis suggest.

Article.Title: Multi-omics and spatial analysis of microgravity-grown glioblastoma organoids reveal superior modeling of advanced disease after long-term spaceflight
Article.Authors: Burchett Darantiere A.; Zarodniuk M.; Giza S.; Rexroat J.; Kuehl P.; Clements T.; Balraj K.; Marco H.; D’Souza A.; Najera J.; Bhargava R.; Datta M.
Article.Abstract: Creating accurate organoid models remains a challenge, particularly for diseases like glioblastoma (GBM), an aggressive, treatment-resistant brain cancer with an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Microgravity-grown GBM+monocyte organoids exhibit increased secretion of proteins such as CXCL12 and LOX-1, associated with more aggressive disease. Infrared chemical imaging confirms spatial chemical gradients of DNA, protein, and lipid species in both space- and terrestrially-grown organoids. In summary, this work presents not only an advanced model of glioblastoma for basic and translational research but also demonstrates methods to acquire diverse data from organoids compatible with the unique constraints of in-space systems, helping establish a working model for orbital oncology.

Article.Title: Unveiling the structure of Leishmania flagella through cryoelectron tomography
Article.Authors: Wilburn D.; Pinskey J.; Zhu H.; Nepal B.; Phan N.; Wetzel D.; Nicastro D.
Article.Abstract: Leishmania are unicellular parasites that cause the serious disease leishmaniasis, presenting ongoing global challenges as existing treatments face issues with resistance and toxicity. Leishmania contain a single motile flagellum, essential for transmission, which has the conserved [9 + 2] microtubule arrangement. While the overall structure, including three broad radial spokes and two-headed outer dynein arms, resembles other eukaryotes like Trypanosoma brucei, Tetrahymena, and Opisthokonts, the Leishmania flagellum also exhibits unique and asymmetrical features. These include asymmetrically shaped radial spoke heads similar to T. brucei , suggesting this may represent a kinetoplastid-specific feature. Further, Leishmania contain an additional inner-junction and 8-nm wide A2 protofilament hole. Strikingly, Leishmania have many doublet-specific structures such as outer dynein arm tethers, interdoublet linkers, and heterogeneous connections to the paraflagellar rod. In this work, we show that divergent structural traits of Leishmania flagella highlight lineage-specific adaptations within eukaryotes.

Article.Title: Structure of a sparsely populated chimeric intermediate that facilitates fold-switching of a metamorphic protein
Article.Authors: Nandi B.; Sekhar A.
Article.Abstract: Metamorphic proteins challenge the single-sequence-structure-function paradigm by switching between distinct folds that often adopt complementary functions. This state is a chimera that integrates the secondary and tertiary structure of one fold with the quaternary assembly of the other. Locking lymphotactin into a single conformation abolishes access to this state, supporting its role as an on-pathway intermediate in metamorphosis. Article.Authors: Soulier N.; Datta D.; Schwarz R.; Pokorski J.; Golden J.; Golden S.
Article.Abstract: Cyanobacteria provide a promising platform for light-driven heterologous protein production. These findings streamline recombinant protein production in cyanobacteria and facilitate environmental interactions with cell products, expanding the potential applications of both free-living and material-encapsulated cyanobacteria.

Article.Title: Compensation of the effects of temperature on a motor system in the crab, Cancer borealis
Article.Authors: Jacquerie K.; DiMartino J.; Dalal A.; Zeng J.; Marder E.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how warming affects life-critical physiological processes is increasingly important as ocean temperatures rise at unprecedented rates. We study the stomatogastric system of the crab Cancer borealis . Movement depends on multiple temperature-sensitive processes, from motor pattern generation to neuromuscular transmission and contraction. We simultaneously recorded motor neuron activity, muscle fiber membrane potential, and contraction force. As temperature increased, the pyloric rhythm frequency increased, the excitatory junctional potential amplitudes remained constant, and muscle contraction diminished and failed. Increasing motor nerve stimulation frequency to mimic neuronal activity at warm temperatures partially rescued contraction. This shows that the temperature-dependent increase in neuronal firing provides partial compensation but is insufficient to prevent the loss of contraction at high temperatures. Because warming hyperpolarized muscle fibers, it moved the membrane potential further from the contraction threshold, and decreased synaptic integration, thus protecting against overexcitability. However, high-potassium-induced contractures revealed that the contractile machinery remained functional at high temperature, but the nerve-evoked depolarizations were apparently not large enough to cross the threshold for muscle contraction. Thus, a variety of temperature-dependent compensatory mechanisms overlap to extend the temperature range over which the neuromuscular system remains functional over a broad temperature range.

Article.Title: Molecular fossils of an ancestral code revealed by large-scale analysis of tRNAs
Article.Authors: Nova Royo A.; Martín-Cabezas P.; Ovchinnikov S.; Schimmel P.; Ribas de Pouplana L.
Article.Abstract: Modern tRNAs are thought to have evolved from simpler RNA minihelices resembling acceptor stems, some of which could be specifically aminoacylated. A central and testable prediction of minihelix-based models is that vestiges of ancestral coding relationships should remain embedded within the acceptor stems of contemporary tRNAs and should persist after correction for structural constraints. Here, we ask whether cognate anticodon-like triplets are statistically enriched in nonanticodon regions of modern tRNAs beyond what would be expected from structural and compositional constraints alone. Using a curated dataset of 77,335 canonical tRNA sequences and a structure-aware statistical framework, we find that for a subset of amino acids cognate anticodon-like triplets are significantly enriched in acceptor stems and, to a lesser extent, in other structural domains. Notably, these amino acids include those previously shown to support specific minihelix aminoacylation [Y. M. Hou, P. Schimmel, Nature 333 , 140–145 (1988); C. Francklyn, P. Schimmel, Nature 337 , 478–481 (1989)]. The strongest acceptor-stem signals survive structure-preserving null models, and cluster nonrandomly against proposed chronologies of amino acid incorporation into the genetic code. Together, these findings identify molecular fossils within modern tRNAs consistent with the persistence of an ancestral operational code, and provide refined statistical support for the notion that extant codon–amino acid relationships evolved from early aminoacylation systems involving RNA minihelices.

Article.Abstract: Developing insight into liquid–liquid phase separation in complex polyelectrolyte mixtures has acquired new urgency considering the role this process plays in the formation of biomolecular condensates, which are involved in diverse processes including, stress response, signal transduction, metabolism, gene regulation, and many human diseases. Condensates can be viewed as a biological membraneless structure situated, in scale and function, between macromolecules and cells. The physical properties of, and the physico-chemical environments within, condensates are very important determinants of their biological function. These properties and environments are determined by the phase separation process. Earlier experimental work in one of our laboratories characterized in detail a phase separation process in solutions of oppositely charged polypeptides. Considering new information being developed on macromolecular association in homogeneous solutions of oppositely charged polyions, we have revisited our earlier data looking into the influence of intermolecular association on the outcome of the phase transition. We demonstrate that dispersity of species in homogeneous solution owing to macromolecular association affects phase separation by creating an open miscibility gap, leading to a dependence of the phase compositions on the initial polymer volume fraction. It is very likely that this plays a significant role in the formation of condensates in the biological context that may have been overlooked.

Article.Title: Harry L. Swinney: Nonlinear science and chaos pioneer
Article.Authors: Lathrop D.; Schatz M.; Sreenivasan K.
Article.Abstract: Harry Leonard Swinney passed away peacefully at his home in Austin, Texas, on July 13, 2026, at the age of 87. Harry was an exceptional experimental physicist, well-known for elegant studies of instabilities, nonlinear dynamics, chaos and pattern formation in a wide variety of fluid, chemical, and granular systems, work whose influence propagated into numerous scientific and engineering disciplines well beyond the particular problems that prompted it. The late Russell Donnelly of the University of Oregon used to say, “Harry is a prince”; Russ meant it, in the spirit of the tenth-century Persian poet Ferdowsi, as a compliment affirming the nobility, dignity, integrity, and grace with which Harry pursued his science and treated everyone he worked alongside.

Article.Title: Ecological, physiological, and evolutionary drivers of stoichiometry in insects
Article.Authors: Laborieux L.; Knecht R.; Fagan W.; Sanders N.; Swain A.
Article.Abstract: The elemental composition of organisms links physiology to biogeochemical cycles, yet the relative contributions of evolutionary divergence, ecology, and allometry to stoichiometric variation remain incompletely resolved. Phylogenetically corrected models recover trophic enrichment across successive trophic levels, consistent with previously documented patterns, and positive scaling between body mass and both C:P and N:P, in line with the general predictions of the Growth Rate Hypothesis. Temperature was the strongest ecological predictor of insect stoichiometry, with positive effects on C:P and N:P ratios and a negative effect on C:N, highlighting the thermal underpinnings of previously observed geographic patterns. Finally, our models recover higher P and lower C in terrestrial insects relative to their aquatic counterparts, contrary to classic expectations that invoke differences in structural constraints and autotrophic composition across habitats. Together, our work shows that variation in insect stoichiometry emerges from the interacting influences of evolutionary divergence and ecological and physiological variation, which can be disentangled through appropriately scaled, phylogenetically informed analyses.

Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Gong H.; Zhang Z.; Ying P.; Zhang C.; Xu W.; Kong L.
Article.Abstract: Respiratory infections remain a major global health challenge, further compounded by antibiotic resistance. Article.Title: Disentangling the evolving effects of climate change and technology diffusion on building electricity demand
Article.Authors: Shi M.; Wei Z.; Lehner F.; Craig M.
Article.Abstract: Climate change and technology diffusion will jointly drive future growth in building electricity demand. Our framework drives 209,352 machine learning models of building electricity demand with 100 spatiotemporally downscaled climate realizations across four climate models and three emissions scenarios, and 18 technology diffusion pathways of air source heat pumps and insulation. We find that the combined response of peak demand to climate change and technology diffusion diverges substantially from the sum of their individual responses, with distinct patterns across hot and cold grid regions. In cold regions, climate change and technology diffusion drive roughly up to 10 times larger peak demand growth than climate change alone by 2060. Conversely, in hot regions, technology diffusion counteracts climate-change-driven peak demand growth. Across regions, climate-change-induced warming reduces or eliminates a shift toward winter peaking driven by technology diffusion. Via uncertainty partitioning, we find climate-related uncertainty dominates near-term peak demand uncertainty, while technology-diffusion-related uncertainty increases to 10 to 80% of uncertainty by 2060. Internal variability accounts for a much larger share of climate-related uncertainty in peak demand than in temperature itself. Our results demonstrate that capturing nonadditive responses between climate change and technology diffusion is important for planning reliable power systems.

These results reveal a qualitative reorganization of dynamical couplings across thermodynamic conditions, implying that molecular liquids at thermal equilibrium can exhibit an emergent directionality in their fluctuation couplings. As a consequence, our analysis reveals that external perturbations acting on specific degrees of freedom can induce a stronger arrow of time in the causal relations between translational and orientational modes.

Article.Title: Meta-analysis of 990 EBV genomes identifies EBER2 SNP7048 and its interaction with HLA-A*11:01 driving nasopharyngeal carcinoma risk
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Yao F.; Zhang X.; Wang L.; Sia Y.; Ong E.; Yeo E.; Rio A.; Siow C.; Goh H.; Chin Z.; Ng R.; Tan Y.; Chee J.; Teo W.; Zhai W.; Chen Y.; Xu M.; Loh K.; Lim W.; Chua M.; Tay J.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a major health burden in East and Southeast Asia (SEA). While EBV infection is a primary driver, the specific viral strains responsible for NPC development and their interaction with host genetics across geographically diverse endemic regions remain poorly understood. We performed a whole-genome sequencing of 388 EBV isolates and matched host whole-exome sequencing in a Singaporean cohort. To define the global significance of these findings, we conducted a meta-GWAS and phylogenetic analysis across three independent cohorts (Singapore, Hong Kong, and Guangdong and Guangxi provinces of China), totaling 990 EBV genomes. Our study identifies high-risk EBV strains—carrying a core variant in the EBER2 locus (SNP7048)—as the key viral determinator of NPC risk, accounting for approximately 68% of the attributable risk in SEA. Meta-analysis reveals these strains are consistently associated with NPC across all populations, resolving previous regional genetic discordances. We demonstrate a potent synergistic interaction between these EBV risk strains and the host HLA-A*11:01 protective allele; individuals lacking this protection while carrying a high-risk strain exhibit a 30.9-fold increase in NPC risk. Phylogenetic analysis further reveals that these high-risk lineages populated SEA through clonal expansion from Southern China, following historical migration routes. These findings establish that NPC development is driven by the distribution of specific high-risk EBV lineages and their synergistic interaction with host immune susceptibility. This provides a definitive genetic framework for precision population screening and early diagnosis of NPC in the endemic regions.

Article.Title: Multiple sources contribute to predictive tactile attenuation in the mouse whisker system
Article.Authors: Gupta K.; Chakrabarti S.; Schwarz C.
Article.Abstract: The brain predicts action outcomes using interacting neuronal systems that integrate sensory feedback, movement, and rewards. In the mouse whisker system, we investigated whether two presumed predictive mechanisms jointly attenuate ascending tactile signals during movement. To this end, we employed an open-loop whisker-reach task that monitored facial nucleus motor activity and presented experimental tactile consequences while measuring tactile attenuation in the barrel cortex. Experimentally manipulating sensory consequences revealed two distinct systems. Sensory gating, a previously documented but functionally unclear mechanism of tactile attenuation, appeared graded but persisted during and after movement. In contrast, a second system was found to be temporally precise, generate suppression when stimuli are omitted, and capable of being learned within hundreds of trials. We label it state estimation as its characteristics—active suppression of expected tactile input—aligns well with the classical reafference principle, previously overlooked in the whisker system.

Article.Title: Mechanism of HIV-1 capsid rupture and uncoating by reverse transcription
Article.Authors: Ghosh K.; Gupta M.; Voth G.
Article.Abstract: One of the key events in the HIV-1 life cycle is reverse transcription (RT), during which single-stranded viral RNA (ssRNA) is converted into double-stranded DNA (dsDNA). This process occurs inside the mature HIV-1 capsid and, once it reaches a critical threshold, drives capsid rupture. This uncoating is essential for infection because it releases viral genetic material into the host cell nucleus. Despite its importance, many mechanistic details of this process remain to be fully understood. To address this gap, we develop a multiscale computational method for simulating RT inside the capsid, termed Coarse-Grained Kinetic Monte Carlo (CG-KMC). CG-KMC stochastically adds deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs) to the coarse-grained RNA model, enabling stepwise growth of DNA inside the HIV-1 capsid. We implement this method within an integrative coarse-grained framework that combines a “bottom-up” capsid model with a “top-down” representation of the viral RNA/DNA genome. Our simulations phenomenologically capture and predict diverse capsid rupture pathways during RT. The resulting ruptured structures closely match previously identified cryo-ET images. We further perform an extensive analysis of the rupture process, examining its mechanistic and kinetic aspects as well as the role of capsid–DNA interactions. Our findings illuminate how different capsid–DNA conditions give rise to distinct rupture pathways, which differ from ruptures due to simple outward pressure expansion models from within the capsid.

Article.Title: Heterogeneous amyloid β dimerization revealed by single-molecule FRET and MD simulation
Article.Authors: Meng F.; Pantelopulos G.; Kim J.; Best R.; Chung H.
Article.Abstract: The correlation between specific amyloid fibril polymorphs and diseases suggests that characterization of heterogeneity in the aggregation process is key to understanding disease mechanisms. In this work, we use single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation to quantitatively characterize dimerization of amyloid β (Aβ), the first step of the aggregation process. We find that dimerization is extremely rare, with a high dissociation constant of >16 mM, yet there are multiple dimer states with distinct FRET efficiencies and stabilities, many of which survive for milliseconds to seconds. The dimer population increases with the increasing ionic strength and decreasing pH, indicating the importance of nonspecific electrostatic interactions in dimer formation. MD simulations with enhanced sampling demonstrate the formation of diverse bound states having a range of FRET efficiencies and flexible N termini, compatible with the experimental observations. There are conformational clusters represented by the formation of three mixed parallel/antiparallel β strands forming Greek key-like motifs and the formation of antiparallel β strands, which may be representative of dimers with longer and shorter lifetimes, respectively, observed in the FRET experiment. This structural and kinetic heterogeneity, resulting from transient interactions, reflects the rugged energy landscape of amyloid formation and may be related to the great diversity of fibrils ultimately formed in the aggregation process.

Article.Title: Structure of bovine viral diarrhea virus E2 glycoprotein in complex with CD46 reveals the molecular basis of virus–receptor recognition
Article.Authors: Duan Y.; Lin S.; Wang F.; You Y.; Chen Z.; Guo L.; Gong W.; Liang L.; Tang S.; Yu H.; He Y.; He B.; Wan Z.; Cao Y.; Yang F.; Lu G.
Article.Abstract: Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) is a major contagious pathogen of ruminants and imposes substantial economic burdens on the global livestock industry. The viral envelope glycoprotein E2 mediates host cell attachment by recognizing the CD46 receptor; however, the molecular basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here, we report the crystal structure of BVDV-1 E2 in complex with bovine CD46 at 3.1-Å resolution. The structure reveals that the SCR1-2 domains of CD46 engage the DII-DIV domains of E2 in a roughly antiparallel orientation. Atomic interactions at the E2/CD46 interface are dominated by van der Waals contacts, accompanied by only a limited number of hydrogen bonds, which explains the observed low-affinity binding between the two molecules. Structural analysis and mutagenesis studies identify key receptor features that govern host susceptibility to the virus and propose an interesting bipartite model: The D′/D interloop within SCR1 of CD46 likely serves as the “molecular determinant,” and key interface residues within SCR2 function as the “affinity regulator.” We further engineered CD46 decoy proteins exhibiting over 1,800-fold higher apparent binding to E2 than the wild-type receptor and demonstrated their potent virus-neutralizing activity. Collectively, these findings elucidate the molecular basis of CD46 recognition by BVDV, provide a structural framework for understanding the viral host range, and establish a receptor-based strategy for potential antiviral intervention.

Article.Title: Programmable chemoenzymatic synthesis of a keratan sulfate N -glycan library for glycocode decoding
Article.Authors: Wang K.; Ma W.; Zhang W.; Hao T.; Zhang M.; Li W.; Zhao W.; Xu Z.; Li T.
Article.Abstract: Keratan sulfate (KS) is a unique and widely distributed glycosaminoglycans family implicated in diverse biological processes. KS features branched glycan architectures with diverse sialylation and sulfation patterns, encoding a vastly expanded chemical and biological space. The limited accessibility of well-defined structures has hindered precise investigations into the KS biological functions. Here we report a programmable chemoenzymatic platform for assembling a 106-membered library of KS N -glycans and their nonsulfated counterparts, featuring length-variable oligo- N -acetyllactosamine (LacNAc) extensions and encompassing diverse sulfation and sialylation patterns. The synthetic strategy integrates length-controlled iterative glycosylation to assemble versatile precursors, orthogonal deprotection for site-specific sulfation, and modular enzyme-driven diversification. Glycan microarray analysis of this comprehensive library reveals that glycan–protein recognition is governed by the interplay of sulfation and sialylation patterns, oligo-LacNAc chain length, and terminal epitope presentation, providing insight into the functional versatility of KS glycans.

Article.Title: Molecular basis for discrimination of cGAMP linkage isomers by a c-di-GMP-II riboswitch variant
Article.Authors: Xu X.; Cheng W.; You H.; Hu Z.; Bao X.; Li H.; Zhang J.; Patel D.; Ren A.
Article.Abstract: Riboswitches are noncoding RNA regulatory motifs predominantly found in bacteria. Signaling molecules such as c-di-GMP, c-di-AMP, and 3′,3′-cGAMP have been reported to be recognized by riboswitches. In contrast, 2′,3′-cGAMP functions as a second messenger in mammalian cells, yet its interaction with RNA molecules remains unclear. Here, we report the crystal structures of a c-di-GMP-II riboswitch variant, c-di-GMP-II-Bh, bound to 2′,3′-cGAMP and 3′,3′-cGAMP. Both complexes adopt a similar overall RNA scaffold with an identical binding pocket composition. However, the ligand bases adopt inverted orientations in the binding pocket, resulting in distinct interaction patterns with residues A64 and G68 and differences in base-pair stacking against the phosphodiester backbone. Structural comparison together with ligand-binding assays of structure-guided mutants using isothermal titration calorimetry reveals the molecular principles by which an RNA riboswitch discriminates among cyclic dinucleotide linkage isomers, highlighting the remarkable sensitivity of RNA binding pockets to subtle ligand structural variations and provides a mechanistic framework for understanding ligand specificity in RNA–small molecule recognition.

Article.Title: A tunable immune-evasion function of Zika virus NS5 governs viral fitness and pathogenesis
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhang Y.; Liu C.; Ren W.; Zhao Y.; Li C.; Guo Y.; Bai L.; Wang P.; An J.; Liu J.; Ding Q.
Article.Abstract: Type I interferon (IFN) signaling is a central antiviral defense, with STAT2 driving the expression of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) to restrict viral infection. Zika virus (ZIKV) and dengue virus evade this pathway through nonstructural protein 5 (NS5)-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of STAT2, yet the contribution of this immune-evasion strategy to viral fitness and pathogenesis remains incompletely defined. Here, using a multistep mutational scanning strategy that jointly assessed STAT2 degradation and viral RNA replication, we identified a single NS5 residue, L162, as uniquely permissive to substitution that abolishes STAT2 degradation without compromising intrinsic replication functions. Substitution of L162 with alanine or glycine (L162A or L162G) selectively disrupted NS5 recruitment of the ZSWIM8-CUL3 E3 ubiquitin ligase, thereby preserving STAT2 stability and restoring IFN signaling. Recombinant ZIKV carrying these mutations exhibited reduced replication and enhanced ISG induction in human cells, defects fully rescued by STAT2 knockout. In A129 mice (type I IFN receptor deficient), mutant and WT viruses replicated comparably, but in human STAT2 knock-in mice, ZIKV-NS5 L162G exhibited markedly reduced viral loads and disease. In pregnant human STAT2 knock-in mice, the mutant also reduced placental and fetal viral burdens and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Notably, infection with ZIKV-NS5 L162G elicited robust neutralizing antibody and T cell responses that conferred protection against WT challenge. Together, these findings establish NS5-mediated STAT2 degradation as a central determinant of ZIKV immune-evasion, viral fitness, and pathogenesis and highlight disruption of NS5–STAT2 antagonism as a promising strategy for antiviral intervention and rational attenuation.

Article.Title: Widespread plasma jets in the Martian magnetosheath revealed by dual-spacecraft observations
Article.Authors: Tadlock A.; Dong C.; Zhang C.; Raptis S.; Zhou H.; Li X.; Gao J.
Article.Abstract: Plasma jets in planetary magnetosheaths are transient, high dynamic pressure structures capable of strongly perturbing downstream magnetospheres and modulating solar wind energy transfer. Although recently identified at Mars, their formation mechanisms and global occurrence remain poorly constrained. Using dual-spacecraft observations from Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN and Tianwen-1, we show that magnetosheath jets occur throughout the Martian magnetosheath, in striking contrast to Earth where jet occurrence is strongly controlled by interplanetary magnetic field orientation and largely confined to quasi-parallel shock regions. We propose that this widespread distribution is linked to Mars’ extended hydrogen corona, which generates pickup ions that drive proton-cyclotron waves upstream of the bow shock. Because this mechanism is generic to any body with an extended corona (or exosphere) embedded in a stellar wind, this finding bears on solar–wind interactions at comets and other small bodies, and on the space environments of unmagnetized terrestrial exoplanets. These results indicate that magnetosheath jet formation can be governed not only by external solar wind forcing but also by intrinsic planetary properties, pointing to a previously unrecognized pathway for solar wind–planet coupling at unmagnetized worlds.

Article.Title: Unique features of EIGHT fold—Proteins with the most complex 8 <sub>3</sub> knotted topology
Article.Authors: Mozajew M.; Sikora M.; Fortunka M.; Perlinska A.; Kluza A.; Niewieczerzal S.; da Silva F.; Lukaszewicz M.; Sikorska J.; Mikulska L.; Jackson S.; Sulkowska J.
Article.Abstract: Herein, we present three crystal structures of the most complex knotted protein to date, an 8 3 knot with eight crossings, which belongs to a clasp knot family. The fold of this protein is also unique, and we call it the EIGHT fold (Extraordinarily Intricate Globular Helical Tangled fold). The 8 3 knot is found only in a certain group of bacteria, where it is strictly conserved, despite sequence identities as low as 10%. The 8 3 structure shows a high level of internal symmetry, with structurally analogous halves. It is possible that the EIGHT fold evolved from a single unknotted “half” that duplicated and formed a complex protein. Based on an in vitro study of three selected 8 3 proteins, we estimated their thermal and thermodynamic stability, and showed that they follow a two-state unfolding model under equilibrium conditions and their refolding occurs to a compact, nonnative state. Unfolding kinetics of 8 3 knotted proteins reveal a complex, multiphase process spanning milliseconds to days. Six kinetic phases were resolved using stopped-flow fluorescence and far-ultraviolet absorbance circular dichroism spectroscopy, highlighting both rapid early events and slower rearrangements in secondary and tertiary structures. Finally, with a structure-based model, we showed that proteins with an 8 3 knot can self-tie through a 6 1 knotted intermediate state. They can also self-untie, albeit via an additional intermediate knot such as 4 1 . Nevertheless, these proteins do not seem to fit with current folding theories known to date and require the development of a new approach.
