Article.Title: Recombination shapes the dynamics of selective constraint in global populations of human gut bacteria
Article.Authors: Liu Z.; Good B.
Article.Abstract: The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) encodes important information about the selection pressures acting on protein-coding genes. In bacterial populations, dN/dS often declines with the sequence divergence between strains, but the mechanisms responsible for this broad empirical trend are still debated. Existing models have primarily focused on de novo mutations, overlooking the older genetic variants that are continually introduced through horizontal gene transfer and recombination. Here we introduce a phenomenological model of dN/dS in recombining populations of bacteria, which allows us to disentangle the effects of recombination among pairs of closely related strains. We find that clonally inherited regions of the genome exhibit consistently higher dN/dS ratios, and that the accumulation of recombined segments can quantitatively explain the majority of the decline in dN/dS. We use these observations to re-examine models of purifying selection and adaptive reversion in human gut bacteria, and uncover evidence for widespread weak selection at a large fraction of protein-coding sites. Our findings show that horizontal gene transfer can be an important factor in shaping genome-wide patterns of selective constraint, and raise new questions about the effectiveness of natural selection in complex bacterial populations.

Article.Title: FuChi is a cell cycle biosensor for tracking cell cycle dynamics during avian development
Article.Authors: Sudderick Z.; Briggs T.; Mubarak S.; Van Kerckvoorde M.; Hernandez Rodriguez A.; Panda S.; Riddell J.; Batho-Samblas C.; Taylor L.; McTeir L.; Meunier D.; Findlay A.; Roberts F.; Raper A.; Sakaue-Sawano A.; Miyawaki A.; Rainger J.; Schoenebeck J.; Weijer C.; McGrew M.; Headon D.; Davey M.; Mort R.; Glover J.

This was first made possible by fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator (Fucci) technology, which distinguishes specific cell cycle phases through the reciprocal degradation of fluorescently tagged, truncated forms of human CDT1 and GMNN proteins. Fucci genetic systems have been successfully implemented in transgenic mice, zebrafish, and axolotls. To date, no viable, stably expressing Fucci line has been developed in an avian species. Although a range of continuously improving Fucci constructs have been developed in recent years, existing in vivo Fucci models remain limited because they rely on older reporter technology that fails to distinguish cells in S, G2, and M phases or to label cells in early G1. As a result, these models can be challenging to interpret and their utility for continuous cell tracking and precise analysis of cell-cycle dynamics is limited. These latter experiments revealed that transition from S phase may be a key morphogenetic event during gastrulation as mesendoderm cells egress from the primitive streak to form embryonic structures including the prechordal plate. Article.Authors: Zhao B.; Bhagwat S.; Ferreira J.; Ruff K.; Swain D.; Pappu R.; Santi C.; Fu Z.; Lishko P.

Functional validation using electrophysiology and calcium imaging in mouse sperm shows that capacitation-associated partial removal of the CatSper1 N-terminus selectively impairs temperature-dependent activation. Article.Title: Implicit sensorimotor adaptation comprises distinct mechanisms for action selection and execution
Article.Authors: Wang T.; Lam T.; Taylor J.; Ivry R.
Article.Abstract: The sensorimotor system is continuously adjusted to minimize error. Current theories assume that this adaptation process entails the operation of multiple learning systems, with a key division between implicit and explicit components. Recent studies have revealed several inconsistencies regarding the characteristics and constraints of the implicit system, suggesting that the current framework is incomplete. Here, we propose that these conflicting findings can be understood by recognizing that there are multiple implicit subcomponents, each with distinct computational goals. One well-studied component is implicit recalibration, a process critical for action execution which uses sensory-prediction errors to automatically refine the sensorimotor map. In the current study, we describe a second, novel component, implicit aiming, a process which contributes to action selection to achieve specific goals. Through a series of studies using human participants, we find compelling evidence that those two implicit processes show a clear separation in their temporal stabilities and contextual modulations. These distinct properties correspond to different computational frameworks attributing learning dynamics to either contextual inference or cancellation of competing neural populations, respectively. Together, these findings suggest an alternative framework for sensorimotor adaptation based on the computational goals of the system rather than phenomenology.

Article.Title: Type III effectors of symbiotic Rhizobia include diverse predicted transcriptional and post-transcriptional modulators
Article.Authors: Teulet A.; Schornack S.
Article.Abstract: Rhizobia are soil bacteria that establish nitrogen-fixing symbioses with legumes. While many rhizobia use a Type III Secretion System to deliver “Nodulation Outer Protein” (Nop) effectors, some uniquely use these proteins to initiate nodule organogenesis, bypassing classical signalling. The molecular functions of these effectors remain largely unknown due to extreme sequence divergence. Using AlphaFold2-mediated structural proteomics, we identified a modular architecture in rhizobial effectors composed of 22 distinct structural units. We reveal that many Nop effectors are cryptic transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulators, harbouring unrecognised nucleic acid–binding modules and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase domains. Crucially, these modules are conserved in specific plant pathogens, such as gall-inducing Pantoea , where our predicted structural units align with experimentally validated DNA-binding domains. Furthermore, we discovered the BPN (B3 and PUA-like nucleic acid binding) domain as a structural mimic of plant B3-domain transcription factors, pointing to a direct mechanism for hijacking legume development. Our findings strongly suggest that rhizobia employ a modular domain-fusion strategy to act as direct genetic modulators, uncovering a conserved mechanism used by both symbionts and pathogens to hijack host developmental programmes.

Article.Title: The histone methyltransferase complex subunit RBBP5 serves as a central epigenetic regulator of proteostasis dynamics
Article.Authors: Kubra S.; Sun M.; Dion W.; Bian Y.; Catak A.; Luong H.; Wang H.; Pan Y.; Liu J.; Ponna A.; Liu L.; Sipula I.; Luo J.; Jurczak M.; Liu S.; Zhu B.
Article.Abstract: Proteostasis is essential for cellular health, with its disruption contributing to aging, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disorders. While the upstream proteotoxic stress-sensing and protein-folding mechanisms in the ER and cytosol are well studied, the transcriptional regulation of proteostasis remains incompletely understood, particularly concerning the temporal epigenome dynamics, chromatin landscapes, and co-regulatory networks underlying dynamic proteostasis control. Traditionally, proteotoxic stress responses were viewed as acute reactions to noxious stimuli, but recent evidence shows that many proteostasis genes exhibit ~12-hour ultradian rhythms under physiological conditions, driven by an XBP1s-dependent oscillator independent of the canonical circadian clock and cell cycle. By mapping the chromatin landscape of the murine 12-hour oscillator, we identified RBBP5—an essential subunit of the COMPASS complex responsible for H3K4 trimethylation—as a pivotal epigenetic regulator of proteostasis dynamics. In contrast, histone acetyltransferases and H3K9 acetylation were dispensable for dynamic proteostasis gene expression. RBBP5 is not only indispensable for the 12-hour oscillator but also essential for the transcriptional regulation of diverse proteotoxic stresses response, by coactivating XBP1s and promoting H3K4me3 deposition at the promoters of proteostasis genes. As a result, loss of RBBP5 sensitizes cells to proteotoxic stress in part due to impaired autophagy. Proximity labeling of H3K4me3 further uncovered a dynamic chromatin-associated proteomic architecture, including components of COMPASS, the Integrator complex and SWI/SNF remodelers, that constitutes the transcriptional response to proteotoxic stress. Together, these findings establish RBBP5 as a central regulator of proteostasis dynamics, essential for maintaining cellular resilience.

Article.Title: Better antibodies, better science
Article.Authors: Duchêne J.
Article.Abstract: Poorly validated antibodies generate misleading results and waste research resources. Two new studies in PLOS Biology quantify the ethical costs of this issue, examine why unvalidated antibodies are still used, and identify solutions to reduce their use.

Article.Title: Inadequate antibody validation places substantial numbers of animal and human tissue samples at risk of waste
Article.Authors: Biddle M.; Cooper J.; Blades K.; Ruddy D.; Krockow E.; Virk H.
Article.Abstract: Lack of antibody validation by researchers frequently misdirects biomedical research, yet the ethical consequences—particularly avoidable use of animal and human biological materials—remain unquantified. Using focus groups ( n = 12), surveys ( n = 107), and systematic analysis of 785 publications, we examined how researchers select and validate antibodies, and quantified the downstream ethical costs. Antibody selection is substantially influenced by social factors such as previous laboratory use and peer recommendations, while systematic evaluation of performance characteristics remains limited. From a dataset of 614 antibodies subjected to rigorous characterisation using knockout controls, 97 (15.8%) failed across all tested applications; we systematically searched for publications linked to these antibodies. Within the 760 publications (those where validation status could be confirmed), only 120 (15.8%) presented any validation evidence—despite 72.0% of surveyed researchers reporting having used at least one recommended validation method. The remaining 640 papers reported a minimum of 8,064 animal samples and 4,424 human tissue samples used with antibodies of demonstrated poor performance and without evidence of fitness for the specific experimental purpose; we describe these as samples at risk of waste. Reserving the term waste for samples used with reagents since withdrawn from sale, and therefore irreproducible, conservative extrapolation gives lower-bound, order-of-magnitude estimates of millions of animal and human tissue samples consumed globally. Researchers identified time, cost, and lack of supervisor support as primary barriers, whilst strongly supporting open data sharing, dedicated validation funding, and publisher requirements as solutions. These findings provide a first quantification of the ethical costs of inadequate antibody validation and highlight the need for coordinated stakeholder interventions to reduce avoidable biological sample waste in biomedical research.

Article.Title: Actionable solutions to address antibody validation failures
Article.Authors: Blades K.; Biddle M.; Froud R.; Krockow E.; Virk H.
Article.Abstract: The experimental use of antibodies that have not been validated for context-specific use frequently misdirects biomedical research. Experimental results that derive from the use of inadequately validated antibodies are estimated to waste over $1 billion annually in the United States alone and to consume millions of animal and human biological samples in experiments whose conclusions may be unreliable. Community validation frameworks, reporting standards, and independent characterisation initiatives have made important progress, and multi-stakeholder coordination efforts are emerging. However, the research community lacks a formally developed, consensus-based action plan that specifies what each stakeholder group should do, by when, and with what priority. We conducted a modified Delphi study with international experts representing academic researchers, scientific publishers, research funders, antibody manufacturers, and institutional research leaders to develop actionable recommendations for improving antibody validation, selection, and reporting practices. Thirty-two participants rated 33 proposed actions on effectiveness and feasibility using 9-point scales, with consensus assessed using the RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method. Over two rounds, the panel achieved consensus on 15 items as both effective and feasible for implementation by 2030. These spanned institutional actions (training in antibody validation, integration into research integrity frameworks, support for local expertise networks), funder actions (dedicated validation budgets, grant application requirements, endorsement of community reporting standards), publisher actions (complete antibody reporting packages, clear validation standards), manufacturer actions (assignment of unique identifiers at source), and cross-stakeholder coordination (a shared roadmap for improvement). An additional 15 items were rated as effective but with uncertain feasibility, reflecting a consistent pattern in which the panel agreed on the value of proposed interventions but expressed reservations about realistic implementation timelines. One item was rejected by the panel with concerns around effectiveness and feasibility. Participants described four interconnected barriers to progress: diffuse ownership of the problem across stakeholders; market dynamics that inadequately reward antibody quality; difficulty justifying investment when returns are distributed across the research system; and coordination challenges among actors with different incentive structures. These barriers are addressable through coordinated action, and the findings complement existing technical and data-sharing initiatives by providing the structured, expert-informed policy framework to help translate awareness of the problem into concrete practice and policy changes.

Article.Title: A binding-activated CRISPR/dCas13X imaging system enables precise RNA tracking in plants
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Tao Y.; Zhao Y.; Lei M.; Shen Y.; Li Q.; Liu C.; Bai J.
Article.Abstract: Visualizing the spatiotemporal dynamics of native RNA molecules with single-transcript-level sensitivity in living plant cells remains a formidable challenge due to the high background noise caused by the unique cellular architecture of plants. Here, using transiently transformed Nicotiana benthamiana cells and stable Arabidopsis thaliana lines, we present a high-signal-to-noise RNA imaging platform that couples CRISPR–dCas13X with a binding-associated fluorescence stabilization strategy. We identified a novel plant-specific degron that selectively targets unbound probes for proteasomal degradation while preserving target-associated signal in a manner consistent with binding-dependent protection, enabling high-fidelity detection of endogenous mRNA puncta with minimal perturbation. Leveraging this platform, we characterized dynamics of FT mRNA trafficking in living plant cells, including plasmodesmata-targeting, cell-to-cell trafficking, and long-distance movement. Loss-of-function analysis further identified the established RNA-binding protein GRP7 as a factor that contributes to efficient FT mRNA transport. This work establishes a useful toolkit for investigating plant RNA biology and provides mechanistic insight into the systemic transport of florigenic signals.

Article.Title: Why are some neurons spared in neurodegeneration? Cellular subtype identity maintenance as a candidate threshold-setting mechanism
Article.Authors: Kim D.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases often damage some neuronal populations while sparing closely related neighbors. But instead of asking why some neurons die, should we be asking why some survive? This Essay proposes that a neuron’s capacity to sustain the gene-regulatory machinery that maintains its subtype identity helps set the stress threshold beyond which recovery fails. The initiating insult may be metabolic, proteostatic, inflammatory, or arise from the surrounding tissue, but it is the cell’s capacity for maintenance that will determine where the tipping point lies: above a critical level, the identity program recovers, whereas below it, regulatory loss becomes self-sustaining. Such a framing could have implications for how neuronal vulnerability to neurodegeneration is understood.

Article.Title: Moral and perceptual conflict processing are implemented by distinct brain activation and functional connectivity patterns
Article.Authors: Zhu R.; Grueschow M.; Moisa M.; Liu C.; Ruff C.
Article.Abstract: While humans resemble other primates in terms of motor and perceptual abilities, our behavior is uniquely characterized by morality—the ability to choose our actions based on specific ethical values. The evolutionary origins and neurobiological basis of moral behavior are debated intensely, with opposing proposals about whether moral decisions rely on domain-general decision-making neural circuitry (neural common currency hypothesis) or on unique neural processes that were shaped by evolutionary pressures associated with life in groups (social brain hypothesis). Here we examine the potential overlap between moral and perceptual decision-making, by combining functional magnetic resonance imaging with computational modeling of behavior in a novel task requiring human participants to make alternating moral and perceptual choices on identical stimuli. At the algorithmic level, we found that moral and perceptual choices were well fit by the same sequential sampling model, which allowed us to quantify and directly compare conflicts between the choice alternatives for both types of decision-making. At the implementational level, moral and perceptual choice conflicts were represented by distinct neural activity patterns; in fact, neural signals in some brain areas (e.g., temporoparietal junction) encoded the strength of the two types of conflict in opposite directions. Our findings suggest that while similar computational decision mechanisms underlie both moral and perceptual choices, their neural implementation is fundamentally different, supporting the social brain hypothesis.

Article.Title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals the molecular landscape and therapeutic strategies in Chinese cervical cancer patients
Article.Authors: Pan T.; Zhuang X.; Zhang Y.; Guo J.; Li S.; Zhang C.; Han L.; Li F.; Gao Y.; Yu J.; Li Y.; Sun C.
Article.Abstract: Genomic or transcriptomic sequencing guides the precision of cervical cancer (CC) diagnosis; however, the molecular profile of Asian patients remains poorly understood. We established a comprehensive multi-omics cohort comprising 112 tumor-normal adjacent tissue pairs from Chinese CC patients. Our integrated analysis revealed a mutational burden comparable to other populations, with three major mutational signatures primarily attributed to APOBEC-associated, age-associated, and DNA repair-associated biological categories. Multi-omics profiling elucidated the functional consequences of somatic mutations and copy number variations, identifying PIK3CA, EP300, and MPRIP as key driver events. We further uncovered both concordant and discordant activation patterns across cancer-related signaling pathways. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses nominated cell cycle regulation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and LAMC2 as promising diagnostic and therapeutic targets. Comprehensive immune characterization enabled stratification of patients into three major immune phenotypes with varying microenvironmental profiles. This study provides valuable resources and novel insights into the molecular architecture of cervical cancer in the Chinese population, identifying potential biomarkers to guide precision detection and immunotherapy strategies.

Article.Title: Uracil-driven ROS signaling and larval TrpA1-B neuron activation are required for priming the adult Drosophila gustatory response to bacteria
Article.Authors: Milleville R.; Manière G.; Berthelot-Grosjean M.; Lamotte O.; Grosjean Y.; Royet J.; Kurz C.
Article.Abstract: Animals perceive their immediate environment through their sensory systems. While these systems rely on well-defined neuronal circuits and receptor proteins encoded by the genome, they can also be modulated by internal physiological conditions or exogenous factors. We have previously shown that the presence of certain pathogenic bacteria in the larval gut can alter the specificity of bacterial peptidoglycan recognition in the adults that emerge from these larvae. However, the nature of the bacterial signal and the host cells and molecules involved in receiving and transducing this signal remained unknown. Our results identify uracil as the bacterial metabolite responsible for this priming and demonstrate that the effect is mediated by Duox-dependent production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the larval gut. We further show that specific expression of TrpA1 isoforms in a Gr66a-expressing neuron of the larval terminal organ is required for the adult response. Together, these findings reveal uracil as the bacterial cue and the Duo/ROS signaling and TrpA1/Gr66a modules as key mediators linking larval gut microbial signals and host integration to subsequent sensory system modulation in the adult.

Article.Title: Sequential TPRX1 and HERVL activation delineates a progression toward the totipotent-like state
Article.Authors: Huang A.; Jiang N.; Luo S.; Kong X.; Yi S.; Yin S.; Peng J.; Jiang Y.; Xie H.; Xie B.
Article.Abstract: The in vitro induction of 8-cell-like cells (8CLCs) from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) provides a model to study the regulatory principles of totipotency and zygotic genome activation (ZGA). However, the cellular dynamics underlying 8CLC emergence remain poorly understood. Here, we generate a TPRX1-EGFP/HERVL-tdTomato dual-reporter hPSC line to resolve the stepwise acquisition of totipotent-like identity. We show that 8CLC induction follows an ordered trajectory in which TPRX1 activation precedes the emergence of TPRX1+HERVL+ cells, which most closely resemble the in vivo 8-cell embryo transcriptionally. Single-cell transcriptomics and time-resolved flow cytometry further define a continuous transition from the primed state through a TPRX1+ intermediate to the HERVL+ 8CLC state. CRISPRi and RNA-directed perturbations support functional contributions of HERVL elements and HERVL-derived RNA to this transition, while potential locus-dependent mechanisms remain unresolved. Together, these findings establish sequential TPRX1 and HERVL activation as a defining feature of human 8CLC induction.

Article.Title: The conserved NUS-1/DHDDS-1 complex links N-glycosylation to lipid and lysosomal homeostasis in C. elegans
Article.Authors: Gong M.; Zhao W.; Du Y.; Zhu L.; Zhai Y.; Xie Y.; Liu C.; Li W.; Zhao P.; Zhang Z.
Article.Abstract: N-glycosylation is essential for proteome integrity, yet the systemic roles of the cis-prenyltransferase (cis-PT) complex remain poorly defined. Using Caenorhabditis elegans, we demonstrate that this complex is a dual regulator of global lipid and lysosomal homeostasis. Mechanistically, NUS-1 physically associates with the core oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex to coordinate N-glycan transfer. Loss of NUS-1/DHDDS-1 triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, lysosomal collapse, and systemic lipopenia. This lipid defect arises from impaired N-glycosylation of the SREBP cleavage-activating protein (SCAP). cis-PT deficiency causes unglycosylated SCAP to undergo massive degradation and absolute physical entrapment within the ER, preventing SREBP nuclear translocation and downstream lipid synthesis. Furthermore, pathogenic mutations cause dysfunction through distinct molecular mechanisms: pocket integrity disruption or catalytic impairment. These findings uncover an essential crosstalk between protein glycosylation and global lipid metabolism, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding the systemic pathophysiology of congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG).

Article.Title: Polycystin-2 functions as a calcium leak channel under endoplasmic reticulum stress to protect against myocardial ischemia
Article.Authors: Vuchkovska V.; Paluru S.; Knutila R.; Simoens D.; Márquez-Nogueras K.; DiNello E.; Cao Q.; Kirk J.; Kuo I.
Article.Abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress activates the unfolded protein response (UPR) to enhance metabolism and restore homeostasis by increasing mitochondrial calcium at mitochondrial-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites (MERCs). Unresolved ER stress is deleterious and contributes to the severity of diseases such as myocardial infarction (MI). The identity of the MERC calcium source and its interplay with the UPR is unclear. We find that ER-localized polycystin-2 (PC2), a calcium channel, is upregulated in cardiomyocytes with MI. Cardiomyocyte PC2-knockout mice with MI exhibit worsened heart function and decreased PERK. ER stress induces a PC2-facilitated adaptive ER calcium leak and PC2 localization to MERCs. PC2 requires PERK phosphorylation for mitochondrial calcium transfer. PC2 mutations impair ER calcium leak, restored by full-length PC2 expression. Thus, PC2 functions in a PERK-dependent manner under ER stress to provide mitochondrial calcium, and its upregulation is cardioprotective in MI.

Article.Title: METTL4 interacts with histone methylation readers MRG1/2 to regulate alternative splicing and promote thermomorphogenesis in Arabidopsis
Article.Authors: Zhu X.; Li X.; Liang Z.; Wang J.; Shen W.; Su W.; Yu Y.; Wang H.; Wu J.; Dong A.
Article.Abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) functions in thermomorphogenesis, but how AS is regulated during this process remains unclear. Here we show that METTL4 physically interacts with MRG1/2 in Arabidopsis thaliana. The mettl4-1, mrg1 mrg2, and mettl4 mrg1 mrg2 mutants exhibit reduced hypocotyl elongation under warm temperature conditions (28°C), indicating that METTL4 and MRG1/2 cooperatively promote thermomorphogenesis. Transcriptome analysis revealed that both METTL4 and MRG1/2 are required for warm temperature-induced reprogramming of gene transcription and AS. Further analysis showed that METTL4 and MRG1/2 modulate the AS of key brassinosteroid (BR)-signaling genes BES1, GSK1, and SBI1 in thermomorphogenesis. In addition, METTL4 promotes MRG2 binding to the chromatin of BES1 and GSK1 loci. METTL4 also promotes hypocotyl elongation and regulates the AS of BR signaling genes independently of its methyltransferase activity. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that METTL4 and MRG1/2 co-regulate AS and BR signaling to promote thermomorphogenesis in Arabidopsis.

Article.Title: The TCF-1-E-protein axis preserves stem-like Th17 identity and prevents autoimmune pathology
Article.Authors: Han X.; Wang X.; Li C.; Zhai X.; Gao P.; Liu X.; Zhou X.; Song J.; Zhang F.
Article.Abstract: T helper 17 (Th17) cells exhibit plasticity, transitioning from homeostatic cells to pathogenic effectors in autoimmune diseases. Although TCF-1 restrains Th17 pathogenicity by binding RORγt, mechanisms sustaining TCF-1 expression in mature Th17 cells and the transcriptional architecture governing the switch between states remain unknown. Using an interleukin 17 (IL-17) fate-mapping system deleting Tcf7 in cells with IL-17 history, we show that TCF-1 maintains homeostatic Th17 identity. TCF-1 deficiency does not impair Th17 generation but destabilizes the non-pathogenic state, causing loss of stem-like markers (SLAMF6 and CD27), acquisition of pathogenic features (CXCR6, T-bet, and IFN-γ), and exacerbated experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. Mechanistically, TCF-1 and E-proteins form a reciprocal feedback loop establishing a self-reinforcing transcriptional circuit; disruption of either collapses this circuit and unleashes pathogenicity. Single-cell transcriptomics reveals that TCF-1 downregulation is an early event in pathogenic conversion. Thus, the TCF-1-E-protein axis sustains TCF-1 expression and prevents pathogenic conversion.

Article.Title: SMURFs regulate mesendoderm differentiation through SMAD2-dependent ubiquitination of CDK9
Article.Authors: Shin J.; Xu X.; Xiao T.; Tang Y.; Molla M.; Chen T.; Chen Q.; Du Y.; Liu C.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Precise control of transcriptional timing is essential during embryonic development, where dynamic gene expression programs govern lineage specification. Promoter-proximal pausing of RNA polymerase II (Pol II) and its regulated release into productive elongation constitute a critical checkpoint in transcriptional regulation. Nodal, a transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) family morphogen, promotes mesendoderm differentiation through SMAD2-dependent transcription, in part by promoting cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9)-mediated release of paused Pol II. While mechanisms of transcriptional activation downstream of Nodal are well characterized, how this transcriptional program is attenuated during gastrulation remains unclear. Here, we show that E3 ubiquitin ligases SMAD Ubiquitination Regulatory Factor (SMURF) 1 and SMURF2 are critical regulators of SMAD2-driven transcription. SMURF1/2 ubiquitinate CDK9 and promote its proteasome-mediated degradation, thereby restraining CDK9-dependent promoter-proximal pause release and productive transcription of SMAD2-dependent genes. Loss of SMURF function stabilizes CDK9, increases its occupancy at SMAD2 target genes, and enhances Pol II pause release, thereby sustaining mesendodermal gene expression. These findings reveal a ubiquitin-dependent mechanism that restricts morphogen-induced gene expression and ensures timely developmental progression.

Article.Title: An engineered probiotic for diagnosis and mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel disease
Article.Authors: Zhao Y.; Sun Y.; Zhu X.; Hu W.; Chen S.; Peng G.; Yang S.; Ma D.; Mao X.; Yi S.; Tian L.; Han K.; Tang X.; Zheng J.; Zhou J.
Article.Abstract: Early diagnosis and timely treatment of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are critical to limit disease progression, yet integrated diagnostic-therapeutic strategies remain limited. Here, we design a synthetic probiotic system that responds to reactive oxygen species (ROS) to enable noninvasive detection of intestinal inflammation. We further engineer EcN-IL22, a therapeutic strain that conditionally expresses interleukin 22-fragment crystallizable (IL-22-Fc) fusion protein in situ to mitigate colitis-associated tissue damage. Mechanistically, EcN-IL22 activates epithelial IL-22 receptor 1/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (IL-22R1/STAT3) signaling, promoting epithelial barrier restoration and intestinal stem cell proliferation. We identify thyroid hormone receptor-interacting protein 13 (Trip13) and fidgetin-like 1 (Fignl1) as IL-22R1-responsive candidate genes associated with epithelial repair. Importantly, replacing the diagnostic output of the ROS-responsive circuit with IL-22-Fc enables inflammation-triggered therapeutic delivery and significantly alleviates colitis. Finally, EcN-IL22 demonstrates robust protective efficacy in a piglet colitis model, supporting its translational potential. Together, this work establishes an integrated probiotic platform for IBD diagnosis and regenerative therapy.

Article.Title: A MADS51 allele is associated with flowering-time divergence and contributes to ecological adaptation during wild rice speciation
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Han J.; Li Y.; Qiang C.; Yu L.; Jiao Z.; Yu W.; Jing C.; Zhou L.; Ren N.; Zheng X.; Zhang F.; Ge S.
Article.Abstract: Flowering-time divergence can contribute to ecological speciation, but causal genes and mutations remain largely unknown in wild plants. Here, we investigate flowering-time divergence between the wild rice species Oryza rufipogon and O. nivara. By establishing a transformation system for wild rice and combining genome scans, population genomics, and functional assays, we identify MADS51 as a contributor to flowering-time divergence. Knockout of MADS51 in O. rufipogon accelerates flowering, whereas overexpression delays flowering. A functional haplotype (functional haplotype 2 [FH2]), defined by three nonsynonymous substitutions and a 4-bp frameshift, is nearly fixed in Southeast Asian O. nivara. Complementation assays confirm that FH2 promotes earlier flowering than ancestral haplotypes. Population genetic analyses reveal a selective sweep associated with FH2, which appears to have arisen de novo in O. nivara. These findings provide insights into how de novo mutation can contribute to phenotypic differentiation in wild rice.

Article.Title: Multi-omics profiling of the choroid plexus reveals developmental cellular remodeling, early immune gene activation, and epithelial cell heterogeneity
Article.Authors: Fernandes M.; Andersson-Li L.; Correia E.; Vieira A.; Alves-Afonso D.; Álvarez-López A.; Campos J.; Mahmud N.; Meijer M.; Agirre E.; Marques F.; Nobrega C.; Castelo-Branco G.; Sousa J.; Falcão A.
Article.Abstract: Brain development and function are influenced by the choroid plexus, whose dynamic cellular and transcriptional changes shape immune cell trafficking and cerebrospinal fluid composition. Here, we performed a comprehensive multi-omics analysis-including bulk and single-cell transcriptomics and epigenomics-of the lateral ventricle choroid plexus across postnatal and adult stages in mice and rats. We identified changes in the choroid plexus cellular composition and gene expression profiles, including early and progressive activation of several immune related genes in main cell types from early postnatal to young adult stage. Epithelial cells exhibited developmental remodeling over time, characterized by distinct gene expression programs, locus-specific changes in chromatin accessibility, and cellular diversity. In addition, we uncovered an epithelial cell population characterized by a distinct transcriptional signature. Our study offers a comprehensive atlas of transcriptional activity and chromatin accessibility in choroid plexus cells, providing a valuable resource to guide future research.

Article.Title: Organization of retrosplenial cortex projections at the single-neuron level
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Jiang T.; Gong H.; Li A.; Li X.; Ren M.
Article.Abstract: The retrosplenial cortex (RSP) supports spatial cognition, memory, and brain-wide information integration, yet its output architecture remains poorly resolved at single-neuron resolution. Using fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography (fMOST), we reconstruct sparsely labeled neurons sampled predominantly from the anterior RSP across the whole brain. We find three major projection routes-cortical-restricted (CR), thalamic-restricted (TR), and thalamic-brainstem collateral (TBC)-and classify neurons into ten projection subtypes with distinct target-selective profiles. Somatic location and volumetric features are associated with axonal projection patterns. TR-pattern neurons show subregion-dependent thalamic targeting, whereas TBC-pattern neurons display greater axonal complexity and subtype-specific collateralization toward thalamic, midbrain, and hindbrain targets. Bilaterally projecting neurons across distinct projection patterns show cross-network projection modes with an overall ipsilateral preference and laminar-specific commissural architectures. Together, these findings provide a single-neuron anatomical map of RSP cortical, thalamic, and cortico-subcortical output patterns and a framework for examining distributed information processing across brain-wide networks.

Article.Title: Pharmacological blockade of p65 palmitoylation modulates NF-κB transcriptional activity
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Hu L.; Sun L.; Che J.; Yates J.; Park J.; Wu X.
Article.Abstract: Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) regulates inflammation and immunity and is frequently dysregulated in autoimmune diseases, inflammatory disorders, and cancers. Cytokines and pathogens activate NF-κB transcription factors, and nutrients and metabolites, including fatty acids, also modulate its activation, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we report that RelA (p65), a major component of the NF-κB transcription complex, is autopalmitoylated at cysteine 197 and 206. Palmitoylation of p65 enhances its nuclear localization and p65-p50 complex formation, thereby increasing NF-κB transcriptional activities. We further show that licochalcone D, a small-molecule anti-inflammatory compound, directly inhibits RelA/p65 autopalmitoylation, suggesting it may act through an additional mechanism. These results indicate that fatty acid metabolism can directly regulate NF-κB activity through p65 palmitoylation and suggest that targeting p65 autopalmitoylation may be a therapeutic strategy for diseases with dysregulated NF-κB signaling.

Article.Title: BATF condensation drives gastric cancer metastasis via chromatin association and transcriptional regulation
Article.Authors: Feng T.; Deng Z.; Deng K.; Zhang L.; Yang L.; Lu Y.; Chen H.; Kerr D.; Yao X.; Yang J.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: While liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is understood to be relevant with various types of cancers, the relationship between LLPS and gastric cancer (GC) remains ambiguous. In this study, we demonstrate that the basic leucine zipper ATF-like transcription factor (BATF) shows increased DNA-binding activity and expression in GC tissues and cell lines, based on assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analyses. Additionally, in GC cells, BATF forms droplet-like nuclear condensates. Using combined approaches of chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq), ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq, we find that BATF condensation promotes its binding to the TM4SF1 promoter and enhancer regions, thereby regulating TM4SF1 transcription and prompting the TM4SF1-driven formation of focal adhesions and GC metastasis. Thus, we unveil a role for BATF LLPS in GC metastasis through its modulation of chromatin association and transcriptional regulation, highlighting the relevance of LLPS to GC progression and potential treatment approaches.

Article.Title: Optogenetic reduction of theta oscillations induces remapping of time cells without memory impairment
Article.Authors: Yong H.; Chang H.; Brandon M.
Article.Abstract: In a delayed alternation spatial working memory task, hippocampal time cells fire during specific moments of the delay period to form a sequential representation of the entire delay interval. The causal relationship between these sequences and working memory remains unclear. Similarly, hippocampal theta oscillations are thought to support working memory, primarily through the generation of time cell sequences. To causally examine these relationships, we optogenetically silence the medial septal GABAergic theta-generating circuit during the delay portion of a delayed spatial alternation task. With hippocampal theta oscillations substantially reduced, many time cells exhibit remapping, and new time cells are recruited. Despite partial remapping of time cell sequences, behavioral performance remains intact and trajectory-specific coding is preserved, suggesting that task-relevant information remains available under theta disruption.

Article.Title: Structural remodeling and activation of the hdeAB and proVWX operons in response to pH and salt stress
Article.Authors: Ge P.; Rashid F.; Gaarthuis L.; Cajili M.; Tan M.; Pang B.; Schnetz K.; Dame R.
Article.Abstract: Escherichia coli is highly sensitive to acid and osmotic stress but adapts by modulating the expression of stress-responsive genes. Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in DNA organization and sensing environmental changes. The histone-like nucleoid structuring protein H-NS is an NAP acting as a global regulator of stress genes. H-NS may alter local chromatin structure to modulate the expression of such genes in response to environmental stress. The H-NS homolog suppressor of td phenotype A (StpA) co-regulates several target genes, but its role is poorly defined. To investigate the regulatory interplay between these two proteins, we examined transcription, DNA binding, and chromatin structure at two regulated operons, hdeAB and proVWX, in E. coli following exposure to acid and salt shock. Our results show that H-NS senses pH and osmotic cues to remodel chromatin and relieve repression, while StpA-in part-compensates for H-NS loss, particularly at proVWX, highlighting a coordinated regulatory network.

Article.Title: Programmed DNA breaks drive chromatin reconfiguration and facilitate transcriptional potentiation at neuronal early response genes
Article.Authors: Heady L.; Fenelon K.; Delint-Ramirez I.; Rueda R.; Segev A.; Morton K.; Briseno S.; Madabhushi R.
Article.Abstract: Neuronal activity causes topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2B) to form DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within the promoters of early response genes (ERGs), such as Fos and Npas4. Despite their purported risk, recurrent DSB cycles progressively potentiate ERG induction in mouse cortical neurons and HEK293T cells, evoking the effects of transcriptional memory. Potentiated ERG inducibility following recurrent DSBs persists through intervening cell cycles, occurs even when DNA repair is likely mutagenic, and correlates with a substantial loss of cis- and a gain of trans-, chromosomal interactions with ERG promoters. Together, these results reveal how activity-induced DSBs impact transcription by regulating chromatin dynamics at ERG promoters.

Article.Title: TIA1 is required for microglial activation in tauopathy
Article.Authors: Webber C.; van der Spek S.; Cruz A.; Puri S.; Shao Y.; Zhang C.; Aw J.; Papadimitriou G.; Roberts R.; Jiang K.; Tran T.; Zhang L.; Taylor A.; Wang Z.; Tobunluepop K.; Ellini M.; Porter J.; Sotiropoulos I.; Emili A.; Silva J.; Li H.; Wolozin B.
Article.Abstract: The RNA-binding protein T cell intracellular antigen-1 (TIA1) regulates cellular stress responses and tau pathology, key contributors to the pathophysiology of tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). TIA1 acts in peripheral monocytes to inhibit inflammation, but its function in central microglia, critical to neuroinflammation and disease progression, remains unknown. Proteomic analyses show TIA1 interaction with the microglial proteins C1Q, previously implicated in microglial activation. Article.Title: Proline transporters coordinate immune activation and regenerative capacity after injury in plants
Article.Authors: Xu D.; Belew Z.; Ferreira Dias N.; Wang L.; Zhang A.; Stephanie Chen Y.; Newton C.; Kong F.; Zheng Y.; Yao Y.; Brewer M.; Pereira Lima Teixeira P.; Nour Eldin Auis H.; Xu D.; Yang L.
Article.Abstract: Effective survival after injury requires the precise coordination of immune activation and tissue regeneration, yet the molecular mechanisms balancing these opposing processes remain poorly understood. Here, we identify proline transporters as key regulators of this trade-off in plants. Mechanistically, a ProT3-CPK1 complex modulates wound-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS), sustaining a ROS level that restricts de novo root regeneration (DNRR) after wounding. Article.Title: ALKBH8 promotes acute myeloid leukemia progression by coupling codon-dependent translation elongation to mRNA stability
Article.Authors: Li S.; Hong Y.; Deng S.; Wu X.; Jia Z.; Liu Y.; Liu Y.; Wu G.; Chen Y.; Wu A.; Gao X.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: Dysregulated mRNA translation is a critical driver of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) progression. ALKBH8 is required for the proliferation and leukemogenic capacity of human and murine AML cells in vitro and in vivo. Article.Title: AREG mediates transient hepatocellular carcinoma resistance to receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors
Article.Authors: Lou L.; Feng H.; Zhang X.; Wang H.; Fan Y.; Tao Y.; Zhang Z.; Lin C.; Sun Y.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Lenvatinib is a first-line therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Emerging studies suggest resistance evolves through dynamic multi-step processes. Here, using multi-timepoint and multi-omics sampling, we characterized the trajectory of lenvatinib resistance in HCC cells and identified three adaptive states marked by state transitions. Multi-omics analyses and functional validation identified amphiregulin (AREG) as a key transient mediator of resistance in our models. AREG is a sufficient and dominant ligand to promote cell survival through epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) activation. Pharmacological inhibition of the AREG-EGFR axis specifically targeted early-resistant cells. Furthermore, AREG upregulation was validated in additional replicate experiments and another HCC cell line. Mechanistically, a focal deletion on chromosome 3p may contribute to NF-κB activation and AREG expression. This study delineates a recurrent yet transient adaptive mechanism and suggests new therapeutic opportunities-such as combination therapies targeting transient resistance mechanisms-to prevent or overcome drug resistance.

Article.Title: Hexokinase-2 moonlights as a suppressor of STING-mediated innate immunity
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Li F.; Gao M.; Ma J.; Wang S.; Xiao B.; Zhong B.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic enzymes are increasingly recognized for "moonlighting" functions beyond their primary metabolic roles. While such non-canonical activities are well characterized in cancer biology, their roles in innate immunity remain poorly defined. Here, we show that Hexokinase II (HK2), a rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, suppresses STING-mediated innate immune responses independently of its enzymatic activity. Upon STING activation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) trigger the dissociation of HK2 from the mitochondria to the cytosol. Cytosolic HK2 then interacts with STING, impeding its oligomerization and translocation to the Golgi apparatus, thereby dampening downstream immune signaling. Notably, HK-TAT, a peptide that induces HK2 release from the mitochondria, effectively inhibits STING-dependent immune activation and ameliorates disease phenotypes in STING-driven autoimmune mouse models. Our findings highlight the moonlighting role of HK2 as a negative regulator of STING signaling and provide a potential therapeutic approach for treating autoimmune diseases driven by STING dysregulation.

Article.Authors: Gaevert J.; Mayer-Blackwell K.; Pogorelyy M.; Schattgen S.; Kirk A.; Duan S.; Van de Velde L.; Souquette A.; Awad W.; St. James D.; Clark N.; Duque D.; Allen E.; Lythe G.; Molina-Paris C.; Crawford J.; Fiore-Gartland A.; Bradley P.; Minervina A.; Thomas P.

Article.Title: E2 displacement of CIP2A from TOPBP1 activates the DNA damage response during papillomavirus life cycles

Article.Title: BCLAF1 and responses to RAG-induced DNA breaks enforce pre-B cell checkpoint
Article.Authors: Schmidt H.; Yang W.; Crowley S.; White L.; Russell L.; Zhang R.; Tran T.; Kolicheski A.; Taylor S.; Chen B.; Bednarski J.
Article.Abstract: During early B cell development, pre-B cells encounter signaling from pre-B cell receptor (pre-BCR) and DNA damage responses (DDR) triggered by RAG-induced DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs) generated during immunoglobulin light chain (Igl) recombination. These signals drive cooperative and antagonistic programs to promote pre-B cell checkpoint. Here, we show in vivo that pre-B cells transition between distinct subpopulations predominated by either pre-BCR or RAG DSB-induced DDR signals. Article.Authors: Wang J.; Jiang W.; Yan P.; Huang D.; Chen L.; Hou T.; Asara J.; Inuzuka H.; Toker A.; Wei W.
Article.Abstract: AKT hyperactivation is a hallmark of many human cancers and contributes to poor clinical outcomes, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Article.Title: Baseline microbial ecology encodes probiotic responsiveness through distinct metabolic and network configurations
Article.Authors: Li J.; Özkurt A.; Baertschi I.; Wang J.; Aeschlimann L.; Goepfert C.; Misselwitz B.; Sokollik C.; Yilmaz B.
Article.Abstract: Probiotic efficacy in inflammatory bowel disease varies widely between individuals, and the sources of that variability remain poorly understood. D-lactate is a microbiota-derived metabolite that accumulates during intestinal inflammation and is associated with epithelial barrier dysfunction, which motivated our use of a consortium selected to contribute none of it. Here we show that its benefit is not an intrinsic property of the administered strains but is determined by the pre-existing ecological state of the recipient microbiome. Across three independent mouse resources, preventive administration reduced disease severity and histopathological damage only where baseline communities carried higher diversity and more complex co-occurrence architecture; in those animals the consortium preserved community structure and metabolic output, restoring disease-disrupted metabolites, and selectively raising butyrate and propionate. Article.Title: RAStoERK: A reference interaction atlas for insights into signaling and disease
Article.Authors: Vucak G.; Didusch S.; Cannizzaro L.; Santiago A.; Hartl M.; Menche J.; Baccarini M.
Article.Abstract: The RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway has been extensively studied for its roles in physiology and disease, yet a systems-level view of its interplay with the broader cellular context is lacking, limiting insight into paralog-specific roles, mutation-driven rewiring, and cross-pathway integration. To address this, we simultaneously mapped the interactomes of all pathway components and their activating and inactivating mutations, identifying 2,500 high-confidence interactors, 88% of which previously unreported, and generating a high-confidence, comprehensive reference map of the pathway in resting and activated states. Dataset exploration uncovers paralog- and mutation-specific interaction signatures and pathway-level crosstalk, including previously unknown connections to mRNA metabolism and WNT signaling. Article.Title: Mechanisms of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 modulation by amphetamines and lobeline
Article.Authors: Wu D.; Liu C.; Wang H.; Chi C.; Wang Y.; Zhang W.; Wang X.; Jiang D.
Article.Abstract: Amphetamine-type stimulants (ATSs) disrupt the brain monoaminergic system and strongly stimulate motivation, movement, and addiction. Here, we report the cryo-EM structures of human VMAT2 in complex with four ATSs (AMPH, METH, MDMA, and MDA) and the inhibitor lobeline, revealing the molecular mechanisms underlying ATS recognition and modulation. ATSs mimic monoamines and occupy the substrate-binding site of VMAT2, indicating that ATSs function as substrates and thus redistribute the vesicular monoamine pools to the cytosolic pools. Lobeline adopts an unexpected dual-binding mode and locks VMAT2 in a lumen-facing conformation, inhibiting monoamine and ATS uptake. Our dopamine release assay revealed that lobeline regulates AMPH-induced dopamine release by modulating both VMAT2 and DAT. This study provides important mechanistic insights into VMAT2 modulation by amphetamines and lobeline.

Article.Authors: Wang C.; Xie J.; Shen Z.; Ehrmann J.; Yu C.; Fang M.; Wu H.; Fu T.
Article.Abstract: Like mammalian nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain receptors (NLRs), bacterial NLR-like proteins mediate antiviral defense. In the resting state, ATP-bound Avs5 is monomeric and subsequently forms a SIR2-mediated dimer that likely represents an intermediate in a stepwise activation pathway. Upon activation, ATP-dependent conformational remodeling of the NBD promotes conversion of these dimers into active filaments. Structure-guided mutagenesis, biochemical assays, and functional analyses show that filament assembly is required for efficient NAD+ hydrolysis and antiphage defense. These findings reveal an effector-driven activation mechanism and extend the principles by which NLR proteins couple higher-order assembly to immune defense across domains of life.

Article.Title: Role of Leu and Val synthesis in sensing mitochondrial nutrient and energy availability
Article.Authors: Phan J.; Gay L.; Dokládal L.; De Virgilio C.; Salcedo L.; Tha S.; Wandvik C.; Babst M.
Article.Abstract: How cells integrate nutrient availability to coordinate metabolism and growth remains poorly understood. Here, we identify branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) synthesis as a metabolic sensing system linking mitochondrial activity to translational and transcriptional control. Reduced Val synthesis activates Gcn2, whereas reduced Leu synthesis inhibits TORC1, together decreasing translation efficiency and restricting growth. Thus, BCAA synthesis couples mitochondrial anabolic capacity to Gcn2 and TORC1 activity and, through translational control of transcription factor abundance, shapes cellular metabolism.

Article.Authors: Walker S.; van der Veeken J.; Rudensky A.; Pritykin Y.
Article.Abstract: T cells differentiate into functionally distinct subsets in response to pathogens, yet essential immune functions such as self-renewal, expansion, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity are common to multiple subsets and therefore must be programmed via shared regulatory mechanisms. Article.Authors: Zeng W.; Liu W.; Caudal A.; Liu L.; Kong X.; Zhu W.; Kim H.; Lee A.; Alamana C.; Melesio J.; Cao X.; Howell K.; Chen K.; Pang P.; Day J.; Wu J.

Article.Authors: Striepen J.; Culibrk L.; Dananberg A.; Rozowsky J.; Petljak M.; Maciejowski J.

We also provide the first causal evidence that endogenous APOBEC3A generates the indel signature InD9a, linking it to uracil excision following cytosine deamination. In this study, we demonstrated that exercise-induced exerkine clusterin mediates the pro-regenerative effects of running plasma on cardiac repair and cardiomyocyte proliferation following myocardial infarction (MI). Cardiac-specific Clu knockout attenuated, whereas clusterin overexpression enhanced, post-MI cardiac regeneration. Recombinant clusterin administration promoted heart regeneration in adult mice after MI. Mechanistically, clusterin activated NF-κB via proteasome-dependent IκBα degradation through direct binding with IκBα. Furthermore, the liver was identified as the major source of exercise-induced circulating clusterin; hepatocyte-specific Clu knockdown abolished the stimulatory effect of exercise plasma on cardiac regeneration. This study reveals a liver-heart crosstalk mechanism by which exercise-induced clusterin promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation, positioning clusterin as a potential therapeutic target for post-MI heart failure.

Article.Title: Pot1a maintains mesenchymal stem cell niche function to support hematopoietic stem cells
Article.Authors: Esaki Y.; Hosokawa K.; Yao H.; Adachi S.; Baba Y.; Arai F.
Article.Abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) maintain their function through interactions with niche cells in the bone marrow. We previously demonstrated that protection of telomeres 1a (Pot1a), a shelterin component, maintains HSCs and neuron-glial antigen 2-expressing (NG2+) mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) by suppressing DNA damage response (DDR) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. However, the role of Pot1a in leptin receptor-expressing (LepR+) MSCs, a primary HSC niche component, remains unclear. LepR-specific Pot1a knockout mice showed decreased LepR+ MSC numbers, increased DDR and ROS production, reduced HSC quiescence, and impaired long-term hematopoietic reconstitution. In contrast, cell-permeable Pot1a enhanced the hematopoietic-supporting function of LepR+ MSCs. Pot1a deficiency reduced pleiotrophin (Ptn) expression, whereas Pot1a overexpression increased its expression. These findings suggest that Pot1a preserves LepR+ MSC function by limiting stress-associated changes, maintaining MSC numbers, and regulating hematopoietic-supportive factor expression, including PTN.

Article.Title: A competitive PDLIM1-USP14 axis destabilizes ACTN4 to disturb the invasive homeostasis of trophoblast in preeclampsia
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Zhang X.; Chen R.; Xiang Y.; Gong E.; Tong H.; Sun X.; Yin H.; Qi H.
Article.Abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by insufficient extravillous trophoblast (EVT) invasion, but the cytoskeletal mechanisms restraining EVT motility remain unclear. TMT-based placental proteomics identified the cytoskeletal adaptor PDLIM1 as markedly upregulated in PE. In primary trophoblasts and cell lines, PDLIM1 depletion remodeled the actin cytoskeleton and enhanced migration and invasion, whereas trophoblast-restricted Pdlim1 overexpression impaired trophoblast invasion and placental development in mice. Mechanistically, PDLIM1 bounds the rod domain of α-actinin-4 (ACTN4) and competitively displaced USP14, limiting ACTN4 deubiquitination and shifting ACTN4 toward RNF38-associated K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Importantly, placenta-targeted chondroitin sulfate A-binding nanoparticles delivering Pdlim1 short hairpin RNA (shRNA) alleviated PE-like maternal and fetal phenotypes in mice. Collectively, these findings define a PDLIM1-USP14-ACTN4 proteostatic axis controlling trophoblast invasive homeostasis and identify PDLIM1 as a potential therapeutic target in PE.

Article.Title: Arbitrium crosstalk enables shared signaling among phages
Article.Authors: Lomeli-Ortega C.; Balcázar J.
Article.Abstract: The arbitrium system has transformed our understanding of phage biology by demonstrating that temperate phages communicate through extracellular peptides to coordinate lysis-lysogeny decisions. Initially considered a highly specific signaling pathway restricted to individual phage lineages, arbitrium communication has now been shown to extend beyond lineage boundaries in some phage systems. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of the molecular basis of arbitrium signaling, the structural determinants of peptide-receptor specificity, and the potential ecological and evolutionary consequences of inter-phage communication. We suggest that arbitrium crosstalk may shape phage ecology by mediating competitive and potentially cooperative interactions within shared signaling environments. We also discuss its potential uses in engineered phage systems, synthetic biology, and microbiome engineering. Collectively, the available evidence broadens the concept of viral communication beyond lineage-specific signaling, while the ecological significance and practical applications of arbitrium crosstalk remain to be established.

Article.Title: Cysteine promotes islet α-cell glucagon secretion by limiting oxidative inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels
Article.Authors: Behera S.; Dickerson M.; Dadi P.; Dobson J.; Gibson S.; Peachee S.; Kim R.; Agarwal S.; Lucerne A.; Stiadle B.; Nallagatla S.; Dean E.; Jacobson D.
Article.Abstract: Cysteine serves as a robust α-cell secretagogue. While diabetes alters both plasma cysteine and glucagon levels, the mechanisms of α-cell cysteine action remain unclear. Here, we identified cysteine as a key regulator of islet glucagon secretion through redox control of α-cell electrical excitability. Short-term cysteine depletion markedly suppressed hypoglycemia-stimulated glucagon secretion from both human and mouse islets. Moreover, cysteine-depleted islets showed reduced hypoglycemia-stimulated α-cell calcium (Ca2+) influx. Islet glucagon secretion and α-cell Ca2+ influx rapidly normalized following cysteine restoration. Cysteine depletion also reduced α-cell voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV) conductance and action potential amplitude. Importantly, reducing agents restored NaV currents and glucose control of α-cell Ca2+ handling in islets without cysteine. Together, these findings identify reductive amplification of NaV channels as a key mechanism required for hypoglycemia-stimulated glucagon secretion, highlighting cysteine as a critical regulator of α-cell redox state, electrical excitability, and glucagon secretion.

Article.Title: Fatigue links sociodemographic risk to pain intensity and spread in 2 surgical cohorts
Article.Authors: Sun M.; Ansari B.; Clauw D.; Harris R.; Sluka K.; Kaplan C.; Brummet C.; Lindquist M.; Wager T.; N/A N/A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Why some surgical patients develop pain that extends beyond the original site of injury while others do not remains poorly understood. The recently proposed Risk of Pain Spread (ROPS) framework integrates multiple psychosocial risk factors associated with widespread pain, but its generalizability to surgical populations has not been established. Using 2 large presurgical cohorts of participants undergoing total knee arthroplasty or thoracic surgery, we evaluated the generalizability of the ROPS framework and examined relationships among psychosocial and sociodemographic factors, surgical-site pain, nonsurgical-site pain, and widespread pain using complementary latent-variable, regression, Bayesian network, and mediation analyses. Across cohorts and analytical approaches, fatigue emerged as the most consistent correlate of pain outcomes, independent of other measured risk factors. Fatigue also occupied a central position within the conditional dependency structure of psychosocial and pain variables and accounted for substantial shared variance linking sleep disturbance, depressive symptoms, neuroticism, adverse childhood experiences, and socioeconomic disadvantage with pain intensity. Nonsurgical-site pain consistently occupied a position linking pain intensity with widespread pain across complementary analyses. Together, these findings externally validate the ROPS framework in clinically relevant surgical populations and identify fatigue as a central correlate linking biopsychosocial vulnerability with pain burden.

Article.Title: Astrocyte Orai1 signaling promotes spinal excitatory synaptic potentiation and neuropathic pain after nerve injury in male mice
Article.Authors: Tsujikawa S.; Shetti A.; Grant R.; Novakovic M.; Prakriya M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neuropathic pain after peripheral nerve injury is a multifactorial condition mediated partly by inflammation in the spinal cord that results in potentiation of excitatory synaptic transmission in nociceptive circuits. Glial cells including astrocytes are key mediators of the underlying inflammation, but the signaling checkpoints that regulate astrocyte-driven spinal cord inflammation and sensitization of nociceptive circuits are not well understood. Here, we identify Orai1-mediated store-operated Ca 2+ entry (SOCE) as an important regulator of spinal astrocyte cytokine production, metabolic reprogramming, and pain hypersensitivity in mice. Conditional deletion of Orai1 in astrocytes attenuated mechanical allodynia after nerve injury in male but not female mice, despite comparable SOCE suppression in both sexes. Orai1 deficiency also attenuated production of proinflammatory cytokines after SOCE activation, including TNFα, IL-6, and IL-33, both in vivo and in vitro. Electrophysiological recordings revealed that astrocyte Orai1 deletion prevented injury-induced enhancement of glutamatergic synaptic transmission in dorsal horn neurons, linking astrocytic Ca 2+ signaling to central sensitization. Metabolomic profiling showed that Orai1 loss disrupted glycolysis and TCA cycle intermediates while promoting accumulation of immunomodulatory metabolites such as itaconate, consistent with a less inflammatory astrocyte metabolic state. These findings identify Orai1 channels as integrators of astrocyte Ca 2+ signaling, immunometabolism, and excitatory synaptic potentiation after nerve injury, and identify a sexually dimorphic astrocyte mechanism governing neuropathic pain pathogenesis. Targeting astrocyte Orai1 channels may provide a selective therapeutic strategy for male-predominant chronic pain.

Article.Title: Mineralocorticoid receptor signaling reduces somatostatin expression in developing sensory neurons and drives neonatal pain after early-life stress
Article.Authors: Eid F.; Serafin E.; Muniz M.; Woodke S.; Booher J.; Zhang J.; Baccei M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Early-life stress (ELS) causes pain hypersensitivity in neonatal mice and alters the transcriptional profile of the immature dorsal root ganglia (DRG), highlighted by a marked reduction in the expression of a neuropeptide, somatostatin (Sst), which is known to constitutively suppress peripheral nociceptive transmission during adulthood. However, the mechanisms that drive plasticity in gene expression within the developing DRG and neonatal pain after ELS remain unclear. Here, we investigated the degree to which ELS-induced neonatal pain was mediated by corticosterone signaling onto sensory neurons and potential changes in peripheral Sst transmission. The conditional knockout of the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR), but not the glucocorticoid receptor, from immature DRG neurons prevented ELS-evoked neonatal pain. In contrast, the systemic administration of the selective MR antagonist eplerenone failed to acutely influence pain after ELS, thus suggesting that MR activation enhances pain during the neonatal period via canonical effects on gene transcription. Meanwhile, hind paw injection of the Sst receptor antagonist cyclo-somatostatin increased spontaneous nocifensive behaviors in control pups, but not in pups previously subjected to ELS, raising the possibility that a disruption in tonic antinociception mediated by peripheral Sst contributes to neonatal pain after ELS. Furthermore, administration of the peripherally restricted Sst analog octreotide reversed noxious cold and pressure hypersensitivity in neonatal mice after ELS. Finally, the selective deletion of MR from sensory neurons prevented the ELS-induced decrease in Sst expression. Collectively, these results provide novel mechanistic insight into the effects of chronic early-life adversity on nociceptive processing in the developing nervous system.

Article.Title: Targeting GPR183 to reduce peripheral sensitization: evidence from rodent and human tissue analyses
Article.Authors: Oberkrom K.; Braden K.; Li E.; Shah S.; Maric D.; Mannes A.; Pacifico P.; Jayaraj N.; Arnatt C.; Menichella D.; Sapio M.; Salvemini D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Peripheral sensitization is a key process in the development of painful inflammatory conditions, driven in part by immune-cell mediator release following tissue injury. The G protein–coupled receptor, GPR183, predominantly expressed on immune cells, regulates their migration, positioning, and mediator production. However, its role in peripheral sensitization and the specific immune cells involved remains insufficiently understood. In rats, intraplantar injection of 7α,25-dihydroxycholesterol (7α,25-OHC), the most potent endogenous GPR183 ligand, produced long-lasting nociception that was prevented by the selective GPR183 antagonist SAE-14. As GPR183 activates extracellular signal-regulated kinase signaling, which influences pain pathways including nitric oxide synthase (NOS) activity and NO formation, we used NOS inhibitors and knockout animals to test the contribution of inducible and neuronal NOS isoforms to 7α,25-OHC-induced sensitization. We found that both isoforms influence this response, independent of cyclooxygenases. In a well-characterized rat incisional injury model, GPR183 protein expression increased in injured paw tissue, and SAE-14 reversed hypersensitivity. Meta-analysis of human postsurgical skin samples similarly showed elevated GPR183 expression and transcriptional changes favoring 7α,25-OHC production after injury. We identified macrophages, Langerhans cells (LCs), and T cells as the principal GPR183 -expressing cell types in human skin. Ablation of LCs and removal of mature B and T cells revealed that 7α,25-OHC-evoked hypersensitivity does not depend on these cell types, leaving GPR183 + macrophages as the most likely drivers of GPR183-induced hypersensitivity. Overall, our findings define the cellular and molecular pathways linking GPR183 to peripheral sensitization and highlight GPR183 antagonism as a promising strategy for pain management.

Article.Title: Pain education in Brazilian medical schools: a national curriculum analysis
Article.Authors: Silva T.; Domingues F.; Medeiros D.; Gandolfi A.; Reis F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide, yet undergraduate medical education remains insufficient to prepare future physicians for its assessment and management. The International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) has proposed a competency-based curriculum framework; however, its implementation in Brazilian medical education is unclear. The aim of this study was to evaluate the availability of pain education in Brazilian medical schools and assess its alignment with the IASP Curriculum Outline on Pain for Medicine. We conducted a national cross-sectional documentary analysis of all medical schools registered in the Brazilian Ministry of Education database between May 2024 and December 2025. Institutional websites were systematically screened for publicly available curricular documentation, and data were independently extracted by 2 reviewers. Variables included the presence of pain-related content, existence of a dedicated pain course, course workload, timing within the curriculum, and type of offering. Among 447 identified schools, 277 (62.0%) provided accessible curricular information. Only 47 institutions (16.9%) offered a stand-alone pain course, and 29 had detailed syllabi for item-level analysis. Most analyzed courses were mandatory and delivered in the early years of training. Alignment with IASP competencies was incomplete across all domains, with greater coverage of neurobiological and pharmacological content and limited inclusion of pain assessment and measurement, psychosocial and behavioral management, public health, ethics, and care for special populations. Pain education in Brazil is inconsistently structured and only partially aligned with international recommendations, indicating the need of comprehensive, competency-based curricular reform.

Article.Title: The analgesic efficacy of opioids in different application modalities for the treatment of breakthrough cancer pain—a systematic review with network meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Dinges H.; Thiedmann S.; Weyland J.; Volberg C.; Schmitt F.; Wulf H.; Schubert A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Breakthrough cancer pain episodes often require oral immediate release opioids or parenteral opioid treatment. Different formulations and application modalities have been approved for this condition. This study aimed to identify the most effective of the available substances and applications to treat breakthrough cancer pain. We conducted a comprehensive systematic review with network meta-analysis. The database search included MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible were randomized controlled trials comparing opioids and application modalities for the treatment of breakthrough cancer pain episodes. Primary end points were the pain intensity difference (PID) at 15 and 30 minutes. Secondary end points were side effects and adverse events, as well as dichotomous outcomes of treatment success. Frequentist network meta-analysis was conducted using the package netmeta in R. From 5133 records initially identified by the literature review, 23 studies were eligible for quantitative analysis. Compared with placebo, the most effective interventions at 15 minutes (PID) were intravenous or subcutaneous applications of morphine, and intranasal fentanyl or sublingual fentanyl tablets. After 30 minutes (PID), the most effective interventions were still subcutaneous and intravenous morphine, but also sublingual fentanyl tablets. Intranasal fentanyl spray was equally effective as buccal and other transmucosal applications by 30 minutes. The quality of evidence on the topic is poor as most studies are phase III trials for drug approval. The risk of publication bias is therefore high. Sublingual fentanyl tablets were as effective as intravenous or subcutaneous morphine and are a practical modality for self-administration.

Article.Title: Evoked alpha oscillatory activity is suppressed by prolonged elbow pain and modulated by repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
Article.Authors: Chowdhury N.; Hoddinott J.; Chang W.; Cheng D.; Manivasagan N.; Schabrun S.; Seminowicz D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Alpha-band oscillatory activity, assessed using electroencephalography (EEG), is among the most widely studied neurophysiological markers of pain. However, the literature has focused predominantly on resting-state measures, leaving unclear whether pain also alters evoked alpha-band dynamics, measured via cortical perturbation using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Here, we examined whether prolonged pain alters TMS-evoked alpha event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) and intertrial coherence (ITC), reflecting cortical reactivity and phase consistency, and whether 10-Hz repetitive TMS (rTMS) modulates these responses. We performed a secondary analysis on 2 previous experiments, which used nerve growth factor (NGF) injection to induce prolonged elbow muscle pain. In experiment 1, participants underwent primary motor cortex (M1) TMS-EEG at baseline (day 0) pre-NGF injection and day 2 (peak pain) and day 7 (pain resolution) post-injection. In experiment 2, M1-TMS-EEG was assessed on day 0 before NGF injection and again on day 4 after injection, with active or sham 10-Hz rTMS delivered to M1 between these assessments. In experiment 1, M1 TMS-EEG showed reductions in alpha ERSP ( P = 0.014) and alpha ITC ( P = 0.041) from day 0 to day 2. In experiment 2, active rTMS produced a more positive pre-to-post change in alpha ERSP ( P = 0.006) relative to sham but did not alter alpha ITC ( P = 0.804). Our findings suggest that prolonged experimental pain is associated with diminished evoked alpha oscillatory activity, whereas high-frequency rTMS modulates this activity in the positive direction. These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked alpha metrics warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of pain state and response to neuromodulation.

Article.Title: Beyond intensity: pain distribution shapes healthcare- and treatment-seeking beliefs in individuals with and without clinical pain
Article.Authors: Frankenstein T.; Intert S.; Szikszay T.; Katra M.; Elsner B.; Coghill R.; Luedtke K.; Adamczyk W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain is commonly described in sensory terms, yet its spatial characteristics are rarely quantified. We investigated whether lay beliefs about pain distribution influence theoretical decisions to seek care and treatment preferences. In a cross-sectional survey (N = 503; 49% reporting pain), participants completed thought experiments in which both visually presented pain distribution patterns (small, moderate, or large) and pain intensity (Numerical Rating Scale scores: 2, 5, 8/10) were systematically varied. For each scenario, they rated the likelihood of (1) seeking professional help (LoSH) and (2) taking analgesic medication (LoTM) on 0 to 100 scale. Participants also completed a spatial–intensity trade-off task, in which they chose between a fixed 20% reduction in intensity and variable reductions in pain distribution (20%-80%). A reversed version contrasted a fixed 80% reduction in pain distribution with variable reductions in pain intensity. LoSH and LoTM increased significantly with greater pain distribution ( P < 0.001), mirroring the gradient observed for pain intensity. In the spatial–intensity trade-off task, participants' choice followed a sigmoid-like function ( P < 0.001): 1% reduction in intensity was treated as equivalent to approximately a 3% reduction in distribution, indicating a systematic valuation of pain distribution. This ratio was lower in individuals experiencing pain compared with pain-free individuals. Moreover, 61% reported that pain distribution should be routinely considered in pain management alongside intensity. Results suggest that pain distribution is not merely a trivial descriptor, but a meaningful determinant of healthcare-related decision-making beliefs. Incorporating spatial metrics into clinical assessment and research may better capture how individuals implicitly evaluate pain severity.

Article.Title: A mMono-Bac1.0 system for recombinant adeno-associated virus vectors with higher flexibility, throughput and yield
Article.Authors: Wang P.; Qi Y.; Han D.; Deng J.; Zhu Z.; Chen P.; Zhu X.; Liu L.; Ren Q.; Qiu Y.; Wang J.; Li C.; Liu J.; Wu Y.; Liu Q.; Jia F.; Wang H.; Wen P.; Xu F.
Article.Abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) holds immense promise for therapeutic applications, but high production costs limit its widespread clinical use, underscoring the urgent need for manufacturing breakthroughs. Here, we establish a modular Mono-Bac system with the p24 -NanoLuciferase (Nluc) reporter Bacmid for rAAV production, named mMono-Bac1.0, enhancing manufacturing flexibility, throughput and yield simultaneously. The system introduces two key technology to the pFD/Cap-(ITR-GOI)-Rep transfer vector-based Mono-Bac framework. First, a modular pGB-AAV Donor construction strategy enables one-step all-in-one AAV transfer vector assembly and effortless switching of capsids or GOIs, thus facilitating high-throughput combinatorial production. Second, an engineered p24 -Nluc Bacmid enables rapid (<5 min) quantification of infectious recombinant baculovirus (rBV) titers and real-time monitoring of Nluc activity in culture supernatants to determine the optimal harvest point (log RLU ~ 6.5), thereby maximizing rAAV yield. This system has the potential to advance baculovirus expression vector (BEV)-based rAAV manufacturing into a data-driven era, supporting efficient industrial-scale production.
