Article.Title: Leptin-Driven Distinct Transcriptional Reprogramming in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer: Implications for Racial Disparities
Article.Authors: Sudan S.; Sharma A.; Anand S.; Challagundla L.; Kaur J.; Craft B.; Singh A.; Singh S.
Article.Abstract: Obesity is an established risk factor for breast cancer (BC), and leptin, an adipocyte-derived hormone, may link obesity to tumor progression. However, the role of leptin in the molecular heterogeneity of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), particularly across racial groups, remains unclear. Here, we examined circulating leptin levels in Black and White women with and without BC and characterized leptin-induced transcriptional changes in TNBC cell lines of White and Black racial backgrounds using RNA sequencing. Functional enrichment analyses were performed using Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway annotations, and clinical relevance was assessed using publicly available datasets. Circulating leptin levels were significantly elevated in women with BC and were relatively higher in Black than White women and associated with increased odds of luminal A and TNBC diagnoses. Several leptin-responsive genes showed concordant expression in clinical specimens and exhibited race- and subtype- associated differences and prognostic significance. Collectively, these findings identify distinct, context-dependent leptin-responsive transcriptional programs in TNBC and provide insight into their potential contributions to tumor heterogeneity and breast cancer disparities.

Article.Title: Beyond Sequence Optimization in Enzyme Engineering: Protein Maturation and Operational Stability
Article.Authors: Paik S.; Han S.
Article.Abstract: Enzyme engineering commonly focuses on catalytic performance and recombinant protein production. Neither focus alone reveals how much expressed protein becomes an active catalyst or how long it remains functional. This review discusses engineering strategies for catalyst formation and maintenance using four representative enzyme groups. Cytochrome P450 enzymes illustrate the roles of cofactor incorporation and redox-system organization. Zymogenic proteases show how precursor maturation and autolysis control the active-enzyme population. Fungal cellulases demonstrate how post-translational modifications and host processing shape the final proteoform. Lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) link active-site maturation to protection against oxidative damage. Together, these examples point to common strategies for improving catalyst formation and catalytic lifetime. Emerging approaches extend these principles to accessory maturation machinery and controlled activation. Conformational engineering and state-resolved measurements provide further opportunities for enzyme design.

Article.Authors: Dec M.; Hauschild T.; Urban-Chmiel R.
Article.Abstract: The aim of this study was to elucidate the molecular basis of β-lactam resistance in Ligilactobacillus salivarius, with a focus on mutations in genes encoding penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). Twelve L. salivarius strains (2 reference strains and 10 turkey-derived isolates) were analyzed. Susceptibility to β-lactams was determined by the broth microdilution method. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) analyses and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were used to detect resistance genes. Alterations in 3 PBPs (FtsI, PBP2x-like, and PBP1A) were identified by comparative analysis of presumptive amino acid (aa) sequences. Phylogenetic relationships between strains were assessed using multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Six strains were resistant to ampicillin (MIC ranging from 32 to ≥128 mg/L) and showed elevated MICs for cephalosporins. No β-lactamase genes were detected in any strain. Resistant strains exhibited distinct patterns of aa alterations in the transpeptidase domains of FtsI and PBP2x-like proteins, whereas susceptible strains with elevated ampicillin MICs (2–4 mg/L) showed only partial alteration profiles. PBP1A displayed limited variation and no clear association with resistance phenotype. Taken together, these findings are consistent with an association between β-lactam resistance in L. salivarius and alterations in high-molecular-weight (HMW) PBPs, particularly FtsI and PBP2x-like proteins, in the absence of detectable β-lactamase production. However, further studies, including functional analyses, are needed to clarify the role of these PBP alterations in the observed resistance phenotype.

Article.Title: Ecological Responses of Cyanotis arachnoidea C.B. Clarke and Its Rhizosphere Microbiome in Zinc Mine Tailings: Insights for Post-Mining Restoration
Article.Authors: Kutrasaeng N.; Kawicha P.; Sangdee A.; Nakbanpote W.
Article.Abstract: Mining activities severely disrupt soil ecosystems through heavy metal contamination. This study evaluated the phytoremediation potential and rhizosphere microbial dynamics of Cyanotis arachnoidea C.B. Clarke (confirmed via rbcLa and trnH–psbA barcoding), a native plant from Thai zinc mines. Pot experiments demonstrated that plants grown in tailings-contaminated soil exhibited reduced growth and distinct leaf reddening, accompanied by significantly elevated anthocyanin levels. Conversely, proline levels decreased, whereas chlorophyll content and antioxidant parameters (total phenolic content (TPC), total flavonoid content (TFC), and free radical scavenging activity (FRSA)) changed only slightly. Based on zinc (Zn) and cadmium (Cd) uptake and translocation profiles, growth characteristics, and physiology, C. arachnoidea was classified as a highly Zn-tolerant phytostabilizer and a high-translocating Cd excluder. Furthermore, high-throughput sequencing (HTS) and culture-dependent analyses demonstrated that metal toxicity reduced bacterial alpha diversity but selectively enriched stress-tolerant taxa—such as Sphingomonas, Bacillus, Bacteroidota, and Chloroflexi—compared with the nutrient-cycling Acidobacteriota that dominated the cover soil. Collectively, its physiological adaptability, capacity for Zn phytostabilization, effective Cd exclusion strategy, and association with a stress-resilient microbiome make C. arachnoidea a promising candidate for the ecological restoration of multi-metal-contaminated sites.

Article.Title: Comparative Transcriptomic and Physiological Profiling Reveals Species-Associated Differences Across Five Duckweed Species
Article.Authors: Thingujam D.; Tan Z.; Wang Y.; Pajerowska-Mukhtar K.; Mukhtar M.
Article.Abstract: Duckweeds (Lemnaceae) are fast-growing aquatic monocots with potential for biomass production and phytoremediation, but baseline molecular and physiological differences among species remain poorly characterized. We assembled de novo transcriptomes of five duckweed species, Lemna minor, Lemna japonica, Lemna gibba, Landoltia punctata, and Lemna aequinoctialis, grown on basal Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium (three biological replicates per species), and evaluated for completeness with Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) against Viridiplantae, Embryophyta, and Liliopsida reference sets. Orthogroup-level expression divergence was characterized by species signature scoring and Pearson correlation analysis; Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) annotations were examined using descriptive composition analyses and formal overrepresentation tests. In an independent experiment, biomass, protein content, glucose accumulation, peroxidase activity, and chlorophyll a/b concentrations were measured after 7 days under four nutrient regimes (Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium, Hoagland solution, Gamborg’s B5 medium, and nitrogen-free MS (MS–N) medium). All assemblies were highly complete (≥89% complete BUSCOs). Replicates clustered by species (median within-species r = 0.99 versus between-species r = 0.40; label-permutation p = 1 × 10−4), and species signatures selected on training replicates correctly assigned every held-out sample. GO and KEGG annotation composition differed among species, but no term reached a false discovery rate (FDR) ≤ 0.10 in species-specific enrichment tests. Medium effects were species-dependent: relative to basal MS, MS–N lowered protein and chlorophyll a and raised glucose and chlorophyll b in all species, and increased peroxidase activity in four of five species. Because the media differ in several components, these effects cannot be attributed to nitrogen alone. The five species have distinct, reproducible baseline transcriptomes and differ in their physiological responses to nutrient media, providing a hypothesis-generating resource for comparative duckweed research.

These findings describe a heterogeneous germline spectrum and exploratory genotype–phenotype associations in a Brazilian cohort. Heterogeneous genetic testing coverage and the absence of individual genomic ancestry assessment limit interpretation; the findings should not be considered ancestry-specific or nationally representative. Article.Title: Structural Determinants Underlying the Interplay Between Fatty Acid Binding and S-Nitrosylation of Human Serum Albumin
Article.Authors: Batalova A.; Samodurova K.; Vovk M.; Belinskaia D.; Jenkins R.; Goncharov N.
Article.Abstract: Human serum albumin (HSA) is a multifunctional protein whose biological properties are determined not only by its amino acid sequence but also by a complex interplay of functional sites, post-translational modifications, and endogenous ligands. However, the structural mechanisms by which these regulatory factors influence the functional state of HSA remain insufficiently understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the structural basis of the interplay between HSA functional regions, using Cys34 S-nitrosylation and fatty acid (FA) binding as model regulatory processes. For this purpose, the structural features and conformational dynamics of FA-free and FA-loaded native and nitrosylated HSA, as well as their interactions with glutathione (GSH) and S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO), were studied using molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Changes in the overall structure of HSA after incubation with GSNO were assessed by 1H NMR spectroscopy. MD analysis revealed that FA binding alters the conformational dynamics of HSA and affects the structural environment of Cys34 and other functionally significant regions. These FA-induced effects were further modulated by S-nitrosylation, which influenced the conformational landscape of albumin in a manner dependent on its fatty acid-bound state. The similarity of the one-dimensional 1H NMR spectra of HSA before and after incubation with GSNO suggests the absence of pronounced changes in the overall protein structure upon interaction with the nitrosylating agent. The obtained data provide insights into how FA binding and S-nitrosylation shape the conformational properties of HSA through modulation of the structural environment of Cys34 and other functionally significant regions. The results highlight the importance of considering post-translational modifications and endogenous ligands as key determinants of HSA structure–function relationships.

Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Li Z.; Wang M.; Li L.; Lim K.; Cui W.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive neurovascular dysfunction and neuroinflammation, in which perivascular macrophages (PVMs) serve as key immune sentinels that regulate cerebrovascular homeostasis and disease progression. However, the transcriptional remodeling, genetic susceptibility, and functional mechanisms of PVMs in the pathogenesis of PD remain unclear. In this study, we integrated human midbrain single-nucleus RNA sequencing, genetic association datasets, and transcriptomic analyses to characterize PVM alterations in PD. Through multi-omics analyses, including Mendelian randomization, colocalization, and trajectory inference, we identified PD-associated PVM genes and regulatory pathways, which were further validated in a rotenone-induced PD model. We found extensive transcriptional remodeling of PVMs in PD, manifested by inflammatory activation, altered complement signaling, and aberrant neurovascular interactions. Genetic analyses identified HLA-DRA, OSBPL3, and RIN3 as PD-associated PVM genes that were enriched in PVMs and exhibited dynamic changes during disease progression. Functional analyses suggested that these genes are involved in immune regulation, lipid metabolism, and intracellular trafficking. The rotenone-induced model further confirmed the upregulation of Osbpl3 and Rin3. These findings reveal that PVM-centered neurovascular immune remodeling is a feature of PD and identify HLA-DRA, OSBPL3, and RIN3 as candidate genes supported by genetic evidence, linking PVM dysfunction to PD susceptibility.

Article.Title: A Modular and Pd-Free Synthesis of Fluorescent Phenoxazine and Pyridobenzoxazine Heterocycles
Article.Authors: Kontra B.; Rózsa B.; Mucsi Z.; Dunkel P.
Article.Abstract: Phenoxazine and pyridobenzoxazine derivatives are privileged heterocyclic scaffolds with relevance in fluorescence science, redox chemistry and medicinal chemistry. However, modular access to structurally diverse analogs, particularly heteroaryl-fused systems, is often limited by harsh reaction conditions, metal-catalyzed protocols or substrate-dependent outcomes. In this work, we describe a palladium-free strategy based on aryl ether formation followed by intramolecular SNAr-type ring closure and N-dealkylation. The method tolerates a range of aryl and heteroaryl halides and can be performed under conventional heating or accelerated by microwave irradiation. Reaction optimization revealed the importance of solvent, base, leaving group and substrate electronics. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations support a three-stage pathway consisting of endergonic ether formation, intramolecular quaternization/ring closure and final N-dealkylation. The methodology provides access to a focused library of phenoxazine derivatives and creates a platform for further development of redox-active and bioimaging-relevant dyes.

Article.Title: Molecular Mechanisms of Therapeutic Resistance in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Li K.; Sun F.; Chan S.; Leung R.; Li B.; Wong J.; Fung T.; Lo J.; Chan A.; Yau T.
Article.Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major global health burden, and therapeutic resistance continues to limit the benefit from systemic treatment. Despite advances in systemic therapies, including immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations, antiangiogenic agents, and multitargeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors for patients with advanced HCC, primary non-response and acquired resistance are common. This review summarizes the mechanisms that underlie resistance to contemporary HCC therapies, including tumour heterogeneity, molecular pathway rewiring and crosstalk, tumour microenvironment and immune escape, epigenetic alterations, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and cancer stem cell expansion. We discuss how these mechanisms limit the efficacy of current doublet and triplet regimens, and why biologically rational combinations do not consistently translate into clinical benefit. Emerging strategies to overcome resistance, including biomarker-enriched trial designs and liquid biopsy are also discussed. A deeper integration of mechanistic insights with translational biomarkers will be essential to improve treatment durability and clinical outcomes for patients with HCC.

Article.Title: Beyond the Neuron: TDP-43 and the Challenge of Pre-Analytical Quality in Platelet Biomarker Development
Article.Authors: Malkamu B.; Buratti E.; Cappelli S.
Article.Abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is the primary pathological hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Yet, despite two decades of intensive research, a reliable peripheral TDP-43 biomarker remains elusive. Recognizing platelets as a major blood reservoir of TDP-43 opens new diagnostic avenues but may also reveal potential vulnerabilities. In this narrative review, we first trace the evolving understanding of TDP-43 from a nuclear RNA-binding protein to a molecule whose functions and disease-associated alterations extend beyond the neuron. We then examine recent breakthroughs demonstrating that TDP-43 function is shaped by its cellular environment and how it may be uniquely concentrated in platelets. Next, we argue that pre-analytical variables, such as hemolysis, clotting, cold-chain failures, and biobank protocols, are not mere “noise” but potential confounders that distort molecular integrity and should be taken into account. Finally, we discuss the biological and methodological uncertainties surrounding platelet TDP-43 and highlight how standardized handling and systematic pre-analytical reporting can improve reproducibility and support future biomarker validation. More broadly, the methodological standards outlined in this review may extend beyond TDP-43 to other disease-related proteins that are present in platelets and similarly sensitive to pre-analytical variability.

Article.Title: Prometheus’s Fire, Part III: The Forge of Hephaestus—Non-Pharmacological and Pharmacological Interventions Targeting Adipose Tissue Immunometabolism in Obesity
Article.Authors: Grudniewska A.; Mrozikiewicz-Rakowska B.; Wiszniewski K.; Filipiak K.; Kuryłowicz A.
Article.Abstract: There is a growing recognition of obesity as a chronic immunometabolic disease in which impaired adipose tissue expandability contributes to a self-amplifying inflammatory network that extends across multiple organs. This state-of-the-art narrative review, the third and final part of the Prometheus’s Fire series, considers how lifestyle interventions, bariatric surgery and pharmacological therapies may disrupt this network and support the restoration of immunometabolic homeostasis. We introduce the concept of therapeutic convergence, describing how interventions with different primary mechanisms can influence shared processes, including NOD-, LRR- and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activity, adipokine dysregulation, adipose tissue remodelling, mitochondrial stress and inter-organ inflammatory signalling. Evidence from randomised controlled trials, meta-analyses and mechanistic studies shows that these interventions differ considerably in the extent and breadth of their effects. Bariatric surgery, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and double GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonists (tirzepatide) have the most consistent evidence for coordinated effects on adipose tissue inflammation, metabolic dysfunction and inter-organ signalling. Other interventions appear to influence more selected components of the network and may therefore have greater value as complementary rather than comprehensive approaches. This perspective also highlights a limitation of relying on body weight as the primary measure of therapeutic success. Weight loss remains an important clinical goal, but it may not fully reflect the extent or durability of immunometabolic recovery. The therapeutic convergence framework therefore offers a way to understand how mechanistically distinct interventions can produce overlapping systemic benefits and may help identify treatment strategies that more effectively restore adipose tissue function while disrupting the inflammatory processes that sustain metabolic disease.

Article.Title: Photocatalytic Oxidative Desulfurization of H2S: A Review of Photocatalysts, Reaction Mechanisms, and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zhou M.; Kong H.; Wang S.; Samy M.; Yuan S.
Article.Abstract: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a highly toxic, corrosive, and malodorous sulfur-containing pollutant emitted from diverse industrial and agricultural activities. Its low concentration, dispersed distribution, and intermittent emission characteristics often limit the effectiveness and economic feasibility of conventional desulfurization technologies. Photocatalytic desulfurization has emerged as a promising approach for H2S removal owing to its ability to utilize light energy under ambient conditions without generating secondary pollution. Among the various photocatalysts investigated, TiO2 remains the most extensively studied material. To improve photocatalytic performance, strategies such as elemental doping, defect engineering, heterojunction construction, and support coupling have been widely adopted to enhance visible-light absorption, promote charge separation, and improve resistance to deactivation. In addition, emerging photocatalysts, including metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4), conjugated polymers, and carbon-based composites, have shown considerable potential for improving H2S adsorption, activation, and visible-light utilization. Photocatalytic H2S oxidation generally proceeds via sulfate or elemental sulfur formation pathways; however, both can result in sulfur accumulation on catalyst surfaces, leading to performance deterioration. Consequently, developing photocatalytic systems with efficient solar-light utilization, high sulfur tolerance, and long-term operational stability remains a critical challenge. This review summarizes recent advances in photocatalytic H2S oxidation, focusing on photocatalyst design, H2S removal performance, reaction mechanisms, and catalyst deactivation behaviors. Future challenges and research directions for the development of efficient and durable photocatalytic desulfurization technologies are also discussed.

Article.Title: Modification of the HIV-1 Fusion Inhibitor 2P23 via N-Glycosylation Sites Enhances Its Cell Membrane Level and Antiviral Activity
Article.Authors: Borovikova S.; Tvorogova A.; Shepelev M.; Kruglova N.
Article.Abstract: HIV (Human immunodeficiency virus) gene therapy represents a promising strategy to suppress viral replication and potentially achieve long-term control of infection. One of the effective strategies is based on the generation of the genetically modified virus-resistant T cells by expressing peptide inhibitors of viral fusion on the cell membrane. These peptides, such as MT-C34 and 2P23, are derived from HIV gp41 protein and inhibit HIV entry into modified cells. We previously demonstrated in cell-to-cell viral transmission experiments that the 2P23 peptide showed lower protective activity than the MT-C34 peptide. In this study, we hypothesized that the difference in protective activity may arise from the differential N-glycosylation of the peptides. To test this, the 2P23 sequence was modified by introducing the N-glycosylation site (NDT) at the N-, C-, or both termini. These modifications significantly enhanced the plasma membrane expression and protective activity of the 2P23 peptide, with the NDT-2P23-NDT variant being the most potent. The validity of this peptide engineering approach was confirmed with the highly similar HP23L peptide, demonstrating an increased cell membrane expression and antiviral potency of the modified variant. Experiments with the N-glycosylation inhibitor tunicamycin provide indirect evidence that this effect is glycosylation-dependent. These findings suggest that introducing N-glycosylation sites is a versatile approach to improve the potency of membrane-bound antiviral peptides for HIV gene therapy.

Article.Title: Research Progress of Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 in Major Neurodegenerative Diseases
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Xia J.
Article.Abstract: Major neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) represent a large category of disorders characterized by the progressive loss of structure, function, or eventual death of neuronal cells in the brain and spinal cord. Current conventional therapeutic strategies for NDDs primarily focus on symptomatic relief. In contrast, IGF-1 is a pleiotropic protein with neurotrophic, synaptogenic, and anti-apoptotic properties, and its neuroprotective potential has been demonstrated in various preclinical models of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other NDDs. However, the clinical efficacy of IGF-1-based interventions—whether for symptomatic relief or disease modification—has not been established in humans. Research on IGF-1 as a therapeutic target for NDDs remains predominantly preclinical, and its translation into effective clinical treatments requires further validation. This narrative review summarizes the mechanisms of action and therapeutic advances of IGF-1 in the progression of NDDs, encompassing the following four aspects: (1) Strategies based on signaling pathway regulation that target key pathways such as IGF-1/PI3K/Akt to reduce neuronal loss, promote synaptogenesis and structural remodeling, correct anomalous tau hyperphosphorylation, and improve amyloid-β (Aβ) clearance impairment. (2) Strategies based on restoring central sensitivity that focus on ameliorating cerebral insulin/IGF-1 resistance and utilizing agents to indirectly restore the neuroprotective function of IGF-1, thereby delaying cognitive decline. (3) Strategies based on delivery systems: in animal models, these employ viral vectors or nanomaterials to achieve targeted brain delivery of IGF-1, effectively promoting the survival of dopaminergic and motor neurons. (4) Future research directions that further elucidate the dynamic evolution of IGF-1 signaling across different disease stages and the development of stage-specific regulatory strategies. This review discusses approaches to restoring central IGF-1 signaling, ameliorating cerebral insulin resistance, and improving brain-targeted delivery, while emphasizing that their therapeutic relevance remains predominantly preclinical and requires validation in human studies.

Article.Title: Genome Editing for Earliness and Plant Architecture in Cucurbit Crops: Recent Advances and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Wan L.; Wang Z.; Ren J.; Wei J.; Zeng H.; Li X.; Qu J.; Xiong J.; Tang M.
Article.Abstract: Earliness and plant architecture are major breeding targets in cucurbit crops because they influence crop duration, early yield, planting density, canopy management, and production efficiency. This review summarizes genetic, molecular, and genome-editing advances related to flowering, sex expression, fruit development, stem elongation, branching, and canopy architecture in cucumber, melon, watermelon, Cucurbita species, and other cucurbits. Current evidence shows that earlier flowering or increased femaleness does not necessarily lead to earlier commercial maturity, while compact growth must be evaluated together with yield, fruit quality, and environmental adaptation. CRISPR/Cas9 knockout remains the most established editing approach, whereas base editing, cis-regulatory editing, multiplex editing, developmental-regulator-assisted regeneration, and DNA-free RNP delivery offer promising routes toward more precise trait optimization. Major constraints include genotype-dependent transformation, pleiotropic effects, limited validation in elite germplasm, and scarce direct evidence for shortening fruit-development duration. An evidence-guided framework is proposed that links trait definition, functional genomics, target prioritization, tailored genome editing, whole-plant evaluation, and breeding deployment. Future progress will depend on quantitatively tuned alleles and coordinated optimization of reproductive timing, canopy architecture, productivity, fruit quality, and environmental stability.

Article.Title: Cross-Tissue Concordance of a T1D Blood-Derived B-Cell Signature with Hashimoto Thyroiditis Tissue: Exploratory Spatial Immune-Topic Analysis
Article.Authors: Joo E.; Lee S.
Article.Abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) and Hashimoto thyroiditis (HT) share autoimmune features, but cross-tissue concordance of B-cell transcriptional programs remains uncertain. Using 24 retained cohort–pathway effect estimates, we recalculated T1D blood summary-level meta-analysis statistics and separately report the previously generated frozen 14-gene HT thyroid association. The T1D meta-analysis yielded Hedges’ g = 0.51 (95% CI 0.18–0.85; q = 0.022; I2 = 0%). In HRA001684 (16 HT, 50 non-HT), the frozen score was associated with HT (HC3-adjusted β = 2.65, 95% CI 2.37–2.94; permutation P = 2 × 10−5). Single-cell data (6512 cells; three HT and three immune-checkpoint-inhibitor-associated thyroiditis libraries) lacked healthy controls and were analyzed descriptively. In five spatial sections, the frozen-signature contrast was nonsignificant (Δ = 0.459; exact P = 0.10; matched-gene P = 0.085), with no preferential correspondence to B/plasma-cell topics (reported P = 0.90). Independently inferred thyroid immune topics showed regional variation but did not localize the frozen score. These reported findings are compatible with partial T1D blood–HT thyroid transcriptional concordance but do not establish systemic HT activation, a shared cell-intrinsic program, or validated spatial localization. In the reported sensitivity analysis, joint B-cell/plasma-cell marker adjustment attenuated the HT association by approximately 90%, with the fully adjusted confidence interval including zero. Comparisons with equal weighting and other B-cell reference signatures did not establish a statistically significant advantage of the T1D-derived weights. The public GitHub workflow verifies summary-level pooling of retained effects only; source-to-result reconstruction of the HT bulk, spatial, single-cell, and marker/weight analyses has not been established.

Article.Title: Avocado (Persea americana Mill.) Genomic Divergence Across the Victoria, Tanganyika and Rukwa Lake Basins of Tanzania
Article.Authors: Cortés A.; Hussein J.; Juma I.
Article.Abstract: Avocado (Persea americana Mill.) is a crucial horticultural tree crop for food security and rural income in Tanzania. Despite its importance, the genomic divergence of avocado populations in the country’s Lake Zone, Western Zone, and the Southern Highlands region of Rukwa has not previously been investigated. While the Southern Highlands are recognized as a major production hub, a significant knowledge gap exists regarding the genomic diversity, population stratification and racial ancestry of landraces in the Western Rift and Lake Victoria Basin, areas characterized by unique microclimates and historical transboundary trade routes with neighboring Great Lakes nations. Therefore, this study aimed to characterize the genomic diversity of avocado germplasm through low-coverage whole-genome resequencing (lcWGS) of 105 trees from five key regions: Mara, Mwanza and Kagera in the Lake Zone and Lake Victoria Basin; Kigoma in the Western Zone and Lake Tanganyika Basin of the Western Rift; and Rukwa in the Southern Highlands’ Lake Rukwa Basin adjacent to the Lake Tanganyika Basin and Western Rift. The study sought to identify patterns of local differentiation and gene flow. We hypothesized that the avocado populations in these regions are not panmictic but are structured by geographic and ecological barriers, where (i) regions bordering the Albertine Rift (i.e., Kigoma and Kagera) exhibit distinct West Indian types likely shaped by transboundary exchange and climate heterogeneity and (ii) the Lake Victoria Eastern Basin regions of Mwanza and Mara harbor unique intermediate genotypes resulting from inter-racial hybridization with lowland genotypes. The lcWGS screening generated more than 63,577,355 SNPs across a total of 405 studied trees, after compilation with published lcWGS reads from 300 avocado trees from Tanzanian Morogoro and the Southern Highlands of Iringa, Mbeya and Ruvuma (95) and racial control groups in the Americas (205). Phylogenetic, unsupervised principal component and ADMIXTURE analyses found that germplasm from Rukwa clustered with Southern Highlands germplasm from Iringa, Mbeya, and Ruvuma. In contrast, accessions from Kigoma and Kagera formed a distinct Western Rift lineage enriched for West Indian ancestry, and populations in Mara and Mwanza occupied intermediate positions, suggesting extensive inter-racial admixture in the eastern Lake Victoria Basin. These genetic clusters may guide the utilization of East African avocado landraces.

Article.Title: Hippocampal Glial Alterations Are Associated with Mitochondrial Changes and Reduced Glucocorticoid Receptor Density in Suicides
Article.Authors: Vázquez-Hernández A.; Escribano-Cadena Y.; Morales-Medina J.; Flores A.; Mendoza-Larios L.; Mendoza-Morales R.; Nicolini H.; Tendilla-Beltrán H.; García-Dolores F.; Flores G.
Article.Abstract: Suicide is a major public health concern frequently associated with depressive disorders and neurobiological alterations within the hippocampus. This study investigated biomarkers related to neuroinflammation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and mitochondrial labeling in the CA1 region of the hippocampus of young and adult individuals of Mexican ancestry who died by suicide. Postmortem hippocampal CA1 samples were obtained from young and adult suicide cases and age-matched controls. Cellular markers of microglia (ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1, Iba1) and astrocytes (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP), neuronal density, glucocorticoid receptor expression, and mitochondrial labeling were evaluated and compared among groups. Suicide cases exhibited increased microglial and astrocyte cell density indicated by increased Iba1 and GFAP immunoreactivity in both age groups. In contrast, mitochondrial labeling and glucocorticoid receptor immunoreactivity were reduced in suicide cases, regardless of age. Additionally, a significant reduction in neuronal density was detected exclusively in young individuals who died by suicide. Together, these findings indicate age-independent alterations in glial immunoreactivity, mitochondrial labeling, and glucocorticoid receptor expression, alongside reduced neuronal density in the hippocampal CA1 region of younger suicide cases, supporting the involvement of neuroinflammation-related processes in suicide. Despite the limited sample size, these findings provide insight into potential neurobiological mechanisms underlying suicide and may contribute to the identification of biomarkers and therapeutic targets for individuals at risk.

Article.Title: Use of 16S rRNA Gut Microbiome Analysis to Identify Shared Microbial Signatures Across Metabolic Syndrome Components in Obese Subjects
Article.Authors: Antonetti L.; Longo S.; Cardellini M.; Casagrande V.; Menghini R.; Cicalini I.; Pieragostino D.; Poggiogalle E.; Frigerio F.; Piciocchi C.; De Laurenzi V.; Savastano S.; Donini L.; Mingrone G.; Federici M.
Article.Abstract: Gut microbiota (GM) alterations and related metabolic outputs have been implicated in metabolic syndrome (MetS) and early cardiometabolic risk. However, the associations between GM alterations and MetS, and their relationship with the marked interindividual variability in cardiovascular risk, remain incompletely defined. Prevalence of individual MetS traits was 37.4% for hyperglycemia, 23.4% for hypertriglyceridemia, 54.0% for hypertension, and 52.1% for low HDL cholesterol, with 51.1% of participants meeting criteria for MetS overall. Comparative analysis of 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data identified a shared gut microbial signature comprising 45 ASVs across MetS clinical components. Members of Prevotellaceae and Ruminococcaceae were consistently reduced in MetS, whereas Veillonella and Streptococcus were enriched. Reduced microbial alpha diversity was observed in individuals with MetS. PICRUSt2-based functional inference indicated lower representation of pathways related to complex carbohydrate utilization and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) metabolism in MetS-positive individuals. Our results, derived from two independent datasets, indicate that MetS is associated with a depletion of bacterial taxa involved in complex carbohydrate metabolism and SCFA production.

Article.Title: Serum Fatty Acid Profiles Across Normoglycemia, Prediabetes, and Type 2 Diabetes: Associations with Glycemic and Cardiometabolic Parameters in a Kazakh Population
Article.Authors: Toishimanov M.; Shokan A.; Voitsekhovskiy I.; Kanapiyanov B.; Myrzabayeva N.; Nurtazina A.
Article.Abstract: Population-specific data on serum fatty acids across the progression to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are limited. In this exploratory cross-sectional study, serum fatty acids were determined by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry in 177 adults from Kazakhstan (45 normoglycemic, 114 with prediabetes, 18 with T2DM) and expressed as percentages of the quantified profile of the 13 components detected in ≥50% of samples. No fatty acid differed between glycemic groups after false discovery rate correction. In controls and participants with prediabetes, oleic and palmitoleic acids correlated with serum triglycerides (ρ = +0.65 and +0.32; q ≤ 0.005), and both associations persisted after adjustment for age, sex and adiposity and after exclusion of implausible profiles arising from a peak-assignment inconsistency. Across all participants, linoleic acid correlated inversely with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c; ρ = −0.21, q = 0.033) in unadjusted analyses only. An association of heptadecanoic acid with HbA1c depended on its non-detection in part of the samples and was neither established nor excluded. Covariates were not recorded for the T2DM group, HbA1c was recorded with limited precision for most participants, and adjusted analyses were restricted to 107 participants without diabetes. The study describes serum fatty acid composition in this population and generates hypotheses.

Article.Title: Kallmann Syndrome and MSI-H Colorectal Cancer in a Patient with a Germline PROKR2 Variant: A Case Report with Exploratory Cohort Analysis
Article.Authors: Lu Y.; Li D.; Liang W.; Tong Z.; Zhang X.; He Y.; Yu N.; Weng S.; Yuan Y.; Yang M.
Article.Abstract: PROKR2 is an established gene associated with Kallmann syndrome (KS), and preclinical studies have suggested a possible role in tumor development. In this study, we report a patient with KS and microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) colon cancer and aim to explore the potential association between PROKR2 variants and MSI-H status in colorectal cancer (CRC). Peripheral blood samples from the proband and his parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (WES) to identify germline variants. The WES revealed that both the proband and his father carried a likely pathogenic variant in the KS-associated gene PROKR2 (NM_144773.4:c.337T>C, p.Tyr113His). To place this case in a broader context, we performed exploratory bioinformatic analyses of somatic PROKR2 variants in two public CRC cohorts, DFCI-CRC and TCGA-CRC, although these cohort analyses cannot inform germline risk. In the DFCI-CRC cohort, PROKR2 somatic variant status showed no statistically significant association with MSI-H status in either the unadjusted or TMB-adjusted analysis. In the TCGA-CRC cohort, PROKR2 somatic variants were associated with higher unadjusted odds of MSI-H (OR = 5.50, 95% CI = 1.003–30.20, p = 0.0248, BH-adjusted q = 0.0495). After TMB adjustment, this positive association was not retained and the adjusted estimate was in the opposite direction (adjusted OR = 0.093, 95% CI = 0.014–0.549, p = 0.00875, BH-adjusted q = 0.0175). Accordingly, this case report describes the co-occurrence of PROKR2-related KS and MSI-H CRC in a single patient, although a causal relationship between PROKR2-related KS and CRC remains unestablished.

Article.Title: Immunotargeting of Cervical Cancer Cells with the Adaptor CAR T-Cell Platform RevCAR
Article.Authors: Jones-Cifuentes N.; Arndt C.; Loureiro L.; Berndt N.; von Jutrzenka-Trzebiatowski A.; Feldmann A.; Bachmann J.; Seliger B.; Rincon-Orozco B.; Bachmann M.
Article.Abstract: The Prostate Stem Cell Antigen (PSCA) is not only overexpressed in prostate cancer (PC) but also in many other tumors, including cervical cancer (CC). The adaptor chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) platform RevCAR can be used for immunotargeting of PSCA-expressing tumor cells. We found that the CC cell line SiHa natively expresses PSCA. The expression was sufficient for redirection of RevCAR T-cells using recently described RevCAR target modules (RevTMs) directed against PSCA. Like almost all PC cell lines, however, SiHa cells also downregulate their PSCA expression in cell culture. To overcome this limitation, we established artificially PSCA-overexpressing SiHa cells. Retargeting of RevCAR T-cells strictly depends on PSCA-directed RevTMs and PSCA-expressing target cells. It leads to (i) upregulation of CD69, Perforin and Granzyme B, (ii) lysis of target cells with EC50 values in the picomolar range, and (iii) cytokine secretion of IFN-γ, TNF-α, GM-CSF and IL-2. Phenotypic analysis shows a prominent increase in memory RevCAR T-cells but only a slight increase in exhausted cells, indicating a low level of tonic signaling of RevCAR T-cells. Together, our data supports an efficient and safe immunotargeting of PSCA-expressing CC cells with the RevCAR technology.

Article.Title: Clinical and Genetic Spectrum of OPN1LW/OPN1MW-Associated Disorders in a Chinese Cohort: Contribution of Long-Read Sequencing
Article.Authors: Wei X.; Li Y.; Li H.; Li W.; Zhou Y.; Sui R.
Article.Abstract: The highly homologous OPN1LW/OPN1MW gene cluster poses substantial challenges for molecular diagnosis. Article.Title: Integrated Host Genome Rumen Microbiome Metabolome Prediction of Low-Methane, High-Feed-Efficiency Sheep Under Climate Stress
Article.Authors: Rehman S.; Tharwat M.; Shaukat A.; Alkheraif A.; Ali R.
Article.Abstract: Sheep are well adapted to marginal grazing systems and provide important products such as wool, milk and meat. However, microbial fermentation in the rumen and reticulum generates enteric methane, which contributes to greenhouse gas emissions from livestock production. Both methane emissions and feed efficiency show heritable variation, while host genetics can also shape rumen microbial composition through complex host–microbe interactions. This review explores how host genomics, rumen microbiome profiles, methanogenic archaeal communities, and rumen and blood metabolomics can be combined to identify biomarkers of low methane emissions and improved feed efficiency, particularly under environmental stress. Evidence suggests that methane production is repeatable and genetically influenced, and that rumen microbiome composition is associated with methane emission and feed efficiency, although current evidence does not show that specific microbial taxa directly cause these traits. Integrating host genotype with microbial and metabolic information may therefore improve statistical prediction of methane emissions and residual feed intake, which is not the same as identifying validated biomarkers or showing biological causation. Nevertheless, reliable microbial biomarkers have yet to be established, and validation across breeds, diets, and production environments remains limited. Heat stress adds further complexity by altering rumen fermentation, oxidative status, and microbial community structure, yet integrated omics research under climatic stress remains scarce. Future studies should prioritize longitudinal, multi-breed designs, standardized methane phenotyping, and coordinated multi-omics analyses to develop robust biomarkers for sustainable, low-emission sheep production.

Article.Title: Low MATR3 Expression Is Associated with Poor Prognosis in Endometrial Carcinoma: An Integrated Immunohistochemical and Transcriptomic Analysis
Article.Authors: Podemski J.; Grzanka D.; Podemska E.; Skoczylas-Makowska N.; Jerka D.; Gagat M.; Antosik P.
Article.Abstract: Endometrial carcinoma (EC) is the most common malignancy of the female genital tract, yet reliable prognostic biomarkers remain limited. Matrin-3 (MATR3), a nuclear matrix protein involved in genome stability and RNA processing, has been implicated in various cancers, but its role in EC has not been described. Here, we performed an integrated analysis combining immunohistochemical evaluation of MATR3 protein expression in a retrospective institutional cohort of 112 patients with EC and in silico analysis of MATR3 mRNA expression in 172 TCGA cases. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed nuclear MATR3 expression in both EC and normal endometrial tissues, with significantly lower protein levels in EC compared to control tissues (p < 0.0001). MATR3 mRNA was significantly reduced in EC tumour tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues (p < 0.0001). Low MATR3 protein expression was associated with shorter OS after adjustment for age, histological grade, pT, pN and pM in an LVSI-stratified Cox model (HR = 2.296; 95% CI: 1.284–4.104; p = 0.0050). Low MATR3 mRNA expression was associated with improved overall survival in TCGA (median OS = 110.1 months; HR = 2.174; 95% CI: 1.066–4.43; p = 0.0303). Co-expression analysis identified BCLAF1 and TOP2B as key positive correlates, while TRAPPC5 and FASTK showed the strongest negative correlations. Genes positively correlated with MATR3 mRNA expression were enriched for nuclear transcription and RNA-processing annotations, whereas negatively correlated genes were enriched for mitochondrial processes. These associations do not establish a mechanistic link between MATR3 and pathway activity. Our findings support further investigation of MATR3 as a candidate prognostic marker in EC, with independent validation and functional studies required.

Article.Title: Natural Bioactive Compounds in Cosmeceuticals: Challenges and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Kavosh Tehrani F.; Masi M.
Article.Abstract: The global cosmetic market is experiencing dramatic growth, and it is shifting significantly toward the use of natural substances rather than synthetic ingredients in cosmetic formulations. Natural bioactive compounds, obtained from plants, are used in the modern cosmetic industry in order to enhance skin appearance and provide biological bene-fits. These compounds include flavonoids, terpenoids, steroids, fatty acids, and vitamins with anti-aging, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties. Most previous studies have focused on plant extracts and their general effects on human skin, without bridging the gap between systematic classification of bioactive compounds and their cosmetic applications. Therefore, the aim of this article is to provide a novel framework for bioactive compounds which are utilized in cosmeceuticals. Additionally, it discusses biological activities of each compound associated with skin well-being, its applications in the cosmetic industry, as well as its general challenges and limitations in cosmetic formulations.

Article.Title: Short-Chain Fatty Acids as Modulators of the Gut–Immune Axis in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Linking Metabolism, Immune Regulation, and Epithelial Barrier Function
Article.Authors: Piątek D.; Sokal-Dembowska A.; Strycharz-Dudziak M.; Jarmakiewicz-Czaja S.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), which include Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), are chronic conditions associated with abnormalities in the immune response, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and disruption of the intestinal barrier homeostasis. A growing body of evidence suggests that the gut–immune axis plays a key role in the pathogenesis of IBD, and that metabolites of microbial origin influence the regulation of the immune response and the maintenance of intestinal barrier integrity. Particular importance is attributed to short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate. The aim of this review is to present the current knowledge regarding the role of SCFAs as modulators of the gut–immune axis in IBD, with particular emphasis on their mechanisms of action and therapeutic potential. Physiologically, SCFAs are produced through the fermentation of dietary fiber by the gut microbiota. However, in IBD, the composition of the gut microbiota is often disrupted. SCFAs influence the expression of inflammatory genes and regulate the function of immune cells. Furthermore, butyrate in particular strengthens the integrity of the intestinal barrier by improving the function of tight junctions (TJs), increasing mucus production, and supporting epithelial regeneration. SCFAs represent an important link between diet, the gut microbiota, and immunity. Strategies to increase their availability may represent a promising approach to supporting IBD treatment, but they require further evaluation in well-designed clinical trials involving humans.

Article.Title: Simple, Fast and Cheap Pb2+ and Hg2+ Detection in Liquid Media Using EGOFET-Based Aptasensors
Article.Authors: Keshek A.; Skvortsov D.; Poimanova E.; Orlov V.; Oleynikov I.; Stiazhkina M.; Turashev A.; Zavyalova E.; Agina E.
Article.Abstract: Lead and mercury are among the most dangerous environmental pollutants due to their high toxicity to humans and other living organisms. They are also ubiquitous in our ecosystems as a result of industrial waste. Therefore, it is essential to develop a simple and inexpensive method to rapidly detect low concentrations of these metals in various liquids, including wastewater. Aptamer-based electrolyte-gated organic field-effect transistors (EGOFETs), which are traditionally used to detect large biomolecules such as viruses and proteins, are a promising concept for heavy-metal detection. To achieve this, we chose several aptamers with high affinity for and specificity to Pb2+ and Hg2+ ions, determined the dissociation constants and stoichiometry of the complexes, investigated the kinetics of complex formation and cross-specificity and proposed structures for the aptamer–cation complexes. Based on these aptamers, we developed EGOFET-based aptasensors for Pb2+ and Hg2+. The fabricated EGOFET devices have been shown to be sensitive to low concentrations of lead (from 30 nM to 2.5 μM) and mercury (from 250 nM to 2.5 μM) cations. These ranges correspond to the maximum permissible concentrations in drinking and wastewater for lead, which are 144 nM and 1.2 μM, respectively, and exceed the range of maximum permissible concentration in drinking and wastewater for mercury, which is 5 nM. Despite this, it was possible to detect mercury cations at a concentration of 5 nM within five minutes in a model system that simulates liquid flow using the EGOFET device. This demonstrates the potential for fast and selective detection of Pb2+ and Hg2+ ions at maximum permissible concentrations in drinking water using EGOFET-based aptasensors. This is a significant step forward in the development of flow sensors for detecting heavy metals in liquid media.

Article.Title: Emerging Therapeutic Strategies for Targeting Hyaluronan in Metabolic Disease from Molecular Design to Clinical Translation
Article.Authors: Feng M.; Hu X.; Zhou H.
Article.Abstract: Hyaluronan (HA) is increasingly implicated as a contributor to metabolic disease; however, the strongest causal evidence still derives from preclinical models, and no HA-directed treatment has reached the metabolic clinic. That gap points to a weakness in the underlying therapeutic logic. Clinical results for systemic removal of HA have been mixed rather than uniformly negative. In the phase II HALO-202 trial, PEGPH20 improved progression-free survival in patients with hyaluronan-high pancreatic tumors, whereas the phase III HALO-301 trial, which enrolled only hyaluronan-high patients, showed no overall survival benefit; depletion alone was therefore insufficient, and this outcome cannot be attributed to unselected treatment or to molecular size. Its biological activity is not determined by molecular size alone. Concentration, preparation purity, receptor context, tissue location, and the balance between high-molecular-weight HA (HMW-HA, generally above 1000 kDa) and smaller fragments, which range from oligosaccharides of about ten saccharides or fewer to low-molecular-weight HA in between, jointly influence whether the matrix mainly protects or injures metabolic tissues. The argument here is that the field should move away from bulk depletion and toward precision delivery and biomarker-guided patient selection. The therapeutic landscape is organized around four strategies: pharmacological inhibition of HA synthesis, enzymatic degradation, HA-based biomaterials, and defined-molecular-weight HA fragments. Throughout, we distinguish interventions that modify endogenous HA biology from platforms that use HA as a carrier or scaffold, because improved drug delivery or wound healing does not by itself demonstrate correction of pathological HA signaling. Their translational obstacles are then assessed, including patient stratification by HA size and CD44 signature, standardization of size-resolved HA quantification, thromboembolic risk, manufacturing and regulatory hurdles for drug–device combinations, and the design of trials with composite metabolic endpoints. HA is best viewed as an amplifier of metabolic stress rather than a bystander, and the route to clinical translation lies in restoring the equilibrium between HA synthesis and degradation rather than eliminating the molecule, a goal that remains a translational hypothesis rather than a demonstrated clinical outcome.

Article.Title: Noncoding RNAs in Nuclear Condensates and RNA Processing in Skeletal Muscle
Article.Authors: Ngo T.; Lee W.
Article.Abstract: Spatial organization in the nucleus is an active layer of RNA regulation in skeletal muscle, yet localization is often interpreted more strongly than the evidence permits. This critical review compares physiological nuclear RNA compartments with pathological repeat-RNA assemblies using a graded evidence framework. NEAT1-associated paraspeckles provide the clearest muscle-linked example of an RNA-marked nuclear body, although isoform-specific architectural causality remains untested in muscle. MALAT1 regulates speckle-associated splicing-factor and chromatin states but is dispensable for gross speckle formation, and muscle studies report opposing differentiation phenotypes. Nucleolar FRG2 transcripts in facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy connect spatial RNA organization to rDNA transcription and translational capacity. Expanded DMPK CUG and CNBP CCUG RNAs in myotonic dystrophy sequester processing factors and drive spliceopathy, although calibrated imaging in patient-derived DM1 myotubes indicates that most apparent foci are individual retained transcripts rather than bulk condensates. The framework distinguishes spatial association, molecular participation, functional necessity, in vivo relevance, and therapeutic target engagement. It also maps interventions to toxic-RNA abundance, RNA–protein binding, repeat-locus transcription, downstream splicing, or compartment state. Together, this evidence-based synthesis identifies which nuclear RNA mechanisms are established in muscle, which remain extrapolated from non-muscle systems, and which experiments are required before therapeutic modulation can be interpreted mechanistically.

Article.Title: ENO1 Is More Abundant than ENO2 on the Surface of Metastatic and Neuroendocrine Prostate Cancer Cells and Upregulated in High-Risk Prostate Tumors
Article.Authors: Santiago K.; Durán A.; Nyirendah L.; Soliz J.; Morcos A.; Makamure A.; Manrique N.; Escobar-Acuña K.; Whitley K.; Roy S.; Wall N.; Das B.; Almaguel F.; Casiano C.
Article.Abstract: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remains lethal, and lineage plasticity drives a subset of tumors to neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), most often treatment-emergent (t-NEPC). Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA), the target of radioligand therapies for advanced prostate cancer (PCa), is heterogeneously expressed across metastatic sites but lost during neuroendocrine differentiation, excluding many patients from these therapies. The glycolytic enzyme Enolase 1 (ENO1) is a promising alternative target because it localizes to the surface of human tumors and promotes cancer growth and metastasis. However, it remains understudied in advanced PCa compared with ENO2 (neuron-specific enolase), a canonical neuroendocrine marker. We report here that total and cell surface ENO1 are more abundant than ENO2 in PSMA-negative mCRPC and NEPC cells. ENO1 silencing reduced cell proliferation and clonogenic growth even when triggering ENO2 upregulation. Targeting cell surface ENO1 with a monoclonal antibody decreased proliferation, clonogenicity, and tumorsphere formation in mCRPC cells, including docetaxel-resistant cells. This was associated with S-phase accumulation, elevated phospho histone p-H2A.X, and increased apoptosis. Significantly higher transcript expression of ENO1 than ENO2 was observed in clinical prostate tumors, including high-Gleason and neuroendocrine tumors, concomitant with elevated expression of their transcriptional regulator MYC. These findings position cell-surface ENO1 as a therapeutic and theranostic target for PSMA-low, treatment-refractory PCa.

Article.Title: Widely Targeted Lipidomics of Nasal Fluid Across Upper-Airway Inflammation: Phenotype-Associated Remodeling in Allergic Rhinitis and Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Han J.; Wang X.; Wang W.; Wang L.; Zha Y.; Lv W.; Zhu Z.
Article.Abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) share overlapping inflammatory mechanisms while retaining distinct disease biology. Although lipid metabolism is increasingly implicated in airway inflammation, the nasal fluid lipidomic landscape across AR and CRSwNP and its relationship to local eosinophilic inflammation and clinical burden remain incompletely understood. We performed widely targeted liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) lipidomics on nasal fluid from 73 participants, including 22 controls, 23 patients with AR, and 28 patients with CRSwNP. Group differences were evaluated using multivariate analysis and models adjusted for age, sex, and smoking status, followed by trajectory clustering and residual-correlation network analysis. Within CRSwNP, adjusted models were used to assess lipid associations with tissue eosinophilia, the 22-item Sinonasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22), overall visual analog scale (VAS), and Lund–Mackay computed tomography score. Lipid subclass patterns were examined by ranked enrichment and focused subclass score analyses. AR was characterized mainly by higher relative abundances of TG species, whereas CRSwNP showed broader increases involving triacylglycerol species, plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamines, and lysophospholipids. Exploratory clustering of 147 lipids showing nominally significant differences (p < 0.05) in at least one covariate-adjusted pairwise group comparison yielded four modules with differing biochemical compositions, although the partition was sensitive to the input lipid set. Among these, the diacylglycerol–lysophosphatidic acid-related module displayed strong internal network connectivity, suggesting coordinated variation within the identified module. Within CRSwNP, ranked analysis of lipid associations with tissue eosinophilia showed negative enrichment of plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamine, sphingomyelin, and ether-linked lysophosphatidylcholine, and positive enrichment of glycerolipid and acylcarnitine subclasses. Clinical burden showed only partial overlap with this pattern: plasmalogen phosphatidylethanolamine was inversely associated with both tissue eosinophilia and patient-reported symptom burden, whereas conventional lysophosphatidylcholine showed stronger positive associations with symptomatic and radiographic burden. These findings suggest distinct and coordinated nasal fluid lipidomic features associated with the upper-airway inflammatory phenotype, local eosinophilic inflammation, and clinical disease burden.

Article.Title: Rapid FAK Phosphorylation and Progressive Tight-Junction Protein Alterations Under Hyperosmotic Stress in Corneal Epithelial Cells
Article.Authors: Zhou Y.; Ma C.; Gao Y.; Wang Y.; Zhang Z.; Shi M.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Dry eye disease (DED) is characterized by tear hyperosmolality and ocular surface injury, but the contribution of focal adhesion kinase (FAK)-related signaling to tight junction (TJ) protein alterations remains unclear. We combined a scopolamine hydrobromide (SCOP)-induced desiccating stress mouse model with human corneal epithelial (HCE-T) cells exposed to NaCl-induced hyperosmolarity, together with transcriptomics, immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, pharmacological inhibition, and siRNA-mediated FAK knockdown. RNA sequencing identified 823 significant large-effect differentially expressed genes; analysis of the 3741 FDR-corrected significant genes revealed significant enrichment of focal adhesion, extracellular matrix–receptor, cell adhesion, and tight junction pathways. In HCE-T cells, hyperosmotic stress increased FAK Tyr397 phosphorylation as early as 1 h without changing total FAK. At 24 h, p-FAK declined while total FAK protein levels remained stable, consistent with dephosphorylation at Tyr397; by 48 h, total FAK protein was lost, accompanied by cell injury. TJ protein abundance and junctional continuity decreased progressively with increasing osmolarity and exposure duration. PF-562271, a dual FAK/Pyk2 inhibitor, produced a concentration-dependent reduction in FAK Tyr397 phosphorylation and, at 2.5 μM, also reduced Pyk2 Tyr402 phosphorylation while partially preserving ZO-1, claudin-1, and occludin abundance. FAK knockdown independently attenuated TJ protein loss and partially preserved ZO-1 junctional continuity under 500 mOsm/L hyperosmotic stress. These findings support a time-dependent contribution of FAK-related signaling to hyperosmotic stress-induced TJ protein remodeling.

Article.Title: Endogenous Retrovirus-Targeted Immunotherapy for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Supported by Cellular HERV-K Expression, Dependency and Efficacy of ERV Therapy in a Murine Model
Article.Authors: Perez-Penco M.; Scott T.; Engdal E.; Picon Jara C.; González G.; Barfod L.; Rohrberg K.; Bagger F.; Neukirch L.; Andersson A.; Holst P.
Article.Abstract: Human endogenous retrovirus-K (HERV-K/HML-2) has been associated with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but its functional relevance and the potential for HERV-directed immunotherapy remains unresolved. Here, we characterized HERV-K expression across 207 advanced NSCLC patient biopsies by total RNA-seq observing widespread expression of HERV-K Gag and Env antigen encoding sequences. Immunotherapeutic targeting was performed using the ASB-XIV mouse NSCLC cell line and a murine ERV surrogate antigen using adenovirus to express murine leukemia virus (MLV) antigen on a mouse β-retroviral particle structurally related to HERV-K. This immunization was able to elicit significant protection against tumor challenge and additive benefit with anti-PD-L1 in therapeutic treatment, establishing proof-of-concept for ERV-targeted immunotherapy in a murine surrogate system rather than direct evidence of HERV-K-targeted efficacy. Our findings suggest an important role of HERV-K in NSCLC immunobiology and that adaptive immunity targeting HERV-K should be explored in the treatment of NSCLC patients.

Article.Title: Various Aspects of Antimicrobial Properties of Populus Propolis
Article.Authors: Okińczyc P.; Widelski J.; Szperlik J.; Sroka Z.
Article.Abstract: Propolis is a bee product which is composed of plant resins and bee glue. In temperate climatic zones, the main sources of resins are buds of different species of the Populus genus. Propolis is known to have multiple medicinal properties, especially antimicrobial (including antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains), anti-inflammatory, and wound treatment properties. Due to growing antibiotic resistance, new antibacterial agents and therapies solutions are still needed. For this reason, this article summarizes the results of research related to the antibacterial activity of Populus genus propolis. We discuss the main types of Populus genus propolis (aspen, aspen–poplar and poplar), propolis’s general effect against different bacterial strains, the classes of antibacterial agents, the mechanism of antibacterial action of propolis, and interactions of propolis with antibiotics. Our analysis of the literature reveals that Populus propolis is a valuable antibacterial agent. However, its activity varies due to the instability of its composition. Therefore, before it can be designated for medicinal use biological and phytochemical standardization is required. Clinical data reveal the efficiency of propolis preparations in mild external infectious diseases in oral cavity and wound treatment. These data are limited only to poplar propolis. Similar efficiency may be possible using aspen and aspen–poplar propolis, but there is no direct clinical data to support this assertion. Combined therapy using propolis with antibiotics remained controversial due to the lack of sufficient clinical data and unclear data from in vitro research. Administering Populus propolis preparations to treat internal bacterial diseases requires further clinical research and should not be a standard therapy at this moment.

Article.Title: Antidepressant-like Activity of a Triple Combination of Venlafaxine, Codeine and Nor-Binaltorphimine in the Mouse Tail Suspension Test
Article.Authors: Lungu C.; Muntean C.; Păunescu H.; Marin R.; Lungu F.; Costescu M.; Ghiță C.; Fulga I.; Coman O.
Article.Abstract: About one-third of patients with major depressive disorder do not remit on conventional monoaminergic antidepressants. Venlafaxine (VEN) is a classic antidepressant that inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake. Venlafaxine does not bind opioid receptors, yet its antidepressant-like action requires intact µ-opioid signalling. The dynorphin/κ-opioid axis exerts an opposing, dysphoria-promoting influence. A possible question is whether combining serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition, µ-opioid receptor activation by codeine (COD) and sustained κ-opioid receptor blockade produces an antidepressant-like effect larger than that of the components given alone. Male NMRI mice were tested in the forced swim test (FST) (one experiment) and in the tail suspension test (TST) (three experiments) using a parallel-design (n = 10 to 17 per group; 277 animals), as follows: VEN 10 to 40 mg/kg in both tests—FST and TST; COD 10 to 40 mg/kg added to VEN 20 mg/kg in TST; and nor-binaltorphimine (norBNI) 10 mg/kg, given 24 h before, combined with VEN 20 mg/kg and COD 20 mg/kg and compared with norBNI alone, COD alone and norBNI + VEN, with amitriptyline (AMI) 20 mg/kg as the positive control in the TST. The three agents and two reference ligands were also docked into eight experimental human structures of the monoamine transporters and of the μ, κ and δ opioid receptors. VEN did not reduce FST immobility at any dose but produced a dose-dependent reduction in the TST, reaching −66.2% at 40 mg/kg. COD did not potentiate VEN 20 mg/kg at any of three COD doses. The triple combination, in the TST, reduced immobility by 65.7% relative to saline (Dunnett p = 0.013), an effect of similar magnitude to AMI with no significant difference detected between them, whereas norBNI alone, COD alone and norBNI + VEN did not reach significance. The design was underpowered for intermediate effects (the calculated n should be about 36 per group, unapproved because of ethical considerations). The triple combination was not significantly more effective than norBNI + VEN (p = 0.375), so the contribution of codeine remains undetermined. Docking reproduced the experimental pose of all eight co-crystallised ligands and was consistent with VEN occupying the transporter S1 site, COD the μ-opioid pocket and norBNI the κ receptor. A triple serotonin-adrenergic and opioid combination produced an antidepressant-like effect that none of the single treatments tested in the same cohort reached, but the fixed-dose design does not establish cooperativity between all three mechanisms. The docking results are consistent with, but do not prove, engagement of three separate sites.

Article.Title: Folate Receptor Alpha (FRα/FOLR1) in Cancer: Diagnostic, Prognostic or Predictive Biomarker? A Critical Review of Its Clinical Utility
Article.Authors: Kapczuk P.; Marcinowska Z.; Kołodziejczak M.; Szubert D.
Article.Abstract: Folate receptor alpha (FRα) plays a key role in folate homeostasis. Folate is involved, among other processes, in nucleotide biosynthesis, and the marked difference between FRα expression in certain cancers and under physiological conditions gives this receptor potential as a cancer biomarker. However, the current state of knowledge points to a specific role for this marker and defines its potential place in cancer diagnosis and treatment. This review aims to critically evaluate the available evidence regarding the clinical utility of FRα. Analysis of the literature indicates that despite differences in expression, the sensitivity and specificity of FRα are insufficient for its use as a standalone diagnostic marker. In contrast, its potential as a prognostic marker is strongly dependent on cancer type. The strongest evidence of clinical utility concerns membranous FRα protein expression assessed by a validated immunohistochemical companion diagnostic assay for selecting patients with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer for mirvetuximab soravtansine treatment. In contrast, the predictive relevance of FRα for other targeted therapeutic strategies remains under investigation. Overall, FRα should be regarded as a clinically actionable biomarker in a defined therapeutic setting and as a promising, but not universally validated, diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive candidate in other oncological applications.

Article.Title: Microbial Siderophores for Sustainable Agriculture: Stress Tolerance, Biocontrol, Mechanism, and Omics Integration
Article.Authors: Akhtar N.; Ahlawat Y.; Singh A.; Wani A.; Panda S.; Kumar A.; Patel L.; Stevanato P.; Celletti S.
Article.Abstract: Microbial siderophores play an important role in improving plant tolerance to abiotic and biotic stresses. Beyond iron acquisition, they support plant health by regulating oxidative stress, chelating toxic metals, and mediating beneficial plant–microbe interactions. This review highlights the role of siderophore-producing microbes in mitigating salinity, drought, alkaline stress, and metal toxicity, as well as in the improvement of nutrient solubilization and uptake. It also delineates environmental and physiological factors affecting siderophore production. The review additionally explores how the microbial interactions within soil consortia moderate siderophore biosynthesis and bio-control activity. Advances in multi-omics and genome editing approaches are discussed for identifying important genes and pathways associated with siderophore-mediated stress tolerance. The mechanisms behind siderophore-mediated stress tolerance are discussed, mainly their involvement in pathogen suppression through iron competition and activation of induced systemic resistance. Furthermore, it addresses the commercialization challenges and integration of siderophore applications into precision agriculture, aligning their agricultural and environmental benefits with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

Article.Title: The Seminal Microenvironment as a Potentially Tractable Interface Between Metabolic Disease and Sperm Damage
Article.Authors: Yao Y.; Zhang X.; Li L.; Fei C.; Zhang Y.; Huang S.; Zong Y.; Zhu L.; Cao Y.; Li T.; Shao M.; Zheng Y.
Article.Abstract: Male reproductive disorders are increasingly linked to metabolic diseases, but mechanistic research remains predominantly focused on the testis. The seminal microenvironment, shaped by epididymal and accessory-gland secretions, contains metabolites, lipids, ions, cytokines, extracellular vesicles, and microbial products, and may act as a metabolically responsive post-testicular interface that continues to influence sperm after spermatogenesis. Obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and chronic inflammation can remodel this environment by disrupting secretory activity, redox homeostasis, immune signaling, and microbial ecology. These changes may converge on oxidative and inflammatory pathways, promoting membrane lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired motility and capacitation, oxidative DNA base lesions, DNA fragmentation, and potentially epigenetic alterations. Mouse studies separately report obesity-associated epididymal vesicle remodeling and RNA-dependent changes in embryonic gene expression. In this Review, we examine the regulation and metabolic remodeling of the seminal microenvironment, how these changes may translate systemic metabolic stress into sperm injury, and emerging interventions including metabolic correction, antioxidant strategies, and microbiome-targeted approaches. Overall, current evidence remains largely observational and cross-sectional, with additional technical limitations in low-biomass seminal microbiome studies. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies are therefore needed to determine whether the seminal microenvironment is a causal mediator of metabolic infertility and a clinically tractable target for mechanism-guided preconception care.

Article.Title: PCSK9 in the Immunometabolism of Type 2 Diabetes
Article.Authors: Villari P.; Labate A.
Article.Abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibition reduces cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes, while experimental studies implicate PCSK9 in immune activation, platelet function and organ-specific metabolism. Whether these mechanisms contribute clinically beyond atherogenic lipoprotein lowering remains uncertain. This critical narrative review integrates an original corpus of 108 appraised publications, with targeted additions during revision. It evaluates whether findings from different compartments and experimental perturbations can be transferred to particular treatments and clinical outcomes. Mechanistic evidence implicates receptor trafficking, intracellular cholesterol, mitochondrial stress and inflammatory signalling. Effects vary by cell type and compartment: local PCSK9 promotes injury in some models but preserves pancreatic, glomerular or cardiac function in others. Global knockout, tissue-specific deletion, extracellular antibodies and hepatic silencing are therefore distinct exposures. Human biomarker and imaging studies provide translational signals but generally cannot isolate direct effects from concomitant lipoprotein changes. Randomised antibody trials establish cardiovascular efficacy and an overall reassuring glycaemic profile, without demonstrating clinically meaningful glucose lowering. PCSK9 has broader immunometabolic functions, but the available evidence does not quantify an additional clinical benefit independent of atherogenic lipoprotein lowering. Tissue-specific mechanisms and causal mediation require further investigation.

Article.Title: Colon Effects of 7-Day Whole-Body Inhalation Exposure of Fischer 344 Rats to Emissions from First- and Second-Generation Biodiesel Fuels with and Without a Particle Filter
Article.Authors: Wilczak J.; Dziendzikowska K.; Gromadzka-Ostrowska J.; Oczkowski M.; Sapierzyński R.; Czerwińska M.; Lankoff A.
Article.Abstract: Biodiesel is projected to reduce greenhouse gas and particulate matter emissions relative to petrodiesel, but biodiesel engine emissions (DEEs) contain higher levels of nitrogen oxides, nano-sized particles, and specific oxygenated volatile organic compounds and aromatics that may increase health risks. Most research on DEE health effects has focused on respiratory, cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and reproductive outcomes, leaving a considerable knowledge gap regarding gastrointestinal effects. We therefore examined and compared the colon effects of DEE produced by combustion of first-generation B7 biofuel (7% v/v fatty acid methyl esters, FAMEs) or second-generation SHB20 biofuel (7% v/v FAME plus 13% v/v hydrotreated vegetable oils, HVOs), with or without a diesel particle filter (DPF). Male Fischer 344 rats were exposed to DEE for 7 consecutive days (6 h/day; seven exposure sessions, 42 h in total) in whole-body inhalation chambers, at measured particulate matter concentrations of 2.19 and 2.13 mg/m3 without DPF and 0.17 and 0.19 mg/m3 with DPF for B7 and SHB20, respectively. Whole-body DEE exposure induced lipid peroxidation, oxidative-stress-associated and redox-related changes, mobilisation of the antioxidant defence system, and an inflammatory-associated response in colon tissue. These colon effects were blend-specific and only partly and endpoint-dependently mitigated by DPF use, with SHB20 DEE without DPF producing the most pronounced responses.

Article.Title: Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Angiogenesis in Peripheral Artery Disease: Context-Dependent Effects in Ischemic Limbs and Atherosclerotic Plaques
Article.Authors: Tamaru Y.; Yoshioka Y.; Kikuchi S.; Ochiya T.
Article.Abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is most commonly caused by atherosclerotic arterial stenosis or occlusion, which reduces downstream tissue perfusion and causes tissue ischemia. In response to ischemia, reparative angiogenesis is activated and may support tissue perfusion recovery and skeletal muscle protection. In contrast, neovascularization within atherosclerotic plaques may promote intraplaque hemorrhage and plaque destabilization. Thus, angiogenesis has dual roles in PAD-related ischemia and atherosclerotic plaques. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane-bound particles that carry various cargo, including proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and metabolites. Through the transfer of bioactive cargo and surface-mediated signaling, EVs can modify recipient-cell functions and thereby influence angiogenic signaling. Investigation of EV-mediated communication may therefore help elucidate the mechanisms underlying angiogenic regulation in vascular disease. In addition, disease-promoting EVs may be therapeutically targeted, whereas engineered EVs may be developed as therapeutic agents or delivery platforms. Recent studies have shown that EVs regulate angiogenic responses in preclinical murine hindlimb ischemia models. However, these effects in ischemic limbs and the potential involvement of EVs in atherosclerotic plaque neovascularization have rarely been reviewed in an integrated manner. This narrative review discusses these contrasting angiogenic processes from a context-dependent perspective. Understanding this context dependency may help develop EV-based strategies that promote functional vascular repair in ischemic tissues while suppressing or normalizing pathological neovascularization in atherosclerotic plaques.
