Article.Title: Does Thymoma Plus Hypogammaglobulinemia Define Good Syndrome? A 30-Year Longitudinal Study of a Single Patient with Persistent B-Cell Preservation
Article.Authors: Iguasnia Portilla D.; Castillo Castillo I.; Franco Figueroa V.; Fernández Cabrera H.; Romero Chala S.; Sobieschi I.; Cordero H.; Fernández Pereira L.
Article.Abstract: Good syndrome is commonly diagnosed when thymoma and hypogammaglobulinemia coexist, although universally accepted diagnostic criteria are lacking. Profound B-cell lymphopenia is one of its most consistent immunological features. We describe a woman followed for 30 years in our unit whose severe antibody deficiency preceded thymoma detection by 14 years. Circulating B cells were preserved before thymectomy and throughout 16 years of subsequent follow-up, with maintained class-switched memory B cells despite persistent antibody deficiency. Her clinical course was favorable under immunoglobulin replacement, without documented major opportunistic infections. T-cell differentiation abnormalities were present despite preserved absolute counts. These findings suggest that patients currently classified as Good syndrome may represent a more heterogeneous group than traditionally assumed. Although preserved B cells do not exclude Good syndrome under existing definitions, the present observation should be considered hypothesis-generating and supports further studies evaluating potential biological heterogeneity among patients diagnosed with Good syndrome. This case highlights the need for consensus diagnostic criteria that consider the temporal relationship between both conditions, B-cell numbers, and the accompanying immune abnormalities, rather than relying on the coexistence of thymoma and hypogammaglobulinemia alone.

Article.Title: Molecular and Translational Anti-Inflammatory Strategies After Abdominal and Liver Surgery: From Immunonutrition to Cell-Based Therapies
Article.Authors: Pietrzyk B.; Pierzchała W.; Mikolajczyk J.; Lis P.; Heliasz A.; Kaczmarczyk B.
Article.Abstract: Postoperative inflammation influences recovery after abdominal and liver surgery. This narrative review critically synthesizes clinical and translational evidence on inflammation-modulating strategies using a structured search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library for publications from 2015 to 2025. Case reports, pediatric studies, and publications lacking clinical or translational relevance were excluded. Immunonutrition and early enteral nutrition are the most established approaches, with benefits for postoperative recovery and infectious complications. Perioperative corticosteroids in liver resection and short-course antibiotics following adequate source control offer procedure- and indication-specific benefits. Emerging interventions, including microbiota modulation, N-acetylcysteine, activation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2/heme oxygenase-1 signaling, and cell-based therapies, show biological promise but lack sufficient high-quality clinical evidence for routine implementation. Established strategies should be integrated into Enhanced Recovery After Surgery pathways according to patient risk and surgical context. Personalized management requires prospective validation of emerging therapies and candidate biomarkers, including interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, and heme oxygenase-1, with standardized assays and sampling schedules.

Article.Title: Arecoline Induces Testicular Injury and Impairs Spermatogenesis in Rats Through Notch Signaling-Mediated Oxidative Stress
Article.Authors: Yang Y.; Li W.; Ge P.; Lv M.; Sun Y.; Chen Q.; Zhang J.; Sun R.; Zhou D.; Liu M.
Article.Abstract: Millions of people chew areca nut to boost work efficiency and relieve stress. Areca nut contains arecoline, which adversely affects reproductive function, although the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Herein, we evaluated arecoline-mediated reproductive toxicity using Sprague–Dawley (SD) rat models and an in vitro GC-1 cell model. Molecular docking, quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR), Western blot, cell-based assays, and functional rescue experiments were used to investigate the mechanisms involved. Dose-dependent spermatogenic damage was observed in male rats receiving 50, 100 and 200 mg/kg arecoline, with reduced sperm counts and quality, higher testicular MDA and lower activity of antioxidant enzymes superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione peroxidase (GPx). Molecular docking predicted a possible interaction between arecoline and Notch1. qRT-PCR and Western blot analyses showed that the expression of Notch1 and its ligands, Jagged-1 and Dll-1, was downregulated in testicular tissues and GC-1 cells following arecoline exposure. Notch1 expression was strongly positively correlated with seminiferous tubule diameter and seminiferous epithelium height. In vitro, arecoline induced ROS accumulation, inhibited proliferation and promoted apoptosis in GC-1 cells. Rescue experiments showed that the Notch activator valproic acid, used to enhance Notch signaling, alleviated arecoline-induced toxicity, whereas Notch inhibitor FLI-06 worsened cell injury. These findings support a role for altered Notch signaling and oxidative stress in arecoline-induced spermatogenic injury and provide insight into the molecular mechanisms of its reproductive toxicity.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial ROS and Mitophagy in Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: Mechanistic Interplay and Links to Regulated Cell Death
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Cao K.; Cheng H.; Fang Z.
Article.Abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) develops through interacting mechanical, matrix, nutritional, inflammatory and age-related processes. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and mitophagy participate in some of these contexts, but current evidence does not place mitophagy failure at the start of every degenerative trajectory. Most mechanistic studies have been performed in nucleus pulposus (NP) cells. In these models, mechanical overload, inflammatory mediators and oxidant stress can depolarize mitochondria, disturb fission–fusion balance and increase mtROS. Mitophagy can limit injury when damaged cargo is selected and delivered through a competent lysosomal pathway; accumulation of pathway markers during blocked flux, or mitochondrial clearance that is not matched by renewal, need not be protective. The most extensive mechanistic literature concerns apoptosis and senescence. Evidence linking mitochondrial quality control to pyroptosis and ferroptosis is growing but remains model-dependent, whereas direct evidence for necroptosis is comparatively sparse. We use a capacity-matching framework to organize these findings around damage burden, cargo selection, lysosomal completion and mitochondrial renewal within the regional metabolic constraints of the disc. This is an interpretive framework rather than a newly identified pathway. Its purpose is to define testable conditions under which mitophagy is likely to be protective, insufficient or maladaptive, while preserving the distinction between NP-derived evidence and the more limited evidence from annulus fibrosus and cartilage endplate cells.

Article.Title: Oxysterols Are Not Functionally Equivalent: Cell-Type- and Territory-Specific Responses in Human Models of Atherosclerosis
Article.Authors: Truffin D.; Marchand F.; Chatelais M.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to compare the biological activities of major oxysterols, including 7-ketocholesterol (7KC), 7α-hydroxycholesterol (7α-HC), 7β-hydroxycholesterol (7β-HC), and 27-hydroxycholesterol (27HC), as well as oxidized LDL (oxLDL), in complementary human models representative of the atherosclerotic microenvironment: monocyte-derived macrophages (MΦs), vascular endothelial cells (v-ECs), and vascular smooth muscle cells (v-SMCs) isolated from the carotid artery and abdominal aorta. Cellular responses were strongly dependent on both cell type and vascular territory. Among the oxysterols tested, 7KC exerted the strongest biological effects, markedly reducing cell viability, increasing oxidative stress and apoptosis, promoting endothelial dysfunction, and profoundly altering lipid homeostasis pathways. Spectral Nile Red analysis further revealed distinct patterns of neutral-lipid- and phospholipid-associated fluorescence, indicating oxysterol-specific remodeling of intracellular lipid compartments. In vascular smooth muscle cells, 7KC was associated with increased CD36 expression and reduced ABCA1/ABCG1-mediated cholesterol efflux, whereas macrophages responded predominantly through SREBP1- and NR1H4-associated metabolic reprogramming rather than enhanced lipid uptake. In contrast, oxLDL was the strongest inducer of neutral lipid accumulation and classical foam-cell formation in macrophages. Although 27HC increased intracellular 7KC levels, it induced comparatively limited effects on viability, oxidative stress, and macrophage functions. Moreover, oxLDL promoted a distinct macrophage activation state and altered polarization trajectories depending on the timing of exposure. These findings demonstrate that major oxysterols exert distinct and complementary biological effects across vascular and immune cell populations, highlighting their differential contribution to atherosclerotic plaque development and progression, and support the development of therapeutic approaches targeting multiple oxysterol species rather than a single oxidized cholesterol derivative.

Article.Title: Identification of Novel Plasma Protein Biomarkers for Early Clinical Stage Colorectal Carcinoma by High-Throughput Proteomics
Article.Authors: Yin G.; Chen Z.; Feng G.; Lu J.; Jiao C.; Zhu Z.; Liu L.; Xu C.
Article.Abstract: Early detection is critical for improving survival in colorectal carcinoma (CRC), underscoring the need for reliable early-stage biomarkers. Plasma protein biomarkers may support the detection of early-stage CRC. In this study, we profiled plasma from 24 patients with stages I–III CRC and 10 non-tumor participants, together with paired tumor and distant-normal tissues from the patients with CRC, to identify proteins preferentially elevated in stage I disease. Seven plasma proteins had higher abundance in stage I CRC than in stages II and III CRC and non-tumor participants; three of these proteins, HSPA8, ALDOA, and PDLIM1, were also elevated in stage I tumor tissues. In the discovery comparison of stage I CRC with non-tumor participants, HSPA8 alone achieved an internally cross-validated random forest classification accuracy of 88.9%, matching the three-protein model. Tissue upregulation was further supported by Western blotting. ELISA assessment included 32 participants with matched proteomic measurements and was subsequently expanded to 108 participants. The HSPA8-score was calculated by dividing the dilution-corrected HSPA8 concentration by the total protein amount in 10 μL of plasma. In the expanded cohort, random forest classification using this score achieved internally cross-validated accuracies of 74.47% for stage I versus stages II–IV CRC and 56.67% for stage I CRC versus non-tumor participants. The corresponding exploratory reference cutoffs were 0.066 and 0.029. These findings identify HSPA8 as a potential plasma protein biomarker for stage I CRC detection.

Article.Title: Host Ubiquitin-Specific Proteases Regulate All Stages of Herpesvirus Infection
Article.Authors: Maarouf M.; Peterson C.; Mohni K.
Article.Abstract: Herpesviruses are a large group of double-stranded-DNA viruses that replicate their genomes in the nucleus, forming large replication compartments during lytic infection. Herpesviruses are known to modulate host DNA replication and DNA damage-repair proteins to promote their replication. Ubiquitination is a cellular process that can alter protein stability, localization, and availability, including that of multiple proteins involved in genome maintenance. Ubiquitin-specific proteases (USPs) are a class of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) that counter this process by removing ubiquitin chains, thus acting as another level of regulation. Proteins from each of the three herpesvirus subfamilies (alpha-, beta-, and gammaherpesviruses) have been reported to interact with at least one host USP, and USP7 in particular is reported as a target in representatives of all three subfamilies. In this review, we give an up-to-date summary of herpesviruses–USPs interactions, with special emphasis on DNA replication, and how these interactions could shape infection outcomes. We also examine published proteomic datasets for herpesvirus-driven host-proteome modulation and offer a framework for future directions to prioritize potentially important, understudied USPs. Lastly, we visit herpesvirus-encoded DUBs and highlight their roles in viral replication by remodeling ubiquitin signaling, discussing viral DUBs and virus–USP interfaces as proposed antiviral targets.

Article.Title: Genetically Predicted Blood DNA Methylation Reveals Putative Regulatory Signals Associated with ALS Risk
Article.Authors: Zhao T.; Hoffman M.; Wu G.; Belzil V.
Article.Abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder whose genetic architecture and molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood, particularly in sporadic disease. To investigate whether genetically regulated DNA methylation may help interpret ALS susceptibility, we conducted a methylome-wide association study of genetically predicted blood methylation using the PrediXcan framework. Using S-PrediXcan, we evaluated 192,378 unique CpG sites. At nominal p < 0.05, 3741 CpGs were associated with ALS risk using ARIES models and 13,127 using Understanding Society models. After Bonferroni correction, 25 CpGs across eight genomic regions remained significant, including signals near established ALS and ALS–frontotemporal dementia loci (C9orf72, TBK1, SCFD1, and MOB3B). Three CpGs mapped to WHAMM at 15q25.2, a region not previously implicated by ALS GWAS. Predicted methylation was positively associated with risk at 18 CpGs and inversely associated at seven. Complementary whole-blood transcriptome-wide association analysis identified 11 significant genes, including C9orf72. Together, these findings prioritize regulatory candidates for functional investigation without establishing that methylation changes cause ALS.

Patients with metastases in two or more organs had more detectable oncogenic alterations than those with one metastatic site (median, three versus two; adjusted q = 0.00184; rank-biserial correlation = 0.687). Article.Title: Molecular Dynamics Simulations Reveal a Broadly Open Solution Ensemble for the DNA Holliday Junction: Mg2+ Crossover Bridging and Weak Force-Field Sensitivity
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhou Y.
Article.Abstract: Holliday junctions, four-way DNA crossovers central to DNA origami and key intermediates of homologous recombination, must be accurately modeled for rational DNA-nanodevice design, yet their solution conformational ensemble remains incompletely characterized. We characterize this ensemble for the experimental junction d(TCGGTACCGA)4 by all-atom molecular dynamics, comparing the AMBER force fields parmbsc1, OL21, and OL24 in OPC water with matched ionic conditions. In every force field, the junction explores a broad, nearly flat inter-arm-angle landscape, with <1 kcal/mol variation across inter-arm angles of 2–90°: the open state is favored by 0.45–0.63 kcal/mol, the crystallographic-like inter-arm angle occurs in 2–5% of frames, and the crossover remains coaxially stacked whether open or compact. A Mg2+ ion occupies the crossover pocket in 92–94% of frames, specifically bridging the A- and C-strand phosphates (Li–Merz CM Mg2+ set). Stacking-isomer exchange between the A/C-continuous and crystallographic B/D isomers proceeds at ~0.5 ns−1 in this minimal short-arm construct, independent of force field, with A/C-continuous favored ~2:1. parmbsc1 yields a more open junction than OL21 and OL24, which reproduce the crystallographic inter-arm angle of 39–43°; the sugar-pucker shift targeted in OL24 is also visible at the junction. These results establish a force-field-robust baseline for simulation-guided design of crossover-containing nanostructures.

Article.Title: Integrative Single-Cell and Radiomics Analyses Identify N-Acetylneuraminate Synthase (NANS)-High Signature Associated with Adverse Prognosis and Immune Remodeling in Glioblastoma
Article.Authors: Chen J.; Wu Q.; Cardenas H.; Bernard K.; Berglund A.; Sun Y.; Macaulay R.; Mulé J.; Etame A.
Article.Abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by marked heterogeneity and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Cell–cell communication analysis revealed enhanced outgoing signaling toward malignant tumor states and T-cell subsets, with LGALS9-centered interactions representing the dominant differential communication program. MRI radiomics may noninvasively predict this NANS-high BMDM state, supporting imaging-based risk stratification and therapeutic selection.

Article.Title: RyR2 Gain-of-Function Increases Ca2+ Spark and Ca2+ Wave Activity in Vascular Smooth Muscle Cells
Article.Authors: Alves D.; Zhai Q.; Lu L.; Chu Z.; Tsvetkov D.; Chen S.; Gollasch M.; Kassmann M.
Article.Abstract: Ca2+ sparks in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) regulate vascular function, and their dysregulation with ageing may contribute to vascular disease. However, it is still unclear which RyR isoform (RyR1, RyR2, or RyR3) primarily drives these Ca2+ signals in arterial VSMCs, as all three are present. VSMCs from young RyR2R4496C mice exhibited a significantly higher frequency of Ca2+ sparks and a greater percentage of cells displaying Ca2+ sparks and propagating Ca2+ waves compared with controls. The RyR2R4496C mutation enhanced RyR2 sensitivity to caffeine, resulting in larger increases in intracellular [Ca2+]i and arterial contractions in older mice. These findings demonstrate that RyR2 gain-of-function increases Ca2+ spark and Ca2+ wave activity in VSMCs, supporting a role for RyR2 in the regulation of local and propagating Ca2+ signals. Dysregulated RyR2 activity may therefore contribute to altered vascular Ca2+ signaling and could represent a potential mechanistic link to vascular dysfunction associated with ageing and metabolic stress.

Article.Authors: Lee C.; Park S.; Lee G.; Moon H.; Choi J.; Lee J.; Martinez-Sobrido L.; Almazán F.; Ryu E.; Baek Y.; Park J.

Relative LD intensity strongly correlated with viral intensity in both models (Pearson r = 0.951 and 0.956, respectively; both p < 0.0001). These findings demonstrate that concurrent pharmacological modulation of host lipid metabolism exerts synergistic anti-ZIKV effects, highlighting highly curated transcriptomic repurposing as a mechanistic prioritization strategy for host-directed antiviral discovery.

Article.Title: A Tailored Sequencing Approach for Identifying SARS-CoV-2 Variants in Challenging Samples from Mink
Article.Authors: Giza A.; Iwan E.; Bomba A.; Orłowska A.; Smreczak M.; Pietruk M.; Chudzik A.; Olejnik M.; Domańska-Blicharz K.
Article.Abstract: High-throughput sequencing (HTS) is an essential tool for genomic surveillance of infectious agents, including SARS-CoV-2 in farmed mink. In this study, six mink-origin SARS-CoV-2-positive samples were sequenced using two hybrid-capture methods (commercial and custom) and a shotgun metagenomic approach. All methods consistently identified SARS-CoV-2 variants. The metagenomic approach yielded the lowest mapping rate (up to 0.35%), breadth of coverage (97–100%), depth of coverage (9–932×), and mean mapq (30–59), and one sequence did not meet the quality criteria. In contrast, both hybrid-capture methods achieved higher mapping rates (47–99%), breadth of coverage (99.9–100%), and depth of coverage (508–115,846×). The custom hybrid-capture approach was selected because of its superior coverage uniformity, the lowest number of ambiguous bases (N), adjustability to low RNA levels and degraded material, and streamlined laboratory workflow. To further evaluate its applicability, it was applied to 35 clinical samples collected as part of routine genomic surveillance. This method generated sequencing data with high mapping rates (median 95%), depth of coverage (median 13,238×), breadth of coverage (median 100%), and mean mapq (median 60). These findings demonstrate that the custom hybrid-capture approach is a useful tool for genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 in mink-origin samples.

Article.Title: Computational Discovery of Plant-Derived Peptides with Therapeutic Potential: A Scoping Review
Article.Authors: Maphumulo S.; Mpofana N.; Ojewole E.
Article.Abstract: Computational methods are increasingly applied to the discovery of plant-derived peptides, but the extent, composition and reporting practice of this literature have not been mapped. Following PRISMA-ScR and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect and PubMed were searched for records published between 2021 and 2026. Of 5062 unique records, 593 were screened at title and abstract, 88 full texts were assessed, 80 sources met all five eligibility criteria and 79 were charted. Overall, 49 (62.0%) were primary studies, 12 (15.2%) described a tool or database and 18 (22.8%) were narrative reviews. Antimicrobial peptides were the commonest class (33, 41.8%), followed by antioxidant (21, 26.6%) and ACE-inhibitory peptides (18, 22.8%). Only 11 sources (13.9%) trained and evaluated a model of their own, whereas 23 (29.1%) combined prediction with molecular docking. Of 61 empirical sources, 14 (23.0%) reported at least one quantitative prediction-task performance figure and 13 (21.3%) benchmarked a named comparator; the metrics used were not mutually comparable. Moreover, 18 of 62 applicable sources (29.0%) confirmed their own prediction experimentally; 70 (88.6%) named a plant source, most often Arabidopsis thaliana; and 8 (10.1%) linked their material to documented traditional medicine. No source applied machine learning to African plant peptides, an absence within the literature sampled rather than proof that none exists.

Article.Title: Real-Time Automated Fluorescence Imaging Assay for Quantifying GFP-Expressing Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis
Article.Authors: Badia-Bringué G.; Prado-López A.; Alonso-Hearn M.
Article.Abstract: Measurement of Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) load within macrophages using a mycobacterial growth inhibition assay (MGIA) is an accurate indicator of host immune control of MAP infection. Real-time fluorescent microscopy allows the continuous analysis of infected cells and the quantification of fluorescence intensity, which directly correlates with concentration of fluorescent bacteria. The objective of this study was to develop an automated and real-time live-cell imaging assay using the IncuCyte SX1® platform for quantifying green fluorescence protein (GFP)-expressing MAP (MAP-GFP) within infected macrophages. The fluorescence of serially diluted free MAP-GFP was quantified using the IncuCyte SX1® demonstrating that the fluorescence signal of 3 × 107 CFU was significantly different from lowest MAP concentrations. Significant differences between uninfected and infected BOMAC cells (MOI; 1:10) in DMEM-F12, DMEM-F12 supplemented with fetal bovine serum (FBS), and RPMI-1640 supplemented with FBS were observed, indicating the suitability of these culture media for measuring MAP-GFP-host cell interaction in the IncuCyte SX1®. For the optimization of the MOI and cell density, bovine monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and the BOMAC cells were seeded at different cell densities and infected with MAP-GFP at different MOIs. After 2 h of infection, the supernatant was removed, the cells were washed three times with HBSS, and fresh RPMI-1640 supplemented with FBS was added to the cells. Then, the fluorescence was quantified in the IncuCyte SX1® at different times p.i. Our results demonstrated that MAP phagocytosis is pathogen number- and cell density-dependent. Overall, the results showed that infection of 1 × 106 cells at an MOI of 1:10 maintained a stable fluorescence signal of approximately 400 to 500 GCU ⋅ μm2/image across 2 h to 4 days p.i. In addition, good correlations between MAP-GFP (logCFUs) estimated in the BACTEC MGIT™ 960 system and fluorescence intensity measured in the IncuCyte SX1® were observed for free MAP-GFP bacilli and from MAP-GFP within infected BOMAC cells, r = 0.79 and r = 0.78, respectively. In conclusion, real-time fluorescent microscopy enables continuous monitoring of MAP-GFP within infected macrophages.

Article.Title: Preliminary Evaluation of the Anticancer Activity of a PGK1 Small Molecule Inhibitor in Ishikawa Endometrial Cancer
Article.Authors: Cao H.; Xue S.; Xue M.; Li F.; Feng L.; Zheng W.; Ding H.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: To investigate the roles of a phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) small-molecule inhibitor in Ishikawa endometrial cancer. The expression levels of PGK1 in cancer cells treated with various concentrations of the PGK1 small molecule inhibitor at 48 h and 72 h were determined via Western blotting. Xenograft mouse models were established through subcutaneous tumor transplantation, and immunofluorescence analysis of PGK1 and apoptosis in tumor tissue was performed. The results of the cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay revealed that NG52 inhibited the activity of human endometrial carcinoma Ishikawa, HEC-1-A, and HEC-1-B cells in a concentration-dependent manner. Moreover, NG52 significantly reduced the migration ability of the Ishikawa cell line in a dose-dependent manner. Flow cytometry (FCM) demonstrated that NG52 affected the survival of endometrial carcinoma cells by arresting the cell cycle at the G1 phase and inducing apoptosis in a dose-dependent manner. Western blot analysis also revealed that the apoptosis-inducing effects of NG52 were accompanied by a reduction in PGK1 expression after 48 h and 72 h of NG52 treatment. Moreover, NG52 partially suppressed tumor growth in a human Ishikawa xenograft model, and transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) showed an increasing trend of NG52-treated tumor tissue apoptosis, with a decreasing trend in PGK1 expression in the treatment group. NG52, a PGK1 small molecule inhibitor, can serve as a structural basis for developing potential anti-endometrial carcinoma agents. Article.Title: Evaluation of Dihydropyridine Derivatives as Aldose Reductase Inhibitors: Enzymatic Screening, Molecular Docking and Ex Vivo Assessment of a Selected Compound in a Lens Model
Article.Authors: Alonso-Hurtado K.; Méndez-Pérez T.; Hernández-Gallegos Z.; Cajero-Juárez M.; Navarro-Santos P.; Virgen-Ortíz J.; Martínez-Pacheco M.
Article.Abstract: Aldose reductase (AR) is a key enzyme in the polyol pathway and has been widely implicated in the development of diabetic complications, including cataract formation. Treatment reduced glucose-induced lens opacity by 89.1%, estimated by image-based analysis, and decreased sorbitol accumulation by 57.48% relative to hyperglycemic control, indicating modulation of the polyol pathway at the tissue level. In contrast, no significant changes were detected in calcium content. These findings support the potential of DHP derivatives as a scaffold for aldose reductase inhibition and highlight their ability to attenuate early alterations associated with hyperglycemia in lens tissue. Article.Title: Ovariectomy Exacerbates Chronic Constriction Injury-Induced Neuropathic Pain Through Dysregulation of Spinal Estrogen Receptor Balance in Rats
Article.Authors: Chan Y.; Lin S.; Huang C.; Zheng T.; Wang Y.; Tsai Y.
Article.Abstract: Estrogen depletion after menopause has been associated with altered pain sensitivity; however, the spinal mechanisms linking estrogen deficiency to neuropathic pain remain incompletely understood. Female Sprague Dawley rats underwent OVX or sham surgery, followed 5 weeks later by median nerve CCI or sham CCI. Mechanical withdrawal thresholds and thermal withdrawal latencies were evaluated using von Frey filaments and the plantar test, respectively. ERα and ERβ expression in the spinal dorsal horn was assessed via immunofluorescence staining and Western blotting. Rats in the OVX/CCI group exhibited more pronounced pain behaviors than those in the Sham/CCI group, indicating that OVX exacerbated CCI-induced neuropathic pain. In the spinal dorsal horn, ERα expression was increased in the OVX/Sham, Sham/CCI, and OVX/CCI groups, with the greatest increase observed in the OVX/CCI group. In contrast, ERβ expression was decreased in the Sham/CCI and OVX/CCI groups, with no significant difference between these groups. These findings suggest that OVX-induced estrogen depletion exacerbates CCI-induced neuropathic pain, potentially through a shift toward ERα-dominant signaling relative to ERβ in the spinal dorsal horn. Article.Title: Vitamin K2 and Cardiovascular Calcification: Mechanistic Foundations, Conflicting Clinical Evidence, and Unresolved Questions
Article.Authors: Kothari C.; Chowdhary R.; Babazade S.; Egoavil A.; Abuirmaileh W.; Kapadia S.; Wimalawansa S.
Article.Abstract: Cardiovascular calcification is an active, complex process involving osteogenic transformation, inflammation, extracellular vesicle release, and impaired mineral buffering. These changes result from mineral imbalance and reduced levels of calcification inhibitors. Vitamin K supports the γ-carboxylation of matrix Gla protein (MGP) and other mineralization inhibitors, though some calcification defenses do not depend on vitamin K. Vitamin K deficiency and warfarin therapy increase circulating dephosphorylated-uncarboxylated MGP (dp-ucMGP), which is linked to greater vascular calcification. Preclinical studies demonstrate that disruption of the vitamin K-MGP axis promotes calcification. Supplementation with vitamin K1 or K2 can reduce, prevent, or partially reverse mineralization in certain animal models. In contrast, evidence from human studies is less consistent. Observational studies have identified an association between menaquinone (vitamin K2) intake and cardiovascular outcomes, but causality has not been established. Most randomized trials have shown neutral results for aortic-valve and chronic kidney disease-associated calcification, while the VitaK-CAC and DANCODE studies reported slower progression of coronary artery calcium in selected populations with moderate or severe baseline coronary calcification. These discrepancies may be due to differences in calcification phenotypes, disease stage, vitamin K forms, dosing regimens, vitamin D status, renal function, and response to vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin. Coronary intimal, valvular, and arterial medial calcification should be regarded as phenotypically distinct entities. This review evaluates the mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence linking vitamin K2 to cardiovascular calcification and highlights population groups that warrant further clinical investigation. Large, adequately powered, and phenotype-specific clinical trials are needed to determine whether appropriately dosed vitamin K2 is a safe and cost-effective intervention for slowing valvular and vascular calcification.

Article.Title: Conserved Hepatospora eriocheir Sequences in Chinese Mitten Crabs from Poland, Germany and Belgium: A Comparative Molecular Study
Article.Authors: Stachnik M.; Normant-Saremba M.; Ewers C.; Keirsebelik H.; Schoelynck J.

The study provides the first specimen-linked, sequence-confirmed molecular characterisation of infections in the sampled German and Belgian crab populations, together with new Polish infections from 2022 and a comparative two-locus reference dataset. The repeated Baltic detection, combined with shared Polish–German host COI haplotypes and existing evidence of North Sea–Baltic connectivity, is consistent with the arrival of infected migrating crabs, although the parasite’s precise source remains unresolved.

Article.Title: Biomodulators and Skin Boosters in Skin Rejuvenation: Mechanisms, Applications, and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Ding Z.; Jin C.; Ming H.; Shim J.; Huy V.; Chien P.; Heo C.
Article.Abstract: Biomodulators and skin boosters comprise heterogeneous preparations whose biological activity and clinical effects require separate evaluation. This structured narrative review distinguishes mechanistic plausibility from human comparative findings for skin aging, skin quality, and atrophic acne scars. Risk-of-bias assessments classified 123 results as High and 36 as Some concerns; none was Low overall. Selected formulations and procedure-assisted regimens showed benefits for particular outcomes, whereas other comparisons were null or discordant. Hydration, tissue remodeling, clinical appearance, and patient satisfaction were treated as distinct outcomes. Retrospective result selection, heterogeneous interventions and outcomes, four access-unresolved reports, and the absence of a prospective protocol constrain confidence. Clinical claims should remain specific to the product, protocol, indication, comparator, and outcome investigated.

Furthermore, the −1012 bp proHSPII fragment retained an inducible GUS expression under heat, drought, and combined heat and drought stress conditions. Article.Title: Pyrrolocytosine as a Fluorescent Sensor of RNA–Small Molecule Interactions
Article.Authors: Coulson T.; Valdez G.; Widom J.
Article.Abstract: Fluorescent base analogues have proven to be valuable probes of RNA structure. We utilized complementary fluorescence spectroscopy methods to understand the functional impacts and ligand sensitivity of pC substitutions distal to and within the binding pocket. When placed in the ligand binding pocket, pC exhibits a moderately decreased affinity for the ligands guanine (G) and hypoxanthine (Hx) while maintaining high specificity for G. We found that pC behaves as a turn-off sensor, with distinct changes in fluorescence upon G or Hx binding. These differences are dependent on the number of hydrogen bonds formed with pC and are resolvable in both time-dependent and steady-state fluorescence measurements. Our results show that pC can be used to study RNA–small molecule interactions and can discriminate between similar ligands even when they have identical binding modes.

Article.Title: From Oxyntomodulin to Retatrutide: A Translational Review of Metabolic Polyagonism
Article.Authors: Saldívar-Cerón H.; Maldonado-Trejo D.; Chavez-Castañeda Q.; Mercado-Guzmán A.; León-Barrita A.; López-García I.; Hernández-Solís A.; Ramírez-Mendoza A.; Terrazas-Delgado D.; Castañeda-Ramírez A.; Quiñones-Lara E.; Jay-Jímenez B.; Pozo-Molina G.; León-Cabrera S.
Article.Abstract: Oxyntomodulin (OXM), an endogenous proglucagon-derived peptide with dual glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and glucagon receptor (GCGR) agonism, provides a physiological precedent for contemporary multi-receptor pharmacology. Recognition that GCGR signaling regulates not only hepatic glucose production but also amino acid turnover, lipid metabolism, substrate oxidation, and energy expenditure prompted the development of engineered GLP-1R/GCGR co-agonists, including cotadutide, mazdutide, survodutide, and pemvidutide. Retatrutide extends this strategy by integrating GIPR, GLP-1R, and GCGR agonism within a single long-acting peptide and has produced substantial improvements in body weight, glycemic control, and cardiometabolic parameters in phase 2 and phase 3 trials. This review examines the evolutionary and structural relationships of the proglucagon–Class B1 GPCR system, OXM biosynthesis and receptor pharmacology, the mechanistic rationale for therapeutic GCGR agonism, and the molecular and clinical development of dual and triple agonists. We further address receptor balance, the GIPR agonism–antagonism paradox, receptor-specific causal attribution, and the unresolved limitations of translating molecular pharmacology into durable clinical benefit. Finally, we propose an Activity–Exposure–Context framework for interpreting polyagonist pharmacology and discuss prospective enteroinsular phenotyping using standardized mixed-meal testing as a testable strategy to investigate interindividual variability in therapeutic response.

Article.Title: ssDNA Wrapping of Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes and the Role of Sequence Periodicity: A Critical Review
Article.Authors: Al Nissafi L.; Emjeida M.; Venkatesan R.; Vetcher A.
Article.Abstract: Noncovalent hybrids of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are central to chiral sorting and near-infrared biosensing, yet no quantitative rule connects the periodicity of a natural sequence to the geometry of a given nanotube. Earlier reviews treat the sequence as a tool for sorting or sensing; this critical review asks what the published evidence up to 2026 establishes about periodicity. We compare base–wall affinities from calculation, calorimetry and force spectroscopy; the periods reported by cryo-electron microscopy, scanning tunnelling microscopy, atomic force microscopy (AFM) and X-ray scattering in solution; the recognition sequences used for single-chirality sorting; and the few studies of genomic DNA. The experimental order of base affinities depends on the method and on whether the surface is flat or curved. Helical pitches of 1.6–3.3 nm, spacings of 8.6–14.3 nm between strands in solution and the AFM period of about 14 nm are different quantities. Recognition depends on sequence pattern, length, chiral angle and handedness in addition to diameter. To our knowledge, base spacing at fixed composition has been varied only in covalently cross-linked hybrids; for noncovalent wrapping, this test is still missing. We outline the next experiments and the reporting standards and open data they require.

Article.Title: Hormone-Mediated Signaling of Reactive Oxygen Species Under Abiotic Stress
Article.Authors: Fedoreyeva L.; Bursakov S.; Molchanova T.; Muratova O.; Zakharova E.
Article.Abstract: Abiotic stresses trigger the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in various subcellular compartments of plant cells, where they perform a dual function: acting as cytotoxic agents during acute stress and as highly specific signaling modulators under mild or chronic stress. However, the fundamental question of how the cell distinguishes between toxic and signaling ROS pools—and how phytohormones coordinate this distinction—remains unresolved. This review re-examines the molecular logic of the hormone-redox interface, focusing on the post-translational modifications of NADPH oxidases (RBOHs) and antioxidant enzymes as a key mechanism for the rapid tuning of signals. Moving beyond traditional linear cascade models, we propose the concept of a “dynamic hormonal code,” in which abscisic acid acts as the primary initiator of apoplastic ROS bursts via SnRK2-dependent phosphorylation, while salicylates and jasmonates modulate the duration and amplitude of these bursts, thereby determining the outcome—ranging from programmed cell death to systemic resistance. Known mechanisms of the hormonal code have been established (e.g., ABA → SnRK2 → RBOH; SA/JA antagonism mediated by NPR1; and the redox relay involving PRXIIB/GPX3 → ABI2). This review goes beyond simple hormone combinatorics by proposing a conceptual framework: the hormonal code encodes ROS signals through parameters of time, amplitude, and cellular compartment. Particular attention is paid to recent discoveries regarding the roles of auxin and brassinosteroids in reconfiguring chloroplast redox homeostasis during flooding and heat shock. Generalizing these data, we propose an integrated model of spatiotemporal regulation that explains how feedback loops involving ROS, Ca2+ waves, and hormone receptors facilitate systemic acclimation. Thus, targeting key crosstalk nodes—specifically SnRK2 and TOR kinase complexes—offers new strategies for engineering stress-resilient crops in the face of climate change.

Article.Title: Exercise Modalities, Training Dose, and Circulating Myostatin and Follistatin in Adults: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Qiao C.; Yang C.; Guo S.; Yang S.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Exercise-associated changes in circulating myostatin (MSTN) and follistatin (FST) across training modalities remain uncertain. Seven bibliographic databases were searched for controlled exercise interventions lasting at least four weeks in adults (PROSPERO CRD420261492548). Multilevel random-effects models used study-clustered CR2 inference. Renewed retrieval enabled assessment of 203 of 220 reports. The review included 79 reports from 78 study families; 39 studies contributed primary effects. Exercise was associated with lower MSTN (57 effects; 33 studies; Hedges’ g = 1.25, 95% CI 0.68–1.82) and higher FST (42 effects; 23 studies; g = 1.58, 95% CI 0.92–2.23). Heterogeneity remained high and reference-model prediction intervals crossed zero. Excluding extreme effects attenuated the pooled magnitudes. Graph-exclusion and leave-one-study-out analyses retained positive average-effect intervals. Exploratory modality and dose analyses did not establish superiority or an optimal prescription. GRADE certainty was low for both outcomes. Exercise may alter circulating MSTN and FST, but assay differences, retrieval restrictions and heterogeneous protocols limit interpretation. These findings do not establish a confirmed intracellular mechanism or validated clinical surrogate endpoint.

Article.Title: 2B9-Fc Ameliorates Immune Thrombocytopenia by Suppressing STAT1-Mediated M1 Macrophage Polarization and Expanding Regulatory T Cells
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Xing S.; Shen X.; Zhu W.; Ge M.; Xiao H.; Yu K.; Yu Z.
Article.Abstract: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune bleeding disorder in which enhanced platelet destruction and impaired platelet production coexist, and a substantial proportion of patients remain refractory to available therapies. Here, we evaluated 2B9-Fc, a thrombopoietin (TPO) mimetic peptide engineered from a cyclic peptide with high affinity for both human and mouse c-MPL, in passive (anti-CD41 monoclonal antibody R300) and active (guinea pig anti-mouse platelet serum, GP-APS) immunization male C57BL/6J and humanized c-MPL receptor transgenic mouse models of ITP. 2B9-Fc (500 μg/kg, subcutaneously) significantly elevated peripheral platelet counts in both models (p < 0.01), without affecting WBC, RBC, or hemoglobin, and alleviated skin purpura and bleeding scores in the active model. In addition, 2B9-Fc treatment was associated with a reduced splenic M1/M2 macrophage ratio, increased regulatory T cells (Tregs), downregulated IL-6 and iNOS while upregulating TGF-β1 and Foxp3, and suppressed STAT1 phosphorylation. In humanized c-MPL receptor transgenic (MT) mice, 2B9-Fc promoted CD41+ megakaryocyte generation in vitro and sustained platelet recovery in vivo through day 14. These results indicate that 2B9-Fc ameliorates ITP and is associated with promotion of megakaryocyte maturation and restoration of immune tolerance, likely involving inhibition of STAT1-mediated M1 polarization and Treg expansion, supporting its potential for clinical translation.

Article.Title: Raffinose in Brassica Crops: Integrating Plant Stress Physiology, Food Quality, Nutrition and Precision Breeding
Article.Authors: Czernicka M.; Czernicka M.
Article.Abstract: Raffinose-family oligosaccharides (RFOs) have nutritional and physiological significance that cannot be inferred from concentration alone. In Brassica, interpretation of their food value and definition of breeding targets require consideration of edible organ, environmental history, analytical resolution, and intended use. This critical review integrates evidence on RFO composition, plant physiology, food quality, and nutrition with an evidence-weighted assessment of conventional breeding, genetic transformation, and new genomic techniques. Direct Brassica experiments are distinguished from evidence derived from soybean and Arabidopsis and from prospective applications. Direct studies demonstrate that RFO metabolism in Brassica is manipulable, but they do not support a universal strategy for improving vegetable or meal quality. Genome-editing studies in soybean further show that reductions in total RFOs may coexist with increased raffinose and that lower RFO concentrations do not themselves demonstrate nutritional benefit. Tissue-specific regulation may offer a route to balance seed composition with stress responses, although genotype-dependent regeneration remains an important constraint. A three-tier framework is therefore proposed in which raffinose is interpreted as a stress-responsive metabolite, a potential food-quality indicator, and a context-dependent nutritional component. Compound-specific phenotyping, functional validation, and product-relevant physiological testing should precede deployment of low-RFO or stress-responsive Brassica material.

Article.Title: Functional Characterization of Glycosyltransferases from Saussurea involucrata Involved in Rutin Biosynthesis
Article.Authors: Yi P.; Huang B.; Zhan R.; Ma D.
Article.Abstract: Saussurea involucrata is a medicinal plant rich in flavonoids, but the glycosyltransferases (GTs) responsible for flavonoid glycosylation in this species remain largely uncharacterized. Here, five GT genes (SiUGT03, SiUGT09, SiUGT60, SiRhaT68-1, and SiRhaT68-2) were identified. Four of the five proteins (SiUGT03, SiUGT09, SiUGT60, and SiRhaT68-1) possessed an intact PSPG-box, and phylogenetic analysis placed SiUGT03 in the 3GT clade and SiRhaT68-1 in the 1,6GT clade. Recombinant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli as soluble maltose-binding protein (MBP) fusions and purified. In vitro enzymatic assays showed that SiUGT03 catalyzed the 3-O-glucosylation of quercetin to isoquercetin (quercetin-3-O-glucoside), whereas SiRhaT68-1 catalyzed the 1,6-rhamnosylation of isoquercetin to rutin. Among the substrates tested, SiUGT03 was active only toward the flavonols quercetin and kaempferol, while SiRhaT68-1 was active toward isoquercetin and one of the four tested flavone 7-O-glucosides, diosmetin-7-O-glucoside. Kinetic analysis revealed an apparent difference in catalytic efficiency between the two enzymes under the conditions tested (SiUGT03: Km = 36.08 μM, kcat/Km = 0.01983 μM−1·s−1; SiRhaT68-1: Km = 184.70 μM, kcat/Km = 0.0005755 μM−1·s−1); however, since the Km of SiRhaT68-1 was close to the highest substrate concentration tested, this difference should be regarded as preliminary. These results, obtained from separate in vitro assays, demonstrated that the two enzymes catalyze two consecutive terminal glycosylation steps of rutin biosynthesis and represent promising candidates for further exploration of rutin biosynthesis in S. involucrata.

Article.Title: Fluorophore-Conjugated Diphenylalanine Peptides Reveal Self-Sorting in a Multicomponent Supramolecular System
Article.Authors: Dan Y.; Shelef O.; Buzhor M.; Shimon L.; Satchi-Fainaro R.; Shabat D.; Adler-Abramovich L.
Article.Abstract: The interplay between distinct molecular building blocks in multicomponent supramolecular systems can lead to co-assembly or self-sorting, yet distinguishing between these modes of organization remains challenging. These findings establish fluorophore-conjugated short peptides as intrinsically traceable building blocks for investigating multicomponent supramolecular organization, while highlighting that fluorophore conjugation can simultaneously enable visualization and influence the assembly.

Article.Title: Targeted Regulation and Treatment Application of Liquid–Liquid Phase Separation in Human Diseases
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Xu Q.; Liu Y.; Yao K.; Chen N.; Sui G.; Li D.; Zheng J.
Article.Abstract: Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) is widely recognized as a fundamental mechanism underlying the formation of membraneless organelles, which are critical for maintaining spatiotemporal precision in cellular function. Dysregulation of LLPS has become increasingly recognized as a key driver underlying the development of multiple human diseases, thereby establishing this process as a rapidly growing focus in biomedical research. In this review, we examine the contributions of LLPS to cellular pathophysiology. We start by outlining the fundamental biophysical and molecular principles that govern LLPS formation. We further explore how aberrant phase transitions contribute to disease mechanisms across different organ systems. Building on this mechanistic framework, we assess current and potential therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting LLPS for clinical intervention. Overall, this review aims to synthesize current understanding of LLPS in disease etiology and to highlight its potential as a novel target for future therapeutic development.

Article.Title: The Impact of Intratumoral Bacterial Response to Vaccine Therapy in Cancer Treatment
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Sun Z.; Qi H.; Zhao D.; Xing X.; Jiang J.; Gao T.
Article.Abstract: Therapeutic Human papillomavirus (HPVs) vaccines are designed to enhance the immunogenicity of HPV and promote the elimination of tumor cells effectively. Mounting evidence implies that tumor-resident microbiomes may influence therapeutic outcomes through immune modulation. In this study, we evaluated whether the intratumoral microbiota affects the efficacy of the therapeutic HPV vaccine. We analyzed RNA sequencing data from tumor tissues of C57BL/6N female mice treated with a DNA vaccine incorporating HPV16 E6/E7 antigens fused with the chemokine CCL11. Microbial community data were acquired using the PathSeq bioinformatics pipeline. Alpha diversity was estimated using the Shannon index and the number of observed taxonomic features, while beta diversity was assessed via principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on Bray–Curtis distance. Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) analysis was performed to identify differentially abundant microbial taxa. Immune cell infiltration was characterized using the xCell deconvolution method. The analysis revealed significant divergence in both the alpha- and beta-diversity metrics of intratumoral microbiota, associated with treatment responsiveness. Vaccinated groups exhibited enriched abundances of the phyla Proteobacteria, together with a concomitant reduction in Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, and were associated with a positive response to cancer immunotherapy. Additionally, intratumoral microbiome composition and diversity correlated with the increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells, natural killer T (NKT) cells, and myeloid cells. This study identifies intratumoral microbiota remodeling as a key feature of therapeutic HPV vaccine response. The observed coordination between bacterial signatures and immune cell infiltration is associative and raises the hypothesis that intratumoral bacteria may modulate, rather than drive, antitumor immunity. These findings support the development of intratumoral microbiota profiling and highlight the potential for microbiota-targeted strategies to enhance cancer immunotherapy efficacy.

Article.Authors: Bukhanov E.; Gaevsky N.; Poznakhareva O.; Tikhomirov A.; Ushakova S.; Shabanov V.
Article.Abstract: Photosynthetic acclimation involves coordinated changes in the structural organization and functional activity of the photosynthetic apparatus. However, the structural basis underlying enhanced photosynthetic activity following biostimulant treatment under non-stress conditions remains insufficiently understood. Siberian. These changes occurred without evidence of pronounced PSII photoinhibition, indicating that the observed changes in PSII photochemistry were not a response to experimentally induced stress. Structural and functional changes were accompanied by increases in plant and leaf biomass. Taken together, these findings indicate that leaf biostimulation is associated with coordinated remodeling of thylakoid architecture and PSII excitation-energy partitioning under the experimental conditions studied.

Article.Authors: Arima T.; Takahama K.; Suetsugu K.; Kobae Y.; Iwai H.; Takasaki I.; Kurihara T.; Terazono H.

Article.Title: Immunometabolic Memory in Obesity: Nutritional Drivers, Persistence, and Reversibility
Article.Authors: Reytor-González C.; Zambrano-Villacres R.; Andrade Mejia N.; Duran-Agüero S.; Simancas-Racines D.
Article.Abstract: Obesity reshapes immune function across adipose tissue, circulation, and hematopoietic compartments. Weight reduction improves cardiometabolic health, yet emerging evidence indicates that prior obesity can leave persistent cellular, transcriptional, and epigenetic changes. Whether nutrition can reverse this biological imprint remains uncertain. We conducted a critical narrative review informed by structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and Epistemonikos, complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. We prioritized mechanistic human studies, controlled dietary interventions, longitudinal weight-loss studies, and experiments that tested persistence after stimulus withdrawal or response to re-exposure. Evidence was interpreted according to biological compartment and study design rather than pooled statistically. Obesogenic exposures can alter innate immune metabolism, inflammasome signaling, hematopoiesis, and chromatin states. Animal studies provide the strongest evidence that these changes can persist after weight normalization and amplify responses during weight regain. Human studies show incomplete normalization of adipose immune states, persistent adipocyte programs, and durable methylation changes in T lymphocytes after weight loss. Dietary interventions can lower inflammatory tone and modify immune metabolism, microbial metabolites, and lipid mediator pathways, but no dietary pattern has been shown to erase established obesity-associated immune memory in humans. An evidence map built on a core set of 47 studies showed that experimental work dominates the induction, persistence and re-challenge domains, whereas human evidence clusters in post-weight-loss remodelling and dietary modulation; human re-challenge data were absent and no study provided a direct test of reversal in humans. Obesity-associated immunometabolic memory appears to be distributed across hematopoietic, immune, adipose, stromal, and microbial compartments. Nutrition can modulate mechanisms implicated in this persistence, but human evidence of reversal is lacking, and whether pharmacologically induced weight loss leaves a comparable imprint has not been tested. Mechanistic trials should separate energy deficit, diet composition, adiposity change, and weight-loss modality and include a weight-stable follow-up and functional re-challenge where feasible.

Article.Authors: Lan R.; Weng L.; Cao B.; Li A.; Zhang J.; Shi H.; Yang L.; Lv Y.

Spatial analyses showed AEIC-enriched regions forming an extracellular matrix-rich barrier associated with NK_CD16− cell exclusion, M2-like macrophage polarization, and increased genomic instability. Finally, an AEIC-derived 16-gene signature stratified prognosis across independent cohorts and was associated with distinct drug-sensitivity patterns, including increased predicted sensitivity to Bortezomib and AZD4547. Article.Title: Physiological and Transcriptome Analysis of Polygonatum Cyrtonema Under Continuous Drought Stress
Article.Authors: Xu X.; Cheng S.
Article.Abstract: Against the backdrop of global warming and the increasingly uneven distribution of water resources, drought has emerged as a critical abiotic stressor limiting the growth and quality formation of medicinal plants. In this study, Polygonatum Cyrtonema was subjected to a continuous drought treatment experiment by withholding water for 5, 10, and 20 days, alongside a well-watered control (CK), to preliminarily investigate its physiological responses and transcriptomic alterations under water-deficit conditions. Physiological measurements revealed that prolonged drought stress significantly increased the concentrations of malondialdehyde (MDA) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) in leaves, accompanied by elevated in superoxide dismutase (SOD) and peroxidase (POD) activities, as well as increased chlorophyll content. RNA-seq analysis identified a substantial number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with 11,835, 12,110, and 11,416 DEGs in the D5, D10, and D20 vs. CK comparisons, respectively, including 6133 shared core DEGs. KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that these DEGs were primarily involved in starch and sucrose metabolism, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and plant hormone signal transduction. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a specific gene module (black module) containing 1681 genes that was highly positively correlated with drought duration (r = 0.95). Protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis of this module highlighted several candidate hub genes, including WRKY33 (BMK_Unigene_251623), EDA39(BMK_Unigene_034545), OHP (BMK_Unigene_221621), and RD20 (BMK_Unigene_149641). Furthermore, genes within the black module were significantly enriched in metabolic pathways such as anthocyanin, phenylpropanoid, and isoflavonoid biosynthesis, as well as phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, arginine, and proline metabolism. RT-qPCR validation confirmed the expression patterns of these candidate genes, supporting the reliability of the transcriptomic data. Collectively, these findings provide transcriptomic insights into the continuous drought response in P. cyrtonema, and identify candidate genes and pathways for future functional validation and stress-resilience improvement in this species.

Article.Title: Pre-Treatment CD44 and CD47 Expression and Pathological Complete Response After Neoadjuvant Therapy in Breast Cancer: An Exploratory Single-Center Study
Article.Authors: Asoglu H.; Asarkaya E.; Aykut A.; Cavusoglu G.; Aydinalp Camadan Y.; Kidi M.; Biter S.; Yaslikaya S.; Asoglu R.; Toyran T.; Ergin M.; Bayram E.; Kara I.; Sahin B.; Paydas S.; Koseci T.
Article.Abstract: CD44, a stem cell-associated adhesion molecule, and CD47, an anti-phagocytic checkpoint, have been implicated in breast cancer chemoresistance, but their relationship to neoadjuvant response is poorly defined. We assessed both markers by immunohistochemistry in pre-treatment core biopsies from 43 women treated with neoadjuvant therapy at a single center. Total pathological complete response (pCR; ypT0/is ypN0), designated the primary endpoint during peer review, occurred in 12 patients (27.9%), and breast pCR (ypT0/is) in 14 (32.6%). Total pCR rates were 18.2% in CD44-positive and 38.1% in CD44-negative tumors (odds ratio, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.09–1.46; Fisher exact p = 0.185). CD44 positivity was concentrated in rarely responding hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative tumors, and stratification by subtype moved the odds ratio toward the null (0.62; exact 95% CI, 0.07–5.25). For CD47, the odds ratio per one-point increase in immunoreactivity score was 0.80 (95% CI, 0.54–1.19; p = 0.264), but immunoreactivity was low (only two tumors reached the prespecified high-expression threshold) and possibly technically compromised, so these findings are inconclusive. No statistically detectable association was observed between either marker and total or breast pCR; treatment could not be adjusted for, and only very large effects were detectable. These exploratory data do not provide sufficient evidence to support CD44 or CD47 as response markers.

Article.Title: Beyond DNA Demethylation: Curcumin as a Context-Dependent Remodeler of the Epigenetic Landscape
Article.Authors: Costa S.; Ragusa M.; Nicosia A.
Article.Abstract: Curcumin has attracted considerable attention for its pleiotropic effects on cellular signaling, inflammation, metabolism, and cancer biology. A growing body of evidence indicates that these effects coincide with alterations in the epigenetic landscape; however, a causal contribution of such alterations has seldom been established experimentally. Although curcumin has frequently been described as an epigenetic demethylating agent, accumulating evidence suggests more complex, context-dependent mechanisms, which involve DNA methylation, hydroxymethylation, histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and non-coding RNAs. These changes may affect the accessibility and transcriptional activity of genes involved in cell identity, proliferation, differentiation, inflammation, and therapeutic response. The few genome-wide methylomic and transcriptomic studies available, mostly performed in a single cell line and at micromolar concentrations that exceed those reached in vivo, suggest that curcumin-induced epigenetic changes depend on cellular context, dose, and exposure conditions. This narrative review summarizes evidence published mainly from 2004 onward on the effects of curcumin on DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation, while integrating its interactions with histone modifications, chromatin organization, and non-coding RNA networks. We further discuss how these interconnected mechanisms contribute to the rewiring of gene regulatory programs and may underlie the biological and therapeutic effects of curcumin. Finally, we highlight the current limitations, including the poor bioavailability of curcumin, the non-specific chemistry of the molecule, and the scarcity of integrative multi-omics data, and we discuss what would be required to establish whether curcumin-induced epigenetic changes are relevant at pharmacologically attainable concentrations.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: curcumin; chromatin remodeling; histone modifications; DNA methylation; non-coding RNA; DNA hydroxymethylation; epigenetics; multi-omics integration; curcumin bioavailability; gene regulatory networks

Article.Title: Nasopharyngeal Microbial Signatures Associated with Anti-VEGF Therapeutic Outcomes in Exudative Age-Related Macular Degeneration: A Pilot Study
Article.Authors: Cebatoriene D.; Bruzaite A.; Vilkeviciute-Petraite A.; Zaliuniene D.; Lukosevicius R.; Skieceviciene J.; Kupcinskas J.; Liutkeviciene R.
Article.Abstract: Exudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is driven by choroidal angiogenesis, and the response to anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy varies between patients. In this pilot study, we investigated whether the pretreatment nasopharyngeal microbiota differs between patients with exudative AMD and controls and whether it is associated with treatment response. Nasopharyngeal swabs were analysed by 16S rRNA gene (V3–V4) amplicon sequencing; after removal of host-derived, chloroplast and contaminant sequences and rarefaction, 55 samples (25 patients and 30 controls) were retained. Treatment response was assessed six months after starting therapy. Community composition was compared using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) adjusted for age, sex and statin use. Alpha and beta diversity did not differ between patients and controls (Shannon index, p = 0.892; PERMANOVA, p = 0.067). Pretreatment community composition differed between 19 responders and five non-responders (Bray–Curtis R2 = 0.057, p = 0.015; weighted UniFrac R2 = 0.143, p = 0.006), and non-responders had lower diversity (observed ASVs, p = 0.004). Non-responders had a higher relative abundance of Corynebacterium (median 71% vs. 19%; p = 0.009), which did not remain significant after correction for all genera tested. Pretreatment nasopharyngeal microbiota composition was associated with the response to anti-VEGF therapy but not with AMD status. These preliminary findings require confirmation in larger, independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Gut Microbiota-Mediated SN-38G Metabolism In Vitro: Effects of Murraya koenigii and Ruta graveolens
Article.Authors: Scheithauer T.; Olgiati E.; Verheij E.; van Butselaar W.; Ossendrijver M.; van der Wurff M.; Schuren F.
Article.Abstract: The influence of the human microbiome on health and disease has been extensively studied over the past two decades. More recently, the microbiota has also been implicated in modulating the efficacy and toxicity of various drugs, including cancer therapies. This study focuses on irinotecan, a chemotherapeutic prodrug used in colorectal cancer treatment. Irinotecan is converted to the active metabolite SN-38, which is then glucuronidated in the liver to form the inactive metabolite SN-38G. Following biliary secretion into the intestine, microbial enzymes can cleave the glucuronide group and release SN-38, a process that may contribute to gastrointestinal toxicity. Human fecal microbiota converted SN-38G to SN-38 in vitro. Antibiotic treatment markedly reduced conversion, indicating that microbial activity accounted for most of the conversion under these conditions. In an exploratory screen, extracts from Murraya koenigii and Ruta graveolens reduced SN-38G conversion. Differences in community composition and beta-glucuronidase gene abundance were observed after extract exposure. These results show microbiota-dependent SN-38G conversion in vitro and identify compounds and plant extracts that delay or inhibit this conversion. Whether this effect is caused by direct inhibition of microbial beta-glucuronidase or by more generic microbiota effects is open for future research.

Article.Title: An Oxidized Mogrol Derivative Alleviates LPS-Induced Acute Lung Injury in Association with Reduced NLRP3 Inflammasome-Associated Inflammatory Responses in Mice
Article.Authors: Feng G.; Tuo Y.; Su J.; Huang F.; Li D.; Huo L.; Xia X.
Article.Abstract: Acute lung injury (ALI) is a severe inflammatory pulmonary disorder with high morbidity and limited treatment options available in clinical settings. Mogrosides, natural products derived from Siraitia grosvenorii, have been shown to exhibit protective effects against ALI, but structural optimization of their aglycone moiety, mogrol, may provide opportunities to improve pharmacological efficacy. In this study, oxidized mogrol derivatives (MG-COOH and MG-CHO) were synthesized, and their anti-inflammatory activities were initially compared with those of natural mogrosides in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated MH-S cells. MG-COOH exhibited pronounced anti-inflammatory activity and was designated for comprehensive analysis of its protective potential and underlying mechanisms in the LPS-induced ALI model. MG-COOH effectively alleviated LPS-induced injury in lung, decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and reduced oxidative stress, showing a tendency toward greater efficacy relative to natural mogrosides at equimolar doses. Transcriptomic analysis indicated that MG-COOH modulated genes involved in the HIF-1, JAK-STAT, MAPK, PI3K-Akt, NF-κB, NOD-like receptor, and Toll-like receptor signaling pathways. Furthermore, MG-COOH reduced the expression of NLRP3, ASC, caspase-1, and IL-1β mRNA and protein in lung. In conclusion, the oxidized mogrol derivative MG-COOH exhibits pronounced anti-ALI activity, which is associated with reduced NLRP3 inflammasome-related inflammatory responses in the lung, which serves as a pivotal node in multiple inflammatory signaling cascades.

Article.Title: Integrated Physiological and Transcriptomic Analyses Reveal Secondary Metabolic Responses of Prunella vulgaris Seedlings to Sodium Nitroprusside Treatment
Article.Authors: Gong Z.; Zhu M.; Zuo Q.; Zou X.; Hu X.; Li Y.; Ergu W.; Deng R.; Chen T.; Xing B.; Zhu Z.; Cao L.; Chen Y.
Article.Abstract: Prunella vulgaris L. is a valuable edible and medicinal industrial crop widely cultivated and used in Asia and Europe. Although exogenous sodium nitroprusside (SNP, a NO donor) is known to increase the biosynthesis of bioactive polyphenols and triterpenoids in this plant, its precise regulatory network remains unclear. Here, we integrated physiological and transcriptomic analyses to decipher how exogenous sodium nitroprusside (SNP, 100 μM) reprograms secondary metabolism in P. vulgaris seedling leaves at 2, 24, and 48 h post treatment. The results indicated that SNP treatment significantly altered antioxidant and redox responses, elevated osmotic regulators, and increased accumulation of key bioactive compounds (such as rosmarinic acid and ursolic acid), accompanied by increased in vitro antioxidant activity. At 24 h post treatment, our comparative analysis revealed 4341 differentially expressed transcripts (DETs). Exogenous SNP treatment is associated with phytohormone signal transduction, Ca2+ signaling, and secondary metabolite biosynthesis. SNP treatment markedly increased endogenous jasmonic acid (JA) levels and upregulated the expression of core transcription factors (MYBs, bHLHs, WRKYs, and NACs), along with increased expression of JA biosynthesis transcripts (e.g., PvLOXs, PvAOC, and PvACX), as well as key transcripts involved in polyphenol biosynthesis (e.g., PvPAL, PvTAT, and PvRAS) and triterpenoid biosynthesis (e.g., PvHMGS, PvDXS, and PvSQS). Our findings provide a systematic view of the physiological, hormonal, and transcriptional responses through which SNP is associated with changes in secondary metabolism in P. vulgaris and provide a theoretical basis for future studies on foliar SNP application to improve the pharmaceutical quality.

Article.Title: Quantitative Bioluminescent Imaging of AHR Activity Using a Thermostable Variant of the Fungal Luciferase nnLuz
Article.Authors: Gleneadie H.; Veland N.; Markina N.; Sardini A.; Fadeeva A.; Webster Z.; Gao F.; Merkenschlager M.; Fisher A.; Sarkisyan K.
Article.Abstract: Bioluminescent reporters are important tools in biomedical research. Luciferase enzymes, expressed as part of transgenes or inserted into endogenous genomes, can be used to visualise molecular events with minimally invasive experiments. However, the reaction requires addition of the substrate, luciferin. Organisms with self-sustained luminescence that both express the luciferase and produce the luciferin would allow continuous, convenient and affordable acquisition of physiological information. The Neonothopanus nambi fungal bioluminescence pathway has been harnessed in this way to produce autoluminescent plants. However, progress into mammalian models has been hindered by temperature sensitivity of the wild-type fungal luciferase (nnLuz). We tested the efficacy of a thermostable variant of nnLuz (nnLuz_v3) in vivo at physiologically relevant levels, by generating a reporter of endogenous Cyp1a1 expression as a measure of aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) activation. Previously published Cyp1a1-Fluc mice allowed a comparison between the novel luciferase nnLuz_v3 and the established firefly luciferase (Fluc). In Cyp1a1-nnLuz_v3 mice, the bioluminescence signal was sufficiently stable to enable well-resolved luminescence images to be captured on standard in vivo imaging equipment and consumer-grade cameras. These results derisk the use of nnLuz_v3 as an in vivo molecular reporter whilst providing a novel tool for AHR drug discovery and research.

Article.Title: Early Toxicities of CAR-T Cell Therapy: Mechanisms, Prediction, and Management
Article.Authors: Srikantan S.; Weiss A.; Muslehuddin Z.; Farhan S.
Article.Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has completely reshaped the therapeutic landscape for some blood cancers, including B-cell lymphoma, myeloma, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia. However, the complications associated with this powerful therapy are preventing it from being used more widely. This review explores the underlying biology, clinical signs, and current treatments for the three major early CAR-T cell therapy-associated toxicities: cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, and immune effector cell-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome. Here, we outline key findings from preclinical animal models, data from multicenter clinical trials, and real-world patient cohort study data to delineate how infused cells and different host-derived and blood–brain barrier disruptions contribute to these adverse effects. A growing body of evidence is revealing that the patient’s own monocytes and macrophages, not just the infused CAR-T cells, may contribute to driving systemic toxicities primarily by releasing interleukin-1 (IL-1) and IL-6. A more thorough and mechanistically detailed understanding of CAR-T cell therapy-associated toxicity is needed to develop better predictive tools and treatment strategies so that patients derive the greatest antitumor benefits with the lowest risk of severe treatment-related complications.

Article.Title: Trichoderma-Synthesized Iron Oxide Nanoparticles Confer Vanadium Tolerance in Rice Through Multiple Defense Responses
Article.Authors: Shahbaz H.; Ulhassan Z.; Shahbaz Z.; Kaleem Z.; Shah A.; Mohammed A.; Alotaibi M.; Alkhalifah D.; El-Keblawy A.
Article.Abstract: Vanadium (V) toxicity severely restricts plant growth and yield. The mechanistic basis by which Trichoderma-synthesized iron oxide nanoparticles (nFe) can improve V stress tolerance in rice remains unclear. To bridge this gap, we evaluated the protective efficacy of nFe in rice seedlings exposed to vanadium (V) stress. Results revealed that nFe lowered V-induced toxic impacts by minimizing V, MDA, H2O2, and O2•− accumulation in leaves and roots. These reductions were correlated to improved photosynthesis phenomics, biomass, and membrane integrity, and reduced oxidative stress. Furthermore, nFe significantly increased the antioxidant enzyme activity and their gene expressions, and partially restored the amino acid (such as glycine, GABA, and proline) accumulation in V-treated seedlings, underscoring its crucial roles in plant defense. Additionally, nFe modulated the subcellular distribution of V by facilitating cell wall fixation and vacuolar sequestration by regulating chelator genes (OsPCS1, OsMT2b, OsPCS2 and OsGSH). Moreover, nFe recovered V-inducede cellular damages by preserving mesophyll structures, mainly chloroplast and thylakoids membrane. V accumulation, Fe uptake, photosynthesis, redox homeostasis and amino acid metabolism serve as key physiological indicators for evaluating crop cultivation under V-stressed conditions. Practically, the foliar application of biogenic nFe offers a promising and sustainable agricultural strategy to improve crop resilience and ensure food security in metal-contaminated soils.

Article.Title: The Tryptophan Operator Acts as a Portable Downstream Enhancer for Recombinant Protein Expression in Escherichia coli
Article.Authors: Su B.; Lai P.; Xiong X.; Wang Y.; Li M.; Zhu H.; Deng M.
Article.Abstract: Downstream enhancer-like regulatory elements remain largely unexplored in prokaryotes. The tryptophan operator sequence (trpO), an 18-bp near-palindromic element from the Escherichia coli trpEDCBA operon, is conventionally defined as the binding site for the TrpR repressor, which blocks transcription initiation. Here, we report a previously unrecognized function of trpO: it can serve as a portable, orientation-dependent downstream enhancer that increases recombinant protein expression in E. coli. Inserting trpO downstream of multiple constitutive promoters increased eGFP reporter expression, with the reverse orientation (retrpO) conferring the most prominent enhancement, yielding a 1.56-fold expression increase. Adding L-threonine further raised expression to 3.98-fold. After screening plasmid replicons and host strains, the combination of the CloDF13 replicon and W3110 host, together with L-threonine supplementation, achieved a cumulative 9.57-fold enhancement in protein expression. Together, these findings challenge the long-standing notion that trpO functions exclusively as a negative regulatory element and establish trpO as a portable tool for increasing protein yields in E. coli.

Article.Title: Transcriptional Responses to Fire in Three Savanna Grass Species: Candidate Pathways for Fire-Stimulated Flowering
Article.Authors: Ghimire U.; Fill J.; Yu F.; Crandall R.; Tie L.
Article.Abstract: Aristida beyrichiana (wiregrass) is a grass species in the southeastern U.S. that exhibits pronounced fire-stimulated flowering, an adaptive trait in fire-prone ecosystems. Although fire-stimulated flowering has been well documented morphologically in this species, its molecular basis remains largely unknown. To investigate species-specific drivers of this adaptation, we performed comparative transcriptomic analyses under natural field conditions, before and approximately seven weeks after a prescribed fire, on wiregrass and two other grass species, Aristida spiciformis (bottlebrush threeawn) and Sporobolus junceus (pineywoods dropseed), which are not known to rely on fire to induce flowering. All species showed upregulation of conserved stress-related genes after fire, yet wiregrass exhibited a more focused transcriptional response. Notably, genes involved in nitrogen remobilization (ASN1, GDH2) and carbohydrate metabolism (SUS4, TPS10, DPE2) were uniquely upregulated in wiregrass, suggesting candidate metabolic adaptations that may support rapid post-fire regrowth and flowering. We also detected non-coding RNAs among the differentially expressed genes in wiregrass, pointing to a possible additional layer of regulation in fire-induced responses. Collectively, these results provide new transcriptomic insight into post-fire responses in wiregrass and identify candidate genes and regulatory pathways that require functional validation; because the observed expression differences integrate fire-induced, developmental and seasonal effects, they should not be interpreted as direct fire-specific responses.

Article.Title: Azadirachta indica (Neem) in Wound Healing: A Review of Bioactive Compounds, Mechanisms, and Current Translational Evidence
Article.Authors: Alomari R.; El-Zohri M.; Alharbi S.
Article.Abstract: Chronic wounds are significantly increasing the risk of morbidity and amputation in diabetic patients and older people worldwide. Moreover, the widespread use of antibiotics has led to an increase in drug-resistant infections, complicating the healing process, prolonging hospitalization, and increasing the financial burden on healthcare systems. Consequently, plant-derived therapeutics have attracted considerable interest as accessible, biocompatible adjuncts in regenerative medicine. The neem plant (Azadirachta indica) is traditionally known as the “village pharmacy” due to its extensive pharmacological effects, such as antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and regenerative activities. This review covers the properties of different neem parts and extracts, their applications, and the molecular mechanisms of its essential bioactive compounds. In addition, it summarizes recent in vitro, in vivo, and emerging clinical findings across different wound types. Furthermore, it critically appraises key translational bottlenecks, including a primary technical barrier related to the lack of phytochemical standardization, non-linear dose responses, and the paucity of well-controlled human trials. Overall, while heterogeneous preclinical evidence supports the biological plausibility and wound-healing activity of A. indica, definitive clinical utility remains unproven across diverse patient cohorts. Future prospective methodology incorporating systematic chemical profiling and adequately powered randomized controlled trials will be essential to establish its clinical utility and safety profile in contemporary wound management.
