Article.Title: Repeated TRPA1 Blockade Reduces Nociception and Neuroinflammation in a Relapsing–Remitting Mouse Model of Multiple Sclerosis
Article.Authors: Luiz A.; Peres D.; Kudsi S.; Moraes R.; Antoniazzi C.; Pereira L.; Brito H.; Pillat M.; Flores M.; Rodrigues P.; Trevisan G.
Article.Abstract: Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) is a chronic autoimmune and neurodegenerative disease characterized by neuroinflammation and demyelination. Neuropathic pain is a frequent and poorly managed symptom associated with oxidative stress. Transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1), which is activated by oxidative mediators, contributes to nociceptive signaling and neuroinflammatory processes in the relapsing–remitting experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (RR-EAE) model. This study investigated the effects of repeated pharmacological blockade of TRPA1 on nociceptive behaviors and disease-associated pathological mechanisms using an RR-EAE mouse model. Female C57BL/6 mice received the TRPA1 antagonist A-967079 (30 mg/kg, intragastric) from day 16 to day 36 post-induction. Behavioral, molecular, and biochemical analyses were performed. Repeated administration of A-967079 attenuated mechanical and cold allodynia without impairing locomotor function or altering body weight. TRPA1 antagonism modulated glial marker expression and plasma pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. A-967079 attenuated oxidative stress, reducing hydrogen peroxide, 4-hydroxynonenal, advanced oxidation protein product levels (TRPA1 endogenous agonists), and NADPH–cytochrome c reductase activity. These findings demonstrate that repeated TRPA1 antagonism effectively modulates neuropathic pain-like behaviors and targets key pathological mechanisms associated with RRMS. This approach closely reflects clinical management, as treatment was initiated after disease onset, when symptoms were already present. Our results support TRPA1 antagonism as a promising therapeutic strategy for pain management in RRMS.

Article.Title: HESD: A Database of Candidate Reactions and Enzymes for Metabolic Engineering of Corynebacterium glutamicum
Article.Authors: Ivanisenko T.; Demenkov P.; Kleshchev M.; Venzel A.; Khlebodarova T.; Volyanskaya A.; Kolchanov N.; Ivanisenko V.
Article.Abstract: The effect of a heterologous enzyme depends on the position of its reaction within the host metabolic network. We present HESD, a database of candidate reactions for heterologous introduction into Corynebacterium glutamicum ATCC 13032 with assessments of network position and feasibility. Rhea release 141, ChEBI and UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot data were integrated with the genome-scale model iCGB21FR, linking reaction variants to 32,619 protein records, with taxonomic assignments for 32,577 records from 3149 taxa. HESD contains 846 variants with both main substrate–product pair metabolites represented in the model and 3642 with one represented metabolite. Variants were classified topologically and assessed for stoichiometric balance, flux feasibility and energy-generating cycles. After excluding variants forming energy-generating cycles, 406 of 525 fully mapped variants retained feasible flux under loopless flux balance analysis. Topological classification agreed for 87.5% of variants shared with the independent model iCW773. Reaction RHEA:79573, catalyzed by ArcE from Thermococcus kodakarensis, replaced two consecutive steps catalyzed by ArgG and ArgH and increased predicted maximum L-arginine flux by 22.7% in iCGB21FR supplemented with Ddh and 12.5% in iCW773 with native Ddh, at a minimum growth rate of 0.05 h−1. HESD supports candidate selection for modeling and experimental validation.

Article.Title: Apical Periodontitis and Blood–Brain Barrier Compromise: Biological Mechanisms and Current Evidence—A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Bucchi C.; Hernández M.; Chaparro A.; de Anta J.; Bordagaray M.
Article.Abstract: This narrative review explores the potential link and the associated biological mechanisms between apical periodontitis (AP) and blood–brain barrier (BBB) integrity. An electronic literature search to identify publications related to AP and BBB integrity was conducted using the Scopus and PubMed databases. Both experimental and clinical studies were included and qualitatively analyzed. Available evidence shows that serum inflammatory marker levels are elevated in patients with AP compared to healthy controls, including proteins associated with endothelial barrier disruption such as ZO-1 and Claudin-5. Indirect evidence shows that disruption of the BBB can occur due to circulating inflammatory cytokines and pathogen insults. BBB cells express receptors that respond to circulating insults by upregulating pro-inflammatory cytokines, necroptosis, and proteolytic activity, which compromise BBB integrity. Elevated baseline levels of inflammatory markers from other chronic oral diseases, particularly periodontitis, have been linked to an increased risk of neurological disorders. Although similar pathophysiological mechanisms may be involved and recent in vitro experimental evidence suggests that the systemic inflammatory milieu associated with AP may compromise BBB function, direct in vivo and clinical evidence establishing a causal link remains lacking. Although biological plausibility supports a role for AP in BBB disruption, and recent in vitro experimental evidence has provided the first preliminary support for this association, in vivo preclinical studies and prospective clinical longitudinal studies are still needed to establish a clear causal relationship. Given the global burden of neurological disorders, elucidating the potential impact of AP on BBB integrity represents an important avenue for research.

Article.Title: Functional Classification of Zn2+-Dependent Histone Deacetylase Homologs and Variants Using Chemical Profiling
Article.Authors: Kopranovic A.; Münster H.; Rosowski A.; Groll L.; Almstätter F.; Attenhauser E.; Meyer-Almes F.
Article.Abstract: Zinc-dependent histone deacetylases (HDACs) are found in all species, ranging from bacteria to eukaryotes. They catalyze the removal of acetyl groups or various organic acid residues, including fatty acids, from proteins or polyamines. These enzymes are located in various cellular compartments, and their function is modulated by their ability to form different protein complexes. HDACs are prominent targets in the study of human diseases and infections, but they have also recently been considered as targets for fungicides. The active sites of HDACs are highly conserved, both structurally and sequentially. Therefore, the development of isoenzyme-selective inhibitors poses an exceptionally great challenge. In this study, a chemical profiling approach was used to classify human HDAC isoenzymes, bacterial homologs, and mutant variants by function and to identify specific ligand-binding patterns. While the recognition profiles generally reflected established HDAC classes, HDAC8 exhibited significant differences from HDAC1–3. In contrast, HDAC6 demonstrated substantial similarity with HDAC1–3 despite their low sequence identity, distinguishing itself from the sequentially closely related HDAC10. These findings demonstrate that sequence similarity alone is not a reliable predictor of ligand recognition and underscore the importance of local active-site architecture and physicochemical properties. Zebrafish HDAC10 closely resembles human HDAC10, supporting its use as a functional surrogate, while bacterial homologs display distinct profiles that suggest opportunities for species-selective inhibitor development. A single active-site substitution in class IIa HDAC4 (H976Y) shifted its recognition profile from HDAC class IIa toward class I. Engineered HDAC11 variants showed substantially improved recombinant expression and comparable stability while retaining wild-type-like ligand recognition. This supports their use in screening, biophysical, and structural studies. Together, these results establish ligand recognition profiling as a practical approach for functionally classifying HDACs and guiding the development of selective inhibitors.

Article.Title: Metal Oxide Semiconductor Gas Sensors for Amine-Based Carbon Capture: A Mini Review
Article.Authors: Ye Y.; Fan W.; Liu L.; Ning C.; Huang L.; Zhao X.; Zheng J.
Article.Abstract: Carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) is indispensable for achieving global carbon neutrality, and amine-based chemical absorption remains the most mature and widely deployed technology. However, amine emissions during operation result in absorbent loss, secondary pollution and potential public health risks, while conventional offline detection methods are unable to satisfy the requirements of real-time monitoring. This review systematically summarizes recent progress in metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) gas sensors for monoethanolamine (MEA) detection, with particular emphasis on AOx-based systems. The effects of the base material, microstructure and modification strategies, including noble metal decoration and heterojunction construction, on sensing performance are critically compared. Through such modifications, AOx-based sensors have achieved markedly improved sensing performance, and several are capable of detecting MEA at room temperature. The feasibility of existing sensing materials is further evaluated in the context of post-combustion amine capture. Among the reported systems, SnO2-based sensors exhibit clear advantages for MEA detection, including high sensitivity, favorable selectivity, rapid response and recovery, and satisfactory stability and repeatability. In contrast, studies on ABO3 perovskite-based sensors remain limited; although these materials show fast response, they continue to suffer from poor stability and insufficient humidity resistance. Future research should therefore focus on low-temperature operation, enhanced humidity tolerance and long-term durability, so as to accelerate the industrial translation of MOS gas sensors and support the sustainable development of CCUS.

Article.Title: Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptors Modulate T-Tubule Architecture Under Sympathetic Overstimulation
Article.Authors: He C.; Zeng Q.; Zhao J.; Meng Y.; Guo Y.; Wang H.; Wang S.; Li X.; Hou T.
Article.Abstract: Pathological remodeling of transverse tubules (T-tubules, TTs) is commonly observed in cardiac disease and may be promoted by sustained adrenergic stimulation. Although cholinergic signaling has been associated with cardioprotective effects, it remains unclear whether it directly modulates TT integrity in cardiomyocytes. Here, we examined how cholinergic receptor activation affects TT organization during acute β-adrenergic stimulation in isolated adult rat cardiomyocytes. Cells were exposed to isoproterenol (ISO), alone or in combination with acetylcholine (ACh) or nicotine (Nic). Confocal imaging showed that ISO disrupted TT organization and reduced the cellular length-to-width (L/W) ratio. ACh or Nic alone altered TT architecture, primarily by reducing TT power and increasing longitudinal tubule density; however, co-treatment with either agonist was associated with altered TT remodeling responses to ISO in TT structure and cell morphology. The muscarinic receptor agonist xanomeline (Xano) did not reproduce these effects. These results suggest a cardiomyocyte-autonomous role for nAChR signaling in limiting acute β-adrenergic stimulation-induced TT remodeling. Further studies are required to identify the nAChR subtype and downstream signaling mechanisms involved and to determine the relevance of these findings in vivo.

Article.Title: Theoretical Considerations Regarding the Role of Hyperinsulinemia and Insulin/IGF Signaling in Cancer Metabolic Reprogramming: Potential Mechanisms and Therapeutic Vulnerabilities
Article.Authors: Chae B.
Article.Abstract: Hyperinsulinemia is increasingly recognized as a systemic factor that can promote tumor progression by amplifying insulin receptor and insulin-like growth factor (IGF) signaling, reshaping cancer-cell metabolism, and influencing the tumor microenvironment. Commonly associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, persistent hyperinsulinemia can enhance insulin/IGF receptor signaling and downstream PI3K–AKT–mTOR and RAS–MAPK pathways. These pathways interact with stress-response networks, including NRF2-dependent redox control and AMPK–autophagy signaling, thereby supporting metabolic plasticity under nutrient and microenvironmental stress. Hyperinsulinemia-associated signaling may increase glucose utilization, pentose phosphate pathway activity, glutaminolysis, de novo lipogenesis, and antioxidant capacity, collectively promoting anabolic growth, survival, and treatment adaptation. Metabolic remodeling extends beyond aerobic glycolysis and involves context-dependent alterations in mitochondrial function, oxidative metabolism, lactate production, and metabolic crosstalk among cancer, stromal, and immune cells. Consequently, hyperinsulinemia-associated signaling may contribute to lactate-rich, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, tumor progression, and heterogeneous therapeutic responses across cancer types. This review integrates experimental, epidemiological, and translational evidence linking persistent hyperinsulinemia and insulin/IGF signaling with cancer metabolic reprogramming. It critically examines strategies to reduce systemic insulin exposure, inhibit insulin/IGF signaling, or co-target tumor-specific metabolic dependencies, including the metabolic consequences of PI3K-pathway inhibition. By advancing a hyperinsulinemia-centered framework, this review identifies mechanistic gaps and translational priorities for more precise metabolic interventions in cancer.

Article.Title: Transcriptome-Guided Identification of Two GPCR Candidates Contributing to Trap Formation in Arthrobotrys oligospora
Article.Authors: Liu J.; Li Y.; Zhan F.; Deng M.; Wang Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) connect environmental cues to fungal development, but the functions of many candidate receptors in nematode-trapping fungi remain unresolved. Deletion of AoGrn1 or AoGrn2 reduced nematode-induced trap formation, and complementation partially restored the phenotype. AoGrn3 deletion produced no statistically detectable change in trap density under the tested conditions. In HEK293F cells, nematode extract elicited bioluminescence resonance energy transfer responses in the AoGrn1–AoGpa2 and AoGrn2–AoGpa1 combinations. AlphaFold2-Multimer models suggested intracellular receptor–Gα interfaces, although model score preferences did not consistently match the observed response profiles. These findings support roles for AoGrn1 and AoGrn2 in trap formation and identify receptor–Gα combinations for further investigation of prey-associated signaling. The active extract components and the corresponding coupling relationships in the native fungus remain to be established.

Article.Title: Divergent Reactions of Coumarin- and 7-Azacoumarin-3-Carboxylic Acids with Azomethine Ylides: Spirocyclization and Ring Expansion
Article.Authors: Trifonov A.; Appazov N.; Kibardina L.; Gazizov A.; Voloshina A.; Luybina A.; Dobrynin A.; Litvinov I.; Tolegen A.; Burilov A.; Pudovik M.; Turmanov R.; Akylbekov N.; Alabugin I.; Chugunova E.
Article.Abstract: A series of new spiro-fused polycyclic systems has been synthesized via cascade reactions of 7-azacoumarin-3-carboxylic acid and coumarin-3-carboxylic acid derivatives with azomethine ylides generated in situ from L-proline or sarcosine and various carbonyl components (ninhydrin, aceanthrenequinone, isatin, and substituted isatins). For the conventional cycloaddition products (derived from isatin with L-proline or sarcosine), the cascade reactions contain a 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition with a decarboxylation step, affording a single detectable diastereomer in each case. For those products for which single-crystal X-ray structures were obtained, the crystals belong to centrosymmetric space groups, so the compounds are racemic. The reaction of 7-azacoumarin-3-carboxylic acids with the ylides derived from L-proline and ninhydrin or aceanthrenequinone provides the first example of a pyrrolidine-to-piperidine ring expansion (5→6); this transformation is currently demonstrated only for a limited set of substrates and should be regarded as a proof-of-concept rather than a general method. Transformation differs mechanistically from the conventional cycloaddition–decarboxylation; the proposed mechanism is presented as a working hypothesis. The effect of the solvent on the structure of the final products of reaction of 7-azacoumarin-3-carboxylic acid with ylides based on sarcosine and isatins is shown: in methanol, ring-opened esters are formed, whereas in acetonitrile the coumarin fragment is retained. For compounds 10 and 17d, the IC50 values against M-HeLa cells were numerically similar to those of the reference drug 5-fluorouracil, while compound 6b gave an IC50 against HuTu80 cells numerically similar to that of 5-fluorouracil. Compound 10 gave a numerically lower IC50 value than 5-fluorouracil against A549 lung carcinoma cells. These results should be regarded as a preliminary cell-viability screening rather than evidence of therapeutic potential; the spirocyclic scaffolds provide a starting point for further structure–activity investigation.

Article.Title: Protecting Neurons in Retinal and Optic Nerve Diseases: The Role of Ferroptosis-Associated Pathways
Article.Authors: Xiang L.; Ye X.; Lo A.
Article.Abstract: Retinal ischemia (RI) is a prominent pathological feature of several ocular diseases, including diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and retinopathy of prematurity. These diseases are major causes of adult and childhood blindness worldwide. Retinal and optic nerve degeneration also involves non-ischemic mechanisms. Severe or sustained RI can cause irreversible retinal injury and visual impairment. RI can trigger oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and mitochondrial dysfunction, which can contribute to cell death. Ferroptosis is a distinct form of regulated cell death characterized by the iron-dependent accumulation of lethal lipid peroxides in membrane phospholipids. Accumulating preclinical evidence indicates that ferroptosis-associated processes may contribute to retinal and optic nerve injury. Targeting ferroptosis-related pathways may offer promising approaches to mitigate cellular damage in these diseases. In this review, we summarize the ferroptosis mechanisms relevant to retinal and optic nerve injury and evaluate evidence from experimental models, cell types, pharmacological rescue studies, and genetic approaches. By comparing experimental models, cell types, and mechanistic evidence, we distinguish direct neuronal findings from non-neuronal ocular responses and assess whether the results support ferroptosis or broader oxidative stress. We also identify the evidence needed to assess the translational relevance of ferroptosis-targeted strategies in retinal and optic nerve diseases.

Article.Title: A Novel Glucocerebrosidase Allosteric Activator Prevents MPTP-Induced Neurodegeneration in Mice
Article.Authors: Emelyanov A.; Kopytova A.; Lavrinova A.; Rychkov G.; Rudenok M.; Rybolovlev I.; Ibatullin F.; Pidyurchina V.; Artynyuk A.; Nikolaev M.; Bezrukova A.; Stepakov A.; Boitsov V.; Baydakova G.; Grigor’eva E.; Pavlova S.; Partevian S.; Semenova E.; Miliukhina I.; Nesterov M.; Abaimov D.; Bezrukikh V.; Timofeeva A.; Kvanchiani V.; Sergeeva E.

Furthermore, we demonstrate for the first time that N2 exerts robust neuroprotective effects in an in vivo 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced mouse model of PD. Specifically, N2 treatment attenuated MPTP-induced hexosylsphingosine accumulation in the prefrontal cortex, and ameliorated both tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neuronal loss in the substantia nigra and dopamine depletion in the striatum. Article.Title: Following the Central Dogma: A Review of Fluoroquinolone Resistance Mechanisms in Aquatic Pathogenic Bacteria
Article.Authors: Zhu L.; Dai C.; Wang M.; Zhu X.; Ma J.; Zhang Y.; Zhao Y.; Li H.; Zhang Z.
Article.Abstract: Fluoroquinolone resistance in aquatic bacterial pathogens is a growing concern in aquaculture worldwide. Multidrug-resistant isolates are increasingly reported across major farming regions, and the potential transmission of resistance genes to humans through the food chain and environmental exposure has attracted attention beyond aquaculture. Most existing reviews discuss individual resistance mechanisms, such as target-site mutations, plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance (PMQR), efflux pumps, and altered membrane permeability, as discrete topics, with limited consideration of their interrelationships. This review takes a different approach. Using the central dogma of molecular biology as an organizing framework, it organizes fluoroquinolone resistance into four interconnected levels: gene, transcription, protein, and phenotype. Gene-level resistance involves point mutations in the quinolone resistance-determining region (QRDR) and the acquisition of PMQR genes. Transcriptional responses include coordinated upregulation of efflux pumps and downregulation of porins, which together reduce intracellular drug accumulation. Protein-level mechanisms include altered drug targets, target protection by Qnr proteins, drug efflux, and enzymatic modification of the drug. At the phenotypic level, PMQR-mediated low-level resistance provides a survival window during which subsequent QRDR mutations accumulate, whereas efflux pump overexpression confers higher-level resistance. Biofilm formation and metabolic reprogramming further stabilize the resistance phenotype at the population level. This framework highlights how resistance mechanisms interact across different molecular and cellular levels, rather than functioning independently or following a strictly linear sequence. Key gaps remain in understanding the regulatory roles of non-coding RNAs, the structural biology of PMQR proteins, and the use of multi-omics approaches to clarify regulation across these levels. Further research is needed to address these gaps.

Article.Title: An Endothelial Address for the Sphingosine 1-Phosphate Axis: Cell-Type Attribution of 171 Sphingolipid Targets Across 27 Human Cancers
Article.Authors: Ding T.; Li W.; Yi Y.; Fan X.; Tan J.; Han A.; Tang Y.
Article.Abstract: Sphingolipid enzymes have been nominated as cancer targets for three decades. CTAI reproduces at Spearman +0.30 against the protein index and +0.50 against the spatial one. S1PR1 and SPNS2 rank endothelium first in 23 of 31 and 22 of 31 datasets. Normal tissue immune fraction declines as CTAI rises (ρ = −0.52 core set, −0.60 genome-wide). Modelability, the proportion of genes yielding a dependency model that meets the predictability criterion, falls across the four functional groups (Cochran–Armitage p = 0.0024). Matched control genes fall the same way (p = 7.9 × 10−7), indicating that the gradient is not specific to sphingolipids. Clinical-stage targets sit in the low-attribution, low-dependency quadrant of our set, but genome-wide, with the target development level and literature volume held constant, that quadrant carries no advantage (odds ratio 1.05, 95% confidence interval 0.89 to 1.24). Attribution splits this pathway into a cell-autonomous arm, which cell-line dependency screens measure directly, and a sphingosine 1-phosphate arm expressed mostly outside the malignant compartment, in cells those screens do not contain.

Article.Title: Ceramides as Biomarkers of Risk Prediction and Prognosis in Cardiovascular and Other Diseases: Are We There Yet?
Article.Authors: Garikipati T.; Dubey P.; Work D.; Oli S.; Sharma D.; Chatterjee S.
Article.Abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, yet roughly 70% of major adverse cardiovascular events occur in statin-treated patients with optimized Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), a gap that cholesterol-based risk panels do not close. Ceramides are bioactive sphingolipids whose plasma species and ratios carry risk information absent from standard lipid panels, and ceramide-based scores (CERT and CERT2) are already in clinical use. Whether this value extends beyond CVD is unclear. We reviewed ceramide species and ratios as biomarkers for disease prediction, prognosis, and disease activity across cardiovascular, metabolic, autoimmune rheumatic, inflammatory bowel, pulmonary, kidney, and oncologic contexts, searching PubMed and Scopus from January 1990 to June 2026 and extending the search for the historical literature. In CVD, CERT and CERT2 predicted cardiovascular events and mortality independently of LDL cholesterol, including in statin-treated and kidney disease populations. In metabolic and autoimmune rheumatic disease, ceramide profiles tracked cardiovascular risk and disease activity. In inflammatory bowel disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and most cancers, the evidence is mechanistically strong but limited to single-cohort or observational studies. Ceramides are emerging biomarkers that complement, not replace, established risk tools. Broader clinical use requires prospective validation, diverse cohorts, standardized assays, and demonstrated cost-effectiveness.

Article.Title: Deciphering Cancer-Specific H3K27ac Landscapes Through Systematic Multi-Omics Integration and Development of Open-Access Genomic Annotation Platform
Article.Authors: Zhuang Y.; Gao Y.; Zhang Z.; Wang Z.; Liu J.; Zhang L.; Bateer S.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: H3K27ac epigenetically modulates gene expression and serves as an indicator of cancer status. These cancer-specific H3K27ac gains were predominantly enriched in non-coding regions, where they were associated with increased chromatin accessibility and chromatin interactions, enabling the recruitment of oncogenic transcription factors to activate target genes. Conversely, cancer-specific H3K27ac losses preferentially occurred in promoters and correlated with chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression. Mechanistic multi-omics analyses in leukemia further demonstrated this epigenetic-structural coupling. Leukemia-specific H3K27ac gains established a permissive chromatin environment that facilitated oncogenic GATA1 binding and activation of its target gene TAL1. Within this context, TAL1 exhibited increased interaction with STIL, a well-known fusion partner implicated in leukemogenesis. To enable broader application of these findings, we developed an open-access web server for genomic annotation. Collectively, our study provides a comprehensive landscape of cancer-specific H3K27ac modifications, defining them as a functional epigenetic signature of oncogenic chromatin remodeling and offering an annotation resource for understanding the regulation of the cancer genome.

Article.Title: Targeting Dendritic Cells in Cancer Immunotherapy: From Immune Priming to Tumor Microenvironment Reprogramming
Article.Authors: Zanotta S.; Galati D.
Article.Abstract: Dendritic cells (DCs) are specialized antigen-presenting cells that shape antitumor immunity by integrating antigen uptake, processing, presentation, co-stimulation, and cytokine-mediated T-cell instruction. Their function is therefore critical for generating tumor-specific T-cell responses and may influence responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Although early ex vivo DC vaccines established feasibility, safety, and immunogenicity, clinical efficacy has been heterogeneous. Sipuleucel-T demonstrated an overall-survival benefit in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, whereas DCVax-L produced encouraging but methodologically debated survival signals in glioblastoma. More recently, individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccination combined with pembrolizumab has shown durable recurrence-free survival benefit in resected high-risk melanoma. This review examines the biological rationale for DC-directed immunotherapy, tumor-induced DC dysfunction, next-generation DC platforms, in vivo DC targeting, DC-derived extracellular vesicles, negative and controversial clinical evidence, and rational combinations with checkpoint blockade and tumor-microenvironment-modulating strategies. The field is evolving from the use of DCs as cellular vaccine vehicles toward programmable immune-priming approaches that integrate antigen quality, DC functional state, spatial organization, and tumor microenvironment features.

Article.Authors: Yang Z.; Jiang S.; Cui W.; Zhou J.; Li W.
Article.Abstract: Podocyte injury is a central pathological event in diabetic kidney disease (DKD), but the mitochondrial regulatory mechanisms underlying podocyte dysfunction remain incompletely defined. We integrated single-nucleus RNA-seq data from human renal biopsies in GSE195460 with podocyte-specific differential expression, functional enrichment, mitochondrial gene annotation, co-expression network analysis, machine learning feature selection, pseudotime analysis, in silico knockout, transcription factor enrichment, motif analysis, and molecular docking; findings were externally evaluated in GSE209781. Thirty-one mitochondrial-related differentially expressed genes were identified, and OXR1 was prioritized as a candidate regulatory hub based on consistent downregulation, network centrality, machine learning selection, and external validation. HNF4A was predicted as an upstream regulator linked to OXR1 and other mitochondrial targets. In silico OXR1 perturbation increased the predicted injured-state probability from 15% to 82%, while promoter motif analysis provided additional computational support for a putative HNF4A–OXR1 regulatory relationship. These findings highlight OXR1 as a candidate associated with podocyte mitochondrial dysfunction in DKD and suggest a putative HNF4A–OXR1 regulatory relationship.

Article.Title: Fenofibrate and Lomitapide in PNPLA2-Related Neutral Lipid-Storage Disease with Myopathy: A Single-Patient In Vitro Approach
Article.Authors: Merkevicius K.; Preston G.; Larson S.; Houssin N.; Houten S.; Kozicz T.; Morava E.
Article.Abstract: Neutral lipid-storage disease with myopathy (NLSD-M), caused by pathogenic PNPLA2 variants, has no established treatment. We report a single-patient in vitro study in a 32-year-old female evaluating fenofibrate and lomitapide in patient-derived fibroblasts, selected based on prior therapeutic evidence. Therapeutic endpoints included lipid-droplet (LD) burden, quantified by volumetric z-stack imaging, and bioenergetic profiling, performed by Seahorse respirometry, citrate synthase (CS) activity, cellular NADH capacity, and complex II activity. Fibroblasts were treated with fenofibrate (20 µM) and lomitapide (5 nM) for two weeks. PNPLA2-mutant fibroblasts exhibited LD burden of median 56 droplets per cell, reduced CS activity, a proxy for mitochondrial content, and a hypometabolic profile. Preserved total NADH oxidase and Complex II activities indicated unaffected intrinsic electron transport chain function. Under fenofibrate exposure, most measured bioenergetic parameters in the patient-derived line were closer to the corresponding values in treated controls, but paradoxically increased LD count 1.5–1.9-fold. Lomitapide did not reduce LD burden and further worsened bioenergetic parameters. Loss of PNPLA2-mediated lipolysis produces a dual phenotype of LD accumulation and bioenergetic impairment. Fenofibrate and lomitapide produced divergent and partially adverse effects across these two endpoints. These findings informed precautionary, patient-specific clinical management decisions. Combined LD and metabolic profiling in patient-derived fibroblasts may complement therapeutic decision-making in NLSD-M, pending validation in larger cohorts.

Article.Title: From Molecular State to Clinical Outcomes After Spinal Cord Injury: A Scoping Review of Selected Fluid Biomarkers and Rehabilitation Relevance
Article.Authors: Calabrò R.; Quartarone A.; Calderone A.; Ardizzone A.; Raciti L.; Morini E.
Article.Abstract: Human fluid biomarkers may complement neurological assessment after spinal cord injury (SCI), but their relevance to rehabilitation depends on the clinical relationship tested. This scoping review mapped selected neuroendocrine, inflammatory, neurotrophic and neural injury biomarkers in serum, plasma or cerebrospinal fluid. Five databases were searched on 8 October 2026; 17,317 records yielded 41 included reports. Findings were charted by phenotype, sampling window, assay, outcome and analytical denominator, with question-appropriate critical appraisal. Two reports randomized interventions, and 39 reports contributed nonrandomized biomarker analyses. Acute neural injury markers mainly addressed initial severity and later neurological status. Prognostic signals included neurofilament light, glial fibrillary acidic protein and tau, but all 10 prediction-model reports had high overall risk of bias; independent validation remained insufficiently established. Chronic endocrine, mobility and pain studies examined different constructs. Partial integration included biomarker–imaging models and trial-embedded associations; no identified report validated biomarker-guided rehabilitation dosing or a causal molecular–circuit–functional pathway. Reports with age-related eligibility uncertainty or combined neurotrauma were interpreted separately. Heterogeneous assays, overlapping cohorts, incomplete follow-up and incompletely quantified rehabilitation exposure limited inference. These data support focused prospective validation rather than routine biomarker-directed rehabilitation. Mandatory marker, matrix and outcome search terms constrain coverage; absence claims apply to the identified reports.

Article.Title: Diabetes Mellitus: Review of the Common, Rare, and Uncommon (Conceptual and Metaphorical) Types
Article.Authors: Pliszka M.; Szablewski L.
Article.Abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) comprises a complex heterogeneous group of chronic metabolic disorders that affect various organ systems, resulting in a number of complications, including kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, immune dysfunction, retinopathy, neuropathy, and cancer. Uncontrolled DM may also lead to a coma and confusion, and if untreated, death due to ketoacidosis or nonketotic hyperosmolar syndrome. In 2019, DM was directly responsible for 1.5 million deaths, with an additional 460,000 due to kidney disease, as well as about 20% of cardiovascular-associated deaths. In addition to the well-known types—viz. type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)—several other rare conceptual/metaphoric forms have been described, although they are not regarded as formal diagnoses. The aim of this review is to present the various types of DM and summarize their characteristics, clinical features, diagnosis, pathophysiology, risk factors, management, and therapy.

Article.Title: A Semi-In Vivo System Reveals Impairment of Cell-Cycle Machinery upon Derailment of Polarity and Cellular Differentiation in In Vitro-Fertilised Egg Cells of Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.)
Article.Authors: Pónya Z.; Mirmazloum I.; Keszthelyi S.; Farkas S.; Hoffmann R.; Bázár G.; Cresti M.
Article.Abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are central regulators of cell-cycle progression and play essential roles in coordinating DNA replication, mitosis and cytokinesis. Although their involvement in cell proliferation has been extensively investigated, considerably less is known about their contribution to developmental pattern formation during the earliest stages of plant embryogenesis. This question is particularly relevant in angiosperms, where the first zygotic division is intrinsically linked to cell differentiation and formation of the apical–basal body axis. In the present study, the localisation and functional significance of the wheat CDC2 (Cell Division Cycle 2) homologue, p34cdc2, the key regulator of the G2/M transition, were investigated in in vivo- and in vitro-fertilised egg cells of wheat (Triticum aestivum L.). An affinity-purified antibody raised against a synthetic peptide corresponding to the C-terminal region of wheat CDC2 enabled the immunolocalisation of p34cdc2 during zygote development and early embryogenesis. Double-labelling experiments with tubulin showed stage-associated differences in p34cdc2 localisation and its apparent association with the preprophase band, a cytoskeletal structure involved in division-plane determination. Functional analyses showed that pharmacological and antibody-based perturbations were associated with marked changes in early embryonic development. Microinjection of anti-CDC2 and anti-PSTAIRE antibodies into in vitro-fertilised egg cells revealed a critical developmental window shortly after fertilisation during which antibody-mediated interference markedly reduced subsequent cell division. Likewise, inhibition of CDKs by purine derivatives, including olomoucine, disrupted normal morphogenesis and prevented establishment of characteristic embryonic organisation. Oryzalin-mediated disruption of microtubules was accompanied by loss of detectable p34cdc2 localisation to the future division plane, whereas genistein treatment induced severe polarity defects and aberrant embryonic pattern formation. An elaborate semi-in vivo re-implantation system indicated that maternal ovular tissues can support the maintenance of polarity and embryogenic competence during zygote and proembryo development. Taken together, our findings indicate that CDC2-associated processes are closely linked to cell-cycle progression and may be coordinated with polarity establishment and embryonic pattern formation. These results support a model in which interference with CDC2-associated processes can be accompanied by disrupted cell-cycle progression and abnormal embryonic patterning during early wheat embryogenesis.

Article.Title: High Intratumoral PROS1 Expression Is Associated with Improved Survival, Reduced Hypoxia Score Markers, and Alterations in Gene Expression Associated with Oncogene Signaling and Cell Cycle Signaling in Selected Solid Tumors
Article.Authors: Prouse T.; Majumder R.; Majumder S.
Article.Abstract: Protein S (PS), encoded by PROS1, is a vitamin K-dependent physiological anticoagulant with emerging, context-dependent roles in tumor biology. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), exogenous PS suppresses tumor growth and intratumoral hypoxia in preclinical models. Notably, high intratumoral PROS1 expression is associated with improved survival and attenuation of oncogenic, hypoxia-responsive, and EMT-related transcriptional programs in PDAC. Here, we examined associations between intratumoral PROS1 expression and overall survival, hypoxia-associated signaling, and genomic instability across nine cancer types using publicly available cBioPortal datasets. Tumors were stratified by low versus high PROS1 expression. Genomic instability was assessed using tumor mutational burden, aneuploidy, and tumor break load, where available. High PROS1 expression was associated with improved survival in ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma and lung adenocarcinoma in exploratory, unadjusted Mantel-Haenszel hazard ratio analyses. It was also inversely associated with genomic instability markers in ovarian, lung adenocarcinoma, and PDAC. Meta-analyses in select genes under low and high PROS1 expression conditions revealed shifts in pathways linked to oncogenic signaling, cell-cycle regulation, hypoxia, and EMT. Collectively, these findings position PROS1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker in selected cancers and support further investigation of PROS1’s roles in limiting tumor progression and preserving genomic stability.

Article.Title: Comorbidities in Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria: Integrating Disease Drivers and Systemic Consequences
Article.Authors: Kim J.; Kim M.; Ye Y.
Article.Abstract: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is a mast cell-driven inflammatory skin disorder traditionally considered self-limiting and non-life-threatening. However, accumulating evidence suggests that CSU is associated with multiple comorbidities, reflecting systemic immune and neuroinflammatory dysregulation. These comorbidities may act as both triggers and consequences of disease activity, forming a complex network centered on mast cell activation. Autoimmune diseases, particularly autoimmune thyroid disease, are strongly associated with CSU, especially in the type IIb autoimmune endotype. By contrast, type I autoallergic CSU is associated with immunoglobulin E (IgE) autoantibodies. Atopic diseases, neuroimmune interactions, and psychiatric conditions may further contribute to disease persistence through mechanisms involving IgE signaling and substance P-mediated mast cell activation via Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2. Metabolic and cardiovascular comorbidities have also been reported, with recent large-scale cohort studies strengthening the evidence for an association with cardiovascular risk, although causality remains unestablished. Associations with malignancy remain uncertain, whereas recent real-world studies suggest increased mortality among patients with CSU, potentially reflecting the underlying comorbidity burden rather than direct disease effects. Importantly, effective disease control may improve CSU outcomes and associated comorbidities. A comprehensive, mechanism-based approach that integrates comorbidity assessment into clinical management is essential for optimizing patient care.

Article.Title: Computational Evaluation of Necrostatin-1 Analogues as Potential RIPK1 Inhibitors
Article.Authors: Petsas E.; Chasapis C.
Article.Abstract: Receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) regulates necroptotic cell death and sterile inflammation, representing an established therapeutic target for degenerative and inflammatory disorders. Here, three putative hydantoin-based analogues bearing distinctive N-substitutions—an ethylcyclobutyl derivative (Compound 1), an ethoxyphenylethyl analogue (Compound 2), and a 5-chloroindole (3-fluoro-4-methylbenzyl) derivative (Compound 3)—were investigated against the prototypical inhibitor Necrostatin-1 using virtual screening, induced-fit docking, 500 ns molecular dynamics simulations and pharmacokinetic profiling. Induced Fit Docking within the RIPK1 kinase domain indicated that Compound 3 (−9.1 kcal/mol) and Compound 1 (−7.9 kcal/mol) achieved favorable predicted binding scores surpassing Necrostatin-1 (−7.3 kcal/mol), whereas Compound 2 displayed a considerably weaker binding score (−4.1 kcal/mol). All-atom molecular dynamics simulations revealed that Compound 1 maintained high dynamic stability with ligand RMSD constrained to 1.2–2.0 Å and sustained hydrogen bonding with Leu157. Conversely, Compound 2 dissociated from the primary binding pocket, while Compound 3 deviated from its initial docking pose (RMSD 7.0–9.2 Å) to engage a secondary interaction network with Asn170, Glu171 and Lys45. In silico ADME profiling predicted that all three candidates comply with Lipinski and Veber drug-likeness criteria with high predicted intestinal absorption. These computational findings provide putative structural insights into kinase-ligand interactions, prioritizing candidate molecules for chemical synthesis and in vitro biological evaluation.

Article.Title: Light Intensity and Gibberellic Acid Differentially Shape Primary Metabolism and Ginsenoside Profiles in Panax ginseng Sprouts
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Choi B.; Na H.; Jang J.; Song S.; Lee J.; Lee Y.; Kim K.; Lee D.; Yoon D.
Article.Abstract: Ginseng sprouts (Panax ginseng C.A. Meyer) are mostly cultivated under controlled indoor conditions, allowing modulation of growth and phytochemical composition through environmental and hormonal treatments. In this study, 1H NMR and UPLC-QTOF/MS were used to investigate the independent and interactive effects of light intensity and gibberellic acid (GA3) on primary metabolism and ginsenoside profiles. While GA3 promoted shoot growth, high light reduced plant height but increased root dry weight. Multivariate analysis of 42 identified primary metabolites and 26 ginsenosides revealed that the primary metabolite profiles are primarily distinguished by GA3, whereas ginsenoside profiles are more clearly differentiated based on light intensity. GA3 broadly increased soluble carbohydrates and decreased free amino acids, whereas light intensity had a selective effect on some primary metabolites. In contrast to the limited interaction effects in primary metabolism, significant interactions between light and GA3 were detected for eight ginsenosides. High-intensity light increased the content of several ginsenosides, including Re, Rg1, Rd, Rb2, and Rc, while decreasing protopanaxadiol (PPD)-type ginsenosides that lack a sophorosyl moiety at C-3. Correlation analysis across the experimental conditions revealed coordinated variation between primary metabolites and ginsenosides, with the most prominent pattern corresponding to the light-response axis. Overall, GA3 and light intensity exerted distinct but interconnected effects across metabolic layers, providing a framework for understanding how cultivation factors determine growth and phytochemical composition in ginseng sprouts.

Article.Title: TFAM Expression, rs1937 Variant, and Mitochondrial DNA Copy Number in Egyptian Myocardial Infarction Patients
Article.Authors: El naidany S.; Khader H.; Kenawy A.; Elhelbawy M.; Abouelatta Z.; Abdelmoneim H.; Aboukhalil R.; Tawfik W.; Abouelenin M.
Article.Abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a fatal condition that causes damage to the heart muscle by abruptly stopping blood flow and oxygenation. Mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtDNA CN) show an increased rate of association with development of several human diseases and malignancies. This paper, therefore, aims to identify the possible relation among mtDNA CN and its regulating gene TFAM (expression of the gene and rs1937 polymorphism) as markers in myocardial infarction among Egyptians. A total of 200 participants were enrolled and divided into two groups. Group 1 included 100 myocardial infarction patients with ST-segment elevation (STEMI) recruited from from the Coronary Care Unit (CCU) of Menoufia University Hospitals, while group 2 included 100 Controls. Blood samples were collected from all participants immediately after diagnosis of MI and before beginning therapy. TFAM SNP (rs1937) was determined by the allelic discrimination TaqMan technique, and mtDNA CN and TFAM gene expression were detected using real-time quantitative PCR in 100 MI patients and 100 controls. TFAM mRNA expression and mtDNA copy number were profoundly reduced in MI patients than controls. Analysis of genotype showed that the TFAM rs1937 variant distribution was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. The C allele and the GC genotype were substantially more frequent in the patients’ cohort (p = 0.006 and 0.005, respectively). The GC genotype of the TFAM polymorphism (rs1937) showed a preliminary association with MI in STEMI patients. Limitations of this study are the absence of longitudinal pre-MI or post-recovery data. TFAM mRNA expression and mtDNA copy number were measured in whole blood without adjustment for leukocyte subpopulations or platelet counts. Small number of C carriers of TFAM rs1937 variant and absence of CC genotype limited statistical power and requires replication in larger Egyptian cohort. These findings suggest that decreased TFAM gene expression and mtDNA CN were significant biomarkers associated with acute myocardial infarction in STEMI patients.

Article.Abstract: 3,4-Dihydropyrimidin-2(1H)-ones (DHPMs) are privileged heterocyclic scaffolds with broad biological activities. Docking, 200 ns molecular dynamics, and MM/PBSA estimates were compatible with this hypothesis but did not constitute experimental target validation. These data identify 4m as a starting point for DHPM-based antiproliferative agents and TOP2A as a hypothesis to be tested experimentally.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics Analysis of Phytolacca acinosa Fruit Fermentation Broth Against Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Evaluation of Phytolaccagenin as a Candidate Bioactive Constituent
Article.Authors: Zou Y.; Li Z.; Cao J.; Shu Y.; Zhou Y.; Zhang B.
Article.Abstract: Phytolacca acinosa Roxb. is a traditional Chinese medicine. In traditional practice, its root has long been used for “promoting diuresis to reduce edema” and “detoxifying and resolving masses”, and certain constituents of the root have been reported to exhibit in vitro anti-tumor activities. However, the fruit of Phytolacca acinosa represents a newly explored medicinal resource, and the anti-hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) activity of its fermentation broth (PAFFB) remains largely unexplored. This study evaluated the anti-HCC efficacy of PAFFB and its underlying mechanisms by integrating pharmacodynamics, multi-omics (transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics), and UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS profiling. In a diethylnitrosamine (DEN)-induced HCC rat model, PAFFB (0.75, 1.5, and 3 g/kg/d for 4 weeks) dose-dependently improved body weight and survival, alleviated liver injury, reduced tumor burden, and restored liver function, while exhibiting less apparent toxicity than cyclophosphamide in the parameters assessed (body weight, survival, and hepatic function and histopathology). Joint pathway enrichment analysis revealed that PAFFB modulated DEN-induced pathological alterations through the coordinated regulation of cholesterol–bile acid metabolism, inflammatory signaling, and energy metabolism. Mechanistically, PAFFB restored TLR-4/MYD88 expression, suppressed p65 and p38 phosphorylation, and upregulated CYP7A1, PPARα, and FXR. Among the 120 identified constituents, 21 compounds were absorbed into the bloodstream; phytolaccagenin suppressed Hepa1-6 proliferation, colony formation, and migration, induced apoptosis, ROS accumulation, and lipid peroxidation in vitro, and inhibited Hepa1-6 syngeneic tumor growth in mice without obvious toxicity. In conclusion, PAFFB exerts anti-HCC effects by regulating metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory signaling, and phytolaccagenin represents a candidate bioactive constituent of PAFFB.

Article.Title: Role of Ferroptosis in Anticancer Drug Resistance in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Systematic Review of Preclinical Studies
Article.Authors: Marques C.; Morais E.; Felipe-Moreira N.; Costa B.; Oliveira L.; Graner E.; Al-Samadi A.; Coletta R.
Article.Abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC) frequently develop anticancer drug resistance, limiting treatment efficacy. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation, is dysregulated in drug-resistant HNSCC cells and may contribute to tumor survival. This systematic review synthesized preclinical evidence on the role of ferroptosis in HNSCC anticancer drug resistance. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261286567). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched without language or date restrictions, and preclinical studies evaluating ferroptosis in HNSCC drug resistance were included. Study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment were independently performed by two reviewers. Out of 1870 records, 22 studies published between 2016 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Most used acquired cisplatin-resistant cell lines. Resistant cells consistently exhibited enhanced antioxidant defenses and reduced lipid peroxidation, primarily involving the SLC7A11/xCT–GSH–GPX4 axis and KEAP1–NRF2 signaling. Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of these defenses restored drug sensitivity in several models. Causal evidence was strongest in studies using ferroptosis-inhibitor rescue or in vivo validation, although methodological reporting was frequently insufficient. In conclusion, ferroptosis suppression contributes to HNSCC drug resistance, supporting ferroptosis induction as a potential resensitization strategy. Clinical translation requires validation in clinically relevant models.

Article.Title: Natural Medicines Targeting Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3: A Narrative Review of Cellular and Molecular Events
Article.Authors: Kmail M.; Suaidi N.; Chin J.; Lim L.; Wong K.
Article.Abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also known as Machado-Joseph disease, is the most common autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia and is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration for which no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapeutics are currently available. Mitochondrial dysfunction has emerged as a central pathogenic mechanism in SCA3, making it a promising therapeutic target. This narrative review aims to evaluate the published evidence on the therapeutic potential of natural medicines and their active compounds targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3. This review summarizes published evidence on the therapeutic potential of natural medicines and their active compounds targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3 in preclinical studies. The reviewed studies suggest the therapeutic potential of Glycyrrhiza inflata, Codonopsis pilosula, Ginkgo biloba, Poria cocos, Pueraria lobata, Rehmannia glutinosa, Curcuma longa, Hericium erinaceus, Astragalus membranaceus, Hemerocallis citrina, caffeic acid, and resveratrol in targeting mitochondrial dysfunction in SCA3. These natural medicines were reported to regulate multiple mitochondrial-associated pathways, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane potential, mitochondrial bioenergetics, mitochondrial dynamics, mitochondrial quality control, and mitochondria-mediated apoptosis, thereby improving neuronal survival and mitochondrial function in experimental SCA3 models. In conclusion, natural medicines targeting mitochondrial dysfunction represent promising preclinical candidates for further investigation in SCA3. However, further mechanistic investigations, well-designed clinical trials, and optimization of pharmacokinetic properties are required to facilitate their translation into clinical practice.

Article.Title: Multi-Omics and RNAi Reveal a Role for the Ubiquitin-Proteasome Pathway in Muscle Fiber Development of Common Carp (Cyprinus carpio)
Article.Authors: Gong Y.; Luo M.; Zhang X.; Qin N.; Wang L.; Zhu W.; Fu J.; Dong Z.
Article.Abstract: To investigate the molecular mechanisms of muscle fiber development underlying locomotion differences between two common carp (Cyprinus carpio) strains cultured in a rice-fish symbiosis system, we conducted comparative transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of muscle tissues collected from indolent Congjiang (CJ) and active FFRC No. 2 (FR) strains cultured under identical paddy field conditions. RNA-seq revealed 3708 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), and proteomic analysis identified 108 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs). Functional enrichment and protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analyses highlighted key genes (psma3, ppargc1a, ube3a) and proteins (Myh, Ckmt2b, Suclg2) associated with proteasome activity, adipocytokine signaling, and ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation. Quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis of ubiquitin-proteasome pathway-related genes confirmed significantly higher expression levels in the muscle tissue of CJ compared with FR. After a 21-day interference experiment, ube3a knockdown increased average muscle fiber area and diameter and reduced muscle fiber density in juvenile CJ, indicating that ube3a knockdown might promote muscle development in common carp. Subsequent swimming performance measurements can be conducted to further explore the impact of ube3a on fish locomotion. These results provide molecular insights into fish locomotion capacity related to behavioral adaptation in agroecological systems.

Article.Title: Association of GHRL and CYP19A1 Variants with Uterine Leiomyoma: An Exploratory Case–Control Study with In Silico Annotation
Article.Authors: Akbaba E.; Sezgin B.; Demirtaş A.; Özdemir Ç.; Edgünlü T.
Article.Abstract: Uterine leiomyomas (ULMs) are common benign gynecological tumors associated with estrogen signaling and metabolic–endocrine pathways. This study investigated the associations of CYP19A1 (cytochrome P450 family 19 subfamily A member 1; rs2414096) and GHRL (ghrelin and obestatin prepropeptide; rs34911341, rs696217) polymorphisms with leiomyoma risk and evaluated their potential functional effects in silico. This case–control study included 65 women with uterine leiomyoma and 72 healthy controls. Genotyping was performed using polymerase chain reaction–restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP). Associations were assessed using Firth’s penalized-likelihood logistic regression under additive, dominant, and recessive models, with adjustment for age, body mass index (BMI), and parity. Functional predictions employed CADD, PolyPhen-2, SIFT, SpliceAI, and I-Mutant v2.0. Cases and controls were comparable in age, BMI, and parity (all p > 0.05). CYP19A1 rs2414096 was not associated with leiomyoma risk. Conversely, GHRL rs34911341 showed a significant association under the adjusted additive model (OR = 2.85, 95% CI: 1.59–5.45, p = 0.0003; FDR q = 0.001) and remained independently associated in the joint multivariable model (OR = 2.75, 95% CI: 1.52–5.30, p = 0.0006). GHRL rs696217 showed a nominal additive association (adjusted OR = 2.11, p = 0.037), which did not remain significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction or in the joint model. Recessive associations for both GHRL variants were affected by complete separation. In silico analyses classified rs2414096 as benign, whereas both GHRL variants were computationally predicted to be potentially deleterious and to reduce protein stability. These findings suggest a candidate association between GHRL rs34911341 and leiomyoma susceptibility. Given the modest sample size, control-group Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium deviations, and absence of biochemical peptide measurements, larger multicenter studies are needed for validation.

Article.Title: Exploratory Association of 12S-HETE with Postprandial Hyperinsulinemia Rather than HOMA-IR in Women with PCOS/PMOS
Article.Authors: Szczuko M.; Skórka-Majewicz M.; Żwierełło W.; Pęcak A.; Rudak L.; Szczuko U.; Pokorska-Niewiada K.
Article.Abstract: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) is one of the most commonly diagnosed endocrine disorders among women of reproductive age. The proposed term more accurately reflects the pathophysiology of the condition, emphasizing its multisystem nature rather than restricting it to ovarian dysfunction. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is estimated to affect approximately 6–20% of women of reproductive age. The condition is characterized by considerable clinical heterogeneity, including menstrual irregularities, hyperandrogenism, difficulties conceiving, and abdominal obesity. In addition to hormonal disturbances, an important and often underestimated aspect of PMOS is its association with insulin resistance and chronic low-grade inflammation. Current evidence indicates that insulin resistance represents an important component of the pathogenesis of PMOS. In this context, the identification of biomarkers reflecting metabolic and inflammatory disturbances in affected women is of particular interest. Pro-inflammatory lipid mediators, such as hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids (HETEs) and hydroxyoctadecadienoic acids (HODEs), are products of fatty acid oxidation and act as active modulators of the inflammatory response. Increased concentrations of these metabolites have been reported in individuals with type 2 diabetes, excessive body weight, cardiovascular diseases, and in women with PMOS. The study included 45 women diagnosed with PMOS, who were divided into groups according to the presence of insulin resistance assessed using the HOMA-IR index. Venous blood plasma was used as the biological material, and the concentrations of selected HETE and HODE metabolites were determined using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The obtained data were subjected to statistical analysis to assess the associations between lipid mediator concentrations, parameters of carbohydrate metabolism, and selected metabolic indices. Statistical analysis revealed no significant differences in the concentrations of the analyzed oxylipins (HETE and HODE) between patient groups stratified according to HOMA-IR. No significant direct correlations were observed between most of the analyzed metabolites and body mass index (BMI) or fasting blood glucose levels. However, a nominally significant association was identified for 12S-HETE (p = 0.0258), which did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction (adjusted p = 0.1806). Its concentration was nearly twofold higher in patients with PMOS who exhibited postprandial hyperinsulinemia, assessed two hours after an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), compared with women who had a normal insulin response. Among the seven oxylipin metabolites analyzed, only 12S-HETE showed a nominal association with postprandial hyperinsulinemia. At the same time, the findings suggest that HOMA-IR and glycemic parameters may not fully reflect changes in the oxylipin profile in patients during the early stages of metabolic dysfunction. The concentrations of several analyzed oxylipins were strongly correlated, whereas 16RS-HETE showed only weak correlations with the other metabolites. Further studies are needed to clarify the relationship between oxylipin concentrations and metabolic dysfunction in women with PCOS/PMOS.

Article.Title: Whole Genome Resequencing Reveals High Genetic Homogeneity and Localized Candidate Differentiation Signals in Saxidomus purpuratus Along the Yellow and Bohai Sea
Article.Authors: Xu S.; Zhao C.; Han H.; Wu Y.; Ren L.; Wu B.; Xie C.; Li J.; Yu T.
Article.Abstract: Saxidomus purpuratus (S. purpuratus) is an economically important bivalve along the northern coast of China, where intensifying fishing pressure threatens its wild stocks. Its genome-wide population genetic variation remains poorly characterized. We resequenced 75 wild individuals from five populations spanning the northern Yellow Sea (Donggang, DDDG; Ganjingzi, DLGJ; Huancui, WHHC) and the Bohai Sea (Changdao, YTCD; Laizhou, YTLZ). The sampled populations exhibited relatively low genetic diversity (He = 0.1301–0.1324), weak among-population differentiation (Fst = 0.0035–0.0040), and heterozygosity deficiency (Fis = 0.0480–0.0831). PCA, NJ, and ADMIXTURE detected no geographic structure. PSMC revealed concordant demographic histories, with a sustained decline following a Middle Pleistocene expansion, consistent with historical allele exchange. Selection scans (DDDG as the target population; WHHC and YTCD as references) identified 1268 candidate genes, of which 197 were shared across the two comparisons. After masking a tandem histone gene cluster, the remaining 155 non-histone genes fell into five functional categories: receptor and signal transduction, membrane transport and ion channels, innate immunity and defense, extracellular matrix and adhesion, and detoxification and metabolism. These signals recurred in both comparisons, identifying DDDG as a candidate population for genotype–environment association testing. Together, these results indicate that the five populations constitute a single genetically connected unit, while pinpointing a small set of candidate loci that may underpin local adaptation and should inform stock-enhancement programmes.

Article.Title: Environmental Ligands of the Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor in Allergic Rhinitis: Immune and Neuroimmune Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Xiong Y.; Han J.; Yang Z.; Liu Y.; Ding P.; Bian X.; Yan B.; Fang Y.
Article.Abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is an immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated chronic inflammatory disease. Although type 2 immune responses are central to AR, environmental exposures, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and neuroimmune interactions also contribute to disease development. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is a ligand-activated transcription factor that links environmental signals to immune responses. Elevated AhR expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with AR has been associated with clinical severity. In non-AR experimental systems, AhR suppresses histamine-associated interleukin-6 (IL-6) production in macrophages, whereas 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) reduces acetylcholinesterase (AChE) expression and activity in neuronal cells. These findings suggest possible links to nasal inflammation and cholinergic regulation, but their contribution to nasal symptoms in AR remains to be established. In addition, AhR modulates mast-cell, B-cell, and T-cell responses in a ligand- and cell-dependent manner. Overall, AhR may exert protective or pathogenic effects depending on the activating ligand and target cell type, suggesting that its therapeutic potential in AR lies in ligand- and cell-specific modulation.

Article.Title: Molecular Markers of Agronomic Traits and Superior Germplasm of Spring Wheat in Northern Kazakhstan and Siberia
Article.Authors: Chernook A.; Divashuk M.; Ermolaev A.; Shamanin V.; Savin T.; Shelaeva T.; Chudinov V.; Fedorenko E.; Shepelev S.; Tajibayev D.; Morgounov A.
Article.Abstract: Spring bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is the principal crop of the vast rainfed region spanning Northern Kazakhstan, the Urals, and Western Siberia, where productivity is limited by moisture stress, diseases, and the slow adoption of genomic tools in traditional breeding. We performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of 142 spring wheat genotypes from the Kazakhstan–Siberia Network for Spring Wheat Improvement (KASIB), evaluated at four sites in Russia and Kazakhstan during 2020–2022. The analysis identified 23 significant marker–trait associations (SNPs), of which 21 were stable across at least two environments, and 11 showed pleiotropic effects on two or more traits. Grain yield was associated with two SNPs (1A_12366171_G_A and 1B_15284504_C_T), each also affecting heading and maturity. Heading and maturity were controlled by a cluster of SNPs on chromosomes 1B, 2B, 5A, and 7B, with effects of up to 5.1 days. Plant height was associated with SNPs on 1A, 5A, and 6B, including one marker (5A_585412831_A_G) that was pleiotropic with 1000-kernel weight. Spike productivity was associated with loci on 1A, 3D, 4A, 4D, 5B, and 7B (grain weight and grains per spike, spikelets per spike, and spike harvest index). Grain size and 1000-kernel weight were linked to SNPs on 1B, 5A, and 6B, and protein and gluten content to two loci on 3A and 4B, which raised protein by up to 0.62% and gluten by up to 1.39%.

Article.Title: Cholesterol- and Biosurfactant-Stabilized Ethosomes for Betanin: Formulation, Encapsulation and Controlled In Vitro Release
Article.Authors: Chudzińska-Skorupinska J.; Wawrzyńczak A.; Feliczak-Guzik A.
Article.Abstract: Betanin is a hydrophilic antioxidant with limited physicochemical stability, motivating the development of vesicular carriers to improve its retention and regulate release. This study employed a systematic, stepwise formulation-screening approach to develop and characterize cholesterol-containing ethosomes, including biosurfactant-modified formulations, for betanin encapsulation. The effects of preparation conditions, surfactant type and concentration, cholesterol content, and betanin loading on colloidal properties and storage stability were evaluated. Encapsulation efficiency, loading capacity, and in vitro release were also investigated. Formulations containing 2.5% (w/w) phospholipid, 30% (w/w) ethanol, 10% (w/w) ethylene glycol, 1% (w/w) cholesterol, and 0.625% (w/w) Tween 20 or Tween 20/Mirasoft® SL L60 mixture, prepared by 3 min homogenization, showed the most favorable performance. Betanin incorporation altered vesicle organization, while encapsulation and release strongly depended on surfactant composition and betanin loading. The highest encapsulation efficiency was 87.87 ± 3.22%, whereas the maximum loading capacity was 0.0271 ± 0.0026%. Release was incomplete and composition-dependent, ranging from 5.67 to 34.49% after 90 min at pH 5.8. The limited release indicated formulation-dependent betanin retention, which may favor controlled delivery but could also restrict active-compound availability. As skin permeation and biological safety were not evaluated, the relevance of these findings for dermal delivery remains to be established. Weibull analysis adequately described the nonlinear release profiles. These findings demonstrate that biosurfactant-modified ethosomes are tunable lipid nanocarriers with composition-dependent encapsulation and in vitro release properties.

Article.Title: Neuroinflammation and Anxiety-Related Pathology: Apoptosis, Pyroptosis, and the Preclinical Potential of Paeoniflorin
Article.Authors: Li C.; Dong Q.; Hou Y.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety disorders have a multifactorial pathophysiology involving neurotransmitter signaling, stress-responsive neuroendocrine systems, and distributed neural circuits. Neuroinflammation has emerged as an important component of this network, although its contribution varies across anxiety phenotypes and experimental contexts. Apoptosis and pyroptosis may contribute to cellular injury in selected preclinical models, but their causal roles in human anxiety disorders remain incompletely established. This review examines inflammatory signaling and cell-death pathways relevant to anxiety-related pathology and critically evaluates the evidence for paeoniflorin (PF), a monoterpene glycoside derived from Paeonia species. Particular attention is given to the tryptophan–kynurenine pathway, regional differences across amygdala, hippocampal, and prefrontal networks, and interactions among the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, glucocorticoid signaling, and peripheral-to-central immune communication. PF-related changes in inflammatory, apoptotic, and pyroptotic markers are considered alongside neurochemical, neuroendocrine, and behavioral outcomes, with direct PF findings distinguished from evidence involving other interventions or disease models. Available studies support further investigation of PF as a preclinical candidate, rather than establishing clinically meaningful anxiolytic efficacy. Limitations in model validity, causal inference, dosing, bioavailability, and biomarker validation are discussed to guide mechanistic research and future clinical translation.

Article.Title: Efficacy of Platelet-Rich Plasma in the Treatment of Chronic Plantar Fasciitis Compared with Other Conventional Treatments (Corticosteroids and Shockwave Therapy): A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Ortiz-Romero M.; Parra-Aguado E.; Gordillo-Fernández L.
Article.Abstract: Plantar fasciitis is a degenerative condition of the plantar fascia characterized by collagen fiber degeneration, increased ground-substance (extracellular matrix) proteins, focal fibroblast proliferation and increased vascularity; it is for ≥3 months and affects around 10% of the general population. This review compared the efficacy of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), an autologous source of growth factors, with corticosteroid (CS) injection, which acts through anti-inflammatory mechanisms, and extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT), which acts through mechanotransduction. Following a protocol registered retrospectively in Open Science Framework (OSF) Registries, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and Dialnet were searched from January 2020 to September 2026 for comparative studies of PRP versus CSs and/or ESWT in adults with chronic plantar fasciitis. Screening was performed independently by two reviewers. Because of heterogeneous outcome scales, time points and reporting, pooling was not appropriate and results were synthesized narratively by comparator and follow-up period. Twenty-two primary studies (1915 patients) were included: 20 compared PRP with CSs and two compared PRP with ESWT. Short-term (≤6 weeks) results for PRP versus CSs were inconsistent, with some studies favoring CSs. From approximately 3 months onward, most studies reported lower pain (visual analogue scale), better function (American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS), Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM), Foot Function Index (FFI)) and a greater reduction of ultrasonographic plantar fascia thickness with PRP; three studies found no difference or favored CSs. The two studies comparing PRP with ESWT reported mixed results. The available evidence suggests that PRP may provide greater medium- to long-term improvements in pain and function than CS injection, whereas short-term results are inconsistent. Evidence comparing PRP with ESWT is insufficient to draw conclusions. According to Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE), the certainty of the evidence was low for long-term pain and plantar fascia thickness and very low for the remaining outcomes and for the comparison with ESWT.

Article.Title: Hereditary Angioedema with Normal C1-Inhibitor in Children: Diagnostic Challenges, Novel Mutations in MYOF, F12, and HS3ST6, and the Role of Bioinformatics Analysis
Article.Authors: Denisova A.; Kolosova N.; Geppe N.; Denisova V.; Podzolkova V.; Ozerskaia I.; Shatalina S.; Shakhnazarova M.; Ostankova Y.; Pechnikova N.
Article.Abstract: Hereditary angioedema with normal C1 inhibitor (HAE-nC1INH) lacks validated biochemical biomarkers, complicating diagnosis and interpretation of rare genetic variants, particularly in children. All 23 patients underwent whole-exome sequencing, followed by integrated in silico assessment of candidate variants. A rare heterozygous MYOF p.Arg1590Gln variant was identified in one patient and classified as a VUS, with computational analyses suggesting potential functional relevance. Homozygous F12 p.Ala207Pro was identified in two unrelated patients; however, its high population frequency and benign ClinVar classification do not support a causative role. Four HS3ST6 missense variants were detected in five patients; p.Pro199Leu showed the strongest computational evidence of potential functional relevance, whereas the clinical significance of the remaining variants remains uncertain. These findings expand the molecular spectrum of pediatric HAE-nC1INH and support combining sequencing with prioritization of variants in relevant genes. Functional studies are required to confirm causality before clinical implementation.

Article.Title: Integrated Transcriptomic Analysis Identifies a Ferroptosis-Related Gene Signature Underlying Macrophage Heterogeneity and Immune Dysregulation in Rheumatoid Arthritis Synovium
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Zhang R.
Article.Abstract: Ferroptosis contributes to rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the key regulators and their cell-specific functions in the synovial microenvironment remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify robust ferroptosis-associated biomarkers and define their cellular context through an integrated transcriptomic framework. Bulk synovial transcriptomic datasets were integrated using differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and a curated ferroptosis gene set. Candidate genes were prioritized using three feature-selection algorithms and validated across twelve models. Immune infiltration, single-cell RNA sequencing, pseudotime, CellChat, and virtual gene perturbation analyses characterized their cellular and functional context. Six ferroptosis-related genes (AIM2, HCP5, CAPG, ALOX5, TYMS, and RUNX3) formed a diagnostic signature discriminating RA from healthy synovium (mean leakage-free test AUC 0.977 across five training-only re-derivations; 0.9375 in the primary split), with consistent leave-one-dataset-out and osteoarthritis-control validation. These genes linked to adaptive immune and ferroptosis-associated transcriptional programs. Single-cell analysis localized this transcriptional score to macrophages, where ferroptosis-signature-high macrophages occupied a central communication-network position and showed collagen-pathway enrichment; because RA and healthy samples were not fully independent of dataset origin, this finding is hypothesis-generating. Pseudotime analysis suggested progressive induction of these genes toward an inflammatory NF-κB/TNF/IL-17 terminal state, and virtual perturbation suggested convergence on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation networks that persisted after removing sex-chromosome genes, though residual sex-associated effects cannot be fully excluded. This study identifies a biologically interpretable ferroptosis-related gene signature and suggests ferroptosis-associated macrophage reprogramming may contribute to immune dysregulation in RA synovium. The single-cell findings are hypothesis-generating given the cohort design, while the diagnostic signature was supported by leakage-free, cross-cohort, and disease-specificity analyses, providing candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets for RA.

Article.Title: Induction of Oral Immune Tolerance Enables Sequential AAV9/AAV8 Gene Therapy in Mucopolysaccharidosis IVA
Article.Authors: Saikia S.; Musini K.; Khan S.; Tomatsu S.
Article.Abstract: Mucopolysaccharidosis IVA (MPS IVA) results from deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase (GALNS), leading to progressive keratan sulfate accumulation, and current treatments have limited efficacy. Although adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy can restore systemic enzyme activity, immune responses to the transgene and viral capsid restrict durability and prevent vector re-administration. We evaluated a combined strategy of antigen-specific oral immune tolerance and sequential AAV serotype delivery. Neonatal MPS IVA mice received a mixture of three immunodominant GALNS-derived T- and B-cell epitopes on alternate days for 20 days, followed by AAV9 at 4 weeks and redosing with either AAV9 or AAV8 at 10 weeks. Peptide-treated tolerized MPS IVA mice showed a 2–3-fold increase in circulating GALNS activity after the first dose and a 7–8-fold increase after redosing, whereas non-tolerized MPS IVA mice developed anti-GALNS antibodies that reduced enzyme levels. No cross-reactive neutralizing antibodies were detected between AAV9 and AAV8. Peptide-treated mice showed normalization of plasma and hepatic keratan sulfate (KS) and significant improvements in skeletal and cardiac histopathology, with the greatest benefit in the peptide-treated AAV9→AAV8 group. These findings demonstrate that oral immune tolerance enables safe AAV re-administration, enhances systemic enzyme bioavailability, and improves tissue correction, supporting a clinically translatable approach for durable treatment of MPS IVA.
