Article.Title: Characterization of the Aromatic Profile of Mature-Green Tomato Fruit (‘Fen Junmei’) in Response to Supplemental LED Light Quality and Intensity During Ripening
Article.Authors: Yang J.; Yu X.; Wang Q.; Xia Z.; Yin P.; Zhang X.; Zhang J.; Jeong B.; Song J.
Article.Abstract: Light quality and light intensity, as important environmental signals, can regulate the ripening process and flavor compound synthesis in tomato fruits. Chitosan oligosaccharides, as natural bio-stimulants, can improve postharvest quality of fruits and vegetables. However, how varied LED light quality–intensity regimes modulate ripening and aroma metabolism in chitosan-oligosaccharide-pre-treated mature-green tomato fruit remains unclear. This study used mature-green tomato fruits as experimental material, which were pre-treated by immersion in chitosan oligosaccharide solution. Subsequently, different combinations of supplemental light qualities (white light, blue light, and 1:1 red–blue composite light) and varying light intensities were applied for continuous illumination. The effects of these lighting conditions on the postharvest physiological quality and volatile aroma components of tomatoes were systematically investigated, and the molecular regulatory mechanisms were analyzed through transcriptome sequencing. The results showed that light quality and intensity significantly regulated tomato fruit color change, firmness, pigment accumulation, and sugar–acid quality. High-intensity red–blue combined light treatment (RB-H) effectively accelerated fruit ripening, promoted carotenoid accumulation, significantly increased the content of terpenes and aromatic volatile compounds, and improved fruit flavor. Transcriptome analysis revealed that different light treatments induced a large number of differentially expressed genes, with transcription factors from the WRKY, MYB, AP2/ERF, bHLH, NAC, and C2H2 families widely involved in light signal responses. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified two key modules associated with light response. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed that the biosynthesis of the terpenoid backbone, monoterpenoid biosynthesis, sesquiterpenoid and triterpenoid biosynthesis, as well as tyrosine metabolism pathways, are the core pathways regulating the production of volatile aroma compounds in tomatoes. In summary, RB-H treatment promotes the accumulation of characteristic aromatic compounds and enhances overall tomato quality by activating key genes involved in terpenoid biosynthesis and tyrosine metabolism pathways. This study reveals the transcriptional regulatory network by which light quality and intensity shape postharvest tomato ripening and flavor development in chitosan-oligosaccharide-pre-treated fruit, providing theoretical support for precise LED light environment control and targeted improvement of flavor quality in postharvest tomatoes.

Article.Title: Lens Capsule microRNA Profiling Across the Primary Angle-Closure Disease Spectrum: Association with Anterior Segment Crowding
Article.Authors: Park H.; Cho H.; Yeon Y.; Cha M.; Lee J.; Ryu S.; Yoon J.; Kim Y.; Lee W.
Article.Abstract: We aimed to compare anterior lens capsule microRNA (miRNA) expression across the primary angle-closure disease (PACD) spectrum and a control group, and to examine associations between differentially expressed miRNAs and anterior segment biometric parameters. Higher miR-188-5p expression correlated with greater LV (r = −0.64, p = 0.033), narrower AOD500 (r = 0.50, p = 0.015), and shorter AXL (r = 0.41, p = 0.032). miR-146b-5p and miR-335-5p showed subgroup-specific differences and correlated with LV and AXL/AOD500, respectively, though these findings were exploratory. However, these findings did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing. Article.Title: Discovery of Novel HDAC8 Inhibitors Through Shape-Based Virtual Screening: Experimental Validation and Characterization of a Promising Quinoline-Based Hit Scaffold
Article.Authors: Gargano A.; González-Bakker A.; Puerta A.; Maggisano V.; Bulotta S.; Rocca R.; Padrón J.; Alcaro S.
Article.Abstract: Histone deacetylase 8 (HDAC8) is overexpressed in several solid tumors and, unlike other Class I HDACs, functions independently of large corepressor complexes, making it an attractive target for structure-based drug design. Here, we aimed to identify novel natural compounds capable of targeting the human HDAC8 catalytic site. A library of 307,814 natural products from ZINC15 was screened by shape-based virtual screening using five structurally diverse co-crystallized HDAC8 ligands as templates, followed by molecular docking and Molecular Mechanics-Generalized Born Surface Area (MM-GBSA) binding free energy calculations. Seven commercially available hits were selected for enzymatic validation, leading to the identification of 4-((7-methoxyquinolin-4-yl)amino)benzamide (ZINC000054202375, compound 2) as a promising HDAC8 inhibitor. In vitro antiproliferative assays across multiple human solid tumor cell lines demonstrated significant growth inhibition by compound 2, further supported by colony formation assays. Mechanistic studies using label-free live-cell imaging, Annexin V staining, DAPI (4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) nuclear morphology, and DCFDA (2′,7′-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate) assays revealed membrane blebbing, mitotic failure, increased reactive oxygen species, and nuclear fragmentation, consistent with apoptosis induction. Finally, 1 μs molecular dynamics simulations supported the formation of a persistent ligand–receptor interaction network within the HDAC8 catalytic pocket. Overall, compound 2 represents a promising non-hydroxamate hit scaffold with promising HDAC8 inhibitory activity, serving as a starting point for the development of novel HDAC-targeted anticancer agents.

Article.Title: Metabolomic Differences Between Wild and Cultivated Ophiocordyceps sinensis Identify Source-Associated Metabolites with Predicted Antifibrotic Relevance
Article.Authors: Jin M.; Li J.; Lan J.; De B.; Wei D.; Zhang L.; Zhou X.
Article.Abstract: Ophiocordyceps sinensis (O. sinensis), a precious traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), exhibits remarkable hepatoprotective effects. We combined untargeted ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography–Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry with targeted liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry to compare wild type (WT) and artificially cultivated (AC) specimens. Adenosine, cordycepin, and ergosterol were more abundant in AC extracts, whereas hypoxanthine, deoxyguanosine, guanosine, and guanine were more abundant in WT extracts. These findings reveal source-associated metabolic differences between the analyzed WT and AC samples and provide mechanistic insights into their potentially divergent roles in liver fibrosis regulation, which warrant further experimental validation.

Article.Title: Combining Ligand- and Structure-Based Approaches to Develop Haloacetamide-Derived Di(hetero)arylmethanes as Potential Anticancer Agents
Article.Authors: Shibaeva K.; Smolobochkin A.; Chugunova E.; Nguyen H.; Shakirov A.; Gibadullina E.; Lyubina A.; Sapunova A.; Voloshina A.; Aleksandrova Y.; Neganova M.; Gazizov A.; Burilov A.; Pudovik M.; Sinyashin O.

Article.Title: Genetic Variants in HSP70 Family Genes and Their Co-Chaperones Are Associated with Ischemic Stroke Susceptibility and Gene Expression During Acute and Early Recovery Phases
Article.Authors: Ivenkov M.; Snezhkina A.; Shilenok I.; Medvedenko N.; Zarubin A.; Bushuev E.; Dubinina U.; Kobzeva K.; Kudryavtseva A.; Nechipurenko Y.; Bushueva O.

Additional variants were associated with age at IS onset, lipid levels, coagulation parameters, body mass index, and number of IS episodes. Functional analyses linked associated loci to pathways relevant to atherosclerosis, inflammation, apoptosis, oxidative stress, autophagy, mitochondrial dysfunction, and angiogenesis. Transcriptomic analysis identified associations of rs1043618 HSPA1A with C4B expression during acute IS and DDR1 expression on day 7, while rs1042665 HSPA9 was associated with genotype-dependent changes in HSPA9 expression. Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and In Silico Characterization of the Salt Overly Sensitive 3/Calcineurin B-like (GhSOS3) Gene Family in Upland Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) and Expression Profiling of Two Members Under Drought, Salt and Heat Stress
Article.Authors: Iqra L.; Shahid M.; Shah M.; Akram U.; Božić D.; Haider I.; Hu Y.; Junaid M.; El-Hendawy S.
Article.Abstract: Upland cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) is a global cash crop cultivated extensively for its high-quality fiber and oil-rich seeds. Several gene families are involved in the regulatory pathways that enable plants to acclimate to adverse abiotic stresses. One such gene family is the Calcineurin B-like (CBL)/Salt Overly Sensitive-3 (SOS3) family of calcium-sensor proteins associated with plant signaling. The encoded proteins showed conserved EF-hand-related motifs, with differences in gene structure, predicted physicochemical properties, and motif composition. Putative abscisic acid-responsive (ABRE), salicylic acid-responsive (SARE), drought stress-responsive (DSRE) and gibberellin-responsive (GRE) elements predicted in the promoters suggest that the GhSOS3 genes may be transcriptionally responsive to abiotic stress-related signals; however, these predictions require experimental validation. Experimentally, qPCR analysis showed stress- and time-dependent changes in the transcript abundance of GhSOS3-2 and GhSOS3-3 under drought, salt, and heat treatments in three cotton genotypes, indicating differential transcriptional responses to these stress conditions. Collectively, these findings establish a genomic and expression framework for future functional studies of GhSOS3 candidates in calcium-mediated stress responses in cotton.

Article.Title: Icariin, a Multi-Target Natural Neuroprotectant, and a Comprehensive Review on Its Synthetic Methods, Pharmacological Evaluation and Pharmacokinetic Characteristics
Article.Authors: Zhang K.; Li J.; Ban W.; Chen P.; Ding X.; Lv L.; Guo B.; Yang Z.
Article.Abstract: Epimedii Folium (Yinyanghuo), a unique and traditional Chinese medicinal plant used in medicine for more than a thousand years, has been traditionally used to tonify the liver and kidneys, strengthen the muscles and bones, and eliminate rheumatism. Its principal active ingredient, icariin, has long been used clinically for impotence and spermatorrhea, weakness of muscles and bones, rheumatism and arthralgia pain, and has recently attracted growing attention for its therapeutic potential against central nervous system diseases. This review summarizes advances over the past five years in the preparation, neuroprotective effects, and pharmacokinetics of icariin. The literature was retrieved from Pubmed, CNKI (China National Knowledge Infrastructure), Web of Science, and Google Scholar using keywords including “icariin”, “Epimedii Folium”, “neuroprotection”, “biosynthesis” and “pharmacokinetics”, and studies were screened for relevance to preparation methods, pharmacological evaluation, and pharmacokinetic properties. Although extraction from plant sources remains the main preparation method, chemical synthesis and biosynthesis are emerging in response to resource scarcity. Accumulating evidence indicates that icariin exerts neuroprotective effects through multiple mechanisms, including anti-neuroinflammation, mitochondrial protection, antioxidant effects, inhibition of neuronal apoptosis, promotion of neuronal proliferation and differentiation and regulation of synaptic plasticity. Its rapid absorption, ability to cross the blood–brain barrier, and low cumulative toxicity provide a favorable pharmacokinetic basis for central nervous system applications. This review highlights synthetic strategies, pharmacological evaluation and pharmacokinetic characteristics of icariin, aiming to support its broader application in CNSDs.

Article.Title: Cardiac Atrial Appendage Stem Cells Embedded in Elastin-like Recombinamer Hydrogel for Cardiac Repair After Acute MI: A Pilot Study
Article.Authors: Heeren E.; Vastmans L.; Deluyker D.; Delaet A.; Steegen L.; Vandenboer V.; Van der Wee I.; Puertas Bartolomé M.; Duwé S.; Dhont S.; Volders P.; Cardilli A.; Rodríguez-Cabello J.; Bronckaers A.; Hendrikx M.; Bito V.

MI+C+H significantly improved anterior wall thickness versus MI+H, with favorable trends for MI+C. Wall motion score index showed a similar large, non-significant effect. Transcriptomics suggested the MI+C+H molecular profile reflected complementary contributions of both monotherapies rather than distinct synergistic mechanisms. These preliminary findings support ELR-mediated CASC delivery and suggest potential benefits for preserving cardiac function and limiting adverse remodeling, warranting confirmation in adequately powered studies.

Article.Title: Transcriptomic Alterations in Peripheral Blood of Patients with Metabolic Syndrome
Article.Authors: Medetalibeyoglu A.; Oyaci Y.; Senkal N.; Sayin S.; Guzel Dirim M.; Senkal H.; Pehlivan M.; Tukek T.; Pehlivan S.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is a complex cardiometabolic disorder characterized by interconnected abnormalities in glucose and lipid metabolism, adiposity, and vascular regulation. This study aimed to identify peripheral blood gene expression changes in MetS using RNA sequencing and to evaluate selected candidate genes by RT-qPCR in an independent cohort. RNA sequencing was performed in 15 patients with MetS and 10 healthy controls; after exclusion of three MetS samples based on PCA, differential expression analysis included 12 patients with MetS and 10 controls. Among 19,668 protein-coding genes, 730 showed nominal differential expression (p < 0.05), whereas only FKBP1B and EVA1C remained significant after FDR correction. In the RT-qPCR cohort, FKBP1B, ARVCF, and NAA40 showed significantly higher expression in MetS, corresponding to 6.33-, 1.87-, and 2.34-fold increases, respectively; all remained significant after FDR correction. No significant differences were observed for PLIN2, ALOX15B, or MUSTN1. Exploratory analyses identified no robust associations between candidate-gene expression and metabolic or cardiovascular clinical parameters after multiple-testing correction. FKBP1B remained significant after transcriptome-wide FDR correction and showed concordant upregulation in the independent RT-qPCR cohort, while the nominal RNA-seq candidates ARVCF and NAA40 also showed significantly increased expression by RT-qPCR. Article.Title: Quantification of Enzyme–Inhibitor Pharmacological Actions
Article.Authors: Masson P.; Pashirova T.
Article.Abstract: Quantitative measurement of enzyme–drug interactions has become a key step in the process of drug discovery. More and more studies refer to the determination of the operational index, IC50, the half-maximal inhibitory concentration, from dose–response curves, instead of the determination of the exact dissociation constant, Ki, a true thermodynamic parameter that measures the affinity and provides information on binding mechanisms. Although knowledge of IC50 is useful for rapid screening and comparison of new molecules, it depends on experimental conditions, in particular substrate and enzyme concentration, type of inhibitor, and incubation time with inhibitor. Thus, IC50 values can be misleading in cases of allosteric inhibition, partial inhibition, slow-tight binding and progressive inhibition (covalent inhibition). As a consequence, the relationships between IC50 and Ki strongly depend on catalytic and inhibition mechanistic models and experimental conditions. The present review provides relationships between IC50 and Ki for simple and complex mechanisms of enzyme inhibition and highlights the interest of a thorough analysis of binding processes and irreversible reactions with inhibitors to describe the potentialities of new pharmacologically active compounds, acting either on Michaelian or non-Michaelian enzymes.

Article.Title: RNA m6A Modification in Immunometabolism: Context-Dependent Mechanisms and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Fang Q.; Li W.; Cai Y.; Zhang S.; Tang X.; Chu C.; Zhou M.; Li F.; Zhang Z.; Li X.
Article.Abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) regulates RNA fate and has been linked to immune cell function and metabolic adaptation. This narrative review examines selected studies across innate, adaptive, and tissue-resident immune populations, focusing on the cellular origin, target transcript, and experimental evidence supporting each mechanism. Metabolic inputs, including α-ketoglutarate, lactate, and D-2-hydroxyglutarate, can influence m6A regulatory pathways, while m6A-dependent RNA regulation can alter metabolic enzymes, transporters, and immune responses. We discuss these findings within a proposed metabolite–m6A–immune framework; reciprocal relationships demonstrated in separate settings do not establish a closed feedback circuit in every cell population or disease model. We distinguish direct metabolic measurements from changes in signaling, survival, differentiation, and inferred pathway activity, and consider how tissue context and target selection may account for contrasting effects of the same regulator. Representative pharmacological studies of METTL3, FTO, and YTH domain readers are considered alongside interventions with less well-defined target specificity and early clinical development of METTL3 inhibition. The available evidence supports context-dependent mechanisms and therapeutic hypotheses, while clinical benefit, cellular selectivity, and long-term safety remain unresolved for the applications discussed.

Article.Title: Chloroplast Genome Variation and Phylogenetic Relationships of Lavandula angustifolia and Lavandula × intermedia
Article.Authors: Popov A.; Petrova K.; Patrushev M.; Toshchakov S.; Sharko F.
Article.Abstract: Plant chloroplast genomes are characterized by high conservatism and a well-described organization, making them a convenient basis for analyzing evolutionary dynamics and constructing phylogenetic hypotheses. The assembled genomes ranged from 151,431 to 151,480 bp, which is consistent with the expected chloroplast genome organization and indicates high structural stability within the genus. All six genomes exhibited the typical quadripartite structure of angiosperm chloroplast genomes, with a large single-copy (LSC) region of 82,682–82,837 bp, a small single-copy (SSC) region of 17,579–17,580 bp, and two inverted repeats (IRa and IRb) of 25,532–25,586 bp each. They contained 113 genes in total, including 79 protein-coding genes, 30 tRNA genes and 4 rRNA genes. Nucleotide diversity analysis revealed several variable intergenic regions that could serve as potential candidate molecular markers. Each sample harboured 56–57 simple sequence repeat (SSR) loci, unevenly distributed across the genome. Phylogenetic analysis based on whole chloroplast genome alignments confirmed the placement of the newly assembled Lavandula sequences within the family Lamiaceae. The six chloroplast genomes obtained in this work provide a robust reference set for future comparative genomic, phylogenetic and population-level studies in Lavandula.

Article.Title: Association of GSTM1 and GSTT1 Deletion Variants with Susceptibility to Behçet’s Disease in a Saudi Population: A Case Control Study
Article.Authors: Mustafa M.; Alkathiri S.; Alrashidi S.; Algoblan S.; Alokaily F.
Article.Abstract: Behçet’s disease (BD) is a chronic multisystem inflammatory disorder in which genetic susceptibility and oxidative stress may contribute to disease pathogenesis. Article.Title: Mechanism-Matched Pharmacology of Resistance in EGFR-Mutant NSCLC: Genomic Bypass, Lineage Plasticity, Antibody-Drug Conjugates, and Candidate Biophysical Targets
Article.Authors: Seo Y.
Article.Abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) often responds to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors but develops heterogeneous resistance. This structured narrative review integrates clinical and experimental evidence on resistance after osimertinib and intensified EGFR-directed therapy. It distinguishes on-target EGFR alterations, MET and ERBB-family bypass, downstream signaling, oncogenic fusions, histologic transformation, epithelial–mesenchymal plasticity, and drug-tolerant persistence, linking each mechanism to an appropriate assay and treatment context. We evaluate next-generation EGFR inhibitors, EGFR-MET combinations, bispecific antibodies, platinum-pemetrexed intensification, and antibody-drug conjugates directed at HER3, TROP2, or HER2. Clinical validation is assessed separately from mechanistic causality, with attention to allelic phase, central nervous system exposure, target engagement, unbound drug concentration, predictive biomarkers, and safety. Ion channels and transporters, including ANO1/TMEM16A, LRRC8/VRAC, KCa3.1, hERG, STIM-ORAI, TRP, and pH regulators, remain exploratory candidate targets. Available evidence for their role in acquired osimertinib resistance is largely indirect; expression or general tumor biology does not establish disease-specific dependency. A mechanism-matched development pathway using paired tissue and plasma sampling, relevant resistant models, causal perturbation, and pharmacodynamic validation is proposed. Clinical decisions should follow validated mechanisms rather than extrapolated biophysical hypotheses.

Article.Title: Duration-Dependent Ketone Body Responses to Fasting: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression
Article.Authors: Ulupınar S.; Terzi M.; Malkoç N.; Çamli A.; İnce İ.; Gençoğlu C.; Özbay S.
Article.Abstract: Prolonged fasting with no caloric intake induces a metabolic shift characterized by increased fat oxidation and ketone production. However, the magnitude of circulating ketone responses and their dependence on fasting duration have not been quantitatively synthesized. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of water-only fasting and other prolonged fasting protocols involving complete caloric abstinence on circulating ketone biomarkers and examined whether fasting duration moderates these responses. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched for human studies published between 2000 and 2025. Eligible studies reported pre–post measurements of β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), acetoacetate, or total plasma ketones following water-only or other non-caloric fasting protocols. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using Hedges’ g. Duration effects were assessed through subgroup analyses (≤3 days vs. >3 days) and random-effects meta-regression with study-level cluster-robust standard errors. Thirty studies providing 44 effect sizes were included. Fasting significantly increased BHB (g = 2.794), total plasma ketones (g = 3.260), and acetoacetate (g = 1.731). Greater elevations in BHB and total plasma ketones were observed with fasting durations exceeding three days. Meta-regression indicated significant positive associations between fasting duration and responses for BHB and total plasma ketones, whereas no significant association was detected for acetoacetate. Despite substantial heterogeneity for BHB and total plasma ketones, sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the pooled effects. Small-study effects were detected for BHB, whereas funnel-plot asymmetry for total plasma ketones was considered exploratory because of the limited number of studies. Water-only fasting and other prolonged fasting protocols involving complete caloric abstinence are associated with marked increases in circulating ketone bodies, with a clear duration-dependent pattern observed particularly for BHB and total plasma ketones.

Article.Title: Effect of the rs12249854 Polymorphism in the HECTD2 Gene and Selected Clinical Variables on the Response to Intradetrusor Injection of Botulinum Neurotoxin Type A in Female Patients with Overactive Bladder: A Single-Center Prospective Study
Article.Authors: Ciećwież S.; Lewandowska K.; Boroń A.; Kotlęga D.; Kociszewski J.; Ciechanowicz A.
Article.Abstract: The HECTD2:rs12249854 polymorphism may be associated with a weaker response to an intradetrusor injection of botulinum neurotoxin type A (BoNT/A) in patients with overactive bladder (OAB). This prospective study analyzed the link between the HECTD2:rs12249854 polymorphism and the response to BoNT/A treatment in 156 OAB patients, based on changes in urodynamic parameters and ICIQ-OAB and ICIQ-LUTS-QoL scores six months after the injection. BoNT/A treatment contributed to improvements in all parameters except the average flow rate. Wild-type homozygotes (TT, n = 137) differed from TA heterozygotes (n = 19) solely in terms of pretreatment ICIQ-OAB Part A and ICIQ-LUTS-QoL Part A scores, both of which were higher in the heterozygotes. Thus, the HECTD2:rs12249854 polymorphism does not appear to be associated with the response to BoNT/A treatment. Patients with neurogenic OAB (n = 60) had a higher pretreatment detrusor pressure at maximum flow than those with idiopathic OAB (n = 96), but this difference was no longer observed after BoNT/A treatment. Good responders to the BoNT/A injection (defined as at least 50% decrease in the ICIQ-LUTS-QoL Part A score, n = 50) had a higher body mass index and parity and a lower pretreatment maximum flow rate than poor responders (n = 106). Before formulating any definitive conclusions, the results of this exploratory study should be verified in an adequately powered multicenter cohort.

Article.Title: Optimizing Nystatin Biosynthesis Through Targeted Manipulation of nysL and nysGtf in Streptomyces noursei
Article.Authors: Shi J.; Song D.; Yang J.; Ni X.; Xu Y.; Wang F.; Ylihonko K.; Metsä-Ketelä M.; Song M.; Xu W.
Article.Abstract: Nystatin, a polyene macrolide antifungal agent produced by Streptomyces noursei, exists as three major derivatives (nystatin A1, A3, polyfungin B) with distinct C-10 and C-35 modifications. Although the core catalytic functions of NysL and NysGtf have been established, the metabolic crosstalk between the C-10 hydroxylation and C-35 digitosylation branches, together with the in vivo substrate promiscuity of NysGtf in industrial S. noursei, remains poorly understood. In this study, we constructed gene-disruption, complementation and overexpression mutants of S. noursei 72-22-1 to characterize nysL and nysGtf. While NysL has previously been established as the C-10 hydroxylase, we characterized its role in the industrial derivative strain 72-22-1. nysL disruption abolished C-10 hydroxylation, eliminated nystatin A1/A3 and caused accumulation of 10-deoxynystatin and polyfungin B, while complementation and/or overexpression restored A1/A3 formation. nysGtf inactivation blocked C-35 glycosylation, raising nystatin A1 titer to 0.587 mg/mL and decreasing polyfungin B to 0.027 mg/mL. Its overexpression enhanced nystatin A3 production to 1.195 mg/mL. Our findings define the physiological roles of NysL and NysGtf in nystatin biosynthesis, identify polyfungin B as the key antifungal component, and provide a feasible strategy for metabolic engineering of S. noursei to generate high-activity nystatin derivatives.

Article.Title: Helicobacter pylori-Derived Outer Membrane Vesicles Promote Hepatocellular Carcinoma Cell Proliferation with PI3K/AKT/mTOR Activation and Cyclin D1 Upregulation
Article.Authors: Zhou J.; Song X.; Li J.; Huang H.; Chen H.; Tang H.; Li H.
Article.Abstract: Accumulating evidence suggests an association between Helicobacter pylori infection and liver diseases; however, it remains unclear whether H. pylori or its extracellular products directly influence hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) biology. Here, we examined the effects of viable H. pylori, sterile H. pylori-conditioned supernatant (Hp-CS), and isolated H. pylori-derived outer membrane vesicles (Hp-OMVs) on HCC cells. H. pylori adhered to and invaded Huh7 and Hepa1-6 cells, increased Cyclin D1 expression, and enhanced the growth of tumors derived from bacteria-exposed Hepa1-6 cells in immunocompetent C57BL/6J mice. Hp-CS increased HCC cell metabolic activity, colony formation, migration, and invasion. Hp-OMVs were characterized by transmission electron microscopy and nanoparticle tracking analysis. Exposure to Hp-OMVs increased HCC cell metabolic activity, colony formation, cell-cycle progression, and tumor growth in a syngeneic mouse model. Hp-OMVs also increased PI3K, AKT, and mTOR phosphorylation and elevated Cyclin D1 expression. The PI3K inhibitor LY294002 attenuated these molecular changes and reduced Hp-OMV-induced cell-cycle progression and colony formation. These findings show that H. pylori and its extracellular products promote proliferation-associated phenotypes in experimental HCC models. Hp-OMVs are biologically active extracellular components of H. pylori, and pharmacological inhibition supports the involvement of PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling and Cyclin D1 upregulation in their growth-promoting effects.

Article.Title: Research Trends, Knowledge Evolution and Pharmacological Advances of Cordyceps cicadae: A Bibliometric Analysis
Article.Authors: Du S.; Luo R.; Liu A.; Yang T.; Wang N.; Duan J.
Article.Abstract: Cordyceps cicadae (C. cicadae), an entomopathogenic medicinal fungus widely used in traditional Chinese medicine, has attracted growing scientific interest due to its diverse reported pharmacological activities. Despite increasing research activity, a comprehensive bibliometric assessment of global publication trends and research hotspots remains limited. This study aimed to analyze publication trends, research characteristics, and thematic developments in English-language publications on C. cicadae indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC). Relevant publications covering the period 1990–2025 were retrieved, yielding 192 eligible records, including 188 original articles and four reviews. Bibliometric analyses were performed using VOSviewer(version 1.6.20), CiteSpace(version 6.3.R1), and Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny(version 4.3.3) to evaluate publication output, contributing countries, authors, journals, co-citation networks, keyword co-occurrence patterns, and thematic evolution. Annual publication output remained relatively low in the early years but increased markedly after 2018. China accounted for the largest proportion of publications, while researchers such as Chen Chin-Chu, Li Wei, and Ouyang Zhen were among the notable contributors. Co-citation and keyword analyses identified the isolation and characterization of bioactive constituents and the investigation of pharmacological activities as major research themes. More recent research topics included immunomodulation, antioxidant activity, renal and hepatoprotective effects, gut microbiota modulation, and multi-omics-based mechanistic investigations. Overall, this study provides a systematic overview of the research landscape of C. cicadae and identifies emerging topics that may inform future investigations into cultivation strategies, bioactive constituents, pharmacological mechanisms, and potential biomedical applications.

Article.Title: α-Carbonic Anhydrase 1 Affects Photosynthetic CO2 Assimilation and Stomatal Conductance in Arabidopsis thaliana Plants
Article.Authors: Rudenko N.; Ruppert M.; Mitenko G.; Nadeeva E.; Kozuleva M.; Ignatova L.; Ivanov B.
Article.Abstract: Arabidopsis thaliana plants of two mutant lines with a knockout of the At3g52720 gene, encoding stromal α-carbonic anhydrase 1, αCA1 (αCA1-KO), and wild-type plants of the Columbia ecotype (Col), were grown under 450 ppm (NCO2) and 150 ppm (LCO2) CO2 in the air. The CO2 assimilation rate (ACO2) in plants grown under NCO2 was lower in the αCA1-KO plants than in Col plants at CO2 concentrations from 600 to 1200 ppm in the measurement chamber. In LCO2-grown plants, ACO2 values were lower than in NCO2-grown plants both in Col and mutants, with the same values in mutants and Col. Water use efficiency (WUE) in NCO2-grown mutant plants was lower than in Col at a CO2 concentration of 600 ppm and above, and in LCO2-grown mutants WUE became lower than in Col at 1200 ppm. The starch content was lower in leaves of mutants than in Col under both NCO2 and LCO2 conditions due to its reduced synthesis during the daytime photosynthesis. Under NCO2, the content of hydrogen peroxide was 55% higher in αCA1-KO plant leaves than in Col. Under LCO2, the content of H2O2 in Col increased to more than three times its level under NCO2, and became 2.5 times higher than in αCA1-KO, in which it decreased by 34% compared to that in NCO2 plants. Under NCO2 conditions, the contents of the stromal, cytosolic, and peroxisomal forms of ascorbate peroxidases (APXs) were about twice higher in αCA1-KO than in Col plants. Contrariwise, in LCO2-grown plants the contents of APXs were lower in mutants than in Col. The total protein amount, as well as the level of ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, were the same in Col and mutants under NCO2 conditions, but were 35% and 45–50%, respectively, lower in αCA1-KO than in Col under LCO2 conditions. In the leaves of NCO2-grown plants, the stomatal conductance was higher in αCA1-KO than in Col with slower stomatal opening and delayed closure in response to decreases and increases in CO2 level, respectively. At the same time, in the absence of αCA1, both the total number of stomata per unit leaf surface area, and the relative number of open stomata were higher than in Col leaves. In the protoplasts isolated from NCO2-grown αCA1-KO plants, the steady-state rates of oxygen evolution were 30% lower in mutants than in Col and were reached at a lower HCO3− concentration (5 mM) than in protoplasts from Col (8 mM). The apparent half-saturating bicarbonate concentration was approximately 2 mM for αCA1-KO and 4 mM for Col. Our data demonstrate the involvement of the stromal chloroplast αCA1 in providing A. thaliana cells with CO2, and imply the significance of αCA1 in supplying inorganic carbon for starch and protein synthesis in plants. The increase in the total number of stomata per unit of leaf surface area and in the relative proportion of open stomata, as well as the reduced rate of stomatal responses in plants lacking αCA1, suggests the possible involvement of this enzyme in signaling processes regulating both stomatal movement and development.

Article.Title: DNA Damage in Diabetes: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Implications
Article.Authors: Vernì F.; Angioli C.; Ferriero A.; Agostini B.
Article.Abstract: A growing body of evidence indicates that diabetes is associated with pronounced DNA damage, ultimately leading to genomic instability. Chronic hyperglycemia induces the production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS and RNS), which trigger a cascade of oxidative stress through multiple pathways. These reactive species attack DNA, causing mutations as well as single- and double-strand breaks. Hyperglycemia also promotes the non-enzymatic glycation of DNA causing the formation of advanced glycation end products (AGEs) adducts. Binding of AGEs to the receptors for AGEs (RAGEs) stimulates additional ROS production, thereby amplifying oxidative stress. This state of genomic instability is further promoted by a decline in antioxidant defenses, which allows ROS-induced damage to accumulate, and is sustained by compromised DNA repair mechanisms. Accumulating DNA damage contributes to the development of diabetic micro- and macrovascular complications by triggering destructive mechanisms such as apoptosis, fibrosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis that compromise organ function. Additionally, persistent DNA damage elevates the risk of diabetes-associated malignancies and compromises male reproductive health. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular mechanisms driving hyperglycemia-induced genomic damage and highlights its broad clinical implications. Understanding the multifaceted impact of DNA damage in diabetes provides a comprehensive framework for its role in disease progression and associated comorbidities.

Article.Title: ITGB1 Contributes to Matrix Stiffness–Induced Lipid Raft Organization and Promotes Hepatocellular Carcinoma Cell Migration
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Liu X.; Liu Y.; Song G.
Article.Abstract: Matrix stiffening is a characteristic pathological feature of the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) microenvironment and promotes HCC cell migration. Lipid rafts are cholesterol–enriched plasma membrane microdomains involved in cell adhesion and migration. However, whether matrix stiffness promotes lipid raft organization and whether lipid rafts contribute to stiffness–promoted HCC cell migration remain unclear. Using two HCC cell lines cultured on polyacrylamide hydrogels with distinct stiffnesses, we found that stiff matrix enhanced cell migration, increased Area-normalized GM1 fluorescence, and upregulated Caveolin-1 and Flotillin-1 protein expression, consistent with enhanced lipid raft–associated membrane organization. Cholesterol depletion with methyl-β–cyclodextrin (MβCD) reduced GM1 fluorescence and attenuated migration on the Stiff matrix. Cholesterol replenishment partially restored GM1 fluorescence and wound closure after MβCD treatment. To explore how extracellular matrix stiffness is coupled to lipid raft organization, we next examined integrin β1 (ITGB1), a major extracellular matrix mechanoreceptor. The Stiff matrix increased ITGB1 protein expression, ITGB1–GM1 colocalization, and ITGB1 levels in raft-enriched fractions. ITGB1 knockdown reduced GM1 fluorescence, decreased Caveolin-1 and Flotillin-1 levels in raft-enriched fractions, and suppressed migration under Stiff–matrix conditions. These findings support a contributory role for ITGB1 in stiffness-associated lipid raft organization and HCC cell migration.

Article.Title: Ligand-Dependent Associations of the Bovine TLR2 R152Q Variant with Neutrophil Oxidative Burst, Extracellular DNA Release, and Innate Immune Gene Expression
Article.Authors: Sadowska J.; Tobolski D.; Polak Z.; Krupa M.; Wójcik R.; Brym P.
Article.Abstract: The bovine Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) R152Q substitution lies in an extracellular leucine-rich repeat domain and may alter pathogen-associated molecular pattern recognition, but its association with neutrophil function remains unknown. We genotyped 267 Polish Holstein–Friesian cows and evaluated isolated polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) after stimulation with the TLR2 agonist peptidoglycan (PGN) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)–a well-documented PMN activator. The oxidative burst was assessed by the nitroblue tetrazolium reduction assay, extracellular double-stranded DNA release as an indirect index of neutrophil extracellular trap (NET)-associated DNA release by PicoGreen fluorescence, and the abundance of eight innate immune transcripts by RT-qPCR. Genotype frequencies were 0.59 for GG (coding for arginine), 0.39 for GA (heterozygotes), and 0.02 for AA (coding for glutamine), showing a significant deviation from Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. In silico structural modeling predicted an allosteric destabilizing effect of the R152Q substitution. Functional responses of PMNs were both ligand- and concentration-dependent. The heterozygous GA PMNs exhibited the highest oxidative activity and extracellular dsDNA release following PGN stimulation. Conversely, AA PMNs demonstrated altered effector responses, including lower dsDNA release under LPS stimulation, accompanied by elevated basal transcript levels of recognition genes (TLR2, TLR4, NCF1, PADI4) but reduced IRAK4 expression upon stimulation. These findings suggest that the TLR2 R152Q polymorphism is associated with ligand- and concentration-dependent variation in bovine PMN functional responses. Overall, the enhanced responses in GA PMNs point toward a potential heterozygote-associated functional advantage, whereas the predicted structural destabilization and altered effector responses in the rare AA genotype (n = 3) suggest possible selective constraints against mutant homozygotes, though these latter findings remain preliminary and require confirmation in larger cohorts.

Article.Title: Epimedium: A Versatile Player in Bone Tissue Engineering
Article.Authors: Xu T.; Zhang R.; Hu J.; Jiang J.; Qiao L.; Deng S.; Li X.; Zhang W.; Zhou Z.; Xu K.; Mu C.
Article.Abstract: Epimedium is a traditional herb that has been investigated for its potential osteogenic and bone-regenerative effects, yet systematic analyses of its multi-component, multi-target mechanisms in bone metabolism and tissue engineering applications are limited. To address this knowledge gap, this narrative review systematically summarizes more than 20 bioactive constituents extracted from various parts of major medicinal Epimedium species. We elaborate on their pivotal roles in modulating osteogenic differentiation, suppressing osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption, regulating inflammatory responses, exerting antioxidant effects, promoting angiogenesis, demonstrating antitumor activity, exerting chondroprotective effects, and exhibiting antibacterial activity during bone defect repair. Furthermore, we highlight recent advancements and current trends in applying these bioactive constituents within the field of bone tissue engineering. Additionally, we compared the osteogenic and osteoprotective potentials of three metabolically related flavonoids (icariin, icaritin, and icariside II). Network pharmacology was utilized to elucidate their multi-target mechanisms in modulating bone metabolism, providing insights for future mechanistic studies. Despite the long-standing clinical use and extensive scientific investigation of Epimedium, this review identifies several challenges associated with its application in bone tissue engineering and offers constructive recommendations to overcome these limitations.

Article.Title: Food-Associated Xenobiotics and Innate Immunity: Molecular and Cellular Effects of Imazalil, TBHQ (Tert-Butylhydroquinone), Carrageenans, and Monosodium Glutamate
Article.Authors: Sayareh F.; Zwierzchowski G.; Wójcik R.
Article.Abstract: Food-associated xenobiotics may influence innate immune responses, but the relevance of experimental findings to human dietary exposure remains uncertain. This narrative review critically examines evidence concerning imazalil, tert-butylhydroquinone (TBHQ), carrageenans, and monosodium glutamate (MSG), representing a post-harvest fungicide, a synthetic antioxidant, a hydrocolloid, and a flavor enhancer, respectively. Experimental findings are compared across cellular and humoral innate immune endpoints, with attention to chemical form, dose, administration route, exposure duration, and the distinction between biomarker changes and adverse functional outcomes. Reported effects involve redox-sensitive signaling, cytokine regulation, macrophage and neutrophil responses, NK-cell activation and effector-associated markers, and intestinal barrier–microbiota interactions. These overlapping processes do not establish equivalent mechanisms or immunotoxic potential. TBHQ has a comparatively well-characterized connection to Nrf2 activation, although Nrf2 dependence has not been established for every reported immune effect. Imazalil evidence is narrower and requires independent replication, whereas findings for carrageenans depend strongly on material characterization and experimental context. MSG findings vary with dose, route, life stage, and metabolic conditions. Moreover, the predominantly preclinical literature includes exposure conditions whose correspondence to human dietary intake is uncertain. Consequently, available evidence supports context-dependent innate immune modulation but does not establish clinically meaningful immune impairment at customary dietary exposure. Further progress requires exposure-informed studies linking molecular and cellular changes to persistent functional effects and adverse outcomes, supported by human-relevant systems and human investigations where feasible. Such evidence would clarify the contribution of innate immune endpoints to food-safety assessment.

Article.Title: Ascorbic Acid Potentiates Cisplatin-Induced Antitumor Activity in HeLa Cervical Cancer Cells: Oxidative Stress, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, Apoptosis, and 3D Spheroid Responses
Article.Authors: Ayağ M.; Tolunay H.; Tuncer M.; Öztürk Ş.
Article.Abstract: Cisplatin is widely used in cervical cancer chemotherapy; however, dose-limiting toxicity and the development of treatment resistance restrict its therapeutic efficacy. Ascorbic acid (AsA) may exert pro-oxidant and anticancer effects at pharmacological concentrations and has the potential to enhance the activity of conventional chemotherapeutic agents. This study aimed to investigate whether AsA enhances the anticancer activity of CDDP in HeLa cervical cancer cells and to characterize the underlying mechanisms, with particular emphasis on oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptotic signaling, and the persistence of the combination effect in a three-dimensional (3D) tumor spheroid model. The effects of AsA and CDDP, alone and in combination, were evaluated in HeLa cells using cell viability and Chou–Talalay combination index (CI) analyses. Apoptosis, cell-cycle distribution, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), N-acetylcysteine (NAC)-mediated antioxidant rescue, mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) using JC-1 (5,5′,6,6′-tetrachloro-1,1′,3,3′-tetraethylbenzimidazolylcarbocyanine iodide), caspase-3/7 activity, and apoptosis-related gene expression were assessed. The antitumor activity of the combination was further evaluated in 3D HeLa spheroids by assessing spheroid morphology, diameter, adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-based viability, and Live/Dead fluorescence staining. AsA and CDDP exhibited 48-h half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 3.73 mM and 3.93 µM, respectively, and their combination produced synergistic cytotoxicity (CI = 0.72). Total apoptosis increased from 6.8% in control cells to 47.6% following combined treatment, accompanied by increased ROS generation, caspase-3/7 activity, and G2/M accumulation. AsA + CDDP markedly decreased ΔΨm and increased the BAX/BCL2 ratio and TP53 expression, supporting activation of the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway. NAC attenuated ROS accumulation and partially rescued cell viability, supporting the involvement of oxidative stress in the combination response. In the 3D spheroid model, AsA + CDDP produced the greatest reduction in spheroid diameter and ATP-based viability, accompanied by marked structural disintegration and an increased relative EthD-1 red fluorescence-signal fraction. These findings identify AsA as a potential CDDP-sensitizing strategy and support further preclinical investigation. Because the study was limited to in vitro cell and spheroid models and did not establish in vivo efficacy or safety, future studies should validate the combination in more representative cervical cancer models and assess its efficacy and safety in vivo before clinical translation.

Article.Title: Nucleated Erythrocytes: Linking Structure, Mechanics, Function, and Stress Responses
Article.Authors: Yu T.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Red blood cells have traditionally been studied through mature mammalian erythrocytes, which provide a model of highly deformable enucleated cells. However, nucleated erythrocytes retained by birds, fish, amphibians, and reptiles represent a distinct circulating cell strategy that integrates membrane–skeleton organization, cytoplasmic properties, nuclear structure, organelle function, and stress responses. This review uses human mature red blood cells as a mechanical reference rather than a replacement model to examine how conserved and nucleus/organelle-associated mechanisms link erythrocyte structure, mechanics, and function. Current evidence indicates that nucleated erythrocytes can be considered composite cellular systems in which the nucleus may contribute to local mechanical heterogeneity and deformation behavior, although direct causal links to whole-cell mechanical phenotypes remain insufficiently established. Comparative studies across vertebrate models reveal complementary insights into nuclear regulation, metabolic adaptation, immune responses, and stress tolerance. The major challenge is to establish causal relationships between structural remodeling, mechanical changes, and physiological outcomes using integrated mechanical, imaging, and molecular approaches. This review highlights nucleated erythrocytes as valuable models for understanding the relationships among cellular architecture, mechanics, and function beyond the conventional enucleated red blood cell paradigm.

Article.Title: Lip Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Molecular, Immune and Microenvironmental Drivers
Article.Authors: Alicka Y.; Topi S.; Gaxhja E.; Baldini G.; Orsini G.; Pietropaoli D.; Cifone M.; Giuliani M.; Altamura S.
Article.Abstract: Lip squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) is a distinct subtype of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma strongly associated with ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure and characterized by unique molecular, immune, and microenvironmental features. Although UV-induced photodamage represents the principal initiating event, increasing evidence indicates that LSCC progression results from complex interactions among genetic and epigenetic alterations, dysregulated signaling pathways, chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, host–microbiome dynamics, and tumor microenvironment (TME) remodeling. Recent advances have expanded the traditional view of LSCC by highlighting the contributions of UV-induced DNA damage, tumor protein p53 (TP53) alterations, epigenetic reprogramming, aberrant activation of key signaling pathways, and progressive immune escape mechanisms. In parallel, growing attention has focused on the role of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), stromal remodeling, microbial dysbiosis, and disruption of the microbiome–immune–metabolic axis as important modulators of disease progression and biological heterogeneity. Emerging biomarkers, including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), epigenetic signatures, liquid-biopsy analytes, immune-related markers, and microbiome-associated profiles, together with artificial intelligence (AI)-based analytical approaches, are creating new opportunities for diagnosis, risk stratification, disease monitoring, and precision oncology. Rather than providing a conventional descriptive overview, this review proposes an integrated conceptual framework in which molecular, immune, microbial, and microenvironmental drivers interact through continuous bidirectional crosstalk to shape LSCC initiation, progression, therapeutic responsiveness, and clinical heterogeneity. This system-oriented perspective may provide a foundation for future biomarker-guided and biologically informed approaches to LSCC management.

Article.Title: Convergent Early Dysregulation of Sarcopenia-Associated Genes in Skeletal Muscle During Aging and SOD1G93A ALS Models
Article.Authors: Aparicio P.; Dobrowolny G.; Lupoli M.; Moreno-Martínez L.; López-Royo T.; Musarò A.; Manzano R.; Osta R.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal muscle undergoes structural and functional decline due to aging and neuromuscular disorders such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), both of which impact protein expression and contribute to muscle atrophy. This study investigates how aging and the SOD1G93A ALS-related mutation affect the expression of eight genes previously linked to sarcopenia (PF4, OIT3, MMRN1, MASP1, C1R, SVEP1, VCAN and SPTB) but not yet characterized in muscle tissue. All eight target genes were expressed in skeletal muscle and most of them showed increased transcription with aging. In ALS models, gene expression was significantly overexpressed at early stages, particularly in muscle-specific (MLC/SOD1G93A) and systemic (SOD1G93A) models, mimicking aging-related profiles. These alterations attenuated with disease progression, suggesting an early transient muscle response to ALS-linked SOD1 mutations. Hence, this study demonstrates that sarcopenia-associated proteins are actively expressed and modulated in skeletal muscle during aging and ALS and suggests convergent response mechanisms.

Article.Title: Integrated Plasma snoRNA–Protein Network Analysis Identifies Circulating Molecular Signatures Associated with High-Risk Benign Breast Lesions and Early Breast Cancer
Article.Authors: Jijiwa M.; Khadka V.; Huo M.; Higa L.; Young S.; Deng Y.
Article.Abstract: High-risk benign breast lesions increase subsequent breast cancer risk, yet circulating molecular patterns that distinguish them from early breast cancer remain poorly defined. We profiled plasma small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) and small Cajal body-specific RNAs (scaRNAs) using UMI-based small RNA sequencing in 32 plasma samples from patients with low-risk benign lesions (Be; 9), high-risk benign lesions (HB; 14), or early breast cancer (CA; 9), and integrated matched data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics in a subset of 20 samples (HB; 11, CA; 9). Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) of 475 molecular features identified 11 modules. The Yellow module contained 25 snoRNAs/scaRNAs and 26 proteins and was enriched for extracellular matrix (ECM), blood microparticle, platelet, and serine-type endopeptidase inhibitor functions. An exploratory Yellow-module-focused analysis identified 10 snoRNAs with nominally lower abundance in CA than in HB (p < 0.05), showing concordant directions of differential abundance with the global analysis. The strength of differential RNA evidence correlated with mean intramodular RNA–protein correlation (Spearman ρ = 0.788, p = 2.85 × 10−6). External snoDB target mapping supported 28.6% of the exploratory network edges, including SNORD38A–FN1, SNORA73B–LAMB1, SNORD22–LAMB1, and SNORD22–NCAM1. Integration of differential plasma snoRNA profiling, cross-omic network analysis, and experimentally observed snoRNA interaction data indicated convergence on ECM/collagen and platelet/coagulation biology. These candidate snoRNA–protein axes may characterize differences in the circulating molecular states of CA and HB.

Article.Title: Moderately High Nutrient Solution Electrical Conductivity Re-Shapes Stage Specific Carbon Metabolism Linked to Flavor For-Mation in Tomato Fruit
Article.Authors: Shao Z.; Ma Y.; Wang T.; Nie Z.; Guo S.; Zheng J.
Article.Abstract: Modulating nutrient-solution electrical conductivity (EC) is an important strategy for improving the fruit flavor of tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) in soilless culture. Previous salinity studies have typically elevated EC through NaCl supplementation, which is physiologically distinct from raising EC via basal nutrient concentrations. Moreover, whether the quality-improving effect of moderately high electrical conductivity (HEC) arises from passive osmotic concentration or active metabolic reprogramming remains unclear. Tomato cultivar ‘Hangza 602′ was grown under CK (2.0 mS cm⁻¹) and HEC (3.0 mS cm⁻¹). Fruits were sampled at mature-green, breaker, pink and red-ripe stages for integrated transcriptomic, enzymatic and metabolomic analyses. HEC increased total soluble solids across ripening stages and promoted sugar and organic acid accumulation at pink and red-ripe stages, with a greater organic-acid increment reducing the sugar-acid ratio. Sugar transporter genes were induced at the breaker stage. At the pink stage, HEC elevated the activities of phosphofructokinase, citrate synthase and NADP-malate dehydrogenase without altering sucrose-phosphate synthase, indicating enhanced catabolic flux rather than sucrose biosynthesis. Sugars and citric acid accumulated persistently, whereas malic acid rose transiently then declined at red-ripe. Multiple downstream pathways were altered in HEC-treated red-ripe fruits. Collectively, HEC initiates stage-specific carbon-metabolic reprogramming combining osmotic and active effects, providing experimental insights for precision EC management in protected tomato production. Future work will further identify key regulatory genes governing this stage-specific metabolic response and validate the combined effects of EC and other environmental factors to develop robust soilless culture strategies for flavor improvement.

Article.Title: Targeting the ERK2 D-Recruitment Site with Anticancer Peptides from the DRAMP Database: An Integrated In Silico Study
Article.Authors: Almansour N.; Ibrahim M.
Article.Abstract: ERK2 is a central regulator of the MAPK pathway, governing cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival, and its aberrant activation is a recognized driver of cancer progression. ATP-competitive ERK2 inhibitors suffer from limited selectivity owing to the highly conserved kinase active site, whereas the ERK2 D-recruitment site (DRS), a non-catalytic docking surface mediating substrate recruitment, offers a more selective route to pathway modulation. Herein, the DRAMP database was screened, yielding 31 peptides with putative anticancer activity within the 5–15 residue range, which were docked towards the ERK2 DRS employing HADDOCK2.4. The protocol was first validated by reproducing the crystallographic binding mode of the co-crystallized KIM-MAP3 peptide. Peptides meeting the applied docking-score threshold were advanced to molecular dynamics simulations, followed by MM-GBSA binding energy calculations. Over 200 ns trajectories, DRAMP03987, DRAMP03983, and DRAMP03985 bound ERK2 more favorably than the reference KIM-MAP3 peptide, with ΔGbinding values of −71.2, −65.1, and −63.1 kcal/mol, respectively, versus −51.5 kcal/mol. Energetic and structural analyses indicated sustained occupancy of the DRS throughout the simulations, while in silico physicochemical profiling revealed preliminary physicochemical characteristics. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of the identified peptides as ERK2 DRS-binding candidates, warranting further experimental investigation.

Article.Title: Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) and Fungal Antigen Presentation: Immunological Mechanisms and Their Role in Anti-Fungal Immunity
Article.Authors: Shu F.; Khamto N.; Amsri A.; Youngchim S.; Nosanchuk J.; Chum-in T.; Deng Q.; Pruksaphon K.
Article.Abstract: Cellular-mediated immunity against invasive fungal infections is fundamentally governed by Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) restriction, whereby T cells detect fungal invasion indirectly through peptide fragments displayed on host MHC molecules rather than by recognizing intact fungal pathogens. In contrast to B cells, which bind native microbial antigens, T lymphocytes monitor antigen-presenting cells for processed fungal peptides presented by MHC class I and class II molecules. This review examines the molecular mechanisms underlying fungal antigen processing and presentation, emphasizing the pivotal contributions of MHC class II-restricted CD4 T-helper (TH1/TH17) cells and cross-presented, MHC class I-restricted CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes to antifungal host defense. We also summarize key experimental approaches, including overlapping peptide libraries, ELISpot assays, and peptide–MHC multimers, for defining MHC function and identifying immunodominant fungal antigenic determinants. Evidence from representative pathogenic fungal antigens, including Asp f16, Crf1, Eng2, and the multivalent rCpa1 vaccine, highlights both the promise and complexity of achieving cross-protective cellular immunity. Importantly, amino acid sequence similarity alone is insufficient to predict T-cell cross-reactivity, indicating that computational prediction and experimental epitope mapping should be employed as complementary approaches for the accurate identification and validation of immunologically relevant epitopes. Finally, elucidating the molecular principles governing fungal peptide presentation establishes a rational foundation for the development of broadly protective epitope-based vaccines and next-generation immunotherapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: A Shared Epithelial Barrier Program Across Mucocutaneous Lichen Planus: A Compartment-Aware Multi-Cohort Transcriptomic Reanalysis
Article.Authors: Alothman L.; Alameen A.; Eltahir M.
Article.Abstract: Oral lichen planus (LP) is widely described as molecularly distinct from cutaneous LP, yet most supporting transcriptomic evidence compares mucosal epithelium with full-thickness skin. We reanalysed four public microarray series covering oral, genital and cutaneous LP (101 arrays) with matched microRNA arrays, using covariate-adjusted models, meta-analysis, cross-platform integration, a within-platform site-by-disease interaction model, pathway and deconvolution scoring and a test of experimentally supported microRNA–target interactions. Eighty-five genes were differentially expressed at both discovery sites, 83 concordantly, dominated by cornified-envelope and keratinisation genes; BPIFC, CDSN and WFDC12 replicated in all four cohorts. A 52-gene barrier score separated lesional from control tissue in the discovery and genital cohorts (AUC 0.98–1.00, partly in-sample), and panels derived at one LP site transferred across study, platform and site (AUC 0.95–0.99), but the score did not reach significance in the only fully independent oral cohort (AUC 0.76, p = 0.13). In comparator series, the programme was also induced in psoriasis and partly in cutaneous lupus, but not in atopic dermatitis, eosinophilic oesophagitis or periodontitis, so it is shared rather than LP-specific. Interferon and MYC-target activity and several immune populations were higher in cutaneous LP, but an epithelial:immune compartment proxy showed that cutaneous biopsies were full-thickness whereas mucosal biopsies were epithelium-only, confounding this contrast. Within one platform, 292 genes showed an oral-versus-genital interaction. Neither miR-20a-5p nor miR-34a-5p tracked barrier expression, and across 222,203 supported microRNA–target pair correlations were predominantly positive rather than inverse. Across LP sites, a reproducible epithelial barrier programme is the most consistent shared feature, although it is not specific to LP and its transfer to independent cohorts remains provisional; reported immune divergence cannot be separated from the biopsy compartment.

Article.Title: The Role of D-3-Phosphoglycerate Dehydrogenase (PHGDH) in Chemoresistance in Ovarian Cancer: Molecular Insights and Therapeutic Potential
Article.Authors: Velázquez-Moreno J.; Mejía-Aguayo M.; Casarrubias-Jaimes F.; De la Fuente-Hernández M.; Apolonio-Sánchez D.; Sosa-León R.; Álvarez-Gómez R.; Leyva-Vázquez M.; Pedroza-Torres A.; Garibay-Cerdenares O.
Article.Abstract: Ovarian cancer (OC) is often diagnosed at advanced stages, and resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy remains one of the leading causes of treatment failure. This resistance is sustained in part by metabolic plasticity, particularly through the de novo serine synthesis pathway (SSP), orchestrated by D-3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), which diverts glycolytic carbon toward serine, glycine, and one-carbon (1C) units that fuel nucleotide biosynthesis, epigenetic regulation, and redox homeostasis. Elevated PHGDH expression in OC is associated with advanced International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) stage and poorer overall survival; conversely, a subset of tumors downregulates PHGDH at relapse and shifts toward NAD+-dependent pathways that sustain poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) activity and DNA repair, creating a distinct therapeutic vulnerability. Rather than a contradiction, this bidirectional behavior reflects the metabolic plasticity through which OC adapts to treatment pressure. Therefore, this review analyzes the context-dependent role of PHGDH in OC, the mechanistic basis of divergent associations with therapy resistance, and the current status of pharmacological inhibitors. Preclinical evidence indicates that PHGDH inhibition with CBR-5884 increases oxidative stress, reduces stemness, and restores platinum sensitivity in PHGDH-high models. We further identify the relationship between PHGDH and radiotherapy response as an unexplored question in OC, despite evidence of SSP-dependent radioresistance in other tumor types. Together, these observations position PHGDH as an actionable, but biomarker-dependent, metabolic target in OC.

Article.Title: Phenotypic and Genomic Characterization of Bacillus sp. DLB3, a Black Pepper Rhizosphere Isolate with Antagonistic, Abiotic Stress-Tolerant, and Antibiotic-Susceptible Traits
Article.Authors: Vu A.; Hoang S.; Ho C.; Le C.; Hoang H.; Nguyen H.; Le L.
Article.Abstract: Rhizosphere bacteria combining biocontrol activity with resilience to environmental stress are valuable candidates for sustainable agriculture. This study characterized strain DLB3, isolated from black pepper rhizosphere soil, through dual-culture and disk-diffusion antagonism assays, enzymatic and siderophore screening, physiological tolerance tests, antibiotic susceptibility testing, whole-genome sequencing, and genome mining. Phylogenomic analysis and average nucleotide identity (>97%) and digital DNA–DNA hybridization (>79%) values identified the isolate as Bacillus velezensis. The strain inhibited Fusarium falciforme, Fusarium oxysporum, and Colletotrichum gloeosporioides (47.6–71.2% radial growth inhibition) and produced an inhibition zone (8.4 mm) against Ralstonia solanacearum, alongside extracellular protease, amylase, CMCase, and catecholate-type siderophore production. DLB3 tolerated a broad range of temperatures (20–50 °C, with optimal growth at 25–40 °C, peaking at 35 °C), pH (5–9), and salinity (up to 10% NaCl), and exhibited minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 1800, 500, 450, and 250 mg L−1 for Pb, Zn, Cu, and Cr, respectively, while remaining susceptible to all nine antibiotics tested. The 3,913,361 bp draft genome was assembled into 44 contigs (N50 = 990,239 bp; L50 = 2), with 99.81% completeness and 0.12% contamination according to CheckM. It harbored 18 biosynthetic gene clusters, carbohydrate-active enzymes, peptidases, and genes associated with heavy metal resistance, broadly consistent with the observed phenotypes, as well as a homolog of the cfr methyltransferase gene (97.4% identity) that was not phenotypically expressed. These findings provide a comprehensive genomic and phenotypic profile of strain DLB3 and its biocontrol-related potential.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial Biogenesis in Human Skeletal Muscle: High-Intensity Interval Training Versus Moderate-Intensity Continuous Training
Article.Authors: Bischof K.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial biogenesis is a hallmark adaptation to endurance exercise with broad implications for metabolic health and athletic performance. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) both stimulate mitochondrial remodeling in human skeletal muscle, yet whether exercise intensity or total work performed is the principal determinant remains contested. This mini review synthesizes current evidence on the intensity-dependent activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK), and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α)—a central transcriptional coactivator in mitochondrial biogenesis. The author critically examines the distinction between mitochondrial content and respiratory function, discusses how study design—particularly work-matched versus time-matched protocols—shapes comparative conclusions, and identifies key unresolved questions including sex-based differences, fiber-type specificity, and the role of mitochondrial dynamics. The evidence indicates that both modalities are effective but operate through overlapping yet intensity-sensitive mechanisms; the metabolic-stress hypothesis provides a testable explanatory framework. Practical implications for exercise prescription are discussed. The review further considers the coordination of mitochondrial translation and turnover, mitochondrial Ca2+ handling, sex-specific evidence limitations, and translational outcomes in cardiometabolic disease.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial Dynamics in Cancer Therapy Response: Context-Dependent Adaptation, Cell Death, and Therapeutic Opportunities
Article.Authors: Do Y.; Bui K.; Kim J.; Shin S.; Seo J.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial plasticity has emerged as a central determinant of cancer therapy response, enabling tumor cells to adapt to diverse metabolic, environmental, and therapeutic stresses. Among its key features, mitochondrial dynamics contributes to the balance between mitochondrial stress burden and compensatory capacity that shapes cell fate. We propose an adaptive-lethal threshold as a context-dependent conceptual framework describing the transition from reversible mitochondrial dynamics and cellular adaptation to persistent mitochondrial dysfunction and irreversible cell death commitment. Rather than representing a fixed molecular cutoff, this boundary reflects a context-dependent transition in which overall mitochondrial stress can no longer be adequately compensated to maintain cellular homeostasis. Furthermore, how this threshold is defined and reprogrammed in therapy resistance remains unresolved. In this review, we synthesize current advances to propose a framework in which mitochondrial dynamics govern cell fate through threshold-dependent mechanisms. We highlight key pathways across multiple cancer types, including reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling, mitophagy, metabolic reprogramming, retrograde signaling, evasion of cell death, and interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Importantly, we discuss how context-dependent alterations in these processes can shift the balance between cytoprotective adaptation and irreversible mitochondrial dysfunction, contributing to therapy resistance or cell death. We further highlight emerging therapeutic strategies targeting mitochondrial dynamics and consider how modulation of mitochondrial dynamics can alter mitochondrial stress responses and influence the adaptive-lethal threshold, leading to cell sensitivity. Finally, we discuss key limitations and future directions in defining the context-dependent determinants of the adaptive-lethal transition and their implications for mitochondria-targeted therapies in cancer treatment.

Article.Title: MicroRNAs in Neurodevelopment and Their Relationship with Neurological, Neuropsychiatric and Neurodegenerative Diseases
Article.Authors: Catalano-Iniesta L.; Díez-Castro D.; García-Barrado J.; Carretero-Hernández M.; Hernández-González D.; Vicente-García T.; Torres L.; Carretero J.
Article.Abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression at the post-transcriptional level and play important roles in the development and function of the nervous system. Through the coordinated regulation of multiple target genes and signalling pathways, miRNAs participate in key neurodevelopmental processes, including neural progenitor proliferation and differentiation, neuronal specification and migration, morphological maturation, synaptic development, and circuit formation. Their functions are strongly dependent on developmental stage, cell type, brain region, and expression level, and the extent of mechanistic characterization varies considerably among individual miRNAs. This review examines well-characterized and emerging neurodevelopment-related miRNAs, including members of the miR-9, miR-34, miR-107, miR-124, miR-132, miR-134, miR-137, miR-181, miR-185, miR-191, miR-200, miR-218, and miR-344 families, integrating evidence on their molecular mechanisms and functions during nervous system development. Their dysregulation is further considered in neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric, neurological, and neurodegenerative disorders, as well as in selected rare and metabolic or endocrine disorders with neurological involvement. We also examine the potential of circulating and tissue-associated miRNAs as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers and the emerging therapeutic possibilities of miRNA modulation. Current evidence supports important roles for miRNAs in neurodevelopment and neurological disease but also highlights substantial differences between mechanistic and associative evidence. Methodological heterogeneity, differences between central and peripheral miRNA profiles, limited independent validation, and challenges associated with targeted delivery and off-target effects remain major barriers to their clinical translation.

Article.Title: Evaluation of Dwarf Tomato Germplasm for Dual-Purpose Use: Breeding and Rootstock Potential
Article.Authors: Mascarenhas Maciel G.; Alves Ribeiro A.; Medeiros Pereira L.; Arantes Mendonça H.; Villani Purquerio L.; Parrella N.; Ferreira da Silva A.; Silva Siquieroli A.; Ribeiro de Oliveira O.; Augusto Pereira V.; Gomes Barbosa F.
Article.Abstract: Tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum L.) productivity is threatened by biotic and abiotic stresses, exacerbated by climate change. The use of rootstocks is an effective strategy to enhance tomato resilience. Interest in characterizing dwarf tomato germplasm has increased, though its potential as a rootstock remains unexplored. The objective was to validate the use of dwarf tomato germplasm for: (1) characterizing dwarf tomato genotypes for morphoagronomic traits relevant to hybrid development and (2) evaluating their potential as rootstocks. Two greenhouse experiments were conducted. Experiment I assessed a recurrent parent (normal-architecture tomato), a donor parent (dwarf tomato), and twelve dwarf tomato lines. Morphoagronomic traits of fruits, shoots, and roots were evaluated, allowing the selection of the best dwarf tomato candidate for rootstock use. Experiment II was performed after grafting onto the selected dwarf tomato rootstock (UFU MC TOM1) from Experiment I. Commercial hybrids (Xanthus, Luan, Vivacy, and Bento) were used as grafting material, resulting in four graft combinations: Vivacy/UFU MC TOM1, Xanthus/UFU MC TOM1, Luan/UFU MC TOM1, and Bento/UFU MC TOM1. Both experiments followed a randomized block design in a greenhouse. Data were analyzed using univariate and multivariate approaches. The evaluated dwarf tomato germplasm exhibited relevant morphoagronomic traits, standing out as a promising source for hybrid development. The use of dwarf tomato genotypes as rootstocks proved viable, as grafting significantly increased root volume, overcoming potential limitations associated with the dwarf plant’s root system. These findings highlight the potential of dwarf tomatoes for both breeding programs and grafted seedling production, contributing to crop sustainability and efficiency.

These findings support further investigation of FGP for diabetic wound repair, while tissue-level mechanisms and long-term outcomes remain to be established.

Article.Title: LLM-Guided Adaptive Cost Calibration in Active Learning for Parkinson’s Disease Biosignals
Article.Authors: Gülez B.; Güneş A.; Kocabıçak E.
Article.Abstract: Confirmatory labels for Parkinson’s disease (PD), from expert examination or, prospectively, biological assays, are costly, and missed cases and false alarms carry unequal consequences. ClinRisk-LLM is a framework for label-efficient, cost-aware learning from gait and speech signals in which a large language model (LLM) translates a predefined safety specification into a frozen policy setting the positive-class weight of a support vector machine and the priority of potential missed cases for annotation. Cost-sensitive training, risk-aware querying and the LLM policy were ablated on gait (n=165) and speech (n=252) data and benchmarked against post hoc thresholding, a refer-all policy, held-out gait studies and an independent speech cohort. With half of the labels, cost-sensitive active learning reduced the 4:1 asymmetric cost by 34.1% (gait) and 5.7% (speech) relative to standard active learning, at the expense of specificity. ClinRisk-LLM translated the predefined safety specification into a frozen, auditable policy that adjusted risk settings during label acquisition. Component-wise analyses indicated that classifier weighting accounted for most of the observed cost reduction, while the incremental benefit of LLM-guided adaptation varied across datasets and comparison settings. A threshold-tuned symmetric model came within 1.3 cost points for gait, and gait remained roughly level with referring everyone. ClinRisk-LLM reached a gait cost of 47.60 versus 46.10 for fixed cost-sensitive learning; 40 policies generated across three LLMs from a reconstructed specification yielded gait costs of 52.1–75.8. Applications to molecular triage remain prospective. Code and data availability details are provided in the Data Availability Statement.

Article.Title: Gut Microbiome Alterations in Alzheimer’s Disease: A Shotgun Metagenomic Case–Control Study
Article.Authors: Issilbayeva A.; Kozhakhmetov S.; Kushugulova A.; Askarova S.; Kaiyrlykyzy A.; Tuigunov D.; Dolmatova O.; Zholdassova Z.; Omarov Y.; Nurgozhin T.
Article.Abstract: The gut microbiome has been proposed as a contributor to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathogenesis via the microbiota–gut–brain axis, but findings across cohorts are inconsistent and scarce data exist from Central Asian populations. We used shotgun metagenomic sequencing to compare the gut microbiome of AD patients and cognitively healthy controls from Kazakhstan. In a cross-sectional case–control study (35 AD, 39 Control), we profiled taxonomic and functional (HUMAnN pathway) composition, and compared alpha/beta diversity, individual taxa and pathways, and their association with clinical and demographic variables (Mann–Whitney U test, PERMANOVA/PERMDISP, OLS regression, all BH-FDR corrected, sensitivity analysis using ANCOM-BC2), with sensitivity analyses adjusting for age and BMI and applying Bonferroni correction. Within the AD group, circulating adiponectin—measured only in this group—was examined for associations with microbiome features in an exploratory analysis. Alpha diversity was lower in AD (q < 0.05). Community composition also separated by group on PERMANOVA (R2 = 8.6%, p = 0.001), and this separation held after adjusting for age and BMI. A total of 178 taxa differed significantly between groups (BH-FDR; 37 were also Bonferroni-significant), most prominently depletion of Faecalibacterium and enrichment of Eisenbergiella and Desulfovibrio in AD; 100 pathways differed significantly (20 Bonferroni-significant). Three clinical/demographic variables (total bilirubin, atherogenic index, BMI) were associated with specific taxa or pathways. Within the AD group, adiponectin correlated negatively with the pathway assimilatory sulfate reduction IV (rho = −0.60, q = 0.015). AD in this Central Asian cohort was associated with a less diverse, compositionally distinct gut microbiome, with depletion of butyrate-producing Firmicutes and enrichment of sulfate-reducing taxa, alongside other taxa whose direction of association differed from prior reports.
