Article.Title: Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts and Prostaglandin E2 Signaling in Gastric Cancer: Immunometabolic Mechanisms and Implications for Immunotherapy Resistance
Article.Authors: Xu C.; Wang Y.; Zhang Q.; Dong Y.; Yuan M.; Li D.; Deng S.; Du J.
Article.Abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) signaling have each been implicated in resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in gastric cancer. CAFs are associated with immune exclusion, whereas PGE2 can suppress CD8+ T-cell responses through prostaglandin E receptors 2 and 4 (EP2 and EP4) and alter dendritic-cell and myeloid-cell function. Whether PGE2 produced by CAFs directly contributes to ICI resistance in gastric cancer, however, remains unclear. To distinguish association from functional involvement, we synthesize the available literature into a conceptual continuum describing the possible contribution of PGE2 to CAF-associated immunotherapy resistance. At the Model A end, PGE2 may accompany CAF activation or local inflammation, whereas other CAF-associated mechanisms, including extracellular matrix remodeling, lactate, and CXCL12 signaling, may account for much of the resistance phenotype. At the Model B end, PGE2 may make an identifiable functional contribution to resistance beyond these alternative mechanisms, although the cellular source of the relevant PGE2 remains unresolved. These models represent interpretive endpoints derived from the available evidence rather than experimentally validated resistance subtypes or an established CAF-derived PGE2 pathway. Clinical findings with the EP4 antagonist ONO-4578 support the therapeutic potential of receptor blockade but do not identify the cellular source of PGE2 involved. Key unresolved questions concern the cellular sources of PGE2, its relationship with immune exclusion, and whether PGE2-related markers improve the prediction of ICI response beyond established indicators.

Article.Title: Targeting JAK/STAT Signaling Attenuates Postoperative Recurrence in an HLA-B27 Transgenic Rat Model of Crohn’s Disease
Article.Authors: Blondeaux A.; Valibouze C.; Titécat M.; Letarouilly J.; Dubuquoy C.; Danes M.; Dubuquoy L.; Zerbib P.; Foligné B.; Desreumaux P.; Speca S.
Article.Abstract: Postoperative recurrence (POR) remains a common complication following ileocecal resection (ICR) in patients with Crohn’s disease (CD), and no therapy is currently approved. This study aimed to study the benefits of JAK/STAT pathway inhibition in preventing POR using an ICR model in HLA-B27 transgenic (Tg) rats. Twenty-nine Tg rats underwent ICR at 12 weeks of age (W12). TOFA (15 mg/Kg/day) or placebo was administered at W10 as a preventive intervention. Disease extent and severity were assessed by monitoring body weight, stool consistency, performing endoscopy (W15) and evaluating macroscopic and histologic scores (W18). Ileal STATs phosphorylation was assessed by Western blotting and immunohistochemistry, while inflammatory cytokine expression was quantified by qRT-PCR and ELISA. In the placebo-treated Tg group, 57% of rats exhibited mucosal ulcerations in at least 20% of the anastomotic area (macroscopic score ≥2), which correlated with an endoscopic score ≥9. In contrast, only 13% of TOFA-treated Tg rats had a macroscopic score ≥2 and all had endoscopic scores ≤9. TOFA reduced mucosal inflammation and decreased ilealSTAT3 phosphorylation and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression. These findings provide a preclinical rationale for further investigating JAK inhibition as a potential preventive strategy against POR in CD.

Article.Title: Checkpoint Pathways in Childhood Cleft Lip and Palate—Associations of PD1 and CTLA4 with Clinical Parameters
Article.Authors: Budner M.; Torres K.; Opoka-Winiarska V.; Lasota A.; Gdak M.; Mertowska P.; Mertowski S.; Gosik K.; Kang M.; Urbanowicz T.; Grywalska E.
Article.Abstract: Cleft lip and/or palate (CL/P) is associated with recurrent upper respiratory tract complications, yet the immunoregulatory mechanisms accompanying this defect remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to characterize cellular and soluble parameters associated with PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 in children with CL/P and to analyze their associations with selected clinical and hematological characteristics. This single-center cross-sectional study included 32 children with CL/P and 16 healthy children as controls. Serum concentrations of sPD-1, sPD-L1, and sCTLA-4 were measured, and the percentages of cells expressing PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 within T-lymphocyte (CD3+ CD4+ and CD3+ CD8+) and B-lymphocyte (CD19+) populations were assessed using flow cytometry. We analyzed relationships between immunological and clinical parameters, as well as differences between subgroups by gender and mode of delivery. Children with CL/P exhibited significantly higher serum concentrations of sPD-1, sPD-L1, and sCTLA-4, as well as higher percentages of T and B lymphocytes expressing these immune checkpoint molecules, compared to the control group (p < 0.0001 in all cases). We observed significant associations among selected immune checkpoint-related parameters, including a positive correlation between sPD-1 and sCTLA-4 and an inverse correlation between the percentages of CD19+ PD-L1+ and CD19+ CTLA-4+ B lymphocytes. The markers clearly distinguished children with CL/P from healthy children in the study cohort; however, we found no consistent differences by gender or mode of delivery. Children with CL/P exhibited distinct cellular and soluble immune checkpoint-related profiles compared to the control group. However, given the limited sample size and the study’s cross-sectional design, these results should be considered preliminary and require confirmation in larger, independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Advances and Future Perspectives on Chitosan-Based Hydrogels for Bone Regeneration in Periodontitis-Associated Defects
Article.Authors: Li Z.; Yang Y.; Zheng Y.; Su X.; Wen J.; Liang H.; Guo M.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis-triggered alveolar bone loss is an irreversible pathological lesion that remains challenging to regenerate in clinical practice. Functionally modified chitosan (CS) hydrogels combine favorable biocompatibility, tunable biodegradability, intrinsic antibacterial activity, and immunomodulatory properties, rendering them promising scaffolds for the repair of inflammatory bone defects. This review summarizes advances over the past five years in the development of functionalized CS hydrogels for periodontitis-associated alveolar bone regeneration. We categorize and compare four mainstream modification strategies for CS: biomimetic structural design, inflammatory immunoregulation, stimuli-responsive controlled release, and mechanical microenvironment adaptation. Beyond hydrogels, chemically modified CS in diverse forms (membranes, bulk scaffolds, micro/nanoparticles, and surface coatings) is also discussed. Furthermore, we comprehensively elaborate on the core regenerative mechanisms of modified CS hydrogels, including antibacterial defense, immune microenvironment remodeling, osteogenic activation, and angiogenesis–osteogenesis coupling. Unlike most previous reviews covering CS biomaterials, the present work specifically focuses on the challenges of bone regeneration under periodontitis-related inflammatory conditions, with a small set of other bone regeneration studies included as supporting references. It examines the key limitations of current investigations—particularly those concerning mechanical matching, sustained anti-inflammatory efficacy, and clinical translatability—and outlines targeted research directions involving structural optimization, multistage cascade regulation, and personalized clinical translation. Overall, this review provides a theoretical framework and practical design strategies for developing high-performance CS-based hydrogels toward periodontal bone defect regeneration.

Article.Title: Kabuki Syndrome: Epigenetic Mechanisms, DNA Methylation Signatures, and Diagnostic Advances
Article.Authors: Zabudskaya K.; Ryzhkova O.
Article.Abstract: Kabuki syndrome (KS) is a rare multisystem developmental disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, developmental delay, hypotonia, and variable congenital anomalies. Most molecularly confirmed cases are associated with pathogenic variants in KMT2D (KS type 1) or KDM6A (KS type 2), genes encoding regulators of chromatin modification and gene expression. However, a subset of individuals with a clinical diagnosis of KS remains molecularly unresolved, while variants of uncertain significance may complicate diagnostic interpretation. DNA methylation episignatures have emerged as complementary molecular biomarkers that may support the interpretation of uncertain genetic findings and help clarify selected diagnostically unresolved cases. This review examines the molecular and epigenetic mechanisms underlying KS, summarizes the evidence for KS-associated DNA methylation episignatures, and discusses their potential applications in clinical diagnostics. Particular attention is given to the interpretation of episignature classifier results, the available evidence on diagnostic performance, and methodological limitations, including the representation of different variant classes and the interpretation of negative or inconclusive results. The review also considers genotype–phenotype correlations, genetic counseling, and clinical management in the context of current diagnostic approaches. Although episignature analysis may provide valuable functional evidence complementary to genetic testing, its results should be interpreted alongside clinical findings and molecular data. Further validation in well-characterized cohorts is needed to define its diagnostic utility across the full spectrum of KS-associated genetic variation.

Article.Title: TNF rs1800629 Genotype and Motor Response to Intensive Rehabilitation in Parkinson’s Disease: An Exploratory Study
Article.Authors: Agliardi C.; Guerini F.; Bolognesi E.; Zanzottera M.; Saibene F.; Salvatore A.; Arcuri P.; Castagna A.; Cattaneo D.; Bowman T.; Anastasi D.; Navarro J.; Meloni M.; Clerici M.

Possible associations between genotype, treatment group and MDS-UPDRS III score at T1 were analyzed using ANCOVA and linear mixed-effects models, adjusting for baseline MDS-UPDRS III score, age, sex, disease duration and levodopa equivalent daily dose (LEDD). A significant treatment group x TNF rs1800629 genotype interaction was observed (p = 0.033). Longitudinal analyses revealed a significant time × treatment group × TNF rs1800629 genotype interaction (p = 0.010), with GG homozygotes showing an approximately 10-point reduction in MDS-UPDRS III score (40.87 to 30.87; p < 0.001). Article.Title: Transendothelial Transport of Low-Density Lipoproteins in Atherosclerosis: Mechanisms of Activation and Possible Therapeutic Targets
Article.Authors: Tanyanskiy D.; Denisenko A.
Article.Abstract: Despite advances in the prevention of cardiovascular events in recent decades, the risk of developing atherosclerosis and its complications remains a major challenge. One promising way to reduce this risk is to develop measures to inhibit the activated transport of low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) through the endothelium, which is the initial stage of atherosclerosis. Recent research has provided some molecular details of the mechanism, including the roles of caveolin-1, LDL receptors, and certain motor proteins. This review summarizes data on recent advances in studying of LDL endothelial transcytosis, focusing on its role in atherogenesis as well as on its regulation by hemodynamics, lipoproteins, cytokines, and metabolic factors. Data on potential targets for inhibiting transendothelial LDL transport are also presented. A better understanding of the mechanisms of endothelial LDL transcytosis and the development of drugs to inhibit it may lead to improved treatment of atherosclerosis and more effective prevention of cardiovascular events.

Article.Title: Regulatory Elements and Splicing Factors Govern Mutually Exclusive Splicing of DmRdl Exon 3
Article.Authors: Song Z.; Zhang Y.; Lin K.; Wang X.; Duan Y.; Bao J.; Bass C.; Zhao C.
Article.Abstract: Ionotropic γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors are major inhibitory receptors in insect central nervous systems, with their diversity partly generated by alternative splicing. The results of RNA pull-down, mass spectrometry, and RNAi demonstrated that the splicing factors, CG30122 and Rbp1-like bind to the ERE and exert opposite effects on E3b inclusion. The results of STRING network analysis supported the functional interaction between CG30122 and Rbp1-like, while molecular docking provided structural support for their potential interaction with the ERE-containing RNA sequence. This study reveals the molecular regulatory network underlying the MEAS of DmRdl E3, and and provides a foundation for investigating other MEAS exons, such as E6 and E9 in insect Rdl.

Article.Authors: Mahmood T.; Al-Samydai A.; Al-Mamoori F.; Alqaraleh M.; Abu Hajleh M.; Mayyas A.; Moshawih S.; Al-Sanabrah A.; Qtashat Q.; AlMafrachi R.; Kassim H.; Ali Agha A.; Al-Hussaniy H.; AlShaer W.

At 48 h, release reached 87.30% and 73.24%, respectively; Weibull best described β-sitosterol and Higuchi naringenin, revealing asynchronous release and a time-dependent delivery ratio. Across 1200 augmented profiles, first-4-h measurements predicted 6–48-h release with R2 = 0.976–0.996, while parameter-based reconstruction reproduced compound-specific trajectories. Exploratory reconstructed-replicate assessment yielded a pooled R2 of 0.938 (mean absolute error (MAE) = 3.32%; root-mean-square error (RMSE) = 4.78%). Naringenin docked across all targets (7.58 to −8.40 kcal/mol), whereas β-sitosterol showed weaker binding and no COX-2 pose. Article.Authors: Lima B.; Dantas L.; Silva R.; Melo N.; Yano-Melo A.

Notably, PeWRKY was induced in all treatments at seven days and showed particularly high expression in FoP-challenged plants. Mycorrhizal and arbuscular intensities were strongly positively correlated with PePR-12 expression at 24 h, while at seven days PeLecRK expression was strongly correlated with PeSERK1, PeWRKY, and PePR-12. These results reveal a dynamic temporal reprogramming of defense-related gene expression in P. edulis and indicate that AMF colonization is associated with modulation of molecular responses to FoP. The identified genes provide candidates for further functional investigation of mycorrhiza-mediated defense responses in passion fruit.

Article.Authors: Lori L.; Fiorilla I.; Ghezzi B.; Pedrazzi M.; Todesco A.; Mazzola F.; De Tullio R.; Cresta F.; Castellani C.; Patrone M.; Raffaelli N.; Audrito V.; Averna M.

In vitro, recombinant NAMPT increased MMP-9 expression and enzymatic activity in PBMCs from healthy donors. Pharmacological treatment with FK866 reduced endogenous eNAMPT release and attenuated NAMPT-induced MMP-9 production. Mechanistically, eNAMPT triggered rapid AKT activation followed by sustained ERK1/2 phosphorylation. Article.Title: Nitrate Versus Ammonium Assimilation in Neochlorella semenenkoi: 15N-Tracking Study of Metabolomic Dynamics
Article.Authors: Vishnevskaya A.; Sinetova M.; Malyshev N.; Malyukova A.; Nikolaev E.; Kostyukevich Y.
Article.Abstract: Microalgae of the Chlorellaceae family are promising producers of valuable metabolites, yet the choice of nitrogen source significantly modulates their physiology and biochemistry. Targeted analysis revealed that ammonium-fed cells restored their amino acid pools substantially within 1 day, with a pronounced accumulation of glutamate and glutamine, whereas nitrate-fed cells exhibited a slower and only partial recovery of their free amino acid pool, with several amino acids remaining undetectable even after 3 days. Untargeted metabolomics identified 308 unique metabolites, and the heatmaps of the most variable compounds highlighted a marked early upregulation of TCA cycle intermediates, stress-signaling molecules, and nucleotide precursors in AA cultures, in contrast to a delayed, lipid-centric response in nitrate cultures. The 15N tracing confirmed near-complete (>96%) enrichment of amino acids in both sources, demonstrating that recovery is driven by de novo synthesis rather than recycling, and that isotopic enrichment extends to nucleotides and the NAD+ precursor nicotinamide. These findings reveal the metabolic advantages of ammonium over nitrate for rapid metabolic recovery and restoration of nitrogen-rich compound pools, and provide a foundation for optimizing cultivation strategies for this biotechnologically relevant alga.

Article.Title: Crystalloid-Dependent Modulation of Aquaporins and Molecular Stress Pathways During Acute Normovolemic Hemodilution in Rat Heart and Aorta
Article.Authors: Erkalp K.; Şengelen A.; Demirgan S.; Aksüt Y.; Önay-Uçar E.; Yelmen N.
Article.Abstract: Acute normovolemic hemodilution (ANH) maintains circulating volume with replacement fluids, but its harmful effects and whether crystalloid composition alters cardiovascular tissue stress remain unclear. Correlation analysis showed tissue-specific aquaporin–injury coupling: cardiac AQP1 was associated with reduced apoptosis and inflammation, cardiac AQP3 with increased oxidative injury, and aortic AQPs with predominantly inverse injury relationships. Consequently, crystalloid composition influenced cardiovascular adaptation to ANH. RL reduced apoptotic and vascular inflammatory activity, limited aortic oxidative stress, and produced distinct Hsp90 and aquaporin profiles. Article.Title: Modeling Celiac Disease: From Pathogenesis to Therapy
Article.Authors: Aufiero V.; Treppiccione L.; Luongo D.; Mazzarella G.; Camarca A.
Article.Abstract: Celiac disease (CeD) is a common gastrointestinal disorder triggered by the ingestion of gluten in genetically predisposed individuals. It is characterized by a complex immune response involving both adaptive and innate immunity, ultimately leading to intestinal mucosal damage and a broad range of extraintestinal manifestations. Although great progress has been made in understanding the pathogenesis of CeD, several questions remain unanswered. Furthermore, the only treatment currently available is a gluten-free diet, and research is actively working to find therapies that can at least complement dietary treatment. Understanding the complexity of the mechanisms underlying CeD has required the development and use of different experimental models, which allowed the investigation of specific pathways and cell populations. In this review, we provide a critical and updated overview of the main in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo models used to investigate CeD-related pathways, including human cell lines, ex vivo culturing of duodenal biopsies, intestinal organoids and mouse models. For each model, we highlight its specific characteristics, advantages and limitations, as well as its potential applications in translational research.

Article.Title: Integrated Multi-Omics Convergence Scoring Reveals Modular Network Architecture with Age-Associated Mitochondrial Signatures in Sarcopenia
Article.Authors: Park D.; Park J.; Chun O.; Kwon E.; Bae H.
Article.Abstract: Sarcopenia arises from convergent genetic, epigenetic, transcriptomic, metabolic, and microbiome-associated perturbations, yet conventional multi-omics analyses often yield fragmented, layer-specific feature lists. We developed an integrated multi-omics convergence scoring framework that calculates an Integrated Convergence Score (ICS) by combining standardised layer-level statistical evidence, layer-specific pathway context, network features and sarcopenia-specific disease-relevance evidence. We applied it to skeletal muscle transcriptomes from five independent cohorts (208 participants), ageing-associated muscle DNA methylation, and genome-wide association studies of muscle mass and strength, each analysed against its own null distribution. Gene-level changes were few and did not replicate, whereas mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial translation and contraction pathway scores were lower in sarcopenia in the pooled analysis. These mitochondrial signatures were also lower in ageing-, frailty-, and pre-sarcopenia-related comparisons, indicating a component shared with muscle ageing. The three layers implicated largely distinct mechanisms. Compared with rank-based combined statistics, the ICS top-ranked genes formed a more connected network, which partly reflects the network component of the score. A context map placed the modules within mitochondrial respiration, creatine-based energy buffering, and NAD–PGC-1α signalling. This framework organises fragmented multi-omics evidence into a systems-level gene network associated with sarcopenia and prioritises candidate genes and mechanisms for future functional studies.

Article.Title: Development of a Novel Amplicon-Based Whole-Genome Sequencing Approach for Improved Surveillance of Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense 2026
Article.Authors: Rueca M.; Specchiarello E.; Smoquina F.; Colavita F.; Gruber C.; Chillemi G.; Maggi F.; Carletti F.
Article.Abstract: Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) remains one of the least genomically characterized filoviruses, partly due to the absence of primer schemes specifically optimized for its full genome amplification. Existing amplicon-based protocols developed for the Zaire Ebola virus or other orthoebolaviruses provide incomplete coverage when applied to BDBV, limiting genomic surveillance during outbreaks. In this study, we present a newly designed multiplex PCR primer scheme tailored to the genomic features of BDBV and optimized for sequencing on the Ion Torrent platform. The panel comprises 37 overlapping primer pairs spanning the entire ~19 kb BDBV genome, designed to minimize amplicon dropouts and ensure uniform coverage across regions with variable GC content and sequence divergence. Validation using BDBV RNA, derived from a diluted aliquot of a clinical specimen collected from a patient who tested positive for BDBV during the 2026 outbreak, demonstrated >99% genome recovery, high coverage uniformity, and robust performance even in low-titer samples. This represents, to the best of our knowledge, the first experimentally validated primer scheme specifically developed for BDBV. The protocol provides a reliable and accessible tool for genomic surveillance, outbreak investigation, and evolutionary studies, supporting improved diagnostic and public health responses to BDBV disease.

Article.Title: Autophagy–Gut Microbiota–Epigenetic Interactions in Disease Pathogenesis: Focus on Neurodegenerative and Neuropsychiatric Disorders and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Mashayekhpour M.; Amani H.; Hajizadeh Moghaddam A.; Moradi A.; Nohesara S.; Mostafavi Abdolmaleky H.
Article.Abstract: Autophagy is a key cellular process that participates in numerous physiological functions, including maintaining epithelial barrier integrity, regulating intracellular degradation pathways, modulating immune responses, and enhancing antimicrobial defense. Impaired autophagy may contribute to the accumulation of misfolded proteins and insoluble aggregates in the neuronal cytoplasm, defective clearance of damaged organelles and proteins, and the buildup of toxic metabolites. In the gut, these alterations may disrupt the balance between beneficial and potentially harmful microorganisms, contributing to gut dysbiosis, chronic inflammation, and epigenetic alterations in intestinal cells that may indirectly affect the brain. Here, we review the current evidence on the interplay among autophagy, the gut microbiota, and the epigenome in the pathogenesis of diseases, particularly neuropsychiatric disorders (NPDs) and neurodegenerative diseases (NDs). First, we briefly discuss autophagy and its roles in health and disease. We then examine the association between impaired autophagy, inflammation, and epigenetic aberrations in the pathogenesis of NPDs and NDs. Next, we focus on the relationships among gut dysbiosis, defective autophagy, and epigenetic alterations in NPDs and NDs, and discuss microbiota-based therapeutic strategies that may influence epigenetic regulation and autophagic function. Finally, we highlight the current challenges and future directions for investigating the critical role of these interactions in the pathogenesis and treatment of NPDs and NDs.

Article.Title: DOPA-Substituted KLVFFA Peptides Potently Inhibit Amyloid-β Aggregation and Mitigate Neurotoxicity
Article.Authors: Fukuhara K.; Mori K.; Okiyama Y.; Takaki T.; Misawa T.; Tsuchiya K.; Demizu Y.; Shibanuma M.; Ohno A.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is driven primarily by the self-assembly of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides, a process stabilized by intermolecular π–π stacking interactions involving Phe19 and Phe20 residues of adjacent Aβ molecules. To competitively disrupt these interactions, we designed novel peptide inhibitors derived from the Aβ recognition motif KLVFFA (Aβ16–21), in which phenylalanine residues were replaced with L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA), featuring a catechol moiety capable of enhanced aromatic stacking and hydrogen bonding. The DOPA-substituted peptides effectively inhibited Aβ1–42 (Aβ42) aggregation, as demonstrated via Thioflavin T fluorescence assays, circular dichroism spectroscopy, and transmission electron microscopy. These complementary analyses collectively revealed substantial suppression of β-sheet formation and fibril elongation. Notably, the anti-aggregation potency was dependent on the substitution position, with the Phe19-substituted analog (KDF) exhibiting stronger inhibitory activity than the Phe20-substituted analog (KFD). The dual-substituted analog (KDD) displayed the greatest overall anti-aggregation activity. Molecular simulations further supported the superior activity of KDF over KFD, revealing a more favorable binding free energy for KDF compared to the parent peptide. Furthermore, the DOPA peptides potently mitigated Aβ42-induced neurotoxicity in SH−SY5Y cells, with the dual-substituted analog (KDD) providing the highest level of cytoprotection. Collectively, these findings validate that targeted modulation of aromatic interactions through DOPA substitution represents a powerful molecular strategy for controlling Aβ42 self-assembly, positioning these peptides as promising therapeutic tools for the treatment of AD.

Article.Title: Toward an Integrative Understanding of Dianthus gratianopolitanus: Genetics, Physiology, Ecology, and Conservation
Article.Authors: Zielińska K.; Kołodziejczyk I.; Michalska E.
Article.Abstract: Effective conservation of endangered species under increasing anthropogenic pressure requires a thorough understanding of their biology. However, the growing specialization of modern biology has fragmented botanical science into separate disciplines, characterized by its own terminology, methods, and conceptual frameworks. As a result, researchers working on the same taxon may struggle to integrate findings. Yet, some of the most important biological questions arise precisely at the intersection of studies in genetics and physiology and field ecology. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genetics, physiology, and ecology of Dianthus gratianopolitanus (Cheddar Pink). Despite its widespread horticultural use, the species remains rare in its natural habitats and is red-listed in multiple countries. The aim of this review is to identify integrative research directions relevant to its effective conservation. The published literature on D. gratianopolitanus was reviewed, focusing on chloroplast genomics, population genetics, physiological adaptations, population ecology, and habitat requirements. Attention was given to research questions emerging at the intersection of disciplines. D. gratianopolitanus displays apparent ecological flexibility alongside strong microhabitat dependence; population-level differentiation reflects a combination of edaphic adaptation, phenotypic plasticity, and biogeographic history, while chloroplast genomic analyses reveal positive selection in photosynthesis- and stress-related genes, whose functional significance remains to be experimentally validated. Major knowledge gaps persist in the mechanisms translating environmental conditions into physiological performance, the relative contributions of genetic fixation versus plasticity to local adaptation, long-term demographic dynamics, and the criteria for genotype-informed conservation translocations. This review proposes that bridging ecological, physiological, genomic, demographic, and biotechnological research is both feasible and necessary for the long-term conservation of the species.

Article.Title: Ferroptosis-Mediated Radiosensitization in Glioblastoma: Preclinical Insights and Translational Opportunities
Article.Authors: Gilbert O.; Fowler H.; Madarapu A.; Reed M.; Fahim A.; John S.; Shen C.; Higgins D.
Article.Abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains the most common and most aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults, and despite maximal safe resection with adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) and temozolomide (TMZ), median overall survival remains 12–15 months with near-universal recurrence. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by the accumulation of lipid peroxides, has emerged as a distinctive vulnerability in GBM, whose iron-avid phenotype, polyunsaturated fatty acid-rich milieu, and high oxygen consumption create a permissive substrate for lipid peroxidation. In this review, we synthesize preclinical evidence positioning ferroptosis as a determinant of GBM radiosensitivity and evaluate strategies to exploit it. We first outline core ferroptosis biology and GBM-specific modifiers of ferroptotic susceptibility, including TFR1-mediated iron import, grade-dependent glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) expression, acyl-coenzyme A synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) levels, transsulfuration, NRF2, p53, non-coding RNAs, and the relative resistance of mesenchymal tumors and glioma stem cells. We then examine mechanisms of radiation-induced ferroptosis, in which RT upregulates ACSL4 and depletes glutathione (GSH) while simultaneously provoking adaptive responses that induce the cystine transporter solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) and GPX4, alongside hypoxia-, IFI16/HMOX1-, and lncRNA-mediated programs that sustain radioresistance, noting that recurrent tumors display a ferroptosis-primed profile after chemoradiation. Radiosensitization strategies are reviewed across pharmacologic ferroptosis inducers (classes I-IV), repurposed agents, NRF2 inhibition, genetic targeting of ferroptosis mediators, and blood–brain barrier-penetrant nanoplatforms that couple iron delivery, high-Z radiation deposition, and antioxidant disruption. We further address the immunologic consequences of ferroptosis within the immunosuppressive GBM microenvironment, the countervailing problem of radiation-induced brain injury and candidate neuroprotective approaches, the potential convergence of FLASH RT with iron-dependent differential sparing, and comparative evidence of ferroptosis-RT synergy in other treatment-resistant malignancies. Finally, we appraise candidate biomarkers and ferroptosis-related gene signatures, and close by addressing open questions and current translational hurdles facing the field.

Article.Title: Blood–CSF MiRNA Signatures in Alzheimer’s Disease Reveal Novel Biomarker Candidates: A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Benchohra A.; Juárez-Alía C.; Serrano G.; Segura T.; Peinado J.; Rabanal-Ruiz Y.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as promising regulators of AD-related pathways and potential minimally invasive biomarkers. However, existing meta-analyses have yielded inconsistent results, and whether miRNA signatures are conserved across biological fluids remains unclear. The present work aimed to systematically review studies performing miRNA discovery or multi-candidate profiling in blood and CSF during the last 15 years, in order to identify miRNAs showing significant and consistent differential expression across independent studies. By systematically comparing the direction and consistency of miRNA dysregulation across independent studies and biological sources, we identified 80 miRNAs consistently dysregulated in both blood and CSF, revealing a reproducible cross-fluid signature of AD-associated molecular alterations. Notably, miR-451a and miR-16-5p emerged among the most consistently dysregulated miRNAs across fluids. In contrast, several miRNAs displayed divergent or compartment-specific patterns, highlighting that blood and CSF may capture distinct aspects of AD-related molecular changes. Among these, miR-484, miR-3200-3p and miR-598 were identified as novel CSF candidates, while miR-20a-5p, miR-363-3p and miR-5006-3p represented novel blood-specific candidates. Furthermore, a substantial proportion of detected miRNAs was associated with extracellular vesicle/exosomal fractions, supporting their potential stability and biological relevance. Overall, our findings demonstrate that AD-associated miRNA dysregulation comprises both conserved and biofluid-specific signatures. From a clinical perspective, the current evidence primarily supports further evaluation of miRNAs as diagnostic/discriminative biomarkers rather than validated tools for early detection, disease monitoring, or prognosis. Their clinical translation remains limited by biofluid and methodological heterogeneity and requires harmonized cross-cohort and longitudinal validation.

Article.Title: Unlocking the Power of Metaproteomics: A Novel Tool for Enhancing Shorebird Conservation and Blue-Economy Management
Article.Authors: Escobar-Niño A.; Calcis-Marzán M.; Forján-Miguéns A.; Punta-Sánchez I.; Coste O.; Pérez-Hurtado A.; Fernández-Acero F.
Article.Abstract: Metaproteomics, the large-scale analysis of proteins from environmental or host-associated samples, has emerged as a transformative tool for characterizing microbial communities and their functional roles. Unlike metagenomics or metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics directly captures phenotypic expression, linking molecular function to ecological and physiological outcomes. Beyond its established applications in human microbiome and dietary research, metaproteomics enables the precise identification of food-derived protein biomarkers, including the discrimination of tissue-specific origins. This level of resolution is not attainable through DNA-based approaches. Here, we applied metaproteomics for the first time to analyze the feces of shorebirds in the salt flats and salt marshes of Cadiz Bay, aiming to determine their diet with unprecedented resolution. Conventional methods, based on direct observation or fecal inspection, are labor-intensive and risk losing critical dietary information. By contrast, metaproteomics provides rapid, high-resolution insights, offering a robust alternative for ecological monitoring. Our results demonstrate the potential of this technique to transform natural area management, optimize conservation strategies for avian species, and support the sustainable development of the blue economy. This study highlights metaproteomics as an innovative, cross-sectoral approach capable of advancing both fundamental ecological research and practical conservation outcomes.

Article.Title: Betulinic Acid-Derived HIV-1 Maturation Inhibitors: Bridging Chemical Design, Molecular Dynamics, and Experimental Evidence
Article.Authors: Sapiyeva A.; Sadykov N.; Omari A.; Akpayeva K.; Aipova G.; Zhakipbekov K.
Article.Abstract: Betulinic acid-derived human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) maturation inhibitors connect natural-product medicinal chemistry with inhibition of capsid–spacer peptide 1 (CA–SP1) processing. This critical narrative review examines how chemical modifications relate to target structure, conformational dynamics, antiviral activity and development limitations. C-3 pharmacophore replacement and modification of the C-28/C-17 region improved antiviral breadth and exposure, but improved cellular potency alone did not establish clinical differentiation. Cryo-electron microscopy, microcrystal electron diffraction and nuclear magnetic resonance support engagement of the CA–SP1 six-helix bundle and restriction of its dynamics. Molecular simulations offer an ensemble-based explanation whose interpretation depends on assembly state, cofactors, sampling and experimental validation. Binding kinetics and cleavage measurements provide particularly informative connections between molecular observations and antiviral activity. Later-generation compounds demonstrate that broader susceptibility coverage and favorable pharmacokinetics must be evaluated alongside tolerability, resistance and regimen requirements. Progress therefore depends on aligning compound identity, relevant target assemblies, experimentally constrained dynamics, and functional processing and exposure, while retaining negative and discordant findings.

Article.Title: Spatial Transcriptomics in Chronic Rhinosinusitis: Deciphering Tissue Architecture, Immune Niches, and Precision Therapeutics
Article.Authors: Ghosh S.; Madar I.; Bardhan K.; Muruganantham P.
Article.Abstract: Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is a heterogeneous inflammatory disorder in which epithelial injury, immune activation, and stromal remodelling are organised into local tissue niches. Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing have defined important cell states, but dissociation removes the anatomical relationships needed to determine where those states coexist. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) addresses this gap by mapping RNA, and in some platforms, protein, onto intact sinonasal tissue. This review provides an evidence-graded synthesis organised around a single translational chain: spatial niche to molecular signature to plausible biological mechanism to CRS phenotype/endotype to clinical implication to therapeutic relevance to validation status. Direct CRS ST evidence is separated from single-cell RNA sequencing support, computational prediction, protein or in situ evidence, experimental perturbation, clinical validation, and extrapolation from other inflammatory diseases. Current CRS studies support spatial compartmentalisation of eosinophil-rich epithelial lesions, ALOX15-positive macrophage programmes, GZMK-positive CD8 T-cell-fibroblast neighbourhoods, and treatment-associated epithelial and stromal changes. However, most ligand-receptor calls remain predictive, and spatial association alone does not establish functional causality. ST is therefore best viewed as a discovery and mechanistic-prioritisation technology whose clinical promises—biomarker selection, biologic matching, and response monitoring—require independent cohorts, locked assays, patient-level reproducibility, and prospective outcome studies. We compare study designs and platforms, examine statistical issues including spatial autocorrelation and pseudoreplication, and propose a cautious translational framework in which orthogonal and clinical validation convert spatial observations into actionable evidence.

Article.Title: The Molecular, Genetic, Pathological Basis and Clinical Perspectives of Endometrial Cancer: A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Chang C.; Chen J.; Chen K.
Article.Abstract: Endometrial cancer (EC) is the most common gynecologic malignancy in high-income regions, with a rising global incidence driven by population aging and obesity. Management of EC is undergoing a paradigm shift from traditional histopathological classification (Bokhman Types I and II) to a molecularly integrated model. Key driver alterations include mutations in PTEN, PIK3CA, PIK3R1, ARID1A, KRAS, and TP53, alongside focal amplifications of CCNE1 and ERBB2, all of which drive oncogenesis through dysregulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin, MAPK/ERK, and p53 signaling cascades. Integrated genomic profiling via The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and practical surrogates like ProMisE classifies EC into four distinct molecular subgroups: POLE-ultramutated (POLEmut), mismatch repair-deficient (MMRd/MSI-H), copy-number low/non-specific molecular profile (NSMP), and copy-number high/p53-abnormal (p53abn). These subgroups display unique biological features, tumor microenvironments, and prognostic trajectories, and have been formally incorporated into the FIGO 2023 staging system. Crucially, molecular classification directly informs biomarker-driven systemic management. MMRd may predict profound responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., pembrolizumab, dostarlimab) in both frontline and recurrent settings. For MMR-proficient disease, combination strategies such as anti-angiogenic/immunotherapy (lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab), hormone/mTOR or CDK4/6 inhibitor combinations, and nuclear export inhibitors (selinexor in TP53 wild-type) seem to offer substantial benefit. Furthermore, novel modalities including HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugates (trastuzumab deruxtecan), PARP inhibitors, and G2/M checkpoint inhibitors (adavosertib) are actively expanding the therapeutic armamentarium. Integrating multi-omics techniques, artificial intelligence, and novel systemic therapies into clinical workflows emerge to refine risk stratification, avoid over- or undertreatment, and establish a new standard of precision oncology in endometrial cancer.

Article.Title: Attenuation of Diabetes-Induced Defects in Cardiac Sarcoplasmic Reticulum and Myofibrils by Propionyl L-Carnitine Therapy
Article.Authors: Tappia P.; Gill J.; Elimban V.; Tandon R.; Dhalla N.
Article.Abstract: Our previous work showed that treatment of diabetic rats with propionyl L-carnitine (PPLC), a metabolic intervention, improved cardiac function and depressed the occurrence of Ca2+-overload in addition to attenuating sarcolemmal defects in Na+-K+ ATPase, Na+-Ca2+ exchange and Ca2+/Mg2+-ecto ATPase activities. This study was undertaken to examine the efficacy of PPLC treatment on changes in sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+-uptake and Ca2+-stimulated ATPase as well as myofibril (MF) Ca2+-ATPase activities by employing male Sprague-Dawley rats injected with streptozotocin (65 mg/kg) for the induction of diabetes. Three days after inducing diabetes, diabetic rats were treated with or without PPLC (250 mg/kg/day) for 8 weeks. PPLC treatment was observed to improve cardiac function and attenuate depressions in both SR Ca2+-uptake and Ca2+-pump ATPase activities without affecting depressions in MF Ca2+-stimulated or Mg2+-ATPase activities as well as myosin Ca2+- or actin-stimulated ATPase activities in diabetic hearts. PPLC treatment also reduced the increased content of cardiac long-chain acylcarnitine as well as the plasma levels of free fatty acids and triglycerides without affecting the elevated levels of plasma glucose or depressed levels of plasma insulin in diabetic animals. The depression in cardiac carnitine content was corrected by PPLC treatment. Under in vitro conditions, palmitoyl L-carnitine (PMLC; a long-chain acylcarnitine) did not affect MF Ca2+-stimulated ATPase in the absence or presence of PPLC, whereas the inhibitory effect of PMLC on SR Ca2+-stimulated ATPase activities was antagonized by PPLC. These data suggest that the beneficial effects of PPLC in diabetic cardiomyopathy may be associated with attenuation of SR Ca2+-handling defects rather than with any action regarding depressed MF ATPase activity.

Article.Title: Impaired Mitochondrial Translation and Bioenergetic Dysfunction Associated with the MT-RNR1 m.1014A>G Variant
Article.Authors: Marrone I.; Ura B.; Celsi F.; Zupin L.; Sommella E.; Golino V.; Peruzzo P.; Ciardi C.; Bonati M.; Genova E.; Zeviani M.; Spinelli A.; Capaci V.
Article.Abstract: Pathogenic variants in MT-RNR1 are classically associated with aminoglycoside-induced sensorineural hearing loss through disruption of the mitochondrial 12S rRNA decoding center. Their contribution to pediatric neurological disease remains poorly defined. We identified a novel homoplasmic MT-RNR1 variant, m.1014A>G, in a patient with drug-resistant focal epilepsy beginning at 9 months of age who remained undiagnosed after trio whole-exome sequencing filtered using an extensive epilepsy gene panel. The variant was also detected in her mother. Structural modeling suggests that the variant, affecting a highly conserved region of the mitochondrial 12S rRNA, may alter the mitochondrial small ribosomal subunit assembly. To investigate its pathogenicity, we performed comprehensive functional studies in patient-derived fibroblasts. Unlike canonical MT-RNR1 variants, m.1014A>G did not confer aminoglycoside toxicity. Functional in vitro studies on patients’ fibroblasts demonstrated increased 12S/16S rRNA ratios, reduced abundance of both mitoribosomal subunit proteins, decreased levels of mitochondrially encoded respiratory-chain subunits, and impaired oxidative phosphorylation. These abnormalities were accompanied by mitochondrial network fragmentation, increased mitochondria–lysosome colocalization suggestive of enhanced mitophagy and reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number. Altogether, the findings are consistent with defective mitoribosome assembly and altered mitochondrial translation, resulting in a bioenergetic defect. Our study points to a previously unrecognized candidate pathogenic mechanism associated with MT-RNR1 and may expand the phenotypic spectrum of MT-RNR1-related disorders to include maternally inherited infantile-onset epileptic encephalopathy. These findings highlight the importance of dedicated mitochondrial DNA analysis in children with unexplained early-onset epilepsy despite negative nuclear genomic testing.

Article.Title: Central Responses to SGLT2 Inhibition: Distinguishing Direct CNS Pharmacology from the Brain–Kidney–Metabolism Axis
Article.Authors: Kim D.; Lee M.; Lee S.; Kim J.; Bae J.; Khang A.; Kang Y.; Yi D.
Article.Abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors improve cardiovascular and kidney outcomes through mechanisms that extend beyond glycemic control. Emerging studies report changes in hypothalamic and brainstem physiology following SGLT2 inhibitor administration, but the evidentiary meaning of these observations remains uncertain. This review critically evaluates clinical, in vivo, ex vivo, and cellular evidence linking SGLT2 inhibition to central metabolic regulation. We distinguish three claims that are often conflated: central pharmacological capacity after direct neural exposure, central nervous system (CNS) adaptation after systemic treatment, and therapeutically relevant CNS target engagement with causal mediation. Candidate pathways include hypothalamic nutrient sensing, insulin responsiveness, melanocortin signaling, ketone availability, glial inflammation, redox regulation, and autonomic activity. We propose a bidirectional brain–kidney–metabolism framework in which renal glucose and sodium loss generate metabolic, hormonal, inflammatory, hemodynamic, and potentially neural signals that are integrated by hypothalamic and brainstem circuits. These circuits may then convey autonomic and neuroendocrine outputs to peripheral organs. Current evidence supports central responsiveness and CNS adaptation to systemic treatment, but not a unified direct SGLT2-dependent brain mechanism. Compound-specific unbound CNS pharmacokinetics, orthogonal cell-specific target validation, compartment-restricted models, selective renal-afferent manipulation, and longitudinal human phenotyping are required to establish causality. The proposed framework complements, rather than replaces, established renal and tissue-specific mechanisms.

Article.Title: High-Density Culture and Lipopolysaccharide Cooperatively Activate TAK1–MAPK Signaling to Promote Osteogenic Differentiation in Human Dental Pulp Stem Cells
Article.Authors: Pwint K.; Kawashima N.; Okada Y.; Noda S.; Okiji T.; Yahata Y.
Article.Abstract: Human dental pulp stem cells (hDPSCs) are promising for regenerative medicine because of their multipotent differentiation capacity and ease of isolation from extracted teeth. We previously reported that high-density culture enhanced their osteogenic potential; however, the inflammatory environment at the transplantation site may influence osteogenic differentiation. This study investigated the effects of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) on the osteogenic differentiation of hDPSCs cultured at high density. hDPSCs were seeded at either low or high density and stimulated with LPS. High-density culture increased focal adhesion kinase (FAK) phosphorylation, a well-established marker of integrin signaling activation, and enhanced osteogenic differentiation. Under high-density culture conditions, LPS further increased the expression of the osteogenic markers bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2) and runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) and promoted mineralized nodule formation. Moreover, LPS stimulation induced the phosphorylation of transforming growth factor-β-activated kinase-1 (TAK1), p38 and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) exclusively under high-density culture conditions. TAK1 inhibition suppressed the phosphorylation of p38 and JNK and reduced BMP2 and RUNX2 expression. TAK1 phosphorylation was attenuated by a FAK inhibitor in LPS-stimulated hDPSCs cultured at high density. These findings suggest that FAK signaling associated with high-density culture facilitates LPS-induced TAK1–MAPK activation, contributing to increased BMP2 and RUNX2 expression and enhanced mineralized nodule formation in hDPSCs.

Article.Title: Sargassum horneri Fucoidan Suppresses the Early-Stage Amyloid Fibrillation of Insulin
Article.Authors: Amishiro N.; Miwa A.; Kariya S.; Ito Y.; Yasaski Y.; Funakoshi M.; Ohshiro T.; Yagi H.
Article.Abstract: Amyloid fibril formation is implicated in numerous protein misfolding disorders. Fucoidan, a sulfated polysaccharide primarily derived from brown algae, exhibits diverse biological activities. In this study, we investigated the inhibitory effect of Sargassum horneri fucoidan (S-fucoidan) on insulin amyloid fibrillation in vitro. Initial screening of fucoidans derived from Cladosiphon okamuranus, Kjellmaniella crassifolia, and S. horneri identified S-fucoidan as the most effective inhibitor of insulin fibrillation. Therefore, we characterized the inhibitory effect of S-fucoidan using Thioflavin T fluorescence, transmission electron microscopy, circular dichroism spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography, and cell viability assays. Both S-fucoidan and low-molecular-weight S-fucoidan inhibited fibrillation in a concentration-dependent manner. When present from the onset of the reaction, S-fucoidan prevented detectable fibril formation, preserved the initial secondary structure of insulin, and maintained insulin in a monomeric or near-monomeric state. In contrast, addition during nucleation or elongation did not effectively halt ongoing fibrillation. These findings indicate that S-fucoidan predominantly suppresses the early stage of insulin amyloid fibrillation and provide a basis for investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying its anti-fibrillation activity.

Article.Title: Differentiation of Human Glioblastoma Stem Cells as a Prospective Tool to Find New Biomarkers and Molecular Targets: A Proteomic and Lipidomic Approach
Article.Authors: Cardoso A.; Serra D.; Xavier C.; Monteiro J.; Morais C.; Correia I.; Domingues M.; Vasconcelos M.; Jurado A.; Lima M.
Article.Abstract: Although glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) constitute a small subpopulation of this highly heterogeneous brain cancer, they are widely recognised as key drivers of tumour recurrence after surgical resection and resistance to radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Differentiation of GSCs has, therefore, emerged as a strategy to increase glioblastoma susceptibility to therapeutic and surgical interventions. Cellular and molecular heterogeneity of glioblastoma limits the effectiveness of any treatment that relies on single molecules identified as disease-specific biomarkers. In this context, lipidomic and proteomic profiles constitute a source of information that can be translated into the identification of clinically relevant diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers, and novel therapeutic targets towards eradication of this lethal disease. Our initial studies demonstrated that BMP4 induced differentiation of the human glioblastoma stem cells G144 with approximately a 30-fold increase in expression of the astrocytic marker GFAP, which was coupled with a reduction in cell proliferation (33% decrease in EDU incorporation), invasion (61% decrease) and tumoursphere growth (53% decrease in area), and enhanced senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity (5.9-fold increase). Lipidomic and proteomic analysis (using data from 3 and 4 independent experiments, respectively) was then performed, allowing the identification of specific lipids and proteins exclusively detected or predominant in stem or differentiated G 144 cells. Importantly, our findings, which revealed a 6-fold increase in GFAP expression upon downregulation of a specific protein detected only in stem cells (SPRY4), pave the way for the employment of the RNAi-mediated knockdown strategy as a mechanistically distinct alternative to the use of BMP4, and highlight this protein as a candidate regulator associated with the G144 stem-like phenotype.

Article.Title: Analysis of Local Free Volume and Hydration in Pharmaceutical Polymer Films Using Positron Annihilation Lifetime Spectroscopy
Article.Authors: Shokoya M.; Süvegh K.; Vilimi Z.; Kállai-Szabó N.; Zelkó R.; Sebe I.
Article.Abstract: The relationship between the nanoscale free volume of pharmaceutical polymer films and their hydration behavior remains poorly understood. Eight pharmaceutical polymers were screened at three concentration levels within a quality-by-design framework; only two poly(vinyl alcohol) grades (PVA EG-30P and EG-40P), hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC), and sodium alginate (Na-alginate) formed continuous films. These were characterized by positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS), loss on drying (LOD), and swelling analysis. PALS clearly differentiated HPC, Na-alginate, and PVA, whereas the two PVA grades were similar and the concentration had only a minor effect. HPC showed the largest free volume holes (86.7–89.5 Å3), and Na-alginate the smallest holes (36.9–39.6 Å3) together with the highest LOD (20.2–21.6%). Across the 12 polymer–concentration combinations, the free volume hole volume correlated inversely with LOD (Spearman ρ = −0.85) but not with the equilibrium swelling index, as both HPC and Na-alginate swelled considerably more than PVA. Thus, PALS discriminates film-forming pharmaceutical polymers and reflects their residual water content, but the free volume of the air-dried films does not predict their swelling capacity.

Article.Title: Towards Integrative and Multi-Scale Imaging with Recent Advances in Cryo-Electron Tomography
Article.Authors: Corroyer-Dulmont S.; Masson C.; Quemin E.
Article.Abstract: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) enables the three-dimensional visualization of molecular architectures within complex biological environments in a near-native state. In recent years, major advances in sample preparation, instrumentation, data acquisition, and computational processing have considerably expanded the scope of cryo-ET. Workflows that were once low-throughput and largely restricted to a small number of thin specimens and use cases can now be applied to many different samples from isolated macromolecular assemblies to cells, organoids, or tissues. In parallel, the advent of (i) automatic procedures for cryo-focused ion beam milling used for sample thinning as well as streamlined tilt series acquisition, (ii) improved methods for high-pressure-frozen specimens including lift-out, (iii) together with increasingly integrated reconstruction and processing pipelines are all contributing to improve throughput, reproducibility, and accessibility of the technique. Emerging deep learning tools further facilitate target identification, quality control with feedback loops, tomogram reconstruction, and downstream analysis by sub-tomogram averaging. Here, we discuss recent developments on different aspects of the cryo-ET workflow that are progressively bridging molecular and cellular scales in conjunction with multi-modal imaging. We also highlight current limitations and emerging technologies that may further extend cryo-ET capabilities, particularly in combination with complementary approaches toward integrative structural cell biology.

Article.Title: β-Ionone for Cancer Therapy: Molecular Mechanisms, Apoptotic Signaling, Preclinical Evidence, and Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: Kumar A.; Sharma P.; Goyal S.; Saini S.; Kaur D.; Bhatia G.; Sharma S.; Tuli H.; Alharbi H.; Rahmani A.
Article.Abstract: β-Ionone is a naturally occurring C13-norisoprenoid apocarotenoid which is mainly derived from carotenoid cleavage and has gained significant attention due to its potential anticancer activity. Experimental investigations have shown that β-ionone has the ability to arrest the proliferation of cancer cells and to induce programmed cell death by several mechanisms depending on the type of tumors and experimental conditions. Mitochondrial apoptosis, such as Bax/Bcl-2 balance, cytochrome c release, activation of caspases, and p53-associated signaling, is the most consistently supported evidence for β-Ionone. Other mechanisms include modulation of the PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK signaling pathways, regulation of cell-cycle progression, generation of oxidative stress, and increased sensitivity to death-receptor-mediated apoptosis. Moreover, recent experimental studies have provided further support for the role of β-ionone in ferroptosis, as it was found to modulate the ferroptosis-associated proteins and Wnt/β-catenin signaling in gastric cancer models. By contrast, other mechanisms such as autophagy and the JAK/STAT3 signaling pathway are proposed mechanisms that need to be directly tested. Most importantly, evidence collected using β-ionone derivatives (such as esters and endoperoxides) differs from that collected from the parent. While promising preclinical results have been observed, translation is hampered by the lack of human pharmacokinetic data, uncertainties in bioavailability, and a lack of toxicity data and clinical trials. Target validation, characterization of the PHPD profile, safety assessment, formulation optimization, and clinically relevant in vivo validation should thus be given special attention in future studies.

Article.Title: Therapeutic Targeting of Hepatic Stellate Cell Inactivation and Collagen Degradation by IC-2 Mitigates Liver Fibrosis
Article.Authors: Itaba N.; Abe K.; Kono Y.; Shimizu H.; Oka H.; Morimoto M.; Nanba D.; Shiota G.
Article.Abstract: Liver fibrosis, characterized by excessive accumulation of the extracellular matrix (ECM), is caused by an imbalance between fibrogenesis and fibrolysis. Effective antifibrotic therapy requires the regulation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) through the production of collagen and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). The TGF-β/Smad and Wnt/β-catenin pathways play central roles in this regulation. In this study, we investigated whether IC-2, a Wnt/β-catenin inhibitor derived from ICG-001, reduces TGF-β/Smad and Wnt/β-catenin signaling in HSCs in vitro. We further examined the anti-fibrotic effects in two fibrosis models: carbon tetrachloride (CCl4)-treated mice and high-fat diet (HFD)-fed ob/ob mice. IC-2 markedly suppressed the TGF-β/Smad and Wnt/β-catenin pathway in HSCs. Furthermore, IC-2 markedly ameliorated liver fibrosis in CCl4-treated mice, accompanied with suppressed HSC activation and enhanced collagenolytic activity. IC-2 also attenuated fibrosis in the livers of HFD-fed mice. Co-immunoprecipitation analysis confirmed that IC-2 disrupts the β-catenin/CREB-binding protein (CBP) complex. IC-2 specifically induced MMP-1 expression in human HSCs, while the JNK inhibitor SP600125 suppressed IC-2-mediated MMP-1 induction at 48 h, but not at 24 h. It is suggested that this delayed effect may be due to a delayed transcriptional response or indirect signaling cascade downstream of JNK activation. These findings demonstrate that IC-2 mitigates liver fibrosis by inhibiting HSC activation and promoting collagenolysis, highlighting its therapeutic potential in cirrhosis.

Article.Title: A Hydrophobic Ion-Paired Self-Microemulsifying System Enhances Jejunal Absorption and Acute Glycemic Control of Semaglutide in Rats
Article.Authors: Wang K.; Hu Y.; Jiang Y.; Fan R.; Bao Y.; Wang S.; Liang Q.; Lu K.; Xue J.; Yan Y.; Liu X.; Liu W.; Zhu Y.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: Oral delivery of semaglutide offers a promising strategy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) by improving patient adherence. However, its clinical translation is limited by low oral bioavailability, resulting from the peptide’s hydrophilicity, instability in gastrointestinal environments, and poor intestinal permeability. To address these challenges, semaglutide was converted into a hydrophobic ion-pair (HIP) complex with the cationic lipid DODAB (termed SEDAB), which was subsequently incorporated into a self-microemulsifying drug delivery system (SMEDDS), yielding SEDAB-SME. A comparative screen of two cationic amphiphiles identified DODAB as the selected counterion, which forms a stable complex with semaglutide. Ion pairing with DODAB markedly increased the lipophilicity of semaglutide, and the resulting SEDAB-SME formulation enhanced its stability in simulated intestinal fluid, effectively protecting the peptide from enzymatic degradation. In vitro, FITC-semaglutide delivered by SEDAB-SME showed markedly greater cell association than native FITC-semaglutide, and inhibitor studies suggested the involvement of a cholesterol-sensitive, raft-associated internalization route. In an intra-jejunal (i.j.) regional intestinal absorption study in SD rats, SEDAB-SME enhanced jejunal absorption of semaglutide (Frel = 0.12%) by approximately 28-fold compared with native semaglutide administered via the same i.j. route. In an acute single-dose pharmacodynamic study in STZ-induced T2DM rats, oral administration of SEDAB-SME enteric-coated capsules significantly reduced blood glucose levels. These results demonstrate that the HIP-SMEDDS strategy markedly enhanced regional jejunal absorption and produced acute glucose-lowering effects in a rodent model. This proof-of-concept study highlights a promising approach that warrants further validation of direct oral pharmacokinetics and long-term safety.

Article.Title: Inhibition of miR-148a-3p Ameliorates Prion Accumulation by Restoring ATP6AP2-Mediated Lysosomal Acidification
Article.Authors: Xu R.; Chen C.; Sun T.; Li J.; Zhai X.; Xu B.; A R.; Zhang X.; Ning F.; Liang D.; Cao R.; Zhou W.; Gao L.; Xiao K.; Shi Q.; Dong X.
Article.Abstract: Prion diseases (PrDs) are fatal neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the accumulation of misfolded prion protein (PrPSc) and progressive impairment of protein quality-control systems. Lysosomal dysfunction and defective autophagic flux contribute to PrPSc accumulation, but the upstream regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely defined. In this study, we investigated the regulatory role of miR-148a-3p during prion infection. We found that miR-148a-3p expression is markedly increased in ME7- and 139A-infected mouse brains and prion-infected SMB-S15 cells. Dual-luciferase assays confirmed that miR-148a-3p directly targets the PRNP 3′UTR, negatively regulating cellular PrP expression. In prion-infected cells, inhibition of miR-148a-3p reduced proteinase K (PK)-resistant PrP (PrPres), delayed RT-QuIC conversion, and decreased PMCA-amplified PrPres. Through bioinformatic prediction and experimental validation, we identified ATP6AP2, a V-ATPase-associated regulator of lysosomal acidification, as a high-confidence target of miR-148a-3p. ATP6AP2 expression was significantly decreased in sCJD transcriptomic data, scrapie-infected mouse brains, and prion-infected cells. Importantly, inhibition of miR-148a-3p restored ATP6AP2 expression, which improved lysosomal acidification and alleviated impaired autophagic flux. Furthermore, overexpression of ATP6AP2 directly reduced PrPSc accumulation in SMB-S15 cells and diminished prion seeding capacities in RT-QuIC and PMCA assays. These findings identify miR-148a-3p as an upstream regulator of ATP6AP2-dependent lysosomal dysfunction in prion infection. Inhibition of miR-148a-3p may restore lysosomal clearance capacity and reduce PrPSc accumulation, suggesting a potential regulatory strategy for PrDs.

Article.Title: Hypoxia Alters Polymeric Immunoglobulin Receptor Expression and Cell Differentiation in the Airway Epithelium
Article.Authors: Gerard L.; Lecocq M.; Detry B.; Bouzin C.; Hoton D.; Carlier F.; Plante-Bordeneuve T.; Gohy S.; Lacroix V.; Pilette C.
Article.Abstract: Secretion of immunoglobulin A (IgA), actively transported across the airway epithelium (AE) by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR), represents a key defense of the lung against pathogens. Dysregulation of the IgA/pIgR system has been reported in respiratory diseases, but the underlying mechanism, and particularly the effects of hypoxia, remains poorly characterized. The effects of hypoxia were investigated using the model of human AE reconstituted in vitro upon culture in the air/liquid interface (ALI). AE was exposed to 1% O2, upon resting or inflammatory conditions. Mechanistic studies included pharmacological stabilization of HIF-1α and inhibition of TGF-β signaling. Additionally, HIF-1α and TGF-β pathways were analyzed by multiplex fluorescence immunostaining of lung tissue from patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and controls. In ALI AE cultures from 22 subjects, hypoxia significantly reduced pIgR expression (mRNA and proteic), regardless of inflammation. Hypoxia also altered AE structure and cell differentiation, leading to a loss of ciliated and goblet cells. Both hypoxia and pharmacological stabilization of HIF-1α recapitulated these effects and induced increased TGF-β2 expression. In lung tissue from ARDS patients, the AE exhibited reduced pIgR expression, associated with increased HIF-1α stabilization and TGF-β2 expression. Hypoxia induced pIgR downregulation and impaired cell differentiation, through HIF-1α stabilization and subsequent autocrine TGF-β2 signaling, providing a novel pathway underlying altered lung IgA immunity in disease.

Article.Title: Influence of Small Changes in Intermolecular Distances on Results of Interaction Energy Decomposition for Stacking Interactions, Hydrogen Bonds, and Antiparallel Interactions
Article.Authors: Blagojević Filipović J.; Zarić S.
Article.Abstract: A SAPT (Symmetry-Adapted Perturbation Theory) decomposition analysis was performed for various types of noncovalent interactions (stacking, hydrogen bonds, and antiparallel) for various distances of interacting fragments. Although the total interaction energy does not significantly change within the small range around the optimal distance, the energy contributions can significantly change in some systems. This is particularly pronounced for stacking interactions, while for hydrogen bonds and antiparallel interactions the energy contributions do not significantly change around the optimal distance. Thus, the nature of interactions should be carefully interpreted, as small alterations in distances between the interacting fragments can sometimes lead to significant changes in energy contributions, especially for stacking interactions.

Article.Title: Novel Palladium(II) β-Diketonate Complexes: Synthesis, Dual Antimicrobial/Anticancer Activity, and Molecular Insights into DNA/Protein Interactions
Article.Authors: Trifunović Stevanović M.; Joksimović N.; Petronijević J.; Stojanović S.; Đorđević S.; Stanković J.; Bufan B.; Božić D.
Article.Abstract: This study reports the synthesis and biological evaluation of four novel palladium(II) complexes (B1–B4) with O,O-bidentate β-diketo ester ligands. Spectroscopic characterization confirmed their structures, while biological assays revealed substituent-dependent activity. Complexes B3 and B4 showed the most consistent antimicrobial activity, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 312–1200 μM across the tested microorganisms. B3 exhibited the highest antiproliferative potency, with IC50 values of 2.3, 5.2, and 5.4 μM against K-562, HeLa, and HaCaT cells, respectively. However, its selectivity varied with the cell model, reaching a selectivity index (SI) of 5.17 against K-562 cells relative to MRC-5 fibroblasts and 2.35 relative to HaCaT cells. B2 showed a more moderate activity profile, with some selectivity towards K-562 cells. Flow-cytometric analysis revealed increased sub-G0/G1 populations following treatment, consistent with the induction of apoptosis. Biophysical assays and molecular docking indicated structure-dependent interactions with DNA, while fluorescence studies revealed differences in the apparent binding affinities of the complexes toward human serum albumin (HSA). These findings highlight the influence of ligand structure on the biological activity and biomolecular interactions of palladium(II) complexes, identifying B3 as the most promising candidate for further investigation based on its antiproliferative potency and selectivity.

Article.Title: Platinum-Induced Toxicity and Zinc-Based Interventions: A Systematic Review of Preclinical Evidence
Article.Authors: Tseriotis V.; Ampazis D.; Karachrysafi S.; Papamitsou T.; Kouvelas D.; Stergiou K.; Fouskas V.; Pavliis P.; Hatzibougias D.; Chatzianagnosti S.; Dimaki E.; Konstantinidis I.; Tsiptsios D.; Lallas K.; Sič A.; Keramidas V.; Tastanis C.; Papadopoulou K.; Cheva A.; Arnaoutoglou M.
Article.Abstract: Zinc may mitigate platinum-induced toxicity through antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects. We systematically reviewed preclinical in vivo evidence on zinc-based interventions, focusing on organ protection, mechanisms and antitumour efficacy. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and supplementary sources were searched for studies in rats and mice. Risk of bias was assessed using SYRCLE, and the findings were synthesised narratively. Database searches identified 1552 records; 25 studies were included following database and supplementary screening. The risk of bias was frequently unclear for sequence generation, allocation concealment and blinding. Most studies investigated cisplatin; fewer evaluated carboplatin, oxaliplatin or combination chemotherapy. Zinc interventions included salts, dietary supplementation, organic complexes and nanoformulations, predominantly administered before platinum exposure. Protective findings were reported across renal, reproductive, nervous, hepatic, haematopoietic and cardiovascular systems. Proposed mechanisms included metallothionein induction, enhanced antioxidant defences and modulation of inflammation and apoptosis. Heterogeneity precluded conclusions about formulation superiority. Limited tumour-bearing evidence indicated that zinc-induced metallothionein may reduce cisplatin activity, whereas bismuth zinc citrate preserved tumour control within the tested model. Methodological weaknesses, heterogeneity and scarce tumour-bearing evidence limit confidence in efficacy and oncological safety. These findings support further preclinical investigation rather than clinical implementation.

Article.Title: Quorum Quenching and Quorum-Sensing Interference in Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Molecular Mechanisms, Host Protection, and Translational Barriers
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Zou W.; Pei L.
Article.Abstract: Quorum sensing (QS) coordinates virulence expression, biofilm-associated behavior, and persistence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, making its signaling network a potential target for adjunctive anti-virulence therapy. Quorum quenching (QQ) directly degrades, modifies, or sequesters signaling molecules, whereas broader QS interference encompasses inhibition of signal synthesis, receptor antagonism, and disruption of downstream regulatory interactions. Experimental studies of N-acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL)-degrading enzymes and PqsR antagonists have demonstrated suppression of selected virulence-associated phenotypes, with several infection models showing reductions in host injury or persistence-associated outcomes. The PqsE–RhlR regulatory interface has gained substantial molecular and genetic support as a distinct intervention target, but its pharmacological development remains limited. Responses to QS interference vary with bacterial strain, regulatory network adaptation, environmental conditions, and infection stage. Reductions in virulence-factor production or biofilm biomass do not consistently correspond to bacterial clearance or host protection. Available human studies involving agents with proposed QS-modulatory activity have not established clinical benefits specifically attributable to QS inhibition. Clinical translation requires validated target engagement, efficacy assessment in established and polymicrobial infections, and characterization of delivery, pharmacological exposure, safety, and resistance evolution.

Article.Title: Sugar Depletion in Korean Pine Infected with Cronartium ribicola, Alongside Metabolic Reprogramming by the T6P–Tre Signaling Module
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Wang B.; Yu Q.; Zhang R.; Tan B.; Feng Z.; Wang F.; Li D.
Article.Abstract: In diseased Korean pine trees (Pinus koraiensis), Cronartium ribicola develops aecia only in the bole, where sugar is initially sufficient. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying sugar depletion in diseased Korean pine trees remain unelucidated, hindering sugar-targeted control strategies. Focusing on host responses, this study integrated metabolomics, transcriptomics, and targeted glycomics based on spatial partitioning to investigate sugar metabolic reprogramming in the bole of diseased pines. Multi-omics revealed severe sugar depletion in the blister area, which was significantly correlated with relative C. ribicola DNA level. However, the transcription of sugar synthesis genes was upregulated, while sugar degradation genes were downregulated, indicating decoupling between sugar metabolism and transcription. Concurrently, T6P–Tre-centered reprogramming was identified: Pktppd and Pktpp4, encoding enzymes that convert T6P into Tre, were downregulated, leading to elevated T6P and reduced Tre levels. This T6P–Tre shift likely acts as a signal to activate genes related to sugar accumulation in response to sugar depletion, thereby explaining the observed transcriptional-metabolic decoupling. Targeting the T6P–Tre module to modulate host sugar allocation and restrict sugar availability to the pathogen may offer a novel strategy for the targeted control of Korean pine blister rust (KPBR).

Article.Title: Structural and Biophysical Profiling of HLA Class II Mismatches Using AlphaFold 3: A Computational Study
Article.Authors: Bardash V.; Samchuk O.; Tolstyak Y.; Demydenko H.; Sklyarov E.
Article.Abstract: Conventional linear eplet-matching algorithms (HLAMatchmaker, HLAMM) evaluate primary sequence polymorphisms across human leukocyte antigen (HLA) loci without integrating three-dimensional (3D) steric accessibility and local physicochemical constraints. Here, we developed an exploratory computational antigenicity pipeline using AlphaFold 3 to evaluate 10,000 simulated European donor–recipient pairs across pre-computed, full-length HLA class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) and heterodimeric class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) complexes modeled in a standardized peptide-free conformation. Candidate eplets were sequentially screened using a spatial solvent-accessible surface area threshold (SASA ≥ 10.0 Å2) and an empirical biophysical exclusion gate (5th percentile of absolute net charge |Qnet| ≥ 0.3326 e and hydropathy Htotal ≥ −7.265, calibrated on N = 170 antibody-verified eplets). Across the simulated cohort (n = 10,000), filtration reduced median [Q1; Q3] eplet counts from 19 [12; 26] to 17 [10; 23] for HLA-A, 22 [15; 29] to 18 [12; 24] for HLA-B, 12 [7; 17] to 10 [7; 15] for HLA-C, 15 [10; 19] to 11 [7; 14] for HLA-DR, 12 [6; 17] to 9 [4; 14] for HLA-DQ, and 7 [3; 12] to 6 [2; 9] for HLA-DP. Component ablation demonstrated that 3D steric accessibility (SASA ≥ 10.0 Å2) accounted for the vast majority of eplet exclusions—87.8% in HLA-DR and HLA-DP and 58.2% to 69.1% across HLA-DQ and class I loci—whereas the registry-calibrated biophysical gate acted as a secondary refinement. Within the subset of simulated pairs initially exceeding the arbitrary ≥10-eplet linear cutoff, the proportion dropping below 10 eplets after filtering was low for class I (HLA-A: 4.4%, HLA-B: 8.0%, HLA-C: 13.2%) but substantially higher for class II high-load subsets: HLA-DQ (21.8%), HLA-DR (26.0%), and HLA-DP (33.7% of 3693 baseline high-load pairs). Furthermore, class II loci, particularly HLA-DP, exhibited weakened covariance between heuristic charge and hydropathy indices that persisted after 1:1 count-matched subsampling (ρmatched = −0.268) and partial correlation adjustment (ρpartial = −0.385). This dual-filter pipeline defines a restricted mathematical subset of spatially accessible and biophysically suprathreshold candidate eplets. Because this is a hypothesis-generating in silico framework, multicenter retrospective registry analyses and prospective clinical trials evaluating de novo donor-specific antibody formation, biopsy-proven rejection, and allograft survival are strictly required before clinical translation.

Article.Title: Endocrine Signaling and Tissue Remodeling in Gynecomastia: Implications for Treatment Response
Article.Authors: Deng J.; Tong S.; Liu S.; Zhou H.; Ren M.
Article.Abstract: To critically synthesize evidence on treatment response in gynecomastia using a framework that distinguishes biological response, structural response, and patient-important benefit. We searched PubMed, PubMed Central, and targeted journals through 11 September 2026. Priority was given to gynecomastia-specific human studies; evidence from other breast systems, animal models, and general biomarker methodology was treated as indirect. The randomized anastrozole trial showed an endocrine effect but did not demonstrate superiority over placebo on the prespecified structural endpoint. Receptor expression in surgical specimens provides biological plausibility but does not establish receptor functionality, endocrine dependence, or predictive value. Stromal composition may influence lesion regression, but this remains a hypothesis requiring direct testing. Ultrasonography and elastography may support pretreatment characterization, but current studies do not validate imaging features as surrogates for fibrosis or endocrine responsiveness. Gynecomastia-derived organoids offer a disease-relevant model for functional studies, although donor numbers are small and endocrine responsiveness, cellular representativeness, and reproducibility across patients require further evaluation remain uncertain. Biological response, structural response, and patient-important benefit need not occur together or in a fixed sequence. Further research should link tissue and model findings to pretreatment markers, compare treatment benefits, and establish clinical utility before marker-guided care.
