Article.Title: Curcumin Sensitizes Colorectal Cancer Cells to TRAIL-Mediated Apoptosis
Article.Authors: Rimondi E.; Manfredini M.; Nigro F.; Gonelli A.; Milani D.; Celeghini C.; Previati M.; Marcuzzi A.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major clinical challenge due to resistance to conventional cell death-inducing therapies. TRAIL selectively induces apoptosis in cancer cells via death receptors, but its effectiveness in preclinical models is limited by tumor resistance mechanisms. Curcumin, a natural polyphenol, modulates multiple survival and apoptotic pathways and has been proposed as a sensitizing agent to overcome TRAIL resistance. Here, we investigated the combinatorial effects of TRAIL and curcumin in the HCT116 colorectal cancer cell model. Cells were treated with TRAIL, curcumin, or their combination for 24 and 48 h, evaluating apoptosis, viability, and underlying mechanisms. Curcumin significantly enhanced TRAIL-induced apoptosis (p < 0.0001) and further reduced MTT-derived metabolic activity (p < 0.01) compared with TRAIL treatment alone. This effect remained evident after 48 h, although the stability and persistence of TRAIL activity were not directly assessed. Mechanistically, combined treatment enhanced PARP cleavage, γ-H2AX phosphorylation, and BAX and Caspase-3 cleavage, while downregulating anti-apoptotic IAP family members. Notably, cotreatment also promoted pyroptosis, shown by characteristic morphological changes (p < 0.0001) and increased Gasdermin-E cleavage. These findings indicate that curcumin sensitizes CRC cells to TRAIL by engaging both apoptotic and pyroptotic pathways, suggesting a potential approach to counteract both TRAIL and multidrug resistance in colorectal cancer.

Article.Title: The Broadly Neutralizing DEV_K57 Antibody, Isolated from a Convalescent Patient, in Complex with the SARS-CoV-2 RBD
Article.Authors: Sinitsina E.; Imatdinov I.; Tuyrin V.; Shipovalov A.; Zaykovskaya A.; Osinkina I.; Yanshin A.; Radchenko N.; Ryzhykau Y.; Sudarev V.; Kuklina D.; Onkhonova G.; Ivleva E.; Agafonov A.; Gladysheva A.
Article.Abstract: The continuous evolution of SARS-CoV-2 necessitates broadly neutralizing antibodies for robust therapeutics. In this study, we isolated 1824 single B cells from a COVID-19 convalescent donor and obtained 91 pairs of nucleotide sequences potentially encoding VH/VL domains. From this library, we generated and evaluated a panel of 38 recombinant monoclonal antibodies. Among this panel, we identified DEV_K57 as a broadly neutralizing human IgG1 antibody targeting the SARS-CoV-2 RBD. DEV_K57 exhibited in vitro neutralization breadth against diverse variants, demonstrating subnanomolar IC50 values. This in vitro efficacy was translated in vivo. In a Syrian hamster model of SARS-CoV-2 Delta infection, DEV_K57 significantly reduced viral RNA and infectious titers in both the upper and lower respiratory tracts, conferring a favorable safety profile with minimal histopathological damage. To elucidate its mechanism, we performed comprehensive biophysical and structural analyses. Biolayer interferometry revealed a high picomolar binding affinity to the RBD Delta. Furthermore, size-exclusion chromatography coupled with small-angle X-ray scattering and computational modeling uncovered a unique, stable dimeric architecture of the DEV_K57 Fab-RBD complex in solution, with a binding interface distinct from previously characterized structures. These findings underscore the value of rapid antibody isolation for pandemic preparedness against future emerging biological threats.

Article.Title: Phylogenetic Analysis of Rare Crepis Species of the Crimean Flora (C. purpurea (Willd.) M. Bieb. and C. callicephala Juz.) Through Plastid Genome Reconstruction
Article.Authors: Emirsaliev A.; Afonnikov D.; Mitrofanova I.; Salina E.; Kochetov A.
Article.Abstract: One of the largest genera within the Cichorieae tribe of the Asteraceae family is Crepis, comprising ∼200 species. The diversity of numerous local forms is of interest for adaptation studies. There are two rare closely related species within the Lagoseris clade of the genus Crepis which occupy highly divergent habitats—C. callicephala Juz. and C. purpurea (Willd.) M. Bieb.—both occurring in the Crimean Peninsula. The habitats differ in environmental conditions and are isolated by location and altitude, restricting opportunities for gamete exchange. The species are similar morphologically but demonstrate different phenological patterns, representing a notable natural model for investigating how isolation and habitat conditions may shape genetic differentiation and local adaptation. We sequenced the total DNA of C. callicephala and C. purpurea. Relying on both short-read and long-read data, we assembled plastid genomes of these species and reconstructed the phylogeny of the subtribe Crepidinae. The assembled plastid genomes are 149,980 bp (C. callicephala) and 150,007 bp (C. purpurea), and the two species were recovered as a closely related pair on a long common branch within the sampled Crepidinae. We also noted an unusual structural rearrangement in the rbcL–psaI locus shared by the studied accessions of both species, affecting the accD gene (encoding the β-carboxyltransferase subunit of acetyl-CoA carboxylase), which has not been reported in other members of Cichorioideae. Together with the shifts in the inverted-repeat boundaries, these features provide molecular data relevant to the taxonomic status and relationship of C. callicephala and C. purpurea.

Article.Title: Multiple Myeloma Measurable Residual Disease: Spotting Three Different Detection Methods
Article.Authors: Tartaglione S.; Tagliaferro M.; Scerpa M.; Basile V.; D’Ambrosio F.; Natali P.; Marino M.; Equitani F.; Maurillo L.; Basile U.
Article.Abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) is the second most common hematologic malignancy. It is still largely incurable, but treatment has changed greatly with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, monoclonal and bispecific antibodies, autologous stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T cells. Most patients now achieve a complete response. As a result, conventional criteria, based on monoclonal protein, serum free light chains and bone marrow plasma cell counts, can no longer distinguish different depths of response. Measurable residual disease (MRD) has therefore become the reference endpoint. The International Myeloma Working Group defines MRD negativity as the absence of clonal plasma cells among at least 100,000 bone marrow cells. MRD negativity predicts progression-free and overall survival, independently of cytogenetic risk and disease stage. The US Food and Drug Administration has also accepted it as an early endpoint for accelerated approval. This review examines the three main technologies now used to assess MRD in MM. Next-generation flow cytometry is standardized through the EuroFlow two-tube, eight-color protocol. It gives same-day results and can be applied to all patients without a baseline sample. Next-generation sequencing of clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangements is more sensitive and can be used on stored samples. It can also follow clonal evolution and the appearance of resistance mutations. Mass spectrometry is performed on peripheral blood. It detects the patient-specific clonotypic immunoglobulin with much higher sensitivity than electrophoretic methods and allows frequent, minimally invasive monitoring. For now, however, it complements marrow-based testing and does not replace it. For each method, we discuss analytical principles, sensitivity, standardization, pre-analytical requirements, clinical validation and limitations, and we briefly consider the growing contribution of artificial intelligence. The review also covers the role of cytogenetics and fluorescence in situ hybridization in baseline risk assessment. Finally, we discuss the limits of MRD testing in a disease that is often unevenly distributed between marrow, extramedullary sites and peripheral blood. Current evidence suggests that combining marrow-based and blood-based assays may identify residual disease most accurately. This combined approach has not yet been validated prospectively, and for now it should be used within clinical trials.

Article.Title: Dual-Metal Oxide on Cellulose Nanofibers for Advanced Supercapacitors
Article.Authors: Bathula C.; Singh A.; Mane S.; Naik S.; Kim H.
Article.Abstract: The effective use of cellulose-based materials in energy applications has attracted significant global attention because of their potential contribution to environmental sustainability. However, the use of eco-friendly materials for energy storage remains challenging because of limitations in cycling stability. In this study, bimetallic oxides such as copper oxide (CuO)–manganese oxide (MnO2) was deposited on cellulose nanofibers (CNFs) through a simple one-step synthesis, and the resulting composite was evaluated for supercapacitor applications. The prepared material, referred to as the cellulose nanofiber/CuO–MnO2 composite (CCM), was characterized using field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). TEM images confirmed the formation of a robust interfacial architecture. The electrochemical performance of the prepared materials was subsequently evaluated for energy storage applications. At a current density of 0.5 mA/cm2, pristine CNF exhibited a specific capacitance of 81.25 F/g, whereas CCM achieved 266 F/g at the same current density and retained 96.1% of its capacitance after 10,000 cycles. These results demonstrate the potential of CCM as an energy-storage material owing to its cycling stability, cost-effectiveness, and environmentally friendly nature, making it a potential alternative to conventional metal oxide-based materials for energy applications.

Article.Title: Licochalcone A Attenuates Oxidative Stress and Inflammation to Promote Second-Degree Burn Healing Through Nrf2/HO-1 Activation in Mice
Article.Authors: Xu M.; Zhou H.; Li S.; Li Y.; Wang Q.; Guan H.; Luo X.
Article.Abstract: Burn injury represents one of the most prevalent accidental traumas worldwide, contributing to substantial morbidity and mortality. Second-degree burns are frequently complicated by bacterial infection, excessive inflammation, and oxidative stress, which collectively impede wound healing. Licochalcone A (LCA), a bioactive flavonoid isolated from licorice, exhibits anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, yet its therapeutic role in burn wounds remains unexplored. Here, we evaluated the effects of a topical LCA-containing hydrogel on wound healing in a mouse dorsal second-degree scald model (100 °C, 5 s) and explored the associated molecular changes. In vivo, LCA-hydrogel treatment was associated with increased collagen deposition, reduced expression of interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), reduced neutrophil and macrophage infiltration, and upregulated Ki67 and vascular endothelial growth factor C (VEGF-C). In hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-stimulated fibroblasts, LCA attenuated reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, improved cell viability and migration, preserved mitochondrial integrity, and restored antioxidant enzyme activities. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses identified 227 co-differentially expressed genes/proteins enriched in the reactive oxygen species pathway. Western blotting showed that the effects of LCA were associated with increased nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) expression and decreased Kelch-like ECH-associated protein (Keap1) expression. These exploratory findings suggest that the LCA-containing hydrogel is associated with accelerated second-degree burn healing, and that the antioxidant effects of LCA are associated with modulation of Keap1/Nrf2/HO-1 signaling, supporting further evaluation of its potential as a burn therapeutic candidate.

Article.Title: Thymol Regulates the Expression of Antioxidant-Related Messenger RNAs and Improves Bovine Secondary Follicles Development and Antrum Formation In Vitro
Article.Authors: Nascimento D.; Barroso P.; Azevedo V.; de Assis E.; Martins S.; Araújo V.; Gomes G.; Donato M.; Peixoto C.; Silva J.
Article.Abstract: This study investigated the effects of 1, 10, or 100 μg/mL thymol on bovine secondary follicles cultured in vitro for 18 days at 38.5 °C with 5% CO2. After culture, the following parameters were evaluated: (1) the follicular growth, antrum formation, viability, and ultrastructure, (2) the levels of malondialdehyde, reduced glutathione, and nitrite in the culture medium, and (3) mRNA levels of catalase (CAT), glutathione peroxidase 1 (GPX1), superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6), proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), and growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF-9). The results showed that 10 μg/mL thymol increased cell viability, antrum formation and follicular development. At day 18, nitrite levels were higher in medium of follicles cultured with 10 μg/mL thymol than those found in control medium alone or with 1 μg/mL thymol. Gene expression analysis revealed that 10 μg/mL thymol increased catalase and glutathione peroxidase 1 mRNA levels, while the expression of other transcripts was unaffected. Transmission electron microscopy showed that granulosa cells exhibited rounded nuclei, elongated mitochondria, and sparse cytoplasmic vacuoles in all treatments, except for those cultured in control medium that had signs of degeneration. In conclusion, 10 μg/mL thymol increased mRNA expression of catalase and glutathione peroxidase 1, stimulated antrum and preserved granulosa cells of bovine secondary follicles in vitro.

Article.Title: Lessons from Plant–Microbe Interactions: Concepts for Improving Plant Nutrition and Stress Tolerance
Article.Authors: Yaish M.; Mithöfer A.
Article.Abstract: Plant-associated microorganisms, particularly plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB), enhance plant nutrition and stress tolerance and offer potential complementary approaches to conventional fertilization and crop protection. However, inconsistent field performance, ecological concerns associated with introducing non-native bacterial strains, and the need for formulations tailored to specific plant genotypes and soil conditions limit their agricultural application. These challenges have stimulated research into complementary strategies for promoting plant growth under favorable and stressful conditions. Here, we review advances and limitations of PGPB-based biofertilizers, focusing on multi-strain consortia, endophytic versus epiphytic microorganisms, and precision agriculture approaches integrating soil microbiome dynamics with plant-genotype-specific formulations. We also examine molecular mechanisms through which PGPB influence plant gene expression, stress signaling, nutrient acquisition, and rhizosphere communication. Building on these insights, we discuss strategies for using beneficial microbial mechanisms to improve abiotic stress tolerance and nutrient uptake. Integrating microbiome-informed biofertilizer development with genetic engineering, crop breeding, and precision agriculture could improve plant resilience. However, successful application requires functional validation and field testing under variable environmental conditions. Such approaches may reduce dependence on external agricultural inputs while improving crop productivity and sustainability. Together, these complementary strategies provide a framework for harnessing plant–microbe interactions to support climate-resilient agriculture and future food security worldwide.

Article.Title: Potential Effects of Naringenin on Hepatic Lipid Accumulation and Lipogenesis-Related Gene Expression in High-Fat Diet-Fed Rats
Article.Authors: Alshehri S.; Osman M.; Alnafisah G.; Asiri S.; Arzoo S.; Al-Harbi L.
Article.Abstract: This study investigated the protective effects of naringenin (NAR) against metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) in male Wistar rats fed a high-fat diet (HFD). We fed rats a high-fat diet for a total of 12 weeks, with oral NAR administered daily from weeks 9–12 (n = 8 rats/group). The HFD group (from week 9) were divided into four experimental groups: HFD (control); HFD+ 50 mg/kg NAR; HFD+ 100 mg/kg NAR; and HFD+ 200 mg/kg NAR. In addition, rats receiving standard diet (from week 9) were divided into two groups: a normal control (NC) group (i.e., standard diet + vehicle) and an NC+ 200 mg/kg NAR. NAR was orally administered for the last 4 weeks. We observed that the increasing doses (100 and 200 mg/kg) of NAR decreased body mass index (BMI), liver function markers, fasting plasma glucose and insulin, and HOMA-IR, and improved hepatic and serum lipid profiles. At 200 mg/kg, NAR reduced body weight by about 20.4%, BMI by 19.2%, serum ALT by 24%, AST by 43%, fasting glucose by 21%, fasting insulin by 44%, HOMA-IR by 56%, serum TG by 37%, TC by 41%, and LDL-c by 25%, and it increased HDL-c by 20%, relative to the HFD group. Similarly, it lowered the hepatic TG by 35.1%, TC by 28.4%, and LDL-C by 30.3%, while raising HDL-C by 31.8%. Histopathological examination of the liver revealed enhanced hepatocellular structure, reduced cytoplasmic vacuolation, decreased immune cell infiltration, and reduced injury scores. Furthermore, NAR was associated with improved antioxidant status, demonstrated by increasing the levels antioxidant mediators such as mRNA Nrf2, GSH, GSH-Px, SOD, and CAT in the liver. Moreover, it suppressed inflammatory mediators, including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and mRNA NF-κB, while elevating the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10. NAR was associated with increased hepatic SIRT1 and decreased PPARγ, ChREBP, and SREBP-1c mRNA levels. The more pronounced effect of NAR was observed at 200 mg/kg. These results of our study suggest the potential of NAR as a therapeutic candidate for MASLD, improving metabolic parameters and reducing hepatic lipid accumulation and inflammation associated with MASLD- like model, alongside improved antioxidant status and changes in SIRT1 and ChREBP/SREBP-1c expression.

Article.Title: STAT3 Signaling Contributes to Chemokine Production in E2-Induced Dermal Inflammation
Article.Authors: Ancona N.; Li Y.; Renaud L.; Fierkens R.; Kear K.; Pinckney K.; Baker Frost D.
Article.Abstract: Scleroderma (SSc) is characterized by dermal inflammation and fibrosis. Patients with SSc have elevated circulating levels of estradiol (E2) that contribute to dermal fibrosis. Using bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), we investigated inflammatory pathways in E2 or ethanol (ETOH, vehicle)-treated human skin tissue for 48 h to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and enriched pathways. Among the 90 DEGs responsive to E2 treatment, many were associated with enriched inflammatory pathways. Likewise, cytokine and chemokine activities were among the most significantly enriched molecular function terms. qPCR and protein analyses demonstrated increased cytokine and chemokine expression in primary dermal fibroblasts. CIBERSORTx deconvolution using a skin single-cell reference suggested an activated fibroblast transcriptional signature in E2-treated human skin tissue. In this tissue, E2-induced IL-6 and CXCL8 transcript levels were positively correlated. Pharmacologic STAT3 inhibition reduced E2-induced CXCL2, CXCL3, CXCL8, and CCL20 transcript levels in human skin tissue. In SSc dermal fibroblasts, anastrozole treatment significantly decreased CXCL3 and CXCL8 transcript levels. Together, these data suggest that E2 contributes, in part, to increased CXCL2, CXCL3, CXCL8, and CCL20 transcripts and that IL-6/STAT3 signaling may be important in this dermal inflammatory response.

Article.Title: Engineering Silk and Silk-like Proteins into High-Performance Fiber Materials
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Zhang F.
Article.Abstract: Silk and silk-like proteins emerge as programmable building blocks for high-performance fiber materials because they can integrate mechanical robustness, biological compatibility, environmental responsiveness, and degradability within genetically defined polymers. Synthetic biology now enables precise control over protein sequence, repeat number, molecular weight, and modular architecture, creating opportunities to design fibers beyond naturally harvested silks. However, application-ready protein fibers require coordinated control across multiple length scales, from sequence-encoded motifs and molecular assembly to spinning-induced alignment, hierarchical network formation, and final property profiles. This review discusses recent advances in engineering silk and silk-like proteins into mechanically and functionally optimized fibers. We highlight how crystallite-forming motifs, amorphous domains, terminal domains, and folded or dynamic modules contribute to fiber strength, toughness, extensibility, damping, shape recovery, humidity stability, biodegradation, and recyclability. We further connect these sequence–structure–property relationships to applications in structural textiles, biomedical fibers, smart and protective systems, and sustainable materials. Finally, we discuss future opportunities in scalable recombinant production and data-driven sequence design. These advances are expected to accelerate the translation of engineered protein fibers into practical high-performance materials.

Article.Title: Hassall’s Corpuscles as Dynamic and Functionally Specialized Structures
Article.Authors: Odaka C.; Hub E.; Rot A.
Article.Abstract: Hassall’s corpuscles were first described in 1846 by the British physician and anatomist Arthur Hill Hassall. During histological observations of the human thymus, he discovered distinctive concentric epithelial structures within the medulla, which he termed “Hassall’s corpuscles”. Hassall’s corpuscles are also called Hassall’s bodies. These structures share morphological and molecular features with the epidermis. Since Hassall’s corpuscles express late keratinization markers such as involucrin, keratin 10, and filaggrin, they are considered to be composed of terminally differentiated medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs). Recent fate-mapping and single-cell transcriptomic analyses have demonstrated that Hassall’s corpuscles originate from post-Aire mTECs, and their differentiation has been suggested to be Aire-dependent. Hassall’s corpuscles are now recognized as heterogeneous structures that play a role in central tolerance and regulatory T cell (Treg) development. In this review, we summarize recent advances in our understanding of the development of Hassall’s corpuscles within the mTEC lineage. We further describe that Hassall’s corpuscles undergo dynamic changes in size and number during thymic involution and regeneration. Thus, we propose that Hassall’s corpuscles should no longer be regarded as merely regressive structures but rather as functionally active bodies with critical immunological roles.

Article.Title: Self-Amplifying RNA Vaccines After the First Approvals: Technology, Development Landscape, and Regulatory Science Considerations
Article.Authors: Yi S.; Seo E.; Hong K.; Park P.
Article.Abstract: Self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) is a next-generation nucleic acid vaccine platform that enhances antigen expression through intracellular amplification of replicon RNA without producing infectious virions. saRNA constructs encode an alphavirus-derived replicase comprising nonstructural proteins nsP1–nsP4 and can elicit robust immune responses at low RNA doses. Replication intermediates may activate RIG-I, MDA5, and endosomal TLR3/7/8, contributing adjuvant-like activity. Kostaive (ARCT-154; zapomeran) became the first saRNA vaccine to receive full marketing approval in Japan in 2023, followed by authorization in the European Union in 2025 and the United Kingdom in 2026, demonstrating the platform’s clinical and regulatory feasibility. Development now extends beyond COVID-19 to seasonal and pandemic influenza, rabies, Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever, Nipah virus disease, and individualized cancer vaccines. However, the longer transcripts and additional replicase and subgenomic-promoter elements make in vitro transcription efficiency, full-length RNA content, double-stranded and truncated RNA impurities, lipid nanoparticle encapsulation, and potency testing particularly important. Regulatory assessment increasingly focuses on correct replicase and antigen expression, the magnitude and duration of self-amplification, biodistribution and persistence, and comparability. This review synthesizes the scientific basis, development landscape, manufacturing challenges, and regulatory science considerations of saRNA vaccines.

Article.Title: Converging Paths: Artificial Intelligence for Integrating Biological and Digital Biomarkers in Personalized Longevity Medicine
Article.Authors: Saliev T.; Singh P.
Article.Abstract: Ageing is a multidimensional biological process characterised by interacting molecular, physiological, functional, and environmental changes that chronological age alone cannot adequately represent. The rapid development of epigenetic clocks, proteomic and metabolomic signatures, imaging-derived biomarkers, wearable sensors, and digital phenotypes has created an increasingly rich but fragmented landscape of aging biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a potential integrative framework that can combine these heterogeneous data streams and convert them into multidimensional estimates of biological age, health risk, functional reserve, and potentially treatment response. Recent studies demonstrate that molecular and clinical information can be integrated into composite aging measures, while independent work shows that wearable movement data, retinal imaging, and speech characteristics can provide non-invasive digital representations of aging-related phenotypes. The emerging concept of multimodal aging clocks extends these approaches by integrating physiological, clinical, imaging, and molecular measurements into a common representation of biological aging.

Article.Title: Large-Scale Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis of Mouse Liver Responses to High-Fat Diet Identifies a Reproducible Core and Duration-Associated Variation
Article.Authors: Chung O.; Seong K.; Shim S.
Article.Abstract: High-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice are widely used to investigate hepatic responses relevant to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but reproducibility across experiments remains unclear. We performed a multilevel meta-analysis of 64 mouse liver RNA-sequencing GEO Series (GSEs) comprising 105 HFD-versus-control contrasts and compared the results with three human liver cohorts relevant to MASLD. Among 18,234 mouse genes, 6920 showed significant pooled HFD effects, whereas only 59 met all three study-defined reproducibility criteria: pooled FDR < 0.05, a 95% prediction interval excluding zero, and ≥80% of evaluable GSEs matching the pooled-effect direction (GSE-balanced directional consistency). These 59 genes constituted a high-confidence reproducible subset. Twenty-five Hallmark pathways showed significant pooled enrichment, and HFD duration was associated with 2744 gene-level effects and multiple Hallmark pathways. Mouse–human correspondence was weak, but among 10,658 one-to-one orthologs, mouse directional consistency was associated with the odds of a same-direction human effect (OR 1.075 per 10-percentage-point increase; 95% CI 1.035–1.115; p = 1.5 × 10−4). The hepatic HFD response therefore includes a small reproducible core within a broader duration-sensitive transcriptional response, while greater cross-experiment recurrence in mice was associated with modestly higher directional concordance in MASLD-relevant human liver cohorts, without constituting direct model validation.

Article.Title: Reporter Virus-Based High-Throughput Screening Identifies LM-10 as a Novel Inhibitor Targeting KRM1 for Coxsackievirus A10 Blockade
Article.Authors: Li H.; Gai W.; Yao H.; Gu Y.; Li Y.; Chen M.; Luo G.; Zhou J.; Tang Y.; Wang Z.; Li D.; Cui Y.
Article.Abstract: Enteroviruses causing hand, foot, and mouth disease, including currently circulating Coxsackievirus A10 (CVA10) and Coxsackievirus A6 (CVA6), rely on KREMEN1 (KRM1) for cell entry, making the virus–KRM1 interface a potential target for antiviral intervention. We screened GLMarNP, an in-house library of about 3000 natural products and derivatives. Candidates targeting the KRM1 ectodomain were selected by blind docking, drug-likeness assessment, and scaffold diversity analysis. To enable high-throughput antiviral screening, we inserted eGFP into a full-length infectious CVA10 cDNA clone to generate a reporter virus designated eGFP-A10. The virus was rescued in HEK293T cells and produced robust fluorescence in RD cells over serial passages. Among 29 candidate compounds, LM-10 showed the strongest antiviral activity and exhibited low cytotoxicity. Mechanistically, LM-10 bound KRM1 and acted early in the viral life cycle. Molecular docking suggested that LM-10 binds the KR domain at a site overlapping the VP2 EF-loop contact region. KRM1 also acts as a DKK1 receptor to regulate Wnt/β-catenin signaling. LM-10 did not significantly affect this pathway in the TOP-GFP reporter assay or in transgenic zebrafish embryos. These findings establish a practical CVA10 reporter-virus platform and support steric blockade of the receptor interface as a potential antiviral strategy.

Article.Title: Clinical Utility of lncRNAs in Urothelial Carcinoma of the Bladder: Diagnostics, Risk Stratification, and Treatment Guidance
Article.Authors: Ławiński J.; Franczyk B.; Sagr A.; Popek K.; Tabarkiewicz J.
Article.Abstract: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder remains challenging to assess in real time. Standard tools such as white-light cystoscopy and urine cytology are essential, but both have recognized limitations, particularly for carcinoma in situ, low-grade disease and repeated long-term surveillance in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). Conventional risk models also show imperfect performance in contemporary practice, contributing to both overtreatment and delayed escalation in biologically aggressive disease. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are emerging as attractive biomarkers because of their context-specific expression, measurable expression in tumor tissue and detectability in urine and blood, including within extracellular vesicles (EVs), such as exosomes that protect RNA from degradation. The potential clinical role of lncRNAs is determined by the specimen, molecular compartment, disease setting, and intended use. Urinary cell-free and urinary EV-associated lncRNAs currently have the strongest translational evidence for hematuria triage diagnostic support, recurrence-risk assessment, and longitudinal molecular monitoring. Tissue lncRNAs are most relevant to biological classification and prognostic refinement after transurethral resection or cystectomy, whereas blood-based lncRNAs may provide complementary information on systemic disease burden and treatment-associated response, particularly in muscle-invasive or advanced disease. Although several urinary multi-lncRNA panels have functioned as stand-alone statistical classifiers in development cohorts, no lncRNA assay has been prospectively validated to replace cystoscopy, cytology, histopathology, or established treatment-selection biomarkers in routine care. Repeatedly studied candidates include UCA1 and several exosomal/uEV-associated lncRNAs (e.g., TERC, SNHG16), while multi-lncRNA panels and combined strategies (including integration with established urine tests such as NMP22) may stabilize performance across biological and pre-analytical variability. Evidence also supports the concept of longitudinal “molecular response” monitoring using liquid-based lncRNA readouts, although truly predictive, treatment-interaction evidence remains limited. Across studies, performance is strongly influenced by the urine compartment analyzed (pellet/sediment, cell-free urine, or urinary EVs (uEVs)/exosomes) and by pre-analytical handling and normalization choices. lncRNA assays are unlikely to replace cystoscopy in the near term, but they have clear potential as decision-support tests that complement clinical risk assessment, cytology, and other urine-based platforms. This work synthesizes mechanistic and clinically annotated evidence on lncRNAs in bladder cancer, with an emphasis on urine-based and uEV/exosomal assays. The search strategy covered publications from 1 January 2015 to 30 December 2025, with emphasis on most recent clinically relevant studies, and included mechanistic studies with functional validation, liquid biopsy/urine studies, and evidence syntheses.

Article.Title: Cyanidin-3-O-Glucoside in Anthocyanin-Rich Fraction Combined with Atorvastatin Mitigates Kidney Injury via Attenuating Renal Lipotoxicity and Oxidative Stress and Preserving Mitochondrial Function in Obese Rats
Article.Authors: Lalichatsakul C.; Phatthapong P.; Pengrattanachot N.; Sutthasupha P.; Laorodphun P.; Nakrat S.; Sookwong P.; Mahatheeranont S.; Lungkaphin A.
Article.Abstract: Obesity-related kidney injury is associated with renal lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress. This study investigated the potential renoprotective effects of cyanidin-3-O-glucoside (C3G) in an anthocyanin-rich fraction from black glutinous rice (Oryza sativa L.) bran in combination with atorvastatin (ATO) in obese rats. Rats were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 16 weeks, followed by 8 weeks of treatment with C3G (100 or 200 mg/kg BW/day) combined with ATO (5 mg/kg BW/day) or ATO alone (10 mg/kg BW/day). HFD increased renal lipid accumulation and oxidative stress and altered mitochondrial-related proteins and renal structure. Both C3G doses combined with ATO 5 mg/kg BW/day improved selected metabolic and renal outcomes. Based on the overall responses, C3G 100 mg/kg BW/day + ATO 5 mg/kg BW/day was selected for subsequent molecular analyses. This combination was associated with reduced renal lipid accumulation and favorable changes in proteins related to lipid metabolism, mitochondrial homeostasis, and oxidative stress, including PPARα, Sirt-1, PGC-1α, MFN2, Parkin, NOX4, Keap1, and Nrf2. Renal MDA levels were also reduced, accompanied by preservation of renal architecture and attenuation of glomerular, tubular, and fibrotic injury. Across several measured outcomes, the renoprotective effects of C3G 100 mg/kg BW/day + ATO 5 mg/kg BW/day were broadly comparable to those of ATO 10 mg/kg BW/day. These findings support further investigation of C3G combined with ATO as a potential adjunctive strategy for obesity-associated kidney injury.

Article.Title: Chlorogenic Acid-Rich Fraction from Green Coffee Beans and Its Combination with Paclitaxel Attenuate Porphyromonas gingivalis LPS-Stimulated Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma Related to the NF-ĸB and p38 Pathways
Article.Authors: Panyathep A.; Punturee K.; Chewonarin T.
Article.Abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is linked to Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg). Pg lipopolysaccharide (LPS-PG) triggers inflammatory responses contributing to cancer progression. Paclitaxel (PTX) is frequently used in combination regimens for ESCC therapy. This study aimed to investigate the role of a chlorogenic acid (CGA)-rich fraction from green coffee bean extract, known as the ethyl acetate-insoluble fraction (EIF), in inflammatory responses and cancer progression in LPS-PG-triggered ESCC (KE5 and T.T cells), as well as its combination with PTX. Both EIF and pure CGA were assessed for their effects on LPS-pretreated ESCC cell lines. Cell survival, adhesion, migration, and invasion assays were performed. Key inflammatory and metastatic mediators were measured using Western blotting, ELISA, and zymography. The study also examined the effects of combining PTX with EIF. Our results showed that LPS-PG stimulated inflammatory responses and malignant phenotypes in ESCC. EIF effectively diminished these effects by involving the NF-κB and p38 MAPK pathways. Furthermore, in T.T cells, the combination of EIF (25 μg/mL) and PTX (3 μg/mL) reduced the expression of cancer- and inflammation-related markers compared with PTX alone, without further reducing cell viability. Therefore, EIF represents a candidate agent, either alone or in combination with PTX, to attenuate Pg-driven ESCC progression.

Article.Title: Genetic and Molecular Regulation of Seed Size in Brassica napus: Current Knowledge and Breeding Perspectives
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Ashraf S.; Han Y.; Long X.; Jiang W.; Atar H.; Ahmad M.; Ma L.; Zhang Q.
Article.Abstract: Brassica napus L. (rapeseed), a member of the family Brassicaceae, is the world’s third most important oilseed crop for edible oil production, after soybean and palm. Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping is a powerful strategy for dissecting the genetic basis of seed weight. In this review, Previous studies summarized a total of 1905 candidate genes associated with seed weight in Brassica napus. Five candidate genomic regions harboring 204 seed-weight-related genes were identified, among which 21 genes were characterized as differentially expressed genes via transcriptomic analysis. Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) mutant libraries targeting genes related to silique and seed size have been constructed in Brassica napus, revealing that BnaHRD genes play critical roles in seed development. These differentially expressed genes are involved in developmental processes, cell division. and nutrient storage, supporting their functions in seed size regulation. SHB1 and HAIKU2 modulate endosperm proliferation through the IKU pathway, thereby affecting seed weight. BZR1 (brassinazole-resistant 1) acts as a master regulator of seed growth via maternal tissues. Thidiazuron (TDZ), a cytokinin analogue, simultaneously promotes cell proliferation and cell expansion, thereby increasing cell number and cell size. Multiple phytohormone signaling pathways, including auxin, gibberellin (GA), and brassinosteroid (BR), as well as transcription factors such as LEC2, participate in the regulatory network of seed size. Here, we review current advances in the genetic and molecular regulation of seed size and discuss future perspectives for rapeseed breeding.

Article.Title: Aldosterone-Mediated Atrial Remodeling and Atrial Fibrillation: Molecular Mechanisms, Translational Insights and Implications for Cardiac Surgery
Article.Authors: Torre D.; Pirri C.
Article.Abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) has heterogeneous mechanisms, including structural atrial cardiomyopathy, electrical remodeling and primary ion-channel abnormalities. Aldosterone–mineralcorticoid receptor (MR) signaling may contribute to an arrhythmogenic atrial substrate through redox-sensitive, inflammatory, profibrotic and electrophysiological pathways; however, their direct demonstration in human atria varies. Primary aldosteronism is associated with excess AF risk, but circulating aldosterone, renin-independent secretion, tissue MR activation and MR-antagonist exposure are not interchangeable biological measures. This narrative review critically distinguishes evidence from human atrial tissue, atrial experimental systems and extrapolation from other cardiovascular models, with particular emphasis on the cardiac surgical setting. Preoperative aldosterone has been associated with postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF), whereas perioperative MR-antagonist studies have reported discordant findings and observational analyses remain susceptible to confounding. We propose a testable, rather than established, two-hit framework in which a pre-existing endocrine-associated atrial substrate may interact with perioperative inflammation and hemodynamic stress. The review identifies gaps in endocrine phenotyping and the need for adequately powered prospective and interventional studies before aldosterone-directed POAF prevention can be recommended.

Article.Title: Comparative Plastome Analysis of Two Viburnum Species from East Asian Islands: Genome Conservation, Localized Divergence, and Plastome-Based Phylogenetic Placement
Article.Authors: Jiang D.; Shen X.
Article.Abstract: The genus Viburnum represents an evolutionarily informative lineage of woody angiosperms, but plastome variation in the two focal species remains insufficiently characterized. In this study, we assembled and compared one complete plastome from each of V. suspensum and V. taitoense to characterize genome conservation, sequence divergence, codon-usage patterns, and plastome-based phylogenetic placement. The complete plastomes of V. suspensum and V. taitoense were 158,577 bp and 158,544 bp in length, respectively, and both contained 133 annotated genes with an identical quadripartite architecture and the same GC content (38.1%). Comparative analysis with 52 additional publicly available Viburnum plastome records revealed highly conserved genome organization across the sampled records, whereas sequence divergence was unevenly distributed among genomic regions. The inverted-repeat regions showed higher conservation than the single-copy regions, and sliding-window analysis of 98 plastomes identified the ndhF–rpl32 intergenic region as the only major variable region exceeding the predefined threshold (maximum Pi = 0.06171). Both focal plastomes exhibited highly similar codon-usage patterns, with 29 preferred codons, 28 ending in A or U and UUG as the only preferred codon ending in G, and weak overall codon bias (ENC = 50.26 and 50.24). Complete-plastome phylogenetic analysis recovered the sampled plastomes of V. suspensum and V. taitoense as a sister pair, although this node received only moderate bootstrap support (BS = 72). These findings provide plastome-level evidence for the sampled accessions of V. suspensum and V. taitoense and establish a basis for broader population-level and phylogenomic investigations.

Article.Title: Gamete Cryopreservation: Molecular Mechanisms of Cellular Injury and Epigenomic Alterations in Human and Animal Models
Article.Authors: Zhu X.; Todorov P.; Gaydarova L.; Isachenko V.
Article.Abstract: In human spermatozoa, freezing and thawing are consistently associated with impaired membrane integrity, reduced motility, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative imbalance and alterations in DNA/chromatin stability. Regulated cell death pathways may additionally contribute to post-thaw deterioration; however, the strength of evidence differs among individual pathways, and emerging mechanisms such as ferroptosis remain less extensively characterized in human spermatozoa than conventional oxidative and apoptosis-associated injury. Evidence for cryopreservation-associated epigenomic alterations is similarly heterogeneous. Experimental and animal studies demonstrate changes in DNA methylation, histone modifications and non-coding RNA profiles. In contrast, human evidence is generally more reassuring and has not demonstrated consistent persistent abnormalities in major imprinting-associated methylation patterns. Accordingly, observations from animal models should not be directly extrapolated to human reproductive outcomes. By integrating human and experimental evidence while explicitly considering these differences in evidentiary strength, this review identifies established mechanisms, emerging molecular pathways and major unresolved questions in contemporary gamete cryobiology.

Article.Title: Taxifolin Attenuates Bacterial Pathogenicity and Thereby Enhances Antibacterial Efficacy in Clinically Relevant Bacteria
Article.Authors: Yoon J.; Kim Y.; Kim K.
Article.Abstract: Biofilm formation is an important pathogenic process that contributes to bacterial virulence, persistence, and reduced susceptibility to antimicrobial treatment. Therefore, taxifolin was evaluated as a potential antibiofilm agent. Taxifolin was assessed for its effects on biofilm formation, planktonic growth, antibiotic susceptibility, and the expression of biofilm- and virulence-associated genes. Taxifolin inhibited biofilm formation by Enterococcus faecalis, Enterococcus faecium, Escherichia coli, Streptococcus mutans, Streptococcus sobrinus, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Cutibacterium acnes, and Porphyromonas gingivalis (IC50, 0.065~0.79 µg/mL). In E. faecalis and E. faecium, taxifolin did not substantially affect planktonic growth at 10 µg/mL. Taxifolin enhanced the antibacterial activity of commercially available antibiotics, and downregulated the expression of cytolysin-associated genes (cylR, cylM, and cylLs), quorum-sensing genes (fsrB and fsrC), biofilm-associated genes (gelE, acm, scm, ebpA, ebpB and bps), and the biofilm-associated virulence gene Esp. Taxifolin inhibited biofilm formation, enhanced bacterial susceptibility, and attenuated virulence-associated gene expression, supporting its potential as an adjunctive antibiofilm therapy for the management of biofilm-associated bacterial infections. Further studies are required to define its mechanism of action, activity against established biofilms, pharmacological properties, safety, and efficacy in appropriate in vivo models.

Article.Title: Cell Wall-Formed Dietary Fiber in Tartary Buckwheat Governs Selective Enrichment of Phytochemicals to Enhanced Postprandial GLP-1 Response
Article.Authors: Jiang M.; Chen Y.; Zhang G.
Article.Abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is well-known for its biological functions in glucose homeostasis which aligns closely with the antidiabetic function of whole grain foods (WGFs). Although postprandial GLP-1 responses to WGF have been extensively studied, the influence of cell wall-formed dietary fiber (CW-DF), as the main functional component of WGFs, on the GLP-1 response remains poorly understood. Here, Tartary buckwheat flour fractions with different particle sizes (small particle size (SF: 0.2 mm), middle particle size (MF: 0.6 mm), and large particle size (BF: 0.9 mm)), reflecting different degrees of cell wall integrity, were used to investigate how particle size modulates GLP-1 secretion. The in vivo mouse study showed that intact endosperm cells from Tartary buckwheat grains significantly increased the postprandial GLP-1 response. Further study demonstrated that only the hydrolysate from BF augmented GLP-1 secretion from enteroendocrine STC-1 L-cells, which is all positively correlated with the selectively enriched phytochemicals in BF particles (ononin, ginkgolide C, pristimerin, and pentadecanoic acid). Significant correlations between particle size, phytochemical profiles and GLP-1 release demonstrated that the integrity of CW-DF is essential to the nutritional properties of WGFs. Molecular docking simulations suggested putative interactions between phytochemicals and bitter taste receptors in GLP-1 secretion. Thus, cell wall integrity is a pivotal regulator of the health benefits of WGFs, offering a mechanistic rationale for minimal processing to harness the health benefits of WGFs through targeted endogenous GLP-1 production.

Article.Title: Genetic Variations in Neuroinflammatory Chemokine Receptor Genes in Patients with Epilepsy: An Exploratory Study
Article.Authors: Pekkoc-Uyanik K.; Agay E.; Uzun H.
Article.Abstract: Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder in which genetic and neuroinflammatory mechanisms may contribute to differences in seizure control. Chemokine receptor signaling plays an important role in inflammatory processes, and genetic variations in neuroinflammatory chemokine receptor genes may potentially influence the prognosis of epilepsy. This study aimed to investigate genetic variations in the neuroinflammatory chemokine receptor genes CCR5 and CXCR4 in patients with epilepsy and to explore their potential association with seizure control during treatment. Targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) was performed to investigate genetic variations in the CCR5 and CXCR4 genes using genomic DNA obtained from 22 patients with epilepsy receiving antiseizure medication (ASM) treatment with levetiracetam and/or valproic acid. Patients were classified into two groups according to seizure frequency to evaluate the association between genetic variation and clinical prognosis. A total of seven genetic variants were identified in the CCR5 and CXCR4 genes, including three variants in CCR5 and four variants in CXCR4. However, sufficient genotype variation for group-wise comparisons was available only for CCR5 rs1799988 and rs1800023. No significant differences were observed in the genotype or allele distributions of the CCR5 and CXCR4 gene variants between the responsive and persistent groups. The two CCR5 variants, rs1799988 and rs1800023, showed strong linkage disequilibrium (D′ = 1.000, r2 = 0.913) and were included in a single haplotype block. None of the identified CCR5 haplotypes was significantly associated with seizure control. In this preliminary cohort, no statistically significant associations were detected between the analyzed genetic variations and seizure control during treatment; however, the limited sample size may have reduced the statistical power to detect potential associations. Strong linkage disequilibrium was observed between rs1799988 and rs1800023 (D′ = 1.000, r2 = 0.913), consistent with previously reported patterns. Given the small sample size and the limited number of informative variants, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than as evidence for or against a genetic contribution to seizure control. Larger, independent cohorts are needed to assess the potential clinical relevance of CCR5 and CXCR4 variation in epilepsy.

Article.Title: IL-10 Beyond Immunosuppression: Unraveling Spatial, Cellular, and Metabolic Mechanisms of Gut Protection
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Liu X.; Wang B.; Yin H.; Tian X.; Zhao J.; Xin S.; Wang H.; Ren Y.; Liu X.; Liu J.; Bian Y.; Gu S.; Zhang H.; Wei T.; Gao L.; Lu X.; Shang H.; Xu J.
Article.Abstract: Intestinal homeostasis requires immune tolerance, barrier integrity, tissue repair, and microbiota mutualism. Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is essential, but not merely as an immunosuppressant. Although IL-10 signals via the IL-10R—JAK1/TYK2—STAT3 axis, its outputs are cell-type and context dependent. In macrophages, IL-10 restrains IL-23 production, inflammasome activation, IL-1β release, and metabolic reprogramming. In T cells, it limits pathogenic T helper 17 cell (Th17) responses while stabilizing regulatory cells and promoting metabolically driven IL-10 production. In the epithelium, IL-10 maintains barrier integrity by limiting apoptosis, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and mucus defects. IL-10 and the gut microbiota engage in reciprocal regulation: microbial metabolites and structural components enhance IL-10 production and receptor responsiveness, whereas IL-10 signaling preserves microbial diversity and ecological resilience. This may help to explain why systemic recombinant IL-10 failed in Crohn’s disease (CD)—increasing ligand abundance alone is unlikely to recapitulate endogenous localization or restore refractory target cells. Emerging strategies aim to tune IL-10 signaling through gut-selective delivery, engineered cytokines, conditionally activated prodrugs, regulatory cell approaches, and microbiome or metabolic interventions. Clinical translation requires biomarkers of IL-10R expression, STAT3 responsiveness, macrophage metabolic state, microbial signatures, and acquired IL-10 hyporesponsiveness. Despite the established role of IL-10 in intestinal homeostasis, systemic IL-10 therapy has failed in clinical trials, and there is a lack of effective strategies to restore IL-10 signaling in a spatially and cell-specific manner. The spatially organized, metabolically conditioned homeostatic IL-10 signaling—largely inferred from model systems and awaiting direct spatial validation in human intestine—offers a roadmap for more precise therapy in inflammatory bowel disease and related intestinal disorders.

Article.Title: Dermatoprotective Potential of Hibiscus sabdariffa L.: A Systematic Review of Preclinical Evidence
Article.Authors: Abimbola O.; Bolawa O.; Sarandy M.; Novaes R.; Gonçalves R.; Gouveia Peluzio M.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory and degenerative skin disorders are associated with persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, tissue dysfunction, and impaired wound healing. This systematic review synthesized preclinical evidence on the biological effects and molecular mechanisms of Hibiscus sabdariffa L. in inflammatory and degenerative skin disorders and was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251013303). Eligible studies were original, peer-reviewed in vitro or in vivo investigations evaluating H. sabdariffa L. extracts, formulations, or isolated bioactive compounds and relevant dermatological outcomes; non-original publications, human studies, other Hibiscus species, and studies without appropriate controls were excluded. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase were searched on 24 March 2025. Study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers, with methodological quality assessed using the SYRCLE Risk of Bias tool supplemented with criteria relevant to preclinical phytopharmacological research. Sixteen studies were included: nine in vitro, six in vivo, and one combined study. Because of substantial heterogeneity, results were synthesized narratively using mechanistic mapping and comparative assessment rather than meta-analysis. Anti-inflammatory effects were reported in 13 studies (81.3%), antioxidant effects in 12 (75.0%), and wound-healing/tissue-regenerative effects in 9 (56.3%); anti-fibrotic/photoaging effects occurred in 7 (43.8%), and anti-melanogenic activity in 4 (25.0%). Heterogeneity and methodological limitations restrict direct comparison and condition-specific conclusions. These findings indicate dermatoprotective potential, but standardized preclinical and clinical studies are warranted. Funding was provided by the Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de Minas Gerais (FAPEMIG), the Coordination for the Improvement of Higher Education Personnel (CAPES), and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development (CNPq).

Article.Title: Comprehensive Genomic Profiling of Relapsed Interdigitating Dendritic Cell Sarcoma Reveals Novel Molecular Insights in a Patient Achieving Durable Remission After Autologous Stem Cell Transplantation
Article.Authors: Riemma C.; Cavatorta C.; Salvesi C.; Garbetta J.; Angeli D.; Fonzi E.; Lo Schiavo F.; Molinari C.; Simonetti G.; Malaspina F.; Rosa J.; Musuraca G.; Ferrari A.
Article.Abstract: Interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma (IDCS) is an extremely rare hematologic malignancy with no standardised therapeutic approach, particularly in the relapsed setting. We report a case of a 69-year-old woman with multifocal relapsed IDCS, KRAS/BRAF/SMARCA4 mutated, successfully treated with CHOP chemotherapy followed by consolidation with high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), achieving a durable complete remission. This case supports the potential role of intensive chemotherapy and ASCT in selected patients with aggressive or relapsed disease.

Article.Title: Functional Autoantibodies Against G-Protein-Coupled Receptors: Insights into Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Relevance and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zwerenz R.; Lakatos P.; Flecks M.; Wallukat G.; Hohberger B.
Article.Abstract: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) represent the largest superfamily of membrane-bound receptors in the human organism and are involved in the regulation of numerous physiological processes in almost all organ systems. Characterized by seven transmembrane domains and coupling to heterotrimeric G-proteins, they mediate signal transduction between extracellular stimuli and intracellular responses. Through these mechanisms they regulate critical processes such as cardiovascular function, neurotransmission, immune function, endocrine secretion, and metabolic homeostasis. Growing evidence suggests that functional autoantibodies directed against GPCRs (GPCR-fAAbs) may contribute to the pathophysiology of various diseases. By binding to extracellularly accessible regions of their target receptors, these antibodies can directly modulate receptor function and intracellular signaling. Depending on the receptor, epitope, and functional properties of the autoantibody, GPCR-fAAbs can act as agonists and activate receptor function or as antagonists and inhibit receptor function or alter the receptor signaling. Importantly, the presence of GPCR-directed autoantibodies does not necessarily indicate functional activity or pathogenicity, and their biological effects may depend on both autoantibody-specific and cellular factors. The potential role of GPCR-fAAbs has been described in a growing number of autoimmune and non-autoimmune diseases affecting various organ systems. This review article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current knowledge on GPCRs and GPCR-fAAbs focusing on their molecular mechanisms, functional characteristics, and potential pathophysiological roles in various diseases. Furthermore, current detection methods, clinical findings and established and emerging therapeutic strategies, including immunoadsorption (IA), aptamer-based neutralization, receptor blocking, and targeted B cell modulation, are critically discussed. Although all these approaches present certain challenges in their application, specific prospects for clinical implementation can be highlighted. Overall, GPCR-fAAbs represent an increasingly recognized pathophysiological factor with potential clinical implications, while their targeted therapeutic modulation remains an evolving area of translational research.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Characterization of the CAMTA Gene Family in Paulownia fortunei and Potential Role of PfCAMTA5 in Salt-Stress Responses
Article.Authors: Cao Y.; Sun H.; Liu C.; Liu J.; Cao S.; Zhao Z.
Article.Abstract: Calmodulin-binding transcription activator (CAMTA) transcription factors play key roles in plant stress responses, but their functions in Paulownia fortunei remain largely unknown. Here, we identified eight CAMTA family genes in P. fortunei and investigated their structural features, evolutionary relationships, and expression patterns under salt stress. All PfCAMTA proteins contain the conserved CG-1, ANK, and IQ domains, although their gene structures and physicochemical properties differ. Phylogenetic and synteny analyses revealed close paralogous pairs and orthologous relationships with Arabidopsis CAMTAs. Under salt stress, the eight PfCAMTA genes displayed distinct tissue-specific expression patterns, with PfCAMTA5 emerging as the most prominent salt-responsive candidate, showing broad induction across tissues and the highest transcript abundance. Molecular docking and Y2H assays suggested a potential interaction between PfCAMTA5 and the salt-responsive calcium sensor PfCML28. Transient overexpression of PfCAMTA5 in tobacco improved salt tolerance, as reflected by enhanced photosynthesis, higher antioxidant enzyme activities, and reduced membrane damage, and up-regulation of stress-responsive genes. Together, these findings suggest that PfCAMTA5 may play a potential role in salt tolerance and provide a foundation for further investigation of the CAMTA-mediated salt stress regulatory network in P. fortunei.

Article.Title: Pyridine Regioisomerism and Aryl Substitution Govern the Divergent Cyclization of Isoniazid-Derived Thiosemicarbazides: Mechanistic DFT Analysis and Antimycobacterial Evaluation
Article.Authors: Paneth A.; Trotsko N.; Głogowska A.; Augustynowicz-Kopeć E.; Paneth P.
Article.Abstract: Isoniazid is an established antitubercular pharmacophore widely used as a structural platform for developing compounds with potential activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This study investigated isoniazid-derived thiosemicarbazides as precursors for the synthesis of thiazolidin-4-one derivatives, focusing on the influence of pyridine regioisomerism and aryl substitution on cyclization outcomes. Thiosemicarbazides containing 2-, 3-, or 4-pyridyl moieties and fluoro- or chloro-substituted phenyl groups were synthesized and subjected to cyclization with ethyl bromoacetate. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to compare the competing pathways leading to thiazolidin-4-one and 1,3,4-oxadiazole formation, and the resulting heterocyclic compounds were evaluated against four M. tuberculosis strains. An initial control experiment using a 2-pyridyl/2-fluorophenyl thiosemicarbazide yielded the target thiazolidin-4-one as the sole product. However, investigation of the broader substrate series revealed pronounced substrate-dependent differences in cyclization selectivity. Most substrates afforded 1,3,4-oxadiazoles, whereas 2-pyridyl thiosemicarbazides bearing ortho-fluoro or ortho-chloro substituents selectively formed thiazolidin-4-ones. DFT calculations provided an energetic rationale for the observed divergence in cyclization pathways. Despite systematic structural diversification, none of the investigated 1,3,4-oxadiazole or thiazolidin-4-one derivatives, including ester-functionalized analogues, exhibited appreciable antimycobacterial activity (MIC ≥ 512 µg/mL). These findings demonstrate that pyridine regioisomerism combined with aryl substitution strongly influences the cyclization pathways of isoniazid-derived thiosemicarbazides. However, the pronounced structure–reactivity relationship governing cyclization was not accompanied by a meaningful structure–activity relationship against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The combined experimental and computational results provide insight into the factors governing cyclization selectivity and inform the design of future INH-derived analogues.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Association Study Identifies Loci and a Candidate Gene Regulating Tomato Seed Germination
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Zhu Y.; Miao J.; Wan H.; Yao Z.; Ruan M.; Ye Q.; Li Z.; Zhou G.; Cheng Y.; Zhang X.; Wang R.
Article.Abstract: Seed germination is the first critical transition in the plant life cycle, strongly influencing seedling establishment, crop uniformity, and subsequent productivity. However, the genetic basis of seed germination in tomato remains incompletely understood. Here, we performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) using 319 diverse tomato accessions to identify new loci and candidate genes associated with seed germination. Five significant variants were detected across the genome. Among them, SNP_59508294 on chromosome 3 was consistently associated with the seed germination index (SGI), and accessions carrying the GG haplotype exhibited a significantly higher SGI than those carrying the TT haplotype. Seven α-expansin (EXPA) genes were located within or near the associated interval. Integration of transcriptomic data from contrasting accessions and expression profiles across tomato tissues showed SlEXPA10 to be the most plausible candidate gene. The InDels in the SlEXPA10 promoter were highly associated with its low expression level in low SGI varieties. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of SlEXPA10 significantly reduced the rate and speed of seed germination relative to the wild type. Collectively, these results identify SlEXPA10 as a positive regulator of tomato seed germination and provide a candidate locus for improving seed vigor and emergence uniformity.

Article.Title: Explainable AI for Network Pharmacology: A Critical Framework for Interpreting Multi-Target Drug Discovery on Biological Graphs
Article.Authors: Allemailem K.; Almatroudi A.; Alnajim A.
Article.Abstract: Network pharmacology examines drug action across interacting targets, pathways, and disease modules. Increasingly, however, the graph neural networks and knowledge-graph models used for this purpose are difficult to inspect. This critical narrative review considers feature attribution, attention, counterfactual and rule-based explanation, explainable graph neural networks, Bayesian and causal methods, and path-based knowledge-graph reasoning. We assess these approaches against three demands imposed by biological graphs: preservation of heterogeneous node and relation semantics, support for multi-hop reasoning, and concordance with evidence excluded from model training. Among the methods reviewed, none has yet been shown to satisfy all three demands consistently. A model-faithful explanation may still emphasize node degree, network hubs, or heavily studied entities instead of a disease-specific mechanism. To address this problem, we propose five evaluation domains: faithfulness, stability, external biological concordance, bias sensitivity, and translational utility, together with a six-item reporting standard. Both are conceptual proposals; they remain unweighted, uncalibrated, and unevaluated empirically. An exploratory, literature-based application to TxGNN, DDI-GCN, and MINERVA shows that transparency-related reporting is useful but incomplete. This exercise demonstrates how the criteria might be used; it is not an empirical evaluation or calibration of the framework. We did not retrain or rerun any model or conduct new quantitative benchmarking. The field still lacks a unified biomedical benchmark that evaluates prediction and explanation together under heterogeneous, cold-start, and provenance-aware graph settings. Progress will depend on task-matched evaluation, explicit treatment of uncertainty, and experiments designed to distinguish what a model uses from what biology actually does.

Article.Title: Functional Humanization of Mouse Alox15 Does Not Alter Early Vascular Lipid Deposition in ApoE-Deficient Mice
Article.Authors: Yang J.; Borchert A.; Mangarova D.; Zhao Z.; Wang B.; Kühn H.
Article.Abstract: Arachidonic acid 15-lipoxygenases (ALOX15) have previously been implicated in atherogenesis, and functional inactivation of the Alox15 gene protected mice from arterial lipid deposition. However, translation of these results into humans was criticized since human and mouse ALOX15 orthologs exhibit distinct catalytic properties. We recently created Alox15 knock-in mice (Alox15ki/ki), which express an enzyme variant (Leu353Phe mutant) exhibiting a reaction specificity similar to that of human ALOX15. To make these animals athero-susceptible, we crossed them with ApoE−/− mice yielding Alox15ki/ki+ApoE−/− animals and compared the degree of hypercholesterolemia, the extent of arterial lipid deposition, and the expression patterns of inflammation-related genes with the corresponding parameters of age- and sex-matched outbred control animals (Alox15wt/wt + ApoE−/−) keeping the mice for different time periods on regular chow diet. Peritoneal macrophages of Alox15ki/ki + ApoE−/− mice oxygenated arachidonic acid mainly to the 15S-hydroperoxy derivative (15S-HpETE) and this data indicates systemic functional humanization of the reaction specificity of the Alox15 pathway. In 14- and 25-week-old animals of either sex, we observed consistent genotype-specific differences neither in the extent of aortic lipid deposition nor in the vascular expression patterns of inflammation-related gene products. This data suggests that the reaction specificity of Alox15 may not be of major relevance for early mouse atherogenesis.

Article.Title: Tuning the Brain: How Acoustic Energies Modulate Neural and Glial Phenotypes
Article.Authors: Cipriano G.; Agostinelli E.; Floramo A.; Argento V.; Spinelli S.; Calabrò M.; Anchesi I.
Article.Abstract: The traditional view of neuronal communication is shifting toward a mechanobiological paradigm. This review examines how mechanical energy from diverse acoustic stimuli—audible sound and whole-body or vibrotactile vibration, low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS), low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU), high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), and extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT)—translates into biochemical signals. Evidence is stratified throughout by model system (in vitro, animal in vivo, human) and by reported exposure dose, and sensory-pathway or network-level effects of audible sound are kept distinct from direct cellular mechanotransduction. Acoustic forces are directly detected by primary mechanosensitive ion channels, such as Piezo1 and TRPV4, and experimental evidence links this mechanotransduction to neurotrophic signaling (mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR); p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK); brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)) that supports neurite outgrowth and structural repair, whereas a continuous signaling axis running from the cytoskeleton through the linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton (LINC) complex to epigenetic regulation remains a mechanistic hypothesis that has not been demonstrated in any acoustically stimulated neural cell. Furthermore, glial cells act as active mechanosensors, and emerging evidence suggests that acoustic stimulation can promote microglial polarization toward neuroprotective M2 phenotypes and may support Schwann cell-mediated peripheral nerve regeneration. We discuss the emerging concept of “acoustic pharmacology,” in which specific waveforms and frequencies dictate distinct therapeutic outcomes. From targeted amyloid clearance in Alzheimer’s disease to the non-invasive neural circuit control offered by sonogenetics, acoustic stimulation is a tunable but still predominantly preclinical frontier in regenerative medicine and neuromodulation: of the 144 sources cited here, seven report human studies, and the only randomized, sham-controlled evidence with a clinical endpoint concerns ablative high-intensity focused ultrasound; for the non-ablative neuromodulatory, neuroprotective, and regenerative regimes that are the subject of this review, no such trial is present in this evidence base.

Article.Title: Exploring FTIR Spectroscopy as an Orthogonal Approach for Detecting Processing-Induced Changes in Extracellular Vesicle Preparations
Article.Authors: Tursunović M.; Filipović L.; Mitić N.; Popović M.
Article.Abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) require complementary methods for their comprehensive characterization. This study investigates the potential of attenuated total reflectance Fourier-transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy to provide orthogonal information on alterations in EV preparations subjected to different processing conditions. EVs were isolated using a previously established nanobody-based immunoaffinity approach, and further subjected to lyophilization, repeated freeze–thawing, or heat treatment followed by sonication. The EV preparations were characterized using nanoparticle tracking analysis, transmission electron microscopy, biochemical assays, flow cytometry and ATR-FTIR spectroscopy. Although the overall FTIR spectral profiles remained broadly similar, multivariate and targeted spectral analyses revealed differences in the heat-and-sonicated preparation, which also showed the most pronounced changes observed by complementary characterization methods. The findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that ATR-FTIR can provide orthogonal information for the assessment of processing-induced changes in EV preparations.

Article.Title: Calculated Serum Antioxidant Capacity Masks Opposite Associations of Urate and Unconjugated Bilirubin with Leukocyte Count: A Ten-Year Cross-Sectional Hospital Laboratory Study Including 25-Hydroxyvitamin D
Article.Authors: Osredkar J.; Godnov U.; Jerin A.; Siuka D.
Article.Abstract: Calculated total antioxidant capacity (cTAC), a weighted sum of albumin, urate and bilirubin, is often interpreted as a single antioxidant dimension. We asked whether its constituents share the same association with leukocyte count, a routine but nonspecific marker of the inflammatory, oxidant-generating cell compartment, and examined 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D]. In this retrospective cross-sectional study of routine records from a tertiary university hospital laboratory (2014–2023; 20,525 patient-years, 14,152 adults), cTAC was calculated with Trolox-equivalent coefficients (0.63·albumin + 1.02·urate + 1.50·bilirubin). Patient-clustered models of log leukocyte count, leukopenia (<4 × 109/L) and leukocytosis (≥10 × 109/L) were adjusted for age, sex, season and era, and additionally for estimated glomerular filtration rate and alanine aminotransferase. Urate accounted for 90% of the variance of cTAC. cTAC showed a U-shaped association with leukocytosis, whereas its components diverged. Per standard deviation, urate was associated with more leukocytes (+4.2%, 95% CI 3.2–5.2; leukocytosis odds ratio [OR] 1.23, 1.14–1.32) and calculated unconjugated bilirubin with fewer (−4.3%, −5.7 to −2.9; OR 0.71, 0.63–0.82). Both associations were similar after multiple imputation of missing covariates. Platelet adjustment attenuated the bilirubin estimate to −1.4%, whereas haemoglobin adjustment did not; with platelet counts of 150–400 × 109/L and no anaemia, it was −3.8% (−5.0 to −2.7). 25(OH)D was weakly inversely associated (−1.2%, −1.8 to −0.6), without evidence of effect modification. In this cross-sectional setting, in which residual confounding is likely, a single calculated antioxidant capacity statistically conceals opposite-signed associations of its constituents with leukocyte count.

Article.Title: An Integrative Phosphoregulatory Landscape of FAK Signaling
Article.Authors: George M.; Dcunha L.; Ahmed M.; Mahin A.; Gopalakrishnan A.; Modi P.; Velikkakath A.; Raju R.
Article.Abstract: Focal adhesion kinase (FAK) is a protein tyrosine kinase that plays a major role in regulating cell adhesion, proliferation, motility, and survival. While FAK-regulatory phosphosites play significant roles in cancer progression and metastasis, the broader perspective of its phosphorylation remains largely unknown. Therefore, mapping the phosphoregulatory networks provides significant insights into targeted therapies. To characterize the phosphorylations of FAK, we systematically retrieved PubMed-indexed studies and compiled large-scale cellular mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomics datasets. An integrative, data-driven analysis was performed on 678 qualitative and 235 quantitative cellular phosphoproteomic datasets to map the signatures of FAK phosphorylation. The study observed that the S910 modification is the most frequently detected phosphorylation outside the catalytic kinase domain. This predicts a broader regulatory role of S910 in signaling than previously understood. Further, by integrating phosphosite co-detection patterns across diverse biological contexts, we characterized FAK phosphorylations and their co-regulated Phosphosites in Other Proteins (PsOPs). The phospho-coregulatory analysis of S910 and FAK activation phosphosites Y576, Y577, and Y861 provided distinct potential phosphosite cross-talks. Furthermore, the study predicts several potential candidate substrates and interactor PsOPs, providing a framework for prioritizing phosphosites for future experimental investigation. Moreover, the study also illustrated a hypothesized model of potential FAK phosphosite-specific coregulatory associations within gastrin-associated signaling. Taken together, these large-scale observations provide a data-driven foundation for future FAK-centered experimental approaches and understanding of its multifaceted role as a potential target.

Article.Title: Pilomatricoma in Turner Syndrome: Association with Renal Malformations and Analysis of the Vitamin D Pathway
Article.Authors: Rios R.; Rodríguez-Jurado R.; Torres Espíndola L.; Sáez-de-Ocariz M.; Velázquez Aragón J.; Pérez González Ó.; Villarroel Cortés C.; Rodríguez Morales M.; Frías S.; Velázquez Cruz R.
Article.Abstract: Pilomatricoma is a rare benign cutaneous neoplasm that may occur more frequently in syndromic conditions such as Turner syndrome (TS). This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence and clinical characteristics of pilomatricoma and its association with clinical factors, serum vitamin D (VD) levels, and genetic variants in the VD pathway in patients with TS. Clinical variables and serum VD levels were obtained from medical records, and single-nucleotide variants in the GC, NADSYN1, and VDR genes were analyzed by allelic discrimination using real-time polymerase chain reaction. Among 97 patients with TS, six cases of histopathologically confirmed pilomatricoma were identified, corresponding to a prevalence of 6.2%, with lesions predominantly located on the head and upper extremities. Four patients (66.7%) had renal malformations. In exploratory multivariable analysis, renal malformations were significantly associated with pilomatricoma (adjusted OR = 14.2; 95% CI: 2.1–95.4; nominal p = 0.008; FDR-adjusted p = 0.032). No significant associations were observed with serum VD levels or the analyzed genetic variants. These findings suggest that pilomatricoma may be more frequent in TS than previously reported and identify an exploratory association between pilomatricoma and renal malformations. Given the small number of pilomatricoma cases, this association requires confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

Article.Title: Mesenchymal Stem Cell-Derived Exosomes for Bone Regeneration: Modification Strategies and miRNA-Mediated Modulation of Osteogenic Signaling
Article.Authors: Meglei A.; Paymeteva D.; Nedorubova I.; Basina V.; Goldshtein D.; Bukharova T.
Article.Abstract: Bone tissue regeneration remains a major clinical challenge, and exosomes secreted by mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as attractive cell-free therapeutic tools. To enhance their efficacy and local action, exosomes can be modified to enrich them with regulatory factors and impregnated into biocompatible matrices. This review summarizes recent advances in engineering MSC-derived exosomes for bone regeneration. Strategies analyzed include physicochemical modification of donor MSCs, direct exosome modification, and genetic modification of MSCs to enrich exosomes with therapeutic molecules such as bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP-2), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and regulatory miRNAs. In addition, the role of these miRNAs in osteogenic signaling was analyzed. Modified exosomes demonstrate enhanced osteogenic, angiogenic, and immunomodulatory effects in vitro and in vivo, particularly when combined with biomaterial scaffolds for sustained release. Thus, engineered MSC-derived exosomes constitute an effective approach for bone tissue engineering and show potential for clinical translation.
