Article.Title: Development and Evaluation of the 40K Liquid SNP Array for Population Genetic Analysis in Golden Pompano (Trachinotus ovatus)
Article.Authors: Liu B.; Gao Y.; Guo H.; Zhu K.; Xian L.; Zhang N.; Zhu T.; Zhang D.
Article.Abstract: Single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays provide efficient and scalable platforms for genetic diversity assessment, population genomic analysis, and molecular breeding in aquaculture species. However, a high-throughput SNP genotyping platform specifically developed for golden pompano (Trachinotus ovatus), an economically important marine aquaculture fish, remains limited. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a liquid SNP array for T. ovatus and assess its applicability in population genetic analyses. Genome-wide SNP resources were generated from 200 individuals representing 10 cultured populations of T. ovatus. Following SNP discovery, quality filtering, probe evaluation, and marker optimization, a 40K liquid SNP array, designated Changxin-I, was constructed. The performance of Changxin-I was evaluated using an independent validation cohort of 144 individuals from five cultured populations with both WGS-derived and array-derived genotype data available. The array exhibited high genotyping performance, with an average SNP detection rate of 99.94% and a genotype concordance rate of 96.23% with WGS data. Genetic diversity and population structure analyses were performed using Changxin-I genotype data, and the inferred population patterns were compared with those obtained from whole-genome resequencing (WGS) data from the same individuals. A total of 40,476 SNPs were selected for the final Changxin-I array, including 40,442 genome-wide background markers and 34 trait-associated SNPs. The validation results showed high genotyping quality, with an average mapping rate of 98.87% and a mean SNP detection rate of 99.94%. Most SNP markers (99.93%) exhibited minor allele frequencies (MAF) greater than 0.10. Changxin-I successfully revealed genetic diversity and population differentiation among cultured populations, and the population structure patterns were consistent with those obtained from WGS-based analyses. Changxin-I represents a reliable and efficient genomic tool for large-scale SNP genotyping in golden pompano. This array provides a practical platform for population genetic studies, germplasm characterization, and future genomic-assisted breeding applications in T. ovatus.

Article.Title: Neuromuscular Junction Degeneration in Skeletal Muscle Atrophy: Disease-Specific Mechanisms, Evidence-Informed Stratification, and Therapeutic Windows
Article.Authors: Li S.; Liu M.; Zhang P.; Ma X.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal muscle atrophy involves not only the loss of muscle mass and fiber size, but also a significant decline in contractile performance. Force decline often occurs before visible fiber atrophy, suggesting that early defects in neuromuscular transmission might trigger or exacerbate the wasting process. Therefore, we argue that neuromuscular junction (NMJ) degeneration is not a universal, conserved pathway across all atrophy syndromes. Instead, it should be viewed as a stage- and disease-specific event, with its actual contribution varying based on specific evidence. To explore this, we compare NMJ maintenance and degeneration across a broad spectrum of conditions, ranging from primary neuromuscular diseases (like denervation and motor neuron disorders) to systemic states such as aging, cachexia, and metabolic or respiratory diseases. Based on this, we propose a framework to evaluate NMJ involvement by timing, lesion type, and reversibility, drawing on diverse evidence from morphological, electrophysiological, and biomarker studies. Crucially, this approach distinguishes primary synaptic disorders from systemic conditions where NMJ damage acts merely as a secondary modifier. Ultimately, aligning specific molecular lesions with practical intervention windows will help refine patient stratification and guide the design of more targeted NMJ therapies.

Article.Title: Modulation of the Liver–Brain Axis by Ondansetron in Thio-Acetamide-Induced Acute Hepatic Encephalopathy
Article.Authors: Sari F.; Bilgin Y.; Cicek B.; Kurt E.; Ozkaraca M.; Gungor A.; Kurt N.; Bilgin A.
Article.Abstract: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a severe neurological complication of liver failure characterized by hyperammonemia, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and progressive neuronal dysfunction. Ondansetron (OND), a selective 5-hydroxytryptamine-3 (5-HT3) receptor antagonist, has reported anti-inflammatory and neuroactive properties, but its effects in HE remain poorly defined. This study evaluated OND in a thioacetamide (TAA)-induced acute HE model in female Sprague-Dawley rats. Animals were assigned to Control, TAA, OND, TAA+OND (0.5 mg/kg), and TAA+OND (1 mg/kg) groups. Serum and cerebral glutamine, oxidative and antioxidant parameters, histopathological alterations, and TLR2, NF-κB, IL-1β, GFAP, NLRP3, and caspase-1 immunoreactivity were assessed in liver and brain tissues. TAA increased glutamine accumulation, produced tissue injury, altered redox parameters, and increased several inflammation-related markers. OND significantly reduced cerebral glutamine and attenuated selected biochemical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical alterations, with generally more pronounced effects at 0.5 mg/kg. These findings indicate that OND administration is associated with partial modulation of metabolic, oxidative, inflammatory, and structural alterations in TAA-treated rats, warranting further receptor-specific and functional studies to clarify its mechanisms and therapeutic relevance.

Article.Title: Safety and Antitumor Activity of the Usnic Acid Derivative OL9-116, a TDP1 Inhibitor, as an Adjunctive Therapy in Combination with Topotecan
Article.Authors: Kornienko T.; Zakharenko A.; Chernyshova I.; Chepanova A.; Dyrkheeva N.; Firsova A.; Rogachev A.; Luzina O.; Popova N.; Maksimova V.; Vlasova O.; Deryagina V.; Rodnyy A.; Salakhutdinov N.; Lavrik O.
Article.Abstract: Topotecan inhibits topoisomerase 1 (TOP1) by trapping the enzyme in a DNA-cleavage complex, which can be repaired by tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 1 (TDP1). The usnic acid derivative OL9-116 inhibits TDP1 and thereby enhances the antitumor activity of topotecan, making it a promising combination partner. However, the safety and optimal administration schedule of OL9-116 with topotecan have not been characterized. We demonstrated that OL9-116 has no genotoxic or epigenetic effects using Ames and CBMN assays, as well as HeLa trichostatin A-inducible cells with an epigenetically repressed GFP gene. Intraperitoneal administration was found to provide higher bioavailability than intragastric administration. We showed on the RShM-5 cervical cancer model that repeated topotecan administration in a clinically relevant low single-dose regimen was more effective than a single injection, and addition of topotecan at the Tmax of OL9-116 enhanced tumor growth inhibition. In the Lewis lung carcinoma model, the OL9-116–topotecan combination reduced primary tumor mass and lung metastases, enhancing both antitumor and antimetastatic effects. Monitoring of hematological parameters, liver, and spleen indices revealed no clinically significant toxicity. Moreover, peripheral blood parameters improved with the OL9-116–topotecan combination compared with topotecan monotherapy. Collectively, these findings support OL9-116 as a promising safe TDP1 inhibitor for combination with topotecan.

Article.Title: Terminalia buceras (Syn. Bucida buceras) and Retinal Oxidative Stress: A Critical Review of Published Evidence and Its Relevance to Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration
Article.Authors: Lewis-Luján L.; Iloki-Lewis A.; Guerrero-Magaña D.; Galvez-Ruiz J.; Perez-Martinez C.; Vargas-Durazo J.; Trujillo-López S.; Iloki-Assanga S.
Article.Abstract: Dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD) is a multifactorial retinal disorder involving oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic para-inflammation, complement dysregulation, and progressive retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) failure. This critical review evaluates the published evidence concerning Terminalia buceras (L.) C.Wright (syn. Bucida buceras L.; Combretaceae), hereafter referred to as T. buceras, and its relevance to dry age-related macular degeneration. The evidence is organized into five categories: species-specific chemical evidence, species-specific retinal evidence, species-specific non-retinal biological evidence, external isolated-compound evidence, and hypothesis-generating comparisons with related plants or experimental systems. The evidence base remains preliminary. Species-specific retinal data are restricted to in vitro observations, and there are currently no epidemiological studies linking T. buceras use to AMD outcomes, no validated animal studies demonstrating efficacy in dAMD, and no clinical studies. Moreover, phytochemical standardization, ocular exposure, metabolism, and retinal bioavailability remain insufficiently characterized. Accordingly, this review does not propose T. buceras as a preventive or therapeutic intervention and does not claim superiority over better-characterized medicinal plants. Instead, this review critically synthesizes published species-specific chemical and biological findings and evaluates their methodological limitations. The direct retinal evidence supports partial cytoprotection in an ARPE-19 oxidative-injury model, whereas the non-retinal inflammatory findings concern different preparations and experimental systems. Chemical characterization, cellular responses, and contextual mechanistic evidence are, therefore, considered separately. The available findings do not establish a disease-modifying effect on dAMD, clinically achievable retinal exposure, or chronic ocular safety.

Article.Title: Comparing the Composition of Small RNA in Blood Plasma Fractions Containing Exomeres and Supermeres
Article.Authors: Aronov A.; Artamonov A.; Chekrigin S.; Grigoryev E.; Vezo O.; Glushakov R.; Kondratov K.
Article.Abstract: It is known that small RNAs contained within extracellular vesicles can serve as agents of intercellular signaling. However, recent studies have shown that these molecules are carried not only by vesicles but also by smaller, non-membranous particles known as exomeres and supermeres. At the same time, the specific repertoire of small RNAs in these particles, as well as the extent to which the RNA profiles of exomeres and supermeres in human blood plasma differ—remains insufficiently studied. The aim of this study was to compare the small RNA patterns in blood plasma fractions containing these particles. Extracellular vesicles were first pelleted from platelet-poor plasma via ultracentrifugation (170,000× g, 4 h); subsequently, a fraction containing exomeres (FCE; pellet from 170,000× g, 20 h centrifugation) and a fraction containing supermeres (FCS; pellet from 370,000× g, 20 h centrifugation) were sequentially isolated. Subsequently, the small RNA composition was analyzed (FCE from eight donors and FCS from fourteen donors). It was found that the FCE and FCS fractions differed significantly in their non-coding RNA composition. Compared to FCE, FCS showed a significantly higher GC content in the small RNA fraction, as well as higher proportions of rRNA, tRNA, snoRNA, and snRNA, and lower proportions of miRNA, piRNA, lncRNA, and scaRNA. Analysis of the sequenced fragments length distribution revealed that, compared to FCE, the FCS sample contained a higher proportion of sequences shorter than 20 nucleotides (17–20 nt) and longer than 24 nucleotides (24–50 nt). A comparison of the major sequences showed that miRNA-451a accounts for approximately 50% of the total miRNA in FCE and 25% in FCS, while piRNA-45195 constitutes about 50% of the total in both FCS and FCE. A comparison of the levels of various miRNAs in the two fractions showed that the levels of 184 miRNAs were significantly higher (p-adj < 0.05, fold change > 2) in the FCE fraction, while 3 miRNAs were significantly higher in the FCS fraction. Additionally, the levels of 13 piRNAs were significantly higher in FCE, and 34 in FCS. Thus, despite the fact that the patterns of the most abundant small RNAs in these fractions are quite similar, FCS and FCE most likely exhibit different signaling functions.

Article.Title: Precision Pharmacotherapy for Childhood Obesity: Molecular Targets Beyond Single GLP-1 Receptor Agonism and a Framework for Disease Modification
Article.Authors: Dauleh H.; Hussain K.
Article.Abstract: Childhood obesity is a heterogeneous chronic disease shaped by genetic susceptibility, neuroendocrine signaling, energy homeostasis, adipose dysfunction, insulin resistance, and environmental exposure. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have markedly improved treatment efficacy, but heterogeneous response, weight recurrence after withdrawal, residual organ risk, and limited long-term pediatric data expose the limitations of a single-pathway, weight-centered model. This narrative review integrates the molecular rationale and clinical evidence for precision pharmacotherapy beyond single GLP-1 receptor agonism. It examines glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 and GLP-1/glucagon co-agonism, triple agonism, amylin combinations, fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) analogues, leptin replacement, and melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) agonism, separating established pediatric evidence from adult proof-of-concept and preclinical inference. Genotype-directed treatment for monogenic and syndromic obesity and lesion-directed treatment for acquired hypothalamic obesity provide the clearest examples of causal pathway correction. For common obesity, treatment selection should integrate developmental stage, hyperphagia, insulin resistance, ectopic fat, body composition, genetic context, treatment burden, and early response. Disease modification should be evaluated across growth, puberty, bone and lean tissue, beta cell and hepatic health, physical function, psychosocial well-being, safety, and durability. A dynamic cycle of phenotyping, mechanism-based treatment, multidomain monitoring, adaptation, and longitudinal re-phenotyping may improve the clinical relevance of pediatric obesity care.

Article.Title: The Interplay Between Pediatric Atopic Dermatitis and Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Emerging Evidence, Mechanistic Insights, and Clinical Implications
Article.Authors: Ma X.; Chen Z.; Anstey A.; Wan P.; Deng D.
Article.Abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common chronic inflammatory skin disease in children and is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder with potential consequences beyond the skin. Growing evidence links pediatric AD to neurodevelopmental disorders, particularly attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but the mechanisms and clinical implications remain incompletely understood. Systemic and neuroimmune inflammation, altered T-helper-cell and cytokine signaling, and genetic and epigenetic susceptibility may contribute to this association. Sleep disruption and psychosocial stress represent additional potential pathways linking skin inflammation with neurodevelopment. Stronger associations have been reported in children with severe or early-onset AD, multiple atopic comorbidities, and persistent sleep disturbance, highlighting the importance of disease heterogeneity. This narrative review integrates epidemiologic evidence and proposed mechanisms to examine the skin–brain axis in pediatric AD, with particular attention to high-risk phenotypes and implications for developmental surveillance and multidisciplinary management. Although current evidence supports an association, causality remains uncertain. Prospective studies integrating AD phenotypes, biomarkers, and neurodevelopmental assessments are needed to clarify these relationships and determine whether early effective AD treatment can modify long-term neurodevelopmental trajectories.

Article.Title: A Thermophilic Bacteriophage TP-84 Surrogate System for Validating Photocatalytic and Ultraviolet Inactivation of Airborne Viruses, Including SARS-CoV-2
Article.Authors: Sobolewski I.; Łubkowska B.; Mazierski P.; Gołąbiewska A.; Zaleska-Medyńska A.; Skowron P.
Article.Abstract: The airborne transmission of SARS-CoV-2 has renewed interest in engineering controls for indoor air; photocatalytic oxidation over titanium dioxide (TiO2) under ultraviolet (UV) light is an attractive, reagent-free basis for such controls. Rational development requires a biosafe, quantifiable challenge organism usable at biosafety level 1 (BSL-1). We validated the thermophilic bacteriophage TP-84 (host Geobacillus stearothermophilus) as a surrogate for airborne viruses, characterising its stability, aerosolisation, recovery from photocatalytic supports and inactivation on TiO2 surfaces under UVA, UVC and UVA + UVC by a reference-normalised mass balance. TP-84 was stable in a simulated saliva matrix, survived ultrasonic nebulisation, and was recovered from porous ceramic supports at 66.0–91.7%. Five minutes of UV on TiO2 surfaces—UVC (254 nm, 540 mJ cm−2) or combined UVA + UVC (2040 mJ cm−2)—inactivated 87.4–89.4% and 61.6–76.5% of phage, respectively; bulk liquid was strongly protective (94.6–97.5% recovery), whereas desiccation reduced recovery to 4.3–16%. Flow-through aerosol assays provided a device test bed. Because TP-84 is a hardy, non-enveloped dsDNA virus, these values are conservative lower bounds that must not be equated with SARS-CoV-2 efficacy; validation with an enveloped surrogate and authentic virus is the next step.

Article.Title: Irreversible Inhibition of Human Ornithine Aminotransferase: A Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics Study
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Guan X.; Gong A.; Wang G.; Zhang Q.; Li Y.; Wang W.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Human ornithine aminotransferase (hOAT) is overexpressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and participates in glutamine anabolic metabolism, making it a promising therapeutic target. Although (1S,3S)-3-amino-4-(hexafluoropropan-2-ylidenyl)-cyclopentane-1-carboxylic acid (named here as BCF3 after the (bis)trifluoromethyl feature) has been proposed as a potent inhibitor of hOAT, previous experimental studies have characterized an external aldimine intermediate and the static end-state adduct, but the elementary fluorine-elimination steps and their modulation by the active-site environment remain incompletely understood. Herein, molecular dynamics (MD) and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations were employed to systematically explore the irreversible inhibitory mechanism mediated by external aldimine II—the key reaction intermediate of BCF3—against hOAT. Conserved active-site water molecules act as proton-shuttling bridges, and residue-dependent electrostatic effects control fluorine elimination. External aldimine II forms a stable covalent adduct with Lys292 and sequentially releases fluorine atoms from the –CF2 moiety via water-mediated Fα− and Fβ− elimination, with feasible barriers of 10.8 and 16.0 kcal/mol, respectively. Negative overall reaction energies indicate that the elimination products are energetically favored in the system. Electrostatic and noncovalent interaction analyses suggest that Arg180 and Gly42 promote fluorine elimination whereas Phe177 suppresses it, providing an atomistic explanation for the superior inhibitory potency of the bis-trifluoromethyl scaffold. The atomistic inhibitory mechanism uncovered in this study provides a theoretical foundation for the future rational design of hOAT-targeted drugs for hepatocellular carcinoma therapy.

Article.Title: What a Near-Perfect AUROC Does Not Show: Random-Panel and Label-Permutation Controls for a Sepsis Blood-Transcriptome Signature
Article.Authors: Kolev M.; Naskinova I.; Lazarova M.; Klisurov V.; Kalinov H.
Article.Abstract: Sepsis blood-transcriptome signatures are usually judged against healthy controls. Two questions are rarely separated: whether the classifier exceeds chance, and whether its genes outperform an arbitrary list of equal size. We tested both on public microarray data (discovery GSE65682, n = 359; validation GSE57065, n = 53), using the 9983 of 11,222 genes measurable on both platforms. A 10-gene signature was selected by nested cross-validation and applied to validation without refitting. It separated sepsis from health perfectly (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUROC, 1.000). The pipeline exceeded chance: no label permutation in 1000 matched it (p = 0.001). The genes did not outperform random lists: 12.5% of 2000 random 10-gene panels matched or exceeded the signature, as did 67.6% of panels drawn from the same 300 preselected candidates. Against non-infected intensive care patients, cross-fitted AUROC fell to 0.730 (95% confidence interval 0.642–0.818), unchanged after age and sex matching. At a threshold of 0.5, the cross-fitted model called 70 of these 75 patients septic. Selection was unstable: 200 bootstrap resamples gave a median of 6 genes, from 109 distinct genes. A near-perfect AUROC against healthy controls reflects an easy benchmark, not a specific gene list.

Article.Title: Beyond Targeted Delivery: The Emerging Immunomodulatory Landscape of Antibody-Oligonucleotide Conjugates
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Wang S.; Wang H.
Article.Abstract: Antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates (AOCs) are usually viewed as delivery vehicles that carry nucleic-acid payloads to defined cell populations for gene silencing or gene regulation. Existing reviews concentrate on delivery systems, tumour-directed therapy and extrahepatic oligonucleotide delivery, while the intrinsic immunomodulatory activity of AOCs has received far less attention. Conjugation couples antibody-mediated targeting with the innate immune-stimulating activity of the payload, a property that most current AOCs seldom exploit. This review repositions AOCs as active immune regulators. Three emerging immunoregulatory applications are examined in detail: vaccine-adjuvant construction, neutrophil-driven innate immune activation, and immunometabolic reprogramming. Structure–activity relationships linking AOC design to immune potency are summarized, and their immune mechanisms are distinguished from those of free oligonucleotides and unconjugated antibodies. Based on preclinical and in vitro evidence, AOCs act as multifunctional immunomodulators rather than passive cargo carriers. Two sources of immune activity are distinguished: direct immunostimulation by the conjugated payload, and effects secondary to targeted delivery. These findings still await clinical confirmation. Key barriers to translation, including conjugation efficiency, mechanistic gaps and manufacturing bottlenecks, are discussed. Prospective applications include engineered vaccines, anti-infective innate therapy, tumour microenvironment remodelling and autoimmune intervention, pending further validation. This review provides a conceptual framework for developing next-generation AOC-based immune adjuvants and precision immunotherapeutics.

Article.Title: Maternal Plasma Proteomic Signatures Distinguish Preeclampsia from Healthy Pregnancy but Not Early-Onset from Late-Onset Subtypes: A Leakage-Free Machine-Learning and Explainability Study
Article.Authors: Yasar S.; Melekoglu R.; Basak Turkmen N.; Safarova A.; Colak C.; Alzakari S.; Alkhalifa A.; Yagin F.
Article.Abstract: Early-onset (EOPE) and late-onset (LOPE) preeclampsia are clinically distinct, but their molecular differences are incompletely defined. Using a strictly leakage-free pipeline, we re-examined maternal plasma proteomes of EOPE, LOPE, and healthy pregnancy (HP) and asked whether the subtypes are separable at the proteome level. Label-free LC–MS/MS proteomes comprising 370 proteins from 46 women (HP, n = 18; EOPE, n = 17; LOPE, n = 11) were analysed using limma and fully nested cross-validation, in which feature selection, class balancing, and tuning were confined to the outer training folds; model explanations used SHAP and feature-selection stability. Observed selection frequencies far exceeded a random-selection null (for example, complement factor D was selected in all 15 outer folds, Wilson 95% confidence interval 0.80 to 1.00, against an expected frequency of 0.07), indicating that the stability was not a chance artefact. Discrimination is summarised as the mean ± standard deviation across the 5-fold × 3-repeat (15) outer test folds; because the single best-performing classifier was chosen on outer-fold performance, the reported area under the curve is modestly optimistic (on average by 0.04, and by up to 0.10 relative to the median of the three classifiers), even though the leakage-free procedure was applied identically to each classifier. Disease-versus-healthy contrasts were strong and concordant, with 10 and eight differentially abundant proteins identified for EOPE and LOPE, respectively, and AUROCs ranging from 0.88 to 0.90. EOPE showed a complement/acute-phase/coagulation signature, whereas LOPE showed an apolipoprotein/lipid signature, with limma, stability analysis, and SHAP yielding convergent findings. By contrast, the EOPE-versus-LOPE comparison identified no differentially abundant proteins and showed no reliable multivariate separation. A post hoc sensitivity analysis (two-sample t-test, two-sided, α = 0.05) indicated that the discovery cohort (early-onset n = 17, late-onset n = 11) had 80% power only for very large per-protein standardised differences (Cohen’s d ≥ 1.13, or d ≥ 2.10 after Bonferroni correction across the 370 proteins), and only 24% and 51% power to detect medium (d = 0.5) and large (d = 0.8) effects; the absence of a detectable early-versus-late difference is therefore consistent with limited power for small-to-moderate effects rather than proven biological equivalence. In an independent ELISA cohort (n = 87), EOPE differed from HP for seven of nine analytes, with AUCs of up to 0.82, led by sFlt-1 (fold-changes paralleled these areas under the curve: the largest early-onset median disease-to-control ratios were fibronectin 2.9, soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 2.8 and α1-antitrypsin 2.5, whereas placental growth factor decreased to 0.6 and apolipoprotein E was unchanged at 1.0); however, the subtypes again did not separate. On adjustment for maternal age, body mass index and smoking, the leading early-onset markers remained significant (soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1, serum amyloid A and fibronectin robust; complement factor D and alpha-1-antitrypsin borderline), whereas maternal chronic hypertension, diabetes and thyroid disease were not recorded and could not be modelled. Benchmarked against soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (DeLong test), no novel candidate exceeded its discrimination and several were significantly lower; only glycoprotein hormones alpha chain added cross-validated incremental value in early-onset disease (cross-validated area under the curve 0.71 to 0.76), and none improved on soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 in late-onset disease; apolipoprotein E did not validate, and placental growth factor decreased as expected. Plasma proteomics distinguishes preeclampsia from healthy pregnancy and recovers coherent subtype-leaning signatures but provides little evidence of a sharp EOPE–LOPE boundary; the prioritised panel warrants validation in larger cohorts.

Article.Title: Prognostic Value of lncRNA H19 in Gastric Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Song S.; Li Y.; Gao C.; Li S.; Jin S.; Liu S.
Article.Abstract: LncRNA H19 is a crucial regulatory player in GC and could operate as an attractive biomarker for patient prognosis. This meta-analysis aims to gauge the link between lncRNA H19 expression levels and patient prognosis, as well as clinicopathological features. HR and 95%CI were utilized to evaluate the connection between lncRNA H19 expression and prognosis, as well as clinicopathological features in GC patients. Bioinformatics analysis, potential molecular mechanisms and drug therapy involving lncRNA H19 were predicted through databases. The expression of lncRNA H19 in GC cells was verified through qRT-PCR. High expression of lncRNA H19 is correlated with a lower overall survival rate in GC patients, as well as TNM stage, lymph node metastasis and tumor invasion. Bioinformatics analysis confirmed that lncRNA H19 is significantly expressed in GC and related to poor prognosis. Function prediction analyses suggested that lncRNA H19 may contribute to GC progression through ceRNA regulatory networks, TFs, and predicted interactions with RBPs. Nutlin-3, PD-0332991, and Topotecan were predicted as preliminary candidate drugs. LncRNA H19 was confirmed to be highly expressed in GC cells. LncRNA H19 might act as a feasible biomarker for prognostic prediction in GC, warranting further validation in clinical studies.

Article.Title: A 3D-Printed BCP/PLGA-PEG-PLGA Scaffold for LNC000133-Loaded BMSC-Derived Exosome Delivery Promotes Repair of Steroid-Induced Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head
Article.Authors: Xia T.; Yang C.; Li X.; Chen T.; Xu Y.
Article.Abstract: Dysfunction of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and impaired exosome-mediated intercellular communication are recognized as critical contributors to the pathogenesis of steroid-induced osteonecrosis of the femoral head (SONFH), although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Moreover, the development of novel biomaterials and therapeutic strategies capable of improving SONFH treatment remains an urgent clinical priority. Previous studies have demonstrated that LNC000133-modified exosomes derived from human BMSCs (hBMSCs) promote osteoblastic differentiation and enhance exosome uptake by osteoblasts, thereby exerting therapeutic effects in SONFH. Building on these findings, we developed a 3D-printed biphasic calcium phosphate (BCP)/poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA)- polyethylene glycol (PEG)-PLGA scaffold loaded with LNC000133-modified hBMSC-derived exosomes (LNC000133-Exos) to facilitate the clinical translation of this gene-based therapeutic approach for SONFH. The biological effects of this composite scaffold on hBMSCs were subsequently evaluated in vitro. Furthermore, the BCP/PLGA-PEG-PLGA scaffold loaded with LNC000133-Exos was applied for the treatment of SONFH in a rabbit model. Our results demonstrated that transplantation of the LNC000133-Exos-loaded BCP/PLGA-PEG-PLGA scaffold markedly enhanced bone repair and structural reconstruction within the necrotic region of the femoral head in vivo. Collectively, these findings indicate that the BCP/PLGA-PEG-PLGA scaffold and LNC000133 synergistically promote hBMSC proliferation and osteogenic differentiation while suppressing adipogenic differentiation, providing a strong theoretical foundation and a promising therapeutic strategy for targeted SONFH treatment.

Article.Title: Ferroptosis-Related GPX4 and CD71 and Immune Checkpoint PD-L1 in Cutaneous Melanoma: Associations with Clinicopathologic Features and Survival Outcomes
Article.Authors: Güner R.; Yüceer R.; Ünsal A.; Akyol M.; Eğilmez H.
Article.Abstract: Ferroptosis-related pathways and immune checkpoint signaling may contribute to melanoma progression, but their clinicopathologic and prognostic interplay remains incompletely characterized. To investigate GPX4, CD71, and PD-L1 expression in primary cutaneous melanoma and evaluate their associations with clinicopathologic features and survival outcomes. This retrospective single-center cohort included 44 patients with primary cutaneous melanoma. PD-L1, GPX4, and CD71 expressions were assessed immunohistochemically. Associations with clinicopathologic parameters were analyzed, and overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS) were evaluated using Kaplan–Meier and Cox regression analyses. PD-L1, GPX4, and CD71 positivity was were observed in 25.0%, 38.6%, and 36.4% of tumors, respectively. PD-L1 expression was associated with Breslow thickness (p = 0.004), whereas CD71 expression was associated with perineural invasion, Clark level, and disease stage (p = 0.019, p = 0.034, and p = 0.045, respectively). GPX4-positive tumors showed significantly shorter OS (40 vs. 103 months; p = 0.003) and DFS (42 vs. 86 months; p = 0.009). Triple-positive tumors (PD-L1+/GPX4+/CD71+) demonstrated significantly shorter OS and DFS than triple-negative tumors (p = 0.035 and p = 0.040, respectively). In multivariable analysis, GPX4 positivity remained independently associated with poorer OS. GPX4 expression was associated with adverse survival outcomes in cutaneous melanoma, while combined GPX4, CD71, and PD-L1 expression identified a subgroup with particularly unfavorable outcomes. These findings support further investigation of ferroptosis-related markers alongside immune checkpoint pathways as candidate prognostic biomarkers in melanoma.

Article.Title: Distinct Molecular Relationships and Partial Pathway Convergence of Anserine and RRR-α-Tocopherol in Human Diabetic Kidney Disease
Article.Authors: Mosaoa R.
Article.Abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) involves interacting metabolic, inflammatory, vascular, and fibrotic disturbances. This study investigated the molecular relationships of anserine and RRR-α-tocopherol with human DKD using a disease-centered computational framework in which compound–target evidence was established independently before integration with kidney transcriptomic data. Stage-associated transcription was analyzed in 36 human kidney samples spanning Control, Early DKD, and Advanced DKD, with external assessment in two independent cohorts, followed by evidence-based prioritization, pathway analysis, renal single-cell localization, and sensitivity analyses. Predefined target sets comprised 100 anserine and 111 RRR-α-tocopherol targets, with only 16 shared. Integration yielded 21 prioritized compound–DKD relationships involving 20 unique genes. Despite limited target overlap, the primary pathway analysis identified shared enrichment in Class A G protein-coupled receptor, Gαi, interleukin, and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling; only receptor tyrosine kinase signaling remained shared under conservative target-confidence restriction. The 20 genes localized across diverse tubular, immune, vascular, and stromal populations. Sensitivity analyses retained 17 of 21 relationships under stricter target-confidence criteria and showed external gene–DKD replication for 18 of 21 relationships in at least one cohort. These findings define a transparent, hypothesis-generating framework for experimental testing without implying therapeutic efficacy or a confirmed mechanism of action.

Article.Title: Terpenoids: A Comprehensive Review on Biosynthesis, Applications and Enhancement Strategies for Translational Research
Article.Authors: Irum N/A.; Tripathi G.; Ahmad S.; Fatima N.; Puri P.; Ahmad N.; Dissanayake K.; Ahmad K.; Ahmad S.; Farooqui A.
Article.Abstract: There is growing interest in natural bioactive compounds as potentially safer and more sustainable sources of therapeutic agents. Terpenoids, one of the most structurally diverse and biologically active classes of natural products, are derived from repeating isoprene units and possess a broad range of pharmacological and industrial applications. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in terpenoid biosynthesis, structural classification, and therapeutic applications. It also discusses emerging approaches for enhancing large-scale production, improving functional efficacy, and overcoming pharmacokinetic limitations. Attention is given to terpenoids currently undergoing clinical evaluation, along with their progress toward commercial development. Despite substantial preclinical evidence supporting their therapeutic potential, the clinical translation of many terpenoids remains limited. Key challenges include poor aqueous solubility, low permeability, slow dissolution, and high lipophilicity, which can collectively restrict systemic bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, only a relatively small proportion of biologically active terpenoids have progressed to advanced stages of clinical development, highlighting a considerable gap between experimental findings and clinical application. This review integrates current knowledge of terpenoid biosynthesis, biological activities, production strategies, and translational development while highlighting sustainable and scientifically driven approaches that may facilitate their future therapeutic and commercial utilization.

Article.Title: TNF-α and IL-8 Are Helpful in the Prediction of Late Post-COVID-19 Venous Thromboembolic Disease—Single-Center Prospective Study
Article.Authors: Wyrostkiewicz D.; Lewandowska K.; Jankowska E.; Dybowska M.; Jędrych M.; Zimna K.; Roży A.; Szturmowicz M.; Tomkowski W.; Sobiecka M.
Article.Abstract: Post-COVID-19 syndrome is associated with persistent inflammation and an elevated risk of late venous thromboembolism (VTE). The role of proinflammatory cytokines has been well documented in the acute phase of the disease, but their potential role in late post-COVID-19 VTE remains unknown. What is the prevalence of VTE among symptomatic post-COVID-19 patients, and which laboratory parameters could enhance the diagnostic accuracy for VTE in these patients? Consecutive patients with objectively confirmed previous SARS-CoV-2 infection, admitted to a single department of lung diseases in a tertiary hospital due to sustained symptoms of dyspnea and/or exercise intolerance, were included. Clinical assessment and laboratory testing, including cytokine profiling (Il-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, TNF-α), PAI-1, and ferritin, were performed. VTE events (pulmonary embolism and/or deep vein thrombosis) were confirmed by standard imaging. Clinical and laboratory parameters were compared between participants with and without VTE. 108 patients: 69 (63.9%) males and 39 (36.1%) females, entered the study. VTE episodes were diagnosed in 39.8% (16.7% in the course of COVID-19 and 23.1% after the acute phase of the disease). Patients who entered the study ≤6 months and >6 months from acute COVID-19 infection were compared. Median D-dimer concentration was higher in patients with VTE that occurred within 6 months from the COVID-19 diagnosis compared to the non-VTE group (607 ng/mL vs. 428 ng/mL, borderline significance, p = 0.0595). Median_IL-8 concentration was significantly higher in those who developed VTE more than 6 months after COVID-19 compared to non-VTE patients: 10.19 pg/mL vs. 6.61 pg/mL, respectively, p = 0.048. The same was noted for TNF-α (39.02 pg/mL vs. 24 pg/mL, respectively, p = 0.011). The best diagnostic utility for VTE prediction was obtained for TNF-α concentration in symptomatic patients diagnosed >6 months from acute COVID-19 infection (ROC AUC 0.73, 95% CI 0.57–0.91). TNF-α was an independent risk factor of VTE episodes in the whole study group. Detection of elevated IL-8 and TNF-α levels later than 6 months from acute COVID-19 disease may help to identify patients at increased risk of late venous thromboembolism; nevertheless, further studies are needed to validate this observation.

Article.Title: Lineage-Associated Dichotomous Patterns in Codon Usage of Parasitic Cestodes
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Yang D.; Bae Y.
Article.Abstract: Genome remodeling, accompanied by modifications in base composition and translational architecture, may systematically reshape codon usage patterns, contributing to adaptation to changing biological demands through altered translational efficiency. In the present study, codon usage and genomic tRNA profiles were comparatively investigated in species representing two cestode lineages with contrasting genome organizations and biological characteristics. Despite relatively well-preserved amino-acid frequencies, these cestode species exhibited clear inter-lineage divergence in synonymous codon usage. Diphyllobothriideans preferentially utilized C-ending synonymous codons, whereas cyclophyllideans favored the corresponding T-ending alternatives, forming distinct lineage-associated codon dialects. These divergent patterns were consistently retained across coding-sequence datasets ranging from genome-wide to highly curated orthologous sets. Nucleotide composition contributed substantially to codon usage, while multiple lines of evidence indicated additional selective and translational constraints. Genomic tRNA gene pools were greatly reduced in cyclophyllideans, particularly taeniids. However, relationships between synonymous codon preferences and corresponding tRNA gene counts varied among codon families, indicating that their evolutionary associations may not be uniform. Collectively, these findings suggest that distinct codon usage patterns have evolved in cestode lineages with contrasting genomic architectures, shaped by lineage-specific compositional environments and, potentially for certain codon families, translational factors. They provide a framework for investigating how such diversifications contribute to translational adaptation to nutritional and environmental changes.

Article.Title: Exercise-Mediated Regulation of Ferroptosis in Diabetic Cardiomyopathy: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Bo W.; Guo Q.
Article.Abstract: Exercise is an important non-pharmacological intervention for the prevention and management of diabetes and its cardiovascular complications; however, the underlying mechanisms by which exercise confers cardiometabolic protection remain incompletely understood. Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cardiovascular complication of diabetes, characterized by progressive myocardial structural and functional abnormalities associated with oxidative stress, dysregulated lipid metabolism, chronic inflammation, and miochondrial dysfunction. Ferroptosis, a form of regulated cell death characterized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, has emerged as a potential pathological link between metabolic disturbances and myocardial injury in DCM. Accumulating evidence suggests that exercise may modulate ferroptosis through multiple interconnected mechanisms, including restoration of iron homeostasis, suppression of lipid peroxidation, enhancement of endogenous antioxidant defenses, and improvement of mitochondrial function and quality control, thereby contributing to myocardial protection. In this review, we systematically summarize the cardioprotective benefits of exercise in the context of DCM and critically discuss the potential associations between exercise characteristics, including exercise modality, intensity, duration and the regulation of ferroptosis. By integrating current evidence on the molecular mechanisms underlying exercise-mediated ferroptosis regulation, this review provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how exercise may counteract ferroptosis in DCM and highlights the potential of ferroptosis-informed, precision exercise strategies for the prevention and management of diabetic cardiomyopathy.

Article.Title: Conditional Proximity Labeling in Complex Biological Systems: Design Principles, Emerging Platforms, and Applications
Article.Authors: Yang J.; Zhu M.; Liu S.; Yang L.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Proximity labeling (PL) enables covalent capture of biomolecules near a defined target in living systems, providing a route to map molecular proximity in situ. Conventional PL usually relies on a single targeting cue and may therefore lack the selectivity required to resolve defined molecular events or dynamic processes in complex biological systems. Conditional PL addresses this limitation by coupling labeling activity to additional inputs, including interaction-dependent enzyme reconstitution, localization of catalytic modules at cell–cell interfaces, light-regulated catalysis, and multiple orthogonal labeling reactions. These designs allow labeling to respond to specified spatial, temporal, or molecular conditions. We group conditional PL into four designs—split complementation, interface localization, light control, and multiple labeling—based on what activates labeling and what the labels reveal. We examine their use in studying protein complexes, trafficking, and intercellular communication. We also consider what each strategy encodes, the experimental boundaries of the resulting proximity information, and trade-offs among selectivity, labeling efficiency, temporal control, and compatibility with native biological contexts. Remaining challenges include expanding catalyst and probe diversity, improving in vivo compatibility, and integrating conditional PL with single-cell analysis, spatial omics, and high-resolution imaging.

Article.Title: Natural Antioxidant-Derived Compounds and Materials as Emerging MALDI Matrices: Applications, Evidence, and Perspectives
Article.Authors: Bania K.; Bartusik-Aebisher D.; Dynarowicz K.; Smolak B.; Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Antioxidants constitute a chemically diverse group of compounds that are widely studied in food, natural products, and biological systems, creating a continuing need for analytical methods capable of their reliable characterization. Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (MALDI-MS) provides rapid molecular analysis with minimal sample preparation and has been increasingly applied to low-molecular-weight compounds, natural products, food constituents, and biological samples. However, the analysis of small molecules by MALDI-MS is often limited by matrix-derived background signals, differences in ionization efficiency, heterogeneous crystallization, and difficulties in achieving reliable quantitative measurements, highlighting the need for alternative matrix systems with improved and more controllable analytical properties. In this context, naturally occurring antioxidants are of particular interest because many possess aromatic and conjugated structures, UV-absorbing groups, acid–base and redox properties, and functional groups capable of matrix–analyte interactions, which may support their function as MALDI matrices. This review summarizes the use of MALDI-MS for the analysis of antioxidant compounds in purified samples, plant extracts, food products, and biological materials, while critically evaluating the emerging concept of using naturally occurring antioxidants as alternative MALDI matrices. Particular emphasis is placed on the structural and physicochemical features relevant to matrix performance, including aromaticity, UV absorption, acid–base properties, redox behavior, crystallization, and matrix–analyte interactions. Conventional organic matrices are discussed alongside emerging alternatives, including ionic liquid matrices, nanomaterial-based systems, carbon-based materials, and matrix-free approaches. Importantly, the available evidence indicates that only a limited number of natural antioxidant-derived compounds and materials have been experimentally demonstrated as MALDI matrices, whereas evidence for other candidates remains preliminary or theoretical. Their potential analytical value is further considered in relation to reproducibility, background interference, matrix selectivity, and quantitative performance, together with future opportunities involving rational matrix design, mass spectrometry imaging, and computational approaches. Natural antioxidant-derived compounds and materials therefore represent an emerging and still insufficiently explored class of MALDI matrices that could expand the range of matrix chemistries available for small-molecule analysis, although their analytical value will ultimately depend on compound-specific experimental validation rather than antioxidant activity alone.

Article.Title: Hydatid Cyst Fluid of Echinococcus granulosus Alleviates Experimental Ulcerative Colitis by Suppressing Inflammation and Oxidative Stress and Regulating the Gut Microbiota
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Baota A.; Wang F.; Didaer Y.; Shan J.
Article.Abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic recurrent inflammatory disease of the colonic mucosa, with a rising global incidence. Hydatid cyst fluid of Echinococcus granulosus (EgHCF) has been shown to alleviate UC inflammation, but how it exerts this protective effect is not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigated the protective efficacy of EgHCF using a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced acute colitis model in mice and an NCM460 intestinal epithelial cell line. In vivo, EgHCF treatment significantly ameliorated the clinical signs of DSS-induced colitis, counteracted colon shortening and weight loss, and mitigated colonic histopathological damage; furthermore, it enhanced intestinal barrier integrity, suppressed inflammatory responses, reduced oxidative stress, and activated the Keap1/Nrf2 signaling pathway. Gut microbiota analysis revealed that EgHCF attenuated gut microbial dysbiosis by increasing α-diversity and the abundance of Firmicutes and Verrucomicrobiota. Metabolomics analysis further indicated that the tryptophan metabolic pathway plays a prominent role in the treatment of DSS-induced UC mice with EgHCF. In vitro, EgHCF protected the epithelial barrier function of NCM460 cells, significantly inhibited the expression of pro-inflammatory factors iNOS and COX-2, attenuated intracellular ROS levels, and activated the Keap1/Nrf2 pathway in DSS-stimulated NCM460 cells. These findings suggest that EgHCF alleviates DSS-induced colitis by mitigating inflammation and oxidative stress, as well as regulating the gut microbiota, providing novel insights into its role in repairing the intestinal barrier.

Article.Title: Effects of μ-Agatoxin-Aa1a in Cellular and Rat Models of Myocardial Ischemia–Reperfusion Injury
Article.Authors: Iurova E.; Dolgova D.; Mikheeva N.; Ermakova A.; Sugak D.; Gilmutdinova A.; Fomin A.; Saenko Y.
Article.Abstract: Myocardial infarction is one of the common cardiovascular diseases. Sodium overload in the myocardium is another of the most important mechanisms underlying ischemia/reperfusion injury. Na+ entry into the cell through ion channels can be controlled using peptide toxins targeting ion channels. In our work, we analyze the use of mu-agatoxin-Aa1a, as a sodium channel modulator, as a cytoprotective agent in ischemia/reperfusion injury. For IRI modeling in vitro, the H9C2 culture was placed under oxygen-glucose deprivation conditions followed by reperfusion. Cell death and ion dynamics were recorded using a fluorescent plate reader. Reversible myocardial ischemia of rats in vivo was created by applying an occluder under the main branch of the left coronary artery. Histological and biochemical changes were recorded. The study demonstrated the ability of mu-agatoxin-Aa1a myocardial cells to adapt to rapidly changing extracellular conditions upon restoration of normal blood flow after a period of ischemia. Thus, the study allows us to consider mu-agatoxin-Aa1a as a biologically active molecule with a targeted effect to enhance the adaptation of cardiomyocytes to OGD/reperfusion conditions.

Article.Title: Transcriptomic and Epigenetic Reprogramming in Solanum tuberosum L. Micropropagation: A Systematic Review of Elicitor-Driven Acclimatization and Scalable Biofactories
Article.Authors: Sarchi G.; Sarchi S.; Ortega J.; Hernández F.; Martínez R.
Article.Abstract: Solanum tuberosum L. relies heavily on in vitro propagation for pathogen-free seed tuber production; however, the transition to ex vitro environments causes severe plantlet mortality due to transplant shock. Exogenous elicitors have emerged as pivotal preconditioning tools, but their underlying molecular mechanisms remain fragmented. This systematic review aims to elucidate the translational architecture of elicitor-driven preconditioning in Solanum tuberosum, systematically organized across a tripartite continuum—(1) epigenetic chromatin plasticity, (2) transcriptomic defense reprogramming, and (3) scalable biofactory platforms (temporary immersion bioreactors and sensor-actuated aeroponics)—required to validate ex vitro physiological competence. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines for systematic reviews, we conducted a structured search across Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect (January 2010 to August 2026). Inclusion criteria targeted original research evaluating transcriptomic or epigenetic responses to in vitro elicitation in S. tuberosum. Following quality appraisal, data from 58 high-quality studies were synthesized using a critical narrative approach. The evidence is clearly stratified into our three core layers. (1) Transcriptomic Reprogramming: Exogenous elicitors systematically reactivate dormant defense networks prior to ex vitro transfer, converging strictly on salicylic acid (SA), jasmonic acid (JA), and ethylene (ET) signaling pathways alongside reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. (2) Epigenetic Plasticity: Concurrently, morphological adaptation is heavily modulated by reversible chromatin remodeling; specifically, transient DNA hypomethylation and histone acetylation ensure in vitro cellular totipotency and stress memory. (3) Translational Scalability: Automated bioreactors and aeroponic platforms provide the essential physical microenvironment to validate these molecular outcomes and reverse vitrotype disorders at commercial scales. Elicitors drive an integrated tripartite preconditioning continuum that mitigates transplant shock and enables scalable hardening. We delineate a comprehensive translational framework to the transition from empirical micropropagation to targeted, genomics-informed biofactory platforms.

Article.Title: In Vitro Assessment of Chemically Modified Probiotic Bacteria as Receptor-Mimic Decoys for Cholera Toxin B Subunit
Article.Authors: Mainero Rocca I.; Stuhr-Hansen N.; Blixt O.; Goletz S.
Article.Abstract: Gastrointestinal infections remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Conventional antibiotic treatment can be ineffective or inappropriate in some settings, particularly in the context of increasing antimicrobial resistance. In many enteric infections, an early step in pathogenesis involves binding of pathogens or their toxins to oligosaccharide receptors on host–cell surfaces, making these interactions attractive targets for antimicrobial strategies that do not rely on conventional antibiotics. Here, we developed a non-recombinant, microbiome-based chemical engineering approach in which cholesteryl-peptides serve as flexible chemical scaffolds for displaying GM1 receptor mimics on probiotic bacteria. After incubation with the GM1-cholesteryl-peptides, GM1 signals accessible to the cholera toxin B subunit (CTB) were detected on both the Gram-positive probiotic Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 and the Gram-negative probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917. These findings establish an in vitro proof-of-concept for a modular, non-recombinant bacterial decoy platform and may provide a basis for the future development of receptor-mimic strategies against toxin-mediated gastrointestinal infections.

Article.Title: CRMP4-Mediated Regulation of Cav1.3 Protein Stability and Apoptosis Resistance in Endometriosis
Article.Authors: Huang Y.; Wang Y.; Li R.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: Endometriosis (EMs) is a common chronic gynecological disorder characterized by the ectopic implantation and growth of endometrial-like tissue. The abnormal survival of ectopic endometrial cells, including their reduced susceptibility to apoptosis, plays an important role in the development of EMs. Cav1.3 is aberrantly upregulated in EMs and contributes to disease progression; however, the mechanism responsible for its increased expression remains unclear. In this study, protein stability and ubiquitination assays were performed in hEM15A cells. Cav1.3-interacting proteins were screened by co-immunoprecipitation coupled with liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry, and the regulatory pathway was further examined using in vitro experiments and animal models. We found that reduced ubiquitin–proteasome-mediated degradation increased Cav1.3 stability in hEM15A cells. Our results further showed that ZNF460 increased CRMP4 expression by activating its transcription. CRMP4 associated with Cav1.3 and reduced RNF138–Cav1.3 association, accompanied by decreased Cav1.3 ubiquitination and increased protein stability. ZNF460-dependent CRMP4 expression promoted Cav1.3 accumulation and was associated with reduced apoptosis in hEM15A cells. These findings clarify the post-translational mechanism underlying Cav1.3 upregulation in EMs and suggest that the ZNF460/CRMP4/RNF138/Cav1.3 axis may serve as a potential molecular target for EMs treatment.

Article.Title: Telomere-Independent Associations of hTERT Promoter Polymorphisms with Metabolic Phenotypes and Diabetic Complications
Article.Authors: Sawicki K.; Suchecka M.; Matysiak-Kucharek M.; Kruszewski M.; Wojtyła-Buciora P.; Dziemidok P.; Kapka-Skrzypczak L.
Article.Abstract: This study investigated association of three hTERT promoter polymorphisms (rs2735940, rs7712562, rs2853669) with leukocyte relative telomere length (RTL) and clinical characteristics, in patients with type 1 (T1DM) and type 2 (T2DM) diabetes. Covariate-adjusted ANCOVA revealed no significant direct association between hTERT variants and leukocyte RTL in either cohort. However, nominally significant, RTL-independent clinical associations emerged in T2DM patients. Multivariate logistic regression associated the rs2853669 CC genotype with lower odds of diabetic neuropathy (OR = 0.324, 95% CI: 0.106–0.989, raw p = 0.048). Furthermore, the rs2735940 TT genotype was associated with a favorable lipid profile (lower TC, LDL, and non-HDL; raw p < 0.05), while rs7712562 CC carriers exhibited higher waist circumference (raw p = 0.016). While hTERT variants were not directly associated with RTL under severe metabolic stress, they exhibited clinically relevant phenotypic associations. Although these exploratory secondary findings did not survive False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction, the nominal association of rs2853669 CC with lower neuropathy odds suggests potential non-telomeric pathways associated with mitochondrial protection. These hypothesis-generating observations warrant independent validation in larger, prospective cohorts.

Article.Title: Analysis of Multi-Site Bile Acid Metabolic Profile Reveals an Association Between Bile Acid–FXR Signaling and Visceral Hypersensitivity in Heterotypic Intermittent Stress-Induced IBS
Article.Authors: Jiang S.; Gao C.; Song Y.; Zhang N.; Zhang Z.; Liu X.; Su Y.; Wang X.; Li T.
Article.Abstract: Visceral hypersensitivity (VH) is a hallmark of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), establishing a reliable VH model is vital for investigating the disorder. While the impact of chronic stress on bile acid (BA) metabolism remains unclear. The exploratory study aimed to evaluate a heterotypic intermittent stress (HIS)-induced rat model of VH and characterize associated alterations in BA metabolism and farnesoid X receptor (FXR) signaling. Rats underwent a 9-day HIS regimen, and VH was assessed by electromyographic recording of the visceromotor response to colorectal distension. BA profiles in feces, colon, and serum were quantified by HPLC-MS/MS, and colonic FXR and CGRP expression were examined by Western blot, immunohistochemistry, and three-dimensional confocal reconstruction. HIS induced significant VH without organic colonic pathology, accompanied by increased CGRP-positive nerve fibers. The bile acid pool composition region-specific alterations in feces, colon, and serum. Specifically, the free-to-conjugated BA ratio was significantly increased in the colon and decreased in the serum of HIS rats, whereas no significant difference was detected in feces, while species-level changes were compartment-specific. Colonic FXR was upregulated and spatially associated with CGRP-positive fibers; in a preventive guggulsterone-treated group, both signals were reduced. These findings indicate that HIS-induced VH is associated with region-specific alterations in BA metabolism and colonic FXR signaling change, identifying the BA–FXR axis as a candidate pathway meriting functional validation as a potential therapeutic target for IBS.

Article.Title: From Phenotype to Genome: A Critical Evidence-Based Synthesis of Frosty Pod Rot (Moniliophthora roreri) Resistance in Cacao and a Proposed Evidence-Gated Framework to Support Genetic Gain
Article.Authors: Pineda-Rodriguez Y.; Navas J.; Jarma-Orozco A.; Oviedo-Zumaque L.; Rodríguez-Páez L.
Article.Abstract: Frosty pod rot (FPR), caused by Moniliophthora roreri, severely constrains cacao production in the Neotropics, yet evidence supporting molecular breeding for resistance remains fragmented and is often conflated with findings from witches’ broom disease. We conducted a structured critical review, not a systematic review, and classified each FPR-related claim with an author-developed, multidimensional evidence classification system (E0–E5) separating directness, genetic replication, mechanistic inference and breeding utility. The evidence supports a quantitative, partial and context-dependent architecture of resistance. The strongest QTL have been re-detected only within the Pound 7 × UF273 pedigree (E2a), and no FPR locus replicated in genetically independent material (E2b) was identified in the literature retrieved and verified. Genomic predictive ability reached 0.60–0.67 under random cross-validation within one clonal panel but averaged approximately 0.16 when models were transferred among related populations; these values answer different questions and are not directly comparable. Host and pathogen transcriptomics provide correlative evidence (E3a), and recombinant M. roreri effectors show biological activity in heterologous or cacao tissues (E3b-i), but no stable genetic manipulation altering FPR in a pod-challenge assay (E4) and no documented breeding utility (E5) were identified. We propose a Phenotyping and Reporting Guideline for FPR (PRG-FPR) and MIGGA, a modular, evidence-gated decision framework illustrated with a retrospective worked example; its effect on realised genetic gain remains to be tested.

Article.Title: Micronized Acellular Dermal Matrix and Synthetic Polymers: Temporal Macrophage Transition as a Mechanistic Framework
Article.Authors: Jin Z.; Jin C.; Ding Z.; Hai D.; Ming H.; Seo S.; Choi M.; Shim J.; Huy V.; Chien P.; Heo C.
Article.Abstract: Injectable biodegradable polymers and micronized acellular dermal matrix (mADM) have potentially complementary regenerative properties, but how their combination shapes the host response remains poorly defined. In many systems, polymers provide persistent material-associated stimulation that may sustain macrophage-driven foreign-body responses, whereas mADM provides tissue-derived extracellular matrix (ECM) cues that support cellular infiltration, vascularization, and remodeling, with persistence dependent on processing and host-mediated replacement. This narrative review evaluates whether changes in macrophage population states could help explain potential polymer–mADM synergy. Across the reviewed polymer–ECM hybrid studies, most evidence is indirect, and temporal sampling rarely resolves sequential state changes. No included study establishes temporal coupling as a causal mechanism. We therefore propose a temporal macrophage-switching model in which both components act from implantation and their relative contributions change over time; their spatiotemporal overlap may shape macrophage population trajectories and remodeling outcomes. We further define a functional macrophage polarization window using biological landmarks rather than fixed time points. The model remains a testable hypothesis whose applicability depends on material and tissue context. Validation requires polymer-only, mADM-only, and hybrid comparisons across independent mADM lots, with systematic variation in polymer persistence, mADM processing, component ratio, spatial organization, and degradation/remodeling kinetics.

Article.Title: Coincident Detection of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) in the Oral and Genital Regions in a Young Adult Male with Oral Lichen Planus: A Case Report
Article.Authors: Petrović A.; Popović Ž.; Pokimica B.; Vučić V.; Čanković M.
Article.Abstract: Oral lichen planus (OLP) is an atypical presentation in young males, and its co-occurrence with human papillomavirus (HPV) raises clinical concerns regarding malignant transformation. This case report describes a 27-year-old sexually active male with OLP and potentially persistent, synchronous oral and multigenotypic genital HPV co-infections. A 27-year-old male presented for follow-up 19 months after surgical excision of an oral papilloma with lichenoid features and histopathologically confirmed OLP. Molecular detection and genotyping were performed using oral and genital swabs via CFX96 real-time PCR. Results revealed potentially persistent oral co-infection with high-risk HPV 31 and low-risk HPV 44. Genital screening detected these same oral genotypes alongside four additional strains, consisting of high-risk HPV 18, 35, and 73 (classified per IARC standards), and low-risk HPV 81, with clinically evident condylomata acuminata. The long-term detection of high-risk HPV 31 in the oral swab in the presence of OLP highlights a hypothetical “dual-hit” oncogenic framework, where inflammation-induced oxidative stress may synergize with viral E6 and E7 oncoproteins to disrupt cell cycle regulation and elevate malignant transformation risks, though this remains entirely speculative in the absence of mechanistic biomarkers. Synchronous oral and anogenital HPV co-infections in young patients with OLP warrant a comprehensive multidisciplinary diagnostic protocol and cautious oncologic surveillance recommendations to prevent malignant progression and further transmission.

Article.Title: Natural Phenolic Antioxidants from Micromeria aybalae: Solvent-Dependent Composition and Bioactivity
Article.Authors: Karakus Z.; Sarikurkcu C.
Article.Abstract: Micromeria aybalae H.Duman & Dirmenci is a recently described endemic Lamiaceae species from southwestern Türkiye whose non-volatile phytochemistry and biological properties remain largely unexplored. This study comparatively evaluated ethyl acetate, methanol, and water extracts of its aerial parts for phenolic composition, antioxidant capacity, and enzyme inhibitory activity. Targeted Targeted liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) screening of 31 phenolics detected 23 compounds, with rosmarinic acid as the predominant constituent, reaching 19,650.23 µg/g extract in the water extract. The water extract also showed the highest extraction yield (11.14%), total phenolic content (71.62 mg gallic acid equivalents (GAE)/g extract), and activities in the phosphomolybdenum, 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), 2,2′-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS), cupric reducing antioxidant capacity (CUPRAC), and ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assays. In contrast, the methanol extract exhibited the highest total flavonoid content (17.73 mg RE/g extract) and the strongest tyrosinase and α-amylase inhibitory activities. Verbascoside was markedly enriched in the ethyl acetate extract (1288.60 µg/g extract), which also displayed the greatest metal-chelating activity. These findings provide the first comprehensive phenolic and bioactivity profile of M. aybalae and highlight extraction-condition-dependent differences in phenolic composition and in vitro activities, establishing a foundation for future investigations of this endemic species.

Article.Title: Reconsidering Mineral Formulations in Human Health and Disease: Molecular Mechanisms, Bioavailability and Metabolic Fates
Article.Authors: Ye M.; Rhie S.; Park Y.; Kim W.; Shim I.
Article.Abstract: Minerals are essential nutrients involved in enzymatic catalysis, signal transduction, cellular bioenergetics, and the maintenance of structural integrity. However, much of the existing research in mineral nutrition has evaluated physiological effects primarily at the elemental level, without adequately distinguishing whether a mineral is ingested as part of an organic matrix in natural foods or enters the biological system as an ionized species from inorganic salts or aqueous solutions. This review examines the criteria by which the conceptual definitions of organic and inorganic minerals have been established and explores the historical, analytical, and methodological factors underlying the lack of clear distinctions between these categories. In addition, it analyzes how the chemical form of minerals governs intestinal transport pathways, systemic bioavailability, tissue-specific accumulation, and intracellular metabolic handling. Using vanadium, silicon, zinc, and selenium as representative paradigms, this review contrasts the distinct molecular and toxicological fates of organic complexes versus inorganic salts-highlighting critical pathways such as protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTPase)-mediated insulin signaling, collagen cross-linking, mitochondrial mitochondrial aconitase (m-aconitase) regulation, and selenoprotein-dependent redox homeostasis. Furthermore, this review addresses the pharmacological and toxicological windows associated with high-dose inorganic salt exposure versus sustained food-bound assimilation. The purpose of this review is not to assert the absolute superiority of one mineral form over another, but rather to clarify poorly defined conceptual boundaries, reassess the interpretative scope of existing findings, and emphasize the necessity for future nutritional and biomedical research to adopt precise, form-specific molecular frameworks.

Article.Title: Effects of β-Glucans on Pro-Inflammatory Markers and Behavioral Phenotype in a Valproic Acid (VPA)-Induced Autism Model in Zebrafish
Article.Authors: Camussi D.; Marchese M.; Ogi A.; Fronte B.; Nicoletti F.; Santorelli F.; Mero S.
Article.Abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a multifactorial neurodevelopmental condition in which neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and synaptic dysfunction act as converging mechanisms. Prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA), an antiepileptic drug and histone deacetylase inhibitor, is a recognized environmental risk factor associated with ASD-like phenotypes. Zebrafish, with conserved neuroimmune pathways, rapid development, and quantifiable social behavior, represents a robust model for investigating ASD pathophysiology and testing therapeutic candidates. This study aimed to assess if a previously selected concentration of VPA is capable of inducing persistent alterations from early development through adulthood, and to assess the potential of β-glucans, natural polysaccharides with antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties, to mitigate VPA-induced alterations. A multimodal approach included morphological evaluation, mitochondrial respiration, quantitative PCR of inflammatory markers, and behavioral assays targeting locomotion, anxiety-like responses, and social preference. Low-dose VPA (25 μM) induced developmental and behavioral difficulties, accompanied by a transient reduction in mitochondrial respiratory capacity. β-glucan supplementation attenuated selected VPA-induced alterations, including inflammatory gene-expression changes in larvae and behavioral alterations in adulthood. Overall, these findings provide preclinical evidence that β-glucans can modulate selected VPA-induced inflammatory, molecular and behavioral alterations and support further investigation of their potential effects in neurodevelopmental models.

Article.Title: Lipid Metabolism and Ferroptosis in Cancer: Regulatory Mechanisms, Alternative Splicing, and Therapeutic Implications
Article.Authors: Procopciuc L.; Hangan A.; Lucaciu R.
Article.Abstract: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation and is increasingly recognized as an important vulnerability in cancer. Its sensitivity is determined by the interplay between membrane lipid composition, iron availability, oxidative stress, and antioxidant defense. Cancer cells can adapt to these pressures by altering the balance between polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fatty acids, thereby shifting toward either ferroptosis sensitivity or resistance. Emerging evidence indicates that alternative splicing provides an additional regulatory layer by generating functionally distinct isoforms of genes involved in cystine transport, iron metabolism, oxidative stress, antioxidant protection, and lipid remodeling. Functionally validated splice events affecting the cystine/glutamate antiporter subunit, transferrin receptor, spermidine/spermine acetyltransferase 1, SCL/TAL1 interrupting locus protein, and cluster of differentiation 44 demonstrate that isoform switching can influence ferroptotic susceptibility independently of total gene expression. This review integrates current knowledge on the biochemical basis of ferroptosis, the lipid determinants of ferroptosis sensitivity, and splicing-dependent mechanisms that shape vulnerability and resistance in cancer. Therapeutic strategies targeting ferroptosis defense systems, lipid metabolism, and alternative splicing are also discussed. Finally, we highlight the potential of integrating long-read ribonucleic acid sequencing, lipidomics, proteomics, and functional ferroptosis assays to develop multidimensional vulnerability signatures for patient stratification and precision cancer therapy.

Article.Title: IGF2BP3 Orchestrates Metabolic Reprogramming via Stabilizing m6A-Modified PLK1 mRNA to Promote Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression
Article.Authors: Ji G.; Liu R.; Ding Y.; Wu S.; Luo Y.; Gao C.; Cui X.
Article.Abstract: Epigenetic dysregulation, particularly N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification, drives hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression, yet the oncogenic role of the m6A reader IGF2BP3 remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to elucidate the functional contributions and molecular mechanisms of IGF2BP3 in HCC. Multi-omics databases and tissue microarrays were employed to evaluate IGF2BP3 and PLK1 expression, clinicopathological associations, and prognostic value via Kaplan–Meier, Cox regression, and ROC analyses. Molecular interactions were probed by RIP, luciferase reporter, MeRIP, dot blot, and actinomycin D assays. In the TCGA-LIHC discovery cohort, each showed an independent prognostic association with unfavorable outcomes after adjustment for established clinical covariates. PLK1 mRNA was validated to carry m6A modifications and directly bind IGF2BP3, an interaction abolished by cycloleucine. Functionally, IGF2BP3 upregulated m6A-modified PLK1 by enhancing its mRNA stability, leading to elevated HK2 expression, increased glucose-6-phosphate and lactate levels, and enhanced ECAR, while suppressing mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes, ROS production, and OCR. In conclusion, IGF2BP3 is overexpressed in HCC and tightly associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and adverse outcomes. Altogether, these findings suggest that IGF2BP3 may enhance the stability of the m6A-modified PLK1 transcript, orchestrating a metabolic rewiring from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis, revealing a potential IGF2BP3–m6A–PLK1 axis driving HCC aggressiveness and offering potential therapeutic targets for precision intervention.

Article.Abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are important post-transcriptional regulators of cardiac responses to hypoxia, but how breed and altitude interact to shape cardiac miRNA expression remains unclear. Pairwise comparisons revealed greater breed-related divergence at high altitude and a stronger altitude-associated miRNA response in Tibetan pigs than in Yorkshire pigs. K-means clustering further identified a Tibetan high-altitude-enriched miRNA module whose predicted targets were associated with hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1), mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), adrenergic, calcium, and metabolic pathways. Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), correlation analysis, and miRanda prediction prioritized three candidate regulatory pairs: ssc-miR-671-5p–ATP1B2, novel-miR-212–ADCY6, and ssc-miR-296-3p–PFKM. Article.Title: Disruption of Placental Immune Privilege by Complications of Pregnancy: Consequences for Maternal and Child Health
Article.Authors: Mixtega-Ruiz W.; Contreras Escamilla M.; Sevilla-Montoya R.; Olmos-Ortiz A.; Zaga-Clavellina V.; Castro-Rodríguez D.
Article.Abstract: Maternal chronic conditions, including obesity, diabetes, hypertensive disorders, and autoimmune diseases, promote a systemic proinflammatory environment characterized by oxidative stress and chronic inflammation. These alterations lead to reduced expressions of human leukocyte antigen-G (HLA-G) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), decreased regulatory T (Treg)cell activity, and increased T helper (Th)1/Th17 responses, disrupting placental immune privilege and resulting in increased production of proinflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, trophoblastic dysfunction, and placental senescence. This change in immune privilege contributes to fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, congenital anomalies, and long-term cardiometabolic programming in offspring. Understanding the mechanisms underlying placental immune dysregulation may facilitate the development of targeted therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring immune tolerance and reducing inflammatory and hypoxic signaling pathways to improve maternal and neonatal outcomes. This review summarizes the current state of the field of placental immunological privilege and how maternal chronic conditions like obesity, diabetes, hypertensive disorders, and autoimmune diseases can disrupt it and its possible consequences on the progeny.

Article.Authors: Shan S.; Choy K.; Ling C.; Li H.; Lung H.; To C.; Do C.

Article.Title: Immunomodulatory Effects of MSC-Derived ExtracellularVesicles in Celiac Disease
Article.Authors: Ciccocioppo R.; Mottola I.; Zuliani V.; Adamo A.; Vitale S.; Krampera M.; Camarca A.; Rotondi Aufiero V.; Pisapia L.; Capuano F.; Mazzarella G.; Del Pozzo G.; Gianfrani C.
Article.Abstract: Coeliac disease (CeD) is the most frequent chronic enteropathy, in which intestinal lesions are caused by a dysregulated immune response to gluten proteins.
