Article.Title: The Functional Molecular Biopsy: Exercise-Induced Transpulmonary Multi-Omic Profiling in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
Article.Authors: Oliveira F.; Menezes T.; Mickael C.; Oliveira R.
Article.Abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a disease in which diverse pathogenic drivers converge to promote inflammatory vascular remodeling, ultimately leading to right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and heart failure. Exercise right heart catheterization (RHC) reveals abnormal pulmonary vascular responses early in the disease course and improves diagnosis and risk stratification in PH. Despite major advances in PH research, direct access to the biological processes driving pulmonary vascular remodeling remains limited. Existing clinical assessments predominantly capture the consequences of disease rather than its causes, while tissue-based studies are constrained by limited access to early-stage human samples and the inability to perform serial measurements. This creates a critical need for methodologies capable of interrogating pulmonary vascular biology in vivo and across the disease continuum. We propose that combining exercise RHC with paired transpulmonary omics measurements may provide such an opportunity. The strategy of measuring the change in molecular concentrations across the pulmonary circulation during physiological stress has the potential to function as a dynamic molecular biopsy of the pulmonary vasculature, linking abnormal exercise hemodynamics to the biological pathways that drive disease, although current supporting evidence remains limited to small, heterogeneous proof-of-concept cohorts. In this review, we examine the physiological basis, technical framework, biological insights, and translational implications of this emerging approach for PH.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial Metabolic Reprogramming and Immune Evasion in Colorectal Cancer: Research Advances and Mechanistic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Ding D.; Hu J.; Wang Y.; Jiang L.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most prevalent malignancies of the gastrointestinal tract worldwide. Notably, most patients with microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumors show primary resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), creating an unmet clinical need. The mechanisms underlying immune evasion and strategies to overcome therapeutic resistance have therefore become important topics in CRC immunology research. Recent studies indicate that mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion in CRC. Tumor cells display metabolic plasticity through dynamic shifts between glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), which can intensify the depletion of critical nutrients, particularly glucose and glutamine, within the tumor microenvironment (TME). These metabolic changes can also promote the accumulation of immunosuppressive metabolites, including lactate, thereby impairing the function of effector cells such as CD8+ T cells and dendritic cells (DCs) and supporting the expansion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Lactate may further reshape the immune landscape through hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 1 (HCAR1) signaling and histone lactylation. In parallel, mitochondrial quality control can regulate tumor immunogenicity by influencing mtDNA availability and cGAS-STING signaling. Therapeutic approaches targeting glycolysis, glutamine metabolism, fatty acid oxidation, lactate transport, and mitochondrial dynamics have shown immune-sensitizing activity in preclinical models. Nanodelivery systems and gene-editing technologies may improve the spatial and cellular specificity of these interventions. This review summarizes how mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion in CRC and evaluates mitochondria-directed strategies for improving treatment responsiveness, particularly in MSS CRC.

Article.Title: Co-Regulation Analysis of Domain-Specific Phosphosites Reveals Insights into the Phosphoregulation-Directed Functional Diversity of Nucleolin
Article.Authors: Shaji M.; Thomas J.; Sekhar P.; Subair S.; Mahin A.; Dcunha L.; Sambreena A.; Raju R.; Soman S.
Article.Abstract: Nucleolin (NCL) is a highly phosphorylated, multilocalized, pleiotropic nucleolar protein involved in chromatin organization, DNA damage response, the cell cycle, RNA metabolism, and ribosome biogenesis. A large-scale integration of publicly available human cellular phosphoproteome datasets led to the identification of 18 frequently detected/reported phosphosites across 1266 profiling and 507 differential datasets. Amidst various strategies currently being considered to target NCL in cancers, multi-domain distribution of these phosphosites differentially regulated across distinct cancers highlighted its plausible involvement in tumor-associated regulatory mechanisms. This demands the exploration of the potential kinases and interactors associated with these phosphorylation events. We performed a co-occurrence analysis to explore potential coordinated phosphorylation events among them and across other phosphoproteins. An integrative analysis of phosphosite-specific co-regulation, upstream kinases, and interaction networks was employed to explore potential phosphosite-specific signaling associations. Intriguingly, our analysis inferred the association of the predominant phosphosites within the acidic tract with chromatin organization and histone-related functions, whereas TPxKK motif phosphosites were linked to NCL localization, chromosome segregation, and nucleolar reorganization. Phosphosites in the RRM domain showed a potential association with RNA-binding proteins and metabolic pathways. Collectively, these findings suggest a domain-specific phosphosite-centric regulatory network of NCL, providing a valuable reference framework for future experimental studies and phosphosite-directed therapeutic strategies in cancers.

Article.Title: Acute Postprandial Glycemic and Antioxidant Responses to Maqui Berry Gummies in Adults with Overweight/Obesity: A Small Within-Subject Pilot Study
Article.Authors: Acevedo-Hernández P.; Valero-Jara V.; Jara-Gutiérrez C.; Ibacache-Quiroga C.; Jorquera G.; Thomas-Valdés S.
Article.Abstract: Maqui berry is rich in anthocyanins and has attracted interest as a functional food ingredient with potential metabolic and antioxidant effects. In the reported analyses, co-consumption of gummies was associated with lower glucose concentrations (p < 0.05), and total glucose AUC was lower under MMBG than under Control (p < 0.0207). Insulin at 120 min was higher under both gummy conditions (p < 0.01), and GLP-1 was higher under MMBG (p < 0.05); however, changes in GLP-1 from baseline did not differ significantly among conditions (p > 0.05). Direct comparisons of baseline-adjusted analyses in antioxidant biomarkers established a differential response among gummies formulations, with UMBG exhibiting better TRAP results with decrement of SOD activity when adjusted for the corresponding baseline value. Article.Title: Metabolic Dysfunction and T-Cell Exhaustion in Colorectal Cancer: Mechanisms, Microenvironment Remodeling, and Therapeutic Opportunities
Article.Authors: Jeon J.; Baek H.; Park K.; Park M.; Heo N.; Cheon S.; Kim G.; Kim S.
Article.Abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide. Metabolic disorders such as obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome are associated with CRC risk. Metabolic abnormalities may contribute to colorectal tumorigenesis and reshape the tumor immune microenvironment, which in turn influence immune dysfunction and therapeutic resistance. Exhausted CD8+ T cells exhibit impaired effector function, sustained inhibitory receptor expression, and transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. Metabolic stressors within the CRC microenvironment may modulate T-cell function and exhaustion-associated states. Additionally, other immune populations (natural killer cells, macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, dendritic cells, and regulatory T cells) may develop distinct dysfunctional or immunosuppressive states. Recent single-cell and spatial studies have indicated the heterogeneity of these immunometabolic interactions in CRC. This review examines the interactions of the systemic and tumor-associated metabolic alterations with T-cell exhaustion and other forms of immune dysfunction in CRC. We discuss the influence of glucose, lipid, amino acid, and mitochondrial metabolism, hypoxia, microbiota-derived metabolites, and chronic inflammation in shaping tumor–immune interactions. Finally, we reviewed therapeutic strategies targeting immunometabolic pathways and their potential integration with immune checkpoint blockade. Overall, understanding these interactions may help identify immunometabolic vulnerabilities for informing precise therapeutic strategies for CRC.

Article.Title: Genomic Characterization of Clinical Staphylococcus aureus Isolates from Ecuador Reveals Diverse Lineages and Genomic Similarity Among Sequence Type 2625 Isolates
Article.Authors: Vinueza A.; Šefcová M.; Mejía Limones I.; Bejarano L.; Szaboová R.; Herich R.; Andrade Mena G.; Rosero-Tixicuro A.; Barba P.; Larrea-Álvarez M.
Article.Abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is characterized by substantial genomic diversity, with lineages differing in antimicrobial resistance, virulence-associated determinants, and accessory genetic content. However, genomic data from Ecuador remain comparatively limited. Here, we characterized five clinical S. aureus isolates recovered in Ibarra, Ecuador, using phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequencing, and compared them with publicly available Ecuadorian genomes. The isolates represented four sequence types (ST8, ST30, ST72, and ST2625), including four MRSA isolates and one MSSA isolate. Whole-genome analysis identified differences in antimicrobial resistance determinants, virulence-associated genes, and replicons, while phenotypic susceptibility profiles generally corresponded with the detected resistance traits. The Ecuadorian collection showed a diverse population structure, with ST8 predominating. Placement within globally circulating lineages showed that the ST8 isolates clustered with USA300-LV (CA12), the ST30 isolate with G2-Sg2-Pr, and the ST72 isolate with clade B. A focused phylogenomic analysis of ST2625 showed limited genomic divergence among Ecuadorian and international isolates, with broadly similar resistance and virulence-associated profiles. These findings add genomic data from northern Ecuador and illustrate variation in the genetic composition of circulating S. aureus lineages. Continued genomic surveillance across additional geographic settings may help clarify the distribution and diversity of S. aureus in the country.

Article.Title: Antibiotic Perturbation and Gut Symbiont Recolonization Affect the Cold Tolerance of Apis cerana
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Zhao J.; Jiang L.; Zuo C.; Guo Y.; Guo Z.
Article.Abstract: The gut microbiota contributes to host stress tolerance, yet its role in cold adaptation in the Eastern honey bee (Apis cerana) remains poorly understood. Here, A. cerana workers were treated with three antibiotics (tetracycline, streptomycin sulfate, and tylosin) at 50 μg/mL for 3 and 7 days, followed by cold survival assessment at 10 °C and 16S rRNA sequencing of the gut microbiota. Five cold tolerance-associated symbionts were subsequently evaluated in bacterial recolonization assays. Three days of antibiotic treatment significantly reduced bee survival under cold stress at 10 °C compared with the control, with the median survival time decreasing to 60 h across all groups. Seven days of streptomycin sulfate treatment further shortened the median survival time to 48 h. Antibiotics markedly depleted key symbionts, including Apibacter (from 23.89% to as low as 1.30%), Snodgrassella, and Lactobacillus. Recolonization with Apilactobacillus kunkeei and Gilliamella apicola significantly extended the cold median survival time to 92 h (p < 0.01 and p < 0.001, respectively), whereas Providencia rettgeri, Klebsiella oxytoca, and Bifidobacterium indicum extended it to 88 h. These findings indicate that gut symbionts modulate cold tolerance in A. cerana and that A. kunkeei and G. apicola can improve bee survival under low-temperature stress.

Article.Title: Association of Glucagon-like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists Versus Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 Inhibitors with Tuberculosis and Mortality in Adults with Diabetes
Article.Authors: Hsu C.; Chang R.; Chen C.; Chu K.; Jiang Y.; Hong W.; Chen I.; Lin M.
Article.Abstract: Diabetes is associated with an increased risk of tuberculosis (TB), but whether the class of glucose-lowering therapy is associated with TB outcomes remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study to examine the association between glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) use versus dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i) use and the risk of TB and mortality. We used de-identified records from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults with diabetes who had a qualifying record for either a GLP-1 RA or a DPP-4i between 2016 and 2024 were eligible. Cohort entry was defined as the first qualifying drug-class record during this period. Patients with prior-year use of the comparator drug class, a history of TB, or death before cohort entry were excluded. Propensity score matching was performed at a 1:1 ratio. Outcomes assessed during days 1–365 included TB (ICD-10-CM A15–A19), the platform-defined death outcome, and a composite outcome of gastrointestinal and hepatobiliary diagnoses. After matching, 466,903 patients remained in each group. GLP-1 RA exposure was associated with fewer recorded TB events, deaths, and gastrointestinal/hepatobiliary events than DPP-4i exposure during the first year after cohort entry. TB was recorded in 155 GLP-1 RA users and 320 DPP-4i users (HR, 0.472; 95% CI, 0.390–0.572). The corresponding numbers for the platform-defined death outcome were 7575 and 14,572 (HR, 0.505; 95% CI, 0.492–0.520), and those for gastrointestinal/hepatobiliary diagnoses were 15,914 and 20,559 (HR, 0.750; 95% CI, 0.735–0.766). The analysis restricted to patients with type 2 diabetes (ICD-10-CM E11) yielded a similar association for TB. Residual imbalance in body mass index (BMI) and residual confounding, including confounding by indication, limit a causal interpretation.

Article.Title: Profiling of Bioactive Metabolites and In Vitro Multifunctional Properties of Postbiotic Cell-Free Supernatant Derived from Probiotic Lactic Acid Bacteria Isolated from Fermented Olives
Article.Authors: Abouloifa H.; Maiouet I.; Bouqafa A.; Mouhtadi N.; Bouzzit M.; Bentouhami N.; Ghabbour N.; Mellouki F.; Karboune S.
Article.Abstract: This work aims to characterize the bioactive metabolite profile and in vitro multifunctional properties of postbiotic cell-free supernatants (Postbiotic-CFSs) derived from three lactic acid bacteria (Levilactobacillus brevis S27, Lactiplantibacillus pentosus S42, and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum S62) isolated from fermented green olives. The postbiotic-CFSs were analyzed for their bioactive metabolites, emulsification index E24%, and antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antidiabetic activities. The bioactive metabolites identified in all postbiotics included organic acids (lactate, citrate, and oxalate), SCFAs (acetate), hydrogen peroxide, diacetyl, exopolysaccharides (EPSs), proteins, biosurfactants, polyphenols, and flavonoids. The postbiotic-CFSs exhibited emulsification index (E24%) values ranging from 21.5% to 38.2%. Furthermore, they demonstrated antimicrobial properties with inhibition diameters ranging from 14.10 to 16.9 mm against pathogenic bacteria and from 15.8 to 23.50 mm against yeast, while fungal mycelial growth was inhibited by 35.77 to 45.09%. All postbiotics demonstrated antioxidant activities of DPPH from 65.91 to 68.55% and FRAP values from 1707.31 to 1765 µg AAE/mL, as well as anti-inflammatory activity (11.83–12.88%) and antidiabetic activity (34.38–93.75%). These findings highlight the significant potential of postbiotic-CFSs as natural bio-preservative agents in food products and as a source of bioactive metabolites with multifunctional health benefits for consumers.

Article.Title: Vascular Smooth Muscle Cell Plasticity in Atherosclerosis: From Macrophage-like Transdifferentiation to Therapeutic Targeting
Article.Authors: Zhang M.; Wang Z.; Lu M.; Hao J.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Atherosclerosis remains the leading cause of cardiovascular mortality worldwide. Vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) were long regarded as passive structural elements of the arterial wall, but they are now recognized as highly plastic cells capable of transdifferentiating into macrophage-like cells (MLCs). This conversion promotes plaque inflammation, matrix degradation, and necrotic core expansion, yet the mechanisms that control it remain poorly defined. This review synthesizes current understanding of the multilayered regulatory networks that govern VSMC-to-MLC transdifferentiation. These networks couple upstream signaling through MAPK, Notch, TGF-β, and PI3K/AKT to master transcription factors such as KLF4, IRF7, and ZEB2. They further extend to epigenetic mechanisms encompassing DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding RNAs, and metabolic reprogramming involving cholesterol efflux and lipophagy. We then assess therapeutic strategies that prevent or reverse this conversion, including miRNA replacement, kinase inhibition, LXR activation and autophagy induction. We further highlight unresolved questions on MLC heterogeneity, reversibility, and targeted delivery, outlining priorities for translating these insights into clinical benefit.

Article.Title: Integrated Genetic Mapping, Transcriptomic, and Small RNA Analysis of Fruit Bitterness in Melon
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Yuan G.; Lu M.; Han W.; Zhang H.; Wang J.; Zhang H.; Li C.; Ma J.
Article.Abstract: Melon fruit bitterness, mainly caused by cucurbitacin B (CuB), is a major quality defect that reduces consumer acceptance and market value. However, the genetic and regulatory mechanisms underlying fruit bitterness remain largely unclear. In this study, two thin-skinned melon inbred lines, A54 (bitter leaves and fruit) and B15 (bitter leaves but non-bitter fruit), were used to dissect the genetic basis of fruit bitterness. Genetic analysis revealed that fruit bitterness in A54 is controlled by a single dominant locus. Through bulked-segregant analysis sequencing (BSA-seq) and fine mapping, the candidate region was delimited to a 133-kb interval on chromosome 9, which contains four bHLH genes. Among them, MELO3C005610 (formerly designated CmBr) exhibited 25.5-fold higher expression in A54 than in B15 and was identified as the most plausible positional candidate gene. We further developed a near-isogenic line with bitter fruit (B15NIL) and performed integrated transcriptome, small RNA, and degradome sequencing. Twelve CuB biosynthetic genes were significantly up-regulated in B15NIL fruits, indicating coordinated activation of the cucurbitacin biosynthetic pathway. In addition, small RNA and degradome analyses identified candidate miRNA-target interactions that may contribute to post-transcriptional regulation of CuB biosynthesis, although these interactions require further functional validation. Together, these findings provide a framework for understanding the genetic basis of fruit bitterness in melon and suggest candidate targets for future functional validation and breeding of non-bitter cultivars.

Article.Title: Concentration-Associated DNA Methylation Remodeling of Oncogenic Signaling Networks Following Moringa oleifera Treatment in Metastatic PC3 Prostate Cancer Cells
Article.Authors: Mancuso F.; Lilli C.; Bellucci C.; Ceccarelli V.; Stabile A.; Gambelunghe C.; Pugliese L.; Cecchetti M.; Antognelli C.; Baroni T.
Article.Abstract: PC3 prostate cancer (PCa) cells exhibit high metastatic potential, androgen independence, and activation of multiple oncogenic signaling pathways. Although Moringa oleifera has recognized anticancer properties, its effects on DNA methylation in aggressive PCa remain largely unexplored. Here, PC3 cells were treated with Moringa oleifera extract (MO) at 100 or 200 μg/mL and evaluated using functional and molecular analyses alongside genome-wide DNA methylation profiling. Both concentrations reduced AKT phosphorylation and the expression of mesenchymal and invasion-associated markers, whereas increased apoptosis was observed at 200 μg/mL MO. ERK1/2 phosphorylation differed between the two concentrations but was not significantly reduced relative to untreated controls. Methylation profiling revealed concentration-specific pathway-enrichment profiles among genes associated with differentially methylated regions (DMRs). At 100 μg/mL, hypermethylated DMR-associated genes were enriched mainly in small GTPase signaling, focal adhesion, cytoskeletal organization, axon guidance, MAPK, Rap1, and RHO signaling. At 200 μg/mL, enrichment involved cell adhesion, Wnt signaling, RAC1/CDC42 GTPase cycles, and VEGF/VEGFR2-mediated signaling. Hypomethylated DMR-associated genes showed distinct but partly overlapping enrichment profiles. In the direct comparison, DMRs with higher methylation at 100 μg/mL were associated with axon guidance, focal adhesion, actin cytoskeleton regulation, MAPK, and EPH–Ephrin signaling, whereas those with higher methylation at 200 μg/mL were associated mainly with NOTCH and RHOB/RHOC signaling. These findings identify concentration-specific DNA methylation changes in genes belonging to networks relevant to aggressive PCa, accompanied by molecular and cellular responses, without establishing a causal relationship between methylation changes and those responses.

Article.Title: Discovery of Putative Phosphorylation Sites in Cre1 and Ace1 as Engineering Targets for Enhanced Cellulase Production in Trichoderma reesei
Article.Authors: Liu J.; Wang S.; Gao X.; Chen Y.; Wang W.
Article.Abstract: In the filamentous fungus Trichoderma reesei, cellulase production is subject to carbon catabolite repression (CCR) mediated by the key repressors Cre1 and Ace1. In this study, we identified two previously unreported phosphorylation sites—S204 in Cre1 and S145 in Ace1—through phosphoproteomic profiling. Site-directed mutagenesis revealed that dephosphorylation-mimicking mutations (Cre1S204A and Ace1S145A) significantly relieved CCR and promoted cellulase biosynthesis, while phosphomimetic mutations exerted opposite effects. Notably, the Cre1S204A/Ace1S145A double mutant exhibited a combined enhancement in cellulase activity, achieving a 0.7-fold increase in pNPCase activity compared to the parental strain, along with substantially upregulated cellulase gene transcription and increased extracellular CBH1 accumulation. These results demonstrate that S204 and S145 are functionally relevant phosphorylation sites that negatively modulate cellulase production. Our findings provide novel engineering targets for strain improvement and, more broadly, open new avenues for investigating the phosphorylation-based regulatory mechanisms of Cre1 and Ace1 in future studies. From an applied perspective, the work offers a straightforward and effective genetic strategy for the rational design of high-performance fungal strains for lignocellulose bioconversion.

Article.Title: Potential Molecular Links Between Triclosan Exposure and Prostate Cancer: An Integrative Computational Analysis
Article.Authors: You H.; Zou Y.; Liu J.; Xiao Y.; Li J.; Xu J.; Xu W.
Article.Abstract: Triclosan (TCS) is a widely used antimicrobial and endocrine-disrupting chemical whose potential relevance to prostate cancer (PCa) biology remains insufficiently understood. We integrated multi-omics and computational analyses to identify candidate targets that overlap between predicted TCS-related molecular targets and PCa-related transcriptomic alterations. Cross-database target mapping, differential expression, and network analyses were combined with machine learning, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, Mendelian randomization, and single-cell transcriptomic profiling. Pathway analyses highlighted oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation as key processes shared between predicted TCS-related targets and PCa-associated transcriptomic alterations. Machine learning prioritized five candidate genes—FERMT2, F5, PRKCA, ABCC4, and ACOX2—with discriminative value for PCa classification in the analyzed cohorts. Docking and molecular dynamics simulations supported plausible binding compatibility of TCS to ABCC4 and ACOX2. Mendelian randomization suggested that genetically predicted ABCC4 expression may be associated with PCa risk. Single-cell analysis further showed cell-type-specific expression of candidate genes in tumor-enriched epithelial populations. These findings provide an integrative framework for generating mechanistic hypotheses on how TCS-related molecular targets may be associated with PCa biology.

Article.Title: Heat-Induced HSAT3 Transcription and Nuclear Stress Body Assembly in Human Myeloid Cells
Article.Authors: Ponomartsev N.; Enukashvily N.
Article.Abstract: Heat shock activates heat shock factor 1 (HSF1), which induces classical heat shock genes and promotes transcription of pericentromeric HSAT3 repeats that contribute to nuclear stress body (nSB) formation. Although well characterized in epithelial cells, this response remains poorly understood in myeloid cells. We compared heat-induced HSAT3 transcription and nSB assembly in epithelial and monocytic cell lines, using A549 and THP-1 as models. pHSF1 (Ser326) levels, HSPA1A and HSAT3 expression, and nSB formation were assessed by Western blotting, qPCR, immunofluorescence, RNA-FISH, and 5-ethynyluridine labeling. Heat shock increased pHSF1 (Ser326) levels and HSPA1A expression in both models. A549 cells showed increased HSAT3 transcript levels and prominent nSB formation, whereas undifferentiated THP-1 cells showed little immediate change in HSAT3 transcript levels and did not form prominent nSBs. 5-EU labeling revealed discrete nascent RNA foci in heat-shocked A549, but not THP-1, cells. These foci overlapped with HSF1 and were associated with HSAT3-related hybridization signals. However, click chemistry increased accessibility of genomic satellite sequences, limiting RNA-specific interpretation of the HSAT3 probe signal. PMA-induced differentiation enabled an increase in HSAT3 transcript levels during heat shock and nSB assembly. These findings identify cellular state as a determinant of heat shock-induced satellite transcription and nSB assembly.

Article.Title: Harnessing Neurogenic Potential of Glial Cell Types as an Emerging Strategy for Treating Epilepsy
Article.Authors: Chesnokova E.; Kotova I.; Reznikova A.; Balaban P.; Bal N.
Article.Abstract: In every third case of epilepsy, anti-seizure drugs are ineffective, so the search for new therapies for this disease is ongoing. In recent years, new methods for generating cells with desired properties, as well as for the targeted expression of genes in specific cell types in situ within the brain, were designed. These methods allowed researchers to consider the idea of transforming resident glial cells into neurons in conditions like epilepsy; in such pathologies it may rescue both neuronal loss and gliosis. In this review, we describe epilepsy-associated pathological changes in glial cells, the neurogenic potential of different glial types (their similarities to neural stem cells and their inherent limited ability to produce neurons in response to brain damage), and existing methods of neuronal transdifferentiation starting with different cell types with varying proximity in lineage distance to neurons. Based on overlaps between these topics, we make conclusions about the applicability of glia-to-neuron conversion in treating epilepsy and the most important challenges that should be considered in designing experiments and clinical trials for this strategy.

Article.Title: Tissue Factor Expression Is Associated with Distinct Pattern of Immune-Cell Infiltration in the Ovarian Tumor Microenvironment
Article.Authors: Mohiuddin T.; Binte Hafiz F.; Sheng W.; Zhang C.; Al-Rawe M.; Zeppernick F.; Tchaikovski S.; Meinhold-Heerlein I.; Hussain A.
Article.Abstract: Tissue factor (TF) has been implicated in tumor progression and immune regulation, but its cellular sources and relationship with immune infiltration in ovarian cancer remain incompletely defined. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (GSE232314), analyses of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) ovarian cancer cohort, and multiplex immunofluorescence in an independent 25-case tissue microarray (TMA). Single-cell analysis showed that TF expression was concentrated in tumor epithelial cells and a discrete endothelial subpopulation, with minimal expression in immune and other stromal compartments. In the TCGA cohort, TF expression was not significantly associated with tumor stage, grade, disease-free survival, or overall survival. In TF-stratified analyses, however, high CD8+ T cell infiltration was associated with improved survival in the low-TF expression subgroup (HR = 0.60) but with worse survival in the high-TF subgroup (HR = 1.72); high M1 macrophage infiltration was associated with improved survival only in the low-TF subgroup. TF expression correlated negatively with estimated CD8+ T cell, memory B cell, and M1 macrophage infiltration and positively with naïve B cell infiltration. In the TMA cohort, high-TF tumors showed significantly lower CD56+ NK-cell and CD68+ macrophage infiltration and a lower CD68/CD163 ratio. Together, these findings show cross-sectional associations between TF expression and reduced measured abundance of several antitumor immune populations and a stratum-dependent association between CD8+ T cell infiltration and survival. These associations were not fully concordant between the transcriptomic (TCGA) and protein-level (TMA) cohorts and require prospective, formally tested validation. TF warrants further investigation as a candidate immune-context biomarker in ovarian cancer.

Article.Title: Immune Dysregulation as a Driver of Coronary Heart Disease
Article.Authors: Chu S.; Zhou H.; Wan H.
Article.Abstract: Coronary heart disease (CHD) affects millions of individuals worldwide and remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. It compromises quality of life primarily through myocardial ischemia resulting from progressive coronary arterial narrowing and contributes to a wide range of adverse clinical outcomes. Although current therapeutic strategies, including coronary revascularization, lipid-lowering therapy, and plaque stabilization, have substantially improved patient prognosis, they do not fully address the underlying immunopathological mechanisms driving disease progression. Increasing evidence suggests that immune-mediated inflammation and vascular injury play critical roles in the initiation, progression, and destabilization of atherosclerotic plaques, highlighting the immune system as a potential therapeutic target in CHD management. In this review, we summarize recent advances in our understanding of the contributions of innate and adaptive immune responses to CHD pathogenesis. Collectively, current evidence indicates that immune dysregulation is a central driver of atherogenesis and its clinical manifestations, supporting the development of targeted immunomodulatory strategies as promising approaches for the prevention and treatment of CHD.

Article.Title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Analysis Reveals Shared Macrophage-Associated Inflammatory Signatures in MASLD/NAFLD and Rheumatoid Arthritis
Article.Authors: Yu W.; Nie Q.; Wu Y.; Lan X.; Liu J.; Xu D.; Guan S.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease/nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) may share inflammatory mechanisms, although their common cellular basis remains unclear. We integrated bulk transcriptomic datasets (GSE66676 and GSE55235), single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from murine RA synovium (GSE192504) and NASH liver (GSE129516), disease-association analysis, molecular docking, and in vitro experiments in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages. Bulk transcriptomic analysis identified 630 shared differentially expressed genes, including 344 concordantly upregulated genes enriched in immune response, cytokine and chemokine signaling, phagosome, Toll-like receptor signaling, and Fc receptor-mediated phagocytosis; a strict dual-dataset intersection further defined 18 core genes significantly upregulated in both diseases. Immune-signature analysis indicated altered myeloid cell-associated inflammatory activity in both diseases, and several shared genes, including S100A8, S100A9, FCER1G, FCGR3A, LYZ, and MS4A7, correlated positively with monocyte/macrophage-related signatures. Single-cell analysis identified macrophage subsets with high S100a9 expression and elevated shared myeloid inflammatory signature scores in both RA synovium and NASH liver. Triptolide showed favorable predicted binding to the S100A8/A9 complex and reduced LPS-induced inflammatory cytokine secretion and expression of the six-gene signature in RAW264.7 cells, supporting the hypothesis that S100A9-associated inflammatory macrophage activation represents a candidate target for further investigation. These findings support a shared S100A9-positive inflammatory macrophage-associated program in MASLD/NAFLD and RA, and support the hypothesis that the S100A8/A9 complex represents a candidate target for further investigation.

Article.Title: Evaluation of Two Combined Analytical Approaches to Assess the Impact of Rare Variants on Severe COVID-19
Article.Authors: Rosamilia F.; Recchi G.; Cangelosi D.; Decherchi S.; Lantieri F.; Croci S.; Salvarani C.; Cavalli A.; Rusmini M.; Ceccherini I.; Uva P.
Article.Abstract: Severe COVID-19 displays substantial inter-individual variability that cannot be fully explained by common genetic variants, suggesting a contribution of rare functional variation. We performed whole-genome sequencing in 191 Italian patients (96 moderate, 95 severe) to investigate rare coding variants (minor allele frequency <1% and <5%) via complementary network-based and machine learning approaches. Classical single-variant and burden tests did not identify significant associations after multiple testing correction. However, Network-based Heterogeneity Clustering (NHC) revealed that multiple gene clusters were enriched in severe cases, particularly those involving RNA polymerase II–mediated transcription, RNA metabolism, and vesicle-mediated transport pathways. Gene-level rare variant analysis via the variable threshold method identified five genes significantly associated with severe disease (FDR < 0.05), namely, EIF4G3, GTF2F2, LY96, COX6A1, and STK11, which are involved in transcriptional and translational regulation, innate immune signaling, and mitochondrial function. Unsupervised biclustering significantly stratified patients by severity, and a decision tree model highlighted the burden of DOCK10 variants as a key discriminator between phenotypes. Convergence between the network-based and machine learning results further supported the robustness of the identified signals. Overall, our integrative framework underscores the contribution of rare variants to COVID-19 severity and highlights the coordinated perturbation of interconnected molecular pathways as a determinant of clinical outcome.

Article.Title: Nanoencapsulation of Essential Oils for Food Preservation and Agricultural Applications: A Systematic Review of Biological Efficacy, Safety, and Technological Challenges
Article.Authors: Diogo Gonçalves S.; Silva L.
Article.Abstract: Essential oils (EOs) are promising natural bioactive compounds for food preservation and sustainable agriculture because of their antimicrobial, antifungal, antioxidant, and insecticidal properties. However, poor water solubility, high volatility, and chemical instability limit their practical application. Nanoencapsulation has emerged as an effective strategy to improve EOs stability, bioavailability, controlled release, and biological performance. This systematic review evaluated the efficacy, safety, and technological challenges of nanoencapsulated EOs for food and agricultural applications. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science were systematically searched, and original experimental studies reporting at least one safety-related outcome were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment Tool for In Vitro Studies, and results were synthesized narratively. Of 776 records identified, 19 studies met the inclusion criteria. Nanoencapsulation generally improved EOs stability, controlled release, and biological persistence while frequently enhancing antimicrobial, antifungal, antioxidant, insecticidal, and preservation efficacy. Preliminary safety assessments, including cytotoxicity, hemolysis, phytotoxicity, sensory evaluation, and nanoparticle migration, were generally favourable. However, methodological heterogeneity, predominantly laboratory-based evidence, and limited long-term toxicity and industrial validation reduce the certainty of the evidence. Overall, nanoencapsulation represents a promising approach for enhancing the practical application of EOs, although standardized safety assessments and large-scale validation studies are needed before widespread commercial implementation.

Article.Title: Maternal Circulating Angiogenic Biomarkers for Predicting Fetal Growth Restriction and Small-for-Gestational-Age Birth Without Preeclampsia
Article.Authors: Kim M.; Lee E.; Lee H.; Choi A.
Article.Abstract: Maternal circulating angiogenic factors are established biomarkers in preeclampsia, but their early profiles in fetal growth impairment without preeclampsia remain unclear. We quantitatively synthesized data from observational studies measuring maternal serum placental growth factor (PlGF), soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), or their ratio before 29 weeks and before clinical recognition of growth impairment in singleton pregnancies without preeclampsia, subsequently classified as fetal growth restriction (FGR), small for gestational age (SGA), or unaffected. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched through April 2026; 22 studies were included. In random-effects meta-analysis, PlGF was lower in affected pregnancies (standardized mean difference [SMD] −0.38; 95% CI −0.63 to −0.13; I2 = 92.0%; 19 studies), whereas sFlt-1 did not differ (SMD 0.03; 95% CI −0.27 to 0.34; I2 = 79.5%; 12 studies) and the ratio was higher in the primary analysis (SMD 0.39; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.70; I2 = 80.0%; seven studies). This pattern suggests that the ratio signal was influenced largely by lower PlGF. Bivariate analysis of five PlGF accuracy studies yielded a summary sensitivity of 0.29 and specificity of 0.86. Despite substantial heterogeneity, reduced PlGF was the most consistent early angiogenic feature in pregnancies subsequently classified as FGR/SGA without preeclampsia. Its low sensitivity does not support its use as a stand-alone screening test, but these findings warrant further evaluation of PlGF within multimarker prediction models.

Article.Title: Amino Acid Profiles in Dried Blood Spots and Clinical Outcomes in Selective Fetal Growth Restriction: A Twin-Pair Study
Article.Authors: Chagovets V.; Tokareva A.; Frankevich N.; Novoselova A.; Yushina M.; Hajjar F.; Eldarov C.; Michailova O.; Karapetyan T.; Ryumina I.; Frankevich V.; Sukhikh G.
Article.Abstract: Selective fetal growth restriction (sFGR) remains a leading cause of perinatal morbidity in multiple pregnancies; however, its pathogenesis is not yet fully elucidated. Investigating amino acid metabolism in weight-discordant twins may uncover critical metabolic pathways involved in this condition, given the essential roles of amino acids in fetal growth and energy supply. The use of dried blood spots (DBSs) enables the minimally invasive, retrospective evaluation of neonatal metabolic profiles, providing a unique opportunity to identify sFGR-associated signature and clarify differences between monochorionic (MC) and dichorionic (DC) placentation. In the present study, we profiled 23 amino acids in DBS from 23 twin pairs (11 discordant and 12 non-discordant, defined by postnatal birth-weight discordance), stratified by chorionicity, to identify specific metabolic signatures associated with sFGR and to evaluate their temporal dynamics and clinical significance. Our findings suggest that chorionicity is associated with distinct amino acid signatures of postnatal birth-weight discordance. In MC twins, the larger co-twin displayed significantly elevated glycine, α- and γ-aminobutyric acids, serine, asparagine, and citrulline, alongside reduced proline and tryptophan. In DC twins, the larger co-twin exhibited higher α-aminobutyric acid, valine, leucine, arginine, and citrulline, whereas glycine was elevated in the smaller co-twin. Pathway enrichment analysis further suggested the enrichment of amino acid transport and protein synthesis pathways in MC postnatal discordance and nitric oxide (NO)-dependent signaling in DC postnatal discordance. Longitudinal follow-up showed a statistically significant attenuation of intrapair differences for several amino acids by the second time point. All 11 discordant pairs were retrospectively confirmed to fulfil the Delphi criteria for sFGR. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

Article.Title: Identification of SOD1 Gene Variants in Mexican Patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Article.Authors: Gómez-Pérez C.; Ramírez-García M.; Ruiz-Sánchez E.; Romero-Hidalgo S.; Ochoa-Morales A.; Jara-Prado A.; Méndez-Armenta M.; Nava-Ruiz C.; Yescas-Gómez P.
Article.Abstract: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing, fatal neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. Clinical manifestations include progressive muscle weakness, amyotrophy, fasciculations, dysphagia, and fatal respiratory failure. The median survival after symptom onset is typically 2 to 5 years. Despite its severity, the epidemiological profile and genetic landscape of ALS in Latin American populations, particularly in Mexico, remain unclear. In this study, we evaluated the mutational spectrum of the SOD1 gene in a Mexican cohort of 156 ALS patients. Using high-resolution melting (HRM) analysis and Sanger sequencing, we identified 22 SOD1 variants in 42 of 156 patients (overall variant carrier frequency, 26.92%). Pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants were found in 21 patients (13.5%). Notably, 5 of the 22 variants were novel, expanding the spectrum of SOD1 variants. The variant carrier frequency identified in this study is higher than that reported for European populations but similar to frequencies observed in Asian populations. Our results highlight the distinct genetic heterogeneity of ALS in Mexico and demonstrate that HRM is a rapid and effective method for identifying SOD1 gene variants.

Article.Title: Loss of Sidt2 in Mice Resembles Danon Disease and Results in Induction of a Type I Interferon Response with Increased Apoptosis
Article.Authors: Barrios M.; Nguyen T.; Houweling P.; Frank D.; Garton F.; Lidov H.; Tsui E.; Garnham A.; Ambardekar A.; Smyth G.; Mestroni L.; Cleveland J.; Taylor M.; North K.; Hunter C.; Pang K.
Article.Abstract: SIDT2 is a lysosomal membrane protein that—together with LAMP2—has been implicated in a recently described process known as RNAutophagy. Mutations in LAMP2 have long been known to cause Danon disease, a rare lysosomal storage disorder that affects multiple organ systems including brain and skeletal muscle. Recently, we have shown that loss of SIDT2 function in both humans and mice causes brain dysfunction, and it has been previously observed that loss of SIDT2 in mice also leads to muscle damage and reduced muscle strength. Here, we show that changes in the skeletal muscle of Sidt2−/− mice are reminiscent of those seen in Danon disease as evidenced by accumulation of autophagic vacuoles with sarcolemmal features, selective atrophy of fast twitch fibers, and a shared alteration in gene expression. Moreover, we find that loss of SIDT2 not only leads to impaired autophagy in skeletal muscle as previously described but also stimulates a type I interferon response and increased apoptosis.

Article.Title: Provenance-Associated Confounding in Cross-Collection Comparisons of Urease Inhibitors: A Quantified Reference Scale and a Domain-Aware Alternative
Article.Authors: Farías-Abarca J.; Urra G.; Henríquez C.; Yáñez O.; Osorio M.; Palma J.; Morales-Quintana L.; Suardíaz R.; Bustos D.
Article.Abstract: Reference-library comparisons are widely used in target-focused cheminformatics to characterize the chemical space occupied by bioactive compounds. The separation obtained from such comparisons may, however, reflect differences in library provenance rather than target-related chemistry. The present study quantifies this effect using UI-Ref, a curated reference set of 1218 compounds reported in urease assays in ChEMBL, BindingDB and PubChem, for which assay- and document-level provenance was retained. Within this single target-focused collection, a random forest trained on 25 physicochemical descriptors predicted the depositing database with a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC) of 0.954 (95% confidence interval, CI, 0.939–0.968) and the source publication with a median one-versus-rest AUC of 0.997, providing an empirical reference scale for provenance-associated separability. Under a conventional pairwise design, comparisons between UI-Ref and external reference libraries yielded AUCs of 0.956–0.982. After property matching and publication-grouped cross-validation, the corresponding AUCs decreased to 0.762–0.841. Because the two tasks differ in terms of class priors, sample size and validation structure, this reference scale is reported as a diagnostic covariate rather than as a decision threshold, and the residual separation was compared against null models constructed within the same design. A null using only features that describe a molecule’s relative position within its source library, rather than its absolute physicochemical descriptor values, reached AUCs of 0.995–0.996 in that same task and exceeded the observed models by 0.154–0.234 (paired bootstrap; DeLong Z = −20.1 to −24.6). Models predicting an administrative provenance label within an external library achieved AUCs of 0.740–0.749, close to but below the 0.762–0.841 range obtained for collection membership. This similarity indicates that descriptor-based predictability is not specific to target-related chemistry. The residual separation exceeded the within-pair label-permutation null by 0.263–0.341, which indicates a detectable difference; however, the design cannot distinguish target-related chemistry from residual provenance structure. Following conditioning on provenance predictability, approximately 1% of compound pairs remained comparable. Matching on four physicochemical properties, moreover, left 25 to 27 of the 39 covariates visible to the models imbalanced, including thiourea and chelating motifs. Nearest-neighbor rankings changed after sample-size balancing, and the apparent overlap with approved drugs corresponded to a median nearest-neighbor Tanimoto similarity of only 0.355. Clusters in the joint chemical spaces were associated more strongly with source publication than with collection membership (adjusted mutual information 0.814 versus 0.187, respectively). No association between a structural motif and potency survived hierarchical estimation using a document-level random intercept and false discovery rate control. A revised classification cascade was therefore developed, incorporating explicit label definitions, probability calibration, a prespecified applicability domain and conformal prediction. Between 92.8% and 97.0% of the compounds in each external library fell outside the ECFP4-based applicability domain, and only 10.3% of an external screening cohort completed the cascade with an informative prediction. The measured-active-against-measured-inactive stage is reported as a narrow-scope diagnostic rather than as a general predictive stage, and every model-based stage reports empirical coverage without a conformal guarantee, because exchangeability across source publications is rejected. Provenance-associated confounding can therefore dominate conventional cross-collection comparisons and should be quantified before chemical or biological interpretations are drawn. The curated data, analysis code, trained models and domain-aware application are publicly available.

Article.Title: Multiscale Computational Prioritization of Chromone-Based Acetylcholinesterase Ligands
Article.Authors: Khibech O.; Abdelfattah B.; Bouhrim M.; Alqahtani M.; Alqahtani J.; Miantezila Basilua J.; Boulouiz A.; Touzani R.
Article.Abstract: Identifying acetylcholinesterase (AChE) ligands for Alzheimer’s disease research requires integrating molecular recognition with pharmacokinetic and safety considerations. Here, four designed chromone derivatives (M1–M4) were investigated to determine how conformational sampling and complementary molecular descriptors refine docking-based prioritization. Donepezil redocking in human AChE and cross-docking into Torpedo californica AChE recovered the crystallographic and transferred reference orientations, respectively, with RMSDs of 0.942 and 1.074 Å. Molecular docking was integrated with 800 ns molecular dynamics, MM/PBSA, electronic-structure calculations, and pharmacokinetic/toxicity predictions. M4 achieved the most favorable chromone docking score (−9.6 kcal mol−1), whereas M3 yielded the most favorable chromone MM/PBSA estimate within the 775–800 ns window (−23.90 ± 2.31 kcal mol−1). Donepezil retained a more favorable MM/PBSA estimate (−41.00 ± 2.75 kcal mol−1). M4 exhibited the highest electronic hardness, while predicted toxicity profiles revealed distinct liabilities across the series. The divergence between docking and sampled energetics highlights the value of integrating complementary criteria when selecting compounds for experimental evaluation. These protocol-dependent findings prioritize M3 and M4 as complementary computational candidates requiring experimental confirmation of AChE inhibition, selectivity, and safety.

Article.Title: Distinct Post-Exposure Metabolic States Following Pharmacological Perturbation of Mitochondrial Respiratory Complexes I–V in SH-SY5Y Cells: A Positional 13C-NMR Study
Article.Authors: Li H.; Baykal A.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a recurring mechanism in neuronal vulnerability and in the toxicity of several neuroactive compounds, yet lesions at different respiratory-chain nodes are commonly treated as a single bioenergetic defect. Whether pharmacological perturbation at distinct nodes leaves neuronal cells in distinguishable metabolic states has not been examined across all five complexes in one system. Undifferentiated SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells were exposed to five compounds selected as pharmacological perturbagens nominally directed at Complexes I–V: MPTP, 3-nitropropionic acid (3-NP), antimycin A, sodium azide and oligomycin, each titrated to approximately 80% viability (24 h, except 3-NP at 12 h). Inhibitors were then removed, and cells were labelled for 24 h with [U-13C6]glucose. Positional 13C-NMR was combined with pyruvate carboxylase (PC) and pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) enzyme-capacity assays in parallel extracts from the same biological replicates (n = 3 per group). The design is a single-factor, six-level layout in which five exposures share one vehicle control; labelling data were log2-transformed and analysed by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett many-to-one contrasts (error df = 12), with Hedges’ g and 95% confidence intervals, and group structure was tested by permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA). PERMANOVA demonstrated a significant overall effect of exposure group on the multivariate labelling matrix (pseudo-F = 18.77, p = 0.0001, 9999 permutations), and principal component analysis of the seven complete-case metabolites showed visually distinct group structure (PC1 65.9%, PC2 19.3%; 85.3% cumulative). Oligomycin produced the most distinct positional phenotype, preserving the PDH-associated glutamate C4 readout (107.2% of control, p = 0.971) while nearly doubling the PC-associated glutamate C3 readout (197.7%, p = 0.004; Hedges’ g = 17.8, 95% CI 5.3–30.2), concordant with PC capacity at approximately 138% and PDH capacity at approximately 60% of control. Azide produced the strongest reduction in glutamate C4 labelling (31.9%, p < 0.001; g = −8.3); antimycin A produced the broadest suppression of labelling; 3-NP produced accumulation of 13C-labelled succinate that was undetectable in the control. MPTP gave the weakest phenotype, with most of its individual comparisons not surviving the shared-control analysis. Exposure to compounds directed at different respiratory nodes leaves neuronal cells in non-equivalent post-exposure 13C-labelling states that positional 13C-NMR resolves. Because tracing followed washout, because the compounds are not fully selective and because the enzyme assays report capacity rather than flux, these are compound-defined post-exposure metabolic states and not measurements of complex-specific flux.

Article.Title: Identification of Candidate MYB Regulators of Seed Coat Color and Oil Content in Brassica napus
Article.Authors: Zheng L.; Gao X.; Wang F.; Zhao X.; Liu X.; Zhang L.; Huang J.; Chao H.; Zhao W.
Article.Abstract: Yellow-seeded Brassica napus varieties are highly desirable for breeding due to their superior oil content and seed quality. Proanthocyanidins (PAs) are the major flavonoids determining seed coat color, which is closely associated with oil accumulation. MYB transcription factors, especially R2R3-MYBs, act as important regulators of flavonoid biosynthesis and multiple developmental processes and may be associated with variation in PA accumulation and oil content. In this study, we performed a genome-wide identification and characterization of PA biosynthesis-related genes and MYB transcription factors in B. napus, and a total of 102 PA biosynthesis-related genes (BnaPABGs) and 416 high-confidence R2R3-MYBs (BnaMYBs) were identified and characterized. Transcriptome profiling of yellow- and black-seeded accessions at distinct developmental stages uncovered divergent expression patterns of both PA-related genes and MYBs. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a central module that co-enriched the majority of PA biosynthesis-related genes along with numerous lipid metabolism-related genes, suggesting a potential co-expression relationship between flavonoid metabolism and oil accumulation during seed maturation. By integrating co-expression networks with previously reported quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for seed coat color and oil content, we identified candidate BnaMYBs potentially associated with seed coat pigmentation and oil accumulation. Among these candidates, BnaA08.MYB61, BnaC06.MYB63, and BnaC03.MYB56 were prioritized as candidate genes based on their expression patterns and co-expression relationships, while haplotype analyses provided additional support for BnaC03.MYB56 and BnaA08.MYB61. Haplotype analyses further revealed supported associations between natural variation at BnaC03.MYB56 and BnaA08.MYB61 loci and seed oil content, whereas BnaC06.MYB63 showed limited haplotype diversity. Collectively, our findings provide new insights into the potential relationship of flavonoid and lipid metabolism in B. napus seeds and provide candidate genetic resources for further functional investigation of seed coat pigmentation and oil accumulation in B. napus.

Article.Title: Changes in Serum MMP-9 and TIMP-1 Concentrations in Children with Inflammatory Bowel Disease over a Six-Month Observation Period
Article.Authors: Zdanowicz K.; Lebensztejn D.; Daniluk U.
Article.Abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic condition with a long-term and often unpredictable course. The aim of our study was to evaluate serum levels of matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1 (TIMP-1) in children with IBD at diagnosis or disease exacerbation and during follow-up to assess their changes during the course of the disease. Patients were assessed at the time of inclusion (T0), after 3 months (T1), and after 6 months of follow-up (T2). At each time point, clinical disease activity was evaluated, along with routine laboratory tests and measurement of fecal calprotectin (fCal). Serum concentrations of MMP-9 and TIMP-1 were determined using the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay method. Fifty-nine children with IBD were included in the study (19 with Crohn’s disease and 40 with ulcerative colitis; 39 with newly diagnosed disease and 20 with disease exacerbation). During the six-month follow-up, patients received anti-TNF-α therapy with infliximab or adalimumab; at T1, 8 patients received infliximab and 5 received adalimumab, whereas at T2, 17 patients received infliximab and 7 received adalimumab. At T0, significant differences in MMP-9 and TIMP-1 were observed between IBD patients and controls. In the IBD group, a significant decrease in MMP-9 (p < 0.001), TIMP-1 (p < 0.001), and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio (p = 0.006) was observed over the six-month follow-up. At T1, only TIMP-1 levels differed between groups, while at T2 no significant differences were observed. Patients who achieved clinical remission showed a significant decrease in MMP-9 (p = 0.001) and TIMP-1 (p < 0.001) levels, whereas no significant changes were observed in patients who did not achieve remission. However, the percentage change in MMP-9 did not differ significantly according to clinical remission status (p = 0.50). Similarly, patients who achieved fCal-defined biochemical remission showed significant reductions in MMP-9 (p = 0.005), TIMP-1 (p = 0.003), and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio (p = 0.01) over time. In patients without fCal-defined biochemical remission, MMP-9 (p = 0.04) and TIMP-1 (p = 0.01) also decreased significantly over time, whereas the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio did not change significantly. However, direct comparisons showed no significant differences in the percentage changes in MMP-9 (p = 0.28) or TIMP-1 (p = 0.37) according to fCal-defined biochemical remission status. In conclusion, serum MMP-9 and TIMP-1 levels change over six months in children with IBD, reflecting changes in disease activity. Changes in these biomarkers were not significantly associated with fCal-defined biochemical remission. A significant difference in TIMP-1 percentage change was observed according to clinical remission status. However, this finding should be considered exploratory and interpreted with caution.

Article.Title: Spatial Molecular Signatures of Canine Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma with and Without Locoregional Metastasis with Cross-Species Comparison to Human Samples
Article.Authors: Goldschmidt S.; Tepper C.; Soltero-Rivera M.; Brady R.; Aleman J.; Rebhun R.; Wang X.; Birkeland A.; Meiklejohn K.; Todebusch R.; Lui C.; Murphy B.; Vapniarsky N.
Article.Abstract: Accurate diagnosis of locoregional spread in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is critical for prognosis and treatment planning. However, the currently available pre-surgical staging modalities often fail to detect occult nodal metastasis, necessitating nodal extirpation for accurate pathologic staging. This approach carries no clinical benefit and introduces unwarranted morbidity in patients with nonmetastatic lymph nodes (pN0 neck). The aim of this study was to define the molecular landscape of HNSCC in a spontaneous model of disease (pet dogs) with and without pathologically confirmed locoregional metastasis to identify biomarkers that may improve risk stratification and guide nodal management. Spatial transcriptomic profiling revealed a distinct metastatic tumor signature characterized by downregulation of PTEN, EPSTI1, CD99, MAPKAPK2, OAZ1, and upregulation of LOC477699. The tumor microenvironment of metastatic tumors demonstrated reduced JAK1 and trends consistent with T-cell exhaustion. Metastatic lymph node deposits conserved transcriptomic signatures matched to the primary tumor, and peri-metastatic lymph nodes displayed potentially permissive molecular alterations, including reduced F13A1 and DLA88 expression. Cross-species comparisons with human datasets identified conserved molecular and pathway-level features. Collectively, these findings identify candidate biomarkers and biological pathways associated with locoregional metastasis and support future prospective validation in canine and human HNSCC.

Article.Title: Molsidomine Pretreatment Modulates Renal Redox and Endothelial Activation Markers in Experimental Polymicrobial Sepsis
Article.Authors: Kose A.; Keser Z.; Gul M.; Yasar S.; Ozhan O.; Ulutas Z.; Dogru F.; Kurucay E.; Levent A.; Balkar M.; Parlakpinar H.
Article.Abstract: Sepsis-associated renal injury involves oxidative, inflammatory, and microvascular disturbances. This study evaluated renal changes associated with molsidomine pretreatment in cecal ligation and puncture (CLP)-induced polymicrobial sepsis. Forty Wistar rats were randomly allocated to Sham (n = 8), molsidomine (MOL; n = 8), CLP (n = 12), or MOL+CLP (n = 12) groups. Molsidomine (10 mg/kg/day) was administered orally for 14 days before surgery. Four animals in each septic group died before 24 h, leaving eight survivors per group. The primary outcome was total renal histopathological damage score; secondary outcomes included renal biochemical and immunohistochemical markers and serum renal indices. The total histopathological score differed across groups (overall p < 0.001) and was lower in surviving MOL+CLP than CLP animals (2.22 ± 0.97 vs. 5.38 ± 1.06). All four injury components were numerically lower, but adjusted pairwise differences were significant only for glomerular capillary collapse and renal tubular injury. Compared with CLP, MOL+CLP showed lower renal malondialdehyde (106.41 ± 9.03 vs. 136.45 ± 20.27 nmol/g), higher superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase activities, and lower VEGF and P-selectin immunoreactivity. Renal nitric oxide, other redox and inflammatory markers, and serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and urea did not differ significantly between septic groups after multiplicity adjustment. Among survivors, molsidomine pretreatment was associated with less pronounced renal structural injury and tissue-level abnormalities, without significant differences in conventional serum renal indices. Its effects when initiated after sepsis onset remain unknown. Further studies should evaluate post-sepsis dosing, antimicrobial and supportive care, and longer-term renal functional outcomes.

Article.Title: Molecular Targeting of the Peripheral Nerve–Tumor Axis in Extracranial Solid Cancers: Eight Signaling Systems, One Effect—Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Tudorașcu D.; Vere C.; Petrescu M.; Ciurea A.; Pană R.; Dan A.; Târtea E.; Greșiță A.; Hădăreanu D.; Obleagă C.; Târtea G.
Article.Abstract: The peripheral nerves that innervate solid tumors communicate with the malignant cells through a restricted set of molecular signaling systems: adrenergic and muscarinic receptors, sensory neuropeptides, neurotrophins and their tyrosine kinase receptors, axon guidance molecules, and nociceptor ion channels. Each has been proposed separately as a therapeutic target but never quantitatively compared with the others. The question is whether one of them dominates—or whether the real target is the axis as a system. We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, with four query modules per database, without year or language restriction. We included in vivo studies in mammals, on extracranial solid cancers, with an intervention that modulated tumor innervation, peripheral nerve activity, or neural signaling, and with at least one tumor burden outcome. Of 16,649 unique records, 362 were included, with 1291 experiments and 1437 effects. Blockade of the peripheral nerve–tumor axis reduced tumor burden by −44.8%. In the prespecified primary analysis, on established tumors, the reduction was −52.0% with no significant difference from preventive interventions (p = 0.17). All eight molecular signaling systems responded to blockade, with estimates ranging from −34.3% for TRP channels to −70.2% for glutamatergic signaling. Interventions that activate the axis produced the opposite effect, with a 52.1% increase (95% CI: 32.1 to 75.1) across 253 effects, and bidirectionality was demonstrated within the same molecular system for the adrenergic compartment (−42.8% for blockade vs. 58.1% for activation), axon guidance molecules, and TRP channels. Egger’s test indicated marked small-study effects (slope −1.12; p < 0.001); the estimate remained stable when low-confidence digitized values were excluded (−42.6%). Eight distinct molecular signaling systems, disrupted by methods with nothing in common, produce reductions of a similar magnitude in tumor burden, and stimulation of three of them produces the opposite effect.

Article.Title: HDAC Inhibitors Potentiate Doxorubicin Cytotoxicity in HepG2 Cells and Alter DNA-Repair- and p53-Associated Transcriptional Programs
Article.Authors: Guo K.; van Herwijnen M.; Caiment F.; van den Beucken T.
Article.Abstract: Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACis) can enhance responses to DNA-damaging chemotherapy, but how they alter doxorubicin (DOX)-induced transcriptional programs remains incompletely understood. We investigated the effects of valproic acid (VPA) and vorinostat (SAHA) on DOX cytotoxicity and associated molecular responses in HepG2 cells. HDAC inhibition, cell viability, apoptosis, and DOX IC50 values were assessed using histone H3 acetylation, cell counting, Alamar Blue assays, and cleaved caspase-3 immunofluorescence. Transcriptomic responses were analyzed by RNA sequencing, differential expression analysis, and Hallmark gene set enrichment analysis, with selected findings evaluated by RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and comparison with published CRISPR/Cas9 DOX-response data. Both HDAC inhibitors increased histone H3 acetylation and enhanced DOX cytotoxicity, markedly reducing DOX IC50 values. VPA co-treatment also increased DOX-induced cleaved caspase-3 signaling. RNA-seq showed broad transcriptional remodeling, including depletion of the DNA-repair gene set following VPA treatment and attenuation of canonical p53-responsive genes during HDACi–DOX co-treatment. Several HDACi-repressed DNA-repair genes overlapped with genes whose loss sensitized cells to DOX in a published CRISPR screen. HDAC inhibition therefore enhances DOX cytotoxicity and is accompanied by alterations in DNA-repair-associated and p53-responsive transcriptional programs.

Article.Title: Chronic Ultrasound (‘Emotional’) Stress in Mice Exacerbates Colitis Through GSK3β-Mediated Neuroimmune Dysregulation and Is Ameliorated by Probiotic Intervention
Article.Authors: Gorlova A.; Haque A.; Reid N.; Inozemtsev A.; Askarova S.; Umriukhin A.; Obleukhova A.; Zakharova E.; de Munter J.; Dudchenko A.; Kushugulova A.; Deykin A.; Cherdyntseva T.; Pavlov D.; Strekalova T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Growing evidence supports a bidirectional relationship between ‘emotional’ (psychological) stress and intestinal inflammation. ‘Emotional stress’, a form of stress that is triggered by negative information and experiences of non-physical nature, is an established risk factor for the development of subclinical intestinal inflammation, called irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). However, the underlying mechanisms of this transition remain unclear, owing to the limited availability of appropriate animal models. Glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β), a molecular hub of ‘emotional stress’ response, as shown particularly in the ultrasound stress (US) model, and an important player in gut inflammation, may underlie this transition. Here, we propose a mouse paradigm for the progression from IBS to IBD-like syndrome by combining the US with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis paradigm in mice and investigate the role of GSK3β signaling under these conditions. Methods: C57BL/6 mice were subjected to a 21-day US consisting of irradiation of alternating ‘negative’ and ‘neutral’ frequencies, followed by 5 days of 0.5% DSS exposure via drinking water. A standardized anti-inflammatory probiotic VSL#3 whose efficacy was shown in DSS-based models was administered to a subgroup of mice. Behavioral, histological, and molecular outcomes previously established in US and IBS models were evaluated. This included parameters of anxiety, anhedonia, time of intestinal transit, fecal water content, and brain and gut neutrophil infiltration, as well as gene expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and of GSK3β, and serum levels of pro-inflammatory molecules. Given the important role of the nervus vagus in brain–gut interactions, molecular changes were studied in the nervus vagus as well. Results: Mice exposed to the combined US and DSS challenge had impaired intestinal transit and increased fecal water content, neutrophil infiltration, the upregulation of pro-inflammatory mediators and GSK3β in the gut that together manifested the IBD-like state. In this group, upregulated gene expression of these markers was found in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus, as well as in the vagus. The combined US and DSS challenge exacerbated anxiety- and anhedonia-like behaviors and elevated blood cytokine and chemokine levels. In comparison to these changes, solitary exposures to US or DSS exerted smaller effects on the majority of measured parameters. Probiotic treatment attenuated most of the physiological, inflammatory, and behavioral abnormalities induced by the combined US and DSS intervention. Conclusions: The mouse model employed here using both US and DSS recapitulated the progression of IBS to the IBD associated with ‘emotional stress’ and demonstrated upregulated gut and brain Gsk3β expression accompanying this transition. The described model provides a useful paradigm for investigating the mechanisms underlying the disease development from IBS- to IBD-like pathology.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide DNA Methylation Sequencing Identifies Methylation-Associated Genes Related to Porcine Skeletal Muscle Fiber Diversity
Article.Authors: Zha C.; Li B.; Yang W.; Hou L.; Chao Z.; Wu W.
Article.Abstract: Alterations in skeletal muscle fibers are closely linked to human diseases, yet the mechanisms by which DNA methylation drives muscle fiber diversity remain unclear. Here, we performed whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) to generate single-base-resolution DNA methylomes of fast-twitch Biceps Femoris (Bf) and slow-twitch Soleus (Sol) muscles and integrated transcriptomes to reveal associations between DNA methylation and gene expression. The global methylation level in skeletal muscle averaged 4.22%, with context-specific rates of 70.0% (CG), 1.16% (CHG), and 1.12% (CHH). The distribution of methylation levels of the mCs in CG and CHG contexts was similar but distinct from that in the CHH context. Furthermore, 152,286 DMCs and 51,079 DMRs were identified between Bf and Sol muscles. Bf showed higher global methylation (4.54%) than Sol (3.90%), and distinct differences in DNA methylation occurred throughout the genomic regions and gene functional element regions. CG-context DMCs and DMRs were mainly located in CpG islands and introns, while CHG and CHH DMCs and DMRs were exon-enriched. DMR-associated genes were significantly enriched in pathways related to muscle growth and remodeling and disease-related pathways. Moreover, five DMR-linked differentially expressed genes—HSPB6, ATP2A2, TNNI1, HOXA11, and PTPN3—were identified as critical candidate regulators of muscle fiber diversity. In addition, a context-dependent (CG, CHG, CHH) relationship between DNA methylation patterns and gene expression was observed across different genomic regions in the two muscle types. Our findings highlight the essential role of DNA methylation in skeletal muscle fiber diversity and identify potential epigenetic targets and pathways.

Article.Title: Circulating Tumour Cell GALNT13 Expression Is Associated with Prognosis and Treatment Response in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
Article.Authors: Fernández Armúa E.; Serrano M.; Santana D.; Carrasco M.; Molina M.; Aznar I.; Acosta M.; Villar B.; Ferrari J.; Touya D.; Osinaga E.; Berois N.
Article.Abstract: Reliable circulating biomarkers for prognosis and treatment monitoring in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain limited. Liquid biopsy offers a minimally invasive approach to identify clinically informative tumour-derived markers. Given the emerging role of GalNAc-transferases in cancer biology, we evaluated GALNT13 expression in peripheral blood as a potential biomarker for prognosis and disease monitoring in lung cancer patients. Sensitive molecular assays (nested and digital RT-PCR) were developed to detect GALNT13 mRNA in circulating tumour cells (CTCs). These methods were applied to peripheral blood samples from non-small cell lung cancer patients to assess prognostic value and enable longitudinal monitoring. A cohort of 143 NSCLC patients was analysed, of whom 60% were GALNT13-positive in peripheral blood at baseline. During a five-year follow-up, GALNT13 positivity was significantly associated with reduced overall survival. In several patients, increases in GALNT13 levels preceded radiologic evidence of disease progression. GALNT13 expression in CTCs emerges as a promising biomarker for prognosis and treatment monitoring in NSCLC. Prospective studies in larger cohorts are warranted to validate its clinical utility.

Article.Title: Endothelial Redox Dysregulation in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: Compartmentalized Mechanisms and Therapeutic Implications
Article.Authors: Moreno-Caceres S.; Marciano D.
Article.Abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive pulmonary vasculopathy in which endothelial dysfunction drives increased pulmonary vascular resistance and arterial remodeling. Redox signaling is central to endothelial homeostasis, and its disruption in PAH reflects changes in the magnitude, source, and subcellular location of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, as well as the molecular targets they engage. In healthy endothelium, compartmentalized redox signaling supports adaptive responses while preserving nitric oxide bioavailability. Loss of this spatial control in PAH can convert normally transient redox signals into persistent endothelial dysfunction, although the strength of evidence for this conversion differs substantially between pathways. This review examines how disease-associated stressors reshape endothelial redox signaling through NADPH oxidases, mitochondria, eNOS, iron-dependent chemistry, and nuclear pathways and how these compartments communicate. We also examine emerging circulating markers of redox and endothelial dysfunction and evaluate redox-directed therapies across experimental pulmonary hypertension and PAH. Throughout, we grade each mechanism according to whether it is supported by evidence from human PAH vascular tissue, patient-derived pulmonary arterial endothelial cells, experimental pulmonary hypertension models, and pulmonary endothelial models or by extrapolation from other relevant disease systems, and we identify where compartment-specific evidence is inferred from enzyme localization rather than measured directly. Current evidence supports moving beyond broad antioxidant approaches toward strategies that selectively target pathogenic redox signaling within the relevant endothelial compartment.

Article.Title: The Screening and Identification of Potential Probiotics in Misgurnus anguillicaudatus Intestine
Article.Authors: Sui Z.; Shu M.; Zhang R.; Yu J.; Dai Z.; Sun Y.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: We characterized the intestinal microbiota of Misgurnus anguillicaudatus using 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V4 region). Strains secreting extracellular digestive enzymes were functionally screened, identified by 16S rRNA sequencing, and evaluated for biosafety. Microbial diversity analysis revealed that the intestinal microbiota of M. anguillicaudatus was dominated by the genera Vibrio, Pseudoalteromonas, and Aeromonas as core predominant taxa. Functional screening yielded four strains. Three non-hemolytic strains secreting amylase, lipase, and protease were identified as Aeromonas hydrophila, Shewanella xiamenensis, and Cedecea neteri, respectively. A. veronii was excluded due to its β-hemolytic activity. Biosafety assessment indicated that all three strains exhibited satisfactory biosafety. The three strains, A. hydrophila, S. xiamenensis, and C. neteri, obtained in this study possess potential probiotic functions in aiding host digestion and promoting nutrient absorption, and provide candidate strains for the development of microecological preparations for aquatic animals.

Article.Title: Effects of Losartan on Renal Dopaminergic and Renin–Angiotensin System Alterations Induced by a High-Fat Diet in Sprague-Dawley Rats
Article.Authors: Cantú S.; Lee H.; Höcht C.; Donoso A.; Valtuille R.; Puyó A.; Choi M.
Article.Abstract: The renal dopaminergic system (RDS) promotes natriuresis, diuresis, and exerts anti-inflammatory effects. High-fat diet (HFD) intake triggers the renin–angiotensin system (RAS). The aim of this study was to determine whether losartan (L) prevents RDS-RAS alteration and its impact on blood pressure and renal injury induced by HFD. Male Sprague–Dawley rats studied for 8 weeks were assigned to four groups: control (C; n = 4); HFD (n = 6): 50% w/w of bovine fat added to the standard diet; control + losartan (CL; n = 4): 30 mg/kg/day of L dissolved in drinking water; and HFD + losartan (HFDL; n = 6): HFD + CL. (Mean ± SD; p < 0.05). L prevented the following: HFD-induced increases in systolic blood pressure (SBP) and L-Dopa/dopamine urinary index (HFD vs. C, p < 0.01; HFDL vs. HFD, p < 0.01); lower expression of OCTN-1/2/3 (HFD vs. C, p < 0.01; HFDL vs. HFD, p < 0.05); overexpression of D1DR and Na+/K+-ATPase (HFD vs. C, p < 0.01; HFDL vs. HFD: D1DR p < 0.01; Na+/K+-ATPase p < 0.05), NF-κB1 and TGF-β1 (HFDL vs. HFD, p < 0.01). L mitigated proximal tubular alterations and interstitial fibrosis (HFDL vs. HFD, p < 0.01). Under chronic HFD intake, early L administration prevented renal dopaminergic system alterations and SBP elevation, and attenuated renal inflammation and interstitial fibrosis, reflecting its nephroprotective effects.
