Article.Title: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Data in Metastatic Melanoma with Pre-Existing Autoimmune Disease: A Real World Experience
Article.Authors: Vitale M.; Mallardo D.; Sparano F.; Festino L.; Vanella V.; Trojaniello C.; Ottaviano M.; Cioli E.; Mallardo M.; Facchini B.; Simeone E.; Ascierto P.
Article.Abstract: Patients with pre-existing autoimmune disease (AID) are underrepresented in trials of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). We retrospectively compared 41 patients with stage IV melanoma and pre-existing AID with 162 contemporaneous controls without AID who received ICI treatment between November 2016 and April 2023. In the AID and control cohorts, respectively, the objective response rates were 46.3% and 32.7%, and the disease control rates were 80.5% and 51.2%. Treatment interruption attributed to worsening of the baseline AID was recorded in 11/41 patients, while 13/41 interrupted treatment because of toxicity distinct from the baseline AID. The full cohort contributed 114 progression-free survival (PFS) events and 92 deaths. In models adjusted for age, sex, ICI regimen and M category, AID was associated with PFS (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.24–0.99; p = 0.046), whereas the association with overall survival (OS) was not statistically significant (adjusted HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.29–1.34; p = 0.232). These findings support the feasibility of ICI therapy in carefully selected patients with clinically stable AID, while the observational design and residual confounding require cautious interpretation of comparative outcomes.

Article.Title: Comparison of SERS Substrates in Direct Analysis of Urine Samples for Detection of Albuminuria: Relatively Large Gold Nano-Spheroids Outperform Gold Nanorods on Gold Film
Article.Authors: Boranova A.; Kabyl A.; Tuleuov B.; Kassymaly M.; Makhammajanov Z.; Gaipov A.; Bukasov R.
Article.Abstract: Proteins found in human urine can be used as a source of information on kidney function and as possible biomarkers for diseases such as chronic kidney disease (CKD). Focusing on differentiating between high and low albumin concentrations in urine samples, this study examines the roles of various substrates in detecting albuminuria as a specific form of proteinuria using surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS). Using gold nanorods (AuNRs) and gold spheroidal nanoparticles (AuNPs) on various substrates to optimize the identification of albuminuria, we studied urine samples from 77 and 124 patients with albumin concentrations above and below 0.3 g/L. SERS spectra were analyzed using principal component analysis—linear discriminant analysis (PCA-LDA), partial least squares with linear discriminant analysis (PLS-LDA), and support vector machine (PLS-SVM)—to differentiate between high- and low-urinary-albumin groups. PLS-LDA was the best-performing method among the three methods. The largest of all tested nanoparticles, 200 nm diameter (D200 nm) AuNPs on gold substrates, performed best in distinguishing between high and low concentrations of albumin in urine, with a maximum average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.97, 100% sensitivity, 92% specificity, and 96% accuracy and a higher enhancement factor of 5.4 × 107 in comparison to the same parameters obtained with λ650 nm and λ750 nm AuNRs on gold, which demonstrated average AUC values of 0.86 and 0.77 and EFs of 11 and 3 × 106, respectively. These larger NPs create hot spots in nanogaps between nanoparticles, which may have better accessibility to protein molecules compared to hot spots created in gaps between smaller nanorods and nanoparticles. This study highlights the role of nanoparticle size and shape in determining optimal SERS substrate parameters, thereby yielding more accurate results in the detection of high concentrations of albumin in urine by direct SERS.

Article.Title: Celastrol in Rheumatoid Arthritis: Immunomodulatory Mechanisms, Multicellular Convergence, and Translational Challenges
Article.Authors: Corona-Meraz F.; Martín-Márquez B.; Cobos-Puc L.; Guzmán-Alemán E.; Aguayo-Morales H.; Hernández-Ortega L.; Rosales-Gómez R.; Castañeda-Arellano R.; Sandoval-García F.; Tovar-Cuevas A.
Article.Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) arises from interactions among immune, stromal, and osteoimmune compartments, supporting interest in agents with multilevel activity, such as celastrol. This narrative review critically integrates evidence on its chemical–pharmacological basis, immunomodulatory mechanisms, cellular effects, and translational potential in RA. Preclinical data show inhibition of inflammatory programs in macrophages and neutrophils, modulation of T- and B-cell responses, suppression of pathogenic fibroblast-like synoviocyte (FLS) functions, and reduced osteoclastogenesis and structural damage. COMM domain-containing proteins 3 and 8 (COMMD3/8) provide the strongest causal validation, while insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 3 (IGF2BP3) has biophysical and functional support; numerous inflammatory and metabolic nodes primarily represent downstream signaling. Multicellular models support functional convergence, but intercellular causation in RA remains limited; directional functional evidence for dendritic cell–T-cell modulation comes from non-rheumatoid models, and no persistent synovial reprogramming has been demonstrated. Low bioavailability, multitarget covalent pharmacology, a narrow therapeutic window, and contributions from delivery carriers constrain translational interpretation. Addressing these translational challenges explicitly can help guide future research to improve celastrol’s safety and efficacy, which is essential for clinical application.

Article.Title: Water Inside the Carbon Cage—H2O@C60 and Related Fullerene Structures: Synthesis, Experimental Characterization, Computational Insights, and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Zielińska-Pisklak M.; Kuś Z.; Gackowski M.; Szeleszczuk Ł.
Article.Abstract: The encapsulation of a single water molecule inside C60 has established H2O@C60 as a benchmark system for investigating molecular behavior under precisely defined subnanometer confinement. This review integrates advances in the synthesis, experimental characterization, theoretical description, and emerging applications of H2O@C60 and selected related water-containing fullerenes. Particular attention is given to molecular-surgery strategies, in which the fullerene cage is opened, loaded with water, and subsequently reconstructed, as well as to improvements that have increased encapsulation and cage-closure efficiencies and enabled isotopically labeled and heterofullerene derivatives. Structural, nuclear magnetic resonance, infrared, terahertz, neutron-scattering, dielectric, photoelectron, and single-molecule transport studies collectively show that the C60 framework remains highly rigid, while the confined water molecule retains pronounced translational, rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin dynamics. At the same time, weak but measurable host–guest interactions produce symmetry breaking, rotational-level splitting, electrostatic screening, modified vibrational responses, and environment-dependent ortho–para conversion. Computational studies, ranging from density functional and correlated wave-function methods to multidimensional quantum-dynamical and molecular-dynamics approaches, have been essential for interpreting these observations and defining the underlying potential-energy landscape. Related systems, including H2O@C70, H2O@C59N, charged azafullerenes, and isotopically substituted endofullerenes, provide routes to tune cage geometry and electrostatic interactions. Although technological applications remain largely at the proof-of-principle stage, these systems offer promising platforms for quantum spectroscopy, molecular electronics, and the rational design of functional host–guest nanomaterials.

Article.Title: Targeting the Microbiota–Metabolism–Immunity Axis: Active Components of Traditional Chinese Medicine in Colitis-Associated Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Chen Q.; Zhang H.; Fu L.; Liu F.; Yang Q.; Zhang G.; Huang Y.; Yang Y.; Yao C.; Wang Y.; Du Z.; Luo H.
Article.Abstract: Colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC) develops in the setting of long-standing intestinal inflammation and remains a major complication of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Although effective control of inflammation may reduce cancer risk, approaches that specifically prevent the progression from chronic colitis to neoplasia remain limited. Disruption of the gut microbiota–metabolism–immunity axis is increasingly implicated in this process, as microbial dysbiosis and altered metabolite production can compromise epithelial barrier integrity, sustain inflammatory signaling, and disturb mucosal immune homeostasis. This review examines how active components derived from traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), particularly flavonoids, alkaloids, saponins, and polysaccharides, influence this interconnected network in CAC-related models. Rather than treating these constituents as a single group, we compare the mechanistic patterns and evidence base associated with each class. Flavonoids and alkaloids have been studied mainly in relation to inflammatory signaling and epithelial barrier protection, whereas saponins are more often linked to regulation of the immune microenvironment. Polysaccharides have been studied most frequently in relation to microbiota remodeling, short-chain fatty acid production, and mucosal immune balance. These distinctions are not absolute, and substantial overlap exists across component classes. Moreover, most evidence is derived from animal or cell-based studies, with marked variation in experimental models, compound characterizations, dosing, and outcome assessments. The microbiota–metabolism–immunity axis provides a coherent framework for interpreting the multi-level actions of TCM-derived components, but their causal mechanisms and clinical relevance to human CAC require further validation.

Article.Title: ISG15 Is a Key Multidirectional Regulator of Cytosolic RNA- and DNA-Sensing Pathways and Type I Interferon Feedback Loops
Article.Authors: White M.; Iordanskiy S.
Article.Abstract: Activation of cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathways that normally recognize viral nucleic acids triggers the expression and release of type I interferons (IFN-I). This release drives the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) that activate acute inflammation and counteract viral replication at various stages. Recent studies have highlighted how interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15), a small, ubiquitin-like modifier, regulates cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathway proteins to control the antiviral response and inflammation. ISG15 is a multifunctional protein that acts as a secreted cytokine, binds freely to intracellular proteins, and covalently modifies proteins in a reversible process termed ISGylation. A dual regulatory molecule, ISG15 can both stabilize and destabilize proteins that promote and inhibit IFN-I signaling. Conversely, viruses have evolved strategies to disrupt and exploit ISG15-dependent antiviral responses to evade the host immune system. In this review, we examine how ISG15 regulates cytosolic RNA and DNA sensing pathway proteins to control IFN-I signaling and the antiviral response, highlighting it as a master regulator that fine-tunes IFN-I signaling and feedback. Recognizing the multifaceted action of ISG15 is essential for designing balanced therapeutic strategies across antiviral drug development, cancer immunotherapy, and chronic inflammatory disease management.

Article.Title: Biopsy-Based Molecular Signatures Predicting Therapeutic Response in Ulcerative Colitis
Article.Authors: Grassi I.; Liso M.; Mastronardi M.; Valentini A.; Curlo M.; Armentano R.; Cavalcanti E.
Article.Abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with marked molecular heterogeneity, resulting in highly variable responses to biologic therapies. Despite the efficacy of Infliximab (IFX), many patients fail to achieve sustained remission. Identifying biomarkers predictive of treatment response is essential for advancing precision medicine in UC. Gene expression profiling of colonic mucosal biopsies from IFX responders, IFX non-responders, and healthy controls was performed using a multiplex array, followed by technical confirmation by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemical assessment to further characterize tissue expression and biological relevance. IFX non-responders displayed a stromal–immune molecular signature marked by extracellular matrix remodeling, stromal remodeling, integrin-mediated signaling, and persistent inflammatory pathways. SPARC and SPP1 emerged as the most prominent biomarkers, with significantly increased gene and protein expression in non-responder patients, highlighting their association with chronic tissue remodeling and therapeutic resistance. Mucosal resistance to IFX is associated with a specific stromal–immune profile characterized by SPARC and SPP1 upregulation. These findings suggest that both molecules may serve as promising candidate markers for patient stratification, highlighting the need for future prospective studies to explore their role in personalized management strategies for ulcerative colitis.

Article.Title: Cynaroside Attenuates Ethinylestradiol-Induced Cholestatic Liver Injury by Modulating the FXR/BSEP/CYP7A1/SHP Axis
Article.Authors: Hamed A.; Al-Nouri D.; Mahrous N.; Bassit A.; Abouelella A.; Hassan A.; Mokhtar G.; Ahmad G.; Osman A.; Ahmed A.; Mahgoob A.; Thabet S.; Abdel-Latif H.; Shamlan G.; Zhao H.; Al-Farga A.; Soliman S.
Article.Abstract: Cholestatic liver diseases are characterized by disrupted bile acid homeostasis, oxidative stress, and inflammation, ultimately leading to progressive hepatic injury. Although ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) remains the standard pharmacological therapy, its therapeutic efficacy is limited in several cholestatic conditions. This study investigated the hepatoprotective effects of cynaroside (CYN), a naturally occurring flavonoid glycoside, against ethinylestradiol (EE)-induced cholestatic liver injury and explored its underlying molecular mechanisms. Female Wistar rats were randomly allocated into four groups (n = 7): control, EE, EE + CYN, and EE + UDCA. Liver function indices, bile acids, cholesterol, oxidative stress and inflammatory biomarkers, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, Western blotting, qRT-PCR, and molecular docking analyses were performed. EE administration induced pronounced cholestatic liver injury, as evidenced by impaired liver function, hepatic accumulation of bile acids and cholesterol, oxidative imbalance, inflammatory responses, and marked histopathological alterations. CYN significantly ameliorated these biochemical and histological abnormalities, reduced hepatic bile acid and cholesterol accumulation, restored redox homeostasis, and attenuated inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, CYN modulated the hepatic FXR/BSEP/CYP7A1/SHP regulatory network, modulated hepatic FXR and Nrf2 protein expression, suppressed NF-κB activation, and favorably regulated TNF-α, IL-1β, and BCL2 expression. Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings further confirmed substantial preservation of hepatic architecture following CYN treatment. Molecular docking revealed favorable interaction of CYN with the FXR ligand-binding domain, with a predicted binding free energy of −8.18 kcal/mol, comparable to that of UDCA (−7.95 kcal/mol). Cynaroside attenuated EE-induced cholestatic liver injury by improving bile acid homeostasis and mitigating oxidative and inflammatory responses, potentially by modulating FXR-associated signaling and its downstream regulatory network. Collectively, the results provide a rationale for continued investigation of cynaroside in the context of cholestatic liver injury.

Article.Title: Conformational Sampling of CPT1A Enables Dynamic Structure-Based Ligand Screening
Article.Authors: Zhang S.; Zhang Y.; Zhao J.; Long J.; Zhang L.; Yang Z.
Article.Abstract: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) catalyzes a rate-limiting step in fatty acid β-oxidation and is a target for studies of metabolic disease and cancer. However, the structural dynamics of CPT1A remain poorly understood due to the lack of full-length structure. In this study, we employed an integrated computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Markov state models (MSMs), and binding free energy calculations to elucidate the conformational landscape of human CPT1A. We performed an all-atom MD simulation of CPT1A embedded in a realistic outer mitochondrial membrane, and root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF)-guided local region analysis coupled with MSM transition-path analysis and GROMOS clustering convergently identified a representative conformation. The pathway probabilities reported here describe dominant local transitions within specific mobile segments rather than the global equilibrium population of the full-length protein. Using this representative conformation, we performed a virtual screening of over 1.23 million compounds from the ChemDiv library, followed by Lipinski filtering, yielding five candidates with docking scores below −10 kcal/mol. Subsequent MD simulations and binding free energy calculations confirmed stable binding, with Compound 2 exhibiting the most favorable free energy of −25.99 kcal/mol. Principal component analysis (PCA) and secondary-structure analyses revealed ligand-specific modulation of CPT1A dynamics. A preliminary in vitro CPT1 activity assay revealed candidate-specific responses, and the free-energy and activity data were partially consistent. These results provide a dynamically informed structural basis for CPT1A ligand recognition, identify candidates with distinct energetic and functional profiles, and establish an integrated strategy for ligand discovery in structurally uncharacterized proteins.

Article.Title: Recycled PET/Sepiolite Composite Adsorbent for Methylene Blue Removal: Formulation, RSM Optimisation, Reusability, and Adsorption Mechanism
Article.Authors: Mohd Din S.; Khan Z.; Mohsin M.; Mousa S.; Othman N.; Younes M.; Mohamad Z.; Hossain S.
Article.Abstract: This study explores the valorisation of post-industrial recycled polyethylene terephthalate (rPET) via incorporation of sepiolite clay to develop a composite adsorbent for methylene blue (MB) dye removal. The composite formulation was evaluated by varying the rPET concentration, TFA:DCM solvent ratio, sepiolite content, and blending time. The selected formulation had an average particle size of 267.10 nm, a specific surface area of 0.67 m2/g, and a pore volume of 0.003925 cm3/g. Adsorption conditions were then optimised using a five-factor, three-level Box–Behnken design, considering contact time, MB concentration, adsorbent dosage, pH, and temperature. The resulting quadratic model was statistically significant (F = 114.18, p < 0.0001), with R2 = 0.9892, adjusted R2 = 0.9805, and predicted R2 = 0.9568; however, the lack-of-fit was also significant (F = 90.90, p < 0.0001), indicating that model predictions should be interpreted within the investigated factor ranges. At the selected conditions of 62.5 min, 25.5 mg/L MB, 2.55 g/50 mL adsorbent, pH 7, and 55 °C, the model predicted an MB removal efficiency of 99.03%. The adsorbent retained at least 93% reusability efficiency after six adsorption–washing–reuse cycles. The kinetic data were described more closely by the pseudo-second-order model, whereas the Freundlich model provided a better representation of the equilibrium data (R2 = 0.9976). Thermodynamic results indicated that adsorption was favourable and exothermic within the investigated temperature range. Overall, the results show that post-industrial PET can be converted into a value-added sepiolite-containing adsorbent for MB removal.

Article.Title: Biofluid Biomarkers of Neuronal and Glial Injury in Epilepsy and Seizures: A Comprehensive Review
Article.Authors: Moroșanu V.; Maier S.; Roman-Filip I.; Moroșanu S.; Bălașa R.
Article.Abstract: Epilepsy is one of the most common chronic neurological disorders worldwide, affecting millions of individuals and imposing a substantial cognitive, psychological, social, and economic burden. Despite significant advances in epilepsy research, key questions remain unresolved regarding the mechanisms underlying drug resistance, cognitive impairment, depression, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, as well as the contribution of recurrent seizures in promoting neuronal and glial injury. Addressing these challenges requires reliable biomarkers capable of accurately reflecting disease activity and detecting ongoing brain damage. In this review, we summarize the current evidence on biofluid biomarkers of neuronal and glial damage in epilepsy and seizures and discuss their potential clinical relevance. Particular attention is given to biomarkers associated with major pathways involved in epileptogenesis, including neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, neurodegeneration, blood–brain barrier disruption, altered gene expression, and synaptic remodeling. Emerging evidence suggests that circulating and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers may provide valuable insights into seizure-related brain injury and the molecular mechanisms underlying epilepsy. Although none of these markers has yet been adopted in routine clinical practice, they represent promising tools for improving diagnosis, prognostic assessment, patient stratification, and the development of more personalized therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Exploring the Role of Umbilical Cord Blood Leptin and Visfatin in Fetal Growth: Associations with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and Neonatal Anthropometric Measurements

Article.Abstract: Leptin and visfatin are adipokines involved in metabolic regulation and fetal development, but their associations with maternal gestational diabetes mellitus and neonatal growth remain incompletely understood. In multivariable regression analysis, the models explained 9.3% and 20.5% of the variability in leptin and visfatin concentrations, respectively. GDM status was independently associated with cord blood leptin concentration, whereas neonatal weight category was independently associated with visfatin concentration. Article.Title: Circular RNAs in Skeletal Muscle Aging and Sarcopenia: Mechanistic Evidence, Biomarker Potential, and Therapeutic Readiness
Article.Authors: Ngo T.; Lee W.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal muscle aging arises from interacting defects in proteostasis, mitochondrial quality control, inflammatory signaling, neuromuscular integrity, regenerative capacity, and mechanical–metabolic plasticity, and may culminate in sarcopenia. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are plausible regulators and biomarker candidates, but most evidence derives from developmental myogenesis, expression profiling, or non-aging atrophy models. This critical review organizes the literature around skeletal muscle aging and applies a four-level framework encompassing discovery, mechanistic support, in vivo causality, and functional intervention. We assess human linkage, species, treatment timing, locus of action, and endogenous or engineered modality separately. circSnd1 and circDdb1 currently provide the strongest combination of functional preclinical evidence and association with aged human skeletal muscle. circFUT10, circBBS9, circNEB, and circGLIS3 define less mature regenerative, discovery, histological, or muscle-quality domains. Non-aging atrophy studies, including circTmeff1 and engineered circmiR-29b, test whether proposed mechanisms remain active under defined catabolic stress. Human blood and serum-vesicle studies provide discovery-level associations with strength or mobility, but clinical validation of a circulating circRNA biomarker for sarcopenia remains insufficient. Therapeutic development is constrained by quantitative target credibility, systemic skeletal-muscle exposure, post-onset functional efficacy in aged organisms, safety, reversibility, and independent replication. The field should now prioritize rigorous validation over additional descriptive cataloging.

Article.Title: Folate Deficiency Drives Metabolic Dysfunction, Oxidative Stress, and Inflammation in HK-2 Renal Tubular Cells
Article.Authors: Chiu T.; Liu H.; Lin B.
Article.Abstract: The growing aging population has been accompanied by an increasing prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD), highlighting the need to better understand modifiable dietary and metabolic factors that contribute to renal injury. Folate deficiency and excessive fructose intake have been implicated in renal inflammation; however, the underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Folate deficiency markedly increased the secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokines interleukin-6 (IL-6) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), accompanied by enhanced NF-κB activation, both in the presence and absence of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation. Exogenous lactate supplementation or modulation of lactate production using the LDH inhibitor oxamate further demonstrated that elevated lactate promoted IL-6 and transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) production, NF-κB activation, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Consistent with these findings, folate deficiency significantly reduced the oxygen consumption ratio (OCR), indicating impaired mitochondrial function and a metabolic shift away from oxidative phosphorylation toward increased lactate production. High fructose exposure also enhanced IL-6 and MCP-1 secretion, particularly following LPS stimulation, while both LPS exposure and folate deficiency further increased lactate production. Collectively, these findings identify lactate accumulation as a potential metabolic link between folate deficiency, inflammation, oxidative stress and fibrotic signaling in renal tubular HK-2 cells. This metabolic-inflammatory pathway may contribute to the initiation and progression of CKD and highlights folate status and lactate metabolism as potential targets for preventing diet-associated renal injury.

Article.Title: Red Blood Cells Beyond Oxygen Transport: Dynamic Regulators, Disease Biomarkers and Therapeutic Platforms—A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Vives-Corrons J.
Article.Abstract: Red blood cells (RBCs) have traditionally been regarded as passive carriers of respiratory gases. Increasing evidence, however, indicates that they are active participants in vascular homeostasis and respond to mechanical, metabolic, and oxidative stimuli. This narrative review examines the interconnected roles of RBCs as regulators of vascular physiology, indicators of hereditary and systemic disease, therapeutic targets, and delivery platforms. RBC deformability, membrane organization, ion-water balance, metabolism, and redox capacity support microcirculatory flow, while ATP release, nitric oxide handling, adhesion, and extracellular-vesicle formation influence vascular function. RBC morphology, mechanics, hydration, metabolism, oxidative status, and vesiculation can provide clinically relevant information, although emerging functional and molecular biomarkers require further standardization and validation. RBC-directed treatments and RBC-based carriers offer additional therapeutic opportunities. Automated image analysis and machine-learning-assisted microfluidic classification are the most substantiated artificial-intelligence applications; broader multimodal decision-support systems remain exploratory.

Article.Title: Extraction, Structure–Activity Relationships, and Modification of Plant-Derived Polysaccharides: An Integrated Framework for Evidence-Based Method Selection and Bioactivity Optimization—A Review
Article.Authors: He Y.; Xin Y.; Zhang X.; Han D.; Liang Q.; Kong L.; Guan Y.; Sun H.; Liu C.; Han Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Extensive research has been conducted on plant-derived polysaccharides, yet three interrelated challenges remain insufficiently explored: extraction methods are often selected without systematic validation; the structure–activity relationship (SAR) remains fragmented; and modification strategies are rarely designed on the basis of SAR knowledge. We critically compare various extraction techniques and clarify that method selection requires consideration of source characteristics and application orientation. We also demonstrate that extraction conditions may affect structural integrity and, consequently, influence biological activity. Subsequently, we analyze SAR by examining molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, uronic acid content, and chain conformation to identify structural determinants of biological functions. Finally, we review chemical modification strategies and illustrate how their efficacy depends on structural features initially determined by extraction. By integrating evidence from these three stages, this review offers a practical framework to support rational, evidence-based development of plant-derived polysaccharides for applications in medicine, food, and biomaterials.

These findings establish the Np–EndoA1–GluA1 axis as a key epileptic pathway, whereby Np negatively regulates EndoA1 to promote GluA1-AMPAR internalization and suppress excitability. Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by selective and progressive degeneration of specific neuronal populations, often accompanied by glial dysfunction. Spatial omics technologies preserve anatomical context and enable interrogation of cell-type composition, molecular heterogeneity, and intercellular interactions within neural systems. We highlight emerging insights into pathology-associated gene modules, neuron-glia interactions, and mechanisms underlying regional vulnerability. Finally, we discuss multimodal data integration and future directions for translating spatially resolved molecular maps into mechanistic understanding.

Article.Title: Theta-Band Temporal Interference Stimulation Modulates Food Reward Prediction Error Encoding in Individuals with Elevated Food Addiction Symptoms
Article.Authors: Wen Y.; Wang M.; Dong X.; Gola M.; Liu Q.; Tu Y.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Prediction error (PE) signals support feedback evaluation and adaptive updating, and are closely linked to medial frontal theta dynamics, particularly within dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)-centered networks. However, evidence linking these oscillatory mechanisms to the modulation of PE encoding remains limited. Here, we tested whether theta-band modulation of a dACC-centered medial frontal network altered trial-level PE encoding during food-reward processing. In a single-blind, sham-controlled pre-post design, individuals with elevated food addiction symptoms performed a food incentive-delay task while undergoing electroencephalographic recordings combined with theta-band temporal interference stimulation. Single-trial analyses revealed that feedback-related negativity (FRN) amplitudes varied as a function of both behavioral and model-derived prediction errors. Critically, theta-band modulation altered FRN-PE coupling, with the effect most pronounced for unfavorable outcomes, whereas anticipatory activity remained unchanged. These findings support the hypothesis that theta-band modulation can alter feedback-related PE encoding within this population and task context.

Article.Title: Cystatin C and its Role in the Neuro-Glial-Vascular Unit: Implications for Cerebrovascular Diseases and Neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Li M.; Wang Z.; Huang Z.; Guo X.; Wang Q.; Wei X.
Article.Abstract: Cystatin C (CysC) is emerging as a key regulator and intercellular signaling mediator within the neuro-glial-vascular unit (NGVU). This review comprehensively examines its multifaceted roles across NGVU components, detailing mechanisms by which CysC preserves blood-brain barrier integrity, modulates neuroinflammation, and influences pathological protein aggregation. Rather than providing a merely descriptive catalogue, we emphasize its context-dependent nature. In cerebrovascular and neurodegenerative diseases, CysC exhibits functional duality along the neuron-glia axis, either restraining or perpetuating inflammation and proteinopathy depending on cellular context and disease stage. Similarly, along the endothelial-oligodendrocyte precursor cell crosstalk, its coordination of angiogenesis and myelination may shift from protective to detrimental under chronic hypoperfusion. We evaluate its dual utility as a clinical biomarker and therapeutic target, addressing challenges in brain delivery, target selectivity, and safety. This integrative synthesis provides a critical perspective on unresolved controversies and future research priorities regarding CysC in neurological disorders.

Article.Title: Normative Modeling of Amygdala Subfields and Disease-Specific Vulnerabilities Across Neurological Disorders
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Bai L.; Shi D.; Li W.; Ai L.; Ao F.; Bai Y.; Bai Y.; Bao H.; Cai Q.; Cao J.; Chai L.; Chen F.; Chen F.; Chen K.; Chen Y.; Cheng D.; Cole J.; Cui Z.; Dai H.; Deng D.; Du X.; Du Y.; Duan X.; Fu Y.
Article.Abstract: As an integrative center of the limbic system, the amygdala and its subfields participate in diverse neural functions and demonstrate heterogeneous structural changes in various neurological disorders. In this study, three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI data from 22,258 healthy participants were analyzed using normative modeling to establish normative references for the volumes of the amygdala and its subfields. These models elucidated the developmental and aging curves of the amygdala and identified distinct ages at peak volume across subfields, ranging from 24.6 to 43.7 years. Based on these references, individual centile scores were calculated for 4132 patients with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, cerebral small vessel disease, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. These centile scores not only captured disease-specific deviation patterns of the amygdala subfields but also demonstrated utility in disease classification. Moreover, the centile scores correlated with clinical measures of cognitive function, emotional state, and motor performance across disorders. These findings suggest that normative references of the amygdala subfields provide insights into cross-disease alteration patterns and offer potential neuroimaging biomarkers to aid differential diagnosis and clinical assessment.

Article.Title: Non-suicidal self-injury in adolescents and young adults: an expert review
Article.Authors: Kaess M.; Reichl C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is highly prevalent among community and clinical adolescent populations and is associated with substantial psychiatric comorbidity, psychosocial impairment, and elevated suicide risk. This review synthesizes key findings on the development and maintenance of adolescent NSSI and discusses the clinical implications of this transdiagnostic behavioural phenomenon. It examines the prevalence and developmental course of NSSI, environmental and biological risk factors, proximal mechanisms, its conceptualization as an independent diagnosis versus a transdiagnostic risk marker, and current treatment approaches including their limitations. Current evidence indicates that adolescent NSSI emerges from interacting environmental risk factors (e.g. adversity and interpersonal stress) and neurobiological mechanisms related to emotional dysregulation, stress responsivity, and altered pain processing. While NSSI prospectively predicts suicidal behaviour, associations with other psychiatric disorders remain probabilistic and diagnostically non-specific. Overall, findings support conceptualizing NSSI as a transdiagnostic risk marker and behavioural phenotype linked to emotion dysregulation rather than as a distinct diagnostic entity. Adolescent NSSI reflects a dynamic biopsychosocial process involving emotional, neurobiological, and interpersonal mechanisms. Early detection and accessible intervention are essential to reduce chronicity, relapse, and the escalation of suicidal behaviour. Future research should prioritize mechanism-informed and personalized treatment approaches, improved identification of at-risk adolescents, and integration of developmental, neurobiological, and digital methodologies to advance prevention and intervention.

Article.Title: Integrative neuroimaging-transcriptomic analysis of neurodevelopment in adolescent-onset mental health problems
Article.Authors: Hou J.; van Wingen G.; van de Mortel L.; Smit D.; Liu S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mental health problems often emerge in childhood and adolescence, yet the neurodevelopmental and molecular processes underlying their onset remain poorly understood. Using longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, we examined structural and functional brain cortical changes in youth who developed ADHD, conduct, anxiety, depressive, oppositional defiant, or somatic problems over a two year follow up period compared to healthy controls in five neuroimaging modalities (including structural MRI, resting-state fMRI, and task-based fMRI). We applied partial least squares (PLS) regression to link spatial patterns of neurodevelopmental changes to cortical gene expression profiles derived from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Pathway enrichment was assessed using spin-permutation-derived gene rankings. Significant neurodevelopmental alterations were observed in the ADHD and conduct groups only. PLS analysis further revealed significant spatial associations between their neurodevelopmental changes and gene expression distributions (Spearman rₛ >0.64). In ADHD, pathway enrichment highlighted mitochondrial respiration, oxidative phosphorylation, aerobic electron transport, ATP synthesis, and mitochondrial organization, with additional negative-end enrichment for synaptic protein interaction pathways. In conduct problems, all significant pathways were enriched among genes whose cortical expression patterns were inversely aligned with the conduct-problem imaging phenotype and involved translational machinery, ribosomal function, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial translation, protein targeting to mitochondria, and broader RNA/protein regulatory processes. These findings reveal distinct cortical transcriptomic patterns associated with adolescent-onset ADHD and conduct problems, with mitochondrial energy metabolism emerging as a prominent molecular correlate of ADHD-related cortical development and a distinct inverse transcriptional pattern characterizing conduct-related development. Together, our findings suggest that these externalizing problems are associated with neurodevelopmental alterations embedded within distinct cortical molecular contexts.

Article.Title: TCF7L2 functionally relevant genetic variation with clinical implications in bipolar disorder with impaired glucose metabolism
Article.Authors: Miola A.; Winham S.; De Filippis D.; Gardea Resendez M.; Romo-Nava F.; Bond D.; Singh B.; Veldic M.; Ozerdem A.; Pendegraft R.; Pazdernik V.; Ercis M.; Sanchez-Ruiz J.; Prieto M.; McElroy S.; Biernacka J.; Frye M.; Cuellar-Barboza A.
Article.Abstract: Impaired glucose metabolism (IGM) and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) are common in bipolar disorder (BD). Genome-wide association studies have identified variation (rs7903146) in the gene encoding transcription factor 7-like 2 ( TCF7L2 ) as a well-established risk factor for T2DM in the general population and variation (rs12772424) showing a significant association with BD when accounting for BMI. Evaluating T2DM- and BD-associated TCF7L2 SNPs within bipolar IGM groups, along with their clinical correlates, could provide translational insights for future clinical practice. IGM was operationalized as evidence of prediabetes (fasting glucose of 100-125 mg/dL or glycated hemoglobin of 5.7%-6.4%) or T2DM. We compared sociodemographic, genetic, clinical characteristics, and course of illness measures between BD groups with and without IGM, then within BD subgroups (prediabetes, T2DM, and no IGM). Out of 850 BD patients included (mean age 49, SD = 13, 57% female, 8% non-White) 280 (33%) individuals had IGM. Compared to BD patients without IGM, those with IGM were older (p < 0.001), more likely to be non-White (p = 0.005), and obese (p < 0.001). The minor allele for the rs7903146 SNP (T2DM-associated SNP) was significantly greater in the IGM group compared to the group without IGM (11% vs. 5%, p = 0.009). There was no significant association between rs12772424 SNP (BD-associated SNP) with bipolar course of illness measures. Further investigation examining the complex interactions between functional genetic variants, molecular markers, environmental influence, and clinical phenotypes in BD is needed to better understand the mechanistic underpinnings to the high rate of T2DM bipolar comorbidity and identify early targets for treatment of both disorders.

Article.Title: Electroacupuncture alleviates chronic pain and comorbid depression through Gut-Metabolite-Brain axis remodeling to restore mPFC Glu/GABA balance
Article.Authors: Li S.; Huang J.; Lin D.; Luo D.; Fu W.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The comorbidity of chronic pain and depression is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder involving dysregulated microbiota–gut–brain communication. Although electroacupuncture (EA) has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy for both pain and depression, the mechanisms linking peripheral microbial-metabolic remodeling to central neurotransmitter regulation remain incompletely understood. Here, we employed an integrated multi-omics approach in a spared nerve injury (SNI) rat model to investigate the gut–metabolite–brain mechanisms underlying EA’s efficacy. EA significantly alleviated mechanical hypersensitivity and depressive-like behaviors while restoring mPFC Glu/GABA balance, accompanied by normalization of the glutamate transporter EAAT2 and the GABA-synthesizing enzyme GAD67. Metagenomic analysis showed that EA remodeled the gut microbial ecosystem by increasing microbial diversity, suppressing opportunistic pathobionts, including Bacillus cereus, Alistipes onderdonkii , while enriching SCFA-associated genera, including Butyricimonas and Romboutsia . These alterations were accompanied by coordinated remodeling of amino acid and butanoate metabolism. Correlation network analysis identified Pipecolic acid as a central metabolic node linking gut microbial alterations with mPFC GABAergic neurotransmission and behavioral recovery. Although individual bacterial genera did not significantly mediate its restoration, causal mediation analysis demonstrated that the Pipecolic acid–GABA axis significantly mediated improvements in both mechanical allodynia and anhedonia, supporting Pipecolic acid as a functional metabolic hub linking peripheral metabolic remodeling to central GABAergic regulation. Collectively, these findings identify peripheral metabolic remodeling as a key mechanistic interface through which EA coordinates gut microbial ecology and central neurochemical homeostasis, providing a systems-level framework for understanding the therapeutic mechanisms of acupuncture in pain–depression comorbidity.

Article.Title: Large-scale EEG reveals shared and distinct neural oscillatory features across major psychiatric disorders
Article.Authors: Rao S.; Xie J.; Niu M.; Pan Y.; Li Y.; Yu H.; Xie J.; Zhang Y.; Zhao S.; Pan G.; Guo W.; Li T.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: Major psychiatric disorders are leading contributors to global disability, yet robust biomarkers to inform diagnosis and treatment remain elusive. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a scalable, noninvasive approach to capture neural dysfunction, but prior findings have been inconsistent due to small, single-disorder cohorts. Here, we report a large-scale, two-site comparative study of resting-state EEG in schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder (BD), and major depressive disorder (MDD) compared with healthy controls (HC). Across 9751 participants’ EEG recordings, standardized preprocessing and feature generation yielded spectral power and functional connectivity (FC) measures tested with both statistical and machine-learning approaches. We identified convergent transdiagnostic alterations—reduced alpha power and increased gamma-band FC, implicating shared disruptions in inhibitory control and large-scale network coordination. Additional spectral differences included more pronounced delta-theta elevation in SCZ and a graded delta-theta continuum (SCZ > BD > MDD), suggesting a dimensional progression of neural dysregulation. Machine-learning models robustly distinguished individuals with psychiatric diagnoses from healthy controls within sites, but cross-site generalization and inter-disorder discrimination remained limited, underscoring challenges of heterogeneity. These findings identify reproducible EEG features that capture both shared and disorder-distinct neural alterations, advancing efforts towards early detection and individualized treatment in major psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Episodic memory-associated weighted atrophy network mapping in mild cognitive impairment and subjective cognitive decline: a multi-center study
Article.Authors: Huang A.; Jiang K.; Chi L.; Qiao M.; Yang X.; Wu H.; Chen S.; Fan J.; Wang H.; Chen Y.; Tong Z.; Lin X.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: This study localizes episodic memory-associated impaired networks in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and subjective cognitive decline (SCD) using a weighted key atrophy network mapping method, and investigates whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can modulate them. Replicability was assessed across three independent cohorts involving 1312 subjects. First, single-subject key atrophy maps were constructed by comparing cortical thickness with cognitively normal groups and retaining regions showing significant thickness-memory correlations. Second, these maps served as seeds for functional connectivity analysis in a large normative connectome, generating atrophy networks weighted by atrophy extent. Third, group-level comparisons identified impaired networks in MCI and SCD, and methodological reliability was further validated against a memory network derived from patients with focal brain lesions. Finally, the impaired networks were experimentally modulated via a 4-week rTMS intervention (25 MCI, 13 SCD). Despite substantial individual-level heterogeneity, atrophied regions in most MCI patients were functionally connected to a common episodic memory-associated impaired network. This phenomenon was not significant in SCD patients. Both lesion-memory network mapping and cross-dataset validation confirmed consistency across cohorts. Critically, rTMS can modulate the impaired network in MCI patients, primarily reflected by enhanced functional connectivity within this network. In conclusion, this study developed a robust weighted key atrophy network mapping method, localizing common episodic memory-associated impaired networks in MCI/SCD. Modulation of this impaired network may serve as a potential therapeutic strategy to delay MCI progression.

Article.Title: Serum B-cell activating factor and delayed memory in first-episode drug-naïve schizophrenia: a case-control study
Article.Authors: Yang Q.; Jin T.; Jin S.; Jiang F.; Qiu J.; Yang X.; Wang P.; Yan Q.; Tian Q.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive impairment in schizophrenia has been linked to immune dysregulation, but the role of humoral immune regulators remains unclear. We examined serum B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) in 90 first-episode drug-naïve schizophrenia (FES) patients and 90 matched healthy controls (HCs). Cognitive performance was assessed using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS), and symptom severity was assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). Serum BAFF and APRIL were measured using Luminex technology. After adjustment for age, sex, education, BMI, and smoking status, serum BAFF and APRIL levels were significantly lower in FES patients than in HCs (BAFF: F = 131.935, P < 0.001; APRIL: F = 59.772, P < 0.001). In the hypothesis-driven primary analytic model focusing on RBANS delayed memory, the Group × BAFF interaction was significant ( F (1,171) = 13.524, P < 0.001), with a positive BAFF slope in HCs ( B = 0.015, P = 0.017) but a negative slope in FES patients ( B = -0.022). This interaction remained robust in sensitivity analyses. Exploratory analyses suggested a nominal Group × BAFF interaction for RBANS total score ( F = 5.866, P = 0.016, FDR-adjusted q = 0.082), which was interpreted cautiously. No analogous Group × APRIL interaction was observed, and BAFF/APRIL levels were not significantly associated with PANSS symptom dimensions. These cross-sectional findings identify peripheral BAFF as a hypothesis-generating correlate of delayed memory in early untreated schizophrenia, but do not establish temporality, causality, or central immune-cognitive mechanisms.

Article.Title: Aerobic exercise prevents neuroinflammation and ameliorates depressive-like behaviors via suppression of HMGB1/NF-κB pathway-mediated reactive microglial states in mice exposed to chronic mild stress
Article.Authors: Jiang L.; Zhang C.; Yang D.; Liu S.; Liao R.; Xu E.; Yu Y.; Liu L.
Article.Abstract: Aerobic exercise is shown to have a positive effect on depressive-like symptoms; however, the associated mechanisms have not yet been fully elucidated. The role of neuroinflammation in the pathogenesis of depression is well-documented. High mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), a late mediator of inflammation, can promote the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines in various inflammation-related diseases. This study aimed to investigate the antidepressant effects of aerobic exercise by regulating hippocampal neuroinflammation via the HMGB1/NF-κB pathway-mediated microglial reactivity state. We assessed the depressive-like behaviors of the mice through behavioral tests. It was found that aerobic exercise significantly alleviated chronic mild stress (CMS)-induced depressive-like behaviors in mice. Furthermore, aerobic exercise reduced the total number of microglia and altered microglial morphology and reactive states in the hippocampus, accompanied by down-regulation of pro-inflammatory markers. These effects were observed to be regulated by HMGB1. We found a significant nuclear-to-cytoplasmic translocation of HMGB1 in the hippocampus, in the absence of apoptotic alterations (pyknotic nuclei, karyorrhexis, karyolysis), indicating an active release in the brain after CMS stimulation. Interestingly, aerobic exercise could reverse these alterations by inhibiting the HMGB1/NF-κB pathway. These findings not only enhance the understanding of the processes driving neuroinflammation in the hippocampi of mice exposed to CMS, but also highlight the potential of aerobic exercise as an anti-depression therapeutic strategy.

Article.Title: Neurobehavioral changes in fear generalization in clinical high risk for psychosis
Article.Authors: Clauss J.; Babadi B.; Tuominen L.; Deng W.; Leathem L.; Holt D.
Article.Abstract: Changes in basic associative learning processes have been identified in several psychiatric conditions. However, it remains unknown whether these findings result from ongoing psychopathology or represent an underlying transdiagnostic risk factor for multiple clinical states. In this study, 72 participants with subclinical psychopathology, 23 of whom met criteria for the Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis syndrome (CHR+) and 49 who did not meet these criteria (CHR-), completed a fear conditioning and generalization paradigm while functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data were collected. During this procedure, participants were presented with face stimuli that were either paired (CS+) or not paired (CS-) with a mild electrical shock, as well as eight face “morphs” (stages between the CS+ and CS-) tailored to each participant’s perceptual discrimination ability. Following the scan session, participants rated the likelihood that each stimulus had been previously followed by a shock. Fear generalization-related neural responses (in a subset of the sample, 16 CHR+ and 40 CHR- participants) and the memory ratings were then examined using both categorical and individual-level psychometric modeling approaches. Expected patterns of fear generalization-related responses were observed in the anterior insula and superior frontal gyrus and in the memory ratings. The psychometric modeling analysis revealed a significantly greater threshold in responses of the left anterior insula, representing a wider fear generalization curve, in the CHR+, compared to the CHR-, group. Moreover, across the whole sample, symptoms of anxiety were associated with a wider fear generalization gradient. These findings suggest that specific features of a basic associative memory process, fear generalization, may be linked to CHR status and transdiagnostic risk for psychiatric illness.

Article.Title: Association between tirzepatide use and risk of suicidal ideation among individuals with obesity and major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Liu T.; Chu C.; Liu C.; Wu J.; Tsai Y.; Chang H.; Lai C.
Article.Abstract: Obesity and major depressive disorder (MDD) frequently co-occur and confer mutually reinforcing risks, including elevated suicidality. Tirzepatide has demonstrated substantial metabolic benefits, yet its psychiatric safety in high-risk populations with MDD remains uncertain. This study aimed to compare suicidal ideation outcomes among adults with comorbid obesity and MDD initiating tirzepatide versus non–GLP-1RA anti-obesity medications. This retrospective, propensity score–matched cohort study used deidentified electronic health record data from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults (≥18 years) with diagnosed obesity and MDD who initiated tirzepatide or non–GLP-1RA anti-obesity medications were included. The primary outcome was suicidal ideation. Secondary outcomes included anxiety disorders, insomnia disorders, all-cause mortality, and emergency department or inpatient encounters. Among 24,103 matched pairs, tirzepatide use was associated with lower risk of suicidal ideation (HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.42–0.93), anxiety disorders (HR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.81–0.86), insomnia disorders (HR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.86–0.98), all-cause mortality (HR, 0.38; 95% CI, 0.25–0.58), and emergency department visits or hospitalizations (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89–0.99). Risk reduction was generally consistent across prespecified subgroups. Control outcome analyses supported the internal validity of the findings. In conclusion, this study provides real-world evidence that tirzepatide initiation was associated with a lower recorded risk of suicidal ideation, as well as reduced anxiety, insomnia, all-cause mortality, emergency department visits, and hospitalizations, among adults with comorbid obesity and MDD. This observational association should not be interpreted as evidence of a direct antisuicidal effect. These findings support the potential for tirzepatide to serve as a metabolically favorable treatment option associated with a lower risk of suicidal ideation in this vulnerable, high-risk population.

Article.Title: Altered GABAB receptor sensitivity in heavy drinkers indexed using a TMS-based biomarker: a randomized controlled experimental medicine trial
Article.Authors: Montemitro C.; Donahue D.; Costumati A.; Maruottolo F.; Terezza S.; Sjoberg C.; Perini I.; Roman M.; Kugelberg F.; Heilig M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Metabotropic γ-aminobutyric acid type B receptors (GABA B Rs) are implicated in alcohol use disorder (AUD) and represent a promising therapeutic target. However, robust biomarkers of GABA B Rs target engagement and sensitivity in humans are lacking. We examined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)–derived cortical inhibition and growth hormone (GH) release as measures of GABA B R function, and whether heavy alcohol use is associated with altered responses to pharmacological GABA B R activation. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 31 healthy volunteers (16 heavy drinkers, 15 light drinkers) received baclofen 30 mg, baclofen 60 mg, or placebo across three sessions. Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI), short-interval intracortical inhibition, and intracortical facilitation were assessed with paired-pulse TMS at baseline and ~60 min post-dose. Baclofen blood concentrations and plasma GH levels were measured. Baclofen produced dose-dependent increases in GH release, confirming neuroendocrine GABA B R engagement. The LICI response to baclofen differed between groups: In light drinkers, baclofen at 30 mg potentiated LICI, and a similar potentiation was seen at 60 mg, indicating that a plateau may have been reached. In contrast, in heavy drinkers, a potentiation of LICI similar to that in light drinkers was seen at 30 mg baclofen, but was absent at the 60 mg dose despite comparable pharmacokinetics, suggesting altered GABA B R function. Effects were selective for GABA B R–mediated inhibition, with no consistent modulation of short-interval intracortical inhibition or corticospinal excitability. Acute baclofen administration reveals altered GABA B R sensitivity in heavy drinkers, with preserved responses at lower doses but reduced response under stronger agonist stimulation. LICI and GH release provide complementary biomarkers of central and peripheral GABA B Rs engagement and may support translational development of mechanism-based treatments for AUD.

Article.Title: Aberrant single-subject cortical morphological networks and their associations with multiple symptoms in generalized anxiety disorder
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Hu X.; Deng R.; Cao L.; Chai S.; Wang Y.; Li H.; Gao Y.; Gong Q.; Qiu C.; Huang X.
Article.Abstract: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is a prevalent disorder associated with disrupted topological organization of large-scale brain networks. However, the morphological basis for network disruption and its clinical relevance remains unexplored. We constructed single-subject cortical morphological networks for 58 drug-free GAD patients and 86 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) separately based on cortical thickness, surface area, cortical volume, mean curvature, sulcal depth and local gyrification index. Between-group differences in local morphology and network topology were analyzed using general linear models. Partial correlation analyses were conducted to examine the relationship between brain alterations and clinical characteristics in GAD patients, while controlling for age, sex, education years and intracranial volume. Compared with HCs, GAD patients showed increased thickness in the left middle temporal gyrus and decreased local gyrification index in the left superior frontal gyrus. At the network level, GAD patients exhibited increased local efficiency, normalized clustering coefficient, and small-worldness, alongside decreased characteristic path length in cortical volume-based networks. Local morphology and network topological properties were associated with clinical characteristics such as illness duration, age of onset, anxiety severity, and personality traits. Our findings revealed both region-specific cortical abnormalities and global network reorganization in GAD patients. In particular, the shift toward stronger small-world configurations suggests enhanced local integration and global communication efficiency. These results highlight that GAD is associated not only with focal cortical alterations but also with systemic structural network changes that ma y underlie excessive anxiety and personality traits associated with the disorder.

Article.Title: Efficacy and safety of long-acting injectable aripiprazole in bipolar disorder: a multinational real-world target trial emulation
Article.Authors: Hsu C.; Hung K.; Carvalho A.; Berk M.; Tseng P.; Lai Y.; Lin Y.; Liang C.; Chen Y.
Article.Abstract: Long-acting injectable (LAI) aripiprazole is approved for maintenance treatment of bipolar disorder (BD), but real-world efficacy and safety evidence remains limited. Using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, we conducted a target trial emulation among patients with BD who initiated oral aripiprazole between 2017 and 2023. Patients switching to LAI within one month were compared with those continuing oral therapy. After 1:1 propensity score matching on demographics, comorbidities, prior treatments, and laboratory data, hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for nine efficacy and safety outcomes were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models, with prespecified sensitivity and subgroup analyses. After matching, 1814 LAI and 1814 oral aripiprazole users were followed for a mean of 1.6 years. LAI use was associated with reduced all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.77, 95%CI 0.69–0.85) and emergency department visits (0.88, 0.79–0.98), with no difference in suicidal ideation or behavior (0.90, 0.75–1.08) or all-cause mortality (0.86, 0.55–1.37). Risks were higher for obesity (1.17, 1.06–1.29) and extrapyramidal symptoms (2.20, 1.38–3.50), but lower for major adverse cardiovascular events (0.73, 0.55–0.95) and hyperlipidemia (0.83, 0.72–0.97). Efficacy benefits were most pronounced in females and middle-aged or older adults; in adolescents, suicidal ideation or behavior was markedly reduced (0.49, 0.35–0.68). Sensitivity analyses showed similar trends. In BD, LAI aripiprazole was associated with better clinical outcomes without increased mortality compared with continued oral aripiprazole. The favorable benefit–risk profile supports broader consideration of LAI in maintenance care, with active monitoring of obesity and extrapyramidal symptoms.

Article.Title: Cyclopurine DNA lesions and repair in individuals with bipolar disorder and their unaffected siblings
Article.Authors: Arat Çelik H.; Tuna G.; Akşahin İ.; Yılmaz S.; Fettahoğlu İ.; Eslami Abriz A.; Gör C.; Çörekli E.; Kök Kendirlioğlu B.; Dal Bekar N.; Çelik Ö.; Yorguner N.; Ceylan D.
Article.Abstract: Oxidative stress plays a key role in bipolar disorder (BD). 8,5’-cyclopurine-2’-deoxynucleosides (cPUs), including R- and S-cdA, are tandem oxidative lesions that distort the DNA helix, impair replication and transcription, and are primarily repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway. To date, cPU levels and NER gene expressions have not yet been studied in BD. This study assessed cPU levels and the expression of NER genes ( XPB, XPC, XPD, XPF, ERCC1 , and CSB ) in individuals with BD (n = 44), their unaffected siblings (n = 37), and healthy controls (HC; n = 46). Urinary cPU levels were quantified using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Expression of NER pathway genes were assessed in peripheral blood samples using quantitative reverse transcription PCR. cPU levels were significantly elevated in both BD and sibling groups compared to HCs, with R-cdA concentrations highest in siblings. NER gene expressions were also increased: XPB, XPF, ERCC1 , and CSB were upregulated in siblings, while XPC was elevated in both BD and sibling groups. XPB, XPF , and CSB levels were significantly higher in siblings than in the BD group, whereas XPD expression was increased in the BD group compared to both siblings and HCs. Elevated nucleotide damage and increased NER gene expression in individuals with BD and their unaffected siblings support prior evidence implicating oxidative DNA damage and repair mechanisms in BD pathogenesis. The identification of cPU lesions and distinct NER expression patterns highlights additional molecular markers and suggests a potential familial vulnerability contributing to the development of BD.

Article.Title: Exploring the effect of maternal autoimmune diseases on behavioral and social difficulties risk in children born preterm: evidence from EPIPAGE-2 study
Article.Authors: Ellul P.; Marchand-Martin L.; Salmon F.; Ancel P.; Pierrat V.; Letouzey M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Maternal immune activation (MIA) and preterm birth have both been associated with increased risk of autism spectrum disorder but their combined impact in preterm children is unclear. This prospective population-based cohort study used data from the French EPIPAGE-2 study, which included liveborn infants delivered at 22 to 34 weeks’ gestation in 2011 and followed them to 5 years of age. Neurodevelopmental outcomes at 2 years’ corrected age and at 5 years were assessed. Among 3609 children (155 [4.3%] exposed), maternal autoimmune diseases were initially associated with more impaired personal-social skills on the Ages & Stages Questionnaire at 2 years and a lower prevalence of high Social Communication Questionnaire scores at 5 years, but these associations were no longer statistically significant after adjustment. No significant associations were found between maternal autoimmune diseases and global developmental delay, ASD risk, or behavioral difficulties at 2 or 5 years in adjusted analyses. Subgroup analyses by gestational age and by exposure to immunosuppressive therapy also showed no increased risk. In this national preterm birth cohort, maternal autoimmune diseases during pregnancy were not associated with increased early behavioral or social communication difficulties in offspring. However, given the small number of exposed children, the predominance of endocrine autoimmune diseases, and the lack of immune activation biomarkers, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and warrant confirmation in larger, mechanistically informed studies

Article.Title: Predicting trail-making test performance using 7-Tesla structural cerebral MRI
Article.Authors: Schnellbächer G.; Rajkumar R.; Veselinović T.; Ramkiran S.; Hagen J.; Collee M.; Shah N.; Neuner I.; Dammers J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Psychopharmaceutical therapy has seen a lack of improvement in efficacy, highlighting the need for a more individualized treatment approach that optimally leverages pharmaceutical effects. To achieve this, it is necessary to identify factors that can predict psychological attributes and treatment outcomes. We hypothesize that brain morphology may serve as a predictor of performance in psychological tests. A 7-Tesla-MRI system was used to measure 74 transdiagnostic patients and 41 healthy controls. Values for grey matter volume (GMV), cortical thickness and gyrification based on the Schaefer 100 Atlas for parcellation were determined. Using this morphological data, performance in a Trail-Making Test (TMT) - A and B was predicted with the help of a deep learning model. A SHAP analysis was conducted to identify the key variables important for the model. The accuracy in predicting TMT performance was very good at 0.795. The most decisive feature influencing predictions was gyrification. Areas indicating inter-group differences were focused in the frontal cortex, as well as in temporal and parietal regions. Morphological characteristics can predict test performance with high accuracy. These results support the implementation of a transdiagnostic approach in clinical practice to better address the underlying pathophysiology. Symptom prediction based on neuroimaging data appears to be an achievable goal.

Article.Title: Distinct cocaine- and shock-responsive ensembles in the nucleus accumbens
Article.Authors: Correia R.; Domingues A.; Aguiar L.; Cunha-Macedo M.; Vilasboas-Campos D.; Vieitas-Gaspar N.; Jungmann R.; Teixeira E.; Coimbra B.; Rodrigues A.; Soares-Cunha C.
Article.Abstract: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) responds to both natural and non-natural rewards as well as aversive stimuli; however, it remains unclear how motivationally relevant rewarding and aversive experiences are represented within NAc neuronal ensembles. Here we used Fos-CreER T2 -based activity-dependent tagging to label NAc neuronal ensembles activated by a potent non-natural reward, cocaine, or by foot shock. We found that the cocaine ensemble consists predominantly of dopamine D1 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-MSNs), whereas the foot shock ensemble contains both D1- and D2-MSNs. One-photon calcium imaging in freely moving mice revealed that acute cocaine primarily excites D1-MSNs while inhibiting most D2-MSNs, whereas foot shock induced excitatory responses in both types of MSNs. Optogenetic reactivation of the cocaine-ensemble elicited a strong behavioral preference, whereas reactivation of the shock-ensemble produced only modest behavioral effect. Together, these findings indicate that rewarding and aversive experiences recruit partially overlapping NAc ensembles with distinct cellular composition, activity dynamics, and behavioral outcomes. While both stimuli engage shared neuronal populations, only reactivation of cocaine-responsive ensembles change behavioral preference and reinforcement, highlighting functional differences in how motivationally relevant experiences are represented within the NAc.

Article.Title: Environmental factors and polygenic risk score for psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders in children with dyslexia
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Fan H.; Liu R.; Zhu K.; Xiang Z.; Zhao S.; Chen Q.; Zhang J.; Wang T.; Liang X.; Song R.
Article.Abstract: Developmental dyslexia (DD) impacts learning achievement and psychosocial development and is associated with various environmental factors and also genetic factors. Here, we conducted a multi-center case-control study by screening 29,820 primary school students between 2–6 grades in four cities in China and enrolled 948 dyslexia cases who meet the criteria of dyslexia and 948 controls with matching age and sex. We comprehensively investigated the environmental factors using the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) machine learning model and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) algorithm. The most important risk factors in dyslexia are the proactive learning habit, the age of child’s literacy, maternal education level, out-migrant workers, and prolonged screen exposure during pregnancy. The home literacy environment accounted for most of the variance within both groups. Then we examined shared polygenic risks between DD, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorders, schizophrenia, major depressive disorder, and bipolar disorder using polygenic risk score (PRS) analyses. The results showed that the highest PRS DD quartile had a 2.13-fold risk than the lowest quartile with risk factors adjusted (95% CI: 1.08, 4.18). The individuals with the highest PRS ASD quartile and PRS SCZ quartile (OR: 2.13; 95% CI: 1.14, 3.98 and OR: 2.41; 95% CI: 1.23, 4.72) were associated with increasing dyslexia risks. This study identified the importance of screening personalized environmental factors among dyslexia and highlighted the shared genetic architecture between dyslexia and other disorders. These findings offered novel insight into the etiology of dyslexia, contributing to the advancement of early prevention strategies.

Article.Title: Ketamine induces synaptic and monoaminergic remodeling in human iPSC-derived neurons
Article.Authors: Pagano J.; Mangano E.; Eminente S.; Marcatili M.; Krivosova M.; Colombo M.; Tritto V.; Bordoni R.; Boeckers T.; Conti L.; Sala C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of global disability, and a substantial proportion of patients develop treatment-resistant depression (TRD), highlighting the urgent need for mechanistically novel and fast-acting antidepressants. Ketamine has emerged as a paradigm-shifting therapy due to its rapid and robust antidepressant effects, yet its molecular mechanisms in human neurons remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the cellular and transcriptomic effects of ketamine in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived forebrain neurons. Neuronal cultures were treated with ketamine (1 µM) for 72 h and analyzed using immunocytochemistry, western blotting, and RNA sequencing. Ketamine treatment did not alter gross neuronal morphology or presynaptic organization but significantly increased synaptic localization of the postsynaptic scaffolding protein PSD-95, suggesting molecular changes associated with synaptic remodeling. At the signaling level, ketamine selectively modulated the Akt pathway without inducing changes in BDNF protein levels or MAPK activation, and without broadly altering excitatory or inhibitory synaptic protein expression. Transcriptomic profiling revealed 604 differentially expressed genes, with significant enrichment of pathways related to serotonergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission. Notably, ketamine upregulated genes involved in monoamine synthesis and signaling, including DDC and DRD1 , while downregulating genes associated with GPCR ligand binding and neurotransmitter transport. SynGO analysis further identified selective regulation of synapse-associated genes, predominantly affecting presynaptic and neurotransmitter uptake mechanisms. Together, these findings indicate that ketamine induces molecular and transcriptional changes in human neurons that are consistent with synaptic remodeling and with activation of transcriptional programs enriched for monoaminergic signaling pathways. This hiPSC-based model provides a platform to investigate the molecular responses of human neurons to ketamine and to explore patient-specific mechanisms in future studies.

Article.Title: GPR84 exacerbates blood-brain barrier disruption after ischemic stroke via cAMP/CREB-dependent tight junction suppression
Article.Authors: Lu H.; Ying M.; Hu C.
Article.Abstract: Compromise of the blood-brain barrier represents a pivotal event in ischemic stroke pathology, though the specific inflammatory mediators involved remain incompletely characterized. We postulated a role for the inflammatory G protein-coupled receptor GPR84 in driving this process. Experimental cerebral ischemia in mice provoked a marked increase in cortical GPR84 expression. A corresponding upregulation was observed in human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation and recovery. Mice lacking the Gpr84 gene demonstrated a pronounced protective phenotype following ischemic insult, featuring limited tissue infarction, diminished brain swelling, superior performance on neurological assessments, and significantly reduced vascular leakage. Preservation of the structural proteins Claudin-5 and ZO-1 at the neurovascular unit was evident. Application of selective GPR84 agonists to endothelial monolayers recapitulated barrier failure, an effect abrogated by co-administration of a cell-permeable cAMP analogue. Silencing of GPR84 expression conferred resistance to barrier dysfunction and was linked to maintained phosphorylation of the transcription factor CREB. This work delineates a cell‑autonomous GPR84‑cAMP‑CREB signaling cascade that directly impairs brain endothelial barrier function. The integrated contributions of GPR84 expressed on immune cells within the neurovascular unit in vivo remain to be defined. These results suggest GPR84 as a candidate mechanistic target for barrier preservation strategies.

Article.Title: Blunted cerebello-basal ganglia-thalamic circuit connectivity in melancholic depression
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Xia Y.; Wang Y.; Shen N.; Sheng J.; Chen W.; Bao J.; Yan R.; Yao Z.; Lu Q.
Article.Abstract: Melancholic major depressive disorder (MDD-M), characterized by anhedonia, is a clinically distinct subtype with poor treatment response and impaired social function. This study aimed to investigate abnormal patterns of inter-regional neural communication in MDD-M. This study included 1541 participants who underwent resting-state fMRI scans across three independent datasets: an exploration dataset (n = 1175), a validation dataset (n = 216), and a longitudinal clinical cohort ( n = 150) with at least two scans per participant. Granger causality analysis was used to evaluate directed information flow between brain regions. In the exploration cohort, we applied directed Network-Based Statistics to identify melancholic-specific network features and correlate these features with clinical characteristics. These features were then used to construct a classification model in the validation dataset. Finally, we assessed the stability of these features in the longitudinal cohort via repeated-measures ANOVA. MDD-M exhibited a hypo-connectivity network pattern compared to the control group. Specifically, MDD-M reported weakened bidirectional connectivity between the thalamic ventrolateral nucleus (ThalVL) and the nucleus accumbens, as well as diminished causal outflow from the cerebellar vermis to both the globus pallidus and the ThalVL. This hypo-connectivity network pattern achieved an AUC of 0.81 in the validation set. Longitudinal analysis further confirmed the stability of the hypo-connectivity pattern in MDD-M. We identified a connectivity pattern of diminished directed information flow within the cerebello-basal ganglia-thalamic circuit that may represent a potential circuit-level feature of MDD-M. This stable and directional brain network feature may help identify the subtype and develop targeted treatments.

Article.Title: Epigenetic signatures of different types of childhood maltreatment in a high-risk sample: a preregistered replication study
Article.Authors: Meier M.; Gurri L.; Beck K.; d’Huart D.; Jawinski P.; Boonmann C.; Stadler C.; Schmid M.; Bürgin D.; Unternaehrer E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Childhood maltreatment (CM) has long-lasting effects on physical and mental health with CM type specific effects being reported. Epigenetic processes, like deoxyribonucleic acid methylation (DNAm), might mediate this link, and CM types might be linked to differential alterations in DNAm. While a study by Cecil et al. [1] suggests that different forms of CM share common but also exhibit distinct epigenetic signatures, it is unclear whether these results are generalizable to other high-risk samples. The aim of this preregistered study was to replicate the study of Cecil and colleagues [1] in a sample of N = 116 previously out-of-home placed young adults (32% women, age mean = 26.38, SD = 3.49). Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire - Short Form (CTQ-SF), DNA was extracted from whole blood and DNAm was assayed using the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip Microarray. Using state-of the-art processing pipelines, we failed to replicate the original finding of common and shared epigenetic signatures by CM type. When using a pipeline that was closely matched to the original study, we found that DNAm of cg07032930 was significantly linked to emotional neglect, but in the reverse direction as in the original report. Overall, replication rates per CM subtype were only modest. These findings highlight challenges in independently replicating reported epigenetic associations in high-risk samples and underscore the importance of replication attempts in the field of behavioral epigenetics. Further research is needed to clarify the robustness and specificity of DNAm signatures linked to distinct CM types.
