Article.Title: Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids differentially regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation during Western diet feeding in male Ldlr −/− mice
Article.Authors: Kim S.; Noh S.; Ji M.; Vence T.; Gao L.; Otoko O.; Nichols F.; Blesso C.; Kwon O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Western diet (WD) is associated with skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism, redox imbalance and inflammation. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiome‐derived metabolites contribute to host metabolic regulation, yet the role of Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids in skeletal muscle remains unknown. This study tested whether two structurally related bacterial glycine lipids, lipid 654 (L654) and lipid 1256 (L1256), regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial remodelling in WD‐fed Ldlr −/− mice. Male Ldlr −/− mice were fed a normal chow or WD and administered L654, L1256 or vehicle control for 8 weeks. Skeletal muscle glycine lipid accumulation, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial biogenesis markers, mitophagy‐associated signalling, inflammatory and antioxidant proteins and muscle fibre cross‐sectional area were assessed. L1256, but not L654, accumulated in skeletal muscle. Functionally, L1256 selectively enhanced fatty acid‐supported mitochondrial respiration and increased respiratory control ratio. L1256 also increased peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC‐1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and electron transport chain complexes IV and V, suggesting enhanced oxidative mitochondrial remodelling. In parallel, L1256 altered markers associated with mitochondrial quality control signalling, increased nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), suppressed nuclear factor kappa‐light‐chain‐enhancer of activated B cells (NF‐κB) signalling and preserved muscle fibre cross‐sectional area. L654 upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis transcripts without altering protein abundance. These findings identify L1256 as a microbiome‐derived lipid retained within skeletal muscle that enhanced oxidative metabolism and preserved mitochondrial quality signalling under metabolic stress. The data suggest that tissue retention of bacterial lipids may be an important determinant of skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation. image Key points Western diet contributes to skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism and chronic inflammation. Microbiome‐derived glycine lipids are bioactive molecules from Bacteroidota species, but their effects on skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism remain poorly understood. Bacteroidota‐derived glycine lipids produce distinct skeletal muscle responses in Western diet‐fed Ldlr − / − mice, where lipid 1256 accumulated in skeletal muscle and enhanced fatty acid‐supported respiration, whereas lipid 654 primarily induced transcriptional responses without detectable tissue accumulation. Lipid 1256 increased peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator 1‐alpha (PGC‐1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain together with restoration of Parkin, nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) while reducing nuclear factor kappa‐light‐chain‐enhancer of activated B cells (NF‐κB) and interleukin 6 (IL‐6) expression and preserving skeletal muscle cross‐sectional area. These findings suggest that gut microbiome‐derived glycine lipids are regulators of skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism, and that tissue retention of bacterial lipids influences mitochondrial oxidative remodelling during metabolic stress.

Article.Title: Breathing‐evoked potentials in humans during wakefulness and sleep
Article.Authors: Grassion L.; Andrillon T.; Niérat M.; Wattiez N.; Patout M.; Njlagni Voutsa J.; Oudiette D.; Arnulf I.; Gonzalez‐Bermejo J.; Similowski T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Breathing modulates cortical activities and cognitive functions, but the neurophysiological basis of the brain–breathing relationship is incompletely understood. We aimed to determine whether breathing at rest evokes scalp EEG‐detectable potentials (as inspiratory occlusions do in the respiratory‐related evoked potential model), whether these signatures persist during sleep and whether they are linked to sleep‐organizing processes. We examined recordings from 729 participants in the Cleveland Family Study to identify cortical activity time‐locked to inspiration during wakefulness and sleep, with a median of 7871 respiratory cycles analysed per participant. Breathing‐related cortical responses were assessed in the time and frequency domains. Quiet breathing evoked a reproducible sequence of cortical potentials during wakefulness, including a pre‐inspiratory component ∼300 ms before inspiration and several post‐inspiratory peaks ≤3 s after. These responses persisted during non‐rapid eye movement stages 2 and 3 (N2 and N3) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, in which they showed simplified morphology resembling K‐complexes and co‐occurred with increased spindle‐range activity. The pattern was present irrespective of body mass index and was qualitatively unchanged in the 203 participants free of sleep‐disordered breathing, arguing against obesity or sleep apnoea as its origin. Scalp EEG can detect breathing‐evoked potentials during quiet breathing in awake humans. These potentials persist during sleep with a morphology that resembles cortical activities previously associated with sleep stabilization. Further studies are needed to determine the physiological and clinical significance of these observations in health and disease. image Key points Spontaneous breathing at rest evokes reproducible breathing‐related cortical potentials detectable with scalp EEG. These potentials persist during sleep. They are associated with time‐locked modulation of cortical oscillatory activity.

Article.Title: Making sense of touch: Spatial tactile cues promote efficient visuo‐somatosensory integration and restore motor accuracy under sensory conflict
Article.Authors: Vlachou M.; Lafaverges E.; Mouchnino L.; Blouin J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Effective interaction with complex environments relies on the integration of somatosensory and visual signals into coherent spatial representations of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, as during goal‐directed hand movements under mirror‐reversed visual feedback, motor performance deteriorates. Despite this conflict, the visual mapping between the hand and the environment remains preserved, and visual information typically facilitates motor performance, whereas tactile feedback impairs it. Here, we tested whether providing tactile input with explicit spatial structure renders visuo‐somatosensory integration functionally relevant and stabilizes motor behaviour under sensory conflict. Healthy adults performed a mirror‐tracing task, tracing a shape's contour with the index finger while tactile feedback conveyed either motion‐related cues alone or additional discrete spatial landmarks aligned with the outline. Spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness relative to motion‐related tactile input, indicating more effective online motor control. EEG source analyses further revealed that, when spatial tactile cues were present, somatosensory activity increased and functional connectivity was largely restricted to sensorimotor areas. In contrast, when tactile cues did not convey spatial information, sensory conflict was associated with widespread reductions in cortical activity, including in somatosensory and parietal areas, and with a diffuse functional connectivity pattern consistent with elevated sensorimotor uncertainty. Together, these findings indicate that providing spatial structure to tactile input can mitigate the detrimental effects of visuo‐somatosensory conflict on motor performance and support more efficient integration of visual and somatosensory information during action. image Key points Accurate movements depend on combining visual and somatosensory information to estimate the position of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, motor performance usually deteriorates and tactile feedback can become disruptive. We tested whether tactile feedback becomes useful for movement control when it provides explicit spatial landmarks, rather than only motion‐related information from finger–surface contact. During a tracing task under visuo‐somatosensory conflict, spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness compared with when touch conveyed motion cues alone. Spatial tactile cues were associated with increased somatosensory cortical activity and a more spatially restricted pattern of functional coupling within sensorimotor networks, whereas their absence was associated with reduced somatosensory and parietal activity and a more distributed connectivity profile. Spatial structure in touch promotes multisensory integration, helping stabilize motor control under sensory conflict and highlighting how tactile cue design may improve sensorimotor function.

Article.Title: Prolonged rod photoresponse and enhanced cone sensitivity in the transgenic mouse retina lacking arrestin and guanylate cyclase activating proteins
Article.Authors: Sato S.; Frederiksen R.; Sampath A.; Kefalov V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Light activates visual pigments and downstream G protein signalling cascades in rod and cone photoreceptor cells. Timely response inactivation requires visual pigment inactivation by arrestin and restoration of cellular cGMP by guanylate cyclase activating proteins (GCAPs). Using GCAP‐deficient mice, we previously showed that apo‐opsin produces photoresponse‐like signals. To investigate the inactivation of apo‐opsin by arrestin, we generated GCAP‐deficient mice lacking arrestin ( Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− ). Using ex vivo electroretinography, we found that the dim flash responses of Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− rods were ∼100‐fold slower than those of control Gcaps −/− rods. As a result, even brief dim light exposure during sample preparation resulted in prolonged rod saturation, so that only cone responses were initially observed in Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− retinas. In contrast, rod responses were observed immediately when Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− retinas were dissected under infrared light to avoid rod photoactivation. Microspectrophotometry showed that the rate of production and decay of the active rhodopsin photoproduct, Meta II, was comparable between Gcaps −/− and Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− rods. However, the rate of photoproduct Meta III decay was 3‐fold slower in Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− rods, supporting a role for arrestin in accelerating the decay of photoactivated rhodopsin. To evaluate the effect of rod saturation on cone responses, we compared photopic cone responses from wild‐type and Gnat1 −/− retinas lacking rod signalling. Cone photoresponses were larger and more sensitive in wild‐type retinas, suggesting the potentiation of cone function by the saturation of rod phototransduction. Together, our results demonstrate that the very slow deactivation of rod responses in Gcaps −/− Arr1 −/− retinas might result in selective and potentiated cone signalling in darkness. image Key points Arrestin and guanylate cyclase activating proteins (GCAPs) play an important role in inactivation of the phototransduction cascade and termination of the light response in rod photoreceptors. The deletion of arrestin and GCAPs results in ∼100‐fold slower dim flash responses in rods so that even brief dim light exposure produces saturation of the rods for tens of minutes. The decay of the rhodopsin photoactivated intermediate Meta III was slowed down 3‐fold by the deletion of arrestin in Gcaps −/− rods, supporting a role for arrestin in accelerating the decay of photoactivated rhodopsin. Cone photoresponses were smaller and less sensitive in retinas lacking rod signalling, suggesting potentiation of cone function by the saturation of rod phototransduction. Together, these results demonstrate that the very slow deactivation of rod responses in arrestin‐ and GCAP‐deficient retinas can result in selective and potentiated cone signalling in darkness.

Article.Title: SGIP1 limits cannabinoid receptor signalling in spinal nociceptive synapses and modulates analgesia during neuroinflammation
Article.Authors: Dresslerova D.; Pontearso M.; Muzik D.; Bhattacharyya A.; Slepicka J.; Vasconcelos D.; Palecek J.; Spicarova D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The endocannabinoid system is important for pain modulation, whereas its utilization for analgesia is restricted due to the limited efficacy of cannabinoids and side effects. Cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB 1 ) in the spinal dorsal horn provides presynaptic inhibition of nociceptive neurotransmission. CB 1 regulatory protein, SH3‐containing GRB2‐like protein 3‐interacting protein 1 (SGIP1), controls its functional availability, while its role in pain modulation remains poorly understood. We examined the role of SGIP1 in nociceptive signalling under control and inflammatory conditions, using behavioural tests, patch‐clamp recordings in spinal cord slices and calcium imaging of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. SGIP1 knockout (KO) mice of both sexes showed a selective reduction in heat sensitivity, with no change in mechanical withdrawal threshold. Following carrageenan‐induced inflammation, both wild‐type (WT) and KO mice developed mechanical allodynia, whereas thermal hyperalgesia in KO mice reached only the control values of WT mice. Intrathecal application of cannabinoid agonist WIN55,212‐2 produced analgesia in both WT and KO mice, with enhanced effect of the lower dose (5 µg vs . 10 µg) in KO animals. WIN55,212‐2 (1 µM) in slices from inflamed SGIP1 KO mice induced significantly greater reduction in miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) frequency, without amplitude change, indicating enhanced presynaptic inhibition in KO mice. These enhanced inhibitory effects of WIN55,212‐2 in KO mice after inflammation were further demonstrated in DRG cultured neurons. Our results establish SGIP1 as a state‐dependent negative modulator of CB 1 function and identify SGIP1–CB 1 interaction as a candidate target for selective enhancement of cannabinoid analgesia under inflammatory pain conditions. image Key points SGIP1 deletion reduced basal heat sensitivity in mice of both sexes without altering mechanical threshold, suggesting a sex‐independent role in thermal nociception. Inflammation increased mechanical and thermal sensitivity in both SGIP1 KO and WT mice, whereas the increased thermal sensitivity of KO reached only the baseline levels of WT mice. Intrathecal cannabinoid agonist WIN55,212‐2 produced analgesia in both genotypes, with a bigger effect of the lower dose (5 vs . 10 µg) in SGIP1 KO mice. WIN55,212‐2 induced strong inhibition of miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) frequency in dorsal horn neurons that was selectively potentiated by SGIP1 deletion under inflammatory, but not control, conditions, consistent with a presynaptic locus of action. These effects were further confirmed by calcium imaging in DRG cultured neurons. SGIP1 acts as an inflammation‐dependent presynaptic CB 1 modulator of spinal nociceptive transmission, positioning the SGIP1–CB 1 interaction as a candidate target for selective enhancement of cannabinoid analgesia.

Article.Title: Non‐steady‐state modelling reveals reduced skeletal muscle protein synthesis as the primary driver of disuse‐atrophy in young, healthy females
Article.Authors: Pufahl C.; Mcleod J.; Ferguson E.; Boileau K.; Ross B.; Tripp T.; Wilkinson J.; Simpson C.; Gurd B.; McGlory C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Skeletal muscle mass reflects the balance between muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and muscle protein breakdown (MPB). In healthy humans, a decline in MPS is recognized as the primary driver of muscle disuse‐atrophy, with limited contribution from increased MPB. However, disuse‐induced declines in protein pool size directly influence the calculation of muscle protein turnover. We examined how accounting for changes in protein pool size impacted MPS and MPB rates assessed using deuterium oxide in healthy humans. Fourteen females (21 ± 2 years of age; 24.5 ± 3.0 kg/m 2 ) had one leg subjected to 10 days of unloading, whilst the contralateral leg underwent loading in the form of resistance exercise. Steady‐state and non‐steady‐state modelling approaches were used to calculate MPS and MPB rates. In response to unloading, there was a significant decline in MRI‐derived vastus lateralis volume, and thus non‐steady‐state equations were applied exclusively to this limb. Regardless of whether steady‐state or non‐steady‐state approaches were applied, mixed MPS rates were significantly reduced in response to unloading, whilst mixed MPB rates remained unchanged. Notably, unloading elicited protein fraction‐specific responses, whereby myofibrillar MPS rates declined significantly whilst sarcoplasmic MPS rates were unaltered. We also found that in response to loading, mixed, myofibrillar and sarcoplasmic MPS rates remained unchanged compared with basal rates. Our findings show that unilateral unloading in females induces muscle disuse‐atrophy driven by reductions in MPS rates, rather than by elevations in MPB rates, a response that was protein fraction specific and preserved irrespective of whether steady‐state or non‐steady‐state equations were used. image Key points In humans, short‐term muscle disuse‐atrophy is generally attributed to reduced muscle protein synthesis (MPS) rates, but integrated tracer approaches to measure protein turnover can be influenced by changes in protein pool size. We used deuterated water ( 2 H 2 O) to measure rates of MPS and muscle protein breakdown (MPB) during 10 days of unilateral unloading in young, healthy females. Steady‐state and non‐steady‐state equations were applied to account for changes in the protein pool size that occur with disuse‐atrophy. Unloading reduced muscle size and MPS rates, whereas MPB rates were unchanged. Accounting for the change in the protein pool size using non‐steady‐state equations did not alter this conclusion. These findings refine our interpretation of the mechanisms driving muscle disuse‐atrophy in healthy humans that might differ from more severe clinical or preclinical scenarios of muscle wasting.

Article.Title: K <sub>V</sub> channels contribute to thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans
Article.Authors: Ruiz‐Pick Y.; Wagle‐Babb S.; Kichloo A.; Olivencia‐Yurvati A.; Dick G.; Romero S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Localized application of heat is used therapeutically to reduce skeletal muscle pain and improve mobility and recovery in various populations. The efficacy of this thermal therapy is considered to be partly a result of increased blood flow in the skeletal muscle directly exposed to heat (i.e. thermal hyperaemia). However, the mechanisms mediating thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans remain poorly understood. Voltage‐dependent potassium (K V ) channels play a pivotal role linking upstream vasodilatory signals to electro‐mechanical mechanisms that mediate vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Therefore, the present study aimed to test the hypothesis that K V channel antagonism would attenuate thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans. We used microdialysis to directly measure local blood flow via the ethanol washout technique at two sites in the vastus lateralis muscle of 10 healthy adults (seven women). One probe was perfused with 0.9% saline, whereas the other was perfused with the K V channel antagonist 4‐aminopyridine (26.6 m m ). Pulsed short‐wave diathermy was used to induce deep heating of the vastus lateralis for 90 min. Muscle temperature was measured midway between the microdialysis probes via a thermocouple. Baseline blood flow did not differ between probes ( P = 0.684). Pulsed short‐wave diathermy increased skeletal muscle temperature through 90 min of heating ( P < 0.001). However, the accompanying increase in blood flow at 90 min was attenuated when perfused with 4‐aminopyridine ( P = 0.0222). These data suggest that K V channels substantially contribute to thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans. image Key points The efficacy of thermal therapy is considered to be partly a result of increased blood flow in the skeletal muscle directly exposed to heat (i.e. thermal hyperaemia). However, the mechanisms mediating thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle remain poorly understood. Voltage‐dependent potassium (K V ) channels play a pivotal role as downstream effectors that mediate vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Therefore, we tested the hypothesis that K V channel antagonism would attenuate thermal hyperaemia in skeletal muscle of humans. Using microdialysis, we found that K V channel antagonism with 4‐aminopyridine attenuated thermal hyperaemia at 90 min of localized heating, when this vasodilatory response was the greatest. We identified a critical role for K V channels in human skeletal muscle thermal hyperaemia, establishing these channels as important downstream effectors of this vasodilatory response.

Article.Title: Progesterone does not modulate myofibrillar protein synthesis at rest or following acute resistance exercise in premenopausal females
Article.Authors: D'Souza A.; Shea A.; Dunlop C.; Lees M.; Ali H.; Houtkamp D.; Prowting J.; Newbold J.; Phillips S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Progesterone has been proposed to modulate skeletal muscle protein turnover, although direct support for this hypothesis is lacking. We examined whether acute elevation of progesterone alters myofibrillar protein synthesis (MyoPS) at rest and following resistance exercise (RE) in naturally menstruating females. Twenty premenopausal females (21 ± 3 years of age) were randomised in a double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial to receive oral micronized progesterone (400 mg) or matching placebo at −34 and −10 h before a stable isotope infusion on days 1–5 of their menstrual cycle. One leg performed RE while the contralateral leg remained rested, followed by ingestion of 30 g whey protein. MyoPS was quantified using the l ‐[ring‐ 1 3 C 6 ]‐phenylalanine precursor–product method across fasted–rested, fed–rested and fed–exercised conditions. Progesterone elevated serum concentrations well above the luteal‐phase range (185 ± 105 vs . 1.0 ± 0.2 ng mL −1 ). Despite this, we detected no difference in MyoPS groups in any conditions, including the exercise‐induced increment (treatment × leg interaction, P = 0.945). Both protein feeding ( P = 0.00459) and RE ( P < 0.001) independently stimulated MyoPS above resting fasted levels. Progesterone was associated with modestly lower total amino acid concentrations, but not essential amino acid or leucine specifically; postprandial kinetics did not differ between groups. Acute elevation of circulating progesterone above the luteal‐phase range does not detectably modify the skeletal muscle anabolic response to RE or protein feeding in premenopausal females. These findings challenge the characterisation of progesterone as catabolic (or anabolic) to skeletal muscle and indicate that menstrual cycle phase‐based training recommendations predicated on a progesterone‐driven effect warrant critical re‐evaluation. image Key points Progesterone has been proposed to exert catabolic effects on skeletal muscle, yet direct evidence in premenopausal adult females is absent. We examined whether pharmacological elevation of progesterone augments myofibrillar protein synthesis (MyoPS) at rest and following resistance exercise. Oral micronized progesterone administered at 34 and 10 h before testing successfully elevated serum progesterone to well above the luteal‐phase range (185 ± 105 vs . 1.0 ± 0.2 ng mL −1 ) during the early follicular phase. Despite this, MyoPS did not differ between progesterone and placebo in fasted–rested, fed–rested or fed–exercised conditions. Resistance exercise robustly elevated MyoPS above the fed–rested conditions, confirming model sensitivity. Neither postprandial amino acid availability nor individual progesterone exposure was associated with MyoPS. These findings challenge the characterisation of progesterone as pro‐catabolic/anti‐anabolic to skeletal muscle and indicate that menstrual cycle phase‐based training and nutrition recommendations predicated on progesterone‐driven effects on skeletal muscle are not supported by direct mechanistic evidence.

Article.Title: Developmental mechanisms contributing to non‐linear firing dynamics in spinal motoneurons of the postnatal mouse
Article.Authors: Sharples S.; Miles G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The intrinsic properties of spinal motoneurons support flexible movement, including the maintenance of postural tone. Motoneurons can produce sustained action potential output that outlasts synaptic input, a phenomenon traditionally attributed to persistent inward currents (PICs) mediated by sodium and calcium channels. Using whole‐cell patch‐clamp electrophysiology, we examined how specific ion channels contribute to PIC maturation and non‐linear firing dynamics that allow motoneurons to sustain their output in fast and slow lumbar motoneurons across postnatal development in mice. PIC amplitude and non‐linear firing dynamics increased after weight‐bearing in fast but not slow motoneurons. Blocking Na V 1.6 channels reduced PIC amplitude at both pre‐ and post‐weight‐bearing stages, whereas L‐type calcium channel blockade only reduced PICs after weight‐bearing emerged. However, reducing PIC amplitude by blocking these channels, either individually or in parallel, did not abolish sustained firing hysteresis, which may be because PICs are not yet fully established at this stage of postnatal development. Unexpectedly, activation of muscarinic receptors increased PIC amplitude while promoting adaptive firing dynamics, suggesting that PICs alone do not account for sustained firing hysteresis. We also found that pharmacological manipulation of potassium currents mediated by KCNQ and K V 1.2 channels produced substantial changes in firing dynamics. Strikingly, blocking hyperpolarization‐activated cyclic nucleotide‐gated channels promoted sustained firing dynamics and led to the emergence of self‐sustained firing in fast motoneurons. These results indicate that PICs and non‐linear firing dynamics mature together and extend the current framework on non‐linear firing dynamics of motoneurons to include additional voltage‐gated ion channels. image Key points Persistent inward currents (PICs) and recruitment–derecruitment hysteresis increase in parallel in fast, but not slow, motoneurons following the onset of hindlimb weight‐bearing. Increased expression or function of L‐type calcium channels may contribute to enhanced PIC amplitude in fast motoneurons after weight‐bearing emerges. Blocking Na V 1.6 or L‐type calcium channels did not reduce sustained firing hysteresis in fast motoneurons. KCNQ channels oppose PICs and, together with K V 1.2 channels, shape recruitment–derecruitment asymmetry, thereby modulating firing hysteresis in fast motoneurons. Hyperpolarization‐activated cyclic nucleotide‐gated channels generate a resting H‐current that delays recruitment, modulates firing hysteresis, and prevents the emergence of self‐sustained firing in fast motoneurons.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial electron transport chain activity is not essential for the acute hypoxic response of spinal oxygen sensors
Article.Authors: Sartori M.; Amir A.; Wilson R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Spinal sympathetic preganglionic neurons (SSPNs) are oxygen sensitive. These spinal oxygen sensors (SOS) increase sympathetic output when subjected to acute hypoxia, orchestrating cardiorespiratory responses to protect against the deleterious effects of oxygen deprivation. Most other oxygen‐sensing systems rely on mitochondrial mechanisms to detect and signal decreases in oxygen. Here, we apply pharmacological blockers of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and a mitochondrial‐targeted antioxidant to a rat perfused in situ spinal cord preparation to test the role of mitochondria in the SOS. We demonstrate that, unlike other oxygen‐sensitive cells, the mitochondrial respiratory chain is not essential for the SOS. Nonetheless, blockade of mitochondrial respiratory complexes augments SSPN activity. These results indicate that mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) can increase SSPN activity but do not appear to drive the SOS. We propose that, in chronic diseases prone to oxidative stress and/or frequent hypoxic events, SSPN mitochondrial ROS directly contribute to sympathetic overactivity. image Key points Decreases in oxygen concentration are detected by oxygen‐sensitive cells that orchestrate cardiorespiratory and vascular adjustments to avoid oxygen deprivation to vital tissues. Recently discovered spinal oxygen sensors (SOS) increase sympathetic and respiratory activity in response to hypoxia. Unlike other oxygen‐sensitive cells, here we report that the SOS do not rely on the mitochondrial electron transport chain for oxygen sensing. Our findings show that pharmacological blockade of mitochondrial respiratory complexes can increase sympathetic activity but does not inhibit the hypoxic response. These results indicate that mitochondrial reactive oxygen species can affect sympathetic activity, but that mitochondria do not appear to play a key role in spinal oxygen sensing.

Article.Title: Identification of TREK channels in mouse intracardiac ganglion neurons
Article.Authors: Campos‐Rios A.; Herrera‐Perez S.; Rodriguez‐Castañeda M.; Ameal‐Tedin D.; Alvarez‐Rodriguez M.; Blanco‐Remesar D.; Rodriguez‐Tebar A.; De Miguel E.; Covelo A.; Lamas J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The intracardiac nervous system is a complex neural network formed by a diffuse plexus, the so‐called intracardiac ganglion (ICG). These ganglia locally innervate and control heart function, but little is known about how ICG neuronal activity is regulated. Although various ionic currents have been characterized in cardiac tissue, the expression and role of TWIK‐related K + (TREK) channels in ICG neurons remain unexplored. TREK channels, members of the two‐pore domain potassium channel family, are essential regulators of neuronal membrane resting potential and excitability, with recognized neuroprotective functions. In this study, we have characterized different ionic currents present in mouse ICG neurons, including tetrodotoxin‐sensitive Na + currents, delayed K + rectifiers, Ca +2 ‐dependent K + currents and A, H and M currents. Notably, we provide the first evidence of functional TREK channel expression in these neurons. Our findings suggest that TREK channels contribute to excitability control and cellular homoeostasis in ICG neurons, highlighting their potential relevance to cardiac physiology and disease. image Key points This study provides the first evidence of functional TWIK‐related K + (TREK) channel expression in intracardiac ganglion (ICG) neurons. Comprehensive profiling of ionic currents shaping excitability in ICG neurons. Neuroprotective TREK channels might emerge as potential therapeutic targets for cardiac disorders.

Article.Title: Infra‐slow brain–heart–gut electrophysiological interactions reveal a co‐ordinated multisystem physiological network in humans
Article.Authors: Sitti G.; Pitti L.; Candia‐Rivera D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Growing evidence indicates that brain continuously interacts with other physiological systems through neural and non‐neural pathways. The brain–heart and brain–gut axes play a central role in homoeostasis, allostasis and behaviour, but also in cognitive aspects, including emotion and decision‐making. Disruptions in these axes have been linked to a wide range of cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric disorders. Despite this evidence, triadic crosstalk between the brain, heart and gut remains largely unexplored. Brain activity, cardiac autonomic fluctuations and gastric rhythms all exhibit slow temporal components in resting state, suggesting that brain–heart–gut electrophysiological interactions may occur over time scales from the infra‐slow (0.01–0.1 Hz) physiological range. Using open‐access electrophysiological recordings from 28 healthy subjects at rest, we extracted time‐varying power dynamics describing the activity of the three organs: brain alpha power, cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic indices, and the power of the gastric rhythm. Statistical associations among these organs were quantified using the maximal information coefficient across the extended temporal delay range. Physiological interactions were confirmed using surrogate‐based testing, which allowed us to construct the network topology of interactions between the three organs. Our findings show that triadic brain–heart–gut interactions form a multidirectional network primarily at infra‐slow time scales during resting state. This study offers one of the first insights into the physiology of brain–heart–gut interplay, providing a methodological baseline for the development of more comprehensive biomarkers based on network dynamics capable of linking pathological conditions to dysregulation across multiple organ systems. image Key points First in‐human, non‐invasive investigation of parallel brain–heart–gut electrophysiological interactions in awake, healthy subjects. We analysed simultaneous electroencephalographic (EEG), electrocardiographic (ECG) and electrogastrographic (EGG) recordings and quantified strength and temporal scale of the derived time series associations to construct a large‐scale network of interactions. We found that brain–heart–gut interactions extend into the infra‐slow range (0.01–0.1 Hz), indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in the electrophysiological activity of one organ at rest are typically followed by corresponding changes in the other two. We consistently found a robust brain–heart–gut network topology across subjects, with multidirectional interactions and bodily dynamics converging towards midline central‐posterior EEG regions. These findings provide one of the first endeavours in characterizing the physiology of brain–heart–gut interactions and a methodology with strong biomarker development potential.

Article.Title: The three‐element Windkessel parameters have empirical relations that uniquely define the mechanoenergetics of cardiac muscle shortening
Article.Authors: Kohombakadawala C.; Pham T.; Tran K.; Taberner A.; Han J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The three‐element Windkessel model of the systemic circulation comprises terms that represent the resistance of peripheral vessels ( R p ), compliance of the arteries ( C ) and characteristic impedance ( Z c ) of the aorta. It is widely used to represent the biophysics of the arterial system, and can be used to model the vascular load that can be experimentally presented to isolated hearts or muscles. Reported values of the three Windkessel parameters span several orders of magnitude. By collecting literature data across species, we found empirical relationships that are naturally preserved among the three Windkessel parameters. We applied these empirical relationships in our experiments when prescribing loads to isolated cardiac muscles, and compared the results with loading protocols that do not preserve these empirical relationships. Thus, in our loading protocols, R p was varied, whereas C and Z c were either held constant or varied according to their empirical relationship with R p . Muscles responded to the prescribed loads and generated force–length work‐loops that were unique to the various loading protocols. The differences in work‐loops were most evident during muscle shortening in terms of the force achieved to commence shortening, the dynamics of the force during shortening and the force reached at the completion of shortening. With these loading protocol‐specific shortening, muscles liberated distinct amounts of shortening heat and performed different amounts of work, resulting in different levels of mechanical efficiency. In conclusion, the three‐element Windkessel parameters have empirical relationships that uniquely define the load and mechanoenergetics of cardiac muscle shortening. image Key points The heart pumps blood into the aorta against the arterial load imposed by the systemic vasculature. The biophysical properties of the vasculature are characterised by resistance, compliance and impedance. By compiling literature data across multiple species, we identified a relation that is rather ‘universal’ linking resistance and compliance, and another linking resistance and impedance. We conducted experiments on isolated cardiac muscles subjected to contract against loads that either conformed to or departed from the relations. We found that when the loads conformed to the relations, the mechanics, kinetics and energetics of muscle contraction and shortening were distinct from those loads that deviated from the relations. These findings establish a fundamental link between arterial load and cardiac muscle mechanoenergetics, demonstrating that presenting isolated muscles with loading conditions that conform to the empirical relations is essential for understanding the physiological mechanics of cardiac contraction.

Article.Title: Altitude‐induced plasticity of respiratory central–peripheral chemoreflex interaction
Article.Authors: Guluzade N.; MacKenzie B.; Day T.; Wilson R.; Keir D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Stable breathing depends on the integrated action of central and peripheral chemoreceptors, but the nature of this interaction in humans and its physiological importance remain controversial. Previous studies reported additive, hypo‐additive and hyper‐additive responses across species, preparations and protocols. Here, we used a novel method to quantify peripheral chemoreflex sensitivity across graded levels of central chemoreceptor activation to test whether central–peripheral chemoreceptor interaction in awake humans is fixed or state dependent. At low altitude, the form of interaction varied across individuals, with most showing additive responses (12/17) and a substantial subset showing hypo‐additivity (5/17). After 7–10 days of acclimatization to 3500 m, all five hypo‐additive individuals became additive, and four additive participants became hyper‐additive. This shift in interaction towards hyper‐additivity provides the first evidence that central‐peripheral chemoreceptor integration is plastic. Plasticity during wakefulness was not associated with individual differences in central sleep apnoea severity at high altitude. Thus, our findings confirm that central–peripheral chemoreceptor interaction differs among individuals and suggest that the form of interaction can be reshaped by hypobaric hypoxic stress. image Key points How central and peripheral chemoreceptor drives to breathe interact in humans and whether this process is plastic remains uncertain. We quantified peripheral chemoreflex sensitivity to hypoxia (PChS) across graded levels of central chemoreceptor activation at low altitude and after 7–10 days of high‐altitude exposure (3500 m). Seventeen participants performed repeated modified rebreathing tests with end‐tidal fixed at 150 (hyperoxia), 60 and 45 mmHg (hypoxia). PChS was computed at 1 mmHg intervals of end‐tidal () from linear regression of the difference in ventilation between hypoxic and hyperoxic conditions vs . calculated arterial oxygen saturation (ScO 2 ) (L·min −1 ·mmHg −1 ·%ScO 2 −1 ). At low altitude, PChS increased with in all individuals; the relationship was linear (no interaction) in 12 participants, and 5 showed hypo‐additivity. After acclimatization, central and peripheral chemoreflex sensitivities increased. All hypo‐additive individuals became additive; four additive individuals became hyper‐additive. Central–peripheral chemoreceptor interaction is plastic in humans and can shift towards hyper‐additivity with sustained hypobaric hypoxia.

Article.Title: Harnessing the ion transportome to treat cancer
Article.Authors: Capatina A.; Malcolm J.; Ahmed A.; Bruce J.; Buchanan P.; Eykyn T.; Fitzgerald E.; Foust A.; Hales T.; Hayashi Y.; Higgins S.; Huang A.; Jackson A.; James A.; Jones F.; Lilley S.; McCloskey K.; Moodad S.; Robinson H.; Salvage S.; Soyer O.; Yerlikaya S.; Ashmore J.; Murrell‐Lagnado R.; Brackenbury W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Despite significant advances in early detection and therapeutic opportunities, cancer remains a critical global health challenge. The greatest barrier to reducing cancer‐associated mortality is the persistent problem of therapeutic resistance and metastasis. Standard treatment approaches, including surgery combined with chemotherapy and radiation, are effective for many patients with localised disease. However, a substantial proportion of patients will experience recurrence and therapy resistance, leading to treatment failure and poor outcomes. This adverse prognosis for patients highlights the critical need to identify new therapeutic targets capable of improving long‐term survival. The ion transportome comprises ion channels, solute transporters and pumps that regulate controlled movement of sodium (Na + ), potassium (K + ), calcium (Ca 2+ ), chloride (Cl − ) and hydrogen (H + ) across cell membranes. Ion transport is central to many cellular processes, including cell growth, volume regulation, proliferation and migration. In many solid tumours, the finely tuned ionic balance becomes dysregulated, with aberrant expression or activity of membrane transport proteins being closely linked to many of the hallmarks of cancer. Ion channel modulation using pharmacological agents designed to treat channelopathies has demonstrated promise in suppressing cancer progression in preclinical models. Thus, targeting ion‐driven vulnerabilities within solid tumours may complement existing therapies to overcome resistance and improve patient outcomes. The dynamic nature of ion transport mechanisms means that addressing critical research questions regarding their suitability as pharmacological targets is challenging, highlighting the need to develop innovative approaches to study these processes in oncology. image

Article.Title: Channelrhodopsin ion selectivity determines mechanisms and efficacy of optogenetic defibrillation in human atria and ventricles
Article.Authors: Ohnemus S.; Dasí A.; Ramadan A.; Greiner J.; Wülfers E.; Stoyek M.; Tillert L.; Vierock J.; Quinn T.; Kohl P.; Boyle P.; Timmermann V.; Schneider‐Warme F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cardiac re‐entrant arrhythmias are a major cause of sudden cardiac death. Optogenetic defibrillation has emerged as a promising anti‐arrhythmic strategy based on photoactivation of channelrhodopsins, yet the efficacy and potential adverse consequences of activating different classes of light‐gated ion channels have not been systematically evaluated. Previous studies assessed either cation (e.g. ChR2) or anion (e.g. GtACR1) non‐selective channels, both of which depolarize resting cardiomyocytes. Recently identified light‐gated K + channels (e.g. WiChR) suppress cardiomyocyte activity while maintaining the membrane potential near its resting state, but their defibrillation potential remains unexplored. We used computational simulations to compare ChR2, GtACR1 and WiChR. Single‐cell simulations showed that ChR2 and GtACR1 markedly increased diastolic intracellular Ca 2+ (by 42.6% and 52.6%, respectively), whereas WiChR induced only minimal changes (by 4.0%), suggesting lower pro‐arrhythmogenic risk. WiChR, however, slightly increased intracellular Na + (by 15.1% vs . 0.1% and 3.4% for ChR2 and GtACR1), consistent with the residual Na + permeability of currently available K + ‐conducting channelrhodopsins. Simulations in human ventricles and atria showed that GtACR1 most effectively terminated re‐entrant arrhythmias at low light intensities, whereas WiChR achieved comparable efficacy at ≥5 mW/mm 2 . Complementary tissue‐scale simulations revealed that defibrillation occurs through depolarization within the excitable gap followed by fast Na + channel inactivation (ChR2 and partly GtACR1), or through reduced membrane resistance at sufficiently high light intensities (large‐conductance channels GtACR1 and WiChR). Overall, we demonstrate that channelrhodopsin ion selectivity is a key determinant of both optogenetic defibrillation efficacy and its underlying mechanisms. image Translational perspective Re‐entrant arrhythmias are a leading cause of sudden cardiac death. Standard therapies, including the activation of implantable cardioverter‐defibrillators, carry burdens such as pain and myocardial injury. Optogenetic defibrillation has been suggested as a potentially gentler alternative, replacing high‐voltage electrical shocks by photoactivation of light‐gated ion channels expressed in cardiac cells. Determining which light‐gated ion channel optimally balances efficacy and adverse effects on cardiac electrophysiology is critical for clinical translation. We addressed this question using computational simulations and validation experiments in zebrafish hearts. We identify ion selectivity as a key determinant of both the success rate for arrhythmia termination and the underlying mechanisms: non‐selective cation‐ and anion‐conducting channels terminate re‐entry efficiently while promoting intracellular Ca 2+ accumulation, a plausible substrate for pro‐arrhythmic side effects that could undermine therapeutic safety. K + ‐conducting channels largely avoid this pro‐arrhythmic risk by holding cardiomyocytes near their resting potential, albeit at the cost of requiring transmural illumination, while also causing mild Na + accumulation attributable to residual Na + permeability. Together, these trade‐offs define clear clinical implications: K + ‐conducting channels may provide the safest option for optogenetic defibrillation, particularly once variants with further enhanced K + selectivity and red‐shifted activation spectra for improved operation within blood‐perfused myocardium become available. Key points We use computational simulations to compare cation non‐selective (ChR2), anion non‐selective (GtACR1) and K + ‐selective (WiChR) channelrhodopsins for optogenetic termination of re‐entrant arrhythmia. Single‐cardiomyocyte simulations suggest that ChR2 and GtACR1 activation can cause progressive accumulation of intracellular Ca 2+ , which is minimized when using WiChR. Intracellular microelectrode recordings from hearts of transgenic adult zebrafish validate the simulated voltage dynamics seen with ChR2, GtACR1 or WiChR activation. Simulations of human left ventricles and atria indicate that GtACR1 is most effective in terminating re‐entrant arrhythmia at low light intensities, whereas WiChR becomes similarly effective at higher intensities. Tissue‐scale simulations indicate distinct defibrillation mechanisms: excitable gap extinction by de novo action potential initiation followed by inactivation of fast Na + channels for depolarizing channelrhodopsins (ChR2, GtACR1), and reduction in membrane resistance for the large‐conductance channels (GtACR1, WiChR), effectively clamping the membrane potential at each channel's reversal potential at high light levels.

Article.Title: Warburg redefined: Metabolites, mitochondria and macrophages in immune regulation
Article.Authors: Min Y.; Henry Ó.; O'Neill L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nearly 100 years ago, Otto Warburg observed that cancer cells preferentially use glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen, supporting rapid cell growth. Since then, the concept of the Warburg effect has expanded far beyond tumour bioenergetics and is now recognised as a key feature of immune cell activation. A notable example is in macrophages, which, following pro‐inflammatory stimulation, undergo Warburg‐like metabolic reprogramming, characterised by increased glycolysis. Recent studies have shown that accumulated metabolites such as lactate have a range of immunoregulatory functions that shape macrophage inflammatory responses. In addition, glycolytic enzymes have been found to exert non‐canonical functions that directly regulate macrophage immune signalling. Mitochondria, once considered suppressed during Warburg reprogramming, also undergo profound changes, with the electron transport chain generating reactive oxygen species and metabolites such as succinate, fumarate and itaconate playing complex immunoregulatory roles, and mitochondrial dynamics actively shaping metabolism and immune responses. Together, these findings redefine the Warburg effect in macrophages as a coordinated metabolic and signalling process that integrates glycolysis, mitochondrial function and immunometabolite signalling to optimise context‐dependent immune responses. image

Article.Title: Ascending infection of Gardnerella spp. and compartmentalized inflammatory response in fetal–maternal interface organ‐on‐chip model
Article.Authors: de Castro Silva M.; Sena Baptista Ferreira J.; Gomes Barnabé R.; Tesini Rocha M.; Yonezawa de Souza L.; Ribeiro de Andrade Ramos B.; Menon R.; Guimarães da Silva M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Preterm birth is a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality worldwide, with ascending infection and inflammation at the fetal–maternal interface recognized as major contributors to its pathophysiology. Gardnerella spp., key species associated with bacterial vaginosis, have been implicated in adverse pregnancy outcomes; however, the mechanisms underlying their ability to ascend and trigger inflammatory responses remain poorly understood. In this study, we used a fetal–maternal interface organ‐on‐chip model to investigate the ascending infection of Gardnerella spp. and the resulting compartmentalized cytokine response. The device integrated decidual, chorionic trophoblast, amniotic mesenchymal and amniotic epithelial cells to mimic the in vivo architecture of the fetal membranes. Quantitative PCR revealed progressive bacterial ascension, with a significantly higher load of Gardnerella spp. in the amnion mesenchymal layer after 48 h of stimulation. Cytokine analysis demonstrated increased production of interleukin (IL)‐1β, IL‐6, C‐X‐C motif chemokine ligand 8 and IL‐10 across cellular compartments, indicating a coordinated pro‐inflammatory and compensatory anti‐inflammatory response. These findings provide direct evidence of Gardnerella spp. invasion dynamics and immune activation at the fetal–maternal interface, supporting the use of microphysiological systems as translational tools to study infection‐driven mechanisms of spontaneous preterm birth. image Key points Gardnerella spp. ascend rapidly across the fetal–maternal interface. Ascending infection induces compartmentalized inflammatory cytokine responses. Amnion mesenchymal cells exhibited the highest bacterial burden after 48 h. The fetal–maternal interface organ‐on‐chip provides a translational model for studying infection‐driven preterm birth.

Article.Title: Ionizing radiation‐induced remodelling of the heart: Cellular pathways and crosstalk relevant to stereotactic arrhythmia radioablation (STAR)
Article.Authors: Nys L.; Goethals E.; Saint‐Martin‐Willer A.; Vandenberk B.; Dries E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Stereotactic arrhythmia radioablation (STAR) has emerged as a promising non‐invasive therapy for refractory ventricular tachycardia, yet its biological mechanisms remain poorly defined. While conventional catheter ablation achieves arrhythmia control through structural remodelling, radiotherapy was initially assumed to act similarly. However, STAR reduces ventricular arrhythmia burden within weeks, preceding the development of radiation‐induced structural remodelling. This temporal mismatch indicates that early anti‐arrhythmic effects are probably driven by functional adaptations. Human tissue findings and preclinical large‐ and small‐animal models have provided the first insights into how the myocardium responds to focal high‐dose radiation, yet experimental data on STAR's underlying cellular mechanisms remain limited. Across these studies, a consistent observation is the temporal dissociation between early functional effects and delayed structural remodelling, which provides a key framework for interpretating STAR's anti‐arrhythmic action. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on cell‐type‐specific responses to ionizing radiation by integrating insights from the emerging STAR literature, oncology and radiation heart disease models. By linking time‐resolved cellular responses to clinical observations, we aim to distinguish mechanisms most relevant to early therapeutic effects from those contributing to delayed remodelling, and to define key knowledge gaps for guiding safe and effective clinical implementation. image

Article.Title: microRNA‐145‐5p regulates P‐glycoprotein and breast cancer resistance protein in primary human fetal brain endothelial cells
Article.Authors: Lye P.; Bloise E.; Ivanovski N.; Nadeem L.; Casciaro C.; Matthews S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp, encoded by ABCB1 ) and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP/ ABCG2 ), present in the blood–brain barrier, protect the fetal brain from exposure to neurotoxicants. P‐gp and BCRP are modulated by microRNA‐145‐5p (miR‐145‐5p) in cancer cells. In the present study, we hypothesized that miR‐145‐5p modulates P‐gp and BCRP in human fetal brain endothelial cells (hfBECs) and in an adult BEC line (human cerebral microvascular endothelial cell line; hCMEC/D3). miR‐145‐5p mimic and inhibitor were transfected into hfBECs ( n = 6, mid‐gestation) and hCMEC/D3 cells. P‐gp and BCRP mRNA, protein expression and efflux activity were assessed using qPCR, Western blotting, immunofluorescence and calcein‐AM and chlorin e6 assays. Target specificity was evaluated using luciferase reporter assays. hfBECs exhibited lower ABCB1 and ABCG2 mRNA and protein expression and reduced P‐gp activity, but significantly increased BCRP activity, compared with hCMEC/D3 cells. The miR‐145‐5p mimic reduced luciferase activity of an ABCB1 3′‐untranslated region (3’‐UTR) reporter but had no effect on the ABCG2 3′‐UTR. In hfBECs, miR‐145‐5p overexpression reduced P‐gp and BCRP levels and efflux activity. In contrast, miR‐145‐5p overexpression in hCMEC/D3 cells increased P‐gp activity while reducing BCRP activity. Inhibition of miR‐145‐5p in hfBECs increased P‐gp protein levels and exhibited a trend towards increased P‐gp activity, without altering BCRP levels, although BCRP activity significantly increased. miR‐145‐5p directly modulates the expression and activity of P‐gp and indirectly modulates BCRP in fetal and adult human BECs. These data suggest that miR‐145‐5p plays an important role in the regulation of key drug transporters at the BBB in fetal brain and may modulate BBB function in adulthood. image Key points microRNA‐145‐5p (miR‐145‐5p) directly targets the 3′‐untranslated region (3′‐UTR) of ABCB1 , but not ABCG2 , as shown by luciferase assays. In human fetal brain endothelial cells (hfBECs), miR‐145‐5p mimic reduces P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp) and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) levels and transporter activity. Inhibition of miR‐145‐5p in hfBECs increases P‐gp and BCRP activities. In adult human cerebral microvascular endothelial cell line (hCMEC/D3) cells, miR‐145‐5p mimic increases P‐gp activity and decreases BCRP activity, indicating developmental differences in regulation. miR‐145‐5p directly modulates P‐gp and indirectly modulates BCRP, suggesting a key role in blood–brain barrier (BBB) transporter regulation during fetal development and potentially in adulthood.

Article.Authors: Morelli A.

(1992).They demonstrated how one hemisphere can transiently suppress the excitability of the other, a method introduced through transcallosal connections.Since then, IHI has become one of the principal experimental models for investigating functional connectivity in the human brain. Article.Title: Dyssynchrony without dysfunction: Left bundle branch block does not acutely reduce cardiac output
Article.Authors: Kruthoff C.; Krauß J.; Sánchez J.; Gerach T.; Barrios Espinosa C.; Duhme J.; Loewe A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Left bundle branch block (LBBB) describes a disruption or delay in electrical conduction through the left bundle branch of the His‐Purkinje system (HPS). While new‐onset LBBB commonly emerges in individuals with a history of hypertension, cardiomegaly or coronary artery disease, it can also occur in the absence of other cardiovascular abnormalities. Whether LBBB is a cause or a consequence of heart failure remains unclear. In this work, we used six different electromechanical in silico heart models with an integrated HPS to simulate both a healthy control and a pure LBBB case for each geometry, affecting only the HPS in the absence of other cardiovascular pathologies. We compared electrophysiological, mechanical and haemodynamic metrics between both cases. Despite exhibiting a severe delay of up to 87 ms in left ventricular activation, all six virtual patients showed almost no acute change in ejection fraction (EF) due to LBBB. However, an absolute increase in septal flash of 1.4 mm to 2.7 mm indicated mechanical dyssynchrony. Furthermore, we observed a relative strain increase of 12.3–30% in the left ventricular free wall across all models. The load imbalance marked by the strain increase could drive LBBB‐induced remodelling, leading to a major reduction in EF over time. Regardless of variations in heart geometry, this study shows that electrical dyssynchrony immediately affects mechanics more than haemodynamics. In line with clinical data, our findings suggest that patients with LBBB might benefit from an earlier application of cardiac resynchronization therapy to prevent strain‐induced remodelling and preserve cardiac output. image Key points Left bundle branch block (LBBB) describes an impairment of electrical conduction in the left bundle branch of the His‐Purkinje system, causing a delay in left ventricular activation. While LBBB has been discussed as a risk factor for the progression of heart failure, the exact relationship of acute and chronic effects of LBBB in heart failure is not fully understood. In this study, we simulated both a healthy and a pure and acute LBBB scenario in six different electromechanical in silico heart models. Pure LBBB induced mechanical dyssynchrony, increasing septal flash and left ventricular free wall strain, while the ejection fraction remained virtually unchanged. The strain‐induced load imbalance may cause long‐term remodelling, reducing ejection fraction over time. In line with clinical data, our results suggest an early application of cardiac resynchronization therapy in patients with LBBB to prevent remodelling and sustain cardiac output.

Article.Title: Cancer‐associated fibroblast heterogeneity across solid and haematological malignancies: Lessons from colorectal cancer and multiple myeloma
Article.Authors: Mo H.; Han H.; O'Dwyer M.; Reidy E.; Ryan A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Although substantial advances have been made in cancer immunotherapy, the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME) continues to pose a significant obstacle to the achievement of sustained clinical responses. Cancer‐associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are increasingly recognised as pivotal regulators in the TME. Their functional adaptability shapes immune responses through extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling, metabolic reprogramming and the secretion of immunomodulatory factors. This review explores the heterogeneity and plasticity of CAFs, characterising them as dynamic functional states, including myofibroblastic (myCAF), inflammatory (iCAF), antigen‐presenting (apCAF) phenotypes and hypoxia‐induced senescent fibroblasts (hsCAF), which transition fluidly in response to microenvironmental cues and oncogenic signalling. Through a comparative analysis of colorectal cancer (CRC) and multiple myeloma (MM), this review highlights how stromal regulation is adaptive across solid and haematological malignancies. In CRC, CAFs establish dense, collagen‐rich ECM barriers that exclude effector T cells, whereas, in MM, they establish adhesion‐dependent niches within the bone marrow to spatially segregate immune cells from malignant plasma cells. This review also discusses how oncogenic drivers such as KRAS and TP53 ‘educate’ the stromal microenvironment and explores emerging immune evasion mechanisms, including the sialic acid‐Siglec glyco‐immune checkpoint. Current therapeutic approaches are shifting from non‐selective stromal depletion toward normalising phenotypes, blocking secretome factors and disrupting metabolic interactions. The integration of spatial multi‐omics and artificial intelligence provides a framework for mapping these functional landscapes. In conclusion, harnessing CAF heterogeneity in multimodal combination therapies may help shift the tumour microenvironment from an immunosuppressive to a more pro‐immune state. image

Article.Title: Hexagonal modulation of theta rhythmic attentional sampling of visual space
Article.Authors: Kienitz R.; Moroz M.; Martini J.; Helfrich R.
Article.Abstract: Spatial attention improves visual perception by selecting behaviorally relevant sensory signals. Traditionally, attention has been conceptualized as a static spotlight, while recent evidence posited that attention operates as a moving spotlight that samples visual space sequentially in discrete snapshots that are clocked by theta rhythms (∼3-8 Hz). While theta rhythmic attentional sampling has mainly been observed in fronto-parietal and occipital areas, theta oscillations also hallmark entorhinal-hippocampal grid-cell networks, which encode physical space in hexagonal patterns that guide overt exploration and navigation. We hypothesized that visual attention might rely on the same underlying principles and sample visual space in a hexagonal, grid-like configuration. To test this hypothesis, twenty participants (10 females and 10 males) performed a cue-guided attention task that probed behavioral performance as a function of space and time. Reaction times were assessed as a function of spatial location and varying cue-target intervals, which displayed spatially-structured theta rhythms. Specifically, higher theta power occurred at spatial locations that were aligned to multiples of 60°, consistent with an underlying hexagonal organization. Participants that exhibited stronger hexagonal sampling relied less on the spatial cue to guide their attentional allocation. In sum, these findings suggest that covert visual attention is organized in a hexagonal pattern that might be consistent with the grid-like structure known from the entorhinal-hippocampal system and highlight that theta rhythms could reflect a common organizing principle for spatial cognition. Significance Statement Attention prioritizes sensory inputs to optimize behavior. But how does attention sample the environment in space and time? Here, we demonstrate that attentional sampling of visual space is not uniform, but might preferentially explore locations that are oriented along a hexagonal pattern, reminiscent of the spatial configuration of entorhinal-hippocampal grid cells. Moreover, covert attentional sampling exhibited oscillatory theta signatures (3-8 Hz). In sum, these findings suggest that spatial attention and navigation may share a common organizing principle, and indicate that theta rhythms may orchestrate sampling behaviors in space and time as a unifying principle underlying spatial cognition.

Article.Title: Bivalent habenula modulation of human monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways
Article.Authors: Hudson L.; Davey C.; Steward T.; Kung P.; Dai Y.; Unsworth L.; Jamieson A.; Moffat B.; Glarin R.; Harrison B.
Article.Abstract: The habenula is implicated in signaling negative reward prediction errors (RPE), yet direct evidence demonstrating its influence on downstream human brain circuits is limited. Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling across two negative RPE-inducing experimental tasks, we characterize habenula-directed connectivity with monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways in healthy adults (n = 47, 24 males and 23 females; n = 43, 23 males and 20 females). Negative feedback drove habenula inhibition of ventral tegmental area and dorsal raphe nucleus activity, while positive feedback had an excitatory effect. These core effects are replicated across reversal learning and perceptual decision uncertainty tasks, establishing a generalizable mechanism for behavioral adaptation. Task-specific modulatory effects emerged in pathways between the subcortical and cortical regions (ventral tegmental area→dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal raphe nucleus→medial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex→habenula), revealing context-dependent cortical elaboration of negative RPE-driven habenula signals. This provides the first evidence in humans, using model-based effective connectivity, for bivalent modulation of habenula function on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical pathways, demonstrating how the brain integrates negative and positive signals to guide adaptive behavior. Significance Statement The habenula – an epithalamic brain region – plays a key role in the encoding of reward and punishment. Animal studies have demonstrated the habenula to be bivalently modulated by aversive and appetitive stimuli, resulting in the bidirectional modulation of monoaminergic brain region activity. Despite this evidence, the directional impact of bivalently modulated habenula activity on its circuitry has yet to be investigated in humans. This study leverages ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and dynamic causal modelling to reveal the impact of bivalent habenula modulation on monoaminergic midbrain and cortical regions across two distinct tasks. Through these methodologies, we demonstrate the habenula to have a key role in guiding adaptive behavior.

Article.Title: Perception of tones versus tone streams under random multi-tone masking and its representation in auditory cortex
Article.Authors: Kistenmacher F.; Doll L.; Gutschalk A.
Article.Abstract: When repeated tones are presented among random masker tones, their perceptual organization is often variable. In some trials, they cannot be segregated from the masker tones. In other trials, often with a delay, they form coherent streams, segregated from the masker tones. A strong awareness-related negativity is evoked by each segregated tone of the stream in auditory cortex. A similar negative-going response has been observed when subtle, isolated tones are detected versus missed, raising the question of whether target tones that do not form a stream under informational masking are still perceived or not. Here a paradigm is introduced to probe this question while activity in auditory cortex was recorded with magnetoencephalography. Human listeners (13 female, 8 male) were instructed to indicate when they detected an isochronous stream of tones under multi-tone masking while listening to the stimulus. Thereafter, they indicated if a cue tone, presented subsequently to each trial, was comprised in the target and masker combination. Results confirmed that target tones could still be perceived in the subset of trials where they did not form a coherent stream, but the detectability in the cued frequency report was higher for tones forming a stream. A prominent awareness-related negativity was only observed when the tones formed a stream, suggesting that this response reflects the perceptual organization of the tones into streams and beyond the pure perception of the tones themselves. We speculate that the perceptual organization into a stream further enhances the detectability of the tones comprised in the stream. Significance Statement Tone sequences may form streams that segregate from competing aspects of the auditory scene, a phenomenon considered comparable to visual object grouping. In multi-tone masking, hearing out streams of repeated tones seemingly enhances tone detectability by a degree that makes it difficult to judge whether these tones could at all be perceived if they had not formed a coherent stream. We present a paradigm that allows for probing both, the perception of target-tone frequency and the formation of coherent streams in the same trials. Applying this setup in magnetoencephalography showed that the perceptual organization into a stream is more strongly represented in auditory cortex than the ability to correctly detect a tone frequency within a random tone masker.

Article.Title: Macaque Area LIP Reflects Confidence-Dependent Changes in Decision Policy
Article.Authors: Tu M.; Vivar-Lazo M.; Fetsch C.
Article.Abstract: The process of forming a decision gives rise to an estimate of its quality or likelihood of success. This graded sense of confidence is important for guiding subsequent decisions, but a neural mechanism linking subjective confidence to formation of the next decision has not been identified. We trained two male rhesus macaques to report a perceptual choice and simultaneous confidence judgment in a reaction-time (RT) motion discrimination task. Monkeys were more likely to repeat a rewarded choice when they reported low confidence on the previous trial, and showed greater changes in RT after a surprising outcome (low-confidence correct or high-confidence error). Neural activity in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) encoded the previous trial's choice and confidence more strongly after a low-confidence correct trial, and the strength of history encoding was correlated with a trial-by-trial estimate of choice bias. Ramping dynamics of the decoded decision variable also depended systematically on the conjunction of confidence and reward on the previous trial, in a manner that reflected individual differences between animals. The findings suggest that LIP not only reflects the formation of the current decision but could participate in confidence-guided learning via adjustments of the subsequent decision process. Significance statement Decision confidence is of primary interest in the study of metacognition, yet it also plays a key role in learning, serving as a graded prediction of accuracy that modulates the response to feedback. Reanalyzing data from nonhuman primates performing a reaction-time (RT) motion discrimination task with explicit confidence reports, we found that adjustments of choice bias and RT were gated by the animal’s self-reported confidence on the previous trial. The interaction of confidence and outcome (reward or punishment) was reflected in the activity of parietal (LIP) neurons on the subsequent trial, in ways largely consistent with the behavioral effects. The results and accompanying computational model suggest plausible functional links between the neuronal substrates of perceptual decision making and reinforcement learning.

Article.Title: PTPRO restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors through TrkB dephosphorylation
Article.Authors: Li J.; Yasumura M.; Iguchi T.; Taniguchi M.; Oka Y.; Tsai C.; Sato M.
Article.Abstract: The structural complexity of axon collateral terminal arbors shapes synaptic connectivity. In corticospinal projections, individual axon collaterals exhibit distinct patterns of terminal arborization, ranging from sparse local branches to dense, highly complex arbors in target regions such as the pontine nuclei. How this complexity is controlled remains poorly understood. Here, using corticopontine projections in male and female mice, we show that protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) selectively restricts higher-order branching of terminal arbors in the pontine nuclei without affecting collateral number. This function requires the intracellular phosphatase domain of PTPRO but not its extracellular region. We demonstrate that PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), and that the excessive terminal arborization caused by acute PTPRO loss is rescued by TrkB depletion or phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibition. Together, these findings reveal that PTPRO-mediated TrkB dephosphorylation acts as a molecular brake on corticopontine terminal arbor elaboration. Significance Statement How individual axons regulate terminal branching within target regions is a fundamental question in neural circuit development. This study identifies protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO), a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase that negatively regulates signaling through tyrosine phosphorylation, as a selective regulator of higher-order branching in corticopontine terminal arbors. PTPRO dephosphorylates tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a neurotrophin receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes neuronal growth and branching, thereby restricting terminal arbor complexity without affecting collateral number from the main axon. Given that terminal arbor architecture determines the synaptic territory of each cortical input, PTPRO-dependent constraint on arbor elaboration may represent a general principle by which projection-specific arbor complexity is established across long-range circuits in the central nervous system.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: PTPRO; corticopontine projections; pontine nuclei; PI3K inhibition; protein tyrosine phosphatase; synaptic connectivity

Article.Title: State-Dependent Modulation of Corticospinal and Cortical Responses by Closed-Loop Paired-pulse TMS
Article.Authors: Choi D.; Güth M.; Ma M.; Harmon M.; Wischnewski M.; Park J.; Blenker A.; Lee S.; Opitz A.
Article.Abstract: Brain oscillations shape cortical excitability in a phase-dependent manner. Cortical excitability reflects the net output of intracortical circuits, including inhibitory and facilitatory pathways. However, whether the phase of ongoing brain rhythms differentially modulates inhibitory and facilitatory responses remains unknown. Paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (ppTMS) can selectively engage these circuits, providing a unique tool to dissociate their contributions. We combined real-time EEG-guided closed-loop TMS with single- and paired-pulse TMS in 24 healthy adults (13 female) to probe how sensorimotor mu (8–13 Hz) and beta (14–30 Hz) oscillatory phase shapes responses associated with intracortical inhibitory and facilitatory processes. Single-pulse TMS (spTMS), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were delivered at four phases (peak, falling, trough, rising). Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) and TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs) were recorded to assess corticospinal and cortical responses, respectively. We found that MEP amplitude was phase-dependent across all three stimulation types, with spTMS-evoked and ICF-conditioned MEPs showing the largest amplitudes at the rising phase, whereas SICI-conditioned MEPs were largest at the peak phase of the mu oscillation. TEP P60-N100 amplitude was modulated by oscillatory phase across all stimulation types, with maximal responses at the trough phase. SICI showed opposing phase patterns between the two measures, revealing a dissociation between cortical and corticospinal responses. MEP and TEP preferred phases were correlated across participants only in the ICF condition. These findings extend phase-dependent spTMS effects to paired-pulse stimulation and show that ongoing mu phase differentially shapes responses to SICI and ICF across cortical and corticospinal levels. Significance Statement Ongoing brain oscillations are known to shape cortical excitability across their phase cycle. However, whether this effect differentially influences inhibitory and facilitatory responses has remained unresolved. Here, using closed-loop EEG-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation in healthy adults, we probed how SICI- and ICF-conditioned responses vary across different phases of the sensorimotor mu and beta rhythms. We show that corticospinal and cortical responses to inhibitory and facilitatory paired-pulse protocols exhibit distinct phase-dependent patterns in the sensorimotor mu rhythm. These findings extend phase-dependent stimulation effects beyond single-pulse TMS and reveal that the relationship between cortical state and stimulation response differs across paired-pulse protocols.

Article.Title: Area MT carries acceleration information in a quickly and directly decodable representation
Article.Authors: Chen P.; Huk A.
Article.Abstract: We sought to better understand the neural representation of visual motion acceleration. A straightforward estimation of acceleration would involve calculating the rate of change of velocity, which itself would be calculated from change in position over time. As it is well-established that neurons in area MT encode velocity, the brain could thus indirectly estimate acceleration by calculating the change in MT’s velocity representations. An alternative mechanism, however, could operate more rapidly and directly. In this case, the brain could exploit interactions between MT’s standard motion encoding and idiosyncratic temporal dynamics of neural responses. Such direct decoding would thus exploit nonlinearities usually ignored in studies of MT coding. We tested between these two theories by measuring from ensembles of MT neurons while two male awake fixating macaques viewed linearly accelerating motion stimuli. Direct decoding of acceleration from MT was possible on faster time scales, and could be done with higher fidelity, than indirect decoding. Distinct motion acceleration information could thus be efficiently read out from rich and heterogeneous MT ensemble responses, regardless of the mechanisms that give rise to various forms of motion tuning that it exhibits. A similar analysis of activity in the medial superior temporal area (MST) did not suggest that this later stage of motion processing has a more refined acceleration representation. Together, these results suggest that the brain may opportunistically exploit nonlinear idiosyncrasies of neural responses to efficiently extract behaviorally relevant information on fast time scales, instead of performing explicit calculation of certain variables. Significance Statement This study aims to understand if linear acceleration information of visual motion is extracted and represented in primate visual motion areas MT and MST. By combining large-scale multi-area neuronal recordings, population-level analyses, and a rich set of moving stimuli, we show that linear acceleration can be decoded from MT activity. Specifically, our results demonstrate that (1) motion acceleration is encoded in MT, and can be directly and quickly decoded from MT ensemble activity, and (2) area MST, despite being a later stage of motion processing, does not refine acceleration representations. These findings call for revisiting how brain areas might efficiently extract behaviorally relevant information from the environment and highlight the importance of temporal dynamics in visual motion processing.
