Article.Title: Punishment Enhances Reward Learning through Striatal Prediction Errors
Article.Authors: Blades R.
Article.Abstract: A gazelle cautiously approaches a watering hole, eyeing its surroundings for predators. It is driven by two simultaneous needs: to drink water and to avoid danger. Its survival depends on balancing these opposing forces: approach motivation, which drives reward seeking, and avoidance motivation, which drives evasion of punishment. Reinforcement learning is the process by which animals learn to make decisions through trial and error using rewards and punishments as feedback. Over time, animals learn to select actions that maximize rewards and minimize punishments. Behaviors followed by rewarding outcomes become more likely to be repeated due to approach motivation, whereas behaviors followed by negative outcomes become less likely to occur through avoidance motivation. These dynamics play out continually in day-to-day life as all animals, including humans, learn from these trade-offs. Although rewards and punishments frequently co-occur in real-world environments, little research has investigated how receiving a mix of rewards and punishments influences learning processes. Reinforcement learning paradigms often study them separately, creating siloed research domains that mirror the classic “carrot and stick” metaphor in which rewards and punishments are treated as independent tools for shaping behavior. However, behavioral evidence suggests that they are not discrete learning processes; for example, conditioned suppression studies show that cues signaling a potential punishment can disrupt approach behavior directed toward rewards (Allcoat et al., 2015). This finding demonstrates that reward and punishment systems dynamically interact rather than operate in isolation. One possibility is that experiences of reward and punishment influence each other, because reinforcement learning shares a neural substrate: dopamine. Dopaminergic neurons calculate prediction errors: the difference between what was expected and what actually occurred. Better-than-expected outcomes produce positive prediction errors through increased firing of dopaminergic neurons, whereas worse-than-expected outcomes produce negative prediction errors through reduced dopamine release. Article.Title: Learning from Error Predictions Rather Than Prediction Errors: A Perspective on Self-Supervised Learning in the Brain
Article.Authors: Meirhaeghe N.
Article.Abstract: Humans learn by doing and observing but also by imagining the result of simulated actions in their mind. When learning from executed or observed actions, traditional theories posit that behavior improves by minimizing the difference between (1) the perceived outcome derived from sensory feedback and (2) the desired outcome (performance error) or the outcome predicted by an internal model (prediction error, PE). Supporting these theories, decades of electrophysiological studies have documented the role of the dopaminergic system and cerebellum in generating activity patterns compatible with the hypothesized error signals. In comparison, our understanding of the neural basis underlying the ability to learn from simulated actions is far more limited. Here, I argue that this form of self-supervised learning is best described in terms of a quantity known as the predicted performance error (PPE), theorized more than 30 years ago and yet largely overlooked ever since. Complementary to PEs, PPEs reflect error predictions between predicted and desired outcomes. Unlike PEs, however, PPEs exist even in the absence of sensory feedback and can in principle serve to evaluate actions without executing them, based on an efference copy of the underlying motor plan. I review evidence supporting the computation of PPEs in the brain and propose a network implementation based on a corticobasal ganglia loop interacting at multiple timescales with prefrontal, parietal, and hippocampal areas. I then connect PPEs to recent discoveries on motor planning and formulate novel predictions linking PPEs to various high-level brain functions such as metacognition, problem-solving, and deception.

Article.Title: Object detection through dynamic motor-sensory convergence in freely moving rats
Article.Authors: Nelinger G.; Saraf-Sinik I.; Ahissar E.
Article.Abstract: To detect objects in natural environments, animals must coordinate movement and sensation. This process unfolds dynamically, as perceivers actively shape sensory input through ongoing motor actions in a closed loop. In this study, we use precise tracking of behavioral kinematics to investigate the initial phase of object interaction, asking: what motor-sensory strategies support object detection during natural approach? Using high-speed videography and advanced tracking tools, we tracked whisker and head dynamics as male rats approached and contacted objects. We found that whisker-object interactions converged toward a distinct ratio between changes in whisker angle and curvature, denoted $\alpha ^\ast $ . In a motor-sensory phase plane this ratio appears as a line, reflecting a regime in which small motor adjustments produce large curvature changes during contact. This motor-sensory ratio cannot stabilize during free-air whisking and thus can serve as a signature for object presence. Rats gradually converged toward this object-dependent mechanical signature across contacts, and proximity to $\alpha ^\ast $ predicted subsequent head movements and the termination of object approach. Convergence to $\alpha ^\ast $ was invariant to object shape and texture and to whisker’s length. Moreover, touch-induced pumps both signaled and reinforced convergence. The results suggest that rats use successful convergence to this object-dependent motor-sensory contingency as a signature of object presence. Object detection thus emerges as a closed-loop dynamical process in which action, mechanics, and sensation jointly shape perceptual inference. Significance Statement How does a rat know it is touching an object with its moving whiskers? We trained freely moving rats to discriminate objects while tracking whisker kinematics at high resolution. We found that the detection phase involved whisker-object interactions that converged toward a distinct ratio between changes in whisker angle and curvature. This ratio can arise mechanically only when whiskers contact an external object, making its attainment a reliable indication of object presence. During object approach, rats steered their exploratory movements to seek this motor-sensory contingency, marking the transition to focused exploration or disengagement. These findings reveal a dynamical, closed-loop mechanism for object detection in freely moving rats.

Article.Title: Neurocognitive characteristics of perceptual feedback processing differ in autism
Article.Authors: Zuk N.; Slobodskoy-Plusnin J.; Weiss Y.; Sampath V.; Düsterwald K.; Akrami A.; Ahissar M.
Article.Abstract: Autistic individuals often show reduced adaptation to changing environmental demands, but the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We asked whether it may be explained by reduced sensitivity to external feedback and changes in task difficulty. Autistic and non-autistic adults of either sex, matched for cognitive ability, performed a pitch discrimination task in which their response was immediately followed by feedback. Accuracy was similar between the two groups, yet autistic participants exhibited a markedly reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an event-related EEG potential differentiating explicit negative versus positive feedback. They also showed weaker modulation of feedback-evoked EEG responses by perceptual difficulty. Lastly, they showed reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up experiment conducted 1–2 years later. When combined they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with about 80% accuracy. Together, our findings indicate that multiple processes for evaluating perceptual decisions and adjusting subsequent behavior differ in autism and likely contribute to slow updating in changing contexts. Significance Statement Autism is associated with reduced adaptation to changing environments in both behavior and neural signals, but the underlying neurocognitive mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that autistic individuals exhibit a reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an EEG component that is present when receiving negative instead of positive feedback. They also show weaker neural modulation by perceptual difficulty and reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up study. When combined, they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with high accuracy. These findings suggest that reduced flexibility in autism is associated with reduced processing of external feedback and task difficulty.

Article.Title: One-shot learning of paired association navigation with biologically plausible schemas
Article.Authors: Kumar M.; Tan C.; Libedinsky C.; Yen S.; Tan A.
Article.Abstract: After learning a multiple paired-association (MPA) navigation task, rodents can rapidly learn new cue–location associations after a single exposure, a phenomenon proposed to be facilitated by cognitive schemas. However, it remains unclear what schemas support this behavior and how they could be implemented in biological neural circuits. Here, we identify a set of schemas sufficient for gradual then one-shot paired-association navigation, and implement them in a fully neural agent using biologically plausible plasticity rules. The agent gradually acquires a low-dimensional spatial metric representation using a path-integration based temporal-difference error, enabling self-localization across different environments. It also contains a memory network that forms one-shot associations between sensory cues and goal locations, implemented using reward-modulated exploratory Hebbian (EH) plasticity. A third network performs vector subtraction between the agent’s current and goal location to compute goal-directed actions. Supplementing these schemas with an actor–critic enables one-shot navigation past obstacles. Lastly, learning a working-memory gating mechanism using the temporal-difference error enables one-shot learning even with brief cue and distractor presentation. The model reproduces key behavioral features of rodent learning in the MPA task and generates testable predictions about the neural mechanisms underlying schema-based one-shot learning. Significance Statement Schema-dependent learning is exemplified by better recall of a lecture when one already has a schema for understanding. A rodent navigation task showing a shift from slow to rapid learning has been proposed to reflect such schema use, yet how schemas are neurally implemented and enable faster learning is poorly understood. We clarify this gap in this computational study by describing several schemas and implement them as neural networks with biologically plausible learning rules. Composing them into an agent reproduces schema-dependent rodent learning behavior. Because schemas also shape self beliefs, clarifying their neural basis has implications for psychopathology. At the same time, understanding how biological schemas support rapid learning may inform advances in machine learning.

Article.Title: Emotional Content Enhances Attentional Tracking of Conversations through Context-Sensitive Modulation of Auditory-Language Networks
Article.Authors: Heikkinen P.; Lepistö S.; Wikman P.; Koskinen E.; Peräkylä A.; Ravaja N.; Harjunen V.
Article.Abstract: Engagement in conversation often requires continuous monitoring of relevant speech in a continuously evolving auditory environment. Emotional salience of semantic content may influence this process, but its role in attentional tracking of continuous speech remains unclear. We address this question using an audiovisual “Cocktail-party” paradigm combined with source-localized magnetoencephalography and encoding–decoding analyses. Participants (18 female, 14 male) selectively attended to one dialogue while ignoring a concurrent distractor dialogue, with both emotional salience and semantic coherence of the conversations manipulated independently. Decoding analyses revealed that negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant semantic content strengthened neural speech tracking, but only for attended dialogues. This effect depended on semantic structure, emerging earlier in semantically coherent than incoherent dialogues. Encoding analyses further showed latency- and region-specific effects across temporal, parietal, and frontal cortical regions. Emotional salience and coherence jointly modulated mid-latency (100 - 250 ms) responses, whereas late-latency (270 - 450 ms) responses were driven primarily by emotional salience. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning enhances neural prioritization of attended speech and semantic coherence shapes the temporal dynamics of this enhancement. Together, these results indicate context-sensitive emotional modulation of auditory–language processing during selective listening of continuous speech. Significance Statement Understanding how the brain prioritizes and selectively processes information in naturalistic, continuously evolving audiovisual scenes such as conversations is a central challenge in neuroscience. Here, we show that conversations conveying negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant content enhance neural tracking of attended speech in a noisy cocktail-party setting. This enhanced tracking depends on the semantic structure of the conversation, emerging earlier for coherent dialogues that are easy to follow. Furthermore, we show that emotional content strengthens mechanisms related to speech comprehension and sharpens segregation of relevant from irrelevant talk. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning and semantic continuity jointly shape cortical processing of continuous speech, providing new insight into how the brain selects and processes meaningful information during a conversation.

Article.Title: Aperiodic EEG activity is a domain-specific marker of attentional aging in neurotypical adults
Article.Authors: Cazares C.; Rigby A.; Kang L.; Getzmann S.; Arnau S.; Wascher E.; Voytek B.
Article.Abstract: Aperiodic neural activity has been reliably shown to be reduced among older adults, and these reductions are associated with age-related cognitive decline. These results suggest that aperiodic activity, as measured by the spectral exponent, might be a viable electrophysiological biomarker for cognitive aging. However, this has not been tested longitudinally, within participants, during normal aging. Here, we used a longitudinal cohort of either sex to test whether changes in aperiodic activity between two sessions, approximately 5 years apart, track behavioral change across two domains: sustained attention (Psychomotor Vigilance Test) and executive function (modified Simon task). We found that aperiodic activity declined within individuals after the interval, independent of age at baseline. This within-person change tracked concurrent changes in reaction times during sustained attention but was not associated with changes in any Simon task measure. Within a resampling framework, the aperiodic-PVT association was stable across cohort resamples and independently fitted partitions, though it was not confirmed in a small, frozen held-out set. These findings suggest the longitudinal decline in aperiodic activity tracks attentional processing speed rather than executive function, supporting its potential as a domain-specific biomarker of attentional aging in neurotypical populations. Significance Statement Aperiodic (non-oscillatory) neural activity, indexed by the aperiodic exponent, is known to decline in older adults, but whether this happens within individuals over just a few years, and in step with cognitive change, remains unclear. Here we leveraged scalp EEG and cognitive-behavioral data from 276 neurotypical adults, tested twice approximately five years apart, and found that the aperiodic exponent declines within individuals over this interval, independent of age at baseline. This decline tracked concurrent slowing on a sustained attention task, but not change on an executive function task, and only in EEG recorded before, not after, cognitive testing. Based on this dissociation, we propose that aperiodic exponent decline indexes attentional processing speed rather than general cognitive decline in neurotypical aging.

Article.Title: Early life stress leads to detectable aberrant spread of neuron avalanches in the prefrontal-amygdala network in males but not females
Article.Authors: Kharybina Z.; Palva J.; Palva S.; Lauri S.; Hartung H.; Taira T.
Article.Abstract: Development of the brain networks is highly vulnerable to stressful events. Early life stress (ELS) has been linked to multifaceted cognitive and emotional deficits in adulthood. Despite a growing body of evidence showing ELS-induced structural and functional changes in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), a circuit crucial for emotional processing, our knowledge of the resulting changes in the network dynamics is incomplete. Here, we investigate how maternal separation (MS) affects prefrontal-amygdala network in terms of neuronal avalanches, spatiotemporal clusters of activity, using simultaneous multielectrode recordings in the medial PFC (mPFC) and the BLA of urethane-anaesthetized juvenile (postnatal day (p) 14 – p15) and young adult (p50 – p 60) rats. Firstly, we show that MS leads to an intensified spread of activity within both regions as reflected in the higher mean branching ratios of the avalanches. Next, we demonstrate that most of the avalanches occur locally in one region, however, a small percentage of avalanches have clusters of activity in both regions simultaneously. We show that in MS animals prefrontal clusters followed by activity in the amygdala tend to be larger compared to controls and each event in the mPFC is followed by smaller number of events in the BLA, pointing towards impaired spread of activity from the mPFC to the BLA. Interestingly, avalanche spread from the BLA to the mPFC remains unaffected by MS. Abovementioned effects manifest only in adulthood and, intriguingly, only in males highlighting prolonged developmental and sex-dependent nature of ELS outcome. Significance statement Brain criticality describes the brain’s ability to maintain a balanced state in which neural activity spreads efficiently without becoming too weak or overly chaotic. This balance can be measured through neuronal avalanches, bursts of cascading activity across interconnected neurons. Here, we show that early life stress (ELS) — adverse experiences during early brain development — disrupts the development of avalanche patterns in the connection between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), brain regions involved in emotion and stress regulation. These effects were detected in males but not females. Our findings improve understanding of how stable brain activity develops in emotional brain networks and suggest that early life stress is an important factor influencing this critical balance.

Article.Title: Probing the neural geometry of conscious object perception in time
Article.Authors: Hachisuka A.; Baumgarten T.; Spector D.; Koenig L.; He B.
Article.Abstract: Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a “coarse-to-fine” sequence or a “fine-to-coarse” sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. By contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level. Significance statement Despite significant interests, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious perception remains unclear. Here, we investigated the unfolding of neural events in time that support perceptual awareness of visual objects. Using a threshold-level object perception task involving three image conditions (normal, low-pass filtered, masked) and high-density EEG, we reveal that basic and superordinate category information both emerge early in the neural activity (at ∼100 ms), but only the basic-level category representation positively contributes to awareness. By contrast, the early superordinate category representation negatively correlates with perceptual awareness. At ∼300 ms, an abstract superordinate category representation emerges, which also positively correlates with perceptual awareness. Therefore, category-level neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate level.

Article.Title: The Roles and Uses of Extracellular Vesicles in Neuroimmunologic Diseases
Article.Authors: Kammeyer R.; Coughlan C.
Article.Abstract: Neuroimmunology is a field of neurology focused on the diagnosis and treatment of diseases where the immune system causes inflammation or injury to the nervous system. This includes diseases such as multiple sclerosis, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, autoimmune encephalitis, autoimmune ataxia, stiff person syndrome spectrum disorder, and neuro-rheumatologic diseases such as neuropsychiatric lupus. Over the past couple decades, there have been significant advancements in the diagnostic methods for several neuroimmunologic diseases. Despite these achievements, major needs remain for additional methods to facilitate earlier diagnosis, monitor disease activity and treatment, and elucidate disease mechanisms to aid in the development of novel or tailored treatment strategies. Currently, there is often a trade-off between the invasiveness of neurodiagnostic testing and the level of detail that can be obtained from the test without causing an iatrogenic injury. Here, we discuss the potential of extracellular vesicles (EVs), especially CNS-derived EVs obtained from peripheral blood, as a promising avenue for advancing research and clinical care in neuroimmunology. This article provides a review of the key clinical features and approaches to care for the most common neuroimmunologic diseases. We identify gaps that remain in our current understanding of these conditions. We then highlight how ongoing research in the EV field may address these existing gaps. Finally, we examine the challenges that must be overcome before EV analysis can be more widely adopted in both research and clinical care in this field.

Article.Title: Fast corrective responses in redundant motor control are shaped by intrinsic constraints of movement patterns
Article.Authors: Kobayashi T.; Nozaki D.
Article.Abstract: In real-world motor tasks, body movements unfold in a high-dimensional space, whereas task errors are defined in a lower-dimensional space. How such low-dimensional errors propagate across redundant motor degrees of freedom to generate rapid corrective responses remains poorly understood. To address this question, we developed a redundant bimanual task in which human participants (males and females) manipulated a virtual stick with both hands to move its tip to a visual target. By shifting the tip position (task-relevant perturbation) or rotating the stick with the tip position fixed (task-irrelevant perturbation), we separated task-space errors from redundant-dimension errors. Participants rapidly corrected both types of perturbations using highly stereotyped movement patterns. Corrections to task-relevant errors consistently involved coordinated changes across redundant dimensions, and even perturbations that did not affect task success elicited systematic corrective responses. Together, these results demonstrate that fast corrective responses in redundant motor control are shaped by intrinsic coordination constraints that govern how visual errors propagate through the motor system. Significance Statement The motor system can correct a movement error within 200 ms of its occurrence. However, the compensatory movement pattern is not uniquely determined because of the many degrees of freedom in the body. How does the motor system rapidly select and execute an appropriate corrective pattern? Our bimanual stick-tip reaching task, in which participants controlled a cursor located at the tip of a virtual stick, allowed us to dissociate tip-displacing errors from stick-rotation errors. Tip displacements triggered fast corrections, but surprisingly, rotation-only perturbations also evoked rapid responses and biased the tip along its usual coordination between tip motion and stick tilt. Our findings show that fast corrections are constrained by intrinsic coordination patterns, limiting the ability to ignore goal-irrelevant perturbations.

Article.Title: Prefrontal ensembles represent freezing of conspecifics
Article.Authors: Miranda B.; Torossian A.; Reis F.; Patel N.; Liu X.; Walker E.; Leeds H.; Hilgert E.; Gudipati R.; Adhikari A.
Article.Abstract: Social buffering is a process in which the presence of other members of the same species (conspecifics) decreases stress reactions during threat exposure. In parallel, prior reports showed that groups of individuals display synchronous actions in non-threatening situations. However, it is unknown if individuals also synchronize actions when facing threats. Prior studies showed social buffering of freezing in pairs of subjects. We now expand these findings and show social buffering of freezing during exposure to a predator and a shock grid in mice of both sexes in a larger group of four conspecifics. Furthermore, mice also displayed synchronized freezing. The presence of freezing synchrony suggests the existence of a neural representation of conspecific freezing. We reasoned that this encoding might be in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), as this region has been implicated in social behaviors and freezing. Strikingly, mPFC neural activity represented the average level of freezing across conspecifics. MPFC ensembles displayed differential encoding of self and conspecific freezing, and during predator exposure the mPFC encoded the number of conspecifics freezing and conspecific freezing bout duration. These data show, for the first time, neural representation of conspecific freezing, and suggest that the mPFC may coordinate behavioral responses to threat across conspecifics. Significance Statement Social animals display attenuated threat-elicited responses when encountering threats as a group. However, it is unknown how freezing signals from conspecifics are encoded by the brain when facing threats, as prior work has been limited to studies of pairs, or assays without social interactions. We identify a neural population in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) that represents conspecific freezing during grouped threat exposure, and these cells dynamically represent the duration of other animals' freezing bouts. Strikingly, the activity of these ensembles also represents the number of conspecifics freezing. These findings uncover a previously unknown function of the mPFC to encode conspecific freezing.

Article.Title: Insulin regulates activity-dependent mitochondrial depolarization and calcium dynamics in dentate granule cells
Article.Authors: Ferrán B.; Rose H.; Gray J.; Redwine T.; Pham S.; Rubin O.; Rice H.; Sonntag W.; Díaz-García C.
Article.Abstract: Systemic insulin resistance is associated with reduced hippocampal energy metabolism and cognitive impairment both in humans and animal models. However, whether insulin rapidly regulates neuronal metabolic stability during activity remains unclear. Here, we examined insulin signaling and queried the corresponding mitochondrial responses in dentate granule cells (DGCs) of adult female mice. This layer of excitatory neurons within the hippocampus plays an essential role in learning and memory. Insulin robustly increased Akt phosphorylation in dentate gyrus tissue when insulin degradation was inhibited, and this response was attenuated by genetic deletion of the insulin receptor in DGCs, consistent with cell-autonomous signaling. We found that insulin did not alter mitochondrial membrane potential at rest, but significantly limited activity-evoked mitochondrial depolarization induced by neuronal stimulation. However, this change had no measurable impact on cytosolic ATP availability and was instead associated with Ca 2+ dynamics. Removing Ca 2+ ions from the extracellular solution, or disrupting mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake, prevented insulin modulation of the mitochondrial membrane potential. Furthermore, insulin limited cytosolic Ca 2+ accumulation through an insulin receptor-dependent mechanism that persisted despite Akt inhibition. Insulin also accelerated the clearance of mitochondrial Ca 2+ transients in active neurons, which occurred without changes in either neuronal excitability or pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphorylation. Together, these findings identify endogenous insulin degradation as a key regulator of hippocampal insulin signaling, and reveal a previously unrecognized interaction between insulin and Ca 2+ signaling in stimulated DGCs. This work also establishes a direct link between central insulin signaling and the maintenance of mitochondrial electrochemical homeostasis in the adult brain. Significance Statement Insulin signaling is known to influence synaptic plasticity, yet its direct effects on neuronal metabolism remain poorly defined. Here, we show that endogenous insulin degradation limits insulin signaling in adult hippocampal tissue. This finding suggests that inhibitors of the insulin degrading enzyme may hold the potential to improve the efficacy of insulin-based interventions aimed at improving learning and memory. Acute insulin signaling does not modify neuronal excitability, or cytosolic ATP availability. Instead, it stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces calcium accumulation in active dentate granule cells. By identifying an insulin-dependent mechanism that regulates the electrochemical homeostasis of mitochondria in active neurons, this work provides insight into how brain insulin resistance may contribute to cognitive dysfunction in aging and neurometabolic disorders.

Article.Title: Wide dynamic range of contrast-encoding in neural responses in macaque V1
Article.Authors: Yoshida H.; Chen Y.; Geisler W.; Seidemann E.
Article.Abstract: The dynamic range of contrast-encoding in the early visual system has been investigated at both single-neuron and population levels in animals using oriented stimuli such as gratings and Gabor patches. However, contrast-encoding of unoriented stimuli such as Gaussians has been less explored, even though such stimuli can evoke a large population response. In studies that employ Gaussians, contrast response functions (CRFs) of neurons and neural populations in primary visual cortex are typically characterized across a limited range of Weber contrasts up to 100%, which may not adequately reflect the statistics of contrast in natural scenes. Indeed, our preliminary analysis shows that locations with center-surround contrasts far exceeding the level comparable to a Gaussian stimulus of 100% Weber contrast are ubiquitous in natural scenes. Thus, our current understanding of contrast encoding remains incomplete in the context of natural environments. Here, we measured spiking activities of individual neurons using electrophysiology and population responses using widefield calcium imaging in V1 of fixating male macaques ( Macaca mulatta ) while Gaussian stimuli were presented over a wide range of Weber contrasts, up to 900%. Both the average spiking response and the average population response continued to increase robustly above 100% Weber contrast. Only a small minority of neurons saturated below 100% Weber contrast. These results demonstrate that the dynamic range of contrast-encoding in V1 is broader than previously assumed and aligns more closely with the statistics of contrast in natural scenes. Significance Statement The dynamic range of contrast-encoding in V1 has typically been characterized using only a limited range of contrasts, often excluding the high contrasts commonly found in natural scenes. We measured contrast response functions of individual neurons and neural populations in V1 across a much wider range of contrasts. We found that the responses of the majority of neurons, as well as the overall population, increased robustly up to extremely high contrasts. These findings suggest that the dynamic range of contrast encoding in V1 extends well beyond the commonly tested range.

Article.Title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis
Article.Authors: Xu J.; Wang Y.; Nomura T.; Van H.; Zhu Y.; Castillon C.; Chiesa M.; Marshall J.; Armstrong J.; Zhu Y.; Savas J.; Contractor A.
Article.Abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1 A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time. Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature “silent” synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

Article.Title: Representation of emotional expressions across the face and voice brain networks
Article.Authors: Mattioni S.; Falagiarda F.; Arya T.; Gau R.; Rezk M.; Battal C.; Van Audenhaege A.; Collignon O.
Article.Abstract: Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is fundamental to successful social interaction, yet how the brain represents emotional information across sensory systems remains unclear. Here, we systematically mapped the contribution of individually-defined face- and voice-selective cortical regions in 24 human participants of either sex to unimodal and crossmodal emotion expressions. Using multivariate pattern classification, we show that emotional expressions are robustly decodable from the dominant sensory modality across all individually defined face- and voice-selective areas, and that these representations cannot be accounted for by low- and mid-level stimulus properties alone. Strikingly, emotional information from the non-dominant modality—vocal expressions within face networks and facial expressions within voice networks—was also represented throughout the network, with the exception of the occipital face areas. Crossmodal decoding further revealed a shared neural code for facial and vocal emotions in the temporal voice areas, posterior superior temporal sulcus, and precentral gyrus, indicating that these regions contain emotion representations that generalize across sensory modalities. Furthermore, in most face- and voice-selective regions, audiovisual emotional expressions could be distinguished from representations elicited by the dominant unimodal modality, indicating that bimodal signals are not simply represented as their strongest sensory component. Together, these findings reveal that emotion representations are distributed broadly across face- and voice-selective regions and identify temporo-frontal regions as key sites supporting modality-independent emotion representations. Significance statement Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is essential for everyday social interaction, yet the brain mechanisms that integrate these signals remain poorly understood. Using functional MRI (fMRI) and advanced pattern analyses, we show that emotional expressions are represented widely across both face- and voice-selective brain regions-even when conveyed through a non-preferred sensory modality. Strikingly, specific temporo-frontal regions encode facial and vocal emotions using a partially shared, modality-independent neural code. We further demonstrate that seeing and hearing emotions together reshapes how emotional information is organized in the brain, revealing a graded transition from sensory-specific to multisensory representations. These findings challenge strictly segregated models of emotion processing and provide a more integrated account of how the brain supports social understanding.

Article.Title: Late Integration of Prior Expectations During Precision-Weighted Perceptual Decisions
Article.Authors: Gastrell T.; Rangelov D.; Mattingley J.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive perceptual decision-making relies on the ability to combine sensory evidence with prior expectations in a precision-weighted manner. Although Bayesian inference provides a clear normative account of how such integration should occur, the neural mechanisms through which the brain represents and combines priors and likelihoods remain poorly understood. Across two preregistered experiments, we investigated how the precision of learned priors and sensory likelihoods influence visual motion judgements and associated neural activity patterns during a random-dot motion estimation task. Neurotypical adult participants (N=80, 58 female) reported directions of visual motion stimuli, with motion coherence varying randomly across trials. Prior expectations over the continuous motion direction space were manipulated block-wise by implicitly varying the probabilities with which different motion directions were presented. Consistent with precision-weighted inference, response accuracy improved as motion coherence increased with robust response biases toward the expected motion direction. Neural activity measured using electroencephalography (EEG) revealed reliable effects of prior expectation on the univariate central-parietal positivity (CPP), consistent with reduced accumulation of sensory evidence under informative priors. Multivariate analysis using inverted-encoding models revealed robust effects of prior precision on stimulus-specific neural representations, but only late, during response planning stages. Together, these findings suggest that priors learned over a continuous space do not modulate the encoding of sensory evidence and are instead integrated later in the decision-process. Significance Statement Perceptual decisions require combining noisy sensory input with prior expectations about what is likely to occur. It remains unclear how the brain integrates prior expectations with incoming sensory evidence. Using a visual motion task and concurrent brain imaging, we show that expectations do not alter early stimulus-encoding, but are instead integrated at later stages of decision formation and action planning. These findings add nuance to influential theories proposing that learned expectations directly affect stimulus representations and instead highlight their contribution to later decision-related processes. This work advances understanding of how the brain uses experience to optimise perceptual decisions under uncertainty.

Article.Title: Specific regulation of transsynaptic nanoalignment and postsynaptic assembly by a novel NCAM family synaptic adhesion molecule
Article.Authors: Van der Linden Costello P.; Wennerberg M.; Rydbom J.; Gratz S.; Terry J.; Fennema L.; O’Connor-Giles K.; Broihier H.
Article.Abstract: Synapse formation underlies the organization of neurons into functional circuits and requires precise alignment and coordinated maturation of pre- and postsynaptic compartments. Many synaptogenic adhesion molecules have been identified that drive target recognition and sustained adhesion between appropriate synaptic partners. Yet the degree to which individual molecules serve distinct functions in synapse formation and maturation remains poorly understood. In particular, how exquisite nanoalignment of pre- and postsynaptic specializations flows from micron-scale adhesive interactions between synaptic partners remains a key unanswered question. Here we shed new light on this question by establishing a specialized set of synaptic functions for Epithelial limiter of Fasciclin II function (Elff ), an NCAM family member with previously unknown roles in the nervous system. Our structural and functional studies at the glutamatergic Drosophila NMJ of both sexes indicate that Elff is required for postsynaptic function and maturation as well as transsynaptic alignment; however, it is not required for presynaptic function, bouton formation, or developmental expansion of the NMJ. NMJs in elff null mutants display reduced glutamate receptor clusters beginning at the embryonic stage when NMJ synapses first form. Using super-resolution STED microscopy, we demonstrate that these poorly defined postsynaptic specializations are frequently out of register with presynaptic release sites. Surprisingly, the striking defects in elff nulls occur in the context of both normal active zone number and developmental expansion of the NMJ. These findings suggest an unexpected degree of specialization among transsynaptic adhesion complexes and demonstrate that Elff-mediated signaling is critical for transsynaptic nanoarchitecture of glutamatergic synapses. Significance Statement This work reveals a surprisingly selective role for a novel NCAM family member called Elff in coordinating postsynaptic assembly and precise transsynaptic nanoalignment without altering NMJ formation, expansion or presynaptic active zone number. This separation of phenotypes is new and provides crucial insight into molecular specialization of adhesion complexes during synaptogenesis. Because NCAM family member dysfunction linked to multiple neurological disorders, most notably schizophrenia, illuminating the molecular mechanisms by which they orchestrate synaptic organization and function is an important goal.

Article.Title: A novel nitric oxide (NO)-dependent ‘molecular switch’ mediates LTP in the Octopus vulgaris brain through persistent activation of nitric oxide synthase (NOS)
Article.Authors: Turchetti-Maia A.; Shomrat T.; Bidel F.; Koren I.; Stern-Mentch N.; Nesher N.; Hochner B.
Article.Abstract: Cephalopod mollusks provide a striking example of the independent evolution of advanced cognitive abilities in invertebrates. In octopuses, learning and memory are mediated by the vertical lobe (VL), whose visual input synapses undergo robust activity-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP). Here, we used Octopus vulgaris of either sex to show that persistent activation of nitric oxide synthase (NOS) mediates both LTP expression and maintenance, independently of de novo protein synthesis. Contrary to the prevailing view, NO signaling is not required for LTP induction, as LTP can still be induced in the presence of NOS inhibitors. Remarkably, however, NOS inhibitors blocked presynaptic LTP expression, while NO donors induced only short-term potentiation, together suggesting that LTP expression depends on persistently elevated NO levels. The effective NO concentrations, estimated both pharmacologically and amperometrically, were more than three orders of magnitude higher than those required for activation of the canonical sGC–cGMP pathway, suggesting that NO acts through direct covalent modification of proteins, such as S-nitrosylation. In a subset of synapses, the NOS inhibitor L-NNA rapidly and completely erased established LTP; however, following washout, full potentiation could be reinstated by renewed tetanic stimulation. We therefore propose a ‘molecular switch’ mechanism in which an NO-dependent positive feedback loop persistently reactivates NOS, thereby maintaining LTP. These findings reveal an unprecedented form of convergent evolution in which molecular innovations equip the octopus VL network with the computational properties required for associative learning. Significance Statement Long-term potentiation (LTP) is a central cellular mechanism of learning and memory. While extensively studied in vertebrates, its mechanisms in octopuses—animals that independently evolved sophisticated cognitive abilities—remain poorly understood. Here, we uncover a novel form of LTP involving activity-dependent activation of nitric oxide synthase (NOS) in the postsynaptic cell. The produced nitric oxide (NO) mediates LTP maintenance through persistent NO-dependent reactivation of NOS (a “molecular switch”) and simultaneously mediates LTP expression by retrogradely facilitating presynaptic transmitter release. These findings reveal a striking example of convergent evolution in which distinct molecular mechanisms independently evolved to implement associative (Hebbian) learning rules within a neural network.

Article.Title: The hypothalamic orexin–medial prefrontal cortex pathway modulates susceptibility to depression in the learned helplessness paradigm in male mice
Article.Authors: Mi T.; He Z.; Yu B.; Li Q.; Lu G.; Hao J.; Niu J.; Ma S.; Rong W.; Niu J.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a prevalent psychiatric disorder primarily characterized by behavioral despair and helplessness. The orexinergic system plays a crucial role in stress-induced depression; however, the precise mechanisms remain unclear. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a major target of orexinergic projections, is essential for emotional regulation. This study suggests that impaired orexinergic input to the mPFC underlies depression-like behaviors in murine models. In the learned helplessness (LH) paradigm, the majority of male mice subjected to inescapable foot shocks developed depression-like behaviors (classified as LH-susceptible), whereas a subset displayed resilience (classified as LH-resilient). LH-susceptible mice exhibited a reduced number of orexin + neuronal somata in the hypothalamus, along with decreased expression of prepro-orexin mRNA . Correspondingly, the mPFC of these mice displayed decreased density of orexinergic terminals and lower Orexin A levels. In contrast, LH-resilient mice maintained stable hypothalamic orexin neuron counts, exhibited increased prepro-orexin mRNA expression, and preserved orexinergic terminal density in the mPFC. Chemogenetic activation of the hypothalamic orexin–mPFC pathway alleviated depression-like behaviors in LH-susceptible mice through Orexin A signaling. Conversely, inhibition of this pathway induced depression-like behaviors in LH-resilient mice. Additionally, LH-susceptible mice showed decreased excitatory synaptic transmission in layer V pyramidal neurons of the mPFC, which was improved by activation of hypothalamic orexinergic inputs; this improvement was attenuated by administration of an orexin receptor 1 (OX1R) antagonist. Collectively, these findings implicate the hypothalamic orexin–mPFC pathway as a pivotal regulator of excitatory synaptic transmission and suggest its involvement in modulating individual variability in susceptibility and resilience to depression. Significance statement Depression is a highly prevalent emotional disorder characterized by behavioral despair and helplessness under stress. This study demonstrates that the orexinergic system is critical for modulating resilience to aversive stimuli. Using the learned helplessness (LH) mouse model, we found that LH-susceptible mice, but not LH-resilient mice, show compromised hypothalamic orexinergic projections to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), together with decreased excitatory synaptic transmission in layer V pyramidal neurons. Activation of the hypothalamic orexin–mPFC pathway alleviates depression-like behaviors in susceptible mice through Orexin A, while inhibition of this pathway induces depression-like phenotypes in resilient mice. These findings identify orexinergic signaling as a promising therapeutic target for depression.

Article.Title: Microglial Presenilin-1 modulates neuronal function and memory-associated behaviors
Article.Authors: Frost P.; Martinez C.; Millet A.; McWhirt J.; Cheng J.; Bamkole M.; Kim Y.; Silva H.; Lafaille J.; Azevedo E.; Stevens B.; Ledo J.
Article.Abstract: Microglial cells, the macrophages of the brain parenchyma, are increasingly recognized to play a key role in synaptic plasticity and function. Presenilin 1 (PS1) is an essential protein involved in learning and memory; the loss of neuronal Presenilin function causes cognitive deficits and impaired synapse plasticity in mice. Here we show memory enhancement in male mice lacking PS1 in microglia (PS1 ΔMG ). Leveraging high-throughput RNA sequencing with single-cell deconvolution-analysis, we estimate that PS1 ΔMG increases Cd52-lo microglial population, a proliferative group enriched in AP-1 responsive genes; and increases chemokines Ccl7 and Ccl8 . In silico prediction of binding partners showed that microglial CCL7 may act via inhibition of neuronal CCR5, a receptor known to negatively regulate learning and memory. By profiling active neuronal populations via PhosphoTRAP the data showed a non-autonomous cell effect of microglial PS1 by modulating genes involved in neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity . Ex vivo electrophysiology and in vivo calcium imaging in freely behaving mice confirm these effects with functional changes in CA1 hippocampus as seen by increased NMDA/AMPA ratios and increased amplitude of neuronal Ca2+ transients in freely behaving animals, respectively. Remarkably, PS1 ΔMG mice exhibited increased memory retention in contextual fear conditioning and novel object recognition. Together, these data suggest a novel mechanism where microglial PS1 negatively regulates neuronal activity through modulation of NMDAR and memory-associated behaviors. Significance Statement Microglia are increasingly recognized as active regulators of neuronal function, yet the molecular mechanisms that constrain their influence on synaptic activity remain incompletely defined. This study identifies microglial Presenilin-1 (PS1) as a key regulator of neuron-microglia signaling that shapes synaptic transmission and learning. We show that loss of microglial PS1 shifts microglia toward a transcriptional and signaling state that enhances NMDA receptor-dependent synaptic activity and improves memory, demonstrating that microglial molecular programs can directly modulate neuronal excitability. These findings establish microglial PS1 as a physiological brake on circuit plasticity and reveal that altering microglial signaling alone is sufficient to influence cognition. Targeting microglial regulatory pathways may therefore provide new strategies to enhance synaptic resilience and cognitive function in brain disorders.

Article.Title: Time <sup>2</sup> : A Framework for the Neural Dynamics of Visual Perception
Article.Authors: Caplette L.; Gosselin F.
Article.Abstract: Whenever we look at an object, we seem to perceive it immediately. However, this is not the case for two reasons. First, it takes hundreds of milliseconds for the brain to process visual information reaching the retina. Second, perceiving an object requires fixating it for some duration—typically hundreds of milliseconds—during which the retina continuously receives new visual information. These facts together imply that visual information is both processed and received through time. These two temporal facets of perception, which we term processing time and stimulus time, are often conflated in the literature, and rarely considered together in experiments. Here, we argue that, to obtain a more complete portrait of visual perception and further constrain models of vision, it is essential to consider and measure both temporal facets simultaneously. We present a new method designed to do so that is based on reverse correlation: Time 2 . We show that this method allows us to precisely characterize many neural phenomena, including rhythmic perception, predictive processing, and coarse-to-fine sampling.

Article.Title: Voluntary movement initiation is associated with cardiac input in Libet’s task
Article.Authors: Germanova K.; Studenova A.; Bredikhin D.; Gippert M.; Kapralov N.; Klucharev V.; Villringer A.; Herrojo Ruiz M.; Nikulin V.
Article.Abstract: ​​The relationship between motor intention and initiation of voluntary movement remains a fundamental topic in neuroscience, originating from the seminal framework of B. Libet, introduced in 1983. Libet’s paradigm significantly influenced discussions on intentionality, motor control, and free will. However, methodological critiques continue to challenge its interpretations, specifically the accuracy and validity of the ‘urge to move’ phenomenon. One understudied factor in this debate is the potential influence of interoceptive signals—such as cardiac activity—in shaping the experience of motor intention and movement initiation. In our study, we addressed this gap by examining whether cardiac signals modulate participants' experience of the ‘urge to move’, using behavioural and electrophysiological measures in 39 healthy human participants (17 males and 22 females) performing Libet's task. Crucially, when participants were asked to follow the ‘urge to move’, their button press timings were predominantly aligned with the diastolic phase of the cardiac cycle, indicating cardiac modulation of movement initiation. However, analysing heart evoked potential (HEP) amplitudes as a measure of cardiac input perception, we observed no differences in HEP amplitudes associated with changes in introspective demands during the task in both source and sensor spaces. Our results suggest that implicit perception of cardiac signals biases voluntary action initiation in Libet’s task, independently of cortical interoceptive markers. These findings have implications for models of motor preparation, intentionality, and the bodily basis of voluntary action, challenging conventional interpretations of motor intention and informing debates on volition and interoception. Significance Statement Our study provides evidence that implicit perception of cardiac signals influences movement initiation in Libet’s task. We demonstrate, for the first time, that when attending to the ‘urge to move’, participants tended to initiate voluntary movements during the diastolic phase of the cardiac cycle. These findings challenge traditional views on factors affecting motor initiation in Libet’s task, suggesting the relevance of interoceptive processing. By highlighting the role of cardiac input in experiencing motor intention, our findings expand on existing debates on volition, agency, and free will, further underscoring the importance of integrating bodily signals into these theoretical frameworks.

Article.Title: Cerebellar climbing fibers signal flexible, rapidly adapting reward predictions
Article.Authors: Vignali C.; Mutersbaugh M.; Hull C.
Article.Abstract: Classical models of cerebellar computation posit that climbing fibers (CFs) operate according to supervised learning rules, correcting movements by signaling the occurrence of motor errors. However, recent findings suggest that in some behaviors, CF activity can exhibit features that resemble the instructional signals necessary for reinforcement learning, namely reward prediction errors (rPEs). Despite these initial observations, many key properties of reward-related CF responses remain unclear, thus limiting our understanding of how they operate to guide cerebellar learning. Here, we have measured the postsynaptic responses of CFs onto cerebellar Purkinje cells using two-photon calcium imaging in mice of both sexes to test how CFs respond to learned stimuli that either do or do not predict reward. We find that CFs can develop generalized responses to similar cues of the same modality, regardless of whether they are reward predictive. However, the extent of this generalization depends on temporal context, and generalization does not extend across sensory modalities. Further, learned CF responses are flexible, and can be rapidly updated according to new reward contingencies. Together these results reveal two properties of learned CF responses: their generalization across similar cues is graded by the temporal and sensory context in which the cues are learned, and, when reward contingencies are reversed, they update rapidly to track new learning rules. Significance Statement The cerebellum is best known for coordinating movement, and the climbing fiber teaching signals thought to instruct cerebellar motor learning were long thought to report movement errors exclusively. Recent work has shown that these instructional signals can also convey information about reward. Here, by recording from these climbing fiber inputs in mice learning which cues predict reward, we find that they carry flexible, context-sensitive reward predictions. Notably, these signals do not simply track which cue an animal should respond to: they generalize across similar cues depending on context, and they rapidly reorganize when reward associations change. These properties resemble those of midbrain dopamine neurons, the brain's canonical reward system. These findings reframe how cerebellar teaching signals contribute to reward-guided learning.

Article.Title: Machine Learning Framework for Integration of Video and EEG Reveals Distinct Seizure Phenotypes in Mouse Models of Epilepsy
Article.Authors: Liu C.; Martin C.; Lee A.; Sands T.; Frankel W.; Makinson C.
Article.Abstract: Video-electrocorticogram (VEEG) recordings are the gold-standard diagnostic tool for detecting and characterizing seizures in rodent models of seizure and epilepsy. Manual/visual scoring remains the prevailing strategy despite significant limitations. Alternatively, automated and semi-automated analyses have been applied to either EEG or video features alone but integrating these disparate data forms presents a challenge that has not been sufficiently addressed. Here, we introduce an integrated machine learning pipeline that jointly leverages EEG and behavioral video data to enable scalable and objective event classification. Integrated video-EEG analysis was initially validated using a well-established pharmacologically induced seizure paradigm in male mice, where overt generalized motor seizures provide a clear benchmark. We then tested the pipeline on a genetic mouse model of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) that displays a complex spike-wave discharge (SWD) seizure phenotype that poses significant challenges for traditional scoring methods. Machine learning-powered integrated analysis of video-EEG recordings outperformed unimodal EEG- or video-based approaches and performed favorably to experienced rodent EEG electrophysiologists while also uncovering distinct phenotypic relationships, including classes of atypical behavioral and typical non-behavioral SWD events. This framework provides a flexible tool for high-throughput, precise analysis of VEEG data, with potential to accelerate discovery in epilepsy and seizure research. Furthermore, this approach represents a generalizable strategy for the integration of diverse neurobehavioral time series data types. Significance Statement Seizure detection in animal models of epilepsy has relied heavily on manual analysis of video-EEG recordings, a process that is slow and subjective. We present a machine learning pipeline that integrates EEG and video data from mice to classify seizures with high accuracy. This work was validated across two models, first a pharmacologically induced generalized seizure model, and second, a spontaneous spike-wave discharge (SWD) model in genetic epilepsy. Our approach detected events missed by human reviewers and revealed previously uncharacterized SWD subtypes distinguished by their behavior. By combining open-source tools in a flexible framework, this work lowers the barrier to high-throughput, unbiased seizure phenotyping, and also offers a broadly applicable strategy for linking neural activity to behavior in neuroscience research.

Article.Title: iGABASnFR Imaging Reveals that GABA Clearance is rapidly overwhelmed in the Cerebral Cortex
Article.Authors: Gariepy R.; Blackman J.; Gupte A.; Diamond J.; Dulla C.; Armbruster M.
Article.Abstract: Both phasic and tonic GABAergic activity in the cortex, is shaped by the clearance of GABA from the extracellular space by GABA transporters (GATs). However, estimates of the time-course of GAT activity from GAT currents, GABA A , and GABA B electrophysiological recordings range from tens of milliseconds to multiple seconds. These estimates may reflect receptor properties rather than extracellular GABA dynamics. Understanding how long GABA is free in the extracellular space is key to understanding how inhibition controls activity, but has been technically challenging. Here, we utilize the fluorescent GABA sensor, iGABASnFr, to enable us to optically assay extracellular GABA dynamics following bursts of synaptic activity. In the mouse cerebral cortex of either sex, we show that GABA rapidly disperses from release sites via diffusion, with very little role for active transport by GATs. Following diffusion from the sites of release, GABA then accumulates in the extracellular space, where GATs require hundreds of milliseconds to remove it. For areas of high density GABA release or during bursts of activity, this clearance is further slowed. Continued GABA release and summation in the extracellular space for bursts of activity contrasts with recorded Inhibitory post-synaptic current (IPSC) signals, which rapidly depress with additional stimuli, suggesting a disconnect between IPSCs and extracellular GABA. Lastly, the resulting extracellular accumulation of GABA can act hetero-synaptically by activating and/or desensitizing GABA A receptors. Together, this raises new questions about how GABAergic inhibition works to shape network function and suggests a spatiotemporal continuum of extracellular GABA. Significance Statement We use combined iGABASnFr neurotransmitter imaging, electrophysiology, and modeling to show that with trains of synaptic activity, GABA clearance is slowed and GABA rapidly accumulates in the extracellular space. Additionally, we demonstrate that GABA largely diffuses from release sites rather than being captured by GABA transporters and that these transporters have only a small role in shaping extracellular GABA dynamics in the mouse cortex. Lastly, we show that extracellular GABA accumulation can heterosynaptically desensitize GABA A receptors, modulating local phasic inhibition.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: GABA transporters; phasic inhibition; cerebral cortex; inhibitory postsynaptic currents; neurotransmitter imaging

Article.Title: Enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals and musicians is due to reduced internal noise
Article.Authors: Park W.; Awad J.; Fine I.
Article.Abstract: Although it is commonly assumed that early blind individuals have enhanced pitch perception, the literature to date has been contradictory. We measured performance on two tasks known to recruit early versus late stages of auditory frequency tuning in early blind and sighted human adults of both sexes with matched years of musical training. The two groups showed equivalent performance on a tone detection in notched-noise task that assesses cochlear frequency selectivity. In contrast, early blind individuals showed enhanced performance in a pitch discrimination task thought to be mediated by cortical mechanisms. Computational modeling revealed that this enhancement was best explained by reduced internal noise rather than narrower frequency tuning, with both blindness and years of musical training predicting a reduction in internal noise. These findings identify internal noise as a key factor in experience-driven auditory plasticity as a result of both musical experience and early blindness. Significance Statement For centuries, early blindness has been associated with superior auditory abilities. Here we find that the enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals is best explained by reduced internal noise at higher levels of auditory processing, rather than sharper frequency tuning. Years of musical training similarly resulted in lower internal noise, suggesting a shared mechanism through which experience improves auditory perception. These findings identify internal noise reduction as a key component of experience-dependent auditory plasticity.

Article.Title: Estradiol-dependent memory and hippocampal spine remodeling require proteasomal protein degradation
Article.Authors: Beamish S.; Gross K.; Kuehn R.; Frank K.; Valentine E.; Jarome T.; Frick K.
Article.Abstract: Although 17β-estradiol (E 2 ) is a critical neuromodulator of hippocampus-dependent memory and synaptic plasticity, the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Previous studies showed that E 2 enhances dorsal hippocampus-dependent memory consolidation by activating signaling pathways that promote protein synthesis and dendritic spine formation. However, these studies largely overlooked the contribution of protein degradation mediated by the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), despite extensive evidence implicating UPS activity in long-term memory and synaptic plasticity. Here, we combined temporally specific dorsal hippocampal infusions of the proteasome inhibitor β-lactone with three-dimensional spine morphometry to examine the role of UPS-mediated protein degradation in E 2 -induced memory consolidation and CA1 spinogenesis. Immediate post-training bilateral infusion of β-lactone into the dorsal hippocampus of ovariectomized female mice blocked E 2 -induced enhancement of object recognition memory and attenuated E 2 -associated improvements in spatial memory. Arbor-wide Golgi-based analyses revealed robust E 2 -induced increases in spine number across the apical dendritic tree and smaller parallel effects within the basal arbor. Segment-level analyses showed that E 2 produced the greatest structural changes on tertiary apical dendritic segments, increasing total, mushroom, and thin spine density and enhancing multiple morphometric features, including mushroom spine surface area and head-to-neck ratio. Secondary basal dendritic segments exhibited smaller, more variable changes. Many E 2 -associated structural effects were attenuated or abolished by β-lactone. Together, these findings provide the first evidence that proteasomal protein degradation contributes to estrogenic enhancement of hippocampus-dependent memory and CA1 dendritic spine remodeling, identifying UPS-mediated protein degradation as a previously unrecognized mechanism regulating estrogenic memory consolidation and structural plasticity. Significance Statement 17β-estradiol (E 2 ) rapidly enhances hippocampal memory consolidation and promotes CA1 dendritic spinogenesis, yet the molecular mechanisms that support these effects remain unclear. Here, we combine temporally specific dorsal hippocampal proteasome inhibition with three-dimensional Golgi-based spine analyses to show that proteasomal protein degradation is required for E 2 -induced enhancement of object recognition memory and contributes to E 2 -associated improvements in spatial memory in ovariectomized female mice. We further demonstrate that proteasome activity contributes to E 2 -induced increases in apical CA1 spine density and morphology. These findings reveal new insights into estrogenic modulation of cognition that may provide novel protein targets whose levels could be regulated to reduce memory dysfunction related to menopause, depression, and other conditions for which women are at greater risk.

Article.Title: The central melanocortin system regulates growth hormone secretion
Article.Authors: Sousa L.; do N. Vicente V.; Alves G.; Metzger M.; Frazao R.; Donato J.
Article.Abstract: The central melanocortin system is crucial for controlling food intake and metabolism. It includes neurons that produce pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), a prohormone that generates the melanocortin receptor (MCR) agonist alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), and neurons that produce agouti-related protein (AgRP), an endogenous MCR antagonist. This system also influences neuroendocrine neurons, thereby impacting pituitary hormone secretion. However, it remains unclear whether the central melanocortin system also modulates growth hormone (GH) secretion. Here we showed that arcuate nucleus (ARH) GH-releasing hormone (GHRH) neurons receive inputs from α-MSH and AgRP axons. α-MSH activates a subset (∼25%) of ARH GHRH neurons. Serial blood GH measurements were taken before and after systemic saline or clozapine N-oxide injections in mice expressing the excitatory hM3Dq-Gq receptor in POMC-expressing cells. Activation of POMC-expressing cells elevated blood GH levels compared with baseline or saline-injected mice, in both males and females. To determine whether AgRP neurons inhibit GH secretion, mice expressing the hM3Dq-Gq receptor simultaneously in AgRP- and GHRH-expressing cells were created. While chemogenetic activation of GHRH neurons caused a strong GH secretion, co-activation of AgRP neurons inhibited this response in both sexes. Additionally, Fos expression in GHRH-activated neurons was blunted when AgRP neurons were co-stimulated. Mice expressing the hM3Dq-Gq receptor only in MC4R-expressing cells were also investigated; however, activation of MC4R neurons did not alter GH levels. In conclusion, the central melanocortin system modulates the activity of GHRH neurons and GH secretion possibly through MC4R-independent pathways. These findings highlight a critical hypothalamic neurocircuit that integrates metabolic cues to regulate the somatotropic axis. Significance Statement The central melanocortin system processes both short- and long-term nutritional signals to regulate metabolism and various neuroendocrine axes. Here, we show that growth hormone (GH) secretion is controlled by hypothalamic neurons of the central melanocortin system, including populations that express POMC and AgRP. This regulation occurs, at least in part, through modulation of GH-releasing hormone neuron activity, a key group of cells that control pituitary GH secretion. Overall, these findings reveal a hypothalamic circuit that links nutritional status to the regulation of the GH axis, providing new insights into how growth is adaptively controlled by energy availability.

Article.Title: Pooled versus structured inhibition drives stimulus competition across distinct spatial scales in the superior colliculus
Article.Authors: Banerjee A.; Kothari N.; Mysore S.
Article.Abstract: Competitive stimulus interactions across the space map of the midbrain superior colliculus (SC) are critical for spatial decision-making among multiple options. Here, using electrophysiological recordings from the intermediate and deep layers of the SC (SCid) in mice of either sex, we discovered that the rules and spatial profiles of these competitive interactions are different between local within-receptive field (RF), versus global across-RF-boundary, spatial scales. When one visual stimulus was centered in the RF and a second one was located within the RF’s classical inhibitory surround, we found that stimulus interactions followed an averaging rule. This classical surround was spatially restricted, and the strength of inhibition underlying these within-RF interactions decreased with distance from the RF center. By contrast, when the second stimulus was located outside the RF, stimulus interactions followed a divisive rule. Strikingly, this extra-classical inhibitory surround was spatially global, and the strength of competitive inhibition underlying these across-RF-boundary interactions was distance-invariant while being dependent on the relative strengths of the competing stimuli. Computational modeling revealed that whereas within-RF interactions are well-explained by a normalization-like mechanism driven by pooled inhibition, across-RF-boundary interactions are not, and instead, are well-explained by a winner-take-all-like mechanism driven by structured, donut-like inhibition. Combined, our results reveal the mechanistic logic of stimulus competition across the space-map of mammalian SCid. Significance statement Selecting one target among many is essential for diverse cognitive functions, and requires neural circuits to compare priorities of competing stimuli. Using electrophysiological recordings in the mouse superior colliculus, a critical brain area for spatial decision-making, we show that stimulus competition follows fundamentally different rules at local versus distant spatial scales. Nearby stimuli within a receptive field (RF) engage spatially restricted, decaying inhibition, enacting an averaging rule. By contrast, distant stimuli separated by the RF boundary engage spatially global, distance-invariant inhibition, enacting a divisive, relative strength-dependent rule. Computational modeling reveals that local interactions are explained by a pooling normalization mechanism, whereas global interactions are explained by a donut-like winner-take-all mechanism. Results resolve long open questions about stimulus competition in the SC.

Article.Title: Revisiting post-stimulus theta activity: evidence for a broadband rather than narrowband spectral origin
Article.Authors: Vanneau T.; Quiquempoix M.; Voytek B.; Gyurkovics M.; Molholm S.
Article.Abstract: The aperiodic, 1/f-like component of electrophysiological activity is increasingly recognized as a meaningful feature of neural function rather than background noise. Meanwhile, many EEG studies interpret transient post-stimulus changes in oscillatory power as signatures of attention, salience, or cognitive control. Such interpretations typically depend on baseline normalization, which assumes aperiodic activity remains stable from pre- to post-stimulus periods. Using high-density EEG from typically developing children, we tested this assumption across two paradigms: an audiovisual simple reaction-time task (n = 36, 19 males and 17 females) and a visual oddball task (n = 38, 20 males and 18 females). In each, conventional spectral analyses were compared with analyses that explicitly modeled and removed aperiodic activity in both windows. Across tasks, stimulus onset produced robust increases in aperiodic exponent and offset, indicating systematic 1/f changes. In the audiovisual task these were modality-specific, with central, parieto-occipital, or combined topographies by stimulus type. They diminished but persisted after ERP removal, suggesting they were not fully explained by phase-locked activity. Critically, once aperiodic activity was accounted for, the apparent theta increase was largely abolished in both tasks, including the canonical fronto-central enhancement to infrequent targets. The conventional method also overestimated beta desynchronization, especially in the induced signal, indicating a spurious consequence of spectral slope steepening. By contrast, alpha desynchronization remained robust and was enhanced, reflecting genuine suppression. Together, these findings suggest many conventional time-frequency effects, particularly apparent theta synchronization, may reflect stimulus-driven aperiodic changes rather than robust narrowband changes, challenging core assumptions of these analyses. Significance statement Frequency-domain neural activity comprises both narrowband oscillations and broadband aperiodic activity. Conventional time–frequency analyses use baseline normalization to isolate oscillatory responses, implicitly assuming that aperiodic activity remains stable following stimulus onset. Across two EEG paradigms, we show that stimulus presentation systematically alters aperiodic activity in a sensory- and attention-dependent manner. These changes can produce apparent increases in theta-band power that do not reflect genuine narrowband oscillations and can exaggerate beta desynchronization. In contrast, alpha desynchronization remained robust after accounting for aperiodic activity. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-related aperiodic changes can substantially influence conventional time–frequency measures and should be explicitly considered when interpreting post-stimulus oscillatory responses.
