This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of routinely available complete blood count (CBC)–derived indices, particularly the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), as potential low-cost surrogate markers for infection in resource-constrained healthcare settings. A multicenter cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study was conducted in primary and secondary healthcare facilities in two conflict-affected governorates in southern Yemen (Al-Dhalea and Lahej) between January and December 2025. A total of 700 consecutive patients aged ≥ 5 years for whom a complete blood count was clinically indicated (including those presenting with fever, fatigue, or general malaise) were enrolled. Patients with chronic hematological disorders, active malignancy, recent blood transfusion, pregnancy, or critical illness were excluded. Diagnostic performance of NLR and PLR was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess their independent predictive value. Among 700 participants (mean age 34.5 ± 14.2 years; 52% female), 217 (31%) had confirmed malaria. Median NLR was significantly higher in malaria infected compared with non-infected individuals (4.1 [IQR 3.2–5.3] vs. 1.6 [IQR 1.2–2.1], p < 0.001). NLR showed good diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.81, 95% CI 0.77–0.85). An optimal cut-off value of NLR ≥ 3.0 yielded 82% sensitivity and 76% specificity. PLR also demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.74, 95% CI 0.70–0.78). In multivariable analysis, NLR remained a strong independent predictor of malaria (adjusted OR = 5.6, 95% CI 3.9–8.1), followed by PLR (adjusted OR = 3.4, 95% CI 2.5–4.7). CBC-derived inflammatory indices, particularly NLR and to a lesser extent PLR, may serve as practical and low-cost triage markers for detecting malaria in conflict-affected and resource-limited settings. The NLR threshold of ≥ 3.0 showed good diagnostic accuracy and could be incorporated into clinical triage algorithms to support early identification of malaria and strengthen diagnostic capacity in peripheral health systems in fragile settings.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Malaria Research and Control; Medicine > Oncology > Inflammatory Biomarkers in Disease Prognosis; Medicine > Epidemiology > Sepsis Diagnosis and Treatment

Article.Title: Conjugation of metal-organic framework (MIL-125) to NiFe2O4@CdS nanoparticles for enhanced photocatalytic hydrogen generation
Article.Authors: El-Taib Heakal F.; Abdelhamid H.; Frrag M.; El-Bery H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Harnessing solar energy with semiconductors offers a feasible path toward sustainable hydrogen production via photocatalytic water splitting. In this study, a ternary photocatalyst, MIL-125(Ti)/NiFe 2 O 4 @CdS, was fabricated by integrating a Ti-based metal–organic framework with a green-synthesized NiFe 2 O 4 @CdS binary core–shell heterostructure for visible-light-driven hydrogen evolution. Illicium verum Hook. f. (star anise) extract was used as a natural reducing and stabilizing agent for NiFe 2 O 4 nanoparticles preparation prior to the fabrication of the binary photocatalyst. The ternary composite was comprehensively characterized by structural, morphological, optical, and photoelectrochemical techniques. Compared with the individual components, the ternary photocatalyst exhibited enhanced visible-light absorption, a reduced band gap (2.42 eV), and a mesoporous structure with a BET surface area of 148.62 m²/g, pore volume of 0.5721 cm 3 /g, and a mean pore diameter of 15.0 nm. Photoelectrochemical analyses revealed improved charge separation, the lowest charge-transfer resistance, the highest photocurrent response, the largest electrochemically active surface area, and favorable band alignment. Consequently, MIL-125/NiFe 2 O 4 @CdS achieved an initial hydrogen evolution rate of 1.62231 mmol g − 1 h − 1 and a cumulative hydrogen production of 10.20386 mmol g − 1 after 5 h, significantly outperforming CdS and the binary NiFe 2 O 4 @CdS. The photocatalyst retained approximately 60% of its initial activity after four reaction cycles, demonstrating good stability. The enhanced performance is attributed to the synergistic effects of MIL-125, which increase surface area, improve light harvesting, and promote efficient charge separation and transfer through a dual direct Z-scheme heterojunction. These findings highlight MIL-125/NiFe 2 O 4 @CdS as a promising photocatalyst for sustainable hydrogen production.
Article.TopicFields: Energy > Renewable Energy, Sustainability and the Environment > Advanced Photocatalysis Techniques; Energy > Renewable Energy, Sustainability and the Environment > TiO2 Photocatalysis and Solar Cells; Energy > Renewable Energy, Sustainability and the Environment > Metalloenzymes and iron-sulfur proteins

Article.Title: A novel Hybrid Beetle Swarm Optimization-based MPPT strategy for PV battery-based microgrid with real-time OPAL-RT validation
Article.Authors: Kumar G.; Verma S.; Bhushan R.; Routray A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Use of renewable energy sources in achieving sustainable solutions to reliable and uninterrupted supply of electricity is becoming a dominant trend, and solar photovoltaic (PV) technology is playing a central role with regard to this trend. Nevertheless, the nature of solar energy intermittency due to changes in solar irradiance and temperature, as well as the fact that most solar panels do not convert all the energy incident to the panel, and thus requires the introduction of sophisticated Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) methods. This research proposes an improved, robust, and high-performance Hybrid Beetle Swarm Optimization (BSO)-based MPPT strategy for solar PV systems. A high-fidelity MATLAB/Simulink-based microgrid model integrating a solar PV array with a battery energy storage system is developed to evaluate the proposed control scheme. The performance of the hybrid BSO-MPPT algorithm is strictly tested under various conditions of operation, such as a dynamic change of irradiance and temperature. The comparative performance analysis with the traditional optimization methods, including Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Dung Beetle Optimization (DBO) proves to be more accurate in tracking, faster in reacting to changes, less oscillation in steady-state, and more robust in the proposed method. The detailed graphical and tabular outputs of the results also confirm better efficiency of the algorithm. Besides, the suggested controller is tested and proven on an OPAL-RT OP4510 hardware in the loop (HIL) platform with real-time performance and latency requirements in mind. The similarity between the real-time HIL performance and the actual hardware performance validates the strength, computational performance, and real-time feasibility of the suggested hybrid strategy of BSO with MPPT to microgrids.
Article.TopicFields: Energy > Renewable Energy, Sustainability and the Environment > Photovoltaic System Optimization Techniques; Engineering > Control and Systems Engineering > Microgrid Control and Optimization; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithms Research

Article.Title: Terahertz sensor with parity time symmetry for enhanced detection of frozen oral cancer tissues
Article.Authors: Zaky Z.; Hennache A.; Panda A.
Article.Abstract: In this work, we present a defect-engineered one-dimensional photonic crystal (1D-PhC) operating in the terahertz regime, designed on the principle of parity-time (PT) symmetry for highly sensitive detection of frozen oral cancer cells. The proposed sensor is a one-dimensional parity–time-symmetric photonic crystal consisting of repeated silicon dioxide/porous silicon bilayers surrounding a central defect layer on a substrate, where the defect layer serves as the sensing region for frozen oral tissues. The transfer matrix method is employed to investigate the shift in the defect mode characteristics in the transmittance spectrum. By incorporating a complex refractive index distribution that fulfills PT-symmetric conditions, the system acquires non-Hermitian characteristics, resulting in sharp resonances and tunable defect mode responses. The simulation results reveal that the introduction of PT-symmetric gain and loss (Q) layers remarkably enhances the sensitivity compared to conventional PhC-based sensors. The proposed design achieves transmittance-based sensitivity of $$\:2.4\times\:{10}^{11}\:\%/RIU$$ and $$\:1.7\times\:{10}^{10}\:\%/RIU$$ , whereas spectra-based sensitivity of $$\:68.8\:GHz/RIU$$ and $$\:68.8\:GHz/RIU$$ for Q = 10.695 and 7.85, respectively. Along with its high sensitivity, the simplicity and fabrication feasibility of the structure make it a promising platform for real-time, label-free early-stage oral cancer detection.
Article.TopicFields: Physics and Astronomy > Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics > Photonic Crystals and Applications; Materials Science > Electronic, Optical and Magnetic Materials > Metamaterials and Metasurfaces Applications; Engineering > Biomedical Engineering > Plasmonic and Surface Plasmon Research

Article.Title: Estimated fat mass and body mass index z-score in relation to locomotion-related components of physical fitness in Japanese elementary schoolchildren
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Shoji K.; Miyata H.; Ma J.; Hazar F.; Kim H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Whether anthropometrically estimated fat mass explains variation in physical fitness beyond body mass index z-score remains unclear. This school-based cross-sectional study examined these associations in 3,259 Japanese elementary schoolchildren aged 7–12 years. Fat mass was estimated as measured body weight minus anthropometrically predicted fat-free mass and analyzed with height adjustment because conventional fat mass index showed residual height dependence. The assessed locomotion-related components of physical fitness comprised the 20-m shuttle run, 50-m run, side-step test, and standing long jump. The composite fitness score was calculated as the mean of their sex- and age-standardized scores, with the 50-m run reverse-coded. Sex-stratified models adjusted for age, survey year, and school fixed effects. Higher body mass index z-score and estimated fat mass were associated with lower composite fitness scores in boys and girls. Adding estimated fat mass to models containing body mass index z-score and height increased explained variance by 4.4% points in boys and 2.7% points in girls. Estimated fat mass provided modest additional explanatory information within this sample; these findings do not establish clinical predictive utility.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Obesity, Physical Activity, Diet; Medicine > Physiology > Physical Activity and Health; Medicine > Physiology > Body Composition Measurement Techniques

Article.Title: Design of an in-situ CONOSEAL sealing surface repairing equipment for nuclear reactor thermocouple column
Article.Authors: Li H.; Duan H.; Cheng P.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: The CONOSEAL seal for the nuclear reactor thermocouple column belongs to the boundary seal of the primary circuit. When the sealing surface suffers from scratches, damages, or other defects, it will directly affect the sealing reliability and result in leakage. However, replacing the thermocouple column is a complex process with huge workload and long period. To address these issues, an in-situ reactor thermocouple column CONOSEAL sealing surface repairing device is designed. Due to the in-situ structure and operation conditions, the repairing device is designed in a compact modular and light weighted manner. Repair tests have been conducted on a thermocouple column to verify the repair capability of the CONOSEAL sealing surface repairing device. A prototype of cycling test platform is established to simulate the in-situ conditions of the thermocouple column. The CONOSEAL sealing surface is repaired to achieve a surface roughness of Ra 1.712 μm and pressure tests according to RCC-M standard and thermal cycling tests are both performed on the thermocouple column. For the pressure tests, the measured pressure drops do not exceed 0.2 MPa during a 10 min pressure maintenance. In the thermal cycling tests, the pressure is maintained for 10 min under the pressure of 15.5 MPa and the temperature is 310 ℃ and there are no leaks. The test results show that the dimensions and roughness of the sealing surface after repairing by the repair device meet the requirements of the in-situ operation conditions. This verifies the capability of the CONOSEAL sealing surface repairing equipment.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Safety, Risk, Reliability and Quality > Nuclear and radioactivity studies; Engineering > Aerospace Engineering > Nuclear reactor physics and engineering; Engineering > Aerospace Engineering > Nuclear Engineering Thermal-Hydraulics

Article.Title: User perceptions of serendipity-control, cognitive-level labelling, and explanation features in an LLM-based academic article recommender: a single-institution pilot study
Article.Authors: Afridi A.; Johar S.; Ahmad N.; Jan T.; Khalil R.
Article.Abstract: Serendipity in recommender systems has been studied mainly as an algorithmic property rather than as an interface-design question. This pilot study examined how undergraduates perceived three interface features of ScholarMind, a prototype in which a large language model (LLM) generates article recommendations directly: accuracy and serendipity sliders, LLM-assigned Bloom’s taxonomy labels, and an explanation panel of LLM-generated weights labelled as SHAP values. Forty-one students at one institution in Pakistan completed a task requiring use of all three features, followed by a self-report battery (ResQue, SUS, UEQ-S and three unvalidated feature scales). Mean feature ratings lay on the agreement side of the midpoint (3.62–3.80 on 5-point scales), but reverse-worded items correlated negatively with their scales, indicating acquiescent responding. Exploratory correlations linked explanation-panel perceptions with perceived trust (rₛ = 0.47, 95% CI [0.18, 0.68]) and Bloom’s-label perceptions with perceived usefulness (rₛ = 0.51, 95% CI [0.23, 0.71]). Perceived usability was below benchmark (SUS = 56.6 vs. 68), and preference relative to Google Scholar was evenly split. Inspection of the source code showed that the sliders only reorder a fixed set of generated articles. The findings describe perceptions of an interface prototype, not recommender performance.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Information Systems > Recommender Systems and Techniques; Computer Science > Human-Computer Interaction > Usability and User Interface Design; Computer Science > Information Systems > Information Retrieval and Search Behavior

Article.Title: On reliable cost-efficient data-driven modelling of microwave passives in reduced-dimensionality domains with co-kriging
Article.Authors: Koziel S.; Pietrenko-Dabrowska A.
Article.Abstract: Data-driven surrogate modeling has seen a rise in attention in microwave engineering over the recent years. It has been primarily employed to expedite electromagnetic (EM)-based design procedures, e.g., parametric optimization or robust design. However, behavioral modeling of microwave components becomes problematic due to their nonlinear characteristics, often large numbers of geometry parameters, as well as broad ranges thereof. This work proposes an unconventional approach to resource-efficient and accurate modeling of microwave passive circuits. Our methodology is founded on reducing the design space dimensionality carried out via fast global sensitivity analysis, and also the incorporation of variable-resolution simulation data. The surrogate domain extends alongside the most significant directions reflecting the highest circuit response variability. The surrogate model is rendered using a mixture of densely sampled low- and sparsely allocated high-resolution EM simulation training points, which are blended together using co-kriging. The aforementioned mechanisms ensure remarkable computing performance of the modeling process and greatly improve the surrogate’s predictive power as compared to surrogates established in a full-dimensionality domain. Comparative studies carried out using three circuits and a number of recent benchmark methods corroborate the competitive performance of the introduced methodology, in particular, its ability to yield design-ready behavioral models featuring relative RMS error of a few percent at the cost corresponding to less than a few hundred of high-fidelity training points.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Microwave Engineering and Waveguides; Computer Science > Computational Theory and Mathematics > Advanced Multi-Objective Optimization Algorithms; Physics and Astronomy > Statistical and Nonlinear Physics > Model Reduction and Neural Networks

Article.Title: MCD–Huber based control chart for contaminated multivariate process monitoring
Article.Authors: Zaagan A.; Alzahrani A.; Alamri A.; Alharbi M.; Nabi M.
Article.Abstract: The SAMEWMA–VSS chart combines support-vector-regression-based adaptive smoothing with a variable sample size within a Mahalanobis-form multivariate EWMA statistic, but neither this mechanism nor the classical multivariate charts it builds on were designed for contaminated data: a single gross measurement error can distort the estimated shift magnitude that drives the chart’s adaptive smoothing constant and sample size, and classical Phase-I moment estimates are well known to suffer from masking under contamination. This paper proposes MCD–Huber SAMEWMA–VSS, which replaces the classical Phase-I mean and covariance with robust minimum covariance determinant (MCD) estimates and replaces each subgroup’s raw contribution with a Huber-weighted one, while retaining the original chart’s SVR-based adaptive smoothing and variable-sample-size mechanisms. An extensive Monte Carlo study compares the proposed chart against the original SAMEWMA–VSS chart and against an Isolation-Forest-weighted (IF-weighted) alternative across clean shifts, gross-error contamination at varying rates and magnitudes, and a range of correlation structures. The results show a clear contrast between the two robust alternatives: the IF-weighted chart’s more aggressive weighting substantially improves contamination resistance but masks genuine large shifts, never signaling at all for the largest shifts examined, whereas MCD–Huber SAMEWMA–VSS achieves a substantial but partial gain in contamination resistance — the in-control average run length under 10% gross-error contamination rises from 27.19 for the original chart to 67.42, still well below the clean target of 370—while retaining detection speed close to the original chart for small and moderate clean shifts (within about 13% up to δ = 1.5), at the cost of slower detection of large shifts (δ ≥ 3), where its ARL levels off near 7. An illustrative NASA IMS bearing feature-based simulation, using real Phase-I vibration-feature statistics as the reference model with simulated Phase-II shifts and contamination, demonstrates the proposed chart’s behavior under both clean and contaminated conditions. Supplementary analyses examine the run-length distribution, the precision of the control limits, the Huber cutoff, the Phase-I sample size and contamination, the delayed-shift metrics FAP τ and CDD τ , dimensions up to 20, serial correlation and computing time.
Article.TopicFields: Decision Sciences > Statistics, Probability and Uncertainty > Advanced Statistical Process Monitoring; Engineering > Control and Systems Engineering > Fault Detection and Control Systems; Mathematics > Statistics and Probability > Advanced Statistical Methods and Models

Article.Title: Timing of vancomycin initiation and mortality in critically Ill patients with sepsis and type 2 diabetes: A clone–censor–weighting analysis
Article.Authors: Song C.; Dong Y.; Zhang K.; Qin Y.; Shi L.; Zheng L.; Zheng C.; Sun Q.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Sepsis in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with high mortality. While early antibiotics are crucial, the optimal timing for initiating Gram-positive coverage with vancomycin remains uncertain in this high-risk population. Observational analyses of treatment timing are susceptible to immortal time and time-dependent confounding. We therefore aimed to evaluate the associations between vancomycin initiation timing and mortality and ICU length of stay among critically ill patients with sepsis and T2DM who ultimately received vancomycin. We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis using data from the MIMIC-IV database, including ICU patients with sepsis and T2DM who received systemic intravenous vancomycin during the index ICU stay. A cloning–censoring–weighting (CCW) framework was applied within this treated cohort to compare initiation at < 48 h versus ≥ 48 h after ICU admission, with exploratory analyses across four 12-h initiation windows. The primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality; secondary endpoints were 7-, 30-, and 90-day mortality and ICU length of stay. Sensitivity analyses evaluated alternative confounding, weighting, timing-cutoff, and missing-data specifications. A total of 4,019 ICU patients with sepsis and T2DM were included, of whom 72.3% received vancomycin within 48 h of ICU admission. Initiation at ≥ 48 h, compared with < 48 h, was associated with higher in-hospital mortality within the selected treated cohort (adjusted OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.23–1.71; P < 0.001). Exploratory refined-window analyses showed a non-monotonic pattern, and estimates for the later initiation windows should be interpreted cautiously because of the small subgroup sizes. ICU length of stay did not differ significantly among the four < 48-h initiation windows (all P > 0.05), but was longer when vancomycin was started ≥ 48 h (adjusted mean difference 2.1 days; P < 0.001). Among septic patients with T2DM who ultimately received vancomycin, initiation at ≥ 48 h was associated with higher mortality and longer ICU stay within this selected treated cohort. These observational findings should not be interpreted as evidence that earlier vancomycin initiation improves outcomes and require validation in prospectively defined populations.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Epidemiology > Sepsis Diagnosis and Treatment; Medicine > Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism > Hyperglycemia and glycemic control in critically ill and hospitalized patients; Medicine > Pharmacology > Antibiotics Pharmacokinetics and Efficacy

Article.Title: A harmonised protocol for generating human extracorporeal photopheresates for research
Article.Authors: Stepien J.; Arella F.; Veltman H.; Riquelme P.; Schmidt T.; Glehr G.; Iglesias Escudero M.; Brosig A.; Haehnel V.; Martinez Caceres E.; Eggenhofer E.; Hutchinson J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Extracorporeal photopheresis (ECP) is an established second-line therapy for T cell-mediated immune diseases such as graft-versus-host disease and organ transplant rejection. The ECP procedure induces apoptosis in autologous leucocytes using 8-methoxypsoralen (8-MOP) and UVA irradiation, which are then reinfused into patients leading to immunomodulatory effects. To ensure the comparability and relevance of investigations into these immunomodulatory actions, we developed and validated an ECP protocol for research purposes that closely reproduces the apoptotic profile of clinical ECP products from the CELLEX system. We optimised key parameters, including 8-MOP concentration, UVA dose and sample preparation, such that apoptosis rates matched clinical ECP products. An 8-MOP concentration of 400 ng/ml and UVA dose of 2 J/cm 2 resulted in consistent T cell apoptosis rates (84.7 ± 2.1% at 48 h). Analysis by flow cytometry confirmed similar kinetics of early and late apoptosis in research-grade and clinical photopheresates. Our research-grade protocol, which was validated by an independent laboratory, establishes a reliable and therapeutically relevant model for harmonised mechanistic and translational ECP research.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Hematology > Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation; Immunology and Microbiology > Immunology > T-cell and B-cell Immunology; Medicine > Transplantation > Organ and Tissue Transplantation Research

Article.Title: Morphometric changes in foramen rotundum before adulthood: a CT study
Article.Authors: Inci M.; Selcuk M.
Article.Abstract: The aim of this study is to evaluate the morphometric characteristics of the foramen rotundum (FR) during childhood and adolescence using computed tomography (CT) scans, to identify age-related developmental changes, the effect of sex and bilateral asymmetry, and to present age-specific normative data. A total of 600 FRs were retrospectively analyzed on head CT scans of 300 individuals under 18 years of age (150 females, 150 males) from a Central Anatolian population. Cases were categorized into five developmental stages. Canal length (CL), mid-sagittal distance (MD), foramen width (FW), and foramen height (FH) were measured. Age was an independent predictor for all parameters ( p < 0.005), whereas the effect of sex was negligible (d ≤ 0.17). Mean MD was 12.5 mm in the 1–2-year group and 17.9–18.0 mm in the 14–17-year group, while mean CL was 4.0 mm and 8.5 mm, respectively. Regression analysis predicted approximately 2.8 mm greater CL and 3.5–3.7 mm greater MD per 10-year difference in age. The largest relative differences between consecutive age groups were observed in MD in early childhood, in FH around school age, and in CL in adolescence. CL, FW, and FH values were significantly higher on the left side ( p ≤ 0.001); asymmetry was highest for CL (5.65%) and lowest for MD (0.84%). FR morphometry exhibits marked age-dependent changes during childhood and adolescence; thus, adult reference values cannot be directly applied to pediatric cases. The age-specific normative data presented in this study may serve as a reference for the anatomical assessment of the pediatric skull base; their diagnostic and surgical utility requires confirmation in clinical studies.
Article.TopicFields: Arts and Humanities > Archeology > Forensic Anthropology and Bioarchaeology Studies; Medicine > Surgery > Nasal Surgery and Airway Studies; Dentistry > Oral Surgery > Dental Radiography and Imaging

Article.Title: The impact of age-friendly smart homes on care burden, out-of-pocket costs and their distributional inequality among urban older households in China
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Ibrahim F.; Wang Y.; Liu J.; Liu Y.; Zhao S.
Article.Abstract: Population ageing and ageing-in-place policies leave more frail older adults at home, raising family care burden and costs and calling for more equitable home-based care. Age-friendly smart homes are increasingly installed to share this care. We ask whether such technology substitutes for care uniformly and how its benefits are distributed across households. Using a prospective matched cohort of 640 older households in 24 urban communities in Hefei, China, we estimate the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) of installation with propensity-score weighting, test its variation with interaction models, and relate the passive and active functions configured in each treated home to outcomes in within-treatment dose models. Installation is associated with lower care burden and out-of-pocket costs and with fewer fall-related visits. The gains are unevenly captured. Hospital-day reductions concentrate among older adults living alone, a gradient that survives false-discovery-rate control across 15 moderator tests. Out-of-pocket savings narrow as human care availability rises, a gradient that survives the same control under the normal reference distribution and falls short of it under a small-cluster t reference. No gradient is detected for care-burden relief. Within treated homes, wider passive-monitoring coverage goes with caregivers withdrawing from device-mediated supervision. The out-of-pocket difference lies mainly in recorded inpatient and other medical spending, adjusting for hospital days changes it little, and the medical estimates are sensitive to assumptions about households without records. Allocation can combine need-based eligibility with priority for households facing care scarcity, with the balance set by the policy goal.
Article.TopicFields: Social Sciences > Demography > Technology Use by Older Adults; Health Professions > General Health Professions > Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues; Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Aging, Health, and Disability

Article.Title: Work-intensity demands, autonomous motivation, and school support show distinct associations with perceived distress and low perceived coping in teachers
Article.Authors: Pânișoară I.; Ursu A.; Lazăr I.; Piele M.
Article.Abstract: Teacher stress may involve distinct experiences of perceived distress and low perceived coping that relate differently to working conditions and motivational resources. This cross-sectional study examined work-intensity demands, school support, autonomous motivation, and two facets of perceived stress among 5,312 Romanian teachers. Partial least squares structural equation modelling estimated the formative work-intensity composite, higher-order constructs, indirect associations, and the interaction term; covariance-based analyses supplemented the assessment of the reflective measurement structure. A two-factor PSS-10 specification fit better than a unidimensional model under both estimators. Work-intensity demands were positively associated with autonomous motivation, strongly associated with perceived distress, and weakly associated with low perceived coping. School support was associated with a weaker work-intensity slope for perceived distress, whereas the interaction with low perceived coping was small and positive, contrary to the proposed buffering pattern. Four indirect associations through autonomous motivation were negative and significant; those involving work-intensity demands were opposite in sign to the corresponding direct associations at mean school support. School support and autonomous motivation were negatively associated with both stress facets, with stronger associations with low perceived coping. These findings support distinguishing the two stress facets and considering both demanding working conditions and school-level resources when examining teacher stress.
Article.TopicFields: Health Professions > Occupational Therapy > Occupational Health and Burnout; Psychology > Social Psychology > Stress and Burnout Research; Health Professions > General Health Professions > Workplace Health and Well-being

Article.Title: A multimodal characterization of early monoarthritis in rats using an MBSA/CFA-induced model
Article.Authors: Pereira M.; da Silveira L.; Ferian P.; Utuari F.; Velosa A.; de P. Faria D.; Massironi S.; Massoco S. G. C.; Mori C.; Teodoro W.; Fantoni D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A detailed characterization of the initial inflammatory events in arthritis is essential to improve experimental models and accelerate translational research. In this study, we comprehensively established and characterized a monoarthritis model in male Wistar rats, induced by intra-articular injection of methylated bovine serum albumin (mBSA) combined with Freund’s complete adjuvant (CFA). Animals were allocated into a control group and two groups with arthritis, evaluated at early (8 days) and late acute phase (13 days). Arthritis induction resulted in pronounced synovial inflammation, characterized by increased cellular infiltration composed predominantly of CD68 + macrophages, extracellular matrix remodeling with elevated collagen I and V deposition, and increased intra-articular glucose metabolism, assessed by PET/CT with [18F]FDG. Biochemical analysis revealed significantly elevated levels of prostaglandin E 2 in the synovial lavage fluid of arthritic joints. These pathological changes were accompanied by transient clinical and behavioral changes, including reduced limb-use impairment, decreased body weight gain, and increased pain scores, which were attenuated by tramadol administration. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that a single mBSA/CFA challenge followed by an mBSA booster is sufficient to induce consistent monoarthritis with measurable pathological, metabolic, clinical, and behavioral correlations. This model provides a robust platform for investigating early inflammatory mechanisms and evaluating diagnostic and therapeutic strategies targeting joint inflammation.“
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Rheumatology > Rheumatoid Arthritis Research and Therapies; Medicine > Rheumatology > Osteoarthritis Treatment and Mechanisms; Medicine > Complementary and alternative medicine > Natural Compounds in Disease Treatment

Article.Title: Assessing the reliability of accelerated quantitative susceptibility mapping sequences in memory clinic patients
Article.Authors: Di Nardo F.; Iandolo R.; Cavaliere C.; Di Cecca A.; Salvatore E.; Pappatà S.; Salvatore M.; Aiello M.
Article.Abstract: Alterations of iron and other chemical species in brain tissue, measurable with Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM), are associated with various neurodegenerative diseases. QSM relies on 3D multi-echo gradient-echo sequences with long acquisition times, potentially reducing patient comfort and increasing susceptibility to motion artifacts. This study evaluated the reliability of susceptibility maps obtained from an accelerated QSM sequence compared with a conventional protocol in memory clinic patients. Thirty-six patients underwent a 3 T brain MRI protocol including conventional and accelerated 3D-T1 weighted and QSM acquisitions. The standard QSM acquisition was itself accelerated using parallel imaging SENSE, whereas the accelerated QSM used CS-SENSE; Image preprocessing comprised registration, segmentation, and susceptibility map reconstruction, followed by extraction of magnetic susceptibility metrics from the cerebral cortex and deep grey matter nuclei. Within-subject differences were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, while equivalence was evaluated using a paired two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure with a predefined ± 0.025 ppm margin. Consistency and absolute agreement were assessed using ICC(C,1) and ICC(A,1), respectively, while Bland–Altman analysis and interscan coefficient of variation evaluated agreement and reproducibility. Image similarity was evaluated using the structural similarity index and mean square error. No significant differences were observed between conventional and accelerated acquisitions for any metric. TOST demonstrated equivalence for most ROI-metric combinations, with exceptions limited to weighted susceptibility measures in the pallidum and putamen. Overall, measurements showed good consistency, low interscan variability, and high image similarity between methods. Sensitivity analyses using alternative QSM map reconstruction and common T1-weighted segmentation yielded consistent results. These findings support accelerated QSM as a reliable alternative to conventional acquisitions. Although further clinical validation is warranted, the shorter acquisition time may facilitate integration into routine dementia imaging protocols.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Radiology, Nuclear Medicine and Imaging > Advanced MRI Techniques and Applications; Medicine > Radiology, Nuclear Medicine and Imaging > Advanced Neuroimaging Techniques and Applications; Physics and Astronomy > Nuclear and High Energy Physics > NMR spectroscopy and applications

Article.Title: Mitigating the effect of traps in p-GaN HEMTs through field plate and doping optimization
Article.Authors: Muktadir M.; Ahmad M.; Mech B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract This work presents a complete analysis of normally-off p-GaN High Electron Mobility Transistors (HEMTs) with field plate using TCAD simulations in conjunction with physics-based analytical model. The study focuses on maximizing the breakdown voltage ( $$V_{BR}$$ ) through the integrated optimization of field plate (FP) length and Magnesium (Mg) doping concentration in the p-GaN cap layer under the influence of thermally assisted traps. The analyses were performed taking the reported experimental values of Mg and TAT (Trap Assisted Tunneling) concentrations. Implementation of the field plates successfully suppresses the crowding of electric field and enhance the channel breakdown voltage. The numerical length of the field plate is optimized for the highest breakdown voltage which was achieved at 978V when the field plate length (LFP) was 1.5 $$\mu $$ m in combination with high Mg doping.TCAD results also reveal that, Mg concentration significantly modulates the device’s threshold voltage ( $$V_{TH}$$ ), power density and leakage current. Explicitly, increasing the parametric value of Mg active concentration to $$1\times 10^{18}$$ $$cm^{-3}$$ increases the DC peak output current from 12 mA/mm to a saturation value of 67 mA/mm for V $$_{GS}$$ = 10V, while shifting the threshold voltage $$V_{TH}$$ from 4.91V to 1.6V. Furthermore, the TCAD results are compared with a physics-based analytical models specially developed for p-GaN HEMTs. These comparisons demonstrate strong agreement between the TCAD and the theoretical results in terms of DC characteristics for the proposed device. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, the combined optimization of field-plate length and Mg doping under trap-assisted tunneling conditions has not been previously investigated in detail. With the analytical cross-validation against experimentally-calibrated TCAD simulation, this approach also offers various performance parameter configurations, helping designers select the ideal combination for reliable high-power applications.
Article.TopicFields: Physics and Astronomy > Condensed Matter Physics > GaN-based semiconductor devices and materials; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Silicon Carbide Semiconductor Technologies; Engineering > Electrical and Electronic Engineering > Advancements in Semiconductor Devices and Circuit Design

Article.Title: Life cycle assessment of vertical flow constructed wetlands vs. conventional treatment in hot-arid climates: a Saudi Arabian case study
Article.Authors: Kamal M.; Alali A.
Article.Abstract: Water scarcity and the carbon intensity of conventional treatment are coupled constraints in arid regions, where reclaimed effluent is a strategic resource under Saudi Vision 2030. Vertical flow constructed wetlands (VFCWs) perform well in hot climates, but no life cycle assessment (LCA) has compared them with conventional treatment using primary kinetic data measured in a hot-arid setting, and none has adjusted the conventional benchmark for the same climate. This study reports the first comparative cradle-to-grave LCA of a pilot VFCW and a functionally equivalent conventional activated sludge (CAS) system treating institutional wastewater in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, over a 20-year design life. The functional unit is 1.0 m³ of wastewater entering the treatment system and treated to the Saudi standard for restricted irrigation; every inventory flow, including the reuse credit, is expressed on this influent basis. The systems were compared on the operational elements that distinguish them: aeration and pumping electricity, chemical dosing, sludge production and handling, direct methane and nitrous oxide emissions, construction media and haulage, and end-of-life management. Primary kinetics and measured material quantities were combined with a regionalized inventory: grid carbon intensity of 0.69 kg CO₂-eq·kWh⁻¹, aeration energy raised by 15% for reduced oxygen transfer at high temperature, and avoided seawater desalination credited in proportion to the reusable effluent each system delivers (0.935 m³ for the VFCW after evaporative loss; 1.00 m³ for CAS). Excluding the reuse credit, the VFCW returns a global warming potential of 0.39 kg CO₂-eq·m⁻³ against 0.67 for CAS, a 42% reduction rising to 52% at community scale (10 m³·day⁻¹); paired Monte Carlo simulation over 1,000 iterations gives a discernibility proportion above 99.9%. Because the VFCW delivers less reusable water, crediting avoided desalination by effluent volume halves the absolute margin, from 0.28 to 0.14 kg CO₂-eq·m⁻³, without reversing it. The wetland removed 92.7% of ammonia-nitrogen, but total nitrogen was not measured; under a conservative nitrogen mass balance in which nitrified nitrogen leaves as nitrate, the marine eutrophication potentials of the two systems are similar (0.022 and 0.020 kg N-eq·m⁻³), and no nitrogen advantage is claimed. Net water savings through displaced desalination are 0.93 m³ (VFCW) and 0.98 m³ (CAS) per m³ treated. The advantage is conditional rather than general: phosphorus retention of 59% produces a freshwater eutrophication potential about 6.5 times that of chemically dosed CAS, the carbon advantage is lost where aggregate haulage exceeds approximately 180 km, and it disappears where the conventional plant is supplied by solar photovoltaic electricity. The findings rest on a single pilot in one climate and on a design-based conventional benchmark, and are bounded accordingly.
Article.TopicFields: Environmental Science > Waste Management and Disposal > Constructed Wetlands for Wastewater Treatment; Environmental Science > Waste Management and Disposal > Wastewater Treatment and Reuse; Environmental Science > Environmental Engineering > Environmental Impact and Sustainability

Article.Title: Castor oil plus sweeping membrane maneuver versus oral misoprostol for labor induction: a prospective observational study
Article.Authors: Francesca C.; Alessia M.; Eleonora M.; Laura M.; Pietro S.; Francesca O.; Sofia R.; Silvana A.; Alberto R.
Article.Abstract: Labor induction is a common procedure in obstetric practice, required to terminate pregnancy in several clinical conditions. Oral prostaglandins are frequently used, but require close monitoring of maternal-fetal well-being. Combination of oral castor oil administration plus membrane sweeping maneuver could represent an initial strategy, but its comparative effectiveness and resource implications require further evaluation. A prospective observational study was conducted on 169 term pregnant women indicated for labor induction: 100 received 60 mL oral castor oil plus membrane sweeping (combined strategy); 69 received oral misoprostol. Primary outcome was active labor onset within 24 h; other outcomes included maternal-fetal safety parameters, induction-to-delivery time and secondary medical interventions. Labor onset within 24 h was achieved in 54/100 patients (54.0%) of the combined strategy group versus 37/69 patients (53.6%) of the misoprostol group. The crude risk difference was + 0.38% points (95% CI − 14.51 to + 15.37), while the adjusted risk difference was − 2.59% points (95% bootstrap CI − 17.97 to + 14.31). Given a no difference detected in induction-to-delivery interval, the combined strategy was associated with a significantly less use of secondary medical interventions (oxytocin use, amniorexis, epidural analgesia). Overall, delivery mode and neonatal outcomes were comparable; the misoprostol group had a higher incidence of meconium-stained amniotic fluid (5,0% versus 13,0%), but the association was exploratory. Crossover to misoprostol was described as a treatment pathway and was not used to infer comparative efficacy. This prospective observational study did not detect a difference in the proportion of women entering active labor within 24 h between the two initial strategies; however, the study was not designed to establish equivalence or non-inferiority. Lower use of some intrapartum interventions was observed in the combined strategy group, but residual confounding cannot be excluded. Larger randomized studies should assess clinical outcomes, safety and costs.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Obstetrics and Gynecology > Maternal and Perinatal Health Interventions; Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Reproductive Health and Contraception; Medicine > Epidemiology > Preterm Birth and Chorioamnionitis

Article.Title: Antiglycation activity of nonvasodilatory beta blockers highlights acebutolol with reduced glycation markers and altered phosphoprotein expression
Article.Authors: Drygała S.; Karpienko K.; Drygalski K.; Żendzian-Piotrowska M.; Zalewska A.; Maciejczyk M.
Article.Abstract: Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) contribute to diabetic vascular injury through oxidative and pro-inflammatory signaling, but the anti-glycation potential of non-vasodilatory β-blockers (NVBBs) is unclear. To evaluate the anti-glycation activity of selected NVBBs (alprenolol, nadolol, penbutolol, sotalol, acebutolol, and bisoprolol) using in vitro and in silico models. Protein glycation was assessed in bovine serum albumin (BSA) models using six glycating agents. Acebutolol, selected from the comparative BSA screen, was docked against 21 glycation- and signaling-associated protein structures and evaluated in hyperglycemic human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) for glycation, oxidation, apoptosis-related, and PI3K/Akt/mTOR-associated phosphoprotein readouts. All NVBBs reduced multiple AGE subtypes in carbohydrate induced models. Acebutolol showed the broadest observed activity profile across the tested conditions, including reductions in argpyrimidine of 55.71%, pentosidine of 53.36%, and vesperlysine of 41.88%, and exceeded aminoguanidine for selected readouts. In HUVECs, 100 µg/mL acebutolol reduced selected glycation and oxidation-associated readouts, including total AGEs by 28.1%, advanced oxidation protein products by 40.5%, and NADPH oxidase activity by 23.2%. At 20–80 µg/mL, marked changes were observed in several measured phosphoproteins, including p-mTOR, p-S6RP, and p-BAD. Acebutolol showed a broad anti-glycation profile in the comparative BSA screen and altered selected glycation, oxidation, and signaling-associated readouts in hyperglycemic HUVECs. The molecular docking and cellular findings warrant confirmation in direct mechanistic studies.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Clinical Biochemistry > Advanced Glycation End Products research; Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Food Science > Potato Plant Research; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Protein Interaction Studies and Fluorescence Analysis

Article.Title: CAMELOT-IDS: a multi-scale transformer with empirical uncertainty diagnostics for IoT intrusion detection
Article.Authors: Qureshi A.; Bajwa I.; Sarwar N.; Hamdi M.; Samad A.
Article.Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) intrusion detection must address severe class imbalance, heterogeneous traffic, and potential distribution shift while providing interpretable information about predictive uncertainty. CAMELOT-IDS integrates semantic local-global Transformer encoding, hierarchical supervision, Label-Distribution-Aware Margin loss with deferred reweighting (LDAM-DRW), deterministic Mondrian Regularized Adaptive Prediction Sets (RAPS), and stream-oriented monitoring. On the reported CICIoT2023 analysis subset, the reference model achieved 99.20% fine-class accuracy, 76.76% fine-class macro-F1, and 99.79% malicious-class F1. At α = 0.10, the deterministic RAPS implementation produced 99.95% empirical coverage with a mean prediction-set size of 1.60. Because probability scaling and RAPS-threshold estimation reused the same labeled calibration pool, these set-valued results are interpreted as empirical diagnostics rather than as a formal split-conformal validity result. Batch throughput was 18,141.6 samples/s on an NVIDIA RTX 3060 and 1062.3 samples/s on the tested dual-Xeon platform. Fine-class performance remained highly uneven, with the Uploading Attack class yielding an F1 score of 4.96%. The stream-monitoring pathway produced no trigger during the held-out stream replay. These findings support further provenance-aware external validation, dependence-aware calibration, and controlled distribution-shift evaluation.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Computer Networks and Communications > Network Security and Intrusion Detection; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

Article.Title: Post-stroke cognitive impairment in an Alzheimer’s disease mouse model
Article.Authors: Gens R.; Testaferrata R.; Verhoye M.; Kooijman R.; Engelborghs S.; De Raedt S.; De Bundel D.
Article.Abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) is a major risk factor for dementia and may accelerate Alzheimer’s disease (AD) progression, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We investigated whether cortical IS influences AD-related pathology, including hippocampal gliosis, neurogenesis, and amyloid deposition, and whether it worsens cognitive decline in a preclinical AD model. Permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (pMCAO) was induced in 4-month-old wild-type (WT) and triple-transgenic AD (3xTg-AD) mice. Stroke severity and motor function were assessed one week post-surgery, followed by behavioral and histological analyses at the age of 5–6 months. pMCAO produced comparable infarct size and motor outcomes in WT and 3xTg-AD mice, with lesions restricted to the sensorimotor cortex and sparing the hippocampus. Histological analyses revealed reduced hippocampal neurogenesis and mildly increased astrogliosis in 3xTg-AD mice, whereas pMCAO did not significantly affect microgliosis, neurogenesis, or amyloid burden in either genotype. Behaviorally, 3xTg-AD mice showed impaired remote contextual fear memory, consistent with early AD-related deficits. In WT mice, pMCAO impaired contextual memory retrieval when conditioning occurred after stroke, but did not further worsen cognition in 3xTg-AD mice. At the time point examined, early cortical IS did not induce detectable additional AD-related pathology or cognitive impairment in 3xTg-AD mice. Cognitive impairments in 3xTg-AD mice coincided with reduced hippocampal neurogenesis.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: post-stroke cognitive impairment; Alzheimer's disease; mouse model; stroke; neurodegeneration
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Neurology > Neurological Disease Mechanisms and Treatments; Medicine > Psychiatry and Mental health > Dementia and Cognitive Impairment Research; Medicine > Physiology > Alzheimer's disease research and treatments

Article.Title: CSqL-m-H2LA-GRBiTM: categorical square loss-based multi-head hierarchical location attention enabled deep learning mechanism for smishing detection
Article.Authors: Shoaib M.
Article.Abstract: Smishing detection is an effective research area that remains essential in the recent decade. Detection of SMS phishing is decisive due to adversaries evolving in the network simultaneously. Several existing researches worked to perform accurate smishing detection but failed due to certain challenges. Shortage of large datasets, improper classification of legitimate and malicious messages, high computational resource utilization, and high false positive rates were the major challenges addressed in the conventional researches. Thus, the Categorical Square Loss-based multi-head Hierarchical Location Attention-enabled Gated Recurrent Unit with Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (CSqL-m-H2LA-GRBiTM) model is proposed in the research that presents robust smishing detection, leveraging the power of artificial intelligence (AI). The model captures information concerning spatial and temporal features, which elevates the efficiency in handling complex patterns in smishing detection. The proposed m-H2LA mechanism focuses on the relevant messages and their features to boost interpretability. Moreover, the deployment of a CSqL loss function enables robust detection by balancing maximum separation with probabilistic calibration and heavily penalizes misclassifications that cross the safety boundary. Overall, the CSqL-m-H2LA-GRBiTM model attains the accuracy, F1-score, and log-loss of 98.36%, 96.84%, and 5.09 with the SMS phishing dataset and 98.43%, 97.41%, and 5.23 with SMS Smishing Dataset at K-fold-10 respectively, which depicts high efficiency in comparison with the traditional methods.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Information Systems > Spam and Phishing Detection; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Hate Speech and Cyberbullying Detection; Social Sciences > Sociology and Political Science > Misinformation and Its Impacts

Article.Title: Satisfaction with social support as a mediating resource between trait emotional intelligence and self-care agency among healthcare professionals: a cross-sectional study in Spain
Article.Authors: Urtubia-Herrera V.; Navarta-Sánchez M.; Palmar-Santos A.; Collado-González B.; Luis E.; Sarrionandia A.; Fernández-Berrocal P.; Bermejo-Martins E.
Article.Abstract: Healthcare professionals are exposed to occupational stressors that threaten their well-being. Supporting healthcare professionals’ self-care is important in demanding clinical environments. Trait emotional intelligence (EI) and interpersonal resources may be relevant to self-care agency, but the pathways linking these factors remain insufficiently understood. This study examined the associations of trait EI with self-care agency, focusing on the potential mediating roles of dispositional mindfulness and satisfaction with social support. This cross-sectional study included healthcare professionals from four regions of Spain who completed an online survey. Regression analysis and structural equation modelling were used to examine five hypotheses concerning the direct, indirect, moderating and mediating associations among trait EI, dispositional mindfulness, satisfaction with social support, and self-care agency. In the parallel mediation model, trait EI was positively associated with self-care agency, and satisfaction with social support showed a significant indirect association between trait EI and self-care agency. The indirect association through dispositional mindfulness was not statistically significant. The direct association between trait EI and self-care agency remained significant after accounting for both mediators. No significant moderating effect of satisfaction with social support was found in the model. These findings highlight satisfaction with social support as a potentially relevant interpersonal resource in understanding self-care agency among healthcare professionals. However, the indirect association through social support was modest, and dispositional mindfulness did not show a significant mediating role in the parallel model. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the relationships between these resources and self-care agency and to determine their implications for supporting healthcare professionals’ well-being.
Article.TopicFields: Psychology > Social Psychology > Emotional Intelligence and Performance; Psychology > Social Psychology > Stress and Burnout Research; Health Professions > General Health Professions > Healthcare professionals’ stress and burnout

Article.Title: A hybrid bio-inspired optimization framework for modeling infant neurodevelopment from maternal mental health and biometric data
Article.Authors: Ramachandran R.; Muthusamy A.; Balaji C.; Gupta S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The primary identification and marking of infants at risk of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes constitutes a critical public-health challenge, especially in resource-limited environments. This work builds on a hybrid (mimicking the actions of both whales and fireflies) optimization model, Hybrid Whale–Firefly Optimization with Enhanced Extreme Gradient Boosting (HWFO-EXGBoost), and introduces a set of biometric and maternal mental-health determinants, along with longitudinal clinical predictors, to enhance and accelerate the prediction of 12-month developmental status. A multimodal maternal–fetal monitoring framework combining psychometric scores, characteristics of the mothers' blood chemistry and obstetric history, and physiological parameters and infant anthropometry connected with the mother-infant dyad is used to produce the dataset, which consists of 199 mother–infant dyads. Hybrid Whale-Firefly Optimization mechanism allows for better feature selection and model hyperparameters to get better discrimination and calibration. The metrics that are used to evaluative comparative development include 12 performance measures, such as MCC, AUROC, AUPRC, and calibration metrics as per two established benchmarks NBTV-ND 1 and ML-PND-SR 2 . HWFO-EXGBoost always achieves better performance with 94.47% accuracy, 96.34% specificity, AUROC of 0.953, 88.57% sensitivity and AUPRC of 0.742, and excellent calibration properties. The results illustrate how maternal mental health scores overlaid on biometric baselines in an optimised institutional learning system is a powerful decision-making tool for detecting early neurodevelopmental risk, allowing planning of interventions in maternal-child health care systems.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Pediatrics, Perinatology and Child Health > Infant Development and Preterm Care; Health Professions > Health Information Management > Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare; Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Maternal Mental Health During Pregnancy and Postpartum

Article.Title: Characterization and multi-response optimization of epoxy–castor oil composites reinforced with coconut shell and marsh barbel powders
Article.Authors: Balaji A.; Prabhu P.; Arunkumar A.; Purushothaman R.; Kumar P.; Maideen A.; Anand Raj M.; Gebreyohannes D.
Article.Abstract: The increasing demand for sustainable polymer composites has led to the use of agricultural waste and natural materials as alternative reinforcements. The present work deals with the characterization and multi response optimization of epoxy castor oil composites reinforced with coconut shell powder (CSP) and marsh barbel powder (MBP). Hand lay-up casting technique was used to prepare six formulations with different loadings of natural powder and with 20 wt% castor oil, cured at room temperature. The composites were evaluated for mechanical, tribological, electrical voltage, water absorption, chemical, morphological and soil-burial properties. Preliminary electrical voltage measurements, water absorption test and Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy were used to evaluate the composite properties. The electrical voltage of the unfilled epoxy–castor oil matrix (S1) was low, from 15 to 20 V. General performance of MBP reinforced composites was inferior to CSP reinforced composites. The optimum formulation, S6 with 60 wt% epoxy resin, 20 wt% castor oil and 20 wt% CSP had maximum tensile strength of 39.3 MPa, impact strength of 4.35 kJ/m 2 , hardness of 29.7 BHN and interlaminar shear strength of 39.8 MPa. Also, S6 exhibited minimum specific wear rate of 0.018 mm 3 /Nm, coefficient of friction of 0.55 and water absorption of 1.5%. The FTIR analysis revealed the presence of functional groups. SEM showed relatively uniform distribution of the filler and improved interfacial contact. Multi-response optimization showed that S6 is the best formulation, indicating the potential of coconut shell powder in the development of sustainable particulate polymer composites.
Article.TopicFields: Materials Science > Polymers and Plastics > Natural Fiber Reinforced Composites; Engineering > Mechanical Engineering > Polymer Science and Applications; Engineering > Mechanics of Materials > Tribology and Wear Analysis

Article.Title: Differential epithelial requirements for Escargot define Dpp-dependent and Dpp-independent pathways in Drosophila head appendage formation
Article.Authors: Rosales-Bravo F.; Sánchez-Díaz I.; Martínez-Méndez R.; Reynaud E.; Narváez-Padilla V.
Article.Abstract: The development of Drosophila head appendages requires precise coordination between distinct imaginal-disc primordia. While the transcription factor Escargot (Esg) is known to maintain epithelial integrity and progenitor identity in several imaginal tissues, its role in anterior head morphogenesis has remained unclear. Here we show that esg regulates the growth and patterning of the antennal and labial discs through layer- and tissue-specific mechanisms. Using RNAi knockdown driven by two independent esg -Gal4 lines and a peripodial-specific driver (c311-Gal4), we demonstrate that esg depletion causes severe malformations of head appendages, including antennal loss and absence of the distal proboscis. In the antennal disc, esg activity in the peripodial membrane is required for normal antennal-disc organization and to maintain compartmental organization, whereas in the labial disc, esg function within the disc-proper epithelium drives disc growth and normal adult proboscis formation. Moreover, decapentaplegic (dpp) knockdown phenocopies the esg -RNAi phenotype, and esg loss reduces dpp mRNA levels in labial discs, while ectopic dpp expression restores labial-disc size. Thus, esg acts upstream of Dpp signaling during proboscis development. These findings reveal a context-dependent mechanism by which a single transcription factor coordinates morphogenesis across epithelial layers, integrating esg -dependent transcriptional regulation with morphogen signaling.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Developmental Biology and Gene Regulation; Neuroscience > Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience > Neurobiology and Insect Physiology Research; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Cell Biology > Hippo pathway signaling and YAP/TAZ

Article.Title: Salivary and blood measurement of hs-cTnI and an adipokine panel in acute myocardial infarction: an exploratory paired-matrix study
Article.Authors: Gul H.; Sahin L.; Dolanbay T.; Karakayali M.; Sagin F.; Guraslan A.; Gul U.; Can I.; Ciftci H.; Ataozden T.; Yurtseven M.; Alagoz B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) requires rapid biochemical confirmation, and saliva offers a non-invasive alternative to venous sampling. We measured high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI), Apelin, Elabela, Endoglin, Irisin and ischaemia-modified albumin (IMA) in paired blood and saliva from 60 selected AMI patients presenting within six hours of symptom onset and 30 healthy controls. In blood, Irisin, Elabela and Apelin were lower in patients and Endoglin higher (all p ≤ 0.020). In saliva, Endoglin was higher and Irisin lower (both p < 0.001), and only these differences survived Bonferroni correction and age restriction ( p ≤ 0.030); IMA differed in neither matrix. Blood and salivary values correlated strongly (Spearman rs 0.773–0.979, all p < 0.001), but Bland–Altman analysis showed proportional differences and wide limits of agreement. Salivary hs-cTnI assay signals completely separated the two groups; because elevated serum hs-cTnI was an inclusion criterion and no salivary assay was matrix-validated, this reflects case selection rather than diagnostic accuracy. The adipokine panel did not demonstrate an improvement over hs-cTnI in an exploratory cross-validation analysis. These findings provide preliminary evidence that the six analytes generate measurable assay signals in saliva and support further investigation, including matrix-specific validation and prospective evaluation in undifferentiated chest pain.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Cardiology and Cardiovascular Medicine > Acute Myocardial Infarction Research; Medicine > Physiology > Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control; Medicine > Cardiology and Cardiovascular Medicine > Cardiac Fibrosis and Remodeling

Article.Title: Multi-omic cancer subtype clustering with random-walk-refined cross-view contrastive learning
Article.Authors: Zhang L.; Li Z.; Mallory X.
Article.Abstract: Cancer heterogeneity complicates precision oncology, and robust multi-omic subtyping remains challenging. Existing contrastive integration methods often force heterogeneous omics into a single shared latent space and treat all non-matching samples as negatives, which can suppress modality-specific structure and separate biologically similar patients. We present Subtype-DIVIDE, a self-supervised multi-view contrastive framework for integrative cancer subtyping. The model encodes each omic modality separately and performs target-conditioned cross-view alignment, using the target modality’s affinity structure to guide inter-view consistency. To reduce false negatives, Subtype-DIVIDE further refines contrastive supervision with per-omic random-walk soft-positive masks constructed from modality-specific affinity graphs. Across nine TCGA cohorts spanning copy number, DNA methylation, mRNA, and miRNA data, Subtype-DIVIDE achieved statistically significant survival separation in all datasets and the highest mean number of clinically enriched variables among the compared methods. Cox models, leave-one-cluster-out analyses, and technical covariate tests supported the clinical relevance and robustness of the inferred subtypes. Ablation studies showed that cross-view alignment is essential, while diffusion-based soft positives improved robustness. A KIRC case study identified coherent subtype programs involving metabolism, vascular and inflammatory signaling, extracellular-matrix remodeling, and epithelial transport. External validation on two independent cohorts, performed without hyperparameter retuning, supported the generalizability of the inferred subtypes. In 222 CPTAC-3 clear-cell renal carcinoma cases, the subtypes were significantly associated with pathologic stage and T category across all training repeats and recapitulated the KIRC subtype programs. In 1,980 METABRIC breast tumors, they consistently showed significant survival separation and enrichment for age, nodal status, and stage across all repeats.
Article.TopicFields: Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Bioinformatics and Genomic Networks; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Molecular Biology > Gene expression and cancer classification; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Cancer Research > Cancer Genomics and Diagnostics

Article.Title: A predictive modeling approach for determining optimal PPF content in concrete under specific mixture parameters using ANN and RSM
Article.Authors: Mousavinia S.; Dastan Diznab M.
Article.Abstract: The incorporatison of polypropylene fibers (PPF) enhances concrete’s flexural performance but often reduces workability, creating a critical trade-off in mix design. This study employs ANN and RSM to predict FSV and SV, comparatively evaluate the two modeling approaches, and determine the optimal PPF content by balancing flexural strength enhancement and workability retention. During cross-validation, the ANN models achieved R 2 of 0.887 for FSV and 0.842 for SV, compared to 0.720 and 0.773 for RSM, respectively; the final models fitted to the complete dataset achieved R 2 of 0.935 and 0.852 (ANN) and 0.885 and 0.896 (RSM). A multi-objective optimization approach identifies PPF contents that balance strength improvement with minimal workability loss, providing practical guidance for the design of fiber-reinforced concretes in construction applications.
Article.TopicFields: Engineering > Civil and Structural Engineering > Innovative concrete reinforcement materials; Engineering > Building and Construction > Structural Behavior of Reinforced Concrete; Engineering > Civil and Structural Engineering > Concrete and Cement Materials Research

Article.Title: Sexual dimorphism and sex estimation in the cuneiform bones from a Chilean modern osteological series
Article.Authors: Álvarez I.; Arroyo E.; Retamal R.; Saldías E.
Article.Abstract: In challenging forensic contexts, reconstructing the biological profile with insufficient evidence remains a significant endeavor to achieve human identification. In contemporary osteological series, foot bones are often protected by footwear that may preserve their integrity, providing an alternative for sexual dimorphism studies. Despite the interest in the largest tarsal bones, the midtarsal bones are seldom the focus. This study evaluates the three cuneiform bones from 167 adult individuals (100 males, 67 females) from the Colección Osteológica Subactual de Santiago de Chile using linear measurements. Sex estimation was performed using binary logistic regression models for each bone separately and combined. Results indicated that males display larger dimensions than females, but with lower classification by overlap of small samples. The medial cuneiform achieved the highest accuracy (80%) utilizing two variables, followed by the lateral cuneiform (72.5%), and the intermediate cuneiform with 60%. The pronounced dimensions of the medial cuneiform, whose sexual differences are better expressed in size, could explain the difference in the correct classification between these bones. This research highlights local biological variability through a low-cost, replicable approach, providing population-specific data essential for contemporary forensic investigations when classic tools are unavailable.
Article.TopicFields: Arts and Humanities > Archeology > Forensic Anthropology and Bioarchaeology Studies; Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology > Genetics > Forensic and Genetic Research; Social Sciences > Anthropology > Pleistocene-Era Hominins and Archaeology

Article.Title: Screening Aegilops tauschii accessions for salinity tolerance at the seedling stage using multi-trait-based indices
Article.Authors: Moradkhani H.; Jadidi O.; Jamshidi B.; Mehrabi A.; Türkoğlu A.; Bocianowski J.; Pour-Aboughadareh A.; Etminan A.
Article.Abstract: Genetic diversity provides a critical foundation for the development of stress-resilient crops. Aegilops tauschii , the diploid progenitor and D‑genome donor of bread wheat ( Triticum aestivum L.), is an important source of genetic variation for wheat improvement, including the enhancement of salinity tolerance. Despite its breeding potential, the physiological basis of salinity adaptation in Ae. tauschii and the extent to which these responses vary among geographically distinct populations remain insufficiently resolved. In this study, geographically diverse Ae. tauschii accessions collected from Iran, Turkey, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Afghanistan were evaluated under control conditions without NaCl and under salinity stress imposed with 200 mM NaCl. Plant growth, ion accumulation, photosynthetic performance, and a range of physiological traits associated with stress responses were characterized. The salinity treatment significantly affected multiple traits, resulting in reductions in shoot and root dry weight, shoot K⁺ concentration, root and shoot K⁺/Na⁺ ratios, relative chlorophyll content, membrane stability index, stomatal conductance, net photosynthetic rate, maximum quantum efficiency of photosystem II, and maximum photochemical performance. Conversely, the salinity treatment increased root Na⁺ and K⁺ accumulation and initial fluorescence compared with the respective control conditions. To identify genotypes exhibiting superior and balanced performance across multiple traits, multi-trait selection was performed using the multi-trait genotype–ideotype distance index (MGIDI) and the factor analysis and ideotype-design approach based on best linear unbiased prediction (FAI-BLUP). Iranian and Turkish accessions generally had the best performance under salinity, as observed by better biomass retention, preservation of photosynthetic activity, and maintenance of membrane stability. In contrast, several Afghan accessions exhibited comparatively favorable photochemical responses. The combined analysis indicated clear geographic differentiation in the physiological responses of Ae. tauschii to salinity stress and demonstrated that superior salinity tolerance was associated with the coordinated maintenance of several physiological processes rather than a single trait response. Seven Iranian accessions (26, 37, 38, 39, 40, 42, and 44) were consistently identified as the highest-performing genotypes across the analytical approaches. These accessions constitute promising sources of salinity-adaptive variation for wheat pre-breeding and may serve as priority donors for the targeted introgression of potentially beneficial D-genome alleles into cultivated wheat. The breeding value of these accessions should be further assessed through field-based evaluation and genomic characterization before their deployment in wheat improvement programmes.
Article.TopicFields: Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Plant Stress Responses and Tolerance; Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Genetics and Plant Breeding; Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Wheat and Barley Genetics and Pathology

Article.Title: Prior institutional contact and hospitalization risk after telemedicine visits for acute respiratory infections
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Miyawaki A.; Iwagami M.; Komiyama J.; Miyata J.; Tamiya N.
Article.Abstract: The rapid expansion of telemedicine during the COVID-19 pandemic increased telemedicine consultations without prior contact to the same medical institution, raising concerns about continuity of care. This study examined whether prior institutional contact was associated with hospitalization after telemedicine visits for acute respiratory infections. Using a nationwide claims database in Japan, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of 189,377 initial telemedicine visits between April 2020 and April 2024. Prior institutional contact was defined as at least one visit to the same institution in the preceding 12 months. The primary outcome was all-cause hospitalization within 14 days. Overall, 24.7% of visits involved prior institutional contact; hospitalization occurred in 0.4% of these visits and 0.9% of visits without prior contacts. Prior institutional contact was associated with a lower hospitalization risk (adjusted risk ratio, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.58–0.87). These findings suggest the potential importance of prior institutional contact when selecting a provider for initial telemedicine consultations for acute respiratory infections.
Article.TopicFields: Medicine > Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health > Telemedicine and Telehealth Implementation; Health Professions > General Health Professions > Primary Care and Health Outcomes; Business, Management and Accounting > Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management > Healthcare Systems and Technology

Article.Title: Visual tagging frequency influences SSVEP and early ERP responses during detection and working memory
Article.Authors: Yang J.; Carter O.; Shivdasani M.; Grayden D.; Hester R.; Barutchu A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) are widely used to track selective attention by tagging different visual objects at distinct flicker frequencies. However, whether the choice of tagging frequency itself influences neural and cognitive measures beyond the SSVEP response remains unclear. Here, 27 participants performed detection and 1-back working memory tasks while a central target and peripheral distractors flickered at either 8.6–12 Hz, with the location of each frequency counterbalanced across participants. The working memory task produced slower responses, more errors, and greater perceived difficulty than detection. Tagging frequency strongly influenced neural responses, with 8.6 Hz eliciting higher SSVEP signal-to-noise ratios than 12 Hz regardless of stimulus location. Nevertheless, stronger SSVEP responses for centrally attended stimuli were associated with fewer working memory errors, while SSVEPs for attended and distractor stimuli were negatively correlated. In addition, the working memory task produced a larger P1-N1 peak-to-peak difference, and tagging frequency modulated the amplitude of early ERP responses. Together, these findings indicate that tagging frequency can influence SSVEP and early ERP measures and should be treated as an active design factor in frequency-tagging studies.
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > EEG and Brain-Computer Interfaces; Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Neural dynamics and brain function; Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Neural and Behavioral Psychology Studies

Article.Title: Modeling the relationships between intolerance of uncertainty, autistic symptoms, and anxiety in autistic and non-autistic adults
Article.Authors: Sapey-Triomphe L.; Melis K.; Lemmens L.; Wagemans J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Autistic adults often report difficulties dealing with uncertain situations, potentially due to atypical predictive mechanisms. In this context, they show heightened intolerance of uncertainty (IU), defined as a tendency to perceive uncertainty as distressing. This study examined how intolerance of uncertainty relates to autistic traits and symptoms, anxiety, and sleep quality, and compared two models of these relationships. A total of 384 adults, including 68 autistic individuals, completed seven questionnaires assessing IU, autistic traits, social and non-social autistic symptoms, anxiety and sleep quality. Correlation matrices were computed across and within diagnostic groups. Structural equation modeling compared a Neurodevelopmental Model , which posits directional paths from autistic traits to core symptoms and IU, with an Evolutionary Stress Model , which posits an alternative ordering of these constructs. Logistic regression analyses evaluated whether combinations of questionnaire scores could distinguish autistic from non-autistic participants. Autistic adults reported higher IU, anxiety, and sleep difficulties, alongside elevated autistic traits and symptoms. All questionnaire measures were positively correlated, with particularly strong associations between IU and autistic traits, social difficulties and repetitive behaviors, and anxiety. Structural equation modeling supported the Neurodevelopmental model , in which autistic traits preceded core autistic symptoms and IU, which were in turn specified as predicting anxiety and sleep difficulties. These relationships varied by group and gender. Finally, combining measures of autistic traits, IU, and anxiety yielded high classification specificity. These findings, discussed within the predictive coding framework, highlight the central role of IU in autism, as well as the contribution of anxiety and sleep issues. They underscore the need to develop strategies and programs to alleviate these difficulties.
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Autism Spectrum Disorder Research; Psychology > Experimental and Cognitive Psychology > Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes; Medicine > Psychiatry and Mental health > Child Nutrition and Feeding Issues

Article.Title: Economic growth targets, energy consumption constraints, and transboundary PM2.5 pollution: empirical evidence from China
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Ge T.
