Article.Title: Single-housed, but not pair-housed, male and female rats demonstrate social conditioned place preference
Article.Authors: Bensing P.; Bowers C.; Moosa I.; Leong K.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the factors that modulate social reward has important implications for conditions characterized by social dysfunction, including autism spectrum disorder and social anxiety disorder. Social isolation is particularly relevant, given rising rates of subjective loneliness and social disconnection in the United States. The present study investigated the impacts of isolation on social reward by testing the effects of single- versus pair-housing on social conditioned place preference (sCPP) in adult male and female Sprague-Dawley rats. Across a ten-day paradigm with eight conditioning days, rats were trained in a two-chamber apparatus in which one chamber was repeatedly paired with a same-sex, weight-matched littermate, while the other chamber served as an unpaired control. Pair-housed rats were co-housed with their conditioning partner for the duration of the study. Single-housed, but not pair-housed, rats of both sexes developed a significant preference for the social-paired chamber. These findings indicate that housing condition modulated sCPP expression in adult male and female rats.

Article.Title: Prior trauma shapes the effects of psilocybin on stress sensitization in mice
Article.Authors: Ottofaro S.; Maltman J.; González-Maeso J.
Article.Abstract: Exposure to traumatic events induces persistent alterations in defensive behavior that extend beyond associative fear memories, including heightened responses to novel stimuli (stress sensitivity) and sustained defensive states in neutral contexts (stress sensitization). While serotonergic psychedelics such as psilocybin have been shown to facilitate fear extinction in associative paradigms, their effects on trauma-induced non-associative stress adaptations remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a behavioral paradigm in mice that dissociates contextual fear recall from stress sensitivity and stress sensitization within the same subjects. Male C57BL/6J mice were exposed to an acute foot-shock stressor, followed by assessment of trauma recall, administration of psilocybin (1 mg/kg) or vehicle, and subsequent evaluation of responses to a novel auditory stimulus and context. Trauma-exposed mice displayed robust associative fear and increased freezing in response to a novel auditory stimulus, consistent with enhanced stress sensitivity. However, psilocybin did not significantly alter this stimulus-evoked response. In contrast, psilocybin produced bidirectional, experience-dependent effects on stress sensitization - it reduced baseline freezing in non-traumatized mice but increased freezing in trauma-exposed animals when re-exposed to a novel context in the absence of a stimulus. Together, these findings demonstrate that psilocybin does not uniformly attenuate trauma-related behaviors, but instead modulates non-associative defensive responses in a manner dependent on prior experience. This work highlights the importance of distinguishing between associative and non-associative components of fear and suggests that psychedelic-induced plasticity may amplify latent trauma-related states under certain conditions.

Article.Title: Left DLPFC activation in the association between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Wu Y.; Yang M.; Xi M.; Si S.; Zhang W.
Article.Abstract: The prevalence of depressive symptoms among college students continues to rise. It has been shown that individuals with higher psychological resilience generally exhibit fewer depressive symptoms. The aim of this study is to examine potential associations between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students and to explore the statistical mediating role of brain activation in this relationship. 140 college students received functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) scans while completing a verbal fluency task (VFT). Psychological scales, oxyhemoglobin (HbO) concentration, partial correlation and mediation analyses were processed. Partial correlation analysis showed that psychological resilience was significantly negatively associated with depressive symptoms. The activation of HbO in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC; CH23), right DLPFC (CH3), and right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; CH6) were significantly positively correlated with psychological resilience and negatively correlated with depressive symptoms. Further mediation analyses demonstrated a significant indirect association between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms through activation in the left DLPFC (CH23). The findings suggest that the left DLPFC may be involved in the relationship between psychological resilience and depressive symptoms in college students. Future longitudinal or intervention studies are needed to further clarify the causal relationships among these variables.

Article.Title: Efficacy of chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine on seizures induced by pentylenetetrazole kindling
Article.Authors: Roudini F.; Kohsari I.; Derakhshan M.; Nazemi S.; Azhdari-Zarmehri H.; Mohammad-Zadeh M.
Article.Abstract: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced kindling is an established model for investigating seizure mechanisms and evaluating the efficacy of antiepileptic drugs. Novel drug delivery systems, such as nanoparticles, offer improved therapeutic outcomes by enhancing brain bioavailability and reducing adverse effects. This study investigated the effects of chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine nanoparticles on seizure activity in PTZ-kindled mice compared with the free form of the drug. Male BALB/c mice were divided into three groups: PTZ-kindled control, PTZ + free carbamazepine, and PTZ + chitosan-encapsulated carbamazepine. Seizure stage, Stage latencies 1 and 4, seizure duration, and mortality were assessed using a modified Racine scale. The results showed that while free carbamazepine temporarily reduced seizure stage, its effect diminished over time. In contrast, the chitosan-encapsulated formulation significantly reduced seizure stage, seizure duration, prolonged latencies, and completely prevented seizure-induced mortality. Characterization of the optimized nanoparticles revealed a mean particle size of 65 nm, a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.21, a zeta potential of -34.5 mV, and an entrapment efficiency of 55.35 %, indicating favorable stability and delivery properties. Overall, this study demonstrates that chitosan‑based nanoencapsulation of carbamazepine enhances its antiepileptic efficacy in a PTZ‑kindling model, suggesting its promise as a potential therapeutic strategy for epilepsy.

Article.Title: Varlitinib attenuates neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neurodegeneration in experimental Parkinsonism
Article.Authors: Lim H.; Park J.; Lee W.; Park G.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation mediated by microglial activation plays a critical role in Parkinson's disease (PD), with the NLRP3 inflammasome contributing to dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Varlitinib, a clinically developed pan-human epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor, has been investigated as an anticancer agent; however, its therapeutic potential in PD remains unknown. Here, we evaluated the neuroprotective effects of varlitinib in in vitro and in vivo PD models. BV2 microglial cells were stimulated with α-synuclein and 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium and treated with varlitinib. Varlitinib significantly improved cell viability, reduced lactate dehydrogenase release, and suppressed IL-1β and IL-18 production. Co-treatment with the selective NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 produced no additional anti-inflammatory effects, suggesting that NLRP3 inflammasome signaling contributes, at least in part, to varlitinib's actions. In a 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine-induced mouse model of PD, varlitinib significantly improved motor performance, reduced microglial activation in the substantia nigra and striatum, and preserved tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons. Collectively, these findings support varlitinib as a potential drug-repurposing candidate for PD.

Article.Title: Analysis of the participation and influence of the cerebellum in emotion and emotional memory processing in mice through c-Fos expression
Article.Authors: Prati J.; de Russo T.; Lepesteur Gianlorenço A.
Article.Abstract: The cerebellum's involvement in non-motor functions, such as emotional and cognitive processes, has been gaining attention. The functional topography of the cerebellum remains inconclusive, and both clinical and preclinical studies have aimed to identify it to achieve a better understanding of cerebellar neurophysiology and its influence on other brain structures in different functions. The aim of this study was to analyze activation in cerebellar lobules IV-V, VI and VII under different context and temporal conditions of an inhibitory avoidance (IA) task, and to assess the association between c-Fos expression in these lobules and in other brain regions involved in emotional and memory processing. Thirty-three naïve Swiss Albino mice were exposed to the IA box for 1, 4, and 8 days. After the final exposure of each group to the evaluation apparatus, euthanasia was performed, followed by transcardiac perfusion and brain removal. Immunofluorescence analysis of c-Fos in pre-established structures was performed. Significant c-Fos/DAPI ratio was observed in cerebellar lobules IV-V and VI in animals that performed IA task for 4 days. No significant difference in c-Fos expression was found in the other regions of interest. Spearman's Correlation Coefficient test did not indicate any associations between the c-Fos/DAPI ratios across the regions of interest. These results suggest that cerebellar lobules IV-V and VI may be differentially recruited during the IA task, although their specific involvement in emotional and emotional memory processing remains to be determined.

Article.Title: Anillin functions in distinct glial subtypes to support larval locomotion in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Huynh M.; Dang T.; Thao Dang T.; Yoshida H.
Article.Abstract: Anillin (Ani)/Scraps has a well-characterized function in cytokinesis and has recently been shown to play a role in the nervous system. Ani is expressed in neuroblasts, axons, and neuromuscular junctions in the Drosophila larval nervous system, and pan-neuronal ani knockdown impairs both larval and adult behaviors. However, despite the expression of ani in glial cells, its function in these cells remains unclear. In the present study, we therefore investigated the role of ani in Drosophila glial cells by performing pan-glial ani knockdown and assessing the subsequent effects on larval and adult behaviors. Ani was expressed in a subset of glial cells, including in the central and peripheral nervous systems, and expression levels varied across individual cells. Pan-glial knockdown of ani significantly impaired larval and adult locomotion, larval learning ability, and adult activity; however, it did not affect lifespan. Although ani depletion decreased the number of glial cells in the central nervous system, it did not disrupt neuropil formation. In the peripheral nervous system, ani knockdown increased the total length of neuromuscular junctions. Subtype-specific knockdown analyses suggested that Ani functions in endoreplicating subperineurial and wrapping glia to support larval locomotion. The results also suggested a possible role for Ani in astrocyte-like and ensheathing glia, although the evidence is inconclusive. In contrast, Ani did not appear to have an obvious role in cortex glia or actively proliferating perineurial glia for larval locomotion. Together, these findings indicate that ani exerts both canonical and non-canonical roles in Drosophila glial cells.

Article.Title: Increased CCR2-immunopositive myeloid cells in the putamen and cerebellar white matter with blood–brain barrier disruption in multiple system atrophy
Article.Authors: Okada N.; Togawa N.; Ishimoto T.; Ayaki T.; Maki T.; Matsumoto R.
Article.Abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, and autonomic dysfunction. Recently, a close relationship of neuroinflammation to MSA pathogenesis was identified. Studies in mouse models of MSA have indicated that peripheral-type myeloid cells and endogenous microglia promote neuroinflammation in MSA. However, their distinct roles in MSA pathogenesis remain unknown. We performed immunohistochemical analyses of brain tissues obtained at autopsy from patients with MSA and age-matched controls to examine the putamen and cerebellar white matter with antibodies against CCR2 (a chemokine receptor expressed by monocyte-lineage cells), TMEM119 for microglia, and fibrinogen for blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage. The CCR2-immunopositive area was significantly increased in both regions in MSA patients compared to controls (putamen, p = 0.0043; cerebellar white matter, p = 0.0438); however, the TMEM119-immunopositive area showed no significant between-group difference (putamen, p = 0.4220; cerebellar white matter, p = 0.8152). The densities of CCR2-immunopositive areas in the putamen and cerebellar white matter were positively correlated (Pearson's r = 0.7325, p = 0.0248). In the putamen, fibrinogen immunoreactivity and perivascular leakage were increased and showed a distribution similar to that of CCR2 immunostaining (p = 0.0398). These findings suggest that CCR2-immunopositive myeloid cell accumulation in regions with BBB dysfunction may involve recruitment of peripheral monocyte-lineage cells.

Article.Title: Neural mobilization combined with a polylactic acid conduit enhances functional and morphological recovery following median nerve repair
Article.Authors: Cardoso F.; Pestana F.; Taboada T.; Silva B.; Campos N.; Souza D.; Oliveira J.; Abreu C.; Mendonça H.; Almeida F.; Blanco Martinez A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Peripheral nerve transection repaired with a poly(lactic acid) (PLA) conduit remains associated with incomplete functional recovery. Neural mobilization (NM) may enhance nerve regeneration, but its optimal timing and effects remain unclear. This study investigated how NM timing affects nerve regeneration and functional recovery after median nerve transection and PLA conduit repair. Methods: Nineteen young adult female Wistar rats underwent median nerve transection and repair using a 10-mm PLA conduit to bridge an 8-mm gap. Animals were assigned to control (no mobilization) or NM groups initiated 1, 5, or 30 days after surgery. Mobilization consisted of scapular depression and forelimb movements for 10 min, three times weekly. Recovery was assessed using von Frey and grip strength tests, electrophysiological, histological, morphometric, and muscle analyses 8 weeks after surgery. Results: NM effects were time-dependent, with mobilization initiated 5 days after surgery producing the most favorable functional and electrophysiological outcomes. This timing improved grip strength, mechanical sensitivity, and CMAP amplitude without affecting latency. NM also enhanced axonal regeneration and increased the proportion of myelinated fibers, but did not significantly affect angiogenesis, myelin thickness, or muscle atrophy. Conclusions: Initiating NM 5 days after nerve repair may represent a favorable therapeutic window following severe peripheral nerve injury. NM at this time point improved functional, electrophysiological, and structural outcomes, although it did not significantly affect muscle atrophy or myelin thickness. These findings support NM as a time-dependent therapeutic approach and provide a basis for further investigation of its translational potential future clinical studies and applications.

Article.Title: Selective vulnerability of the spinal cord in a rat model of asphyxia-induced cardiac arrest
Article.Authors: Lee S.; Shin H.; Kim R.; Lee J.; Sabuj M.; Kim I.; Ahn D.; Tae H.; Kim S.; Yoon J.; Lee J.; Park B.
Article.Abstract: Spinal cord injury after cardiac arrest (CA) can cause devastating neurological deficits, including paraplegia. Although lumbar spinal cord injury is clinically important, regional comparisons remain limited. In this study, we examined region-associated vulnerability of the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord using a rat model of asphyxial CA (ACA). Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent sham surgery or ACA, and thoracic and lumbar spinal cord tissues were collected 24 h after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) from ACA survivors with hindlimb paralysis. Histopathological analysis demonstrated significantly fewer surviving neurons in the lumbar compared with the thoracic spinal cord after ACA. The lumbar spinal cord also showed higher BAX/BCL2 ratios and cleaved caspase-3 expression, together with increased phosphorylation of NF-κB and mitogen-activated protein kinases, including p38, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK). Exploratory transcriptomic comparison between ACA-L and ACA-T identified 292 upregulated and 187 downregulated DEGs. Enrichment analyses indicated that upregulated DEGs were associated with extracellular matrix-receptor interaction, focal adhesion, integrin signaling, and PI3K-Akt signaling, whereas downregulated DEGs were associated with nervous system development and myelination. Collectively, these findings demonstrate region-dependent molecular and histopathological alterations at 24 h after ROSC, with a more pronounced injury-associated inflammatory and apoptosis-related profile in the lumbar spinal cord of paralyzed ACA survivors.

Article.Title: Serum CitH3 and PTX3 levels for early prediction of acute respiratory distress syndrome following severe traumatic brain injury
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Lang M.; Zhen C.; Liu B.; Pang Z.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: Objective: To evaluate the predictive value of serum citrullinated histone H3 (CitH3) and pentraxin 3 (PTX3) for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) after severe traumatic brain injury (sTBI). Methods: This prospective observational study enrolled 395 consecutive sTBI patients admitted between April 2025 and February 2026. Patients were categorized into ARDS (n = 111) and non-ARDS (n = 284) groups. Serum CitH3 and PTX3 were measured by ELISA. Candidate predictors were selected by LASSO regression. Spearman correlation, multivariable logistic regression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed. The DeLong test, category-free net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) assessed incremental predictive value over the conventional model. Results: Serum CitH3 and PTX3 were significantly higher in the ARDS group (both p < 0.001) and were positively correlated with each other but negatively with oxygenation indices and albumin. Multivariable analysis identified pulmonary contusion, shock, fluid balance within 12 h of admission, APACHE II and SOFA scores, and elevated CitH3 and PTX3 as independent risk factors (all p < 0.05), whereas a higher GCS score and elevated albumin were protective. Their combination yielded an AUC of 0.841, superior to either alone. When added to the conventional model, biomarkers increased the AUC from 0.926 to 0.943 (p = 0.025), with category-free NRI of 0.554 (95% CI: 0.320-0.778, p < 0.001) and IDI of 0.072 (95% CI: 0.040-0.105, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Combined serum CitH3 and PTX3 demonstrate early predictive potential for ARDS after sTBI but require external validation.

Article.Title: Myrtenol mitigates seizure activity and oxidative imbalance in a mouse model of PTZ-induced seizure
Article.Authors: Rasouli F.; Hojjat S.; Shakeri F.
Article.Abstract: Aim: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced seizures are strongly associated with oxidative imbalance, and the monoterpenoid alcohol myrtenol has been proposed to exert antioxidant and neuroprotective effects. This study investigated whether myrtenol attenuates PTZ-evoked seizure activity and oxidative disturbances in the mouse hippocampus and cerebral cortex. Methods: Sixty male mice were assigned to six groups: control, PTZ-only, three myrtenol pretreatment doses (25, 50, 100 mg/kg), and diazepam. Seizure susceptibility was evaluated by measuring latencies to minimal clonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures following PTZ administration. Oxidative stress markers, including malondialdehyde (MDA), nitric oxide (NO), superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and total thiol content, were quantified in brain homogenates. Results: PTZ reliably induced seizures and oxidative alterations. Myrtenol pretreatment increased seizure latencies in a dose-dependent manner, although diazepam produced the greatest protection. Myrtenol, particularly at 100 mg/kg, reduced PTZ-induced elevations in MDA and NO, restored SOD and CAT activities, and improved thiol levels, with effects approaching those of diazepam. Lower myrtenol doses produced partial or nonsignificant biochemical improvements. Conclusion: These findings indicate that myrtenol mitigates PTZ-induced seizure expression and oxidative stress, with the highest dose demonstrating the most consistent neuroprotective profile.

Article.Title: Trans-vatabnet: transcriptomic signatures for Parkinson’s disease detection using deep learning
Article.Authors: Vishwakarma P.; Vishwakarma P.; Avanti S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Early detection of Parkinson's disease (PD) is essential for timely clinical intervention. However, transcriptomic-based diagnosis faces challenges associated with high-dimensional gene expression data, redundant features, class imbalance, and limited interpretability. Objective: This study proposes TransVaTabNet, an integrated framework for PD detection and biomarker identification using transcriptomic analysis, deep learning, and explainable artificial intelligence. Methods: RNA-seq data were preprocessed using low-expression gene filtering, Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) normalization, and voom transformation. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using limma-voom, followed by stage-specific gene analysis and functional enrichment to investigate disease-associated pathways. A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) generated compact latent representations, while the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) addressed class imbalance. TabNet classified the derived features using sequential attention, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) supported model interpretation and potential biomarker identification. Results: Evaluation on the GSE216281 RNA-seq dataset achieved an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) of 90.95%, outperforming the classical machine learning models evaluated in this study.Conclusion: TransVaTabNet combines dimensionality reduction, attention-based classification, and explainability to support PD detection and potential biomarker discovery. The framework offers an interpretable approach to identifying disease-associated transcriptomic patterns and may support future precision diagnostic research.

Article.Title: Benchmarking 3D U-Net variants for volumetric segmentation of the substantia nigra and brain ageing related analysis using 7T MRI
Article.Authors: Haridhas A.; Alfred L.
Article.Abstract: Unlabelled: Objective: Accurate segmentation of the substantia nigra (SN) is essential for assessing its structural integrity and volumetric changes in Parkinson's disease and brain aging. However, it remains challenging due to SN's small size, deep location, and low contrast on conventional MRI. This study benchmarked six U-Net variants baseline 3D U-Net, ResU-Net, SE-U-Net, Attention U-Net, U-Net++, and U-Net 3+ for SN segmentation using ultra-high-field 7 T MRI. Methods: T1-weighted MP2RAGE images from the ATAG dataset (53 healthy subjects: 31 train, 7 validation and 15 test). Six architectures were evaluated: 3D U-Net, ResU-Net, SE-U-Net, Attention U-Net, U-Net++, and U-Net 3+.Performance was evalauted with Dice score, IoU, 95% HD95, ASSD, and also age-stratified analysis was considered for analysing the robustness of model across young, middle-aged, and elderly cohorts. Results: While ResU-Net achieved the highest overlap metrics (Dice = 0.763, IoU = 0.618), where the baseline 3D U-Net outperformed all variants in boundary accuracy (HD95 = 13.85 mm, ASSD = 20.15 mm). The U-Net 3+ and SE-U-Net complex models relatively underperformed, indicated that architectural complexity does not enhance the segmentation performance of small subcortical structures. Descriptive Age-stratified analysis shows, ResU-Net maintained consistent performance across different age groups and 3D U-Net revealed strong age-invariance, however no statistically significant age-group differences were exhibited. Conclusions: This study findings demonstrates architecture selection influences overlap, boundary detection and volume estimation small-structure segmentation and highlights the importance of evaluating model robustness to demographic variability. The findings offer a methodological benchmark for developing reliable SN volumetry tools for neurodegenerative research.

Article.Title: Multimodal based Brain Tumor Classification using Clustered Federated Learning in Edge based IoT Network
Article.Authors: C R.; B M.
Article.Abstract: A brain tumor is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells that causes a severe impact on the quality of life. Nowadays, various methods based on multimodal medical images are used to identify brain tumors. Meanwhile, these methods require extensive amounts of labeled information to identify disease tissues and often encounter various challenges based on privacy and accuracy. This paper establishes a Taylor-based Focal Log-cosh Entropy Network (TFLE-Net) to classify brain tumors from demographic data and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) images by utilizing clustered federated learning in an edge-based Internet of Things (IoT) network. The detection process is executed in clustered federated learning concerning two entities: server and nodes. In a local training model, an input MRI scan is pre-processed, further brain tumor areas are segmented, and then, the mining of various features is performed. Simultaneously, the normalization of input demographic data is done, and the suitable features are selected using information gain. Further, the extracted features and chosen features are subjected to TFLE-Net to classify brain tumors. Additionally, the TFLE-Net yielded Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.057, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.047, True Positive Rate (TPR) of 97.789%, and accuracy of 96.987%.

Article.Title: Medial temporal atrophy and posterior cingulate structural covariance in mild cognitive impairment
Article.Authors: Yang X.; Lyu J.; Wang J.; Quan Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is associated with structural abnormalities in regions vulnerable to Alzheimer's disease, but the relative contributions of medial temporal, posterior midline, and association cortices remain unclear. We compared regional gray matter volumes between individuals with MCI and cognitively normal (CN) participants and examined their associations with clinical measures, structural covariance, and apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOE ε4) status. Methods: We analyzed 264 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Gray matter volumes were extracted from seven predefined regions of interest. Group differences and clinical associations were assessed using multivariable regression models adjusted for age, sex, education, and total intracranial volume. Structural covariance analyses examined interregional relationships. Exploratory analyses evaluated ROI-by-APOE ε4 interactions, and sensitivity analyses assessed robustness. Results: Individuals with MCI had smaller hippocampal volumes than CN participants, whereas parahippocampal reductions were less consistent. Smaller hippocampal volume was consistently associated with greater cognitive impairment and poorer functional performance; associations involving the parahippocampal gyrus weakened after adjustment for hippocampal volume. The posterior cingulate cortex showed limited evidence of local volumetric differences but more prominent alterations in structural covariance with medial temporal and temporal association regions. Exploratory APOE ε4 interactions were nominally suggestive but did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Main findings were generally robust across sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: Hippocampal volume showed the most consistent local volumetric and clinical associations in MCI, whereas posterior cingulate abnormalities were more evident in structural covariance patterns. Regional atrophy and altered interregional structural covariance may provide complementary information about brain structural changes in MCI.
